Initially created: 2025-12-09T20:44:11.714+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: My sister-in-law's ancestor,
Gōng Sòng (宋公), whose given name was Táo (燾),
was a *lǐnshēng* (廩生) from our district.
One day,
he lay ill in bed
when he saw an official holding a document,
leading a white-headed horse,
who said:
"Please come to take an examination."
Gōng Sòng said:
"The Provincial Education Commissioner (Wénzōng 文宗) has not yet arrived;
how can there be an examination so soon?"
The official did not speak,
but merely urged him on.
Gōng Sòng, despite his illness, mounted the horse and followed.
The road was very unfamiliar.
They arrived at a city,
which resembled a royal capital.
After some time, they entered a government office,
where the palace buildings were magnificent.
Ten or so officials were seated in the upper part;
Gōng Sòng did not know who any of them were,
except for Guān Zhuàngmiào (關壯繆), whom he recognized.
Under the eaves, two desks and two stools were set up.
A *xiùcai* (秀才) was already sitting at the far end,
and Gōng Sòng sat beside him.
On each desk were writing brushes and paper.
Presently, a piece of paper with a topic flew down. Looking at it,
it contained eight characters:
"One person, two people,
with intention, without intention."
When the two gentlemen had finished their essays,
they presented them to the main hall.
In Gōng Sòng's essay, there was a passage that said:
"If one does good with intention,
though it is good, it is not rewarded;
if one does evil without intention,
though it is evil, it is not punished."
All the deities praised it endlessly.
Gōng Sòng was summoned forward,
and it was decreed:
"Hénán (河南) is missing a City God (Chénghuáng 城隍);
you are fit for this position."
Gōng Sòng then understood,
bowed his head, and wept, saying:
"I am honored to receive this noble command;
how dare I decline?
However, my elderly mother is seventy years old,
and there is no one to care for her.
I ask to be allowed to let her live out her natural lifespan,
and then I will submit to your appointment."
The one seated above, who resembled an emperor,
immediately ordered an inquiry into his mother's lifespan records.
A long-bearded official
held up a ledger and flipped through it,
then reported:
"She has nine more years in the mortal realm."
While they were contemplating this,
Emperor Guān (Guāndì 關帝) said:
"It would not be a problem to let Zhāng Shēng (張生) temporarily hold the seal for nine years;
then he can replace him."
Then he said to Gōng Sòng:
"You should proceed to your post immediately;
but now, out of consideration for your filial piety,
you are granted a nine-year leave.
When the time comes, you will be summoned again."
He also encouraged the *xiùcai* with a few words.
Both gentlemen bowed and descended together.
The *xiùcai* clasped Gōng Sòng's hand and
saw him off to the outskirts of the city,
introducing himself as Zhāng Mǒu (張某) from Chángshān (長山).
He presented a farewell poem,
the words of which Gōng Sòng completely forgot,
but it contained the lines:
"With flowers and wine, spring forever stays,
without candles or lamps, night is naturally bright."
After Gōng Sòng mounted his horse,
he bade farewell and departed.
Upon reaching his village,
it was as if he had woken from a dream.
At that time, he had been dead for three days.
His mother heard groaning from the coffin,
helped him out,
and it was half a day before he could speak.
Inquiring about Chángshān,
there indeed was a Zhāng Shēng,
who had died on that very day.
Nine years later,
his mother indeed passed away.
After the burial was completed, Gōng Sòng
washed himself, entered his room, and died.
His father-in-law's family lived inside the west gate of the city.
They suddenly saw Gōng Sòng, adorned in embroidered robes and vermilion headgear,
with many carriages and horses.
He ascended their ancestral hall,
made a bow, and departed.
They were all surprised and bewildered,
not knowing he was a deity.
They rushed to inquire in the village,
only to find that he had already passed away.
Gōng Sòng had written a brief autobiography,
but it was unfortunately lost after the chaos;
this is merely a summary of it.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
Tán Jìnxuán (譚晉玄),
was a *zhūshēng* (諸生) from the district.
He firmly believed in the art of *dǎoyǐn* (導引),
and practiced it without ceasing in hot or cold weather.
After several months of practice,
he seemed to have achieved something.
One day,
as he was sitting in meditation,
he heard a tiny voice in his ear, like a fly,
saying:
"You can see me now."
When he opened his eyes, he heard it no more;
when he closed his eyes and composed his breath,
he heard it again as before.
He thought his elixir was about to be completed,
and secretly rejoiced.
Thereafter, whenever he sat, he would hear it.
So he waited for it to speak again,
intending to respond and observe.
One day,
it spoke again.
He then faintly responded:
"You can see me now."
Immediately, he felt a rustling sensation in his ear,
as if something was emerging.
He slightly glanced at it,
and saw a small person, about three inches tall,
with a fierce and malevolent appearance like a *yèchā* (夜叉),
spinning on the ground.
He was secretly surprised by this,
and so concentrated his mind to observe its transformation.
Suddenly, a neighbor came to borrow something,
knocking on the door and calling out.
When the little person heard this,
it became flustered,
spinning around the room
like a mouse that had lost its hole.
Tán Jìnxuán felt his spirit completely lost,
and no longer knew where the little person had gone.
He then suffered from an epileptic illness,
crying out incessantly.
After half a year of medicine,
he gradually recovered.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Yángxìn, there was an old man surnamed Wēng,
who lived in Càidiàn village.
The village was five or six *lǐ* from the city,
where his father and son ran a roadside inn
for traveling merchants.
Several cart drivers,
who frequently traveled and traded,
often lodged at their home.
One evening,
four men came together,
seeking lodging at their door.
However, Wēng’s inn was full.
The four men, having no other recourse,
insisted on being accommodated.
Wēng mused and thought of a place,
but seemed concerned it might not suit the guests.
The guests said:
“We only seek a spot under a roof,
and dare not be particular.”
At that time, Wēng’s daughter-in-law had recently died,
and her body was awaiting burial in a room.
His son had gone to purchase lumber and had not yet returned.
Wēng, finding the spiritual chamber quiet,
led the guests across the path.
Entering the dwelling,
a lamp dimly lit the table;
behind the table, clothes were draped over a screen,
and a paper quilt covered the deceased.
Upon inspecting the sleeping quarters,
they found conjoined beds in an inner room.
The four guests were quite exhausted from their travels,
and as soon as they lay down,
their snoring gradually grew louder.
Only one guest remained drowsy.
Suddenly, he heard a rustling sound on the spiritual bed,
and quickly opened his eyes.
The lamp in front of the spiritual bed
illuminated everything clearly: the female corpse had already uncovered herself,
and risen;
shortly after, she descended
and gradually entered the bedroom.
Her face was a pale golden color,
and a raw silk band covered her forehead.
She bent close to the front of the bed,
and blew three times on each of the sleeping guests.
The guest was greatly terrified,
fearing it would soon reach him.
He stealthily pulled the quilt over his head,
held his breath, and suppressed a gasp to listen.
Not long after,
the woman indeed came,
and blew on him as she had on the other guests.
He felt her leave the room,
and immediately heard the rustling of the paper quilt.
He cautiously peeked out from under the quilt,
and saw her lying stiffly as before.
The guest was extremely frightened,
and dared not make a sound.
He secretly nudged the other guests with his foot;
but none of them stirred in the slightest.
He considered his options and realized he had no plan,
other than to put on his clothes and escape.
Just as he rose and shook his clothes,
the rustling sound began again.
Frightened, the guest
again lay down,
tucking his head into the quilt.
He felt the woman return,
and she blew several times in succession before leaving.
After a short while,
he heard the spiritual bed creak,
knowing she had lain down again.
He then slowly reached his hand from under the quilt and retrieved his trousers,
quickly put them on,
and rushed out with bare feet.
The corpse also rose,
as if to pursue the guest.
By the time it left the curtained bed,
the guest had already unbolted the door and fled.
The corpse pursued him at a run.
The guest ran and shouted,
but no one in the village was roused.
He wanted to knock on the host’s door,
but feared he would be overtaken if he delayed.
So he fled with all his might
towards the city road.
Upon reaching the eastern suburbs,
he glimpsed a Buddhist temple,
and heard the sound of a wooden fish drum.
He quickly knocked on the monastery gate.
The Daoist priest, surprised by the unusual hour,
did not immediately admit him.
Turning around,
the corpse had already arrived,
a mere foot away from him.
The guest became even more desperate.
Outside the gate stood a white poplar tree,
about four or five *chǐ* in circumference.
He used the tree to shield himself;
if it moved to his right, he moved to its left,
if it moved to his left, he moved to its right.
The corpse grew even angrier.
However, both gradually grew tired.
The corpse stopped abruptly.
The guest, breathing heavily and with stifled breath,
sheltered behind the tree.
The corpse suddenly surged forward,
stretching its arms around the tree to grab and claw at him.
The guest cried out and fell.
The corpse failed to grasp him,
and embraced the tree, stiffening.
The Daoist priest listened secretly for a long time,
and hearing no sound,
gradually emerged.
He saw the guest lying on the ground.
He checked him with a candle and found him dead,
but a faint trace of breath still stirred in his chest.
He carried him inside,
and he revived only at dawn.
The priest gave him hot water and questioned him,
and the guest recounted everything.
By this time, the morning bell had ceased,
and the morning light was hazy.
The Daoist priest observed the tree,
and indeed saw the stiff female corpse.
Greatly alarmed,
he reported it to the county magistrate, *zǎi*.
The magistrate personally came to investigate.
He ordered men to pull the woman’s hands,
but they were firmly clasped and could not be opened.
Upon closer inspection,
all four fingers on both hands
were curled like hooks,
embedded in the wood up to the nails.
Several more men pulled with all their strength
before they could detach her.
The finger holes looked as if they had been chiseled.
An official was dispatched to Wēng’s home,
where they were in an uproar and commotion
over the missing corpse and the dead guest.
The official informed them of what had happened.
Wēng then went along,
and carried the corpse home.
The guest, weeping, told the magistrate, *zǎi*:
“Four of us set out,
but now only one returns.
How can I explain this to my hometown?”
The magistrate provided him with a document
and then saw him off on his journey home.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
When Mr. Sòng Yùshū of Láiyáng was a Department Official (*bùcáo*),
the residence he rented
was quite desolate.
One night,
two maids accompanied his wife, *tàifūrén*, to sleep in the hall.
They heard a flapping sound in the courtyard,
like a tailor spraying water.
The *tàifūrén* urged the maids to get up,
and peeking through a window crack,
saw an old hag,
short and hunchbacked,
with white hair like a broom,
wearing a bun
about two *chǐ* long.
She walked around the entire courtyard,
alternating between slow and hurried crane steps,
spraying as she went,
with water ceaselessly emerging.
The maids were astonished and reported back.
The *tàifūrén* also rose in alarm,
and the two maids supported her as they gathered to watch from under the window.
The hag suddenly approached the window,
and sprayed directly inside the latticework;
the window paper tore,
and all three fell dead,
though the family members were unaware.
When the sun rose,
all the family members gathered,
but knocking on the door received no response,
which alarmed them.
Prying open the door,
they found the mistress and two maids
lying dead in one room.
One maid’s diaphragm was still warm.
They helped her and revived her,
and after some time she awoke
and recounted what she had seen.
When Mr. Sòng arrived,
he was so grieved and enraged he nearly died.
Investigating the place of their demise carefully,
they dug down more than three *chǐ*,
and gradually revealed white hair;
digging further,
they found a corpse
exactly as described,
with a face so swollen and fat it looked alive.
He ordered it to be struck,
but the bones and flesh were all rotten,
and the skin was filled entirely with clear water.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Cháng'ān, there was a scholar named Fāng Dòng.
He had quite a reputation for talent,
but he was frivolous and unobservant of proper decorum.
Whenever he saw young women strolling in the streets,
he would flippantly follow them.
The day before Qīngmíng,
he happened to be walking in the suburbs
when he saw a small carriage,
with scarlet banners and embroidered curtains.
Several servants in blue clothes
followed it at a leisurely pace.
One maid,
riding a small horse,
was exquisitely beautiful.
He gradually approached to observe,
and saw that the carriage curtains were wide open,
with a maiden of sixteen inside,
her red makeup stunningly vibrant,
such as he had never seen in his life.
His eyes were dazzled and his spirit captivated;
he gazed and lingered, unable to leave.
Sometimes ahead, sometimes behind,
he followed for several *lǐ*.
Suddenly, he heard the maiden call a maid to the side of the carriage,
saying:
"Draw the curtain for me.
What boisterous fellow is this,
peeking so often!"
The maid then lowered the curtain
and angrily glared at the scholar, saying:
"This is the new bride of the Seventh Young Master of Fúróng Chéng returning to her parents' home;
she is not like a village woman
to let a scholar stare at her wantonly!"
Having spoken,
she scooped up dust from the road and threw it at the scholar.
The scholar squinted, unable to open his eyes.
As soon as he wiped them and looked,
the carriage and horses had vanished.
He returned, astonished and puzzled.
He felt his eyes were constantly uncomfortable.
He asked someone to open his eyelids and examine them,
and found a small film had grown over his pupils.
Overnight, it worsened,
tears flowing ceaselessly.
The film gradually grew larger,
and after several days, it was as thick as a coin.
His right eye developed a spiral pattern,
and all medicines were ineffective.
Distraught and desperate,
he felt remorse.
He heard that the *Guāngmíng Jīng* could alleviate misfortune.
He took a volume
and asked someone to teach him to recite it.
Initially, he was restless,
but in time, he gradually found peace.
Morning and evening, with nothing else to do,
he would only sit cross-legged and count prayer beads.
He persevered for a year,
and all worldly attachments became pure.
Suddenly, he heard a faint whisper like a fly from his left eye,
saying:
"It's as black as lacquer;
it's unbearable!"
His right eye responded, saying:
"We can go out for a little stroll
and escape this stuffiness."
He gradually felt a蠕動 (wriggling) sensation and itchiness in both nostrils,
as if something was emerging,
and then left his nostrils.
After a while, they returned,
entering his eye sockets again through his nostrils.
Then they spoke again, saying:
"We haven't peeked into the garden pavilion for so long;
the pearl orchids have withered and died!"
The scholar had always loved fragrant orchids and
planted many in his garden.
He watered them himself daily;
since he lost his sight,
he had long neglected them.
Suddenly hearing this,
he quickly asked his wife:
"Why have the orchids withered and died?"
His wife questioned how he knew,
and he then told her the reason.
His wife hurried to check,
and indeed, the flowers had withered.
She was greatly astonished.
She quietly hid in the room to wait for them,
and saw tiny people emerge from the scholar's nostrils,
no bigger than beans,
buzzing out the door.
As they moved further away,
she lost sight of them.
A moment later,
they returned arm-in-arm,
flying onto his face,
like bees and ants entering their nests.
This continued for two or three days.
Again, he heard the left eye say:
"The tunnel is circuitous,
and coming and going is very inconvenient;
it's better to open our own door."
The right eye responded, saying:
"My wall is thick,
it's very difficult."
The left eye said:
"I'll try to break through;
then we can both go."
Immediately, he felt a faint sensation of scratching and tearing inside his left eye socket.
After a short while,
he opened his eyes to look,
and clearly saw several objects.
He happily told his wife.
His wife examined it
and found that the membrane had a small hole,
through which the black pupil gleamed
like a split pepper.
After another night,
the film completely disappeared.
Upon closer inspection,
it was actually a double pupil,
but the spiral pattern in his right eye remained,
thus he knew that both pupils had gathered in one socket.
Although the scholar had one blind eye,
compared to those with both eyes,
he saw much more clearly.
From then on, he became even more disciplined,
and the villagers praised his great virtue.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"There was a scholar in the countryside
who, with two friends, was on a road
when they saw a young woman riding a donkey ahead of them.
He jokingly recited: 'There is a beauty!'
Then, looking at his two friends, he said: 'Chase her!'
They laughed and galloped after her.
Soon, they caught up,
and it turned out to be his daughter-in-law.
He felt ashamed and disheartened,
remaining silent.
His friends pretended not to know,
and commented about her with great disrespect.
The scholar blushed,
and stammered, saying: 'This is my eldest son's wife.'
They each suppressed a laugh and stopped.
Frivolous people often bring insult upon themselves,
which is truly laughable.
As for the squinting and blindness,
that is a cruel retribution from spirits and gods.
The lord of Fúróng Chéng,
I do not know what god it is,
could it be a Bodhisattva manifesting?
Nevertheless, the young gentleman opened his own door;
even though spirits and gods are stern,
why would they not allow people to reform themselves?"
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
Jiāngxī Mèng Lóngtán
and Zhū Xiàolián were sojourning in the capital.
They happened to visit a Buddhist monastery.
Its halls and meditation chambers
were not particularly grand or spacious.
Only an old monk was lodging there.
Seeing the guests enter,
he adjusted his robes and came out to greet them,
then guided them to sightsee.
In the hall was a statue of Zhìgōng.
The paintings on both walls were exquisite,
the figures lifelike.
On the east wall was a painting of celestial maidens scattering flowers.
Among them, one with unbound hair
held a flower and smiled,
her cherry lips seemingly about to move,
her eyes about to flow with emotion.
Zhū gazed at it for a long time,
unconsciously losing himself in thought, his spirit captivated,
and fell into a trance-like contemplation.
His body suddenly felt light and airy,
as if riding on clouds and mist,
and he had arrived on the wall.
He saw layers of halls and pavilions,
no longer the human world.
An old monk was expounding the Dharma on a platform,
many people with bared shoulders circling and listening.
Zhū also stood mixed among them.
A short while later,
someone seemed to subtly pull his skirt.
He looked back,
and it was the girl with unbound hair,
who smiled sweetly and went off.
Zhū immediately followed her.
Passing through a winding balustrade,
they entered a small chamber.
Zhū hesitated and dared not go forward.
The girl turned her head,
raised the flower in her hand,
and made a distant beckoning gesture.
He then hurried after her.
Inside the chamber, it was utterly silent and empty;
he suddenly embraced her,
and she did not resist much,
so they became intimate.
Afterward, she closed the door and left,
instructing him not to make a sound,
and returned only at night.
This continued for two days.
Her companions all noticed it,
and together they found Zhū.
Jokingly, they said to the girl:
"The little lad in your belly is already so big,
yet you still wear unbound hair, pretending to be a maiden?"
They all took up hairpins and ornaments,
urging her to tie her hair into a bun.
The girl was shy and said nothing.
One girl said:
"Little sister, elder sisters,
let us not stay long,
lest someone be displeased."
They all laughed and left.
Zhū looked at the girl.
Her cloudy bun was piled high,
her locks softly drooped,
making her even more dazzling than when her hair was unbound.
Looking around, there was no one else,
and they gradually indulged in intimacy.
The scent of orchid and musk filled their hearts,
their joy was not yet exhausted.
Suddenly, they heard the clanking of boots, very loud,
and the jingle of chains;
soon after, there were noisy shouts and arguments.
The girl startled up,
and she and Zhū secretly peeped.
They saw a golden-armored messenger,
his face black as lacquer,
holding chains and carrying a hammer,
surrounded by the other girls.
The messenger said:
"Is everyone here?"
They replied:
"Everyone is here."
The messenger said:
"If anyone is hiding a person from the lower realm,
you must all confess together,
do not bring yourselves trouble."
Again, they unanimously said:
"No."
The messenger turned his head and looked around like an eagle,
as if about to search for hidden people.
The girl was greatly frightened,
her face ashen,
and she anxiously said to Zhū:
"You must quickly hide under the bed!"
Then she opened a small door in the wall
and abruptly fled.
Zhū lay prostrate,
not daring to breathe for a moment.
Soon, he heard the sound of boots entering the room,
then leaving.
Not long after,
the noise gradually receded, and his heart felt a little safer;
however, there were always people coming and going outside the door, conversing.
Zhū had been cramped for so long
that he felt cicadas buzzing in his ears,
and fire flashing in his eyes.
His state was almost unbearable.
He only listened quietly, waiting for the girl to return,
and actually no longer remembered how he had gotten there.
At this time, Mèng Lóngtán was in the hall,
and in a blink, Zhū was gone.
He asked the monk with suspicion.
The monk smiled and said:
"He has gone to listen to the Dharma."
He asked:
"Where?"
He replied:
"Not far."
A short while later,
he tapped the wall with his finger and called out:
"Zhū Tányuè, why do you linger so long and not return?"
Then, a painting of Zhū appeared on the wall,
standing reverently with his ear cocked,
as if listening and observing.
The monk called out again:
"Your traveling companion has waited for a long time."
Then, he floated down from the wall,
his heart lifeless, standing like wood,
his eyes wide and his legs weak.
Mèng was greatly alarmed,
and calmly asked him.
It turned out that he had been lying prostrate under the bed,
heard a knocking sound like thunder,
and so had come out of the room to peek and listen.
They all looked at the girl holding the flower;
her snail-bun was now prominent,
no longer unbound hair.
Zhū was astonished and bowed to the old monk,
asking him the reason.
The monk smiled and said:
"Illusions arise from human minds;
how can this humble monk explain it?"
Zhū felt a lump in his throat and could not speak,
Mèng was amazed and speechless, his mind bewildered.
They immediately rose,
walked down the steps, and left.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Illusions are created by humans –
this saying is like that of an enlightened one.
When a person has a lustful mind,
a defiled realm is born;
when a person has a defiled mind,
a terrifying realm is born.
Bodhisattvas enlighten the ignorant,
creating a thousand illusions simultaneously.
All these are activated by the human mind itself.
The old monk's compassion was deep,
it is a pity that Zhū did not achieve great enlightenment from his words
and enter the mountains with unbound hair."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Sūn Tàibái once said that his great-grandfather studied at Liǔgōu Temple on Nánshān.
When the wheat harvest came, he returned home
and did not come back until after a period of ten days.
Upon opening the study door,
he found the desk covered in dust,
and the windows filled with cobwebs.
He ordered his servant to sweep and clean.
By evening, it finally felt clean and fit to sit in.
He then brushed the bed, laid out his bedding,
closed the door, and lay down on his pillow.
The moonlight already filled the window.
After tossing and turning for some time,
all sounds became silent.
Suddenly, he heard a booming wind sound,
and the mountain gate creaked open.
He secretly thought that the temple monk had forgotten to close it.
While he was preoccupied with this thought,
the wind sound gradually approached his dwelling,
and soon, his room door opened.
He was greatly perplexed.
Before he could collect his thoughts,
the sound had already entered the room;
then, there was the clanking sound of boots,
gradually approaching the bedroom door.
Fear began to seize his heart.
Soon, the bedroom door opened.
He looked quickly,
and a huge ghost, bowing, squeezed in
and stood abruptly before the bed,
almost reaching the beam.
Its face was the color of old melon skin;
its eyes gleamed and flashed,
looking around the room;
it opened its enormous mouth like a basin,
its sparse teeth about three inches long;
its tongue moved, its throat roared,
and the sound of its “hē lā”
resounded against the four walls.
Gōng was extremely frightened;
he also considered that in such a small space,
there was no escaping,
so it would be better to stab it.
He secretly drew the dagger from under his pillow,
quickly pulled it out and hacked at it,
hitting its belly,
which made a sound like a stone jar.
The ghost became furious,
stretched out its giant claw and grabbed at Gōng.
Gōng shrank back slightly.
The ghost grabbed the quilt,
pulled it,
and angrily departed.
Gōng fell with the quilt,
lying on the ground and crying out.
His family rushed in with lights.
The door was closed as before.
They forced open the window and entered.
Seeing the situation,
they were greatly alarmed.
They helped him back onto the bed,
and only then did he tell them what had happened.
Together they examined it,
and found the quilt stuck in the gap of the bedroom door.
They opened the door and inspected it with a light,
seeing claw marks like a winnowing basket,
where all five fingers had pierced through.
When morning came,
he dared not stay any longer,
and carried his satchel home.
Later, he asked the monks,
but there were no other strange occurrences.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Shěn Língshēng said that his friend, a certain old man,
was taking a nap one summer day.
In a daze,
he saw a woman lift the curtain and enter.
Her head was wrapped in white cloth,
and she wore mourning clothes and a hemp skirt,
heading towards the inner room.
He suspected she was a neighbor visiting his wife;
then, he reconsidered,
why would she enter someone’s house dressed in mourning clothes so abruptly?
While he was still bewildered,
the woman had already exited.
Examining her closely,
she appeared to be over thirty,
her complexion sallow and swollen,
her brows and eyes furrowed,
her expression frightening.
She then lingered, not leaving,
gradually approaching his bed.
He feigned sleep
to observe what would happen.
Before long,
the woman gathered her clothes and climbed onto the bed,
pressing down on his belly.
It felt as heavy as a hundred *jūn*.
Though his mind was clear,
when he tried to raise his hand,
his hand felt bound;
when he tried to raise his foot,
his foot felt paralyzed.
He urgently wanted to cry for help,
but struggled to make a sound.
The woman sniffed the old man’s face with her mouth,
almost covering his cheekbones, nose, eyebrows, and forehead.
He felt her mouth was as cold as ice,
and her breath was bone-chilling.
In his distress and urgency, the old man
devised a plan: when she sniffed his chin and cheeks,
he would bite her then.
Soon after,
it indeed reached his chin.
The old man seized the opportunity and bit her cheek forcefully,
his teeth sinking into the flesh.
The woman, in pain, pulled away,
struggling and whimpering.
The old man bit harder.
He only felt blood covering his chin,
wetting the pillow.
While they were locked in this bitter struggle,
suddenly his wife’s voice was heard from outside the courtyard,
urgently shouting that there was a ghost.
With one moment of relaxation, the woman had already floated away.
His wife rushed in,
saw nothing,
and laughed at his false dream of a nightmare.
The old man recounted the strange event,
and also mentioned there was bloody evidence.
They inspected it together,
and indeed, like water leaking from a roof,
it flowed over the pillow and soaked the mat.
He bent down and sniffed it,
and the腥臭 (xīngchòu) was unusually strong.
The old man then vomited violently.
After several days,
there was still a lingering stench in his mouth.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Old man Sūn,
my wife’s family's Qīngfú’s paternal uncle,
was known for his courage.
One day,
while taking a nap,
he vaguely felt something climb onto the bed,
and then felt his body sway as if riding on clouds and mist.
He secretly wondered, could it be a fox pressing him down?
He peeked slightly:
the creature was as big as a cat,
with yellow fur and a green mouth,
coming from his feet.
It crawled along,
as if fearing the old man would restrain it.
It gradually attached itself to his body: where it touched his feet, his feet became weak;
where it touched his thighs, his thighs became limp.
As soon as it reached his belly,
the old man suddenly rose,
pressed down and grabbed it,
gripping its neck.
The creature cried out urgently and could not escape.
The old man quickly called his wife
to tie its waist with a belt.
Then, holding both ends of the belt,
he smiled and said,
“I hear you are good at transforming.
Now, I’m watching you here,
let’s see how you transform.”
As he spoke,
the creature suddenly shrank its belly,
making it as thin as a pipe,
almost slipping away.
The old man was greatly alarmed
and immediately bound it tightly.
Then, it puffed up its belly again,
making it thicker than a bowl,
and unyieldingly firm;
when his grip loosened slightly,
it would shrink again.
Fearing it would escape, the old man
ordered his wife to kill it quickly.
His wife frantically looked around,
unsure where the knife was.
The old man glanced to his left to show her where it was.
By the time he turned his head back,
the belt was in his hand like a ring,
and the creature had vanished.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Zhǎngshān Ānwēng
loved farming.
When the buckwheat ripened in autumn,
it was cut and piled by the embankment.
At that time, there were crop thieves in a nearby village,
so he ordered his tenant farmers
to transport it to the threshing ground by moonlight;
when they had loaded it and returned,
he stayed to guard it himself.
He then lay down in the open, using his spear as a pillow.
His eyes had just closed
when he suddenly heard someone trampling the buckwheat roots,
making a rustling sound.
He suspected a violent bandit.
Hastily raising his head,
he saw a huge ghost,
over a zhàng tall,
with red hair and tangled beard,
already close to him.
Greatly frightened,
with no time for other plans,
he leaped up abruptly
and fiercely stabbed it.
The ghost shrieked like thunder and vanished.
Fearing it might return,
he carried his spear and went home.
He met the tenant farmers on the way,
told them what he had seen,
and warned them not to go.
The others did not fully believe him.
The next day,
while drying wheat on the threshing ground,
they suddenly heard a sound from the sky.
Wēng cried out in alarm:
"The ghost has come!"
He ran,
and the others ran too.
After some time, they reassembled,
and Wēng ordered many bows and crossbows to be set up to await it.
The next day,
it indeed returned.
Several arrows were fired simultaneously,
and the creature, afraid, fled.
For two or three days, it did not return.
Once the wheat was stored in the granary,
the leftover stalks were mixed together.
Wēng ordered them to be piled into a stack,
and he personally climbed up to tread it firm,
making it several feet high.
Suddenly, he looked into the distance and cried out in alarm:
"The ghost has arrived!"
The others hastily searched for bows and arrows,
but the creature had already rushed to Wēng.
Wēng fell,
and it bit his forehead before leaving.
Everyone climbed up to look,
and saw that a piece of his forehead bone the size of a palm was gone.
He was unconscious.
They carried him home,
where he subsequently died.
It was not seen again afterward.
No one knew what kind of monster it was.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zhǎngshān Lǐ Gōng
was the nephew of the Grand Minister of Justice (Dà Sīkòu).
His residence was often home to strange phenomena.
He once saw a spring bench (chūndèng) in the hall,
flesh-colored,
very smooth and glossy.
Lǐ knew there was no such object there,
so he approached and touched it.
It bent with his hand,
almost as soft as flesh.
Startled, he recoiled.
When he looked back,
its four legs were moving,
gradually entering the wall.
He also saw a white staff (báitǐng) leaning against the wall,
clean and lustrous, long and slender.
He approached to steady it,
but it fell limply,
snaking into the wall,
and only disappeared after some time.
In the seventeenth year of Kāngxī,
Wáng Jùnshēng, a scholar (shēng), was teaching at his house.
At dusk,
when the lamps were first lit,
Wáng Shēng lay on his couch wearing his shoes.
Suddenly, he saw a small person,
about three cùn tall,
enter from outside.
After a brief turn,
it left again.
A moment later,
it returned carrying two small stools,
which it placed in the hall,
looking just like those made from sorghum pith by children.
After another moment,
two small people carried in a coffin,
about four cùn long,
and placed it on the stools.
Before the interment was complete,
a woman arrived leading several servants (sī bì),
all as small as the figures before.
The woman was in mourning clothes,
with a hemp rope tied around her waist,
and her head wrapped in cloth;
she covered her mouth with her sleeve,
weeping faintly,
her voice like a giant fly.
Wáng Shēng stared for a long time,
his hairs stood on end,
as if covered in frost.
He then shouted loudly,
and abruptly ran,
falling off the bed,
trembling and unable to get up.
The people in the guesthouse heard the sound and gathered,
but the figures in the hall had already vanished.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A man surnamed Xǔ,
lived in the northern suburb of Zī,
and was a fisherman.
Every night,
he would carry wine to the river,
drinking and fishing.
When he drank, he would pour a libation on the ground,
praying:
"May the drowned ghosts in the river get a drink."
This was his habit.
Other people fished
but caught nothing,
while Xǔ alone filled his basket.
One evening,
as he was drinking alone,
a young man came
and lingered by his side.
Xǔ offered him a drink,
and they generously shared the wine.
However, for the entire night, he did not catch a single fish,
and felt rather disheartened.
The young man rose and said:
"Please allow me to drive them for you from downstream."
Then he drifted away.
A short while later,
he returned again,
saying:
"Many fish are coming."
Indeed, they heard a gulping sound.
He cast his net and caught several,
all over a chǐ long.
Overjoyed,
he thanked him repeatedly.
When he was about to leave,
he offered fish as a gift,
but the young man refused,
saying:
"I have repeatedly enjoyed your fine wine;
how can these trifles be considered a recompense?
If you do not disdain me,
I would like to be your long-term companion."
Xǔ said:
"We have only spent one evening together;
why do you speak of 'repeatedly'?
If you are willing to stay forever,
that is truly my deepest wish;
but I am ashamed that I have nothing to offer in return for your affection."
He inquired about his name,
and the young man replied:
"My surname is Wáng,
I have no courtesy name (zì),
you may call me Wáng Liùláng when we meet."
Then they parted.
The next day,
Xǔ sold his fish
and bought more wine.
In the evening, when he reached the riverside,
the young man was already there,
and they drank joyfully together.
After a few cups, the young man would always drive fish for Xǔ.
Thus passed half a year.
Suddenly, he told Xǔ:
"I have known Qīngyáng
for a long time, and our affection is deeper than flesh and blood.
However, the day of our separation is near."
His words were very mournful.
Xǔ asked in surprise.
He tried to speak but stopped twice,
then said:
"Our friendship is as close as it gets;
perhaps you will not be surprised if I tell you?
Now that we are about to part,
there is no harm in telling you clearly: I am actually a ghost.
I used to be fond of alcohol,
and drowned while heavily intoxicated,
several years ago, right here.
The fish you caught earlier,
which were always more plentiful than others',
were all secretly driven by me
to repay your libations.
Tomorrow, my karma will be fulfilled,
and there will be a substitute,
and I will go to be reborn.
We only have this evening together,
hence I cannot help but feel emotional."
When Xǔ first heard this, he was very startled;
however, having been intimate for so long,
he was no longer afraid.
So he also sighed,
poured a drink, and said:
"Lìuláng, drink this;
do not be sorrowful.
That we meet only to part so suddenly
is indeed cause for sorrow,
yet with your karma fulfilled and liberation from your predicament,
it is precisely a cause for congratulation;
sorrow is therefore inappropriate."
Thereupon, they drank heartily.
He then asked:
"Who is the substitute?"
He replied:
"You will see him by the riverside;
at noon,
a woman will cross the river and drown –
that will be her."
Hearing the village roosters crowing,
they shed tears and parted.
The next day,
Xǔ respectfully waited by the riverside
to observe the unusual event.
Indeed, a woman came carrying a baby,
and fell into the river upon reaching it.
The baby was thrown onto the bank,
waving its arms and kicking its legs while crying.
The woman floated and sank repeatedly,
then suddenly climbed out onto the bank, drenched,
rested briefly on the ground,
and carried her child directly away.
When the woman was drowning,
Xǔ's heart felt truly unbearable,
and he thought of rushing to save her,
but then changed his mind, realizing this was the substitute for Lìuláng,
so he stopped and did not save her.
When the woman came out herself,
he doubted that the ghost's words were accurate.
Towards evening,
he fished at the usual spot.
The young man returned again,
saying:
"Now we meet again,
and let's not speak of parting anymore!"
Xǔ asked him the reason.
He replied:
"The woman has already substituted for me;
but I pitied the child in her arms.
To substitute for one younger brother
would effectively end two lives,
so I let her go.
I do not know when the next substitute will be.
Perhaps our destiny together is not yet exhausted?"
Xǔ sighed and said:
"Such a benevolent heart
can surely reach the Supreme Being!"
From then on, they gathered as before.
A few days later,
he came again to bid farewell.
Xǔ suspected that there was another substitute.
He said:
"No, that is not it.
My previous moment of compassion
indeed reached the Emperor of Heaven.
Now I have been appointed as the Tǔdì of Wūzhèn, in Zhāoyuǎn County,
and will assume office on the appointed day.
If you do not forget our old friendship,
you should come and visit me;
do not mind the long and difficult journey."
Xǔ congratulated him, saying:
"For you to be an upright god
is very comforting to the heart.
However, there is a barrier between humans and gods;
even if I do not mind the long and difficult journey,
what then can I do?"
The young man said:
"Just come;
do not worry."
He exhorted him repeatedly and then departed.
Xǔ agreed,
and immediately wished to pack up and go east.
His wife laughed and said:
"A few hundred *lǐ* from here,
there is indeed that place.
I fear that clay figures cannot converse with people."
Xǔ did not listen,
and eventually arrived at Zhāoyuǎn.
He asked the residents,
and indeed there was a Wūzhèn.
He soon reached the place,
rested his shoulders at an inn,
and asked where the shrine was.
The innkeeper was surprised and said:
"Might your surname be Xǔ?"
Xǔ said:
"It is.
How did you know?"
He then said:
"Might your hometown be Zī?"
He said:
"It is.
How did you know?"
The innkeeper did not answer,
and quickly went out.
Soon, husbands carrying children,
and daughters-in-law peeking from doors,
came crowding in,
surrounding him like a wall.
Xǔ was even more astonished.
The crowd then told him:
"Several nights ago,
we dreamt that the deity said: 'Xǔ Yǒu from Zīchuān will arrive soon.
You may assist him with travel expenses.'
We have been waiting for a long time."
Xǔ also found this extraordinary,
so he went to offer sacrifices at the shrine and prayed, saying:
"After parting with you,
you have never left my thoughts, day or night.
I have traveled far to fulfill our old promise.
I am also grateful that you revealed this to the residents in a dream,
your kindness is deeply etched in my heart.
I am ashamed that I have no good offerings,
only a cup of wine;
if you do not reject it,
it will be like our drink by the river."
After the prayer,
he burned spirit money.
Suddenly, a wind rose from behind the seat,
swirling for a moment,
then dispersed.
That night, he dreamt that a young man came,
elegantly dressed,
greatly different from usual.
He thanked him, saying:
"It was a long journey for you to visit,
my tears of joy flow.
However, I hold a minor position,
and it is inconvenient to meet face-to-6face.
Although our homes are close,
I feel deeply saddened by this.
The residents have given you a small gift,
as a token to repay our old friendship.
If you have a departure date,
I will still come to see you off."
After several days,
Xǔ wished to return.
The crowd cordially urged him to stay,
inviting him morning and evening,
to a different host each day.
Xǔ firmly declined, wishing to leave.
The crowd then folded letters and held bundles,
vying to present him with farewell gifts.
Before the morning was over,
the gifts filled his satchel.
Old men and young children all gathered,
to see him off outside the village.
Suddenly, a whirlwind arose,
following him for over ten *lǐ*.
Xǔ bowed twice and said:
"Liùláng, take care!
Do not trouble yourself with a long journey.
Your heart is kind and loving,
you can naturally bring blessings to this area,
there is no need for your old friend's admonition."
The wind swirled for a long time,
then departed.
The villagers also sighed in amazement and returned.
When Xǔ returned,
his family was slightly richer,
so he no longer fished.
Later, when he saw people from Zhāoyuǎn and asked them,
they said the spirit's response was as quick as an echo.
Some say it is Shíkēngzhuāng in Zhāngqiū.
It is not known which is correct.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"To be placed in high office,
yet not forget the humble,
this is why it is divine.
Today's noble officials in their carriages,
would they still recognize those who wore bamboo hats?
In my hometown, there was a recluse,
whose family was extremely poor.
He had a childhood friend
who held a lucrative position.
He calculated that if he sought him out, he would surely be taken care of.
He exhausted his efforts to prepare for the journey,
traveling a thousand *lǐ*,
but was greatly disappointed;
he had to empty his satchel to sell his horse,
only then could he return.
His cousin was very witty,
and composed a monthly calendar to mock him, saying:
'In this month,
Big Brother arrived,
his sable hat was removed,
the umbrella was not unfurled,
the horse turned into a donkey,
his boots finally ceased their sound.'
Recalling this brings a smile.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
When I was a child and went to the prefectural examination,
it was during the Spring Festival.
According to old custom,
on the day before,
merchants from all trades,
with decorated floats and drums, would go to the Provincial Administration Commissioner's office,
named
"Yǎnchūn".
I followed my friends to watch.
On that day, sightseers were packed like a wall.
In the hall, the four officials,
all dressed in red,
sat facing each other, east and west.
At that time, I was still young,
and did not understand what offices they held.
But I heard the clamor of people's voices,
and the drums and wind instruments deafening.
Suddenly, a man,
leading a bare-headed boy,
carrying a pole with baskets, came up,
as if to make a report;
a myriad of voices surged,
and I could not hear what was being said.
But I saw the officials in the hall laughing.
Immediately, a green-clad attendant loudly ordered a performance.
The man agreed to the order and was about to begin,
when he asked:
"What play should I perform?"
The officials in the hall looked at each other and exchanged a few words.
An attendant came down to ask what he was skilled at.
He replied:
"I can turn living things upside down."
The attendant reported this to the palace.
A moment later, he came down again,
ordering him to fetch peaches.
The magician assented.
He removed his outer garment and covered his basket with it.
He deliberately put on a mournful expression,
saying:
"The official is truly confused!
The solid ice has not yet melted;
how can one obtain peaches?
If I don't get them,
I fear I will incur the wrath of the one who sits facing south.
What is to be done!"
His son said:
"Father has already assented,
how can you refuse now?"
The magician was lost in thought for a long time,
then said:
"I have considered it thoroughly.
In early spring, with snow still piled up,
where in the human world can they be found?
Only in Xīwángmǔ's (西王母) garden,
where plants never wither throughout the four seasons,
might there be some.
I must steal them from heaven,
then it will be possible."
The son said:
"Alas!
Can heaven be ascended by steps?"
He replied:
"There is a magical technique."
Then he opened his basket,
took out a coil of rope,
approximately ten *zhàng* (丈) long.
He straightened one end,
and threw it towards the sky.
The rope immediately stood suspended in mid-air,
as if something had caught it.
Before long,
the more he threw, the higher it went,
disappearing into the clouds;
the rope in his hand was also completely gone.
Then he called his son, saying:
"Come, my boy!
I am old and feeble,
heavy and clumsy,
unable to go;
you must make the trip."
Thereupon, he handed the rope to his son,
saying:
"You can ascend by holding this."
The son took the rope,
with a look of difficulty,
and complained:
"Old man, you are truly muddled!
With such a thin rope,
you want me to cling to it
to ascend to the high heavens, ten thousand *rèn* (仞) tall.
Should it break midway,
what will become of my bones!"
His father again strongly urged him and patted him,
saying:
"I have already spoken rashly,
and regret is useless.
Please make this trip, my son.
Don't be distressed, my boy.
If you manage to steal them,
there will surely be a reward of a hundred pieces of gold,
and I will arrange for you to marry a beautiful woman."
The son then took the rope,
and spiraled upwards.
His hands moved, his feet followed,
like a spider chasing its thread.
He gradually entered the clouds,
and could no longer be seen.
After a long while,
a peach fell,
as large as a bowl.
The magician was delighted.
He held it and presented it to the official's hall.
It was passed around the hall for a long time,
but no one knew if it was real or fake.
Suddenly, the rope fell to the ground.
The magician exclaimed in alarm:
"Alas!
Someone up there has cut my rope,
what will become of my son!"
A moment later,
something fell.
Looking at it,
it was his son's head.
He held it and wept, saying:
"He must have stolen the peach
and been discovered by the guards.
My son is finished!"
Another moment later,
a foot fell;
soon after,
limbs fell one after another,
nothing remained whole.
The magician was greatly saddened.
He picked up each piece and placed it in his basket, closing it,
saying:
"This old man has only this one son,
who traveled with me north and south every day.
Now, following a strict command,
I did not expect him to suffer such a horrific tragedy!
I must carry him away and bury him."
Then he ascended the hall and knelt,
saying:
"For the sake of a peach,
my son has been killed!
If you would pity this humble person and assist with the burial,
I will tie grass to repay your kindness."
The seated officials were astonished,
and each gave him some gold.
The magician received it and tied it around his waist.
Then he tapped the basket and called out:
"Bābā'ér (八八兒),
why don't you come out and thank them for the reward,
what are you waiting for?"
Suddenly, a shaggy-haired boy's head emerged from under the basket lid,
bowed to the north,
and it was his son.
Because his magic was so extraordinary,
it is still remembered to this day.
Later, I heard that the Báiliánjiào (白蓮教) could perform this trick,
I wonder if this is their descendant?
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異) manuscript:
There was a countryman selling pears in the market,
they were quite sweet and fragrant,
and their price was high.
A Taoist monk, in a tattered turban and patched clothes,
begged in front of his cart.
The countryman yelled at him,
but he would not leave.
The countryman grew angry,
and added insults and curses.
The Taoist monk said:
"There are hundreds of pears in your cart,
this old monk only begs for one;
it will not cause you, the householder, much loss,
why are you so angry?"
Onlookers advised him to give the monk a poor quality one and let him leave,
but the countryman adamantly refused.
A servant in a nearby shop,
seeing the incessant chattering was unbearable,
then paid money to buy one,
and gave it to the Taoist monk.
The Taoist monk bowed in thanks,
and said to the crowd:
"We who have renounced the world do not know how to be stingy.
I have a fine pear,
please allow me to offer it to my guests."
Someone said:
"Since you have it,
why don't you eat it yourself?"
He said:
"I specifically need this core for planting."
Thereupon, he held the pear and ate it heartily.
When he had almost finished,
he held the core in his hand,
took the spade from his shoulder,
dug a hole several inches deep in the ground,
put the core in, and covered it with soil.
He asked the market people for hot water to irrigate it.
A curious person got boiling water from a shop by the roadside.
The Taoist monk received it and poured it into the pit.
Thousands of eyes watched intently,
and saw a hook-shaped sprout emerge,
gradually growing larger;
suddenly, it became a tree,
with lush branches and leaves;
in an instant, it bloomed,
and in an instant, it bore fruit,
large and fragrant,
hanging heavy on the tree.
The Taoist monk then immediately plucked from the treetop and gave them to the onlookers.
In a short while, they were almost all gone.
Afterward,
he used the spade to cut down the tree.
With a *ding-ding* sound for a long time,
it finally broke. He carried it with its leaves on his shoulder,
and walked away slowly and calmly.
Initially,
when the Dàoshì performed his magic,
the villagers also stood among the crowd,
stretching their necks and watching intently,
completely forgetting their work.
After the Dàoshì left,
they first looked back at their cart,
and found the pears were already gone.
Only then did they realize that what had just been distributed
were all their own belongings.
They then carefully inspected the cart and found one shaft missing;
it had been freshly chopped off.
Their hearts were filled with great indignation.
They quickly traced its path,
and turning a corner,
found the broken shaft discarded at the foot of the wall.
Only then did they realize that the pear tree that had been cut down
was that very item.
The Dàoshì was nowhere to be found.
The entire market burst into laughter.
Yìshǐshì said:
"The villagers are confused and muddle-headed,
their foolishness is truly pitiable.
That they were laughed at by the market people
is certainly understandable.
Whenever I see people in the countryside who are said to be wealthy but unranked officials,
if a good friend asks for rice,
they become displeased,
and even calculate, 'This is several days' provisions.'
If someone advises them to help someone in danger,
or feed a lonely person,
they become indignant,
and again calculate, 'This is food for ten or five people.'
Even between father and son, brothers,
they haggle over every trifle.
Yet when lust and gambling blind their minds,
they don't hesitate to empty their purses;
when a knife or saw is at their neck,
they can't afford to delay in ransoming their lives.
Such instances
are too numerous to recount;
how can these foolish villagers
be surprising?"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
In Yì there was a Shēng surnamed Wáng,
who was the seventh child,
from a prominent family.
He had admired the Dao since childhood,
and hearing that Láoshān had many immortals,
he carried his satchel and went to travel there.
He ascended a peak,
where there was a Dàoguān,
which was very secluded.
A Dàoshì sat on a pútuán,
his white hair hanging down to his collar,
but his spirit was radiant and unrestrained.
Wáng knelt and spoke with him,
and his reasoning was profound and subtle.
Wáng asked to be his disciple.
The Dàoshì said:
"I fear you are delicate and lazy and cannot endure hardship."
Wáng replied:
"I can."
His disciples were numerous,
and by dusk they had all gathered.
Wáng bowed to them all,
and then stayed in the Dàoguān.
At dawn,
the Dàoshì called Wáng to him,
gave him an axe,
and told him to join the others in gathering firewood.
Wáng respectfully accepted the instruction.
After more than a month,
his hands and feet were covered in calluses,
and he could not bear the hardship,
secretly developing a desire to return home.
One evening,
Wáng (王) returned and saw two guests drinking with his master.
It was already dusk,
yet there were no lamps or candles.
The master then cut paper into a mirror shape
and stuck it on the wall.
In an instant,
the moonlight illuminated the room,
its brilliance revealing even the finest hairs.
The disciples gathered around, listening and moving about.
One guest said:
“This fine evening and its excellent pleasures
should not be enjoyed alone.”
He then took a pot of wine from the table
and distributed it to the disciples,
urging them to drink their fill.
Wáng (王) thought to himself: with seven or eight people,
how could one pot of wine be enough for everyone?
So they each sought bowls and cups,
eagerly drinking, fearing the pot would run out;
but as they repeatedly drew and poured,
it didn't diminish at all.
His heart found this strange.
Soon,
another guest said:
“Having been granted the illumination of the moon,
we are drinking so solitarily.
Why not summon Cháng'é (嫦娥)?”
Then he threw a chopstick into the moon.
A beautiful woman appeared,
emerging from the light.
Initially, she was less than a foot tall,
but upon reaching the ground, she became human-sized.
With a slender waist and graceful neck,
she danced gracefully
the “Níshang Wǔ (霓裳舞).”
Afterwards, she sang:
“Oh immortal one,
will you return,
and confine me to Guǎnghán (廣寒)?”
Her voice was clear and resonant,
as intense as a flute or pipe.
After the song,
she whirled and rose,
leaping onto the table,
and in the blink of an eye,
she had turned back into a chopstick.
The three men laughed heartily.
Yet another guest said:
“Tonight is most joyful,
but I can't hold my liquor much longer.
Would it be possible to see me off in the Moon Palace?”
The three men moved their seats,
gradually entering the moon.
The onlookers saw the three men
sitting in the moon, drinking,
their beards and eyebrows clearly visible,
like reflections in a mirror.
After a while,
the moon gradually darkened;
the disciples brought candles,
and then the Daoist priest sat alone, his guests gone without a trace.
The dishes and nuts on the table were still as before.
The moon on the wall
was merely a round piece of paper, like a mirror.
The Daoist priest asked the disciples:
“Have you drunk enough?”
They replied:
“Enough.”
“If you've had enough, you should go to bed early,
don't delay your woodcutting.”
The disciples agreed and withdrew.
Wáng (王) secretly admired and longed for this,
and his desire to return home ceased.
Another month passed,
the hardship became unbearable,
yet the Daoist priest had not taught him a single skill.
He could not wait any longer,
and so he took his leave, saying:
“This disciple traveled hundreds of *lǐ* (里) to seek instruction from the immortal master;
even if I cannot obtain the art of immortality,
if I could learn even a small skill,
it would comfort my heart's desire for teaching;
yet after two or three months,
it's been nothing but cutting wood in the morning and returning in the evening.
At home, this disciple
was not accustomed to such hardship.”
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
“I knew you couldn't endure hardship,
and now it has proven true.
Tomorrow morning I shall send you on your way.”
Wáng (王) said:
“This disciple has toiled for many days;
if the master would just impart a small skill,
this journey would not have been in vain.”
The Daoist priest asked:
“What skill do you seek?”
Wáng (王) said:
“I often see the master pass through places
that walls cannot obstruct;
if I could obtain this method, that would be enough.”
The Daoist priest smiled and consented.
He then imparted a spell,
told Wáng (王) to chant it himself,
and then called out:
“Enter!”
Wáng (王) faced the wall,
not daring to enter.
The priest said again:
“Try to enter.”
Wáng (王) indeed walked calmly toward it,
but was blocked by the wall.
The Daoist priest said:
“Lower your head and enter quickly,
don't hesitate!”
Wáng (王) then stood a few steps from the wall,
ran into it;
upon reaching the wall,
it was as if nothing was there;
looking back,
he was indeed outside the wall.
Greatly delighted,
he entered to give thanks.
The Daoist priest said:
“When you return, you must maintain purity,
otherwise, it will not work.”
He then provided Wáng (王) with travel money
and sent him home.
Upon arriving home,
he boasted of meeting an immortal,
and that solid walls could not obstruct him.
His wife did not believe him.
Wáng (王) imitated his actions,
stood a few feet from the wall,
ran into it,
and struck his head against the hard wall,
suddenly falling down.
His wife helped him up and examined him;
a swelling had risen on his forehead,
like a giant egg.
His wife mocked him.
Wáng (王) was ashamed and angry,
and merely cursed the old Daoist priest for his treachery.
Yìshǐshì (異史氏) says:
“Upon hearing this story,
none can help but laugh;
yet, they do not realize that in this world, those who are like Wáng Shēng (王生)
are quite numerous.
There are now vulgar people
who delight in affliction and fear medicine;
thus there are those who lick sores and suck hemorrhoids,
offering methods of displaying power and violence
to please their masters,
and deceiving them by saying: 'If you go forth with this method,
you can act without hindrance.'
The first attempt might achieve a small success,
and then they believe that the entire world
can be managed in this manner,
not stopping until they hit a hard wall and fall down.”
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì (聊齋誌異)
A monk from Chángqīng (長清),
whose conduct was noble and pure.
Though over seventy, he was still strong.
One day,
he fell and could not rise;
the monastery monks rushed to help,
but he had already attained *parinirvāṇa*.
The monk did not realize his own death;
his soul drifted away
and reached the border of Hénán (河南).
In Hénán (河南), there was the son of a former gentry member,
who led more than ten horsemen,
hunting rabbits with hawks.
His horse bolted,
and he fell and died.
The monk's soul happened to encounter him,
and abruptly merged with him,
then gradually revived.
The servants returned and questioned him.
He opened his eyes and said:
“How did I get here!”
The crowd helped him home.
Upon entering the gate,
fair-faced and elegantly dressed women
flocked to him, inquiring about his well-being.
He was greatly alarmed and said:
“I am a monk,
how did I get here!”
The family thought he was delusional,
and together they pulled his ears to make him understand.
The monk did not try to explain himself,
but simply closed his eyes and said nothing more.
They offered him coarse rice, and he ate it;
but he refused wine and meat.
At night, he slept alone,
and would not accept service from his wife or concubines.
A few days later,
he suddenly thought of taking a short walk.
Everyone was pleased.
As soon as he went out,
he settled down for a moment,
then many servants came rushing in,
with money ledgers and grain registers,
asking for various accounts.
The young master pleaded illness and fatigue,
and dismissed them all.
He only asked:
"Do you know Chángqīng Xiàn
in Shāndōng?"
They all replied:
"We know it."
He said:
"I am depressed and bored,
and wish to go there for sightseeing.
You should prepare for the journey immediately."
The servants believed he had only recently recovered,
and should not travel far.
He did not listen,
and departed the next day.
Upon arriving in Chángqīng,
the scenery was just as before.
Without needing to ask directions,
he went straight to the monastery.
Several disciples, seeing a distinguished guest arrive,
bowed in humble reverence.
Then he asked:
"Where has the old monk gone?"
They replied:
"Our master passed away long ago."
He asked about the burial place.
The group led him there,
and it was a three-foot lone grave,
where the wild grass had not yet grown together.
The monks did not know what he meant.
Presently, he ordered his horse to prepare for return,
and instructed them:
"Your master was a monk of strict discipline and conduct.
The writings he left behind,
you should scrupulously preserve,
and not allow them to be damaged."
The monks assented repeatedly.
Then he departed.
Upon his return,
he sat listlessly, disheartened,
and did not attend to any household matters.
After several months,
he left home and absconded,
going directly to the old monastery,
and told the disciples:
"I am your master."
The monks doubted his claim,
looked at each other and smiled.
Then he recounted the reason for his return from the dead,
and also spoke of his deeds throughout his life,
all of which matched.
The monks then believed him,
and settled him in his old bed,
serving him as they had before.
Later, the young master's family repeatedly sent carriages and horses,
begging him to return,
but he paid them no heed.
After another year or so,
his wife sent Jǐgāng
with many gifts.
He rejected all gold and silk,
accepting only one set of plain robes.
When friends occasionally visited his hometown,
they respectfully called on him.
They saw that he was a silent and sincere man;
though only thirty years old,
he frequently spoke of events from eighty-plus years ago.
Yìshǐshì said:
"When a person dies, their soul scatters.
For it to not scatter over a thousand *lǐ*,
it is because of a steadfast nature.
As for the monk,
I am not surprised by his rebirth,
but I am surprised that a person from a prosperous and luxurious home,
could cut himself off from others to escape the world.
If a mere glance of an eye,
can make one's heart fragrant with musk,
there are those who wish for death but cannot find it,
how much more so for a monk!"
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition.
A snake charmer from Dōngjùn, named So-and-so,
made a living by performing with snakes.
He once kept two tame snakes,
both green: the larger one he called Dàqīng,
the smaller one Èrqīng.
Èrqīng had a red spot on its forehead,
and was especially intelligent and tame;
it coiled and moved exactly as desired.
The snake charmer loved it,
more than any other snake.
After a year,
Dàqīng died,
and he thought of replacing it,
but had not had the time.
One night,
he lodged in a mountain temple.
When dawn broke,
he opened his basket,
and Èrqīng was also gone.
The snake charmer was so heartbroken he wished to die.
He searched diligently and called out repeatedly,
but there was no sign.
However, whenever they were in dense woods and lush grass,
he would often release it to go,
allowing it to roam freely,
and it would soon return: because of this,
he hoped it would come back on its own.
He sat and waited,
but as the sun rose high,
he had already given up hope,
and unhappily set off.
After walking a few steps outside the gate,
he heard a rustling sound
among the firewood and brambles.
He stopped and looked around in surprise,
and there was Èrqīng.
He was overjoyed,
as if he had found a precious jade.
He rested his shoulder by the roadside,
and the snake also settled down.
Looking behind it,
a small snake followed.
He stroked it and said:
"I thought you were gone.
Is this a little companion you recommended?"
He took out food and fed it,
and also fed the small snake.
Although the small snake did not leave,
it cowered and dared not eat.
Èrqīng held food in its mouth for it,
just like a host yielding to a guest.
The snake charmer fed it again,
and then it ate.
After eating,
it followed Èrqīng into the basket.
He carried them away and trained it,
and it immediately twisted and turned according to the rules,
without the slightest difference from Èrqīng,
so he named it Xiǎoqīng.
He showed off his skills everywhere,
and earned countless profits.
Generally, when snake charmers play with snakes,
they only use two *chǐ* as a standard;
if a snake becomes too large and heavy,
they immediately replace it.
— Because the two green snakes were well-trained,
they were not hastily abandoned.
After another two or three years,
they grew to over three *chǐ* long.
When they coiled, they filled the basket,
so it was decided to release them.
One day,
they went to the mountains east of Zīyì,
fed them delicious bait,
offered a prayer, and set them free.
After they left,
a moment later, one returned,
coiling outside the basket.
The snake charmer waved his hand and said:
"Go!
There is no feast in the world that never ends.
From now on, conceal yourself in the great valley,
and you will surely become a divine dragon.
How can you remain long in this basket?"
The snake then left.
The snake charmer watched it go.
After a while, it returned again.
He waved it away, but it wouldn't leave,
instead, it touched the basket with its head.
Xiǎoqīng inside
also trembled and moved.
The snake charmer realized and said:
"Could it be that you want to bid farewell to Xiǎoqīng?"
So he opened the basket.
Xiǎoqīng immediately came out,
and then they intertwined their heads and flicked their tongues,
as if conversing.
After a while, they intertwined and left together.
Just as he thought Xiǎoqīng would not return,
presently it came back alone, walking slowly,
and indeed entered the basket to lie down.
From then on, he searched everywhere
but found no better ones.
And Xiǎoqīng also gradually grew larger,
and could not be played with.
Later, he got another one,
also quite tame,
but ultimately not as good as Xiǎoqīng.
And Xiǎoqīng's body was as thick as a child's arm.
Previously,
when the two green snakes were in the mountains,
woodcutters often saw them.
After several more years,
they grew several *chǐ* long,
and their girth was like a bowl;
they gradually came out and chased people,
so travelers warned each other,
and no one dared to use that path.
One day,
the snake charmer passed through that area,
and a snake suddenly emerged like the wind.
The snake charmer was greatly frightened and ran.
The snake pursued more fiercely.
He looked back, and it was almost upon him.
But looking at its head,
the red spot was clearly there,
and he realized it was Èrqīng.
He put down his load and called out:
"Èrqīng,
Èrqīng!"
The snake immediately stopped.
It raised its head for a long time,
then coiled itself around the snake charmer,
just as in the old days when he played with it.
He felt that its intention was not bad at all,
but its body was huge and heavy,
and he could not bear its coiling;
he fell to the ground and pleaded,
and then it released him.
It also touched the basket with its head.
The snake charmer understood its meaning
and opened the basket to let out Xiǎoqīng.
The two snakes met,
intertwining like sticky candy,
and only separated after a long time.
The snake charmer then addressed Xiǎoqīng:
"I have long wanted to part with you;
now you have a companion."
He said to Èrqīng:
"You brought it here,
now you can take it away.
I have one more thing to say: there is no lack of food and drink in the deep mountains,
do not disturb travelers,
lest you incur Heaven's wrath."
The two snakes bowed their heads,
as if accepting the words.
They suddenly rose,
the larger one in front,
the smaller one behind.
Where they passed, the trees in the forest parted for them.
The snake charmer stood and watched them
until they were out of sight, then left.
From then on, travelers were able to pass as usual,
not knowing where they went.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"A snake,
a simple, foolish creature,
yet it harbors such affection for an old friend.
Moreover, it accepts advice as easily as turning one's hand.
It is only strange that those who appear human,
after ten years of close friendship,
or being favored for generations by a benefactor,
often think of throwing stones after pushing one into a well;
or if not that,
then they meet good counsel with scorn,
and brazenly disregard it,
or even become angry and hostile towards it.
Even this snake would be ashamed of such people."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a person surnamed Hú in Hútiáncūn.
His brothers were woodcutters,
and they ventured deep into a secluded valley.
They encountered a giant python.
The elder brother was in front
and was swallowed by it.
The younger brother was initially startled and wanted to flee,
but seeing his brother being devoured,
he furiously drew his woodcutting axe
and chopped at the snake's head.
The head was injured, but it did not stop swallowing.
However, although the head was already inside,
fortunately, the shoulder region could not pass further down.
The younger brother, in his extreme desperation and without a plan,
held his brother's feet with both hands,
struggling with all his might against the python,
and finally dragged his brother out.
The python, also in pain, left.
Looking at his brother,
his nose and ears were completely dissolved,
and he was on the verge of death.
Carrying him on his shoulder, he walked.
Along the way, he rested more than ten times
before finally reaching home.
After half a year of medical care,
he finally recovered. To this day, his face is covered with scars,
and only holes remain where his nose and ears were.
Alas!
Among farmers,
to have a younger brother like this!
Someone said:
"The python did not cause harm
because it was touched by virtue and righteousness."
Indeed, it is true!
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Jiǎ from Qīngzhōu
was away on business,
often not returning home for a year.
His family kept a large white dog.
His wife led it to mate,
and the dog became accustomed to it.
One day,
the husband returned
and slept with his wife.
The dog suddenly rushed in,
climbed onto the bed,
and bit Jiǎ to death.
Later, the neighbors heard about it
and, feeling it was unjust,
reported it to the authorities.
The official interrogated the woman,
but she refused to confess,
so she was imprisoned.
The official ordered the dog to be tied up and brought forth,
then the woman was brought out.
When the dog suddenly saw the woman,
it went straight to her, tore her clothes, and made mating gestures.
Only then did the woman have nothing to say.
Two constables were sent to escort them to the Provincial Commissioner's court,
one escorting the person and one escorting the dog.
Those who wanted to see them mate
pooled money to bribe the constables,
who then brought them together to mate.
Wherever they stopped,
there were often hundreds of spectators,
and the constables profited greatly from this.
Later, both the woman and the dog were cut into small pieces and died.
Alas!
Vast indeed is the universe,
and truly there is nothing that does not exist.
But are there only such human-faced beasts
as this one woman?
The Historian of the Strange delivered a judgment on this, saying:
"Meeting on the Púshàng,
was scorned by the ancients;
coupling in Sāngzhōng,
people wouldn't even deign to mention.
Yet someone,
unable to bear the hardship of lonely widowhood,
recklessly desired the joy of illicit union.
A Yakṣa lay beneath the bed,
which turned out to be the family's female beast;
Jiéqīng entered the burrow,
and thus became the lover under the covers.
Before the Wūshān platform,
wildly wagging the tail of a dào;
in the land of tenderness,
frequently embracing the waist of an xiàng.
A sharp awl in a leather pouch,
a single thrust of the buttocks, and it pierced through;
a knot of passion at the arrow's neck,
no sooner had it buried its shaft than it took root.
Suddenly thinking of interspecies coupling,
truly belongs to a thought beyond the human.
A dragon barks of adultery and commits adultery,
jealousy, cruelty, and murder,
laws like Xiāo Cáo's cannot govern it;
a human not a beast, yet actually a beast,
adultery, filth, and lewdness,
its flesh not eaten by wolves and tigers.
Alas!
When a human commits adultery and murder,
the woman is condemned to dismemberment;
but as for a dog committing adultery and murder,
there is no such punishment in the living world.
When a human is wicked,
they are punished by becoming a dog;
but as for a wicked dog,
the underworld's laws must be exhausted.
It is fitting to dismember it to pursue its soul,
please escort it to question Yánluó."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wáng Gōngyúncāng,
upon taking office in Chǔzhōng,
intended to ascend Mount Lónghǔ to pay respects to the Heavenly Master.
When he reached the lake,
as he was about to board the boat,
a man immediately came in a small skiff,
asking the people in the boat to announce him.
The Duke saw him;
his appearance was tall and imposing.
From his bosom, he produced the Heavenly Master's calling card,
saying:
"Hearing that your retinue is about to arrive,
I was sent ahead as an armed escort."
The Duke was surprised by his foreknowledge,
and became even more convinced of his divinity,
proceeding with sincere respect.
The Heavenly Master prepared a feast to entertain him.
Among his attendants,
many did not resemble ordinary people in their attire, caps, beards, and manes.
The former messenger also waited by his side.
After a short while,
he whispered to the Heavenly Master.
The Heavenly Master said to the Duke:
"This is your fellow countryman,
do you not recognize him?"
The Duke asked about him.
He replied:
"This is none other than Lǐ Zuǒchē, the Hail God, as transmitted in the world."
The Duke was astonished and changed his expression.
The Heavenly Master said:
"He just said he was instructed to cause hail,
so he came to take his leave."
The Duke asked,
"Where?"
He replied:
"Zhāngqiū."
The Duke, concerned because it bordered his jurisdiction,
rose from his seat to beg for its exemption.
The Heavenly Master said:
"This is an imperial decree from the Jade Emperor;
the hail has a fixed quota,
how can I give way to personal favors?"
The Duke continued to plead.
The Heavenly Master pondered for a long time,
then looked at him and instructed:
"Let it fall mostly in the valleys,
and not harm the crops, that will do."
He also instructed:
"With such a distinguished guest present,
leave peacefully, not forcefully."
The god departed,
and in the courtyard,
smoke suddenly rose from beneath his feet,
filling the ground with mist.
After a delay of more than a quarter of an hour,
he exerted great effort to ascend,
only then reaching higher than the courtyard trees;
then he rose again,
higher than the pavilions.
With a clap of thunder,
he flew northward,
shaking the houses
and causing the banquet vessels to rattle.
The Duke exclaimed in shock:
"His departure is accompanied by thunder and lightning!"
The Heavenly Master said:
"I just warned him,
which is why he lingered;
otherwise,
with a single sound from level ground,
he would have vanished instantly."
The Duke took his leave and returned,
noting the date,
and sent someone to inquire in Zhāngqiū.
Indeed, on that day, there was a great hailstorm,
filling all the ditches,
but there were only a few pieces in the fields.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Yīn Tiāngōng of Lìchéng,
was poor in his youth,
but had courage and resourcefulness.
In the district, there was an old family's residence,
covering dozens of *mǔ*,
with buildings stretching continuously.
Strange occurrences were often seen there,
thus it was abandoned and uninhabited;
over time,
weeds gradually covered it,
and even in broad daylight, no one dared to enter.
One day, Yīn Tiāngōng was drinking with some scholars,
and someone jokingly said:
"Anyone who can spend a night here,
we'll all chip in for a feast."
Yīn Tiāngōng sprang up and said:
"What's so difficult about that!"
He carried a mat and went.
The group escorted him to the gate,
and jokingly said;
"We'll wait for you for a while;
if you see anything,
you should shout urgently."
Yīn Tiāngōng laughed and said:
"If there are ghosts or foxes,
I'll catch them for proof."
So he entered,
seeing long grass covering the path,
and mugwort as dense as flax.
It was the time of the waxing moon,
fortunately the moonlight was dim and yellow,
and the doors and windows were discernible.
He fumbled his way forward several times,
before finally reaching the back building.
He ascended to the moon terrace,
which was clean and lovely,
and so he stopped there.
Looking west at the bright moon,
it was only a sliver clinging to the mountains.
He sat for a long time,
with nothing unusual happening,
secretly laughing at the falsity of the rumors.
He sat on the ground, used a stone as a pillow,
and lay watching the Cowherd and Weaving Maid.
As the first watch was nearing its end,
feeling drowsy and on the verge of sleep,
I heard footsteps downstairs,
rustling upwards.
Feigning sleep, I glanced over,
and saw a man in green clothes,
carrying a lotus lantern.
Suddenly seeing me,
he was startled and retreated.
He told those behind him:
"There's a living person here."
Someone below asked:
"Who is it?"
He replied:
"I don't know."
