Presently, an old man came up,
looked closely at me,
and said:
"This is Shàngshū Yīn,
he is sound asleep.
Just attend to our business;
Xiànggōng is a magnanimous person,
and perhaps won't scold us."
Then they led each other into the building,
and all the doors of the building opened wide.
After a while,
the comings and goings became more frequent.
The lights upstairs shone as bright as day.
I subtly shifted my position,
and coughed and sneezed.
The old man, hearing me awake,
came out,
knelt and said:
"Your humble servant has a daughter,
who is getting married tonight.
I did not expect to disturb your honorable self;
I hope you will not punish us severely."
I rose,
and pulled him up, saying:
"I was unaware of this auspicious ceremony tonight;
I am ashamed to have nothing to offer as a congratulation."
The old man said:
"Your esteemed presence
repels ominous evils;
it is truly fortunate.
If you would trouble yourself to sit with us,
it would greatly add to our honor and glory."
I was pleased,
and agreed.
Entering and looking at the building,
the furnishings were exquisite and beautiful.
Then a woman came out to bow,
about forty years old.
The old man said:
"This is my humble wife."
I bowed to her.
Presently, I heard a cacophony of sheng music,
and someone rushed up,
saying:
"They've arrived!"
The old man hurried to welcome them,
and I also stood waiting.
A short while later,
a cluster of figures veiled in gauze
led the groom in.
He was about seventeen or eighteen,
with a handsome and refined demeanor.
The old man ordered him to first perform the ritual with the esteemed guest.
The young man looked at me.
I acted as an usher,
presiding over half of the ceremony.
Next, the old man and his son-in-law bowed to each other.
After this,
they took their seats.
Soon after,
beautiful women gathered like clouds,
and wine and meat flowed like mist,
with jade bowls and golden goblets
shining brightly on the tables.
After several rounds of wine,
the old man called a maidservant to invite the young lady.
The maidservant assented and went in,
but did not come out for a long time.
The old man got up himself,
pulled aside the curtain, and urged her.
Presently, several maids and matrons escorted the bride out,
her adornments jingling,
and the fragrance of musk and orchids diffused.
The old man instructed her to bow to me first.
After rising,
she sat beside her mother.
I subtly looked at her;
with a kingfisher phoenix headdress and bright earrings,
her beauty was unparalleled.
Then, I was served wine in a golden goblet,
which could hold several dòu.
I thought that this item could be used as proof to my companions,
and secretly put it into my sleeve.
I feigned drunkenness, leaned on the table,
and slumped into sleep.
Everyone said:
"Xiànggōng is drunk."
Not long after,
the groom announced his departure,
the sheng music erupted loudly,
and they all descended the stairs and left.
Afterward, the host collected the wine utensils;
one goblet was missing,
and it could not be found despite a thorough search.
Some secretly discussed the sleeping guest; the old man urgently warned them not to speak,
fearing I would hear.
After a while,
inside and out were completely silent,
and I finally got up.
It was dark without any lights,
only the fragrance of rouge and the smell of wine
filled the four walls.
Seeing that the east was already white,
I calmly went out.
Reaching into my sleeve,
the golden goblet was still there.
At the door,
the students were already waiting,
suspicious that I had gone out at night and returned early.
I took out the goblet to show them.
Everyone was astonished and asked,
and I recounted the situation.
They all thought that such an item was not something a poor scholar would possess,
and thus believed me.
Later, I passed the imperial examination to become a Jìnshì,
and was appointed to Féiqiū.
A prominent family named Zhū hosted me,
and ordered a large wine horn to be brought.
It was long in coming.
A young servant covered his mouth and whispered to the host,
who showed a look of anger.
Presently, a golden goblet was presented to urge the guests to drink.
Looking closely,
its style and carvings
were no different from the fox-spirit's item.
Greatly perplexed,
I asked where it came from.
They replied:
"There are eight such goblets in total.
When our elder was a Jīngqīng,
he sought out skilled craftsmen to supervise their creation.
This is a family heirloom,
carefully preserved for a long time.
Because you, Míngfǔ, honored us with your presence,
we just took them from the chests;
only seven remain.
We suspect a family member stole one;
yet, ten years of dust seal remains intact,
which is truly inexplicable."
I smiled and said:
"The golden goblet has transformed and flown away.
However, a treasured family heirloom must not be lost.
I have one,
quite similar,
which I shall present to you."
After the banquet, I returned to my residence,
selected the goblet, and dispatched it to them.
The host examined it,
and was utterly astonished.
He personally went to thank me,
and inquired about its origin.
I then recounted the entire story.
Only then did they realize that an item from a thousand lǐ away
could be brought by a fox spirit,
but it dared not keep it permanently.
According to the manuscript of 'Liáozhāi Zhìyì'
Kǒng Shēng Xuělì,
was a descendant of Confucius.
He was a refined person,
and skilled in poetry.
A close friend of his was a magistrate in Tiāntái,
who sent a letter inviting him.
Kǒng Shēng went,
but the magistrate had just passed away.
He was stranded and unable to return home,
so he lodged at Pútuó Sì,
working for the monks by copying scriptures.
About a hundred paces west of the temple
was the residence of Shàn Xiānshēng.
Shàn Xiānshēng was formerly a young nobleman,
but due to a major lawsuit, his family became desolate,
his household sparse,
and he moved to live in the countryside,
leaving the mansion empty.
One day,
a heavy snowstorm raged,
and no travelers were to be seen.
As he happened to pass by their gate,
a young man emerged,
of very elegant demeanor.
Seeing Shēng,
he hastened to greet him,
offered a brief welcome and inquiry,
and immediately invited him to descend and enter.
Shēng was delighted with him,
and readily followed him in.
The houses were not very spacious overall,
but everywhere hung brocade curtains,
and on the walls were many ancient calligraphies and paintings.
On the table was a book,
with a label that read:
“Lánghuán Suǒjì.”
He browsed through it once,
and everything was unseen by his eyes before.
Shēng, believing the residence to be the Dān family's home,
thought the young man was the master of the house,
and did not inquire about his official status or lineage.
The young man questioned Shēng in detail about his travels,
pitying him,
and advised him to set up a school and take on pupils.
Shēng sighed and said:
“As a sojourner,
who would act as Cáo Qiū?”
The young man said:
“If you do not reject my mediocrity,
I would like to become your disciple.”
Shēng was pleased,
but dared not accept the role of a master,
and asked to be friends instead.
Then he asked:
“Why has this residence been closed for so long?”
He replied:
“This is the Dān family residence.
Previously, the young master lived in the countryside,
which is why it has been vacant for so long.
My family name is Huángfǔ,
and our ancestors lived in Shǎn.
Because our ancestral home was burned down in a wildfire,
we are temporarily borrowing this place for lodging.”
Shēng then realized it was not the Dān family’s.
That evening,
they talked and laughed very happily,
and he stayed to share a bed.
At dawn,
a servant boy immediately brought charcoal and fire into the room.
The young man rose first and went inside,
while Shēng was still sitting wrapped in his quilt.
The servant boy entered and
announced:
“Tàigōng has arrived.”
Shēng started up in surprise.
An old man entered,
his hair and beard all white,
and he profusely thanked Shēng, saying:
“Sir, you have not spurned my foolish son,
and are willing to impart your teachings.
My little boy is just beginning to scribble;
do not, because of your friendship,
treat him as your equal.”
After this, he presented a set of brocade clothes,
and a sable hat, socks, and shoes, each one item.
After seeing Shēng wash and comb,
he then called for wine and food to be served.
The tables, couches, skirts, and clothes,
he did not know their names,
but they shone with dazzling brilliance.
After several rounds of wine,
the old man excused himself,
and left, leaning on his staff.
After the meal,
the young master presented his schoolwork,
which were all classical literary essays,
with no contemporary examination essays.
When asked about it,
he smiled and said:
“I do not seek advancement.”
When evening came,
they poured more wine and said:
“Tonight we shall make merry,
but tomorrow it will not be permitted.”
He called a servant boy and said:
“See if Tàigōng is asleep yet;
if he is,
you can secretly call Xiāngnú here.”
The servant boy left,
first bringing a pipa in an embroidered pouch.
A little while later,
a maid entered,
resplendent in her red attire.
The young master ordered her to play Xiāngfēi.
The maid plucked the strings with an ivory pick,
producing fervent and sorrowful sounds,
the rhythm unlike anything he had heard before.
He then ordered her to serve wine with large goblets,
and they did not stop until the third watch.
The next day,
they rose early and studied together.
The young master was most intelligent;
what he saw, he could compose into verse,
and after two or three months,
his writing was strikingly brilliant.
They agreed to drink once every five days,
and each time they drank, Xiāngnú was always summoned.
One evening,
when the wine flowed and passions ran high,
Shēng fixed his gaze on her.
The young master understood his intention,
and said:
“This maid is kept by my old father.
Brother, you are far from home and without a family;
I have been planning for you day and night for a long time.
It is time for me to find you a good match.”
Shēng said:
“If you are truly so kind,
she must be like Xiāngnú.”
The young master laughed and said:
“You are truly ‘one who has seen little and is surprised by much’!
If you consider this to be good,
then your desires are easily satisfied.”
After half a year,
the student wanted to stroll in the suburbs,
but when he reached the gate,
the double doors were locked from the outside.
He inquired about it.
The gōngzǐ said:
"My father fears that social interactions might distract your thoughts,
so he declines visitors."
The student also accepted this.
It was mid-summer, hot and humid,
so they moved his study to the garden pavilion.
A lump, like a peach, swelled on the student's chest,
and overnight it grew as large as a bowl,
causing him to moan in agony.
The gōngzǐ visited him day and night,
neglecting his own sleep and meals.
After several more days,
the wound worsened,
and he completely stopped eating and drinking.
The Tàigōng also arrived,
and they sighed facing each other.
The gōngzǐ said:
"Last night, I thought of Xiānshēng's illness,
and my younger sister Jiāonà can cure it.
I sent someone to her maternal grandparents' place to summon her home. Why is she taking so long to arrive?"
Suddenly, a僮 came in and said:
"Nàgū is here,
Yí and Sōnggū came with her."
Father and son hurried inside.
A short while later,
he brought his sister to see the student.
She was about thirteen or fourteen years old,
with charming eyes that flowed with intelligence,
and a slender figure that exuded grace.
Upon seeing her countenance, the student
instantly forgot his pain and moans,
and his spirits were refreshed.
The gōngzǐ immediately said:
"This brother is a good friend,
no less than a sibling;
sister, please heal him well."
The girl then composed her shy expression,
pulled back her long sleeves,
and approached the bed to examine him.
As she took his pulse,
he felt a fragrance more exquisite than orchids.
The girl smiled and said:
"It's natural to have this illness;
his heart pulse is agitated.
However, though the condition is critical,
it is curable;
but since the skin mass has already solidified,
it cannot be treated without cutting the skin and scraping the flesh."
She then took off a gold bracelet from her arm and placed it on the affected area,
slowly sliding it down.
The wound protruded about an inch,
rising high above the bracelet,
while the remaining swelling at the base
was completely confined within,
no longer as wide as a bowl as before.
Then, with one hand, she opened her silk tunic,
unfastened a dagger,
whose blade was thinner than paper.
Holding the bracelet and grasping the blade,
she gently cut at the base of the growth.
Purple blood flowed out,
staining the bed sheets,
but being close to her charming form,
he not only felt no pain,
but even feared that the cutting would finish too quickly,
and he would not be able to linger near her.
Before long,
she cut off the putrid flesh,
which was round and resembled a burl cut from a tree.
She then called for water
to wash the cut area.
She spat out a red pill,
the size of a bullet,
placed it on the flesh,
and pressed and rotated it: after one rotation,
he felt hot steam rising;
after another rotation,
a pleasant itch began;
after three rotations,
his entire body felt cool,
seeping into his bones.
The girl swallowed the pill,
and said:
"It's cured!"
She walked out quickly.
The student sprang up to thank her,
his chronic illness vanished as if it had never been.
But his mind kept replaying her radiant beauty,
unable to stop.
From then on, he abandoned his books and sat in a daze,
finding no solace.
The gōngzǐ, having perceived this,
said:
"I have found a suitable match for you, my brother."
He asked:
"Who is it?"
He replied:
"She is also a member of my family."
The student pondered for a long time,
only saying:
"No need."
He faced the wall and recited:
"Once you've crossed the vast ocean, other waters are not water;
besides Wūshān, there are no clouds."
The gōngzǐ understood his implication
and said:
"My father admires your great talent,
and has always wanted to arrange a marriage.
However, there is only one younger sister,
who is too young.
There is an aunt's daughter, Āsōng,
who is eighteen years old,
and quite refined.
If you don't believe me,
Sister Sōng walks through the garden pavilion daily.
Wait in the front chamber,
and you can see her."
The student followed his advice,
and indeed saw Jiāonà arrive with a beautiful woman.
Her painted eyebrows curved like moths,
her lotus-like feet moved gracefully like a phoenix,
and she was comparable to Jiāonà.
The student was greatly pleased,
and asked the gōngzǐ to act as matchmaker.
The gōngzǐ came out from inside the next day,
and congratulated him, saying:
"It's settled!"
Then, they cleared a separate courtyard
to hold the wedding ceremony for the student.
That evening,
the sounds of drums and wind instruments filled the air,
dust settled and flew,
as if the immortal he had seen
was suddenly sharing his bed,
making him doubt that the Guǎnghán Palace
was necessarily in the clouds.
After the wedding ceremony,
he was very content.
One evening,
the gōngzǐ said to the student:
"Your kindness in teaching and learning together
is something I can never forget.
Recently, the single gōngzǐ has returned from his lawsuit,
and is urgently demanding his house back.
I intend to abandon this place and move west.
It will be difficult for us to meet again,
and thus, feelings of separation weigh on my mind."
The student wished to go with him.
The gōngzǐ advised him to return to his hometown,
which the student found difficult.
The gōngzǐ said:
"Don't worry,
I can send you off immediately."
Before long,
the Tàigōng brought Sōngniáng,
and presented the student with a hundred taels of gold.
The gōngzǐ took the student and his wife by the hands,
and instructed them to close their eyes and not look.
They floated lightly through the air,
only feeling the wind whistling past their ears.
After a long while, he said:
"We've arrived."
When they opened their eyes,
they indeed saw their hometown.
Only then did the student realize that the gōngzǐ was not human.
Happily, he knocked on his family's door.
His mother came out, unexpectedly,
and also saw a beautiful wife,
and they rejoiced together.
When he looked back,
the gōngzǐ had vanished.
Sōngniáng was filial to her mother-in-law;
her beauty and virtuous reputation
were widely known.
Later, Kǒng Shēng passed the imperial examination for jinshì,
and was appointed Judicial Officer of Yán'ān.
He took his family to his post.
His mother, however, did not go, as the journey was too far.
Sōng Niáng gave birth to a son,
named Xiǎo Huàn.
Kǒng Shēng offended the Imperial Commissioner
and was dismissed from office.
He was entangled in difficulties and could not return home.
One day, while hunting in the countryside,
he met a handsome young man,
riding a black horse,
who frequently looked back at him.
On closer inspection,
it was indeed Huángfǔ Gōngzǐ.
Kǒng Shēng reined in his horse and stopped,
filled with mixed emotions of joy and sorrow.
Gōngzǐ invited Kǒng Shēng to his home.
They arrived at a village
where the trees were thick and dark,
shading the sun.
Entering his house,
they found it adorned with gilded nails,
clearly indicating a distinguished family.
He asked about his sister,
who had married;
and his mother-in-law,
who had passed away.
He was deeply saddened and mournful.
After staying the night, they parted.
Kǒng Shēng returned with his wife.
Jiāonà also arrived,
and playfully took Kǒng Shēng's son, saying:
"Sister, you've mixed up our lineage."
Kǒng Shēng bowed in gratitude for her past kindness.
She smiled and said:
"Brother-in-law, you're a high official!
The wound has healed,
but have you forgotten the pain?"
Her brother-in-law, Wú Láng,
also came to pay his respects.
They stayed for two nights before leaving.
One day,
Gōngzǐ looked worried
and said to Kǒng Shēng:
"Heaven is sending a great calamity.
Can you save us?"
Kǒng Shēng did not know what it was,
but eagerly pledged himself to the task.
Gōngzǐ hurried out,
called his whole family to enter,
and they knelt and bowed in the hall.
Kǒng Shēng was greatly alarmed
and urgently asked what was happening.
Gōngzǐ said:
"I am not human;
I am a fox.
Now there is a thunderous tribulation approaching.
If you are willing to risk your life,
our entire family may be spared;
otherwise,
please take your son and leave,
and do not be implicated."
Kǒng Shēng swore to share their life and death.
So Gōngzǐ instructed him to stand guard at the door with a sword,
and warned:
"When the thunder strikes,
do not move!"
Kǒng Shēng did as he was told.
Indeed, dark clouds obscured the sky at midday,
making it as black as night.
Looking back at their former dwelling,
there were no longer any houses or gates,
only a towering tomb standing prominently,
and a bottomless cavern.
While he was still bewildered,
a clap of thunder erupted,
shaking mountains and valleys;
torrential rain and fierce winds
uprooted old trees.
Kǒng Shēng was dizzy and deaf,
but stood firm and did not move.
Suddenly, amidst the dense smoke and black wisps,
he saw a demonic creature
with a sharp beak and long claws,
snatching a person from the cavern
and ascending directly with the smoke.
Glancing at the clothes and shoes,
he thought it resembled Jiāonà.
So he swiftly leaped from the ground
and struck it with his sword,
and it immediately fell.
Suddenly, a violent thunderclap burst,
and Kǒng Shēng stumbled
and died.
After a short while,
the weather cleared.
Jiāonà was already able to revive herself.
Seeing Kǒng Shēng lying dead beside her,
she cried loudly:
"Kǒng Láng died for me!
Why should I live?"
Sōng Niáng also came out,
and together they carried Kǒng Shēng back.
Jiāonà had Sōng Niáng hold his head;
her brother used a golden hairpin to pry open his teeth;
then she herself took his chin,
used her tongue to pass a red pill into his mouth,
and then kissed him and breathed into him.
The red pill entered his throat with his breath,
making gurgling sounds.
After some time,
he awoke and revived.
Seeing his family around him,
it was as if he had just woken from a dream.
Thus, the whole family gathered,
their fear settling into joy.
As Kǒng Shēng felt that the hidden dwelling was not suitable for long-term stay,
he proposed that they all return home.
Everyone in the hall praised the idea,
except for Jiāonà, who was unhappy.
Kǒng Shēng asked if she and Wú Láng would come,
but then worried that her parents would not leave their young son,
and they discussed it all day without resolution.
Suddenly, a small servant from Wú Láng's family
arrived, sweating and out of breath.
Alarmed, they questioned him,
and learned that Wú Láng's family had also suffered the same calamity on the same day,
and the entire family had perished.
Jiāonà stamped her foot in sorrow,
and her tears could not be stopped.
Everyone consoled her.
And so the plan to return together was settled.
Kǒng Shēng entered the city
and took care of matters for several days,
then hurried to pack overnight.
Upon returning,
he housed Gōngzǐ in an unused garden,
always keeping the gate locked from the outside;
only when Kǒng Shēng and Sōng Niáng arrived
would the latch be opened.
Kǒng Shēng and Gōngzǐ's brother and sister
would play chess, drink wine, and feast,
like one family.
Xiǎo Huàn grew up,
handsome and refined,
with a foxy charm.
When he went out into the city,
everyone knew him to be a fox child.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Regarding Kǒng Shēng,
I do not envy him for getting a beautiful wife,
but for getting such delightful friends.
Looking at their faces can make one forget hunger,
and listening to their voices can bring a smile.
To have such good friends,
and occasionally feast and converse,
is indeed 'to have one's soul captivated by beauty,'
far superior to
'flipping one's clothes inside out'
in love."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A man named Zhāng suddenly died
and was taken away by a ghost envoy.
He saw the King of the Underworld.
The King checked his ledger,
was furious that the ghost envoy had seized the wrong person,
and ordered him to be sent back.
Zhāng descended,
privately bribing the ghost envoy
to ask to see the prisons of the underworld.
The ghost led him through the nine abysses,
pointing out the knife mountain and sword forest
one by one.
Finally, they reached a place
where a monk was hanging upside down, with a rope threaded through his thighs,
screaming in unbearable pain.
Upon closer inspection,
it was his elder brother.
Zhāng was shocked and saddened to see this,
and asked,
“What sin led to this?”
The ghost replied,
“This man, though a monk,
extensively collected money
and spent it all on promiscuity and gambling.
Therefore, he is punished.
To escape this calamity,
he must genuinely repent himself.”
When Zhāng revived,
he wondered if his brother had already died.
At that time, his brother resided in the Xīngfú Sì,
so he went to visit him.
Upon entering the gate,
he immediately heard sounds of his brother’s painful cries.
Entering the room,
he saw sores growing between his thighs,
gushing with pus and blood.
His feet were hung on the wall,
exactly like the upside-down hanging in the netherworld.
Horrified, he asked the reason.
He replied,
“Hanging them like this makes it a little better;
otherwise, the pain would pierce my very heart and guts.”
Zhāng then told him what he had seen.
The monk was greatly alarmed,
and consequently abstained from meat and alcohol,
and devoutly recited sūtras and incantations.
He recovered in half a month.
He then became a monk who strictly observed the precepts.
Yìshǐ Shì said:
“The ghost prisons are vague and distant,
and evil people often use this to excuse themselves.
But they do not realize that the manifest calamities
are precisely the punishments of the netherworld.
How can one not fear!”
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Yú Gōng,
in his youth, was chivalrous
and fond of boxing and martial arts.
He was strong enough to hold a large vase
and perform a whirlwind dance.
During the Chóngzhēn reign,
he was in the capital for the palace examination.
His servant fell ill and couldn’t get up,
which troubled him.
It happened that there was a skilled diviner in the market
who could predict people’s life and death.
He intended to ask on behalf of his servant.
When he arrived,
he hadn’t spoken yet.
The diviner said,
“Are you not wishing to ask about your servant’s illness?”
Yú Gōng was amazed and assented.
He said,
“The sick one is not in danger,
but you may be.”
Yú Gōng then divined for himself.
The diviner cast the hexagrams
and said in astonishment,
“You will die in three days!”
Yú Gōng was shocked and perplexed for a long time.
The diviner calmly said,
“I possess a minor art.
If you pay me ten gold pieces,
I shall perform a ritual to avert it for you.”
Yú Gōng thought to himself,
life and death are already determined;
how could an art resolve it?
He refused to respond and stood up,
intending to leave.
The diviner said,
“Pitying this small expense, you will regret it, regret it!”
All who cared for Yú Gōng feared for him
and advised him to empty his purse to beg the diviner.
Yú Gōng did not listen.
Suddenly, the third day arrived.
Yú Gōng sat upright in his inn,
quietly observing,
and was unharmed all day long.
At night,
he closed the door, lit a lamp,
and sat precariously, leaning on his sword.
One watch was almost over,
but there was no sign of death.
Just as he intended to go to bed,
he suddenly heard a sound from a crack in the window.
He looked quickly,
and a small figure bearing a spear entered;
when it reached the ground,
it was as tall as a man.
Yú Gōng grabbed his sword and rose,
striking it quickly,
but it darted about and he missed.
It then swiftly shrank,
and sought the window crack again,
intending to escape.
Yú Gōng quickly followed it,
and it fell at his touch.
He lit it with a candle;
it was a paper figure,
its waist already broken.
Yú Gōng dared not sleep
and sat waiting again.
After some time,
an object entered through the window,
monstrous and hideous like a ghost.
As soon as it reached the ground,
he struck it quickly,
cutting it into two pieces,
both of which squirmed.
Fearing they would rise again,
he struck them repeatedly,
every sword stroke hitting,
their sound not soft.
Upon careful inspection,
it was a clay figurine,
shattered into pieces.
Thereupon, he moved his seat under the window,
his eyes fixed on the crack.
After a long time,
he heard a sound outside the window like a cow breathing heavily;
something pushed against the window frame,
the walls of the room shook,
and it seemed about to collapse.
Yú Gōng feared being crushed
and decided it was better to go out and fight it.
So, he tore off the latch with a clang
and rushed out.
He saw a giant ghost,
as tall as the eaves;
in the dim moonlight,
he saw its face was black as coal,
its eyes glinting with yellow light;
it had no clothes above
and no shoes below,
holding a bow and with arrows at its waist.
As Yú Gōng was still startled,
the ghost had already drawn its bow.
Yú Gōng parried the arrow with his sword,
and the arrow fell;
he tried to strike it,
but it had already drawn again.
Yú Gōng quickly leaped to evade,
and the arrow pierced the wall,
vibrating with a sound.
The ghost was extremely angry,
drew its saber,
swung it like the wind,
and powerfully cleaved towards Yú Gōng.
Yú Gōng darted forward like a monkey,
and the saber struck the courtyard stone,
splitting the stone instantly.
Yú Gōng emerged from between its legs,
and slashed the ghost’s ankle,
with a clanging sound.
The ghost became even angrier,
roaring like thunder,
turned around, and chopped again.
Yú Gōng again stooped down and entered;
the saber fell,
cutting Yú Gōng’s skirt.
Yú Gōng was already beneath its ribs,
and chopped it fiercely,
also with a clanging sound,
and the ghost fell forward and stiffened.
Yú Gōng struck it repeatedly and wildly,
the sound hard like a watchman’s clapper.
He lit it with a candle;
it was a wooden puppet,
as tall as a man.
The bow and arrows were still tied to its waist,
carved with a ferocious expression;
where the sword had struck,
blood emerged.
Yú Gōng then held a candle and waited for dawn,
only then realizing that the ghostly figures were all sent by the diviner,
who wished to cause people’s deaths
to make his art seem divine.
The next day,
he informed all his acquaintances,
and together they went to the diviner's place.
The diviner saw him from a distance,
but then vanished from sight in a flash.
Someone said,
"This is the art of invisibility,
which can be broken with dog's blood."
The man did as he was told,
making preparations and waiting.
The diviner again disappeared as before.
They quickly poured dog's blood on the spot where he had stood,
and saw only the diviner's head and face,
all blurred by dog's blood,
his eyes burning like a ghost standing there.
So they seized him and handed him over to the authorities, who executed him.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"I have always said that buying divination is foolish.
How many people in this world who practice this art are not mistaken about life and death?
If divination is mistaken,
it's as if one hadn't divined at all.
And even if it clearly tells me the arrival of my death,
what more can be done?
Moreover, there are those who borrow others' lives to make their art seem miraculous,
which is even more terrifying!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During Yú Qī's rebellion,
people were slaughtered like hemp.
A villager named Lǐ Huàlóng
fled from the mountains and returned.
When the main army advanced by night,
fearing the disaster of being burned or cut,
and having no place to hide,
he lay stiff among a pile of dead bodies,
feigning death.
After the troops had all passed,
he dared not get up immediately.
Suddenly, he saw headless and armless corpses
standing up like a forest.
One of these corpses, its severed head still attached to its shoulder,
spoke, saying:
"The wild dogs are coming,
what shall we do?"
The群屍 responded unevenly:
"What shall we do!"
A moment later,
they all collapsed abruptly,
and then there was complete silence.
Lǐ was just trembling with fright and about to rise,
when a creature came,
with the head of a beast and the body of a human,
stooping to gnaw on human heads,
sucking out all their brains.
Lǐ was terrified and
hid his head under a corpse.
The creature came and nudged Lǐ's shoulder,
wanting to get Lǐ's head.
Lǐ exerted his strength to stay prostrate,
preventing it from succeeding.
The creature then pushed over a corpse and moved it,
exposing Lǐ's head.
Lǐ was greatly alarmed,
groped at his waist,
and found a large stone like a bowl,
which he gripped.
The creature bent down, wanting to bite.
Lǐ suddenly rose,
let out a loud shout,
and struck its head,
hitting its mouth.
The creature howled like an owl,
covered its mouth in pain, and fled,
spitting blood on the path.
When he went to look,
he found two teeth in the blood,
curved in the middle and sharp at the tip,
more than four inches long.
He took them home to show people,
but no one knew what they were.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liú Xiàolián
could remember events from his previous life.
He was a fellow *tóngnián* with my late elder brother Wénbēn,
and often spoke of them vividly.
In one life, he was a *jìnshēn*,
and his conduct had many flaws.
He died at the age of sixty-two.
When he first met the King of the Underworld,
he was treated with the courtesy due to a village elder,
granted a seat,
and served tea.
He glanced at the King of the Underworld's cup,
where the tea was clear and transparent;
in his own cup,
it was as turbid as fermented liquor.
He secretly suspected, "Could this be the Soul-Confusing Broth?"
Taking advantage of the King of the Underworld's inattention,
he poured his cup onto the corner of the table,
feigning that he had drunk it all.
Soon after,
his evil deeds from his previous life were investigated;
angrily,
the King ordered the ghosts to drag him down
and punish him by turning him into a horse.
Immediately, fierce ghosts seized him and took him away.
They arrived at a house,
where the threshold was very high,
impossible to cross.
While he was hesitating and stumbling,
the ghosts beat him forcefully,
and he fell from extreme pain.
He looked at himself
and found his body already in the stable.
He only heard someone say:
"The black mare has foaled,
it's a male."
His mind was very clear,
but he could not speak.
Feeling extremely hungry,
he had no choice but
to seek milk from the mare.
After four or five years,
his body grew tall and strong.
He greatly feared flogging,
and would run away in terror upon seeing a whip.
When his master rode him,
he would always cover him with a saddle blanket
and hold the reins loosely and slowly,
which was not too painful;
but when servants and stablemen
rode him without a saddle or trappings,
their ankles would clip him,
causing pain that pierced to his heart.
At this, he became extremely indignant,
refused to eat for three days,
and subsequently died.
When he arrived at the Underworld court,
the King of the Underworld found that his period of punishment was not yet complete,
reprimanded him for evading it,
stripped off his hide,
and punished him by turning him into a dog.
He felt remorseful and sad,
and did not want to go.
The ghosts beat him indiscriminately,
and he fled into the wilderness in extreme pain.
He thought to himself that it was better to die,
and indignantly threw himself off a cliff,
falling so that he could not get up.
He looked at himself
and found his body lying in a den,
with a female dog licking and suckling him,
and then he knew that he had been reborn into the human world.
As he grew a little older,
he knew that even excrement was filthy;
however, when he smelled it, it was fragrant,
but he steadfastly resolved not to eat it.
Having been a dog for a year,
he often felt angry and wanted to die,
but also feared being punished for evading his sentence.
Moreover, his master fed and cared for him,
and would not kill him.
So he deliberately bit his master,
tearing off a piece of flesh from his thigh.
The master, enraged,
beat him to death with a stick.
The King of the Underworld investigated the situation,
was angry at his madness,
whipped him several hundred times,
and made him into a snake.
He was imprisoned in a dark room,
where he could not see the sky.
Feeling extremely bored,
he climbed up the wall
and burrowed out of the roof.
He looked at himself
and found himself lying in dense grass,
indeed a snake.
He then vowed not to harm living creatures,
and when hungry, ate wild fruits.
After more than a year,
he often thought of committing suicide but couldn't,
nor could he harm others and die;
he wanted to find a good way to die but had not yet succeeded.
One day,
while lying in the grass,
he heard a carriage passing,
and quickly came out onto the road;
the carriage sped over him,
breaking him in two.
Míngwáng was surprised at his swift arrival.
Thereupon, he prostrated himself and confessed.
Míngwáng, considering that he had been unjustly killed,
pardoned him,
and permitted him to be reborn as a human after his full term.
This was Liú Gōng.
Gōng could speak from birth,
and regarding literature, history, and records,
he could recite anything upon a glance.
In the Xīnyǒu year, he passed the xiàolián examination.
He always advised people: "When riding a horse, always use a thick saddlecloth;
the punishment of being clamped by the thighs
is worse than whipping."
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Among creatures with fur and horns,
there are actually kings and high officials;
the reason for this is that
among kings and high officials,
it may not necessarily be that there are no individuals with fur and horns.
Therefore, when the humble do good,
it is like seeking flowers by planting the tree;
when the noble do good,
it is like cultivating the roots of a tree that is already in bloom: those who plant can grow great,
those who cultivate can endure.
Otherwise,
they will carry salt carts,
be bridled and hobbled,
and become horses for others;
otherwise,
they will eat excrement and urine,
be cooked and butchered,
and become dogs for others;
otherwise,
they will wear scales and armor,
be buried by cranes and storks,
and become snakes for others."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The wife of the Shí clan in Wàncūn
was tormented by a fox spirit,
and suffered from it,
but could not drive it away.
There was a jar behind the door.
Whenever she heard her father-in-law coming,
the fox would immediately hide in it.
The wife observed this repeatedly,
and secretly made a plan but said nothing.
One day,
it sneaked in.
The wife quickly plugged its opening with cotton,
placed it in a pot,
and heated water until it boiled.
The jar became hot,
and the fox cried out:
"It's very hot!
Don't play such a nasty trick!"
The wife did not respond.
Its cries grew more urgent,
then after a long time, there was no sound.
She pulled out the plug to check,
and there was only a pile of fur
and a few drops of blood.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During the rebellion of Xiè Qiān,
the residences of officials all became bandit lairs.
The house of Wáng Xuéshǐ Qīxiāng
had a particularly large gathering of bandits.
When the city fell and the soldiers entered,
they swept away the villains.
Corpses filled the courtyard steps,
and blood flowed out the gate.
When Gōng entered the city,
he moved the corpses and washed away the blood to live there.
Often, he saw ghosts in broad daylight;
at night, phosphorescent lights flew under the bed,
and ghosts cried in the corners of the walls.
One day,
Wáng Shēng Hàodí was staying overnight at Gōng's house.
He heard a small voice under the bed repeatedly calling:
"Hàodí!
Hàodí!"
After a while, the voice grew louder,
saying:
"I died miserably!"
Then it cried,
and the entire courtyard was filled with crying.
When Gōng heard this,
he entered with a sword,
and said loudly:
"Do you not recognize me, Wáng Xuéyuàn?"
Then he heard a hundred snorting sounds,
laughing through their noses.
Thereupon, Gōng set up a land-and-water dharma assembly,
and ordered Buddhist and Daoist monks to perform rituals for their salvation.
When the ghost food was scattered at night,
phosphorescent lights were seen flickering,
appearing everywhere on the ground.
Previously,
a doorkeeper named Wáng had been critically ill,
unconscious for several days.
That evening,
he suddenly stretched and yawned as if waking up.
His wife offered him food.
Wáng said:
"Just now, the master, for some unknown reason,
offered food in the courtyard.
I also ate with the crowd.
I only just returned after eating,
so I didn't mind."
From then on, the ghosts and strange occurrences ceased.
Could it be that cymbals and bells,
and the Yogācāra Flaming Mouth ritual,
are indeed beneficial?
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"For evil and strange creatures,
only virtue can put an end to them.
At the time of the city's fall,
Wáng Gōng's power was at its peak,
and all who heard of it trembled;
yet the ghosts mocked him.
Could it be that the ghosts knew beforehand that he would not have a good end?
I hereby broadly declare to all great men and gentlemen of the world: If even possessing a human face cannot scare away ghosts,
then may you not put on a ghost face to scare people!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In the Zhēndìng area,
there was an orphan girl,
about six or seven years old,
taken in and raised by her husband's family.
After living together for one or two years,
her husband seduced and had intercourse with her, and she became pregnant.
Her abdomen swelled, and she thought it was an illness.
She told her mother.
Her mother asked:
"Is it moving?"
She said:
"It is moving."
Her mother found it even stranger.
However, because the girl was too young,
she dared not make a judgment.
Not long after,
she gave birth to a boy. Her mother sighed:
"I never expected that she, who is so young,
would give birth to a child!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Dǒng Shìdú Mò'ān’s family
was troubled by a fox.
Tiles, pebbles, bricks, and stones
suddenly fell like hail.
The family members would flee and hide together,
and only when the disturbance subsided
dared they come out to work.
The Duke was distressed by this,
and feigned a move to the residence of Sīmǎ Tíngsūn to escape it.
But the fox's disturbance continued as before.
One day,
while waiting for court in the morning,
he happened to mention this strange phenomenon.
Some ministers said: “The Dàoshì Jiāo Míng from Guāndōng,
who lives in the inner city,
is skilled in the art of general incantations [chìlè zhī shù],
and is quite effective.”
The Duke went to his residence and invited him.
The Dàoshì wrote a talisman in red ink,
and told him to return and paste it on the wall.
The fox, however, was not afraid,
and threw more objects than before.
The Duke again reported to the Dàoshì.
The Dàoshì was angered,
and personally went to the Duke’s house,
built an altar, and performed a ritual.
Soon, a giant fox was seen
lying prostrate beneath the altar.
The family members, having suffered abuse for a long time,
harbored deep resentment.
A maid approached and struck it.
The maid suddenly fell to the ground, unconscious.
The Dàoshì said:
"This creature is so rampant [chāngjué],
even I cannot subdue it quickly;
how dare a woman provoke it like that!"
After a while, he said:
"One can also try to interrogate the fox for a confession."
That would also work.
He pointed his finger and chanted for some time,
and the maid suddenly rose,
kneeling long.
The Dàoshì questioned her about her place of origin.
The maid spoke as the fox:
"I am a product of the Western Regions,
and there are eighteen generations of us who have entered the capital."
The Dàoshì said:
"Under the Emperor's chariot,
how can you all reside here for so long?
Leave quickly!"
The fox did not reply.
The Dàoshì struck the table angrily and said:
"Do you intend to obstruct my order?
If you delay again,
the law will not pardon you!"
The fox then looked distressed and fearful,
and expressed willingness to diligently obey the instructions.
The Dàoshì again urged it to leave.
The maid again collapsed and fainted,
and only revived after a long time.
Soon, four or five white lumps
were seen rolling like balls,
moving along the eaves,
one after another, chasing each other.
In an instant, they all departed.
From then on, peace was restored.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
There was a scholar from Huáiyáng named Yè Shēng,
whose given name is lost.
His essays and fu poems
were unsurpassed at the time;
yet, he never found success wherever he went,
and struggled in the examination halls.
It happened that Liǎo Chénghè, from Guāndōng, came to govern this county.
Seeing Yè Shēng's writing,
he marvelled at it;
he summoned him to converse,
and was greatly pleased.
He ordered him to stay at the government office [gōngshǔ]
and study under his guidance;
from time to time, he bestowed money and grain to relieve his family.
During the provincial examination,
the Duke vigorously promoted him to the educational commissioner [xuéshǐ],
and he subsequently achieved the top rank.
The Duke had extremely high hopes.
After the examination,
he asked for Yè Shēng's essay and read it,
striking his desk and praising it.
Unexpectedly, fate limits people,
and talent is envied by destiny [wénzhāng zēngmìng];
when the results were posted,
he was still unsuccessful.
Yè Shēng returned utterly despondent,
ashamed of having disappointed his patron,
wasted to skin and bones,
as foolish as a wooden puppet.
When the Duke heard this,
he summoned him and comforted him.
Yè Shēng wept ceaselessly.
The Duke pitied him,
and made a pact to travel to the capital together after his term of office [kǎomǎn] ended,
taking him north with him.
Yè Shēng was deeply grateful and impressed.
He took his leave and returned home,
shutting his door and not going out.
Not long after,
he fell ill.
The Duke's inquiries never ceased;
but a hundred doses of medicine [bǎoguǒ]
had no effect whatsoever.
The Duke happened to be dismissed for offending a superior official,
and was about to resign his post.
He sent a letter to Yè Shēng,
which roughly said:
"I will be returning east soon;
the reason for my delay [chíchí]
is waiting for you.
If you arrive in the morning,
I will depart in the evening."
The letter was delivered to his bedside.
Yè Shēng held the letter and sobbed.
He sent a message back with the envoy:
"My illness is critical and cannot be cured quickly;
please depart first."
When the envoy returned and reported this,
the Duke could not bear to leave,
and slowly waited for him.
After several days,
the gatekeeper suddenly announced Yè Shēng's arrival.
The Duke was delighted,
went to meet him, and asked him.
Yè Shēng said:
"Because of my illness,
I have troubled you, master, to wait for a long time,
causing endless anxiety.
Now, fortunately, I can follow you."
The Duke then packed his bags and prepared to depart at dawn.
Upon arriving at his hometown [lǐ],
he ordered his son to become Yè Shēng's disciple,
and to be with him day and night.
His son's name was Zài Chāng,
then sixteen years old,
and not yet skilled in writing.
However, he was exceptionally intelligent;
any literary work he saw two or three times
he would remember without forgetting.
After a year of living there,
he could write essays with ease.
With the Duke's support,
he was admitted to the county school [yìxiáng].
Yè Shēng recorded and taught him all the examination essays [jǔzǐyè] he had prepared in his life.
In the examination, seven topics
were all covered without omission,
and he placed second [yàkuí].
He passed the examination.
One day, the Duke said to Yè Shēng:
"You have, with your remaining talent,
enabled a child to achieve fame.
But what about your own talent [huángzhōng], which has long been abandoned?"
Yè Shēng said:
"This is probably fate.
To use your good fortune to give voice to my writings,
and let the world know that my half-life of decline [lúnluò]
was not due to lack of skill [fēi zhàn zhī zuì],
is enough for my wish.
Moreover, a scholar who finds one true friend [zhījǐ]
can have no regrets.
Why must one abandon one's humble abode [báizhù],
and only then call it a good fortune?"
As Yè Shēng had been a guest for a long time,
the Duke feared he would miss the annual examination [suìshì],
and advised him to return home to visit his family.
Yè Shēng looked sad and unhappy.
The Duke could not bear to force him,
and instructed his son to go to the capital
to pay for Yè Shēng's grain tax [nàsù].
His son again passed the metropolitan examination [nángōng],
and was appointed a principal secretary [zhǔzhèng] in a ministry.
He took Yè Shēng to the capital's examination institute [jiān];
and they were together morning and evening.
After a year,
Yè Shēng entered the northern examination [běiwéi],
and indeed won the provincial recommendation [xiāngjiàn].
It happened that his son was dispatched to manage river affairs in the south [nánhé diǎnwù].
He then said to Yè Shēng:
"This journey is not far from your esteemed hometown.
Sir, you have soared to success [fènji yúnxiāo],
returning home in glory [jǐn huán] will be a joy."
Yè Shēng was also pleased,
chose an auspicious day, and set off.
Upon reaching the border of Huáiyáng, he ordered his servants and horses to escort Yè Shēng home.
Upon his return, he saw his home desolate,
and his heart was deeply saddened.
After a moment, he entered the courtyard,
where his wife came out carrying a winnowing basket.
Seeing him,
she dropped the basket and ran away in fright.
He said sadly,
“I am now a high official.
I haven't returned for three or four years;
how can you suddenly not recognize me?”
His wife called to him from a distance,
“You have been dead for a long time.
Why do you speak of being a high official again?
The reason people delayed your burial
was only because our family was poor and our son was young.
Now Ādà has also grown up,
and we are about to choose a burial site.
Do not make strange appearances to frighten the living.”
When he heard this,
he was stunned and melancholy.
He slowly entered the room
and saw his coffin standing there solemnly.
He fell to the ground and vanished.
His wife looked in alarm
to see his clothes, hat, shoes, and socks lying as if cast off.
She wailed loudly,
embracing his clothes and weeping sorrowfully.
His son returned from school
and saw carriages with four horses at the gate.
After inquiring about their origin,
he ran in fright to his mother.
His mother, wiping away tears, told him what happened.
Then, after questioning the attendants in detail,
she finally learned the whole story.
When the attendants returned,
the young master heard the news,
and tears fell upon his chest.
He immediately ordered his carriage and wept in his room. He took out money from his purse to arrange the funeral,
and buried him with the rites of a xiàolián.
He also gave a generous gift to his son,
and hired a teacher to educate him.
He spoke to the xuéshǐ,
and in a year, the son passed the entry examination for the prefectural school.
Yìshǐshì said:
“A soul following its bosom friend,
can it truly forget death?
Those who hear this doubt it,
but I deeply believe it.
A qíngnǚ with a shared heart
can even leave her soul from her pillow;
a good friend a thousand *lǐ* away
can still recognize the path in a dream.
How much more so for those whose silken threads and fly-marks
stir the hearts and livers of scholars;
whose flowing waters and high mountains
connect with our very lives!
Alas!
Opportunities are hard to predict,
and encounters are often missed.
Our paths are solitary,
facing shadows with long sorrow;
our proud bones are stark,
scratching our heads in self-admiration.
We lament the bitterness of our appearance,
which invites ridicule from ghosts.
If one frequently lives among the successful,
then every strand of hair and beard seems ugly;
if one falls outside the ranks of the successful,
then every part of one's writing is flawed.
Among those who have wept bitterly throughout history,
only Biàn Hé comes to mind;
among those who identify exceptional talents,
who is Bólè?
Carrying a recommendation letter close to one's heart,
the characters vanish after three years;
standing on tiptoe to look,
there is no home in the four seas.
In life,
one only needs to close one's eyes and take a step,
and let the Creator determine one's fate, high or low.
There are many in the world who are as aspiring yet fallen as Yè Shēng,
but where can we find Lìng Wēi to return
and let life and death follow him?
Alas!
Alas!”
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wáng Dàsīmǎ of Xīnchéng
had a chief steward whose family was known for its wealth.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a person rushing in,
saying,
“You owe forty thousand *qián*.
It is time to repay it.”
When asked,
he did not reply
but went straight inside.
When he awoke,
his wife had given birth to a son.
Knowing it was a past karma,
he immediately bundled forty thousand *qián* and placed it in a room,
from which all the child’s food, clothing, illness, and medicine
were provided.
After three or four years,
he looked at the money in the room,
and only seven hundred remained.
Just then, the wet nurse brought the child over,
playing and laughing by his side.
So he called out to the child,
“The forty thousand *qián* are almost used up.
You should go.”
No sooner had he spoken
than the child’s complexion suddenly changed,
his neck snapped, and his eyes opened wide.
When he touched him again,
his breath had already ceased.
He then used the remaining money to prepare for the burial and interred him.
This can serve as a warning to those who are in debt.
In the past, there was an old man without a son,
who asked a high monk about it.
The monk said,
“If you owe no one,
and no one owes you,
how can you have a son?”
Indeed, bearing a good son
is to repay the karmic connection;
bearing a troublesome son
is to collect a debt.
The living should not rejoice,
nor should the dead grieve.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wéndēng's Zhōu shēng,
from a young age, shared writing instruments with Chéng shēng,
and thus they became a close, inseparable friendship.
However, Chéng was poor,
so he often relied on Zhōu throughout the year.
By age, Zhōu was older,
and Chéng called Zhōu's wife "sǎo."
On holidays and festivals, he would visit their hall,
as if they were one family.
Zhōu's wife gave birth to a son,
but died suddenly after childbirth.
Zhōu then married Wáng shì.
Because Chéng was young,
he had never sought to meet her.
One day,
Wáng shì's younger brother came to visit his sister,
and they were feasting in the inner chambers.
Chéng happened to arrive.
A servant announced him,
and Zhōu, seated, ordered him to be invited in.
Chéng did not enter,
and excused himself to leave.
Zhōu moved his seat to the outer room,
chased after him, and brought him back.
No sooner had they sat down
than someone reported that a servant from their detached property
had been severely flogged by the Yì zǎi.
Previously,
a herdsman from Huáng Lìbù's household,
whose ox had strayed into Zhōu's field,
had caused an argument.
The herdsman ran to tell his master, who seized Zhōu's servant and sent him to the official,
whereupon he was flogged.
Zhōu questioned and learned the reason,
and was greatly enraged, saying:
"How dare that pig-herding slave from the Huáng family
do this!
His ancestors served my grandfather;
did he quickly gain prominence
and now consider himself unrivaled?!"
Rage filled his throat and chest,
and he rose in anger,
intending to seek out Huáng.
Chéng pressed him down and stopped him,
saying:
"In this violent world,
there is no distinction between right and wrong.
Moreover, half of today's officials are like powerful bandits who don't wield spears and bows!"
Zhōu did not listen.
Chéng remonstrated with him repeatedly,
even to the point of tears,
and only then did Zhōu stop.
His anger, however, remained unreleased,
and he tossed and turned until dawn.
He said to his family:
"The Huáng family has bullied me;
they are my enemy.
Let's put that aside for now.
The Yì lìng is an official of the imperial court,
not an official of powerful families.
Even if there is a dispute,
both parties must be present.
How could he behave like a dog that follows a command?
I will also bring charges against their herdsman
and see how he handles it."
His family all encouraged him,
and the plan was thus decided.
He prepared a complaint and went to the Zǎi,
who tore it up and threw it away.
Zhōu was enraged and
spoke offensively to the Zǎi.
The Zǎi was ashamed and furious,
and consequently arrested and imprisoned him.
After the mid-morning meal,
Chéng went to visit Zhōu,
only to learn that he had gone to the city to litigate.
He rushed to dissuade him,
but Zhōu was already in prison.
He stamped his feet, at a loss for what to do.
At that time, three pirates had been captured,
and the Zǎi and Huáng bribed and instructed them
to falsely implicate Zhōu as an accomplice.
Based on their testimony, Zhōu was stripped of his official's hat and robe
and subjected to cruel torture.
Chéng entered the prison,
and they looked at each other, heartbroken.
They planned to appeal to the emperor.
Zhōu said:
"My body is confined in a heavy prison,
like a bird in a cage: although I have a weak younger brother,
he is only capable of providing prison food."
Chéng eagerly took the responsibility upon himself,
saying:
"This is my duty.
If I don't act urgently in times of difficulty,
what good is friendship!"
So he set off.
Zhōu's brother offered him travel money,
but he had already been gone for a long time.
When he arrived at the capital,
there was no channel for making his complaint.
It was rumored that the emperor was about to go hunting,
so Chéng hid in the timber market beforehand;
soon, the imperial carriage passed,
and he prostrated himself, weeping and wailing,
and thus obtained permission.
He was sent down by post-station,
with instructions for the imperial board and court to review and report.
More than ten months had passed by then,
and Zhōu had already falsely confessed and been sentenced to death.
The court received the imperial rescript,
was greatly alarmed,
and again summoned Zhōu for a personal re-trial.
Huáng was also alarmed
and plotted to kill Zhōu.
He bribed the jailer
to cut off his food and drink;
when Zhōu's brother came to bring food and inquire,
he was severely refused entry.
Chéng again went to the court to voice the injustice,
and only then was Zhōu summoned for questioning,
but he was already too weak from hunger to stand up.
The Yuàn tái was enraged
and had the jailer beaten to death.
Huáng was greatly frightened
and offered several thousand taels of gold,
instructing them to arrange for Zhōu's release,
and thus he was vaguely excused from the charges.
The Zǎi was sentenced to exile according to law.
Zhōu was released and returned home,
feeling even deeper gratitude towards Chéng.
Chéng, having been involved in a lawsuit,
lost all interest in worldly affairs,
and invited Zhōu to retire from the world with him.
Zhōu, however, was infatuated with a young woman,
and often made circuitous visits to her, which Chéng smiled at.
Although Chéng did not speak,
his intention was very clear.
After they parted,
he did not appear for several days.
Zhōu sent someone to inquire at his home,
where the family suspected he was at Zhōu's place;
since neither had seen him,
they began to worry.
Zhōu knew in his heart that something was amiss,
and sent people to track him down,
searching temples, monasteries, ravines, and valleys,
almost everywhere.
At that time, he provided Chéng's son with money and silk.
Another eight or nine years passed,
when Chéng suddenly arrived,
dressed in a yellow turban and a loose robe,
with the dignified air of a Daoist.
Zhōu rejoiced,
grabbed his arm, and said:
“Where have you been,
making me search almost everywhere?”
Chéng smiled and said:
“A solitary cloud and a wild crane
have no fixed dwelling.
Fortunately, I am still robust and healthy since we last met.”
Zhōu ordered wine to be set out,
and they briefly spoke of their separation,
intending to have Chéng change his Daoist attire.
Chéng smiled and remained silent.
Zhōu said:
“How foolish!
Why abandon your wife and children as if they were worn-out rags?”
Chéng smiled and said:
“Not so.
People will abandon me;
how can I abandon people?”
When asked where he resided,
he replied, “On Láoshān, at the Shàngqīng Palace.”
Afterward, they slept foot-to-foot.
Zhōu dreamed that Chéng was lying naked on his chest,
making it difficult for him to breathe.
He asked in surprise what he was doing,
but Chéng did not answer.
Suddenly, he woke up with a start,
called out to Chéng but received no response;
he sat up and searched for him,
but he was nowhere to be found.
After a long while,
he realized he was in Chéng's bed,
and exclaimed in horror:
“I wasn't drunk last night;
how did I get so disoriented?”
Then he called his family.
His family lit a lamp,
and it was indeed Chéng.
Zhōu usually had a full beard,
but when he touched his chin,
there were only a few strands.
He took a mirror and looked at himself,
exclaiming in surprise:
“Chéng is here;
where am I?”
Then he suddenly understood,
realizing that Chéng had used a magic art to lure him into reclusion.
He wanted to return home,
but his younger brother, seeing his changed appearance,
forbade him from entering.
Zhōu also had no way to explain himself.
He immediately ordered a servant and horse to go search for Chéng.
Several days later,
he entered Sūshān.
The horse traveled swiftly,
and the servant could not keep up.
Stopping to rest under a tree,
he saw many Daoist priests coming and going.
One Daoist priest looked at Zhōu,
and Zhōu therefore asked about Chéng.
The Daoist smiled and said:
“I have heard his name;
he seems to be at Shàngqīng.”
Having spoken,
he left directly.
Zhōu watched him go,
and saw him, a bowshot away,
speaking with another person,
also briefly, before leaving.
The person he spoke with gradually approached,
and it was a fellow scholar from his community.
Seeing Zhōu,
he was astonished and said:
“We haven't met for several years,
and people say you are studying the Dao in famous mountains;
are you still wandering in the human world?”
Zhōu recounted his strange experience.
The scholar exclaimed in surprise:
“I just met him,
and I took him for you.
He left not long ago,
so he shouldn't be far.”
Zhōu was greatly surprised and said:
“How strange!
How could I not recognize my own face when seeing it face-to-face?”
The servant soon arrived,
and he galloped off,
but found no trace.
The view was vast and empty,
making it difficult to decide whether to advance or retreat.
He thought to himself that he had no home to return to,
and so he decided to pursue Chéng relentlessly.
However, the terrain was too treacherous to ride,
so he entrusted his horse to the servant to return,
and walked on by himself.
In the distance, he saw a boy sitting alone.
He hurried over to ask for directions,
and also explained his situation.
The boy introduced himself as Chéng's disciple,
offered to carry his clothes and provisions,
and guided him to travel together.
They ate under the stars and slept in the open,
traveling a great distance.
They arrived after three days,
and it was not what the world called Shàngqīng.
It was then mid-October,
and mountain flowers filled the path,
not resembling early winter.
The boy went in to announce the guest,
and Chéng immediately rushed out,
and Zhōu recognized his own form.
Chéng took his hand and led him in,
set out wine, and conversed.
He saw birds of unusual colors,
tame and unafraid of people,
whose songs were like flutes and mouth organs,
and who sometimes came to sing at their seats.
He found this very strange.
However, his worldly thoughts were pressing,
and he had no intention of lingering.
There were two rush mats on the ground;
he pulled one over and sat opposite Chéng.
After the second watch,
all his worries subsided.
Suddenly, he seemed to doze off for a moment,
and felt his body had swapped places with Chéng.
Doubtful,
he stroked his chin,
and his beard was as it used to be.
At dawn,
he had a strong desire to return.
Chéng insisted on keeping him.
After three days,
Chéng finally said:
“Rest a little,
and I will send you off early.”
As soon as his eyelids met,
he heard Chéng call out:
“Your travel preparations are ready!”
So he got up and followed him.
The path taken was utterly unlike the old one.
Before I knew it,
my village was already in sight.
Chéng sat waiting by the roadside,
allowing me to return home alone.
Zhōu tried to persuade him not to, but failed,
so he trudged home to his gate.
He knocked but received no answer.
Thinking of climbing over the wall,
he felt his body float like a leaf,
and with one leap, he was over.
He crossed several walls in total
before finally reaching his bedroom.
The lamp and candle were brightly lit,
and his wife was not yet asleep,
murmuring words to someone.
He licked the window to peek,
and saw his wife drinking from the same cup with a servant,
their manner exceedingly intimate.
At this, his rage burned like fire;
he planned to catch them unawares,
but feared his single strength would be insufficient.
So he quietly slipped out through the door,
ran to inform Chéng,
and begged for his help.
Chéng readily agreed,
and they went straight to the inner chamber.
Zhōu lifted a stone and pounded on the door,
causing great panic inside;
the more furiously he pounded,
the more firmly the door was secured from within.
Chéng pried it open with his sword,
and with a clang, it instantly burst open.
Zhōu rushed in,
and the servant bolted out the door.
Chéng, standing outside the door,
struck him with his sword,
severing his shoulder and arm.
Zhōu seized his wife and interrogated her,
only then learning that she had been having an affair with the servant since the time he was taken.
Zhōu borrowed the sword to cut off her head,
and threw her guts among the courtyard trees.
Then he followed Chéng out,
and traced their way back.
Suddenly he woke up,
finding himself on his bed,
and exclaimed in surprise:
“What a strange and terrifying dream,
it makes one gasp with fright!”
Chéng laughed and said:
“What you, my brother, take for a dream is real,
and what is real you take for a dream.”
Zhōu was astonished and questioned him.
Chéng drew his sword and showed it to him;
the spattered blood was still there.
Zhōu was so shocked he almost fainted,
secretly suspecting Chéng was creating illusions.
Chéng understood his meaning,
so he hastened to prepare to see him off home.
After some time, they reached the village gate,
and Chéng said:
“Wasn’t this the spot
where I waited for you leaning on my sword last night?
I am weary of seeing filth and corruption;
please allow me to return and wait for you here.
If you do not return by late afternoon,
I will depart on my own.”
When Zhōu arrived home,
the doors were desolate,
as if no one lived there.
He returned to his younger brother’s house.
When his brother saw him,
tears immediately streamed down his face,
and he said:
“After you left,
thieves killed your wife at night,
and disemboweled her.
It was so cruel and tragic,
and the authorities have not yet apprehended the culprit.”
Zhōu awoke as if from a dream,
and then recounted the situation,
warning his brother not to investigate further.
His brother was bewildered for a long time.
Zhōu asked about his son,
and an old nanny was instructed to bring him.
Zhōu said:
“This swaddled child
is crucial to the family line.
Brother, please look after him well.
I wish to bid farewell to the human world.”
Then he rose
and walked straight out.
His brother, weeping and crying, tried to hold him back,
but Zhōu walked away laughing, without looking back.
When he reached the wilderness,
he saw Chéng,
and they walked on together.
From afar, Zhōu looked back and said:
“To endure is the greatest joy.”
His brother wanted to speak,
but Chéng merely raised his wide sleeve,
and they instantly vanished from sight.
His brother stood there dejectedly for a while,
then cried bitterly and returned.
Zhōu’s younger brother was simple and unsophisticated,
not skilled at managing family affairs or property.
After several years,
the family became even poorer.
As Zhōu’s son gradually grew older,
they could not afford a teacher,
so his uncle taught him to read.
One day,
he arrived at the study early
and saw a sealed letter on the desk,
very securely fastened,
with the inscription
“For my second brother (Zhòngshì) to open”
Upon examination,
it was his elder brother’s handwriting;
he opened it,
but there was nothing inside,
only a single fingernail,
about two fingers long.
He found this strange.
He placed the nail on the inkstone
and went out to ask his family where it came from,
but no one knew.
Returning,
he saw the inkstone sparkling brilliantly,
having transformed into gold.
He was greatly astonished.
He tried it on copper and iron,
and the same thing happened.
From this, they became immensely wealthy.
He gave a thousand pieces of gold to Chéng’s son,
and so it was said that the two families possessed the art of transmuting base metals into gold.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Méi Xiàolián Óucháng of Jiāngnán
spoke of Gōng Sūn from his village,
who was the magistrate of Dézhōu,
and judged a strange case.
Initially,
a villager had married a wife for his son.
When the new bride entered the home,
relatives and villagers all congratulated them.
They drank until past midnight,
when the groom stepped out
and saw the bride, in her splendid attire,
hurrying behind the house.
He suspected something and followed her.
Behind the residence was a long stream,
crossed by a small bridge.
He saw the bride cross the bridge and go straight away,
which made him even more suspicious.
He called out to her, but she didn’t respond.
From afar, she beckoned to the groom with her hand;
the groom rushed to catch up,
remaining only a foot away,
but could never quite reach her.
After walking several *lǐ*,
they entered a village.
The woman stopped
and said to the groom:
“Your family is lonely,
and I’m not used to living there.
Please, dear husband, stay with me at my family’s house for a few days,
then we can return together to visit your parents.”
After speaking,
she pulled out a hairpin and knocked on a door,
and with a creak, a young girl came out to answer.
The woman went in first.
With no other choice,
he followed her.
Once inside,
he saw his mother-in-law and father-in-law both in the main hall.
They said to the groom:
“Our daughter has been spoiled since childhood,
never once leaving our side.
Once she left her hometown,
her heart was always troubled.
Now that she has come with you,
it greatly relieves our worries.
After a few days’ stay,
we will send you both back.”
Then they prepared a room for them,
with bedding and everything ready,
and so they stayed there.
The guests at home saw that the bridegroom had been gone for a long time,
and together they sought him.
In the air, only the new bride was present,
not knowing where the groom had gone.
Thereupon, they inquired far and wide,
but there was no news.
The old man and woman wept,
thinking he must have died.
Nearly half a year passed,
and the bride's family, lamenting their daughter had no match,
then requested Qūn Rénfù (村人父),
wishing to remarry their daughter.
Qūn Rénfù (村人父) grew even sadder,
saying:
"There are no bones or clothes to verify,
how do we know my son has become a ghost!
Even if he died suddenly,
marrying a year later would still not be too late.
Why are you in such a hurry!"
The bride's father grew even more resentful,
and brought a lawsuit to the court.
Sūn Gōng (孫公) was puzzled and suspicious,
unable to exert his power,
and ruled that they should wait for three years,
then filed the case and dismissed them.
The son of the Qūn (村) family lived at the bride's house,
and the family members also treated him very kindly.
Whenever he discussed returning home with the bride,
the bride also assented,
but procrastinated and did not go immediately.
After more than half a year,
his heart was restless,
and he was extremely anxious.
He wanted to return alone,
but the bride insisted on keeping him.
One day,
the whole family was in a panic,
as if there was an urgent calamity.
In a rush, they said to the groom:
"We originally intended to send the couple back together in two or three days.
Unexpectedly, the wedding attire was not ready,
and suddenly there was a calamity;
we have no choice but
to send you, Lang, back first."
Thereupon, they sent him out the door,
and immediately turned back quickly.
Their movements and speech
were quite hasty.
Just as he was about to find his way,
he looked back and saw that the courtyard was no longer there,
but only saw Gāo Jiā (高家).
Greatly alarmed,
he quickly found his way home.
Upon arriving home,
he recounted the entire story,
and then went to the authorities to make a complaint.
Sūn Gōng (孫公) detained the bride's father and instructed him,
to send the daughter home,
and only then did they perform the wedding ceremony.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
A certain Daoist priest from Cháotiān Guān (朝天觀)
enjoyed the art of breath control.
An old man temporarily resided in the temple,
who happened to share the same爱好,
and thus they became fellow Daoist friends.
After several years,
whenever the suburban sacrifice approached,
he would leave ten days in advance,
and only return after the sacrifice.
The Daoist priest was suspicious and asked him about it.
The old man said:
"We two are intimate friends,
I can tell you the truth: I am a fox.
When the time for the suburban sacrifice arrives,
all the deities cleanse the impurities,
and I have no place to stay,
so I leave."
Another year,
he left on schedule,
but did not return for a long time.
The Daoist priest was suspicious.
One day, he suddenly arrived.
He then asked him the reason.
He replied:
"I almost didn't see you again!
Previously, I wanted to hide far away,
but my heart was quite lazy,
and I saw the sewer was very hidden,
so I hid under a rolled-up jar.
Unexpectedly, the Spirit Official's cleaning came to this place,
and I was glimpsed by him.
He was furious and wanted to whip me.
I was afraid and fled.
The Spirit Official chased very quickly.
When we reached the Yellow River,
he was almost upon me.
In great distress and with no plan,
I burrowed and hid in the dry mud.
The deity detested its filth,
and only then turned back and left.
After emerging,
I was covered in foul stench,
and could no longer wander among humans.
So I jumped into the water to cleanse myself,
and then hid in a burrow for nearly a hundred days,
before the filth finally disappeared.
I come now to bid you farewell,
and also to instruct you: you should also hide elsewhere,
a great calamity is coming,
and this is not a blessed land."
Having spoken,
he bid farewell and left.
The Daoist priest followed his advice and left his disciples.
Not long after, the Jiǎshēn (甲申) Incident occurred.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
Wáng Lán (王蘭) of Lìjīn (利津) died of a sudden illness.
The King of Hell re-examined,
and it was found to be the ghost messenger's mistaken summons.
He was ordered to be sent back to life,
but the corpse had already decayed.
The ghost, fearing punishment,
said to Wáng Lán (王蘭):
"To be human and then a ghost is suffering,
to be a ghost and then an immortal is joy.
If there is joy,
why must one be born?"
Wáng Lán (王蘭) thought it was true.
The ghost said:
"There is a fox here
whose golden elixir has been formed.
Steal its elixir and swallow it,
then your soul will not dissipate,
and you can exist forever.
Wherever you wish to go,
nothing will be unsatisfactory.
Do you desire this?"
Wáng Lán (王蘭) agreed.
The ghost led him,
into a grand mansion,
where they saw magnificent buildings,
but it was utterly deserted.
There was a fox under the moon,
looking up at the sky.
With one exhale,
a pill emerged from its mouth,
went straight up into the moon;
with one inhale,
it would fall back down,
and it would catch it with its mouth,
then exhale it again: this continued without end.
The ghost secretly waited by its side,
and waited for it to spit out the pill.
It quickly snatched it into its hand,
and gave it to Wáng Lán (王蘭) to swallow.
The fox was startled,
and angrily confronted them.
Seeing two people,
it feared it could not contend,
and left in anger and resentment.
Wáng Lán (王蘭) parted with the ghost,
and went to his home.
His wife and children saw him,
and all feared and ran away.
Wáng Lán (王蘭) told them the reason,
and they gradually gathered.
From then on, he lived and slept at home as usual.
His friend, a man surnamed Zhāng [Zhāng],
heard about it and went to visit him.
They met and talked about their well-being.
Then, Wáng [Wáng] said to Zhāng [Zhāng]:
"My family and yours have long been poor.
Now I have a skill
that can make us rich.
Can you accompany me on my travels?"
Zhāng [Zhāng] assented readily.
Wáng [Wáng] said:
"I can heal without medicine,
and prognosticate without divination.
I wish to appear in my true form,
but I fear those who recognize me would be shocked by my strangeness.
Would it be permissible to attach myself to your person and travel?"
Zhāng [Zhāng] again assented readily.
Thereupon, they packed their bags that very day
and traveled to the border of Shānxī [Shānxī].
A wealthy family had a daughter
who fell seriously ill,
dizzy and unconscious.
All previous attempts at medicine and exorcism had failed.
Zhāng [Zhāng] went to their house
and showed off his skill.
The rich old man had only this daughter
and cherished her greatly.
He vowed to reward anyone who could cure her
with a thousand pieces of gold.
Zhāng [Zhāng] asked to see her.
Following the old man into the room,
he saw the girl lying unconscious.
He uncovered her quilt
and stroked her body,
but the girl remained insensible.
Wáng [Wáng] privately told Zhāng [Zhāng]:
"Her soul is lost.
We must find it for her."
Zhāng [Zhāng] then told the old man:
"Although the illness is critical,
it can be cured."
The old man asked:
"What medicine is needed?"
They both said no medicine was needed.
"The young lady's soul has departed to another place.
I have already dispatched a spirit to find it."
After about an hour,
Wáng [Wáng] suddenly returned,
reporting that the soul had been found.
Zhāng [Zhāng] then invited the old man to re-enter,
and again stroked the girl.
A moment later,
the girl stretched and yawned,
her eyes suddenly opening wide.
The old man was overjoyed,
stroking her and asking questions.
The girl said:
"Just now in a pleasure garden,
I saw a young man
with a slingshot, shooting birds.
Several people were leading fine horses,
following behind him.
I wanted to flee quickly,
but was forcibly stopped.
The young man handed me a bow
and taught me to shoot.
Just as I was ashamed and about to scold him,
he carried me onto a horse,
and we rode together.
He laughed and said: 'I enjoy playing with you,
don't be shy.'
We rode several *lǐ* into the mountains,
and I cried and cursed on the horse.
The young man grew angry,
pushed me off by the roadside,
and I had no way to return.
Just then, a person arrived,
grabbed my arm,
and sped like the wind.
In an instant, I was home,
suddenly as if waking from a dream."
The old man deemed it divine,
and indeed presented them with a thousand pieces of gold.
That night, Wáng [Wáng] discussed with Zhāng [Zhāng],
keeping two hundred pieces of gold for their journey expenses,
and taking the rest,
he knocked on the door and gave it to his son.
He also ordered three hundred pieces to be sent to Zhāng's [Zhāng] family,
and then returned.
The next day,
they bid farewell to the old man.
Not seeing where the gold was hidden,
the old man was even more amazed,
and saw them off with generous gifts.
After several days,
Zhāng [Zhāng] met his fellow villager Hè Cái [Hè Cái] in the outskirts.
Cái [Cái] indulged in drinking and gambling, neglecting his livelihood,
and was as poor as a beggar.
Hearing that Zhāng [Zhāng] had acquired a strange skill
and obtained countless gold,
he hurried to find him.
Wáng [Wáng] advised giving him a small sum and sending him away.
Cái [Cái] did not change his extravagant ways,
squandering it all in ten days,
and was about to seek Zhāng [Zhāng] again.
Wáng [Wáng] already knew this,
saying:
"Cái [Cái] is wild and perverse,
he cannot be kept around.
It is only right to bribe him to leave,
so the trouble will be shallower."
The next day,
Cái [Cái] indeed arrived,
insisting on going with them.
Zhāng [Zhāng] said:
"I knew you would come again.
If you spend your days in alcoholism and gambling,
how can a thousand pieces of gold fill a bottomless pit?
If you sincerely change your ways,
I will give you a hundred pieces of gold."
Cái [Cái] agreed.
Zhāng [Zhāng] emptied his purse and gave it to him.
Cái [Cái] left,
and with the hundred pieces of gold, became even more daring in gambling.
He also indulged in visits to brothels,
spending money like dirt.
The town's constables suspected and arrested him,
brought him before the official,
and subjected him to cruel torture.
Cái [Cái] truthfully confessed the source of the gold.
Thereupon, constables were dispatched to escort Cái [Cái] and apprehend Zhāng [Zhāng].
After several days,
Cái's [Cái] wounds became severe,
and he died on the road.
His soul did not forget Zhāng [Zhāng],
and returned to depend on him,
thus meeting Wáng [Wáng].
One day,
they were drinking together at Yāndūn [Yāndūn].
Cái [Cái] got very drunk and started yelling wildly.
Wáng [Wáng] tried to stop him, but he wouldn't listen.
