Just then, an Imperial Censor [Yùshǐ] on tour passed by.
Hearing the shouts, he searched
and apprehended Zhāng [Zhāng].
Zhāng [Zhāng] was afraid
and told the truth.
The Censor was enraged,
had him flogged and reported the matter to the gods.
That night, he dreamt of a golden-armored man who said:
"Upon investigation, Wáng Lán [Wáng Lán] died innocently,
and is now a ghost immortal.
Healing is also a benevolent art,
and should not be governed by the laws of demons and spirits.
I now bear the Emperor's [Dì] command
to appoint him as the Commissioner of Clearing the Way [Qīngdào Shǐ].
Hè Cái [Hè Cái] was dissolute and depraved,
and has already been banished to the Iron Mountain Range [Tiěwéi Shān].
Zhāng [Zhāng] is innocent,
and should be pardoned."
The Censor awoke, finding it strange,
and then released Zhāng [Zhāng].
Zhāng [Zhāng] packed his bags and returned home.
He had several hundred pieces of gold left in his purse,
and respectfully sent half to Wáng's [Wáng] family.
Wáng's [Wáng] descendants
thus became wealthy.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* [Liáozhāi Zhìyì].
The Dōngyuè Temple in the prefectural city
is in Nánguō.
To the left and right of the main gate,
the gods are over a *zhàng* tall,
popularly known as
"Yīng Hǔ Shén,"
ferocious and awe-inspiring.
The Daoist priest in the temple, surnamed Rèn,
would rise at cockcrow
to burn incense and chant scriptures.
A thief, having hidden in the corridor beforehand,
waited for the Daoist priest to rise,
then stealthily entered the bedchamber
to search for valuables.
However, there was nothing of value in the room;
he only found three hundred coins under the mat,
which he put into his waist pouch,
unlocked the door and left,
intending to ascend Qiānfó Shān.
After fleeing south for some time,
he finally reached the foot of the mountain.
He saw a giant man
coming down from the mountain,
with a grey eagle on his left arm,
just meeting him.
Upon closer inspection,
his face was a bronze-green color,
vaguely resembling the one he was accustomed to seeing at the temple gate.
Greatly alarmed,
he crouched down, trembling.
The god exclaimed,
"Where are you taking the stolen money?"
The thief was even more terrified,
and kowtowed incessantly.
The god pulled him back,
into the temple,
made him pour out the stolen money,
and kneel to guard it.
When the Daoist priest finished his lessons,
he looked back, startled and aghast.
The thief recounted everything in detail.
The Daoist priest took his money and dismissed him.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Wáng Chéng,
a descendant of an old family in Píngyuán,
was extremely lazy.
His livelihood declined daily,
leaving only a few dilapidated rooms,
and he and his wife slept in ox-skin clothes,
their poverty being unbearable.
It was the height of summer, hot and humid,
and there had always been a Zhōu family garden outside the village,
whose walls and characters had all fallen,
leaving only a pavilion;
many villagers lodged there,
and Wáng was also among them.
When dawn broke,
all the sleepers left;
when the red sun was three *gān* high,
Wáng finally rose,
and was about to return home hesitantly.
He saw a golden hairpin in the grass,
picked it up and examined it.
It had fine characters engraved, saying:
"Made by Yíbīn Fǔ."
Wáng's grandfather was an *yíbīn* of the Héng Fǔ,
and many old family items
were of this style,
so he held the hairpin, pondering.
An old woman came looking for the hairpin.
Though Wáng was poor,
he was principled by nature,
and immediately handed it to her.
The old woman was delighted,
praising his virtue profusely,
saying:
"What is the value of the hairpin? It is a memento from my late husband."
She asked:
"Who is your husband?"
He replied:
"My late *yíbīn*, Wáng Jiǎnzhī."
Wáng was startled and said:
"He is my grandfather!
How is it that we meet?"
The old woman was also surprised, saying:
"Are you then the grandson of Wáng Jiǎnzhī?
I am a fox immortal.
A hundred years ago,
I had a deep affection for your grandfather.
When your grandfather passed away,
I then went into seclusion.
This lost hairpin
just happened to fall into your hands,
is this not fate?"
Wáng had also heard that his grandfather had a fox wife,
believed her words,
and invited her to visit.
The old woman followed.
Wáng called his wife out to meet her,
dressed in tattered clothes,
her face sallow and dull.
The old woman sighed,
saying:
"Alas!
The grandson of Wáng Jiǎnzhī
has come to such poverty!"
She then looked at the cold, smokeless stove,
saying:
"If the household is like this,
how can you make a living?"
The wife then detailed their impoverished state,
sobbing and weeping.
The old woman handed the hairpin to the wife,
telling her to pawn it for money to buy rice,
and asked to meet again in three days.
Wáng tried to persuade her to stay.
The old woman said:
"Your one wife cannot sustain herself;
if I stay,
living off your roof,
what good would it do?"
Then she left directly.
Wáng told his wife the reason,
and his wife was greatly frightened.
Wáng praised her righteousness,
and told her to serve the old woman,
to which his wife agreed.
After three days,
she indeed arrived.
She took out several pieces of gold,
and bought one *shí* each of millet and wheat.
At night, she shared a short bed with Wáng's wife.
The wife was initially afraid of her;
however, she observed that her intentions were very sincere,
and thus no longer doubted her.
The next day,
she said to Wáng:
"My grandson, you mustn't rely on sentiment.
It is fitting to engage in a small business;
how can one live long by simply eating? "
Wáng told her he had no capital.
She said:
"When your grandfather was alive,
gold and silk were taken as needed.
As someone from beyond this world,
I have no need for such things,
so I never took much.
Forty taels of gold from collected pollen
still remain to this day.
Keeping it long serves no purpose.
You may take it all to buy kāngé,
and set a date to go to the capital;
you might earn a small profit."
Wáng followed her advice,
and bought over fifty bolts of cloth to bring home.
The old woman ordered him to prepare for travel,
calculating that it would take six or seven days to reach Yāndū.
She instructed:
"Be diligent, not lazy;
be swift, not slow: delay even one day,
and regret will come too late!"
Wáng respectfully assented,
packed his goods, and set off.
Midway, he encountered rain,
and his clothes and shoes became soaked.
Wáng, having never experienced hardship in life,
was utterly exhausted.
He therefore temporarily rested at an inn.
Unexpectedly, the torrent continued through the night,
with rain falling from the eaves like ropes.
After staying a night,
the mud became even worse.
He saw travelers coming and going,
treading through mud up to their shins,
and his heart dreaded the hardship.
He waited until noon,
when it gradually dried,
but then dark clouds gathered again,
and the rain started heavily once more.
He traveled after staying two nights.
Approaching the capital,
he heard rumors that the price of kāngé had soared,
and secretly rejoiced.
Upon entering the capital,
he unpacked at an inn.
The innkeeper deeply regretted his lateness.
Before this,
the southern route had just opened,
and kāngé was extremely scarce.
The Bèilè residence was urgently purchasing it,
and the price had suddenly risen,
to about three times the usual.
The day before, they had just finished their purchases,
and those who came later were all disappointed.
The innkeeper informed Wáng of this reason.
Wáng was depressed and frustrated.
The next day,
more kāngé arrived,
and the price fell further.
Wáng, seeing no profit, refused to sell.
After delaying for more than ten days,
calculating the increasing cost of food,
he became even more worried and distressed.
The innkeeper advised him to sell cheaply
and pursue other plans.
He followed the advice.
Having lost more than ten taels of capital,
he sold everything.
Early in the morning,
as he was making plans to return,
he opened his bag to look inside,
and found the gold was gone.
Alarmed, he told the innkeeper.
The innkeeper had no solution.
Someone advised him to report it to the authorities
and demand compensation from the innkeeper.
Wáng sighed and said:
"This is my fate;
how can I blame the innkeeper? "
The innkeeper heard this and appreciated his virtue,
gifting him five taels of gold,
and comforting him to return home.
He thought to himself that he had nothing to show his grandmother,
and paced back and forth,
trapped between advancing and retreating.
Just then, he saw people fighting quails,
with a single bet often reaching several thousand cash;
each quail purchased
constantly cost more than a hundred cash.
His idea suddenly stirred.
Calculating the funds in his bag,
it was just enough to deal in quails.
He discussed it with the innkeeper.
The innkeeper eagerly encouraged him,
and even agreed to provide lodging and food,
without charging him.
Wáng was pleased,
and then set off.
He bought a full load of quails,
and re-entered the capital.
The innkeeper was happy,
congratulating him on a quick sale.
By night,
heavy rain continued until dawn.
At daybreak,
the streets were like rivers,
and the drizzle had not yet stopped.
He stayed, waiting for it to clear.
For several consecutive days,
there was no cessation.
He got up to look into the cage,
and the quails were gradually dying.
Wáng was greatly frightened,
not knowing what to do.
The next day,
even more died;
only a few remained,
which he put into one cage to feed.
After a night, he peeked inside,
and only one quail remained.
He then told the innkeeper,
tears falling unconsciously.
The innkeeper also wrung his hands in sympathy.
Wáng felt that with all his money gone, he couldn't return,
and only wished for death.
The innkeeper comforted him.
Together they went to look at the quail,
and observed it carefully, saying:
"This seems like a valiant creature.
The death of the other quails
might very well be due to this one fighting and killing them.
You have nothing else to do in your spare time,
please take care of it;
if it is indeed good,
gambling with it might also provide a livelihood."
Wáng followed his instruction.
Once it was tamed,
the innkeeper told him to take it to the street,
to gamble for food and drink.
The quail was very strong,
and always won.
The innkeeper was pleased,
gave gold to Wáng,
and had him gamble again with the young masters;
he won all three battles.
In about half a year,
he accumulated twenty taels of gold.
His heart was even more comforted,
and he regarded the quail as his life.
Earlier,
the Grand Prince (dàqīnwáng) was fond of quails,
and every Yuánxiāo Festival,
he would allow commoners with quails to enter his residence to fight them.
The innkeeper said to Wáng:
"Great wealth can now be instantly acquired;
what is unknown
lies in your fate."
He then explained the reason,
and led him to go together.
He instructed:
"If you lose,
then just leave dejectedly.
But if there's a one-in-ten-thousand chance
the quail wins,
the Prince will certainly want to buy it,
you must not agree;
if he insists forcefully,
look only to my head for guidance,
and only respond after I nod."
Wáng said:
"Yes."
Upon arriving at the residence,
quail handlers were shoulder-to-shoulder below the steps.
A moment later,
the Prince came out to the main hall.
His attendants announced:
"Is there anyone who wishes to engage in quail fighting?"
Immediately, a man holding a quail
hurried forward.
The king ordered his quail to be released,
and the visitor also released his;
after just one leap and bound,
the visitor's quail was already defeated.
The king laughed heartily.
Soon, more were called,
and several more came up and were defeated.
The host said,
"Enough."
They invited someone to come forward together.
The king examined it,
saying,
"Its eyes have an angry pulse;
this is a strong-feathered one,
it should not be underestimated."
He ordered the one with the iron beak to confront it.
After one or two leaps,
the king's quail was defeated.
He then selected another good one,
but it was replaced and defeated again.
The king urgently commanded them to fetch the jade quail from the palace.
After a short while, it was brought out.
Its white feathers were like a egret's,
and its spirit and agility were extraordinary.
Chéng's resolve faltered,
and he knelt, begging to stop,
saying,
"Your Majesty's quail
is a divine creature.
I fear it will harm my bird
and ruin my livelihood."
The king laughed and said,
"Let it fight.
If it dies in the fight,
I will compensate you generously."
Chéng then released it.
The jade quail charged straight at it.
But as the jade quail approached,
Chéng's quail lay in wait like an angry chicken;
when the jade quail pecked fiercely,
it rose like a soaring crane to strike it;
advancing and retreating, circling around,
they held each other for about one 'fúshí' (a unit of time).
The jade quail gradually grew tired,
while the other's anger intensified,
and its fighting became more urgent.
Before long,
its white feathers were torn off,
and it fled with drooping wings.
Among the thousand spectators,
there was no one who did not sigh in admiration.
The king then demanded to take it and held it himself,
from its crest to its claws,
examining it thoroughly.
He asked Chéng,
"Can this quail be sold?"
He replied,
"This humble man has no permanent property.
I rely on it for my life,
and I do not wish to sell it."
The king said,
"I will bestow upon you a heavy price,
enough to acquire the property of a middle-class family.
Do you truly wish for it?"
Chéng lowered his head and thought for a good while.
He said,
"I originally did not wish to part with it;
but since Your Majesty truly loves it,
if this humble man can obtain clothing, food, and a livelihood,
what more could I ask for?"
The king asked for the price,
and he replied, "A thousand gold pieces."
The king laughed and said,
"Foolish man!
What kind of rare treasure is this,
that it is worth a thousand gold pieces?"
Chéng said,
"Your Majesty may not consider it a treasure,
but I believe it is no less valuable than the 'liánchéng zhī bì' (a famous jade worth many cities)."
The king said,
"How so?"
He replied,
"When this humble man takes it to the market,
I earn several gold pieces daily,
easily exchanging them for 'shēngdǒu' of grain.
My family of more than ten mouths
has no worries of freezing or starving.
What treasure is like it?"
The king said,
"I will not shortchange you;
I will give you two hundred gold pieces."
Chéng shook his head.
He then increased the amount by a hundred.
Chéng looked at his host,
whose expression did not change.
He then said,
"Obeying Your Majesty's command,
I will reduce the price by a hundred."
The king said,
"Stop!
Who would be willing to exchange nine hundred for one quail?"
Chéng put the quail in his pouch, intending to leave.
The king called out,
"Quail man, come back!
Quail man, come back!
I will actually give six hundred.
If you agree, sell it;
otherwise, so be it."
Chéng again looked at his host,
who remained as before.
Chéng's heart was overflowing with desire,
only fearing to miss the opportunity,
and said,
"To sell it for this amount,
my heart is truly discontented;
but if the deal is not made,
then the offense will be much greater.
I cannot help it,
I will follow Your Majesty's command."
The king was pleased,
and immediately weighed and paid him.
Chéng put the gold in his pouch,
bowed his thanks, and left.
The host complained,
"What did I say?
Why did you rush to sell it yourself?
If you had held out a little longer,
eight hundred gold pieces would have been in your hand!"
Chéng returned home,
threw the gold on the table,
and asked his host to take it himself.
The host refused to accept.
He insisted on offering it again,
so the host calculated the cost of his meals and accepted it.
The king packed his belongings and returned,
and upon arriving home,
recounted what had happened,
taking out the gold to celebrate.
His wife ordered the management of three hundred 'mǔ' of good land,
built houses and made tools,
becoming quite an established family.
His wife rose early,
made Chéng supervise the plowing,
and his wife supervise the weaving;
if they were slightly lazy,
she would scold them.
The couple lived in peace,
not daring to utter a word of complaint.
After three years,
their family became even richer.
His wife bade farewell, wishing to leave.
The couple together tried to persuade her to stay,
even to the point of tears.
His wife then also stopped.
But when they looked for her at dawn the next day,
she was already gone.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Wealth is all obtained through diligence;
this case alone was obtained through idleness,
which is truly unheard of.
I do not know if one, though utterly poor,
whose inherent nature remains unchanged,
is this why Heaven first abandoned him and then finally took pity on him?
Can there truly be wealth and honor in laziness?"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The Gěng clan of Tàiyuán
was formerly a prominent family,
their residence vast and expansive.
Later, it declined,
and the contiguous buildings
were half abandoned.
Consequently, strange occurrences began to happen;
the main gate would open and close by itself,
and the family would constantly be startled awake by shouting in the middle of the night.
The Gěng family was troubled by this,
so they moved to a villa,
leaving an old man to guard the gate.
From then on, the desolation grew worse.
Sometimes, laughter, conversation, singing, and musical sounds were heard.
Gěng Yǒucóngzǐ Qùbìng,
being wild and unrestrained,
instructed the old man that if he heard or saw anything,
he should immediately report it.
That night,
when he saw the lights in the upper story flicker,
the old man ran to report it to Qùbìng.
Qùbìng wanted someone to investigate the strangeness.
He was stopped,
but he did not listen.
He was familiar with the gates and doors from old times,
so he pushed aside the weeds and brambles,
winding his way in.
He ascended the building,
but there was nothing unusual.
Passing through the building,
he heard hushed human voices.
He secretly peered in
and saw two huge candles burning,
their light as bright as day.
An old man, wearing a scholar's cap, sat facing south,
with an old woman opposite him,
both over forty years old.
Facing east was a young man,
about twenty years old;
to his right was a young lady,
just past her capping ceremony.
The table was laden with wine and meat,
and they sat in a circle, laughing and chatting.
Qùbìng burst in,
and, laughing, exclaimed:
"An uninvited guest has arrived!"
The group scattered in surprise and hid.
Only the old man came out
and shouted, asking:
"Who dares enter people's private chambers?"
Qùbìng said:
"These are my family's private chambers,
which you have occupied.
You drink the fine wine by yourselves,
without inviting the host even once.
Isn't that a bit too stingy?"
The old man scrutinized him
and said:
"You are not the host."
Qùbìng said:
"I am the wild scholar Gěng Qùbìng,
the host's nephew."
The old man saluted respectfully and said:
"I have long admired your eminence!"
Then he bowed and invited Qùbìng in,
immediately calling his family to change the food.
Qùbìng stopped him.
The old man then poured wine for the guest.
Qùbìng said:
"We are close friends,
there is no need for the other guests to avoid me.
I still wish to invite them to drink with us."
The old man called:
"Xiào'ér!"
Soon, the young man entered from outside.
The old man said:
"This is my unworthy son."
He bowed and sat down, briefly inquiring about their family backgrounds.
The old man introduced himself:
"My surname is Hú."
Qùbìng was naturally bold and free-spirited,
and his conversation flowed with spirit;
Xiào'ér was also elegant and unrestrained.
In their conversation,
they found each other very agreeable.
Qùbìng was twenty-one,
two years older than Xiào'ér,
so he treated him as a younger brother.
The old man said:
"I heard your ancestor compiled the 'Wàichuán of Túshān,'
do you know about it?"
Qùbìng replied:
"I know it."
The old man said:
"I am a descendant of the Túshān clan.
After the Táng dynasty,
I can still recall the genealogy;
but before the Five Dynasties,
there is no record.
I hope you can enlighten me."
Qùbìng briefly recounted the accomplishments of the Túshān woman in assisting Yǔ,
embellishing it with many words,
with wonderful ideas gushing forth.
The old man was greatly pleased
and said to his son:
"Today, we are fortunate to hear what we have never heard before.
This young master is also not an outsider,
so you may invite mother and Qīngfèng to come,
to listen together,
and also let them know of our ancestors' virtue."
Xiào'ér entered the curtained chamber.
A short while later,
the old woman came out with the young lady.
Qùbìng carefully observed her:
her delicate demeanor gave rise to charm,
her autumnal eyes flowed with intelligence;
there was no beauty like hers in the human world.
The old man pointed to his wife and said:
"This is my old wife."
Then he pointed to the young lady:
"This is Qīngfèng,
my humble daughter.
She is quite intelligent,
and remembers everything she hears and sees,
so I called her to listen."
Qùbìng finished speaking and drank,
gazing at the young lady,
his eyes fixed on her.
The lady noticed this
and lowered her head.
Qùbìng secretly nudged her small feet,
and the lady quickly drew back her feet,
without showing any anger.
Qùbìng's spirit soared,
unable to control himself,
he slapped the table and exclaimed:
"To have a wife like this,
I wouldn't trade it for ruling the world!"
The old woman saw that Qùbìng was getting increasingly drunk
and more wild,
so she and the lady both rose
and abruptly pulled back the curtain and left.
Qùbìng was disappointed,
so he bade farewell to the old man and left.
But his heart was troubled,
unable to forget Qīngfèng.
That night,
he went again.
The scent of orchid and musk was still fragrant,
but though he waited the whole night,
there was not a sound or cough.
He returned and discussed with his wife,
wanting to move his family there to live,
hoping for an encounter.
His wife did not agree,
so Shēng then went by himself
to read downstairs.
As he leaned on his desk at night,
a ghost with dishevelled hair,
its face as black as lacquer,
stared at Shēng with wide eyes.
Shēng smiled,
dipped his finger to grind ink and smeared it on himself,
then glowed and stared back at it.
The ghost was ashamed and departed.
The next night,
when the watch was deep,
he extinguished the candle, intending to sleep,
and heard a door bolt unlatch behind the house,
opening with a clatter.
He quickly got up to peer,
and found the door half-open.
Soon, he heard the soft sound of footsteps,
and a candlelight emerged from the room.
He looked,
and it was Qīngfèng.
Suddenly seeing Shēng,
she was startled and retreated,
quickly closing both doors.
Shēng knelt for a long time and addressed her, saying:
"This humble one does not avoid danger and malice;
it is truly for your sake.
Fortunately, there is no one else;
if I could but shake your hand and share a smile,
I would die without regret."
The maiden replied from afar:
"How could I not know
your deep and earnest affection?
But my uncle's household rules are strict,
and I dare not comply with your request."
Shēng pleaded earnestly,
saying:
"I dare not even hope for intimate contact;
just a glimpse of your countenance would be enough."
The maiden seemed to consent,
opened the door and came out,
then grabbed his arm and pulled him.
Shēng was overjoyed,
and they went together into the downstairs room,
where he embraced her and placed her on his lap.
The maiden said:
"Fortunately, we have a predestined connection;
after this one night,
then lovesickness will be useless."
He asked:
"Why?"
She said:
"My uncle feared your audacity,
so he transformed into a fierce ghost to scare you,
but you were unmoved.
Now he has already chosen another place to live;
the whole family has moved their belongings to the new residence,
and I am left to guard;
tomorrow, I will depart."
Having spoken,
she wanted to leave,
saying:
"I fear my uncle will return."
Shēng forcibly detained her,
wanting to enjoy their time together.
While they were conversing,
the old man abruptly entered.
The maiden was so ashamed and frightened she could not compose herself;
she bowed her head against the bed,
fiddling with her sash and saying nothing.
The old man angrily said:
"Wretched creature, you disgrace our family!
If you don't leave quickly,
the whip will follow!"
The maiden lowered her head and rushed away;
the old man also left.
Shēng followed and listened,
hearing endless scolding and insults.
When he heard Qīngfèng sobbing softly,
Shēng's heart felt as if it were being cut,
and he cried loudly:
"The fault is mine;
what has it to do with Qīngfèng?
If you pardon Qīngfèng,
then saws, chisels, and iron axes,
this humble one is willing to suffer them myself!"
After a long silence,
Shēng then returned to sleep.
From then on, there was absolutely no sound or trace from within the dwelling.
Shēng's uncle heard of it and found it extraordinary,
willing to sell him the residence,
without bargaining the price.
Shēng was pleased,
and moved there with his family.
He lived there for over a year,
very comfortably,
but he never for a moment forgot Fèng.
It happened during the Qīngmíng Festival when a scholar returned home after visiting the graves.
He saw two small foxes
being chased by a dog.
One threw itself into the wilderness and scurried away,
while the other was frantically running on the road.
Seeing the scholar,
it cried mournfully and lingeringly,
its ears flattened and head bowed,
as if begging for help.
The scholar took pity on it,
opened his robe,
picked it up, and brought it home.
He closed the door,
placed it on the bed,
and it turned into Qīngfèng.
Greatly delighted,
he offered comfort and inquired.
The woman said:
"I was just playing with my maidservant
when I encountered this great calamity.
If not for you, my lord,
I would surely have been buried in a dog's belly.
I hope you will not despise me for being of a different species."
The scholar said:
"Every day my heart has been filled with longing,
bound to my soul and dreams.
Seeing you is like obtaining a rare treasure;
how could I speak of despising you!"
The woman said:
"This is fate.
Without this upheaval,
how could we have come together?
But luckily,
the maidservant must now believe me to be dead,
so we can now seal our eternal vow, my lord."
The scholar was pleased
and set up a separate residence for her.
More than two years passed.
One night, as the scholar was reading,
Xiàor entered suddenly.
The scholar stopped reading,
surprised and questioned his visit.
Xiàor prostrated himself,
and tearfully said:
"My master has met with a sudden misfortune,
and no one but you can save him.
He intended to come himself to plead,
but feared he would not be received,
so he sent me."
The scholar asked:
"What is the matter?"
He replied:
"Does the young master know Mò Sānláng?"
The scholar said:
"He is a son of a family friend of mine."
Xiàor said:
"He will be passing by tomorrow.
If he happens to carry a hunted fox,
I hope you will keep it."
The scholar said:
"The shame of the pavilion incident
is still vivid in my mind;
I dare not inquire about other matters.
If you truly wish me to offer my meager help,
Qīngfèng must come!"
Xiàor wept and said:
"Sister Fèng died in the wilderness three years ago!"
The scholar waved his sleeve and said:
"If that is the case,
then my hatred is even deeper!"
He picked up his book and began to recite loudly,
not glancing at Xiàor at all.
Xiàor rose,
cried without a sound,
covered his face, and left.
The scholar went to Qīngfèng's place
and told her the situation.
The woman's face changed color and she asked:
"Will you really save him?"
He replied:
"I will save him;
my refusal just now was merely a way to repay his past offense."
The woman then happily said:
"I was orphaned young
and raised by my uncle.
Although I offended him in the past,
it was in accordance with our family rules."
The scholar said:
"Indeed,
but it makes one unable to be entirely free of resentment.
If you had truly died,
I definitely would not have helped him."
The woman laughed and said:
"How cruel!"
The next day,
Mò Sānláng indeed arrived,
adorned with carved eagle badges and a tiger skin,
his retinue very imposing.
The scholar met him at the gate.
He saw many captured animals,
among them a black fox,
its fur stained with blood;
he touched it,
and its flesh was still warm.
He then pretended his fur coat was damaged
and begged to mend it with the fox's fur.
Mò generously untied it and presented it to him.
The scholar immediately gave it to Qīngfèng
and then drank with his guest.
After the guest left,
the woman held the fox in her arms.
After three days,
it revived,
and then transformed back into the old man.
He looked up and saw Qīngfèng,
doubting if he was still in the human world.
The woman recounted the entire story.
The old man then bowed down,
ashamed and apologetic for his past misdeeds.
Happily, he looked at the woman and said:
"I always said you weren't dead;
now it has come true."
The woman said to the scholar:
"If you care for me,
I beg you to lend me the house and courtyard,
so that I may fulfill my duty of filial piety."
The scholar agreed.
The old man, blushing, thanked them and departed.
As night fell,
his whole family indeed came.
From then on, they were like family,
without any more suspicion or resentment.
When the scholar was in his study,
Xiàor would often join him for discussions and banquets.
As the scholar's legitimate son gradually grew older,
he had Xiàor tutor him;
Xiàor taught patiently and skillfully,
with the manner of a true teacher.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Shēng of Tàiyuán,
was traveling early in the morning
when he met a young woman
carrying a baby and running,
struggling greatly to walk.
He hurried to catch up with her.
She was a beautiful girl of sixteen or so.
His heart was filled with affection for her,
and he asked,
"Why are you walking alone day and night?"
The woman said,
"A traveler like me
cannot resolve her own sorrows,
so why bother to ask?"
The scholar said:
"What sorrows do you have?
Perhaps I can help;
I will not refuse."
The woman sadly said:
"My parents were greedy for bribes
and sold me to a wealthy family.
The legitimate wife was extremely jealous,
scolding me in the morning and humiliating me with physical abuse in the evening,
which I could not bear,
so I am fleeing far away."
He asked:
"Where are you going?"
She said:
"A person on the run
has no fixed abode."
The scholar said:
"My humble dwelling is not far;
please honor me with your presence."
The woman was pleased
and followed him.
The scholar carried her belongings for her,
guiding her home with him.
The woman looked around the room and saw no one,
asking:
"Why do you have no family members?"
He replied:
"This is just a study."
The woman said:
"This place is very good.
If you pity me and give me life,
you must keep it a secret and not reveal it."
The scholar agreed.
Then they slept together.
He hid her in a secret room,
and after several days, no one knew.
The scholar subtly told his wife.
His wife, Chén,
suspected that the woman was an attendant concubine of a wealthy family
and advised him to send her away.
Shēng did not listen.
One day, he went to the market,
where he encountered a Daoist priest.
The priest looked at Shēng and was startled,
asking:
“What have you encountered?”
He replied:
“Nothing.”
The Daoist priest said:
“Evil qi encircles your body;
how can you say nothing?”
Shēng again strongly denied it.
The Daoist priest then left,
saying:
“How deluded!
There are indeed those in the world who are unaware even when death is imminent.”
Shēng, finding his words strange,
began to doubt the woman;
but then he thought, how could such a beautiful woman
be a demon?
He suspected the Daoist priest was merely preying on people with exorcisms and rituals.
Soon after,
he reached the study gate,
but it was bolted from within,
preventing entry.
Suspecting something amiss,
he climbed over the wall.
The room door was also closed.
He tiptoed to the window and peered in,
seeing a fierce ghost,
with a green face
and saw-like teeth.
It spread a human skin on the couch
and painted it with a colorful brush;
then it threw down the brush,
lifted the skin,
as if shaking out clothes,
put it on its body,
and immediately transformed into the woman.
Seeing this,
he was greatly terrified
and crept out like a beast.
He quickly chased after the Daoist priest,
but did not know where he had gone.
He searched everywhere,
and found him in the wilderness.
He knelt and begged for help.
The Daoist priest said:
“Please let me remove it.
This creature also suffers greatly;
it has just managed to find a substitute,
and I cannot bear to harm its life.”
Then he gave Shēng a fly whisk,
telling him to hang it on the bedroom door.
Before parting,
he arranged to meet at Qīngdì Miào.
Shēng returned,
not daring to enter the study,
and instead slept in the inner chamber,
hanging the whisk there.
After about one watch,
he heard rustling sounds outside the door,
but he dared not look himself,
so he made his wife look.
She only saw the woman coming,
who dared not advance when she saw the whisk;
she stood grinding her teeth,
and after a long time, left.
A short while later, she returned,
cursing:
“The Daoist priest scared me!
But I won’t just leave without my mouthful, will I?”
She grabbed the whisk and smashed it,
then broke through the bedroom door and entered.
She went straight to Shēng’s bed,
tore open Shēng’s abdomen,
scooped out Shēng’s heart, and left.
His wife screamed.
A maid came in with a candle,
and Shēng was already dead,
his cavity messy with blood.
Chén, terrified and weeping, dared not make a sound.
The next day,
she sent his younger brother, Èrláng, to inform the Daoist priest.
The Daoist priest angrily said:
“I pitied it,
but this demon dares to act like this!”
He immediately followed Shēng’s brother.
The woman was already nowhere to be found.
After a moment, he looked up and around,
saying:
“Luckily, it hasn’t fled far!”
He asked:
“Whose family is in the South Courtyard?”
Èrláng said:
“It’s where I live.”
The Daoist priest said:
“It’s currently with you.”
Èrláng was startled,
thinking it wasn’t possible.
The Daoist priest asked:
“Has there been an unfamiliar person come recently?”
He replied:
“I went to Qīngdì Miào early,
so I really don’t know.
I should go back and ask.”
He left for a short while and returned,
saying:
“Indeed there has!
In the morning, an old woman came,
wanting to be hired to work for my family.
My household kept her,
and she is still there.”
The Daoist priest said:
“That is the creature.”
So he went with them.
Wielding a wooden sword,
he stood in the center of the courtyard,
and shouted:
“Vicious demon!
Return my whisk!”
The old woman in the room,
pale with panic,
came out the door, trying to flee.
The Daoist priest pursued and struck her.
The old woman fell,
her human skin ripping off,
transforming into a fierce ghost,
lying and howling like a pig.
The Daoist priest coiled his wooden sword around its head;
its body turned into thick smoke,
piling up on the ground.
The Daoist priest took out a gourd,
pulled out its stopper and placed it in the smoke.
It then sucked in air as if through a mouth,
and in an instant, the smoke was gone.
The Daoist priest stoppered the gourd and put it into his bag.
They all looked at the human skin;
eyebrows, eyes, hands, and feet,
all were complete.
The Daoist priest rolled it up,
with a sound like rolling a scroll painting,
and also put it in his bag.
Then he bid them farewell, intending to leave.
Mme. Chén welcomed him at the door,
weeping and begging for a method to revive Shēng.
The Daoist priest declined, saying he could not.
Chén grew even sadder,
prostrating herself on the ground and not rising.
The Daoist priest pondered deeply, saying:
“My art is shallow;
I truly cannot raise the dead.
I can point you to someone
who might be able to,
and if you go and ask, it will surely be effective.”
She asked:
“Who?”
He said:
“There is a madman in the market
who sometimes lies in dung and mud.
Try to entreat him with sorrow.
If he should insult you wildly,
do not be angry.”
Èrláng also knew him well.
So they bid farewell to the Daoist priest
and went together with his sister-in-law.
I saw a beggar singing wildly on the road.
His snot was three *chǐ* long,
and he was so filthy one could not approach him.
Chén knelt and moved forward.
The beggar laughed and said,
“Does the beautiful woman love me?”
Chén told him her reason.
He laughed loudly again and said,
“All men are husbands.
Why keep him alive?”
Chén earnestly implored him.
Then he said,
“Strange!
A person dies, and you beg for life from me.
Am I Yánmó?”
He angrily struck Chén with his staff.
Chén endured the pain and received the blow.
Townsfolk gradually gathered like a wall.
The beggar coughed up a handful of phlegm and spittle,
raised it to Chén’s lips and said,
“Eat it!”
Chén’s face flushed red
and showed difficulty. But recalling the Taoist priest’s instructions,
she forced herself to eat it.
She felt it enter her throat,
hard like a ball of floss,
and it went down with a grating sound,
stopping and knotting in her chest.
The beggar laughed loudly and said,
“The beautiful woman truly loves me!”
Then he got up
and walked away without looking back.
She followed him
into a temple.
She pursued and searched for him,
but did not know where he was.
She searched high and low,
but there was no trace.
Ashamed and resentful, she returned home.
She grieved over the misery of her husband’s death,
and regretted the shame of eating the spittle.
She looked up and down, weeping sorrowfully,
wishing only to die immediately.
Just as she was about to spread the bloodied cloth and prepare the corpse,
her family members stood watching,
none daring to approach.
Chén embraced the corpse and gathered its intestines,
arranging them while crying.
Her crying became hoarse,
and suddenly she felt like vomiting.
She felt something knotted in her diaphragm,
which suddenly rushed out.
Before she could turn her head,
it had already fallen into the cavity.
Startled, she looked at it,
and it was a human heart.
It was still throbbing in the cavity,
steaming with hot vapor like smoke.
She was greatly astonished.
Hastily, she pressed the two halves of the cavity together with her hands,
squeezing with all her might.
If she relaxed a little,
vapor would diffuse out from the seams.
So she tore a piece of silk and tightly bound it.
She stroked the corpse with her hand,
and it gradually grew warm.
She covered it with a quilt.
At midnight, she opened it to look,
and there was breathing.
By dawn,
he was actually alive.
He said,
“It was vague, like a dream,
but I just felt a dull pain in my abdomen.”
She looked at the wound,
a scab had formed like a coin,
and it soon healed.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“How foolish are people of the world!
Clearly it was a demon,
yet they considered it beautiful.
How deluded are the foolish!
Clearly it was loyalty,
yet they considered it madness.
However, if one loves another’s beauty and preys on it,
then his wife will also eat another’s spittle and find it sweet.
The way of Heaven has good retribution,
but the foolish and deluded do not understand it.
How lamentable it is!”
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
An elder from Chǔ,
traded abroad.
His wife lived alone.
She dreamt of intercourse with a person;
upon waking, she looked at him,
and it was a young man.
She observed his behavior,
which was different from humans,
and knew it was a fox.
Not long after,
he got out of bed and left.
The door had not even opened, and he was already gone.
In the evening,
she invited the kitchen maid to keep her company.
Her ten-year-old son,
who usually slept in a separate bed,
was also invited to stay with them.
As night deepened,
the maid and the boy both fell asleep,
and the fox came again.
The wife murmured as if speaking in a dream.
The maid awoke,
called her,
and the fox then left.
From then on,
she felt listless, as if something were missing.
At night,
she dared not extinguish the candle,
and warned her son not to sleep too soundly.
Late into the night,
the boy and the maid leaned against the wall and dozed off briefly.
When they awoke,
the wife was gone.
They thought she had gone out to relieve herself;
they waited a long time and she did not return,
then they began to suspect.
The maid was afraid
and dared not go look for her.
The boy took a lamp and searched everywhere,
and when he reached another room,
his mother was lying naked within;
when he approached and helped her,
she showed no shame or shyness.
From then on, she went mad,
singing, crying, shouting, and cursing,
changing her state ten thousand times a day.
At night, she disliked living with people.
She had her son sleep in a separate bed,
and also sent the maid away.
Whenever the son heard his mother laughing and talking,
he would get up and light a fire.
His mother would instead get angry and scold him,
but the son did not take it to heart,
thus encouraging his boldness.
However, her games were without moderation;
daily she would practice,
piling bricks and stones on the windows,
and she would not listen when stopped.
If one stone was removed,
she would roll on the ground and let out a delicate cry,
and no one dared to provoke her.
After several days,
both windows were completely blocked,
with no light whatsoever.
After this, she mixed mud and plastered the wall holes,
busily working all day,
without tiring of her labor.
Once the plastering was done,
having nothing else to do,
she then sharpened the kitchen knife, *huòhuò*.
Those who saw her all detested her stubbornness,
and did not consider her human.
Èr, at midnight, hid a knife in his bosom.
He covered the lamp with a gourd.
He waited for his mother to murmur in her sleep,
then quickly lit the lamp,
and shouted, banging the door.
When nothing unusual happened for a long time,
he moved away from the door and announced loudly,
pretending he wanted to search.
There was a creature,
like a civet cat,
that suddenly rushed through the door crack.
He quickly struck it,
only cutting off its tail,
about two inches long,
still dripping with wet blood.
Initially,
when he lit the lamp and got up,
his mother immediately cursed him,
but Èr acted as if he didn't hear.
He was frustrated that his strike had missed,
and went to sleep in regret.
He thought to himself that although he hadn't killed it immediately,
he could hope it wouldn't come back.
At dawn,
he saw the bloodstains leading over the wall and away.
Tracking them,
they led into the Hè family garden.
Indeed, that night it did not come,
and Èr was secretly pleased.
But his mother lay listless as if dead.
Not long after,
the jiārén returned,
and went to the bed to inquire.
The fù cursed,
looking at him as if he were an enemy.
Èr recounted the situation.
Wēng was startled,
and invited a doctor to treat her.
The fù rejected the medicine and cursed.
Secretly, the medicine was put into hot water and mixed for her to drink,
and after several days, she gradually improved.
Father and son were both happy.
One night, Èr awoke,
and found his mother gone;
the father and son searched again and found her in another room.
From then on, she became deranged again,
not wanting to share a room with her husband.
Towards evening,
she would run to another room.
If they tried to restrain her,
her curses became even more severe.
Wēng had no recourse,
and locked all the other doors.
But when the fù ran,
the doors opened by themselves.
Wēng was distressed by this,
and performed all kinds of exorcisms,
but to no avail.
At dusk, Èr secretly entered the Hè family garden,
and lay hidden in the undergrowth,
intending to find the fox's whereabouts.
As the moon began to rise,
he suddenly heard human voices.
He stealthily parted the clumps of grass [péng kē]
and saw two people come to drink.
One was a long-whiskered servant [zhǎngliè nú] holding a pot,
dressed in an old brown color.
Their voices were all low and indistinct,
not very discernible.
After a while,
he heard one person say:
"Tomorrow, bring some white wine."
Soon after,
they both left,
only the long-whiskered one remained,
taking off his clothes and lying on a garden stone.
Upon careful observation,
his four limbs were all like a human's,
but a tail hung down from his rear.
Èr wanted to return,
fearing the fox would notice,
so he remained hidden all night.
Before dawn,
he heard the two people return one after another,
muttering as they entered the bamboo grove.
Èr then returned.
Wēng asked where he had been,
and he replied:
"I stayed at my uncle's [ābó] house."
Just as he was following his father into the market,
he saw a fox tail hanging in a hat shop,
and begged Wēng to buy it.
Wēng ignored him.
Èr pulled his father's clothes,
coaxing him noisily.
Wēng could not bear to refuse,
and bought it.
While his father was trading in the market,
Èr played by his side.
When his father looked away,
he stole money and left,
bought white wine,
and left it at a shop's corridor.
He had a maternal uncle [jiùshì] who lived in the city,
who had always been a hunter.
Èr ran to his house.
His uncle was out.
His aunt [jìn] inquired about his mother's illness,
and he replied:
"She has been a little better for the past few mornings.
But mice have gnawed at her clothes again,
and she is angry and distraught,
so she sent me to beg for some hunting medicine."
His aunt searched her trunk,
took out some money,
wrapped it, and gave it to Èr.
Èr thought it was too little.
His aunt wanted to make soup and noodles for him.
Èr, seeing no one in the room,
opened the medicine packet himself,
secretly took a handful, and put it in his bosom.
Then he quickly told his aunt
not to light the fire,
"Father is waiting in the market,
and there's no time to eat."
Then he went straight out,
secretly put the medicine into the wine.
He wandered around the market,
only returning at dusk.
His father asked where he had been,
and he claimed to have been at his uncle's house.
From then on, Èr spent his days roaming the market.
One day, he saw the long-whiskered man also among the crowd.
Èr confirmed it was him,
and secretly followed him.
Gradually he spoke to him,
asking about his residence.
He replied:
"North Village."
He also asked Èr,
and Èr falsely said:
"Mountain Cave."
The long-whiskered man found it strange that he lived in a cave.
Èr smiled and said:
"My family has lived in a cave dwelling for generations,
aren't you the same?"
The man was even more surprised,
and immediately asked for his surname.
Èr said:
"I am a son of the Hú family.
Have you forgotten where I saw you with the two young masters [láng]?
Did you forget it?"
The man observed him carefully,
half believing, half doubting.
Èr slightly lifted his lower garment,
revealing a little of his fake tail,
saying:
"We mix among humans,
but this thing still remains,
which is regrettable."
The man asked:
"What do you want to do in the market?"
Èr said:
"My father sent me to buy."
The man also said he was there to buy.
Èr asked:
"Have you bought it yet?"
He replied:
"My family has many poor people,
so I often have to steal more when there's an opportunity."
Èr said:
"This job is also quite hard,
full of anxiety."
The man said:
"I'm sent by my master,
so I can't help it."
He then asked:
"Who is your master?"
He replied:
"It's the two young masters [láng] whom you saw previously, brothers.
One is having a private affair with the Wáng family's wife in the North Guō,
and the other stays at an old man's [wēng] house in East Village.
The son of that Wēng's family is very malicious;
he had his tail cut off,
and only recovered after ten days.
Now he's gone there again."
Having spoken,
he wished to bid farewell,
and said:
“Do not mess up my affair.”
The boy said:
“Stealing it is difficult;
it is not as easy as selling it.
I will first sell it and send it to your corridor;
I respectfully offer it to you as a gift.
I still have some spare money in my purse,
so I don’t worry about selling it.”
That person was ashamed of having nothing to repay him with.
The boy said:
“We are originally of the same kind;
why be stingy with a little bit?
When we have leisure,
I should still drink heartily with you.”
Then he went with him,
took out the wine and gave it to him,
and then returned home.
That night,
the mother finally slept soundly,
and no longer ran about.
Knowing in their hearts that there was something unusual,
they told the father to go together to verify it.
Then two foxes were found dead on the pavilion,
and one fox died in the grass,
with blood still oozing profusely from its snout.
The wine bottle was still there;
they held it and shook it,
and it was not yet empty.
The father asked in surprise:
“Why didn’t you tell me earlier?”
He said:
“This creature is most spiritual;
if I had leaked it,
they would have known.”
The old man joyfully said:
“My son,
you are the Chén Píng of hunting foxes!”
Thereupon, the father and son carried the foxes home.
They saw one fox with a bald tail,
and knife marks distinctly visible.
From then on, they were at peace.
However, the wife had become exceptionally thin,
her mind gradually became clearer,
but her cough worsened,
and she would vomit several sheng of phlegm,
but then quickly recovered.
The wife of the Wáng family in Běi Guō
had previously been troubled by a fox;
when asked about it now,
the fox was gone and her illness also cured.
The old man, from this, thought his son extraordinary,
and taught him horsemanship and archery.
Later, he became a high-ranking official, reaching the position of Zǒng Róng.
According to the manuscript of Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì
Lǚ Fèngníng, a servant of Wáng Pújīn in my hometown,
had a particular fondness for snakes.
Whenever he got a small snake,
he would swallow it whole,
like eating an onion.
For larger ones,
he would cut them inch by inch with a knife,
before scooping them up to eat.
When he chewed, there was a clanging sound,
and blood stained his cheeks.
Moreover, he had a good sense of smell;
he once smelled the scent of a snake through a wall,
and immediately rushed outside the wall,
and indeed found a snake over a foot long.
At the time, he had no knife,
so he first bit its head,
with its tail still wriggling at the corner of his mouth.
According to the manuscript of Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì
Jīn Shìchéng,
a native of Chángshān.
He had always been unrestrained.
Suddenly he left home to become a monk (tuóluó).
He seemed mad,
and considered unclean things delicious.
Whenever dogs and sheep left their excrement in front of him,
he would immediately prostrate himself and eat it.
He styled himself a Buddha.
Ignorant common women found his behavior extraordinary,
and those who adopted the disciple’s礼 number in the tens of thousands.
Jīn would order them to eat excrement,
and none dared to disobey.
He built halls and pavilions,
the cost of which was considerable,
and people gladly donated for it.
The county magistrate, Nán Gōng, detested his strangeness,
arrested him and flogged him,
ordering him to repair the local Confucian temple (Shèng Miào).
His disciples competed to tell each other:
“The Buddha is in trouble!”
They eagerly raised money to save him.
The palace was completed within a month,
and the collection of money
was even faster than the pursuit and demands of cruel officials.
The Historian of Anomalies (Yì Shǐ Shì) says:
“I heard about the Taoist Jīn;
people all referred to him by his name,
calling him ‘Jīn Shìchéng Fó.’
His behavior reached the point of eating filth;
it was extreme.
Flogging him was not enough to humiliate him,
but punishing him was truly effective;
how good was Magistrate Nán’s method of punishment!
However, for the school temple to be dilapidated and troubled by a heretical Taoist,
is also a shame for the gentry and officials.”
According to the manuscript of Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì
Dǒng Shēng,
courtesy name Xiásī,
was a man from the western border of Qīngzhōu.
One winter evening,
he spread a quilt on his couch and lit charcoal.
Just as he was about to light his lamp,
a friend invited him for a drink,
so he locked his door and left.
At his friend’s place,
there was a doctor in the company,
skilled in reading the Tàisù pulse,
who diagnosed all the guests.
Before seeing Wáng Shēng Jiǔsī and Dǒng, he said:
“I have seen many people,
but no one has a pulse as strange as yours two gentlemen: a noble pulse with ignoble omens,
and a long-life pulse with signs of brevity.
This is not something I dare to understand.
However, Dǒng Jūn’s situation is particularly severe.”
Everyone was surprised and asked him about it.
He said:
“Even I am at a loss with my skill here,
and dare not make a mere conjecture.
I wish you two gentlemen to be careful yourselves.”
The two were initially very alarmed to hear this,
but then thought it was ambiguous talk,
and paid no attention to it.
In the middle of the night,
Dǒng guī
returned to find the gate of his study ajar,
which greatly puzzled him.
Being in his cups, he recalled
that he must have been in a hurry when he left,
and thus forgotten to latch the door.
Entering the room,
he didn't immediately light a lamp,
but first put his hand into the quilt
to feel if it was warm.
As soon as he probed in,
he felt the smooth presence of a person lying there.
Greatly startled,
he withdrew his hand.
He quickly lit a lamp,
and it turned out to be a beautiful woman,
with a youthful face and tender teeth,
no different from an immortal.
He was ecstatic.
Playfully, he probed her lower body,
and found a long, furry tail.
He was terrified
and wanted to escape.
The woman had already woken up and,
reaching out, grabbed his arm,
asking:
"Where are you going, sir?"
Dǒng became even more frightened,
trembling as he pleaded:
"I beg you, immortal, have mercy and forgive me!"
The woman smiled and said:
"What did you see that makes you fear me?"
Dǒng replied:
"I do not fear the head, but I fear the tail."
The woman smiled again and said:
"You are mistaken.
Where is there a tail?"
She took Dǒng's hand
and forced him to probe again,
and this time her thigh flesh was like lard,
and her buttocks were round and smooth.
She laughed and said:
"How about that?
Your drunken eyes were blurry,
you didn't know what you were seeing,
and so you slandered me like this."
Dǒng was already delighted by her beauty,
and now he was even more bewildered,
blaming himself for his previous mistake.
However, he doubted the origin of her sudden appearance.
The woman said:
"Don't you remember the yellow-haired girl from the east neighbor?
Counting on your fingers, it has been
ten years since we moved.
At that time, I had not yet put up my hair,
and you were still a child with a topknot."
Dǒng suddenly realized and said:
"Are you Āsuǒ of the Zhōu family?"
The woman said:
"That's right."
Dǒng said:
"Now that you mention it,
I vaguely remember.
Ten years unseen,
and you've grown so slender!
But how did you manage to come here suddenly?"
The woman said:
"I married a foolish man four or five years ago.
My parents-in-law passed away one after another,
and unfortunately, I also became a Wén Jūn,
leaving me alone,
isolated and without support.
I remembered you were the only one I knew from childhood,
so I came to see you and stay.
It was already late when I arrived,
and someone had just come to invite you to drink,
so I hid to wait for your return.
Having waited for a long time,
my feet were cold and my skin goose-pimpled,
so I borrowed the quilt to warm myself,
I hope you don't suspect me."
Dǒng was delighted,
took off his clothes, and slept with her,
feeling utterly content.
After more than a month,
he gradually became emaciated.
His family asked him curiously,
but he always said he didn't know why.
After a long time,
his face became even more gaunt and haggard,
so he became afraid
and went again to consult a skilled pulse-taker.
The doctor said:
"This is a demonic pulse.
The sign of death from the other day has been confirmed,
and the illness is incurable."
Dǒng wept bitterly,
but did not leave.
The doctor, having no other choice,
acupuncture-needled his hands and cauterized his navel,
and gave him medicine,
advising him:
"If you encounter her again,
exert all your strength to break free."
Dǒng also felt his life was in danger.
Upon returning home,
the woman smiled and beckoned him.
He angrily said:
"Don't entangle me again;
I am about to die!"
He fled without looking back.
The woman was greatly ashamed
and also angrily said:
"Do you still wish to live?"
That night,
Dǒng took the medicine and slept alone.
As soon as he closed his eyes,
he dreamed of intercourse with the woman,
and woke up having ejaculated.
He was even more terrified,
and moved his bed indoors,
where his wife and children kept watch with lamps.
The dream was the same.
He realized the woman was no longer there.
After several days,
Dǒng vomited more than a dou of blood and died.
Wáng Jiǔsī was in his study
when he saw a woman enter.
Charmed by her beauty, he took her as his lover.
He asked where she came from.
She replied:
"I am a neighbor of Xiásī.
He used to be kind to me,
but unexpectedly he was seduced by a fox and died.
The demonic aura of these creatures can be harmful,
so scholars should be especially careful to guard against them."
Wáng was even more impressed by her,
and they continued their joyful companionship.
After a few days,
he became bewildered and emaciated.
Suddenly, he dreamt that Dǒng appeared and said:
"The one you are with is a fox.
She killed me,
and now she wants to kill my friend.
I have already reported this to the underworld,
to vent this deep resentment.
On the seventh night,
you should light incense outside your room,
do not forget!"
He awoke, surprised by the dream.
He said to the woman:
"I am very ill,
and fear I may soon die in a ditch.
Someone advised me not to be married."
The woman replied:
"If one is destined for a long life,
one will live even if married;
if not destined,
one will die even if unmarried."
She sat with him, joking and teasing.
Wáng could not control himself,
and again became intimate with her.
Afterwards, he regretted it,
but could not break away.
When evening came,
he stuck incense by the door.
The woman came,
knocked it over, and discarded it.
That night, he again dreamt that Dǒng came,
reproaching him for disobeying her instructions.
The next night,
he secretly instructed his family
to light the incense stealthily after he had gone to bed.
The woman, on the bed,
suddenly exclaimed:
"Are you lighting incense again?"
Wáng claimed he did not know.
The woman quickly got up, found the incense,
and broke it to extinguish it.
She came back in and asked:
"Who taught you to do this?"
Wáng said:
"Perhaps my household members are worried about my illness and
believe in a sorceress's protective charm."
The woman paced around, unhappy.
His family members, secretly observing the incense extinguished,
lit it again.
The woman suddenly sighed:
"Your good fortune and virtue are truly abundant.
I mistakenly harmed Xiásī and then came to you.
This is indeed my fault.
I will go with him to be judged in the underworld.
If you do not forget our past affection,
please do not destroy my skin-bag."
After a moment, she got down from the bed,
collapsed to the ground, and died.
They lit a candle and saw
that it was a fox.
Still fearing it might revive,
he quickly called his family,
skinned it, and hung it up.
Wáng's illness worsened severely.
He saw the fox come and say:
"I reported this to the judicial officials.
The officials said that Dǒng Jūn was moved by lust
and deserved his death;
but they blamed me for improperly deluding a human,
retrieved my golden elixir,
and ordered me to be reborn.
Where is my skin-bag?"
Wáng said:
"My family did not know,
and has already removed it."
The fox said sadly:
"I have killed many,
and now it is too late for me to die;
but how cruel you are, sir!"
Full of resentment, it left.
Wáng's illness was almost fatal,
and he recovered only after half a year.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript from
the household of the late Elder Wáng Qīnwén of Xīnchéng,
there was a stableman surnamed Wáng.
As a child, he went to Mount Láoshān to study the Dao.
After a long time,
he stopped eating cooked food,
consuming only pine nuts and white stones,
and his whole body grew hair.
After several years,
missing his aged mother, he returned to his village.
Gradually, he resumed eating cooked food,
but still ate stones as before.
If he held them up to the sun,
he could tell the sweetness, bitterness, sourness, and saltiness of the stones,
just like eating taro.
After his mother died,
he returned to the mountains,
and it has now been another seventeen or eighteen years.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript from
the Xīnchéng student Wáng Qǐhòu,
great-grandson of Fangbó Zhōngzì Gōngxiàngkūn.
He saw a woman enter his room,
her appearance fat, dark, and unattractive.
She smiled and approached the bed,
her intentions very disrespectful.
Wáng rejected her,
but she would not leave.
From then on, he saw her whenever he sat or lay down.
But his resolve was firm,
and he never wavered.
The woman grew angry
and slapped his cheek,
with a sound,
but it was not very painful.
The woman tied a sash to the beam
and tried to hang herself alongside him.
Wáng unconsciously threw himself under the beam,
stretching his neck as if to hang himself.
People saw his feet not touching the ground,
standing rigidly in mid-air,
yet he could not die.
From then on, he suffered from madness.
Suddenly, he would say:
"She is going to throw me into the river!"
and would rush madly towards the river,
only stopping when pulled back.
He experienced a hundred such manifestations,
several times daily,
and neither magic nor medicine had any effect.
One day,
he suddenly saw a warrior in chains enter,
who angrily shouted:
"How dare you disturb the honest and sincere!"
He grabbed the woman by the neck,
and she came out from within him.
As soon as she reached outside the window,
the woman no longer looked human;
her eyes flashed like lightning,
and her mouth was blood-red like a basin.
He recalled one of the four clay demons at the gate of the City God Temple,
which was exactly like her.
After this, his illness vanished as if nothing had happened.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
Língyáng's Zhū Ěrdàn,
courtesy name Xiǎomíng.
His nature was unrestrained,
but he was dull-witted by nature.
Though diligent in his studies,
he had yet to make a name for himself.
One day,
the members of his literary society were drinking together.
Someone playfully said to him:
"You have a reputation for bravery!
If you can go to the Shíwáng Diàn late at night,
and carry back the judge from the left corridor,
we will all chip in for a feast."
Now, in Língyáng there was a Shíwáng Diàn,
where the gods and ghosts were all carved from wood,
decorated to look lifelike.
In the east wing stood a judge
with a green face and red beard,
whose appearance was especially fierce and malevolent.
Sometimes at night, sounds of interrogation and torture were heard from the two corridors.
Those who entered
felt their hair stand on end.
Thus, the group used this to challenge Zhū.
Zhū laughed, stood up,
and went straight out.
Before long,
he shouted from outside:
"I have brought the bearded Grand Master!"
Everyone rose.
Soon, he carried the judge in,
placed it on the table,
offered a cup,
and made three libations.
When everyone saw it,
they squirmed uncomfortably in their seats,
and still asked him to carry it away.
Zhū then poured wine onto the ground,
and prayed:
"This student is reckless and unrefined,
but I trust the Grand Master will not take offense.
My humble dwelling is not far,
please do come and seek a drink when the mood strikes you,
and do not treat us as strangers."
Then he carried it away.
The next day,
everyone indeed invited him for a drink.
As evening approached,
he returned half-drunk,
his spirits still high.
He lit a lamp and drank alone.
Suddenly, someone lifted the curtain and entered.
Looking,
he saw it was the judge.
Zhū stood up and said:
"I fear I am about to die!
Did I offend you last night,
and have you come to punish me now?"
The judge parted his thick beard
and smiled, saying:
"Not so.
Last night you kindly invited me,
and as I happened to be free tonight,
I have come to honor the promise made to an understanding person."
Zhū was greatly pleased.
He pulled at his sleeve, urging him to sit,
and he himself got up to wash dishes and make a fire.
The judge said:
"The weather is mild,
we can drink it cold."
Zhū obeyed,
placed the bottle on the table,
and rushed to tell his family to prepare dishes and fruit.
His wife, hearing this,
was greatly alarmed
and warned him not to go out.
Zhū did not listen,
and stood waiting for the preparations before coming out.
They exchanged cups and toasted each other.
Only then did Zhū inquire about his name.
He said:
"My surname is Lù,
but I have no given name."
They discussed classical literature,
and he responded instantly like an echo.
Zhū asked:
"Do you know about 'eight-legged essays'?"
He replied:
"I can quite distinguish between good and bad.
Reading in the underworld
is roughly similar to the human world."
Lù drank heartily,
ten goblets in one go.
Because Zhū had been drinking all day,
he gradually felt his 'jade mountain' collapse
and fell asleep, slumped over the table.
When he awoke,
the residual candle was dim and yellow,
and the ghostly guest had already left.
From then on, Lù would come every two or three days.
Their friendship grew deeper,
and sometimes they would lie down with their feet touching.
Zhū presented his manuscripts,
and Lù always marked them with red ink,
saying they were not good.
One night,
Zhū was drunk
and went to bed first.
Lù was still drinking by himself.
Suddenly, in his drunken dream,
he felt a slight pain in his internal organs.
Waking up, he saw
Lù sitting upright by the bed,
his chest open, his intestines and stomach taken out,
each one being carefully arranged.
Zhū was astonished and said:
"We have no old enmity,
why do you want to kill me?"
Lù smiled and said:
"Don't be afraid,
I am merely replacing your heart of wisdom."
He calmly put the intestines back in,
and closed the incision.
Finally, he bound Zhū's waist with a foot-wrapping cloth.
When he finished,
there were no bloodstains on the bed.
He felt a slight numbness in his abdomen.
He saw Lù place a piece of flesh on the table.
He asked about it,
and Lù said:
"This was your heart.
Your essays were not smooth,
I knew your pores were blocked.
I just went to the underworld
and, among thousands of hearts,
selected a good one
to replace yours.
I left this one to make up the number."
Then he got up,
closed the door, and left.
At dawn, he untied the cloth and looked,
the wound had already closed,
with a red line remaining.
From then on, his literary talent greatly advanced,
and he forgot nothing he read.
A few days later,
he showed Lù another essay.
Lù said:
"It's acceptable now.
However, your fortune is thin,
you cannot achieve great eminence,
only success in the provincial and metropolitan examinations."
Zhū asked:
"When?"
Lù said:
"You will surely be the top candidate this year."
Not long after,
he became the champion in the provincial examination,
and indeed was the top candidate in the autumn imperial examination.
His literary society peers had always ridiculed him;
but when they saw his examination papers,
they looked at each other in astonishment,
and only by detailed inquiry did they learn of his peculiarity.
They all asked Zhū to introduce them,
wishing to befriend Lù.
Lù agreed.
The group prepared a grand feast to await him.
At the beginning of the first watch,
Lù arrived,
his red beard lively,
his eyes sparkling like lightning.
Everyone became pale,
their teeth chattering;
gradually, they withdrew.
Zhū then took Lù home for a drink.
When they were quite drunk,
Zhū said:
"You have already given me much by cleansing my intestines and cutting my stomach.
I have received many favors.
There is still one more thing I wish to trouble you with,
I wonder if it is possible?"
Lù then asked for his command.
Zhū said:
"If the heart and intestines can be changed,
I imagine the face and features can also be altered.
My wife,
my lifelong partner,
her lower body is not bad at all,
but her head and face are not very beautiful.
I still wish to trouble you with your knife and axe,
what do you say?"
Lù smiled and said:
"Yes,
allow me to plan it slowly."
After several days,
Lù came knocking at the gate in the middle of the night.
Zhū quickly rose and invited him in.
He lit a candle,
and saw Lù had something wrapped in his lapel.
When asked what it was,
he said:
"The item you requested the other day,
I had difficulty finding it.
I just obtained the head of a beautiful woman,
and respectfully report to you that your command is fulfilled."
Zhū pushed it aside to look;
the blood on the neck was still wet.
Lù urged him to quickly enter,
without alarming the birds or dogs.
Zhū worried the door was bolted for the night.
When Lù arrived,
he pushed the door with one hand,
and the door opened by itself.
He led Zhū to the bedroom,
where he saw Zhū's wife sleeping on her side.
Lù gave the head to Zhū to hold;
then from his boot he drew a white blade like a dagger,
placed it against Zhū's wife's neck,
pressed with force as if cutting tofu,
and it was severed with one stroke.
The head fell beside the pillow;
he quickly took the beautiful woman's head from his bosom
and placed it on the neck,
carefully aligning it straight,
and then pressed it down.
After a moment, he moved the pillow to support the neck,
ordered Zhū to bury the old head in a quiet place,
and then left.
Zhū's wife awoke,
feeling a slight numbness in her neck,
and her cheeks felt rough like scales.
She rubbed them
and found flakes of blood,
which greatly alarmed her.
She called a maid to draw water for washing;
the maid saw her face covered in blood and was utterly
astonished.
When she washed,
the basin water turned completely red.
She looked up and her face and features were completely different,
again greatly alarming her.
The lady picked up a mirror to look at herself,
and was stunned, unable to comprehend.
Zhū entered and told her;
then he repeatedly examined her closely,
and saw long eyebrows covering her temples,
dimples appearing on her cheekbones,
she was a woman from a painting.
She untied her collar to examine it,
and there was a red line all around,
the flesh above and below it
clearly different.
Before this,
there was a daughter of Censor Wú who was very beautiful,
but before marriage, she had lost two husbands,
so at nineteen she was still unmarried.
During the Yuán Festival, she visited the Shíwáng Diàn,
at which time there were many people,
among whom was a scoundrelly thief who spied on her and desired her.
He then secretly inquired about her residence,
climbed in by ladder at night,
drilled a hole in the bedroom door,
killed a maid under the bed,
and forced the girl to commit adultery;
the girl resisted strenuously and shouted,
the thief became angry
and killed her too.
Madame Wú faintly heard a commotion,
called a maid to check,
and was terrified upon seeing the corpse.
The whole family rose,
placed the body in the hall,
and laid the head beside the neck.
The whole household cried and wailed,
in an uproar all night.
At dawn, when they uncovered the quilt,
the body was there but the head was missing.
They beat all the maids,
accusing them of not guarding properly,
leading to the head being eaten by dogs.
The Censor reported it to the prefecture.
The prefecture set a strict deadline to catch the thief,
but after three months, the culprit was not found.
Gradually, news of the strange head-swap in Zhū's family reached Censor Wú.
Wú suspected something,
and sent an old woman to investigate at Zhū's house;
upon entering and seeing the lady,
she fled in fright to tell Censor Wú.
The Censor saw his daughter's corpse still there,
and was astonished and doubtful, unable to make a decision.
He suspected Zhū had killed his daughter with black magic,
and went to question Zhū.
Zhū said:
"My wife dreamt of having her head changed,
I truly do not understand why;
to say I killed her
is an injustice."
Wú did not believe him,
and sued him.
He had Zhū's family arrested and interrogated,
and they all confirmed Zhū's words.
The Prefect was unable to decide.
Zhū returned home
and sought advice from Lù.
Lù said:
"It's not difficult,
we should make her daughter speak for herself."
Wú dreamt that night that his daughter said:
"Your daughter was murdered by Yáng Dànián of Sūxī,
and has nothing to do with Zhū Xiàolián.
He was not pleased with his wife,
so Lù Pànguān took your daughter's head and exchanged it with hers,
thus your daughter's body died but her head lives.
Please do not hold a grudge."
He awoke and told his wife,
and her dream was the same.
So they reported it to the authorities.
When questioned,
there indeed was a Yáng Dànián;
he was apprehended and shackled,
and confessed his crime.
Wú then went to Zhū,
asked to see his wife,
and from then on they became father- and son-in-law.
Zhū's wife's original head was then reunited with the daughter's corpse and buried.
Zhū entered the imperial examination hall three times,
but each time was disqualified due to examination rules.
He then lost heart in official advancement,
and thirty years passed.
One evening,
Lù informed him:
"Your life will not be long."
When asked about the exact time,
Lù replied, "In five days."
"Can you save me?"
Lù said:
"Only Heaven dictates fate;
how can a person interfere privately?
Moreover, from the perspective of an enlightened person,
life and death are one and the same,
why must life be joy,
and death be sorrow?"
Zhū thought it was so.
He immediately prepared clothing, burial shrouds, coffins, and outer coffins.
When they were ready,
he dressed in formal attire and died.
The next day,
as his wife was扶 (fú) his coffin and weeping,
Zhū suddenly and gently arrived from outside.
His wife was frightened.
Zhū said:
"I am indeed a ghost,
no different from when I was alive.
I was merely worried about you, a widow with an orphaned child,
and felt very attached."
His wife cried loudly,
tears flowing down her chest.
Zhū affectionately comforted her.
His wife said:
"There is an ancient saying about spirits returning to life.
Since you have a spirit,
why don't you revive?"
Zhū said:
"The decrees of Heaven cannot be defied."
She asked:
"What duties do you perform in the underworld?"
He replied:
"Lù Pàn recommended me to supervise archival matters.
I have been granted an official rank,
and suffer no hardships."
His wife wanted to say more,
but Zhū said:
"Master Lù came with me;
you may prepare food and wine."
He hurried out.
His wife prepared according to his words.
She only heard laughter and drinking from inside the room,
with bright spirits and loud voices,
just as when he was alive.
Peeking in at midnight,
he had quietly departed.
From then on, he would come every three to several days.
Sometimes he would stay overnight in intimate company,
and conveniently manage household affairs.
His son, Wěi, was five years old then,
and Zhū would always pick him up and hold him when he came.
When Wěi reached seven or eight years old,
Zhū would teach him to read by lamplight.
The son was also intelligent,
able to write essays at nine,
and entered the county school at fifteen,
completely unaware that he had no father.
After this, his visits gradually became less frequent,
only coming once a month or so.
One evening he came again
and said to his wife:
"Today I bid you a final farewell."
She asked:
"Where are you going?"
He replied:
"I have been ordered by the Emperor to be the Grand Minister of Mount Huà (Tàihuá Qīng).
I am about to set off on a distant journey.
The duties are many and the journey arduous,
so I will not be able to come again."
The mother and son held him and wept,
saying:
"Don't be like this!
Our son is already grown,
and the family's livelihood is still sustainable.
How can there be a phoenix that lives for a hundred years without parting?"
He looked at his son and said:
"Be a good person,
and do not disgrace your father's legacy.
We will meet again in ten years."
He walked straight out the door,
and thus, their connection was severed.
Later, Wěi passed the imperial examination at twenty-five,
and became an official in the Ministry of Rites (Xíngrén).
He was ordered to offer sacrifices at the Western Peak (Xīyuè).
On his way through Huáyīn,
suddenly an entourage with feather canopies
galloped and clashed with his official procession (lǔbù).
He was surprised.
Upon careful inspection of the person in the carriage,
it was his father.
He got out of his carriage and knelt weeping by the roadside.
His father stopped his carriage and said:
"Your official reputation is good;
I can now close my eyes."
Wěi knelt, unable to rise.
Zhū urged his carriage to move,
speeding off without looking back.
After a few steps,
he looked back,
unfastened his sabre, and sent someone to present it.
He said from afar:
"Wearing it will bring you nobility."
Wěi wanted to follow,
but saw the carriage, horses, and entourage
swiftly vanish like the wind,
disappearing in an instant.
He grieved deeply for a long time.
He drew the sabre and examined it.
Its craftsmanship was extremely exquisite,
with a line of characters engraved on it,
saying:
"Be bold in spirit, but cautious in heart;
be adaptable in wisdom, but upright in conduct."
Wěi later rose to the rank of Grand Marshal (Sīmǎ).
He had five sons:
Chén,
Qián,
Yùn,
Hún,
and Shēn.
One evening,
he dreamt his father said:
"The sabre should be given to Hún."
He followed this instruction.
Hún became a Censor-in-Chief (Zǒngxiàn),
and had a good reputation for governance.
The Historian of the Unusual (Yìshǐ Shì) remarks:
"To sever a crane's leg and lengthen a duck's is a misguided attempt at artistry;
to graft flowers and connect trees
is the work of a wondrous innovator.
How much more so for those who chisel and pare at livers and intestines,
and apply knives and awls to necks!
As for Master Lù (Lù Gōng),
he can be said to have put beautiful bones into a skin.
From the late Míng dynasty until now,
not many years have passed.
Does Master Lù of Língyáng still live?
Does he still possess his spiritual power?
I would willingly hold his whip,
for I admire him greatly."
Based on the manuscript of Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio (Liáozhāi Zhìyì)
Wáng Zǐfú,
a native of Luódiàn in Jǔ.
He was orphaned young.
Extremely intelligent,
he passed the preliminary examination at fourteen.
His mother loved him dearly
and usually did not allow him to wander in the countryside.
He was engaged to a Miss Xiāo,
but she died before marriage,
so he had not yet found a spouse.
It was the Lantern Festival (Shàngyuán),
and his maternal cousin, Wú Shēng,
invited him to go sightseeing together.
Just as they reached the edge of the village,
a servant from his uncle's house came
and called Wú away.
Wáng Zǐfú saw throngs of young women like clouds
and, in high spirits, went on alone.
There was a young lady with her maid,
holding a plum blossom branch.
Her beauty was unmatched,
and her smile enchanting.
Wáng Zǐfú stared fixedly,
completely forgetting his inhibitions.
The lady walked a few paces further,
then turned to her maid and said:
"That young man's eyes are as sharp as a thief's!"
She dropped the flower on the ground
and walked away laughing.
Shēng picked up the flower, feeling disheartened,
his spirit lost,
and gloomily returned.
Upon reaching home,
he hid the flower under his pillow,
slept with his head bowed,
speaking and eating nothing.
