His mother worried about him.
His prayers and sacrifices only made his condition worse,
his flesh and skin rapidly diminishing.
Physicians examined him,
prescribing diaphoric remedies,
but he remained dazed and confused.
His mother stroked him, asking the reason,
but he remained silent.
Just then, Wú Shēng arrived,
and she instructed him to question Shēng closely.
Wú approached the bed,
and Shēng, seeing him, burst into tears.
Wú sat by the bed to comfort and console him,
gradually leading to a thorough inquiry.
Shēng fully revealed the truth,
and sought his advice on a plan.
Wú smiled and said:
"Your feelings are truly foolish!
What difficulty is there in fulfilling this wish?
I shall immediately seek her out.
Walking on foot in the wilderness,
she must not be from a prominent family.
If she is not yet betrothed,
the matter will certainly be harmonious; otherwise,
we can try with a heavy bribe,
and the plan will surely be granted.
As long as you recover,
the success of this matter is up to me."
Shēng, hearing this,
could not help but smile.
Wú went out and told Shēng's mother,
looking for the girl's residence in the neighborhood,
but after an exhaustive search,
there was no trace of her.
His mother was greatly worried,
having no plan.
However, after Wú left,
Shēng's face suddenly brightened,
and he ate a little more.
A few days later,
Wú came again.
Shēng asked about the plan.
Wú replied:
"I have found her!
I wondered who she might be,
but she is my aunt's daughter,
that is, your maternal cousin,
and is still awaiting betrothal.
Although there is the suspicion of marriage among close relatives,
if you tell them the truth,
there is nothing that cannot be resolved harmoniously."
Shēng's joy overflowed on his face,
and he asked:
"Where does she live?"
Wú slyly said:
"In the mountains to the southwest,
about thirty *lǐ* from here."
Shēng repeatedly urged him again,
and Wú enthusiastically took on the task and departed.
From then on, Shēng's appetite gradually increased,
and he recovered day by day.
He looked under his pillow,
and although the flower was withered,
it had not yet fallen.
He pondered over it, playing with it,
as if seeing the person herself.
He was surprised that Wú did not come,
so he wrote a letter to summon him.
Wú made excuses and refused to come.
Shēng became angry,
and was unhappy.
His mother, fearing his relapse,
hurriedly discussed marriage for him;
but whenever she suggested something,
he would shake his head, unwilling,
only wishing for Wú daily.
Wú still sent no news,
increasing Shēng's resentment.
He then reconsidered that thirty *lǐ* was not far,
why rely on others?
With the plum blossom in his sleeve,
he impulsively set out by himself,
and his family did not know.
Lonely and walking alone,
he had no one to ask for directions,
but just walked towards the Southern Mountains.
After about thirty *lǐ*,
the chaotic mountains converged,
the clear verdure invigorating his skin,
there were no people walking,
only bird trails.
Looking distantly into the valley,
among clusters of flowers and tangled trees,
there was dimly a small village.
He descended the mountain into the village,
seeing that there were not many houses,
all thatched huts,
but they seemed very neat and elegant.
One house faced north,
with weeping willows in front of the door,
and peaches and apricots were especially abundant inside the wall,
interspersed with slender bamboos;
wild birds chirped within.
He thought it was a garden,
and did not dare to enter hastily.
Looking back at the house opposite,
there was a large, smooth, clean stone,
so he sat on it to rest for a while.
Soon, he heard a girl inside the wall
calling out loudly,
"Xiǎo Róng!"
Her voice was delicate and soft.
While he was listening,
a girl came from east to west,
holding an apricot blossom,
and bowed her head to pin it in her hair.
She looked up and saw Shēng,
then stopped pinning it,
and entered with a smile, holding the flower.
He observed her closely,
and it was indeed the one he had met on the road during the Shàngyuán Festival.
His heart suddenly rejoiced.
But he thought there was no way to approach her;
he wanted to call her "aunt,"
but he had never visited before,
fearing a mistake.
There was no one inside the door to ask.
He sat and stood, pacing,
from morning until sunset,
looking out eagerly,
forgetting hunger and thirst.
Sometimes he saw the girl revealing half her face to peek,
as if surprised that he had not left.
Suddenly, an old woman, leaning on a staff, came out,
and looked at Shēng, saying:
"Where are you from, young gentleman?
I heard you arrived at dawn,
and have been here until now.
What do you intend to do?
Are you not hungry?"
Shēng quickly stood up and bowed to her,
replying:
"I am here to await a relative."
The old woman was deaf and did not hear.
He then said it loudly again.
She then asked:
"What is the surname of your honorable relative?"
Shēng could not answer.
The old woman laughed and said:
"How strange!
You don't even know the name,
what relative can you visit?
I see you, young gentleman,
are just a bookworm.
Why not come with me,
eat some coarse food,
I have a short bed at home where you can sleep.
Tomorrow morning when you return,
find out the surname,
then come back to visit,
it won't be too late."
Shēng was feeling hungry and thinking of food,
and also this would bring him closer to the beautiful lady,
so he was greatly pleased.
He followed the old woman in,
seeing white stone-paved paths inside the door,
red flowers lining the paths,
petals scattered on the steps;
it curved westward,
and another gate opened,
with bean trellises and flower stands filling the courtyard.
He was invited into the house,
where the white walls shone like mirrors;
outside the window, branches of crabapples reached into the room,
covering the tables and beds,
everything was clean and spotless.
As soon as he sat down,
someone outside the window vaguely peered in.
The old woman called:
"Xiǎo Róng!
Please hurry and prepare some millet."
A maid's voice responded from outside.
While sitting,
he fully described his family lineage.
The old woman said:
"Young gentleman's maternal grandfather,
is his surname Wú?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The old woman exclaimed in surprise:
"This is my nephew!
Your esteemed mother
is my younger sister.
For years, due to our family's poverty,
and having no male heir,
our correspondence was cut off.
My nephew has grown so much,
yet I still don't recognize him."
The student said:
"I came here precisely for you, Aunt,
and in my haste, I forgot my surname."
The old woman said:
"My old self is surnamed Qín,
and I have never borne children;
my only surviving child
is also a concubine's offspring.
Her mother remarried
and left her to me to raise.
She's not dull,
but she lacks proper training,
and plays without knowing sorrow.
In a moment,
I'll have her come and pay her respects."
Soon after,
a maidservant served food,
with chicken tails in her grasp.
After the old woman urged him to eat,
the maid came to clear the dishes.
The old woman said:
"Call Yīngníng here."
The maid answered and left.
After a long while,
faint laughter was heard outside the door.
The old woman called again:
"Yīngníng,
your cousin is here."
Outside the door, the snickering did not stop.
The maid pushed her in,
still covering her mouth,
unable to suppress her laughter.
The old woman glared, saying:
"With a guest present,
chattering and scolding,
what kind of behavior is this?"
The girl stifled her laughter and stood,
and the student bowed to her.
The old woman said:
"This is Wáng Láng,
your cousin.
It's laughable that family members don't even know each other."
The student asked:
"How old is my cousin?"
The old woman couldn't understand.
The student repeated it.
The girl laughed again,
unable to look up.
The old woman said to the student:
"I said she lacks proper training,
this is clear now.
She is already sixteen,
but as naive as an infant."
The student said:
"She is one year younger than I."
She said:
"My nephew is already seventeen,
are you by any chance born in the Gēngwǔ year, the Year of the Horse?"
The student nodded in affirmation.
She then asked:
"Who is your niece-in-law?"
He replied:
"I don't have one."
She said:
"With your talent and appearance,
why are you still not betrothed at seventeen?
Yīngníng also has no prospective husband's family,
she is a perfect match;
it's a pity there's the suspicion of being close relatives."
The student remained silent,
his gaze fixed on Yīngníng,
not daring to blink elsewhere.
The maid whispered to the girl,
"His eyes are blazing,
the rogue's nature hasn't changed!"
The girl laughed loudly again,
and turned to the maid, saying:
"See if the green peaches have bloomed yet?"
She suddenly stood up,
covering her mouth with her sleeve,
and walked out with quick, light steps.
Once outside the door,
her laughter finally burst forth.
The old woman also rose,
called the maid to prepare the bedding,
and arranged it for the student.
She said:
"It was not easy for my nephew to come,
you should stay for three or five days,
and I will send you back slowly.
If you find it dull,
there's a small garden behind the house
for your recreation;
there are books you can read."
The next day,
he went to the back of the house;
sure enough, there was a half-acre garden,
with fine grass like a mat,
and willow catkins scattered on the path;
there were three thatched huts,
with flowers and trees surrounding them.
He strolled through the flowers,
and heard a rustling sound in the treetops.
He looked up
and saw Yīngníng up there.
Seeing him approach,
she laughed wildly, almost falling.
The student said:
"Don't do that,
you'll fall!"
The girl descended, still laughing,
unable to stop herself.
Just as she was about to reach the ground,
she lost her grip and fell,
and her laughter ceased.
The student helped her up,
touching her wrist.
The girl's laughter started again,
she leaned against a tree, unable to walk,
and only stopped after a long while.
The student waited for her laughter to subside,
then took out a flower from his sleeve and showed it to her.
The girl took it,
saying:
"It's withered.
Why keep it?"
He said:
"This was left by you, cousin, on the Lantern Festival,
so I kept it."
She asked:
"What is the meaning of keeping it?"
He said:
"To show that my love for you is unforgettable.
Since we met on the Lantern Festival,
my intense longing has made me ill,
I almost thought I would turn into something else;
I didn't expect to see your face again,
please have mercy."
The girl said:
"This is a very trivial matter.
Why be so stingy with a close relative?
When you leave,
I will call the old servant
to cut a huge bundle of garden flowers
and send them with you."
The student said:
"Are you foolish, cousin?"
The girl said:
"Why am I foolish?"
The student said:
"I don't love the flowers,
I love the person who picked the flowers."
The girl said:
"As relatives,
why speak of love?"
The student said:
"The love I speak of
is not the love between relatives,
but the love between husband and wife."
The girl said:
「Is there any difference?」
He said,
「Only that we will share a pillow and bed tonight.」
The girl looked down and pondered for a long time,
then said,
「I'm not used to sleeping with strangers.」
Before her words were finished,
the maid secretly arrived,
and the young scholar fled in alarm.
A short while later,
they met at his mother's place.
His mother asked,
「Where have you been?」
The girl replied that they had been chatting in the garden.
The old woman said,
「Dinner has been ready for a long time.
What long conversation
kept you chatting so roundabout?」
The girl said,
「Big Brother wants me to sleep with him.」
Before her words were finished,
the young scholar was greatly embarrassed,
and stared at her with wide, urgent eyes.
The girl smiled and stopped.
Fortunately, the old woman did not hear,
and still pressed her with rambling questions.
The young scholar quickly covered it with other words,
then quietly reprimanded the girl.
The girl said,
「Was what I just said not supposed to be said?」
The young scholar said,
「Those are words to be kept from others.」
The girl said,
「Kept from others,
but how can they be kept from one's own mother?
Besides, sleeping together is a common thing,
why hide it?」
The young scholar hated her simple-mindedness,
having no way to enlighten her.
Just as they finished eating,
people from his family brought two guards to look for the young scholar.
Earlier,
his mother had waited for the young scholar for a long time and he hadn't returned,
so she began to worry;
they searched the village several times,
but found no trace.
So they went to inquire of Wú.
Wú remembered his previous words,
and so instructed his son to go search the mountain villages to the southwest.
After traversing several villages,
they finally arrived here.
The young scholar stepped out the door,
happened to meet them,
and then went in to inform the old woman,
and asked to take the girl home with him.
The old woman happily said,
「I have wished for this,
not just for a day or two.
But my old body cannot travel far.
For my nephew to take my little sister away,
and for her to get to know her aunt,
that is excellent!」
She called Yīng-níng.
Níng came smiling.
The old woman said,
「What is there to be happy about,
that you laugh without stopping?
If you didn't laugh,
you would be a complete person.」
She then glared at her with anger.
Then she said,
「Big Brother wants to take you with him,
you may pack your things.」
She also provided wine and food for the family members,
then saw them out and said,
「Your aunt's family has abundant fields and property,
enough to support idle people.
Once there, do not return for a while.
Learn poetry and etiquette,
and also serve your parents-in-law well.
I will trouble your aunt
to choose a good match for you.」
The two then set off.
When they reached the mountain hollow,
they looked back,
and could still faintly see the old woman leaning against the door, gazing north.
Arriving home,
his mother saw her exquisite beauty
and asked in surprise who she was.
Shēng replied that she was his maternal aunt's daughter.
His mother said:
"What Wú Láng told you earlier,
was a lie.
I have no elder sister,
how could I have a niece?"
She asked the girl,
who replied:
"I am not my mother's biological daughter.
My father's surname was Qín.
When he died,
I was in swaddling clothes
and cannot remember."
His mother said:
"It is indeed true
that I had a sister who married into the Qín family;
however, she passed away long ago.
How could she still be alive?"
Then she carefully questioned her about her face and birthmarks,
and they matched perfectly.
Again she doubted, saying:
"It is she.
However, she has been dead for many years,
how could she still be alive?"
While she was pondering,
Wú Shēng arrived,
and the girl hid in her room.
Wú inquired about what had happened
and was bewildered for a long time.
Suddenly he said:
"Is this girl's name Yīngníng?"
Shēng affirmed it.
Wú repeatedly called it a strange matter.
Asked how he knew,
Wú said:
"After the Qín family's aunt passed away,
her husband remained a widower.
He was tormented by a fox spirit
and died emaciated.
The fox gave birth to a daughter named Yīngníng,
who lay wrapped in swaddling clothes on the bed,
and everyone in the family saw her.
After the aunt's husband died,
the fox still came occasionally;
later, they sought a Daoist Master's talisman and pasted it on the wall,
and the fox then took the girl away.
Could this be she?"
Both of them were filled with suspicion.
But from the room came Yīngníng's giggling.
His mother said:
"This girl is too silly."
Wú asked to meet her.
His mother entered the room,
the girl was still laughing heartily and paid no attention.
His mother urged her to come out,
and only then did she try her best to suppress her laughter.
She faced the wall for a moment
before coming out.
As soon as she made a bow,
she suddenly turned and rushed back in,
bursting into loud laughter.
All the women in the room
smiled cheerfully because of her.
Wú asked to go investigate her strangeness
and also to act as a matchmaker.
Soon he reached the village,
but there were no houses at all,
only scattered mountain flowers.
Wú remembered where the aunt was buried,
it seemed not far;
however, the graves were overgrown and indistinct,
making them unrecognizable.
He returned astonished and sighing.
His mother suspected she was a ghost.
Someone told the girl Wú's words,
but she showed not the slightest fright;
they also commiserated about her being homeless,
but she showed no sadness either,
only constant, silly laughter.
No one could fathom her.
His mother ordered her to sleep with the young maidservants.
At dawn, she would come to visit and inquire,
and her needlework was exquisitely skilled, beyond compare.
However, she loved to laugh,
and even when restrained, she could not stop;
yet her laughter was enchanting,
wild but not detracting from her charm,
and everyone enjoyed it.
Neighboring girls and young wives
all vied to welcome her.
His mother chose an auspicious day to arrange their wedding,
but still feared she might be a ghost.
Secretly she watched her in daylight,
and her form and shadow were no different at all.
On the wedding day,
she was made to wear splendid attire and perform the bride's rituals;
the girl laughed so much she could not bow or rise,
so the ceremony was halted.
Shēng feared that because of her silliness,
she might reveal private matters of the bedchamber;
but the girl was extremely secretive
and would not utter a single word.
Whenever his mother was worried or angry,
the girl would arrive,
and with a laugh, her worries would dissipate.
When servants committed minor faults,
fearing a whipping,
they would often ask to go and talk with his mother together;
and the offending servants who appeared
were always spared.
She had a passion for flowers,
seeking them out among relatives and friends;
she secretly pawned a gold hairpin
to buy fine seeds.
Within a few months,
the steps, pathways, and even the latrine fence
were covered in flowers.
Behind the courtyard was an arbor of Banksia roses,
which belonged to the family next door to the west.
The girl often climbed up it
to pick them for her hair and to play with.
His mother sometimes saw her
and would scold her.
But the girl never changed.
One day,
the son of the western neighbor saw her,
and was fixated and captivated.
The girl did not avoid him but smiled.
The western neighbor's son thought the girl was interested in him,
and his heart grew more restless.
The girl pointed to the base of the wall, smiled, and climbed down.
The western neighbor's son thought she was indicating a meeting place,
and was overjoyed.
When dusk came, he went,
and the girl was indeed there.
He approached to molest her,
but his genitals felt like they were pricked by an awl,
the pain piercing to his heart.
He cried out loudly and fell down.
Looking closely, it was not the girl,
but a withered tree lying by the wall,
and what he had touched was a water-filled hole.
The neighbor's father heard the sound,
rushed over to investigate,
but the son groaned and could not speak.
When his wife arrived,
he finally told her the truth.
They lit a torch and looked into the hole,
seeing a huge scorpion inside,
like a small crab.
The old man broke the wood and caught and killed it.
He carried his son home,
who died in the middle of the night.
The neighbor sued Shēng,
exposing Yīngníng's strange and demonic nature.
The district magistrate admired Shēng's talent
and knew him to be a man of upright conduct,
so he deemed the neighbor's lawsuit false
and intended to flog him.
Shēng pleaded for his exemption,
and he was released.
His mother said to the girl:
"Your silliness and wildness are thus;
I knew early on that excessive joy would lead to hidden worries.
The district magistrate is discerning,
fortunately, we were not implicated;
had it been a muddled official,
he would surely have apprehended the women for questioning in the public court,
how could my son show his face to relatives and neighbors?"
The girl composed herself
and vowed never to laugh again.
His mother said:
"Everyone laughs,
but it must be at the right time."
And from then on, the girl indeed never laughed again;
even when deliberately provoked,
she would ultimately not laugh;
yet she never showed a sad expression throughout the day.
One evening,
she shed tears before Shēng.
He found it strange.
The woman choked back sobs and said:
"Previously, because our time together was short,
I feared that telling you would cause alarm and surprise.
Today, observing both my mother-in-law and my husband,
I see you both love me dearly and have no ill intentions,
so perhaps it won't be harmful to tell you directly?
I am originally the offspring of a fox.
When my mother was about to leave,
she entrusted me to a ghost-mother.
We relied on each other for over ten years,
and only then did I arrive at this day.
I have no brothers,
and my only reliance is you, my lord.
My old mother lies lonely in the mountain ravines,
with no one to pity her and bury her properly alongside others.
In the netherworld, she must constantly mourn and feel regret.
If you, my lord, would not begrudge the trouble and expense,
and allow the one beneath the earth to dispel this resentment and sorrow,
then those who raise daughters might not bear to abandon them by drowning."
Shēng agreed,
but worried that the grave might be lost amidst the wild grasses.
The woman merely said there was no need to worry.
On the appointed day,
the couple carried the coffin and set off.
Amidst the desolate mists and tangled undergrowth,
the woman pointed out the location of the tomb.
Indeed, they found the old woman's corpse,
its skin and flesh still intact.
The woman stroked it and cried in deep sorrow.
They carried it back,
and soon buried it together with Qín Shì's grave.
That night,
Shēng dreamed that the old woman came to thank him.
He awoke and recounted it.
The woman said:
"I saw her last night;
she merely told me not to startle my lord."
Shēng regretted not having invited her to stay.
The woman said:
"She is a ghost.
There are many living people here,
and the Yang energy is strong;
how could she stay long?"
Shēng asked about Xiǎo Róng,
who replied:
"She is also a fox,
and very clever.
My fox mother left her to look after me,
and she often found food to nourish me,
so her kindness is always in my heart.
Yesterday I asked my mother,
and she said she has already married her off."
From then on, every year at the Cold Food Festival,
the couple would visit Qín's grave,
performing their respects and sweeping without fail.
After more than a year,
the woman gave birth to a son.
While in her arms,
he was not afraid of strangers;
upon seeing people, he would always laugh,
and indeed had much of his mother's demeanor.
The Historiographer of the Strange (Yì Shǐ Shì) remarks:
"Observing her earnest, innocent laughter,
she seems utterly guileless;
yet with her mischievous tricks under the wall,
who could be cleverer than she?
As for her sorrowful devotion to the ghost-mother,
turning laughter into tears,
my Yīng Níng is perhaps one who hides behind laughter.
I secretly heard there is a plant in the mountains
called 'Xiào Yǐ Hū'.
If one smells it,
one cannot stop laughing.
If one plants this kind of plant in a room,
then both 'joyful union' (héhuān) and 'forget sorrow' (wàngyōu)
will lose their luster.
As for 'flower that understands speech' (jiěyǔhuā),
it is precisely their affected mannerisms that are bothersome."
According to the manuscript edition of *Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì*.
Níng Cǎi Chén was
a native of Zhè.
His disposition was generous and straightforward,
and he held himself with dignity.
He often told people:
"In my life, I have never had two intentions."
He happened to be traveling to Jīn Huá
and, upon reaching the northern suburbs,
unpacked his luggage at a Buddhist monastery (lánruò).
The temples and pagodas within the monastery were grand and magnificent;
however, the weeds were taller than a person,
as if no one had set foot there.
The monks' quarters to the east and west
had their double doors half-open;
only a small room to the south
had its lock and key appearing new.
He also noticed, in the eastern corner of the main hall,
a cluster of tall bamboo with thick trunks;
below the steps was a large pond,
where wild lotuses were already in bloom.
He was very pleased with its secluded tranquility.
It happened that the Imperial Education Commissioner (Xuésǐ) was visiting,
and lodging prices in the city were high.
Thinking it convenient to stay there,
he strolled about, waiting for the monks to return.
At dusk,
a scholar arrived
and opened the southern door.
Níng hurried to pay his respects
and explained his intentions.
The scholar said:
"There is no landlord here,
and I am also a temporary resident.
If you can endure the desolation,
your instruction, morning and evening,
would be most welcome."
Níng was delighted.
He used hay as a bed
and propped up a board as a table,
preparing for a long stay.
That night,
the moon was bright and pure,
its clear light like water.
The two sat knee-to-knee on the temple corridor,
each introducing their name and courtesy name.
The scholar said of himself:
"My surname is Yàn,
and my courtesy name is Chì Xiá."
Níng suspected him to be one of the students going for the examinations,
but listening to his accent,
it did not sound like Zhè.
When questioned,
he said of himself:
"I am from Qín."
His words were very simple and sincere.
After a while, they ran out of things to say to each other,
so they bowed and returned to their respective rooms.
Níng moved into a new residence,
and for a long time could not sleep.
He heard soft whispers from north of his dwelling,
as if there were a family.
He got up and went to the stone window in the north wall,
and peered out slightly.
He saw a small courtyard outside a short wall,
where there was a woman of about forty years;
and also an old woman dressed in scarlet,
with a topknot pinned with a bun,
whose hunched back was particularly prominent.
They were chatting under the moon.
The woman said:
“Why has Xiǎoqiàn not come for so long?”
The old woman said:
“She should be arriving soon.”
The woman said:
“Could it be that she has some complaints against Lǎolao?”
She replied:
“I haven’t heard any,
but her mood seems somewhat vexed.”
The woman said:
“Servants should not get too familiar.”
Before she finished speaking,
a girl of seventeen or eighteen came,
remarkably beautiful.
The old woman smiled and said:
“One shouldn’t speak ill of people behind their backs;
we two were just talking,
and the little imp came stealthily, leaving no trace.
Luckily, we weren't criticizing her shortcomings.”
She added:
“My dear girl, you are truly a person from a painting!
Even if I were a man,
my soul would be captivated.”
The girl said:
“If Lǎolao doesn’t praise me,
who else will say I’m good?”
The woman and the girl then said something else which Níng did not understand.
Níng thought they were neighbors,
and went to bed, no longer listening.
After another long while,
it finally became silent.
Just as he was about to fall asleep,
he felt someone approach his bedchamber.
He quickly got up to investigate,
and it was the girl from the north courtyard.
Startled, he asked her.
The girl smiled and said:
“Sleepless on a moonlit night,
I wish to cultivate intimacy.”
Níng sternly said:
“You should beware of public criticism,
and I fear human gossip;
a single misstep,
and our sense of shame and integrity will be lost.”
The girl said:
“No one will know at night.”
Níng rebuked her again.
The girl hesitated as if she had more to say.
Níng shouted:
“Go quickly!
Otherwise,
I will call the scholar living in the south dwelling.”
The girl, frightened,
then retreated.
She reached the doorway but returned,
placing a gold ingot on the mat.
Níng picked it up and threw it onto the courtyard steps,
saying:
“Unrighteous gain will
defile my purse!”
The girl, ashamed,
left,
picked up the gold, and muttered to herself:
“This man must be made of iron and stone.”
The next morning,
a scholar from Lánxī came with a servant to await the examination,
lodging in the east wing.
By night, he suddenly died.
There was a small hole in the sole of his foot,
as if pierced by an awl,
with fine blood oozing out.
No one knew the cause.
After a night,
the servant also died,
with the same symptoms.
Towards evening,
Yàn Shēng returned.
Níng questioned him,
and Yàn thought it was a demon.
Níng, being inherently upright and frank,
did not pay much heed.
Around midnight,
the girl returned,
and said to Níng:
“I have met many people,
but none with a character as unyielding as yours.
You are truly a sage,
and I dare not deceive you.
Xiǎoqiàn,
whose surname is Niè,
died young at eighteen,
and was buried by the temple.
She was threatened by a demonic entity,
and has been forced into menial tasks;
facing people,
she truly finds no joy in it.
Now there is no one left to kill in the temple,
and I fear a Yèchā will come tonight.”
Níng was alarmed and asked for a plan.
The girl said:
“Staying in the same room as Yàn Shēng can prevent it.”
He asked:
“Why don’t you bewitch Yàn Shēng?”
She replied:
“He is an extraordinary person;
I dare not approach him.”
He asked:
“How do you bewitch people?”
She replied:
“For those who are intimate with me,
I secretly pierce their foot with an awl.
They become dazed and confused,
and then I draw blood to provide for the demon's drink.
Or sometimes, with gold—
it is not gold,
but the bones of a Luóchà ghost.
Keeping it can sever one’s heart and liver. These two methods
are simply to suit the current tastes.”
Níng thanked her.
He asked when to prepare,
and she replied, “tomorrow night.”
Before leaving, she wept and said:
“I have fallen into a dark sea,
and cannot find the shore.
Your righteous spirit reaches the clouds,
and you will surely be able to deliver me from suffering.
If you would be willing to bag my decaying bones
and rebury them in a peaceful home,
it would be no less than a second creation.”
Níng resolutely agreed.
He then asked about the burial place,
and she said:
“Just remember, above a white poplar tree,
the one with a crow’s nest is it.”
Having spoken, she stepped out the door
and vanished into thin air.
The next day,
fearing Yàn would go out, he went early to invite him.
After morning, he prepared food and drink,
paying close attention to Yàn.
When he proposed they share a room,
Yàn declined, citing his preference for solitude.
Níng did not listen,
and forcibly brought his bedding over.
Yàn had no choice but
to move his mat and comply,
enjoining:
“I know you are a man of integrity,
and my admiration for you is profound.
However, I have a small secret
that is difficult to reveal immediately.
Please do not open and peek into my satchel,
as violating this will be detrimental to both of us.”
Níng respectfully accepted his instruction.
Soon, they each went to sleep.
Yàn placed a box on the window,
and after lying on his pillow for a while,
he snored like thunder.
Níng could not sleep.
Around the first watch,
a faint human shadow appeared outside the window.
Suddenly, it came closer to the window to peek,
its eyes flashing.
Níng was afraid,
and just as he was about to call Yàn,
something suddenly burst out of the satchel,
shining like a bolt of silk,
hitting and breaking the stone on the window.
It shot out like a whirlwind,
then immediately retracted,
disappearing like lightning.
Yàn woke up,
and Níng feigned sleep to observe him.
Yàn held the satchel and inspected it,
took out an object,
and examined it by moonlight,
sniffing it.
It was crystal clear white,
about two inches long,
and as wide as a chive leaf.
Afterward, he wrapped it tightly in several layers,
and placed it back into the broken satchel.
He mumbled to himself:
"What kind of old demon
dares to be so bold
as to damage my satchel!"
He then lay down again.
Níng was greatly astonished by this,
so he got up and asked him,
also telling him what he had seen.
Yàn said:
"Since we know and love each other,
how dare I hide anything deeply?
I am
a swordsman.
If not for the stone,
the demon would have died instantly;
although,
it is also injured."
Níng asked:
"What is sealed inside?"
He replied:
"It is a sword.
Just now, I smelled
a demonic aura."
Níng wanted to see it.
Yàn generously took it out to show him;
it was a small, glittering sword.
Thereupon, Níng held Yàn in even greater esteem.
The next day,
he looked outside the window
and saw bloodstains.
So he went out north of the temple
and saw numerous desolate graves,
and indeed there was a white poplar tree
with a crow's nest at its summit.
When his arrangements were complete,
he packed his bags, intending to return home.
Yàn Shēng set up a farewell banquet,
expressing deep affection and kindness.
He presented Níng with the tattered leather pouch,
saying:
"This is a sword pouch.
Keeping this treasure can ward off evil spirits."
Níng wanted to learn his techniques.
Yàn said:
"Someone with your trustworthiness and uprightness
could do this.
However, you are still a person of wealth and status,
not a person of this path."
Níng then fabricated a story that he had a younger sister buried there,
excavated the girl's bones,
wrapped them in many clothes,
hired a boat, and returned home.
Níng's study faced the wilderness,
so he set up a grave and buried her outside his study.
He offered a sacrifice and prayed, saying:
"I pity your solitary soul,
buried near my humble abode.
Our songs and cries can be heard by each other,
so you will not be oppressed by powerful male ghosts.
This cup of thin gruel
is not very pure or delicious;
I hope you will not mind!"
After praying, he returned.
Later, someone called out:
"Wait a moment, let's go together!"
He looked back,
and it was Xiǎoqiàn.
Joyfully, she thanked him, saying:
"Your trustworthiness,
even ten deaths would not be enough to repay.
Please let me return with you,
pay my respects to your parents-in-law,
and be your concubine without regret."
He carefully examined her:
her skin glowed like flowing clouds,
her feet were delicate like slender bamboo shoots.
In broad daylight, her proper appearance
was especially captivating and exquisite.
So he went with her to his study.
He instructed her to wait a moment,
and first went to inform his mother.
His mother was astonished.
At that time, Níng's wife had been ill for a long time,
so his mother cautioned him not to speak of it,
fearing it would alarm her.
While they were speaking,
the girl had already gracefully entered
and prostrated herself on the ground.
Níng said:
"This is Xiǎoqiàn."
His mother stared in surprise, unable to respond.
The girl said to his mother:
"I am but a lone soul, adrift,
far from my parents and siblings.
I have received the young master's kindness,
his grace covering my very hair and skin.
I wish to wield the broom and dustpan,
to repay his profound righteousness."
His mother saw her graceful and lovely demeanor,
and only then dared to speak with her,
saying:
"Young lady, for you to favor my son,
this old woman is overjoyed beyond measure.
However, I only have this one son in my life,
to carry on the family line,
and I dare not let him have a ghost as a partner."
The girl said:
"I truly have no ulterior motives.
As one from the underworld,
since I am not trusted by the old mother,
please allow me to serve as a sister,
to reside in your lofty hall,
and attend to you morning and evening.
How would that be?"
His mother pitied her sincerity
and agreed.
She immediately wanted to pay respects to his sister-in-law.
His mother declined, citing her illness,
so she stopped.
The girl then went into the kitchen,
taking over the cooking from his mother.
She entered the room, moving about the bed,
as if she were a familiar resident.
At dusk,
his mother was afraid of her,
and bid her to return to her own sleeping place,
not preparing a bed or bedding for her.
The girl perceived his mother's intention
and left immediately.
Passing the study, she wanted to enter,
but then retreated,
pacing outside the door,
as if fearing something.
Níng called out to her.
The girl said:
"There is a sword aura in the room that frightens me.
The reason I did not appear on the road just now
was precisely because of this."
Níng realized it was the leather pouch,
and took it to hang in another room.
The girl then entered
and sat down by the candle.
After a while,
she did not say a single word.
After a long time,
she asked:
"Do you read at night?
I recited the Lèngyán Jīng when I was young,
but now I have forgotten more than half of it.
May I request a volume,
and during my leisure at night,
I will seek your correction?"
Níng agreed.
She sat again,
silently.
As the second watch was nearing its end,
she did not speak of leaving.
Níng urged her.
With a sorrowful expression, she said:
"As a solitary soul from a foreign land,
I am truly afraid of the desolate grave."
Níng said:
"There is no other bed in the study,
and it is also proper for siblings to maintain a respectful distance."
The girl rose,
her brows furrowed as if about to cry,
her steps reluctant and slow.
She calmly exited the door,
descended the steps, and disappeared.
Níng secretly pitied her
and wanted to let her stay in another bed,
but also feared his mother's anger.
In the morning, the girl paid respects to his mother,
holding up the washbasin for her,
and went downstairs to work,
accommodating all his mother's wishes.
At dusk, when she announced her departure,
she would always pass by the study
and recite sutras by candlelight.
When she sensed that Níng was about to sleep,
she would then sadly leave.
Previously,
Níng's wife had been sick and disabled,
and his mother was burdened beyond endurance.
Since acquiring the daughter,
life had been much easier,
and she felt grateful to her.
Day by day, as they grew closer,
she loved her as if she were her own child,
and actually forgot that she was a ghost.
She couldn't bear to let her leave at night,
so she let her stay and share their bed.
When the daughter first arrived, she never ate or drank,
but after half a year, she gradually began to sip thin gruel.
Both mother and son doted on her,
avoiding mention of her being a ghost,
and others also didn't distinguish her as such.
Not long after,
Níng's wife died.
His mother secretly harbored the intention of taking the daughter in,
but feared it would be detrimental to her son.
The daughter subtly observed this,
and seized an opportunity to tell the mother:
"After living here for over a year,
you must know my heart and intentions.
It was because I didn't want to bring misfortune to ordinary people
that I came with your son.
I have no other trivial intentions,
except that Young Master is so bright and upright,
admired and noticed by heavenly beings,
that I truly wish to stay and assist him for a few years,
to borrow his achievements for official titles and honors,
to bring glory to my abode in the underworld."
The mother also knew she was not malicious,
but simply feared she could not continue the family line.
The daughter said:
"Children are bestowed by Heaven alone.
Your son is blessed in the register of fate,
and will have three sons to carry on the family name;
this will not be taken away simply because of a ghost wife."
The mother believed her
and discussed it with her son.
Níng was delighted,
and so arranged a banquet to inform relatives and friends.
Some asked to see the new wife,
and the daughter, with a generous spirit, appeared in elegant attire.
The whole hall stared,
and rather than suspecting her to be a ghost,
they suspected her to be an immortal.
From then on, the inner family members of the five clans
all held gifts to congratulate her,
eagerly bowing to make her acquaintance.
The daughter was skilled at painting orchids and plums,
and always responded with a small painting,
which those who received it treasured carefully,
considering it an honor.
One day,
she leaned her head by the window, feeling lost and dejected.
Suddenly she asked:
"Where is the leather bag?"
He replied:
"Because you were afraid of it,
I sealed it and put it elsewhere."
She said:
"I have received vital energy for a long time now;
I should no longer be afraid.
You should take it and hang it by the head of the bed."
Níng asked her intention.
She said:
"For the past three days,
my heart has been palpitating without cease.
I fear that the demonic creature from Jīnhuá,
resenting my escape,
might come looking for me morning or night."
Níng indeed brought the leather bag.
The daughter examined it repeatedly,
saying:
"This is what a sword immortal uses to hold human heads.
It is so worn out;
I don't know how many people it has killed!
When I look at it today,
my skin still crawls."
So she hung it up.
The next day,
she again ordered it moved to be hung above the door.
At night, she sat by candlelight,
telling Níng not to sleep.
There was an object
that fell like a bird.
The daughter, alarmed, hid between the double curtains.
Níng looked at it:
the object was like a Yakṣa,
with eyes like lightning and a blood-red tongue,
flashing to seize and advance.
It reached the door and stepped back;
it lingered for a long time,
then gradually approached the leather bag,
picking at it with its claws,
as if to tear it open.
The bag suddenly made a rattling sound,
expanding to the size of a large basket.
In a trance, a ghostly figure
protruded halfway out,
grabbed the Yakṣa and pulled it in.
The sound then ceased,
and the bag also instantly shrank back to its original size.
Níng was terrified and astonished.
The daughter also came out,
greatly relieved, saying:
"We are safe!"
Together they looked inside the bag,
and found only several measures of clear water.
A few years later,
Níng indeed passed the imperial examination and became a *jìnshì*.
The daughter gave birth to a son.
After he took a concubine,
she also gave birth to a son,
and all of them distinguished themselves in official careers.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition.
Yáng Tiānyī said: I saw two rats emerge;
one of them was swallowed by a snake.
The other stared with eyes like peppercorns,
appearing very hateful and angry,
yet it looked on from a distance and dared not advance.
The snake, with a full belly,
writhed into its hole;
just as it was more than halfway in,
the rat rushed forward
and fiercely bit its tail.
The snake was enraged
and retreated.
The rat, being quick,
then fled.
The snake, unable to catch it, turned back.
When it entered the hole,
the rat came again,
biting as before.
When the snake entered, it came;
when the snake exited, it went away.
This continued for a long time.
The snake came out
and spat a dead rat onto the ground.
The rat came and sniffed it,
squeaking as if mourning,
then carried it away.
My friend Zhāng Lìyǒu composed "Ballad of the Righteous Rat" for it.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition.
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the *xū* hour of the seventh year of Kāngxī's reign,
there was a great earthquake.
I happened to be a guest in Jìxià,
drinking with my cousin Lǐ Dǔzhī by candlelight.
Suddenly, we heard a sound like thunder,
coming from the southeast
and moving towards the northwest.
Everyone was astonished and perplexed,
not understanding the reason.
Presently, the tables and benches shook,
wine cups overturned;
the roof beams and rafters
creaked and groaned.
We looked at each other, our faces drained of color.
After a long time,
we finally realized it was an earthquake,
and each rushed out.
We saw pavilions and houses
fall and rise again;
the sound of collapsing walls and houses,
along with children crying and women wailing,
was as tumultuous as a boiling cauldron.
People were dizzy and unable to stand,
sitting on the ground,
tossing and turning with the earth.
River water splashed more than a *zhàng* high,
and ducks quacked and dogs barked throughout the city.
After about an hour,
it gradually settled.
Looking at the streets,
men and women gathered naked,
eagerly telling each other stories,
forgetting that they were unclothed.
Later, we heard that in a certain place, a well tilted,
making it impossible to draw water;
in a certain family's house, a platform shifted from north to south;
Qīxiá Shān split;
and in Yíshuǐ, a hole several *mǔ* wide opened up.
These were truly extraordinary and miraculous transformations.
There was a woman from a town,
who got up at night to urinate.
When she returned, a wolf was carrying off her child.
The woman desperately fought with the wolf.
As the wolf momentarily loosened its grip,
the woman snatched her child back
and held it in her embrace.
The wolf crouched down and did not leave.
The woman cried out loudly.
Neighbors rushed to gather,
and only then did the wolf depart.
After her initial shock, the woman was filled with joy.
She gesticulated wildly,
describing how the wolf had taken her child,
and how she had snatched him back.
After a long while,
she suddenly realized she was not wearing a stitch of clothing,
and then she ran inside.
This is the same emotional state as men and women forgetting each other during an earthquake,
a single shared condition.
How laughable
is the desperation and lack of planning in humans!
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
On Gǔjī Dǎo (Ancient Relics Island) in Dōnghǎi,
there were five-colored winter-blooming camellias,
which bloomed out of season.
Yet there were no inhabitants on the island,
and people rarely visited it.
Zhāng Shēng from Dēngzhōu,
being fond of novelty
and enjoying travel and hunting,
heard of its beautiful scenery.
He prepared wine and food
and paddled a small boat there himself.
When he arrived, the flowers were in full bloom,
their fragrance detectable for several *lǐ*;
some trees were more than ten arm-spans in girth.
He lingered repeatedly,
finding it greatly to his liking.
He opened a bottle and poured a drink for himself,
regretting that he had no companion.
Suddenly, a beautiful woman emerged from the flowers,
her red skirt dazzling,
utterly incomparable.
Seeing Zhāng,
she smiled and said:
"I thought my interest was quite extraordinary,
but I didn't expect to find a kindred spirit here before me."
Zhāng, startled, asked:
"Who are you?"
She replied:
"I am Jiāochāng.
I just came from Hǎi Gōngzǐ.
He flies about seeking beauty,
but I, finding walking difficult,
stayed here."
Zhāng, who was suffering from loneliness,
was overjoyed to find such a beauty.
He invited her to sit and drink together.
The woman's words were gentle and soft,
stirring one's heart and mind.
Zhāng was enamored with her.
Fearing Hǎi Gōngzǐ would arrive
and prevent their full enjoyment,
he then pulled her close to make love.
The woman gladly complied.
Before their intimacy was complete,
they suddenly heard the wind whistling,
and the sound of plants and trees bending and breaking.
The woman urgently pushed Zhāng up,
saying:
"Hǎi Gōngzǐ is here!"
Zhāng hastily straightened his clothes and looked around in astonishment,
but the woman had already disappeared.
Soon after, a large snake appeared
from among the bushes,
thicker than a large barrel.
Zhāng was terrified.
He hid behind a large tree,
hoping the snake would not see him.
The snake came closer
and wrapped its body around the man and the tree,
coiling several times;
Zhāng's arms were pinned straight down to his hips,
unable to bend even slightly.
It raised its head
and poked Zhāng's nose with its tongue.
Blood flowed from his nose,
forming a puddle on the ground,
and then it stooped down to drink it.
Zhāng resigned himself to certain death.
Suddenly, he remembered a sachet hanging from his waist
containing fox-poisoning medicine.
He used two fingers to take it out,
broke open the wrapper, and poured it into his palm;
then he tilted his neck to look at his palm,
allowing blood to drip onto the medicine,
filling his hand in an instant.
The snake indeed came to his palm and sucked the mixture.
Before it had finished drinking,
it suddenly stretched its body,
swishing its tail with a sound like thunder,
hitting a tree.
Half of the tree collapsed,
and the snake lay on the ground like a beam and died.
Zhāng also felt dizzy and couldn't get up;
it was a while before he recovered.
He carried the snake back
and was seriously ill for over a month.
He suspected the woman was also a snake spirit.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dīng Qiánxī
was a man from Zhūchéng.
He was rich in money and grain.
He was a chivalrous and righteous man,
admiring Guō Jiě's character.
An imperial censor's touring envoy came to investigate him.
Dīng fled.
He reached Ānqiū
and encountered rain,
taking shelter in an inn.
The rain did not stop all day.
A young man came,
providing generous food and lodging.
Later, as dusk fell,
Dīng stayed overnight at his house;
soybeans were fed to the animals,
and food was supplied most thoughtfully.
When asked his name,
the young man replied:
"The owner's surname is Yáng,
and I am his nephew by marriage.
The owner is fond of making friends,
and he happens to be out.
Only his wife is home.
We are poor and cannot offer much hospitality,
so I hope you will understand."
When asked what the owner's profession was,
he said their family had no assets,
only setting up a gambling den daily
to make a living.
The next day,
the rain still didn't stop,
but the provisions continued without slackening.
By evening,
fodder was provided;
the bundles of fodder were wet
and quite unevenly bundled.
Dīng found this strange.
The young man said:
"To be frank with you, sir: our family is poor and has nothing to feed the animals.
Just now, my mistress removed the thatch from the roof."
Dīng was even more surprised,
thinking they intended to charge him.
At dawn,
he offered them gold,
but they refused it;
when he insisted,
the young man took it inside.
Soon he came out
and returned it to the guest,
saying:
"My mistress said: 'We are not people who live by charging for meals.
When the master is out,
he often goes for days without bringing back a single coin;
when guests come to our home,
how can we demand payment?'"
Dīng praised them with a sigh and took his leave.
He instructed them, saying:
"I am Dīng Mǒu from Zhūchéng.
When your master returns,
you should inform him.
If he has leisure, I hope he will visit me."
Several years passed without news.
Then a great famine struck,
and Yáng was in dire straits,
with no means of livelihood.
His wife casually suggested visiting Dīng,
and he agreed.
Upon arriving in Zhūchéng,
he reported his name to the gatekeeper.
Dīng had completely forgotten him;
only after further explanation did he remember.
He rushed out
and bowed, inviting the guest in.
Seeing his clothes tattered and heels split,
he housed him in a warm room,
set up a feast to entertain him,
and honored him with extraordinary courtesy.
The next day,
he had him made a cap and clothes,
warm both inside and out.
Yáng Yìzhī;
but on his part, his internal worries grew,
and his narrow mind could not help but feel a little hopeless.
After several days,
he still said nothing about a farewell gift.
Yáng became very anxious
and told Dīng,
"I dare not hide anything: when I came,
I didn't have even a pint of rice.
Now I have been excessively favored with your support and understanding,
which is certainly pleasant;
but what about my wife and children!"
Dīng said,
"There's no need to worry about that;
I have already taken care of their affairs.
Please feel at ease and stay a little longer;
I will assist you with funds."
He then hurried to summon all the gamblers,
made Yáng sit and beg for contributions,
and obtained a hundred gold pieces overnight,
whereupon he sent him back home.
Upon returning, he saw his wife,
her clothes and shoes fresh and neat,
with a small maid attending her.
He was startled and asked about it.
His wife said,
"Since you left,
the next day carts and servants brought bolts of cloth, beans, and millet,
piling them up to fill the house,
saying they were gifts from Mr. Dīng.
Also, ten maids
were sent to serve me."
Yáng was overcome with emotion.
From then on, he was moderately prosperous
and disdained his old profession.
The Historian of Anomalies says:
"Poor but hospitable,
those who drink, gamble, and live a dissolute life are especially capable of this;
the most unusual aspect,
however, is his wife alone.
To receive a benefactor's kindness and not repay it,
how could he be human?
Yet, not forgetting the kindness of a single meal,
Dīng indeed possessed such a quality."
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition
There were originally no mountains by the sea.
One day,
suddenly, towering, overlapping peaks appeared,
stretching for several *lǐ*,
which everyone found astonishing and strange.
Another day,
the mountains suddenly shifted elsewhere,
and vanished into nothingness.
It is said that large fish in the sea,
around the Qīngmíng Festival,
bring their families to worship at its tomb,
which is why they are often seen during the Hánshí Festival.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition
Old Master Zhāng Lǎo Sīxiāng,
a native of Jìn.
He was about to marry off his daughter,
so he brought his family to Jiāngnán
to personally purchase the dowry.
When their boat reached Jīnshān,
Zhāng crossed the river first,
instructing his family to stay on the boat
and to avoid any strong-smelling foods.
This was because there was a monstrous *yuán* in the river
that would emerge whenever it smelled something fragrant,
destroy boats, and swallow travelers,
having caused harm for a long time.
Zhāng left,
but his family forgot his instructions and roasted meat on the boat.
Suddenly, a huge wave overturned the boat,
and his wife and daughter both drowned.
Zhāng returned to his boat,
grieving to the point of wanting to die.
He then ascended Jīnshān,
visited the temple monks,
and inquired about the unusual *yuán*,
intending to seek revenge on it.
The monks, upon hearing this,
said in alarm:
"We, who live near it daily,
fear its calamity,
and can only worship it as a deity,
praying for it not to be angry;
from time to time, we slaughter animals
and throw half their bodies to it,
and it leaps out, swallows them, and departs.
Who could possibly seek revenge against it!"
Zhāng heard this
and immediately thought of a plan.
He then summoned ironworkers,
set up a furnace halfway up the mountain,
and smelted red-hot iron,
weighing over a hundred *jīn*.
Having ascertained its usual lurking place,
he had two or three strong men
lift and throw it with large tongs.
The *yuán* leaped out
and swiftly swallowed it.
A short while later,
waves surged like mountains.
After a moment, the waves subsided,
and the dead *yuán* was already floating on the water.
Travelers and temple monks alike rejoiced,
built a shrine for Old Master Zhāng Lǎo Sīxiāng,
placed his statue inside,
and considered him a water god;
prayers to him were always answered.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition
The *shuǐmǎng*
is a poisonous plant.
It grows as a vine similar to *gě*;
its flowers are purple,
resembling hyacinth beans.
Eating it
causes instant death,
whereupon one becomes a *shuǐmǎngguǐ*.
It is popularly believed that these ghosts cannot reincarnate
until another person is poisoned to death,
who then replaces them.
For this reason, it is said that these ghosts are particularly numerous
in the area of Táohuā Jiāng in Chǔ.
People of Chǔ refer to those born in the same year as *tóngnián*,
exchange calling cards upon meeting,
address each other as *gēng* brother or *gēng* younger brother,
and their children address them as *gēng* uncle;
such is the custom.
There was a student named Zhù who went to visit one of his *tóngnián*.
Midway, he felt parched and wanted a drink.
Soon, he saw an old woman by the roadside,
who had set up a shed offering drinks;
he went towards it.
The old woman welcomed him into the shed
and served him very attentively.
He smelled a strange odor,
not like tea,
so he set it aside without drinking
and rose to leave.
The old woman urgently stopped the guest
and called out,
"Sānniáng,
please bring a cup of good tea."
Soon, a young girl
emerged from behind the shed, holding tea.
She was about fourteen or fifteen years old,
of exquisite beauty;
her finger rings and arm bracelets
were glittering and reflected her image.
The student took the cup, his mind captivated;
he sniffed the tea,
and its fragrance was unparalleled.
He drained it and asked for another.
Seeing the old woman step out,
he playfully grasped her slender wrist
and slipped off a finger ring.
The girl smiled faintly,
and the student was even more enchanted.
He briefly inquired about her family,
and the girl said,
"Sir, when you come tonight,
I will still be here."
The student asked for a pinch of tea leaves,
hid the finger ring, and left.
When he arrived at his *tóngnián*'s house,
he felt sick to his stomach,
suspecting the tea was the cause,
and related the situation to his *tóngnián*.
His *tóngnián* exclaimed in alarm,
"Alas!
This is a *shuǐmǎngguǐ*!
My late father died from this.
It cannot be saved;
what is to be done?"
The student was greatly frightened
and took out the tea leaves to examine them;
they were indeed *shuǐmǎng* plants.
He then took out the finger ring
and described the girl's appearance.
His *tóngnián* imagined it and said:
“This must be Kòu Sānniáng.”
Shēng, seeing that the name perfectly matched,
asked,
“How did you know?”
The other replied,
“The daughter of the wealthy Kòu family in the southern village
has long been renowned for her beauty.
Several years ago,
she died from eating a water hemlock.
This must be her ghost.”
Some said that if one possessed by a ghost
knew the ghost’s surname and given name,
and sought out their old undergarments,
boiling and consuming them could cure the affliction.
Mǒu urgently went to the Kòu residence,
honestly told them the situation,
and knelt for a long time, pleading sorrowfully.
The Kòu family, thinking he would die in place of their daughter,
therefore refused to give them.
Mǒu returned in anger,
and reported this to Shēng.
Shēng also gritted his teeth in hatred,
saying,
“When I die,
I will certainly not let that girl escape rebirth!”
Mǒu carried him,
and he died just as they reached the front door of his home.
His mother wept and buried him.
He left behind one son,
who had just turned one year old.
His wife could not uphold the virtue of a widow,
and remarried six months later.
His mother raised the orphan herself,
enduring unbearable toil and hardship,
weeping morning and night.
One day,
as she was holding her child and weeping in the room,
Shēng quietly and suddenly entered.
His mother was greatly startled,
wiped away her tears, and asked him.
He replied,
“Your son heard his mother weeping in the underworld,
and was greatly pained in his heart,
so he has come to attend to you morning and and evening.
Although your son is dead,
he already has a family,
and she has come with me to share your labors.
Mother, do not grieve.”
His mother asked,
“Who is your wife?”
He said,
“The Kòu family sat by and let your son die,
and your son greatly resented them.
After death, I wanted to find Sānniáng,
but did not know her whereabouts.
Recently, I met a certain Gēng Bó,
who finally pointed the way for me.
When your son went,
Sānniáng had already been reborn into the household of Sīláng Rèn.
Your son sped there
and forcibly seized her and brought her here.
Now she is your son’s wife,
and we get along well,
quite without hardship.”
After a while,
a girl entered from outside the door,
beautifully adorned and glamorous,
and prostrated herself to his mother.
Shēng said,
“This is Kòu Sānniáng.”
Although she was not alive,
his mother looked at her,
and her feelings were somewhat comforted.
Shēng then sent Sānniáng to do household chores.
Sānniáng was entirely unaccustomed to it,
but her obedience was truly pitiable.
From then on, she resided in the old house,
and thus stayed and did not leave.
The girl asked her mother to inform all the families.
Shēng meant not to tell;
but his mother, yielding to the girl’s wishes,
finally told them.
Kòu’s elder and his wife,
hearing this, were greatly startled,
and ordered a carriage to rush there.
They saw,
indeed, it was Sānniáng.
They faced each other and cried uncontrollably,
but the girl persuaded them to stop.
His wife saw that Shēng’s family was quite poor,
and felt very distressed.
The girl said,
“A person who is already a ghost,
why would they mind poverty?
Zhùláng and his mother and son
are full of deep affection and loyalty,
your daughter is already content here.”
Then she asked,
“Who was the tea hag?”
She replied,
“That Ní-surname woman,
ashamed that she couldn’t bewitch travelers,
therefore asked your son for help.
Now she has been reborn into the family of a beverage seller in the prefecture capital.”
Then she looked at Shēng and said,
“Since it is settled,
and you haven’t bowed to your in-laws,
what kind of heart do I have?”
Shēng then prostrated himself in deference.
The girl then went into the kitchen,
took over the cooking for her mother,
and served her parents-in-law.
Her mother-in-law looked at her with a heavy heart.
After they returned,
they immediately sent two maids
to serve them;
one hundred catties of gold, dozens of bolts of cloth;
wine was sent regularly,
somewhat enriching Zhù’s mother.
The Kòu family also invited her home for visits from time to time.
After staying for several days,
she would always say,
“There’s no one at home,
so you should send your son back early.”
If they intentionally delayed her,
she would float away and return on her own.
The elder then built a new house for Shēng,
and provided everything abundantly.
However, Shēng never visited the elder’s home.
One day,
someone in the village who had been poisoned by water hemlock
died and then revived,
which was spread as an extraordinary event.
Shēng said,
“It was I who saved him.
He was harmed by Lǐ Jiǔ,
and I drove away his ghost for him.”
His mother said,
“Why didn’t you take someone to replace yourself?”
He said,
“Your son deeply resents such people,
and is just about to drive them all away.
Why would I care for such a thing!
Moreover, serving Mother is your son’s greatest joy,
and I do not wish to be reborn.”
From then on, those who were poisoned
often prepared lavish banquets,
prayed in his courtyard,
and always saw results.
After more than ten years,
his mother died.
Shēng and his wife also grieved deeply,
but did not face guests;
they simply taught their son Límá Yǒng
rituals and etiquette.
After burying his mother,
two more years passed,
and they arranged a marriage for their son.
The wife
was the granddaughter of Sīláng Rèn.
Before this,
Rèn Gōng’s concubine gave birth to a daughter,
who died young after several months.
Later, hearing of Zhù Shēng’s extraordinary abilities,
he consequently ordered his carriage to their home,
and established the in-law relationship.
By this time,
he thus married his granddaughter to their son,
and their visits were uninterrupted.
One day,
he said to his son,
“The Heavenly Emperor, seeing my merits in the human world,
has appointed me as the Dragon Lord of the Four Rivers.
I must depart now.”
Immediately, they saw four horses in the courtyard,
pulling a yellow-canopied carriage;
all four legs of the horses were covered in scales.
The couple, dressed in splendid attire, came out
and ascended the same carriage.
The son and his wife both wept and bowed,
and in an instant, they vanished.
On that day,
the Kòu family saw their daughter arrive,
bidding farewell to her parents,
also as Shēng had said.
Her mother wept and tried to make her stay,
but the daughter said,
“Zhùláng has already left.”
She went out the door and was never seen again.
Their son, whose name was È,
courtesy name Líchén,
requested from Kòu Wēng
that Sānniáng’s remains be interred with Shēng.
According to the Liaozhai Zhiyi manuscript edition
The arts of
bewitchment are
diverse.
Some involve throwing
a tempting bait to
people, deceiving them
into eating it,
whereupon they become
bewildered and
follow along.
Commonly, this is
called "dá xù bā"
(打絮巴), and in
Jiāngnán (江南)
it is called "chě xù"
(扯絮).
Unknowing children
often fall victim
to it.
There are also those
who transform people
into animals,
which is called
"zào chù" (造畜).
This art is rare
north of the river,
but south of the
river, it is common.
In a lodging house
in Yángzhōu (揚州),
a man led five
donkeys, which he
temporarily tethered
in the stable.
He said,
"I will return
shortly,"
and also instructed,
"Do not let them
drink or eat."
Then he left.
The donkeys brayed
loudly in the sun,
stomping and biting.
The host led them
to a cool spot.
When the donkeys
saw water, they
rushed to it
and drank freely.
With a single roll
in the dust, they
transformed into women.
Astonished, the host
questioned them about
what had happened,
but their tongues
were stiff and they
could not answer.
So he hid them
in a room.
Soon after, the
donkey owner arrived,
driving five sheep
into the courtyard,
and asked in alarm
where the donkeys were.
The host pulled
the guest to sit,
served him a meal,
and said,
"Please eat,
sir, the donkeys
will be here soon."
The host went out,
gave all five
sheep water to drink,
and they all, one
after another,
transformed into boys.
He secretly reported
it to the prefecture,
which sent officials
to capture the man,
who was then shackled
and executed.
According to a manuscript
of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
(聊齋誌異):
A scholar from
Fèngyáng (鳳陽),
carrying his satchel,
traveled far.
He told his wife,
"I will return
in half a year."
More than ten months
passed, but there
was no news.
His wife longed
for him with great
anxiety.
One night, just
as she lay down,
the moon through
the gauze curtain
cast a swaying shadow,
and thoughts of
separation filled
her heart.
As she tossed
and turned,
a beautiful woman,
with a pearl
hairnet and a
scarlet cape,
parted the curtain
and entered,
smiling as she asked,
"Sister,
do you not wish
to see your husband?"
The wife quickly
rose to respond.
A moment later,
wine and fruit were served.
The beautiful woman poured wine and said,
"The pair of phoenixes have been separated for a long time,
but tonight we are reunited.
Let us toast with a cup of wine,
in celebration."
The scholar also held up his cup in return.
Host and guest laughed and chatted,
their shoes intermingling.
The scholar gazed at the beautiful woman,
repeatedly teasing her with playful words.
The husband and wife, though just reunited,
did not exchange a single word of greeting.
The beautiful woman also cast flirtatious glances,
her charming words veiled in mystery.
The wife merely sat silently,
feigning foolishness.
After a long time, as they grew increasingly tipsy,
the two spoke with greater intimacy.
Again, she urged a large cup upon the guest.
The scholar declined, pleading drunkenness,
but she pressed him even harder.
The scholar smiled and said,
"If you play a tune for me,
then I will drink."
The beautiful woman did not refuse,
and immediately played the *tíqín* with an ivory plectrum, singing:
"At dusk, having removed the lingering makeup,
the cold west wind outside the window pierces through the gauze, hearing the sound of plantains,
a drizzle falls in successive bursts.
Where can one go for a casual chat?
My eyes, strained from longing,
see him not returning home,
tears stream like hemp fibers.
Again I miss him,
again I resent him,
holding a red embroidered shoe to divine with ghost-trigrams."
When the song was finished,
she smiled and said,
"This is a common street ballad,
unworthy of your ears.
However, as it is popular among the common folk,
I merely imitate it."
Her voice was languid and alluring,
her manner intimate and suggestive.
The scholar was swayed,
as if unable to control himself.
A short while later,
the beautiful woman feigned drunkenness and left her seat;
the scholar also rose
and followed her away.
After a long time, they did not return.
The maid, tired,
slept slumped on the corridor.
The wife sat alone,
solitary and companionless,
her heart filled with indignation,
which she found hard to bear.
She thought of escaping home,
but the night was dim,
and she could not recall the way.
Unable to control herself, she tossed and turned,
then got up to spy on them.
As she approached their window,
the sounds of 'broken clouds and scattered rain'
were faintly audible.
She listened again,
and heard her husband recounting the intimate details of their usual vulgar acts
to the fullest extent.
At this, the wife's
hands trembled and her heart reeled,
almost beyond control.
She thought it better to run out and die in a ditch.
As she indignantly began to move,
she suddenly saw her younger brother, Sānláng, arrive on horseback.
He immediately dismounted and asked,
and she told him everything.
Sānláng was furious,
and immediately returned with his sister,
going straight into their house.
The room door was locked,
and the murmuring words from the pillow could still be heard.
Sānláng picked up a large stone, as big as a measure,
and threw it, striking the window lattice,
shattering three or five pieces.
Inside, a loud cry was heard:
"My husband's head is broken!
What a disaster!"
When the wife heard this,
she was shocked
and cried bitterly,
saying to her brother,
"I did not intend for you to kill my husband,
what shall we do now?"
Sānláng glared and said,
"You 'woo-woo' urged me to come;
just as I manage to vent this anger in my chest,
you protect your man and resent your brother!
I am not accustomed to being ordered about by women!"
He turned to leave,
but the wife pulled his clothing, saying,
"If you don't take me with you,
where will I go?"
Sānláng pushed his sister to the ground,
broke free, and left.
The wife was suddenly startled awake,
realizing it was all a dream.
The next day,
the scholar indeed returned,
riding a white mule.
The wife found this strange but did not speak.
That night, the scholar also had a dream;
what he saw and experienced,
when he recounted it, completely matched,
and they were mutually astonished.
Later, Sānláng heard that his brother-in-law had returned from afar,
and also came to visit.
During their conversation,
he said to the scholar,
"Last night I dreamt you returned;
now it is true,
which is also very strange."
The scholar smiled and said,
"Fortunately, I was not killed by a large stone."
Sānláng was startled and asked why,
and the scholar told him about his dream.
Sānláng was greatly astonished.
For that very night,
Sānláng had also dreamt of meeting his sister crying and complaining,
and in his indignation, he threw the stone.
The three dreams coincided,
but they did not know who the beautiful woman was.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition.
Gěng Shíbā of Xīnchéng,
was critically ill.
Knowing he would not recover,
he said to his wife,
"Our eternal farewell will be soon.
After I die,
whether you remain a widow or remarry is up to you,
please tell me your intention."
His wife remained silent.
Gěng pressed her,
and said,
"Remaining a widow is indeed good,
but remarrying is also a common human sentiment.
Tell me plainly,
what harm is there?
I am about to bid you farewell.
If you remain a widow,
my heart will be comforted;
if you remarry,
my mind will be at peace."
His wife then sadly said,
"Our family has no provisions,
even with you alive we cannot make ends meet,
how can I remain a widow?"
When Gěng heard this,
he suddenly grasped his wife's arm
and said with a groan of resentment,
"How cruel!"
Having said this, he passed away.
His hand remained clenched and could not be opened.
His wife wailed.
Family members arrived,
two of them pulled at his fingers,
and forcefully separated them
before his hand finally opened.
Gěng did not realize he was dead.
He went out the door
and saw over ten small carts,
each with ten people.
Names were written on square pieces of paper
and pasted on the carts.
The cart driver saw Gěng
and urged him to board a cart.
Gěng saw that there were already nine people in the cart,
making ten with himself.
He also looked at the pasted list
and saw his name was last.
The carts moved with a clattering sound,
the noise echoing in his ears,
and he did not know where he was going.
After a while, they arrived at a place
where he heard someone say:
“This is the place of yearning for home.”
Hearing its name,
he doubted it.
Then he heard the attendants whispering, saying:
“Today, three people were executed.”
Gěng was even more startled.
When he listened carefully to their words,
they were all matters of the underworld,
then he suddenly realized, saying:
“Am I not a ghost?”
Immediately, he thought of his family home;
there was nothing more to worry about,
except his aged mother,
and that after his wife got married,
she lacked proper care;
thinking of this,
tears involuntarily streamed down.
After a while,
he saw a platform,
about several *rèn* high,
with many people visiting;
those with sacks on their heads and shackles on their feet
were weeping and going up and down.
He heard people say it was
the “Wàngxiāng Tái” (Platform for Gazing at Home).
When these people reached this point,
they all stepped down from their carts,
and jostled to ascend.
The attendants sometimes whipped them,
or stopped them,
but when it came to Gěng alone,
they urged him to ascend.
After ascending dozens of steps,
he finally reached the summit.
He raised his head and looked around,
and saw his gates, alleys, courtyards
as if right before his eyes.
But the inner rooms were indistinct,
as if shrouded in smoke and mist.
He was filled with unbearable sorrow.
He looked back,
and a man in short clothes stood below his shoulder,
and immediately asked Gěng for his surname and given name.
Gěng told him everything.
That man also introduced himself as a craftsman from Dōnghǎi.
Seeing Gěng shedding tears,
he asked:
“What matter weighs on your mind?”
Gěng told him again.
The craftsman plotted to leap over the platform and escape.
Gěng feared pursuit from the underworld,
but the craftsman insisted there was no harm.
Gěng also worried about falling from the high platform,
but the craftsman merely told him to follow.
So, he leapt first,
and Gěng indeed followed him.
When they reached the ground,
they were completely unharmed.
They were glad that no one noticed.
He looked at the cart they had ridden,
it was still at the foot of the platform.
The two men ran quickly.
After a few paces,
he suddenly remembered his name was stuck on the cart,
fearing he couldn't escape the pursuit by name;
so he turned back and approached the cart,
used his finger dipped in saliva,
wiped off his name,
and then resumed running,
panting heavily,
not daring to stop for a moment.
After a short while,
they entered an inner gate,
and the craftsman escorted him to his room.
Suddenly, he saw his own corpse,
and awoke with a start.
Feeling tired, agitated, and thirsty,
he urgently called for water.
His family was greatly alarmed,
and gave him water;
he drank until more than a *shí* (peck).
Then he suddenly got up,
bowed and prostrated himself;
afterward, he went out the door, made a formal bow in thanks,
only then returned.
Upon returning, he lay stiffly without moving.
His family, seeing his unusual behavior,
doubted if he was truly alive;
however, they gradually observed him,
and there was no other obvious abnormality.
When they cautiously approached and asked him,
he then clearly recounted the whole story.
They asked:
“Why did you go out the door?”
He said:
“To bid farewell to the craftsman.”
“Why did you drink so much water?”
He said:
“At first, I was drinking,
but afterward, it was the craftsman drinking.”
They gave him soup,
and he recovered in a few days.
Because of this, he became disgusted with his wife,
and no longer shared their bed, it is said.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lǐ Huà, a commoner from Chángzhōu,
was wealthy in land and property.
Over fifty years old,
he had no son.
He had one daughter named Xiǎohuì,
whose appearance was exquisite and beautiful;
his wife and he loved her most dearly.
At fourteen,
she died prematurely from a sudden illness,
leaving their household desolate,
and further diminishing their zest for life.
He then took a maid,
and after more than a year,
she bore a son,
whom they treasured as an arch-jade,
and named him Zhū'ér.
As the child grew,
he was robust and lovable.
However, his nature was utterly foolish;
at five or six years old, he still couldn't distinguish beans from wheat;
his speech was clumsy and hesitant.
Lǐ was also fond of him and unaware of his flaws.
There was once a one-eyed monk,
who begged for alms in the market,
and frequently knew about people's private family affairs,
thus people were startled, considering him divine;
and he also said
he could determine people's life, death, misfortune, and fortune.
Demanding hundreds or thousands [of cash],
he would press for payment by name,
and no one dared to refuse.
He went to Lǐ to solicit a hundred *mín*.
Lǐ found it difficult.
He offered ten *jīn*,
but the monk refused;
gradually it reached thirty *jīn*.
The monk sternly said:
“It must be a hundred *mín*,
not one *wén* less is acceptable!”
Lǐ also became angry,
took back the money, and hastily left.
The monk rose furiously and said:
“Don't regret it,
don't regret it!”
Not long after,
Zhū'ér suddenly suffered severe heart pain,
clawing at the bed sheets,
his face the color of earth and ash.
Lǐ was afraid,
and went to the monk with eighty *jīn* to beg for help.
The monk smiled and said:
“Such a large sum is really difficult!
But what can a mountain monk do?”
Lǐ returned, and his son had already died.
Lǐ grieved deeply,
and reported the situation to the county magistrate.
The magistrate arrested the monk and interrogated him,
but he also argued cleverly without any incriminating words.
They flogged him,
but it was like striking tanned leather.
They ordered a search of his person,
and found two wooden figures, one small coffin, and five small banners.
The magistrate was furious,
and repeatedly made hand gestures, pointing them out to the monk.
The monk then became afraid,
and admitted countless wrongdoings.
The magistrate ignored him,
and beat him to death with a staff.
Lǐ bowed in thanks and returned home.
It was already dusk.
Lǐ sat on the bed with his wife.
Suddenly a small child
entered the room
and said:
"Grandpa, why did you walk so fast?
I tried my best but couldn't catch up."
Looking at his physique,
he appeared to be seven or eight years old.
Lǐ was startled.
Just as he was about to question him,
he saw him appear and disappear as if transparent,
hazy like smoke.
In a moment,
he had climbed onto the bed and sat down.
Lǐ pushed him off.
He fell to the ground without a sound
and said:
"Grandpa, why are you like this!"
Then he darted back onto the bed.
Lǐ was frightened,
and he and his wife both fled.
The child called out "Father, Mother,"
babbling incessantly.
Lǐ entered his concubine's room
and quickly closed the door.
He looked back,
and the child was already at his knees.
Lǐ was shocked
and asked what he was doing.
He replied:
"I am from Sūzhōu,
my surname is Zhān.
I lost my parents at six,
and was not tolerated by my elder brother and his wife,
so I was sent to live with my maternal grandparents.
Once, playing outside the gate,
I was bewitched and killed by an evil monk under a mulberry tree.
I was driven like a ghost-minion,
imprisoned unjustly in the underworld,
unable to be reborn.
Fortunately, with your vindication, Grandpa,
I wish to be your son."
Lǐ said:
"Humans and ghosts walk different paths;
how can we depend on each other?"
The child said:
"Just clear a small room,
set up a bed and bedding for me,
and daily pour a cup of cold thin porridge.
Other than that, there is nothing to do."
Lǐ agreed.
The child was delighted
and then slept alone in the room.
In the mornings, he came in and out of the women's quarters
