as if he were born there.
Hearing the concubine crying for her child,
he asked:
"How many days has Zhū'ér been dead?"
They replied, seven days.
He said:
"The weather is severely cold;
the body should not be decayed.
Try opening the tomb and inspecting it.
If it is not damaged,
the child should be able to live."
Lǐ was delighted.
He went with the child,
opened the grave, and examined it.
The body was as it had been.
Just as he was alarmed by this,
he looked back
and the child was gone.
He found it strange
and carried the corpse home.
As soon as it was placed on the bed,
its eyes began to flutter.
A moment later, it called for soup.
After the soup, it sweated,
and after sweating, it got up.
Everyone rejoiced that Zhū'ér had come back to life,
and moreover, he was clever and astute,
quite different from before.
But at night, he lay stiff,
without any breath.
When they turned him over,
he was utterly still, as if dead.
The crowd was greatly alarmed,
thinking he had died again.
When day was about to break,
he would wake as if from a dream.
The group went to question him.
He replied:
"When I was with the evil monk,
there were two other children,
one named Gēzi.
Yesterday, I couldn't catch up with Father
because I was behind saying goodbye to Gēzi.
Now in the underworld,
he is adopted as an heir by Jiāng Yuánwài,
and lives quite leisurely.
At night,
he always comes to invite me to play.
Just now, Báibí escorted me home."
His mother then asked:
"Did you see Zhū'ér in the underworld?"
He said:
"Zhū'ér has already been reborn.
He has no father-son fate with Grandpa;
he was merely Yán Zǐfāng of Jīnlíng,
who came to collect a debt of a hundred thousand coins."
Initially,
Lǐ had traded in Jīnlíng
and owed Yán for goods, which was unpaid.
When Old Yán died,
no one knew about this matter.
Lǐ was greatly alarmed when he heard this.
His mother asked:
"Did you see Huìjiě?"
The child said:
"I don't know.
I will ask when I go again."
After two or three more days,
he said to his mother:
"Younger Sister Huì is doing very well in the underworld;
she married the young master of Chǔjiāng Wáng,
her hair is covered in pearls and jade.
As soon as she steps out,
hundreds of followers shout 'Hail!'."
His mother said:
"Why doesn't she visit home?"
He said:
"Once a person dies,
they are no longer concerned with their flesh and blood.
Only if someone vividly recounts their past life
will they suddenly be moved to remember.
Yesterday, I entrusted Jiāng Yuánwài
to facilitate a meeting with Sister.
Sister asked me to sit on a coral bed
and told me that our parents were worried about her,
but she was as if asleep.
I said: 'When Sister was alive,
she liked to embroider twin flowers.
Once, she pricked her finger with scissors,
and on the red silk,
Sister embroidered it into red water patterns.
Mother still hangs it on the wall beside the bed,
and thinks of it constantly.
Has Sister forgotten it?'
Sister then felt deeply moved
and said: 'I must tell my husband
and return to visit Mother.'"
His mother asked about the date,
but he said he didn't know.
One day he said to his mother:
"Sister will arrive soon;
her entourage is very numerous,
so we should prepare plenty of gruel and wine."
A moment later,
he ran into the room and said:
"Sister is here!"
He moved the bed to the central hall
and said:
"Sisters, please try to sit and
don't weep too much."
No one else saw anything.
The child led people to burn paper and pour libations outside the gate,
then returned and said:
"The retinue has been sent away for now.
Sister asked: 'The green brocade quilt
that used to cover me,
was it once burned by a candle flame, making a spot the size of a bean?
Is it still there?'"
His mother said:
"It is."
She immediately opened the chest and took it out.
The child said:
"Sister wants me to put it in her old chamber.
She's tired,
so she'll rest a little,
and speak with Mother again tomorrow."
Zhào Shì Nǚ from the eastern neighbor
was formerly Huì's embroidery companion.
That night,
she suddenly dreamed that Huì came to visit, wearing a headscarf and purple cape,
speaking and laughing as in life.
She also said:
"I am a different being;
seeing my parents face to face
is as difficult as crossing mountains and rivers.
I will borrow you, my sister, to speak with my family.
You need not be frightened."
At dawn,
just as she was speaking with her mother,
she suddenly fell to the ground and fainted.
She only awoke after a quarter of an hour
and said to her mother:
“Xiǎo Huì and Auntie haven’t seen each other for several years,
and her hair has suddenly turned white!”
Her mother exclaimed in alarm:
“Is my child deranged?”
The girl bowed in farewell and immediately went out.
Her mother knew something was amiss,
and followed her.
She went straight to Lǐ’s house [where her daughter’s body was],
and hugged her mother, weeping mournfully.
Her mother was shocked and didn’t know what she meant.
The girl said:
“When I returned yesterday,
I was quite exhausted,
and had no time for a single word.
I am unfilial,
abandoning my parents midway,
causing them sorrow and worry.
How can my sin be atoned for!”
Her mother suddenly understood,
and then cried.
After a while, she asked:
“I heard you are now of high status,
which greatly comforts my heart.
But since you reside in the Wáng family,
how were you able to come?”
The girl said:
“My husband and I are very devoted to each other,
and my in-laws also treat me with affection.
They don’t consider me ugly or jealous at all.”
When Huì was alive,
she liked to prop her chin with her hand;
as the girl spoke,
she often made the same gesture,
her expression remarkably similar.
Not long after,
Zhū’ér rushed in and said:
“Those who are coming to pick up my sister have arrived.”
The girl then rose,
bowed in farewell, weeping,
and said:
“I’m leaving.”
After speaking,
she collapsed again,
and after some time, she revived.
Several months later,
Lǐ’s illness became severe,
and medicines were ineffective.
Her child said:
“I fear she won’t be saved morning or evening!
Two ghosts are sitting at the head of the bed,
one holding an iron staff,
the other pulling a ramie rope,
about four or five feet long.
They plead with the child day and night not to leave.”
Her mother cried,
and then prepared burial clothes.
When evening came,
the child hurried in and said:
“You common woman,
move aside for now.
My sister’s husband is coming to see father.”
A moment later,
she clapped her hands and laughed.
Her mother asked her why,
and she said:
“I’m laughing at the two ghosts.
When they heard my sister’s husband was coming,
they both hid under the bed like turtles.”
After a little more time,
she greeted someone in the air,
asking after her sister’s well-being.
Then she clapped her hands and said:
“The two ghost servants pleaded with her not to leave,
but she came here, it’s truly wonderful!”
Then she went out to the door,
returned,
and said:
“My sister’s husband has left.
The two ghosts are locked to the horse’s harness.
Father will surely be well immediately.
My sister’s husband said: he will report back to the Great King,
to beg for a hundred years of life for our parents.”
The whole family rejoiced.
By night,
the illness was much better,
and in a few days, it fully recovered.
A teacher was hired to teach the child to read.
The child was very intelligent,
and entered the county school at eighteen.
She could still speak of matters from the underworld.
When she saw sick people in the village,
she would point out where the evil spirits were,
and burn incense,
and often they would recover.
Later, she suffered a sudden illness,
her skin turned bluish-purple,
and she said herself that ghosts and spirits were blaming her for exposing secrets.
From then on, she no longer spoke of such things.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Grand Scribe Mǒu Gōng,
his surname is forgotten.
One day, he was lying down in his study,
when suddenly a small ceremonial procession
came out from the corner of the hall.
The horses were as big as frogs,
and the people smaller than fingers.
The small honor guard consisted of dozens of teams;
an official, wearing a black gauze cap
and embroidered robes,
rode in a sedan chair,
and they allbustled out the door and departed.
Gōng found this strange,
secretly suspecting it was a hallucination from sleep.
Suddenly, he saw a small person
return into the house,
carrying a felt bag,
as big as a fist,
and go directly under the bed.
He said:
“My master has a humble gift,
respectfully presented to the Grand Scribe.”
Having spoken,
he stood opposite,
but did not present the item.
After a moment,
he laughed to himself again and said:
“It’s a trivial thing,
I imagine the Grand Scribe also has no use for it,
better to bestow it upon this humble person immediately.”
The Grand Scribe nodded.
He happily took it and left.
Afterwards, he was never seen again.
It’s a pity that the Grand Scribe lost his nerve
and never questioned where he came from.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Shàng Shēng,
a native of Tàishān.
Lived alone in a pure study.
It happened to be an autumn night,
the Milky Way shone brightly,
the bright moon was in the sky.
He lingered in the shade of the flowers,
quite lost in thought.
Suddenly a woman climbed over the wall and came,
smiling, she said:
“Why is the xiùcái so deep in thought?”
Shēng went to look,
her beauty was like that of an immortal.
Delighted and surprised, he embraced her,
indulging in extreme intimacy.
She introduced herself:
“My surname is Hú,
my name is Sānjie.”
When asked where she lived,
she only smiled and did not speak.
Shēng also no longer questioned her,
only hoping to be together forever.
From then on,
there was no empty evening.
One night,
as they sat close by the lamp,
Shēng loved her,
his gaze fixed without turning.
The woman smiled and said:
“Why are you staring at me so intently?”
He replied:
“I look at you like red peonies and green peaches,
even if I gaze all night,
I would not be tired of it.”
Sānjie said:
"My humble self,
has thus been favored with your affection;
if you were to see my family's fourth sister,
I don't know how much more infatuated you would become."
Shēng grew even more smitten,
regretting not having seen her face,
and knelt for a long time, pleading sorrowfully.
The next evening,
she indeed came with her fourth sister.
She was just past her coming-of-age ceremony,
with her face powdered and dew-kissed,
and her apricot blossom-like beauty dewy with mist.
She smiled enchantingly,
captivatingly beautiful.
Shēng was overjoyed,
and invited them to sit.
The third sister laughed and chatted with Shēng;
the fourth sister only pulled at her embroidered sash with her hand,
head bowed.
Before long,
the third sister rose to take her leave,
and her sister wished to accompany her.
Shēng pulled her, not letting go,
and turning to the third sister, said:
"My dear, please say something."
The third sister then smiled and said:
"My passionate lad is in a hurry!
Sister, stay a little while."
The fourth sister said nothing,
and her older sister then departed.
The two enjoyed themselves fully,
and then, resting their arms as pillows,
poured out their life stories,
no longer concealing anything.
The fourth sister revealed herself to be a fox.
Shēng, attached to her beauty,
was not surprised by this.
The fourth sister then said:
"My elder sister is cruel and venomous,
having already killed three people.
Those she seduces,
none fail to perish.
I am fortunate to be deeply loved by you,
and cannot bear to see you destroyed,
so you should break off with her early."
Shēng was frightened,
and asked for a way to deal with it.
The fourth sister said:
"Although I am a fox,
I have obtained the correct method from an immortal,
so I should write a talisman and stick it on your bedroom door,
which can ward her off."
So she wrote it.
When dawn broke,
the third sister came,
saw the talisman, recoiled,
and said:
"You ungrateful girl,
you've given your heart to your new lover,
forgetting the matchmaker!
You two are destined to be together,
and I bear you no ill will,
but why must it be like this?"
Then she directly left.
A few days later,
the fourth sister went elsewhere,
promising to return the following night.
On that day,
Shēng happened to go out to look around.
Below the mountain there was an old forest,
and from amidst the dense growth,
emerged a young woman,
also quite charming.
She approached Shēng and said:
"Why does Xiùcai always dote on the Hú family sisters?
They can't even give you a single coin."
She then handed Shēng a string of coins,
saying:
"Take this home first,
and buy some good wine;
I'll bring some small dishes soon,
and we'll have fun together."
Shēng took the money home,
and it was just as she had instructed.
A short while later,
the woman indeed arrived,
placed a roasted chicken
and a cured pork shoulder each on the table,
then drew a knife and finely sliced them into pieces;
she poured wine and bantered playfully,
making the joyous atmosphere extraordinary.
Afterward, they extinguished the candles and went to bed,
engaging in extremely wanton intimacy.
They only rose at dawn.
As they sat by the bed,
swapping slippers by hand,
they suddenly heard human voices;
listening closely,
they were already inside the bed curtains,
and it was the Hú sisters.
The woman, startled,
fled in a panic,
leaving her slipper on the bed.
The two girls then cried out:
"Lewd fox!
How dare you sleep with a human!"
They chased after her,
returning after a while.
The fourth sister complained to Shēng:
"You're incorrigible!
To pair up with a lewd fox,
I can no longer be close to you!"
Then she indignantly wanted to leave.
Shēng, in a panic, threw himself at her,
pleading with sorrowful words.
The third sister interceded from the side,
and the fourth sister's anger somewhat subsided,
and from then on, they were as close as before.
One day,
a man from Shǎnxī riding a donkey arrived at the door, saying:
"I've been searching for the demonic creature,
not just for a day or two,
and only now have I found it."
Shēng's father found his words strange,
and asked about the origin.
He said:
"I, your humble servant, travel the waters daily,
roaming the four directions,
for more than ten months a year,
often leaving my hometown for eight or nine months.
My brother was bewitched and killed by a demonic creature.
When I returned, I grieved deeply,
vowing to find and eradicate it.
I traveled thousands of miles,
but found no trace.
Now it is in your home.
If it is not eliminated,
others will follow my brother in death."
At that time, Shēng was secretly close to the girl,
and his parents had subtly noticed it.
Hearing the guest's words,
they were greatly frightened,
invited him in,
and asked him to perform the ritual.
He brought out two bottles,
arranged them on the ground,
and chanted spells for a long time.
Four black mists appeared,
dispersing into the bottles.
The guest happily said:
"The whole family has arrived."
Then he wrapped the bottle mouths with pig bladders,
sealing them very securely.
Shēng's father was also happy,
and insisted on keeping the guest for a meal.
Shēng felt a pang of sympathy,
and secretly peered into the bottle nearby,
hearing the fourth sister say from inside the bottle:
"Watching without helping,
how heartless are you?"
Shēng was even more moved.
He hastily tried to open the seal,
but the knot could not be undone.
The fourth sister again said:
"You don't need to do that,
just lay down the banner on the altar,
and use a needle to pierce a hole in the bladder,
and I will come out immediately."
Shēng did as she asked.
Indeed, a wisp of white gas was seen,
emerging from the hole,
and ascending to the sky.
The guest came out,
saw the banner lying on the ground,
and was greatly surprised, saying:
"It escaped!
This must have been the young master's doing."
He shook the bottle and listened,
saying:
"Fortunately, only one escaped.
This creature is not meant to die,
and can still be forgiven."
Then he took the bottles and departed.
Later, Shēng was in the fields,
supervising his workers harvesting wheat,
and saw the fourth sister sitting under a tree in the distance.
Shēng approached her,
held her hand, and consoled her.
He also said:
“After ten springs and autumns,
your great elixir has now been completed.
But the thought of you has not been forgotten,
hence I bow once more to inquire.”
The scholar wished to return with her.
The woman said:
“I am no longer what I was;
I cannot be stained by worldly affections.
We will meet again later.”
Having spoken,
she disappeared.
More than twenty years later,
the scholar was living alone
when he saw the fourth sister arrive from outside.
The scholar happily spoke with her.
The woman said:
“My name is now listed in the registry of immortals,
and I should not set foot in the mortal world again.
But moved by your affection,
I respectfully come to report the date of your departure.
You should make arrangements for your posthumous affairs early;
also, do not be sad or worried,
for I will transform you into a ghost immortal,
and there will be no suffering.”
Then she bid farewell and left.
On that day,
the scholar indeed died.
Shàng Shēng (尚生) was a relative of his friend Lǐ Wén-yù (李文玉)
and personally witnessed this.
According to the manuscript edition of *Liáo-zhāi Zhì-yì*
In Zhùcūn (祝村), Jìyáng (濟陽), there was an old man named Zhù Wēng (祝翁)
who was over fifty years old
and died of illness.
His family was busy preparing his burial
when they suddenly heard Zhù Wēng (祝翁) call out very urgently.
They all rushed to the spiritual chamber,
and saw that Zhù Wēng (祝翁) had already revived.
Everyone happily offered comfort and inquired.
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) only said to his wife (媼):
“When I just left,
I had no intention of ever returning.
After walking a few *lǐ*,
I had a change of heart, thinking of leaving your old skin and bones in the hands of our children,
dependent on others for warmth and cold,
with no joy in life left.
It would be better to come with me.
Therefore I returned,
wishing to go together with you.”
Everyone thought he was speaking nonsense due to his recent revival,
and did not deeply believe him.
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) repeated his words.
The wife (媼) said:
“That would also be good.
But I am just alive,
how can I die so suddenly?”
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) waved his hand and said:
“That is not difficult.
The household affairs,
you can quickly take care of them.”
The wife (媼) smiled and did not move.
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) urged her again.
So she went outside the door,
delayed for several *kè* and then entered,
deceiving him by saying:
“Everything has been properly arranged.”
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) ordered her to quickly get dressed.
The wife (媼) did not move,
and Zhù Wēng (祝翁) urged her even more urgently.
The wife (媼) could not bear to refuse his wish,
so she dressed up in skirts and came out.
The daughters-in-law and daughters all secretly laughed.
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) moved his head onto the pillow,
and patted it, telling her to lie down.
The wife (媼) said:
“Our children are all here;
lying stiffly side-by-side,
what kind of sight is this?”
Zhù Wēng (祝翁) pounded the bed and said:
“What is so funny about dying together!”
Seeing Zhù Wēng (祝翁)'s impatience,
the children all urged the wife (媼) to just follow his wishes.
The wife (媼) did as told,
lying stiffly side-by-side on the pillow.
The family members again all laughed at them.
A moment later,
the wife (媼)'s smile suddenly faded,
then gradually both her eyes closed,
and after a long silence,
she appeared to be asleep.
Only then did the crowd draw near to look,
and found her skin already cold and her nose without breath.
They tested Zhù Wēng (祝翁) and it was the same,
only then did they all become alarmed and fearful.
In the twenty-first year of Kāngxī (康熙),
Zhù Wēng (祝翁)'s sister-in-law, who was a servant in Bì Cì-shǐ (畢刺史)'s household,
spoke of it in great detail.
Yì Shǐ Shì (異史氏) says:
“Did Zhù Wēng (祝翁) have some extraordinary conduct in his past life?
The road to the underworld is vast and hazy,
to come and go as you please—
how strange!
And he, a white-headed man, wishing his wife to depart,
could call her to go;
how leisurely he must have been!
At the moment of death,
what one is most reluctant to bid farewell to
are the intimate people by the bedside.
If his art could be widely applied,
then the custom of sharing shoes and perfume
could be dispensed with.”
According to the manuscript edition of *Liáo-zhāi Zhì-yì*
The Pig-Dragon (豬婆龍)
is produced in Xījiāng (西江).
Its form resembles a dragon but is short,
and it can fly horizontally;
it often emerges along the riverbanks to prey on geese and ducks.
If one is hunted and caught,
its meat is sold to the Chén (陳) and Kē (柯) families.
These two families are descendants of Yǒu-liàng (友諒),
who have for generations eaten Pig-Dragon (豬婆龍) meat;
other clans dare not eat it.
A guest came from the west of the river,
obtained one,
and brought it onto his boat.
One day,
his boat docked at Qiántáng (錢塘),
the restraints loosened slightly,
and it suddenly leaped into the river.
Soon after,
great waves surged,
and the merchant ship capsized and sank.
According to the manuscript edition of *Liáo-zhāi Zhì-yì*
A certain master from Shǎnyòu (陝右),
a *jìnshì* in the *Xīncǎo* year (辛丑),
could remember his previous life.
He once said that in his previous life, he was a scholar
who died in middle age.
After death, he saw the King of the Underworld judging cases,
with tripods and oil cauldrons,
just as is commonly described.
In the eastern corner of the hall,
several racks were set up,
upon which were draped the skins of pigs, sheep, dogs, and horses.
A clerk called out names,
and some were punished to become horses,
others to become pigs;
all were stripped naked,
and took skins from the racks to cover themselves.
Soon it was the master's turn,
and he heard the King of the Underworld say:
“This one should be made a sheep.”
A ghost brought a white sheepskin,
and pressed it to cover the master's body.
The clerk reported:
“He once saved a person from death.”
The King examined the register and reviewed it,
then showed it and said:
“Exempt him.
Although his evils are many,
this good deed can redeem them.”
The ghost then tried to remove its fur and skin.
The skin was already stuck to his body,
and could not be moved again.
Two ghosts seized his arms and pressed his chest,
forcibly tearing it off,
the pain was indescribable;
the skin tore into pieces,
and could not be completely removed.
After it was removed,
near his shoulder, a piece of sheepskin as large as a palm still adhered.
After the master was born,
a clump of sheep's wool grew on his back,
which reappeared even after being cut.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of *Liáo-zhāi Zhì-yì*
In the late Míng (明) dynasty,
Jì (濟) prefecture was plagued by many bandits.
Each district deployed soldiers,
and those caught were immediately executed.
Zhāngqiū (章丘) had even more bandits.
There was a soldier whose saber was extremely sharp,
and when he killed, it always found the joints.
One day,
more than ten bandits were captured,
and escorted to the market square.
One of the bandits recognized the soldier,
hesitated, then said:
“I hear your saber is the fastest,
beheading without a second stroke.
Please kill me!”
The soldier said:
“Agreed.
Stay close to me,
do not separate.”
The bandit followed him to the execution site,
he drew his saber and swung it,
and the head fell off with a sound of "huòrán".
Several paces away,
it was still rolling around and exclaimed loudly: “What a fast saber!”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of *Liáo-zhāi Zhì-yì*
Gù Shēng
was from Jīnlíng.
He was learned in various arts,
but his family was extremely poor.
Also, because his mother was old,
he could not bear to leave her side.
So, he earned a living daily by painting and writing calligraphy for others,
receiving payments to sustain himself.
By the age of twenty-five,
he was still without a wife.
Opposite their house, there was an old vacant residence
where an old woman and a young girl lived as tenants.
As there were no men in their family,
he had not inquired as to who they were.
One day,
he happened to enter from outside
and saw the young woman coming out of his mother's room.
She was about eighteen or nineteen years old,
graceful, elegant, and refined,
rarely matched in the world.
Upon seeing him, she avoided him greatly,
and her demeanor was cold and stern.
Gù Shēng went in and asked his mother.
His mother said:
"That is the young woman from the house opposite.
She came to borrow a knife and a ruler from me.
She just said that her family also consists of only a mother.
This girl does not look like she comes from a poor family.
When I asked why she wasn't married,
she used her mother's old age as an excuse.
Tomorrow I should go to visit her mother,
and subtly convey our intention.
If her expectations are not extravagant,
you can support her mother for her."
The next day, she went to their house.
Their mother was merely a deaf old woman.
Looking at her house,
there was not even enough food for the next day.
When asked about their livelihood,
they relied on the girl's ten fingers.
She slowly tested their reaction to the idea of sharing meals,
and the old woman seemed receptive,
but turned to discuss it with her daughter.
The girl remained silent,
showing considerable displeasure.
So his mother returned.
She pondered her appearance and suspected, saying:
"Could it be that the girl dislikes our poverty?
She doesn't speak or smile,
as beautiful as peach and plum blossoms,
yet as cold as frost and snow –
what an extraordinary person!"
Mother and son sighed with speculation and gave up.
One day,
Gù Shēng was sitting in his study.
A young man came to ask for a painting.
His appearance was very handsome,
and his manner quite frivolous.
When asked where he was from,
he
replied, "a neighboring village."
Thereafter, he would come every two or three days.
Gradually, they became familiar,
and he began to tease and joke.
Gù Shēng embraced him familiarly,
and he did not resist much,
so they had a private encounter.
From then on, their comings and goings were very intimate.
Coincidentally, the young woman passed by,
and the young man watched her leave,
asking who she was.
He replied, "the neighbor's daughter."
The young man said:
"So beautiful,
why is her expression so formidable?"
A short while later,
Gù Shēng went inside.
His mother said:
"Just now the girl came to beg for rice,
saying they hadn't lit a fire for a whole day.
This girl is extremely filial,
and her extreme poverty is pitiable.
You should help her a little."
Gù Shēng followed his mother's words,
carried a peck of rice and knocked on their door,
conveying his mother's intention.
The girl accepted it,
without offering any thanks.
She often came to Gù Shēng's house,
and seeing his mother making clothes and shoes,
she would help with the sewing.
She came and went in the hall,
working like a daughter-in-law.
Gù Shēng admired her even more.
Whenever he received offerings of food,
he would certainly share them with her mother,
and the girl would barely acknowledge it.
His mother happened to develop a carbuncle in a hidden place,
crying out day and night.
The girl would regularly come to the bed to check on her,
washing the wound and applying medicine for her,
three or four times a day.
His mother felt very uneasy,
but the girl was not disgusted by the filth.
His mother said:
"Alas!
How I wish for a daughter-in-law like you,
who would serve this old body until death!"
Having said that,
she choked with emotion.
The girl comforted her, saying:
"Your son is very filial,
hundreds of times better than my widowed mother and orphaned daughter."
His mother said:
"The task of attending to one at the bedside,
how can a filial son do that?
Moreover, my life is already approaching its end,
exposed to the elements day and night,
I am deeply worried about the continuation of the family line."
While they were speaking,
Gù Shēng entered.
His mother wept and said:
"You owe the young lady so much;
you must not forget to repay her kindness."
Gù Shēng bowed in obeisance.
The girl said:
"You respect my mother,
I do not need to thank you.
Why should you thank me?"
Thereupon, he respected and loved her even more.
However, her demeanor was stiff and unyielding,
and he could not approach her at all.
One day,
the girl went out,
and Shēng gazed at her.
The girl suddenly turned her head,
and smiled charmingly.
Shēng was overjoyed beyond expectation,
and rushed to follow her to her home.
He propositioned her,
and she did not refuse,
happily engaging in intimacy.
Afterward,
she warned Shēng, saying:
“This deed can be done once, but not again!”
Shēng did not respond and returned home.
The next day,
he invited her again.
The girl sternly ignored him and left.
He came frequently every day,
and they often met,
but she never gave him a friendly word or look.
If he tried to joke with her a little,
she would respond with chilling words.
Suddenly, in an empty space, she asked Shēng:
“Who is that young man who has been coming recently?”
Shēng told her.
The girl said:
“His behavior and mannerisms
have been disrespectful to me many times.
Because of your closeness,
I have ignored it.
Please convey this message again: if he does it again,
it means he does not wish to live!”
Shēng, by evening,
told the young man,
and moreover said:
“You must be careful;
she cannot be offended!”
The young man said:
“Since she cannot be offended,
why did you secretly offend her?”
Shēng declared himself innocent.
He said:
“If you are innocent,
then how did those vulgar words
reach your ears?”
Shēng could not answer.
The young man said:
“Also bother to convey this: Stop being so hypocritical and putting on airs;
otherwise,
I will spread it everywhere.”
Shēng was extremely angry,
his emotions showing on his face,
whereupon the young man left.
One evening,
as he was sitting alone,
the girl suddenly arrived,
and smiled, saying:
“My romantic destiny with you is not yet severed;
is this not fate?”
Shēng was ecstatically happy and held her in his arms.
They heard footsteps rustling,
and the two were startled and rose,
then the young man pushed open the door and entered.
Shēng asked in alarm:
“What are you doing here?”
He smiled, saying:
“I came to observe a chaste person.”
He looked at the girl and said:
“Aren’t you blaming anyone today?”
The girl’s eyebrows bristled and her cheeks flushed,
and she remained silent.
She quickly turned over her upper garment,
revealing a leather pouch,
and something came out at her touch,
which was a foot-long, crystal-clear dagger.
Seeing this, the young man
was terrified and fled backward.
She chased him out the door,
but looking around, he was nowhere to be seen.
The girl threw the dagger into the air,
and there was a sharp clang,
shining like a long rainbow,
and presently an object fell to the ground with a thud.
Shēng quickly lit a candle to examine it,
and it was a white fox,
its body and head separated.
He was greatly alarmed.
The girl said:
“This was your male concubine.
I had indeed forgiven him,
but he was determined not to live!”
She put the blade back into the pouch.
Shēng pulled her to come in.
She said:
“That demonic creature spoiled our mood,
please come tomorrow night.”
She went out the door and departed.
The next evening,
the girl indeed came,
and they became intimate, and he questioned her about her art.
The girl said:
“This is not for you to know.
It is essential to keep it secret;
if revealed, it may not be good for you.”
He then proposed marriage,
but she said:
“Sleeping together,
fetching water and drawing from the well,
what else is a wife but this?
Since we are already husband and wife,
why speak of marriage again?”
Shēng said:
“Are you perhaps disliking my poverty?”
She said:
“You are indeed poor,
but am I rich?
Our gathering tonight
is precisely out of pity for your poverty.”
Before parting, she instructed:
“Such casual encounters
cannot be frequent.
When it is appropriate to come,
I will come myself;
when it is not appropriate,
forcing me will be useless.”
Afterward, whenever they met,
Shēng often wanted to draw her aside for private conversation,
but the girl would always run away and avoid him.
However, mending clothes and gathering firewood,
she managed everything,
no less than a wife.
After several months,
her mother died,
and Shēng put forth his utmost effort to bury her.
The girl consequently lived alone.
Shēng thought her solitary sleep could be disturbed,
so he climbed over the wall and entered,
calling out to her repeatedly through the window,
but she still did not respond.
He looked at her door,
and the room was empty.
He secretly suspected that the girl had another appointment.
That night, he went again,
and it was just as before.
So he left his jade pendant by the window and departed.
The next day,
they met at her mother's place.
After they came out,
he followed her and said:
"Do you doubt me, my lady?
Everyone has their own thoughts,
which cannot be told to others.
Now, if I wanted to make you have no doubts,
how could I?
However, there is one urgent matter for which I need your advice."
When he asked her,
she said:
"I have been pregnant for eight months already,
and I fear I will give birth any day now.
'My status is not yet clear,'
and though I can bear it for you,
I cannot raise it for you.
You should secretly tell your mother
to find a wet nurse,
pretending to be seeking an adopted child,
but do not mention me."
The scholar agreed
and told his mother.
His mother laughed and said:
"How strange this woman is!
She cannot be formally betrothed,
yet she is secretly intimate with my son."
She happily followed her plan and waited.
After another month or so,
the woman did not come for several days.
His mother grew suspicious
and went to check her door,
which was quiet and shut.
After knocking for a long time,
the woman finally came out from inside, with disheveled hair and a dirty face.
She opened the door and let her in,
then closed it again.
When they entered her room,
a baby was crying on the bed.
His mother asked in surprise:
"How long ago was it born?"
She replied:
"Three days ago."
She picked up the swaddling clothes and looked at it,
and it was a boy,
with a full jaw and a broad forehead.
She joyfully said:
"My child, you have already given this old woman a grandson,
but you are alone and helpless;
where will you entrust him?"
The woman said:
"My small hidden grievance
I dare not fully show to my old mother.
When it is night and no one is around,
you can take the child away immediately."
His mother returned and spoke to her son,
and they secretly found it very strange.
That night, they went and brought the child home.
After several more nights,
around midnight,
the woman suddenly knocked on the door and entered,
carrying a leather bag in her hand,
and smilingly said:
"My great task is accomplished;
I bid you farewell from now on."
When he urgently asked the reason,
she said:
"The kindness of my foster mother
is always in my heart.
What I said previously, 'it can be once but not twice,'
was because the repayment was not on the bed.
Because you are poor and cannot marry,
I will extend your lineage.
Originally, I expected to conceive with one attempt,
but unexpectedly, my period returned,
thus breaking my vow and doing it a second time.
Now that your kindness has been repaid [and] my wish fulfilled,
I have no regrets."
He asked:
"What is in the bag?"
She said:
"An enemy's head."
He examined it and peered in;
the hair and beard were matted, and it was covered in blood.
He was absolutely terrified and again pressed for details.
She said:
"I didn't tell you before
because secret matters must not be revealed,
fearing disclosure.
Now that the deed is done,
I can tell you: I am from Zhèjiāng.
My father was an official, a Sīmǎ,
who fell into the trap of an enemy,
and that person confiscated my family's property.
I escaped with my old mother,
concealed my name,
and lived in obscurity
for three years now.
The reason I didn't seek revenge immediately
was simply because my mother was still alive;
after my mother passed away,
there was another piece of flesh burdening my belly,
and so it was delayed for a long time again.
My going out at night before was for no other reason
than that I was not familiar with the roads and doors,
fearing mistakes."
Having spoken,
she went out the door.
She further instructed:
"The child I bore,
take good care of him.
You have little fortune and a short life,
but this child can bring glory to your family.
It's deep night, do not alarm your old mother;
I am leaving!"
Just as he sadly wanted to ask where she was going,
the woman flashed like lightning,
and in a blink, she was gone.
The scholar stood rooted to the spot, sighing in wonder,
as if he had lost his soul.
The next morning, he told his mother,
and they merely sighed in amazement together.
Three years later,
the scholar indeed passed away.
His son became a Jìnshì at eighteen
and still served his grandmother until her old age.
The Grand Historian (Yì Shǐ Shì) says:
"A man must first suppress the valiant woman
before he can keep male lovers.
Otherwise,
you love her beauty,
but she loves you as a fat pig!"
According to the Chuìxuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chē Shēng,
whose family was not wealthy,
was addicted to drink;
at night, he could not sleep without floating 'three whites' [cups of wine],
and so his bedside wine jar was never empty.
One night, he awoke,
and as he turned over,
it felt as if someone was sleeping beside him.
He thought it was just a fallen garment.
He touched it,
and it was a furry object,
like a cat but huge.
He lit a candle,
and it was a fox,
sound asleep like a dog.
He looked at his bottle,
and it was empty.
He then laughed and said:
"This is my drinking buddy."
He couldn't bear to disturb it,
so he covered it with a quilt, extending his arm,
and slept with it.
He left the candle lit to observe any changes.
In the middle of the night,
the fox stretched.
The scholar laughed and said:
"What a beautiful sleep!"
He pulled back the covers and looked at it,
and it was a handsome man in a scholar's cap.
He rose and bowed before the bed,
thanking him for not killing him.
The scholar said:
"I am fond of strong liquor,
and people consider me foolish;
but you,
you are my Bào Shú.
If you do not doubt me,
you shall be a good friend for the wine-hill."
He pulled him onto the bed,
and they slept again.
He also said:
"You can come often;
let there be no suspicion between us."
The fox agreed.
When the scholar awoke,
the fox had already left.
So he prepared a generous serving of fine wine,
specifically waiting for the fox.
By evening,
he indeed arrived,
and they sat knee-to-knee, drinking merrily.
Hú's capacity for drink was prodigious,
and he was skilled at witty conversation,
whereupon they regretted not having met sooner.
Hú said:
"I have repeatedly partaken of your excellent wine,
how can I repay your kindness?"
The scholar said:
"The pleasure of a mere 'dou' of wine
is not worth mentioning!"
Hú said:
"Although that is true,
you are a poor scholar,
and money for wine is extremely hard to come by.
I should devise a small plan for your wine funds."
The next evening,
he came and announced:
"Seven *lǐ* southeast from here,
by the side of the road, there is some lost gold.
You should retrieve it early."
At dawn the next day he went,
and indeed found two pieces of gold.
He then bought fine dishes
to accompany their evening drinks,
and Hú again announced:
"Behind your courtyard there is a hidden cellar.
You should open it."
Following his words,
he indeed found over a hundred thousand cash.
Joyfully, he said:
"I already have money in my purse,
so I don't need to worry about buying wine."
Hú said:
"Not so.
How can the water in a rut be scooped for long?
We must plan for more."
Another day,
he said to the scholar:
"The market price for buckwheat is low,
this is a rare commodity to hoard."
He followed his advice,
and bought over forty *shí* of buckwheat.
Everyone laughed at him.
Not long after,
there was a great drought,
and all the grains and beans withered,
only buckwheat could be planted;
he sold the seeds,
and profited tenfold.
From this, he became even richer,
and managed two hundred *mǔ* of fertile land.
He only needed to ask Hú:
plant more wheat, and there would be a wheat harvest;
plant more millet, and there would be a millet harvest.
All matters of planting timing,
were decided by Hú.
Day by day, their intimacy grew,
and he called the scholar's wife "sister-in-law,"
and treated his children as his own.
Later, the scholar died,
and Hú never returned.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Sāng Shēng,
whose given name was Xiǎo,
and courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was from Yízhōu.
He was orphaned young,
and resided in Hónghuā Bù.
Sāng was a quiet and self-contented man,
who went out twice a day,
to eat with his eastern neighbor,
and for the rest of the time, he simply sat firmly.
The neighboring scholar happened to visit,
and playfully said:
"Do you not fear ghosts or foxes living alone?"
He laughed and replied:
"What does a man fear ghosts or foxes?
If a male comes, I have a sharp sword;
if a female, I would still open the door to let her in."
The neighboring scholar returned,
and conspired with a friend,
using a ladder to get a courtesan over the wall,
who then snapped her fingers and knocked on the door.
The scholar peered out and asked who it was,
and the courtesan claimed to be a ghost.
The scholar was greatly frightened,
his teeth chattering audibly.
The courtesan then slowly left.
The neighboring scholar arrived early at Sāng's study,
Sāng recounted what he had seen,
and also announced his intention to return home.
The neighboring scholar clapped his hands and said:
"Why didn't you open the door and let her in?"
Sāng immediately realized it was a prank,
and so remained peacefully as before.
After half a year,
a woman came knocking at his study door at night.
The scholar thought it was his friend playing a prank again,
opened the door and invited her in,
only to find a beauty capable of overthrowing a kingdom.
Startled, he asked where she came from,
she said:
"I am Liánhxiāng,
a courtesan from the western house."
There were indeed many brothels in the *bù*,
so he believed her.
Extinguishing the candle, he went to bed,
and their intimacy was extreme.
From then on, she would visit every three to five nights.
One evening,
alone, Sānɡ-sheng sat in contemplation,
when a woman gracefully entered.
Sānɡ-sheng took her for Lián,
and reciprocated her greetings.
Upon seeing her face, she was quite different: merely fifteen or sixteen years old,
her sleeves hung low in the summer heat,
her demeanor was graceful and elegant,
and as she walked,
she seemed to waver to and fro.
Sānɡ-sheng was greatly alarmed,
suspecting her to be a fox-spirit.
The woman said:
"I am
a good family's daughter,
surnamed Lǐ.
I admire your noble elegance,
and hope you will favor me with a glance."
Sānɡ-sheng was pleased.
He held her hand,
which was cold as ice,
and asked:
"Why is it so cold?"
She replied:
"Being young and delicate,
exposed to frost and dew at night,
how could it be otherwise!"
Soon, her silken jacket was undone,
and she was clearly a virgin.
The woman said:
"I, for the sake of love,
though delicate in nature,
have now given myself.
If you do not dislike my plainness,
I wish to serve you forever by your pillow and mat.
Is there no one else in your room?"
Sānɡ-sheng replied:
"No one else,
only a neighboring courtesan,
who also doesn't come often."
The woman said:
"You must be careful to avoid her.
I am not like the people of the courtesan district,
so you must keep me secret and not reveal me.
When she comes, I will go;
when she goes, I will come—that will suffice."
When the cock crowed, she wished to leave,
and gave him an embroidered slipper,
saying:
"This is what I wear on my foot,
playing with it can convey my longing.
However, when someone else is present, be careful not to play with it!"
He accepted it and looked at it,
it was curved like a knot-untying awl.
His heart was greatly delighted.
The next evening, when no one was around,
he took it out to examine and admire it.
The woman suddenly arrived, floating in,
and they became intimately affectionate.
From then on, whenever he took out the slipper,
the woman would unfailingly arrive as if in response to his thought.
He found this strange and questioned her.
She laughed and said:
"It's just the right time."
One night, Lián came,
and exclaimed in surprise:
"My lord, why is your spirit so depleted?"
Sānɡ-sheng said:
"I didn't notice."
Lián then bade farewell,
agreeing to return in ten days.
After she left,
Lǐ came every evening without fail.
She asked:
"Why has your lover not been here for so long?"
Sānɡ-sheng then told her about their agreement.
Lǐ laughed and said:
"How do you compare me to Lián in beauty?"
He said:
"Both can be called peerless.
But Lián-qīng's skin is warm and soft."
Lǐ's expression changed, and she said:
"You say 'both beautiful'—that's just what you say to me.
She must be an immortal from the moon palace;
I certainly cannot compare to her."
And so, she was displeased.
Then she counted on her fingers,
the ten-day period was already full,
and she instructed him not to leak anything,
and that she would secretly spy on Lián.
The next night,
Lián-xiānɡ indeed arrived,
and they talked and laughed very harmoniously.
When they went to bed,
she was greatly alarmed and said:
"It's serious!
Not seeing you for ten days,
how have you become so emaciated and weakened?
Are you sure you haven't encountered something else?"
Sānɡ-sheng asked her the reason.
She said:
"I examined your vital energy,
your pulse is like tangled silk threads,
it's a ghost ailment."
The next night,
when Lǐ came,
Sānɡ-sheng asked:
"What did you think of Lián-xiānɡ when you spied on her?"
She said:
"She is beautiful, indeed.
I always said there was no such beauty in the world,
and she is indeed a fox-spirit.
When she left,
I followed her,
and she dwells in a cave in the southern mountains."
Sānɡ-sheng suspected her of jealousy,
and responded vaguely.
The next evening,
he playfully said to Lián-xiānɡ:
"I really didn't believe it,
but some say you are a fox-spirit."
Lián immediately asked:
"Who said that?"
He laughed and said:
"I was just teasing you."
Lián said:
"How is a fox-spirit different from a human?"
He said:
"Those who are bewitched by them fall ill,
and in severe cases, die,
that is why they are frightening."
Lián-xiānɡ said:
"Not so.
For a man of your age,
after three days of intercourse,
your vital essence can be restored;
even with a fox-spirit, what harm is there?
If one were to be depleted daily,
humans can be worse than fox-spirits.
All the consumptive corpses and sickly ghosts in the world,
are they all bewitched to death by fox-spirits?
Nevertheless,
there must be someone speaking ill of me."
Sānɡ-sheng strongly denied it,
but Lián questioned him even more insistently.
Sānɡ-sheng had no choice
but to reveal it.
Lián said:
"I wondered why you were so exhausted!
But how could it come to this?
Could it be that she is not human?
Don't say anything,
tomorrow night,
I will spy on her as she spied on me."
That night, Lǐ arrived,
and after only a few words,
she heard a cough outside the window,
and hurried away.
Lián entered and said:
"My lord, you are in danger!
She is truly a ghost!
If you indulge in her beauty and do not quickly break it off,
the path to the underworld is near!"
Sānɡ-sheng thought she was jealous,
and remained silent.
Lián said:
"I know you cannot forget your feelings,
but I cannot bear to see you die.
Tomorrow,
I will bring medicine
to eliminate the yin poison for you.
Fortunately, the root of the illness is still shallow,
and in ten days your ailment should be cured.
Please share the same bed so I can monitor your recovery."
The next night,
she indeed produced a small dose of medicine and gave it to Sānɡ-sheng to eat.
In a moment,
he experienced three or two bowel movements,
and felt his internal organs become clear and empty,
and his spirit instantly refreshed.
Although he appreciated her kindness,
he still didn't believe she was a ghost.
Liánxiāng shared his bed every night;
he desired to couple with her,
but she always stopped him.
A few days later,
her skin became plump and full.
When she was about to leave,
she earnestly warned him to break off with Lǐ.
He falsely agreed.
When he closed the door and lit the lamp,
he would always grasp Lǐ's slipper and ponder.
Lǐ suddenly arrived.
After several days of separation,
she showed some resentment.
He said:
"She has been my shaman-healer for several nights.
Please do not be resentful;
my affections are with you."
Lǐ was somewhat pleased.
He whispered to her on the pillow:
"I love you very much,
but someone called you a ghost."
Lǐ was tongue-tied for a long time,
then cursed:
"It must be the seductive fox confusing you! If you don't cut her off,
I will not come again!"
Thereupon, she whimpered and cried.
He used a hundred words to comfort and appease her,
and only then did she stop.
The next night,
Liánxiāng arrived.
Knowing that Lǐ had come again,
she angrily said:
"Do you truly wish to die?!"
He smiled and said:
"Why are you so deeply jealous?"
Lián grew even angrier and said:
"You are cultivating a root of death;
I am removing it for you.
If I were not jealous, what then?"
He made an excuse to joke, saying:
"She said that my illness the other day
was due to a fox spirit."
Lián then sighed and said:
"If it is truly as you say,
and you are so deluded and unawakened,
should anything unforeseen happen,
how can I defend myself with a hundred mouths?
Please allow me to take my leave from this moment.
After a hundred days,
I will visit you in your bed."
He could not make her stay,
and she left in a huff.
From then on, he and Lǐ were always together, morning and night.
After about two months,
he felt extremely fatigued.
At first, he still tried to reassure himself;
but day by day, he grew thinner and weaker,
consuming only a bowl of porridge.
He wanted to return home to be cared for,
but still lingered, unable to bear to leave immediately.
After several days of delay,
he became so ill he could no longer rise.
His neighbor, seeing his illness and debility,
daily sent a servant from his residence to deliver food and drink.
It was then that he began to suspect Lǐ,
and said to Lǐ:
"I regret not listening to Liánxiāng's words,
to have come to this!"
After speaking, he closed his eyes and became unconscious.
After a while, he revived,
opened his eyes, and looked around,
but Lǐ had already left,
and from then on, they were estranged.
He lay weak in his empty study,
longing for Liánxiāng as if awaiting the new year.
One day,
as he was deep in thought,
someone suddenly drew aside the curtain and entered—
it was Liánxiāng.
She stood by the bed and smiled, saying:
"My country bumpkin,
was I wrong?!"
He choked with sobs for a long time,
confessed his guilt,
and only begged for salvation.
Lián said:
"The illness has reached the vital organs;
there is truly no cure.
I only came to bid an eternal farewell,
to show that it was not out of jealousy."
He was greatly saddened and said:
"There is an object under my pillow;
please smash it for me."
Lián found the slipper,
held it to the lamp,
and repeatedly turned it over and examined it.
Miss Lǐ entered,
and suddenly seeing Liánxiāng,
turned to flee.
Lián blocked the door with her body,
and Lǐ, distressed and urgent, did not know what to do.
He reproached her,
but Lǐ could not reply.
Lián smiled and said:
"I can finally confront you, Auntie.
You once said that the gentleman's previous illness
might not have been caused by me.
What about now?"
Lǐ bowed her head and apologized.
Lián said:
"So beautiful,
yet you sow enmity with love?"
Lǐ immediately threw herself to the ground and wept,
begging for pity and rescue.
Lián then helped her up
and questioned her in detail about her life.
She said:
"I am
the daughter of Judge Lǐ (Lǐ Tōngpàn),
who died young and
was buried outside the wall.
Like a silkworm that has died,
its threads are not yet exhausted.
To be intimate with the gentleman
is my wish;
to cause the gentleman's death
is truly not my original intention."
Lián said:
"I have heard that ghosts benefit from people's deaths,
as they can then be together forever after death.
Is that true?"
She said:
"Not true.
Two ghosts meeting
have no joy;
if there were joy,
would there be so few young gentlemen in the underworld?!"
Lián said:
"How foolish!
Doing it every night,
even a human cannot endure it,
let alone a ghost!"
Lǐ asked:
"Foxes can cause death;
why are you the only one who does not?"
Lián said:
"Those are of the 'essence-sucking' type;
I am not of that kind.
Therefore, there are foxes in the world that do not harm people,
but there are definitely no ghosts that do not harm people,
because their yin energy is too strong."
He heard her words,
and only then knew that both foxes and ghosts were real.
Fortunately, he was accustomed to seeing them often,
and was not particularly alarmed.
But remembering his remaining breath was like a thread,
he could not help but cry out in great pain.
Lián turned to ask:
"How should Lángjūn be treated?"
Lǐ Nǎnrán demurred and gave thanks.
Lián smiled and said:
"I'm afraid Láng is strong and healthy,
and the jealous wife wants to eat yángméi."
Lǐ adjusted her clothing and said:
"If there were a physician skilled enough to save the country,
to allow this concubine to not fail Lángjūn,
I would readily bury my head in the ground,
how would I dare to act thus in the human world again!"
Lián opened her pouch and took out medicine,
saying:
"I knew early on that this day would come;
after we parted, I gathered herbs from the Three Mountains,
and after three months,
the materials were finally complete.
Even if a person is dying from tuberculosis or an evil enchantment,
there is none who does not revive when given this.
However, how the illness was contracted,
and what it should be taken with,
still requires me to seek assistance."
She asked:
"What is needed?"
She said:
"Just a drop of fragrant saliva from your cherry-like mouth.
When I administer one pill,
please connect your mouth and spit on it."
Lǐ's cheeks flushed,
and she lowered her head, turning to look at her shoes.
Lián playfully said:
"My sister's only pride is her shoes!"
Lǐ became even more ashamed,
looking down and up as if she had no place to hide.
Lián said:
"This is a familiar skill from ordinary times,
why are you so reluctant now?"
So she placed a pill into Shēng's mouth,
and urged her to spit.
Lǐ, having no choice,
spat on it.
Lián said:
"Again!"
And she spat again.
After three or four spits,
the pill had already been swallowed.
A short while later,
her abdomen rumbled like thunder.
Lián placed another pill,
and then put her lips to Shēng's and breathed air into her.
Shēng felt a fiery heat in her Dāntián,
and her spirit was invigorated.
Lián said:
"You are cured!"
Lǐ heard the cock crow,
and anxiously departed.
Lián, because of the recent recovery,
still needed recuperation,
and eating outside was not advisable;
so she locked the door from the outside,
falsely indicating that Shēng had returned,
to cut off visitors,
and guarded her day and night.
Lǐ also came every evening,
attending to her diligently,
treating Lián like an older sister.
Lián also deeply cherished and loved her.
After three months,
Shēng was as healthy as before.
Lǐ then failed to come for several evenings;
occasionally, she would come,
look once and leave immediately.
When they were together,
she was also dejected and unhappy.
Lián often asked her to stay and sleep together,
but she would always refuse.
Shēng chased her out,
picked her up and carried her back,
her body as light as a straw effigy.
The woman could not escape,
so she put on her clothes and lay down,
her body no more than two feet long.
Lián felt even more pity for her,
and secretly encouraged Shēng to embrace her intimately,
but even shaking her could not wake her.
Shēng fell asleep;
when he awoke and looked for her,
she was already gone.
More than ten days later,
she never returned.
Shēng missed her deeply,
and constantly took out her shoes to play with.
Lián said:
"So graceful and delicate,
even I feel pity,
let alone a man."
Shēng said:
"In the past, when I played with her shoes, she would come,
I was indeed suspicious,
but I never expected her to be a ghost.
Now, looking at her shoes and thinking of her face,
I am truly heartbroken."
Thereupon, tears fell.
Formerly,
a wealthy family surnamed Zhāng 張 had a daughter named Yàn’ér 燕兒.
She was fifteen years old
when she died without sweating.
She revived after a full night,
and rose, looking about as if to run away.
Zhāng 張 barred the door,
and she could not go out.
The girl said to herself:
"I am the soul of the Prefect's daughter.
I was touched by Sāng Láng's 桑郎 affection,
and my slippers are still there.
I am truly a ghost,
what good is it to lock me up?"
Because her words seemed to have a reason,
they questioned her about how she came to be there.
The girl looked back and forth,
utterly bewildered and unable to explain herself.
Someone said that Sāngshēng 桑生 had fallen ill and returned home,
but the girl argued fiercely that this was false.
The family grew very suspicious.
A scholar from the east neighbor heard of it,
climbed over the wall to peek,
and saw the scholar speaking to a beautiful woman;
he entered stealthily to get closer,
but in the commotion, she had already disappeared.
The neighbor scholar questioned him in alarm.
The scholar laughed and said:
"I told you earlier,
if it's a female, I will take her in."
The neighbor scholar recounted Yàn’ér's 燕兒 words.
The scholar then opened the gate,
intending to go investigate,
but found no way.
Zhāng Mǔ 張母 heard that the scholar had indeed not returned home,
and was even more surprised.
She then sent a maid to search for the slipper,
and the scholar took it out and gave it to her.
Yàn’ér 燕兒 was delighted to get it.
She tried it on,
but the shoe was an inch smaller than her foot,
which greatly startled her.
She looked in the mirror at herself,
and suddenly realized with a flash of insight that she had borrowed a body to live,
and then explained the whole story.
Only then did the mother believe her.
The girl cried loudly into the mirror, saying:
"My appearance that day
was quite confident,
but whenever I saw Lián Jiě 蓮姊,
I felt even more ashamed.
Now I am like this,
a human is not even as good as her ghost!"
She held the slipper and wailed, and could not be comforted.
She covered herself with a quilt and lay stiffly.
When offered food,
she did not eat either,
and her body and skin became completely swollen;
she did not eat for seven days in all,
but did not die in the end,
and the swelling gradually subsided;
feeling unbearable hunger,
she then ate again.
After several days,
her whole body became itchy,
and all her skin peeled off.
One morning,
she woke up,
her bedroom slipper had fallen off,
she sought to put it on,
but it was now immensely huge.
Then she tried on the previous slipper,
and it fit perfectly,
which made her happy.
She looked in the mirror again,
and her eyebrows, eyes, chin, and cheeks
were exactly like her former self,
making her even happier.
She washed and combed herself and saw her mother,
and all who saw her were struck with wonder.
Liánxiāng 蓮香 heard of her strangeness,
and urged the scholar to act as a matchmaker;
but due to the vast disparity in wealth,
she dared not proceed quickly.
It happened that the old woman was having her first birthday celebration,
and so she went with her son-in-law
to offer congratulations.
The old woman saw the scholar's name,
and so she sent Yàn’ér 燕兒 to peer through the curtain and mark the guests.
The scholar arrived last,
and the girl rushed out,
grabbed his sleeve,
wanting to go home with him.
Her mother scolded her,
and she finally went back inside, ashamed.
The scholar looked closely and saw she was exactly as before,
and could not help but shed tears,
then he prostrated himself and did not rise.
The old woman helped him up,
not taking it as an insult.
When the scholar went out,
he asked the girl's uncle to act as a go-between.
The old woman discussed choosing an auspicious day for the scholar to marry into the family.
The scholar returned and told Liánxiāng 蓮香,
and discussed what to do.
Lián 蓮 was dejected for a long time,
and then wanted to leave.
The scholar was greatly alarmed and cried.
Lián 蓮 said:
"If you perform a wedding ceremony in another's house,
and I follow along,
what face would I have?"
The scholar planned to first return to his hometown with her,
and then welcome Yàn 燕,
and Lián 蓮 agreed.
The scholar explained the situation to Zhāng 張.
Zhāng 張 heard he already had a wife,
and angrily reproached him.
Yàn’ér 燕兒 strongly argued for him,
and so it was done as requested.
On the day,
the scholar personally went to welcome her.
The preparations at home
were quite simple;
but upon returning,
from the gate to the hall,
everything was covered with carpets,
and hundreds and thousands of candles
were brilliantly arranged like brocade.
Liánxiāng 蓮香 helped the new bride into the wedding chamber,
and when the veil was lifted,
they were as happy as they had been in life.
Lián 蓮 accompanied them in drinking the nuptial cup,
and then subtly questioned her about the strangeness of her return from death.
Yàn 燕 said:
"That day I was depressed and bored,
simply because I was a different being,
I felt my form was defiled.
After parting, I was indignant and did not return to my grave,
drifting and floating with the wind.
Whenever I saw a living person, I envied them.
By day I relied on plants and trees,
by night I floated freely.
I happened to come to the Zhāng 張 family's house,
and saw a young girl lying on the bed,
I approached and attached myself to her,
not knowing I could then live."
Lián 蓮 heard this,
and was silently contemplative.
More than two months later,
Lián 蓮 gave birth to a son,
and after childbirth, she suddenly fell ill,
daily growing weaker.
She grasped Yàn's 燕 arm and said:
"I dare to burden you with this illegitimate child,
my son is your son."
Yàn 燕 wept,
and tried to comfort her.
She called for a shaman doctor,
but Lián 蓮 always refused.
Her chronic illness lingered,
her breath hanging by a thread.
The scholar and Yàn’ér 燕兒 both cried.
Suddenly she opened her eyes and said:
"Don't do that!
You enjoy living,
I enjoy dying.
If there is fate,
we may see each other again in ten years."
Having spoken, she died.
When they opened the quilt to prepare the body for burial,
the corpse transformed into a fox.
The scholar could not bear to look at it differently,
and gave it a grand burial.
The son was named Hú'ér 狐兒 (Fox-son),
and Yàn 燕 raised him as her own.
Every Qīngmíng 清明 Festival,
she would certainly hold the child and cry at his grave.
Hòushēng was recommended by his乡 (xiāng) (local community),
and his family gradually prospered.
However, Yàn suffered from infertility.
Hú'ér was quite intelligent,
but frail and often ill.
Yàn often wanted to get a concubine for Hòushēng.
One day,
a maid suddenly announced:
"An old woman is at the gate,
bringing her daughter to sell."
Yàn called them in.
Hòushēng saw her and
exclaimed in great surprise:
"Liánjiě has appeared again!"
Hòushēng looked at her,
she truly resembled Liánjiě,
and he was also astonished.
He asked:
"How old is she?"
She replied:
"Fourteen."
"How much is the bride price?"
She said:
"This old body has only this one piece of flesh.
As long as she finds a good match,
and I can also get a place to eat,
so that my old bones won't be left in a ditch in the future,
that's enough."
Hòushēng paid a generous price and kept her.
Yàn took the girl's hand,
entered a private room,
cupped her chin and smiled, saying:
"Do you recognize me?"
She replied:
"I don't recognize you."
Yàn asked her surname,
and she said:
"My surname is Wéi.
My father was a juice seller in Xúchéng,
and he died three years ago."
Yàn counted on her fingers and pondered;
it had been exactly fourteen years since Lián's death.
She then carefully examined the girl,
whose appearance and demeanor
were strikingly similar in every way.
So she patted her head and cried out:
"Liánjiě,
Liánjiě!
The ten-year promise to meet
must not deceive me!"
The girl suddenly seemed to wake from a dream,
and exclaimed with sudden realization:
"Yí!"
She stared closely at Yàn'ér.
Hòushēng smiled and said:
"This is 'it seems I've met her before, and the swallow has returned'
indeed."
The girl's eyes brimmed with tears as she said:
"It is so.
I heard my mother say
that when I was born, I could speak,
which was considered inauspicious,
so I was made to drink dog's blood,
and consequently forgot my past life's karma.
Only today have I truly awakened as if from a dream.
Madam, are you Lǐ Mèi, who was ashamed to be a ghost?"
They talked about their previous life together,
with both joy and sorrow.
One day,
during the Hánshí (Cold Food) Festival,
Yàn said:
"This is the day every year when my husband and I weep for my sister."
So she went with her husband to her tomb;
the wild grass was luxuriant,
and the trees had already grown thick.
The girl also sighed deeply.
Yàn said to Hòushēng:
"My sister Liánjiě and I
shared a deep affection for two lifetimes,
and I cannot bear to be separated from her.
It is fitting that our bones should rest in the same grave."
Hòushēng agreed,
opened Lǐ's tomb, retrieved the bones,
and carried them back for a joint burial.
Relatives and friends heard of this unusual event,
and came in auspicious attire to the grave.
Hundreds of people gathered unexpectedly.
In the Gēngxū (year), I traveled south to Yí,
was delayed by rain,
and rested in an inn.
There was a Mr. Liú Zǐjìng,
whose cousin was the author Wáng Zǐzhāng,
who wrote the Biography of Sāngshēng,
about ten thousand words,
which I managed to finish reading.
This is merely an outline of it.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"Alas!
The dead seek to live,
and the living seek to die.
What is truly difficult to obtain in this world
is not a human body?
Yet, those who possess this body
often neglect it,
leading to a life worse than a fox,
and a death worse than a ghost."
Based on the Chùxuězhāi (Studio of Stored Snow) manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì (Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio).
Sūn Zǐchǔ from Yuèxī,
was a famous scholar.
He was born with supernumerary fingers.
His nature was hesitant and inarticulate;
when people tricked him,
he would always believe it to be true.
If he happened to be where there were singing girls,
he would invariably look away and retreat.
Some, knowing this about him,
would coax him to come,
and have the girls flirt and press close to him.
Then his face would turn crimson down to his neck,
and drops of sweat would trickle down.
People would laugh at him together.
Thus, they depicted his foolish appearance,
and spread ugly stories about him by post,
calling him
"Sūn Chī" (Foolish Sūn).
In the district, there was a wealthy merchant, a certain old man,
whose wealth rivaled that of princes and nobles.
His relatives were all distinguished gentry.
He had a daughter, Ābǎo,
who was of peerless beauty.
Every day, he selected a good match for her,
and sons of prominent families competed to offer betrothal gifts,
but none pleased the old man.
Sūn Zǐchǔ was unpartnered at the time,
and some, playing a joke on him,
urged him to engage a matchmaker.
Sūn Zǐchǔ, without truly considering his own unsuitability,
indeed followed their advice.
The old man had long heard of his reputation,
but disdained his poverty.
As the matchmaker was leaving,
she happened to meet Ābǎo,
who asked about it,
and the matchmaker told her.
The girl jokingly said:
"If he removes his supernumerary fingers,
I will marry him."
The matchmaker told Sūn Zǐchǔ.
Sūn Zǐchǔ said:
"That's not difficult."
After the matchmaker left,
Sūn Zǐchǔ used an axe to chop off his own fingers,
suffering immense pain that pierced his heart,
and blood poured out profusely;
he was on the verge of death.
After several days,
he was finally able to get up,
and went to see the matchmaker to show her.
The matchmaker was astonished.
She rushed to tell the girl.
The girl was also surprised,
and jokingly asked him to also get rid of his foolishness.
Sūn Zǐchǔ heard this and vehemently argued,
claiming that he was not foolish;
however, he had no way to meet her and explain himself.
He then reconsidered, thinking that Ābǎo might not be as beautiful as a celestial being,
so why did she place herself so highly?
From then on, his former desire cooled considerably.
Shēng, after leaving his sickbed,
sat and stood, lost in thought,
absent-mindedly as if in a daze.
He constantly sought to observe Ābǎo,
hoping to encounter her again.
On the Bathing Buddha Festival,
he heard that she would be coming to Xiāngshuǐyuè Sì,
so he went early in the morning and waited by the roadside,
his eyes strained and weary.
By midday,
the young woman finally arrived,
and from inside her carriage, she caught sight of Shēng.
She used her hand to lift the curtain,
gazing fixedly without turning away.
Shēng's heart pounded even more,
and he followed behind her.
The young woman suddenly ordered a maid in green to come and ask his name.
Shēng earnestly introduced himself,
his soul trembling even more.
When the carriage departed,
he finally returned home.
Upon returning, he fell ill again,
utterly refusing food,
and constantly calling out Ābǎo's name in his dreams.
He frequently regretted that his soul was no longer as efficacious as before.
His family had long kept a parrot,
which suddenly died,
and a child was playing with it by the bed.
Shēng thought to himself: "If only I could become a parrot,
I could fly to the young woman's chamber with a flap of my wings."
As his heart was intently focused on this thought,
his body already transformed into a parrot,
and he quickly flew away,
straight to Ābǎo's abode.
The young woman was delighted and caught it,
locking its leg,
and feeding it hemp seeds.
The parrot loudly cried out:
"Elder Sister, do not lock me!
I am Sūn Zǐchǔ!"
The young woman was greatly startled,
released its leg,
but it still did not leave.
The young woman vowed, saying:
"Deep affection is already engraved in my heart.
But now that we are of different species, human and bird,
how can our marital union be fulfilled again?"
The bird said:
"To be close to your fragrant presence
is already enough to fulfill my wish."
When others fed it,
it would not eat;
but when the young woman fed it herself,
it would eat.
When the young woman sat,
it would perch on her knee;
when she lay down,
it would stay by her bed.
This continued for three days.
The young woman felt great pity for him,
and secretly sent someone to inquire.
It turned out that Shēng was lying stiff,
his breath having ceased for three days,
but his heart was not yet cold.
The young woman then vowed again:
"If you can become a human again,
I will vow to follow you until death."
The bird said:
"You are deceiving me!"
The young woman then swore an oath herself.
The bird tilted its head as if in thought.
After a short while,
the young woman bound her feet,
and took off her shoes beneath the bed.
The parrot suddenly flew down,
picked up a shoe in its beak and flew away.
The young woman urgently called out to it,
but it had already flown far away.
The young woman sent an old woman to investigate,
and Shēng had already woken up.
His family saw the parrot come with the embroidered shoe,
fall to the ground and die,
and they were all surprised by this.
After Shēng recovered,
he immediately asked for the shoe.
No one knew why.
Just then, the old woman arrived,
entered to see Shēng,
and asked where the shoe was.
Shēng said:
"This is the token of Ābǎo's solemn vow.
Please convey this message to her: 'This young man will not forget her golden promise.'"
The old woman returned and reported.
The young woman was even more astonished,
so she had her maid secretly reveal her feelings to her mother.
Her mother confirmed it,
and then said:
"This young man's talent and reputation are not bad,
but he has the poverty of Sīmǎ Xiāngrú.
To choose a son-in-law like this after several years,
I fear we will be laughed at by the prominent families."
Because of the shoe, the young woman
vowed not to marry anyone else.
The old man and old woman (her parents) assented.
They quickly sent word to Shēng.
Shēng was delighted,
and his illness immediately recovered.
The old man suggested he become a live-in son-in-law.
The young woman said:
"A son-in-law should not stay long at his wife's family home.
Moreover, the young man is poor,
and staying longer will only make him more despised.
Since your daughter has given her word,
she will be content to live in a humble dwelling and eat simple fare,
without complaint."
Shēng then personally went to receive her and the wedding ceremony was performed,
they met with joy as if from a past life.
Thereafter, their household gained wealth from Yànzhuāng,
and prospered slightly,
their property increasing considerably.
But Shēng was obsessed with books,
and did not know how to manage household affairs or business;
the young woman was good at accumulating wealth,
and did not burden Shēng with other matters.
After three years,
their family became even wealthier.
Shēng suddenly fell ill with xiāokě (diabetes),
and died.
The young woman wept bitterly,
her tear-filled eyes never clearing,
to the point of forsaking sleep and food.
When advised, she would not listen,
and tried to hang herself during the night.
A maid discovered her,
quickly rescued her, and she revived,
but still did not eat.
Three days later,
relatives and friends gathered,
planning to bury Shēng.
Suddenly, a groan and gasp were heard from the coffin,
they opened it,
and he had already revived.
He said:
"I saw the King of the Underworld,
who, because of my lifelong simplicity and sincerity,
ordered me to serve as a clerk.
Suddenly, someone reported: 'Sūn Bùcáo's wife is arriving.'
The King checked the ghost records,
and said: 'This one is not supposed to die yet.'
Someone then reported: 'She has not eaten for three days.'
The King looked and said: 'Moved by your wife's integrity and loyalty,
I shall grant you rebirth.'
Then he ordered an escort to bring me back on horseback."
From this, his health gradually recovered.
During the imperial examination year,
before entering the examination hall,
some young men played a trick on him,
jointly devising seven obscure and recondite topics,
and took Shēng to a secluded place to speak with him,
saying:
"These are the crucial points from a certain influential family,
which we respectfully and secretly impart to you."
Shēng believed them,
and pondered day and night,
producing seven essays.
The others secretly laughed at him.
At that time, the chief examiner was concerned about the malpractice of plagiarism with familiar topics,
and deliberately went against conventional practices.
When the examination papers were distributed,
all seven essays matched the topics.
Shēng thus achieved the top rank.
The following year,
he passed the imperial examination to become a *jìnshì*,
and was appointed to the literary academy.
The emperor heard of this unusual event,
and summoned him for an audience.
Shēng recounted everything in detail.
The emperor was greatly pleased.
Later, he summoned Ābǎo;
and bestowed upon her generous rewards.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"When one is obsessed, their will becomes focused,
thus a bookworm's writing will surely be skillful,
and an art enthusiast's technique will surely be excellent;
those who drift idly in the world without accomplishment
all claim not to be obsessed.
Furthermore, consider those who squander their family fortune on women,
or ruin their household on gambling —
are these not the acts of the obsessed?
From this, we know that excessive cleverness
is actually true obsession.
How could that Sūn Zǐchǔ be considered obsessed?!"
Ten types of 'obsession' are collected here:
"Hoarding money while people are poor.
Always boasting about one's child's intelligence to guests.
Loving one's child so much that one cannot bear to make them study.
Hiding an illness for fear of others knowing.
Investing money to lead others to prostitution.
Secretly attending banquets to entice others to gamble.
Hiring someone to write essays to deceive one's father and elder brothers."
Fùzǐ zhàngmù tàiqīng.
Jiātíng yòng jīxiè.
Xǐ dìzǐ shàndǔ. ”

Fùzé jù Shāndōng Bówùguǎn cáng 703 hào chāoběn bǔ
Cáozhōu Lǐ xìng zhě,
yì zhūshēng.
Jiā sù ráo.
Ér jūzhái gù bù shèn guǎng;
shè hòu yǒu yuán shù mǔ,
huāngzhì zhī.
Yīrì,
yǒu sǒu láishuō wū,
chū zhí bǎijīn.
Lǐ yǐ wú wū wéi cí.
Sǒu yuē:
“Qǐng shòu zhī,
dàn wú fánlǜ.”
Lǐ bù yù qí yì,
gū shòu zhī,
yǐ zhān qí yì.
Yuè rì,
cūnrén jiàn yúmǎ juànkǒu rù Lǐ jiā,
fēnfēn shèn huǒ,
gòng yí Lǐ dì wú āndùn suǒ,
wèn zhī.
Lǐ shū bù zì zhī;
guī ér chá zhī,
bìng wú jī xiǎng.
Guò shùrì,
sǒu hū lái yè.
Qiě yún:
“Bì zì xià yǐ shù chénxī.
Shìshì dōu cǎochuàng,
qǐ lú zuò zào,
wèi xiá yī xiū kèzǐ lǐ.
Jīn qiǎn xiǎonǚbèi zuò shǔ,
xìng yī chuígù.”
Lǐ cóng zhī.
Zé rù yuán zhōng,
chū jiàn shèyǔ huáhǎo,
zhǎnrán yī xīn.
Rùshì,
chénshè fānglì.
Jiǔ dǐng fèi yú láng xià,
cháyān niǎoyú chú zhōng.
Ér'ér xíngjiǔ jiànzhuàn,
bèi jí gānzhǐ.
Shí jiàn tíng xià shàoniánrén,
wǎnglái shèn zhòng.
Yòu wén érnǚ yóngyóng,
mù zhōng zuò xiàoyǔ shēng.
Jiārén bìpú,
sì yǒu shùshíbǎikǒu.
Lǐ xīnzhī qí hú.
Xí zhōng ér guī,
yīn huái shāxīn.
Měi rù shì,
shì xiāoliú,
jī shùbǎijīn,
àn bù yuán zhōng dàimǎn.
Zhòuhuǒ zhī,
yàn gèng xiāohàn,
rú hēilíngzhī,
fán chòu huīmí bùkě jìn;
dàn wén míngtí háodòng zhī shēng,
cáozá guā'ěr.
Jì xī rù shì,
zé sǐhú mǎndì,
jiāotóulàné zhě,
bùkě shèngjì.
Fāng yuèshì jiān,
sǒu zìwài lái,
yánsè cǎntòng,
zé Lǐ yuē:
“Sù wú xiányuàn;
huāngyuán bàosuì bǎijīn,
fēi shǎo;
hé rěn suì xiāngzúmiè?”
Cǐ qí cǎn zhī chóu,
wú bù bào zhě!”
Fènnán ér qù.
Yí qí zhílì wéi yāng,
ér nián yú wú shǎo guàiyì.
Shí Shùnzhì chūnián,
shānzhōng qúndào qiètā,
xiàojù wànyúrén,
guān mò néng bǔ.
Shēng yǐ jiākǒu duō,
rì yōu líluàn.
Shì cūn zhōng lái yī xīngzhě,
zì hào:
“Nánshān Wēng,”
yán réntǐ jiù,
liǎoruò mùdǔ,
míng dàzào.
Lǐ zhào zhì jiā,
qiú tuī jiǎzǐ.
Wēng èrán qǐjìng,
yuē:
“Cǐ zhēnzhǔ yě!”
Lǐ wén dàhài,
yǐwéi wàng.
Wēng zhèngróng gùyán zhī.
Lǐ yíxìn bàn yān,
nǎi yuē:
“Qǐ yǒu báishǒu shòumìng ér dì zhě hū?”
Wēng wèi:
“Bùrán.
Zìgǔ dìwáng,
lèi duō qǐ yú pǐfū,
shuí shì shēng ér tiānzǐ zhě?”
Shēng huò zhī,
qián xí ér qǐng.
Wēng yìrán yǐ
“Wòlóng”
zìrèn.
Qǐng xiān bèi jiǎzhòu shùqiān jù, gōngnǔ shùqiān shì.
Lǐ lǜ rén mò zhī guī.
Wēng yuē:
“Chén qǐng wéi dàwáng lián zhūshān,
shēn xiāngjié.
Shǐ huāyán zhě wèi dàwáng zhēn tiānzǐ,
shānzhōng shìzú,
yí bì xiǎngyìng.”
Lǐ xǐ,
qiǎn Wēng xíng.
Fā cángqiáng,
zào jiǎzhòu.
Wēng shùrì shǐ huán,
yuē:
“Jiè dàwáng wēifú,
jiā chén sāncùn shé,
zhūshān mò bù yuàn zhíbīanxí,
cóng xì xià.”
Jiáxún zhī jiān,
guǒ guīmìng zhě shùqiān rén.
Yúshì bài Wēng wéi jūnshī;
jiàn dà,
shè cǎizhì ruò lín;
jù shān lì zhà,
shēngshì zhèndòng.
Yì lìng shuàibīng láitǎo,
Wēng zhǐhuī qúnkòu,
dàpò zhī.
Lìng jù,
gàojí yú Yǎn.
Chōng bīng yuǎnshè ér zhì,
Wēng yòu fúkòu jìnjī,
bīng dàkuì,
jiàngshì shāshāng zhě shènzhòng.
Shì yì zhèn,
dǎng yǐ wànjì,
yīn zìlì wèi
“Jiǔshān Wáng.”
Wēng huàn mǎ shǎo,
huì dūzhōng jiě mǎ fù Jiāngnán,
qiǎn yī lǚ yàolù cuànqǔ zhī.
Yóushì
“Jiǔshān Wáng”
zhī míng dàzào.
Jiā Wēng wèi
“Hùguó Dàjiāngjūn.”
Gāowò shāncháo,
gōngrán zìfù,
yǐwéi huángpáo zhī jiā,
zhǐrì kěsì yǐ.
Dōng Fǔ yǐ duómǎ gù,
fāng jiāng jìnjiǎo;
yòu dé Yǎn bào,
nǎi fā jīngbīng shùqiān,
yǔ liù dào héwéi ér jìn.
Jūnlǚ jīngqí,
mímǎn shāngǔ.
“Jiǔshān Wáng”
dàjù,
zhào Wēng móu zhī,
zé bùzhī suǒ wǎng.
“Jiǔshān Wáng”
jiǒngjí wú shù,
dēng shān ér wàng yuē:
“Jīné zhī cháotíng zhī shì dà yǐ!”
Shān pò,
bèiqín,
qīnú lù zhī.
Shǐ wù Wēng jí lǎohú,
gài yǐ zúmiè bào Lǐ yě.
Yìshǐshì said:
