"When a person embraces his wife and children,
shuts his door, and removes his headwear,
where can he be murdered?
Even if he were murdered,
how could his clan be wiped out?
The fox's scheme was indeed clever.
But if the soil does not contain the seeds,
they will not grow, even if watered.
The cruelty of that man in killing the foxes,
a root of thievery already lay in his heart,
so the fox was able to nurture its sprout and enact its revenge.
Now, try to seize a passerby and tell him: 'You are the Son of Heaven!'
None would not be terrified and flee.
Clearly leading him to an act that would exterminate his clan,
yet he still happily listened.
His wife and children were slaughtered,
so what more is there to say?
However, when people listen to false words,
they are at first angry upon hearing them,
then doubtful,
and then they believe them.
By the time their reputation and life are both destroyed,
they finally realize their mistake.
This is generally how it is."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Qīu Gōng of Zhūchéng was the Dào of Zūnhuà.
There were many foxes in his yámen.
In the innermost building,
a large family of foxes lived
as if it were their home.
They often caused trouble for people,
and banishing them only made them more rampant.
Officials who served here only offered sacrifices and prayed to them,
none dared to move them.
When Qīu Gōng took office,
he heard about it and was enraged.
The foxes, also fearing the Duke's resolute nature,
transformed into an old woman and told the family servants:
"Please tell the Master: do not make enemies with us.
Allow us three days,
and we will take our little ones and leave."
The Duke heard this,
and also remained silent.
The next day,
after inspecting the troops,
he ordered them not to intentionally damage anything,
but to have all the large cannons from the various camps quickly carried in,
and fire a thousand rounds simultaneously surrounding the building.
The several-rèn-high building
was instantly reduced to flat ground.
Hides, flesh, fur, and blood
rained down from the sky.
Amidst the dense dust and poisonous mist,
a wisp of white qi was seen,
piercing through the smoke and rising into the sky.
The crowd looked at it and said:
"One fox escaped."
And the yámen was peaceful ever after.
Two years later,
the Duke dispatched trusted servants with a certain amount of silver to the capital,
planning for a promotion.
Before the matter was settled,
he temporarily stored the silver in a yámen runner's house.
Suddenly, a villager went to the imperial court to complain,
stating that his wife and children had been unjustly murdered.
He also accused the Duke of embezzling military provisions,
currying favor with influential people,
and currently storing [the silver] at a certain family's house,
which could be verified.
An imperial decree ordered an investigation.
Upon arriving at the yámen runner's house,
they searched thoroughly but found nothing.
The old man merely tapped the ground with one foot, and they understood his meaning,
dug it up,
and indeed found the silver.
Engraved on the silver were the characters
"Dispatched by a certain commandery."
Afterwards, they looked for the old man,
but he was nowhere to be found.
They inquired about his identity using his village and local name,
but he simply did not exist.
The Duke consequently suffered misfortune.
Only then did he realize that the old man was the escaped fox.
Yìshǐshì said:
"The foxes' harming people
is indeed punishable by death.
However, to subdue them and then let them go
would also complete our benevolence.
The Duke could be said to be
'too excessive in his hatred.'
Furthermore, if Guānxī had done this,
how could a hundred foxes have achieved such excellence!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
There was a man from Yù named Zhāng,
whose ancestors were from Qí.
At the end of the Míng dynasty, Qí was in great chaos,
and his wife was abducted by northern soldiers.
Zhāng often traveled to Yù,
and so settled there.
He married in Yù
and had a son named Nè.
Not long after,
his wife died,
and he remarried,
having a son named Chéng with his second wife.
The second wife, Níu shì, was fierce,
and often resented Nè,
treating him like a slave,
feeding him bad vegetable scraps.
She made him cut firewood,
demanding one shoulder-load of firewood daily;
if he failed, she would beat, scold, and curse him,
which was unbearable.
She secretly kept sweets and delicacies for Chéng,
sending him to study with a tutor.
Chéng gradually grew up,
and was filial and kind to his siblings,
unable to bear his brother's hardship,
he secretly urged his mother.
His mother did not listen.
One day,
Nè went into the mountains to cut firewood,
but before finishing,
he encountered a great storm,
taking shelter under a cliff.
When the rain stopped, it was already dusk.
His stomach was very hungry,
so he carried the firewood home.
His mother inspected it, finding it insufficient,
and angrily refused to give him food.
Hunger burned in his heart,
and he entered his room and lay down stiffly.
Chéng came from the塾 (private school),
saw his brother looking listless,
and asked:
"Are you ill?"
He replied:
"Just hungry."
He asked the reason,
and Nè told him the situation.
Chéng looked distressed and immediately left.
After a moment,
he came back with a cake to feed his brother.
His brother asked where it came from.
He said:
"I stole some flour and asked a neighbor woman to make it;
just eat it and don't tell anyone."
Nè ate it.
He cautioned his brother, saying:
"Don't do this again in the future;
if it's found out, it will trouble you.
Besides, one meal a day,
I won't die of hunger."
Chéng said:
"Brother is naturally weak,
how can you cut so much firewood!"
The next day,
after eating,
he secretly went to the mountain,
to where his brother was cutting firewood.
His brother saw him,
and asked in surprise:
"What are you going to do?"
He replied:
"I'm going to help cut firewood."
He asked:
"Who sent you?"
He said:
"I came by myself."
His brother said:
"Regardless of whether you can cut firewood or not,
even if you could,
it's still not allowed."
So he urged him to return home.
Chéng did not listen,
and used his hands and feet to break firewood to help his brother.
He also said:
"Tomorrow I will bring an axe."
His brother approached to stop him.
Seeing that his fingers were already broken
and his shoes were worn through,
he sadly said:
"If you don't go home quickly,
I will immediately kill myself with the axe!"
Chéng then returned.
His brother saw him halfway,
and then turned back.
After gathering firewood,
he went to the private school,
and instructed his teacher, saying:
"My brother is young;
you should keep him indoors.
There are many tigers and wolves in the mountains."
The teacher said:
"I didn't know where he went before noon,
and I've already punished him with a switch."
[Nè] returned and said to Chéng:
“If you don’t listen to my words,
you’ll suffer a beating.”
Chéng laughed and said,
“No, I won’t.”
The next day,
he took an axe and went again.
His elder brother, Nà, was startled and said,
“I told you not to come;
why are you doing this again?”
Chéng did not answer,
but chopped firewood quickly,
sweat dripping from his chin without a moment’s rest.
When he had gathered a full bundle,
he returned without a word.
His master again rebuked him,
so he told him the truth.
The master sighed at his virtue,
and thereupon no longer forbade him.
His elder brother repeatedly tried to stop him,
but he ultimately did not listen.
One day,
while helping someone cut firewood in the mountains,
a tiger suddenly appeared.
Everyone was afraid and prostrated themselves.
The tiger actually carried Chéng away in its mouth.
The tiger walked slowly with the person on its back,
and Nà caught up.
Nà bravely struck it with his axe,
hitting its hip.
The tiger, in pain, ran wildly,
and could not be found or pursued.
Nà cried bitterly and returned.
The others tried to comfort him,
but his crying grew even more sorrowful.
He said,
“My brother
is not like other people’s brothers;
moreover, he died because of me,
how can I go on living?”
Thereupon, he used the axe to cut his own throat.
Everyone rushed to save him,
but the cut had already penetrated about an inch into the flesh,
blood flowed out like a gushing spring,
and he became dizzy and fainted.
Everyone was alarmed,
tore their clothes to bind the wound,
and together helped him home.
His mother cried and cursed, saying,
“You killed my son!
Do you want to disembowel yourself to make amends?”
Nà groaned and said,
“Mother, do not fret.
If my brother dies,
I will certainly not live!”
He was placed on a bed,
but the wound pain kept him from sleeping.
He only sat by the wall, crying day and night.
His father feared he too would die,
and occasionally went to his bed to feed him a little,
but Nà always cursed and rebuked him.
Nà then stopped eating,
and died three days later.
In the village, there was a shaman (wū) who could journey to the underworld (zǒu Wúcháng).
Nà met him on the way
and tearfully recounted his past suffering.
He then inquired about his brother’s whereabouts,
but the shaman said he hadn’t heard.
So he turned around and led Nà away.
They arrived at a great city (dūhuì),
and saw a man in a black robe (zào shān rén) coming out of the city.
The shaman wanted to stop him and ask on Nà’s behalf.
The black-robed man checked and examined a document from his pouch,
listing over a hundred men and women,
none of whom were listed as having committed a crime and being displayed.
The shaman suspected he was on another document.
The black-robed man said,
“This road is under my jurisdiction;
how could there be a mistake in arrest?”
Nà did not believe him and forced the shaman to enter the inner city.
Inside the city, new ghosts and old ghosts came and went bustling about,
and there were also old acquaintances.
He inquired of them,
but none knew.
Suddenly, they all exclaimed loudly,
“The Bodhisattva has arrived!”
Looking up, they saw in the clouds
a great personage,
whose brilliant light illuminated everything above and below.
The whole world instantly felt clear and bright.
The shaman congratulated him, saying,
“Dàláng, you are truly fortunate! A Bodhisattva enters the underworld (Míngsī) only once every few decades
to relieve all suffering and distress,
and you happen to be here now.”
He then pulled Nà to kneel.
The multitude of ghost prisoners, in a disorderly crowd,
clasped their hands and chanted in unison prayers for compassionate rescue from suffering,
their clamor shaking the earth.
The Bodhisattva sprinkled sweet dew (gānlù) everywhere with a willow branch,
fine as dust.
After a moment, the mist receded and the light gathered,
and he disappeared.
Nà felt dew on his neck,
and the axe wound no longer pained him.
The shaman still guided him to return together.
When they saw the village gate (lǐmén),
they parted.
Two days after Nà’s death,
he suddenly revived,
and recounted everything he had experienced,
saying that Chéng was not dead.
His mother thought he was fabricating a lie
and instead cursed and rebuked him.
Nà felt wronged but could not justify himself,
but when he touched the scar, it was indeed much better.
He managed to get up by himself,
bowed to his father, and said,
“I will soon traverse clouds and enter the sea to search for my brother.
If I cannot find him,
I will not hope to return for the rest of my life.
I wish father would still consider your son as dead.”
The old man (wēng) took him to an empty space and wept with him,
not daring to stop him.
Nà then left.
He would often inquire about his younger brother's whereabouts at busy crossroads.
His provisions and money ran out on the journey,
so he begged as he traveled.
Over a year later,
he reached Jīnlíng,
his clothes in a hundred tatters,
stooped on the road.
He chanced to see more than ten horsemen passing,
so he moved to the side of the road to avoid them.
One of them, like a high official,
was around forty years old,
with strong attendants and spirited horses
leaping back and forth.
A young man rode a small horse,
repeatedly looking at Nà.
Nà, thinking him a noble young master,
dared not look up.
The young man stopped his whip and paused for a moment,
then suddenly dismounted,
and called out:
"Is that not my elder brother?"
Nà raised his head and scrutinized him closely;
it was indeed Chéng.
They grasped hands and wept bitterly,
losing their voices.
Chéng also cried, saying:
"Brother, why have you become so destitute?"
Nà recounted his situation,
and Chéng became even more sorrowful.
The horsemen all dismounted and asked for the reason,
reporting it to the *gūancháng*.
The official ordered them to dismount a horse and carry Nà,
and they rode together back to his home,
where he was questioned in detail.
Initially,
when the tiger carried Chéng away,
it was unknown when it had put him down by the roadside.
He lay on the road for a night.
Just then, Zhāng Biéjià came from the capital.
He passed by and,
seeing his refined appearance,
pitied him and gently stroked him.
Chéng gradually regained consciousness.
When he spoke of his village,
it was already far away.
So, Zhāng Biéjià took him along and returned.
He also applied medicine to his wounds,
which healed after several days.
Zhāng Biéjià had no grown sons,
so he adopted him as a son.
It happened that Chéng was following him on a sightseeing trip.
Chéng fully informed his brother.
During their conversation,
Zhāng Biéjià entered.
Nà bowed and thanked him profusely.
Chéng went inside,
brought out silk clothes,
and presented them to his brother.
Then they set out wine for a banquet to converse.
Zhāng Biéjià asked:
"How many able-bodied men are there in your noble family in Yù?"
Nà replied:
"None.
My father was originally from Qí,
who came to reside in Yù as a wanderer."
Zhāng Biéjià said:
"I am also from Qí.
To which district does your village belong?"
He replied:
"I once heard my father say
it belonged to Dōngchāng's jurisdiction."
Zhāng Biéjià exclaimed in surprise:
"We are from the same hometown!
Why did you move to Yù?"
Nà replied:
"In the late Míng dynasty, Qīng soldiers entered the borders
and abducted my former mother.
My father suffered from the ravages of war
and lost his home and family.
He initially traded in the western regions,
traveling frequently,
so he settled there."
Zhāng Biéjià then asked in surprise:
"What is your esteemed father's name?"
Nà told him.
Zhāng Biéjià stared blankly,
then lowered his head as if in doubt,
and quickly hurried inside.
Before long,
the *tàifūrén* came out.
They all bowed deeply.
Afterward,
she asked Nà:
"Are you the grandson of Zhāng Bǐngzhī?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The *tàifūrén* wept loudly
and said to Zhāng Biéjià:
"This is your younger brother."
Nà and his brothers were unable to understand.
The *tàifūrén* said:
"I married your father for three years,
then was displaced and went north.
I belonged to Hēigùshān for half a year,
and bore your elder brother (Zhāng Biéjià).
After another half a year,
Gùshān died.
Your elder brother (Zhāng Biéjià) was appointed to an official position under the banner and moved here.
Now he has resigned from his post.
Every moment I thought of my hometown,
so I had him removed from that family's register
and restored to our original lineage.
I repeatedly sent people to Qí,
but there was no news to be found.
How could I have known your father moved west!"
Then she said to Zhāng Biéjià:
"You treated your brother as a son;
this will surely shorten your lifespan and lead to death!"
Zhāng Biéjià said:
"When I asked Chéng previously,
Chéng never mentioned being from Qí.
I suppose he was young and did not remember."
Then they arranged themselves by age: Zhāng Biéjià was forty-one,
the eldest;
Chéng was sixteen,
the youngest;
Nà was twenty-two,
making him the elder brother (to Chéng) and the middle brother (to Zhāng Biéjià).
Zhāng Biéjià was very happy to have two younger brothers
and shared a room with them.
He fully understood the reasons for their separation
and planned their return.
The *tàifūrén* was afraid they would not be accepted.
Zhāng Biéjià said:
"If they can accept us, we will share;
otherwise, we will separate.
Is there any country in the world without a father?"
Thereupon, they sold their house and prepared their luggage,
setting a date to depart for the west.
Upon arriving at their village,
Nà and Chéng rode ahead to inform their father.
After Nà had left,
his wife also died soon after;
he was a solitary old widower,
pitying his own shadow.
Suddenly, he saw Nà enter,
overcome with sudden joy,
feeling dazed and surprised;
then he saw Chéng,
his joy was extreme,
he could no longer speak,
and wept profusely.
When told that Zhāng Biéjià and his mother had arrived,
the old man stopped crying, startled,
unable to feel joy,
nor able to feel sorrow,
standing foolishly.
Soon after,
Zhāng Biéjià entered and
bowed.
The *tàifūrén* embraced the old man, and they cried together.
When they saw the maids, old women, and servants
filling the inside and outside,
they did not know what to do, whether to sit or stand.
Chéng did not see his mother
and asked about her.
Only then did he learn she had died.
He wailed until his breath gave out,
and only revived after a short while.
Zhāng Biéjià provided funds
to build pavilions and towers;
he hired a teacher to instruct his two younger brothers.
Horses filled the stable,
people bustled in the house,
and they had indeed become a great family.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"I listened to this matter to the end,
and my tears fell several times: The boy of more than ten years,
chopping firewood to help his brother,
exclaimed with emotion: 'Will Wáng Lǎn truly be seen again?'
At that, my tears fell once.
When the tiger carried Chéng away,
I could not help but cry out wildly: 'Heaven's way is so confused!'
At that, my tears fell once.
And when the brothers met unexpectedly,
I wept with joy;
then a brother was added,
and a sorrow increased,
so I wept for Zhāng Biéjià.
The whole family reunited,
their surprise unexpected,
their joy unexpected,
tears without a clear source,
those were for the old man.
I wonder if later generations
will also be as prone to tears as I am?"
According to the Chùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Zhū Gōng, the Prefectural Judge of Fénzhōu,
had many foxes living in his official residence.
One night, as Gōng sat,
a woman came and went under the lamp.
At first, he thought she was a family woman,
and did not bother to look;
but when he raised his eyes,
he did not recognize her at all,
and her face was strikingly beautiful.
He knew in his heart she was a fox,
but he was fond of her,
and quickly called her over.
The woman paused, smiled, and said:
"Raising your voice at people,
who is your maidservant or old woman?"
Zhū laughed and rose,
pulling her to sit and apologizing for his rudeness.
Thus, they became intimate,
for a long time like husband and wife.
Suddenly, she said:
"Your rank is due for promotion,
the day of our separation is near."
He asked:
"When?"
She replied:
"Right now.
But those who offer congratulations are at the gate,
and those who offer condolences are immediately at the village gate,
so I cannot assume the official position."
Three days later,
the promotion announcement indeed arrived.
The next day,
he immediately received the訃音 (fùyīn) of his honored mother's death.
Gōng resigned his post,
and wished to borrow her for a brief reunion.
The fox refused.
He escorted her to the riverbank.
He urged her to board the boat.
The woman said:
"You yourself don't know,
a fox cannot cross a river."
Zhū could not bear to part,
lingering by the riverbank.
The woman suddenly left,
saying she would visit an old acquaintance.
After a while, she returned,
and immediately a guest arrived to return the courtesy.
The woman spoke with the guest in a separate room.
After the guest left, she came and
said:
"Please board the boat at once,
I will send you across."
Zhū said:
"Before, you said you couldn't cross,
why do you say so now?"
She said:
"The one I visited earlier was none other
than the River God.
For your sake,
I specifically requested him.
He granted me ten days for the round trip,
so I can temporarily rely on that."
So they crossed together.
On the tenth day,
she indeed bid farewell and left.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
In Guǎngdōng, there was a gentry member, Fù Shì,
over sixty years old.
He had one son,
named Lián.
He was very intelligent,
but naturally impotent;
at seventeen,
his penis was as small as a silkworm.
When word spread far and wide,
no one would give their daughter to him.
He believed his family line was severed,
and worried day and night,
but there was nothing he could do.
Lián studied with a teacher.
The teacher happened to go out,
and just then there was a monkey show outside the gate;
Lián watched it,
neglecting his studies.
Fearing the teacher would soon arrive,
he fled.
A few *lǐ* from home,
he saw a woman in plain clothes,
accompanied by a small maid, appear before him.
The woman turned her head once,
unbelievably captivating and beautiful.
Her lotus steps were slow and hesitant;
Lián hurried past her.
The woman looked back at her maid and said:
"Please ask the young gentleman,
is he not by chance like Qióng?"
The maid indeed called out and asked.
Lián inquired what it was for.
The woman said:
"If it is indeed Qióng,
I have a letter,
please trouble him to deliver it conveniently to the village gate.
My old mother is at home,
and can also act as the host."
Lián had no fixed destination when he left,
thinking that even crossing the sea would be fine,
so he agreed.
The woman took out the letter and gave it to the maid,
and the maid in turn gave it to the student.
When asked her name and where she lived,
she said:
"My surname is Huá,
I live in Qínnǚ Cūn,
three or four *lǐ* north of the outer city wall."
The student boarded a boat and immediately left.
Upon reaching the northern suburb of Qióngzhōu,
the sun had already set, and it was dusk.
I inquired about Qínnǚcūn,
but no one knew of it.
I walked north for four or five lǐ,
the stars and moon already shining brightly.
Fragrant grasses obscured my vision,
and there was no inn in the wilderness,
which put me in a great predicament.
Seeing a tomb by the roadside,
I thought of resting beside it,
but greatly feared tigers and wolves.
So I climbed a tree with difficulty,
and squatted atop it.
Listening to the rustling of the pines
and the sad chirping of nocturnal insects,
my heart was restless,
and regret burned like fire.
Suddenly, I heard human voices below.
Looking down,
I saw a courtyard distinctly;
a beautiful woman sat on a stone,
two maidservants with braided hair holding painted candles,
attending her on either side.
The beautiful woman looked to her left and said,
"Tonight the moon is bright and the stars sparse.
The compressed tea given by Huágū
can be brewed into a cup,
to enjoy this beautiful night."
I thought they were ghosts or demons,
my hair stood on end,
and I dared not breathe.
Suddenly, a maidservant looked up and said,
"There's someone in the tree!"
The woman rose in surprise and said,
"Where is this bold fellow,
secretly coming to spy on people!"
I was greatly terrified,
with nowhere to flee or hide,
so I slowly descended,
and prostrated myself on the ground, begging for forgiveness.
The woman approached and gave me a glance,
her anger turning to joy;
she pulled me to sit beside her.
I stole a glance at her;
she was perhaps seventeen or eighteen years old,
her appearance exquisitely beautiful.
Listening to her speech,
it was also not a local accent.
She asked:
"Where are you going, sir?"
I replied:
"I am a letter-carrier for others."
The woman said:
"The wilds have many violent ruffians,
sleeping outdoors can be dangerous.
If you don't mind my humble dwelling,
I invite you to spend the night."
She invited me in.
The room had only one bed,
and she ordered a maidservant to spread two quilts upon it.
I felt ashamed of my shabby appearance,
and wished to sleep on the floor.
The woman smiled and said:
"When a good guest arrives,
how dare a 'woman Yuánlóng' sleep high up?"
Having no choice,
I shared the bed with her,
but was so flustered and anxious I dared not relax.
Before long,
the woman secretly reached in with her slender hand,
gently pinching my shin and thigh.
I feigned sleep,
as if I didn't notice.
Soon after,
she lifted the quilt and entered,
shaking me,
but I remained motionless.
The woman then reached down to my private parts.
She then stopped her hand, looking crestfallen,
and quietly left the quilt.
Immediately, I heard weeping.
I was so ashamed and mortified that I wished for the ground to swallow me,
only regretting the imperfections of fate.
The woman called a maidservant to light a lamp.
The maidservant, seeing her tear stains,
asked in surprise what was troubling her.
The woman shook her head and said:
"I am merely sighing over my own fate."
The maidservant stood before the bed,
gazing at her face intently.
The woman said:
"You can wake the gentleman,
and send him away."
Hearing this,
I felt even more ashamed and embarrassed;
and also feared that in the middle of the night,
I would have nowhere to go in the vast wilderness.
While I was pondering,
a woman pushed open the door and entered.
The maidservant announced:
"Huágū has arrived."
I secretly observed her;
she was about fifty years old,
still stylish.
Seeing the woman was not asleep,
she immediately questioned her.
The woman did not reply.
She then saw someone lying on the bed,
and asked:
"Who is sharing the bed?"
The maidservant answered for her:
"A young gentleman is staying here tonight."
The woman smiled and said:
"I didn't know Qiǎoniáng was having a wedding!"
Seeing that the woman's tears were not yet dry,
she exclaimed:
"On the night of the wedding,
such mournful weeping is unfitting;
could it be that the gentleman is rough?"
The woman did not speak,
and became even sadder.
The woman wanted to pull back the quilt to see me,
but as she shook her sleeve,
a letter fell onto the bed.
The woman picked it up and read it,
exclaiming in shock:
"This is my daughter's handwriting!"
She opened and read it, sighing repeatedly.
The woman asked her about it.
The woman said:
"It's news from Sānjǐ's family,
saying Wúláng has died,
and she is all alone with no one to rely on.
What can be done?"
The woman said:
"He indeed said he was carrying a letter for someone,
fortunately he hasn't been sent away yet."
The woman called me to get up,
and questioned me thoroughly about the origin of the letter.
I explained everything in detail.
The woman said:
"You have troubled yourself to carry this letter from afar,
how can we repay you?"
She then looked at me closely,
and smilingly asked:
"What offense did you commit against Qiǎoniáng?"
I said:
"I don't know my fault."
She then questioned the woman.
The woman sighed and said:
"I pity myself for being born into the family of a eunuch,
and later marrying a castrated man.
That is why I am sad."
The woman looked at me and said:
"Clever boy,
are you indeed a man who is also a woman?
You are my guest,
and should not be disturbed by others for long."
She then led me into the east wing,
and reached into my trousers to examine me.
She smiled and said:
"No wonder Qiǎo Niáng is in tears.
However, fortunately, there is still a root and a base,
so we can still do something."
Lighting the lamp, she rummaged through every box and chest,
and found a black pill.
She gave it to the student,
instructing him to swallow it immediately,
and secretly cautioned him not to speak of it.
Then she left.
The student lay alone, pondering the kindness,
not knowing what illness the medicine was meant to cure.
As it neared the fifth watch,
he awoke for the first time,
feeling a thread of warmth below his navel,
rushing straight to his private parts,
and something squirming as if hanging between his thighs.
He explored himself,
and his body had become that of a strapping man.
His heart was filled with joyful surprise,
like one who has just received the nine imperial awards.
As soon as the light of dawn began to show through the window lattice,
the woman entered,
placing a steamed bun in the student's room,
and urged him to sit patiently,
then locked the door from the outside.
She went out and said to Qiǎo Niáng:
"The young master has a letter of appreciation to send,
and will ask Sān Niáng to come
and become sworn sisters with you.
For now, keep him locked up,
to avoid people's annoyance."
Then she left.
The student paced back and forth, bored,
often peeking through the door crack,
like a bird peering out of a cage.
Seeing Qiǎo Niáng,
he repeatedly wanted to call out and reveal himself,
but was too ashamed and timid, so he stopped.
It was not until midnight
that the woman finally returned with her daughter.
Opening the door, she said:
"You must have been terribly bored, young master!
Sān Niáng, come and pay your respects."
The person from the road cautiously entered,
and curtsied to the student.
The woman ordered them to address each other as brother and sister.
Qiǎo Niáng smiled and said:
"Sisters would also be fine."
They all went out into the hall,
sat in a circle, and had drinks.
During the drinks,
Qiǎo Niáng playfully asked:
"Do eunuchs also feel affection for beautiful women?"
The student replied:
"A cripple does not forget his shoes;
a blind man does not forget his sight."
They all laughed heartily.
Qiǎo Niáng, seeing Sān Niáng was tired,
urged her to rest immediately.
The woman looked at Sān Niáng,
and bade her go with the student.
Sān Niáng, blushing with shyness, would not move.
The woman said:
"This is a man disguised as a woman,
what is there to fear?"
She pressed them to go together.
She secretly instructed the student:
"In secret, be my son-in-law;
in public, be my son.
That will do."
The student was delighted,
took her arm, and went up to the bed.
It was like a new blade being sharpened for the first time;
the pleasure can be imagined.
Afterwards, on the pillow, he asked the girl:
"Who is Qiǎo Niáng?"
She replied:
"She is a ghost.
Her talent and beauty are unmatched,
but her destiny has been unfortunate.
She married the young master of the Máo family,
who was ill and castrated.
At eighteen, he was not able to be a man,
and thus she was depressed and unhappy,
her resentment growing deep as the underworld."
The student was startled,
suspecting Sān Niáng was also a ghost.
The girl said:
"To tell you the truth,
I am not a ghost,
but a fox.
Qiǎo Niáng lives alone without a companion,
and my mother and I are homeless,
so we are borrowing this dwelling."
The student was greatly astonished.
The girl said:
"Do not fear,
although we are old ghosts and foxes,
we are not those who bring harm."
From then on, they talked and feasted together daily.
Although he knew Qiǎo Niáng was not human,
his heart admired her beauty,
but he lamented that he had no opportunity to offer himself.
The student was cultivated
and good at flattering and joking,
which earned him Qiǎo Niáng's affection.
One day,
Huá-shì and her daughter were going elsewhere,
and again locked the student in the empty room.
The student was stifled,
pacing the room and calling Qiǎo Niáng through the door.
Qiǎo Niáng ordered a maid to try several keys,
and finally found one that opened it.
The student whispered in her ear, asking for a private moment.
Qiǎo Niáng sent the maid away.
The student pulled her to the bed,
and nestled close to her.
The girl playfully cupped his navel area,
saying:
"Alas, this darling's spot here is lacking."
Before she finished speaking,
her hand touched something full in her grasp.
Startled, she exclaimed:
"How was it so tiny before,
and now suddenly so substantial!"
The student laughed and said:
"Before, I was ashamed to be seen by guests,
so I retracted it;
now, finding your taunts unbearable,
I'm just showing some frog-like anger."
Thereupon, they embraced intimately.
Afterwards, she angrily said:
"Now I know there was a reason for locking the door.
In the past, when mother and daughter wandered homeless,
we borrowed this dwelling.
Sān Niáng learned embroidery from me,
and I never kept any secrets from her.
Yet she is so jealous!"
The student comforted her
and told her the truth about his situation.
Qiǎo Niáng still resented it.
The student said:
"Keep it secret,
Aunt Huá strictly instructed me."
Before he had finished speaking,
Aunt Huá burst in.
The two quickly got up in a panic.
Aunt Huá glared,
and asked:
"Who opened the door?"
Qiǎo Niáng smiled and took responsibility.
Huá grew angrier,
and kept nagging incessantly.
Qiǎo deliberately sneered:
"Old woman, you laugh at others too much!
He is a man disguised as a woman,
what can he do?"
Sān Niáng saw her mother and Qiǎo Niáng fiercely bickering,
and felt uneasy.
She mediated between the two,
and only then did their stubborn anger turn to happiness.
Although Qiǎo Niáng's words were fiery,
she thenceforth reluctantly served Sān Niáng.
But Aunt Huá's constant vigilance day and night
prevented their affections from fully developing,
only expressing themselves through their eyes.
One day,
Aunt Huá said to the student:
"My two daughters have both served you.
I feel that staying here is not a good plan.
You should return and inform your parents,
and arrange the eternal covenant soon."
She immediately prepared his luggage and urged him to go.
The two girls faced each other,
their faces filled with sorrow;
and Qiǎo Niáng was especially inconsolable,
her tears rolling down like broken strings of pearls,
seeming endless.
Aunt Huá pushed her aside and stopped her,
then dragged the student out.
Outside the gate,
there was no courtyard to be seen,
only desolate tombs.
Aunt Huá escorted him to a boat,
and said:
"After you leave,
I, the old woman, will take my two daughters and rent a house in your esteemed town.
If you do not forget our former affection,
you can wait for us in the abandoned garden of the Lǐ family
to arrange the formal marriage."
The student then returned home.
At that time, Fùfù (傅父) couldn't find his son,
and was experiencing intense anxiety.
When he saw his son return,
his joy was beyond expectation.
The student briefly recounted the cliff incident,
and also mentioned the engagement with the Huá (華) family.
The father said:
"How can you trust such monstrous talk?
The only reason you are still alive
is because you were castrated and rendered useless;
otherwise,
you'd be dead!"
The student said:
"Although she is a non-human entity,
her emotions are still like a human's;
moreover, she is intelligent and beautiful,
marrying her would not cause laughter among relatives and friends."
The father said nothing,
but merely sneered at him.
The student then withdrew, and feeling his old urges return,
unable to stay within his bounds,
he secretly dallied with a maidservant;
gradually, this escalated to open promiscuity during the day,
intending to shock his parents.
One day,
he was spied upon by a young maid,
who ran to tell his mother.
The mother didn't believe it,
but after discretely observing,
she was finally shocked.
She called the maidservant to investigate,
and learned all the details.
She was overjoyed,
and proclaimed it to everyone she met,
to show that her son was not castrated,
and that she would arrange a marriage with a prominent family.
The student secretly told his mother:
"I will not marry anyone but the Huá (華) maiden."
His mother said:
"The world is not short of beautiful women,
why must it be a ghost?"
The student said:
"Without Huá Gū (華姑),
your son would not have known the human way,
abandoning her is not right."
Fùfù (傅父) agreed to it,
and sent a servant and an old woman to scout.
Four or five *lǐ* (里) outside the eastern city wall,
they searched for the Lí (李) family garden.
Amidst broken walls and bamboo trees,
wisps of cooking smoke could be seen.
The old woman dismounted,
went straight to the gate,
and saw the mother and daughter wiping tables and washing,
as if waiting for someone.
The old woman bowed and conveyed her master's message.
Seeing Sānniáng (三娘),
she exclaimed:
"Is this our young mistress?
Even I find her captivating,
no wonder the young master is so smitten with her, dreaming of her day and night."
Then she asked about her elder sister.
Huá Gū (華姑) sighed and said:
"She is my adopted daughter.
Three days ago,
she suddenly died and departed."
Then she offered food and drink to the old woman and the servant.
When the old woman returned,
she fully described Sānniáng's (三娘) appearance and demeanor,
and both parents were pleased.
Finally, she conveyed the news of Qiǎoniáng's (巧娘) death,
making the student feel a pang of sorrow and almost weep.
On the night of the formal wedding procession,
he saw Huá Gū (華姑) and personally asked her about it.
She replied:
"She has already been reborn in the northern lands."
The student sighed for a long time.
He brought Sānniáng (三娘) home,
but he could never forget Qiǎoniáng (巧娘);
whenever anyone came from Qióng (瓊),
he would certainly summon them to ask about her.
Someone said that at Qín Nǚ (秦女)'s tomb, ghost cries were heard at night.
The student was surprised by its strangeness,
and went to tell Sānniáng (三娘).
Sānniáng (三娘) pondered for a long time,
then wept and said:
"I have wronged my sister!"
When he questioned her,
she replied:
"When my mother and I came,
we truly did not let her know.
These resentful cries,
could they be hers?
I wanted to tell you earlier,
but I was afraid of exposing my mother's fault."
When the student heard this,
his sorrow turned to joy.
He immediately ordered a carriage,
traveling day and night without stopping,
and rushed to her tomb.
He knocked on the tomb's wooden marker and cried:
"Qiǎoniáng (巧娘),
Qiǎoniáng (巧娘)!
I am here!"
Presently, he saw a young woman holding an infant
emerge from the grave,
she raised her head and wailed mournfully,
her resentment endless.
The student also shed tears.
He reached into his embrace and asked whose child it was,
Qiǎoniáng (巧娘) said:
"He is your offspring,
born three months ago."
The student sighed and said:
"I mistakenly listened to Huá Gū (華姑),
causing mother and child to suffer sorrow underground,
how can I ever escape this sin!"
So, he traveled with them in the same carriage,
and returned home by sea.
He hugged the child and told his mother.
His mother looked at him,
his physique was robust and handsome,
not at all like a ghost,
and she was even more delighted.
The two women were harmonious,
and dutifully served their mother-in-law.
Later, when Fùfù (傅父) fell ill,
a doctor was invited.
Qiǎoniáng (巧娘) said:
"The illness is incurable,
his soul has already left his body."
She supervised the preparation of funerary items,
and after they were complete, he died.
When the child grew up,
he resembled his father exactly;
he was especially intelligent,
and at fourteen, he passed the prefectural examination.
Wēng Zǐxiá (翁紫霞) from Gāoyóu (高郵),
was a guest in Guǎng (廣) and heard of this.
The place name is missing,
and his final whereabouts are also unknown.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
A certain Magistrate Wú (吳令),
whose surname and given name are forgotten.
He was known for his integrity and uprightness.
The custom in Wú (吳) greatly revered the god of the City God,
sculpting his image from wood,
dressing it in brocade,
with hidden mechanisms that made it seem alive.
On the god's birthday,
residents would collect funds for a gathering,
and parade him through the main streets;
various banners and pennants were erected,
along with ceremonial guards,
forming a dense procession.
Drums and wind instruments played continuously,
a deafening and intricate sound,
the procession stretched for a long way.
This had become a custom,
which no one dared neglect annually.
When the magistrate went out,
he happened to encounter it,
and stopped to ask about it.
The residents informed him.
He also deduced that the expenses were quite extravagant.
The magistrate was furious,
and pointing at the god, he rebuked it saying:
"The City God is truly the master of a district.
If you are dull and without spiritual power,
then you are merely a lewd and ignorant ghost,
not worthy of worship;
but if you have spiritual power,
then resources should be conserved,
how can you, with useless expenses,
squander the people's hard-earned wealth?"
After speaking,
he dragged the god to the ground,
and flogged it twenty times.
From then on, the custom was immediately reformed.
The magistrate was honest and selfless,
but as a young man, he was fond of pranks.
After residing there for more than a year,
he once climbed onto the eaves of his official residence to investigate a sparrow's nest,
lost his footing and fell,
breaking his leg,
and soon after died.
People heard that in the City God temple,
the magistrate was shouting angrily,
as if arguing with the god,
and it did not stop for several days.
The people of Wú (吳) did not forget the magistrate's virtue,
they gathered to pray and appease him,
and built a separate temple to commemorate the magistrate,
and the sound then ceased.
The temple was also named after the City God,
and sacrifices were made to him in spring and autumn,
making him even more prominent than the old god.
To this day, Wú (吳) is said to have two City Gods.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
A girl came to the village.
She was twenty-four or twenty-five years old.
She carried a medicine bag
and sold her medical services.
When someone asked her to diagnose an illness,
the girl could not prescribe a formula herself;
she would wait until nightfall to consult the spirits.
In the evening, she would clean a small room
and shut herself inside.
The crowd would gather around the doors and windows,
listening intently in silence.
They would only whisper,
not daring to cough.
Inside and out, all movement and breathing ceased.
After about half a watch,
suddenly a curtain rustled.
The girl inside said,
"Has Jiǔgū come?"
A girl replied,
"I have come."
She then said,
"Is Láméi with Jiǔgū?"
Like a maid, someone replied,
"Not yet."
The three gossiped,
chattering incessantly.
Soon, the curtain hook moved again,
and the girl said,
"Liùgū has arrived."
A jumble of voices said,
"Has Chūnméi brought the young master too?"
A girl said,
"That naughty boy!
I couldn't get him to sleep by coaxing,
he insisted on coming with his mistress.
He's as heavy as a hundred jūn,
what a burden!"
Then a girl's solicitous voice was heard,
Jiǔgū's voice inquiring,
Liùgū's voice exchanging pleasantries,
the two maids' voices offering comfort,
the little child's joyful laughter,
the cat's meows,
all became a clamor.
Immediately, the girl was heard laughing, saying,
"The young master is also very fond of playing,
carrying the cat all this long way."
After a while, the sounds gradually diminished,
the curtain rustled again,
and the entire room became noisy,
saying,
"Why is Sìgū so late?"
A small girl softly replied,
"The road is a thousand lǐ and more;
it took this long to arrive, walking with my aunt.
My aunt walks rather slowly."
Then various voices exchanged greetings of warmth and coolness,
and the sound of moving seats,
and the call to add seats,
all mingled and started simultaneously,
filling the room with noise
until it settled after a short meal's time.
Immediately, the girl was heard asking about the illness.
Jiǔgū thought it appropriate to use rénshēn,
Liùgū thought it appropriate to use huángqí,
and Sìgū thought it appropriate to use báizhú.
After some deliberation,
Jiǔgū was heard calling for brush and inkstone.
Before long,
the rustling sound of folding paper,
the clanging sound of picking up the brush and dropping the cap,
the rumbling sound of grinding ink;
then the sound of the brush being put down, hitting the desk,
the vibrating brush making a noise,
and then the rustling sound of gathering and wrapping medicine.
After a moment,
the girl pushed aside the curtain,
called the patient, and handed over the medicine and prescription.
Turning back into the room,
the three gū were heard bidding farewell,
the three maids bidding farewell,
the little child gurgling,
the cat meowing,
all starting simultaneously again.
Jiǔgū's voice was clear and soaring,
Liùgū's voice was slow and deep,
Sìgū's voice was delicate and melodious,
and the voices of the three maids,
each had their own distinct sound,
clearly distinguishable by listening.
The crowd marveled, believing it to be truly divine.
However, when tested, the prescriptions
were not very effective.
This is what is called ventriloquism,
merely borrowed to sell her art.
Yet it was indeed extraordinary!
In the past, Wáng Xīnyì once said: In the capital, he happened to pass through a market,
heard string music and singing,
and spectators were packed like a wall.
Peering closer,
he saw a young man singing a tune with a melodious voice.
There were no musical instruments;
he only pressed a finger against his cheek,
pressing and singing;
the sound was clear and resonant,
no different from strings.
This was also a descendant of ventriloquism.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Jiāo shēng,
was the uncle's younger brother of Shíhóng Xiānshēng of Zhāngqiū.
He was studying in the garden.
In the middle of the night,
two beautiful women came,
both of peerless beauty.
One was about seventeen or eighteen,
the other about fourteen or fifteen.
They leaned on the table and smiled.
Jiāo knew they were fox spirits,
and refused them with a stern face.
The elder one said,
"Your beard is like a halberd,
why do you lack a man's spirit?"
Jiāo said,
"Throughout my life, I have never dared to engage with two women."
The woman laughed and said,
"How pedantic!
Are you still adhering to obsolete customs?
In the lower world of ghosts and spirits,
everything is turned from black to white,
let alone trivial matters in the bedchamber?"
Jiāo again reprimanded them.
Knowing he could not be swayed, the woman
then said,
"You are a renowned scholar.
I have a couplet;
please provide the matching line.
If you can match it, I will leave: 'Wù-xū (戊戌) share the same body,
but the belly lacks just one dot.'"
Jiāo pondered deeply but could not complete it.
The woman laughed and said,
"Is a renowned scholar truly like this?
I can provide the match for you: 'Jǐ-sì (己巳) follow in tandem,
why don't you lift both feet?'"
She laughed and left.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Wéiyì, the Lǐ
clan had an detached residence. Suddenly, an old man came to rent it.
He offered fifty liǎng of gold annually,
which was accepted.
After he left, there was no news,
so Lǐ instructed his family to rent it out to someone else.
The next day,
the old man arrived
and said,
“The rental of the house has already been discussed.
Why do you want to lease it to someone else?”
Lǐ explained his doubts.
The old man said,
“I will live here for a long time.
The reason for the delay
is that an auspicious day is ten days away.”
Then he paid a year’s rent in advance,
saying,
“Leave it empty for the entire year,
and don’t ask about it.”
Lǐ saw him out
and asked for the date.
The old man told him.
Several days after the specified date,
he was still nowhere to be seen.
When Lǐ went to check on it,
the double doors were closed from the inside,
cooking smoke rose, and human voices mingled.
Astonished,
he presented his calling card and sought an audience.
The old man hurried out,
greeted him, and led him in,
with a friendly smile and words.
After returning,
Lǐ sent someone to present gifts to his family;
the old man reciprocated with generous rewards.
A few days later,
Lǐ hosted a banquet and invited the old man,
and they conversed happily.
When asked about his residence,
he replied that it was in Qínzhōng.
Lǐ was surprised by the distance.
The old man said,
“Your hometown is a blessed land.
Qínzhōng is not suitable for living;
a great calamity is about to break out.”
At that time, there was peace,
so Lǐ did not inquire further.
The next day,
the old man sent a formal invitation in return for Lǐ’s hospitality,
with splendid decorations and food,
of extreme extravagance and beauty.
Lǐ was even more astonished, suspecting him to be a high official.
As they grew friendly,
the old man
confessed that he was a fox spirit.
Lǐ was utterly shocked
and told everyone he met.
The gentry of the district, hearing of his extraordinary nature,
daily brought their carriages to his gate,
wishing to make friends with the old man,
and he humbly received them all.
Gradually, even the prefectural officials occasionally exchanged visits.
Only the district magistrate sought to communicate,
but the old man always declined, citing reasons.
The magistrate then asked the host to introduce him,
but the old man refused.
Lǐ questioned him about the reason.
The old man left his seat, approached Lǐ, and whispered privately,
“You do not know,
but his previous life was a donkey.
Though he now appears to be a superior among the people,
he is one who drinks and gets drunk.
I am naturally of a different species,
and ashamed to be associated with him.”
Lǐ then made an excuse to the magistrate,
saying that the fox feared his divine authority,
and thus dared not meet him.
The magistrate believed him and stopped pursuing it.
This happened in the eleventh year of Kāngxī.
Not long after,
Qín suffered from war and destruction.
The fox’s foresight was indeed
true.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“The donkey is a large creature.
When angered, it brays and roars;
its eyes are larger than jars;
its breath is coarser than an ox’s.
Not only is its sound difficult to hear,
its appearance is also difficult to behold.
But if one offers it a bundle of hay to entice it,
it will lay back its ears and lower its head,
happily submitting to the bridle.
To place such a creature as a superior among the people,
it is fitting that it drinks coarse liquor and gets drunk.
May those who govern the people
take the donkey as a warning,
and seek wisdom from the fox,
then their virtue will daily advance.”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Féng Wēng of Guǎngpíng had a son,
whose courtesy name was Xiāngrú.
Both father and son were scholars.
The old man was nearly sixty,
of an upright and unyielding nature,
but his family was frequently poor.
Within a few years,
his wife and daughter-in-law passed away one after another,
and he had to manage the household chores himself.
One night,
Xiāngrú was sitting under the moon
when he suddenly saw the daughter of the eastern neighbor peering over the wall.
He looked at her;
she was beautiful.
He approached her;
she smiled slightly.
He beckoned with his hand,
but she neither came nor left.
He earnestly invited her,
and she then used a ladder to cross over,
and they slept together.
When asked her name,
she said,
“My name is Hóngyù, the neighbor’s daughter.”
The scholar was greatly delighted
and pledged eternal devotion with her.
The girl agreed.
They visited each other nightly
for about half a year.
One night,
the old man got up
and heard laughter and voices from his son’s room.
He peeped
and saw the girl.
Enraged,
he called his son out
and scolded him,
“What are you doing, you beast!
You are so desolate,
and yet you don’t work hard,
but instead indulge in licentiousness?
If people know of this,
it will ruin your virtue;
if people don’t know,
it will shorten your life!”
The scholar knelt and prostrated himself,
weeping and admitting his regret.
The old man shouted at the girl,
“A woman who does not uphold the rules of the boudoir
not only defiles herself
but also defiles others.
If this matter comes to light,
it will bring shame not only to our humble dwelling!”
After scolding them,
he returned to his bed in anger.
The girl shed tears and said,
“The parental blame and reprimand
are truly shameful and humiliating!
Our destined relationship has ended!”
The scholar said,
“My father is here, so I cannot act on my own.
If you still have feelings,
you should still endure the disgrace for our good.”
The girl’s words were resolute and final,
and the scholar wept.
The girl stopped him, saying,
“Between you and me, there were no matchmakers’ words
or parents’ decrees.
How can we grow old together by climbing over walls and sneaking through gaps?
There is a suitable match here
whom you can marry.”
He told her about his poverty.
The girl said,
“Wait for me tomorrow night;
I will make arrangements for you.”
The next night,
the girl indeed came
and gave the scholar forty liǎng of silver.
She said,
“Sixty lǐ from here,
in Wú Cūn, there is a Wèi clan with a daughter
who is eighteen years old.
Her price is high,
so she has not yet been married.
If you offer a substantial amount,
it will surely be a harmonious agreement.”
Having said this,
she bid farewell and left.
Shēng seized an opportunity to speak to his father,
desiring to go and arrange the marriage.
But he secretly gave money without daring to tell.
The elder himself estimated that he had no resources,
and for this reason,
he stopped him.
The host (Shēng) then gently said,
“Let me try, and if it works, then so be it.”
The elder nodded.
Shēng then borrowed a servant and horse,
and went to the Wèi family.
Wèi was originally a country farmer.
Shēng called him out,
and led him to speak in private.
Wèi knew Shēng was from a prominent family,
and also saw his distinguished and open demeanor,
so he inwardly approved,
but worried that Shēng would be stingy with the resources (money).
Shēng heard the hesitation in his words and meaning,
understood his intent,
and emptied his purse onto the table.
Wèi was then pleased,
and entreated a neighbor to act as intermediary,
writing on red paper and making an oath.
Shēng entered to bow to the elder woman (Wèi’s wife).
By the side of the room,
the daughter shielded herself behind her mother.
He subtly glanced at her,
and although her adornments were simple and rustic,
her expression was radiant and beautiful,
and he was secretly pleased.
Wèi borrowed a house to entertain his son-in-law,
and then said,
“Young master needs not come for the bridal procession himself.
Once we have prepared a little clothing and makeup,
she will be sent over in a sedan chair.”
Shēng set a date with him and returned.
He cunningly told his father,
saying that Wèi loved his pure family lineage,
and did not ask for resources (money).
The elder was also pleased.
On the appointed day,
Wèi indeed sent his daughter over.
The daughter was diligent and frugal,
and possessed virtuous obedience,
and their conjugal life was very harmonious.
After more than two years,
she bore a son,
named Fú’ér.
During the Qīngmíng Festival, he happened to be carrying his son to visit the graves,
and encountered the local gentry Sòng family.
Sòng had served as a Yùshǐ,
but was dismissed for bribery,
and resided in the countryside,
greatly indulging in tyrannical oppression.
On that day, he also returned from visiting graves,
and saw the daughter's beauty.
He asked the villagers,
and learned that she was Shēng’s wife.
He reckoned Fēng (Shēng) was a poor scholar,
and attempted to tempt him with a heavy bribe,
hoping to sway him,
and had his household members hint at this to him.
Upon hearing this, Shēng was immediately
enraged, his anger showing on his face;
but then he considered that he was no match in power,
so he suppressed his anger into a smile,
and returned to tell his father.
The elder was greatly angered,
and rushed out,
facing Sòng’s household members,
pointing to heaven and drawing on the ground,
uttering myriad curses.
The household members fled like rats.
Sòng Shì was also enraged,
and eventually sent several people into Shēng’s house,
to beat the elder and his son,
causing a commotion like a boiling cauldron.
When the daughter heard this,
she abandoned her child on the bed,
and with disheveled hair, cried for help.
The group seized her and carried her away,
leaving with a clamor.
The father and son were injured and disabled,
groaning on the ground,
while the child cried “guā guā” in the room.
The neighbors all pitied them,
and helped them onto the couch.
After a day,
Shēng could get up with a cane.
The elder, out of indignation, refused to eat,
vomited blood, and soon died.
Shēng wept bitterly,
and carrying his son, initiated legal proceedings,
going up to the Dūdǐng and Fǔ (provincial governors),
suing several times,
but ultimately failed to obtain justice.
Later, he heard that his wife had died rather than submit,
and became even more sorrowful.
His chest was filled with grievances,
with no way to express them.
He often thought of assassinating Sòng in a vital passage,
but worried about his numerous retainers,
and that his child would have no one to rely on.
Day and night, he grieved,
his eyelids never closing.
Suddenly, a man came to mourn in his room,
with a curly beard and broad jaw,
whom he had never met.
He was invited to sit,
and Shēng wished to ask about his family and origin.
The guest abruptly said,
“Do you have a father’s murder to avenge,
and the hatred of a stolen wife,
and yet forget to repay it?”
Shēng suspected he was a spy for Sòng,
and so he pretended to answer.
The guest was enraged, his eyes almost bursting,
and abruptly exited, saying,
“I took you for a man,
but now you are like someone not worth mentioning!”
Shēng perceived his unusualness,
knelt and pulled him back,
saying,
“I truly feared the Sòng family.
Now I will truly open my heart to you: I have been enduring hardship and bitterness
for a long time.
But I pity this babe in arms,
fearing the ancestral line will be broken.
You are a righteous man,
can you avenge my wrong?”
The guest said,
“This is a matter for women and girls,
not something I can do.
What you wish to entrust to others,
please take on yourself;
what you wish to take on yourself,
I wish to do in your stead.”
Upon hearing this, Shēng
fell to the ground, head bowed.
The guest left without looking back.
Shēng chased after him to ask his name,
and he said,
“If I fail,
I am not fit to receive blame;
if I succeed,
I am also not fit to receive gratitude.”
Then he left.
Shēng feared calamity would strike,
and fled with his child.
By night,
the entire Sòng family was asleep,
when someone scaled the high wall and entered,
killing the Yùshǐ, his two sons,
and one daughter-in-law and one maid.
The Sòng family members reported the crime to the officials.
The officials were greatly shocked.
Sòng insisted it was Shēng,
and so officials were dispatched to arrest Shēng,
but Shēng had fled and his whereabouts were unknown,
which made the accusation seem even more credible.
Sòng’s servants and government runners searched everywhere.
That night, they reached Nánshān,
heard a child crying,
tracked and found him,
tied him up and proceeded.
The child cried even more angrily,
so the group seized the child and abandoned him.
Shēng was so full of grief and indignation he felt he would die.
He saw the county magistrate,
who asked,
“Why did you kill?”
Shēng said:
“What an injustice!
Someone died by night,
while I went out by day,
and was even holding a wailing infant.
How could I have climbed over a wall and killed someone?”
The magistrate now said,
“If you didn't kill him,
why did you flee?”
Shēng was at a loss for words,
unable to offer a rebuttal.
So he was imprisoned.
Shēng wept, saying,
“My death is nothing to regret,
but what crime has my orphaned child committed?”
The magistrate now said,
“You have killed many children;
what cause for resentment is there
if your child is killed?”
Shēng, having been stripped of his official status,
repeatedly suffered cruel torture,
but ultimately said nothing.
That night, the magistrate was just lying down
when he heard something strike his bed,
making a thudding sound.
Greatly frightened, he cried out.
His whole family rose in alarm,
gathered together and lit a candle,
and saw a short knife,
sharp as frost,
chopped into the bed wood by more than an inch,
so firmly that it could not be pulled out.
When the magistrate saw it,
his soul was lost.
He had guards search everywhere,
but found no trace.
He was secretly disheartened.
Also, because the Sòng man was dead,
there was nothing more to fear,
so he detailed the matter to the judicial commissioner,
and secured Shēng’s release.
Ultimately, Shēng was set free.
When Shēng returned home,
his jar was without a pint or peck,
and his solitary shadow faced the four walls.
Fortunately, his neighbors, out of pity, provided him with food and drink,
so he barely managed to get by.
When he thought that the great wrong had been avenged,
he smiled broadly with joy;
when he thought of the cruel calamity
that almost wiped out his family,
tears fell profusely;
and when he thought of half a lifetime of bone-deep poverty,
and the discontinuation of his lineage,
he would weep aloud in an uninhabited place,
no longer able to restrain himself.
After half a year of this,
the pursuit and prohibitions became laxer.
So he appealed to the district magistrate,
requesting a judgment to return Wèi’s bones.
After burying them and returning home,
he was so grief-stricken that he wanted to die.
Tossing and turning on his empty bed,
he saw no way to live.
Suddenly, someone knocked at the door.
He concentrated his mind and listened silently,
hearing someone outside the door
muttering to a small child.
Shēng quickly got up and peered out,
and it seemed to be a woman.
As soon as the door was opened,
she asked,
“Your great injustice has been redressed,
I'm fortunate that you are safe and sound!”
Her voice sounded familiar,
but in his haste, he could not recall it.
When he lit a candle to see,
it was Hóngyù.
She was holding a small child
who was playfully astride her.
Shēng did not have time to ask questions,
but embraced the girl and wept aloud.
The girl also looked distressed.
After a while, she pushed the child and said,
“Have you forgotten your father?”
The child tugged at the girl’s clothes,
his eyes shining as he looked at Shēng.
Upon closer inspection,
it was Fú’ér.
Greatly astonished,
Shēng tearfully asked,
“How did my child come here?”
The girl said,
“To tell you the truth: what I said before about being a neighbor’s daughter
was false.
I am actually a fox.
That night, as I was traveling,
I saw the child crying at the mouth of the valley,
and adopted him in Qín.
Hearing that the great calamity had ceased,
I therefore brought him back for you to be reunited.”
Shēng wiped away his tears and bowed in gratitude.
The child was in the girl's arms
as if clinging to his mother,
and could not recognize his father anymore.
Before dawn,
the girl suddenly got up.
When asked why,
she replied,
“I want to leave.”
Shēng knelt naked at the head of the bed,
unable to look up due to his tears.
The girl smiled and said,
“I was just teasing you.
Our household is newly established now,
and it won't do without rising early and sleeping late.”
Then she cleared weeds and piled earth,
performing tasks like a man.
Shēng worried about their poverty,
unable to provide for themselves.
The girl said,
“Just please close your curtains and study;
don't ask about abundance or lack.
Perhaps we won't starve to death.”
Then she took out gold to purchase weaving tools;
she rented dozens of *mǔ* of land
and hired workers to cultivate it.
Clearing thorny bushes
and pulling vines to repair the house
became her daily routine.
The villagers, hearing of the wife’s virtue,
were even more willing to help them.
In about half a year,
their household thrived,
like that of a wealthy family.
Shēng said,
“From the ashes,
you have rebuilt everything from scratch.
However, one matter is not yet settled.
What shall we do?”
When she pressed him,
he replied,
“The examination date is approaching,
and my scholarly attire has not yet been restored.”
The girl smiled and said,
“I previously sent four *jīn* to the instructor,
and your name has already been reinstated in the register.
If I had waited for your words,
it would have been delayed for a long time.”
Shēng was even more impressed by her.
That year, he succeeded in the provincial examination.
He was then thirty-six years old,
with fertile fields stretching for miles,
and a grand house.
The girl was graceful, as if about to float away with the wind,
yet she worked harder than a farm wife.
Even in the severe winter, she toiled,
her face and hands smooth as grease.
She said she was twenty-eight years old,
but people looking at her
always thought she was around twenty.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“His son was virtuous,
his father was moral,
hence his vengeance was chivalrous.
Not only was the man chivalrous,
the fox was also chivalrous.
Their encounter was truly extraordinary!
However, the officials were indifferent.
That a knife struck with a thunderous sound and embedded itself in the wood,
making one’s hair stand on end,
why couldn’t it have shifted half a *chǐ* up the bed?
If Sū Zǐměi had read this,
he would surely raise his wine cup and say,
‘What a pity it missed!’”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the Běizhí region, a dragon fell into a village.
Its movements were heavy and clumsy.
It entered the house of a certain gentry member.
The doorway was just wide enough for its body,
and it squeezed through.
The whole family fled.
They climbed to the upper floor and made a commotion,
firing guns and cannons with a roar.
The dragon then came out.
Outside the gate, stagnant water had collected,
less than a *chǐ* deep.
The dragon entered it,
rolling about,
its body completely covered in mud;
it tried its best to leap,
but would fall back after a *chǐ* or so.
It lay in the mud for three days,
flies swarming on its scales.
Suddenly, a heavy rain fell,
and then it ascended into the sky with thunder and lightning.
Fáng Shēng 房生 and his friends climbed Niúshān 牛山,
entered a temple and looked around.
Suddenly, on a yellow brick among the rafters, a small snake coiled,
thin as an earthworm.
Suddenly it rotated once,
like a finger;
another rotation,
and it was like a sash.
They were all alarmed,
knowing it was a dragon,
and rushed down in a group.
Just as they reached halfway up the mountain,
they heard a thunderclap from the temple,
shaking the mountain valley.
Black clouds in the sky were like a cover,
and a giant dragon twisted and turned within them,
disappearing after a short while.
At Zhāngqiū Xiǎo Xiānggōng Zhuāng 章丘小相公莊,
a common woman went to the fields.
She encountered a strong wind,
and dust and sand blew into her face.
She felt one eye narrow,
as if it contained a barley awn.
She rubbed it and blew on it,
but it did not heal.
Opening her eyelid and examining it carefully,
the pupil was indeed unharmed,
but there was a red line winding in the flesh.
Someone said:
"This is a hibernating dragon."
The woman was worried and afraid, awaiting death.
After more than three months,
there was a torrential rain.
Suddenly, a huge thunderclap sounded,
and it tore through her eye corner and departed.
The woman suffered no harm.
Yuán Xuānsì 袁宣四 said:
"In Sūzhōu 蘇州,
I encountered a cloudy and gloomy day,
and a great thunderclap erupted.
People saw a dragon hanging down from the cloud's edge,
its scales and armor moving.
In its claws, it clutched a human head,
its beard clearly visible from behind.
After a while,
it entered the clouds and disappeared.
Nor was it heard that anyone had lost their head."
According to the Xiěxuězhāi Chāoběn 鑄雪齋抄本 edition of the Liáozhāi Zhìyì 聊齋誌異,
Qīngzhōu Dào Chén Gōng Bǎoyào 青州道陳公寶鑰,
a native of Mǐn 閩,
was sitting alone one night.
A woman lifted the curtain and entered.
He looked at her,
and did not recognize her;
but she was exceptionally beautiful,
wearing long sleeves and court attire.
She smiled and said:
"Sitting alone in the clear night,
are you not lonely?"
Gōng 公 was surprised and asked:
"Who are you?"
She said:
"My home is not far,
very close, in the western neighbor."
Gōng 公 suspected she was a ghost,
but his heart was fond of her.
He took her sleeve and pulled her to sit,
and their conversation was refined and elegant;
he was greatly pleased.
He embraced her,
and she did not resist much.
She looked around and said:
"Are there no other people?"
Gōng 公 quickly closed the door,
saying:
"None."
He urged her to loosen her clothes,
and she appeared quite shy and timid.
Gōng 公 diligently helped her.
The woman said:
"I am twenty years old,
still a virgin,
and your wildness may be unbearable."
After the intimacy was completed,
red fluid stained the mat.
Then, whispering by the pillow,
she identified herself as
"Lín Sìniáng 林四娘."
Gōng 公 questioned her in detail.
She said:
"For a lifetime, I have been firm and chaste,
but now I have been completely defiled by you.
If you truly love me,
just desire our lasting affection,
what is the point of being so wordy?"
Before long,
the rooster crowed,
and she rose and departed.
From then on, she came every night.
Each time, they would close the door and drink elegantly.
When discussing music,
she could always analyze gōngshāng 宮商 in detail.
Gōng 公 then thought she was skilled in composing music.
She said:
"It was what I learned as a child."
Gōng 公 requested her to play a piece.
The woman said:
"It has been a long time since I touched music,
more than half the rhythm is forgotten,
I fear I would be laughed at by those who know."
He pressed her again,
and she bowed her head, tapped the rhythm,
and sang the melody of Yīliáng 伊涼,
her voice mournful and poignant.
After the song,
tears flowed.
Gōng 公 also felt sorrowful,
embraced her, and comforted her, saying:
"My dear, do not sing the music of a fallen kingdom,
which makes people melancholy."
The woman said:
"Voice expresses emotion;
those who are sad cannot be made happy,
just as those who are happy cannot be made sad."
The two were intimate,
more so than zithers and lutes.
After a long time,
the family secretly listened to them.
Those who heard her sing
could not help but shed tears.
His wife secretly saw her face,
suspecting that such enchanting beauty did not exist in the human world;
if not a ghost, then surely a fox;
fearing she might be a malevolent spirit or charm,
she advised Gōng 公 to break off the relationship.
Gōng 公 could not listen,
but firmly questioned the woman.
The woman sadly said:
"I am
a palace maid from the Héngfǔ 衡府.
I died during a disaster,
seventeen years ago.
Because of your noble righteousness,
I entrusted myself to your affection,
but I truly dared not harm you.
If you are suspicious or afraid,
I shall take my leave from this moment on."
Gōng 公 said:
"I do not hold it against you;
but with such intimacy,
one cannot but know the truth."
Then he asked about matters in the palace.
The woman narrated from memory,
making it delightful to listen to.
When speaking of the decline,
she would choke up and be unable to form words.
The woman did not sleep much;
every night she would rise and recite various sutras and mantras like Zhǔntí 准提 and Jīngāng 金剛.
Gōng 公 asked:
"Can you repent from the underworld?"
She said:
"That is one reason.
I reflect on being lost for my entire life,
and I wish to find a better next life."
Also, she often discussed and critiqued poetry with Gōng 公;
she would always point out flaws;
when it came to good lines,
she would sweetly chant them in a lingering voice.
Her temperament was refined and elegant,
making people forget their weariness.
Gōng 公 asked:
"Are you skilled in poetry?"
She said:
"I occasionally composed some during my life."
Gōng 公 requested a poem from her.
She smiled and said:
“A daughter's words
are not worthy of being discussed by a noble person.”
After three years,
one evening,
she suddenly announced her departure with a mournful expression.
Gōng was startled and asked her why.
She replied,
“The King of the Underworld, seeing that I committed no sin during my life
and did not forget the sūtras and dhāraṇīs even in death,
has commanded that I be reborn into the Wáng family.
My departure is tonight,
and we shall never meet again.”
Having said this,
she grew sorrowful.
Gōng also shed tears.
They then poured wine and drank together in sorrow.
The woman sang with deep emotion,
in a melancholic and mournful tone,
each word turning a hundred times;
whenever she reached a sad part,
she would choke with sobs.
She stopped and started several times
before finishing the song,
but they could not drink heartily.
She then rose,
hesitating, wishing to bid farewell.
Gōng earnestly tried to keep her,
so she sat for a little longer.
Suddenly, the rooster crowed,
and she said,
“I must not stay longer.
However, you have always complained that I was unwilling to display my humble talent;
now that we are about to part forever,
I shall compose a stanza.”
She asked for a brush and composed it,
saying,
“My heart is sad and my mind is confused,
I cannot polish it;
the rhythm is off and the structure is flawed,
so be careful not to show it to others.”
She covered her face with her sleeve and departed.
Gōng escorted her outside the gate,
where she vanished into thin air.
Gōng grieved for a long time.
He looked at her poem;
the handwriting was elegant and beautiful,
so he cherished and preserved it.
The poem read:
“Seventeen years peacefully confined in the deep palace,
who will ask the azure sky about my former country?
Idly watching the palace halls overgrown with tall trees,
weeping, I gaze at the king transforming into a cuckoo.
The sea country's waves against the slanting evening sun,
the Hàn house's pipes and drums silence the beacon fires.
With a weak body, difficult to be fierce,
my virtuous heart, sorrowful, only seeks Chan.
Daily reciting a thousand hundreds of Bodhi lines,
idly reading two or three pages of palm-leaf sūtras.
Singing loudly on the pear garden stage, replacing tears with song,
please listen, my lord, and you too will shed tears.”
The poem contains repetitions and disconnections,
suggesting errors.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Wáng Shèngyú was traveling south,
and moored his boat in the middle of the river.
After lying down to sleep,
he saw the moonlight was as bright as silk,
and could not sleep.
He had his boy-servant massage him.
Suddenly, he heard a sound on the boat's roof, like a small child walking,
treading on the reed mat, making a noise,
coming from the stern of the boat and gradually approaching the cabin door.
Fearing it was a thief,
he quickly got up and questioned the boy.
The boy had also heard it.
While they were speaking,
they saw a person lying on the boat's roof,
peering into the cabin with head lowered.
Greatly alarmed,
he gripped his sword and called out to his servants,
and everyone on the boat awoke.
He told them what he had seen.
Some doubted it was true.
Soon, the sound started again.
They all got up and looked around,
but there was no one to be seen,
only bright stars and moon,
and the vast river waves.
As the crowd sat in the boat,
they soon saw a greenish fire, like a lamp,
emerge from the water,
floating with the current;
as it approached the boat,
the fire suddenly extinguished.
Immediately, a dark figure swiftly rose,
standing upright on the water,
climbing onto the boat with its hands.
The crowd shouted,
“This must be the thing!”
They wanted to shoot it.
Just as they drew their bows,
it suddenly plunged into the water,
and could not be seen.
They asked the boatman.
The boatman said,
“This is an ancient battlefield;
ghosts appear and disappear frequently,
so there's nothing strange about it.”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Zhāng Yúdàn of Zhāoyuǎn
was wild and unrestrained by nature.
He studied in Xiāosì.
At that time, the magistrate of the district, Lǔ Gōng,
was from Sānhán.
He had a daughter who was fond of hunting.
Zhāng Yúdàn happened to meet her in the countryside,
and saw her graceful and elegant demeanor,
wearing a brocade sable cloak,
riding a small black horse,
flitting about like a painting.
Upon returning, he recalled her beauty
and yearned for her intensely.
Later, he heard that the girl had died suddenly,
and he lamented almost to the point of collapse.
Since Lǔ Gōng's home was far away,
he placed her coffin in the temple,
which was where Zhāng Yúdàn studied.
Zhāng Yúdàn revered her as a deity,
burning incense every morning
and offering sacrifices at every meal.
Each time he offered a libation, he would pray, saying:
“Having seen but half your face,
my dreams have been forever bound;
I did not expect the jade-like maiden
to suddenly pass away.
Now so near,
yet as distant as rivers and mountains,
my regret is like a question unanswered!
However, the living have constraints,
the dead have no taboos;
if the underworld has spirits,
surely you will gracefully come
to comfort my yearning admiration.”
He prayed day and night,
for nearly half a month.
One evening,
as he was reading by lamplight,
he suddenly looked up
and saw the girl standing by the lamp, smiling.
Zhāng Yúdàn rose in surprise and questioned her.
The girl said,
“Moved by your affection,
I could not restrain myself,
and thus did not shun the suspicion of elopement.”
Zhāng Yúdàn was overjoyed,
and they became intimate.
From then on, not a night passed without their meeting.
She said to Zhāng Yúdàn,
“I was fond of archery and horsemanship in life,
finding pleasure in shooting deer and killing roe,
my sins are grave,
and I have no place to return in death.
If you truly love me,
please recite the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra a number of times for me,
and I will not forget it for generations.”
Zhāng Yúdàn respectfully accepted her instruction,
and every night he would rise
to recite the sūtra with prayer beads before her coffin.
Occasionally, when a festival arrived, he wished to take her home with him.
The girl worried that her feet were weak
and she could not walk far.
Zhāng Yúdàn offered to carry her,
and the girl smilingly agreed.
It was like holding a baby,
not at all heavy or cumbersome.
This became their custom.
He even carried her with him to examinations.
However, they always traveled at night.
When Zhāng Yúdàn was about to attend the autumn examination,
the girl said,
“Your fortune is meager,
it will be a fruitless journey.”
So he listened to her words and stayed.
After four or five years,
Lǔ Gōng was dismissed from office,
and being poor, he could not transport his daughter's coffin.
He intended to bury it where it was,
but struggled to find a burial place.
Zhāng Yúdàn then declared,
“I have a small plot of land near the temple;
I wish to bury your esteemed daughter there.”
Lǔ Gōng was pleased.
Zhāng Yúdàn also vigorously helped arrange the burial.
Lǔ Gōng was grateful,
but did not understand the reason.
After Lǔ Gōng left,
the two continued their intimacy as usual.
One night,
leaning against the student's embrace,
tears fell like beans,
and she said:
"Our five years of affection,
now we must part!
The kindness and righteousness I have received from you,
many lifetimes would not be enough to repay!"
The student was startled and asked her.
She said:
"Thanks to your beneficence, a person from the underworld,
whose scriptures and incantations were fully treasured,
I am now able to be reborn into the household of Hùbù Lú in Héběi.
If you do not forget today,
fifteen years from now,
on the sixteenth day of the eighth month,
please make the effort to meet me."
The student wept and said:
"I am already over thirty years old;
another fifteen years,
I will be near the grave,
what would a meeting achieve then?"
The woman also wept and said:
"I wish to be your slave to repay you."
A little while later, she said:
"Please escort your concubine for six or seven *lǐ*.
The path ahead has many thorns,
and my long robes will be difficult to manage."
Then she embraced the student's neck.
The student escorted her to the main road,
where he saw a cluster of carriages and horses by the roadside.
On horseback, there was sometimes one person,
sometimes two;
