in the carriages, sometimes three, four, or a dozen people;
only one ornate carriage,
with embroidered tassels and vermilion shafts,
had only an old woman in it.
Seeing the woman arrive,
she called out:
"Are you here?"
The woman responded:
"I am here."
Then she turned back to the student and said:
"This is the end,
you may go;
do not forget what I said."
The student agreed.
The woman approached the carriage,
the old woman pulled her hand and helped her up,
then immediately set off,
the carriages and horses moved away with a rumbling sound.
The student returned disheartened,
and marked the date on the wall.
He then thought of the efficacy of scriptures and incantations,
and recited them with even greater devotion.
In a dream, a divine being told him:
"Your aspiration is truly excellent.
But you must go to Nánhǎi."
He asked:
"How far is Nánhǎi?"
It said:
"It is close at hand, within your heart."
He awoke and understood its meaning,
his aspiration for Pútí became fervent,
and his spiritual practice became even purer.
Three years later,
his second son Míng and eldest son Zhèng
successively achieved high ranks in the imperial examinations.
Although the student had become suddenly wealthy,
his good deeds did not cease.
One night, he dreamed that a man in green robes invited him away.
He saw a person sitting in a palace hall,
like a Púsà,
who welcomed him, saying:
"Your good deeds are commendable.
It is a pity you lack longevity,
but fortunately, a request has been made to the Shàngdì."
The student prostrated himself on the ground and bowed.
He was called up and
given a seat;
he was served tea,
which had a fragrance like orchids.
Then a young attendant was ordered to lead him away,
and bade him bathe in a pond.
The pond water was clean,
the swimming fish could be counted,
it was warm when he entered,
and when scooped, it had the scent of lotus leaves.
After a while,
he gradually went into the deeper parts,
lost his footing and sank,
the water submerging him entirely.
He awoke with a start,
finding it strange.
From then on, his body became healthier,
his eyes brighter.
He stroked his beard,
and all the white hairs rustled and fell out,
and after a long time,
the black ones also fell out.
The wrinkles on his face also gradually smoothed out.
After several months,
his chin was bare and his face was like a child's,
exactly as he was at fifteen or sixteen.
He also became fond of playful activities,
just like a child.
He became overly concerned with his appearance;
his sons often tried to correct him.
Not long after,
his wife died of old age and illness.
His sons wanted to find him a new wife from a noble family.
The student said:
"Wait until I reach Héběi,
and only then shall I marry."
Counting the days, the appointed time had arrived.
So, he ordered a servant and horses to Héběi.
Upon inquiry,
there was indeed a Lú Hùbù.
Earlier,
Lú Gōng had a daughter.
She was able to speak from birth,
and as she grew, she became increasingly intelligent and beautiful.
Her parents loved her most dearly.
When noble families proposed marriage,
the daughter invariably refused.
Her parents, puzzled, asked her,
and she recounted in detail the vow made in a previous life.
They calculated her age together,
and Lú Gōng laughed loudly, saying:
"You foolish girl!
Zhāng Láng must be fifty years old this year.
With the vicissitudes of human affairs,
his bones must have decayed;
even if he were still alive,
his hair would be white as a child's and his teeth fallen out like a gully."
The daughter did not listen.
Her mother, seeing that her resolve was unshaken,
conferred with Lú Gōng.
They instructed the gatekeeper not to admit visitors,
hoping to extinguish her hopes by letting the date pass.
Not long after,
the young man arrived,
but the gatekeeper refused him entry.
He retreated to his inn,
feeling dejected and at a loss for what to do.
He idled away his time strolling in the suburbs,
and by chance, secretly inquired about her.
The daughter believed the young man had broken his promise,
and wept, refusing to eat.
Her mother said:
"If he did not come,
he must have passed away;
even if not,
the fault for breaking the vow
does not lie with you."
The daughter said nothing,
but merely lay in bed all day.
Lú Gōng was worried,
and also wished to see what kind of person the young man was.
So, feigning a leisurely stroll,
he met the young man in the countryside.
He looked at him
and saw he was a young man,
which surprised him.
They sat on straw and chatted briefly,
and he found him very gallant.
Lú Gōng was pleased
and invited him to his home.
Just as he was about to inquire further,
Lú Gōng suddenly rose,
instructed the guest to sit alone for a moment,
and rushed inside to tell his daughter.
The daughter was happy,
and struggled to get up.
She secretly observed him and found his appearance did not match,
so she returned, weeping,
and resented her father for deceiving her.
Lú Gōng strenuously explained that he was indeed the one.
The daughter said nothing,
but merely wept incessantly.
Lú Gōng came out,
feeling dejected and dispirited,
and was markedly less cordial to the guest.
The young man asked,
"Is there anyone in your esteemed family who is a Hùbù?"
Lú Gōng answered vaguely,
turning his head to look elsewhere,
as if he wasn't addressing the guest.
The young man felt his slight,
and excused himself.
The daughter wept for several days and then died.
That night, the young man dreamed the daughter came to him and said:
"Was it truly you who looked down upon me?
Our ages and appearances are mismatched,
and meeting face to face led to our separation.
I have died of sorrow and indignation.
Please quickly go to the local Earth God temple and summon my soul;
I may be able to live,
but if you delay, it will be too late."
Upon waking,
he urgently went to inquire at the Lú family's door.
Indeed, there was a daughter
who had died two days ago.
The young man wept bitterly,
and went in to mourn in her room.
Afterward, he told Lú Gōng about the dream.
Lú Gōng followed his words,
summoned her soul, and brought it back.
He opened her quilt,
stroked her corpse,
called her name, and prayed for her.
Suddenly, a gurgling sound was heard in her throat.
Then, her "vermilion cherry" (lips) suddenly parted,
and a phlegm-like塊(mass) dropped out like ice.
They helped her move to the couch,
and gradually she began to moan again.
Lú Gōng was delighted,
respectfully showed the guest out,
and arranged a feast with wine.
After carefully inquiring about his official background,
he learned he was from a prominent family,
which pleased him even more.
They chose an auspicious day and performed the wedding ceremony.
After half a month,
he took his daughter and returned home.
Lú Gōng escorted them to their home,
and stayed for half a year before leaving.
The couple lived in their chambers,
resembling a young married pair,
such that many who did not know them often mistook the daughter-in-law for the parents-in-law.
Lú Gōng died the following year.
His youngest son
was slandered by powerful figures,
and their family property was almost entirely lost.
The young man took him in and supported him,
and so they settled there.
According to the Zhùxuě Zhāi manuscript of 《Liáozhāi Zhìyì》.
Hán Shēng
was from a prominent family.
He enjoyed entertaining guests.
A man named Xú from the same village
often drank at his table.
During a banquet,
a Daoist priest with a begging bowl appeared at the door.
The servants offered money and grain,
but he accepted neither;
nor did he leave.
The servants grew angry
and ignored him.
Hán Shēng heard the sound of knocking for a long time.
When he inquired,
the servants told him the situation.
Before they had finished speaking,
the Daoist priest entered.
Hán Shēng invited him to sit.
The Daoist priest raised a hand to both host and guests,
then sat down.
After a brief exchange of questions,
Hán Shēng learned that the priest had recently taken up residence in a dilapidated temple east of the village.
Hán Shēng said:
"How is it that a crane has come to roost in the eastern monastery
and I was not aware?
I have certainly fallen short in the duties of a host."
The priest replied:
"This humble person has just arrived
and has no acquaintances.
Hearing of the generosity of the respected scholar,
I deeply wished to seek a drink."
Hán Shēng ordered a cup to be offered.
The Daoist priest was a heavy drinker.
Xú saw his soiled and worn clothes,
and was quite arrogant,
not showing much respect.
Hán Shēng, however, treated him like a distinguished guest.
The Daoist priest drank more than twenty cups
before taking his leave.
From then on, at every banquet,
the Daoist priest would always arrive.
When there was food, he would eat;
when there was drink, he would drink.
Hán also became somewhat annoyed by his frequent visits.
During one drinking session,
Xú playfully mocked him, saying:
"Daoist master, you are a guest every day,
would you not host just once?"
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
"Daoists are just like lay Buddhists;
we have only two shoulders supporting one mouth."
Xú was ashamed and could not reply.
The Daoist priest said:
"Nevertheless,
I, a Daoist, harbor a genuine heart towards you,
and will certainly do my utmost to repay your kindness, even if it's just a small gesture."
After the drinking,
he instructed, saying:
"Please honor me with your presence tomorrow afternoon."
The next day,
they invited each other to go together,
doubting that he would have anything prepared.
As they walked,
the Daoist priest was already waiting by the road.
Chatting and walking,
they soon arrived at the temple gate.
Upon entering,
they found the courtyards completely new,
with interconnected pavilions spreading like clouds.
Greatly surprised, they said:
"We haven't been here in a long time.
When was this built?"
The Daoist priest replied:
"It was completed not long ago."
When they entered his room,
the furnishings were luxurious,
such as no wealthy family possessed.
The two men stood up respectfully.
As soon as they sat down,
wine and food were served,
all by handsome young boys of sixteen,
dressed in brocade and red shoes.
The wine and dishes were fragrant and delicious,
and exceedingly abundant.
After the meal,
there were further small servings.
Many rare fruits, too numerous to name,
were served in crystal and jade vessels,
their brilliance illuminating the tables and couches.
They drank from glass goblets,
about a foot in circumference.
The Daoist priest said:
"Call for the Shí family sisters to come."
The boys left for a short while,
then two beauties entered.
One was slender and tall,
like a delicate willow;
the other was short,
and the youngest-looking;
both were enchantingly beautiful.
The Daoist priest immediately had them sing to accompany the wine.
The younger girl tapped a clapper and sang,
while the elder accompanied her with a dòngxiāo,
their voices clear and delicate.
When they finished,
the Daoist priest raised his goblet to urge a toast,
and then ordered everyone to be served.
He then asked the beauties:
"You haven't danced in a long time,
can you still do it?"
Immediately, attendants spread a rug beneath the feast,
and the two girls danced opposite each other,
their long sleeves fluttering,
fragrant dust scattering.
After the dance,
they leaned diagonally against the painted screen.
The two guests felt their hearts expand and spirits soar,
unconsciously becoming drunk.
The Daoist priest also disregarded his guests,
emptied his cup,
stood up and said to them:
"Please help yourselves,
I will rest for a bit,
and be back soon."
He then left.
Against the wall of the south room,
a mother-of-pearl bed was set up,
the girls spread brocade upon it,
and helped the Daoist priest lie down.
The Daoist priest then pulled the elder girl to sleep with him,
and ordered the younger girl to stand by the bed and scratch his back.
Seeing this,
the two guests were quite indignant.
Xú then loudly shouted:
"Daoist priest, you must not be rude!"
He advanced, intending to disturb him.
The Daoist priest quickly got up and fled.
Seeing the young girl still standing by the bed,
Xú, in his drunken state, pulled her to the northern couch,
and openly embraced her to sleep.
He looked at the beauty on the bed,
still asleep on the embroidered couch.
He looked at Hán and said:
"Why are you so rigid?"
Hán then directly went to the southern couch;
wishing to engage in intimacy,
but the beauty was fast asleep,
and would not turn when he pushed her.
So he embraced her and slept with her.
At dawn,
their drunken dreams dissipated,
and they felt a cold object in their arms, chilling them.
Looking at it,
Hán found he was embracing a long stone,
lying on the green steps.
He quickly looked at Xú;
Xú was not yet awake.
He saw him using a stone covered with excrement as a pillow,
sleeping soundly in a dilapidated latrine.
Hán kicked him awake,
and they were both mutually astonished.
Looking around,
they saw only a courtyard of overgrown grass,
and two ruined rooms.
*According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì*
In Zhílì, there was a prominent family
who wished to hire a tutor.
Suddenly, a xiùcái
came to their door, recommending himself.
The master of the house invited him in.
His speech was candid and clear,
and they immediately found each other agreeable.
The xiùcái introduced himself as Hú,
so the master accepted his introductory gift and lodged him.
Hú was diligent in his teaching,
and his extensive knowledge was not inferior to that of eminent scholars.
However, he would sometimes go out,
only returning late at night;
the door would be securely locked,
yet without hearing any knocking, he would already be in his room.
People then began to suspect him of being a fox spirit.
However, perceiving Hú's intentions were certainly not malicious,
the master treated him with respect,
not letting the strange circumstances disrupt their etiquette.
Hú knew that the master had a daughter,
and sought an engagement,
repeatedly hinting at it,
but the master pretended not to understand.
One day,
Hú took leave and departed.
The next day,
a guest came to visit,
bringing a black donkey to the gate.
The master went to meet him and invited him in.
He was over fifty years old,
his clothes and shoes were fresh and clean,
and his demeanor was very calm and refined.
After sitting down,
he introduced himself,
and the master then realized he was a matchmaker for Hú.
The master was silent for a long time,
then said:
"I and Mr. Hú
are already very close friends,
why is marriage necessary?
Moreover, my humble daughter is already betrothed."
He added: "Please convey my thanks to Mr. Hú."
The guest said:
"I am certain your esteemed daughter is awaiting a suitor,
why do you refuse so strongly?"
He spoke repeatedly,
but the master remained unyielding.
The guest showed a look of shame,
and said:
"Hú is also from a prominent family,
why is he suddenly inferior to you, sir?"
The master directly stated:
"Honestly, there is no other reason,
but I dislike those who are not of our kind."
Hearing this, the guest became angry;
the master also became angry,
and their mutual aggression intensified.
The guest stood up
and grabbed the master.
The master ordered his servants to beat and drive him away,
and the guest then fled.
He left behind his donkey;
looking at it,
its fur was black,
its ears flapped, its tail was long,
it was a large animal.
When pulled, it wouldn't move; when driven, it would immediately collapse.
Yet, it was merely an insect that eats grass.
The master, angered by his words,
knew there would certainly be a vendetta,
so he made preparations.
The next day,
a large force of fox soldiers indeed arrived: some mounted, some on foot,
some with halberds, some with crossbows.
Horses neighed and men clamored,
the sound and fury immense.
The master dared not go out.
The foxes threatened to set the house on fire,
which only increased the master's fear.
A brave man,
leading the family, rushed out shouting.
Flying stones and shooting arrows,
the two sides clashed,
and both suffered injuries.
The foxes gradually faltered
and retreated in disarray.
A knife was left on the ground,
gleaming like frost and snow;
when approached and picked up,
it was merely a sorghum leaf.
Everyone laughed, saying:
"Their skill extends only to this!"
However, fearing their return,
they increased their vigilance.
The next day,
as the crowd was gathered chatting,
suddenly a giant descended from the sky: over ten *zhàng* tall,
several *chǐ* wide across the body;
he wielded a great saber like a gate,
chasing and killing people.
The crowd hurled arrows and stones at him in a frenzy,
and he stumbled and fell dead,
but it was only a straw effigy.
The crowd scorned them even more.
The foxes did not return for three days,
and the crowd also slackened their guard a little.
The master happened to go to the latrine
when suddenly he saw fox soldiers
approaching with bows drawn and arrows nocked,
shooting at him wildly;
arrows gathered on his buttocks.
Greatly frightened,
he quickly shouted for the crowd to rush out and fight,
and the foxes then departed.
Pulling out the arrows to look,
they were all mugwort stems.
This continued for over a month,
their coming and going unpredictable.
Although not very harmful,
the daily state of alert
troubled the master greatly.
One day,
Hú Shēng led his followers to the house.
The master came out in person.
When Hú Shēng saw him,
he hid among his followers.
The master called out to him,
and having no choice,
he came out.
The master said:
"I thought I had shown no disrespect to you, sir,
so why the hostility?"
The group of foxes wanted to shoot,
but Hú Shēng stopped them.
The master approached and took his hand,
inviting him into his old study,
where he served wine to entertain him.
Calmly, he said:
"Sir, you are an enlightened person,
and should understand my situation.
Given our good relationship,
would I not be happy to form a marriage alliance?
But, sir, your carriages, horses, and mansions
are mostly not like those of humans.
If my young daughter were to follow you,
even you, sir, should know it is not feasible.
Moreover, the proverb says: 'Fruits picked unripe
are not palatable.'
Why do you insist, sir?"
Hú Shēng was greatly ashamed.
The master said:
"No harm done,
our old friendship remains.
If you do not disdain my worldly impurity,
I have a young son in my household,
who is fifteen years old.
I wish he could lie down under your bed without restraint (as a son-in-law).
I wonder if you have a suitable one (daughter)?"
Hú Shēng joyfully said:
"I have a young sister,
one year younger than your young master,
and quite not uncomely.
How about I offer her to serve with a broom and dustpan (as a wife)?"
The master rose and bowed,
and Hú Shēng returned the bow.
Thereupon, they drank merrily,
forgetting all past grievances.
He ordered wine and food to be brought out,
and generously treated all the followers.
Everyone, high and low, was joyous and comforted.
Then he inquired in detail about Hú Shēng's residence,
intending to offer geese as betrothal gifts.
Hú Shēng declined.
As dusk fell, candles were lit,
and deeply intoxicated, they departed.
From then on, they lived in peace.
Over a year later,
Hú Shēng did not return.
Some doubted his promise,
but the master firmly awaited him.
Another half year passed,
when Hú Shēng suddenly arrived.
After exchanging pleasantries,
he said:
"My sister has grown up.
Please choose an auspicious date
to send her to serve her parents-in-law."
The master was delighted
and immediately agreed on a date with him before he left.
That night,
carriages and horses indeed arrived, bringing the new bride.
Her trousseau was abundant,
filling almost the entire room where it was arranged.
The new bride greeted her parents-in-law
with unusual warmth and grace.
The master was overjoyed.
Hú Shēng and a younger brother came to escort the daughter;
both spoke elegantly
and were good drinkers.
They left at dawn.
The new bride could also foresee the good and bad harvests of the year,
so all plans for livelihood
were based on her predictions.
Hú Shēng, his brother, and Hú Āo
would visit their daughter from time to time,
and everyone saw them.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a conjurer with a bucket;
the bucket could hold one *shēng*;
it had no bottom,
and was hollow inside,
just like in common shows.
The performer placed two mats on the street,
and held a *shēng* measure as he entered the bucket;
he then emerged,
and immediately there was a full *shēng* of white rice,
which he poured onto the mats;
he took and poured again,
and in an instant, both mats were full.
Then he measured it all back in,
and when finished and lifted,
it was still an empty bucket.
The wonder lay in its abundance.
Lǐ Jiàntián from Lìjīn
was casually touring a pottery kiln in Yánzhèn,
wanting to buy a large jar.
He argued with the potter about the price,
could not agree, and left.
That night,
over sixty jars that had not yet been taken out of the kiln,
when opened and inspected, were all empty.
The potter was greatly alarmed,
suspected Lǐ,
and went to his door to seek them.
Lǐ disclaimed any knowledge.
The potter pleaded persistently,
and then Lǐ said:
"I took them out of the kiln for you.
Not a single jar is damaged.
Are they not under the Kuíxīnglóu?"
They went to check as he said,
and indeed, every single one was there.
The tower was on the south mountain of the town,
over three *lǐ* from the kiln.
It took laborers three days to transport them all.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A monk in Jìnán,
his origin unknown.
Barefoot and clad in a patchwork robe,
he spent his days at the Fúróng and Mínghú lodges,
chanting sutras and collecting alms.
He refused any offerings of wine, food, money, or grain;
when asked what he needed,
he would not answer.
He was never seen to eat a meal all day long.
Someone advised him, saying:
"Since you, Shī, do not eat meat or drink alcohol,
you should beg for alms in mountain villages and secluded alleys.
Why do you daily come and go in these noisy, smelly places?"
The monk closed his eyes and chanted,
his eyelashes as long as a finger's breadth,
as if he did not hear.
A moment later,
he was spoken to again.
The monk suddenly opened his eyes and said in a stern voice:
"This is how I must transform (people)!"
Then he continued chanting without stopping.
After a long time,
he went out on his own and left.
Someone followed him from behind,
insistently questioning him about the reason for his insistence on doing things this way,
but he walked without responding.
When pressed several times,
he again said in a stern voice:
"It is not for you to know!
This old monk must transform (people) this way!"
After several days,
he suddenly appeared outside the south city gate,
lying by the roadside as if stiff,
not moving for three days.
The residents feared he would starve to death
and bring trouble to the nearby district.
So they gathered and urged other disciples
to give him food if he wanted food,
or money if he wanted money.
The monk remained motionless with his eyes closed.
The crowd shook him and spoke to him.
The monk grew angry,
took a short knife from his monastic robe,
and cut open his own belly;
he put his hand inside,
pulled out his intestines onto the road,
and then his breath ceased.
The crowd was horrified and reported it to the prefecture,
which buried him in a straw mat.
Another day, a dog burrowed into the grave,
and the mat was visible.
Stepping on it felt hollow;
upon opening and inspecting it,
the mat was sealed as before,
still like an empty cocoon.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
Grand Historian Mǒu
was bewitched by a fox
and became thin and ill.
After exhausting all talismans and prayers,
he requested leave to return home,
hoping to escape.
As the Grand Historian traveled,
the fox followed him.
He was greatly frightened,
having no plan.
One day,
he stopped in Zhuó.
Outside the gate, there was an itinerant doctor
who claimed he could subdue foxes.
The Grand Historian invited him in.
The doctor gave him a medicine,
which was a technique from the bedroom arts.
He urged him to take it immediately,
and the man engaged in intercourse with the fox,
with an unstoppable vigor.
The fox recoiled,
pleading sadly for him to stop;
he did not listen,
and advanced with increasing courage.
The fox writhed and struggled to escape,
but could not get away.
After a while, there was no sound,
and when they looked,
it had taken its fox form and died.
Once, there was a scholar Mǒu from my hometown
who had a naturally critical eye,
claiming he had never found anything truly satisfying in his life.
One night, he stayed in a solitary inn,
with no neighbors around.
Suddenly, a girl rushed in,
entering before the door was even opened;
he knew in his heart it was a fox,
but also happily indulged in intimacy with her.
As soon as her clothes were undone,
he entered directly.
The fox shrieked in pain,
making a squeaking sound,
like a hawk escaping,
and flew out through the window.
Mǒu still looked out the window, making intimate sounds,
and called out plaintively,
hoping she would return,
but she was already gone.
This was truly a fierce general for hunting foxes!
It would be fitting to put up a sign outside his door
"Fox Exorcist,"
which could be a profession.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
Yúlíng Qū Yíntái Gōng
was reading upstairs in his study.
It was dark and gloomy due to rain,
when he saw a small object,
glowing like a firefly,
crawling along.
Where it passed,
it was black like a centipede's trail.
Gradually it coiled upward,
and the scroll it coiled around also became scorched.
Thinking it was a dragon,
he picked up the scroll and carried it out.
When he reached outside the door,
he stood there holding it for a long time,
but it remained motionless, curled like a geometer moth.
The Duke said:
"Could it be that you think I am disrespectful?"
He took the scroll back,
placed it back on the desk,
donned his hat and belt, and bowed deeply as if seeing it off.
Just as he reached the eaves,
he saw it suddenly stretch its head upward,
fly horizontally away from the scroll,
with a hissing sound,
a single thread of light;
a few steps away,
it turned its head towards the Duke,
its head now larger than a jar,
and its body several tens of arm spans in circumference;
then it made another turn,
and with a thunderous clap that shook the ground,
it soared into the sky and departed.
Looking back at where it had been,
it had clearly wriggled out from within a book tube.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
When Gāo Gōngmíngtú was prefect of Chēnzhōu,
there was a common woman, Sū Shì,
who was washing clothes in the river.
There was a large stone in the river,
and the woman sat upon it.
A strand of moss,
green and lovely,
floated and swayed in the water,
circling the stone three times.
The woman looked at it,
and her heart was moved.
Upon returning home, she became pregnant,
her belly gradually growing.
Her mother secretly questioned her,
and the woman told her the situation.
Her mother could not understand.
After several months,
she indeed gave birth to a son.
She wanted to abandon him in a narrow alley,
but the woman could not bear to,
so she hid him in a box and raised him.
She then vowed not to marry,
to show her unwavering resolve.
However, to be pregnant without a husband
was ultimately a source of shame.
When the child reached seven years old,
he had never been taken out to be seen by others.
The child suddenly said to his mother:
"Son is growing up,
how can this confinement last forever?
I will leave,
so as not to be a burden to mother."
She asked where he would go.
He said:
"I am not of human kind;
I will soon ascend to the sky and soar over the ravines."
The woman tearfully asked for his return date.
He replied:
"When mother is on her deathbed,
then son will come.
After I leave,
if you ever need anything,
you can open the box where I was hidden and ask for it,
and it will surely be granted as you wish."
Having said this,
he bowed to his mother and left.
When she went out and looked,
he had already vanished.
The woman told her mother,
who was greatly astonished.
The girl steadfastly held to her former resolve,
relying on her mother for support,
but their household grew increasingly poor.
Occasionally, they lacked morning provisions,
looking at the roof with no ideas.
Suddenly, she recalled her son's words,
went and opened the chest,
and indeed found rice,
relying on it to light the fire.
From then on, whatever was requested was provided.
After more than three years,
her mother fell ill and died;
all funeral accoutrements
were supplied from the chest.
After the burial,
the girl lived alone for thirty years,
never peeking out of the door.
One day,
a neighboring woman who came to ask for fire,
saw her sitting motionlessly in the empty chamber,
and left only after speaking for a while.
Not long after,
suddenly she saw auspicious clouds encircling the girl's dwelling,
standing tall like a canopy,
with a person in splendid attire standing within it.
Upon closer inspection,
it was the girl Sū.
She hovered for a long time,
gradually rising higher until she disappeared.
The neighbors all wondered about this.
Peeking into her room,
they saw the girl beautifully adorned and sitting still,
but her breath had already ceased.
The crowd, considering she had no kin,
discussed preparing her for burial.
Suddenly, a young man entered,
of handsome and majestic bearing,
who thanked the crowd.
The neighbors had previously secretly known that the girl had a son,
and so they did not doubt him.
The young man produced gold to bury his mother,
planted two peach trees at the grave,
and then bid farewell and departed.
A few steps away,
clouds appeared beneath his feet,
and he could no longer be seen.
Later, the peaches bore sweet and fragrant fruit,
which the residents called
the "Sū Xiān Táo,"
and the trees bloomed luxuriantly every year,
never withering or decaying.
The officials of that area
each carried the fruit to present to their relatives and friends.
According to the *Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì* Chù Xuě Zhāi Manuscript:
Lǐ Shēng Bó Yán,
a native of Yí Shuǐ.
He was upright and courageous.
Suddenly, he fell gravely ill,
and when his family offered medicine,
he refused, saying:
"My illness cannot be cured by medicine.
The underworld king of Yán Luó is vacant,
and wants me to temporarily take up his seal of office.
When I die, do not bury me;
you should wait."
On that day, he indeed died.
Attendants escorted him away,
into a palace,
where he was presented with a ceremonial robe and crown;
the clerks and assistants attended with great solemnity.
On the desk, official documents were piled high.
One case involved
a certain person from Jiāng Nán,
who had illicitly violated eighty-two respectable women in his lifetime.
He was interrogated,
and the corroborating evidence was not false.
According to the laws of the underworld,
he deserved to be roasted by fire and branded.
Below the hall was a copper pillar,
eight or nine *chǐ* high,
and about one embrace in circumference;
it was hollow and filled with blazing charcoal,
red hot inside and out.
A group of devils lashed and drove him with iron thorns to climb it,
moving his hands and wrapping his feet as he ascended.
As soon as he reached the top,
smoke and gas flew upwards,
and with a crashing sound like a firecracker,
the person fell;
he lay curled up for a while,
then slowly revived.
They flogged him again,
and he exploded and fell as before.
After falling three times,
he dissipated like smoke across the ground,
no longer able to form a shape.
There was another case.
It concerned a certain Wáng from the same district.
He was accused by his maid's father of stealing and occupying his living daughter.
Wáng was already married into his in-laws' family.
Previously,
a man was selling a maid.
Wáng knew that her origin was not legitimate,
but he was attracted by her cheap price,
so he bought her.
At this point, Wáng died suddenly.
The next day,
his friend Zhōu-shēng encountered him on the road.
Knowing he was a ghost,
Zhōu-shēng fled into his study.
Wáng also followed him in.
Zhōu was frightened and prayed,
asking what Wáng wished to do.
Wáng said:
"I just need you to be a witness in the Underworld Office."
Zhōu-shēng asked in surprise:
"What for?"
Wáng replied:
"I genuinely purchased my maid,
but now I am being falsely accused.
You personally witnessed this matter.
I only need to borrow a word from Jìlù,
nothing else."
Zhōu steadfastly refused him.
Wáng went out and said:
"I fear it may not be up to you."
Not long after,
Zhōu indeed died,
and both went to Yánluó to be questioned and examined.
Lǐ saw Wáng,
and secretly harbored an intention to side with him.
Suddenly, fire broke out in the hall,
its flames burning the beams and pillars.
Lǐ was greatly alarmed,
and stood on one foot.
The clerk urgently stepped forward and said:
"The netherworld is not like the human world;
even a private thought cannot be tolerated.
Quickly dispel other thoughts,
and the fire will extinguish itself."
Lǐ collected his thoughts and calmed his mind,
and the fire immediately went out.
Afterwards, the case was tried.
Wáng and the maid's father repeatedly argued bitterly.
When Zhōu was questioned,
Zhōu told the truth.
Wáng was sentenced as a deliberate offender.
After the verdict,
people were sent to return them both to life.
Zhōu and Wáng both revived after three days.
After Lǐ finished his duties,
he returned by carriage and horse.
On the way, he saw several hundred people with missing heads and broken feet,
lying on the ground, wailing mournfully.
He stopped his carriage to inquire closely.
They were ghosts from a foreign land,
who longed to tread their native soil,
and feared that passes and barriers would block them,
so they begged for a travel permit.
Lǐ said:
"I have only served for three days,
and have already resigned my post.
What can I do?"
The crowd said:
"Hú-shēng of Náncūn
is about to hold a Daoist ritual;
if you ask him on our behalf, it can be accomplished."
Lǐ agreed.
When he arrived home,
all his retinue had left,
and Lǐ then revived.
Hú-shēng, courtesy name Shuǐxīn,
was good friends with Lǐ.
Hearing that Lǐ had revived,
he immediately went to visit him.
Lǐ quickly asked:
"When is the pure offering?"
Hú exclaimed in surprise:
"After the devastation of war,
my wife and children barely survived.
I made this vow with my wife,
and have not told a single person.
How do you know?"
Lǐ told him everything.
Hú sighed:
"A private word in the bedchamber
was thus spread to the netherworld;
how terrifying!"
Then he respectfully agreed and left.
The next day,
he went to Wáng's place.
Wáng was still weakly lying down.
Seeing Lǐ,
he rose with solemn respect,
and expressed gratitude for the protection and blessing.
Lǐ said:
"The law cannot be lenient.
Are you fortunately unharmed now?"
Wáng said:
"There are no other symptoms now,
but the sores from the beating are festering."
It took more than twenty more days for him to recover;
the flesh on his buttocks had rotted away,
leaving scars like those from a staff.
Yìshǐ-shì comments:
"The punishments in the netherworld
are more severe than in the human world;
the demands are also harsher than in the human world.
However, if influence cannot be exerted,
then those who suffer cruelty will not complain.
Who says there is no justice in the underworld?
My only regret is that there is no fire to burn the halls of officials who oppress the people!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Hé Shīcān,
courtesy name Zǐxiāo,
had his study east of Tiáoxī,
with his gate facing a vast wilderness.
One evening at dusk, he happened to go out,
and saw a woman riding a donkey,
with a young man following behind her.
The woman was about fifty years old,
with an elegant and refined demeanor.
Turning to look at the young man,
he appeared to be fifteen or sixteen,
his handsome appearance surpassing even that of a beautiful woman.
Hé-shēng had always had a homosexual inclination.
Upon seeing him,
his spirit seemed to leave his body;
he stood on tiptoe, gazing after him,
and only returned when the shadow disappeared.
The next day,
he waited for him early.
As the sun set and darkness gathered,
the young man finally passed by.
Hé-shēng tried to greet him courteously,
and smilingly asked where he had come from.
He replied,
"My maternal grandmother's house."
Hé-shēng invited him to rest for a while in his study,
but he declined, saying he had no time;
Hé-shēng insisted and pulled him,
so he entered.
After sitting briefly, he excused himself,
and could not be persuaded to stay.
Hé-shēng held his hand and sent him off,
earnestly urging him to stop by if he passed this way.
The young man assented and left.
From then on, Hé-shēng was engrossed in thought as if parched,
coming and going, constantly looking out,
his feet never stopping.
One day,
the sun hung like a half-disk.
A young man arrived.
Hé
was greatly pleased and invited him to enter,
ordering the houseboy to serve wine.
He asked his name.
He replied:
"My surname is Huáng,
and I am Ninth.
A young boy has no personal name."
Hé
asked: "Why do you pass by so often?"
He said:
"My mother is at my maternal grandparents' home,
and she is often ill,
so I frequently visit her."
After a few rounds of wine,
he wished to take his leave.
Hé grabbed his arm to stop him,
and locked the gate.
Jiǔláng had no choice,
and sat back down, his expression calm.
They trimmed the lamp and conversed,
he was gentle like a virgin;
but when the conversation turned playful,
he would blush,
and face the wall.
Soon after,
Hé invited him to share the same bed.
Jiǔláng refused,
firmly excusing himself by saying he had a bad sleeping habit.
Hé urged him repeatedly,
so he took off his outer clothes,
and lay on the bed in his trousers.
Hé extinguished the candle;
after a short while,
he moved to share Jiǔláng's pillow,
bent his arm over Jiǔláng's thigh, embraced him intimately,
and desperately sought intimacy.
Jiǔláng angrily said:
"I treated you as a refined scholar,
and therefore lingered with you;
but to do this,
is like treating a human as an animal, and loving them as a beast!"
Soon after,
as the morning stars twinkled,
Jiǔláng left directly.
Hé feared that he would leave permanently,
and watched for him again,
pacing back and forth, gazing intently,
his eyes piercing the Big Dipper.
After several days,
Jiǔláng finally arrived.
Hé delightedly greeted him and apologized;
he strongly pulled him into his study,
urged him to sit, laughed and talked,
secretly glad that Jiǔláng did not hold a grudge.
Before long,
Hé took off his shoes and got onto the bed,
and again stroked and implored him.
Jiǔláng said:
"The depth of your affection
is already carved into my heart and diaphragm,
but must love necessarily be expressed in this way?"
Hé coaxed and pleaded sweetly,
only wishing to touch his jade-like skin once.
Jiǔláng acquiesced.
Hé waited for him to fall asleep,
then secretly took liberties.
Jiǔláng woke up,
grabbed his clothes, and rose abruptly,
fleeing under the cover of night.
Hé was despondent as if he had lost something,
forgot to eat and neglected his pillow,
gradually wasting away.
He only had his study boy constantly scout for him.
One day,
Jiǔláng passed by the gate,
and immediately intended to leave directly.
The boy pulled his clothes and brought him in.
Jiǔláng saw Hé's emaciated appearance,
was greatly alarmed,
and expressed concern.
Hé truthfully told him his situation,
tears trickling down with his words.
Jiǔláng softly said:
"My humble intention
is truly that my love for you would be of no benefit to me,
but harmful to you,
hence I did not engage in it.
Since you enjoy it,
why should I be reluctant?"
Hé was greatly pleased.
After Jiǔláng left,
Hé's illness immediately diminished,
and he recovered in a few days.
Jiǔláng indeed came,
and they then became intimately attached.
Jiǔláng said:
"Today I reluctantly grant your wish,
but please do not take this as a regular occurrence."
Then he said:
"I have something to ask for,
will you be willing to help?"
Hé asked him about it.
He replied:
"My mother has a severe heart pain,
only Grand Physician Qí Yěwáng's Xiāntiān Dān can cure it.
You are on good terms with him,
you should be able to obtain it."
Hé assented.
Before leaving, Jiǔláng gave further instructions.
Hé went into the city to seek the medicine,
and delivered it in the evening.
Jiǔláng was happy,
and clasped his hands to thank him.
Hé again forced intimacy upon him.
Jiǔláng said:
"Do not entangle me.
I will carefully find a beautiful woman for you,
who will be ten thousand times better than me."
Hé asked who.
Jiǔláng said:
"I have a maternal cousin,
unrivaled in beauty.
If you would be interested,
I shall act as the matchmaker."
Hé smiled faintly and did not reply.
Jiǔláng took the medicine and left.
He came three days later,
and again asked for medicine.
Hé resented his tardiness,
and his words were full of reproach.
Jiǔláng said:
"I originally did not bear to bring misfortune upon you,
hence I distanced myself;
since you do not understand my feelings,
please do not regret it."
From then on, there was no evening without their intimate gatherings.
Every three days, he would ask for medicine.
Qí was surprised by the frequency,
and said:
"No one has ever taken more than three doses of this medicine,
why has the illness not improved after so long?"
He then wrapped three doses together and gave them to him.
He also looked at Hé and said:
"Your complexion is dark,
are you ill?"
He said:
"No."
Qí took his pulse,
and exclaimed in surprise:
"You have a 'ghost pulse',
the illness is in the Shaoyin meridian,
those who are not careful will be in danger!"
Hé returned and told Jiǔláng.
Jiǔláng sighed and said:
"He is truly a good physician!
I am indeed a fox,
and I have long feared that I would not be a blessing to you."
Hé suspected he was lying,
hid some of the medicine,
and did not give it all to him,
fearing he would not come otherwise.
Not long after,
he indeed fell ill.
He invited Qí to examine him,
who said:
"You did not tell me the truth before,
now your vital energy has already wandered into the wilderness,
what can Qín Huǎn do?"
Jiǔláng came daily to visit and attend to him,
saying:
"You didn't listen to my words,
and it has indeed come to this!"
Hé soon died.
Jiǔláng cried bitterly and left.
Previously,
in the district, there was a certain Tài-shǐ,
who, when young, shared a desk and inkstone with Shēng.
At seventeen, he was promoted to the Hàn-lín Academy.
At that time, the Qín Fān was corrupt and tyrannical,
and bribed court officials,
so no one dared to speak out.
Gōng submitted a memorial to impeach his evil deeds,
and was dismissed for "overstepping his bounds."
The Fān promoted this Shěng Zhōng-chéng,
who daily sought out Gōng's weaknesses.
Gōng had been known for his talent since he was young,
and had once been favored by a rebellious Wáng Qīng-pàn.
Thus, (the Zhōng-chéng) acquired old correspondence Gōng had exchanged,
and threatened Gōng.
Gōng, frightened,
hanged himself.
His Fū-rén also threw herself into a noose and died.
A night later, Gōng suddenly awoke,
and said:
"I am Hé Zǐ-xiāo."
When questioned,
all he spoke of were matters concerning the Hé family,
and only then did they realize he had borrowed a body to return his soul.
They could not keep him,
so he fled to his old residence.
Fǔ suspected it was a trick,
and absolutely wanted to frame him,
sending someone to demand a thousand pieces of gold from Gōng.
Gōng falsely agreed,
but was so worried and depressed he almost died.
Suddenly, Jiǔ-láng arrived,
and they conversed happily,
their joys and sorrows intermingling.
When he (Gōng) wanted to resume intimacy,
Jiǔ-láng said:
"Do you have three lives?"
Gōng said:
"I regret that life is toil;
it is better to have the ease of death."
He then recounted his grievances and suffering.
Jiǔ-láng pondered with deep concern.
After a while, he said:
"Fortunately, we are reunited.
You are lonely and without a partner.
My aforementioned female cousin
is intelligent, beautiful, and resourceful,
and will surely be able to share your worries."
Gōng wished to see her face.
He said:
"It's not difficult.
Tomorrow, I will take my old mother as a companion,
and this road passes by here.
You pretend to be a younger brother (of mine) or an elder brother,
and I will feign thirst and ask for a drink.
If you say 'The donkey is gone,'
then it is agreed."
Having made their plan, they parted.
The next day, around noon,
Jiǔ-láng indeed passed by the gate with the young lady.
Gōng bowed with cupped hands and talked with her garrulously.
He glanced at the young lady;
her delicate eyebrows were elegant and beautiful,
truly she was an immortal.
Jiǔ-láng asked for tea,
and Gōng invited them in to drink.
Jiǔ-láng said:
"Sān-mèi, do not be surprised.
This is my sworn brother,
there's no harm in resting a little."
He helped her dismount,
tied the donkey at the gate, and entered.
Gōng himself rose to brew tea.
Then he looked at Jiǔ-láng and said:
"Your previous words were not enough.
Now I have found a place to die!"
The girl seemed to understand that his words were meant for her,
rose from the couch,
and said softly:
"Go away!"
Gōng looked outside and said:
"The donkey is gone!"
Jiǔ-láng rushed out in a panic.
Gōng embraced the girl, seeking intimacy.
The girl's complexion turned purple,
distressed as if imprisoned,
she loudly called for Jiǔ-xiōng,
but received no answer.
She said:
"You already have a wife,
why do you try to ruin a person's integrity?"
Gōng declared that he was unmarried.
The girl said:
"If you can swear by the mountains and rivers,
and not let me be discarded like an autumn fan,
then I will obey your command."
Gōng then swore an oath by "pledging the sun."
The girl no longer resisted.
After the deed was done,
Jiǔ-láng arrived.
The girl angrily reproached him, her face flushed.
Jiǔ-láng said:
"This is Hé Zǐ-xiāo,
a famous scholar of the past,
and now a Tài-shǐ.
He is the best of friends with your brother;
he is a man you can rely on.
Even if your aunt hears of it,
she will surely not blame us."
As evening approached,
Gōng entreated them not to leave, but they did not listen.
The girl feared her aunt would be startled and surprised.
Jiǔ-láng readily took responsibility,
mounted his donkey, and rode straight off.
A few days later,
a woman accompanied by a maid passed by.
She was about forty years old,
and her demeanor and bearing
were gracefully similar to Sān-niáng.
Gōng called the girl out to peek,
and indeed it was her mother.
Catching sight of the girl,
she asked in surprise:
"How did you get here?"
The girl was ashamed and could not answer.
Gōng invited her in,
bowed, and explained.
The mother smiled and said:
"Jiǔ-láng is childish,
why didn't he consult me again?"
The girl herself went into the kitchen,
prepared a meal for her mother,
and after eating, she left.
Gōng got a beautiful companion,
which greatly pleased his heart and expectations;
but evil thoughts tangled his mind,
and he constantly frowned with a troubled expression.
The woman asked him about it,
and Gōng vaguely recounted the whole story.
The woman smiled and said:
“Only the ninth brother can solve this,
why do you worry?”
Gōng questioned her about the reason.
The woman said:
“I heard that Fǔgōng is addicted to singing and music and is as stubborn as a child,
and these are all the ninth brother's strengths.
Present them to him as he likes,
and the resentment can be dispelled,
and revenge can also be exacted.”
Gōng worried that Jiǔláng would be unwilling.
The woman said:
“Just beg him pitifully.”
The next day,
Gōng saw Jiǔláng coming,
and he walked forward to meet him.
Jiǔláng was surprised and said:
“Our friendship spans two generations,
I can only exert myself,
not even my head and heels would I begrudge.
Why suddenly act like this towards me?”
Gōng fully explained the plan to him.
Jiǔláng showed a reluctant expression.
The woman said:
“I lost my virginity to you,
who is really to blame for it?
If I were to perish midway,
where would you put me?”
Jiǔláng had no choice
but to agree.
Gōng's clan conspired with him,
and he galloped a letter to his good friend, Wáng Tàishǐ,
and sent Jiǔláng to him.
Wáng understood his intention,
made a grand feast,
and invited Fǔgōng to drink.
He ordered Jiǔláng to dress up as a young woman,
and perform the Tiānmó Wǔ,
looking exactly like a beautiful woman.
Fǔ was enchanted by her,
and immediately begged Wáng,
wanting to purchase Jiǔláng with a large sum of money,
fearing only that he might not obtain her.
Wáng deliberately pondered deeply to make it difficult.
After a long delay,
he finally brought Gōng's command forward.
Fǔ was delighted,
and his previous troubles were instantly dispelled.
Since he obtained Jiǔláng,
they were inseparable in every movement and rest;
his ten-plus concubines
were regarded as dust.
Jiǔláng's food and provisions were like those of a king;
he was given tens of thousands in gold.
After half a year,
Fǔgōng fell ill.
Jiǔláng knew that his journey to the underworld was near,
so he loaded gold and silk
and falsely claimed to return to Gōng's home.
Soon after, Fǔgōng died.
Jiǔláng invested money,
built houses, bought furnishings,
and raised maids and servants.
His mother, son, and maternal aunt all lived in his household.
When Jiǔláng went out,
his carriage and horses were very magnificent,
and no one knew he was a fox.
I have
a "Laughing Judgment"
which is also recorded:
A man and woman living together
is the great moral principle of husband and wife;
the interchange of dryness and wetness
is the proper channel of Yin and Yang.
Serving the wind and waiting for the moon
still carries the criticism of impropriety;
cutting sleeves and sharing peaches
cannot avoid the shame of covering one's nose.
Only a man of great strength
would dare to carve open a bird's path;
if the cave is not Peach Blossom Spring,
how could a fisherman's pole be allowed to mistakenly enter?
Now someone follows the downstream and forgets to return,
abandoning the proper path and not following it.
Before the clouds and rain have arisen,
he already moves his hands up and down;
Yin and Yang are reversed,
and he actually commits adultery both inside and out.
The magnificent pond is placed in a useless place,
falsely saying an old monk has entered meditation;
the barbarian cave is barren land,
thus a one-eyed commander wields his spear.
Tying the Red Hare at the camp gate,
as if to shoot the halberd;
drawing a great bow from the national treasury,
straight up wanting to break through the pass.
Perhaps it is inspecting the inner Yellow River,
visiting an old friend last night;
clearly it is Wáng family's red plums and plums,
seeking compensation for drilling in the next life.
When the cavalry arrives at the Black Pine Forest,
they are indeed at peace;
but if the tidal wave suddenly arrives at the Yellow Dragon Citadel,
how will it be resisted?
It is advisable to cut off the roots of their drilling and piercing,
and also block their paths of coming and going.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
A certain Zhào, a resident of Yíshuǐ,
returned from the city due to an old matter,
and saw a woman in white clothes crying by the roadside,
very sorrowfully.
He glanced at her,
and she was beautiful.
Pleased by her,
he stared intently, not moving.
The woman, weeping, said:
“My husband, oh my husband,
you do not walk the road but look at me!”
Zhào said:
“I thought the wilderness was empty,
and you were crying so mournfully,
it truly pained my heart.”
The woman said:
“My husband is dead, and I have nowhere to go,
that is why I grieve.”
Zhào urged her to find another good match.
She said:
“Being alone like this,
how can I choose?
If I can find someone to entrust myself to,
I can be a concubine.”
Zhào happily offered himself,
and the woman accepted.
Zhào, knowing his home was far,
was about to look for a ride.
The woman said:
“No need.”
Then she went ahead,
floating like an immortal running.
When they arrived home,
she diligently performed household chores.
After more than two years,
she said to Zhào:
“I am grateful for your affection,
for following me,
and suddenly three years have passed.
Now I should leave.”
Zhào said:
“You previously said you had no home,
where are you going now?”
She said:
“At that time, I just said that casually,
how could I have no home?
My father sells medicine in Jīnlíng.
If you wish to meet again,
you can carry medicine there;
it can help with travel expenses.”
Zhào made arrangements,
and rented a carriage and horses.
The woman declined,
went out the door and left directly;
he chased her but could not catch up,
and she vanished in an instant.
He lived there for a long time,
pondering and reminiscing,
then bought medicine and went to Jīnlíng.
He deposited his goods at an inn for travelers
and visited various street markets.
Suddenly, an old man at a pharmacy, seeing him,
said:
"The son-in-law has arrived."
He invited him in.
The daughter was washing clothes in the courtyard;
seeing him, she neither spoke nor smiled,
and continued washing without pause.
Zhào, harboring resentment, quickly exited.
The old man again pulled him back.
The daughter paid him no heed, as before.
The old man ordered preparations for a meal
and planned to give him a generous gift.
The daughter stopped him, saying:
"His blessings are meager;
too much will not benefit him.
It would be better to slightly alleviate his hardship
and give him a dozen or so medical prescriptions;
he will then have more than enough to use."
The old man asked about the medicine he had brought.
The daughter said:
"It has already been sold;
the money is here."
The old man then took out a prescription and handed over money,
and sent Zhào home.
He tried the prescription,
and it had a miraculous effect.
In Yíshuǐ, there are still those who know its formula.
Using a garlic mortar to collect rainwater from under the thatched eaves
to wash warts
is one of its formulas,
and it is very effective.
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of 《Liáozhāi Zhìyì》.
Tāng Gōng, whose given name was Pìn,
was a *jìnshì* in the *xīnchǒu* year.
He was critically ill.
Suddenly, he felt a warmth in his lower body
gradually rising upwards: when it reached his thighs,
his feet died;
when it reached his abdomen,
his thighs also died;
when it reached his heart,
the death of the heart was the most difficult.
All matters from childhood to long-forgotten trivialities
came with the blood of his heart,
surging through one by one.
If it was a good deed,
his heart felt pure, peaceful, and calm;
if it was an evil deed,
he felt vexed and agitated,
like oil boiling in a cauldron,
a state of unbearable distress
that words could not describe.
He still remembered when he was seven or eight years old,
he had reached into a nest, taken out a chick, and killed it;
just for this one incident,
a hot blood surge welled up in his heart,
passing only after a mealtime.
It was necessary to wait for all the deeds of his life
to surge completely,
then he felt a thread of warmth,
passing through his throat and entering his brain,
exiting from the top of his head,
rising like steam.
After several tens of *kè* (quarter hours),
his soul finally left its orifice,
forgetting its body.
And vaguely, without a place to return,
he drifted in the suburban roads.
A giant came,
nearly a *xún* (eight *chǐ*) tall,
picked him up,
and put him into his sleeve.
Inside the sleeve,
people were stacked shoulder-to-shoulder and pressing on thighs,
and there were many of them.
The suffocation and oppression were
almost unbearable.
Gōng suddenly thought that the Buddha could relieve calamity,
and so he recited the Buddha's name.
After only three or four calls,
he floated out of the sleeve.
The giant again put him in.
After three insertions and three falls,
the giant then departed.
Gōng stood alone, bewildered,
not knowing where best to go.
He remembered the Buddha was in the Western Pure Land,
and so he headed west.
Not long after,
he saw a monk sitting cross-legged by the roadside.
He hastened to bow and ask for directions.
The monk said:
"For the records of life and death of scholars,
Wénchāng and Kǒng Shèng preside over them.
You must have your name removed from both places
before you can go elsewhere."
Gōng asked where they resided,
the monk showed him the way,
and he rushed there.
Before long,
he arrived at the Sage Temple
and saw Xuān Shèng (Confucius) sitting facing south.
He bowed and prayed as before.
Xuān Shèng said:
"The removal of your name from the register
still requires the Imperial Lord."
He then pointed out the way.
Gōng again rushed there.
He saw a palace-like pavilion,
like a king's residence.
He bent down to enter
and indeed saw a divine being,
like the Imperial Lord image described in the world.
He prostrated himself and prayed.
The Imperial Lord checked the name and said:
"Your heart is sincere and upright;
you ought to have a chance to live again.
But your skin-bag (body) is decayed,
and only a Bodhisattva can help."
He then gave instructions, telling him to go quickly.
Gōng followed his teaching.
Soon, he saw dense woods and tall bamboos,
with beautiful and magnificent temple buildings.
Upon entering,
he saw the majestic coiled hair (of the Bodhisattva),
and a golden countenance like the full moon;
willows steeped in a vase,
their verdant green drooping like mist.
Gōng reverently bowed his head
and recounted the Imperial Lord's words.
The Bodhisattva found it difficult.
Gōng continued to plead earnestly.
A *zunzhě* (revered one) nearby spoke, saying:
"If the Bodhisattva employs great supernatural power,
a pinch of earth can become flesh,
and a broken willow branch can become bone."
The Bodhisattva then, as requested,
broke a willow branch,
poured out the water from the vase,
mixed pure earth into mud,
and patted it onto Gōng's body.
He then had a young attendant carry it to the spiritual place
and push it to join with the body.
A groan stirred in the coffin,
and his illness was suddenly gone.
His family, startled, gathered around
and helped him out.
It was calculated that he had been dead for seven days (the *duànqī* period).
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of 《Liáozhāi Zhìyì》.
Lǐ Zhōngzhī, a *xiùcai* from Láiwú,
was straightforward and unyielding by nature.
Every few days,
he would die,
stiff as a corpse,
and would only awaken after three or four days.
If asked what he saw,
he would keep it secret and not reveal it.
At that time, there was a Zhāng Shēng in the district
who also died every few days.
He told people:
"Lǐ Zhōngzhī
is King Yánluó.
When I arrive in the Underworld,
I am also one of his subordinates."
He could even describe the couplets on the doors of his palace hall.
Someone asked:
"What matter did Lǐ attend to in the Underworld yesterday?"
Zhāng replied:
"I cannot fully describe it.
Only that he was presiding over the trial of Cáo Cāo,
and answered twenty times."
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The case of Āmàn (Cáo Cāo)
must have passed through several tens of King Yánluó already.
The realms of beasts, the sword mountain,
and all sorts of torments exist.
What crime should he receive,
without need for capture?
Yet, after several thousand years, it remains undecided.
Why is that?
Is it because a prisoner facing execution
prefers a quick demise,
and so he is made to wish for death but cannot achieve it?
How strange!"
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of 《Liáozhāi Zhìyì》.
Yáng Yúwēi
moved his residence to the banks of the Sìshuǐ River.
His study overlooked a vast wilderness;
outside the wall were many ancient tombs.
At night, he would hear the rustling of white poplars,
their sound like a surging tide.
Late at night, holding a candle,
he often felt desolate and heartbroken.
Suddenly, someone outside the wall chanted:
“A bleak wind in the dark night blows backward,
Fireflies brush the grass, then cling to the curtain.”
They chanted repeatedly,
their voice mournful and sorrowful.
Listening to it,
it was delicate and graceful, like a woman’s.
He was suspicious.
The next day,
he looked outside the wall,
but there were no human traces.
Only a purple sash,
was left in the brambles;
he picked it up,
and placed it on the window.
Towards the second watch of the night,
the chanting resumed as before.
Yáng moved a stool and climbed up to look,
and the chanting abruptly stopped.
He realized it was a ghost,
but his heart yearned for her.
The next night,
he lay in wait on the wall-top.
As the first watch was almost over,
a woman gracefully emerged from the grass,
her hand supporting a small tree,
her head bowed, chanting mournfully.
Yáng lightly coughed,
and the woman suddenly disappeared into the wild grass.
From then on, Yáng waited below the wall,
and after she finished chanting,
he would continue it from behind the wall, saying:
“Who sees my deep feelings and bitter sorrow?
When the moon rises, my green sleeves are thin and cold.”
After a long while,
it was silent.
Yáng then entered his room.
As he was sitting,
he suddenly saw the beautiful one come in from outside,
bowing slightly and saying:
“You, sir, are indeed a refined scholar,
but I have many fears and avoidances.”
Yáng was delighted,
and pulled her to sit down.
She was thin and frail, chilled,
as if she could not bear her clothes.
He asked:
“What is your residence? Have you long sojourned here?”
She replied:
“I am from Lǒngxī,
and followed my father when he was exiled.
At seventeen, I died of a sudden illness;
it has been over twenty years now.
In the desolate wilderness of the underworld,
I am as lonely as a wild duck.
What I chant
is my own composition,
to express my hidden grievances.
My thoughts have long been disconnected;
your continuing it for me
brings joy to the underworld.”
Yáng wished to enjoy her company.
She frowned and said:
“The decaying bones of the underworld
are not like living people;
if there is intimate joy,
it shortens a person’s lifespan.
I cannot bear to bring misfortune upon you, sir.”
Yáng then stopped.
He playfully reached out his hand to touch her chest,
and found the flesh of a chicken’s head,
still like that of a virgin.
He also wanted to see the small bound feet beneath her skirt.
The woman bowed her head and smiled, saying:
“This crazy scholar is too impertinent!”
Yáng playfully handled her,
and saw moon-colored silk stockings,
tied with a single colored thread.
When he looked at the other,
it was tied with a purple sash.
He asked:
“Why are they not both sashes?”
She said:
“Last night, out of fear of you, I fled,
and did not know where I dropped it.”
Yáng said:
“I will exchange it for you.”
Thereupon, he took it from the window and handed it to the woman.
The woman, surprised, asked where it came from,
and he told her the truth.
The woman then removed the thread and tied the sash.
After turning over the books on the table,
she suddenly saw the 《Liánchāng Gōng Cí》,
and sighed with emotion, saying:
“When I was alive, I loved reading this the most.
To see it now
is almost like a dream!”
They discussed poetry and literature;
she was intelligent and charming.
Trimming the candle by the west window,
it was like having a good friend.
From then on, every night, he would only hear her faint chanting,
and a short while later, she would arrive.
She would often instruct him:
“You must keep this secret and not disclose it.
I am timid and easily frightened,
and fear being invaded by evil guests.”
Yáng assented.
The two were intimate like fish and water;
although it did not lead to intercourse,
within the boudoir,
there was indeed something more profound than drawing eyebrows.
The woman often wrote for Yáng under the lamp,
her handwriting elegant and charming.
She also selected a hundred palace poems
and transcribed them for recitation.
She had Yáng prepare a chessboard
and buy a pipa.
Every night, she taught Yáng to play chess,
or plucked the strings of the pipa.
She composed
the tune of
“Rain on Banana Leaves at the Window,”
which wrung one's heart;
Yáng could not bear to listen to it completely.
Then she would play
the melody of
“Oriole Song in the Morning Garden,”
and his heart would immediately feel open and comfortable.
They trimmed the lamp and played,
often forgetting the dawn in their joy.
When they saw the light of dawn at the window,
she would flee in a panic.
One day,
Xuē Shēng paid a visit,
finding Yáng taking a noon nap.
He looked around the room.
A pípá and a qípíng were both there,
and he knew these were not things Yáng excelled at.
He also flipped through a book and found palace lyrics,
and seeing the handwriting was exquisite,
his suspicion grew.
When Yáng woke up,
Xuē asked,
"Where did these props come from?"
He replied,
"I want to learn them."
Xuē then asked about the poetry scroll,
and Yáng claimed it was borrowed from a friend.
Xuē examined it repeatedly and intently,
and on the very last leaf, he saw a line of fine script that read:
"On such-and-such a month and day, liánsuǒ wrote this."
Xuē laughed and said,
"This is a young woman's given name,
why deceive me so much?"
Yáng was greatly embarrassed
and unable to utter a word.
Xuē questioned him even more persistently,
but Yáng would not tell him.
Xuē bundled up the scroll,
Yáng became even more flustered,
and so he finally told him.
Xuē requested to meet her.
Yáng then related what she had instructed him.
Xuē's admiration was fervent;
Yáng, having no choice,
agreed to it.
At midnight,
the woman arrived,
and he conveyed Xuē's regards.
The woman angrily said,
"What did you say?
You have already chattered about it to someone!"
Yáng explained the true situation to clear himself.
The woman said,
"My connection with you is over!"
Yáng tried a hundred ways to comfort and appease her,
but she remained unhappy,
stood up to leave,
and said,
"I will avoid this for a while."
The next day,
Xuē came,
and Yáng conveyed her unavailability on her behalf.
Xuē suspected it was an excuse,
so that evening he came with two of his window-mates,
staying on and refusing to leave.
Thus, they deliberately disrupted them: they constantly made noise all night long,
earning severe disapproval from Yáng Shēng,
but there was nothing he could do.
After several nights passed silently,
the group gradually grew tired of it
and their clamor gradually subsided.
Suddenly, they heard a voice chanting,
and they all listened.
It was mournful and about to break off.
As Xuē was intently listening with ears cocked,
one of the martial students inside, Wáng Mǒu,
picked up a huge stone and threw it,
shouting loudly,
"Putting on airs and not seeing guests,
how can one get good lines?
Wailing and sighing
makes people utterly dejected!"
The chanting immediately stopped.
The group was very resentful of him.
Yáng's anger and indignation were evident in his words and expression.
The next day,
they finally left together.
Yáng slept alone in his empty study,
hoping the woman would return,
but there was no trace of her.
After two more days,
the woman suddenly arrived,
weeping,
"You brought evil guests,
they nearly scared me to death!"
Yáng profusely apologized.
The woman quickly went out and
said,
"I already said our fate is over,
we part ways from now on."
When he tried to hold her back, she had already vanished.
After that, for over a month,
she never returned.
Yáng pined for her
until he was gaunt and emaciated,
unable to get her back.
One evening,
as he was drinking alone,
a woman suddenly drew aside the curtain and entered.
Yáng was overjoyed
and said,
"Are you forgiving me?"
The woman's tears streamed down her chest;
she remained silent.
He urgently questioned her,
she wanted to speak but restrained herself,
saying,
"To leave in a huff,
and then hastily seek help from someone,
I can't help but feel ashamed."
Yáng questioned her again and again,
and then she said,
"I don't know where a dirty servant came from,
forcing me to become his concubine.
Considering I am of pure lineage,
how could I stoop to a ghost of the lower classes?
However, with my delicate and weak frame,
how can I resist?
If you still count me among your cherished ones,
you must not let me fend for myself."
Yáng was furious,
so incensed he wanted to kill;
but he worried that the paths of humans and ghosts were different,
and he would be powerless.
The woman said,
"Sleep early tomorrow night,
I will invite you into my dream."
Thereupon, they talked together again,
sitting until dawn.
As the woman was leaving,
she instructed him not to sleep during the day,
but to wait for their night appointment.
Yáng agreed.
So, in the afternoon, he drank a little,
and, feeling tipsy, got onto his bed,
covered himself with clothes, and lay down.
Suddenly, he saw the woman arrive,
hand him a treasured sword,
and lead him away by the hand.
They arrived at a courtyard.
Just as they closed the door and were speaking,
they heard someone pounding on the door with a stone.
The woman cried out in alarm,
"The enemy is here!"
Yáng opened the door and rushed out,
seeing a man with a red hat and green clothes,
with hedgehog-like hair around his mouth.
He angrily shouted at him.
The servant glared back vengefully,
his words fierce and rude.
Yáng was greatly enraged
and rushed towards him.
The servant grabbed a stone and threw it,
as swiftly as a sudden rain,
hitting Yáng's wrist,
preventing him from gripping the blade.
Just when he was in grave danger,
he saw someone in the distance,
with arrows at his waist, practicing archery in the wilderness.
Upon closer inspection,
it was Wáng Shēng.
Yáng loudly cried for help.
Wáng Shēng drew his bow and swiftly arrived,
shooting the servant in the thigh;
he shot him again,
and he fell dead.
Yáng was delighted and grateful.
Wáng asked for the reason,
and Yáng told him everything.
Wáng was pleased that his previous fault could be redeemed,
so he went with Yáng into the woman's room.
The woman trembled with shyness and apprehension,
standing far away without saying a word.
On the table was a small knife,
only a bit over a foot long,
but adorned with gold and jade: when taken out of its scabbard,
its brilliance reflected shadows.
Wáng admired it endlessly, unable to put it down.
After a brief conversation with Yáng,
seeing the woman's pitiful shyness and fear,
he then left,
parting ways with them.
Yáng also returned by himself,
falling over the wall,
and then he awoke with a start,
hearing the village cocks already crowing wildly.
He felt intense pain in his wrist: when he looked at it in the morning,
his skin and flesh were red and swollen.
When he stopped,
Wáng Shēng came,
and at once spoke of the strangeness of his night dream.
Yáng said:
"Did you not dream of shooting?"
Wáng was surprised at his foreknowledge.
Yáng showed him his hand,
and also told him the reason.
Wáng recalled the dream's appearance,
regretting he hadn't truly seen it;
he congratulated himself on having helped the maiden,
and again pleaded for an introduction.
That night,
the maiden came to express her thanks.
Yáng attributed the credit to Wáng Shēng,
and then conveyed his earnestness.
The maiden said:
"With your assistance,
I dare not forget my gratitude.
However, he is so imposing,
I truly fear him."
A moment later, she said:
"He loves my ornamental knife.
The knife was bought for a hundred taels of silver
by my father when he was on an embassy to Yuèzhōng.
I loved it and kept it,
wrapping it with gold thread,
and inlaying it with bright pearls.
My father, pitying my untimely death,
used it for my burial.
Now I am willing to part with it and give it to you;
seeing the knife will be like seeing me."
The next day,
Yáng conveyed this intention.
Wáng was greatly pleased.
That night,
the maiden indeed came with the knife,
saying:
"Instruct him to cherish it,
this is not a thing of Zhōnghuá."
From then on, their comings and goings were as before.
Several months passed,
when suddenly, by lamplight, she smiled at Yáng,
as if wanting to say something,
blushing and stopping three times.
Yáng embraced and asked her.
She replied:
"Having long enjoyed your affection,
I have received the vital energy of a living person,
daily consuming smoke and fire,
and my white bones have suddenly gained vitality.
But it still requires a living person's essence and blood
to be able to fully revive."
Yáng smiled and said:
"Since you yourself are unwilling,
how could I deliberately withhold it?"
The maiden said:
"After our union,
you will surely have a great illness for the next few days,
but medicine can cure it."
So they made love.
Afterwards, she dressed and rose,
and again said:
"It still requires a drop of living blood;
can you bear the pain for love?"
Yáng took a sharp blade and pricked his arm for blood;
the maiden lay on the couch,
and he dripped it into her navel.
Then she rose and said:
"I will not come again.
You must remember the hundred-day period;
look at my grave,
if there is a bluebird singing on the treetop,
then quickly open the tomb."
Yáng respectfully received the instruction.
As she went out, she again instructed:
"Remember carefully, do not forget,
being either too early or too late is not permissible!"
Then she left.
More than ten days later,
Yáng indeed fell ill,
his abdomen swollen to the point of death.
The physician administered medicine,
and he discharged foul matter like mud,
recovering completely in three days.
Counting to the hundredth day,
he had his servants carry spades to wait.
When dusk arrived,
he indeed saw a pair of bluebirds singing.
Yáng happily said:
"It is time."
Then he cut away the thorns and opened the tomb.
He saw that the coffin was already rotten,
but the maiden's face was as if alive.
Touching her, she was slightly warm.
He covered her with clothes and carried her home,
placing her in a warm place,
her breath was barely audible,
finer than a spider's thread.
Gradually, he fed her broth,
and she revived at midnight.
She often said to Yáng:
"Over twenty years,
it was like a single dream."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Hán Gōngzǐ,
a prominent family in the district.
There was a Daoist, Shàn Dàoshì,
who was skilled in magic.
The young master admired his art
and treated him as an honored guest.
Whenever Shàn sat or walked with people,
he would suddenly disappear.
The young master wished to learn his methods,
but Shàn was unwilling.
The young master earnestly pleaded.
Shàn said:
"I am not stingy with my art,
but I fear it would damage my Way.
If it were transmitted to a gentleman, it would be fine;
otherwise,
some might use it for theft.
You, Gōngzǐ, certainly have no such worries,
but what if you went out, saw beauty and were pleased,
and hid your body to enter someone's boudoir?
That would be aiding evil and promoting licentiousness.
I dare not comply."
The young master could not force him,
but harbored anger,
and secretly plotted with his servants to whip and humiliate him.
Fearing he might escape,
he spread fine ash on the threshing ground: thinking that since this heterodox Daoist could become invisible,
there would surely be footprints where he walked,
and they could quickly strike where the prints appeared.
Thereupon, he lured Shàn there,
and had people stand ready with ox whips to strike him.
Shàn suddenly disappeared,
and indeed there were footprints on the ash;
they struck wildly left and right,
but in a moment, he was lost.
When the young master returned,
Shàn also arrived.
He said to the servants:
"I cannot stay here anymore!
You have toiled in service to me;
now I must leave,
and I should repay you."
From his sleeve, he produced a jug full of fine wine,
and then found a bowl of dishes,
placing them both on the table.
After placing them,
he searched again;
after more than ten searches,
the table was already full.
Then he invited everyone to drink,
and they all became drunk;
he put each item back into his sleeve.
Hán heard of his strangeness
and asked him to perform another feat.
Shàn drew a city on the wall,
and pushing and striking it with his hand,
the city gate suddenly opened.
Then he threw his clothes, bags, and boxes,
everything, into the gate,
then bowed and took his leave, saying:
"I am leaving!"
He leapt into the city,
the city gate then closed,
and the Daoist instantly vanished.
Later it was heard that he was in Qīngzhōushì,
teaching children to draw ink circles on their palms,
and playfully tossing them at people;
wherever they were thrown,
be it face or clothes,
the circle would detach,
leaving an imprint there.
It was also heard that he was good at 'bedroom arts,'
able to make his lower body suck up distilled spirits,
finishing one vessel.
The young master once tested him in person.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wú Qīng'ān,
Jūn,
was famous from a young age.
Gé Tàishǐ saw his writings
and always praised them.
He sent a mutual acquaintance to invite him to his home,
and observed his conversation and demeanor.
He said,
"How can a man as talented as Wú Shēng
remain poor and lowly for long?"
So he had a good neighbor convey a message to him, saying,
"If Qīng'ān strives to reach the clouds,
I shall offer my daughter to serve him."
At that time, Tàishǐ had an exceptionally beautiful daughter.
Shēng was overjoyed when he heard this,
and was truly confident.
However, later he failed the autumn examination,
so he sent someone to tell Tàishǐ:
"Wealth and eminence are inherent,
it's only a matter of when, which is uncertain.
Please wait for me for three years,
and marry her off only if I haven't succeeded by then."
Thereupon, he dedicated himself to studying even more diligently.
One night,
under the bright moonlight,
a xiùcai came to visit.
He was fair-skinned with a short beard,
a slender waist, and long fingernails.
When asked where he came from,
he said,
"My surname is Bái,
and my courtesy name is Yúyù."
They talked briefly,
and his words opened one's heart and mind.
Shēng was pleased with him,
and kept him to stay the night.
As dawn approached and he was about to leave,
Shēng urged him to pass by frequently on his way.
Bái was touched by his fervent feelings
and offered to temporarily reside there immediately,
agreeing on a date before departing.
On the appointed day,
a servant boy first brought cooking utensils.
A short while later,
Bái arrived,
riding a spirited horse like a dragon.
Shēng prepared a separate dwelling for him.
Bái ordered his servant to take the horse away.
Thus, they spent their days and nights together,
happily getting along.
Shēng observed the books he read,
which were neither what he usually saw or heard,
nor were they contemporary examination essays.
Surprised, he asked about it,
and Bái smiled, saying,
"Each scholar has his own aspirations;
I am not one who seeks fame and official position."
At night, he often invited Shēng to drink,
and gave him a scroll,
which contained methods of breath regulation.
Shēng did not understand much of it,
and thus put it aside, delaying its study.
Another day, Bái said to Shēng,
"What I gave you previously
are the essential teachings of 'Huángtíng',
the important path,
the ladder and ferry for immortals."
Shēng laughed, saying,
"What I urgently need is not this.
Moreover, those who seek immortality must sever all emotional ties,
and make all thoughts utterly tranquil,
a sickness I am not yet able to cure."
Bái asked,
"Why?"
Shēng was concerned about continuing the family line.
Bái said,
"Why haven't you married for so long?"
Shēng laughed, saying,
"'The solitary man has a sickness;
the solitary man loves beauty.'"
Bái also laughed, saying,
"'May Your Majesty not love petty beauty.'
What kind of beauty do you like?"
Shēng told him the whole story.
Bái doubted if she was truly beautiful.
Shēng said,
"This is known far and wide,
it is not because my eyes are cheap."
Bái smiled slightly and let the matter drop.
The next day,
