he suddenly packed his bags and announced his departure.
Shēng spoke to him wistfully,
chattering on without stopping.
Bái then ordered his servant boy to carry the luggage ahead.
The two were reluctant to part.
Suddenly, a green cicada chirped and landed on the table.
Bái said,
"The carriage is ready,
let us part here.
If you miss me,
sweep my bed and lie on it."
Just as Shēng was about to ask further questions,
in a blink of an eye,
Bái became as small as a finger,
and lightly straddled the cicada's back,
chirping and flying,
disappearing into the clouds.
Shēng then realized that he was no ordinary person,
and stood dumbfounded for a long time,
feeling lost and disheartened.
After several days,
a fine rain suddenly gathered.
His longing for Bái Qí was extremely strong.
He looked at the couch where he lay;
there were countless traces of rats.
Nevertheless, he swept and cleaned,
laid out a mat, and immediately went to sleep.
Before long,
he saw Bái's houseboy come to summon him,
and he happily followed him.
Presently, a phoenix-like bird (tóngfèng) soared down and landed.
The boy caught it and said to the scholar,
"The black path is difficult to walk;
you can ride this as a substitute. "
The scholar worried it was too small to be capable.
The boy said,
"Try riding it. "
The scholar did as requested,
and there was ample space.
The boy also attached himself to its tail.
With a sharp cry,
it ascended into the sky.
Not long after,
he saw a vermilion gate.
The boy dismounted first,
then helped the scholar dismount.
He asked,
"What place is this? "
He replied,
"This is the Gate of Heaven (Tiānmén). "
By the gate, a giant tiger crouched.
The scholar was startled and terrified.
The boy shielded him with his body.
He saw scenery everywhere
that was extraordinarily different from the mortal world.
The boy led him into the Palace of Broad Cold (Guǎnghán Gōng).
Inside, the stairs were made of crystal,
and pedestrians seemed to be in a mirror.
Two large cassia trees (guìshù)
pierced the sky, their branches entwined;
the fragrance of their flowers followed the wind,
its scent unending.
The pavilions and halls all had red windows,
and from time to time beautiful women went in and out.
Their captivating beauty and refined elegance
were unparalleled in the world.
The boy said,
"The beauties of the Queen Mother's Palace (Wángmǔ Gōng) are even more exquisite. "
However, fearing that the host had waited for a long time,
he had no leisure to linger
and guided him out hastily.
After a while,
he saw Bái Shēng waiting at the door.
They clasped hands and entered,
seeing clear water and white sand outside the eaves,
gently flowing over.
Jade steps and carved balustrades
made him almost mistake it for the Cassia Palace (Guì Què).
As soon as they were seated,
sixteen enchanting maids
came to offer fragrant tea.
After a short while,
wine was ordered.
Four beautiful women,
curtsied and jingled,
serving on either side.
The scholar had just felt a slight itch on his back
when a beautiful woman, with slender fingers and long nails,
reached under his clothes to scratch it for him.
The scholar felt his heart and spirit waver,
unable to settle.
Then, slightly tipsy,
he gradually lost self-control,
smiled, looked at the beautiful women,
and jested with them.
The beauties would often laugh and avoid him.
Bái ordered a tune to be played to accompany the wine.
One woman, dressed in scarlet gauze,
raised a goblet towards the guest,
then, right before the banquet table,
sang a clear song with graceful turns.
The other beauties played the reed pipe (shēng) and flute (guǎn) with flowing grace,
humming in harmonious accompaniment.
When it was over,
another woman, dressed in emerald green,
also poured and sang.
There was still one woman in purple,
who, with one in pale white gauze,
giggled in the shadows,
deferring to each other, unwilling to come forward.
Bái ordered one to pour and one to sing.
The woman in purple then came to hold the cup.
The scholar, pretending to take the cup,
playfully touched her slender wrist.
The woman smiled and lost her grip,
the wine cup tilting and falling.
Bái reprimanded her.
The woman picked up the cup, smiled,
bowed her head, and whispered,
"Cold as a ghost's hand, yet fragrant,
daring to grab a person's arm. "
Bái laughed heartily
and punished her by making her sing and dance herself.
After the dance,
the one in pale white flew another goblet.
The scholar declined, unable to drink the toast.
The woman, holding the wine, showed a look of shame,
so he forced himself to drink it.
He carefully observed the four women;
their elegant charm was exceptional,
not one was anything but a peerless beauty.
He suddenly said to the host,
"Peerless beauties are rare in the human world;
I struggle to find even one.
You have gathered a host of beauties.
Can you truly make me captivated? "
Bái smiled and said,
"You already have a beloved in your heart.
How can these be worthy of your discerning gaze? "
The scholar said,
"Now I realize how limited my vision has been. "
Bái then summoned all the women
and let him choose for himself.
The scholar was overwhelmed and couldn't decide.
Since the woman in purple had the intimate interaction of "grabbing the arm,"
Bái therefore made her serve the guest.
Subsequently, their love in bed
was utterly tender and devoted.
The scholar asked for a keepsake,
and the woman removed a golden bracelet from her wrist and gave it to him.
Suddenly, the boy entered and said,
"The paths of immortals and mortals differ;
you should leave immediately. "
The woman quickly rose
and fled.
The scholar asked the host,
The boy said,
"He went early to attend court (dàilòu);
when he left, he instructed me to see off the guest. "
The scholar reluctantly followed him,
returning along the old path.
As he was about to reach the gate,
he looked back at the boy,
who had disappeared at some unknown time.
A tiger roared suddenly,
and the scholar fled in terror.
He looked down, and it was bottomless,
and his feet had already fallen.
He awoke with a start,
to find the dawn already red.
Just as he was about to straighten his clothes,
something soft and oily fell between the bedding.
He looked at it;
it was the bracelet.
His heart was even more astonished.
From then on, his former aspirations grew cold;
he constantly wished to wander with Chìsōng,
but he still worried about his lineage (yìnxù).
Over ten months later,
while deeply asleep in his daytime nap,
he dreamt the purple-clad lady arrived from outside,
carrying a baby wrapped in her arms. She said,
"This is your flesh and blood.
It is difficult for such a thing to remain in Heaven;
I respectfully bring him to you. "
She then laid him on the bed,
pulled his clothes to cover him,
and hastily intended to leave.
The scholar forced her to enjoy their time together.
She then said,
"One encounter was for our wedding,
this encounter is for our eternal farewell.
A hundred years of marriage
ends here.
If you have aspirations,
perhaps we will meet again. "
The scholar awoke
to see the infant lying between the bedding,
wrapped, and told his mother.
His mother was delighted,
and the wet nurse fed him,
naming him Mèngxiān.
The scholar then sent someone to inform the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ)
that he intended to retire
and asked him to choose another suitable match.
The Grand Historian refused.
The scholar insisted on his resignation.
The Grand Historian informed his daughter,
who said,
"Everyone, near and far, knows that my body is pledged to Wú Láng.
To change it would be like having two Heavens. "
Therefore, she conveyed this message to the scholar.
The scholar said,
"Not only do I have no ambition for fame and official position,
but I have also cut off all affection for romantic relations.
The only reason I have not immediately entered the mountains
is solely because I have an elderly mother. "
The Grand Historian then discussed it with his daughter again.
The daughter said,
"Wú Láng is poor,
I am content with his meager fare;
Wú Láng leaves,
I will serve his parents: I am certainly not going to marry another."
He sent people back and forth three or four times,
but to no avail.
So, a day was chosen, and carriages, horses, and a dowry were prepared,
and she was married into the scholar's family.
The scholar was touched by her virtue,
and his respect and love for her reached its peak.
The wife served her mother-in-law filially,
always seeking to please her,
surpassing even poor village girls.
More than two years later,
her mother-in-law died.
The wife pawned her dowry to prepare for the funeral,
leaving nothing undone in accordance with ritual.
The scholar said:
"Having you like this,
what worries could I have!
Considering that if one person attains the Dao,
the entire household can ascend to immortality.
I shall depart to a distant place,
entrusting everything to you."
The wife was calm,
and made no effort to hold him back.
The scholar then left.
The wife managed the household finances externally,
and internally educated her orphan child,
everything in perfect order.
Mèngxiān gradually grew up,
exceptionally intelligent.
At fourteen,
as a child prodigy, he passed the xiāngjiàn (provincial examination),
and at fifteen, entered the Hànlín Academy.
Whenever an imperial commendation was issued,
he did not know his mother's surname,
so he merely referred to her as Gě Mǔ.
Whenever the time of frost and dew (mourning for parents) arrived,
he would ask about his father's whereabouts,
and his mother would tell him everything.
He then wanted to abandon his official post and go searching.
His mother said:
"Your father left home to become an immortal,
and it has now been more than ten years.
I imagine he has already ascended to immortality;
where can he be found?"
Later, by imperial decree, he was sent to sacrifice at Nányuè,
and on the way, encountered bandits.
In his distress,
a Daoist priest entered wielding a sword.
The bandits all scattered,
and the siege was lifted.
He thanked him,
offered him gold,
but he refused.
He produced a letter,
and entrusted it, saying:
"I have an old friend,
who lives in the same village as your honorable self.
Please convey my regards."
He asked:
"What is his name?"
He replied:
"Wáng Lín."
He recalled that there was no such name in the village.
The Daoist priest said:
"He is humble and obscure,
so your esteemed official self naturally would not know him."
Before leaving,
he produced a bracelet and said:
"This is a lady's accessory.
A Daoist priest has no use for such a thing,
so I offer it to you as a token of gratitude."
He examined it;
its inlay and carving were exquisite.
He took it home and gave it to his wife.
His wife loved it,
and ordered skilled artisans to make a matching one according to its style,
but they could never match its exquisite craftsmanship.
He asked all around the village,
but there was no one named Wáng Lín.
He secretly opened the letter;
it said:
"For three years, we were a loving couple,
then parted, each going our separate ways.
Burying my mother and raising our child,
all depended on your virtue.
Having nothing to repay your kindness,
I offer you a pill;
cut it open and eat it,
and you can become immortal."
At the end, it was written:
"For Lín Niáng, my wife, to read."
After reading it,
he didn't understand who it was for,
so he showed it to his mother.
His mother held the letter and wept,
saying:
"This is a message from your father to his family.
Lín
is my small name (childhood name)."
Only then did he suddenly realize
that 'Wáng Lín'
was a character-splitting riddle.
He was filled with endless regret.
He then showed the bracelet to his mother.
His mother said:
"This is my relic.
When your father was at home,
he often showed it to me."
He then looked at the pill,
which was the size of a bean.
He said joyfully:
"My father is an immortal!
Eating this will surely grant eternal life!"
His mother did not swallow it immediately;
she received it and put it away.
Coincidentally, Gě Tàishǐ came to visit his nephew.
The wife recited Wú Shēng's letter,
then offered the elixir as a longevity gift.
Tàishǐ cut it open and shared it.
In an instant,
his spirit was refreshed and invigorated.
Tàishǐ was then seventy years old,
quite decrepit;
he suddenly felt strength overflowing his flesh and skin,
so he abandoned his carriage and walked.
His pace was vigorous and swift;
his family could only keep up by panting.
More than a year later,
the capital experienced a fire disaster,
and the fire did not cease all day.
That night, no one dared to sleep;
everyone gathered in the courtyard.
They saw the chaotic fire,
encroaching upon neighboring houses.
The whole family paced back and forth,
not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, the golden bracelet on the wife's arm
made a sudden sound,
slipped off her arm, and flew away.
Looking at it,
it was as large as several acres;
it covered the house like a shield,
shaped like a crescent moon;
its opening descended towards the southeast corner,
clearly visible.
Everyone was greatly astonished.
A moment later,
the fire came from the west,
but near the shield, it veered diagonally eastward.
When the fire had receded far away,
they secretly thought the bracelet was lost and could not be recovered;
suddenly, they saw a red light momentarily converge,
and the bracelet clanged as it fell at their feet.
Tens of thousands of private houses in the capital were burned,
those to the left, right, front, and back
all turned to ashes.
Only Wú Dì was unharmed,
except for a small pavilion in the southeast,
which was completely destroyed,
precisely where the opening of the bracelet had descended.
Gě Mǔ was over fifty years old,
but if one saw her,
she still looked like a person of about twenty.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi Manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A man named Xú
from Jiāozhōu
was blown off course by a great storm while sailing for trade.
When he opened his eyes, he was in a place
of deep, wild mountains.
Hoping to find inhabitants,
he moored his boat and went ashore,
carrying dried provisions and cured meat.
As he entered,
he saw cave mouths on both cliffs,
dense as a beehive;
inside, human voices were faintly heard.
He reached outside a cave,
paused to peer in,
and saw two Yèchā
whose teeth were like a dense array of halberds,
eyes flashed like two lamps,
and claws ripped apart raw deer to eat.
His soul scattered in fright,
he wanted to rush back down,
but the Yèchā had already seen him,
stopped eating, and seized him.
The two creatures spoke to each other,
like the calls of birds and beasts,
contesting to tear Xú's clothes,
as if intending to.
Xú was greatly afraid,
took the dried provisions from his pouch
and also some beef jerky and offered them.
They shared and ate, finding it very delicious.
They then flipped over Xú's pouch,
and Xú waved his hand to show that he had nothing left.
The Yèchā were angry,
and seized him again.
Xú pleaded with them, saying:
"Release me!
I have pots and steamers in my boat
that can be used for cooking."
The Yèchā did not understand his words,
and remained angry.
Xú tried hand gestures again,
and the Yèchā seemed to slightly understand.
They followed him to the boat,
took the utensils into the cave,
bound firewood, lit a fire,
and cooked their leftover deer.
When it was cooked, he presented it to them.
The two creatures were overjoyed.
That night, they blocked the door with a huge stone,
as if fearing Xú would escape.
Xú lay curled up in a corner,
deeply fearing he would not escape.
At dawn,
the two creatures went out,
and blocked it again.
A little later,
they brought a deer and gave it to Xú.
Xú skinned it,
and drew water from a stream deep in the cave,
cooking several pots.
Soon, several Yèchā arrived,
gathered and devoured it all.
They all pointed at the pot,
as if complaining it was too small.
After three or four days,
one Yèchā brought a large pot,
similar to those commonly used by humans.
Thereupon, the group of Yèchā each brought wolves and elks.
Once cooked,
they called Xú to eat with them.
After living there for several days,
the Yèchā gradually became familiar with Xú.
They no longer restrained him when he went out,
and gathered together like a family.
Xú gradually became able to discern their sounds and understand their intentions,
and would imitate their calls,
speaking the Yèchā language.
The Yèchā were even more pleased,
and brought a female to be Xú's wife.
Xú was initially fearful
and dared not move;
the female herself opened her legs and approached Xú,
and Xú then had intercourse with her.
The female was greatly delighted.
She would often leave meat to entice Xú,
like a harmonious zither and se.
One day,
the Yèchā woke up early,
each wearing a string of bright pearls around their necks,
and took turns going out,
as if awaiting a distinguished guest.
They ordered Xú to cook more meat.
Xú asked the female,
and she said:
"This is the Tiānshòu Festival."
The female went out
and said to the assembled Yèchā:
"Xú Láng has no 'bone-protuberance beads'."
Each of them plucked five,
and gave them all to the female.
The female also took off ten herself,
making a total of fifty,
and used wild ramie as a string
to thread and hang around Xú's neck.
Xú looked at them,
and each pearl could be worth one hundred and ten gold coins.
Soon, they all went out.
After Xú finished cooking the meat,
the female came and invited him to go,
saying:
"To receive the Heavenly King."
They arrived at a large cave,
several *mǔ* in width.
Inside was a stone,
smooth and flat like a table;
all around were stone seats;
the main seat was covered with a leopard skin,
the others with deer skins.
Twenty or thirty Yèchā
sat in rows, filling the space.
A little later,
a great wind raised dust,
and they all rushed out in a flurry.
They saw a giant creature coming,
also resembling a Yèchā,
it rushed into the cave,
and sat down majestically, looking around.
The group followed in,
standing in rows east and west,
all raising their heads,
crossing their arms to form a cross.
The great Yèchā nodded his head and looked around,
asking:
"Are all the Wòméishān group
here?"
The crowd boisterously responded.
He looked at Xú and said:
"Where did this one come from?"
The female replied with
"Son-in-law."
The crowd also praised his cooking.
Immediately, two or three Yèchā
ran and brought cooked meat, arranging it on the table.
The great Yèchā scooped and ate his fill,
highly praising its excellence and beauty,
and moreover, demanded a regular supply.
He then looked at Xú and said:
"Why are your 'bone-protuberance beads' so few?"
The crowd said:
"He just arrived and was not yet equipped."
The creature took a string of pearls from its neck,
removed ten and gave them to him,
all as big as a fingertip,
and round as bullets.
The female quickly took them,
and threaded them for Xú.
Xú also crossed his arms and thanked him in the Yèchā language.
The creature then left,
treading on the wind,
its speed like flight.
The crowd then enjoyed the leftover food and dispersed.
After living there for over four years,
the female suddenly gave birth.
In one pregnancy, she bore two males and one female,
all in human form,
not resembling their mother.
All the yakṣas rejoiced at the children,
and would often caress and play with them.
One day,
they all went out to hunt for food;
only Xú sat alone.
Suddenly, a female came from another cave,
wishing to be intimate with Xú,
but Xú refused.
The yakṣa grew angry,
and pounced on Xú, pinning him to the ground.
Xú's wife arrived from outside,
and in a furious rage, grappled with the other female,
biting off her ear.
A short while later,
the other two yakṣas also returned,
and intervened, making the female leave.
From then on, the female constantly guarded Xú,
never leaving his side in movement or rest.
Another three years passed,
and the children were all able to walk.
Xú would teach them human speech,
and they gradually learned to speak;
amidst their chirping and babbling,
there was a hint of human nature.
Though still children,
they could run through the mountains as if treading on flat ground;
and there was a clear father-child affection between them.
One day,
the female went out with one son and one daughter,
and did not return for half the day.
A great north wind began to blow.
Xú, with a heavy heart, thought of his homeland,
and took his son to the seashore.
He saw his old boat still there,
and planned to return home with his son.
The son wanted to tell his mother,
but Xú stopped him.
Father and son boarded the boat,
and in one day and night, reached Jiāo.
Upon arriving home,
his wife had already remarried.
He produced two pearls,
which sold for over a million in gold,
making his family quite wealthy.
His son was named Biāo.
At fourteen or fifteen years old,
he could lift a hundred jūn,
and was rough and fond of fighting.
The commander of Jiāo saw him and found him remarkable,
appointing him as a Qiānzǒng.
When there was border unrest,
he achieved success wherever he went,
and at eighteen, became a Fùjiàng.
At that time, a merchant sailing the sea
was also caught in a storm and drifted to Wòméi.
Just as he landed,
he saw a young man,
and was astonished upon seeing him.
Realizing he was a Chinese person,
he immediately asked about his home.
The merchant told him.
The young man pulled him into a small stone cave in a secluded valley;
outside the cave were dense thickets;
and he instructed him not to go out.
After some time,
he brought deer meat to feed Shāng.
He said:
"My father also befriended people."
Shāng questioned him,
and learned that he was Xú,
whom Shāng had met when he was a guest.
Then he said:
"He is my old friend.
Now his son is a fùjiàng."
The young man did not understand what the title meant.
Shāng said:
"This is an official title in Zhōngguó."
He then asked:
"What does it mean to be an official?"
He replied:
"When one goes out, one has carriages and horses;
when one comes in, one has a high hall;
the superior calls out once, and the subordinates respond a hundred times;
those who see him look askance,
and stand on one foot: this is what it means to be an official."
The young man was greatly moved.
Shāng said:
"Since your honored father is in Jiāozhǐ,
why do you remain here for so long?"
The young man told him the situation.
Shāng advised him to return south.
He said:
"I have often had this thought.
But my mother is not a Zhōngguó person,
her speech and appearance are very different;
and if her own kind discover her,
she will surely be harmed: for this reason, I hesitate."
Then he said:
"When the north wind rises,
I will come to send you off.
Please trouble yourself to send a message
to my father and elder brothers."
Shāng hid in the cave for almost half a year.
From time to time, he peered out from behind the thorns,
and saw yèchā moving back and forth in the mountains;
he was greatly afraid
and dared not move slightly.
One day,
the north wind whistled,
and the young man suddenly arrived,
leading him to hurry away.
He urged:
"Do not forget what I said."
Shāng assented.
He also placed meat on the table,
and Shāng then returned.
He respectfully reached Jiāozhǐ,
arrived at the fùzǒngfǔ,
and fully recounted what he had seen.
Biāo heard this and was saddened,
wishing to go look for him.
His father worried about the sea waves and demonic lairs,
which were treacherous and difficult to navigate,
and strongly restrained him.
Biāo pounded his chest and wept bitterly,
and his father could not stop him.
So he informed the Jiāozhǐ commander,
and took two soldiers to the sea.
Headwinds hindered their boat,
tossing it about in the sea for half a month.
They gazed boundless in all directions,
but even at close range they were bewildered,
unable to discern north or south.
Suddenly, surging waves met the heavens,
and their boat overturned.
Biāo fell into the sea,
floating and sinking with the waves.
After a long time,
he was dragged away by something;
he arrived at a place,
and there were indeed houses.
Biāo looked at it,
and saw a creature resembling a yèchā.
Biāo then spoke in yèchā language.
The yèchā was surprised and questioned him,
and Biāo then told him where he was going.
The yèchā joyfully said:
"Wòméi,
that is my old home.
How presumptuous and blameworthy I am!
You have departed from your old path by eight thousand lǐ.
From here it is the nation of Dúlóngguó,
not the way to Wòméi."
Then he sought a boat to send Biāo.
The yèchā pushed it in the water like an arrow,
covering a thousand lǐ in an instant;
after one night,
they had reached the north shore.
He saw a young man
gazing by the stream.
Biāo knew there were no humans in the mountains,
and suspected it was his brother;
approaching him,
it was indeed his brother.
Then they held hands and wept.
Afterward, he asked about his mother and sister,
and they both said they were well.
Biāo wanted to go together,
but his brother stopped him,
and then hastily left.
Turning to thank the yèchā,
it had already departed.
Soon after,
both his mother and sister arrived,
and seeing Biāo, they all wept.
Biāo told them his intentions.
His mother said:
"I fear that if we go, we will be bullied by people."
Biāo said:
"Your son is very honorable and wealthy in Zhōngguó,
people dare not bully him."
The plan to return was decided,
but the headwinds made crossing difficult.
While the mother and son were hesitating,
they suddenly saw a canvas sail moving south,
its sound rustling.
Biāo joyfully said:
"Heaven helps us!"
They successively boarded the boat,
the waves rushed like arrows;
three days later they reached the shore.
All who saw them fled.
Biāo took off his clothes and trousers and distributed them among the three.
Upon reaching home,
the yèchā mother angrily scolded the old man,
resenting his lack of foresight.
Xú apologized profusely.
The family members bowed to the mistress of the house,
all trembling.
Biāo persuaded his mother to learn to speak Huáyán,
wear fine clothes,
and enjoy fine food,
and she was greatly pleased.
Mother and daughter were both dressed in men's attire,
similar to Mǎn style.
After several months, they could somewhat distinguish the language,
and the younger brother and sister also gradually became fairer.
The younger brother was named Bào,
and the younger sister Yè'ér,
both strong and powerful.
Biāo was ashamed of not knowing how to read,
and taught his brother.
Bào was the most intelligent,
mastering classics and history at a single glance.
Yet he did not wish to pursue a scholar's career;
instead, he was made to draw powerful crossbows
and ride furious horses.
He passed the wǔjìnshì examination.
He married the daughter of Āyóujī.
Yè'ér, being of a different species,
had no one to marry.
At that time, Yuánshǒubèi, under Biāo's command, lost his wife,
and forcibly married her.
Yè'ér could draw a hundred-shí bow,
and shoot small birds over a hundred paces away,
without missing.
Whenever Yuán went on campaign,
he always took his wife with him.
He successively served as tóngzhī jiāngjūn,
and half of his extraordinary achievements came from his wife.
Bào assumed office at thirty-four years old.
His mother once accompanied him on a southern campaign,
and whenever facing a formidable enemy,
she would don armor and wield weapons
to support her son,
and all who saw her recoiled in fear.
An imperial edict conferred upon her the title of nánjué.
Bào humbly declined the title on his mother's behalf,
and she was titled Fūrén.
The Yìshǐ Shǐ says:
"A yèchā Fūrén is also rarely heard of,
but upon careful thought, it is not rare: every household has a yèchā at the bedside."
Based on the Chùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
A certain resident of Chángshān,
when at leisure,
would invariably have a 'short guest' visit.
They would chat for a long time.
He had never known the guest's background,
and felt quite suspicious.
The guest said:
"In three or four days, I will move house,
and become your neighbor."
After four or five days,
he again said:
"Now we are in the same village;
I can receive your instruction morning and evening."
He asked:
"Where have you taken up residence?"
The guest did not elaborate,
but merely pointed north with his hand.
From then on,
he would come once a day.
Sometimes he would borrow tools from people;
if they were stingy and wouldn't lend them,
he would lose them himself.
Everyone suspected him of being a fox spirit.
To the north of the village there was an ancient tomb,
sunken to an unfathomable depth,
and they thought he must be living there.
They all took up weapons and staffs and went.
They lay in wait, listening,
but for a long time there was no unusual sound.
As the first watch was nearing its end,
they heard a rustling sound in the hole,
like dozens or hundreds of people whispering.
The crowd remained silent and still.
Suddenly, little people about a foot tall
emerged in a continuous stream,
too numerous to count.
The crowd shouted and rose,
striking them all.
Every staff blow sparked fire,
and in an instant they scattered in all directions.
Only a small topknot was left,
like a walnut shell,
adorned with gauze and gold thread.
When smelled,
it had an indescribable foul odor.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Two monks came from the Western Regions.
One went to Wǔtái,
the other planted his staff at Tàishān.
Their attire, speech, and appearance
were all quite different from those of China.
They said:
"We passed through the Huǒyàn Shān.
The mountains were layered upon layered,
and the air steamed and billowed like a stove.
Every journey had to be made after rain,
with focused minds and attentive eyes,
treading with light steps;
if one accidentally kicked a mountain rock,
fiery flames would soar and scorch.
We also passed through the Liúshā Hé,
in which there was a crystal mountain,
with sheer cliffs piercing the sky.
It was clear and transparent on all sides,
as if nothing was obstructed.
There was also a narrow pass,
wide enough for a single carriage;
two dragons with intertwined horns guarded the entrance with their mouths.
Those who wished to pass first bowed to the dragons;
if the dragons allowed it,
their mouths would open by themselves.
The dragons were white,
their scales and manes all like crystal."
The monks said:
"We endured eighteen cold and hot seasons on the journey.
There were twelve people who left the Western lands,
but only two of us remain upon reaching China.
In the Western lands, four famous mountains of China are spoken of: one is Tàishān,
one is Huàshān,
one is Wǔtái,
and one is Luòjiā.
It is said that the mountains are covered everywhere with gold,
and Guānyīn and Wénshū are still alive there.
If one can reach that place,
one's body will become a Buddha,
and one will live forever without dying."
Listening to their descriptions,
it was similar to how people in this world long for the Western lands.
If by chance a traveler to the West
were to meet a voyager to the East midway,
and each described what they had,
they would surely look at each other and burst out laughing,
saving both the arduous journey.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Xíng Dé,
a native of Zézhōu,
was a hero of the greenwood.
He could draw a powerful crossbow
and fire multiple arrows,
a skill unrivaled at the time.
Yet throughout his life, he was unconstrained
and unsuccessful in his ventures;
every time he left home, he would suffer financial loss.
The great merchants of the two capitals
often liked to travel with Xíng,
relying on him to be fearless on the journey.
It happened in early winter
that two or three merchants
borrowed some capital from him
and invited him to join them in trading;
Xíng again emptied his own purse,
intending to deal in goods together.
He had a friend who was good at divination,
so he visited him.
The friend divined and said:
"This hexagram indicates 'regret',
and the business you undertake,
even if it doesn't lose the principal,
will still incur a loss on the interest."
Xíng was displeased
and wanted to stop,
but the other merchants urged him to go.
When they arrived at the capital,
it indeed matched the divination.
When the twelfth month was halfway through,
he rode out of the capital gate alone on horseback.
He thought to himself that he would have no money for the new year,
and his melancholy intensified.
At that time, there was a morning mist.
I temporarily headed to a roadside inn,
unpacked my gear, and sought a drink.
I saw an old man with white hair,
with two youths,
drinking by the northern window.
A boy servant attended them,
his yellow hair disheveled.
Xíng sat at the southern seat,
resting opposite the old man.
The boy servant was serving drinks,
but accidentally knocked over the utensils,
staining the old man's clothes.
The youths were angry
and immediately grabbed his ear.
They held out a cloth
and wiped for the old man.
Then I saw that the boy servant's thumbs each had an iron dart,
half an cùn thick;
each one,
weighed about two liǎng and more.
After eating,
the old man ordered the youths
to take out money from a leather pouch,
piling it on the table.
They weighed it and counted,
and when it was enough to pay for several cups,
they sealed and wrapped it securely.
The youths led a black lame mule from the stable,
helped the old man mount it;
the boy servant also rode a lean horse to follow,
and they left through the gate.
The two youths each carried a bow and arrows at their waists,
and led their horses out together.
Xíng, seeing the abundance of gold,
stared greedily,
his avarice burning as if scorched.
He stopped drinking
and urgently followed them.
Seeing the old man and the boy servant still leisurely walking ahead,
he then left the road and galloped diagonally to get in front of the old man,
tightly drew his bow,
and angrily confronted them.
The old man stooped and took off his left boot,
smilingly said:
“Do you not recognize an old glutton?”
Xíng drew his bow fully and shot an arrow.
The old man lay back on the saddle,
extended his foot,
opened two toes like tongs,
and clamped the arrow.
He laughed and said:
“Is your skill only this much?
Why must this old man bother to fight with his hands?”
Xíng was enraged,
and displayed his ultimate skill:
as soon as one arrow was fired,
another followed immediately.
The old man picked up one with his hand,
seemingly not guarding against the volley;
the second arrow pierced directly through his mouth,
and he fell prostrate,
lying motionless with the arrow.
The boy servant also dismounted.
Xíng rejoiced,
thinking he was already dead,
and approached him.
The old man spat out the arrow and leaped up,
clapping his hands and saying:
“Our first meeting,
why such a malicious prank?”
Xíng was greatly startled,
and his horse also bolted away in fright.
Because of this, he knew the old man was extraordinary,
and dared not turn back.
After traveling thirty or forty lǐ,
he encountered a local official [gāngjì]
who was transporting goods to the capital;
he decided to rob them,
acquiring roughly a thousand pieces of gold,
and his spirits finally soared.
As he was galloping swiftly,
he heard hoofbeats behind him;
he turned his head,
and saw the boy servant, having switched to the lame mule,
rushing like flight.
He shouted:
“Young man, do not leave!
The goods acquired from hunting
Xíng said:
“Do you know ‘Liánzhūjiàn Xíng Mǒu’?”
The boy servant said:
“I have just now received your instruction.”
Xíng, seeing that the boy servant was unimpressive in appearance
and without a bow and arrows,
thought little of him.
He fired three arrows at once,
in an unbroken stream,
like a flock of falcons flying.
The boy servant was not at all flustered,
catching two with his hands
and holding one in his mouth.
He smiled and said:
“Such skill
is truly humiliating!
My master was in a hurry
and didn't have time to find his bow;
these things are also useless,
please let me throw them back to you.”
Thereupon, he removed the iron darts from his fingers,
threaded the arrows through them,
and threw them with the strength of his hand,
making a whizzing sound in the wind.
Xíng quickly blocked them with his bow;
the string just touched the iron,
snapping with a clang,
and the bow also cracked.
Xíng was utterly astonished.
Before he could look for cover,
an arrow passed through his ear,
and he unconsciously tumbled down.
The boy servant dismounted
and immediately began to search him.
Xíng hit him with the bow he was lying on.
The boy servant snatched the bow.
He broke it in half;
then broke it into four pieces,
and tossed them aside.
After that,
he grasped Xíng's two arms with one hand,
and stepped on Xíng's two thighs with one foot;
his arms were as if bound,
his thighs as if pressed,
and he could not move even slightly with all his might.
The belt around his waist was double-folded,
about three fingers' width thick;
the boy servant pinched it with one hand,
and it snapped like ashes in his grasp.
After taking the gold,
he then vaulted onto his mount,
made a gesture with one hand,
and uttered the word
“Mènglàng”
then abruptly departed.
Xíng returned home
and eventually became a good person.
He often recounted his past experiences to others without reservation.
This is somewhat similar to the story of Liú Dōngshān.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Qiáo Shēng,
a native of Jìnníng.
From a young age, he was renowned for his talent.
When he was over twenty years old,
he was still unlucky and struggling.
He was a man of integrity and courage.
He was good friends with Gù Shēng;
when Gù Shēng died,
he regularly supported his wife and children.
The county magistrate greatly respected him for his literary talent;
when the magistrate died while in office,
his family was stranded and unable to return home.
Qiáo Shēng broke his own assets to help carry the coffin,
traveling over two thousand Lǐ back and forth.
Because of this, the scholarly community respected him even more,
but his family's fortunes declined further as a result.
Xiào Lián Shǐ had a daughter,
named Liánchéng,
who was skilled in embroidery
and educated.
Her father spoiled and protected her.
He displayed her embroidery,
"Juàn Xiù Tú," (Weary Embroidery Picture)
to invite young scholars to compose poems for it,
with the intention of choosing a son-in-law.
Qiáo Shēng presented a poem that read:
"Her languid chignon piled high, green and swaying,
early she embroiders a green lotus by the orchid window;
embroidering the mandarin ducks, her soul is about to break,
secretly she stops her needle and thread, furrowing her twin brows."
He also praised her skill in embroidery, saying:
"Her embroidery stitches are like living sketches,
the flowers and birds in the piece are naturally formed;
back then, weaving brocade was not a superior skill,
fortunately, she used palindrome poetry to impress the enlightened ruler."
The girl received the poem and was delighted,
praising it to her father.
Her father considered him poor.
The girl often spoke of him to others;
she also sent an old woman to feign her father's command,
giving him gold to help with his studies.
Qiáo Shēng sighed and said:
"Liánchéng is my true confidante!"
He poured out his heart and conceived an affection,
like a hungry man craving food.
Before long,
the girl was promised in marriage to Wáng Huàchéng, the son of a salt merchant,
and Qiáo Shēng finally despaired;
however, in his dreams, he still cherished her.
Not long after,
the girl fell ill with consumption,
a chronic illness from which she did not recover.
There was a Buddhist monk (touluó) from the Western Regions
who claimed he could cure her;
but it required one qián of a man's breast flesh,
pounded and mixed with medicinal powder.
Shǐ sent someone to Wáng's house to inform his prospective son-in-law.
The son-in-law laughed and said:
"That crazy old man,
wants me to carve out the flesh from my heart!"
The messenger returned.
Shǐ then announced to people:
"Whoever can cut the flesh, I will marry my daughter to him."
Qiáo Shēng heard this and came forward,
pulling out his own sharp blade,
offering his chest to the monk.
His robes and trousers were soaked with blood,
and the monk applied medicine before it stopped.
He compounded three medicinal pills.
After taking all three within three days,
the illness disappeared as if by magic.
Shǐ intended to fulfill his promise,
first informing Wáng.
Wáng was angry
and wanted to sue him in court.
So Shǐ arranged a banquet and invited Qiáo Shēng,
placing a thousand pieces of gold on the table,
saying:
"I deeply owe you a great debt of gratitude,
please accept this as repayment."
He then fully explained the reason for breaking the engagement.
Qiáo Shēng indignantly said:
"The reason I did not begrudge my breast flesh
was merely to repay a confidante;
how could it be to sell flesh!"
He flicked his sleeves and returned home.
When the girl heard this,
she felt truly unbearable,
and entrusted the old woman to comfort and reassure him.
She also said:
"With his talent,
he will not be obscure for long.
Why worry about not finding a good woman in the world?
My dream was inauspicious,
I am sure to die within three years,
there is no need to contend with others for this thing of the underworld."
Qiáo Shēng said to the old woman:
"'A scholar dies for his confidante,'
it is not for beauty.
I sincerely fear that Liánchéng may not truly know me: what harm is there if we are not together?"
The old woman, on behalf of the young lady, swore her sincerity and explained herself.
Qiáo Shēng said:
"If that is truly the case,
when we meet,
you must smile for me,
and I will die without regret!"
After the old woman left,
several days passed.
Qiáo Shēng happened to go out
and encountered the girl returning from her uncle's house,
and he gazed at her.
The girl's autumn-like eyes turned to meet his gaze,
and she parted her lips in a captivating smile.
Qiáo Shēng was overjoyed and said:
"Liánchéng truly knows me!"
Just then, the Wáng family came to discuss the wedding date.
The girl's previous illness recurred,
and she died within a few months.
Qiáo Shēng went to offer his condolences,
and died from extreme grief.
Shǐ had his body carried to his home.
Shēng knew he was dead,
yet felt no sorrow.
Leaving the village,
he still hoped to see Liánchéng once more.
Gazing into the distance, he saw a road stretching north and south,
with travelers continuous as ants,
so he mingled among them.
In a moment,
he entered an official yáshǔ,
where he met Gù Shēng,
who asked in surprise:
"How did you come here?"
He immediately took Shēng's hand and prepared to send him back.
Shēng sighed deeply,
saying:
"My heart's desires are far from fulfilled."
Gù replied:
"I serve as a clerk here,
and am quite trusted.
If I can be of assistance,
I will spare no effort."
Shēng asked about Liánchéng.
Gù then led Shēng around many places,
where they saw Liánchéng with a woman in white,
her tear-filled eyes dim with sorrow,
sitting on the veranda.
Seeing Shēng arrive,
she rose quickly, seemingly pleased,
and briefly asked how he came.
Shēng said:
"You are dead,
how dare I live!"
Liánchéng wept, saying:
"Such an ungrateful person,
yet you still do not cast him aside.
What is the point of dying for him?
However, I can no longer promise you life,
but I vow for the next life."
Shēng told Gù:
"If you have business, go.
I am happy to die and do not wish to live.
Just bother to inquire where Liánchéng will be reborn,
so I may go with her."
Gù agreed and departed.
The woman in white asked who Shēng was,
and Liánchéng recounted the story to her.
When the woman heard it,
she seemed overcome with grief.
Liánchéng told Shēng:
"This is my kinswoman,
her given name is Bīnniáng,
daughter of Magistrate Shǐ of Chángshā.
We came together along the way,
and thus grew fond of each other."
Shēng looked at her,
her demeanor was pitiful.
Just as he was about to inquire further,
Gù had already returned,
and congratulated Shēng, saying:
"I have settled things for you,
I will immediately have the young lady return to life with you,
how about that?"
Both were delighted.
Just as they were about to bow in farewell,
Bīnniáng cried loudly:
"Sister is leaving,
where shall I go?
I beg for your pity and salvation,
I will serve as your handmaiden, Sister."
Liánchéng looked sorrowful,
and had no plan,
so she turned to Shēng for a solution.
Shēng again pleaded with Gù.
Gù found it difficult,
and sternly refused, saying it was impossible.
Shēng insisted.
Then Gù said:
"Let me try presumptuously."
He left for the duration of a meal and returned,
shaking his head, saying:
"What can I do!
It is truly impossible to help in the slightest!"
When Bīnniáng heard this,
she wept charmingly and desperately,
clinging to Liánchéng's arm,
fearing she would leave immediately.
Sorrowful and helpless,
they faced each other in silence;
and seeing their anxious and sorrowful faces,
made one's heart ache.
Gù Shēng indignantly said:
"Please take Bīnniáng with you.
Should there be any transgression or blame,
I will take responsibility for it with my own life!"
Bīnniáng then rejoiced,
and followed Shēng out.
Shēng worried that the journey was long and she would have no companion.
Bīnniáng said:
"I will follow you,
I do not wish to return."
Shēng said:
"You are very foolish.
If you do not return,
how can you live?
When you reach Húnán someday,
do not hide again,
that would be a great fortune."
Just then, two old women were carrying official documents to Chángshā,
Shēng entrusted Bīnniáng to them,
and Bīnniáng wept as she bade farewell and departed.
On the way,
Liánchéng walked haltingly,
resting every lǐ or so;
after more than ten rests,
they finally saw the village gate.
Liánchéng said:
"After being reborn,
I fear there may be complications.
Please retrieve my skeletal remains,
I will consider your home my own,
and will have no regrets."
Shēng agreed.
They returned to Shēng's home together.
The woman was timid, as if she could not walk,
and Shēng waited for her.
The woman said:
"When I arrived here,
my limbs felt shaky,
as if without a master.
I fear my wish may not be fulfilled,
we should still plan carefully;
otherwise,
how can I be free after rebirth?"
They went into a side room together.
After a moment of silence,
Liánchéng smiled and said:
"Do you dislike me?"
Shēng asked in surprise why.
She blushed and said:
"I fear the matter will not succeed,
and I will again burden you.
Please let me repay you as a ghost first."
Shēng was delighted,
and they reveled in their love.
Because of this, she lingered and dared not be reborn immediately,
staying in the side room for three days.
Liánchéng said:
"There's a proverb: 'An ugly wife must eventually meet her in-laws.'
To remain sorrowful here
is not a long-term plan after all."
So she urged Shēng to enter.
As soon as they reached the spiritual bedchamber,
she suddenly revived.
The family was astonished,
and offered her soup and water.
Shēng then sent someone to summon Shǐ,
asking to obtain Liánchéng's corpse,
claiming he could revive her.
Shǐ was pleased,
and agreed to his words.
As soon as it was carried into the room,
she was seen to be awake.
She told her father:
"Your daughter has already committed herself to Qiáo Láng,
there is no reason to return.
If there is any change,
I will simply die again!"
Shǐ returned,
and sent maids to serve her.
When Wáng heard,
he submitted a petition detailing his claim.
The official accepted a bribe,
and ruled in favor of Wáng.
Shēng was so furious he wanted to die,
but could do nothing.
Liánchéng, at Wáng's house,
refused to eat or drink out of anger,
only begging for a swift death.
When the room was empty,
she would hang a belt from the beam.
The next day,
she grew weaker,
almost at the point of expiring.
Wáng was frightened,
and sent her back to Shǐ.
Shǐ again had her carried back to Shēng.
Wáng, knowing this,
could do nothing,
and so let the matter rest.
When Liánchéng recovered,
she often thought of Bīnniáng,
and wanted to send a letter to inquire about her,
but the distance made it difficult to go.
One day,
a family member announced:
"There are carriages and horses at the gate."
The couple went out to see,
and Bīnniáng was already in the courtyard.
They met with mixed emotions of grief and joy.
The Magistrate himself had come to deliver his daughter.
Shēng ēntered.
The Tàishǒu said,
"My little girl, thanks to you, has come back to life.
She vows not to marry anyone else.
I shall now follow her wishes."
Shēng bowed and thanked him as was proper.
The Xiàolián also arrived,
and they spoke of their ancestral ties.
Shēng's given name was Nián,
and his courtesy name was Dànián.
Yìshǐshì remarks:
"To commit one's life to a person known only through a single smile,
some in the world might consider this foolish.
But were the five hundred men of Tián Héng
all utterly stupid?
This is the preciousness of rare understanding,
that which moves the worthy and heroic to feel deeply and be unable to restrain themselves.
Yet, looking across the vast world,
it is also lamentable
that talented and brilliant individuals
can be so captivated by the smile of a beautiful woman!"
The main text is based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
"Yìshǐshì remarks" is supplemented from the twenty-four scroll manuscript.
Huò Shēng from Wéndēng,
and Yán Shēng were close as boys,
and often joked with each other as they grew older.
Their repartee was sharp and combative,
each fearing their retort would not be clever enough.
Huò had a neighboring old woman
who had once assisted Yán's wife in childbirth.
One day, she happened to speak with Huò's wife,
mentioning that Yán's wife had a wart in her private parts.
Huò's wife told Huò.
Huò conspired with his companions,
and seeing that Yán was about to arrive,
deliberately whispered,
"So-and-so's wife is quite fond of me."
The others didn't believe him.
Huò then fabricated the details,
adding,
"If you don't believe me,
she has a double wart on her private side."
Yán stopped outside the window,
listened to everything,
and without entering, left immediately.
Upon reaching home,
he severely beat his wife;
his wife did not confess,
and he became even more brutal.
Unable to endure the abuse,
his wife hanged herself.
Huò then greatly regretted it,
but also dared not confess his falsehood to Yán.
After Yán's wife died,
her ghost cried every night,
preventing the whole family from getting any peace.
Before long,
Yán died suddenly,
and the ghost then stopped crying.
Huò's wife dreamt of a woman with disheveled hair screaming loudly,
"I died a terrible death,
how can you two be happy?!"
She awoke sick,
and died a few days later.
Huò also dreamt of the woman pointing her fingers and cursing him,
slapping his mouth with her palm.
He woke up startled,
felt a faint pain on his lips,
which swelled up high,
and in three days formed double warts,
which became a chronic illness.
He dared not speak or laugh loudly;
if he opened his mouth too suddenly,
the pain was unbearable.
Yìshǐshì remarks:
"That the dead can become vengeful spirits
is due to their injustice.
That the private ailment was transferred to the lips
is both supernatural and humorous."
In the town, Wáng from the Wáng clan
was close with a classmate.
When his classmate's wife returned to her parents' home,
Wáng, knowing her donkey was easily startled,
first hid in a thicket.
When the wife arrived,
he suddenly jumped out;
the donkey was startled, and the wife fell.
Only one servant boy was accompanying her,
unable to help her mount the donkey.
Wáng then ardently embraced and supported her,
so much so that the wife did not recognize who he was.
Wáng swaggered, feeling proud of this,
telling the servant boy to chase the donkey away,
thus managing to have a private encounter with the wife in the thicket,
describing her trousers and shoes in great detail.
When the classmate heard this,
he was greatly shamed and left.
A short while later,
Wáng saw from a crack in the window
the classmate, one hand grasping a blade,
the other holding his wife,
looking very angry and malicious.
Greatly frightened,
Wáng scaled the wall and fled.
The classmate pursued him,
but after chasing for two or three *lǐ* he couldn't catch him,
and finally returned.
Wáng ran with all his might,
his lung lobes expanding,
and because of this, he developed a roaring sickness,
which did not heal for several years.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wāng Shìxiù,
a native of Lúzhōu.
He was brave and strong,
able to lift a stone mortar.
Both father and son were skilled at *cùjū*.
His father, in his forties,
died when crossing Qiántáng.
Eight or nine years passed,
and Wāng went to Húnán for this reason,
mooring overnight on Dòngtíng Lake.
At the time, they watched the moon rise in the east.
The clear river was like a white ribbon.
While they were gazing,
suddenly five people emerged from the lake,
carrying a large mat,
which they spread flat on the water's surface,
about half an *mǔ* in size.
They busily laid out wine and dishes,
the utensils clattering,
but the sound was mellow and deep,
unlike pottery or tiles.
Presently, three people stepped onto the mat and sat down,
and two served them drinks.
Of those seated, one wore yellow,
two wore white;
the turbans on their heads were all black,
lofty and extending down to their shoulders and backs,
their style utterly strange and ancient,
but the moonlight was dim,
not very clear.
The attendants were all in brown clothes;
one seemed like a boy,
the other like a scribe.
They only heard the man in yellow say,
"Tonight's moonlight is excellent,
enough for a joyful drink."
The men in white said,
"The scenery tonight
is very similar to when Guǎnglì Wáng feasted on Líhuā Dǎo."
The three mutually urged each other,
emptying their cups one after another.
But their voices were slightly soft,
so they could not be heard,
and the boatmen hid themselves,
daring not to move or breathe.
Wāng
scrutinized the attendant; the old man bore a striking resemblance to his father.
However, listening to his voice,
it was not his father's.
As two clepsydra-hours were nearing their end,
suddenly a person said:
"While the bright moon is out,
it would be delightful to kick something."
Immediately, the boy was seen disappearing into the water
and retrieving a sphere,
large enough to fill an embrace,
its interior seemingly full of mercury,
transparent both inside and out.
All those seated rose.
The man in yellow called the old man to kick it together.
It was kicked more than a *zhàng* (about 3.3 meters) high,
its light shaking and dazzling people's eyes.
Soon after, it rose far away
and fell into the boat.
Wāng's
hands itched, and he kicked it with all his might,
feeling it to be unusually light.
Kicking it forcefully, it seemed to break,
soaring several *zhàng* high;
a stream of light leaked from within,
shooting downwards like a rainbow;
then it fell swiftly,
like a comet traversing the sky,
plunging straight into the water,
making a bubbling sound as it disappeared.
All present at the feast angrily said:
"What kind of living person
ruined our elegant pleasure!"
The old man laughed and said:
"Not bad, not bad,
this is my family's 'falling star staff'."
The man in white, angered by his jest,
fumed:
"Everyone is annoyed,
how can this old slave be happy?
Go with Xiǎo Wūpí and capture that madman;
otherwise,
your shins and thighs will be beaten!"
Wāng, realizing there was no escape,
was not afraid,
and gripped his knife, standing in the boat.
Suddenly, he saw the boy and the old man approaching with weapons.
Wāng
looked closely; it was truly his father!
He cried out:
"Father!
Your son is here!"
The old man was greatly alarmed,
and they looked at each other with deep sorrow.
The boy immediately turned and left.
The old man said:
"Son, quickly hide!
Otherwise,
we will all die!"
Before he finished speaking,
three men had suddenly boarded the boat.
Their faces were all pitch black,
their eyes larger than pomegranates,
and they seized the old man.
Wāng
struggled to snatch him back, shaking the boat and breaking the cable.
Wāng
chopped off one of their arms with his knife, and the man in yellow fled.
A man in white rushed at Wāng;
Wāng
chopped off his head, which fell into the water with a splash;
then they all plunged in with a roar.
Just as they were planning to cross the lake by night,
they suddenly saw a giant maw emerge from the water's surface,
as deep as a well.
Lake water rushed into it from all sides,
making crashing sounds.
Soon, with a mighty gush,
waves reached the stars,
and thousands of boats tossed about.
The boatmen were terrified.
There were two stone drums on the boat,
each weighing a hundred *jīn* (about 50 kg).
Wāng
lifted one and threw it, stirring the water with a thunderous roar,
and the waves gradually subsided;
he threw the other,
and the wind and waves completely calmed.
Wāng
suspected his father was a ghost. The old man said:
"I was never dead.
Nineteen people drowned in the river,
all eaten by monsters;
I survived by kicking the sphere.
The creature offended Qíantáng Jūn,
which is why it moved to avoid him in Dòngtíng.
The three men are fish spirits,
and the sphere you kicked was a fish's bladder."
Father and son rejoiced at their reunion,
and rowed away in the middle of the night.
At dawn,
they saw a fish fin in the boat,
about four or five *chǐ* (about 1.3-1.6 meters) across,
and then realized it was the arm they had severed during the night.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Therefore, in Zhūgě Chéng
there was a merchant, Shì Yǔ,
who was a scholar.
In a drunken jest, he offended a local gentry, hào.
The hào incited his household servants to beat Shì Yǔ mercilessly.
He was carried home and died.
Shì Yǔ had two sons,
the elder named Chén,
and the younger named Lǐ.
He also had one daughter named Sānguān.
Sānguān was sixteen years old,
and her wedding date was approaching,
but due to her father's death, it was not carried out.
Her two brothers went to press charges,
but for a whole year, they couldn't get a resolution.
The groom's family sent someone to console the mother
and requested that the wedding proceed expediently.
The mother was about to agree.
The daughter stepped forward and said:
"How can one hold a joyous ceremony while a father's corpse is not yet cold?
Do they not have parents?"
When the groom's family heard this,
they were ashamed and stopped.
Not long after,
the two brothers failed to obtain justice in their lawsuit,
and returned home full of grievance.
The whole family was sad and indignant.
The brothers planned to keep their father's corpse
as a basis for another lawsuit.
Sānguān said:
"A man was murdered and no justice was done;
the state of affairs can be known.
Is Heaven going to specifically give birth to a Judge Bāo Lǎo of the underworld for you brothers?
To leave the bones exposed,
how can the heart bear it!"
The two brothers heeded her words,
and thus buried their father.
After the burial,
Sānguān disappeared during the night,
and her whereabouts were unknown.
The mother was ashamed and worried,
fearing that the groom's family would find out,
and dared not tell her clan members,
but only instructed her two sons to secretly search for her.
For nearly half a year,
she was nowhere to be found.
It happened that the hào's birthday arrived,
and he invited actors for entertainment.
The actor Sūn Chún
brought two disciples to assist.
One of them, Wáng Chéng,
had an ordinary appearance,
but his voice was clear and resonant,
and everyone praised him.
The other, Lǐ Yù,
was as beautiful and delicate as a pretty girl.
When called upon to sing,
he declined, saying he was not skilled;
when forced,
the tunes he performed were half mixed with children's folk rhymes,
and the whole audience applauded.
Sūn was greatly ashamed
and told the host:
"This child has not studied for long,
he only knows how to serve drinks.
Please do not blame him."
He then ordered him to serve wine.
Lǐ Yù moved back and forth serving,
skillful at discerning the host's intentions.
The hào was pleased.
When the banquet ended and people dispersed,
he kept Lǐ Yù to sleep with him.
Lǐ Yù helped the hào dust the bed and remove his shoes,
attending to him with diligent care.
The hào spoke flirtatiously in his drunkenness,
but Lǐ Yù only smiled.
The hào was even more infatuated,
and dismissed all other servants,
keeping only Lǐ Yù.
Lǐ Yù waited until all the servants had left,
then closed and bolted the door.
The servants went to drink in another room.
After a while,
they heard a grating sound in the main hall.
One servant went to investigate,
and saw that the room was pitch black,
and no sound was heard.
Just as he was about to turn back,
suddenly there was a very sharp sound,
like a heavy object being suspended and its rope snapping.
He urgently called out,
but there was no response.
The others shouted and pushed open the door to enter,
and found the master's head and body severed;
Lǐ Yù had hanged himself,
but the rope had broken and he had fallen to the ground,
with a piece of the rope clearly
remaining on the beam and around his neck.
Everyone was greatly alarmed
and reported it to the inner chambers,
and a crowd gathered, unable to understand.
When they moved Lǐ Yù's corpse to the courtyard,
they felt his socks and shoes were empty as if there were no feet;
when they removed them,
they found white embroidered shoes with curved toes,
which meant he was a woman.
They were even more surprised.
They called Sūn Chún to question him.
Sūn was extremely horrified
and didn't know how to answer.
He only said:
"Lǐ Yù joined as a disciple a month ago,
wishing to perform for the master's birthday;
I truly don't know his origins."
Because of her attire of mourning,
they suspected she was an assassin from the Shāng family.
They temporarily assigned two people to guard her.
The woman's appearance was lifelike; when touched,
her limbs were warm.
The two guards secretly plotted to violate her.
One of them hugged the corpse and turned it over,
and just as he was about to loosen her bindings,
his head was suddenly struck as if by something,
and blood gushed from his mouth,
and he died in an instant.
The other was greatly startled
and reported it to the crowd.
Everyone revered her as a deity.
They also reported it to the prefecture.
The prefectural officials questioned Chén and Lǐ,
who both said:
"We don't know.
But our sister disappeared
half a year ago."
They were instructed to go and verify,
and it was indeed Sānguān.
The officials were astonished,
ordered the two brothers to lead the burial,
and commanded the hào's family not to seek revenge.
The Historian of Wonders says:
"If a family has a woman like Yù Ràng and does not know it,
then the caliber of the brothers as men can be known.
However, Sānguān's character,
even the desolate Yì Shuǐ,
would be ashamed and would not flow;
how much more so for those who drift aimlessly with the world!
I wish all women in the boudoirs of the world
would buy silk and embroider her [image],
for her merit would be no less than that of serving the valorous Guān Yǔ."
(According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
Among the villagers of Jiāng,
a father stayed in the fields overnight
and was eaten by wolves.
Jiāng was sixteen at the time,
and when he found his father's remaining shoe,
he was overwhelmed with grief and hatred, wishing to die.
At night, after his mother had gone to sleep,
he secretly took an iron hammer
and went to sleep where his father had been,
hoping to avenge his father's kindness.
After a short while,
a wolf came,
hesitantly sniffing around.
Jiāng did not move.
Before long,
it wagged its tail and brushed his forehead,
then gradually lowered its head to lick his thigh.
Jiāng still did not move.
Presently, it joyfully sprang forward
and tried to seize his collar.
Jiāng quickly struck the wolf's head with the hammer,
killing it instantly.
He got up and placed it in the grass.
After a short while,
another wolf came,
acting as the previous one.
He also killed it.
By midnight,
no more came.
Suddenly, he dozed off,
and dreamed his father said:
"Killing two creatures
is enough to vent my hatred.
However, the one who first killed me
has a white nose;
these are not it."
Jiāng woke up,
lay still and waited for it.
When morning came,
he found nothing else.
He wanted to drag the wolves home,
but feared alarming his mother,
so he threw them into a dry well and returned.
That night he went again,
but no more came.
This continued for three or four nights.
Suddenly a wolf came,
bit his foot,
and dragged him along.
After a few steps,
thorns pierced his flesh,
stones wounded his skin.
Jiāng Ruò seemed about to die.
The wolf then placed him on the ground,
intending to disembowel him.
Jiāng abruptly rose and hammered it,
knocking it down;
then hammered it repeatedly,
killing it.
Upon closer inspection,
it was indeed the white-nosed wolf.
Greatly delighted,
he carried it home
and only then told his mother.
His mother wept and followed him,
probed the dry well,
and found two wolves there.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"A man of the farming class,
could he possess such a hero?
His righteous fervor stems from heartfelt sincerity,
not mere bravery,
and his intelligence is also extraordinary."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Zhào Wàng of Téngyì,
he and his wife worshipped Buddha,
eating no meat or blood,
and in the village they
were known
as "good people."
Their family was said to be comfortably off.
They had a daughter, Xiǎo'èr,
who was exceptionally intelligent and beautiful,
and Zhào cherished her.
At six years old,
he sent her with her elder brother Chángchūn
to study under a tutor;
after five years, she had mastered the Wǔjīng.
Her classmate, Dīng Shēng,
courtesy name Zǐmò,
was three years older than the girl,
and possessed literary talent and a refined demeanor,
and they developed a mutual affection.
He privately expressed his feelings to his mother,
asking for a marriage proposal to the Zhào family.
Zhào hoped to marry his daughter to a prominent family,
and therefore refused.
Not long after,
Zhào was swayed by the Báilián Jiào;
when Xú Hóngrú rebelled,
the entire family fell into banditry.
Xiǎo'èr, being well-read and quick to understand,
became proficient in the arts of paper soldiers and bean horses
as soon as she saw them.
Among the six young women who apprenticed under Xú,
only two were considered the best,
and thus she learned all of his techniques.
Because of his daughter, Zhào
received great trust and responsibility.
At this time, Dīng, eighteen years old,
was studying in Téngpàn,
but he would not discuss marriage,
his heart not forgetting Xiǎo'èr.
He secretly fled
and joined Xú's command.
The girl was pleased to see him,
treating him with exceptional courtesy.
As Xú's top disciple, the girl
managed military affairs;
she was in and out day and night,
her parents could not reach her.
Dīng saw her every night,
often dismissing all other servants,
and they would talk until the third watch.
Dīng privately said,
"I have come here,
does Your Ladyship know my humble intentions?"
The girl said:
"I do not know."
Dīng said:
"I do not presumptuously aspire to greatness;
the reason I came
is truly for Your Ladyship.
The heterodox path is of no avail;
it will only lead to destruction.
You are a wise person,
do you not consider this?
If you can flee with me,
then my heart's sincerity will not have been betrayed."
The girl was taken aback for a moment,
then suddenly awakened as if from a dream,
and said:
"To abandon my parents and leave
is unrighteous;
please inform them."
The two entered and presented the pros and cons,
but Zhào did not understand,
saying:
"My master is a divine person,
how could there be any mistake?"
The girl knew persuasion was futile,
so she changed her braided hair into a bun.
She produced two paper kites
and they each mounted one;
the kites swiftly spread their wings,
like jiānjiān birds,
flying wing to wing.
At dawn,
they reached the border of Láiwú.
The girl used her finger to pinch the kite's neck,
and it immediately folded and descended.
They then put away the kites.
They changed into double guards' uniforms
and rode swiftly to Shānyīnlǐ,
posing as refugees,
and rented a house to live in.
The two people departed hastily,
frugal with their provisions,
and lacking firewood and storage.
Dīng was very worried about this.
They tried to borrow grain from their neighbors,
but no one would lend them even a sheng or dou.
The woman showed no signs of worry,
but merely pawned her hairpins and earrings.
They closed their door and faced each other quietly,
guessing lantern riddles,
and recalling forgotten books,
using these to decide who was superior or inferior;
the loser
would strike their wrist with two fingers.
The old man to their west, surnamed Wēng,
was a hero of the greenwood.
One day,
he returned from hunting.
The woman said:
“‘One who becomes rich through their neighbor,’
why should I worry?
If I temporarily borrow a thousand pieces of gold,
will he give it to me?”
Dīng thought it would be difficult.
The woman said:
“I will make him happily hand it over.”
Then she cut paper into the shape of a Pànguān,
placed it on the ground,
and covered it with a chicken cage.
Afterwards, she took Dīng’s hand and ascended the bed,
boiled some aged wine,
and consulted the Zhōulǐ for their drinking game rules: whoever mentioned a certain page of a certain volume,
and a certain person,
they would all flip to it.
Those whose names contained a radical for food, water, or alcohol would drink;
those whose names were in the “wine section” would drink double.
Presently, the woman happened to get
“jiǔrén” (wine person),
and Dīng urged her on, filling a large goblet.
The woman then prayed:
“If we manage to borrow the gold,
you should get the ‘drink section’.”
Dīng flipped the scroll,
and got
“biērén” (turtle person).
The woman laughed loudly and said:
“The matter is settled!”
She dripped the wine into his cup.
Dīng was not convinced.
The woman said:
“You are an aquatic creature,
you should drink like a turtle.”
Just as they were arguing loudly,
they heard a rattling sound from inside the cage.
The woman stood up and said:
“It’s here.”
She opened the cage and examined it,
and indeed, there was a large amount of gold in a cloth bag,
overflowing.
Dīng was overwhelmed with shock and joy.
Later, the old woman from Wēng’s household came to play with her child,
and secretly said:
“When the master first returned,
he lit a lamp and sat up all night.
The ground suddenly cracked open,
so deep that the bottom could not be seen.
A Pànguān emerged from within.
He said: ‘I am a Sīlì of the underworld.
The Emperor of Tàishān is meeting with all the冥Cáo,
to create an evil for violent guests.
A thousand silver lamps are needed,
each weighing ten liǎng;
if a hundred lamps are offered,
their sins will be expunged.’
The master was terrified,
burned incense and kowtowed,
and offered a thousand pieces of gold.
The Pànguān slowly withdrew,
and the ground also closed up.”
The couple listened to her words,
and exclaimed in amazement.
From then on, they gradually bought cattle and horses,
hired servants and maids,
and built a grand residence.
The scoundrels in the village, coveting their wealth,
gathered other lawless individuals,
climbed over the wall, and robbed Dīng.
Dīng and his wife only woke from their dreams
to find a braided straw mat providing light,
and robbers filling the house.
Two men seized Dīng;
another reached into the woman’s bosom.
The woman bared her chest and stood up,
pointed a finger, and scolded:
“Stop,
stop!”
The thirteen robbers
all stuck out their tongues and stood dumbfounded,
as foolish as wooden puppets.
The woman then put on her trousers and got out of bed,
called her household members together,
tied the arms of each robber behind their backs,
and forced them to confess everything clearly.
Then she reprimanded them, saying:
“People from afar bury their heads in valleys and streams,
hoping for mutual support;
how can you be so inhumane?
Difficult times sometimes happen to people,
those in distress might as well state it clearly;
am I one who hoards wealth and keeps it to myself?
Such acts of wolves and jackals
deserve to be completely exterminated;
but I cannot bear to do so,
so I will release you for now,
but you will not be pardoned if you commit this again!”
The robbers kowtowed in gratitude and left.
Not long after,
Hóngrú was captured,
and Zhào and his wife and children were all executed.
The husband subsequently used gold to redeem Chángchūn’s young son and brought him home.
The child was then three years old,
and they raised him as their own,
making him take the surname Dīng,
and named him Chéngtiāo.
Thus, people in the village gradually knew them to be relatives of the Báilián Jiào.
Just then, locusts damaged the crops,
and the woman released hundreds of paper kites with wings into the fields,
the locusts stayed far away,
not entering their furrows,
thus their crops remained unharmed.
The villagers all resented this,
and collectively reported them to the authorities,
claiming they were remnants of Hóngrú’s faction.
The official, coveting their wealth,
regarded them as a source of profit,
and arrested Dīng.
Dīng bribed the magistrate heavily,
and only then was he released.
The woman said:
“The wealth gained through these illicit means
is indeed destined to be scattered and lost.
However, this place of snakes and scorpions
is not somewhere we can stay for long.”
So they sold their property cheaply and left,
settling on the western border of Yìdū.
The woman was intelligent and
skilled in accumulating wealth.
Her management of finances surpassed that of men.
She often operated a shop in Liúlí Chǎng,
personally guiding the craftsmen who came,
creating all kinds of decorative lanterns.
Their unique styles and dazzling colors
were unmatched by any other shop,
and thus, despite their high prices, they sold quickly.
After several years,
her wealth became preeminent.
However, the woman supervised her maids and servants strictly;
hundreds of mouths were fed without a single idle one.
In her leisure, she would often brew tea and play chess with Dīng,
or read history books for pleasure.
The comings and goings of money and grain,
as well as the work of the maids and servants,
were reviewed every five days.
The woman personally held the tallies,
while Dīng recorded the names and numbers.
Diligent workers were rewarded differentially,
while lazy ones were whipped and forced to kneel.
On that day,
they were given leave and did not work at night.
The couple prepared food and wine,
calling the maids to sing folk songs for entertainment.
The woman was as clear-sighted as a deity,
and no one dared to deceive her.
Yet her rewards often exceeded the labor,
so tasks were easily accomplished.
Among the more than two hundred households in the village,
all the poor were given capital according to their needs,
so there were no idle people in the village.
When a great drought occurred,
the woman instructed the villagers to erect an altar in the fields.
She went out in her carriage to the fields,
performing the Yǔ步 ritual.
Sweet rain poured down,
and within five lǐ, all crops were sufficiently watered.
People increasingly regarded her as divine.
The woman never covered her face when she went out,
and all the villagers saw her.
Sometimes, groups of young men
would secretly discuss her beauty;
but when they met her face to face,
they were all solemn and dared not look up.
Every autumn,
the village children who could not farm
were given money
to collect thistles and sow thistles.
For nearly twenty years,
these accumulated, filling houses.
People secretly laughed at her.
Then a great famine struck Shānzuǒ,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
The woman then brought out the vegetables,
mixing them with millet to feed the starving.
The nearby villages survived because of this,
with no one fleeing.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“The deeds of these two
were perhaps heaven-bestowed,
not human effort.
However, had it not been for a single word of enlightenment,
they would have both died long ago.
From this perspective,
many in the world possess extraordinary talents
but mistakenly go astray and perish.
This must also not be a small number.
How can we know that among the six fellow students,
there were none such persons?
It makes one regret not having met Dīng Shēng.”
According to the Jiùxuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Jīn Dàyòng was
a son from an old family in Zhōngzhōu.
He was engaged to Yóu Tàishǒu’s daughter,
named Gēngniáng,
who was beautiful and virtuous.
Their affection was very deep.
Due to the chaos of the roving bandits,
his family scattered.
Jīn took his family and fled south.
On the way, they met a young man
who was also fleeing with his wife.
He introduced himself as Wáng Shíbā from Guǎnglíng,
and offered to go ahead as their guide.
Jīn was pleased,
and they traveled together.
When they reached the river,
the woman secretly told Jīn:
“Do not share a boat with that young man.
He has repeatedly looked at me,
his eyes moving and his expression changing;
his intentions are unfathomable.”
Jīn agreed.
Wáng diligently sought a large boat,
helped Jīn transport his luggage,
and was extremely laborious.
Jīn could not bear to refuse.
He also considered that Wáng had a young wife with him,
so there should be no other intentions.
Wáng’s wife stayed with Gēngniáng,
and her demeanor was also quite gentle.
Wáng sat at the bow of the boat,
chatting with the boatmen,
seeming very familiar and friendly.
Soon,
the sun set,
and the waterway stretched far into the distance,
vast and indistinguishable as to north or south.
Jīn looked around at the gloomy and dangerous surroundings,
feeling quite suspicious and uneasy.
A moment later,
a bright moon rose,
and all he saw was an expanse of reeds.
Upon docking,
Wáng invited Jīn and his father out for a breath of fresh air,
then took the opportunity to push Jīn into the water.
Jīn’s aged father,
seeing this, tried to cry out.
The boatmen struck him with a pole,
and he also drowned.
His birth mother heard the sound and peeked out,
and was also struck and drowned.
Wáng then started shouting for help.
When the mother came out,
Gēngniáng was behind her
and had already caught a glimpse.
When she heard that the entire family had drowned,
she did not show surprise,
but merely cried,
“My parents-in-law are both gone,
where shall I return?!”
Wáng entered and consoled her:
“My lady, do not worry.
Please come with me to Jīnlíng.
My family’s fields and dwellings
are quite sufficient to support you,
and there will be no cause for concern.”
The woman wiped away her tears and said,
“If it can be like this,
my wish is fulfilled.”
Wáng was greatly pleased,
and treated her very well.
When night fell,
he pulled the woman, seeking intimacy.
The woman feigned illness,
so Wáng went to sleep with his wife.
After the first watch passed,
the couple began to quarrel loudly,
for unknown reasons.
But the wife was heard saying,
“If you do what you intend,
thunder will surely smash your skull!”
Wáng then beat his wife.
The wife cried out,
“I’d rather die!
I truly do not wish to be the wife of a murderer!”
Wáng roared in anger,
and his wife came out.
Then a thud was heard,
followed by clamoring that his wife had drowned.
Not long after,
they arrived at Jīnlíng.
He led Gēngniáng to his home
and entered the hall to see the old woman.
The old woman was surprised that she was not the former wife.
Wáng said,
"My wife drowned,
I just married this one."
Returning to the room,
he again wanted to assault her.
Gēngniáng smiled and said,
"You are a man of thirty,
have you never experienced intimacy before?
Even commoners on their wedding night
still need a cup of light wine.
Your family is rich and prosperous,
so it should not be difficult to arrange.
To face each other sober,
what kind of behavior is that?"
Wáng was pleased
and prepared wine to drink together.
Gēngniáng held the goblet
