and entreated him to drink with sincere earnestness.
Wáng gradually became drunk
and declined to drink more.
Gēngniáng picked up a large bowl
and charmingly urged him.
Wáng could not bear to refuse
and drank it.
Thus, thoroughly drunk,
he stripped naked and quickly went to bed.
Gēngniáng removed the utensils and candles,
feigning she needed to relieve herself.
She left the room,
entered with a knife,
and in the darkness, groped for Wáng's neck.
Wáng still grabbed her arm, making affectionate noises.
Gēngniáng strongly slashed him.
He did not die,
but cried out and got up.
She struck him again,
and only then did he die.
The old woman vaguely heard something,
rushed towards them,
and the girl killed her too.
Wáng's younger brother, Shíjiǔ, awoke.
Gēngniáng knew she could not escape,
so she quickly tried to commit suicide by slitting her own throat.
The knife was dull and could not penetrate.
She opened the door and fled.
Shíjiǔ pursued her.
She had already thrown herself into the pond.
He called out to the residents,
who rescued her, but she was already dead,
her complexion as beautiful as if alive.
Together they examined Wáng's corpse
and saw a letter on the window.
They opened and read it,
and it was the girl's detailed account of her grievances.
Everyone considered her a heroine
and planned to collect funds for her funeral.
At dawn,
thousands of onlookers gathered.
Seeing her appearance,
they all bowed to her.
Throughout the day,
one hundred gold pieces were collected,
so she was buried in the southern suburbs.
Those who were fond of good deeds made her a pearl crown and robes,
and interred her grandly.
Initially,
when Jīnshēng drowned,
he floated on a plank
and managed to survive.
As dawn approached,
he reached the Huái River
and was rescued by a small boat.
The boat belonged to the wealthy elder Yǐn Wēng, who specifically kept it to save drowning victims.
After Jīn recovered,
he went to Wēng to express his gratitude.
Wēng treated him with great kindness
and kept him to teach his son.
Jīn, not knowing his family's fate,
intended to go investigate,
and so was undecided.
Soon after, it was reported,
"A dead old man and old woman have been recovered."
Jīn suspected they were his parents
and rushed to verify; indeed they were.
Wēng arranged for their coffins.
As Jīn was deeply grieving,
it was again reported,
"A drowned woman has been rescued,
who claims Jīnshēng is her husband."
Jīn wiped away his tears and rushed out in surprise.
The woman had already arrived.
She was distinctly not Gēngniáng,
but the wife of Shíbā.
She cried loudly to Jīn,
begging him not to abandon her.
Jīn said,
"My mind is already in chaos,
how can I possibly think of anyone else?"
The woman became even more sorrowful.
Yǐn understood the situation
and was pleased, considering it divine retribution. He
advised Jīn to take the woman in.
Jīn used his mourning as an excuse,
saying, "And I am about to seek revenge;
I fear a frail woman would be a burden."
The woman said,
"If that's what you mean,
if Gēngniáng were still alive,
would you abandon her for revenge and mourning?"
Wēng considered her words good
and asked to temporarily adopt and care for her,
to which Jīn then agreed.
When Wēng and the old woman were buried,
the woman cried
as if mourning her own parents-in-law.
After the burial,
Jīn carried a blade and a begging bowl,
intending to go to Guǎnglíng.
The woman stopped him, saying,
"My surname is Táng,
and my ancestors resided in Jīnlíng.
I am from the same hometown as that scoundrel.
My previous mention of Guǎnglíng
was a lie.
Moreover, many river pirates
are his accomplices.
You will not be able to avenge yourself,
but only invite disaster."
Jīn hesitated, not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, news spread of a woman who had avenged her grievances,
circulating widely along the rivers,
with her name clearly identified.
Jīn felt a momentary relief upon hearing it,
but then became even sadder.
He bid farewell to the woman, saying,
"Fortunately, you were not defiled.
With such a heroic wife in my family,
how can I be so unfaithful as to marry again?"
The woman, because the matter was already settled,
refused to leave,
wishing to remain as a concubine.
It so happened that Vice-General Yuán Gōng,
who was an old acquaintance of Yǐn,
was about to set out westward
and passed by Yǐn's place.
Seeing Jīn,
he took a great liking to him
and invited him to be his secretary.
Before long,
the bandits rebelled against the court,
and Yuán achieved great merit.
Jīn, participating in strategic matters,
was commended for his efforts
and granted the title of guerrilla general before returning.
Only then did he and his wife perform the wedding ceremony.
After a few days,
he took his wife to Jīnlíng
to visit Gēngniáng's grave.
They briefly stopped in Zhènjiāng,
intending to ascend Jīnshān.
As their boat glided in the middle of the river,
another boat passed.
In it were an old woman and a young woman,
and the young woman remarkably resembled Gēngniáng.
Their boat passed swiftly,
but the woman peered at Jīn from the window,
her expression even more alike.
Startled and hesitant to inquire,
Jīn quickly shouted,
"Look, are the ducks flying up to the sky?"
The young woman heard this
and also called out,
"The greedy child wants to eat cat's fish?"
These were their secret jests from their chambers in years gone by.
Jīn was greatly surprised,
turned his boat back to approach her,
and it was indeed Gēngniáng.
The maid helped her transfer to their boat,
and they embraced and wept sorrowfully,
moving the travelers.
Táng Shì formally greeted Gēngniáng as the principal wife.
Gēngniáng asked in surprise,
and Jīn then recounted the entire story.
Gēngniáng took her hand and said,
"We spoke on the same boat,
and I never forgot you;
I didn't expect us to become one family from Wú and Yuè.
You kindly buried my parents-in-law,
for which I should first express my gratitude.
Why do you treat me with such ceremony?"
Then, by age,
Táng was one year younger than Gēngniáng,
so Gēngniáng treated her as a younger sister.
Previously,
after Gēngniáng was buried,
she did not know how many springs and autumns had passed.
Suddenly, a person called out,
"Gēngniáng,
your husband is not dead;
you shall be reunited."
Then, as if waking from a dream,
she looked around
and saw that all four sides were walls.
Only then did she realize that she had died and been buried.
She only felt stifled,
but had no other suffering.
Some ruffians, spying that her burial accouterments were rich and beautiful,
dug up the tomb and broke open the coffin.
Just as they were about to plunder it,
they saw Gēngniáng still alive,
and were all terrified.
Gēngniáng, fearing they would harm her,
pleaded with them, saying,
"Fortunately you all have come,
allowing me to see the light of day.
My hairpins and earrings
can all be taken.
I wish to be sold as a nun,
which might yield a little more money.
I will not leak this secret either."
The bandits bowed their heads and said,
"Madam's chastity and integrity
are admired by gods and men alike.
We wretches are merely poor and desperate,
committing this inhumane act.
As long as there are no leaks,
we are fortunate.
How dare we sell you as a nun!"
Gēngniáng said,
"This is what I wish for myself."
Another bandit said,
"Madame Gěng of Zhènjiāng
is a widow without children.
If she sees you, Madam,
she will surely be overjoyed."
Gēngniáng thanked them.
She took off her pearl ornaments
and gave them all to the bandits.
The bandits dared not accept them;
but she insisted,
and they then bowed and accepted them together.
They then carried her away
to Madame Gěng's house,
fabricating a story that she had been lost in a boat accident.
Madame Gěng was
from a wealthy family,
an old widow living alone.
Seeing Gēngniáng, she was greatly pleased,
thinking she was her own daughter who had come out.
It happened that her son had just returned from Jīnshān.
Gēngniáng related her story in detail.
Then Jīn went to the boat to bow to his mother,
and his mother treated him like a son-in-law.
She invited him to her house,
and he stayed for several days before returning.
Thereafter, their comings and goings were ceaseless.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"When a great change is at hand,
the licentious live,
while the chaste die.
The living tear open people's eyes,
while the dead wipe away people's tears.
As for those who remain undaunted in pleasant conversation,
and personally slay their enemies,
among the valiant heroes of a thousand generations,
how many can compare!
Who says women
cannot rival Yàn Yún?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Liǔ Fānghuá,
a native of Bǎodìng.
He was wealthy enough to dominate his village,
generous and hospitable,
often having a hundred guests at his table.
He was quick to help those in need,
not sparing a thousand pieces of gold.
His guests and friends often borrowed money and never repaid it.
Only one guest, Gōng Mèngbì,
a man from Shǎn,
never asked for anything in his life.
Whenever he visited,
he would stay for a year.
His words and intentions were clear and elegant,
and Liǔ spent the most time with him.
Liǔ's son was named Hé,
then a young boy,
who called him 'uncle'.
Gōng also enjoyed playing with Hé.
Whenever Hé returned from school,
he would always help him pry up floor tiles,
bury pebbles,
and pretend to bury gold for fun.
The five-bay house
was dug up several times for treasure.
Everyone laughed at his childish behavior,
but Hé alone delighted in it,
even more so than with other guests.
More than ten years later,
the family's wealth gradually diminished,
unable to satisfy the demands of many guests,
so guests became scarce;
however, a dozen or so people talking all night
was still common.
As his years advanced,
his fortunes declined further.
He still sold fields for money
to prepare meals.
Hé also spent lavishly,
emulating his father in befriending young companions,
which Liǔ did not forbid.
Before long,
Liǔ fell ill and died,
to the point where there was nothing to pay for the funeral arrangements.
Gōng then took out money from his own purse
to manage Liǔ's affairs.
Hé felt even more indebted to him.
Matters big or small,
all were entrusted to Uncle Gōng.
Whenever Gōng entered from outside,
he would always carry pebbles and broken tiles in his sleeve,
and upon reaching the room, would throw them into a dark corner,
the meaning of which was never understood.
Hé often expressed his worries about poverty to Gōng.
Gōng said:
"You do not know the difficulty of hard labor.
Not to mention having no gold;
even if you were given a thousand pieces of gold,
it could be quickly spent.
A man's trouble is not being self-reliant;
why worry about poverty?"
One day,
he said goodbye, wishing to return home.
Hé wept and urged him to return quickly,
Gōng agreed,
and then left.
Hé was poor and could not support himself,
his pawned and mortgaged items gradually emptied.
He looked forward to Gōng's arrival daily,
thinking he would manage things,
but Gōng disappeared without a trace,
gone like the yellow crane.
Earlier,
during Liǔ's lifetime,
he arranged a marriage for Hé with the Huáng family of Wújí,
who were wealthy gentry.
Later, hearing of Liǔ's poverty,
they secretly had second thoughts.
When Liǔ died,
they were notified of the訃告;
they did not even offer condolences;
they merely excused themselves by saying the journey was too far.
After Hé's mourning period ended,
his mother sent him to his in-laws' place
to set the wedding date,
hoping the Huángs would show pity and consideration.
When he arrived,
the Huángs, hearing of his tattered clothes and worn shoes,
ordered the doorkeeper not to admit him.
A message was sent:
"Go and procure a hundred pieces of gold,
then you may return;
otherwise,
let this be the end of it."
Hé cried bitterly upon hearing this.
Old Woman Liú, who lived across the street,
took pity on him and offered him food,
gave him three hundred cash,
and comforted him, telling him to return home.
His mother was also sorrowful and furious, without a plan.
She then remembered that eight or nine out of ten of their former guests owed them money,
and instructed him to seek help from the wealthy ones.
Hé said,
"Those who associated with me in the past
did so for my wealth.
If your son rode in a four-horse carriage,
borrowing a thousand pieces of gold
would not be difficult.
In such circumstances as these,
who would still remember past kindness and old friendships?
Moreover, father lent money to people
without any written agreements or guarantors,
so collecting debts is also unreliable."
His mother, however, insisted.
Hé followed her instruction,
and for over twenty days,
he could not obtain a single cash;
only the actor Lǐ Sì,
who had previously received his father's kindness,
upon hearing his story,
righteously gave him one piece of gold.
Mother and son wept bitterly,
and from then on, lost all hope.
Huáng-nǚ was already at the age of marriage,
and when she heard that her father had broken off the engagement with Hé,
she secretly felt it was unjust.
Huáng wanted to marry his daughter to someone else.
The daughter wept and said:
"Liǔ Láng was not born poor.
If he were to become doubly rich in the future,
how could those who resent me take him away?
To abandon him now that he is poor,
is unbenevolent!"
Huáng was displeased,
and tried to persuade her with a hundred reasons.
But his daughter remained unmoved.
The old man and his wife were both enraged,
and cursed and spat at her day and night,
but the daughter bore it calmly.
Not long after,
they were robbed by bandits one night,
and Huáng and his wife were tortured and almost died,
their house swept clean.
Three years passed quickly,
and the family became even more impoverished.
A western merchant heard of the daughter's beauty,
and offered fifty taels of silver as a betrothal gift.
Huáng, tempted by the profit, agreed,
and intended to force her will.
The daughter, realizing his scheme,
ruined her clothes and smeared her face,
and fled that night.
She begged for food on the road,
and after two months,
finally reached Bǎodìng,
inquired about Hé's residence,
and arrived at his home.
Hé's mother thought she was a beggar woman,
and therefore rebuked her.
The daughter sobbed and explained herself.
The mother took her hand and wept, saying:
"My child, how have you come to this state!"
The daughter then sadly told her the reason.
Mother and son both wept.
She was then given a bath,
and her complexion became radiant,
her eyebrows and eyes shining.
Mother and son were both happy.
However, with three mouths in the family,
they barely had enough for one meal a day.
The mother wept, saying:
"My son and I are destined for this;
what I pity,
is that I have wronged my virtuous daughter-in-law!"
The daughter smiled and comforted her, saying:
"As a beggar, your daughter-in-law
is very familiar with that life,
and looking at it today,
I feel there is a difference between heaven and hell."
The mother was amused.
One day, the daughter entered an idle room,
and saw clumps of broken grass,
with no clear ground;
as she gradually went into the inner room,
dust had accumulated,
and in a dark corner, something was piled up,
which she kicked with her foot,
and picked up to see that they were all zhūtí.
Startled, she ran to tell Hé.
Hé went with her to inspect,
and found that the broken tiles and rubble that Gōng had thrown away in the past
had all turned into silver.
He then remembered that as a child, he often buried stones in the stone room,
could they all be gold?
But their old house had already been mortgaged to the Dōng family.
They quickly redeemed it.
The broken and missing bricks
revealed the stones they had hidden,
which was quite a disappointment;
but when they opened other bricks,
they were all sparkling white silver.
In an instant,
it amounted to several millions.
From then on, they redeemed land,
bought servants,
and their household became more splendid than before.
Hé then spurred himself on, saying:
"If I don't establish myself,
I will have failed my uncle Gōng!"
He devoted himself to his studies,
and in three years passed the xiāng examination.
He then personally took the silver
and went to repay Liú-ǎo.
His splendid clothes dazzled the eye;
more than ten servants,
all rode spirited horses like dragons.
The old woman only had one house,
and Hé simply sat on the couch.
People shouted and horses galloped,
filling the lanes and alleys.
Since his daughter's disappearance,
and the western merchant's demand for the return of the betrothal money,
Huáng's assets were almost halved,
and he had to sell his residence
to pay off the debt.
Thus, he was as impoverished as Hé had been in the past.
Hearing of his former son-in-law's prominence,
he merely closed his door and grieved.
The old woman bought wine and prepared a feast to entertain Hé,
and then spoke of the daughter's virtue,
and also regretted her flight.
She asked Hé:
"Are you married?"
Hé replied:
"I am."
After eating,
he urged the old woman to visit his new wife,
and took her home with him.
Upon arriving home,
the daughter, elegantly dressed, came out,
surrounded by maids like a celestial being.
They were greatly astonished to see each other,
and then recounted their past,
and solicitously inquired about her parents' well-being.
After staying for several days,
they were entertained with great kindness and generosity,
and given beautiful new clothes,
completely renewed,
before being sent back to their home.
The old woman went to Huáng Xǔ,
reported on his daughter's situation,
and conveyed their greetings.
The couple was greatly surprised.
The old woman advised them to go and seek their daughter,
but Huáng showed a reluctant expression.
However, as the cold and hunger became unbearable,
they had no choice but to go to Bǎodìng.
When they arrived at the gate,
they saw how grand and beautiful the entrance was.
The gatekeepers stared with angry eyes,
and they couldn't get through all day.
A woman came out,
and Huáng, with a gentle expression and humble words,
told her his name,
asking her to secretly inform his daughter.
A short while later,
the woman came out,
led them into a side chamber,
and said:
"My lady earnestly desires to see you;
however, she fears her husband might find out,
so she is still waiting for an opportunity.
When did you, sir, arrive here?
You must be hungry, aren't you?"
Huáng then recounted his sufferings.
The woman brought a jug of wine and two bowls of food,
and placed them before Huáng.
She also gifted five pieces of gold,
saying:
"My lady's husband is feasting in the room,
so my lady might not be able to come.
Tomorrow morning,
you should leave early,
lest the master hears of it."
Huáng agreed.
Early in the morning, as he hurried to pack,
the locks and keys had not yet been opened,
so he remained inside the gate,
sitting on his bag to wait.
Suddenly, the master, Hé, came out with a clamor.
Huáng was about to retreat and hide,
but Hé had already seen him,
and asked suspiciously who he was.
The family servants were all at a loss for words.
Hé angrily said:
"This must be a scoundrel!
Seize him and take him to the authorities!"
Everyone responded,
took out a short rope,
and tied him to a tree.
Huáng was ashamed and afraid, not knowing what to say.
Soon after,
the woman from last night came out,
knelt and said:
"This is my maternal uncle.
Since he arrived late last night,
I haven't yet informed the master."
Hé ordered him to be untied.
The woman escorted him out the gate,
saying:
"I forgot to instruct the gatekeepers,
which led to this misunderstanding.
My lady said: when you miss her,
you can have the old madam pretend to be a flower seller,
and come with Liú Āo."
Huáng agreed,
and returned to relate this to his wife.
His wife longed for her daughter like thirst,
so she told Liú Āo,
and Āo indeed accompanied her to Hé's house.
They opened over ten gates
before finally reaching their daughter's quarters.
The daughter wore a scarf and a topknot,
adorned with pearls, jade, silk, and fine white cloth,
exuding a fragrant scent that wafted over people;
with a soft exclamation,
all the small maids and old women
rushed to surround her.
They moved a golden armchair
and placed two armrests.
A clever maid offered tea;
they exchanged greetings in veiled words,
looking at each other with glistening tears.
In the evening,
a room was prepared to accommodate the two old women;
the bedding was warm,
something they had not experienced even during their prosperous years.
After staying for three or five days,
the daughter's kindness and generosity were profound.
The old woman would frequently lead her to a private place,
and tearfully confess her past wrongs.
The daughter said:
"What wrongs could there be between us mother and child that cannot be forgotten?
It's just that my husband's anger hasn't subsided,
and it's better if he doesn't hear of this."
Whenever Hé arrived,
she would run and hide.
One day,
as they were sitting knee-to-knee,
Hé suddenly entered,
saw them,
and angrily scolded:
"What kind of village old woman
dares to sit so close to my lady!
Her sideburns ought to be plucked clean off!"
Liú Āo quickly stepped forward and said:
"This old woman is my distant relative,
Wáng Sǎo, a flower seller.
Please don't punish her."
Hé then bowed and apologized.
He immediately sat down and said:
"You, old woman, have been here for several days,
and I've been very busy,
unable to properly chat.
Are those old animals of the Huáng family still alive?"
The old woman smiled and said:
"They are all well.
But they are too poor to get by.
You, sir, are so rich and noble,
why not show some regard for your father-in-law?"
Hé slammed the table and said:
"If it weren't for your compassion, old woman, in former years,
giving me a bowl of gruel,
how could I have returned to my homeland!
Now I wish to possess and sleep with her,
what sympathy is there to feel!"
Whenever he reached an angry point in his speech,
he would stomp his foot and start cursing.
The daughter angrily said:
"Even if he is unkind,
he is still my father.
I traveled a long, arduous distance,
my hands chapped and frostbitten,
the toes of my feet all worn through,
yet I still consider myself to have done nothing to wrong my husband.
Why do you curse my father in front of your child,
making it unbearable for me?"
Hé then restrained his anger
and stood up and left.
Huáng's wife was ashamed and pale with distress,
and asked to return home.
The daughter secretly gave her twenty pieces of gold.
After returning home,
all contact ceased,
and the daughter worried deeply about this.
Hé then sent someone to summon them.
The couple arrived,
ashamed and not knowing where to put themselves.
Hé apologized and said:
"Last year you honored us with your presence,
and I didn't make it clear,
thus causing a great deal of offense."
Huáng only uttered 'yes, yes.'
Hé changed their clothes and shoes for them.
After staying for over a month,
Huáng still felt uneasy,
and repeatedly asked to return home.
Hé presented them with one hundred taels of silver,
saying:
"The western merchant offered fifty taels,
and I am doubling it."
Huáng accepted it with a flushed face.
Hé sent them back in a carriage,
and that year, in their old age, they could be called somewhat prosperous.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"After Yōngmén wept,
the pearl-adorned shoes disappeared,
making people feel indignant and close their doors,
not wishing to entertain another guest.
However, a good friend's buried bones
turned stone into gold;
this cannot be said to be anything but the reward for generosity and hospitality.
The woman in the inner chambers enjoyed high status,
like a consort or concubine.
If not for a woman of integrity and exceptional character like Huáng Qīng,
who could be worthy of such a position without shame?
Thus, the Creator does not bestow blessings and fortune without reason."
In a certain village, there was a rich man.
He accumulated wealth to the brim,
calculating every penny with extreme frugality.
He hoarded hundreds of thousands of cash in his cellar,
fearing people would know,
so he wore worn-out rags and ate chaff and husks to feign poverty.
When relatives and friends occasionally came,
he never even prepared a chicken or millet meal.
If anyone suggested his family wasn't poor,
he would glare furiously,
hating them as an irreconcilable enemy.
In his later years,
he ate a liter of elm flour daily.
The skin on his arms hung in folds an inch long,
yet he refused to touch his hoarded wealth.
Later, he gradually became emaciated.
When he was on the verge of death,
his two sons gathered around him, asking,
but he still wouldn't tell them immediately.
When he realized he was indeed in critical danger,
he wanted to tell his sons.
When his sons arrived,
his tongue was already stiff and he couldn't speak,
only scratching at his chest
and muttering "hehe" (sound of distress).
After his death,
his descendants couldn't even afford a coffin,
so they buried him roughly.
Alas!
If hoarding gold makes one rich,
then why couldn't I claim the tens of millions in the imperial treasury
as my own?
How foolish!
(From a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* by Zhùxuězhāi)
Wáng Fénbīn said: In his village, there was a man who raised a mynah bird.
He taught it to speak,
and it was very intimate with him.
When he went out, he always took it with him,
and they had been together for several years.
One day,
as he was about to pass through Jiàngzhōu,
his travel funds were exhausted,
and the man was distraught and at a loss.
The bird said:
"Why don't you sell me?
Take me to the king's residence;
you'll get a good price,
and won't have to worry about funds for your return journey."
The man said:
"How can I bear to?"
The bird said:
"It's fine.
Once the master gets the money, hurry away
and wait for me twenty *lǐ* west of the city, under the big tree."
The man agreed.
He took the bird to the city.
As they conversed,
a crowd gradually gathered.
An eunuch saw them,
and reported it to the king.
The king summoned them,
wanting to buy the bird.
The man said:
"Your humble servant and the bird depend on each other for life;
I don't wish to sell it."
The king asked the bird:
"Do you wish to stay?"
It said:
"I wish to stay."
The king was pleased.
The bird then said:
"Give ten pieces of gold as the price;
don't give more."
The king was even more pleased,
and immediately gave ten pieces of gold.
The man pretended to be regretful and left.
The king spoke with the bird,
and its responses were quick and clever.
He called for meat to feed it.
After eating,
the bird said:
"Your servant wishes to bathe."
The king ordered a golden basin filled with water
and opened the cage for it to bathe.
After bathing,
it flew to the eaves,
preening its feathers,
still chattering incessantly with the king.
After a moment,
its feathers dry, it fluttered up
and, in a Jìn accent, said:
"Your servant is leaving!"
It glanced around and was gone.
The king and his attendants
looked up and sighed.
They urgently sought the man,
but he had already vanished.
Later, someone who traveled to Qínzhōng
saw the man with the bird in Xi'ān market.
(Recorded by Bì Zàijī Xiānshēng.)
(From a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* by Zhùxuězhāi)
Liú Hǎishí,
a native of Pútái,
sought refuge in Bīnzhōu during a time of chaos.
At fourteen years old,
he studied with Liú Cāngkè, a scholar from Bīnzhōu,
becoming good friends and
swearing brotherhood.
Not long after,
Hǎishí lost both parents,
and returned home with their coffins,
after which communication ceased.
Cāngkè's family was quite wealthy.
At forty,
he had two sons: the elder, Jí,
was seventeen years old
and a famous scholar in the district;
the younger son was also intelligent.
Cāngkè also took a woman from the Ní family in the district
as his concubine,
and favored her greatly.
Half a year later,
his elder son suffered a brain headache and died,
causing great sorrow to the couple.
Not long after,
his wife also died of illness;
a few months later,
his elder daughter-in-law also died;
and the deaths of servants and maids
followed one after another. Cāngkè's grief
was almost unbearable.
One day,
as he sat in sorrow,
the gatekeeper suddenly announced Hǎishí's arrival.
Cāngkè was delighted,
and rushed out to welcome him in.
Just as he was about to exchange pleasantries,
Hǎishí suddenly exclaimed:
"Brother, you are facing the calamity of your family's destruction,
do you not know?"
Cāngkè was stunned,
not understanding why.
Hǎishí said:
"It has been a long time since we heard from each other,
and I secretly suspected your recent situation might not be good."
Cāngkè sighed,
and then recounted his situation.
Hǎishí wept.
Then he smiled and said:
"The calamities are not yet over;
I initially came to offer my condolences to you, brother.
However, fortunately you met me,
so allow me to congratulate you."
Cāngkè said:
"We haven't met for a long time;
have you recently become proficient in the 'Yuè-rén art'
of healing?"
Hǎishí said:
"That is not my specialty.
I am quite skilled in the geomancy of dwellings."
Cāngkè was pleased,
and immediately asked him to examine his residence.
Hǎishí entered the house,
observing it thoroughly, inside and out.
After a while, he requested to see all the family members;
Cāngkè followed his instruction,
making his sons, daughters-in-law, maids, and concubines
all appear in the hall.
Cāngkè pointed them out one by one.
When he came to Ní,
Hǎishí looked up at the sky,
laughing uncontrollably.
While the crowd was still in startled disbelief,
they saw Miss Ní tremble, losing all color,
her body suddenly shrinking,
becoming barely two feet tall.
Hǎishí struck her head with a boundary-marker,
producing the sound of a stone jar.
Hǎishí pulled her hair,
inspecting the back of her head,
and found a few white hairs,
which he intended to pull out.
The woman shrank her neck, knelt, and wept,
saying she would leave immediately,
but begged him not to pull them out.
Hǎishí angrily said:
"Is your malicious heart not dead yet?"
He then pulled them out from the back of her neck.
The woman transformed immediately,
turning black like a civet cat.
Everyone was greatly alarmed.
Hǎishí picked her up and put her into his sleeve,
then looked at the son's wife and said:
"Daughter-in-law, you have been poisoned deeply;
there must be something unusual on your back,
please let me examine it."
The wife was shy
and unwilling to bare it.
Liú Zǐgù insisted,
and on her back, they saw white hair,
about four fingers long.
Hǎishí pricked it out with a needle,
saying:
"This hair is already old;
in seven days, it will be incurable."
He then looked at Liú Zǐ,
who also had hair,
only two fingers long.
He said:
"Like this, he can live for about a month before dying."
Cāngkè and his maids and servants
were all pricked by him.
He said:
"If I had not come just now,
your entire family would have been wiped out."
He asked:
"What kind of creature is this?"
He replied:
"It is also a fox-type creature.
It absorbs people's vital essence to gain spiritual power,
and is most keen on people's deaths."
Cāngkè said:
"It's been a long time since I saw you;
how can you be so supernaturally gifted!
Are you not an immortal?"
Hǎishí laughed and said:
"I merely learned a minor skill from my master,
how can I be called an immortal so quickly."
When asked about his master,
he replied:
"Shānshí Dàorén.
As for this creature,
I cannot kill it,
so I will return and present it as a captive to my master."
Having spoken,
he bid farewell.
Feeling his sleeve empty,
he exclaimed in alarm:
"I forgot it!
There was a large hair at the end of its tail that was not removed,
and now it has escaped."
Everyone was greatly astonished.
Hǎishí said:
"All its collar hairs have been removed,
so it cannot transform into a human;
it can only transform into a beast,
and its escape should not be far."
Thereupon, he entered the room to inspect his cat,
and went out the door to urge his dog,
but both indicated it was not there.
He opened the pigsty and laughed, saying:
"Here it is!"
Cāngkè looked and
saw an extra pig.
Hearing Hǎishí's laugh,
it immediately lay down,
not daring to move even slightly.
Hǎishí lifted it by the ear and pulled it out,
seeing a white hair on its tail,
hard as a needle.
Just as he was about to inspect and pull it out,
the pig twisted and turned, whimpering mournfully,
refusing to let him pull it.
Hǎishí said:
"You have committed so many wicked deeds,
yet you are unwilling to let me pull out one hair?"
He seized it and pulled it out,
and it immediately transformed back into a civet cat.
He put it into his sleeve, intending to leave.
Cāngkè earnestly detained him,
so he stayed for a meal.
When asked about their next meeting,
he said:
"That cannot be predetermined.
My master's vow is profound;
he often sends us out into the world
to rescue sentient beings,
so it's not impossible that we will meet again."
After they parted,
upon careful reflection on his name,
Cāngkè finally realized:
"Hǎishí is likely an immortal!
'Shānshí'
combines to form the character 'Yán',
which is the taboo name of Lǚ Xiān."
[According to the manuscript of Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio]
When Shí Mòhuá of Qīngzhōu, Minister of Personnel, was still a student,
outside the gate of his department was a large abyss,
which never dried up even without rain.
In the district, dozens of notorious bandits were captured
and executed by the abyss.
Their ghosts gathered and became malevolent spirits,
often dragging passersby into the abyss.
One day,
a certain Mǒu Jiǎ was in dire straits,
when he suddenly heard a group of ghosts flee in terror, saying:
"Minister Shí is coming!"
Soon after,
the duke arrived,
and Mǒu Jiǎ informed him of the situation.
The duke inscribed on the wall with white chalk, saying:
"Shí Mǒu hereby issues a prohibition: It is recognized that your thoughts were wicked,
leading to the wrath of thunder;
your schemes were rebellious,
thus you suffered execution by axe.
You should only turn back your devious hearts,
vying with each other to repent;
only then can you cleanse the blood from your skulls,
and escape this perdition.
Yet you, having suffered extreme punishment in life,
still gather evil in death.
Leaping and arriving,
disheveled and forming groups;
pacing back and forth,
beating your chests and causing harm.
With yellow mud stopping your ears,
you always unleash the ferocity of demon children;
acting as monsters in broad daylight,
almost blocking the path of travelers!
Outside the three-foot burial mound,
governance belongs to humans;
how can it be that within the vast universe,
you stubborn villains are allowed to act as you please?
Let it be known that from now on, each of you should hide your traces,
and not persist in evil.
The bones by the Wúdìng River
await reincarnation peacefully;
the souls in the golden boudoir dreams
shall yet return to their homeland.
If you repeat your former offenses,
you will surely suffer future regrets!"
From then on, the ghost affliction ceased,
and the abyss soon dried up.
[According to the manuscript of Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio]
Táng Jìwǔ, Grand Historian from my hometown,
when he was a few years old,
had a maternal cousin
with whom he played together in a temple.
The Grand Historian, even as a child, was open and straightforward,
and his courage was the greatest.
He saw a clay ghost in the corridor,
with bright, huge, glazed eyes;
he liked them,
and secretly used his finger to gouge one out,
hiding it and returning home.
Upon reaching home,
his cousin suddenly fell ill,
speechless for a long time.
Suddenly, he rose
and fiercely cried:
"Why did you dig out my eye!"
He continued to shout incessantly.
No one understood,
until the Grand Historian finally confessed what he had done.
His family then prayed, saying:
"The child was ignorant,
and playfully injured your esteemed eye;
we will return it immediately."
Then he loudly said:
"In that case,
I must go."
Having spoken,
he fell to the ground and died.
After a long time,
when asked what he had said,
he had no recollection at all.
So the eye was returned to the demon's eye socket.
Yìshǐshì said:
"To ascend the hall and demand an eye,
how efficacious that clay idol was!
But as for Grand Historian Gù (Gù Tàishǐ) picking out the eye,
why did he transfer his anger to his companion?
It is probably because of his noble status,
and moreover his upright nature;
considering how he presented memorials to the Northern Gate (Běiquè),
and brushed his sleeves at the Southern Mountain (Nánshān),
even the gods feared him,
let alone ghosts!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
The ancestor of Mr. Wáng Chūnjì
was very good friends with his uncle, Lord Zǔ Yùtián (Zǔ Yùtián Gōng).
One night,
he dreamt that Lord Zǔ came to his house,
and they spoke sadly.
He asked:
"Whence do you come?"
He replied:
"I am about to depart for a long time,
so I came to bid you farewell."
He asked:
"Whither do you go?"
He replied:
"Far away."
Then he left.
He escorted him to a valley,
where he saw a crack in a stone wall,
so he cupped his hands in farewell,
turned his back to the crack,
hesitated, and walked backward into it.
He called out but received no reply,
and thus awoke with a start.
When dawn came,
he told Grandfather Jìngyī (Tàigōng Jìngyī),
and had him prepare the funerary rites,
saying:
"Lord Zǔ Yùtián (Zǔ Yùtián Gōng) has passed away!"
Grandfather Jìngyī (Tàigōng Jìngyī) requested to investigate first,
and if it were true,
then proceed.
But he did not listen,
and simply went in mourning clothes.
When he arrived at the gate,
the white mourning banners were already hung.
Alas!
The ancients, concerning their friends,
trusted each other in life and death to such an extent;
that a funeral carriage would wait for a high official to depart,
how could that be false!
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The servant of Hán Guānglù Dàqiān,
sleeping in the inner chambers at night,
saw a light upstairs,
like a bright star.
Not long after,
it flickered and fell,
and upon reaching the ground, transformed into a dog.
He glanced at it,
and it turned and went behind the residence.
He quickly got up,
secretly followed it,
and as it entered the garden,
it transformed into a woman.
He knew in his heart it was a fox,
and returned to his original sleeping place.
Presently,
the woman came from behind,
and the servant feigned sleep to observe her actions.
The woman bent down and shook him.
The servant pretended to wake up,
and asked who she was.
The woman did not answer.
The servant said:
"The light upstairs,
was that not you?"
The woman said:
"Since you already know,
why ask?"
Thereupon they slept together.
They separated by day and met at night,
which became their custom.
When the master learned of it,
he ordered two men to sleep on either side of the servant;
when the two men woke up,
they were lying under the bed,
not knowing when they had fallen.
The master grew angrier,
and said to the servant:
"When she comes,
you must catch her;
otherwise,
there will be a whipping!"
The servant dared not speak,
assented, and withdrew.
He thought: catching her would be difficult;
not catching her,
he feared punishment.
He tossed and turned, without a plan.
Suddenly he recalled that the woman had a small red blouse,
clinging tightly to her body,
which she was unwilling to take off even for a moment,
it must be her vital point;
holding this, he could threaten her.
In the middle of the night,
the woman arrived,
and asked:
"Did your master instruct you to catch me?"
He replied:
"Indeed so.
But we two have such affection,
how could I do such a thing?"
When they lay down,
he secretly grasped her blouse.
The woman cried out in alarm,
struggled free, and left.
From then on, they were separated.
Later, when the servant returned from another place,
he saw the woman sitting by the roadside from afar;
when he approached,
she covered her face with her sleeve.
The servant dismounted,
and called out:
"Why do you act like this?"
The woman then rose,
clasped his hand, and said:
"I thought you had forgotten our old affection.
Since you still have the feelings of an old friend,
our relationship can still be forgiven.
The previous matter was due to your master's command,
and I do not blame you for it.
But our fate together is exhausted;
today I have prepared a small feast,
to bid you farewell."
It was early autumn,
and the sorghum was in full bloom.
The woman led him and entered,
and there was a grand mansion within.
He tethered his horse and went in;
in the hall, wine and dishes were already laid out.
As soon as they sat down,
a group of maids served roasted meat.
As evening approached,
the servant had duties,
wishing to report back to his master,
so he bid farewell.
When he exited,
it was merely fields and ridges again.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Shì Tǐkōng said:
"In Qīngzhōu,
I saw two foreign monks,
with ancient and peculiar appearances;
with double rings in their ears,
clad in yellow cloth,
their beards and hair curly.
They claimed to have come from the Western Regions (Xīyù).
Hearing that the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) revered Buddha,
they sought an audience with him.
The Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) sent two attendants
to escort them to the monastery.
The abbot Língzì
did not treat them with much courtesy.
Those in charge of affairs, seeing that the men were unusual,
privately entertained them,
and they stayed there.
Someone asked: 'The Western Regions (Xīyù) have many extraordinary people,
do the Arhats not possess miraculous techniques?'
One of them smiled broadly,
reached into his sleeve,
and in his palm held a small pagoda,
barely a foot high,
exquisite and lovely.
On the highest part of the wall,
there was a small niche,
and the monk tossed the pagoda into it,
where it stood upright and steady,
without the slightest lean.
One could see relics emitting light from the pagoda,
illuminating the entire room.
After a while,
he beckoned with his hand,
and it returned to his palm.
The other monk then bared his arm,
extended his left arm,
which grew to about six or seven feet long,
while his right arm shrank until it was gone;
then he extended his right arm,
which also became like the left."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Liú Dòngjiǔ of Láiwú,
served as an official in Fénzhōu.
As he sat alone in his yámen,
he heard laughter and chatter from outside the pavilion gradually approaching.
They entered the room,
and there were four women: one about forty,
one perhaps thirty,
one around twenty-four or five,
and the last one a young girl with her hair in a bob.
They all stood before the table,
looking at each other and smiling.
Liú already knew that his yámen had many foxes,
so he ignored them.
After a short while,
the young girl with the bobbed hair took out a red kerchief
and playfully tossed it onto his face.
Liú picked it up and threw it onto the window sill,
still ignoring them.
The four women smiled and left.
One day,
the eldest woman came
and said to Liú,
“My younger sister has a fated connection with you.
I hope you will not despise her as mere wild radish.”
Liú casually agreed.
The woman then departed.
Soon, she returned with a maidservant,
escorting the young girl with the bobbed hair,
and made her sit shoulder to shoulder with Liú.
She said,
“What a perfect pair!
Tonight, you shall have your wedding candles.
Serve Lord Liú diligently,
I shall leave now.”
Liú looked closely at her;
she was incomparably radiant and beautiful.
So, he engaged in intimacy with her.
When he questioned her about her origins,
the woman said,
“I am indeed not human,
yet I am truly human.
I am
the daughter of the former official,
bewitched by foxes,
I died suddenly
and was buried in the garden.
The foxes used their magic to bring me back to life,
and so I float about like a fox.”
Liú then reached out his hand to feel her buttocks.
The woman sensed it
and smiled, saying,
“Are you suggesting that foxes have tails?”
She turned around and said,
“Please, try and feel.”
From then on,
she stayed and did not leave.
Wherever she went or sat,
she was always with her little maidservant.
The household members all treated her with the respect due to a young mistress.
Maids and old women came to pay their respects and were given generous rewards.
When Liú’s birthday arrived,
there were many guests,
totaling over thirty tables,
requiring many cooks.
Orders were sent out in advance to summon them,
but only one or two arrived.
Liú was greatly annoyed.
The woman knew of this
and promptly said,
“Do not worry.
Since the cooks are insufficient,
it would be better to dismiss even those who came.
I may be lacking in talent,
but managing thirty tables is not difficult.”
Liú was delighted
and ordered that fish, meat, ginger, and cinnamon
all be moved to the inner chambers.
The household members only heard the sound of chopping and mincing,
ceaselessly intricate.
A table was set up at the inner door,
and the person serving roasts placed them upon it;
when they looked again,
the dishes and platters were already full.
They went and returned,
more than ten people,
forming a continuous line on the path,
and the supply was inexhaustible.
Finally,
the roast-server came to ask for noodles in soup.
A voice from inside said,
“The master did not give prior instructions;
how can it be prepared so quickly?”
Then it said,
“If there’s no other way,
let’s borrow some.”
After a moment,
it called for the noodles in soup.
When they looked,
there were over thirty bowls,
steaming on the table.
After the guests had left,
she said to Liú,
“You can take out some money
to pay for the noodles from a certain family.”
Liú sent someone to take the money.
Meanwhile, that family had lost their noodles
and were all astonished;
when the messenger arrived,
their confusion was finally resolved.
One evening,
while drinking at night,
Liú happened to think of the bitter wine from Shāndōng.
The woman offered to fetch it.
She then went out the door,
and after some time returned, saying,
“There is a jar outside the door
that can provide drinks for several days.”
Liú looked,
and indeed, he got wine,
which was truly the “spring wine from the jar” from his home.
Several days later,
his wife sent two servants to Fénzhōu.
On the way, one servant said,
“I heard that Mrs. Hú gives generous rewards.
When we get there and receive the gold,
we can buy a fur coat.”
The woman in the yámen already knew this
and said to Liú,
“People from home are coming.
It’s hateful how disrespectful these boorish slaves are.
I must teach them a lesson.”
The next day,
as soon as the servant entered the city,
he got a severe headache.
When he reached the yámen,
he clutched his head and cried out.
Everyone suggested giving him medicine.
Liú smiled and said,
“No need for treatment;
when the time comes, it will heal by itself.”
Everyone suspected he had offended the young mistress.
The servant thought to himself: I just arrived and haven’t even unpacked;
how could I have committed an offense?
With no one to complain to,
he merely crawled on his knees and pleaded mournfully.
A voice from behind the curtain said,
“You called me ‘Madam,’
and that would have been fine,
but why did you call me ‘fox’?”
The servant then understood
and kowtowed repeatedly.
The voice then said,
“Since you wanted a fur coat,
how could you be so disrespectful again?”
Then it said,
“You are healed now.”
As soon as it spoke,
the servant’s illness vanished as if by magic.
The servant bowed, intending to leave,
when suddenly a bundle was thrown out from behind the curtain,
saying,
“This is a lambskin coat;
you may take it.”
The servant unwrapped it and looked,
and found five gold pieces.
Liú asked about the news from home,
and the servant said: Everything is fine,
except that a jar of stored wine was lost one night.
Checking the dates,
it was exactly the night the wine was taken.
Everyone feared her divine power
and called her
“Sacred Immortal.”
Liú had a small portrait painted of her.
At that time, Zhāng Dàoyī 張道一 was the Tíxué Shǐ 提學使.
Hearing of her unusual nature,
he went to Liú 劉 on account of their shared hometown affinity,
wishing to beg for a meeting.
The woman refused him.
Liú 劉 showed him her portrait.
Zhāng 張 forcefully took it away.
He returned and hung it by his seat,
praying to it morning and night, saying:
"With your beautiful looks,
what place is impossible for you?
Yet you entrust yourself to that old man!
This humble official is certainly no worse than Dòng Jiǔ 洞九,
why not favor me with a visit?"
The woman, at the yámen 衙門,
suddenly said to Liú 劉:
"Zhāng Gōng 張公 is impolite,
he should be slightly punished."
One day,
as Zhāng 張 was praying,
it seemed as if someone struck his forehead with a ruler,
with a sudden loud sound and intense pain.
Greatly frightened,
he rolled up the scroll and put it away.
Liú 劉 questioned him about it,
but he concealed the reason and gave a deceptive answer.
Liú 劉 smiled and said:
"Is the master's forehead not aching?"
He could not deceive,
and told the truth.
Soon after,
her son-in-law Qí Shēng 亓生 came,
requesting to meet her.
The woman firmly declined.
Qí 亓 insisted on seeing her.
Liú 劉 said:
"The son-in-law is not an outsider,
why such a deep refusal?"
The woman said:
"When the son-in-law meets me,
I must certainly have something to give him.
His expectations of me are extravagant,
and I estimate that I cannot fulfill his wishes,
so I simply did not want to see him.
Since he insists,
I will allow him to meet me in ten days."
When the time came,
Qí 亓 entered,
bowed to her from behind a curtain,
and briefly expressed his greetings.
Her appearance was indistinct,
he dared not scrutinize it;
after he retired,
a few steps away,
he would constantly turn his head and gaze.
He only heard the woman say:
"My son-in-law is turning his head again!"
After she spoke,
she laughed heartily,
fiercely like a clanging bell.
Hearing this, Qí 亓's
legs and thighs all went soft,
he swayed as if he had lost his soul.
After he went out,
he sat for some time
before he gradually recovered.
He then said:
"Just now I heard a laugh,
like listening to a clap of thunder,
I didn't even feel my body was my own."
A little while later,
a maid, on the woman's orders,
gifted Qí 亓 twenty gold pieces.
Qí 亓 accepted them,
and said to the maid:
"The holy immortal lives with my father-in-law daily,
surely she knows my usual lavish nature,
and that I'm not accustomed to using small amounts of money?"
Hearing this, the woman said:
"I certainly knew that.
My purse is just empty;
previously, I traveled with companions to Biànliáng 汴梁,
its city was occupied by Hé Bó 河伯,
all the treasuries were submerged in the water.
Everyone who entered the water only got a little,
how can it satisfy insatiable demands?
Moreover, even if I could give generously,
his meager fortune would not be able to bear it."
The woman could foresee everything,
when there was doubt or difficulty,
consulting her,
everything would be resolved.
One day,
as they sat together,
she suddenly looked up at the sky and exclaimed in great surprise:
"A great calamity is approaching,
what is to be done!"
Liú 劉 anxiously asked about his family members,
she said:
"All others are safe,
only your two sons are concerning.
This place will soon become a battlefield,
you should seek a distant assignment,
so as to avoid the disaster."
Liú 劉 followed her advice,
begged his superiors,
and obtained an assignment to escort provisions between Yúnnán 雲南 and Guìzhōu 貴州.
The journey was long and distant,
those who heard it grieved for him,
but the woman alone congratulated him.
Soon after,
Jiāng 姜 rebelled,
and Fénzhōu 汾州 fell and became a den of thieves.
Liú 劉's second son came from Shāndōng 山東,
happened to encounter the upheaval,
and was subsequently killed.
When the city fell,
all officials suffered in the calamity,
only Liú 劉 was spared by being on official duty away from the city.
After the bandits were quelled,
Liú 劉 finally returned.
Soon after, he was dismissed due to a major case,
so poor that he could not afford daily meals;
and those in power made many demands,
thus he was distressed and worried to death.
The woman said:
"Don't worry,
there are three thousand pieces of gold under the bed,
which can be used for expenses."
Liú 劉 was greatly pleased,
and asked:
"Where did you steal it from?"
She said:
"Things in the world that have no owner
are inexhaustible,
why would I need to steal?"
Liú 劉 managed to escape and return home through clever means,
and the woman followed him.
A few years later, she suddenly left,
leaving a few items wrapped in paper as gifts,
among which was a small object hung on the gate of a mourning household,
about two inches long,
which everyone considered inauspicious.
Liú 劉 soon died.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* 聊齋誌異.
Yuè Yúnhè 樂雲鶴 and Xià Píngzǐ 夏平子
were fellow villagers in their youth,
and shared a study in adulthood,
their friendship was inseparable.
Xià 夏 was intelligent from a young age,
renowned at ten years old.
Yuè 樂 humbly served him,
and Xià 夏 also tirelessly advised him,
Yuè 樂's literary thoughts progressed daily,
thus their names became equally prominent.
However, they struggled in the examinations,
failing every attempt.
Not long after,
Xià 夏 contracted an epidemic and died,
his family was poor and could not afford a burial,
Yuè 樂 courageously took it upon himself.
He left behind an infant son and a widow,
Yuè 樂 provided for their family regularly;
whenever he obtained even a small amount,
he would divide it in half,
and Xià 夏's wife and child survived because of this.
Thus, the literati and officials admired Yuè 樂 even more.
Yuè 樂 did not have much property,
and also worried about Xià Shēng's 夏生 family,
his family finances deteriorated daily.
He then sighed, saying:
"A man of literature like Píngzǐ 平子
still died obscurely,
how much more so me!
One must seize wealth and honor in life while there's time,
being anxious all year round,
I fear I'll fill a ditch before even dogs and horses,
having lived this life in vain.
It's better to plan early for myself."
Thereupon, he stopped studying and became a merchant.
After half a year in business,
his family wealth became moderately prosperous.
One day,
Lè (樂) was traveling to Jīnlíng (金陵),
and rested at an inn.
He saw a tall, slender man,
with prominent muscles and bones,
sitting idly nearby.
His complexion was dark and dull,
and he wore a sorrowful expression.
Lè (樂) asked:
"Do you want something to eat?"
The man did not speak either.
Lè (樂) offered him food;
he scooped it up with his hands,
and in an instant it was all gone.
Lè (樂) then added a portion for two.
The food was again finished.
So he ordered the host to carve a pork shoulder,
and piled it with steamed buns;
he consumed the meals of several people,
before finally feeling full and saying with gratitude:
"In the past three years,
I have never been so completely sated."
Lè (樂) said:
"You are indeed a strong man,
why are you so adrift?"
He replied:
"I have committed a sin that incurred a heavenly punishment,
it cannot be spoken of."
Lè (樂) asked about his dwelling place,
he replied:
"On land I have no house,
on water I have no boat;
I am in a village in the morning and a city in the evening."
Lè (樂) prepared to depart,
and the man followed him,
reluctant to leave.
Lè (樂) bade him farewell.
The man said:
"You will encounter a great calamity,
I cannot bear to forget the kindness of a single meal."
Lè (樂) found this strange,
and so he allowed him to travel together.
Along the way, he invited him to share meals.
The man declined, saying:
"I only eat a few meals in a whole year."
Lè (樂) found this even stranger.
The next day,
as they crossed the river,
a violent storm arose,
and all the merchant boats capsized.
Lè (樂) and the man were both swallowed by the river.
Soon, the wind subsided,
the man carried Lè (樂) and stepped out onto the waves,
boarded a passenger boat,
and then broke through the waves and left;
after a short while,
he pulled a boat to them,
helped Lè (樂) into it,
instructed Lè (樂) to lie down and guard it,
then leaped back into the river,
emerging with goods clutched in both arms,
which he threw into the boat;
he went in again: several times he entered and exited,
filling the boat with goods.
Lè (樂) thanked him, saying:
"It is enough that you saved my life;
how could I dare to hope for the return of my valuables?"
Upon inspecting his belongings,
he found nothing was lost.
He was even more delighted,
and took him for a divine being.
They set sail, preparing to depart;
the man announced his leave,
but Lè (樂) earnestly urged him to stay,
so they continued their journey together.
Lè (樂) said with a laugh:
"In this calamity,
I only lost a golden hairpin."
The man wanted to search for it again.
Just as Lè (樂) was about to dissuade him,
he had already plunged into the water and disappeared.
Lè (樂) was astonished for a long time.
Suddenly, the man emerged with a smile,
and handed the hairpin to Lè (樂), saying:
"Fortunately, I did not fail in my mission."
Everyone on the river was shocked and amazed.
Lè (樂) took him home,
and they shared living quarters.
He would only eat once every ten-odd days,
but when he ate, he consumed countless amounts.
One day,
the man again spoke of leaving,
but Lè (樂) firmly urged him to stay.
It happened to be a dark day, threatening rain,
and thunder was heard.
Lè (樂) said:
"I wonder what it's like among the clouds?
And what is thunder?
If only I could go up to the heavens to see,
then this doubt could be resolved."
The man smiled and said:
"Do you wish to journey through the clouds?"
After a short while,
Lè (樂) felt very tired,
and lay down on the couch to doze.
When he awoke,
he felt his body swaying,
not like being on a couch;
he opened his eyes,
and found himself in a misty cloud,
his whole body felt like floss.
He was startled and stood up,
feeling dizzy as if on a boat.
He stepped,
but there was no ground.
He looked up at the stars,
which seemed to be between his eyebrows.
He then suspected it was a dream.
He looked closely at the stars in the sky,
like old lotus seeds in a pod,
the large ones like jars,
the next size like small jars,
and the small ones like bowls.
He tried to shake them with his hand,
the large ones were firm and unmovable;
the small stars swayed,
as if they could be plucked down.
So he plucked one,
and hid it in his sleeve.
He pushed aside the clouds and looked down,
the vast silver sea spread out,
and he saw cities and towns like beans.
He thought in dismay: if I were to slip,
how could this body ever be found again?
Suddenly, he saw two dragons writhing,
pulling a plain chariot.
One flick of their tail,
sounded like the crack of a cowherd's whip.
On the chariot was a vessel,
several *zhàng* (丈) in circumference,
filled with water.
There were dozens of people,
scooping water with utensils,
and sprinkling it all over the clouds.
Suddenly they saw Lè (樂),
and were all surprised.
Lè (樂) ascertained that the strong man he was with was among them,
and he said to the crowd:
"This is my friend."
Then he took a vessel,
and handed it to Lè (樂), telling him to sprinkle.
At that time there was a severe drought,
Lè (樂) took the vessel, pushed aside the clouds,
looked towards his hometown,
and poured out the water with all his might.
Not long after,
the man said to Lè (樂):
"I was originally a Thunder Official.
Previously, I made a mistake in bringing rain,
and was banished for three years;
now my heavenly term is complete,
please let us part ways here."
Then he threw a ten-thousand-foot rope from the chariot forward,
and bade Lè (樂) grasp the end and descend.
Lè (樂) found this dangerous.
The man smiled and said:
"No worries."
Lè (樂) did as he was told,
and in an instant reached the ground.
He looked,
and found himself standing outside the village;
the rope gradually retracted into the clouds,
and became invisible.
At that time, there had been a long drought,
and for ten *lǐ* (里) around,
the rain was only finger-deep,
but in Lè (樂)'s village, all the ditches and channels were full.
He returned and searched his sleeve,
the plucked star was still there.
He took it out and placed it on the table,
it was dark and dull like a stone; at night,
it shone with brilliant light,
illuminating all four walls.
He valued it even more,
and stored it carefully, wrapped many times.
Whenever there were esteemed guests,
he would bring it out to illuminate their drinks.
If one looked directly at it,
rays of light would pierce the eyes.
One night,
his wife sat opposite him, holding her hair,
when she suddenly saw the starlight gradually diminish like a firefly,
and move horizontally.
Just as his wife exclaimed in surprise,
it had already entered her mouth,
she tried to cough it out but could not,
and it was ultimately swallowed.
Startled, she ran to tell Lè (樂),
Lè (樂) also found it strange.
After they went to bed,
In a dream, Xià Píngzǐ [夏平子] came,
saying,
"I am the star Shàowēi [少微].
Your kindness and affection
I have not forgotten.
Moreover, I was brought back by you from the heavens,
which can be called fate.
Now I shall be your son
to repay your great virtue."
Lè [樂] was thirty and childless,
and was very happy to have this dream.
From then on,
his wife indeed conceived;
and when she gave birth,
light filled the room,
just as when the star was on the table.
Therefore, he named
him "Xīng'ér" [星兒] (Little Star).
He was exceptionally sharp and intelligent.
At sixteen,
he passed the imperial examination and attained the *jìnshì* degree.
Yìshǐshì [異史氏] remarks:
"Master Lè's [樂] writings were renowned throughout his generation,
but he suddenly realized that the position the heavens assigned him was not this.
So he cast aside his writing brush as if shaking off a hindrance.
How is this different
from those who, with swallow necks, cast aside their brushes?
As for Léicáo [雷曹] being moved by the kindness of a single meal,
and Shàowēi [少微] repaying the understanding of a good friend,
how can this be merely the private reciprocation of divine beings for favors?
Rather, it is the impartial reward of the Creator for the worthy and heroic."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* [聊齋誌異]
Hán Dàoshì [韓道士]
lived in the Tiānqí Miào [天齊廟] in the county seat.
He possessed many magical arts,
and everyone called him
"Immortal."
My late father was very close to him;
whenever he went to the city,
he would always visit him.
One day,
he and my late uncle went to the county seat,
intending to visit Hán [韓],
and happened to meet him on the road.
Hán [韓] handed over a key and said,
"Please go ahead, open the gate, and sit down.
I will be there shortly."
They did as he said.
Upon reaching the temple and unlocking the gate,
Hán [韓] was already sitting inside the room.
There were many such incidents.
Before this,
a relative of our family was fond of gambling,
and through Guāngzǐ [光子] also knew Hán [韓].
A monk arrived at the Dàfó Sì [大佛寺],
specializing in [gambling],
and gambled with great daring.
The relative saw him and was pleased,
gambled away all his money,
and suffered great losses;
his heart grew even more ardent,
he mortgaged his property and went again,
losing everything throughout the night.
Dejected and unsuccessful,
he went directly to Hán [韓],
his spirits miserable,
his speech disordered.
Hán [韓] asked him,
and he told him the whole truth.
Hán [韓] smiled and said,
"In constant gambling, there is no way not to lose.
If you can give up gambling,
I will recover your losses for you."
The relative said,
"If I can recover my pearls like in Hépǔ [合浦],
I will grind my flower-bones into an iron pestle!"
Hán [韓] then wrote a talisman on paper,
and gave it to him to wear tucked in his belt.
He instructed,
"Just recover your original possessions and stop;
do not be greedy for more, like looking to Shǔ [蜀] after gaining Lǒng [隴]."
He also gave him a thousand coins,
agreeing that he would repay them after winning.
The relative was overjoyed and left.
The monk examined his funds,
changed them,
and disdained to gamble with him.
The relative insisted,
asking for just one throw as the agreement.
The monk smiled and agreed.
So he staked the thousand coins as an all-in bet.
The monk threw without gain or loss.
The relative received the dice,
and with one throw, achieved a winning combination;
the monk again staked two thousand,
and again lost;
gradually increasing to over ten thousand,
the dice clearly showed a disadvantageous combination,
but with a breath,
they all turned into *lúzì* [盧雉] (winning combination): in an instant, he recovered
all his previous losses.
Secretly thinking it would be even better to win a few thousand more,
he gambled again,
but the dice combinations gradually became worse;
he found this strange,
stood up and looked at his belt,
and the talisman was already gone.
He was greatly alarmed and stopped.
He carried the money back to the temple.
After repaying Hán [韓],
he calculated,
and including what he had lost at the very end,
it exactly matched the original amount.
He then apologized shamefully for losing the talisman.
Hán [韓] smiled and said,
"It is already here.
I specifically told you not to be greedy,
but you did not listen,
so I took it back."
Yìshǐshì [異史氏] remarks:
"Of all things that ruin families in the world,
none is faster than gambling;
of all things that corrupt virtue in the world,
none is worse than gambling.
Those who enter it
are like sinking into the sea,
and will not know where it ends.
Merchants and farmers
all have their main occupations;
scholars of poetry and books
especially cherish every moment.
Carrying a plow or holding classics
is indeed the proper way to establish a family;
pure conversation and light drinking
are still ways to find joy in life.
But you associate with depraved companions,
entangling yourselves throughout the long night.
Emptying bags and overturning boxes,
hanging gold from the sky;
shouting 'zhì' [雉] and calling 'lú' [盧],
begging for spiritual aid from the bones of depravity and darkness.
Rolling the five pieces of wood [dice],
like rolling round pearls;
holding many 'chapters' [dice in hand],
like holding a round fan.
Looking left at others and right at oneself,
staring through the eyes of demons;
feigning weakness overtly while using strength covertly,
exhausting all the tricks of goblins.
Guests wait at the door,
yet still lingering at the gambling table;
smoke rises from the house,
yet still gazing greedily at the dice bowl.
Forgetting meals and neglecting sleep,
thus deeply immersed and confused;
tongues worn out and lips parched,
thus looking at each other like ghosts.
"When the entire army is annihilated,
and eager eyes stare into emptiness.
Looking at the gambling table, shouts are loud,
the hearts of heroes itch for action;
but looking into the money pouch, it is empty,
chilling the hearts of strong men.
Stretching necks and pacing,
realizing the futility of empty hands;
hanging heads in desolation,
finally returning home in the dark night.
Fortunately, those who are scorned are asleep,
fearing to startle barking dogs;
suffering from long-empty hungry stomachs,
how dare they complain about leftover soup?
Then selling children and mortgaging fields,
hoping for pearls to return to Hépǔ [合浦]: unexpectedly, the fire burns all the fur,
ultimately scooping the moon from the vast river.
Only after suffering defeat do I reflect,
having already become a base person;
if one asks who is best at gambling,
everyone points to the pants-less gentlemen.
Even more, when hunger becomes unbearable,
then taking refuge with violent thugs;
scratching heads unable to devise a plan,
even relying on women's cosmetic boxes. Alas!
Corrupted in virtue and lost in conduct,
ruined in property and perished in body,
which of these is not caused by the path of gambling!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* [聊齋誌異]
Wéndēng Jǐngshēng
had a great reputation from a young age.
He lived as a neighbor to Chénshēng,
separated by a low wall.
One day,
Chén Mù passed a desolate ruin
and heard a girl weeping among the pine and cypress trees;
approaching,
he saw a tree with a horizontal branch and a hanging sash,
as if someone were about to hang herself.
Chén questioned her,
and she, wiping her tears, replied:
"My mother went far away,
entrusting me to my maternal cousin.
I didn't expect that wolf-hearted scoundrel
would not keep me to the end.
So desolate am I,
it's better to die!"
Having spoken,
she wept again.
Chén untied his sash
and advised her to marry someone.
The girl worried she had no one to rely on.
Chén invited her to stay at his home temporarily,
and the girl agreed.
When they returned,
he lit a lamp and scrutinized her,
finding her beauty exceptional.
Greatly pleased,
he wanted to have his way with her.
The girl loudly resisted,
and the commotion
reached the neighboring room.
Jǐngshēng scaled the wall to peek,
and Chén then released the girl.
The girl saw Jǐngshēng,
gazed at him intently,
and after a long moment, ran away.
The two men chased her together,
but didn't know where she went.
Jǐngshēng returned home,
closed his door, intending to sleep,
when the girl gracefully emerged from his room.
Startled, he asked her,
and she replied:
"He has shallow virtue and meager fortune,
I cannot rely on him permanently."
Jǐngshēng was overjoyed
and asked her name.
She said:
"My ancestors lived in Qí.
My family name is Qí,
and my given name is Āxiá."
He spoke playfully to her,
and she smiled, not resisting much,
so they slept together.
Many friends visited his study,
and the girl always stayed hidden in the deep room.
After several days,
she said:
"I must leave for a while.
This place is too busy
and bothersome.
From now on,
please let us meet only at night."
He asked:
"Where is your home?"
She replied:
"It's not far at all."
So she left early.
At night, she indeed returned,
and their love was very devoted.
After a few more days,
she said to Jǐngshēng:
"Although our affection is strong,
it is ultimately an illicit union.
My father is an official serving in the Western Regions,
and tomorrow I will go with my mother.
I will take the opportunity to seek permission
so that we can be together forever."
He asked:
"How many days will you be gone?"
She promised to return in ten days.
After she left,
Jǐngshēng thought that living in the study could not be permanent;
if he moved her inside,
he feared his wife's jealousy.
He decided it would be better to divorce his wife.
Once his mind was made up,
he would scold and curse his wife whenever she approached.
His wife, unable to bear the humiliation,
wept and wished for death.
Jǐngshēng said:
"Your death might cause me trouble,
please go home early."
Thus he urged his wife to leave.
His wife cried and said:
"I have followed you for ten years,
and have never had a moral failing,
why are you so utterly resolute?"
Jǐngshēng did not listen,
and pressed her more urgently.
His wife then left the house.
From then on, he whitewashed the walls and swept away the dust,
eagerly anticipating her return;
but unexpectedly, there was no news from the blue luan,
like a stone dropped into the sea.
After his wife returned to her parents' home,
she repeatedly asked mutual acquaintances
to plead with Jǐngshēng for her return,
but Jǐngshēng refused;
she then married into the Xiàhóu family.
The Xiàhóu family lived in a village adjacent to Jǐngshēng's,
and because of their shared field boundaries,
they had been enemies for generations.
When Jǐngshēng heard this,
he became even more enraged and resentful.
Yet he still hoped Āxiá would return,
which would be some comfort.
Over a year passed,
and there was no trace of her.
At the birthday celebration of the Sea God,
men and women gathered like clouds inside and outside the temple,
and Jǐngshēng was also there.
He saw from a distance a woman
who greatly resembled Āxiá.
Jǐngshēng approached her,
she entered the crowd;
he followed her,
she exited the gate;
he followed her again,
and she floated away.
Jǐngshēng chased but could not catch her,
regretting his slowness, he returned.
Half a year later,
he happened to be walking on the road
when he saw a young lady
dressed in crimson,
accompanied by a servant,
and a dark guard.
Looking at her,
it was Āxiá.
He then asked her attendant:
"Who is that young lady?"
The attendant replied:
"She is the second wife of Master Zhèng of Náncūn."
He asked again:
"How long ago was she married?"
The attendant said:
"Only half a month."
Jǐngshēng thought,
could it be a mistake?
The young lady heard the words,
turned her gaze,
and Jǐngshēng saw
it was truly Āxiá.
Seeing that she had married into another family,
anger filled his chest,
and he cried out:
"Xiániáng!
How could you forget our old promise?"
The attendants heard him call their mistress,
and wanted to raise their fists.
The lady quickly stopped them.
She parted the carriage curtain and said to Jǐngshēng:
"How dare a faithless man show his face to me?"
Jǐngshēng said:
"You betrayed me,
how have I ever betrayed you?"
The lady said:
"Betraying your wife is worse than betraying me!
If you treat your wedded wife like that,
how much more so others?
Previously, because of your profound ancestral virtue,
your name was listed among the successful candidates,
which is why I entrusted myself to you;
now, because you abandoned your wife,
your official rank has been removed in the underworld.
Wáng Chāng, the second-place finisher in this examination,
is the one who took your name.
I have already returned to Lord Zhèng,
so there is no need for you to remember me again."
Jǐngshēng bowed his head submissively,
unable to utter a single word.
He watched the woman
spur her donkey and depart like flying,
left only with regret.
In that imperial examination,
Jǐng failed.
The second-place candidate was indeed Wáng Shìchāng.
Zhèng also passed with distinction.
Because of this, Jǐng acquired a minor reputation.
At forty, he had no spouse,
and his family's fortunes declined further.
He constantly sought food from relatives and friends.
One day, he visited Zhèng.
Zhèng treated him kindly
and kept him overnight.
Zhèng's daughter peeked at the guest,
saw him, and pitied him.
She asked Zhèng,
"The guest in the hall,
is he not Jǐng Qìngyún?"
When asked how she knew him,
she replied,
"Before I was married to you,
I once took refuge in his home,
and he also cared for me deeply.
Although his conduct is humble,
his ancestral virtue is not severed.
Moreover, he is a former adversary of yours,
so you should extend to him the 'padded robe' kindness."
Zhèng agreed.
He replaced Jǐng's tattered clothes
and kept him for several days.
At midnight, as they were about to sleep,
a maid brought over twenty gold pieces and presented them to Jǐng.
The daughter spoke from outside the window, saying,
"This is my private savings;
it is merely to repay a past kindness.
You may take it
and find a good match.
Fortunately, your ancestral virtue is deep,
still sufficient to extend to your descendants.
Do not again be burdened by 'clipping and inspecting,'
thereby shortening your remaining years."
Jǐng thanked her.
Upon returning home,
he used over ten gold pieces to buy a gentry family's maid,
who was very ugly and fierce.
She bore him one son,
who later passed two imperial examinations.
Zhèng rose to the rank of Lìbù Láng.
After he died,
the daughter returned from the funeral.
When she opened the sedan chair, it was empty, and there was no one inside.
Only then did they realize she was not human.
Alas!
When a person is unkind,
abandoning the old to pursue the new,
in the end, the eggs are broken, and the bird also flies away.
Heaven's retribution is indeed tragic!
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
Lǐ Sījiàn,
a *jǔrén* from Yǒngnián.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of the fourth year of Kāngxī,
he beat his wife, née Lǐ, to death.
The local authorities reported it to Guǎngpíng,
which ordered Yǒngnián to investigate.
Sījiàn was in front of the prefectural office
when he suddenly snatched a butcher's knife from under a meat rack,
ran into the Chénghuáng Miào,
climbed onto the stage,
and knelt before the deity.
He declared,
"The deity blames me for not listening to righteous people,
for twisting right and wrong in the community,
and has ordered me to cut off my ear."
Thereupon, he cut off his left ear
and threw it beneath the stage.
He then said,
"The deity blames me for cheating people out of their money,
and has ordered me to chop off my finger."
Thereupon, he chopped off his left finger.
He again said,
"The deity blames me for seducing women,
and has ordered me to cut off my kidney."
Thereupon, he castrated himself
and collapsed unconscious.
At that time, Governor Zhū Yúnmén had already memorialized for his dismissal, stripping, investigation, and sentencing,
and the imperial assent had been received.
But Sījiàn had already suffered divine retribution.
*Dǐchāo*.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
Chàng Tǐyuán of Héjīn,
courtesy name Rǔyù.
When he was a *zhūshēng*,
he dreamt that someone called him
"Wǔgǔ Dàfū,"
and was pleased, taking it as a good omen.
When he encountered the chaos of roving bandits,
they stripped him of all his clothes
and locked him in an empty room at night.
It was the winter month,
and it was very cold.
Fumbling in the dark,
he found several sheepskins to protect his body,
barely avoiding death.
At dawn,
he looked at them
and saw that they were exactly five in number.
He smiled wryly, amused by the deity's trick.
Later, through *míngjīng*, he was appointed Magistrate of Luònán.
Recorded by Mr. Bì Zàijī.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
The farmer Mǎ Tiānróng,
over twenty years old.
His wife died, and he was too poor to remarry.
One day, while weeding in the fields,
he saw a young woman in rich attire
crossing the rice paddies and paths.
Her face was flushed,
and her demeanor was quite charming.
Mǎ suspected she was lost,
and seeing no one else in the fields,
he playfully flirted with her.
The woman also subtly assented.
He wished to have relations with her in the wild.
She laughed and said,
"In broad daylight,
it is surely not appropriate for this.
You go home,
close your door, and wait;
I will come at dusk."
Mǎ did not believe her,
but the woman swore an oath.
Mǎ then fully described the layout of his house and its orientation,
and the woman left.
At midnight,
she indeed arrived,
and they became lovers.
He found her skin exquisitely tender;
lighting a lamp,
he saw her skin was red and thin like an infant's,
with fine hair all over her body, which he found strange.
He also doubted her elusive nature,
wondering, *Could she be a fox?*
So he playfully questioned her.
The woman readily admitted it without evasion.
Mǎ said,
"Since you are an immortal,
you should be able to get whatever you desire.
Since you favor me with your affection,
will you not help my poverty with some gold?"
The woman agreed.
The next night she came,
and Mǎ asked for the gold.
The woman feigned surprise and said,
"I completely forgot."
As she was about to leave,
Mǎ again reminded her.
That night,
he asked,
"Did you perhaps not forget what I requested?"
The woman laughed
and asked for another day.
After several days,
Mǎ again asked for it.
The woman laughed and took out two small ingots of white metal from her sleeve,
weighing about five or six *jīn*,
with upturned edges and fine patterns,
quite lovely to look at and handle.
Mǎ was delighted
and carefully stored them in a chest.
After half a year,
he occasionally needed gold,
so he showed it to someone.
The person said,
"This is tin."
When he bit it,
it crumbled at his teeth.
Mǎ was greatly startled,
put it away, and went home.
That night,
the woman arrived,
and he angrily reproached her.
The woman laughed and said,
"Your fate is meager;
you cannot bear true gold."
She dismissed it with a laugh.
Mǎ
yáng yuē: "I hear that all fox fairies are beauties of the country,
but that's not necessarily true."
The woman said:
