"We all transform ourselves to suit the person.
You don't even have the fortune of a single piece of gold;
how could you afford
With my dull and ugly appearance,
I am certainly not enough to serve the upper class;
but compared to those with large feet and hunchbacks,
I am indeed a national beauty."
After several months,
she suddenly gave Mǎ three pieces of gold,
saying:
"You have asked for it repeatedly,
but I deemed that your fate did not include hidden gold.
Now, a marriage proposal has a date,
so please accept this as the cost of a wife,
also serving as a farewell gift."
Mǎ himself said there was no talk of a betrothal.
The woman said:
"In a day or two, a matchmaker will naturally come."
Mǎ asked:
"What about the appearance you speak of?"
She said:
"If you desire a national beauty,
she will naturally be a national beauty."
Mǎ said:
"I dare not hope for that.
But how can three pieces of gold buy a wife?"
The woman said:
"This is predestined by Yuèlǎo,
not by human effort."
Mǎ asked:
"Why such a sudden farewell?"
She said:
"Living under the moon and stars
is ultimately not a permanent arrangement.
'The gentleman has his own wife'41;
why should I continue to make excuses?"
She left at dawn,
giving him a knife-tip's worth of yellow powder,
saying:
"I fear you may fall ill after I leave;
taking this can cure it."
The next day,
a matchmaker indeed came.
First, Mǎ inquired about the girl's appearance,
and the matchmaker replied:
"She is neither exceptionally beautiful nor ugly."
"How much is the betrothal gift?"
"About four or five pieces."
Mǎ didn't dispute the price,
but insisted on seeing the person himself.
The matchmaker feared that a daughter from a respectable family would not agree to be seen.
Eventually, she arranged for them to go together,
to seize an opportune moment.
When they reached her village,
the matchmaker went ahead,
making Mǎ wait outside the village.
After a long while,
she returned and said:
"It's arranged.
My cousin lives in the same courtyard,
and I just went and
saw the girl sitting in her room.
Please pretend to visit my cousin and pass by,
you can glimpse her from a close distance."
Mǎ followed her advice.
Indeed, he saw a girl sitting in the hall,
lying on the bed,
having someone scratch her back.
Mǎ hurried past,
glancing at her,
and her appearance was indeed as the matchmaker had described.
When discussing the betrothal,
they did not haggle over the price at all,
only asking for one or two pieces of gold to
prepare the girl for marriage.
Mǎ esteemed her even more,
and so he handed over the gold;
he also paid the matchmaker and the scribe who wrote the contract,
totaling three taels, which was all used up,
without spending an extra cent.
He chose an auspicious day to welcome the girl home,
but upon entering the door,
he found her chest and back were both hunched,
her neck retracted like a turtle's,
and looking down at her skirt,
her lotus feet were a full *chi* long.
He then understood that the fox's words had a reason.
The historian Yìshǐ Shì said:
"'Transforming oneself to suit the person'
might be the fox girl's way of making light of the situation; however, her words about fortune
are truly credible.
I often say: without several generations of cultivation by one's ancestors,
one cannot achieve high office;
without several generations of cultivation by oneself,
one cannot obtain a beautiful spouse.
Those who believe in cause and effect
will not dismiss my words as baseless."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Luó Zǐfú
was a person.
His parents both died young.
At eight or nine,
he relied on his uncle, Dàyè.
Dàyè was a Zuǒxiāng of the Guózǐ (Imperial College),
wealthy in gold and silk but childless,
loving Zǐfú as his own son.
At fourteen,
he was lured away by rogues to indulge in dissolute pleasures.
At that time, a prostitute from Jīnlíng
was residing in the prefecture,
and the young man was delighted and enchanted by her.
When the prostitute returned to Jīnlíng,
the young man secretly ran away with her.
After living in the madam's house for half a year,
all his money was spent,
and he was greatly scorned by the other prostitutes.
However, she had not yet completely abandoned him.
Before long,
his venereal sores festered and stank,
soiling the bedclothes,
and he was subsequently expelled.
He begged in the market,
and people in the market would avoid him from a distance upon seeing him.
Fearing he would die in a foreign land,
he begged for food and traveled west;
covering thirty or forty *lǐ* a day,
he gradually reached the outskirts of his homeland.
He then thought that with his tattered clothes and suppurating wounds,
he had no face to enter the village gates,
and still hesitated in the vicinity of the town.
As dusk fell,
he wished to hurry to a mountain temple to stay the night.
He encountered a woman,
whose appearance was like that of an immortal.
He approached and asked:
“Where are you going?”
The man told her the truth.
The woman said:
“I am a renunciant.
I live in a mountain cave.
You can stay there.
I am quite unafraid of tigers and wolves.”
The man was delighted
and followed her.
Entering deep into the mountains,
he saw a cave dwelling.
Upon entering, a stream flowed across the entrance,
with a stone bridge spanning it.
A few more paces,
and there were two stone chambers,
radiantly bright,
requiring no lamps or candles.
She bade the man shed his tattered clothes,
and bathe in the stream.
She said:
“Wash yourself,
and your wounds will heal.”
She then drew back the curtains and fluffed the bedding, urging him to sleep,
saying:
“Please sleep now,
I will make trousers for you, young master.”
She then took large leaves resembling banana leaves,
cut and sewed them into clothing.
The man watched her from his bed.
In no time, the garment was finished,
folded at the head of the bed,
and she said:
“Put these on in the morning.”
Then she lay down on the couch opposite him.
After bathing, the man
felt his sores and wounds were no longer painful.
When he woke,
he felt them,
and found they were thick and calloused.
At dawn,
as he was about to get up,
he doubted that banana leaves could be worn.
He took them and examined them closely,
and found they were exquisitely smooth green brocade.
A short while later,
food was prepared.
The woman took mountain leaves and called them cakes;
when he ate them,
they were indeed cakes.
She then cut leaves into the shapes of chickens and fish and cooked them;
they were all like the real thing.
In a corner of the room was a jar,
containing excellent wine,
from which they frequently drank.
When it ran low,
she would pour stream water into it to replenish it.
After several days,
all his scabs had fallen off,
and he asked the woman to sleep with him.
The woman said:
“You frivolous boy: no sooner have you found a safe place to rest,
than you start having improper thoughts!”
The man said:
“It’s merely to repay your kindness.”
So they lay together,
and shared great joy and affection.
One day,
a young woman entered laughing,
saying:
“What a carefree little devil!
Xiē Gūzǐ, how long will your sweet dream
last?”
The woman greeted her with a smile, saying:
“Huāchéng Niángzǐ,
your esteemed feet have not stepped here for a long time.
Today the southwest wind is strong,
blowing you over!
Have you hugged your little boy yet?”
She replied:
“It’s another little maidservant.”
The woman laughed, saying:
“Huā Niángzǐ, you’re a brick kiln!
Why didn’t you bring her?”
She replied:
“I was just humming her to sleep,
and she’s asleep.”
Thereupon they sat down and drank heartily.
She then looked at the man and said,
“This young master is burning good incense.”
The man looked at her;
she was twenty-three or twenty-four years old,
with ample remaining beauty.
He was fond of her.
He peeled a fruit and accidentally dropped it under the table.
He bent down to pretend to pick up the fruit,
and secretly touched Huāchéng’s phoenix-like coiffure.
Huāchéng looked away and smiled,
as if she did not know.
As the man was utterly engrossed,
he suddenly felt his robe and trousers were cold.
He looked at what he was wearing,
and it had all turned into autumn leaves.
He was nearly scared to death.
He sat upright for some time,
and gradually it returned to normal.
He secretly congratulated himself that the two women had not seen it.
A short while later,
during their exchange,
he again used his finger to scratch her slender palm.
Huāchéng laughed and jested openly,
completely unaware.
Amidst his frantic trepidation,
his clothes had already turned into leaves,
and only after some time did they change back.
From then on, he felt ashamed and suppressed his thoughts,
daring not to harbor improper desires.
Huāchéng laughed and said:
“Our little young master
is very improper!
If it weren’t for the ‘Vinegar Gourd Lady’
I’m afraid he’d leap right into the clouds.”
The woman also sneered, saying:
“Frivolous boy,
he deserves to be frozen to death!”
They clapped their hands together,
and Huāchéng left her seat, saying:
“The little maidservant is awake,
I’m afraid she’ll cry her heart out.”
The woman also got up, saying:
“Greedily enticing another family’s man,
you don’t remember that little Jiāngchéng is crying herself hoarse.”
After Huāchéng left,
he feared reproach and blame;
but the woman ultimately faced him as if it were normal.
Not long after,
autumn aged, and the winds grew cold.
Frost fell, and trees shed their leaves.
The woman then collected the fallen leaves,
storing them as fuel for winter.
Gù Shēng was shriveling with cold,
so she took and gathered white clouds from the cave mouth, turning them into cotton wadding for a new garment.
When he put it on, it was as warm as a padded jacket,
and as light and fluffy as new cotton.
After a year,
a son was born,
exceedingly intelligent and beautiful.
Every day they enjoyed themselves playing with the child in the cave.
However, whenever Gù Shēng thought of his homeland,
he begged her to return with him.
The woman said:
"I cannot go with you;
otherwise,
you may go by yourself."
Thus, two or three years passed.
The child gradually grew,
and was betrothed to Huā Chéng for marriage.
Gù Shēng often worried about his elderly uncle.
The woman said:
"Your uncle, Lǎo, is advanced in years,
but fortunately still strong and healthy,
so there is no need to fret.
After our son's marriage,
you may choose to stay or go."
While in the cave, the woman
often took leaves to write books and taught her son to read,
and he understood them as soon as he saw them.
The woman said:
"This child has the look of good fortune;
if he is allowed into the human world,
he will rise to the highest official ranks without worry."
Not long after,
when the child was fourteen,
Huā Chéng personally came to send off the bride.
The woman, Piānpiān, arrived in splendid attire,
her radiant beauty shining upon everyone.
The couple was greatly pleased,
and the whole family gathered.
Piānpiān tapped her hairpin and sang:
"I have a good son,
I do not envy noble palaces.
I have a good daughter-in-law,
I do not envy fine silks.
Tonight we gather,
all should be joyful.
I pour wine for you,
I urge you to eat more."
Afterward, Huā Chéng departed.
The son and his wife lived in the opposite room.
The new daughter-in-law was filial,
clinging closely to their knees,
as if she were their own child.
Gù Shēng again spoke of returning home.
The woman said:
"You have mortal bones,
and are ultimately not of immortal quality.
Our son is also destined for wealth and honor among men,
you may take him with you,
I will not hinder his life's course."
The new daughter-in-law thought of parting from her mother,
and Huā Chéng had already arrived.
The son and daughter-in-law were reluctant to part,
their eyes filled with tears.
Both mothers comforted them, saying:
"Go for now,
you can come back again."
Piānpiān then cut leaves to make a donkey,
and the three of them rode it home.
Dà Yè had grown old and retired to the forest.
He thought his nephew had died,
but suddenly he returned with a beautiful grandson and a lovely daughter-in-law,
rejoicing as if he had found a treasure.
Upon entering the house,
they each looked at what they were wearing.
All were banana leaves;
when torn open,
the wadding steamed and floated away.
So they immediately changed their clothes.
Later, Gù Shēng missed Piānpiān,
and went with his son to visit her.
But yellow leaves covered the path,
and the way to the cave mouth was lost.
They returned in tears.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Were Piānpiān and Huā Chéng perhaps immortals?
To eat leaves and wear clouds,
how strange!
Yet within the curtained bedchamber,
bearing children in their sleep,
how is it different from the human world?
Fifteen years in the mountains,
though without the 'people and city walls'
of legend;
when the clouds obscure the cave mouth,
leaving no trace,
seeing that scene,
it truly resembled Liú and Ruǎn's return journey."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
I heard Lǐ Tàigōng Jìngyī say:
"A certain Lord was in Shěnyáng,
hosting a banquet on a mountain peak.
Looking down the mountain,
a tiger-like creature came,
dug a hole with its claws,
buried something, and left.
He sent men to investigate what was buried,
and found a dead deer.
So they took the deer and loosely covered the hole.
A short while later,
the tiger led a black beast,
whose fur was several inches long.
The tiger preceded it,
as if inviting an honored guest.
When they reached the hole,
the beast squatted, staring intently.
The tiger probed the hole and found the deer missing,
and trembled, lying prostrate, not daring to move even slightly.
The beast was angered by its deception,
and struck the tiger's forehead with its claws,
killing the tiger instantly.
The beast then walked straight away."
The Historian of the Strange says:
"I do not know the name of this beast.
However, judging by its form,
it was not much larger than a tiger,
so why did the tiger stretch its neck to accept death,
fearing it so greatly?
All creatures have something that controls them;
this principle is inexplicable.
For example, the *yù* (prison) is greatly feared by.
From a distance,
they gather in groups of hundreds,
kneeling in rows,
none daring to flee.
They fix their gaze and hold their breath,
waiting for the *yù* to arrive,
which then feels them all over with its claws to assess their fatness or leanness.
The fat ones are marked on their heads with a small stone.
They lie prostrate with the stones on their heads,
terrified like wooden chickens,
only fearing the stones might fall off.
Once the *yù* has felt and marked them,
it then takes and eats them according to the stones,
and the rest finally disperse.
I once said that corrupt officials resemble this,
also feeling the fatness or leanness of the people and marking them,
and then tearing them apart to eat;
and the people hear themselves being eaten,
not daring to breathe,
their foolish submission,
is also just like this.
How lamentable!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Yǐn Túnán of Wǔchāng
had a separate residence,
which he once leased to a *xiùcai*.
For half a year,
he never inquired about it.
One day,
he met him at his door;
he was very young,
but dressed in guest attire of fur and fine horses,
looking exceedingly elegant and handsome.
Yǐn Túnán approached to speak with him,
and he was immediately found to be charming and refined.
Yǐn Túnán was surprised.
He returned home and told his wife.
His wife sent a maid to make an inquiry, pretending to have left something behind, to peek into his room.
In the room was a beautiful woman,
more enchanting than an immortal;
all the flowers, stones, clothing, and ornaments
were unlike anything seen before.
Yǐn Túnán could not guess who he was,
so he went to his door to pay a call,
but he happened to be out.
The next day,
he came to return the visit.
He presented his calling card and,
only then did Yǐn Túnán learn his surname was Dé and his given name was Yú.
During their conversation,
when Yǐn Túnán subtly probed about his official status,
his words were rather vague.
When pressed firmly,
he said:
"If you wish to maintain our acquaintance,
I dare not cut myself off.
You should know that I am not a bandit, thief, or fugitive;
why must you insist on knowing my origin?"
Yǐn Túnán apologized.
He ordered wine and hosted a banquet,
and their conversation and laughter were very joyful.
Towards dusk,
a Kūnlún servant led a horse and carried a lamp,
guiding him away.
The next day,
I broke off a slip of bamboo to notify the host.
Yǐn arrived at his house,
and saw that the walls of the house were all adorned with bright, glossy paper,
clean as a mirror.
Golden suānní gave off a strange fragrance.
In a jade-green vase,
were two phoenix-tail and two peacock feathers,
each more than two *chǐ* long.
In a crystal vase,
a tree of pink flowers was immersed,
I didn't know its name,
also about two *chǐ* high,
its branches hung down covering the outside of the table;
the leaves were sparse, the flowers dense,
buds still unopened;
the flowers resembled wet butterflies with folded wings;
the calyxes were like filaments.
At the feast, there were no more than eight bowls,
but the food was extraordinarily rich and delicious.
After the meal,
he ordered a young servant to beat a drum to "urge the flowers" as a game.
As the drumbeat began,
the flowers in the vase trembled, as if about to unfurl;
presently, the butterfly wings gradually spread;
then, when the drumming ceased,
with a deep resonant sound,
the calyxes and filaments instantly fell off,
and became a butterfly,
flying down onto Yǐn's clothes.
I laughed and got up,
and poured a huge goblet of wine;
just as the wine was filled to the brim,
the butterfly also departed.
A moment later,
the drum sounded again,
and two butterflies flew and settled on my cap.
I laughed and said:
"My own trick has turned against me!"
I also drank two goblets.
When the third drumming finished,
flowers fell in profusion,
fluttering down,
brushing sleeves and touching lapels.
The drumming servant laughed as he came to count: Yǐn had nine tallies,
I had four tallies.
Yǐn was already slightly tipsy,
unable to finish his tallies,
he forced himself to drink three more cups,
then left his seat and fled.
From this, I found him even more remarkable.
However, he was a man of few acquaintances,
always shutting his door and staying home,
not communicating with the people of the state for condolences or celebrations.
Yǐn would broadcast his story whenever he met someone;
those who heard of his strangeness
eagerly sought my company,
and officials' carriages and caps were constantly visible outside my gate.
I found this quite unbearable,
and suddenly bade farewell to the host and left.
After I left,
Yǐn went to his house,
the empty courtyard was swept clean without a speck of dust;
candle tears were piled up on the green steps below;
scattered pieces of silk and broken threads were in the window,
fingerprints clearly visible.
Only a small white stone jar,
capable of holding about one *shí*, was left behind the house.
Yǐn took it home,
and filled it with water to keep red fish.
After a year,
the water was as clear as when first stored.
Later, a servant moved the stone,
and accidentally broke it.
The stored water did not spill out at all.
Looking at it,
the jar was still there,
but felt hollow and illusory.
When a hand was put into it,
the water would leak out with the hand;
when the hand was withdrawn,
it would close again.
Even in winter, it would not freeze.
One night,
it suddenly crystallized,
and the fish swam as usual.
Yǐn feared people would know,
and always kept it in a secret room,
not showing it to anyone but his son-in-law.
Over time, it gradually spread,
and those seeking to examine it thronged at his door.
On a winter's eve,
it suddenly turned back into water,
wetting the ground everywhere,
and the fish were also gone.
Its old jar's broken stones remained.
Suddenly, a Daoist came to the door seeking it.
Yǐn brought it out to show him.
The Daoist said:
"This is a water container from the Dragon Palace."
Yǐn described its peculiarity of being broken yet not spilling.
The Daoist said:
"This is the soul of the jar."
He earnestly begged for a small piece.
When asked what he would use it for,
he said:
"Mixed with medicine as powder,
it can grant the 'water' aspect of longevity."
I gave him a piece,
and he thanked me joyfully and left.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
When Bì Mínbùgōng (also known as Jiā Qǐ) was preparing for the military campaign in Táo and Mín,
a Qianzǒng, Yáng Huàlín, came to greet him.
As their carriages and caps proceeded along the road,
they happened to see a person defecating by the roadside.
Yáng drew his bow, intending to shoot him,
but Gōng quickly shouted to stop him.
Yáng said:
"This wretch is rude,
he deserves a little fright."
So he shouted from afar:
"You defecator!
I'll present you with a strand of Kuàijī rattan hairpin for your bun!"
Then an arrow flew,
hitting precisely his bun.
The person ran off in a hurry,
leaving faeces and urine on the ground.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In the sixth month of the twenty-sixth year,
in a villager's garden west of the city,
new vines grew from a cucumber plant,
bearing one watermelon,
as large as a bowl.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Chéng Shēng from Báixià,
was a straightforward and magnanimous character,
not given to petty distinctions.
One day,
returning from outside,
as he loosened his belt,
he felt the end of the belt heavy,
as if something had fallen.
He looked,
but saw nothing.
As he turned around,
a woman emerged from behind his clothes,
combing her hair and smiling,
exquisitely beautiful.
Chéng suspected she was a ghost,
but the woman said:
"I am not a ghost,
but a fox."
Chéng said:
"If I can have a beautiful woman,
I wouldn't even fear a ghost,
let alone a fox."
Thus, he became intimate with her.
Two years later,
she bore a daughter,
nicknamed Qīngméi.
She often told Chéng:
"Don't get married,
I will bear you a son."
Chéng believed her,
and so did not marry.
Relatives and friends all ridiculed him.
Chéng's resolve weakened,
and he became engaged to a Ms. Wáng from Húdōng.
The fox heard of it and was furious,
she fed her daughter milk,
then left her with Chéng and said:
"This is your family's money-losing product;
whether she lives or dies,
it's all up to you.
Why should I act as a wet nurse for someone else?"
She walked out the door and left directly.
Qīngméi grew up intelligent;
her appearance was graceful and beautiful,
very much resembling her mother.
Later, Chéng fell ill and died,
and Ms. Wáng remarried and left.
Qīngméi lived as a dependent with her paternal uncle;
the uncle was dissolute and immoral,
wishing to sell her to enrich himself.
Coincidentally, a Jìnshì Wáng,
who was awaiting official appointment at home,
heard of her intelligence,
bought her with a large sum of money,
and made her serve his daughter, Āxǐ.
Āxǐ was fourteen,
and her beauty was unparalleled.
Upon seeing Méi, she was delighted,
and shared her bed and living quarters with her.
Méi was also good at waiting on people,
able to "hear with her eyes"
and "speak with her eyebrows,"
thus the whole family loved and doted on her.
In the district lived a man named Zhāng Shēng,
whose courtesy name was Jièshòu.
His family was impoverished,
without permanent assets,
and they rented a dwelling in Wáng Dì.
He was by nature purely filial,
his conduct was meticulous,
and he was also deeply devoted to learning.
Qīngméi happened to visit his home
and saw Zhāng Shēng sitting on a stone, eating coarse gruel.
She entered the room and chatted with Zhāng Shēng's mother,
and saw pig trotters on the table.
At that time, Zhāng Shēng's father was ill in bed.
Zhāng Shēng entered
and privately embraced his father.
The father's bodily fluids soiled Zhāng Shēng's clothes,
and the father, realizing it, felt ashamed.
Zhāng Shēng concealed the traces,
hurriedly went out to wash them,
fearing his father would know.
Qīngméi was greatly impressed by this.
Upon returning, she recounted what she had seen,
and said to the lady (Wáng Dì's daughter):
"My guest
is no ordinary man.
If you do not wish to find a good match, then so be it;
but if you do wish to find a good match,
Zhāng Shēng is the man."
The lady feared her father would despise his poverty.
Qīngméi said:
"Not so,
it rests with you, my lady.
If you deem it acceptable,
I will quietly inform him
and have him seek an intermediary for marriage.
Madam (Wáng Dì's wife) will surely summon you to discuss it: just respond with 'Yes,'
and then it will be successful."
The lady feared that eventually remaining poor would make her a laughingstock.
Qīngméi said:
"I consider myself capable of discerning worthy gentlemen,
and there will be no mistake."
The next day,
she went to inform Zhāng Ǎo (Zhāng Shēng's mother).
Zhāng Ǎo was greatly surprised
and deemed her words inauspicious.
Qīngméi said:
"The young lady (Wáng Dì's daughter) heard of your son and admired him,
so I probed her intentions and spoke.
When the matchmaker goes,
we two will stand by him,
and the plan will surely be agreed upon and succeed.
Even if it fails,
what shame is there for your son?"
Zhāng Ǎo said:
"Yes."
So she entrusted the flower seller, Hóu Shì, to go.
Madam (Wáng Dì's wife) heard of it and laughed,
and informed Wáng (Wáng Dì).
Wáng Dì also laughed heartily.
He called his daughter to him
and recounted Hóu Shì's intention.
Before the lady could reply,
Qīngméi immediately praised Zhāng Shēng's worthiness
and asserted that he would certainly become eminent.
Madam then asked again:
"This is your lifelong affair.
If you can truly eat coarse gruel,
then I will approve it for you."
The lady was silent for a long time,
looked at the wall, and replied:
"Wealth and poverty are fate.
If one's destiny is abundant,
then poverty will not last long, and the period of not being poor will be endless.
Or if one's destiny is meager,
among those princes in fine silks,
how few are those who lack even enough space to stand?
It rests with the parents."
Initially,
Wáng Dì was consulting with his daughter
intending to make a joke;
but upon hearing his daughter's words,
he was displeased and said:
"Do you wish to marry into the Zhāng family?"
The lady did not reply;
he asked again,
and she did not reply again.
Angrily, he said:
"Worthless creature,
utterly incorrigible!
You want to carry a basket and become a beggar's wife,
would you not die of shame?"
The lady flushed red and choked up,
and left in tears.
The matchmaker also quickly ran off.
Qīngméi, seeing that it wouldn't succeed,
decided to plan on her own.
After several days,
she visited Zhāng Shēng at night.
Zhāng Shēng was reading,
and asked in surprise why she had come;
her words were hesitant.
Zhāng Shēng sternly rejected her.
Qīngméi wept and said:
"I am from a respectable family,
not one who elopes;
it is only because of your worthiness
that I wish to entrust myself to you."
Zhāng Shēng said:
"You love me
and call me worthy.
Such an act in the dark of night
is not something a self-respecting person would do,
so how can you say a worthy person would do it?
If one begins with disorder and ends with success,
a gentleman would still say it is impermissible;
how much more so when success is impossible,
how can either of us conduct ourselves?"
Qīngméi said:
"What if it could succeed,
would you be willing to lend a helping hand?"
Zhāng Shēng said:
"To obtain a person like you,
what other method is there?
But there are three insurmountable obstacles,
so I dare not lightly promise."
She asked:
"What are they?"
He said:
"If you cannot decide for yourself,
then there's nothing to be done;
even if you can decide for yourself, if my parents are not pleased,
then there's nothing to be done;
even if they are pleased,
and your value would necessarily be high,
I am too poor to manage it,
then it is even more insurmountable.
You should leave quickly,
the suspicion of 'melon and plum' is to be feared!"
As Qīngméi was leaving,
she again urged:
"If you are truly interested,
please let us plan together."
Zhāng Shēng assented.
Qīngméi returned.
The lady questioned where she had been,
whereupon Qīngméi knelt and confessed.
The lady was angry at her for running off indecently
and intended to punish her.
Qīngméi wept, explaining there was nothing else,
and then told the full truth.
The lady sighed and said:
"Not to consent improperly is ritual;
to surely inform one's parents is filial piety;
not to lightly give one's word is trustworthiness:
with these three virtues,
Heaven will surely bless him,
and he will be free from the worry of poverty."
Then she said:
"What will you do?"
She replied:
"Marry him."
The lady laughed and said:
"Can a foolish maid decide for herself?"
She replied:
"If I fail,
I shall follow it with my death."
The young woman said,
"I will surely fulfill your wish."
Méi bowed her head and prostrated herself before her.
After a few more days,
she said to the young woman,
"Was what you said earlier a jest,
or do you truly intend to show compassion?
If it is the latter,
there is still a small matter,
and I beg you to take pity on me for it as well."
The young woman asked her about it,
and she replied,
"Zhāng Shēng cannot afford the betrothal gifts,
and I, a maidservant, have no means to redeem myself.
They will surely demand a full payment,
and marrying me would be as good as not marrying me."
The young woman pondered and said,
"This is beyond my power to help.
I said I would marry you off,
but I fear it may not be suitable;
and to say there will surely be no payment
is something my father would certainly not permit,
nor dare I mention it."
Qīngméi heard this,
and tears streamed down her face in several lines,
begging only for pity and rescue.
The young woman thought for a long time,
and then said,
"There's no other way.
I have some private savings of gold,
which I will empty my purse to assist you with."
Méi bowed in thanks,
and then secretly informed Zhāng Shēng.
Zhāng Mǔ was overjoyed,
and by various means begged for loans,
accumulating a certain sum,
and awaited good news.
Just then, Wáng was appointed magistrate of Qūwò,
and in his joy, he took the opportunity to tell his mother,
"Qīngméi is already grown,
and I am about to take up my post.
It would be better to send her away."
Fūrén had always considered Qīngméi too cunning,
fearing she might lead her daughter astray,
and had often wished to marry her off,
but feared her daughter would be unhappy.
Hearing her daughter's words, she was very pleased.
Two days later,
a matchmaker conveyed Zhāng Shì's intention.
Wáng laughed and said,
"She is only fit to be a maidservant's mate.
What nonsense was that before!
However, for a maidservant to be sold to a high-ranking family,
the price should be double what it was before."
The young woman urgently interjected,
"Qīngméi has served me for a long time;
to sell her as a concubine,
I truly cannot bear it."
Wáng then sent word to Zhāng Shì,
agreeing to issue the deed for the original sum,
and marry Qīngméi to Zhāng Shēng.
After entering the household,
she was filial to her parents-in-law,
diligently and thoroughly compliant,
even more so than Zhāng Shēng;
and she was even more diligent in her work,
not minding to eat husks and chaff.
From then on, everyone in the family loved and esteemed Qīngméi.
Méi also took up embroidery work,
which sold quickly,
and merchants waited at the gate to buy it,
fearing they would not get any.
The income she earned helped somewhat to alleviate their poverty.
Moreover, she urged Zhāng Shēng not to let household worries distract him from his studies,
taking on all the domestic affairs herself.
When her husband took up his official post,
she went to bid farewell to Āxǐ.
Āxǐ saw her
and cried,
"You have found your rightful place!
I am certainly not as good as you."
Méi said,
"By whose grace is this?
How dare I forget it?
However, to say you are not as good as a maidservant,
I fear it will shorten the maidservant's life."
Thereupon, they tearfully parted.
When Wáng went to Jìn,
half a year later,
Fūrén died,
and her coffin was temporarily placed in a temple.
Two years later,
Wáng was dismissed from office for bribery,
and fined tens of thousands,
gradually becoming so poor he could not support himself,
and his followers scattered.
At this time,
a great plague broke out,
and Wáng also contracted the disease and died.
Only an old maidservant accompanied the young woman.
Not long after,
the maidservant also died.
The young woman, alone and helpless, suffered even more.
A neighboring old woman advised her to marry,
and the young woman said,
"Whoever can bury my parents,
I will follow."
The old woman took pity on her,
gave her a dou of rice, and left.
After half a month, she returned
and said,
"I have tried my utmost for you, young mistress,
but it is difficult to find a match: the poor cannot afford the burial,
and the rich dislike marrying a descendant of a ruined family.
What can be done?
There is still one plan,
but I fear you may not be able to accept it."
The young woman said,
"What is it?"
She said,
"There is a Lǐ Láng here
who is looking for a secondary wife.
If he sees your beauty,
he will immediately provide for a grand burial,
and will surely not be stingy."
The young woman burst into tears and said,
"I am of gentry lineage; how can I become someone's concubine!"
The old woman said nothing
and left.
With only one meal a day,
she prolonged her life, waiting for an offer.
After half a year,
she could no longer bear it.
One day,
the old woman arrived.
The young woman tearfully reported,
"So distressed am I,
that I often wish to end my life;
yet I cling to life and struggle to survive
merely because there are two coffins.
They are about to be cast into a ditch.
Who will collect my parents' bones?
Therefore, I think it is better to follow your advice."
The old woman then brought Lǐ Láng,
who secretly observed the young woman
and was greatly pleased.
He immediately produced gold to arrange the burial,
and both coffins were properly interred.
After this,
he took the young woman away
to present her to the main wife.
The main wife was inherently fierce and jealous,
so Lǐ Láng had not dared to speak of a concubine at first,
but merely claimed to have bought a maidservant.
Upon seeing the young woman,
she flew into a rage,
drove her out with a stick,
and would not allow her to enter the gate.
The young woman, with disheveled hair and weeping,
had nowhere to go, neither forward nor back.
An old bhikṣuṇī passed by,
and invited her to live together.
She gladly followed.
Upon arriving at the nunnery,
she bowed and requested to have her hair shaven (to become a nun).
The bhikṣuṇī refused,
saying:
"I see, young lady,
that you are not destined to languish in the dust for long.
In this nunnery, with earthenware and coarse rice,
we can barely sustain ourselves.
Just stay here temporarily and wait.
When the time comes,
you will leave on your own."
Not long after she resided there,
some ruffians from the market, coveting the girl's beauty,
would often bang on the door, making rude remarks and playing tricks,
which the bhikṣuṇī could not stop.
The girl cried out, wanting to commit suicide.
The bhikṣuṇī went to seek 吏部某公 (Lìbù Mǒu Gōng) to issue a strict prohibition notice,
and only then did the hoodlums somewhat rein in their behavior.
Later, someone drilled a hole in the nunnery wall at night,
and the bhikṣuṇī's alarm calls finally drove them away.
Therefore, she again reported to the 吏部 (Lìbù),
who caught the ringleader
and sent him to the commandery for a flogging.
Only then did they gradually find peace.
After more than another year,
a noble young master passed by the nunnery,
saw the girl, and was utterly astonished.
He pressed the bhikṣuṇī to convey his courtship,
and also tempted the bhikṣuṇī with a hefty bribe.
The bhikṣuṇī gently said to him:
"She is of an aristocratic lineage
and would not be content as a concubine.
Young master, please return for now;
in due course, there will be a reply to report back to you."
After he left,
the girl wanted to use poison to die.
That night, she dreamed her father came,
and in distress said:
"I did not follow your wishes,
leading you to this point.
It is too late to regret,
but delay your death for a moment;
your former wish can still be fulfilled."
The girl was surprised by this.
At dawn,
after washing,
the bhikṣuṇī looked at her and exclaimed in surprise:
"Seeing your face,
all the turbid aura has vanished.
No perverse misfortunes need be feared.
Good fortune is about to arrive.
Do not forget this old body!"
Before she had finished speaking,
a knocking sound was heard at the door.
The girl's color drained,
thinking it must be the noble family's servant.
The bhikṣuṇī opened the door,
and indeed it was.
He hastily asked about the arrangement.
The bhikṣuṇī sweet-talked and agreed,
but requested a delay of three days.
The servant conveyed his master's words,
that if the matter was not accomplished,
the bhikṣuṇī should report back herself.
The bhikṣuṇī respectfully agreed,
and thanked him, letting him leave.
The girl was greatly saddened,
and again wanted to commit suicide.
The bhikṣuṇī stopped her.
The girl worried that they would return in three days,
with no words to respond.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"With this old body here,
I will personally bear any beheading."
The next day,
around late afternoon,
a sudden torrential downpour ensued,
and suddenly several people were heard banging on the door and shouting loudly.
The girl thought a change had occurred,
and was frightened and did not know what to do.
The bhikṣuṇī braved the rain and opened the gate,
seeing a sedan chair stopped;
several maidservants brought out a beautiful woman;
the retinue was grand and splendid,
with many officials' hats and carriages.
She asked in surprise,
and they said:
"This is the inner family of 司李 (Sīlǐ),
temporarily sheltering from the wind and rain."
They led the people into the main hall,
moved beds, and sat solemnly.
The female family members rushed into the meditation rooms,
each seeking rest.
Upon entering the room, they saw the girl
and were struck by her beauty.
They ran to tell the madam.
Not long after,
the rain stopped.
The madam rose
and asked to look into the meditation room.
The bhikṣuṇī led her in,
and she saw the girl's exquisite beauty,
gazing fixedly without blinking.
The girl also looked back for a long time.
The madam was no other
than 青梅 (Qīngméi).
They both cried out in surprise,
and then recounted their respective journeys.
It turned out that after 張翁 (Zhāng Wēng) passed away
and the scholar had completed his mourning period,
he achieved consecutive successes and was appointed as 司理 (Sīlǐ).
The scholar first took his mother to his post,
and later moved all his family members there.
The girl sighed:
"To see each other today,
how different it is, like heaven and earth!"
梅 (Méi) smiled and said:
"Fortunately, young lady, your setbacks were unmatched.
Heaven truly intended for us two to be reunited.
If it weren't for the rain delay,
how could we have had this encounter?
There are spirits and gods at play in this,
not human effort."
Then she took out a pearl crown and brocade robes,
urging the girl to change her attire.
The girl hesitated at first.
The bhikṣuṇī encouraged her from the middle.
The girl worried that living together would not be proper in name.
梅 (Méi) said:
"In the past, there was already a set destiny.
How dare this maidservant forget your great kindness!
Just think, would 張郎 (Zhāng Láng)
be one who forsakes loyalty?"
She strongly adorned her.
They then bid farewell to the bhikṣuṇī and departed.
Upon arriving at the post,
both mother and son were delighted.
The girl bowed and said:
"Today, I have no face to see mother."
The mother smiled and comforted her.
Then they planned an auspicious day for their reunion.
The girl said:
"If there were even a sliver of hope for survival in the nunnery,
I would not have come here with madam.
If you still remember our old affection,
and I could have a small hut,
enough to accommodate a meditation cushion, that would be sufficient."
梅 (Méi) smiled and said nothing.
When the time came,
she brought elaborate makeup and attire.
The girl was at a loss, not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, music and drums erupted,
and the girl could no longer control herself.
梅 (Méi) led the maidservants and old women, forcefully dressed her,
and helped her out.
Seeing the scholar in court attire bowing,
she, too, involuntarily bowed gracefully.
梅 (Méi) led her into the bridal chamber,
saying:
"This position has been vacant, waiting for you for a long time."
She then looked at the scholar and said:
"Tonight, you get to repay kindness,
so treat her well."
She turned to leave.
The girl grabbed her skirt.
梅 (Méi) smiled and said:
"Don't hold me back;
I cannot substitute for you in this."
She freed her fingers and left.
青梅 (Qīngméi) served the girl respectfully,
not daring to take the main position that night.
But the girl ultimately felt ashamed and uneasy.
So the mother ordered them to address her as夫人 (Fūrén).
梅 (Méi), however, continued to adhere to the etiquette of a maidservant or concubine,
never daring to be negligent.
Three years later,
when 張 (Zhāng) was transferred to the capital,
he passed by the nunnery
and offered five hundred gold coins as a gift to the bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇī refused to accept.
He insisted,
and she finally accepted two hundred gold coins,
which she used to build a Guanyin temple
and erect a stele for 王夫人 (Wáng Fūrén).
Later, 張 (Zhāng) rose to the position of 侍郎 (Shìláng).
程夫人 (Chéng Fūrén) bore two sons and one daughter,
and 王夫人 (Wáng Fūrén) bore four sons and one daughter.
張 (Zhāng) submitted a memorial detailing their situation,
and both were granted the title of夫人 (Fūrén).
Shǐ Shì 曰 (the Historian comments):
“Heaven produces beautiful women,
indeed to reward famous scholars;
but the vulgar kings and dukes of the world
keep them to bestow upon fops.
This is what the Creator must contend with.
And so, through many strange and wondrous circumstances,
it takes infinite efforts to bring couples together,
and even the Creator finds it quite difficult.
Only Lady Qīng, being able to recognize a hero in obscurity,
vowed to marry him,
resolved to die for it;
while those who outwardly dress like officials
instead abandon virtue to seek wealth and luxury.
How much less intelligent they are than a mere maid! ”
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Mǎ Jì,
courtesy name Lóngméi,
was the son of a merchant.
He was handsome in appearance.
In his youth, he was unrestrained
and fond of singing and dancing.
He would often join actors of the Pear Garden,
tying a brocade kerchief around his head,
as beautiful as a fine maiden,
and thus he also had
the nickname
“Jùnrén (Handsome Man).”
At fourteen,
he entered the prefecture treasury
and was already well-known.
His father, being old and frail,
ceased trading and stayed at home.
He said to his son:
“A few scrolls of books
cannot be boiled when hungry,
nor worn when cold.
My son, you should continue your father’s trade.”
Mǎ Jì thenceforth gradually engaged in moneylending.
He traveled with others across the sea
and was carried away by a hurricane,
arriving at a great city after several days and nights.
Its inhabitants were all extraordinarily ugly;
seeing Mǎ Jì arrive,
they took him for a demon,
and all clamored and fled.
Mǎ Jì was initially greatly frightened by their appearance;
but when he realized that the people of the country were scared of him,
he then used this to trick the country folk.
When he encountered people eating or drinking,
he would rush towards them;
when people fled in fright,
he would consume their leftovers.
After some time,
he entered a mountain village.
Among its inhabitants, some had faces somewhat resembling humans,
but they were ragged like beggars.
Mǎ Jì rested under a tree,
and the villagers dared not approach him,
only watching him from afar.
After a long while,
they realized Mǎ Jì was not a man-eater,
and began to cautiously approach him.
Mǎ Jì smiled and spoke with them.
Though his words were strange,
they were half understandable.
Mǎ Jì then introduced himself and his origin.
The villagers were pleased
and spread the word to their neighbors that the guest was not a man-eater.
However, the extremely ugly ones would look and immediately leave,
never daring to approach;
those who came
had their mouths and noses positioned
similarly to those in Zhōngguó.
Together they prepared wine and served Mǎ Jì.
Mǎ Jì asked why they were so startled by him,
and they replied:
“We have heard our ancestors say that twenty-six thousand *lǐ* to the west
there is Zhōngguó,
where the people’s appearance is generally strange and unusual.
We only heard this by word of mouth,
but now we believe it.”
He asked why they were so poor.
They said:
“What our country values
is not literary talent,
but appearance.
Those who are extremely beautiful
become high-ranking officials;
the next serve as local administrators;
and those below that
also gain the favor of nobles,
thus obtaining rich food to support their wives and children.
As for people like us, when we were first born,
our parents all considered us inauspicious
and often abandoned us;
those who couldn’t bear to abandon them
were only kept to continue the family line.”
He asked:
“What is the name of this country?”
They replied:
“It is the Great Luóchà Guó.
Its capital city is thirty *lǐ* to the north.”
Mǎ Jì asked to be guided there for a look.
So, they rose at cockcrow
and led him along.
At dawn,
they arrived at the capital.
The city walls were made of black stone,
the color of ink,
and the towers and pavilions were nearly a hundred *chǐ* high.
However, there were few tiles,
and they were covered with red stone;
picking up a broken piece and grinding it on one’s fingernail
was no different from cinnabar.
It was the time when court had just adjourned,
and officials in caps and robes were emerging from the court.
The villagers pointed and said:
"This is the Prime Minister."
They looked at him;
both his ears grew backwards,
his nose had three nostrils,
and his eyelashes covered his eyes like a curtain.
Then several more riders came out,
saying:
"This is the Grand Master."
One by one, they pointed out their official positions,
all of them strange and grotesque;
however, as their rank gradually lowered,
their ugliness also gradually lessened.
Before long,
Mǎ returned,
and the people in the streets and alleys, seeing him,
shouted, ran, stumbled, and fell,
as if encountering a monster.
It took a hundred mouths of the villagers to explain,
before the townspeople dared to stand at a distance.
Upon his return,
the whole country knew that there was an extraordinary person in the village.
Thereupon, the gentry and grand masters
all vied to broaden their horizons,
so they ordered the villagers to invite Mǎ.
However, each time he arrived at a household,
the gatekeeper immediately closed the doors,
and men and women whispered and peeked through the door cracks;
all day long,
no one dared to invite him in.
The villagers said:
"There is an official here, a Zhícháo Láng,
who once served the former king as an envoy to foreign countries.
He has seen many people,
and perhaps will not be frightened by you."
They went to Láng's door.
Láng was indeed pleased,
and bowed, treating him as an honored guest.
Looking at his appearance,
he resembled a person eighty or ninety years old.
His eyeballs protruded,
and his beard was curled like a hedgehog.
He said:
"As a youth, I received the king's command
and served as envoy most frequently;
only I have never been to Zhōnghuá.
Now I am over one hundred and twenty years old,
and have had the good fortune to see people from the superior country.
This must surely be reported to the Son of Heaven.
However, I have been living in seclusion,
and for over ten years have not trod the court steps.
Early tomorrow,
I will go for you."
Then he prepared food and drink,
observing the rites of host and guest.
After several rounds of wine,
he brought out over ten female musicians,
who sang and danced in turns.
Their appearance resembled Yèchā,
all wrapped their heads with white silk,
and dragged crimson robes to the ground.
They performed songs of unknown lyrics,
with strange and grotesque melodies and rhythms.
The host looked at them and enjoyed it,
asking:
"Does Zhōngguó also have this kind of music?"
Mǎ said:
"Yes."
The host asked him to imitate their sound,
so Mǎ struck the table and performed a piece.
The host delightedly said:
"How extraordinary!
The sound is like a phoenix's cry and a dragon's roar;
I have never heard anything like it before."
The next day,
Láng hurried to court
and recommended Mǎ to the king.
The king joyfully issued an edict,
but two or three grand masters
spoke of Mǎ's strange appearance,
fearing it would alarm the sacred person.
The king then stopped.
Láng came out and told Mǎ,
deeply regretting it.
After staying for a long time,
he drank with the host and became drunk.
He took up a sword and danced,
painting his face with charcoal to imitate Zhāng Fēi.
The host thought it was beautiful,
saying:
"Please, sir, present yourself as Zhāng Fēi to the prime minister;
the prime minister will surely be pleased to employ you,
and a generous salary will not be difficult to obtain."
Mǎ said:
"Alas!
Such antics are permissible,
but how can I change my appearance to seek glory and prominence?"
The host insisted,
so Mǎ agreed.
The host arranged a banquet,
inviting powerful officials to drink,
and ordered Mǎ to paint his face and await them.
Before long,
the guests arrived,
and called Mǎ out to meet them.
The guests marveled, saying:
"How strange!
How was he so ugly before and now so beautiful!"
Then they drank together,
very merrily.
Mǎ sang and danced gracefully
the 'Yìyáng tune',
and everyone present was captivated.
The next day,
memorials were submitted one after another, recommending Mǎ.
The king was pleased,
and summoned him with an official banner and credentials.
Upon meeting him,
he asked about the methods of governance in Zhōngguó.
Mǎ explained in detail,
and was greatly praised and admired.
He was granted a banquet in the detached palace.
When the wine was in full flow,
the king said:
"I hear, my lord, that you are skilled in elegant music;
could you let this solitary one hear it?"
Mǎ immediately rose and danced,
also imitating the white silk head-wrap,
and performed a sensuous melody.
The king was greatly delighted,
and on that very day appointed him as a Grand Master of the Lower Rank.
He frequently held private banquets with him,
and his favor and grace were exceptionally special.
After a long time,
the numerous officials in the bureaucracy somewhat perceived his appearance as false;
wherever he went,
people would whisper to each other,
and not be particularly cordial with him.
By this point, Mǎ was isolated,
and felt uneasy.
So he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but it was not granted;
he then requested leave for rest and bathing,
and was granted three months' leave.
Thereupon, he took a post-chaise laden with gold and treasures,
and returned to the mountain village.
The villagers knelt to welcome him.
Mǎ distributed the gold and resources to those with whom he had previously been on good terms,
and shouts of joy resounded like thunder.
The villagers said:
"We humble folk receive the beneficence of the dàfū.
Tomorrow we go to the Hǎishì [Sea Market],
and shall seek rare curios
to repay the dàfū."
[The scholar] asked:
"Where is the Hǎishì?"
[The villager] replied:
"It's a market in the sea.
Jiāorén from the Four Seas
gather there to trade pearls and treasures;
the twelve kingdoms from the four directions
all come to trade.
Many divine beings play within it.
Clouds and mists obscure the sky,
and waves rise intermittently.
Noble people value themselves highly
and dare not venture into such perils;
they all entrust us with gold and silk
to purchase exotic treasures on their behalf.
The time for it is not far off now."
When asked how he knew,
he replied:
"Every time we see crimson birds flying back and forth over the sea,
in seven days,
the market will open."
Mǎ asked about the departure date,
wishing to go and see for himself,
but the villagers advised him to value his noble status.
Mǎ said:
"I am but a guest of the deep sea;
what do I fear from wind and waves?"
Not long after,
indeed, people came knocking on his door to deposit funds,
so he embarked on a boat with those who had supplied the capital.
The boat could hold dozens of people,
with a flat bottom and high railings.
Ten people rowed,
propelling the water like an arrow.
After three days in total,
they saw a layered structure of towers and pavilions
shimmering in the distant water and clouds;
trading boats
clustered like ants.
A short while later,
they reached the base of the city.
Looking at the bricks on the wall,
they were all as long as a person.
The watchtowers reached high into the clouds and the Milky Way.
Mooring their boat, they entered,
and saw displayed in the market
rare and exotic treasures,
their brilliance dazzling to the eye,
many of which were unknown in the human world.
A young man rode up on a swift horse,
and the market people all scattered,
saying it was
the Dōngyáng Sān Shìzǐ [Third Prince of the Eastern Ocean].
After the shìzǐ passed,
he looked at the scholar and said:
"Is this not a person from a foreign land?"
Immediately, someone on horseback came forward to inquire about his native place.
The scholar bowed by the roadside,
fully disclosing his lineage.
The shìzǐ joyfully said:
"Since you have graced us with your presence,
our缘分yuánfèn is not shallow!"
Thereupon, he offered the scholar a horse to ride,
inviting him to ride alongside.
They then exited the west city.
Just as they reached the island shore,
the horse he was riding neighed and leaped into the water.
The scholar was greatly terrified and cried out,
then saw the seawater part,
standing firm like a wall.
Soon after, he beheld a palace,
with tortoiseshell for beams,
and dace scales for tiles;
the four walls were crystal clear,
reflecting images and dazzling the eyes.
He dismounted and bowed to the people.
Looking up, he saw the Lóng Jūn [Dragon Lord] seated above,
and the shìzǐ reported:
"Your subject, while strolling through the market,
met an eminent scholar from Zhōnghuá [China],
whom I present to Your Majesty."
The scholar came forward and bowed.
The Lóng Jūn then said:
"Sir is a literary scholar,
and must be capable of surpassing Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù.
I wish to trouble your brilliant brush to compose a rhapsody on the 'Hǎishì,'
I hope you will not be sparing with your pearls and jades [words]."
The scholar bowed his head and accepted the command.
He was given a crystal inkstone,
a dragon's mane brush,
paper as bright as snow,
and ink fragrant as orchids.
The scholar immediately composed over a thousand words,
and presented them in the palace hall.
The Lóng Jūn struck the rhythm and exclaimed:
"Sir possesses magnificent talent,
bringing glory to the Water Kingdom!"
He then gathered all the dragon clans
and hosted a banquet in the Cǎixiá Gōng [Palace of Luminous Clouds].
After several courses of wine and roast meat,
the Lóng Jūn raised his goblet and addressed the guest:
"My beloved daughter
has not yet found a worthy match,
and I wish to trouble you, sir.
Sir, would you perhaps be interested?"
The scholar left his seat, feeling ashamed and honored,
merely assenting.
The Lóng Jūn then looked at his attendants and spoke.
Presently,
several palace maids
escorted the maiden out.
Jewelry jingled,
and drums and wind instruments erupted.
After bowing,
he stole a glance at her;
she was truly an immortal.
The maiden bowed and departed.
A short while later, the banquet ended,
and a pair of maids with coiled hair picked up painted lanterns,
leading the scholar to a side palace.
The maiden, heavily adorned, sat waiting.
The coral bed
was decorated with eight treasures;
tassels outside the curtain
were adorned with pearls as large as dippers;
the quilts and mattresses were all fragrant.
As dawn broke,
young maidens and enchanting maids
rushed in and filled the sides.
The scholar rose
and hurried out to offer his thanks in court.
He was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi [Commander of the Imperial Son-in-Law].
His rhapsody was then widely circulated throughout the seas.
All the Lóng Jūn of the seas
came to offer their congratulations;
they vied to send invitations to the fùmǎ for drinks.
The scholar wore embroidered robes,
rode a qíngqiú [green hornless dragon],
and exited with attendants shouting "Make way!".
Dozens of warrior cavalry,
with carved bows on their backs
and white lances carried,
gleamed and thronged around him.
Zithers were played on horseback,
and jade chimes in carriages.
In three days,
he toured all the seas.
From this,
the name "Lóngméi" [Dragon Match]
resounded throughout the Four Seas.
In the palace there was a jade tree,
its circumference about an arm's embrace;
its trunk was clear and transparent,
like white glass,
with a core
of pale yellow,
slightly thinner than an arm;
its leaves resembled green jade,
about one qián thick,
tiny and providing dense shade.
He often recited poetry and sang with his wife beneath it.
Flowers bloomed all over the tree,
shaped like [lacquerware].
Each time a petal fell,
it made a clanging sound.
Picking it up and examining it,
it was like a piece of carved red agate,
bright and lovely.
From time to time, exotic birds came to sing,
their feathers golden and green,
their tails longer than their bodies,
their voices like mournful jade,
piercing one's heart.
When the scholar heard them,
he invariably thought of his homeland.
He then said to his wife:
"It has been three years since I left,
separated from the kindness of my parents.
Every time I think of it,
tears stream down my face and sweat covers my back.
Can you return with me?"
The maiden replied:
"The path between immortals and the mortal world is blocked,
we cannot rely on each other.
I also cannot bear to let the love between husband and wife
deprive you of the joy of being with your parents.
Allow me to gradually plan for it."
When the scholar heard this,
he could not stop his tears.
The maiden also sighed:
"This is a situation where both cannot be had!"
The next day,
the scholar returned from outside.
Lóng Jūn said:
"I hear Dūwèi has thoughts of his homeland.
Will you be ready to depart at dawn? "
The scholar thanked him, saying:
"A lonely official in a foreign land,
I have been excessively favored.
My sincerity in repayment
is deeply rooted in my heart.
Allow me to return home temporarily to visit my parents;
we shall plan to reunite then. "
As night fell,
the woman set out wine to bid farewell.
The scholar made a pact for a future meeting.
The woman said:
"Our destined relationship is over."
The scholar was greatly saddened.
The woman said:
"Return to nourish your parents;
this shows your filial piety.
Human gatherings and partings,
a hundred years are but a day and night.
Why lament like children?
Hereafter, I will be chaste for you,
and you will be righteous for me.
With our hearts united from two places,
we are truly husband and wife.
Why must we be together day and night
to call it growing old together?
If this vow is broken,
the marriage will not be auspicious.
If you are concerned about a lack of help in the household,
taking a maidservant is acceptable.
There is one more thing I wish to entrust to you: from the clothes I have worn
there seems to be a propitious sign;
please name our child."
The scholar said:
"If it is a girl,
she may be named Lónggōng;
if a boy,
he may be named Fúhǎi."
The woman asked for an object as a token.
The scholar took out a pair of red jade lotus flowers he had obtained in Luóchà Guó
and gave them to the woman.
The woman said:
"Three years from now, on the eighth day of the fourth month,
you should sail a boat to Nándǎo;
I will return your descendant to you."
The woman made a bag of fish leather,
filled it with pearls and jewels,
and gave it to the scholar, saying:
"Keep this treasured;
it will be enough for several generations to live on."
As dawn faintly broke,
the king set up an ancestral feast
and offered very generous gifts.
The scholar bowed in farewell and exited the palace.
The woman rode in a white sheep chariot,
seeing him off to the sea.
The scholar disembarked and got off his horse.
The woman bid him to take care,
turned her chariot, and departed,
quickly disappearing from view.
The sea, having parted, closed again,
and she could no longer be seen.
Shēng then returned.
He had gone off, floating on the sea,
and everyone believed him dead;
when he arrived home,
his family members were all astonished.
Fortunately, his parents-in-law were unharmed,
but his wife had already remarried.
He then understood Lóngnǚ's
"uphold righteousness"
words,
which were indeed prescient.
His father wanted Shēng to remarry;
Shēng refused,
and instead took a maidservant.
Mindful of the three-year promise,
he boated to the island.
He saw two children sitting afloat on the water,
splashing and playing, laughing,
neither moving nor sinking.
When he approached and drew them near,
the children, with a gasp, grabbed Shēng's arm,
and leaped into his embrace.
One of them cried loudly,
as if angry that Shēng had not helped him.
He also lifted it up.
Examining them closely,
one was a boy and one a girl,
both with delicate and beautiful appearances.
On their foreheads, flower crowns adorned with jade
bore the red lotus.
On their backs were brocade pouches;
he opened them and looked,
and found a letter that read:
"My esteemed parents-in-law are both well, I trust.
Suddenly three years have passed,
the mortal dust forever separating us;
a vast stretch of water,
and even the blue bird cannot convey messages.
My thoughts coalesce into dreams,
my longing becomes weariness,
in the vast blue expanse,
what can one do with such regret!
Consider Cháng'é, who flew to the moon,
yet her laurel palace is empty;
Zhīnǚ, who casts her shuttle,
still laments the Silver River.
Who am I,
to hope for eternal bliss?
When thoughts turn to this,
I often break into tears and then laugh again.
Two months after we parted,
I gave birth to twins.
Now they are babbling in my arms,
and somewhat understand speech and laughter;
they seek dates and grasp pears,
and cannot live without their mother.
Respectfully, I return them to you.
The red jade lotus flower you gave me
adorns their crowns as a token of faith.
When you hold them on your knees,
it will be as if your concubine is by your side.
I heard you kept your old promise,
and my heart is greatly comforted.
This concubine will never be unfaithful in this life,
until death, I will have no other.
The precious items in my trousseau
do not include orchid ointment;
the new makeup in my mirror
has long abandoned powders and paints.
You are like a man on a campaign,
I am like a abandoned wife,
even if left untouched,
how can it be said that we are not like a qín and sè?
I alone consider that my esteemed parents-in-law have already embraced their grandchildren,
yet have never once seen their daughter-in-law,
judging by sentiment and reason,
this is indeed a deficiency.
A year later, when Mother's funeral takes place,
I will come to the grave
to fulfill a daughter-in-law's duty.
Beyond this,
the 'Lónggōng'
is safe and sound,
and there will be many opportunities to visit;
the 'Fúhǎi'
is eternal,
and there may be a way to return and forth.
I humbly implore you to take care,
I cannot express all I wish to say."
Shēng repeatedly read the letter, clutching it and shedding tears.
The two children embraced his neck and said:
"Let's go home!"
Shēng became even more distraught,
and caressed them, saying:
"Children, do you know where home is?"
The children cried,
babbling about going home.
Shēng looked at the vast, boundless sea,
reaching the sky without limit;
the person with misty hair was distant,
the path through the misty waves was exhausted.
He embraced the children, turned his boat back,
and sadly returned home.
Shēng knew his mother's life would not be long,
so he prepared all her burial items in advance,
and planted over a hundred pine trees in the tomb.
A year later,
his mother indeed passed away.
When the funeral carriage reached the burial ground,
a woman appeared at the grave.
Everyone was surprised and looked around,
when suddenly wind raged and thunder roared,
followed by heavy rain,
and in an instant she was gone.
Many of the newly planted pines and cypresses had withered,
but at this point, they all revived.
Fúhǎi, as he grew older,
often thought of his mother,
and would suddenly throw himself into the sea,
only returning after several days.
Lónggōng, because a woman could not go there,
would sometimes close her door and weep.
One day,
at dusk,
Lóngnǚ suddenly appeared,
and stopped her, saying:
"You have already established your own family,
why do you weep?"
She then bestowed a coral tree eight feet tall,
a block of dragon's brain incense,
a hundred bright pearls,
and a pair of golden boxes inlaid with eight treasures,
as dowry.
Shēng, hearing this, burst in,
and grasped her hand, weeping.
In a moment,
a violent thunderbolt struck the house,
and the woman was already gone.
Yìshǐshǐ says:
"Flowery faces seeking favor,
worldly sentiments are like ghosts.
The habit of indulging in perversions
is the same throughout the world.
'A little shame is a little good,
great shame is great good.'
If one were to openly stroll through the city with a beard and eyebrows,
few would not be shocked and flee.
That foolish boy of Língyáng,
where will he go to weep with his invaluable jade?
Alas!
Glory, prosperity, and wealth
should be sought in mirages and sea markets!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wǔ Chéngxīu,
a person from Liáoyáng.
He enjoyed socializing,
and all those with whom he associated were famous scholars.
One night, he dreamt that a person told him:
"Your acquaintances span the entire realm,
but they are all merely casual friends.
Only one person can share a crisis with you,
why do you not recognize him?"
He asked:
"Who?"
The person said:
"Is it not Tián Qīláng?"
He awoke, finding it extraordinary.
The next morning,
he saw those with whom he was acquainted,
and invariably asked about Qīláng.
Some guests recognized him as a hunter from Dōngcūn.
Wǔ respectfully visited the various households,
knocking on their doors with his horse whip.
Before long,
a person emerged,
in his twenties,
with bee-like eyes and a wasp waist,
wearing a greasy turban,
and a black loincloth,
with many white patches.
He cupped his hands to his forehead and asked Wǔ about his origin.
Wǔ introduced his surname and given name;
and also feigned discomfort from his journey,
asking to borrow a hut to rest.
He asked for Qīláng,
who replied:
"I am he."
So, he invited the guest in.
They saw a few dilapidated rafters of a house,
with wood supporting the walls.
Entering a small room,
tiger skins and wolf pelts
hung between the pillars,
with no bed or couch to sit on.
Qīláng spread a tiger skin on the ground for him.
Wǔ conversed with him,
and found his words simple and unadorned, which pleased him greatly.
He immediately offered him gold to make a living,
but Qīláng refused it.
Wǔ insisted on giving it,
and Qīláng accepted it to show his mother.
Soon after, he was about to return it,
resolutely declining.
Wǔ pressed him repeatedly.
His mother, old and frail,
arrived,
and sternly said:
"This old woman has only this one son;
I do not wish him to serve an esteemed guest!"
Wǔ felt ashamed and withdrew,
tossing and turning on his way home,
unable to understand her meaning.
It so happened that his attendant, having heard the mother's words from behind the house,
told Wǔ about it.
Earlier,
Qīláng had brought the gold to show his mother,
and she said:
"I just saw the young master;
he has a dark mark on his face,
and will surely suffer a terrible calamity.
I have heard: he who receives another's trust shares his worries;
he who receives another's kindness hastens to help him in difficulty.
The rich repay others with wealth,
the poor repay others with righteousness.
To receive a large bribe without cause
is inauspicious,
I fear it may lead to your death to repay him."
Wǔ heard this,
and deeply praised the mother's wisdom;
but he admired Qīláng even more.
The next day,
he set up a banquet and invited him,
but he declined to come.
Wǔ went to his hall,
sat down and asked for a drink.
Qīláng personally served wine,
and laid out venison jerky, treating him with utmost sincerity and courtesy.
The next day,
Wǔ invited him in return,
and he came.
They conversed happily and intimately.
Wǔ offered him gold,
but he immediately refused.
Wǔ then feigned wanting to buy a tiger skin,
and he accepted it.
Returning home to inspect his stock,
he found it insufficient to repay the amount,
and thought of hunting again before presenting it.
He entered the mountains for three days,
but caught nothing.
Then his wife fell ill,
and he stayed to look after her and prepare medicine,
having no time for his work.
Ten days passed,
and his wife suddenly died.
He arranged a vegetarian feast and burial for her,
and the gold he had received gradually ran out.
Wǔ personally attended the condolences and burial,
his courtesy and generosity were abundant.
After the burial,
carrying his crossbow, he entered the mountains and forests,
thinking even more about how to repay Wǔ,
but still found nothing.
Wǔ discovered his reason,
and always advised him not to rush.
He sincerely hoped Qīláng would visit him just once;
but Qīláng remained regretful about his debt,
and refused to come.
Wǔ then first asked for an old tiger skin from his collection,
to hasten his visit,
but when Qīláng inspected the old hide,
it was worm-eaten and damaged,
all the fur had fallen off,
and he became even more dejected.
Wǔ learned of this,
rushed to his courtyard,
and did his utmost to comfort him.
He then looked at the damaged hide,
saying:
"This is fine too.
What I wanted
was not originally for its fur."
So, he rolled it up and took it,
and also invited him to come along.
Qīláng refused,
so Wǔ returned alone.
Qīláng thought that he could never repay Wǔ sufficiently,
so he packed provisions and entered the mountains.
After several nights,
he caught a tiger,
whole, and presented it to him.
Wǔ was delighted,
prepared a feast,
and asked him to stay for three days.
Qīláng firmly declined.
Wǔ locked the courtyard gate,
preventing him from leaving.
The guests, seeing Qīláng's simple and rustic appearance,
secretly thought the young master was associating with unsuitable people,
but Wǔ mingled with Qīláng,
treating him quite differently from the other guests.
He offered him new clothes,
but he refused them;
so, Wǔ secretly exchanged them while he slept,
and he had no choice but to accept them.
After he left,
his son, obeying his mother's command,
returned the new clothes,
and asked for his old patched garment.
Wǔ laughed and said:
"Go tell the old woman that
the old clothes have already been cut up to line shoes."
From then on,
Qīláng sent him rabbits and deer daily,
but when summoned, he no longer came.
One day, Wǔ visited Qīláng,
but he was out hunting and had not returned.
His mother came out,
and spoke from the door, saying:
"Do not bring my son here again,
you have very ill intentions!"
Wǔ respectfully bowed to her,
and retreated in shame.
About half a year later,
his family suddenly reported:
「Qīláng, in a dispute over a hunting leopard,
beat a man to death
and has been arrested and taken to the yamen. 」
Wǔdà was alarmed,
and rode there to see him.
He had already been chained and imprisoned.
He saw Wǔ, but said nothing,
only saying:
「Please take care of my old mother hereafter. 」
Wǔ left with a heavy heart.
He immediately bribed the district magistrate with a large sum of money;
and also bribed the victim's family with one hundred gold coins.
After more than a month, without further incident,
Qīláng was released and returned home.
His mother said with emotion:
「My son's body and skin were received through Young Master Wǔ,
they are not something this old woman could cherish and protect.
I only wish that Young Master Wǔ will be free from calamities for the rest of his hundred years,
that would be my son's good fortune. 」
Qīláng wished to go and thank Wǔ,
but his mother said:
「If you want to live, then go;
but when you see the Young Master, do not thank him.
Small favors can be thanked,
but great kindness cannot be thanked. 」
Qīláng saw Wǔ;
Wǔ comforted him with warm words.
Qīláng simply assented.
All the family members found his aloofness strange;
but Wǔ rejoiced in his sincerity and earnestness,
and treated him even more generously.
From then on, [Qīláng] often stayed at Young Master Wǔ's house for several days.
He always accepted gifts,
no longer declining them,
nor speaking of repayment.
It happened to be Wǔ's first birthday celebration,
and there were many guests and retainers,
so at night, all the rooms were full of shoes.
Wǔ and Qīláng slept together in a small room,
while three servants laid down straw beneath the bed.
As the second watch was drawing to a close,
all the servants had fallen asleep,
but the two men were still chatting.
Qīláng's treasured saber, hanging on the wall,
suddenly sprang out of its scabbard by several inches,
making a "zheng-zheng" sound,
its light flashing like lightning.
Wǔ started up in alarm.
Qīláng also got up,
and asked:
"Who are those lying under the bed?"
Wǔ replied:
"They are all servants."
Qīláng said:
"There must be an evil person among them."
Wǔ asked why,
and Qīláng said:
"This sword was bought from a foreign land.
It has never been stained by blood when killing someone.
I have worn it for three generations now.
It has severed thousands of heads,
yet it is still as if newly sharpened.
When it sees an evil person, it hums and vibrates.
The time for killing must not be far off.
Young master should be close to gentlemen
and keep away from petty people;
perhaps by some chance, disaster can be avoided."
Wǔ nodded.
Qīláng remained restless,
tossing and turning on the bed.
Wǔ said:
"Fortune and misfortune are predetermined.
Why such deep worry?"
Qīláng said:
"I have no fear for myself at all,
it's just that my old mother is still alive."
Wǔ said:
"How could it come to that?"
Qīláng said:
"It would be good if it doesn't."
In fact, there were three people under the bed: one was Lín’ér,
an old favorite
who knew how to please his master;
one was a young servant,
twelve or thirteen years old,
whom Wǔ often employed;
and one Lǐ Yìng,
who was most stubborn and awkward,
often quarreling angrily with the young master over small matters.
Wǔ was constantly annoyed by him.
That night, Wǔ silently thought
that it must be this person.
The next morning,
he summoned him
and gently dismissed him.
Wǔ's eldest son, Shēn,
married a woman named Wáng.
One day,
Wǔ went out,
leaving Lín’ér to guard the house.
The chrysanthemums in the study were blooming brilliantly.
The new bride, thinking her father-in-law was out
and the study courtyard would be quiet,
went there herself to pick chrysanthemums.
Lín’ér suddenly rushed out to tease her.
The woman tried to flee,
but Lín’ér forcibly dragged her into a room.
The woman cried in resistance,
her face pale and her voice hoarse.
Shēn rushed in,
and Lín’ér finally released his grip and fled.
When Wǔ returned and heard of this,
he angrily searched for Lín’ér,
but he was nowhere to be found.
After two or three days,
it was learned that he had taken refuge with a certain Yùshǐ.
That official was in the capital,
and all household affairs were decided by his younger brother.
Wǔ, on the basis of their camaraderie,
wrote a letter demanding Lín’ér's return,
but the brother simply ignored it.
Wǔ grew even angrier,
presenting his case to the Yìzǎi.
Although a summons was issued,
the constables did not arrest him, nor did the Yùshǐ investigate.
As Wǔ was fuming with anger,
Qīláng happened to arrive.
Wǔ said:
"Your words have come true!"
He then told him the story.
Qīláng's face turned grim,
but he said not a word,
and then left directly.
Wǔ instructed his servants to search for Lín’ér.
Lín’ér returned at night
and was caught by the searchers,
who brought him before Wǔ.
Wǔ flogged him severely.
Lín’ér spoke insultingly to Wǔ.
Wǔ Shūhéng,
his uncle, who was an elder,
feared that his nephew's violent anger would lead to disaster,
and advised him that it would be better to deal with him by official law.
Wǔ agreed,
bound him, and sent him to the public court.
However, a letter from the Yùshǐ's family arrived by post;
the Zǎi released Lín’ér,
entrusting him to Jìgāng to depart.
Lín’ér grew even more audacious,
openly spreading rumors among the crowd, slandering the master's wife with illicit relations.
Wǔ was helpless,
so enraged he wished to die.
He rushed to the Yùshǐ's gate,
shouting curses.
Neighbors comforted and persuaded him to return home.
The next night,
a servant suddenly reported:
"Lín’ér has been cut into pieces
and his body dumped in the wilderness."
Wǔ was both surprised and delighted,
feeling somewhat vindicated.
Soon after, he heard that the Yùshǐ's family was suing him and his uncle,
so he went with his uncle to face questioning.
The Zǎi would not listen to their defense
and wanted to flog Shūhéng.
Wǔ loudly protested:
"Killing is a groundless accusation!
As for insulting and slandering Shēn,
I truly did it myself;
my uncle had nothing to do with it."
The Zǎi ignored him.
Wǔ glared, wanting to go forward,
but the constables restrained him.
The constables wielding the whips were all Shēn's household henchmen,
and Shūhéng was also old and frail;
before half the strokes were administered,
he had already died.
Seeing Wǔ's uncle dying,
the Zǎi did not investigate further.
Wǔ wailed and cursed,
but the Zǎi acted as if he heard nothing.
He then carried his uncle home,
lamenting and furious, without any plan.
He then thought of seeking Qīláng's counsel.
But Qīláng did not even pay a single condolence visit.
Wǔ secretly thought: I treated Qīláng not poorly,
why is he suddenly acting like a stranger?
He also suspected that Qīláng must have killed Lín’ér.
He then thought: if that were true,
why didn't he consult me?
So he sent someone to search for his home,
but upon arrival, it was locked and silent,
and the neighbors knew nothing of his whereabouts.
One day,
the Yùshǐ's brother was in the inner office,
lobbying the Zǎi.
While firewood and water were being brought in for the morning,
a woodcutter suddenly appeared before him,
put down his load, drew a sharp blade,
and rushed straight at him.
The Yùshǐ's brother panicked,
trying to block the blade with his hand,
but the blade fell, severing his wrist;
with another slash,
he finally severed his head.
The Zǎi was greatly startled
and fled.
The woodcutter still looked around wildly.
The constables quickly shut the yamen gate
and shouted while brandishing their staffs.
The woodcutter then committed suicide by slitting his own throat.
People gathered in a flurry to identify him,
and those who knew him recognized him as Tián Qīláng.
After the Zǎi calmed down,
he came out again to examine the body.
He saw Qīláng lying stiff in a pool of blood,
his hand still gripping the blade.
As he paused to examine him closely,
the corpse suddenly sprang up,
and severed the Zǎi's head,
then fell back down.
Yamen officials tried to arrest his mother and son,
but they had already been gone for several days.
When Wǔ heard of Qīláng's death,
he rushed to mourn him with utmost grief.
Everyone said that he was the one who instigated Qīláng.
Wǔ spent his fortune and pulled strings with those in power
to finally get exempted.
Qīláng's body lay abandoned in the wilderness for over thirty days,
