surrounded by birds and dogs.
Wǔ collected it and gave him a lavish burial.
His son wandered to Dēng,
changing his surname to Tóng.
He joined the military,
and through his merits rose to the rank of Tóngzhī Jiāngjūn.
When he returned to Liáo,
Wǔ was already over eighty,
and pointed out his father's grave to him.
The Yìshǐ Shǐ said:
"One who does not lightly accept a single coin
is indeed one who dares not forget a single meal.
How virtuous was the mother!
As for Qīláng,
his anger was not fully appeased,
and even in death he sought vindication—
how divine was that?
If Jīng Qīng could have done the same,
then there would be no regrets throughout a thousand years.
If such a person exists,
they can mend the holes in the net of heaven."
The ways of the world are vast and confusing;
I lament that Qīláng is too young.
Alas! "
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
in the *rénxū* year,
a woman of the Lǐ clan from Xíngcūn in the district,
whose husband had died,
was pregnant with a posthumous child.
Suddenly, her belly swelled like an urn;
suddenly, it contracted like a fist.
When she was about to give birth,
she could not deliver for a day and a night.
When they looked,
they saw a dragon's head;
as soon as it was seen, it would retract.
The family was greatly frightened
and dared not approach.
There was an old woman named Wáng Āo,
who burned incense and performed the Yǔ steps,
both pressing and chanting curses.
Soon after,
the placenta dropped,
and the dragon was no longer seen;
only several scales,
each as large as a cup.
Afterward, she gave birth to a girl,
whose flesh was clear and transparent like crystal,
and whose internal organs could be seen.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
before Wú Fān rebelled,
he once instructed his generals and soldiers: "Whoever can single-handedly capture a tiger,
I will generously reward him with emoluments and salary,
and he will be called
'Tiger-Slaying General'."
Among the generals was a man
named Bǎozhù,
as agile and nimble as a monkey.
A tall building was being constructed in the prince's residence,
and the main beams had just been erected.
Bǎozhù ascended by climbing the corner of the building,
reaching the top in an instant;
he stood on the ridge beam,
walked swiftly,
performing three or four circuits;
then,
he leaped down,
standing perfectly upright.
The prince had a beloved concubine
who was skilled at playing the *pípá*.
The *pípá* she used
had pegs made of warming jade,
and holding it would warm the room.
The concubine treasured it,
and unless the prince personally commanded it,
it would not be shown to others.
One evening at a banquet,
a guest requested to see its marvel.
The prince happened to be tired
and promised it for the next day.
At that time, Bǎozhù was at his side,
and said:
"Without receiving the prince's order,
your servant can retrieve it."
The prince sent someone to rush a message to his residence,
ordering internal and external guards to be prepared,
and then dispatched Bǎozhù.
Bǎozhù crossed over more than ten layers of walls
before reaching the concubine's courtyard.
He saw lights shining in the room,
but the door was locked,
and he could not enter.
Under the corridor, a parrot was roosting on a perch.
Bǎozhù then made a cat's meow;
afterward, he imitated the parrot's cry,
urgently shouting,
"Cat is coming!"
The sounds of flapping and struggling became frantic.
He heard the concubine say:
"Lǜnú, quickly go and see,
the parrot is being attacked and killed!"
Bǎozhù hid in a dark spot.
Soon, a maid carrying a lamp came out;
as soon as her body left the door,
Bǎozhù had already slipped in.
He saw the concubine guarding the *pípá* on a table
and promptly carried it out.
The concubine cried out in alarm,
"A thief is here!",
and all the guards rose.
They saw Bǎozhù fleeing with the *pípá*,
pursued him but could not catch him,
and arrows rained down.
Bǎozhù leaped onto a tree.
Below the wall there were originally more than thirty large locust trees;
Bǎozhù moved through the treetops
like a bird shifting branches;
when the trees ended, he climbed onto the roof;
when the roofs ended, he climbed onto the tower;
he flew and ran across halls and pavilions,
no less than if he had wings,
vanishing in an instant without a trace.
The guests were still drinking,
when Bǎozhù flew down with the *pípá* before the banquet,
the door still locked as before,
and the chickens and dogs silent.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
in the case of Yú Qī,
those implicated and executed
were most numerous in Qīxiá and Láiyáng counties.
One day,
hundreds of captives
were all massacred on the military exercise ground.
Blue blood covered the ground,
and white bones reached to the sky.
The kind-hearted officials
donated coffins
to the construction workers in Jǐchéng,
emptying all their timber.
Thus, many of those executed as "Eastern Ghosts"
were buried in the southern suburbs.
Around the *jiǎyín* year,
a scholar from Láiyáng came to Jìxià.
Two or three of his relatives and friends were also among those executed,
so he bought paper money and silk,
and poured libations to them in the overgrown wilderness.
He rented lodging from a monk in the lower monastery.
The next day,
he went into the city for business
and had not returned by dusk.
Suddenly, a young man
came to his room to visit.
Seeing that the scholar was not there,
he took off his hat, climbed onto the bed,
and lay on his back with his shoes on.
The servant asked who he was,
but he closed his eyes and did not answer.
When the scholar returned,
it was already twilight,
and he could not distinguish clearly.
He personally went to the bedside to ask him.
The youth stared and said:
"I am waiting for your master;
why do you pester me with questions?
Am I some rude guest?"
The scholar smiled and said:
"The master is here."
The young man immediately got up, put on his hat,
bowed, and sat down,
exchanging many pleasantries.
Listening to his voice,
it seemed familiar.
He urgently called for a lamp;
it was none other than Zhū Shēng from the same district,
who had also died in the calamity of Yú Qī.
Greatly alarmed, he retreated.
Zhū pulled him, saying:
"I and you are literary friends.
Why are you so heartless?
Though I am a ghost,
the memory of an old friend
burns brightly in my heart.
Now I have something to trouble you with;
I hope you will not scorn me as a strange creature."
The scholar then sat down
and asked what he requested.
Zhū said:
"Now my niece is widowed and without a partner;
I wish for her to manage my household.
I have repeatedly sent matchmakers,
but they always use the excuse of lacking a command from elders.
Please do not begrudge your eloquent favor."
Before this,
the scholar had a niece
who had lost her mother early
and was left to be raised by him,
only returning to her family at fifteen.
When she was brought to Jǐnán as a captive,
she heard her father had been executed,
and died from shock and grief.
The scholar said:
"She has her own father;
why ask me?"
Zhū said:
“Her father, as her paternal cousin, moved her coffin away,
and is not here now.”
He asked:
“Whom does your niece depend on now?”
She replied:
“She lives with an old woman neighbor.”
Shēng worried that a living person could not act as a ghost matchmaker.
Zhū said:
“If you grant your golden promise,
then please honor us with your jade presence.”
He then rose and clasped Shēng’s hand.
Shēng firmly declined,
asking:
“Where are we going?”
He replied:
“Just come along!”
Reluctantly, Shēng followed him.
After walking about a lì north,
there was a large village,
with several hundreds of households.
They arrived at a residence.
Zhū knocked on the door,
and an old woman immediately came out.
She swung open both doors,
and asked Zhū:
“What is it?”
He replied:
“Please inform the young mistress that her maternal uncle has arrived.”
The old woman turned back,
and a moment later reappeared,
inviting Shēng in.
She looked at Zhū and said:
“The two humble thatched rooms are too cramped,
I trouble you, young master, to wait outside the gate for a moment.”
Shēng followed her in.
He saw a half-mǔ wild garden,
with two small rooms arranged.
The niece, sobbing, greeted him at the door.
Shēng also wept.
Inside the room, the lamplight flickered.
The girl’s face was as beautiful and pure as when she was alive.
With fixed gaze and tearful eyes,
she asked about all her maternal aunt’s family.
Shēng said:
“Everyone is well,
but your maternal aunt has passed away.”
The girl then choked up and said:
“As a child, I received foster care from my maternal uncle and aunt,
yet I have not repaid even an inch of it.
I never expected to be buried first in a ditch,
which is truly a great regret.
Last year,
my paternal cousin moved father away,
not sparing a single thought for me;
hundreds of lì away,
I was desolate like an autumn swallow.
My maternal uncle did not consider my departed spirit to be discarded,
and also bestowed gold and silk;
I have already received them.”
Shēng then told her what Zhū had said,
and the girl lowered her head, speechless.
The old woman said:
“This young master previously entrusted Old Woman Yáng three or five times.
I thought it was a very good idea;
but the young lady was unwilling to act hastily on her own,
now that her maternal uncle is in charge,
this desire is finally satisfied.”
As she spoke,
a girl of seventeen or eighteen,
accompanied by a maid in green,
suddenly rushed in;
catching a glimpse of Shēng,
she turned to flee.
The niece pulled her skirt and said:
“There’s no need for that!
This is my maternal uncle,
not someone else.”
Shēng bowed to her.
The girl also curtsied.
The niece said:
“Jiǔniáng
is from the Gōngsūn clan of Qīxiá.
Her father was once from a prominent family,
but now he is also a 'pauper'
and
unhappily isolated.
She comes and goes with my son morning and evening.”
Shēng eyed her,
her smile curved like an autumn moon,
her blush like the morning clouds.
Truly she was a celestial being.
He said,
“One can tell she's from a noble family;
how could a person from a humble dwelling be so beautiful?”
The nephew smiled and said,
“And she's a female scholar,
greatly skilled in both poetry and lyrics.
I just received some instruction from her yesterday.”
Jiǔniáng faintly smiled and said,
“This little maid spoils people for no reason,
making my uncle feel cold.”
The nephew again smiled and said,
“Uncle, your 'broken string' has not yet been reattached.
Would such a young lady
be able to please you?”
Jiǔniáng laughed and ran out,
saying,
“This maid is acting like a lunatic!”
Then she left.
Though the words were close to jest,
Shēng was extraordinarily fond of her.
The nephew seemed to perceive this slightly,
and then said,
“Jiǔniáng's talent and beauty are unparalleled.
If Uncle doesn't suspect her to be 'filth,'
I will ask her mother.”
Shēng was greatly pleased.
However, he worried that a human and a ghost could not be a match.
The girl said,
“No harm.
She has a predestined connection with Uncle.”
Shēng then went out.
The girl saw him off,
saying,
“Five days from now,
when the moon is bright and people are quiet,
I will send someone to welcome you.”
Shēng reached outside the door
and did not see Zhū.
He craned his neck, looking west.
Half of the moon's carriage was in the sky,
and in the twilight he still recognized the old path.
He saw a dwelling facing south,
Zhū sitting on the doorstep.
He rose to meet him, saying,
“I have been waiting for a long time.
My humble abode now has the honor of your visit.”
They then held hands and entered,
expressing sincere thanks.
Zhū brought out a golden goblet and a hundred pearls,
saying,
“I have no other valuables.
This will serve as a token of betrothal.”
After a moment, he said,
“My home has some crude wine,
but it is only suitable for a humble room
and not enough to entertain a distinguished guest.
What can be done?”
Shēng thanked him and withdrew.
Zhū accompanied him midway
before they parted.
When Shēng returned,
his monks and servants gathered to ask questions.
He concealed the truth, saying,
“Those who speak of ghosts
are mistaken.
I just went to drink with a friend.”
Five days later,
Zhū indeed arrived,
tidying his shoes and shaking his clothes,
appearing very happy and comfortable.
As soon as he reached the courtyard,
he bowed immediately.
After a short while,
he smiled and said,
“Since your auspicious ceremony is complete,
and the celebration is tonight,
please trouble yourself to come along.”
Shēng said,
“Since there was no reply,
I have not yet sent the betrothal gifts.
How can the ceremony be suddenly complete?”
Zhū said,
“I have already conveyed them on your behalf.”
Shēng felt deeply grateful
and went with him.
They arrived directly at his sleeping quarters,
where the girl's niece, in splendid attire, was greeting him with a smile.
Shēng asked,
“When did you get married?”
The girl said,
“Three days ago.”
Shēng then took out the pearls he had been given
to help with his niece's dowry.
The girl declined three times before accepting,
and said to Shēng,
“I conveyed Uncle's intentions to Old Madam Gōngsūn,
and she was very pleased.
But she said that being old and having no other direct relatives,
she did not wish Jiǔniáng to marry far away,
and hoped that Uncle would come tonight to be a live-in son-in-law in her family.
Since their family has no sons,
you can go with your bride now.”
Zhū then led them away.
As the village came to an end,
the door of a dwelling opened,
and the two entered its hall.
Soon, someone announced,
“The Old Madam has arrived.”
Two green-clad maids
helped an old woman up the steps.
Shēng wanted to bow,
but the madam said,
“I am old and decrepit,
and cannot perform the rites.
We should dispense with formalities immediately.”
She then gestured to the green-clad maids
to serve wine and begin the feast.
Zhū then called his servants
to bring out separate dishes of food
and arrange them before Shēng;
they also set up a separate pot
to serve wine to the guest.
The dishes served at the banquet
were no different from the human world.
However, the host merely helped herself,
and did not particularly urge the guest to eat.
After the feast concluded,
Zhū returned.
A green-clad maid led Shēng away,
and into a room,
where Jiǔniáng was waiting by a bright candle.
They met and their feelings converged,
enjoying the utmost intimacy.
Originally,
Jiǔniáng and her mother
were being escorted to the capital.
Upon reaching the commandery,
her mother died, unable to bear the hardship,
and Jiǔniáng herself also arrived.
On the bed, recalling past events,
she choked up and could not sleep.
She then recited two quatrains:
“My silk skirt of yesteryear turned to dust,
I vainly regret my past life's karmic fruit.
Ten years of cold dew, moon in maple woods;
this night, first encounter with the spring in a painted chamber.”
“White poplars, wind, and rain surround a lonely grave,
who'd think the Yangtái cloud would form again?
Suddenly opening the carved gold casket to look,
bloodstains still dye the old silk skirt.”
As dawn approached,
she urged him, saying,
“You should leave for now,
lest you alarm the servants.”
From then on, he came by day and went by night,
greatly infatuated.
One evening,
he asked Jiǔniáng,
“What is the name of this village?”
She said,
“Láixiálǐ.
Many new ghosts in the village
gave it its name.”
Shēng heard this and sighed.
The girl said sadly,
“A thousand li of tender soul,
wandering endlessly;
mother and child, isolated and alone,
it is heartbreaking to speak of.
I hope you will remember the kindness of one night,
and collect my bones to bury them beside my mother's grave,
so that for a hundred years I may have a place to rest,
and even in death not perish.”
Shēng assented.
The girl said,
“The paths of humans and ghosts are different;
you should not linger long.”
She then gave Shēng a silk sock
and, shedding tears, urged him to part.
Shēng left sadly,
feeling deeply grieved as if he had lost something,
his heart heavy and reluctant to return.
He therefore passed by and knocked on the Zhū clan's door.
Zhū came out barefoot to meet him;
the nephew also rose,
his cloudy hair dishevelled,
surprised and coming to inquire.
Shēng felt distressed for a while
before finally recounting Jiǔniáng's words.
The girl said:
“My aunt [jìn shì] does not speak,
but I, too, have been contemplating this day and night.
This is not the human world,
and it is truly unsuitable to reside here long.”
Thereupon, they wept facing each other,
and he, too, departed with tears in his eyes.
He knocked at his lodging, returned to his bedchamber,
and tossed and turned until dawn.
He wished to find the tomb of Jiǔniáng,
but had forgotten to ask about its inscription.
When he returned at night,
the thousands of tombs were piled high,
and he completely lost the village path.
He sighed with regret and returned.
He unrolled and looked at the silk socks;
they were torn to shreds by the wind,
decayed like ashes.
So he packed his bags and headed east.
For half a year, he could not console himself.
He returned to Jìmén,
hoping for some encounter.
When he reached the southern suburbs,
the sun was already low.
He rested his carriage by a courtyard tree [tíng shù]
and went to the burial ground.
He saw only countless connecting graves [fén zhào wàn jiē],
his eyes lost in the dense wilderness;
ghost fires and fox cries [guǐ huǒ hú míng]
terrified his heart and eyes.
Startled and mournful, he returned to his dwelling.
Disheartened, he wandered about,
then turned his reins and headed east.
After about a li,
he saw from afar a young woman walking alone among the tombs,
her demeanor and expression
strangely similar to Jiǔniáng's.
He cracked his whip and went to look;
indeed, it was Jiǔniáng.
He dismounted to speak with her,
but the girl ran away,
as if she did not recognize him;
when he pressed closer again,
her face showed anger,
and she raised her sleeve to shield herself.
He suddenly called out
“Jiǔniáng!”,
and she vanished like smoke.
The Historian of the Unusual [yì shǐ shì] says:
“Fragrant grasses sink into the net,
blood fills the chest;
Dongshan [dōng shān] wears a pendant,
tears soak the mud and sand: In ancient times, there were filial sons and loyal officials
who were not understood by their rulers and fathers until death.
How could Gōngsūn Jiǔniáng, having been entrusted with a physical body,
harbor an unreleased resentment in her heart?
What lies between the spleen and diaphragm [pí gé jiān wù]
cannot be scooped out and shown to others.
What an injustice!”
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì [liáozhāi zhìyì shǒugǎo běn].
During the Xuāndé [xuāndé] reign,
the court still enjoyed cricket fighting [cù zhī zhī xì],
and crickets were levied from the populace annually.
This insect was not originally produced in the west;
there was a magistrate of Huáyīn [huáyīn lìng] who wished to flatter his superior,
so he presented one.
When it was tested in a fight and proved skillful,
a regular supply was then demanded.
The magistrate in turn imposed this on the lìzhèng.
Young gallants in the market [shì zhōng yóuxiá ér]
who obtained good ones would cage and raise them,
raising their price,
holding them as rare commodities.
The sly and cunning village headmen [lǐ xū huá xiá]
used this as an excuse to levy taxes on households,
and each time one cricket was demanded,
it would ruin the wealth of several families.
In the district, there was a man named Chéng Míng,
who pursued the profession of a child scholar [tóngzǐ yè]
but had long been unsuccessful.
He was naive and slow-witted,
so he was reported by the cunning headmen to serve as a lìzhèng [lǐzhèng] aide.
He tried every stratagem but could not escape.
Before the year was out,
his meager possessions were entirely depleted.
When the cricket levy came,
Chéng Míng dared not extort from households,
nor did he have anything to compensate with,
so he was distraught and wished to die.
His wife said:
“What good will death do?
It would be better to search for one yourself,
hoping for a one-in-ten-thousand chance.”
Chéng Míng agreed.
He went out early and returned late,
carrying bamboo tubes and copper wire cages,
exploring cracks in ruined walls and digging holes in dense grass patches.
He left no stone unturned,
but all was in vain;
even if he caught two or three,
they were weak and inferior, not meeting the requirements.
The magistrate strictly set a deadline for collection;
after more than ten days,
he was whipped a hundred times.
Pus and blood flowed between his thighs,
and he could no longer even move to catch crickets.
Tossing and turning by his bed,
he thought only of suicide.
At that time, a hunchbacked sorcerer came to the village,
capable of divination by spirits.
Chéng's wife gathered funds and went to inquire.
She saw red-clad young women and white-haired old women
filling the doorways.
Entering his dwelling,
she found a secret chamber with a curtain drawn,
and a perfumed table set up outside the curtain.
Those seeking answers would burn incense in a censer
and prostrate themselves twice.
The sorcerer, from the side, would look up at the sky and offer prayers on their behalf,
his lips moving,
uttering words unknown.
Everyone stood respectfully, listening.
A short while later,
a piece of paper was thrown out from behind the curtain,
which immediately revealed the questioner's inner thoughts,
without the slightest error.
Chéng's wife placed her money on the table,
burned incense and prostrated herself like the previous person.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the curtain stirred,
and a small piece of paper floated down.
She picked it up and looked;
it was not writing but a drawing: in the center, a palace-like pavilion was depicted,
resembling a Buddhist monastery.
Below a small hill behind it,
strange rocks lay scattered,
with dense thorny bushes,
and a black-headed man crouching there.
Beside him was a toad,
as if about to dance.
She examined it, but could not understand it.
However, when she considered crickets,
it seemed to strike a chord within her.
She folded it up and hid it,
and returned home to show it to Chéng.
Chéng repeatedly pondered,
"Could it be instructing me where to hunt for insects?"
He carefully observed the scene depicted,
and it truly closely resembled the Great Buddha Pavilion east of the village.
So he forced himself to get up, chose a staff,
and, holding the drawing, went to the back of the temple.
There was an ancient tomb rising majestically;
walking along the tomb,
he saw rocks crouching like scales,
exactly like those in the painting.
So amidst the weeds,
he listened intently and walked slowly,
as if searching for a needle in a haystack.
But his mind, eyes, and hearing were all exhausted,
and there was no trace or sound.
While he was still searching fruitlessly,
a scabby-headed toad suddenly leaped away.
Chéng was even more startled,
and hastily pursued it.
The toad entered the grass.
Following its tracks and parting the growth,
he saw an insect crouching at the root of a thorn bush;
he quickly pounced on it,
but it went into a stone hole.
He poked it with a sharp blade of grass,
but it wouldn't come out;
he poured water from a bamboo tube into it,
and it finally emerged.
Its appearance was extremely strong and nimble,
and he chased and caught it.
Upon careful inspection,
it had a huge body and a long tail,
a green neck and golden wings.
Overjoyed, he caged it and returned home,
the whole family celebrating as if
it were not merely a city or a precious jade disk.
He placed soil in a basin and nurtured it,
feeding it white crab meat and yellow chestnuts,
protecting and loving it with the utmost care,
keeping it until the deadline,
to fulfill his official obligation.
Chéng had a nine-year-old son,
who, seeing his father was not present,
secretly opened the basin.
The insect leaped out directly,
too swift to catch.
When he finally managed to grab it,
its leg had broken off and its abdomen was split open,
and it died in an instant.
The boy, terrified,
cried and told his mother.
His mother, hearing this,
turned deathly pale,
and cursed loudly, saying:
"You evil offspring!
Your death day has come!
When your father returns,
he will settle the score with you himself!"
The boy left, weeping.
Not long after, Chéng returned.
Hearing his wife's words,
he felt as if struck by ice and snow.
Angrily, he sought his son,
but the boy was nowhere to be seen.
When he found his body in the well,
his anger turned to grief,
and he cried out, almost fainting.
The couple sat in despair,
their cottage smokeless,
silently facing each other,
with no hope left.
As dusk approached,
they prepared to bury their son.
When they drew near and touched him,
he still had a faint breath.
Joyfully, they placed him on the bed,
and he revived in the middle of the night.
The couple's hearts were somewhat comforted.
But the cricket cage was empty.
Looking at it, they were heartbroken and speechless,
and dared not blame their son any further.
From dusk till dawn,
they did not close their eyes.
As the morning sun charioted forth,
they lay stiffly, lost in long sorrow.
Suddenly, they heard an insect chirping outside the door;
startled, they got up to look.
The insect was still there, exactly as before.
Joyfully, Chéng tried to catch it,
but it chirped once and leaped away,
moving quickly.
He covered it with his palm,
but it felt empty, as if there was nothing there;
the moment he lifted his hand,
it had already leaped away again, swiftly.
He hastily pursued it.
It turned a corner by the wall,
and he lost sight of it.
Pacing and looking around,
he saw an insect crouching on the wall.
Upon closer inspection,
it was small,
black and reddish,
definitely not the previous one.
Chéng, thinking it was too small,
dismissed it as inferior.
He hesitated, looking around,
searching for the one he had been pursuing.
The small insect on the wall suddenly leaped into his collar and sleeve.
He looked at it;
its shape resembled an earwig,
with plum-blossom-patterned wings,
a square head and long legs,
suggesting it might be a good one.
Pleased, he kept it.
He was about to present it to the yámen,
but was apprehensive that it might not be satisfactory,
so he decided to test it in a fight to observe it.
Among the village youths, there was one who was fond of such things,
and had tamed and raised an insect,
naming it
"Crab-shell Green,"
which he pitted daily against those of other young men,
always winning.
He wanted to use it to profit,
and so he demanded a high price for it,
but no one bought it.
He went directly to Chéng's house to visit him.
Seeing what Chéng possessed,
he covered his mouth and burst out laughing.
Then he took out his own insect,
and put it into the comparison cage.
Chéng looked at it;
it was enormous and powerful,
and he felt increased shame,
not daring to compete.
The youth insisted on it.
Chéng considered that keeping an inferior creature was ultimately useless,
so he might as well gamble on a laugh.
So they put both into the fighting basin.
The small insect lay motionless,
as stupid as a wooden chicken.
The youth laughed heartily again.
They tried poking its antennae with a pig's bristly hair,
but it still did not move.
The youth laughed again.
After repeatedly provoking it,
the insect suddenly became furious,
charged directly,
and they began to leap and strike each other,
making agitated noises.
In a moment, the small insect was seen leaping up,
spreading its tail and extending its antennae,
directly attacking the opponent's neck.
The youth was greatly alarmed,
and ordered them to stop.
The insect proudly chirped,
as if reporting its victory to its master.
Chéng was greatly pleased,
and as they were all admiring it,
a chicken suddenly darted over,
directly advanced to peck.
Chéng stood terrified, gasping.
Fortunately, the peck did not hit,
and the insect leaped away about a foot;
the chicken advanced aggressively,
pursuing and pressing upon it,
and the insect was already under its claws.
Chéng, in his haste, did not know how to save it,
stomping his foot and losing color.
Soon he saw the chicken stretching its neck, flapping and struggling;
upon closer inspection,
the insect had gathered on its comb,
biting hard and not letting go.
Chéng was even more surprised and delighted,
and picked it up and placed it in a cage.
The next day, he presented it to the magistrate.
The magistrate, seeing its small size,
angrily reprimanded Chéng.
Chéng recounted its unusual qualities,
but the magistrate did not believe him.
He tried having it fight other insects,
and all the other insects were defeated;
he then tried it against a chicken,
and it was indeed as Chéng had said.
So he rewarded Chéng.
He then presented it to the Fǔjūn.
The Fǔjūn was greatly pleased,
and with a golden cage, presented it to the Emperor,
detailing its abilities.
Once it entered the palace,
all the butterflies, mantises, yóulìtà, qīngsī'é… …
and all other unusual creatures contributed from all under Heaven,
were tested against it everywhere,
but none could surpass it.
Whenever it heard the sound of zithers and lutes,
it would dance in rhythm.
This made it even more extraordinary.
The Emperor was greatly delighted,
and issued an edict bestowing famous horses and silk brocades upon the Fǔchén.
The Fǔjūn did not forget its origin;
before long,
the magistrate, because of
"outstanding merit,"
became known.
The magistrate was pleased,
and exempted Chéng from labor service.
He also instructed the Xuésǐ,
to allow him to enter the county school.
From then on, he became famous for his skill in raising insects,
and repeatedly received special favor from the Fǔjūn.
Within a few years,
he had a hundred qǐng of land,
mansions with ten thousand rafters,
and thousands of cattle and sheep.
Whenever he went out,
his furs and horses surpassed those of old aristocratic families.
Yìshǐshì says:
"The Son of Heaven happens to use one object,
and may very well forget about it soon after;
but those who carry out the orders immediately make it a fixed rule.
Furthermore, with corrupt officials and oppressive functionaries,
people daily mortgage their wives and sell their children,
with no end in sight.
Therefore, every single step taken by the Son of Heaven
concerns the lives of the people,
and cannot be neglected.
It is unique that the son of the Chéng family, impoverished by harmful insects,
became rich through a cricket,
with splendid furs and horses.
When he was a lǐzhèng and suffered flogging,
how could he have expected to reach such a state!
Heaven was about to reward the honest and benevolent,
and thus made the Fǔchén and Lìngyǐn
both receive favor and protection because of the cricket.
It is said: when one person ascends to immortality,
even his chickens and dogs follow him to heaven.
Indeed!"
According to the manuscript version of Liáozhāizhìyì.
In the late Míng Dynasty,
locusts appeared between Qīng and Yǎn,
gradually gathering in Yí.
The magistrate of Yí was worried.
He retired to sleep in his office tent,
and dreamt that a xiùcai came to visit,
wearing a tall cap and green robes,
with a tall and imposing appearance.
He claimed to have a plan to control the locusts.
When asked,
he replied:
"Tomorrow, on the road to the southwest,
there will be a woman riding a large-bellied female donkey,
she is the Locust God.
Pity her,
and disaster can be averted."
The magistrate found this extraordinary,
prepared supplies, and went out to the south of the county.
He waited for the person,
and indeed there was a woman with a high topknot and a brown cloak,
riding alone on an old gray donkey,
slowly and haltingly passing north.
He immediately offered incense,
held up a cup of wine,
welcomed her and bowed on the side of the road,
grabbing the donkey so it could not leave.
The woman asked:
"Dàfū, what are you going to do?"
The magistrate then pleaded sorrowfully:
"My humble small county,
I beg you to pity us and free us from the locusts."
The woman said:
"It's regrettable that Liǔ Xiùcai is so talkative,
revealing my secret plan!
He should immediately bear the consequences himself;
as long as the crops are not damaged, it's fine."
She then finished three cups of wine,
and vanished instantly.
Later, when the locusts came,
they flew so thickly that they covered the sky and sun,
but they did not land on the crop fields,
only gathering on the poplars and willows.
Wherever they passed, all the willow leaves were eaten clean.
Only then did he realize that the xiùcai was the Willow God.
Some say:
"This was due to the magistrate's concern for his people."
Indeed it is!
According to the manuscript version of Liáozhāizhìyì.
In the 21st year of Kāngxī,
there was a severe drought,
from spring to summer,
the land was parched with no green grass.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month, there was a light rain,
and only then did people begin to plant millet.
On the eighteenth day, a heavy rain soaked the earth thoroughly,
and then beans were planted.
One day.
In Shíménzhuāng, there was an old man,
who saw two oxen fighting on the mountain in the evening,
and said to the villagers:
"A great flood is coming!"
So he took his family and relocated.
The villagers all laughed at him.
Before long,
rain poured down violently,
not stopping all night,
and the flat ground was several feet deep in water,
submerging all the houses.
One farmer abandoned his two children,
and with his wife, supported his elderly mother and fled to a high mound.
Looking down at the village,
it had already become a watery expanse,
and he no longer thought of his children.
When the water receded, he returned home,
and saw that the entire village had become ruins and graves.
He entered his door to look,
and only one house remained,
with his two children sitting together at the head of the bed,
playing and laughing, unharmed.
Everyone said this was the reward for the couple's filial piety.
This happened on the twenty-second day of the sixth month.
In the 34th year of Kāngxī,
there was an earthquake in Píngyáng,
and seven or eight out of ten people died.
The city walls and outer walls were completely ruined;
only one house remained,
and that was the home of a certain filial son.
Amidst the vast catastrophe,
only the filial descendants were unharmed;
who can say that Heaven is indiscriminating?
According to the manuscript version of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A certain Mǒu Jiǎ, a student of Master Sūn Jǐngxià, related: In his town, a certain Mǒu Jiǎ
encountered a rebellion by wandering bandits [liúkòu]
and was killed,
his head falling onto his chest.
When the bandits retreated,
his family found the corpse
and prepared to carry it away for burial.
They heard a faint breath from him;
upon careful examination,
they found his windpipe was not completely severed, connected by a thread barely a finger's width.
So they supported his head
and carried him home.
He began to groan after a day and a night,
and they gradually fed him food and drink with a spoon and chopsticks.
He fully recovered after half a year.
More than ten years later,
he was chatting with two or three people,
and someone made an amusing remark,
at which everyone burst into laughter.
Mǒu Jiǎ also clapped his hands.
In that instant, as he lowered and raised his head,
the old knife scar violently split open,
his head fell off, and blood flowed.
They all looked at him,
and his breath had already ceased.
His father sued those who had laughed.
The crowd pooled money to bribe him,
and also buried Mǒu Jiǎ.
Only then was the matter settled.
Yìshǐ Shì remarked:
"A laugh that caused a head to drop—
this is the greatest laugh of all time!
To have a neck connected by a single thread and not die,
only to await ten years later to create a 'laughter-induced case'—
surely those two or three neighbors were repaying a debt from a previous life!"
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
Duke Zhāng Huádōng of Zōupíng
was ordered to offer sacrifices at Nányuè.
On his way through the Jiānghuái region,
he was about to lodge at an inn.
His vanguard reported:
"There is something strange at this inn;
staying there will certainly lead to trouble."
Zhāng did not listen.
In the middle of the night,
he sat with his hat and sword.
Soon he heard someone entering;
it was an old man with grizzled hair,
wearing a black gauze hat and a black belt.
Surprised, Zhāng asked him,
and the old man bowed his head, saying:
"I am the treasury official.
I have been guarding your Excellency's treasures for some time.
Fortunately, your high authority [jiéyuè] has arrived from afar,
and your humble servant can be relieved of this heavy burden."
Zhāng asked:
"How much is in the treasury?"
He replied,
"Twenty-three thousand five hundred taels of gold."
Fearing that such a large sum would be a nuisance,
Zhāng agreed to verify it upon his return.
The old man assented and withdrew.
When Zhāng arrived in the Nánzhōng region,
his offerings and gifts were quite abundant.
Upon his return,
he lodged at the inn again,
and the old man reappeared to greet him.
When asked about the treasury's contents,
he said:
"It has already been allocated as military provisions for Liáodōng."
Zhāng was deeply surprised by the discrepancy between the two accounts.
The old man said:
"In the human world, one's fortune and destiny [lùmìng]
all have a fixed amount;
not a fraction can be added or subtracted.
On this journey, your Excellency
has already received the amount you were destined to obtain,
so what more do you seek?"
Having spoken,
he departed.
Zhāng then calculated what he had gained,
and it exactly matched the amount the old man had stated was in the treasury.
He then sighed, realizing that one's sustenance is predestined,
and one cannot seek it presumptuously.
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
Outside Dūxiàn there was a cave,
unfathomably deep,
which was traditionally believed to be the office of Yánluó Tiānzǐ.
All the instruments of torture within it
were made by human hands.
When the stocks and fetters rotted away,
they were thrown at the mouth of the cave,
and the county magistrate would replace them with new ones,
which would disappear overnight.
The cost of these supplies
was recorded in the regular budget.
In the Míng dynasty, there was Censor-in-chief [Yùshǐ Xíngtái] Huá Gōng.
When he inspected Dū,
he heard this account
and did not believe it,
wishing to enter the cave to resolve his doubts.
People repeatedly told him it was impossible.
The Duke did not listen,
and holding a candle, he entered,
accompanied by two servants.
He penetrated about a *lǐ* deep,
when the candle suddenly went out.
He looked around
and saw a wide and bright staircase,
leading to more than ten grand halls,
where respected officials [zūnguān] sat in rows,
solemnly robed and holding their ceremonial tablets; only the seat to the east was empty.
The respected officials, seeing the Duke arrive,
descended the steps to greet him,
and smilingly asked:
"You have arrived?
Are you well since we last met?"
The Duke asked:
"What place is this?"
The respected officials said:
"This is the Underworld [Míngfǔ]."
The Duke was astonished and requested to leave.
The respected officials pointed to the empty seat and said:
"This seat is for you;
how can you return?"
The Duke became even more frightened
and earnestly pleaded for mercy.
The respected officials said,
"How can a fixed destiny be escaped?"
They then pulled out a scroll and showed it to the Duke,
on which was written:
"On a certain month and day,
so-and-so will return to the yin realm with his inner body."
The Duke read it,
trembling as if plunged into ice water.
Thinking of his aged mother and young son,
he wept bitterly.
Presently, a divine figure in golden armor
arrived, bearing a yellow silk book.
The officials all bowed and danced, and after opening and reading it,
they congratulated the Duke, saying:
"You have a chance to return to the yang realm!"
The Duke joyfully asked why.
They replied:
"We have just received an imperial edict [dìzhào]
granting a great amnesty to the Underworld [Yōumíng].
This allows us to make an exception for you;
it is a matter of precedent."
Then they showed the Duke the path out.
A few paces beyond,
it was pitch black,
making the path indistinguishable.
The Duke was in great distress.
Suddenly, a divine general [shénjiàng]
entered majestically,
with a red face and long beard,
radiating light several feet around him.
The Duke greeted him with a bow and appealed to him.
The divine person said:
"Recite Buddhist sūtras, and you can leave."
Having spoken, he departed.
The Duke realized he did not remember many sūtras or incantations,
but he had quite thoroughly studied the *Jīngāng Jīng*.
Thus, he clasped his hands and recited it.
Immediately, he felt a ray of light
illuminating the path ahead.
If he suddenly forgot a line,
the path before him would instantly darken;
after concentrating for a while,
he would recite again, and it would brighten again.
Only then was he able to exit.
As for his two accompanying servants,
they were never seen again.
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
In Yíshuǐ, there was a great rain,
and suddenly a dragon fell from the sky.
Both of its eyes were gone,
but it still had a faint breath.
The county magistrate covered it with eighty mats,
but they were not enough to cover its whole body.
He also set up a rural sacrifice for it.
It still repeatedly struck the ground with its tail,
making a resounding noise.
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
Wàn Fú,
courtesy name Zǐxiáng,
was a native of Bóxīng.
As a child, he studied Confucianism.
His family was not wealthy, and his fortune was exceptionally bad;
at over twenty years of age,
he still could not even pluck a single celery stalk (i.e., pass an entry-level examination).
Among the degenerate customs of his village,
it was common for wealthy households to be nominated for official service,
leading to the ruin of upright individuals.
Wàn Fú was just nominated for service,
so he fled in fear,
to Jǐnán,
renting a room in an inn.
One night, a woman rushed in,
her appearance quite beautiful.
Wàn Fú was pleased and took her as his mistress,
asking her surname.
The woman said of herself:
"I am actually a fox,
but I will not bring harm upon you."
Wàn Fú was delighted and harbored no doubts.
The woman instructed him not to share her with other guests,
and so she came daily,
sleeping and living with him.
All daily necessities
were provided by the fox.
Not long after,
two or three acquaintances
came to visit,
and often stayed overnight, unwilling to leave.
Wàn Fú was annoyed by them,
but could not bring himself to refuse;
having no other choice,
he told the guests the truth.
The guests wished to see the immortal lady's face.
Wàn Fú informed the fox.
The fox said to the guests:
"Why do you want to see me?
I am just like a human."
They heard her voice,
clear and distinct, seemingly right before them,
but looking around, they saw nothing.
Among the guests was Sūn Déyán,
who was good at humor,
and he insisted on seeing her,
further saying:
"Just hearing your sweet voice
makes one's soul fly;
why be so stingy with your beautiful face,
only making people yearn for you by your voice?"
The fox laughed and said:
"How virtuous, young Master Sūn!
Do you wish to create a pleasure painting for your great-grandmother?"
All the guests laughed.
The fox said:
"Since I am a fox,
may I speak with the guests about a fox story?
Would you perhaps like to hear it?"
The crowd assented.
The fox said:
"Once, in an inn in a certain village,
there were many foxes,
who often came out to harass travelers.
Travelers knew of this,
and warned each other not to stay at that inn,
so for half a year,
the place was deserted.
The host was greatly worried,
and was very reluctant to speak of foxes.
Suddenly, a traveler from afar came,
claiming to be from a foreign land,
and stopped at the gate to rest.
The host was overjoyed.
As soon as he invited him in,
a passerby secretly warned him: 'There are foxes in this house.'
The traveler was scared,
and told the host,
wishing to go elsewhere.
The host strongly denied it was true,
so the traveler stayed.
As he was about to lie down in the room,
he saw a group of rats emerge from under the bed.
The traveler was greatly alarmed,
and ran out quickly,
shouting urgently:
'There are foxes!'
The host asked in surprise.
The traveler complained: 'Foxes nest here,
why did you deceive me by saying there were none?'
The host then asked: 'What did you see?'
The traveler said: 'What I just saw,
was tiny and miniature,
if not a fox cub,
it must surely be a fox grandchild!'"
When she finished speaking,
the guests roared with laughter.
Sūn Déyán said:
"Since you will not grant us a sight,
we, who are staying overnight,
should not leave,
and thus obstruct your 'sunny terrace' (a euphemism for marital bed)."
The fox laughed and said,
"Staying over is no harm;
if there is any slight offense or transgression,
I hope you won't take it to heart."
The guests, fearing she would play a trick,
then dispersed.
However, they would come every few days,
seeking the fox's witty banter.
The fox was very humorous;
with every word,
she would confound the guests,
and even the wittiest could not best her.
The group playfully called her
"Hú Niángzi."
One day,
a banquet was held.
Wàn took the host's seat.
Sūn and two guests occupied the seats to the left and right,
with a couch set up above for Qū Hú.
Hú declined, saying she was not good at drinking.
Everyone requested her to sit and converse,
and she assented.
After several rounds of wine,
the company threw dice for a game called "Melon Vine" (guā màn zhī lìng).
When a guest hit the melon color,
it was his turn to drink.
Jokingly, he moved his drinking horn to the seat above and said:
"Lady Hú is very sober,
please lend me a cup for a moment."
Hú laughed and said:
"I truly don't drink.
I'd like to tell a story
to accompany you gentlemen in your drinking."
Sūn covered his ears, displeased to hear it.
The guests all said:
"Whoever insults someone should be punished."
Hú laughed and said:
"What if I insult a fox?"
The company said:
"That's fine."
Thereupon, they all leaned in to listen.
Hú said:
"Once, a high official
was dispatched as an envoy to the Red-haired Country (Hóngmáo Guó).
He wore a fox-fur cap
when he met the king.
The king saw it and was amazed,
asking: 'What kind of fur
is this, so warm and thick?'
The official replied, 'It's fox.'
The king said: 'I have never heard of such an animal in my life.
How is the character for "fox" (hú) written?'
The envoy traced the character in the air and reported: '
The right side is a large melon (dà guā), and the left side is a small dog (xiǎo quǎn).' "
The host and guests burst into laughter again.
The two guests,
the Chén brothers,
one named Suǒjiàn and
the other Suǒwén,
seeing Sūn in great distress,
said:
"Where is the male fox,
to allow such a female to spread venom like this?"
Hú said:
"That story
was not yet finished,
and I was interrupted by a pack of barking.
Please allow me to finish it.
The king saw the envoy riding a mule,
and was greatly astonished.
The envoy told him: 'This is born of a horse.'
The king was again greatly astonished.
The envoy said: 'In China, horses give birth to mules,
and mules give birth to foals (jūjū).'
The king inquired about its characteristics in detail.
The envoy said: 'Horses giving birth to mules
is
"what your humble servant has seen" (chén suǒjiàn);
mules giving birth to foals
is
"what your humble servant has heard" (chén suǒwén).' "
The entire company burst into laughter again.
Knowing they could not outwit her,
they made a pact: whoever initiated a joke next
would be penalized by hosting the next banquet.
A moment later,
when the wine was flowing freely,
Sūn jokingly said to Wàn:
"Please complete this couplet."
Wàn said:
"What is it?"
Sūn said:
"When a courtesan leaves her house to visit her lover,
she says 'Wànfú' when she arrives,
and 'Wànfú' when she leaves."
The whole company pondered but could not come up with a match.
Hú laughed and said:
"I have one!"
Everyone listened intently.
She said:
"The Dragon King issued a decree seeking frank advice,
the soft-shelled turtle said 'dé yán,'
and the hard-shelled turtle said 'dé yán.' "
Everyone present collapsed in laughter.
Sūn, greatly vexed, said:
"Just now we made a pact,
why have you broken the rule again?"
Hú laughed and said:
"The fault is indeed mine;
but without this,
it wouldn't be a perfect match.
I will host a banquet tomorrow morning
to atone for my transgression."
They laughed and dispersed.
Hú's wit
was inexhaustible.
After several months,
she returned home with Wàn.
Upon reaching the border of Bóxīng,
she told Wàn:
"I have a distant relative here.
Our contact has been long interrupted,
so I must pay a visit.
It is getting late,
let's stay overnight together,
and we can leave at dawn."
Wàn inquired about the location.
She pointed and said:
"Not far."
Wàn doubted there had been any villages there before,
but he humored her.
After about two li,
they indeed saw a manor,
which he had never seen in his life.
Hú went and knocked on the gate,
and an old servant came out to answer.
The house had multiple gates and layered pavilions,
just like a noble family's residence.
Soon, the host appeared,
an old man and an old woman,
who bowed to Wàn and invited him to sit.
A rich banquet was laid out,
and Wàn was treated as a family relation.
So he stayed there overnight.
Hú had told him earlier:
"If I return with you suddenly,
I fear it might be shocking to hear.
You should go first,
and I will follow."
Wàn followed her advice,
went first,
and informed his family beforehand.
Not long after,
Hú arrived.
She spoke and laughed with Wàn,
and everyone heard it,
but could not see her.
More than a year later,
Wàn again took up duties in Jǐ,
and Hú went with him.
Suddenly, several people came,
and Hú conversed with them,
exchanging many pleasantries.
Then she told Wàn:
"I am originally from Shǎnzòng.
I had a past affinity with you,
and so I followed you for this long.
Now my brothers have arrived,
and I will return with them.
I cannot continue to serve you."
He tried to persuade her to stay, but could not,
and she eventually left.
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A scholar from Bīnzhōu
was studying in his studio.
Someone knocked on the door.
He opened it to look,
and it was a white-haired old man,
whose appearance was very ancient.
He invited him in
and asked his name.
The old man said of himself:
"My name is Yǎngzhēn,
my surname is Hú,
and I am actually a fox immortal.
Admiring your refined elegance,
I wish to spend mornings and evenings with you."
The scholar was naturally broad-minded,
and was not surprised by this.
So they discussed and debated ancient and modern affairs.
The old man was remarkably knowledgeable;
his intricate and elaborate speech
flowed brilliantly from his teeth.
When he occasionally drew upon the classics,
his theories were profoundly deep,
and particularly beyond what the scholar could have imagined.
The scholar was astonished and impressed,
and kept him for a long time.
One day,
he secretly asked the old man,
"You have treated me very kindly.
Considering how poor I am,
if you just raise a hand,
money could be obtained instantly.
Why not give me a small handout?"
The old man was silent,
as if he did not think it advisable.
After a moment,
he smiled and said:
"This is a very easy matter.
But you need a dozen or so coins to use as a 'mother' coin."
The scholar complied with his request.
The old man then went with him into a secret room,
performed Yǔ steps, and chanted a spell.
In a moment,
millions of coins
clattered down from between the beams,
like a sudden downpour.
In a flash, they were knee-deep;
he lifted his feet and stood,
and they were ankle-deep again.
A room a *zhàng* wide
was filled to a depth of about three or four *chǐ*.
He then looked at the scholar and asked:
"Does this somewhat satisfy your wish?"
He replied:
"It's enough."
The old man waved his hand,
and the money immediately stopped with a sudden sound.
Then they opened the door together and came out.
The scholar secretly rejoiced,
thinking himself suddenly rich.
A little later,
he entered the room to take some,
only to find that all the "stuff" in the room had vanished,
with only the dozen or so "mother" coins sparsely remaining.
The scholar was disappointed,
and angrily confronted the old man,
somewhat blaming him for deceiving him.
The old man angrily said:
"I originally formed a literary friendship with you;
I did not intend to become a thief with you!
If it is as the scholar wishes,
you should only befriend those 'gentlemen on the beams';
this old man cannot obey the command!"
Then he brushed his sleeves and left.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain wealthy family in the western outskirts of Yìdū,
possessing immense wealth,
kept a concubine
who was quite gentle and beautiful.
However, the principal wife abused her,
whipping and lashing her harshly.
The concubine served her with the utmost care.
The master pitied her
and often secretly spoke words of comfort to her.
The concubine never once voiced a complaint.
One night,
dozens of people climbed over the wall and entered,
smashing his house door to pieces.
The master and his wife were terrified and distraught,
trembling and at a loss for what to do.
The concubine rose,
silently,
groped in the darkness of the room,
found a wooden pole for carrying water,
pulled the bolt, and rushed out.
The bandits were as disorderly as tangled hemp.
The concubine brandished her pole, and with a resounding *fèngmínggōu* sound,
struck four or five men to the ground.
The bandits all scattered,
startled and running chaotically towards the wall.
They struggled to climb it,
stumbling and crying out in dismay,
losing their souls and their lives.
The concubine propped her pole on the ground,
looked at them, and laughed, saying:
"These kind of fellows
are not even worth raising a hand to fight;
yet they try to act as thieves!
I will not kill you;
killing you would disgrace me."
She let them all escape.
The master was greatly astonished
and asked:
"How are you capable of this?"
It turned out that the concubine's father was a martial arts master,
and the concubine had inherited all his techniques,
being almost a match for a hundred men.
The wife was even more horrified,
regretting her past blindness to the concubine's true nature.
From then on, she treated the concubine kindly.
The concubine, in turn, never committed the slightest disrespect.
A neighbor woman once asked the concubine:
"Sister-in-law, you strike bandits like pigs and dogs,
yet why do you meekly submit to beatings?"
The concubine said:
"That is my lot;
how dare I speak otherwise."
Those who heard her respected her even more.
Yìshǐshì said:
"To possess extraordinary skills,
yet for several years no one knows of them,
and then eventually to defend against calamity and avert disaster,
transforming a hawk into a dove.
Alas!
When the pheasants are hunted and caught,
the inner woman smiles broadly;
when one wins at board games,
the noble lady shares the carriage.
The necessity of not abandoning one's skills
is truly thus!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Xú Yuǎngōng of Chángshān,
was a scholar in the former Míng dynasty.
After the dynastic change,
he abandoned scholarship and sought the Way,
gradually learning the art of *chìlè*.
His name was widely known far and wide.
A certain magnate from a certain county
prepared gifts,
sent a sincere invitation letter,
and summoned him with a horse.
Xú asked:
"What is the meaning of summoning me?"
The servant replied,
"I do not know.
I was merely instructed to respectfully invite you to come."
Xú then departed.
Upon arrival, there was a feast in the central courtyard;
the reception was exceedingly courteous, yet the reason for the invitation was never stated.
Xú grew impatient
and asked,
"What do you truly wish to do?
Please dispel my doubts."
The host simply said,
"Nothing at all,"
and merely urged him to drink.
His words were evasive
and utterly incomprehensible.
As they spoke,
unconsciously evening approached.
Xú was invited to drink in the garden.
The garden's construction was quite splendid,
but bamboo and trees cast deep shadows,
the scenery was eerie and dim,
and clusters of various flowers
were half-submerged among the weeds.
They reached a pavilion,
where the ceiling boards were covered with intricate spiderwebs,
of all sizes and positions,
too numerous to count.
After a few rounds of wine,
the sky grew dim,
and candles were lit for them to continue drinking.
Xú declined, saying he could not hold his liquor,
so the host immediately stopped the wine and called for tea.
The servants hastily cleared away the dishes
and placed them all on a table in the left room of the pavilion.
Before half the tea was sipped,
the host made an excuse and left.
A servant then held a candle and led Xú to stay in the left room.
The candle was placed on the table,
and the servant quickly turned and left,
quite abruptly.
Xú wondered if someone would bring a quilt and keep him company,
but after a long while,
the sound of people completely vanished.
He then got up and bolted the door to sleep.
Outside the window, the bright moon
entered the room and touched his bed;
night birds and autumn insects
chirped all at once.
His heart was anxious,
and he could not fall asleep.
A moment later,
there was a thumping sound on the boards above,
like footsteps,
very fierce.
Presently, a ladder was lowered,
and then it approached the bedroom door.
Xú was startled,
his hair stood on end,
and he hastily pulled the quilt over his head,
but the door had already swung wide open.
Xú cautiously peeked from under the corner of his quilt.
It was a creature,
with a beast's head and a human body;
its body was covered in fur,
as long as a horse's,
deep black;
its fangs gleamed like a cluster of peaks,
and its eyes glowed like two torches.
It reached the table
and squatted to devour the leftover food in the dishes;
with one swipe of its tongue,
several dishes were cleaned as if swept.
After that, it approached the bed
and sniffed Xú's quilt.
Xú suddenly rose,
flipped the quilt to cover the monster's head,
and pressed down, shouting wildly.
The monster, taken by surprise,
struggled free
and fled through the outer door.
Xú put on his clothes and tried to escape,
but the garden gate was bolted from the outside,
preventing his exit.
He ran along the wall,
chose a low section and climbed over,
finding himself in the host's stable.
The stableman was startled;
Xú explained the situation
and asked for a place to stay.
Just before dawn,
the host sent someone to look for Xú,
was greatly alarmed when he was not found,
and then
discovered him in the stable.
Xú emerged,
greatly resentful,
and angrily said,
"I am not accustomed to performing monster-expelling techniques: you sent for me,
and yet kept silent about it;
I have a rúyì gōu (如意鉤) in my bag,
but you did not deliver it to my sleeping quarters: this was meant to kill me!"
The host apologized, saying,
"I intended to tell you immediately,
fearing you would find it difficult.
Initially, I also did not know you had a hook hidden in your bag.
Please forgive me ten times over!"
Xú remained unhappy
and demanded a horse to return home.
From then on, the monster vanished completely.
Whenever the host held a banquet in the garden,
he would often laughingly say to his guests,
"I will never forget Xú-shēng's (徐生) contribution."
Yìshǐshì (異史氏) says:
"'Whether a yellow cat or a black cat,
the one that catches mice is the champion.'
This is not an empty saying.
If, after the wild shouts under the quilt,
he had concealed his fright,
and publicly claimed the monster's flight as his own achievement,
the world would certainly have deemed Xú-shēng (徐生) a true divine being, beyond compare."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
Máo Gōng (毛公), the Prime Minister from Yè Xiàn (掖縣),
came from a family of humble origins.
His father often herded cattle for others.
At that time, the Zhāng (張) family, a prominent clan in the county,
had a new burial ground on the sunny side of Dōng Shān (東山).
Someone passing by it
heard a scolding voice from within the tomb saying,
"You all quickly move away!
Do not long defile the residence of the noble one!"
Zhāng (張) heard this but
did not fully believe it.
Afterward, he frequently had dreams,
warning him:
"Your family's burial ground
is originally Máo Gōng's (毛公) auspicious resting place,
how can you occupy it for so long?"
Because of this, his family experienced several misfortunes.
A guest advised him to move the burial to an auspicious spot,
Zhāng (張) listened
and moved it.
One day,
the Prime Minister's father, while herding,
passed by the former Zhāng (張) family tomb
and was suddenly caught in the rain,
taking shelter in the abandoned burial pit.
Soon after, the rain intensified, pouring down,
and floodwaters rushed into the pit,
collapsing and filling it,
whereupon he drowned.
The Prime Minister was still a child at that time.
His mother personally went to Zhāng's (張) house,
begging for a small plot of land
to bury her son's father.
Zhāng (張) learned his surname
and found it very strange.
He went to inspect the place where the drowning occurred
and saw that it was precisely where a coffin should be placed,
which further astonished him.
So he had them use the old burial pit.
And he also told her to bring her son.
After the burial,
the mother and son went to Zhāng's (張) house to express their gratitude.
Zhāng (張), seeing the boy,
was immediately pleased,
and kept him in his household,
teaching him to read,
treating him like his own sons.
He also proposed to marry his eldest daughter to the boy.
The mother dared not agree.
Zhāng's (張) wife said,
"Since the words have already been spoken,
how can we change our minds midway?"
Eventually, she agreed.
However, this daughter greatly disdained the Máo family,
her feelings of resentment and shame
manifesting in her words and demeanor.
When anyone mentioned it,
she would immediately cover her ears;
she would often say to people:
“I’d rather die than follow a cowherd!”
When the groom came for the wedding,
the new groom entered the feast,
the bridal carriage was at the gate,
but the daughter covered her face with her sleeves and wept in a corner.
They urged her to get dressed,
but she refused;
they tried to persuade her, but she remained unmoved.
Soon after, the groom announced his departure,
the drums and music played loudly,
but the daughter still had tears in her eyes and her hair was disheveled.
The father stopped the son-in-law
and went in himself to persuade his daughter.
His daughter cried as if she heard nothing.
He angrily forced her,
and she cried even more, losing her voice.
The father had no choice.
Then a family member came to report: the new groom was about to leave.
The father rushed out,
saying:
“Her dressing is not yet complete,
I beg the groom to wait a little longer.”
He then rushed back in to see his daughter.
Those going back and forth
never stopped their steps.
After a delay,
the situation grew more urgent,
but the daughter still showed no change of heart.
The father, at his wit's end,
became frantic and wanted to kill himself.
His second daughter was by his side,
and rather disapproved of her older sister,
bitterly urging her.
The older sister angrily said:
“Little girl,
you also learn to be so garrulous!
Why don’t you go with him?”
The younger sister said:
“Father never promised me to Máo Láng;
if he had promised me to Máo Láng,
why would you need me to persuade my older sister to get into the carriage?”
The father found her words spirited and forthright,
so he secretly discussed with her mother
to substitute the younger for the elder.
The mother then said to the younger daughter:
“Disobedient maid who does not follow her parents’ command,
now we want to substitute you for your older sister,
will you agree or not?”
The daughter readily said:
“If parents tell me to go,
even as a beggar I would not refuse;
moreover, why should marrying into the Máo family necessarily mean starving to death for life?”
When the parents heard her words,
they were overjoyed,
and immediately dressed the younger daughter in the older sister’s attire,
and hastily she got into the carriage and departed.
Upon entering the house,
the couple became very fond of each other.
However, the daughter had always suffered from hair loss,
which slightly bothered Gōng.
After a long time, he gradually learned of the substituted marriage,
and this made him even more appreciate his wife's virtue.
Not long after,
Gōng was appointed a bóshì dìzǐ [Doctoral Student],
and was to sit for the autumn examinations.
On his way, he passed through Wáng Shèrén’s inn,
where the innkeeper had dreamed the previous night that a deity said:
“Tomorrow, Máo Jièyuán will arrive,
and later he will deliver you from misfortune.”
Therefore, he rose early in the morning,
and watched for guests coming from the east.
When he received Gōng,
he was extremely pleased.
He provided abundant and excellent provisions,
without asking for payment.
He especially relied on the dream omen.
Gōng also had some self-regard;
he privately worried that his wife’s hair loss
would make him a laughingstock among the prominent,
and he intended to replace her after becoming rich and noble.
Soon after, when the results were posted,
he unexpectedly failed to pass,
sighing and walking with heavy steps,
regretting and losing his ambition.
Feeling ashamed before the former innkeeper,
he dared not return via Wáng Shèrén’s place,
and took another route home.
Three years later,
he took the examination again,
and the innkeeper waited for him as before.
Gōng said:
“Your words did not come true,
and I am very ashamed of your hospitality.”
The innkeeper said:
“Xiùcai, because you secretly intended to replace your wife,
you were thus dismissed by the underworld officials,
how could the prophetic dream not be fulfilled?”
Gōng was startled and asked why.
It was because the innkeeper had another dream after Gōng left.
When Gōng heard this,
he was alarmed and remorseful,
standing rigid as a statue.
The innkeeper said:
“Xiùcai should cherish himself,
and will eventually become the jièshǒu [top-ranked candidate].”
Not long after,
he indeed passed the civil examination as the first-ranked candidate.
His wife’s hair also grew back quickly,
her cloud-like hair hanging green,
making her even more charming.
The older sister married a rich man’s son in the village,
and was quite conceited.
But her husband was lazy and wasteful,
their family gradually declined,
their house empty without cooking smoke.
Hearing that her younger sister became the wife of a xiàolián,
she felt even more ashamed and inferior.
The sisters would always avoid each other on the road.
Not long after,
her husband died,
and her family fell into ruin.
Soon after,
Gōng was again promoted to jìnshì.
When the older sister heard this,
she hated herself to the core,
and indignantly abandoned secular life to become a nun.
When Gōng returned as a prime minister,
she reluctantly sent her female attendant to the mansion to pay respects and inquire,
hoping for some gift.
Upon arrival,
the madam gave several bolts of luxurious patterned silk,
with gold hidden inside,
which the attendant did not know.
She took it back to her master.
The master was disappointed,
and angrily said:
“If it were gold and money,
it could still be used for firewood and rice;
what use do I have for such ceremonial objects!”
So she ordered it to be returned.
Gōng and the madam suspected something.
They opened and inspected it, and found the gold still there,
only then realizing the intention behind the refusal.
Gōng took out the gold and smiled, saying:
“Your master cannot even bear more than a hundred gold pieces,
how could she have the good fortune to follow my old Shàngshū [Minister]?”
He then gave fifty gold pieces to the nun's attendant to take away,
saying:
“Take this for your master’s expenses.
More than this, a person of shallow fortune would find it hard to bear.”
The attendant returned
and reported everything.
The master silently sighed to herself,
reflecting on her actions throughout her life,
how she had always been confused,
choosing between good and bad,
could it have been by human will?
Later, the innkeeper was arrested and imprisoned for a capital crime,
and Gōng vigorously intervened to clear his name.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
“The old tomb of the Zhāng family,
the beautiful grave of the Máo clan—
this is already remarkable.
I heard that people at the time had a joke: ‘The elder sister’s husband becomes the younger sister’s husband,
the former jièyuán becomes the later jièyuán,’
how could this be calculated by the clever and astute?
Alas!
That azure heaven,
long unanswerable,
why, when it comes to Máo Gōng,
does it respond like an echo?”
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Fújiàn’s Zēng Xiàolián,
when he successfully passed the imperial examination at Nángōng,
was strolling in the suburbs
with a few other new literati.
He happened to hear that at Pílú Chányuàn,
a diviner was staying there.
So, they rode there together to consult him.
They entered, bowed, and sat down.
The diviner saw their high spirits
and flattered them slightly.
Zēng smiled faintly
and asked:
“Do I have the destiny for a ‘mǎngyù’ (python robe and jade tablet)? ”
The diviner straightened his face and promised him twenty years as a peaceful prime minister.
Zēng was greatly pleased,
his spirits rising even higher.
It began to rain lightly,
so he and his companions took shelter in a monk’s cell.
Inside the cell was an old monk,
with deep-set eyes and a high nose,
sitting on a pútuan.
He was reserved and did not offer a greeting.
The group simply raised a hand in salutation,
then sat on the couch and chatted among themselves,
all congratulating Zēng on becoming prime minister.
Zēng’s spirits were exceptionally high,
and he pointed to his companions, saying:
“When I become prime minister,
I will recommend Zhāng Niánzhàng as the Governor of the South,
my cousin as an Assistant Minister,
and my old servant will also receive a minor official position.
Then my wishes will be fulfilled.”
Everyone burst into laughter.
Soon, the rain outside poured down even more heavily.
Zēng, feeling tired, lay down on the couch.
Suddenly, he saw two imperial envoys
bearing an imperial edict from the Son of Heaven,
summoning Grand Councillor Zēng to decide national affairs.
Zēng was delighted
and hurried to court.
The Son of Heaven moved his mat forward,
speaking warmly for a long time.
He ordered that all officials below the third rank
be subject to Zēng’s dismissal or promotion.
He bestowed upon him a ‘mǎngyù’ and a famous horse.
Zēng, dressed in his robes, bowed and exited.
Upon entering his home,
it was no longer his old residence,
but a mansion with painted beams and carved rafters,
of the utmost magnificence.
He himself did not understand
how he had suddenly reached such a state.
Yet, when he stroked his beard and gave a slight call,
the responses were like thunder.
Soon, high officials and ministers sent gifts of rare sea delicacies;
those who were obsequious and respectful
streamed out of his gate.
When the Six Ministers came,
he rushed to greet them;
for the Vice Ministers,
he bowed and conversed with them;
for those below them,
he merely nodded.
The Governor of Jìn presented ten female musicians,
all beautiful women.
Among them, Jìng’er
and Xiānxiān were
especially favored.
He removed his official cap and enjoyed his days off,
spending his time in music and song.
One day,
he remembered that in his humble days, the local gentry Wáng Zǐliáng had helped him.
“Now I am in a high position,
while he is still struggling in his official career.
Why not give him a hand?”
Early the next morning, he submitted a memorial,
recommending him as a Grand Master Remonstrant.
An imperial decree was immediately issued,
and he was promoted and appointed.
He also recalled that Guō Tàipú had once held a grudge against him.
He immediately summoned Assistant Minister Lǚ Jǐjiàn and Censor Chén Chāng and others,
and conveyed his intentions to them.
The next day,
impeachment memorials poured in,
and by imperial decree, Guō Tàipú was dismissed from office.
His grievances were settled clearly,
which greatly pleased him.
One day, he happened to go out to the city outskirts,
and a drunkard inadvertently stumbled into his retinue.
He immediately ordered men to seize him and hand him over to the Metropolitan Prefect,
who was beaten to death on the spot.
Those whose residences bordered his,
all offered their fertile lands out of fear of his power.
From then on,
his wealth could rival a kingdom.
Not long after, Jìng’er and Xiānxiān
died one after another,
and he longed for them day and night.
Suddenly, he remembered seeing the exceptionally beautiful daughter of his eastern neighbor years ago.
He had always wished to buy her to be his concubine,
but his meager means had always prevented him from fulfilling this old wish.
“Today, fortunately, I can fulfill my desire.”
So, he sent several capable servants
to forcefully offer money to her family.
In a moment,
a sedan chair arrived,
and she was even more enchantingly beautiful
than when he had seen her from afar.
Looking back at his life,
his wishes were now truly fulfilled.
Another year passed,
and whispers in the imperial court
suggested dissenters.
However, as each served as a tethered horse,
Zēng also, with lofty sentiments and great spirit,
did not take it to heart.
The Academician of the Dragon Diagram, Bāo, submitted a memorial,
which roughly stated:
“I humbly submit that Zēng Mǒu,
was originally a dissolute gambler,
a street ruffian.
By a chance word,
he received imperial favor,
his father became a high official, and his son a low one,
his imperial grace reached its zenith.
He did not think of sacrificing himself or toiling diligently
to repay even a fraction of it;
instead, he indulged his own whims,
arbitrarily wielding power and influence.
His crimes deserving of death are
too numerous to count!
The court's official positions,
he treated as rare commodities,
weighing their deficiencies and advantages,
to determine their price.
Consequently, dukes, ministers, generals, and soldiers
all rushed to his doorstep,
calculating connections and seeking favors,
just like peddlers,
hanging on his every breath and seeking his attention,
countless in number.
If there were outstanding scholars or virtuous officials
who refused to curry favor,
lightly, they would be relegated to idle positions,
severely, they would be stripped of their status and reduced to commoners.
Even more so, if one did not completely align with him,
they would immediately offend his deer-for-horse treachery;
if a single word contradicted him,
they would be exiled to the land of jackals and wolves.
Court officials were chilled to the bone by this,
and the court consequently became isolated.
Furthermore, the rich lands of common people
were allowed to be devoured at will;
virtuous daughters of good families
were forcefully taken as wives.
Evil omens and a miasma of grievances
darkened the very heavens!
When his servants arrived,
the governors and magistrates would fawn over them;
when his letters were delivered,
the judicial and supervisory officials would bend the law.
Or if it was his stable boys
or distant relatives,
when they went out, they would travel by imperial carriage,
moving with the speed of wind and thunder.
If local provisions were slightly delayed,
the whip would immediately fall upon them.
They poisoned the people,
enslaved the officials,
and wherever their retinue passed,
no green grass remained.
Yet Zēng was still arrogantly and grandly,
presuming upon imperial favor without remorse.
He would summon his opposition to the palace gate,
and then slander them before the emperor,
he would calmly leave his official duties,
and then singing and music would already begin in his rear garden.
He indulged in music, women, dogs, and horses,
day and night in debauchery;
he had no thought for the nation's finances or the people's livelihoods.
How could there be such a prime minister in the world!
Inside and outside, there was alarm and error,
and public sentiment was turbulent.
If he is not promptly punished with the axe,
it will inevitably lead to the calamities of Cáo Cāo and Wáng Mǎng.
Your subject, fearing day and night,
dares not rest in peace,
and risks death to enumerate these charges,
to reach the imperial ear.
I humbly pray that you sever the head of this treacherous villain,
confiscate his ill-gotten gains,
above, to quell Heaven's wrath,
below, to satisfy public sentiment.
If my words are false and erroneous,
may the blade, saw, and boiling cauldron
be immediately applied to my person.”
And so on.
When the memorial was submitted,
Zēng heard of it
and was terrified,
as if he had drunk ice water.
Fortunately, the emperor was lenient
and kept it in the palace without issuing it.
Then, the censorial officials, the Nine Ministers,
all submitted memorials to impeach him;
even those who had once bowed at his gate and called him their foster father
turned against him.
An imperial decree ordered the confiscation of his family's property
and his removal to the Yúnyǔ Army.
His son Rèn, the Prefect of Píngyáng,
had already had an officer dispatched to question him.
Zēng was still shocked and dismayed upon hearing the decree,
when suddenly dozens of armed guards,
carrying swords and spears,
stormed into his inner chambers,
stripped him of his official robes and hat,
and bound him and his wife together.
Soon after, several men carried valuables out into the courtyard,
millions in gold, silver, cash, and paper money,
hundreds of measures of pearls, jadeite, agate, and jade,
thousands of items such as curtains, blinds, and couches,
even a child's swaddling clothes and a woman's slippers,
scattered on the courtyard steps.
Zēng looked at each item,
his heart aching and his eyes stinging.
Then, another man dragged out a beautiful concubine,
her hair disheveled and weeping mournfully,
her beautiful face utterly helpless.
The fire of grief burned in his heart,
but he swallowed his indignation and dared not speak.
Soon, the pavilions, towers, and storehouses
were all sealed.
He was immediately ordered out.
The guards dragged him out.
The couple suppressed their sobs as they set off,
seeking a decrepit, inferior cart
to travel a short distance,
but they could not get one.
Ten *lǐ* later,
his wife's feet grew weak,
and she nearly stumbled,
Zēng constantly supported and pulled her with one hand.
After another ten-plus *lǐ*,
he himself was exhausted.
Seeing a high mountain
that pierced the clouds,
he worried he could not climb over it,
and tearfully looked at his wife.
But the guards stared at them fiercely,
not allowing them to stop for even a moment.
Then, seeing the setting sun,
and nowhere to rest,
they had no choice but to
stagger and hobble forward.
By the time they reached the mountainside,
his wife's strength was completely spent,
and she sat weeping by the roadside.
Zēng also stopped to rest,
ignoring the guards' scolding.
Suddenly, a hundred shouts roared,
and a group of bandits, each wielding a sharp knife,
leaped forward.
The guards were greatly alarmed
and fled.
Zēng knelt down,
saying:
“I am exiled far away, a lone man,
with no valuables in my bag.”
He begged for clemency.
The bandits, their eyes wide with anger, declared:
“We are all innocent people harmed by him,
we only want the head of that treacherous villain,
we want nothing else.”
Zēng angrily shouted:
“Though I await punishment,
I am an official appointed by the court,
how dare you scoundrels!”
The bandit also grew angry
and swung a large axe at Zēng's neck.
He felt his head fall to the ground with a sound,
and his soul was still in shocked disbelief
