when two devils immediately came,
bound his hands behind his back,
and drove him away.
After walking for several *kè*,
he entered a metropolis.
Soon after,
he saw a palace;
on the palace was an ugly-looking king,
leaning on a table to decide crimes and blessings.
Zēng stepped forward,
prostrated himself, and begged for his life.
The king reviewed the scroll,
and after only a few lines,
he angrily roared:
"This crime of deceiving the sovereign and misleading the state
deserves to be put into the oil cauldron!"
Ten thousand ghosts echoed,
their voices like thunder.
Immediately, a giant ghost arrived at the foot of the steps.
He saw a cauldron seven *chǐ* high,
with burning charcoal all around,
its legs completely red.
Zēng trembled and cried mournfully,
finding no way to escape.
The ghost grabbed his hair with its left hand
and his ankle with its right,
throwing him into the cauldron.
He felt his body, a single mass,
bobbing up and down with the oil waves;
his skin and flesh scorched,
the pain piercing his heart;
boiling oil entered his mouth,
cooking his lungs and intestines.
He wished for a quick death,
but by no means could he achieve it.
After about a *shí* (two hours),
the ghost took Zēng out with a giant fork,
and he prostrated himself again below the hall.
The king again examined the registers,
and angrily said:
"Bullying others by relying on power
deserves the Hell of the Mountain of Knives!"
The ghost then flung him away.
He saw a mountain,
not very wide;
but steeply rising like a cliff,
with sharp blades crisscrossing,
dense like bamboo shoots.
Several people already had their intestines pierced and exposed on it,
their cries and screams
were heartbreaking and horrifying to behold.
The ghost urged Zēng to go up,
but Zēng cried loudly and shrank back.
The ghost stabbed his brain with a poisonous awl,
and Zēng endured the pain and begged for mercy.
The ghost became enraged,
grabbed Zēng,
and powerfully threw him into the air.
He felt his body high above the clouds,
then fell dizzily,
a blade piercing his chest,
the pain unspeakable.
After some more time,
his body became heavily weighted,
the knife wounds gradually widened;
suddenly, he fell off,
his four limbs wriggling like an inchworm.
The ghost again pursued and brought him before the king.
The king ordered an accounting of how much gold Zēng had accumulated throughout his life by selling titles and trading fame,
and by bending the law to seize property.
Immediately, a bearded man, holding counting sticks,
calculated and said:
"Three million two hundred and ten thousand."
The king said:
"Since he accumulated it,
make him drink it back!"
After a short while,
gold coins were brought and piled on the steps,
like hills.
They were gradually put into an iron cauldron
and melted with intense fire.
Several ghosts
alternately used hooks to pour it into his mouth,
and when it flowed down his chin, his skin cracked and reeked,
and when it entered his throat, his internal organs boiled furiously.
In life, he worried about having too little of this substance,
now, he worried about having too much of it.
It took half a day for it to be finished.
The king ordered him to be escorted to Gānzhōu
to be reborn as a girl.
After walking a few steps,
he saw an iron beam on a架 (frame/rack),
several *chǐ* in circumference,
with a wheel of fire attached,
its size unknown, perhaps hundreds of *yóujùn*,
its flames five-colored,
its light gleaming into the clouds.
The ghost whipped him, making him climb the wheel.
As he closed his eyes and leaped onto it,
the wheel turned with his feet,
he felt as if he was falling,
and his whole body became cool.
He opened his eyes and looked at himself,
his body was already an infant,
and a girl at that.
He looked at her parents,
who were dressed in patched rags.
Inside the earthen dwelling,
a gourd and a staff were still present.
He knew in his heart he was the child of beggars.
Daily, he followed the beggar children to beg for alms,
his stomach constantly rumbling, never getting a full meal.
Dressed in tattered clothes,
the wind often pierced his bones.
At fourteen,
he was sold to Gù Xiùcai to be a concubine's maid,
and his food and clothing were barely enough to sustain him.
However, the principal wife was extremely fierce,
daily whipping him,
and often branding his chest and breasts with a red-hot iron.
Fortunately, her husband was quite affectionate,
which provided some comfort.
A bad young man from the east neighbor
suddenly climbed over the wall and forced himself upon her.
She then thought about her past evil deeds,
for which she had already been punished by ghosts;
how could she let it happen again now?
Thereupon, she loudly screamed.
The husband and the principal wife all got up,
and the bad young man fled.
Not long after,
the *xiùcai* stayed in her room,
chattering on the pillow,
as she was complaining about her grievances.
Suddenly, with a sharp crack,
the room door burst open,
two thieves with knives entered,
and indeed decapitated the *xiùcai*,
bagging all his clothes and belongings.
She huddled under the quilt,
not daring to make another sound.
After the thieves left,
she ran screaming to the principal wife's room.
The principal wife was greatly alarmed,
and together they wept and investigated.
Then she suspected the concubine of killing her husband with an adulterer,
and thus reported the case to the *cìshǐ*.
The *cìshǐ* severely interrogated her,
and eventually, she was tortured into a false confession,
and sentenced to death by *língchí* according to the law.
She was dragged to the execution ground,
her chest choked with indignant grievances,
jumping and crying out her injustice,
feeling that the Nine Hells and Eighteen Prisons
were not as dark as this.
As she was bitterly wailing,
she heard her companion call out:
"Brother, are you having a nightmare?"
She suddenly woke up,
seeing the old monk still sitting cross-legged on the seat.
His companions competed to say to him:
"It's getting late, and our stomachs are empty,
why are you sleeping so soundly for so long?"
Zēng then got up disconsolately.
The monk smiled and said:
"Did the prediction about the chancellor come true?"
Zēng was even more astonished,
bowed, and asked for instruction.
The monk said:
"Cultivate virtue and practice benevolence,
and there will be green lotuses in the fiery pit.
What would a mountain monk know about it?"
Zēng had arrived full of vigor,
but unconsciously returned disheartened.
His aspiration for high office
thus faded away.
He entered the mountains and his ultimate fate is unknown.
The Historian of the Strange said:
"Blessing the good and bringing misfortune to the wicked
is the constant way of Heaven.
Those who hear of becoming a chancellor and rejoice in their hearts
surely do not do so out of a desire to serve with utmost dedication.
At that time, in his mind,
palaces, wives, and concubines,
there was nothing he didn't have.
However, dreams are inherently illusory,
and aspirations are not real either.
He made a void,
and the spirits reciprocated with an illusion.
When the yellow millet is about to be cooked,
this dream is bound to occur,
and should be appended to the story of Hándān."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
It is popularly believed that dragons draw water from rivers and lakes to make rain,
but this is a doubtful saying.
Xú Dōngchī [徐東癡] was traveling south
and moored his boat by a riverbank.
He saw a grey dragon descend from the clouds,
stirring the river water with its tail.
Waves surged up,
following the dragon's body upwards.
From afar, the gleam of the water
was wider than three bolts of silk.
After a while,
the dragon's tail was withdrawn,
and the water also instantly subsided.
Soon after, a heavy rain poured down,
and all the channels were leveled.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* [聊齋誌異].
When Shānyòu Wèizhōngtáng [山右衛中堂] was a student,
he was annoyed by the disturbances,
so he moved his study to a Buddhist monastery.
He suffered greatly from the many bedbugs, mosquitoes, and fleas in his room,
and could not sleep all night.
After eating,
he lay down to rest on his bed.
Suddenly, a small warrior,
with a pheasant tail feather stuck in his head,
about two inches tall,
rode in on a horse as large as a candle.
On his arm was a blue gauntlet,
with a hawk as small as a fly.
He entered from outside,
circling the room,
moving quickly.
The gentleman was watching intently,
when suddenly another person entered,
similarly dressed,
with a small bow and arrows tied to his waist,
leading a hunting dog as big as a giant ant.
After a short while,
walkers and riders,
hundreds of them, came in succession.
There were also hundreds of hawks on arms,
and hundreds of dogs.
When mosquitoes and flies flew up,
they unleashed their hawks to attack,
killing them all.
The hunting dogs climbed onto the bed and up the walls,
searching for and devouring lice and fleas.
Wherever they were hidden in crevices,
none failed to come out when sniffed.
In an instant,
almost all were killed.
The gentleman pretended to sleep and watched them.
Hawks gathered and dogs scurried over his body.
Then a person in yellow clothes,
wearing a Píngtiān Guān [平天冠] (flat-heaven crown),
like a king,
ascended another couch,
tying his four-horse carriage among the reeds.
All the attendants dismounted,
presenting those that flew and those that ran,
gathering in profusion all around,
speaking a language he could not understand.
Soon after,
the king ascended a small palanquin,
and the guards, in a flurry,
each ordered their saddled horses.
Ten thousand hooves galloped,
like scattered beans,
smoke flew and mist surged,
and in a moment, they all dispersed.
The gentleman saw it all clearly,
astonished and bewildered as to its origin.
He slipped on his shoes and peeked outside,
but there were no traces or sounds.
Turning back to look around the room,
he saw nothing;
only a small dog left on a wall tile.
The gentleman quickly caught it,
and it was tame.
He placed it in his inkstone box,
examining it repeatedly.
Its fur was extremely fine and soft,
and it had a small ring around its neck.
He fed it grains of rice,
but after a sniff, it always discarded them.
It jumped onto the bed,
searching the seams of clothes,
biting and killing nits and lice.
Then it would return to lie down.
After more than a night,
the gentleman suspected it was gone;
but when he looked,
it was curled up as before.
When the gentleman slept,
it would climb onto the bed mat,
devouring any insect it encountered,
and no mosquito or fly dared to land.
The gentleman loved it
more than a priceless jade disk.
One day,
he took an afternoon nap,
and the dog stealthily hid in a fold of his clothes.
When the gentleman woke and turned over,
he pressed it under his waist.
The gentleman felt something,
and indeed suspected it was the dog.
He quickly got up to look,
but it was already flattened and dead,
as if cut from paper.
Nevertheless, from then on, there were no more wall insects of any kind.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Commander Liáng Gōng [梁公], the Dūd-tóng Jiāngjūn [督同將軍] (Inspector-General) of Yángzhōu [揚州],
had retired from office and lived in his hometown.
Daily he would carry chess and wine,
wandering among the woods and hills.
On the Double Ninth Festival, while ascending a height,
he was playing chess with a guest.
Suddenly a man came,
lingering by the chessboard,
absorbed in watching and unwilling to leave.
Looking at him,
his face was cold and poor,
and his clothes were patched like a quail's feathers.
Yet, his demeanor was gentle and elegant,
with the air of a scholar.
The gentleman greeted him courteously,
and he sat down.
He was also very humble.
The gentleman pointed to the chessboard and said,
“Sir must be skilled at this;
why not play a round with my guest?”
The man modestly declined for a while,
then finally sat down at the board.
When the game ended, he lost,
and his expression showed regret and vexation,
as if he could not control himself.
He played again and lost again,
growing even more ashamed and frustrated.
He was offered wine,
but did not drink,
only pressing the guest to play more.
From morning until late afternoon,
he did not even take a break for urination.
As they were contending for a path with one piece,
both chattering at each other,
the scholar suddenly rose from his seat, startled,
his expression sad and dejected.
A moment later,
he bowed at the gentleman's seat,
kowtowing and begging for help.
The gentleman was alarmed and perplexed,
rising to help him and saying,
“It’s just a game,
why such a reaction?”
The scholar said,
“Please instruct the stableman
not to bind my neck.”
The gentleman was again surprised,
and asked,
“Who is the stableman?”
He replied,
“Mǎ Chéng [馬成].”
Before this,
the gentleman's stable attendant, Mǎ Chéng [馬成],
was prone to wandering off,
often entering the underworld for ten-odd days at a time,
taking up official documents and acting as a summoner.
The gentleman found the scholar's words strange,
so he sent someone to check on Chéng [成].
He was found lying stiff for two days already.
The gentleman then scolded Chéng [成] not to be impolite.
In a flash,
the scholar vanished into the ground.
The gentleman sighed in wonder for a long time,
then realized he was a ghost.
The next day,
Mǎ Chéng awoke.
The Master summoned and questioned him.
Mǎ Chéng said:
“The scholar, a native of Húxiāng,
had an obsessive fondness for Go,
and squandered all his property.
His father, worried about him,
locked him in his study.
He would always climb over the wall and go out,
secretly finding an empty place,
and befriending other Go players.
His father heard of this and scolded and cursed him,
but could never stop him.
His father died, consumed by resentment and sorrow.
Yán Mó Wáng, considering the scholar's lack of virtue,
shortened his lifespan
and punished him by sending him to the È Guǐ Yù.
It has been seven years now.
It happened that the Fèng Lóu on Dōng Yuè was completed,
and official documents were sent to all the prefectures
to solicit scholars to write stele inscriptions.
The King released him from prison,
so he could answer the summons and redeem himself.
Unexpectedly, he procrastinated midway,
greatly overshooting the deadline.
The Yuè Dì sent his direct subordinate to question the King about his fault.
The King was angry,
and ordered his lesser subordinates to track him down.
Previously, having received my master’s command,
I dared not bind him with ropes.”
The Master asked:
“What is his situation today?”
He replied:
“He has been returned to the prison guards,
and will forever be without hope of rebirth.”
The Master sighed and said:
“How greatly an obsession can mislead a person!
It is indeed so!”
Yì Shǐ Shì comments:
“Upon seeing Go, he forgot about his impending death;
and when he died,
upon seeing Go again, he forgot about his chance at life.
Was it not that what he desired was more important than a thousand lives?
Yet, with such an obsession,
he had not achieved even one brilliant move;
it merely caused that beneath the Jiǔ Quán,
there is an immortal Go ghost.
How lamentable!”
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Féng Shēng of Guǎngpíng,
lived during the Zhèngdé era.
When young, he was frivolous and unrestrained,
indulging in wine.
One dawn, he happened to be walking
when he encountered a young woman,
wearing a red shawl,
her countenance exquisitely beautiful.
She was attended by a small page,
hurrying through the dew,
her shoes and socks soaked.
He secretly admired her.
At dusk, he returned home drunk.
By the roadside, there was an old Buddhist temple,
long overgrown and derelict.
A woman emerged from inside,
who was the beautiful woman he had seen earlier.
Suddenly seeing Féng Shēng approach,
she turned and re-entered.
He mused, "How can such a beautiful woman be in a ruined temple?"
He tethered his donkey at the gate
and went to investigate this strangeness.
Upon entering, he found broken walls in disrepair,
and fine grass like a carpet on the steps.
While he was wandering,
an old man with speckled hair emerged.
His clothes and hat were neat and tidy.
He asked,
"Where does this guest come from?"
Féng Shēng replied,
"I happened to pass by this ancient temple,
and wished to pay my respects.
Why are you here, elder?"
The old man said,
"I am a wanderer with nowhere to stay,
and am temporarily sheltering my little ones here.
Since you have graced us with your presence,
I have some camellia tea that can serve as wine."
Then he courteously led the guest inside.
They came to a courtyard behind the main hall,
where the stone path was bright
and free of brambles.
Entering the room,
curtains, bed-hangings, and
a fragrant mist assailed one's senses.
They sat down, and the old man introduced himself,
saying,
"My humble surname is Xīn."
Féng Shēng, emboldened by drink, abruptly asked,
"I heard that you have a daughter,
who has not yet found a suitable match.
Presumptuously, I
would like to offer my mirror stand as a token of betrothal."
Xīn smiled and said,
"Let me discuss this with my wife."
Féng Shēng then asked for a brush and composed a poem:
"A thousand pieces of gold to seek a jade pestle,
with earnestness, I personally bring it.
If Yúnyīng has a mind,
I will personally pound the prime frost."
The host smiled and handed it to his attendants.
A short while later,
a maid whispered something to Xīn.
Xīn rose, asked the guest to wait patiently,
and drew back the curtain, going inside.
After a few indistinct words,
he quickly came out again.
Féng Shēng thought there must be good news;
but Xīn merely sat and chatted,
not mentioning the matter again.
Féng Shēng could not endure it,
and asked,
"I don't understand the meaning;
please enlighten me."
Xīn said,
"You are an exceptional gentleman,
whom I have admired for a long time.
But I have a private matter that
I dare not speak of."
Féng Shēng insisted.
Xīn said,
"I have nineteen daughters,
and twelve of them are married.
The betrothal decisions are left to my wife;
I do not interfere."
Féng Shēng said,
"I only want the one who was leading the small page through the dew this morning."
Xīn did not reply,
and they sat in silence.
Hearing soft, murmuring voices from the room,
Féng Shēng, emboldened by drink, pulled back the curtain and said,
"Since marriage is not to be,
let me at least have a look at her face to dispel my regret."
Inside, he heard the sound of hooks being moved,
and a group of women stood up, startled and looking.
Indeed, there was the red-clad woman,
shaking her sleeves and tilting her topknot,
standing elegantly, adjusting her sash.
Seeing Féng Shēng enter,
the whole room was in a flurry.
Xīn became angry
and ordered several people to escort Féng Shēng out.
The wine surged even more,
and he fell into the overgrown weeds.
Tiles and stones rained down like water,
but fortunately did not hit him.
After lying there for a while,
he heard his donkey still munching grass by the roadside.
He then got up, mounted his donkey,
and stumbled along.
The night was dark and confusing;
he mistakenly entered a mountain gorge,
where wolves howled and owls shrieked,
making his hair stand on end with fear.
He hesitated, looking around,
not knowing where he was.
In the distance, among the dark woods,
lights flickered,
which he presumed to be a village,
and he rode towards it.
He looked up to see a high gate
and knocked on it with his riding crop.
Someone inside asked,
"What gentleman is this,
coming here in the middle of the night?"
Féng Shēng explained that he had lost his way.
The questioner said,
"Wait, I will inform my master."
Féng Shēng stood on tiptoe, waiting expectantly.
Suddenly, he heard the clang of bolts and the creak of the door.
A strong servant came out
and took the donkey from him.
Féng Shēng entered
and saw that the room was very beautiful.
Lamps were lit in the hall.
After a short wait,
a woman came out
and asked the guest his name.
Féng Shēng told her.
After an hour,
several attendants in green helped an old lady out,
saying,
"The Lady Commander has arrived."
Féng Shēng stood up,
bowing respectfully as if to prostrate himself.
The old lady stopped him,
sat down, and said to Féng Shēng,
"Are you not the grandson of Féng Yúnzǐ?"
He replied,
"Yes."
The old lady said,
"Then you must be my grand-nephew.
My life is drawing to a close,
my remaining years are almost spent.
Among our kin,
we have been estranged."
Féng Shēng said,
"As a child, I lost my parents,
and among those who associated with my grandparents,
I know hardly one in ten.
I have never paid my respects before;
please kindly instruct me."
The old lady said,
"You will know it yourself."
Féng Shēng dared not ask again,
and sat pondering.
The old lady said,
"Grand-nephew, why have you come here so late at night?"
Féng Shēng, priding himself on his courage,
then recounted his entire experience.
The old lady smiled and said,
"This is a great matter!
Moreover, my grand-nephew is a famous scholar,
and such a match would not disgrace our family.
How dare that wild fox spirit act so haughty?
Grand-nephew, do not worry;
I can arrange it for you."
Féng Shēng thanked her repeatedly.
The old lady looked at her attendants and said,
"I didn't know that Xīn's daughter
was so exquisitely beautiful."
The attendants in green said,
"He has nineteen daughters,
all elegant and stylish.
Which one did the gentleman propose to?"
Féng Shēng said,
"She was about fifteen years old."
The attendant in green said,
"That would be the fourteenth daughter.
In the third month,
she came with her mother to wish the Lady Commander a happy birthday.
How could you forget?"
The old lady smiled and said,
"Wasn't it the one who carved lotus petals for elevated shoes,
filled them with fragrant powder,
and walked veiled?"
The attendant in green said,
"That's right."
The old lady said,
"This maid is truly adept at making herself
attractive and charming.
Indeed, she is graceful and slender;
my nephew's appraisal is not mistaken."
She then said to the *qīngyī*:
"Send a little cat to call her here."
The *qīngyī* assented and left.
After a while,
she re-entered and reported:
"Xīn Jiā Shísì Niáng has been summoned."
Soon after, a red-clad woman was seen
bowing low to the old woman.
The old woman pulled her up, saying:
"Later you will be my nephew's wife;
you must not observe the courtesies of a maidservant."
The woman rose,
standing gracefully,
her red sleeves hanging low.
The old woman tidied her hair,
and touched her earlobes,
saying:
"Shísì Niáng, what have you been doing recently in your boudoir?"
The woman replied softly:
"When idle, I merely do embroidery."
Turning her head, she saw the scholar,
and shrank back, feeling uneasy.
The old woman said:
"This is my nephew.
With good intentions, I wish to arrange a marriage for you with him;
why then did you get lost,
wandering through the ravines all night?"
The woman lowered her head, speechless.
The old woman said:
"I called you for no other reason
than to act as a matchmaker for my nephew."
The woman remained silent.
The old woman ordered a bed to be swept and a mattress laid out,
then arranged for them to drink the nuptial cup.
The woman, however, said:
"I still need to inform my parents."
The old woman said:
"I am acting as your matchmaker;
what could possibly be wrong?"
The woman said:
"The command of the *jùnjūn*,
my parents certainly would not dare to defy.
However, to proceed so hastily,
even if this maidservant were to die,
I would not dare to obey the order!"
The old woman laughed and said:
"A young woman whose will cannot be broken,
truly she is my nephew's wife!"
Thereupon she plucked a golden flower from the woman's hair,
and gave it to the scholar to keep.
She ordered him to return home and consult the almanac,
to fix an auspicious day.
Then she had the *qīngyī* escort the woman away.
Hearing the distant roosters crowing,
she sent someone with a donkey to take the scholar out.
A few steps away,
he looked back,
and the village dwellings were already gone;
he saw only the dark, dense pines and cypresses,
and clumps of bushes covering tombs.
After a long moment of contemplation,
he realized that the place was Xuē Shàngshū's tomb.
Xuē was the younger brother of the scholar's paternal grandmother,
hence they called each other nephew.
He knew in his heart that he had encountered a ghost,
yet he did not know who Shísì Niáng was.
He sighed and returned home,
idly checking the almanac to await her,
but fearing that a ghost's promise could not be relied upon.
He went again to the Buddhist temple,
but the halls were desolate.
He asked the residents,
who said that foxes were often seen in the temple.
He secretly thought: if I can gain a beautiful woman,
a fox would also be fine.
On the appointed day,
he cleaned his house and swept the path,
changing servants to watch out,
but it was still quiet at midnight.
The scholar had lost all hope.
A moment later,
there was an uproar outside the gate.
He slipped out to peek,
and saw embroidered palanquins already stopped in the courtyard,
with two maids with double coiled hair helping the woman into a green sedan chair.
There were no superfluous items in the trousseau,
only two long-whiskered servants carrying a large *pūmǎn* [piggy bank],
as big as a jar,
which they set down in a corner of the hall, resting their shoulders.
The scholar was delighted to obtain a beautiful companion,
not at all suspecting her to be of a different species.
He asked the woman:
"A deceased ghost –
why do your family members obey him so readily?"
The woman said:
"Xuē Shàngshū was commanded to be the Five Prefectures'巡壞使 (*xún huài shǐ*),
so hundreds of miles of ghosts and foxes all serve as his escort,
hence he is often absent from his tomb."
The scholar did not forget his matchmaker;
the next day,
he went to make offerings at her tomb.
Upon returning, he saw two *qīngyī* [maids],
carrying *bèijǐn* [ornate brocade] as a congratulatory gift,
which they simply placed on the table and departed.
The scholar told the woman,
who looked at it and said:
"This is the *jùnjūn*'s possession."
In the town, there was the son of Chǔ Yíntái,
who had studied with the scholar since childhood
and was very familiar with him.
Hearing that the scholar had acquired a fox-wife,
he sent gifts as a congratulation,
and then came to the hall to raise a toast.
A few days later,
he sent another invitation to drink.
The woman heard of it
and said to the scholar:
"When the young master came before,
I peeked through a hole in the wall;
that man has monkey-like eyes and an eagle-like nose,
he cannot be associated with for long.
You should not go."
The scholar agreed.
The next day,
the young master came to the door,
asking forgiveness for breaking the appointment,
and also presented new compositions.
The scholar's critiques involved mockery,
and the young master was greatly shamed,
departing unhappily.
The scholar returned,
laughing as he recounted it in the room.
The woman said sadly:
"That young master is a jackal;
you must not associate with him!
If you do not listen to my words,
disaster will befall you!"
The scholar laughed and dismissed her concerns.
Later, he and the young master would often flatter and joke with each other,
gradually forgetting their previous estrangement.
It happened that the provincial examination was held,
and the young master came in first,
the scholar second.
The young master was utterly pleased with himself,
and rushed to invite the scholar to drink.
The scholar declined, but went after repeated invitations.
Upon arrival, he learned it was the young master's birthday,
and the hall was full of guests,
with a grand array of feasts.
The young master presented his examination paper to the scholar.
Relatives and friends praised it shoulder to shoulder.
After several rounds of wine,
music played in the hall,
with boisterous drums and wind instruments;
host and guests were very joyful.
The young master suddenly said to the scholar:
"The proverb says:
'Do not discuss essays in the examination hall.'
Now I know this saying is wrong.
The reason I, your junior, was presumptuously placed above you
is merely because a few opening phrases
were slightly superior."
After the young master spoke,
everyone present praised him.
The scholar, drunk, could not tolerate it,
and burst out laughing, saying:
"Do you still, even now,
think that essays are judged by that standard?!"
After the scholar spoke,
everyone present changed color.
The young master was shamed and choked with anger.
The guests gradually left,
and the scholar also slipped away.
When he sobered up, he regretted it,
and thus told the woman.
The woman unhappily said:
"You are indeed a fickle fellow from the countryside!
Such a frivolous manner,
when applied to a *jūnzǐ*,
will damage our virtue;
when applied to a *xiǎorén*,
it will cost our lives.
Your misfortune is not far off!
I cannot bear to see you destitute and wandering,
so please allow me to take my leave now."
The scholar was frightened and wept,
and moreover expressed his regret.
The woman said:
「If you wish me to stay,
I make a pact with you: from now on, close your doors, cease all socializing,
and do not indulge in frivolous drinking. 」
The scholar respectfully accepted the instruction.
Shísìniáng was diligent, frugal, and unrestrained.
She spent her days weaving.
Occasionally, she would visit her parents,
but never stayed overnight.
She also sometimes invested money and silk in business.
Each day, if there was a surplus,
she would deposit it into a piggy bank.
Daily, she kept the doors shut.
If visitors called, she would instruct the servant to turn them away with an apology.
One day,
Chǔ Gōngzǐ sent a letter.
The woman burned it without mentioning it.
The next day,
she went out to a funeral in the city
and met Gōngzǐ at the mourner's house.
He seized her arm and earnestly invited her.
The scholar declined, stating his reasons.
Gōngzǐ ordered his stableman to take the reins
and escorted him along.
Upon arriving home,
he immediately ordered a feast to be prepared.
The scholar subsequently excused himself to leave early.
Gōngzǐ persisted in detaining him without end,
bringing out household courtesans to play the zheng for entertainment.
The scholar, who had always been unrestrained,
had recently been confined indoors,
feeling quite bored and disheartened.
Suddenly encountering a lavish drinking party,
his spirits became exceedingly high,
and he no longer had any worries.
Consequently, he drank heavily
and collapsed onto the mat, thoroughly intoxicated.
Gōngzǐ's wife, Ruǎn Shì,
was extremely fierce and jealous.
Her maids and concubines dared not apply makeup.
A few days prior,
a maid had entered the study
and was caught by Ruǎn,
who struck her head with a staff,
splitting her skull and killing her instantly.
Gōngzǐ bore a grudge against the scholar for mocking him
and thought daily of how to retaliate.
He then plotted to get him drunk and frame him.
While the scholar was drunk and asleep,
he carried the maid's corpse into the bedchamber,
closed the door, and left directly.
At the fifth watch, the scholar sobered up
and first realized he was lying on a small table.
He rose to find his pillow and bed,
and there was something slimy,
tangled around his feet.
He felt it;
it was a person. He thought the master had sent a boy to sleep with him.
He kicked it again, but it didn't move and was stiff.
Greatly alarmed,
he went out the door, shouting in surprise.
All the servants rose,
went to look,
saw the corpse,
and seized the scholar, angrily making a fuss.
Gōngzǐ came out to examine it
and falsely accused the scholar of coercing and killing the maid.
He had him seized and sent to Guǎngpíng.
The next day,
Shísìniáng finally learned of it
and tearfully said,
「I knew this would happen today! 」
Thereupon, she regularly sent money to the scholar.
The scholar appeared before the Fǔyǐn,
but had no way to clear his name.
He was flogged day and night until his flesh was torn.
The woman personally went to inquire.
When the scholar saw her,
his grief choked him,
and he could not speak.
The woman knew the trap was already deep
and advised him to falsely confess
to avoid further torture.
The scholar wept and obeyed.
When the woman came and went,
people dared not glance at her from nearby.
Returning home, she sighed and lamented,
then quickly sent the maidservant away.
She lived alone for several days,
then entrusted a matchmaker to purchase a good family's daughter,
named Lù'ér,
who was fifteen years old
and quite beautiful.
She shared sleeping and eating with her,
showing her special affection unlike the other servants.
The scholar was determined to be guilty of accidental murder and sentenced to hanging.
The servant returned with the news,
sobbing uncontrollably.
When the woman heard,
she was calm as if she didn't care.
Soon, the date for the autumn execution was set,
and the woman finally became agitated and restless,
leaving by day and returning by night,
her feet never resting.
Whenever she was in a solitary place,
she would weep bitterly,
to the point of losing sleep and appetite.
One day,
at noon,
a fox-maid suddenly arrived.
The woman immediately rose
and led her to a secluded place to talk.
When she came out, her face was full of smiles,
and she managed the household as usual.
The next day,
when the servant went to the prison,
the scholar sent a message to his wife, saying farewell forever.
The servant reported back.
The woman casually responded,
not showing any sorrow,
and treated it with indifference.
The family secretly discussed her cruelty.
Suddenly, a rumor spread widely: Chǔ Yíntái had his rank stripped;
Píngyáng Guānchá was specially appointed to investigate Fēng Shēng's case.
When the servant heard this,
he happily reported it to his mistress.
The woman was also pleased
and immediately sent him to the yamen to inquire.
The scholar had already been released from prison,
and they met with both sorrow and joy.
Shortly after, Gōngzǐ was arrested
and, after one interrogation,
all the facts were revealed.
The scholar was immediately released to return home.
Upon seeing the people in his inner chambers,
he shed tears.
The woman also looked sorrowful,
but after the sadness, came joy.
However, they still did not know how the case reached the Emperor's ears.
The woman smiled and pointed to the maid, saying:
"This is the benefactor of your lord."
Shēng was astonished and asked why.
Earlier,
the woman had sent her maid to Yāndū,
intending to reach the imperial palace,
to plead Shēng's case.
When the maid arrived,
she found a deity guarding the palace,
and she wandered along the imperial moat
for several months without being able to enter.
Fearing she would fail in her mission,
the maid was about to return to devise a new plan,
when she suddenly heard that the present emperor was going to visit Dàtóng.
The maid then went ahead,
disguising herself as a courtesan.
When the emperor arrived at the brothel,
she received great favor.
The emperor suspected that the maid did not seem like a woman of the demimonde,
so the maid began to weep.
The emperor asked,
"What injustice or suffering do you have?"
The maid replied,
"My ancestral home is in Guǎngpíng,
and I am the daughter of the student FÉNG Mǒu.
My father is about to die from an unjust imprisonment,
so I was sold into a brothel."
The emperor was saddened,
and bestowed upon her a hundred taels of gold.
Before leaving,
he inquired in detail about the whole story,
and recorded her name with paper and brush;
he also said he wished to share wealth and high status with her.
The maid said,
"If only my father and I can be reunited,
I do not desire luxury."
The emperor nodded in agreement,
and then left.
The maid sacrificed herself for this reason.
Shēng quickly bowed,
tears welling in both his eyes.
Not long after,
the woman suddenly said to Shēng,
"If not for the bonds of love,
where would I find such troubles?
When you were arrested,
I ran around among relatives and friends,
but not a single person offered any advice or help.
The bitterness in my heart then
truly cannot be told.
Now, I am increasingly厌苦 [weary and disgusted] with the mundane world.
I have already found a good match for you,
and we can part ways from now on."
Hearing this, Shēng
wept and prostrated himself, unable to rise.
The woman then stopped.
At night, she sent Lù'ér to serve Shēng in his bedchamber,
but Shēng refused to accept her.
In the morning, when he looked at Shísì Niáng,
her youthful radiance had suddenly diminished;
after another month or so,
she gradually became old and infirm;
after half a year,
she was dark and haggard like a village crone: Shēng still respected her,
and never abandoned her.
The woman suddenly spoke of parting again,
and moreover said,
"You already have a beautiful companion,
why do you need this aging hūpán?"
Shēng wept in sorrow as before.
Another month passed,
and the woman suddenly fell gravely ill,
refusing food and drink,
lying emaciated in her boudoir.
Shēng attended to her with medicine and soup,
as if serving his own parents.
The shamans and doctors were of no avail,
and she eventually passed away suddenly.
Shēng was heartbroken to the point of collapse.
He immediately used the gold given by the maid
to arrange a vegetarian feast and burial.
A few days later,
the maid also left,
so he took Lù'ér as his wife.
A year later,
they had a son.
However, year after year the harvests failed,
and the family's fortunes declined further.
The couple, having no recourse,
faced their reflections in long sorrow.
Suddenly, he remembered the piggy bank in the corner of the hall,
where he often saw Shísì Niáng putting coins,
and wondered if it was still there.
Approaching it,
he saw that it was almost full of soy sauce and salt jars.
He removed each one,
and probed inside with a chopstick,
but it was firm and impenetrable;
he broke it open,
and gold coins spilled out.
From then on, their finances became greatly abundant.
Later, the old servant went to Tài Huà Shān,
and met Shísì Niáng,
riding a black mule,
with the maid riding a lame one following her,
and she asked,
"Is FÉNG Láng well?"
And she added,
"Please convey to your master,
that I have already been enrolled in the ranks of the immortals."
Having spoken,
she disappeared.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Frivolous words
often come from the scholar class,
which is regrettable for a gentleman.
I have often taken on the name of 'unpopular'
– to speak of injustice is already circuitous;
yet I have never failed to strive diligently
to align myself with the ranks of gentlemen,
and the theories of fortune and misfortune do not concern me.
As for someone like FÉNG Shēng,
a trivial word,
could lead to death;
had there not been an immortal in his house,
how could he have escaped imprisonment
and been reborn in this world?
How terrifying!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a certain White Lotus sectarian,
a person from Shānxī,
whose name has been forgotten,
but he was likely a follower of XÚ Hóngrú.
He used heterodox methods to delude the masses,
and many who admired his arts became his disciples.
One day, as he was about to go elsewhere,
he placed a basin in the hall,
and covered it with another basin,
instructing his disciples to guard it,
and forbidding them from opening and looking inside.
After he left,
a disciple opened it,
and saw the basin contained clear water,
with a boat made of woven grass floating on the water,
complete with sails and masts.
Surprised, he poked it with his finger,
and it tilted with his touch;
he quickly righted it to its original state,
and covered it again.
Soon after, the master returned,
and angrily chastised him,
"Why did you disobey my command?"
The disciple immediately denied it.
The master said,
"Just now a boat capsized in the sea,
how dare you lie to me?"
Another night,
he burned a large candle in the hall,
strictly admonishing them to guard it,
and not to let the wind extinguish it.
After two drops of wax had fallen,
the master had not yet arrived.
However, feeling tired,
the disciple lay down on the bed for a short nap;
when he awoke,
the candle had already gone out,
and he quickly relit it.
Soon after, the master entered,
and chastised him again.
The disciple said,
"I certainly didn't sleep,
how could the candle have gone out?"
The master angrily said,
"Just now you made me walk more than ten *lǐ* in the dark,
and you still say such things?"
The disciple was greatly astonished.
Such wondrous deeds
were too numerous to write down.
Later, a certain person had a beloved concubine who was having an affair with a retainer.
He discovered it,
but kept silent about it.
He sent the retainer to feed the pigs;
when the retainer entered the sty,
he immediately transformed into a pig while standing.
Mǒu then called a butcher to slaughter it,
and sold its meat.
No one knew about it.
The retainer's father, seeing his son did not return,
came to inquire,
but Mǒu excused himself by saying the son had not been there for a long time.
The retainer's family searched everywhere,
but found no news.
A fellow student,
who secretly knew about the matter,
leaked it to the retainer's father.
The retainer's father reported it to the Yìzǎi.
The Yìzǎi feared that Mǒu would escape,
and dared not apprehend or prosecute him;
he reported it to a superior official,
and requested a thousand armed soldiers [jiǎshì]
to surround Mǒu's residence,
and his wife and children were all taken into custody.
They were confined in cages,
and were to be escorted to the capital [dū].
On the way through Tàihángshān,
a giant emerged from the mountain,
as tall as the trees,
with eyes like basins [àng],
and a mouth like a pot [pén],
and teeth about a foot long.
The soldiers stood aghast and dared not proceed.
Mǒu said:
"This is a demon;
my wife can repel it."
So, following his words,
they untied his wife.
His wife took up a spear [gē] and went forth.
The giant became enraged,
and sucked her in and swallowed her.
The crowd was even more horrified.
Mǒu said:
"Since my wife has been killed,
my son is needed."
So he brought out his son again,
who was also swallowed,
as before.
The crowd looked at each other,
not knowing what to do.
Mǒu wept and angrily said:
"Since my wife was killed,
and then my son was killed,
how can I tolerate such a situation!
However, it won't do unless I go myself."
The crowd indeed released him from the cage,
handed him a blade, and sent him off.
The giant met him with overwhelming force.
They struggled for a while,
the giant seized Mǒu, opened its mouth,
stretched its neck and swallowed him,
and then calmly departed.
Based on the manuscript edition of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Wèi Yùnwàng,
a native of Pénquán in Yìdū,
was originally from a prominent aristocratic family [shìzú dàjiā].
Later, the family declined [shìwēi]
and could not afford his studies.
When he was over twenty years old,
he abandoned his studies [fèixué]
and took up his father-in-law's business of selling wine [gū].
One evening,
Wèi was sleeping alone on the upper floor of the wine shop,
when he suddenly heard thumping and kicking sounds downstairs.
Wèi was startled awake and listened intently [sǒng tīng].
The sounds gradually approached,
then came up the stairs,
with every step making a heavy noise.
Before long,
two maids carrying lamps [tiǎo dēng]
had arrived by the couch.
Following them was a young scholar [shūshēng],
leading a young woman [nǚláng],
who approached the couch with a smile.
Wèi was greatly astonished and bewildered.
He then realized they were foxes,
and his hair stood on end [fāmáo sēnsù],
he bowed his head and dared not look.
The scholar smiled and said:
"Sir, do not be suspicious.
My younger sister has a past connection with you,
and it is proper for her to serve you."
Wèi looked at the scholar,
whose brocade and sable [jǐndiāo] were dazzling to the eyes;
he felt ashamed of his own humble appearance [xínghuì],
and his face showed his embarrassment [yán bùzhī suǒduì].
The scholar led the maids away, leaving the lamp.
Wèi carefully examined the young woman,
who was elegant and beautiful like an immortal [chǔchǔ ruò xiān],
and he was very pleased with her in his heart.
However, he was ashamed that he could not utter flirtatious words [yóuyǔ].
The young woman looked at him and smiled, saying:
"Sir, you are not a country bumpkin [bǎoběntóu],
why do you act like a pedant [cuòdàqì]?"
She then quickly moved close to his pillow and mat,
warming his hands against her bosom.
Wèi finally broke into a smile for her,
jokingly pulled up his trousers,
and then became intimate with her.
Before the morning bell rang,
two maids [shuānghuán] came to lead her away.
They agreed to meet again that night.
In the evening,
the woman indeed arrived,
and smiled, saying:
"What good fortune does this foolish fellow have,
to obtain such a beautiful wife [jiāfù]
without spending a single coin,
who comes to him every night on her own accord?"
Wèi was happy that no one was around,
and set out wine to drink with her,
and played the game of guessing hidden tokens [cángméi].
The woman won nine out of ten times.
Then she smiled and said:
"It's better if I hide the tokens [yuēméizi],
and you guess them yourself;
if you guess right, you win,
otherwise you lose.
If I were to guess,
you would never win."
So, they followed her suggestion,
and enjoyed themselves all night.
When it was time to sleep,
she said:
"Last night, the quilt and mattress were rough and cold [sèlěng],
making it unbearable."
So she called a maid to bring a quilt,
which was spread on the bed,
exuding a fragrant scent of silk brocade [qǐxiāng].
After a moment,
they loosely embraced each other,
her lip rouge [kǒuzhī] deeply perfumed the air,
truly not inferior to the "land of tenderness" [wēnróuxiāng] of the Hàn dynasty.
From then on,
this became their regular routine.
Half a year later,
Wèi returned home.
One moonlight night, as he was talking with his wife by the window,
he suddenly saw the young woman [nǚláng], beautifully dressed [huázhuāng], sitting on the wall,
beckoning with her hand.
Wèi approached her.
The woman helped him [yuán zhī],
they climbed over the wall and left,
holding hands she told him:
"Today I must part with you.
Please walk a few paces [shùwǔ] with me,
to show the affection of our half-year together [chóumóu zhī yì]."
Wèi was surprised and asked for the reason,
the woman said:
"Marriage [yīnyuán] has its own predetermined fate [dìngshù],
why wait for an explanation?"
As they spoke,
they reached outside the village,
where the former maid was waiting with two lamps [shuāngdēng];
they then went towards Nánshān,
and at a high point,
she bid Wèi farewell.
Wèi tried to make her stay but could not,
so she left.
Wèi stood there, bewildered [zhùlì huánghuáng],
and saw the two lamps in the distance flicker,
gradually fading from sight,
he returned feeling dejected and melancholic [yàngyù].
That night, the village people [cūnrén]
all saw the lights on the mountaintop.
Based on the manuscript edition of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Lǐ Gōng Zhùmíng
was the son of Mr. Jīn Zhuó, the magistrate of Suīníng.
He was a brave and resolute person, never timid.
He was the brother-in-law of Mr. Wáng Jìliáng of Xīnchéng.
Mr. Wáng's house had many towers and pavilions,
where strange things were often seen.
Gōng often lodged there during the summer months,
fond of the cool evening air on the pavilion.
When others warned him of strange occurrences,
Gōng laughed and would not listen,
insisting that a bed be set up.
The host complied with his request,
instructing the servants to keep him company during the night.
Gōng declined,
saying:
"I enjoy sleeping alone,
and I have never known fear in my life."
The host then had a calming incense lit in the censer,
asked where he preferred to lie,
and only then extinguished the candle, closed the door, and left.
Gōng lay down and, after a while,
in the moonlight,
saw a teacup on the table,
tilting and spinning,
neither falling nor stopping.
Gōng shouted at it,
and it stopped with a clink.
Then, as if someone had pulled out the incense stick,
it danced and swayed in the air,
forming crisscrossing patterns like threads of flowers.
Gōng got up and shouted:
"What kind of demon dares to do this!"
He threw off his clothes and got out of bed,
wanting to grab it.
He felt under the bed with his foot,
finding only one shoe.
Without time for a thorough search,
he struck at the swaying object with his bare foot.
The incense stick immediately plunged back into the censer,
and all was silent without a trace.
Gōng bent down and felt around all the dark corners.
Suddenly, something flew up and struck him on the cheek,
feeling like a shoe.
He searched for it,
but could not find it at all.
He then opened the door and went downstairs,
calling for his attendants to bring a light.
There was nothing there.
He then went back to bed.
When dawn came,
he had several people search for the shoe,
flipping over mats and overturning the bed,
but its whereabouts were unknown.
The host replaced Gōng's shoe.
The next day,
Gōng happened to look up
and saw a shoe wedged between the rafters.
He poked it down,
and it was his own shoe.
Gōng Yìdū Rén
resided in the Sūn family mansion in Zī.
The mansion was very large,
with many unoccupied, spacious areas, and Gōng only lived in half of it.
The south courtyard faced a tall pavilion,
separated only by a wall.
He sometimes saw the pavilion door opening and closing by itself,
but Gōng paid it no mind.
Once, while talking with his family in the courtyard,
the pavilion door opened,
and suddenly a small person appeared,
sitting facing north,
not more than three feet tall,
wearing a green robe and white socks.
Everyone pointed and looked at it,
but it did not move.
Gōng said:
"This is a fox spirit."
He quickly took out his bow and arrow,
aimed at it, intending to shoot.
The small person saw him,
made a jeering sound like "ya-ya,"
and was no longer seen.
Gōng grabbed a knife and went up to the pavilion,
cursing and searching,
but saw nothing,
so he returned.
The strange occurrences then ceased.
Gōng lived there for several years,
safe and sound.
Gōng's eldest son, Yǒu Sān,
was my relative by marriage,
and these events were seen by him.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"I was born late,
and did not have the opportunity to serve Gōng personally,
but I heard from the elders
that he was generally a generous, resolute, and brave man.
These two incidents
generally show his character.
With such a noble spirit within,
how could ghosts and foxes cause trouble for him?"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lǐ Gōng Zhùmíng
was generous and fond of giving.
A certain villager
was employed in Gōng's household.
This man had been idle in his youth,
unable to work in agriculture,
and his family was very poor.
However, he had a small skill
and often performed tasks,
always being generously rewarded.
When he had no food for breakfast,
he would plead for alms from Gōng,
who would always give him a *shēng* or a *dǒu* (measures of grain).
One day,
he told Gōng:
"I receive generous aid daily,
and my three or four family members are fortunately not starving.
But how can this last?
I beg my master to lend me one *shí* of beans as capital."
Gōng happily ordered them to be given to him immediately.
The man carried them away.
More than a year passed,
and he repaid nothing.
When asked,
the bean capital was already gone.
Gōng pitied his poverty
and did not press for repayment.
Gōng was studying in Xiāo Temple.
Over three years later,
he suddenly dreamed that the man came and said:
"I owe my master for the beans,
and I have come to repay them."
Gōng comforted him, saying:
"If I were to ask for your repayment,
how could I even count
all that you have owed me over the years?"
The man said mournfully:
"That is true.
If a person does something for which they receive a thousand pieces of gold,
they might not need to repay it.
But if one receives assistance for no reason,
even a *shēng* or a *dǒu* cannot be ignored,
much less such a large amount!"
After speaking,
he left.
Gōng became more suspicious.
Soon after, his family informed Gōng:
"Last night, the jenny gave birth to a foal,
and it is quite handsome."
Gōng suddenly realized and said:
"Could the foal be that man?"
He returned home a few days later,
saw the foal,
and playfully called it by the man's name.
The foal ran towards him,
as if it understood.
From then on, it was named after the man.
Gōng rode it to Qīngzhōu.
The eunuch of the Héng Mansion saw it and liked it,
wishing to buy it for a high price,
but the price had not yet been settled.
Gōng happened to have urgent family matters
and could not wait,
so he returned home.
Another year passed,
and the foal, sharing a stable with a stallion,
broke its leg
and could not be cured.
A cow doctor came to Gōng's house,
saw it,
and said to Gōng:
"Please entrust the foal to me.
I will care for it day and night,
which will take months or even a year.
If by some chance it recovers,
we can share the profits from its sale."
Gōng agreed.
Several months later,
the cow doctor sold the donkey,
earning one thousand eight hundred coins,
and presented half of it to Gōng.
Gōng received the money
and suddenly realized
that the amount exactly matched the price of the beans.
Alas!
A debt clearly owed
but repaid in the netherworld—
this is enough to serve as a warning and encouragement.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dù Xiùcai Jiǔwǎn's
wife fell ill.
It was the Double Ninth Festival,
and he was invited by a friend to a Cornel Dogwood Gathering.
He rose early,
washed,
and told his wife where he was going.
As he donned his cap and clothes, about to leave,
he suddenly saw his wife in a daze,
muttering as if speaking to someone.
Dù found this strange,
and went to her bedside to ask.
His wife immediately
called out, "Son!"
to him.
The family knew in their hearts that something was amiss.
At that time, Dù's mother's coffin had not yet been interred,
so they suspected it was her spirit possessing his wife.
Dù prayed, saying,
"Could it be my mother?"
His wife cursed, saying,
"You beast! Why do you not recognize your father?"
Dù said,
"Since you are my father,
why have you come home to trouble my daughter-in-law?"
His wife called him by his pet name and said,
"I came specifically for my daughter-in-law.
Why do you resent it?
My daughter-in-law should have died immediately;
four people came to seize her,
the leader being Zhāng Huáiyù.
I pleaded with them in every possible way,
and only then did they agree to allow it.
I promised a small offering,
which you should pay them."
Dù did as he was told
and burned paper money outside the gate.
His wife then said,
"The four men have left.
They couldn't bear to disrespect my wishes,
so three days from now,
you must prepare a feast to reward them.
Your mother is old
and decrepit, unable to manage the household chores.
When the time comes,
it will still trouble my daughter-in-law to go once."
Dù said,
"The living and the dead walk different paths;
how can she substitute for others in cooking?
I hope father will forgive her."
His wife said,
"Son, do not be afraid.
She will go and return immediately.
This is for their sake,
so she must not shirk the effort."
After speaking,
she fell into a trance,
and only after a long while did she regain consciousness.
Dù asked what she had said,
but she remembered nothing.
She only said,
"Just now I saw four men come,
wanting to seize me.
Fortunately, my father-in-law pleaded for me
and also bribed them with money from his pouch,
and then they left.
I saw that my father-in-law's money pouch still had two ingots left,
and I wanted to steal one ingot
to make a living.
My father-in-law saw it
and scolded, 'What do you want to do!
Is this something you can use!'
So I withdrew my hand and dared not move."
Dù, seeing his wife's critical condition,
was half-believing, half-doubting.
Three days later,
while they were laughing and talking,
she suddenly stared blankly for a long time,
and said,
"Your wife is extremely greedy.
She saw my silver just now
and immediately coveted it.
However, generally speaking, it's due to poverty,
so it's not surprising.
I will take your wife to manage the kitchen duties for me;
don't worry."
No sooner had she spoken
than she suddenly died.
About half a day later,
she awoke,
and told Dù,
"Just now my father-in-law called me to go,
and said,
'I don't need you to cook;
I have someone to prepare the food,
you just need to sit firmly and direct, that's enough.
In the underworld, I like things to be bountiful,
so all the dishes should overflow the containers;
you must remember this.'
I agreed.
When I went to the kitchen,
I saw two women handling knives and chopping blocks inside,
both wearing dark purple cloaks with green borders,
who called me 'sister-in-law.'
Whenever roasted meat was served in the bowls,
they would always ask me to inspect it.
The four men from earlier were all at the banquet.
After the dishes were served,
and the wine utensils were already arranged in the vessels,
my father-in-law then ordered me to return."
Dù was greatly astonished,
and recounted this to everyone he met.
According to the manuscript of _Liáozhāi Zhìyì_:
Zhāng Xūyī of Láiwú
was the second elder brother of Zhāng Dàoyī, the Education Commissioner.
He was naturally bold and unrestrained.
Hearing that a certain residence in the county
was inhabited by foxes,
he respectfully brought his calling card to visit,
hoping to see them.
He presented his card.
After a while,
the door opened by itself.
His servant was greatly astonished
and retreated.
Zhāng straightened his clothes and respectfully entered,
seeing tables and couches distinctly arranged in the hall,
but it was utterly silent and empty of people.
He bowed and prayed, saying,
"This junior student has come after fasting and purification.
Since the immortals do not reject me at their gate,
why do you not grant a clear audience?"
Suddenly, a voice was heard from the empty room, saying,
"It is troublesome for you to make this trip;
your footsteps are indeed a welcome sound.
Please sit and give your instruction."
Immediately, two seats moved by themselves to face each other.
No sooner had he sat down
than a carved lacquer tray,
holding two tea cups,
appeared before his eyes.
Each took a cup and drank opposite each other,
making slurping sounds,
yet he still did not see the person.
After tea,
it was followed by wine.
Upon careful inquiry about his official status,
the voice said,
"My surname is Hú,
and by seniority, I am the fourth;
'Xiànggōng'
is what people call me."
Thereupon, they exchanged toasts and discussed,
and their spirits were quite congenial.
Turtle delicacies and deer jerky,
mixed with fragrant water pepper and smartweed, were served.
Those who offered wine and served roasted meat
seemed to be numerous young attendants.
After drinking, he rather craved tea.
No sooner had the thought stirred slightly
than fragrant tea was already placed on the table.
Whatever he thought of,
it would invariably appear in response to his thought.
Zhāng was greatly pleased,
and only returned home completely drunk.
From then on, he would visit Hú every three or four days,
and Hú would also occasionally come to Zhāng's house,
behaving according to the etiquette between host and guest.
One day,
Zhāng asked Hú:
"The shamaness in Nánchéng,
daily invokes the fox spirit to exploit the sick for profit.
I wonder if you know the fox in her household?"
Hú replied,
saying:
"She's just deluding people;
there's really no fox."
A short while later,
Zhāng got up to urinate,
and heard a small voice say:
"Regarding the fox-shamaness in Nánchéng mentioned just now,
I don't know what kind of person she is.
Your humble servant wishes to follow you, sir, to observe her,
may I trouble you to say a word to the master on my behalf?"
Zhāng knew it was a small fox,
so he replied:
"Agreed."
He immediately returned to his seat and asked Hú:
"I wish to have one or two of your servants
go and investigate the fox-shamaness;
I respectfully request your permission."
Hú firmly said there was no need.
Zhāng repeated his request several times,
and then Hú assented.
Afterward, when Zhāng went out,
his horse arrived by itself,
as if someone were leading it.
After mounting and riding,
the foxes spoke to each other on the way,
and said to Zhāng:
"Later, sir, if you feel fine sand scattering on your collar and sleeves
while on the road,
that means we are following you."
As they spoke, they entered the city
and reached the shamaness's house.
When the shamaness saw Zhāng arrive,
she smiled and greeted him:
"Why has your distinguished self suddenly graced us with your presence?"
Zhāng said:
"I heard that your family's fox child has great spiritual efficacy;
is that true?"
The shamaness straightened her face and said:
"Such prattling talk
is unfitting for a noble person to utter!
Why speak of a 'fox child'?
I fear our family's Huājiě will be displeased!"
Before she had finished speaking,
half a brick flew from the air,
hitting the shamaness's arm,
making her stagger and almost fall.
Alarmed, she said to Zhāng:
"Officer, why did you throw something at this old body?"
Zhāng laughed and said:
"Old woman, you're blind!
When did you ever see someone whose own forehead was broken
falsely accuse a bystander?"
The shamaness was bewildered and didn't know what to say.
Just as she was confused,
another stone fell,
hitting the shamaness,
who stumbled;
foul mud rained down,
smearing the shamaness's face like a ghost.
She could only wail and beg for her life.
Zhāng asked for her to be spared,
and then they stopped.
The shamaness quickly got up and ran,
fleeing into her room,
closing the door and daring not to come out.
Zhāng called out to her, saying:
"Is your fox like my fox?"
The shamaness only apologized.
Zhāng looked up into the air,
admonishing them not to harm the shamaness again.
Only then did the shamaness cautiously come out.
Zhāng smiled and instructed her,
then returned.
From then on, whenever he traveled alone on the road,
feeling fine dust and sand rustle,
he would call out to the fox to speak,
and it would always answer correctly.
He relied on this, fearing neither tigers, wolves, nor violent bandits.
More than a year passed like this,
and he became even closer friends with Hú.
He once asked about Hú's birth cycle,
but Hú couldn't remember it himself,
only saying:
"Seeing Huáng Cháo's rebellion
feels like yesterday."
One evening while they were talking,
suddenly there was a rustling sound on the wall,
the sound was very sharp.
Zhāng found it strange,
and Hú said:
"This must be my elder brother."
Zhāng said:
"Why not invite him to sit with us?"
Hú replied:
"His Dao is quite shallow;
he's only good for catching and eating chickens,
and that's all."
Zhāng said to the fox:
"Our friendship is so good,
like the two of us,
it can be said to be without regret;
yet, never having seen your face,
is truly a regrettable matter."
Hú said:
"It's enough to have a good friendship,
what's the point of meeting?"
One day,
Hú prepared wine and invited Zhāng,
also announcing his departure.
When asked:
"Where are you going?"
Hú replied:
"Your younger brother is from Shǎnxī,
and is returning there.
You always regret not seeing my face,
so I will ask you to recognize a friend of several years,
so that you can recognize me another day."
Zhāng looked around but saw nothing.
Hú said:
"You may try opening the bedroom door;
your younger brother is inside."
Zhāng immediately pushed open the door and peeked,
and there was a handsome young man inside,
who looked at him and smiled.
His clothes were elegant,
and his eyebrows and eyes were like a painting;
in the blink of an eye,
he was no longer seen.
Zhāng turned around and walked,
and immediately there were rustling footsteps following him,
saying:
"Today your regret has been released."
Zhāng was reluctant and couldn't bear to part.
The fox said:
"Separation and reunion have their own destiny,
why be so concerned?"
Then, with a large goblet, he urged Zhāng to drink.
They drank until midnight,
when Hú finally guided Zhāng home with a gauze lantern.
When Zhāng went to visit in the morning,
it was just an empty, desolate house.
Later, it was said that a certain gentleman became the educational commissioner for Sìchuān.
Zhāng, still as impoverished as before,
went to visit his younger brother,
with rather extravagant hopes.
After more than a month, he returned,
his initial hopes greatly disappointed,
sighing on his horse,
dejected as if he had lost his other half.
Suddenly, a young man riding a blue horse
followed behind him.
Zhāng looked back
and saw that his fur robes and horse were very splendid,
and his demeanor was also refined and elegant.
So he engaged him in conversation,
and the young man noticed Zhāng's unhappiness
and questioned him.
Zhāng then sighed and told him the reason.
The young man also comforted him.
They traveled together for about a *lǐ*,
until they reached a crossroads,
where the young man bowed his hands and bid farewell,
saying:
"On the road ahead, there is a person
who carries an item from your old friend for you;
please accept it with a smile."
When Zhāng wanted to ask further,
the young man galloped away.
Zhāng couldn't understand what had happened.
Another two or three *lǐ* later,
he saw an old servant,
carrying a small basket,
which he presented before the horse,
saying:
"Hú Sìxiàngōng respectfully sends this to you, sir."
Zhāng suddenly understood clearly.
He received it and opened it to look,
and it was full of white silver.
When he looked for the old servant,
he was nowhere to be seen.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Yìshǐshì said: Human emotions are like the deceitful practices of goblins and imps,
found everywhere;
especially on major thoroughfares in the north and south,
their harm is even more severe.
For instance, those who forcefully rob travelers with bows and horses,
outside the city gates,
everyone knows about them.
Or there are those who carry needles and bags,
seizing goods in the marketplace;
when travelers turn their heads,
their money and goods are already gone.
Are these not the worst of the goblins and imps?
Yet, there are also those who meet like duckweed on water,
with sweet words like nectar;
their approach is gradual,
their penetration deep.
One mistakenly believes them to be bosom friends [lit. friends who overturned their carriage covers for a chat],
and consequently suffers the disaster of losing wealth.
They set traps according to the situation,
and their methods are not uniform.
People commonly refer to their insidious words
by the name
"Niàn Yāng" [reciting seedlings].
Nowadays, there are many such instances on the northern routes,
and those who fall victim to them are particularly numerous.
Wáng Zǐxùn, from my hometown,
was a scholar in the prefecture.
He had a clan elder who was a Qí Jí Tàishǐ in the capital,
and planned to visit him to inquire about his well-being.
He packed his belongings and headed north.
After leaving Jǐnán,
and traveling a few Lǐ,
a man on a black donkey [Wèi]
galloped to join him.
At the time, he engaged in casual conversation to draw Wáng Zǐxùn in,
and Wáng Zǐxùn somewhat responded.
The man introduced himself:
"My surname is Zhāng,
and I am an official subordinate from Qīxiá.
I have been ordered on an official mission to the capital."
His address was falsely humble,
and his service was diligent.
They traveled together for several tens of Lǐ,
and agreed to lodge together.
If Wáng Zǐxùn was ahead,
he would whip his donkey to catch up;
if Wáng Zǐxùn was behind,
he would wait on the roadside.
The servant suspected him,
and therefore sternly refused to allow him to continue,
not letting him accompany them.
Zhāng was quite ashamed,
waved his whip, and left.
When evening came,
they rested at an inn.
Wáng Zǐxùn happened to stroll in the courtyard,
and saw Zhāng drinking in an outer room.
While he was surprised and suspicious,
Zhāng caught sight of Wáng Zǐxùn,
bowed with hands clasped,
humble as a servant,
and respectfully inquired after him.
Wáng Zǐxùn also considered it merely a chance encounter,
and was not suspicious,
but Wáng Zǐxùn's servant remained vigilant all night.
When the rooster crowed,
Zhāng came to call him to travel together.
The servant sternly rebuked him and refused,
so he left.
After the morning sun had risen,
Wáng Zǐxùn finally set out.
After traveling for about half a day,
a man in front, riding a white donkey [Wèi],
around forty years old,
with neat clothes and hat;
his head was bowed, and he rode his donkey slowly,
dozing and almost falling off.
Sometimes he was ahead,
sometimes behind,
lingering for over ten Lǐ.
Wáng Zǐxùn asked in surprise:
"What did you do last night,
to be so exhausted?"
When the man heard this,
he suddenly stretched and yawned,
saying:
"I am from Qīngyuàn,
my surname is Xǔ.
Gāo Qíng, the magistrate of Línzī, is my relative on my mother's side.
My elder brother teaches in the yámen,
and I went to visit him,
and received some gifts.
Last night at the inn,
I mistakenly lodged with a 'Niàn Yāng' swindler,
and was so alarmed that I dared not close my eyes,
which led to this daytime drowsiness."
Wáng Zǐxùn deliberately asked:
"What does 'Niàn Yāng' mean?"
Xǔ replied:
"You are young and travel little,
so you do not know about such dangers and deceptions.
There are bandits who
use sweet words to entice travelers,
and manage to lodge and rest with them,
thereby seizing the opportunity to swindle them.
Yesterday, a distant relative of mine
lost his money this way.
We should all be vigilant."
Wáng Zǐxùn nodded.
Before this,
the magistrate of Línzī had an old acquaintance with Wáng Zǐxùn,
and Wáng Zǐxùn had once served on his staff,
knowing that there was indeed a man named Xǔ among his retainers.
Thus, he no longer had doubts.
He then spoke of warm regards,
and also inquired about his elder brother's situation.
Xǔ invited him to dine with the innkeeper in the evening,
and Wáng Zǐxùn agreed.
The servant, however, remained suspicious of his falseness,
and secretly conspired with the innkeeper [to delay],
lingering and not advancing,
thus losing him,
and he vanished.
The next day,
at midday,
they encountered another young man,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
riding a strong mule,
his clothes and hat neat and elegant,
and his appearance very handsome.
They traveled together for a long time,
without exchanging a single word.
As the sun set in the west,
the young man suddenly said:
"The Qūlǜ Diàn is not far from here."
Wáng Zǐxùn gave a slight response.
The young man then sighed and choked with emotion,
as if unable to control himself.
Wáng Zǐxùn briefly questioned him.
The young man sighed, saying:
"My surname is Jīn, from Jiāngnán.
For three years, I studied diligently,
hoping to pass the imperial examination,
but unexpectedly, I failed completely!
My elder brother is a Zhǔzhèng in the ministry,
so I brought my family members [Xiǎo] with me,
hoping to find some distraction.
I am not accustomed to long journeys,
and the dust and sand in my face
make me irritable."
Then he took out a red handkerchief to wipe his face,
and sighed incessantly.
Listening to his words,
he spoke with a southern accent,
delicate and charming like a woman.
Wáng Zǐxùn liked him in his heart,
and somewhat comforted him.
The young man said:
"I rode ahead earlier,
and my family has been waiting for a long time without appearing;
why have none of my servants arrived either?
It's almost dusk,
what should I do!"
He lingered and looked around,
walking very slowly.
Wáng Zǐxùn then rode on ahead,
and the distance between them gradually widened.
Late, I arrived at a guesthouse.
As I entered the room,
there was a bed against the wall.
There was already a guest unpacking on it.
Wáng asked the proprietor.
Immediately, a person entered,
took him and led him out,
saying,
"Just please settle in;
he will move to another place immediately."
Wáng looked at him,
and it was Xǔ.
Wáng stopped him and stayed with him in the same room,
so Xǔ remained.
Then they sat and chatted.
A short while later,
another person carrying luggage came in.
Seeing Wáng and Xǔ in the room,
he turned around and hastily exited,
saying,
"There are already guests."
Wáng scrutinizingly looked,
and it was the young man from the road.
Wáng had not yet spoken,
when Xǔ urgently rose and pulled him back to stay,
so the young man sat down.
Xǔ then proceeded to ask about his family and clan,
and the young man again recounted his words from the journey to Xǔ.
In a moment,
he opened his purse and took out money,
a considerable pile;
it weighed more than two liǎng,
and he gave it to the proprietor,
instructing him to prepare dishes and wine
for their night conversation.
The two strenuously tried to dissuade him,
but he ultimately did not listen.
Soon, wine and roasted meat were set forth.
During the banquet,
the young man discussed literature with great elegance.
Wáng asked about the examination topics in the Jiāngnán academy,
and the young man told him everything.
Moreover, he recited his ownchéngpò
and his favorite lines from the essay.
After speaking,
he felt quite indignant.
They all clasped their wrists in shared indignation.
The young man also mentioned that his household had been separated,
and he had no servants at night,
worrying that he couldn't manage his stable.
Wáng then ordered his servant to substitute in tending the stable.
The young man was deeply grateful.
After a short while,
he suddenly spoke with a disappointed air,
"My life has been full of setbacks,
and even traveling abroad brings no good fortune.
Last night, I stayed in an inn with bad people,
throwing dice and shouting,
which grated on my ears and disturbed my heart,
preventing me from sleeping."
In the southern dialect, dice are called 'dōu.'
Xǔ didn't understand,
and insisted on asking about it.
The young man drew its shape with his hand.
Xǔ then laughed,
and took out a die from his pouch,
saying,
"Is this the thing?"
The young man nodded.
Xǔ then used the die as a game,
and they happily drank together.
When the wine was nearly finished,
Xǔ invited them to throw dice together,
to win a host.
Wáng declined, not understanding.
Xǔ then playedhūlú with the young man.
He also secretly instructed Wáng, saying,
"You must not leak word.
This barbarian young master is quite well-off,
and also young,
so he may not deeply understand the 'wǔmùjué.'
I'll win a little,
and tomorrow I'll treat you."
The two then went into the adjacent room.
Soon, they heard the boisterous sounds of gambling.
Wáng secretly peeped,
and saw the servant from Qīxiá was also among them.
Greatly suspicious,
he unrolled his quilt and lay down.
After another while,
everyone together pulled Wáng to gamble.
Wáng firmly declined, not understanding.
Xǔ offered to distinguish thexiāo zhī for him,
but Wáng still refused.
So he forcibly threw the dice on Wáng's behalf.
A short while later,
he came to the bed and reported to Wáng, saying,
"You've won several stakes now."
Wáng answered in his sleep.
Suddenly, several people pushed open the door and entered,
chattering in a foreign tongue.
The leader said his surname was Tóng,
and he was a bannerman patrolling for gamblers.
At that time, gambling prohibitions were very strict,
causing everyone to be greatly alarmed.
Tóng loudly threatened Wáng,
but Wáng also countered him with his title of Grand Historian.
Tóng, angered, then relaxed,
and recounted their shared local origin with Wáng,
smilingly inviting him to gamble again for fun.
Everyone stupidly resumed gambling,
and Tóng also gambled.
Wáng said to Xǔ,
"I don't care about wins or losses.
I just want to sleep,
don't bother me."
Xǔ didn't listen,
still going back and forth to report to him.
After the game dispersed,
each counted their chips,
and Wáng owed a considerable amount.
Tóng then searched Wáng's luggage and purse to collect payment.
Wáng rose in indignation to contend.
Jīn grabbed Wáng's arm,
and secretly advised him, saying,
"Those are all ruffians,
their intentions are unfathomable.
We are literary friends,
we must look out for each other.
Just now in the game, I won a certain amount,
which can offset this;
this amount, which should be collected from you, Mr. Xǔ,
let's ask to exchange it: let Xǔ pay Tóng,
and you pay me.
It's just to briefly mislead people,
after this, I will return it to you.
Otherwise,
would I, a friend of righteousness, actually take your payment?"
Wáng was inherently honest and generous,
and so he believed him.
The young man came out,
and told Tóng about the exchange plan.
Then, in front of everyone, he opened Wáng's belongings,
evaluated them, and put them into his own purse.
Tóng then went on to demand payment from Xǔ and Zhāng and departed.
The youth was then brought,
and shared a pillow with Wáng;
the quilts and bedding were all exquisite.
Wáng also summoned his servant to lie on the bed,
and each silently rested their head on the pillow.
After a long while,
the youth deliberately turned over,
moving his lower body towards the servant.
The servant moved aside to avoid him;
the youth again moved closer to him,
his skin touching the servant's thigh,
smooth and slippery as fat.
The servant's heart was stirred,
and he attempted to flirt;
the youth was extremely eager,
the quilts rustled and moaned.
Wáng heard quite a bit of this,
and though greatly astonished and perplexed,
he ultimately did not suspect there was anything else going on.
At dawn,
the youth immediately rose,
urging them to depart early.
He also said:
"Sir, you are weary and exhausted;
the item entrusted to me last night,
I will return it to you further down the road."
Wáng had not yet spoken,
when the youth had already packed his things and mounted his horse.
Wáng had no choice
but to follow him.
The mules travelled swiftly,
gradually moving further away.
Wáng expected the youth to wait for him further down the road,
and initially paid no mind.
He then questioned his servant about what he had heard during the night,
and the servant truthfully told him.
Wáng then exclaimed in surprise:
"Now I have been tricked by a *niàn'yāng*!
How could a gentleman of an official family
personally proposition a servant?"
He then reconsidered, thinking that the youth's conversation was refined and elegant,
not something a *niàn'yāng* could achieve.
He quickly pursued for dozens of *lǐ*,
but the tracks had completely vanished.
He then realized that Zhāng, Xǔ, and Tóng were all part of the same gang;
one scheme failing,
they tried another,
determined to ensure his entrapment.
The arrangement to repay the debt and change clothes
had already laid a trap for extortion;
if their plan to carry off his belongings failed,
they would certainly seize them based on the previous agreement.
For a few dozen gold coins,
they pursued him for hundreds of *lǐ*;
fearing the servant would expose their deeds,
they engaged in sexual intimacy with him;
their methods were indeed cunning.
Several years later,
the incident involving Wú Shēng occurred.
There was a Wú Shēng in the district,
whose courtesy name was Ānrén.
At thirty, he lost his wife,
and slept alone in an empty study.
A *xiùcai* came to converse with him,
and they became intimately acquainted and pleased with each other.
The *xiùcai* brought a young slave,
named Guǐtóu,
who also got along well with Wú's page, Bào'ér.
After a long time, Wú learned that the *xiùcai* was a fox spirit.
When Wú travelled far,
the fox spirit would always accompany him.
Though in the same room,
people could not see it.
When Wú was a guest in the capital,
about to return home,
he heard that Wáng Shēng had suffered the misfortune of a *niàn'yāng*,
and so he warned his page to be vigilant.
The fox spirit laughed and said:
"No need,
this journey will be without harm."
Upon reaching Zhuó,
