a man was tying his horse and sitting in a tobacco shop,
his fur clothes were neat and elegant.
Seeing Wú pass by,
he also rose,
leaped onto his horse, and followed him.
Gradually, he spoke with Wú,
identifying himself as:
"From Shāndōng, surnamed Huáng,
a director in the Ministry of Revenue.
I am returning east,
and am pleased to have company on the same path, not to be solitary."
Therefore, when Wú stopped, he also stopped;
whenever they ate together,
he would always pay for Wú.
Wú outwardly expressed gratitude but inwardly harbored suspicion.
He privately asked the fox spirit,
who simply said:
"No harm."
Wú's doubts then dissipated.
By evening,
they sought lodging together,
and a beautiful youth was already sitting there.
Huáng entered,
and saluted him with clasped hands.
Happily, he asked the youth:
"When did you leave the capital?"
He replied:
"Yesterday."
Huáng then pulled him to share the lodging.
He said to Wú:
"This is Shǐ Láng,
my maternal cousin,
also a scholar;
he can assist your conversation on poetry and elegance,
your night talks will not be lonely."
Then he took out money
to arrange a meal and drink together.
The youth was elegant and refined,
and thus Wú was greatly pleased with him.
During the drinking,
he often signalled Wú to pretend to make a mistake in drinking games,
to fine Huáng,
forcing him,
clapping and laughing.
Wú was even more pleased.
Subsequently, Shǐ and Huáng plotted to gamble,
together pulling Wú in,
and so each took out money from their pouches as stakes.
The fox spirit instructed Bào'ér to secretly lock the wooden door,
and told Wú:
"If you hear people making a ruckus,
just pretend to be asleep and don't move."
Wú assented.
Whenever Wú threw the dice,
he would lose small bets,
but always win large bets.
After more than a *gēng*,
he counted two hundred gold coins.
Shǐ and Huáng's money bags were almost empty,
so they discussed pawning their horses.
Suddenly, they heard a very loud banging on the door,
Wú quickly got up,
threw the dice into the fire,
covered himself with the quilt and feigned sleep.
After a long while,
he heard the innkeeper searching for the key unsuccessfully,
breaking open the lock and opening the door,
several people rushed in furiously,
searching for and apprehending the gamblers.
Shǐ and Huáng both said there was no one.
One person actually pulled off Wú's quilt,
pointing him out as a gambler.
Wú scolded them.
Several people forcibly searched Wú's belongings.
Just as he was unable to resist them,
suddenly they heard the sounds of carriages and horses outside the door, and attendants shouting to clear the way.
Wú quickly went out and called loudly,
whereupon the crowd became frightened,
pulled him inside,
and only begged him to remain silent.
Wú then calmly paid the innkeeper for his packed belongings.
Once the official procession had gone far,
the crowd then left through the door.
Huáng and Shǐ both put on a surprised and delighted expression,
and then sought a place to sleep.
Huáng instructed Shǐ to share a bed with Wú.
Wú placed his money pouch under his pillow,
and was just about to pull up the quilt and sleep.
Before long,
Shǐ opened Wú's quilt,
entered his embrace naked,
and whispered:
"I admire your magnanimity,
and wish to be intimate with you."
Wú knew in his heart that this was a trick,
but he also thought it was a good plan,
so they embraced each other.
Shǐ served him with great effort,
but did not expect Wú to be a truly robust man,
resulting in a severe mismatch,
he groaned, almost unbearable,
and secretly begged for mercy.
Wú firmly demanded to finish the act.
He felt him with his hand,
and blood flowed like a river.
Then he released him and let him go.
By dawn,
Shǐ was too exhausted to get up,
claiming a sudden illness,
and only asked Wú and Huáng to depart first.
Wú, upon parting,
gave him gold for medicine.
On the road, he spoke with the fox spirit,
and then learned that the official procession last night
had all been arranged by the fox spirit.
Huáng yú tú (黃於途),
became increasingly subservient to Wú (吳).
In the evening, they shared a room again.
The small room was very cramped,
barely fitting a single bed.
It was quite warm and clean,
but Wú (吳) found it too small.
Huáng (黃) said:
"It's cramped if two people sleep here,
but if you sleep alone, it's spacious,
what's the harm?"
After eating,
he left directly.
Wú (吳) was also happy to sleep alone, hoping to meet his fox-friend.
He sat for a long time,
but the fox did not arrive.
Suddenly, he heard a finger-tapping sound
on a small door in the wall.
Wú (吳) unbarred it and peered out.
A gorgeously dressed young woman suddenly entered,
closed the door herself,
and smiled at Wú (吳).
She was beautiful as a fairy.
Wú (吳) happily questioned her,
and found she was the host's daughter-in-law.
Thus, they became intimate,
and greatly loved each other.
The woman suddenly burst into tears.
Wú (吳) was startled and asked why.
The woman said:
"I dare not conceal it,
I am actually sent by the host to bait you.
Before, when I entered the room,
I was immediately seized;
I don't know why he hasn't come for so long tonight?"
She then sobbed:
"I am a woman from a respectable family,
and I am unwilling to do this.
Now I have given my heart to you,
please save me!"
Wú (吳) was horrified and afraid,
having no idea what to do,
but urged her to leave quickly.
The woman only bowed her head and cried.
Suddenly, he heard Huáng (黃) and the host arguing loudly outside the cauldron room.
Then he heard Huáng (黃) say:
"I have respected you all the way,
thinking you were a human,
how could you try to seduce my brother in his room!"
Wú (吳) was afraid and forced the woman to leave.
He heard sounds of scuffling outside the wall-door.
Wú (吳) was flustered, sweating profusely,
and the woman also knelt and cried.
Then he heard someone trying to dissuade the host.
The host did not listen,
pounding on the door more urgently.
The dissuader said:
"May I ask the host,
what do you intend to do?
If you want to kill him,
we have several guests here,
and we will not stand by and watch such violence.
If one of the two escapes,
where will the blame lie?
If you want to take this to the public court,
your family's reputation will be ruined,
and you will only bring disgrace upon yourself.
Moreover, you are an innkeeper,
clearly setting a trap,
how can you guarantee that the woman will not speak out differently?"
The host stared blankly, unable to speak.
Wú (吳) heard this,
secretly admiring him,
but did not know who it was.
Earlier,
just as the shop door was about to close,
a scholar came with a servant
and stayed in the outer chamber.
He brought fragrant wine,
offered it to everyone in the chamber,
and especially urged Huáng (黃) and the host to drink.
The two excused themselves, wishing to leave,
but the scholar tugged at their robes,
insisting they stay.
Later, finding an opportunity to escape,
he rushed with a staff to Wú's (吳) place.
The scholar, hearing the commotion,
then came in to mediate.
Wú (吳) peeped through the window,
and saw it was his fox-friend,
secretly delighted.
He also saw that the host's resolve had wavered slightly,
so he spoke loudly to intimidate him.
He then said to the woman:
"Why are you silent, not saying a word?"
The woman cried:
"I regret not being like other people,
being driven to perform such base tasks!"
When the host heard this,
his face turned ashen.
The scholar shouted and cursed:
"Your bestial nature
is fully exposed,
this is what all guests resent!"
Huáng (黃) and the host both dropped their knives and staffs,
knelt down, and pleaded.
Wú (吳) also opened the door and came out,
suddenly becoming furious and cursing.
The scholar again persuaded Wú (吳) to stop,
and the two sides finally reconciled.
The woman cried again,
preferring death to returning.
From inside, a maidservant rushed out,
threw the woman down, and forced her inside.
The woman lay on the ground,
crying even more sorrowfully.
The scholar advised the host to sell her to Wú Shēng (吳生) for a high price.
The host bowed his head and said:
"Having been a mother for thirty years,
today I'm nursing a child in reverse,
what more can be said?"
So he agreed to the scholar's suggestion.
Wú (吳) was naturally unwilling to pay a heavy price;
the scholar mediated between the host and guest,
and it was agreed at fifty taels of silver.
After the person and money were exchanged,
the morning bell had already sounded.
They then quickly packed their bags
and carried the woman away.
The woman was unaccustomed to riding,
and was quite exhausted from the journey.
At noon,
they rested for a while.
As they were about to leave,
they called for Bàor (報兒),
but didn't know where he was.
The sun was already setting,
still no sign or sound,
which caused some suspicion and surprise.
So Wú (吳) asked the fox.
The fox said:
"Don't worry,
he will arrive on his own."
Stars and moon were already out
when Bàor (報兒) finally arrived.
Wú (吳) questioned him.
Bàor (報兒) smiled and said:
"Young master paid fifty taels to enrich a scoundrel,
I secretly felt it was unfair.
Just now, I conspired with Guǐtóu (鬼頭)
and got it back."
Then he placed the gold on the table.
Wú (吳) was startled and asked for the reason.
It turned out that Guǐtóu (鬼頭) knew the woman only had one elder brother,
who had been away for over ten years and had not returned.
So he transformed into the brother's appearance,
and had Bàor (報兒) pose as the younger brother,
entering the door to demand his sister.
The host was terrified
and falsely claimed to be ill and dying.
The two servants wanted to report him to the officials,
the host became even more afraid,
and bribed them with gold,
gradually increasing it to forty.
The two servants then left.
Bàor (報兒) fully recounted the reason.
Wú (吳) immediately rewarded him.
Wú (吳) returned home,
and their marital harmony was very strong.
His family became even wealthier.
Upon detailed questioning of the woman,
it was revealed that the beautiful young man from before was her husband,
and that Shǐ (史) was in fact Jīn (金).
She wore a silk shawl made of oak leaves,
saying it was obtained from someone named Wáng (王) in Shāndōng (山東).
It turned out that his associates were numerous,
and the innkeepers
were all of his kind.
How unexpected that what Wú Shēng (吳生) encountered
was exactly the person whom Wáng Zǐxùn (王子巽) cried out about as "連天叫苦" (liántiān jiàokǔ),
isn't that delightful!
How profound the ancient saying:
"One who rides well often falls."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異)
Wáng Zǐxùn (王子巽) said:
"When I was in the capital,
I once saw a person performing a show in the marketplace.
He carried a wooden box with compartments,
there were twelve holes;
in each hole lay a frog.
He would tap their heads with a slender stick,
and they would croak.
If given money,
he would strike the frog's heads rapidly,
like playing a cloud gong,
and tunes of gōngshāng (宮商) melodies and lyrics
could be clearly distinguished."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異)
It was also said:
“A man was selling rat shows in the Cháng'ān market.
He carried a bag on his back,
in which he kept more than ten small rats.
Whenever he was among a dense crowd,
he would take out a small wooden frame,
place it on his shoulder,
looking just like a miniature stage.
Then he would beat a drum and clappers,
and sing ancient variety plays.
As soon as his singing began,
rats would emerge from the bag,
wearing假面 (jiǎmiàn),
and small costumes.
They would climb onto the stage from his back,
stand on two legs, and dance.
The joy and sorrow of men and women
all perfectly matched the scenes in the play.”
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Luócūn there was a man named Chén Dài,
who was dull and ugly when young.
He married a woman of the Mǒu clan,
who was quite beautiful.
She herself felt that her husband was not as good as others,
and was constantly dejected and discontented.
However, she maintained her chastity and integrity,
and the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law also lived in peace.
One night, while sleeping alone,
she suddenly heard the wind blowing, causing the door to open.
A scholar entered,
took off his clothes and head covering,
and went to sleep with the wife.
The wife was terrified and afraid,
and struggled to resist him;
but her body became stiff,
and she let him fondle her before he left.
From then on, there was never an empty night.
After more than a month,
her appearance became withered and haggard.
Her mother noticed and asked her about it.
At first, she was ashamed and did not want to speak;
but when pressed,
she finally told her the situation.
Her mother was shocked and said:
“This is a demon!”
They tried a hundred methods of incantations and spells,
but ultimately could not stop it.
So they made Dài hide in the room,
holding a stick to wait.
In the middle of the night,
the scholar indeed came again,
placing his hat on the table;
he also took off his robe,
hanging it on a rack.
Just as he was about to get into bed,
he suddenly exclaimed in surprise:
“Dūodūo!
There is a living person's aura!”
He hurriedly put his clothes back on.
Dài suddenly sprang up from the darkness,
striking him in the waist and ribs,
making a 'tā' sound.
He looked around the four walls,
but the scholar had already vanished.
They lit a bundle of firewood,
and a piece of muddy clothing lay on the ground,
while the muddy head covering on the table was still there.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Qiáo Wáng Bǐng,
upon leaving the village,
saw a beautiful woman emerge from the shrine of the Tǔdì god,
who looked at him very affectionately.
He propositioned her with indecent words,
and she joyfully accepted.
They engaged in intimacy without restraint,
and then arranged a secret rendezvous at night.
Bǐng then told her where he lived.
That night,
she indeed came,
and they were extremely affectionate with each other.
When asked her name,
she refused to tell.
From then on, they met constantly.
Sometimes Bǐng would share a bed with his wife,
and the beautiful woman would also come and have intercourse with him,
yet his wife never noticed her presence.
Bǐng was surprised and asked her about it.
The beautiful woman said:
“I am the wife of the Tǔdì god.”
Bǐng was greatly alarmed,
and urgently wanted to break off the relationship,
but tried a hundred ways and could not stop it.
This continued for half a year,
and he became ill and bedridden.
The beautiful woman came even more frequently,
and his family members could all see her.
Not long after,
Bǐng indeed died.
The beautiful woman still came once a day.
Bǐng's wife scolded her, saying:
“Shameless lewd ghost!
The man is already dead,
why do you still come?”
The beautiful woman then left,
and did not return.
Although Tǔdì is a minor deity,
he is still a god.
How could he allow his wife to run off by herself?
In his muddled state, it shouldn't have come to this.
I don't know what kind of lewd and deluded being
caused this village to be known for having a defiled and disrespectful god through the ages.
What an injustice!
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The Daoist from Jǐnán,
whose origin was unknown,
and whose surname was also unclear.
In winter and summer, he wore a single unlined or lined garment,
tied with a yellow cord,
without an undershirt.
He always used half a comb to comb his hair,
then held it with his teeth at the knot,
like a hat.
During the day, he walked barefoot in the market;
at night, he slept on the street,
and ice and snow would melt
a few feet around his body.
When he first arrived,
he often performed magic tricks for people,
and market-goers competed to give him gifts.
There was a ruffian from Jǐngqū,
who gave him wine,
and asked him to teach his art,
but he refused.
When the Daoist was bathing in a ford,
the ruffian suddenly seized his clothes to threaten him.
The Daoist bowed and said:
“Please return them to me,
and I will not be stingy with my art.”
The ruffian feared he was being deceived,
and firmly refused to let go.
The Daoist said:
“Are you really not going to let me teach you?”
He replied:
“Yes.”
The Daoist silently said nothing more;
presently, the yellow cord transformed into a snake,
about several handfuls in circumference,
coiling around his body six or seven times,
with angry eyes and raised head,
flicking its tongue towards him.
The ruffian was greatly astonished,
knelt down,
his face pale and breath short,
only begging for his life.
The Daoist then simply took the cord.
The cord was no longer a snake;
another snake,
slithered into the city and left.
From then on, the Daoist's name became even more famous.
When gentry heard of his uniqueness,
they invited him to socialize with them.
From then on, he frequented the homes of rural scholars.
The Provincial Surveillance Commissioners (Sī) and Intendants (Dào) all heard his name,
and whenever there was a banquet,
they would take the Dàorén along.
One day,
the Dàorén requested to host a banquet for the various high officials (zhū xiàn) at the Shuǐmiàn Tíng.
On the appointed day,
he found the Dàorén's invitation letters for the guests prepared on the table,
though no one knew how they had arrived.
When the guests arrived at the banquet location,
the Dàorén emerged, stooping, to welcome them.
Upon entering,
they found the hall empty and silent,
with no couches or tables set up.
Some suspected he was being presumptuous.
The Dàorén turned to the officials and said,
"This humble Dàorén has no servants.
May I trouble you to lend me your attendants
to run errands for a while?"
The officials all agreed.
The Dàorén drew two door-curtains on the wall
and struck them with his hand.
Someone within answered the door,
opening it with a rattle.
They all eagerly rushed to look,
and saw a bustling crowd coming and going within;
screens, curtains, beds, and tables
were all there too.
Immediately, someone began delivering items outside the door.
The Dàorén ordered the clerks and scribes to line up in the pavilion,
and also instructed them not to speak with the people inside.
As they passed items to each other,
they merely looked and smiled.
In a short while,
the pavilion was filled with furnishings,
utterly magnificent and luxurious.
Then, fine wine diffused its fragrance,
and hot roasts sent up their steam,
all passed out from within the wall.
None of the guests were not astonished.
The pavilion originally backed onto the lake,
and every June,
dozens of acres of lotus flowers
stretched as far as the eye could see.
It was deep winter at the time of the banquet,
and outside the window, all was vast and desolate,
with only hazy greenness.
An official happened to sigh,
"What a lovely gathering today,
it's a pity there are no lotus flowers to adorn it!"
Everyone murmured in agreement.
A moment later,
a green-clad clerk rushed in to report,
"The pond is full of lotus leaves!"
The entire company was startled.
They pushed open the window and gazed out,
and indeed saw a verdant expanse,
interspersed with unopened lotus buds.
In an instant,
tens of thousands of branches and thousands of blossoms
all opened at once;
the north wind blew on their faces,
and the fragrance of lotus permeated their minds.
Everyone thought it extraordinary.
He sent clerks to paddle a boat to pick lotuses.
They remotely saw the clerks enter the dense flowers;
after a short while, they returned,
and came to present the white lotus roots.
An official questioned them,
and the clerks said,
"When we went by boat,
we saw the flowers in the far distance;
as we gradually reached the north bank,
they again turned and were far away in the south marsh."
The Dàorén smiled and said,
"These are merely empty flowers of an illusory dream."
Before long,
the banquet ended,
and the lotuses also withered;
the north wind suddenly rose,
shattering the lotus leaves,
leaving none.
The Jìdōng Guānchá Gōng was very pleased with him,
and took him back to his yámen,
associating with him daily.
One day,
the Gōng was drinking with guests.
The Gōng had a family-secret excellent wine,
and he always limited it to one dòu,
unwilling to allow excessive drinking.
That day,
the guests found the wine sweet and drank it,
insisting on more.
The Gōng firmly refused, claiming it was all gone.
The Dàorén smiled and said to the guests,
"If you absolutely want to fill your old gluttonous desires,
you can ask for it from this humble Dàorén."
The guests asked him.
The Dàorén put a pot into his sleeve,
and after a moment took it out,
pouring for everyone at the table.
It was no different
from what the Gōng had stored.
They stopped only after enjoying themselves to the fullest.
The Gōng was suspicious,
and went in to check his wine,
only to find the seals intact,
but nothing inside.
Secretly ashamed and angry,
he seized the Dàorén, accusing him of being a demon,
and had him flogged.
As soon as the cane struck,
the Gōng felt a sudden sharp pain in his thigh;
with another blow,
the flesh on his buttocks felt like it would tear.
Although the Dàorén was crying out in a hoarse voice at the foot of the steps,
the Guānchá Gōng was already bleeding profusely on his seat.
He then stopped, made no reply,
and ordered him to leave.
The Dàorén then departed from Jì,
his whereabouts unknown.
Later, someone encountered him in Jīnlíng,
his attire as before;
when questioned, he smiled and said nothing.
According to a manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Miào Yǒngdìng,
a *bágòngshēng* from Jiāngxī.
He was habitually addicted to alcohol,
and his relatives and clan members often avoided him.
He once visited his paternal uncle's family.
Miào was a humorous and witty person,
and the guests enjoyed talking with him,
so they drank heartily together.
When Miào got drunk,
he became abusive with alcohol,
insulting the company,
which offended the guests.
The guests were angry,
and the entire company erupted in an uproar.
His uncle tried to mediate between them.
Miào thought his uncle was siding with the guests,
and became even angrier.
His uncle had no choice but to
rush to inform his family.
His family came
and helped him home.
No sooner had he been placed on the bed than
all his limbs became rigid;
when touched,
he lay lifeless, his breath gone.
When Miào died,
a black-hatted man seized him and took him away.
After a while,
they arrived at a yámen,
with turquoise-green tiles,
whose magnificence was unparalleled in the human world.
When they reached the base of the steps,
it seemed they were waiting to be granted an audience with an official.
He thought to himself: What is my crime?
It must be related to the brawl the guests sued over.
He looked back at the black-hatted man,
whose eyes glared like a bull's,
and he dared not ask.
However, he reasoned: As a *gòngshēng* arguing with someone,
perhaps it's not a major crime.
Suddenly, a clerk in the hall announced,
ordering the litigants to await their turn early the next day.
Thereupon, the people below the hall scattered in a hubbub,
like birds and beasts.
Miào also followed the black-hatted man out,
with nowhere else to go,
so he hunched his shoulders and stood under the eaves of a shop.
The black-hatted man angrily said,
"You drunken rogue!
It's getting dark,
everyone else is going to find food and sleep,
so where are you going?"
Miào trembled and said,
"I don't even know what's going on,
and I haven't told my family,
so I have no money for travel or lodging.
Where can I go?"
The black-hatted man said,
"You drunken thief!
If you buy it yourself,
then you'll have the means!
If you hesitate again,
I'll smash your skull with my fists!"
Miào bowed his head and dared not speak.
Suddenly, a person emerged from inside the door.
Seeing Miào,
he asked in surprise,
"Why have you come?"
Miào looked at him,
recognizing him as his maternal uncle.
Uncle Jiǎ氏
had been dead for several years.
Upon seeing him, Miào
finally realized that his uncle was dead,
and his heart grew even more sorrowful and fearful.
He wept profusely to his uncle, saying,
"Uncle, save me!"
Jiǎ looked at the man in the black cap and said,
"Dōnglíng is no stranger;
it is an honor to have you visit my humble abode."
The two then entered.
Jiǎ bowed deeply to the man in the black cap
and asked for his kind favor.
After a moment,
food and wine were brought out,
and they sat together, drinking.
Jiǎ asked,
"What has my nephew done
to warrant such trouble?"
The man in the black cap said,
"The Great King visited Fúluó-jūn,
and encountered your nephew behaving wildly and cursing,
which caused me to come."
Jiǎ asked,
"Has he seen the King yet?"
He replied,
"Fúluó-jūn is attending to the huāzi'àn case,
and the King has not yet returned."
He further asked,
"What punishment will my nephew receive?"
He answered,
"It is yet unknown.
However, the Great King is quite displeased with such individuals."
Miào, standing by,
heard their conversation,
trembled with fear, and broke into a sweat,
unable to lift his cup or chopsticks.
Before long,
the man in the black cap stood up and
thanked them, saying,
"Thank you for the abundant drinks;
I am quite drunk already.
I entrust your nephew to your care.
When the King returns,
I will come to visit again."
Then he left.
Jiǎ said to Miào,
"Nephew, you have no other brothers;
your parents loved you like a pearl in their palm,
and could never bear to scold you even once.
When you were sixteen or seventeen,
after three cups of wine,
you would mumble and find fault with others;
if things were slightly not to your liking,
you would strike doors and curse nakedly.
Yet, they called it childishness.
I didn't expect that after more than ten years,
nephew, you have not improved at all.
What shall we do now!"
Miào prostrated himself on the ground and cried,
only saying that it was too late to regret.
Jiǎ pulled him up and said,
"I run a wine shop here
and have a fair reputation;
I must do my utmost.
The person who just drank with us is the messenger of Dōnglíng;
I often drink with him,
and we are quite good friends.
The Great King has a myriad of affairs daily,
so he may not necessarily remember this incident.
I will carefully speak with him
and ask him privately to release my nephew;
perhaps he will agree."
Then he changed his mind and said,
"This matter is quite a heavy burden,
and cannot be settled without a hundred thousand."
Miào thanked him,
readily taking responsibility and
agreeing.
Miào then stayed at his uncle's place.
The next day,
the man in the black cap arrived early to observe.
Jiǎ asked for a private word,
spoke for a while,
then came to Miào and said,
"It's arranged.
He will return shortly.
I've already put down all I have
as a down payment;
the rest, when you return,
you can slowly gather and bring."
Miào happily asked,
"How much in total?"
He said,
"A hundred thousand."
Miào asked,
"Where will I get so much?"
Jiǎ said,
"Just a hundred bundles of gold, silver, money, and paper
will be enough."
Miào happily said,
"That's easy to arrange."
As it was nearing noon,
the man in the black cap did not arrive.
Miào wanted to go to the market
for a short stroll and look around.
Jiǎ warned him not to wander far,
and Miào agreed and left.
He saw merchants and peddlers in the street,
just like in the human world.
He came to a place
with a high, impenetrable thorn fence,
which seemed to be a prison.
Opposite the gate was a wine shop,
with many people coming and going.
Outside the shop was a long stream,
with dark, churning sewage
that was unfathomably deep.
Just as he was peeking,
he heard someone in the shop call out,
"Miao-jūn, why have you come?"
Miào quickly looked,
and it was Wēng-shēng from a neighboring village,
a literary friend from ten years ago.
He rushed out and shook hands,
as joyful as if they had met in their lifetime.
They went into the shop for a small drink,
each recounting their long separation.
Amidst his good fortune, Miào
again encountered an old acquaintance
and poured out his heart entirely.
Thoroughly drunk,
he completely forgot that he was dead,
and his old habits resurfaced,
shamefully chattering and finding fault with Wēng.
Wēng said,
"After not seeing you for several years,
are you still like this?"
Miào had always disliked people commenting on his drinking habits,
and hearing Wēng's words,
he became even more enraged,
banging the table and cursing.
Wēng glanced at him,
then flung his sleeve and left.
Miào chased him to the edge of the stream
and snatched Wēng's hat.
Wēng angrily said,
"You truly are an irrational person!"
Then he pushed Miào, who stumbled and fell into the stream.
The stream water was not very deep; but in the water were blades like flax,
piercing his ribs and shins,
firm and unmoving,
causing bone-deep pain.
The dark water was half mixed with filth
and, as he inhaled, it went into his throat,
making it impossible to breathe.
People on the bank watched and laughed like a wall,
with no one offering help.
At this critical moment,
Jiǎ suddenly arrived.
Seeing this, he was greatly shocked,
pulled Miào out and brought him back,
saying,
"You are incorrigible!
Even in death, you don't learn;
you are not fit to be a human again!
I beg you to again accept the axe from Dōnglíng."
Miào was terrified
and tearfully said,
"I know my sin."
Jiǎ then said,
"Dōnglíng arrived earlier
to wait for you to make the agreement,
but you were out drinking and didn't return.
He was busy and couldn't wait.
I have already signed the agreement
and given him a thousand strings of cash to leave;
the remainder is due by the end of the ten-day period.
When you return,
you should quickly arrange it,
and at night, in the vast wilderness outside the village,
call my uncle's name and burn it,
and this wish can be fulfilled."
Miào agreed to all of it.
Then Jiǎ urged him to leave.
He escorted him to the outskirts,
and again instructed,
"You must not break your word and implicate me."
Then he showed him the way home.
At that time, Miáo Jǐ 繆己 lay stiff for three days.
His family thought he was dead drunk,
but his breathing was faintly like a hanging thread.
On that day, he revived,
and vomited greatly,
throwing up several *dǒu* 斗 of black substance,
whose stench was unbearable.
After he finished vomiting,
his bedding was soaked with sweat,
and his body finally felt cool and refreshed.
He told his family of the strange experience.
Soon, the pricked spot felt painful and swollen,
becoming a sore overnight,
though fortunately it didn't fester much.
After ten days, he could barely walk with a cane.
His family jointly begged him to repay his karmic debt.
Miáo Jǐ calculated the expenses,
realizing it couldn't be done without several pieces of gold.
He became rather stingy,
saying:
"Perhaps it was just an illusion from a drunken dream.
Even if it wasn't,
since *Yī* 伊 released me privately,
how dare I let the Lord of the Underworld know again?"
His family advised him,
but he wouldn't listen.
However, his heart was anxious and fearful,
and he dared not indulge in drinking again.
The villagers and relatives all rejoiced at his moral improvement,
and gradually began to drink with him.
After more than a year,
the karmic retribution was gradually forgotten,
his will became increasingly unrestrained,
and his old habits gradually re-emerged.
One day,
he was drinking at the home of a relative,
and again cursed the host at the table.
The host expelled him,
closed the door, and left directly.
Miáo Jǐ made a racket for over an hour.
His son then found out,
and prepared to help him home.
Upon entering the room,
he knelt for a long time facing the wall,
throwing himself down countless times,
saying:
"I'll repay your debt now!
I'll repay your debt now!"
After speaking,
he collapsed to the ground.
They looked at him,
and his breath had already ceased.
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* 聊齋誌異)
*Yángwǔ Hóu* 陽武侯 Xuē Gōng Lù 薛公祿 was
a native of Xuējiā Dǎo 薛家島 in Jiāo 膠.
His father, Xuē Gōng Zuì 薛公最, was very poor,
herding cattle for a village gentleman.
The gentleman had some uncultivated land.
While Xuē Gōng Zuì pastured there,
he often saw snakes and rabbits fighting in the weeds,
which he considered unusual.
He therefore asked his master for that place for a dwelling and burial ground,
and built a thatched hut to live in.
Several years later,
his wife was giving birth
when a sudden heavy rain arrived.
Coincidentally, two commanders, dispatched to inspect the coast,
were passing by
and sought shelter inside the door.
They saw a flock of crows and magpies gathered on the roof,
covering the leaking spot with their wings,
which surprised them.
Soon after, the old man came out.
The commanders asked:
"What happened just now?"
He then informed them of the birth.
They further inquired about the gender of the child,
to which he replied:
"It's a boy."
The commanders were even more astonished,
saying:
"This child must be extremely noble.
Otherwise,
why would he have two commanders like us guarding his doorway?"
They sighed in admiration and left.
When the marquis grew up,
his face was dirty and his snot dripped,
and he was far from intelligent.
The Xuē 薛 clan on the island
traditionally belonged to the military registry.
That year, Xuē Gōng Zuì's 翁家 family was required to provide a male to serve in Liáoyáng 遼陽,
and his eldest son was deeply worried about this.
At that time, the marquis was eighteen years old,
considered by people to be too simple-minded
to find a wife.
Suddenly, he said to his elder brother:
"Big brother, are you fretting
because there's no one to take on the service?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Xuē Gōng Lù 薛公祿 laughed and said:
"If you are willing to give me a maidservant as a wife,
I will undertake this task."
His brother was pleased
and immediately married a maidservant to him.
The marquis then took his family to the garrison.
After traveling only a few dozen *lǐ* 里,
a sudden heavy rain fell.
There was a dangerous cliff by the road,
and the couple ran to take shelter beneath it.
A short while later,
the rain stopped,
and they resumed their journey.
Barely a few paces further,
the cliff stones collapsed.
Residents watching from afar saw two tigers leap out,
closely approaching the two people before disappearing.
From then on, the marquis became extraordinarily brave and strong,
and his demeanor changed dramatically.
Later, he was enfeoffed as *Yángwǔ Hóu* 陽武侯 with a hereditary title for his military achievements.
During the Tiānqǐ 天啟 and Chóngzhēn 崇禎 reigns,
the successor marquis, a certain Mr. Mǒu Gōng 某公, died
without a son,
leaving only a posthumous child.
Consequently, a collateral branch temporarily took over.
For all hereditary enfeoffed families who present themselves at court,
if a woman becomes pregnant, it must be reported to the emperor,
and officials would send a midwife to guard her,
until the birth was complete.
After more than a year,
his wife gave birth to a daughter.
After the birth,
her abdomen still pulsated.
For fifteen years,
several midwives were changed,
and then she gave birth to a son.
This son was eligible to be granted the title as the legitimate heir.
The collateral branch made a clamor,
claiming it was not a child of the Xuē 薛 family.
Officials arrested all the midwives,
subjecting them to all sorts of shackles and torments,
but none changed their story.
The title was then settled.
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* 聊齋誌異)
In Zhào Chéng, there was an old woman,
over seventy years old,
who had only one son.
One day, he went into the mountains
and was devoured by a tiger.
The old woman was heartbroken,
almost not wanting to live,
and she wailed and complained to the magistrate (zǎi).
The magistrate laughed and said:
"How can a tiger be controlled by official law?"
The old woman cried even louder,
unable to stop herself.
The magistrate rebuked her,
but she was not afraid.
Out of pity for her old age,
he could not bear to be stern,
so he agreed to catch the tiger for her.
The old woman remained kneeling, not leaving,
insisting on waiting until an official warrant (gōudié) was issued,
only then would she consent to leave.
The magistrate had no choice,
and immediately asked his subordinates
who could go.
A yá lì named Lǐ Néng,
who was tipsy,
approached the seat
and said:
"I can do it."
After receiving the warrant,
the old woman finally left.
When the yá lì sobered up, he regretted it;
he still thought the magistrate's order was a trick,
just to get rid of the old woman's disturbance,
and so he didn't take it very seriously.
When he handed the warrant back,
the magistrate angrily said:
"You firmly said you could do it,
how can you regret it now?"
The yá lì was in a difficult position,
and requested a warrant to round up hunters.
The magistrate agreed.
The yá lì gathered the hunters,
and they lay in ambush day and night in the mountain valleys,
hoping to catch a tiger,
so that they could fulfill their duty.
More than a month passed,
and he had received hundreds of beatings (shòu zhàng),
his grievances and suffering had nowhere to be expressed.
So he went to the Dōngguō Yuè Miào,
knelt and prayed,
crying until he lost his voice.
Before long,
a tiger came from outside.
The yá lì was startled and confused,
afraid of being bitten and eaten.
The tiger entered,
not looking elsewhere,
and squatted in the middle of the doorway.
The yá lì prayed:
"If you are the one who killed so-and-so's son,
then please allow me to bind you."
Then he took out a rope and tied the tiger's neck,
and the tiger docilely submitted to being tied.
He led it to the county office.
The magistrate asked the tiger:
"Did you devour so-and-so's son?"
The tiger nodded.
The magistrate said:
"A murderer dies,
this is an ancient law.
Moreover, the old woman had only one son,
and you killed him;
her remaining years are almost over,
how will she live?
If you can be like a son to her,
I will pardon you."
The tiger nodded again.
Then he released its bonds and let it go.
The old woman was still resenting the magistrate for not killing the tiger to avenge her son.
The next morning,
when she opened her door,
there was a dead deer;
the old woman sold its meat and hide,
using it to support herself.
From then on, this became a regular occurrence,
and sometimes it would bring gold and silk and throw them into her courtyard.
The old woman thus became prosperous,
her sustenance better than what her son provided.
She secretly felt grateful to the tiger.
When the tiger came,
it would sometimes lie under the eaves,
not leaving all day.
Humans and beast lived in harmony,
without any suspicion.
Several years later,
when the old woman died,
the tiger came and roared in the hall.
The old woman's accumulated wealth
was amply sufficient to arrange a funeral,
and her clansmen buried her together.
Just as the mound was completed,
the tiger suddenly ran over,
and all the guests fled.
The tiger went directly to the tomb,
howling like thunder,
and only left after some time.
The local people erected
"Yì Hǔ Cí"
in the eastern suburbs,
which still exists today.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì*.
A man named Zhāng,
happening to walk through a stream valley,
heard a very fierce sound from the cliff.
He found a path and climbed up to observe,
and saw a giant snake, as thick as a bowl,
thrashing and struggling among a clump of trees,
hitting a willow with its tail,
breaking its branches.
Its twisting, falling, and staggering movements
suggested that something was grappling with it.
However, upon careful examination, he saw nothing unusual,
and was greatly puzzled.
Gradually approaching,
he saw a praying mantis perched on its head,
grabbing its head with its "dagger-like" arms,
making it unable to escape.
After a long time,
the snake finally died.
Looking at the skin and flesh on its forehead,
it was already torn open.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì*.
Lǐ Chāo,
courtesy name Kuíwú,
was from the western border of Zī Prefecture.
He was forthright and generous,
and fond of giving.
One day, a monk came begging for alms,
and Lǐ fed him a full meal.
The monk was very grateful,
and said:
"I come from Shàolín.
I have some minor skills,
and would like to teach them to you."
Lǐ was pleased,
and hosted him in his guest house,
providing him generously,
learning from him morning and evening.
After three months,
his skill was quite refined,
and he was very pleased with himself.
The monk asked:
"Have you improved?"
He replied:
"I have improved.
What my master can do,
I can now do entirely."
The monk smiled,
and bade Lǐ demonstrate his skill.
Lǐ then took off his clothes and spat on his hands,
flying like an ape,
descending like a bird,
leaping and tumbling for a while,
then proudly stood facing the monk.
The monk smiled again and said:
"Very good.
Since you have mastered all my abilities,
please let us compete to see who is superior."
Lǐ gladly agreed,
and they each crossed their arms and took a stance.
After that, they pushed and blocked each other,
Lǐ continually finding the monk's weaknesses;
suddenly the monk threw out a kick,
and Lǐ was already thrown backward more than a zhàng.
The monk clapped his hands and said:
"You have not yet mastered all my abilities."
Lǐ pressed his palms to the ground,
ashamed and disheartened, he asked for further instruction.
A few days later,
the monk departed.
Lǐ thus became famous for his martial arts,
roaming north and south,
with no one to match him.
He once happened upon Lìxià
and saw a young nun
performing her art in the square;
onlookers filled it to overflowing.
The nun addressed the assembled guests, saying:
"To turn oneself upside down
is truly quite a cold spectacle.
If any of you are keen,
you might as well step forward for a playful bout."
She repeated this three times.
The crowd looked at each other,
but no one responded.
Lǐ was at the side,
and feeling his skill itching,
he stepped forward with eagerness.
The nun smiled and clasped her hands together.
As soon as they exchanged a move,
the nun halted him, saying:
"This is the Shàolín sect."
She immediately asked:
"Who is your esteemed master?"
Lǐ initially did not speak.
When she pressed him firmly,
he then named his monastic master.
The nun bowed with clasped hands and said:
"Hān Héshang is your master?
If so,
there's no need to exchange blows;
I am willing to concede defeat."
Lǐ urged her repeatedly,
but the nun refused.
The crowd encouraged her,
and the nun finally said:
"Since you are Hān Shī's disciple,
and we are both from the same fold,
there's no harm in a playful match.
But let it be understood between us."
Lǐ agreed.
However, because of her delicate appearance,
he underestimated her;
and being young and fond of winning,
he wished to defeat her,
to gain a day's renown.
Just as they were sparring,
the nun suddenly stopped.
Lǐ asked why,
but she only smiled and said nothing.
Lǐ thought she was afraid,
and insisted on another round.
The nun then rose.
A moment later,
Lǐ lunged with an ankle kick.
The nun pressed her five fingers down to strike his thigh;
Lǐ felt his knee down as if struck by a blade,
and he stumbled and fell, unable to rise.
The nun smiled and apologized, saying:
"I was presumptuous and offended a guest;
please do not blame me!"
Lǐ was carried home,
and it was over a month before he recovered.
More than a year later,
the monk returned
and recounted the past event.
The monk exclaimed:
"You are utterly reckless!
Why provoke her?
Fortunately, you first mentioned my name;
otherwise,
your thigh would have been broken!"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
During the Kāngxī period,
there was a magician carrying a small case.
Inside the case was a small person,
about a foot tall.
When a coin was given,
he would open the case and let the person out,
who would sing a tune and then withdraw.
Upon arriving in Yè,
the magistrate of Yè ordered the case brought to his office
to closely investigate the small person's origin.
Initially, he dared not speak.
When pressed firmly,
he began to describe his hometown and family.
It turned out he was a schoolboy,
returning home from his tutor's,
when he was enchanted by the magician,
who then gave him a medicine
that caused all his limbs to shrink abruptly;
the magician then carried him away,
using him as a performing prop.
The magistrate was enraged
and killed the magician.
He kept the boy, intending to cure him,
but had not yet found the method.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Qínshēng of Láizhōu
made a medicinal wine,
but accidentally added poisonous ingredients.
Unable to bear pouring it away,
he sealed and set it aside.
More than a year passed.
One night, he happened to crave a drink,
but had no wine available.
He suddenly remembered what he had stored,
opened the seal, and sniffed it.
A fragrant and potent aroma wafted out,
making his insides itch and his mouth water,
irresistibly.
He took a cup and was about to taste it,
but his wife desperately advised against it.
Qínshēng laughed and said:
"To drink quickly and die
is far better than to die of craving and thirst."
Having finished one cup,
he inverted the bottle to pour another.
His wife overturned the bottle,
spilling it all over the room.
Qínshēng prostrated himself on the ground and drank it like an ox.
A short while later,
he suffered abdominal pain and locked jaw,
and died in the middle of the night.
His wife wailed,
prepared a coffin,
and mourners helped with the burial.
The next night,
a beautiful woman suddenly entered,
not three feet tall.
She went directly to the funeral chamber,
poured a bowl of water on him,
and he abruptly revived.
When questioned,
she said:
"I am a fox immortal.
My husband recently went to Chén Jiā,
stole wine, got drunk, and died;
I went to save him and returned.
Happening to pass by your house,
he pitied this gentleman, who suffered the same illness as himself,
and so sent me to revive him with the leftover medicine."
Having spoken,
she vanished.
My friend, the *Gòngshì* Qiū Xíngsù,
was fond of drinking.
One night he craved wine,
but there was no place to buy any,
and he tossed and turned, unable to bear it,
so he thought of substituting it with vinegar.
He consulted his wife,
who scoffed at him.
Qiū insisted,
and so she heated vinegar and presented it.
After finishing the pot,
he finally undressed and slept soundly.
The next day,
he used up the money for a pot of wine
and sent his servant to buy some.
On the way, the servant met his younger cousin Xiāngchén,
who questioned him to learn the reason,
and then suspected that his sister-in-law was unwilling to procure wine for his brother.
The servant said:
"Madam said, 'There isn't much vinegar stored at home;
half of it was used up last night. I'm afraid if another pot is used,
the stock of vinegar will be exhausted.'"
Those who heard this all laughed.
They did not know that when the craving for wine is intense,
even poison would taste sweet,
let alone vinegar!
This too can be passed down.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Student Wáng Wén
was from Dōngchāng.
From a young age, he was sincere and upright.
He traveled for a short while in Chǔ,
and when passing through Liùhé,
he rested at an inn.
He then walked outside the door.
He encountered a relative from his village, Zhào Dōnglóu,
who was a great merchant
and had not returned home for several years.
When Zhào Dōnglóu saw Wáng Wén,
they greeted each other with great joy,
and Zhào Dōnglóu immediately invited him to visit.
Arriving at Zhào Dōnglóu's place,
Wáng Wén saw a beautiful woman sitting in the room,
and he was startled and stepped back.
Zhào Dōnglóu pulled him in,
and then called through the window for the girl to leave.
Only then did Wáng Wén enter.
Zhào Dōnglóu prepared food and drink,
and they conversed about their well-being.
Wáng Wén asked,
"What kind of place is this?"
Zhào Dōnglóu replied,
"This is a small brothel.
Because I have been a long-term guest,
I am temporarily lodging here."
During their conversation,
the girl frequently entered and exited.
Wáng Wén felt uneasy and constrained,
and rose from his seat to bid farewell.
Zhào Dōnglóu strongly held him and made him sit.
Soon after, a young girl
passed by outside the door.
Seeing Wáng Wén,
her beautiful eyes frequently glanced his way,
her eyebrows and eyes filled with affection,
and her demeanor was graceful and gentle.
She was truly a celestial being.
Wáng Wén was usually straightforward and proper,
but at this sight, he was completely bewildered and lost,
and immediately asked,
"Who is that beautiful person?"
Zhào Dōnglóu said,
"This is the old woman's second daughter,
her pet name is Yātóu,
and she is fourteen years old.
Those who pay for her repeatedly tempt the old woman with large sums of money,
but the girl insists she doesn't wish to,
leading her mother to whip and beat her.
The girl pleads for mercy due to her youth.
She is still waiting for a suitor."
Hearing this, Wáng Wén
bowed his head and sat silently in a daze,
utterly failing to respond appropriately.
Zhào Dōnglóu teased him, saying,
"If you are interested,
I will act as a matchmaker."
Wáng Wén responded with a look of dismay, saying,
"I dare not entertain such a thought."
Yet, as evening approached,
he made no mention of leaving.
Zhào Dōnglóu again jokingly offered his help.
Wáng Wén said,
"Your kind intention is deeply appreciated and admired,
but my purse is empty, what can I do!"
Zhào Dōnglóu knew the girl's strong will,
and that she would surely not agree,
so he offered to help with ten pieces of gold.
Wáng Wén bowed in thanks and rushed out.
He emptied his own funds and brought
five pieces of gold, urging Zhào Dōnglóu to present them to the old woman.
The old woman indeed thought it was too little.
Yātóu said to her mother,
"Mother daily blames me for not being a money tree.
Today, I have fulfilled your wish.
I am just beginning to learn how to be a person,
and the day will come when I repay you.
Do not let this trivial sum send away a god of wealth."
The old woman, being stubbornly opinionated as women are,
was very happy once she agreed.
So she consented,
and sent a maid to invite Wáng Láng.
Zhào Dōnglóu found it difficult to go back on his word,
and added more gold to give to the old woman.
Wáng Wén and the girl's love and affection were profound.
Afterwards,
she said to Wáng Wén,
"I am of a lowly profession,
unfit to be your equal.
Since you have shown such deep affection,
my duty to you is of utmost importance.
You emptied your purse for this one night of joy,
what will you do tomorrow?"
Wáng Wén was tearful and choked with sorrow.
The girl said,
"Do not grieve.
My life in the dust
is truly not what I desired.
But I have not met anyone as steadfast and trustworthy as you.
Please let us flee tonight."
Wáng Wén was delighted,
and immediately rose;
the girl also rose.
They heard the watchman's drum strike three times.
The girl quickly changed into men's clothes,
and they hastily went out together,
knocking on the host's door.
Wáng Wén, who always traveled with two guards,
fabricated an urgent matter,
and ordered his servant to depart immediately.
The girl tied talismans to the servant's thigh and the donkey's ears,
and let loose the reins, riding at top speed.
Their eyes could not be opened,
and only the sound of the wind whistled past their ears.
At dawn, they reached the mouth of the Hànjiāng River,
rented a house, and stopped.
Wáng Wén was astonished by her unusual abilities.
The girl said,
"If I tell you,
will you not be afraid?
I am not human,
but a fox.
My mother is greedy and licentious,
and I suffered abuse daily,
accumulating resentment in my heart.
Now I am fortunate to escape this sea of suffering.
A hundred li away,
I am no longer known to them,
so fortunately, we are safe."
Wáng Wén had no doubts whatsoever,
and calmly said,
"My house faces lotuses,
but my home has only four bare walls.
It is truly difficult to console myself,
and I fear I will eventually be abandoned."
The girl said,
"Why do you have this worry?
All market goods are available,
and for three or so mouths,
even a frugal living can be self-sufficient.
You can sell the donkey as capital."
Wáng Wén did as she said,
immediately setting up a small stall in front of the door.
Wáng Wén and his servant personally worked together,
selling wine and juice there.
The girl made shawls
and embroidered lotus pouches,
earning a daily surplus,
providing for them very well.
After more than a year,
they gradually were able to afford maids and old women servants.
From then on, Wáng Wén no longer wore short trousers (of a laborer),
but merely managed and supervised.
One day, the girl suddenly became quietly sad,
saying,
"Tonight there will be trouble,
what shall we do!"
Wáng Wén asked her,
and the girl said,
"Mother knows my whereabouts
and will surely oppress me.
If my elder sister comes,
I have no worries;
I only fear Mother herself will arrive."
It was already midnight,
and she congratulated herself, saying,
"No worries,
my elder sister has arrived."
Shortly after,
the girl pushed open the door and entered.
Yātóu smiled and greeted her.
The girl cursed, saying,
“You brazen
slave, follow and hide!
My old mother ordered me to tie you up and take you away.”
Immediately, she took out a rope and tied it around the girl’s neck.
The girl angrily said,
“What crime have I committed by following one person?”
Nīzǐ grew even more indignant,
and she seized the girl, tearing her collar.
All the household maids and matrons gathered.
Nīzǐ, frightened,
ran out.
The girl said,
“Sister, go back;
Mother will surely come herself.
A great disaster is not far off;
you should quickly make plans.”
So, she hurriedly packed her belongings,
intending to relocate again.
Suddenly, the matron burst in,
her face beaming with rage,
and said,
“I knew that a slave like you would be rude;
I had to come myself!”
The girl went to meet her, kneeling and weeping mournfully.
The matron said nothing,
but grabbed her hair and dragged her away.
Wáng [Wén] wandered around, distraught and sorrowful,
neglecting sleep and food entirely.
He urgently went to Liùhé,
hoping to bribe someone for her redemption.
When he arrived, the gate and courtyard were as before,
but the people were gone.
He asked the residents,
but none knew where they had moved.
He returned, grieving her loss.
Thereupon, he dispersed the travelers
and returned east with his money.
Several years later,
he happened to enter Yāndū,
and passing by the Yùyīngtáng,
he saw a child,
seven or eight years old.
His servant thought the child resembled his master,
and repeatedly gazed at him.
Wáng [Wén] asked,
“What are you looking at, that you say so?”
The servant laughed in reply.
Wáng [Wén] also laughed.
He looked closely at the child,
who had a remarkable demeanor.
He thought to himself that he lacked an heir,
and since the child resembled him,
he loved him and redeemed him.
When asked his name,
he called himself Wáng Zī.
Wáng [Wén] said,
“You were abandoned in swaddling clothes;
how do you know your surname?”
He said,
“My former master once said
that when they found me,
there were characters on my chest,
which read ‘son of Wáng Wén of Shāndōng.’”
Wáng [Wén] was greatly astonished and said,
“I am Wáng Wén;
how could I have a son?”
He thought it must be someone with the same name,
but secretly rejoiced in his heart,
and cherished him greatly.
Upon his return,
those who saw the child knew without asking that he was Wáng [Wén]’s son.
Zī gradually grew up,
strong and powerful,
fond of hunting,
not engaged in production,
and enjoying fighting and killing.
Wáng [Wén] was also unable to restrain him.
He also claimed to be able to see ghosts and foxes,
but Wáng [Wén] did not believe any of it.
It happened that there was someone in the village afflicted by a fox,
and they invited Zī to go and observe it.
Upon arrival, he pointed to where the fox was hidden,
and ordered several people to strike where he pointed.
Immediately, a fox cried out,
and fur and blood fell,
and from then on, the family was at peace.
Because of this, people regarded him with even greater wonder.
Wáng one day was strolling through the market,
when he suddenly met Zhào Dōnglóu,
his turban and robe disheveled,
his face gaunt and dark.
Wáng was startled and asked where he had come from.
Zhào sadly answered.
Wáng then accompanied him home,
and ordered wine.
Zhào said:
“The old woman (Wú Ǎo) acquired Yātóu,
and subjected her to cruel beatings.
After moving north,
she also tried to break her will.
The girl swore she would rather die than be unfaithful,
so she was imprisoned.
She gave birth to a boy,
who was abandoned in a side alley;
I heard he was in an orphanage,
and I imagine he has grown up by now.
This is the heir of your lineage.”
Wáng shed tears and said:
“Heaven be praised, my son has returned.”
He then recounted the whole story.
He asked:
“Why have you fallen so low?”
Zhào sighed and said:
“Now I know that the charms of the pleasure quarters
should not be taken too seriously.
What more can I say!”
Before this,
when Wú Ǎo moved north,
Zhào followed her as a peddler.
Heavy goods that were difficult to transport
were all sold cheaply.
Along the way, travel expenses and supplies
cost an immeasurable amount.
Thus, he suffered great losses.
Nīzi’s demands were especially extravagant.
Within a few years,
ten thousand gold coins were completely gone.
When Wú Ǎo saw the money on the bedside was exhausted,
she began to give him the cold shoulder day and night.
Nīzi gradually started staying at noble households,
often not returning for several nights.
Zhào was furious and could not bear it,
but there was nothing he could do.
Just then, Wú Ǎo went out,
and Yātóu called Zhào from the window, saying:
“There is no true affection in the brothel,
what is interwoven and spoken
is merely for money.
If you linger and do not leave,
you will invite terrible disaster.”
Zhào was frightened,
as if waking from a dream.
Before leaving,
he secretly went to see the girl.
The girl gave him a letter to deliver to Wáng,
and Zhào then returned.
He then recounted this situation to Wáng.
He immediately produced Yātóu’s letter.
The letter read:
“I know Zī’ér is already by your side.
My predicament,
Mr. Dōnglóu can certainly understand in detail.
The karma of a past life,
what more can be said!
I am in a secluded room,
dark and without sunlight,
whip wounds tear my skin,
the fire of hunger torments my heart,
every passing day and night
feels like years.
If you do not forget the single quilt on a snowy night by the Hán River,
when we mutually embraced for warmth,
you should plan with our son,
and surely be able to free me from my distress.
Although my mother and sister are cruel,
they are still my flesh and blood,
I only ask that they not be severely injured or maimed,
that is all I wish for.”
Wáng read it,
and wept uncontrollably,
then gave Zhào gold and silk and departed.
At this time, Zī was eighteen years old.
Wáng recounted the whole story to him,
and then showed him his mother’s letter.
Zī’s eyes burned with rage,
and on that very day he went to the capital.
He inquired about Wú Ǎo’s residence,
and saw carriages and horses filling the courtyard.
Zī went straight in.
Nīzi was drinking with a guest from Hú,
when she saw Zī,
she stood startled, her color changing.
Zī rushed forward and killed her.
The guests were greatly alarmed,
thinking he was a bandit.
When they looked at the female corpse,
it had already transformed into a fox.
Zī held his blade and forced his way in,
seeing Wú Ǎo supervising a maid making soup.
Zī ran to the door of the room,
but Wú Ǎo suddenly disappeared.
Zī looked around,
quickly drew an arrow,
and shot it towards the roof beam;
a fox, pierced through the heart, fell,
and he then decapitated it.
He soon found his mother’s location,
threw stones to break open the flat door,
and both mother and son cried out.
His mother asked about Wú Ǎo,
he replied:
“I have already executed her.”
His mother complained:
“Why didn’t you listen to my words, my son!”
She ordered the corpse to be buried in the countryside.
Zī feigned agreement,
but stripped off its skin and hid it.
He searched Wú Ǎo’s trunks and boxes,
took all the gold and valuables,
and brought them to his mother before returning home.
The couple reunited,
with mingled joy and sorrow.
When his mother asked about Wú Ǎo,
Zī said:
“She is in my bag.”
Startled, she asked,
and he produced two pieces of leather and presented them.
His mother was enraged,
and cursed him, saying:
“Rebellious son!
How could you do this!”
She wailed and beat herself,
writhing as if to die.
Wáng tried his best to comfort her,
and scolded his son to bury the leather.
Zī angrily said:
“Now that you have found comfort and peace,
have you forgotten the beatings and torment?”
His mother grew even angrier,
and continued to weep.
Only when Zī buried the skin and reported back
did she finally calm down a little.
After his daughter returned, Wáng’s
household prospered even more.
He was grateful to Zhào,
and rewarded him with a large sum of money.
Zhào then realized that Wú Ǎo and her daughter were both foxes.
Zī was very filial and respectful;
but if one accidentally provoked him,
he would shout violently and harshly.
The daughter (Yātóu) said to Wáng:
“Our son has a stubborn bone (or ‘twisted sinew’),
if it is not removed,
he will eventually kill people and ruin our wealth.”
That night, while Zī was asleep,
she secretly bound his hands and feet.
Zī awoke and said:
“I am innocent.”
His mother said:
“I am going to cure your violence,
do not suffer.”
Zī cried out loudly,
and writhed, unable to be unbound.
His mother used a large needle to pierce the side of his ankle bone,
about three or four fen deep,
and forcibly snapped it,
with a sudden cracking sound;
she did the same at his elbows and near his brain.
Afterward,
she released his bonds,
and patted him to lie down comfortably.
At dawn,
he rushed to attend to his parents,
and tearfully said:
“My son, night and day, recalls his past actions,
none of which were human!”
His parents were overjoyed,
and from then on, their son was as gentle as a maiden,
and the villagers praised him.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“All courtesans are foxes.
I would not say that there are foxes who are courtesans;
as for a fox who is also a procuress,
that is a beast who is also a bird.
Destroying reason and harming ethics,
what is there to be surprised about?
As for enduring a hundred twists and a thousand trials,
and remaining faithful until death,
this is difficult for humans,
yet it is found in a fox?
Mr. Táng said that Wèi Zhēng was even more charming,
I would say the same of Yātóu.”
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The Liú clan of Chángshān
was stout and fond of drinking.
Every time he drank alone,
he would finish a whole jar.
He owned three hundred *mǔ* of land near the city wall,
half of which was planted with millet;
yet his family was exceedingly wealthy,
and drinking was not a burden to him.
A foreign monk saw him
and said that he had a strange illness.
Liú replied:
"No."
The monk said:
"Have you ever not gotten drunk from your drinking?"
He said:
"Yes."
He said:
"This is a wine worm."
Liú was astonished
and immediately sought medical treatment.
The monk said:
"It's easy."
He asked:
"What medicine is needed?"
The monk said none was needed.
"Just lie face down in the sun today,
with your hands and feet bound;
place a vessel of fine wine
about half a foot from your head."
After a while,
he became parched and thirsty,
desiring a drink intensely.
The aroma of wine entered his nose,
the fire of craving burned strongly,
but he agonizingly could not drink.
Suddenly, he felt an intense itch in his throat,
and something vomited out,
falling directly into the wine.
He unbound himself and looked;
it was a red fleshy thing about three inches long,
wriggling like a swimming fish,
with mouth and eyes fully formed.
Liú was surprised and grateful.
He offered gold as payment,
but the monk refused,
only asking for the worm.
He asked:
"What will you use it for?"
The monk said:
"This is the essence of wine: store water in a jar,
put the worm in and stir,
and it will immediately become fine wine."
Liú had him test it,
and it was true.
From then on, Liú hated wine as an enemy.
His body gradually thinned,
and his family also grew poorer day by day,
later becoming unable to afford even food and drink.
Yìshǐ Shì remarked:
"Finishing one *shí* a day
did not diminish his wealth;
not drinking one *dǒu*
only made him poorer: could it be that one's eating and drinking are predestined?"
"Some say: 'The worm was Liú's good fortune,
not Liú's illness;
the monk fooled him to accomplish his trick.'
Is that true or not?"
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition
The merchant Bái Yǒugōng said:
"On the Luòkǒu River,
I saw a man carrying a bamboo basket
and leading two large dogs.
From the basket, he took out a wooden carving of a beautiful woman,
over a foot tall,
whose hands moved on their own,
with glamorous makeup, lifelike.
He then put small brocade saddlecloths on the dogs' backs,
and made the woman sit astride them.
Once she was positioned,
he shouted for the dogs to run swiftly.
The beautiful woman stood up by herself,
performing various acts like the 'untamed horse,'
with her belly hidden by the stirrups,
and her tail attached to her waist.
She knelt, bowed, and stood up,
her transformations agile and flawless.
He also performed 'Zhāojūn Exiting the Frontier': he took another wooden carving,
inserted pheasant feathers,
wore a sheepskin coat,
and rode a dog to follow her.
Zhāojūn frequently looked back,
and the sheepskin-clad figure cracked a whip and pursued her,
truly as if alive."
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition
Fàn Shíyīniáng was
the daughter of the Libationer of Lùchéng.
In her youth, she was enchantingly beautiful,
and her literary elegance was particularly outstanding.
Her parents doted on her,
and seekers of her hand were always allowed to choose for themselves;
but she rarely found anyone acceptable.
It happened that on the Yuán Festival,
the nuns at Shuǐyuè Temple
held
a "Yúlánpén Assembly."
On that day,
maidens gathered like clouds,
and she also went there.
While she was enjoying herself,
a young woman walked alongside her,
repeatedly gazing at her face,
as if she wanted to speak.
Upon closer inspection,
she was an unparalleled beauty of sixteen.
Delighted and pleased,
Fàn Shíyīniáng turned her gaze upon her.
The young woman smiled and said:
"Sister, are you not Fàn Shíyīniáng?"
She replied:
"Indeed."
The young woman said:
"I have long heard your esteemed name,
and what people say is indeed not false."
Shíyīniáng also inquired about her residence.
The young woman smiled and said:
"My surname is Fēng,
I am the third daughter,
living nearby in the next village."
They held hands and laughed happily,
their words warm and gentle,
and thus they became very fond of each other,
clinging together unwilling to part.
Shíyīniáng asked:
"Why are you without companions?"
She replied:
"My parents died early,
and there is only an old woman at home,
left to guard the house,
so she could not come."
When Shíyīniáng was about to return,
Fēng gazed at her, on the verge of tears,
and Shíyīniáng was also wistful,
so she invited her to visit.
Fēng said:
"Your family lives in a vermilion gate and embroidered household,
while I have no relatives of distant connection,
I fear causing gossip and suspicion."
Shíyīniáng insisted on inviting her.
She replied:
"Another day."
Shíyīniáng then took off a golden hairpin and gave it to her,
and Fēng also took a green hairpin from her bun as a return gift.
After Shíyīniáng returned,
her longing was exceptionally strong.
She took out the gifted hairpin;
it was neither gold nor jade,
and her family members did not recognize it,
finding it very strange.
She waited daily for her to come,
becoming dispirited and falling ill.
Her parents, learning the reason,
sent people to inquire in the nearby village,
but no one knew of her.
It was then the Double Ninth Festival,
and Shíyīniáng, weak and bored,
persuaded her maid to forcefully help her peek into the garden,
setting up a mat under the east fence.
Suddenly, a young woman climbed the wall to peer in;
when she looked closely,
it was Miss Fēng.
She called out:
"Help me down with your strength."
The maid complied,
and she swiftly descended.
Shíyīniáng was both surprised and delighted,
immediately stood up,
and pulled her to sit on the mat,
reproaching her for breaking her promise,
and also asking where she came from.
She replied:
“My family lives still far from here,
and I sometimes come to my maternal uncle’s family to play.
What I said before about a nearby village
was because of my maternal uncle’s family.
After we parted, I suffered quite a bit from longing;
however, when a poor and humble person associates with a noble one,
before their feet have even entered the gate,
they first feel shame and apprehension,
fearing they will be looked down upon by maids and servants,
which is why I did not come.
Just now, I passed outside the wall
and heard a woman’s voice,
so I immediately peered over,
hoping it was Miss.
Today, my wish has indeed come true.”
Shíyīniáng then recounted the origin of her illness.
Fēng cried, her tears falling like rain,
and then said:
“My coming must be kept secret.
Those who fabricate stories and stir up trouble,
spreading gossip and slander,
are unbearable to me.”
Shíyīniáng agreed.
They went back to share the same bed,
happily pouring out their hearts to each other.
Her illness soon healed.
They swore to be sisters,
and their clothes and shoes
were often exchanged and worn.
When someone came,
they would hide between the double screens.
After five or six months accumulated,
Gōng and Fūrén began to hear about it.
One day,
as the two were playing chess,
Fūrén quietly entered.
She observed carefully
and exclaimed in surprise:
“You are truly my daughter’s friend!”
She then said to Shíyīniáng:
“You have such a good friend in your chambers,
which makes us both so happy;
why didn’t you tell us earlier?”
Shíyīniáng then conveyed Fēng’s feelings.
Fūrén looked at Sānniáng and said:
“Having her accompany my daughter
makes me extremely happy and comforted;
why did you keep it a secret?”
Fēng blushed deeply across her cheeks,
silently fiddling with her sash.
After Fūrén left,
Fēng then said goodbye.
Shíyīniáng earnestly tried to make her stay,
so she remained.
One evening,
she rushed in from outside the gate,
crying and saying:
“I insisted I shouldn’t stay,
and now I have indeed suffered this great insult!”
Shíyīniáng asked in alarm.
She replied:
“Just now, I went out to change clothes,
when a young man
brazenly interfered with me.
Luckily, I managed to escape.
Given this,
what face do I have left?!”
Shíyīniáng questioned her closely about his appearance.
She apologized and said:
“You needn’t be upset;
this is my foolish elder brother.
I will tell Fūrén
to punish him with a beating.”
Fēng firmly insisted on leaving.
Shíyīniáng asked her to stay until dawn.
Fēng said:
“My maternal uncle’s family is very close;
you just need to lend me a ladder to get over the wall.”
Shíyīniáng knew she couldn’t be persuaded to stay,
so she had two maids climb over the wall to escort her.
After going about half a *lǐ*,
Fēng thanked them and left by herself.
When the maids returned,
Shíyīniáng lay on her bed, grieving and lamenting, as if she had lost her spouse.
Several months later,
the maid, for some reason, went to Dōngcūn.
Returning in the evening,
she met Fēng Nǚ coming with an old woman.
The maid was delighted
and bowed to greet her.
Fēng Nǚ also felt sympathetic
and inquired about Shíyīniáng's well-being.
The maid grabbed her sleeve and said,
"Sāngū, please come to my place!
My mistress is dying of longing to see you!"
Fēng Nǚ said,
"I miss her too,
but I don't want my family to know.
When you return, open the garden gate,
and I will come myself."
The maid returned and told Shíyīniáng;
Shíyīniáng was overjoyed.
Following her instructions,
Fēng Nǚ was already in the garden.
They met,
each recounting their time apart,
and chatted endlessly through the night.
Seeing the maid sleeping soundly,
Fēng Nǚ rose,
moved to share the same pillow with Shíyīniáng,
and whispered,
"I know that Young Mistress is not yet betrothed.
With your talent, beauty, and family background,
why worry about not finding a noble and distinguished husband?
However, those dissolute dandies
are not worth considering.
If you wish to find an excellent match,
please do not judge by wealth or poverty."
Shíyīniáng agreed.
Fēng Nǚ said,
"The place where we met by chance last year
is now holding a Buddhist ritual again.
Tomorrow, please trouble yourself to go there once more,
and I will let you see a satisfactory gentleman.
When I was young, I read books on physiognomy,
and I am quite accurate."
At dawn,
Fēng Nǚ immediately left,
promising to wait at the Buddhist temple.
Shíyīniáng indeed went,
and Fēng Nǚ was already there.
After surveying for a while,
Shíyīniáng invited her to share her carriage.
As they walked out hand in hand,
they saw a scholar,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
dressed in a simple cloth robe,
but with a handsome and dignified appearance.
Fēng Nǚ secretly pointed and said,
"This is a talent for the Hányuàn."
Shíyīniáng glanced at him briefly.
Fēng Nǚ then said,
"Young Mistress, please go home first,
I will follow shortly."
As dusk fell,
she indeed arrived
and said,
"I just observed him very carefully.
That person is Méng Ānrén from the same village."
Shíyīniáng knew he was poor
and did not consider him suitable.
Fēng Nǚ said,
"Young Mistress, why do you also fall into worldly sentiments?
If this man were to remain poor and lowly forever,
I would pluck out my eyeballs
and never again look at any gentleman in the world."
Shíyīniáng asked,
"Then what should be done?"
She replied,
"I wish to get an object
to present to him as a pledge of alliance."
Shíyīniáng said,
"Sister, why are you so hasty?
My parents are alive;
what if it doesn't work out?"
Fēng Nǚ said,
"The reason I am doing this
is precisely because I fear it might not work out.
If one's resolve is firm,
how can life and death snatch it away?"
Shíyīniáng absolutely refused.
Fēng Nǚ said,
"Young Mistress's marriage karma has been stirred,
but the karmic obstacles have not yet been dispelled.
That is why
I came to repay your former kindness.
Please let us part now,
and I will take the golden phoenix hairpin you gave me
to falsely present it to him."
Just as Shíyīniáng was contemplating discussing it further,
Fēng Nǚ had already left.
At that time, Méng Shēng was poor but very talented.
He intended to choose a spouse carefully,
which is why he was still unbetrothed at eighteen.
On that day,
he suddenly saw two beautiful women,
and returned home lost in thought.
As the first watch was nearly over,
Fēng Sānniáng gently knocked and entered.
By candlelight,
he recognized her as the one he had seen earlier that day
and joyfully questioned her.
She said,
"I am from the Fēng clan,
a companion of Fàn Shíyīniáng."
The scholar was greatly pleased;
without pausing to examine closely,
he rushed forward to embrace her.
Fēng Nǚ refused, saying,
"I am not Máo Suì,
but Cáo Qiūshēng.
Shíyīniáng wishes to forge an eternal bond;
please ask me to be the matchmaker."
The scholar was astonished and disbelieving.
Fēng Nǚ then showed him the hairpin.
The scholar was overjoyed beyond measure
and swore,
"Since I am favored with such attention,
if I cannot have Shíyīniáng,
I would rather remain a widower for life."
Fēng Nǚ then left.
At dawn, the scholar
asked a neighboring old woman to visit Fàn Fūrén.
The lady, seeing his poverty,
did not even consult her daughter
and immediately turned her away.
When Shíyīniáng learned of this,
her heart was disappointed,
and she deeply resented Fēng Nǚ for misleading her;
but the golden hairpin was difficult to retrieve,
so she could only swear to die for it.
A few more days passed,
and a certain high-ranking official sought marriage for his son.
Fearing it might not succeed,
he asked the magistrate to act as matchmaker.
At that time, the official was in a powerful position,
and Fàn Gōng feared him in his heart.
He consulted Shíyīniáng,
but Shíyīniáng was unhappy.
When her mother questioned her,
she remained silent,
but shed tears.
She had someone secretly tell her mother,
"If it's not Méng Shēng,
I will die rather than marry."
When Fàn Gōng heard this,
he grew even angrier
and ultimately agreed to the official's family.
He also suspected Shíyīniáng had a secret affection for the scholar
and therefore chose an auspicious day to hasten the ceremony.
Shíyīniáng, in her indignation, refused to eat
and spent her days merely lying down.
On the eve of the wedding procession,
she suddenly rose
and began to adorn herself before the mirror.
Her mother secretly rejoiced.
Soon after, a maidservant rushed in, reporting,
"Miss has hanged herself!"
The entire household was shocked and wept,
full of regret that could no longer be remedied.
She was buried three days later.
Mèng Shēng returned from his neighbor, the old woman, with her reply,
furious and despairing.
Nevertheless, he traveled far and wide to inquire,
vainly hoping to salvage the situation.
When he learned that the beautiful lady already had a master,
the fire of his anger blazed within him,
and all his myriad thoughts were cut off.
Not long after,
he heard that the beautiful one had been buried,
and he was so grieved
he wished he had died with the lovely woman.
He went out in the evening,
intending to take advantage of the dark night to weep at Shíyīniáng’s tomb.
Suddenly a person came,
and as he drew near,
it was Fēng Sānniáng.
She said to him:
“Congratulations! The marriage can now proceed.”
Mèng Shēng wept, saying:
“Don’t you know that Shíyīniáng is dead?”
Fēng Sānniáng said:
“My saying 'proceed'
is precisely because of her death.
You must quickly call your family to open the grave;
I have a wondrous medicine
that can revive her.”
Mèng Shēng followed her advice,
opened the tomb, broke open the coffin,
and then re-covered the grave.
Mèng Shēng carried the corpse himself
and returned home with Sānniáng,
placing her on the bed;
he administered the medicine to her,
and after an hour, she revived.
She looked and saw Sānniáng,
and asked:
“Where is this?”
Fēng Sānniáng pointed to Mèng Shēng and said:
“This is Mèng Ānrén.”
Then she told her the whole story,
and she gradually woke as if from a dream.
Fēng Sānniáng feared exposure,
so they moved about fifty *lǐ* away
and hid in a mountain village.
Fēng Sānniáng wanted to leave,
but Shíyīniáng tearfully asked her to stay as a companion,
and arranged for her to live in a separate courtyard.
They then sold the burial ornaments
to use as living expenses,
and were considered to be moderately well-off.
Whenever Mèng Shēng came, Fēng Sānniáng
would always avoid him.
Shíyīniáng calmly said:
“We sisters are like flesh and blood,
yet we will not ultimately gather for a hundred years.
It would be better to follow the example of Yīng and Huáng.”
Fēng Sānniáng said:
“When I was young, I learned a unique secret art;
breathing exercises can lead to longevity,
which is why I do not wish to marry.”
Shíyīniáng smiled and said:
“It is said that the techniques for nourishing life
are numerous enough to fill carts,
but who has ever practiced them effectively?”
Fēng Sānniáng said:
“What I have obtained is not known to the world.
What is passed down in the world is not the true secret;
only Huà Tuó’s Five Animal Frolics are relatively not false.
All cultivators
simply desire to have their *qì* and blood circulate smoothly.
If one suffers from an adverse condition,
assuming the tiger posture immediately stops it—
is this not proof?”
Shíyīniáng secretly conspired with Mèng Shēng
to have him pretend to go on a long journey.
At night,
she strongly urged Fēng Sānniáng to drink wine;
once she was drunk,
Mèng Shēng secretly defiled her.
Sānniáng awoke and said:
“My sister has harmed me!
If the precept against lust had not been broken,
