when I achieved the Dao, I would ascend to the highest heaven.
Now I have fallen into this evil plot—
it is fate!”
Then she rose to bid farewell.
Shíyīniáng expressed her sincere feelings and apologized sorrowfully.
Fēng Sānniáng said:
“To tell you the truth: I am a fox.
Because I gazed upon your beautiful face,
I suddenly developed affection,
like a silkworm wrapping itself in its own cocoon,
which led to today.
This is a calamity caused by the demon of love,
not by human power.
If I stay longer,
the demon will grow stronger
without end.
Lady, your blessings are still far-reaching;
please take good care of yourself.”
Having spoken, she vanished,
and the couple was astonished for a long time.
After a year,
Mèng Shēng indeed passed the provincial and metropolitan examinations,
and became a Hanlin academician.
He sent his calling card to visit Fàn Gōng,
who was ashamed and regretted not seeing him.
Mèng Shēng insisted,
and then he was seen.
Mèng Shēng entered,
performed the rites of a son-in-law,
and prostrated himself very respectfully.
Fàn Gōng was ashamed and angry,
suspecting Mèng Shēng of being frivolous and shallow.
Mèng Shēng requested a private audience,
and fully explained the situation.
Fàn Gōng did not entirely believe him,
but sent someone to investigate at Mèng Shēng’s home,
and was then greatly surprised and delighted.
He secretly ordered that it not be divulged,
fearing disaster.
Two more years later,
a certain *shēn*’s illicit connections were discovered,
and his father and son were exiled to the army in Liáohǎi.
Shíyīniáng then returned home to her parents.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
My friend Bì Yī’ān
was unconventional and extraordinary,
proud of his unrestrained and indulgent nature.
He was plump,
with many whiskers.
He was well-known among scholars.
Once, for a certain reason, he went to the separate estate of his uncle, Cìshǐ Gōng,
and rested on the upper floor.
It was rumored that the building had many foxes.
Whenever Bì Yī’ān read *Qīngfèng Zhuàn*,
his heart would yearn,
regretting not having an encounter.
Thus, on the upper floor,
he imagined and contemplated.
Later, he returned to his study;
the sun had already set.
It was a hot and humid summer month,
and he slept facing the door.
In his sleep, someone shook him.
He woke and looked back,
and it was a woman,
over forty years old,
yet still graceful and elegant.
Bì Yī’ān was startled and rose,
asking who she was.
She smiled and said:
“I am a fox.
Because you have focused your thoughts on me,
my heart is secretly touched and grateful.”
Bì Yī’ān was pleased to hear this
and joked with her.
The woman smiled and said:
“I am already advanced in years;
even if others do not dislike me,
I am first ashamed myself.
I have a young daughter who has reached marriageable age,
who can serve you in the bedchamber.
Tomorrow night,
do not let anyone else stay in the room;
she will come then.”
Having spoken, she left.
That night,
Bì Yī’ān burned incense and sat waiting.
The woman indeed arrived with her daughter.
Her demeanor was gentle and graceful,
unparalleled in the world.
The woman said to her daughter:
“Bì Láng has a karmic connection with you from a previous life,
so you must stay.
Return early in the morning;
do not be greedy for sleep.”
Bì Yī’ān took her hand and entered the bed-curtains,
attending to her with utmost affection.
After the deed,
she smiled and said:
“Fat lord, you are so earnest and heavy,
it makes one unable to bear it.”
She left before dawn.
That evening, she came herself
and said:
"My sisters are going to congratulate me on my new groom.
Tomorrow, please come with me."
He asked:
"Where to?"
She replied:
"Dàjiě is hosting the banquet.
It's not far from here."
Bì then waited for her.
After a long time, she didn't arrive,
and his body gradually grew tired and lazy.
Just as he leaned on his desk,
the woman suddenly entered and said:
"I have made you wait for a long time."
Then she took his hand and they left.
They quickly reached a place
with a large compound.
Going straight up to the central hall,
he saw the flickering candlelight,
shining like stars.
Soon, the host arrived,
nearly twenty years old,
with light makeup and exceptional beauty.
After bowing and offering congratulations,
as they were about to take their seats,
a maid entered and announced:
"Èrniángzi has arrived."
He saw a woman enter,
about eighteen or nineteen years old,
who smiled and said to the woman:
"Mèizi has 'broken the melon' [i.e., come of age/married]!
Is your Xīnláng quite to your liking?"
The woman hit her back with a fan
and rolled her eyes at her.
Èrniáng said:
"I remember when we were children, we used to wrestle for fun.
You were afraid of being tickled,
and if I just pointed my finger from afar,
you would laugh uncontrollably.
Then you would get angry at me
and say I should marry a dwarf prince from the Jiāojiāo Kingdom.
I said you, the maid, would marry a man with a big beard someday
who would pierce your small mouth.
And now it has come true!"
Dàniáng laughed and said:
"No wonder Sānniángzi curses you!
With the Xīnláng right here,
you are so boisterous!"
After a moment,
they all sat close together,
and the banquet was filled with joyful laughter.
Suddenly, a young girl,
holding a cat, came in.
She was about eleven or twelve years old,
her hair not yet fully grown,
but she was captivatingly beautiful.
Dàniáng said:
"Does Sì Mèimei also want to see her Zǐzhàng?
There's no place to sit here."
So she lifted her onto her lap
and fed her dishes and fruits.
After a while,
she transferred her to Èrniáng's embrace
and said:
"She's making my legs ache!"
Èrjiě said:
"This maid is so big,
as heavy as a hundred jūn!
I am too weak to hold her.
Since she wants to see her Zǐzhàng,
her Zǐzhàng is strong and robust,
his plump knees can bear her weight."
Then she took her and placed her in Bì's arms.
Once in his embrace, she was fragrant and soft,
light as if nobody was there.
Bì held her and drank from the same cup with her.
Dàniáng said:
"Little maid, don't drink too much;
if you get drunk and lose your composure,
Zǐfū might laugh at you."
The young girl smiled persistently,
playing with the cat with her hands,
and the cat let out a sharp cry.
Dàniáng said:
"Still not putting it down?
You'll get fleas and lice by holding it!"
Èrniáng said:
"Let's use this 'raccoon slave' as a drinking game prop.
Pass it around with chopsticks;
whoever it cries for must drink."
Everyone followed her instruction.
Whenever it reached Bì, it cried.
Bì, being a heavy drinker,
raised several cups in a row.
He then realized the little girl was deliberately making it cry,
which caused a loud burst of laughter.
Èrjiě said:
"Little Mèizi, go rest!
You'll crush Lángjūn to death,
and Sānjiě might resent us."
So the little girl left, holding the cat.
Dàjiě saw that Bì was a good drinker,
so she plucked a *shànzi* (lotus seedpod) and filled it with wine to offer him.
Looking at it, it seemed to hold only about a *shēng* of wine;
however, when he drank it,
it felt like several *dǒu*.
When he looked closely,
it was actually a lotus leaf.
Èrniáng also wanted to offer him a drink in return.
Bì declined, saying he couldn't drink any more.
Èrniáng took out a small lipstick box,
larger than a pellet,
and poured wine, saying:
"Since you can't drink any more wine,
let this merely be a token of my regard."
Bì looked at it;
one sip would empty it: he took a hundred sips,
but it never ran dry.
The woman beside him stealthily replaced the box with a small lotus cup
and said:
"Don't be fooled by villains."
When she placed the box on the table,
it was a giant bowl.
Èrniáng said:
"What business is it of yours?
You've only been Lángjūn for three days, are you already so affectionate?"
Bì held the cup to his mouth and drained it completely.
Holding it, it was soft and greasy;
upon closer examination,
it was not a cup,
but a hook from a silk stocking,
exquisitely crafted in a rustic style.
Èrniáng snatched it back and scolded:
"You sly maid!
When did you steal my slipper? No wonder my feet are cold!"
Thereupon, she got up
and went into the room to change her slippers.
The woman motioned for Bì to leave his seat and say goodbye.
The woman saw him out of the village
and let Bì return by himself.
Suddenly, he awoke with a start;
it was all a dream;
yet his nose and mouth were flushed with drink,
and the strong smell of wine still lingered,
which he found strange.
That evening,
the woman came
and said:
"You didn't die of drunkenness last night, did you?"
Bì said:
"I was just wondering if it was a dream."
The woman said:
"My sisters were afraid you would become boisterous and crazy,
so they made it seem like a dream.
It was not a dream in reality."
Whenever the woman played chess with Bì,
Bì always lost.
The woman smiled and said:
"You enjoy this so much every day,
I thought you would be very skilled.
But now that I see it,
you're just average."
Bì tried to instruct her with hand gestures.
The woman said:
"The art of *bēn zhī* [a type of chess or strategy]
is something one must comprehend oneself;
how can I help you?
With daily immersion,
perhaps there will be a change."
After several months,
Bì felt he had made some progress.
The woman tested him
and smiled, saying:
"Not yet,
not yet."
When Bì went out
to play with those he used to play chess with,
people noticed his improvement
and were all astonished.
Bì was a straightforward person,
with nothing hidden in his heart,
so he subtly revealed it.
The woman already knew
and scolded him, saying:
"No wonder those of our path do not associate with wild scholars.
I repeatedly warned you to be discreet,
why are you still like this?!"
She angrily wanted to leave.
Bì apologized profusely and without delay,
and then the woman somewhat relented;
however, from then on, her visits became increasingly infrequent.
After more than a year,
one night she came,
sitting silently opposite me.
I offered to play chess with her,
but she wouldn't;
I offered to sleep with her,
but she wouldn't.
Disappointed for a long time,
she said:
"Do you think I compare to Qīngfèng?"
I replied:
"You probably surpass her."
She said:
"I am ashamed that I am not her equal.
However, Liáozhāi and you are friends through writing,
please trouble yourself to write a short biography for me,
perhaps a thousand years from now, there will be no one who loves and remembers me as you do."
When she finished, I said:
"I have long had this ambition;
formerly, I followed an old instruction,
hence I kept it secret."
The woman said:
"That instruction was given then,
but now we are about to part,
what more is there to conceal?"
I asked:
"Where are you going?"
She said:
"Your concubine and Fourth Younger Sister are conscripted by Xīwángmǔ to be flower and bird envoys,
and will not be able to come again.
Formerly, an elder sister of mine
was with your elder uncle,
and before parting had already given birth to two daughters,
which debt has not yet been repaid;
your concubine and you are fortunately unburdened."
Bì requested a parting message.
She said:
"When arrogance subsides,
faults become few."
Then she rose,
took my hand and said:
"Please see me off."
After about a lǐ,
we parted with tears,
she said:
"If we both have the will,
it is not impossible that we will meet again."
Then she left.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month of the twenty-first year of Kāngxī,
Bìzǐ and I slept side by side in Chuòrántáng,
and he recounted her strangeness in detail.
I said:
"If there is a fox like this,
then Liáozhāi's writing will have glory."
So I recorded it.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A certain person from Chángqīng,
who made a living as a cloth merchant,
was a guest in Tàian.
Hearing that there was a diviner skilled in astrology,
he went to inquire about his fortunes.
The diviner predicted:
"Your luck is very bad,
you should return quickly."
The man was frightened,
and packed his money to go north.
On the way, he met a short-clad person,
who seemed to be a lowly official.
They gradually conversed,
and became fond of each other.
He frequently bought meals and drinks,
and invited him to share.
The short-clad person was very grateful.
The man asked what he was doing,
and he replied:
"I am going to Chángqīng,
to apprehend someone."
He asked who it was,
and the short-clad person produced a warrant,
showing him to inspect it himself: the first name on it was his own.
Alarmed, he said:
"What have I done to be apprehended?"
The short-clad person said:
"I am not a living person,
but a subordinate official from the Hāolí Mountain eastern district.
I think your lifespan is at an end."
The man wept and begged for help.
The ghost said:
"I cannot.
However, there are many names on the warrant.
It will still take time to gather them all.
You return quickly,
and arrange your affairs,
I will call for you last,
this is how I repay your kindness."
Before long,
they reached a river,
where the bridge was broken,
making it difficult for travelers to cross.
The ghost said:
"You are about to die,
not a single coin will you take with you.
Please build a bridge immediately,
to benefit travelers;
although it will be quite troublesome and costly,
it may not be without some small benefit to you."
The man agreed.
The man returned,
and told his wife to prepare funeral clothes.
He set a date to gather workers and build the bridge.
After a long time,
the ghost did not come.
He secretly doubted it.
One day,
the ghost suddenly came and said:
"I have already reported the matter of the bridge building to the Chénghuáng,
who conveyed it to the underworld,
saying that this good deed could extend your life.
Now your name has been removed from the warrant,
I respectfully report the news."
The man was delighted and grateful.
Later, he went to Tàishān again,
not forgetting the ghost's kindness,
he respectfully burned paper money,
and called out the name for a libation.
As he left,
he saw the short-clad person hurrying over and saying:
"You almost got me into trouble!
Just now Lord Sī was on duty,
fortunately he didn't hear about it.
Otherwise,
what would I do!"
He walked with him for a few paces,
then said:
"Don't come again later.
If you have business going north,
you should detour and visit me."
Then they parted.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
There was a farmer weeding at the foot of the mountain,
his wife brought him a meal in an earthenware pot.
After eating,
he placed the pot by the ridge.
Towards evening, he looked,
and the leftover porridge in the pot was completely empty.
This happened repeatedly.
He grew suspicious,
so he watched stealthily to observe.
A fox came,
and poked its head into the pot.
The farmer, carrying his hoe, crept over,
and struck it forcefully.
The fox was startled and fled.
The pot was stuck on its head,
and it struggled but couldn't get it off;
the fox stumbled and fell,
hitting the pot which shattered and fell off,
its head emerged,
it saw the farmer,
and fled even more urgently,
crossing the mountain and leaving.
Several years later,
a noblewoman on the south side of the mountain
was troubled by a fox's haunting,
and talismans had no effect.
The fox said to the woman:
"What can paper talismans do to me!"
The woman deceived it, saying:
"Your magic is truly profound,
it is fortunate that we can be friends forever.
But I wonder if there is anything in your life that you fear?"
The fox said:
"I fear nothing.
However, ten years ago when I was on the north mountain,
I once stole food by the fields,
and was almost killed by a person wearing a wide-brimmed hat,
carrying a curved-necked weapon,
I still tremble at the thought.
The woman told her father.
Her father thought of finding what it feared,
but he didn't know the person's name,
or where he lived,
so he had no way to inquire.
It happened that I, the servant, went to a mountain village for a reason.
I casually mentioned something to someone,
and a person nearby exclaimed in surprise:
"This perfectly matches an incident I experienced years ago!
Could it be that the fox I drove away back then
is now capable of causing mischief?"
I found this strange,
and returned to tell my master.
My master was pleased,
and immediately ordered me, Wū, to summon the farmer.
He respectfully explained what he sought.
The farmer laughed and said:
"Indeed, I did encounter something in the past,
but it's not necessarily this creature.
Moreover, if it can cause monstrous changes,
would it still fear a mere farmer?"
The noble family strongly urged him,
making him dress and adorn himself as he did that day.
He entered the room, struck the ground with his hoe,
and roared:
"I've been searching for you daily without success,
and you've been hiding here!
Now that we've met,
I'll kill you without mercy!"
As soon as he finished speaking,
the cries of a fox were heard in the room.
The farmer grew even more imposing and angry.
The fox then pleaded for its life.
The farmer shouted:
"Go quickly,
I release you."
The woman saw the fox clutching its head and scurrying away,
and from then on, she was at peace.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Wèi Huī Qī Shēng
was a young man of refined upbringing,
with a bold and responsible spirit.
At that time, a prominent family had a grand residence
where ghosts were seen in broad daylight,
and deaths occurred one after another.
They wished to sell it cheaply.
Shēng, seeing its low price,
bought and resided in it.
But the residence was vast and sparsely populated,
and the pavilions in the East Court
had become overgrown with wormwood,
so they were also left abandoned for a time.
At night, his family members would be startled,
often clamoring about ghosts.
After more than two months,
a maid died.
Not long after,
Shēng's wife went to the pavilions in the evening.
Upon returning, she fell ill
and died a few days later.
His family became even more terrified
and urged Shēng to move elsewhere.
Shēng did not listen.
But he was all alone, without a partner,
feeling sad and pitying himself.
His maids and servants also constantly bothered him with talk of strange occurrences.
Shēng became angry,
and in a fit of pique, he bundled up his bedding
and went to sleep alone in the desolate pavilion,
leaving a candle lit to observe any strange happenings.
For a long time, nothing happened,
and he eventually fell asleep.
Suddenly, someone's hand felt under his quilt,
repeatedly stroking him.
Shēng awoke and looked,
to see an old maid,
with tangled ears and dishevelled hair,
excessively bloated.
Shēng knew it was a ghost.
He grabbed her arm, pushed her away,
and laughed, saying:
"Your esteemed form is not suitable for receiving instruction!"
The maid was ashamed,
withdrew her hands, and shuffled away.
A short while later,
a young woman emerged from the northwest corner,
with a graceful and exquisite demeanor.
She boldly came to the lamp,
and angrily cursed:
"Where is this crazy student,
daring to lie here so comfortably!"
Shēng got up and smiled, saying:
"This humble student is the master of this residence,
waiting for you to collect the rent."
He then stood up,
stripped, and grabbed her.
The woman hurriedly fled.
Shēng quickly headed to the northwest corner first,
blocking her return path.
The woman, having no escape,
sat down on the bed.
He approached her,
and by the light of the candle, she was like a celestial being.
He gradually embraced her.
The woman laughed and said:
"Crazy student, do you not fear ghosts?
I will bring disaster upon you and cause your death!"
Shēng forcefully untied her skirt and jacket,
and she did not resist much.
Afterwards, she introduced herself, saying:
"My surname is Zhāng,
and my given name is Āduān.
I mistakenly married a scoundrel
who was stubborn and unkind,
subjecting me to constant humiliation.
I died of indignation and grief,
and have been buried here for over twenty years.
This house sits entirely on burial mounds."
He asked:
"Who is the old maid?"
She replied:
"She is also an old ghost,
serving me.
When living people reside above,
the ghosts are uneasy in their night chambers,
so I sent her to drive you away."
He asked:
"What was she doing by stroking me?"
She laughed and said:
"That maid has not known a man for thirty years,
her feelings are pitiable;
but she is also too presumptuous.
In short,
the timid are more insulted and toyed with by ghosts;
the resolute,
they dare not offend."
Hearing the sound of the neighboring bell cease,
she dressed and got off the bed,
saying:
"If I am not suspected,
I will return tonight."
As evening fell,
she indeed arrived, and
their intimate joy increased.
The scholar said:
"My wife unfortunately passed away, and
the grief and sorrow are never absent from my heart.
Can you bring her to me?"
The woman, hearing this, became even sadder and
said:
"I died twenty years ago;
who would remember me?
You are truly affectionate,
and I will do my utmost.
However, I heard she has already been reborn,
so I don't know if she is still in the underworld."
The next evening,
she told the scholar:
"Your lady is about to be born into a noble family.
In her previous life, she lost an earring,
beat a maidservant, and
the maidservant hanged herself.
This case is not yet concluded,
which is why she is delayed.
Currently, she is still housed beneath the Yàowáng láng,
with a custodian.
I will send a maid to bribe them,
and perhaps she will come."
The scholar asked:
"Why are you so free?"
She replied:
"For all who died unjustly, if they do not present themselves,
Yánmó Tiānzǐ will not know."
As the second watch was nearing its end,
the old maidservant indeed led the scholar's wife to them.
The scholar clasped her hand with great sorrow, and
his wife, her eyes filled with tears, could not speak.
The woman then departed,
saying:
"The two of you may talk of your long separation;
please meet again on another night."
The scholar inquired about the maidservant's death.
His wife said:
"No matter,
it will be concluded soon."
They went to bed, embraced, and
their joy was as profound as in their lifetime.
From then on, this became their routine.
Five days later,
his wife suddenly wept and said:
"Tomorrow I must go to Shāndōng;
the pain of separation will be long.
What can be done!"
Hearing this, the scholar
wiped away his tears, distressed, and
his sorrow was unbearable.
The woman consoled them, saying:
"I have a plan
that can allow you to be together for a while longer."
They both stopped weeping and asked her about it.
The woman asked for ten bundles of paper money,
to be burned beneath the apricot tree in the south hall,
as a bribe for the custodian,
to extend the time.
The scholar followed her advice.
That evening,
his wife arrived and
said:
"Thanks to Duān Niáng,
we now have ten days together."
The scholar was delighted,
forbade the woman to leave,
kept her in bed with them, and
from dusk till dawn,
they feared their joy would end.
After seven or eight days,
as the deadline approached,
the husband and wife wept all night.
They asked the woman for a plan, and
the woman said:
"It's difficult to scheme further.
However, I will try;
it will require no less than a million in underworld currency."
The scholar burned the exact amount.
The woman came,
joyfully saying:
"I sent someone to intercede with the custodian.
At first, it was very difficult;
but upon seeing so much money,
his heart finally wavered.
Now another ghost has been substituted for your wife."
From then on,
she no longer left even in broad daylight,
telling the scholar to seal the windows and doors, and
keep the lamps and candles burning continuously.
After more than a year of this,
the woman suddenly fell ill,
confused and vexed,
as if seeing ghosts.
The wife caressed her and said:
"This is a ghost sickness."
The scholar said:
"Duān Niáng is already a ghost,
how can a ghost be sickened by another ghost?"
The wife said:
"Not so.
When a person dies, they become a ghost;
when a ghost dies, it becomes a niè.
A ghost's fear of a niè
is like a person's fear of a ghost."
The scholar wanted to hire a shaman-doctor for her.
She said:
"How can a ghost be treated by a human?
Old lady Wáng from next door
is now practicing her art in the underworld;
you can go summon her.
However, it's over ten *lǐ* from here,
and my feet are too weak to walk;
please burn a straw horse for me."
The scholar complied.
As soon as the horse was burned,
they saw a maidservant leading a red stallion,
offering the reins in the courtyard,
and in a flash, she disappeared.
A short while later,
she returned with an old woman riding pillion,
tying the horse to a corridor pillar.
The old woman entered and
pinched the woman's ten fingers.
Soon after, she sat upright.
Her head made gestures.
She lay prostrate for some time,
then sprang up and said:
"I am the Great King Hēishān Dàwáng.
The lady is gravely ill.
Fortunately, you have met this minor deity,
and your blessings are profound indeed!
This is a karmic ghost causing calamity,
but there's no harm,
no harm!
However, if the illness recovers,
you must richly provide for my offerings:
one hundred ingots of gold, one hundred strings of coins,
and one grand feast must be prepared.
None must be lacking."
The wife assented to each point.
The old woman again fell prostrate and revived,
and rebuked the sick person,
then stopped.
Soon after, she wished to leave.
The wife escorted her outside the courtyard,
and presented her with a horse.
She departed joyfully.
When they went in to see the young lady,
she seemed somewhat conscious.
The couple was greatly pleased.
They caressed and questioned her.
The young lady suddenly spoke, saying:
"I fear I cannot tread the human world again.
Whenever I close my eyes, I see vengeful ghosts.
It is fate!"
Thereupon, she wept.
The next day,
her illness worsened and she was near death,
her body bent and trembling,
and seeing hallucinations.
She pulled her husband to lie with her,
her head buried in his embrace,
as if fearing being attacked and seized.
As soon as her husband got up,
she cried out in alarm and was restless.
This continued for six or seven days,
and the couple had no recourse.
At this time, the husband went out.
He returned after half a day
and heard his wife crying.
He asked in alarm,
and then realized that Duānniáng had already died on the bed,
her corpse still present.
When he uncovered it,
white bones were clearly visible.
The husband wept bitterly
and buried her with the rites for the living beside his ancestral tomb.
One night,
his wife sobbed in her dream.
He shook her and asked about it.
She replied, saying:
"Just now I dreamt Duānniáng came,
saying her husband was a nièguǐ,
and was angry that she had changed her fidelity in the underworld,
harboring hatred and coming to claim her life.
She begged me to perform a Dàochǎng."
The husband rose early,
and was about to follow the instruction.
His wife stopped him, saying:
"Saving ghosts is not something you can help with."
Then she got up and left.
She returned after about an hour,
saying:
"I have already ordered someone to invite monks.
We should first burn paper money for the purpose of salvation."
The husband followed her advice.
As the sun was setting,
the monks had all gathered,
with jīnnáo and fágǔ,
exactly like in the human world.
The wife always said it was noisy to her ears,
but the husband remarkably did not hear it.
Once the Dàochǎng was completed,
the wife again dreamt that Duānniáng came to thank her,
saying:
"The grievance has been resolved.
I will be reborn as the daughter of the Chénghuáng.
Please convey this to him."
After three years,
the family members were initially afraid upon hearing this,
but gradually got used to it.
When the husband was not present,
she would report from outside the window.
One night,
she cried to the husband, saying:
"The one who previously escorted me to be reborn,
their malpractices have now been exposed,
and the investigation and punishment are very urgent.
I fear we cannot remain together for long."
After several days,
she indeed became ill,
saying:
"My affection lies here;
I originally wished to remain dead forever,
not wishing to be alive.
Now I will part forever.
Is this not fate!"
The husband frantically sought a solution.
She said:
"This cannot be helped."
He asked:
"Will you be punished?"
She said:
"I will be slightly punished.
However, the sin of illicitly living is great,
while the sin of illicitly dying is small."
After she finished speaking,
she became motionless.
When he carefully examined her,
her face and physical form
gradually vanished.
The husband always slept alone in the pavilion,
hoping for another encounter,
but in the end, there was nothing.
His heart then found peace.
According to the manuscript edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Hán Shēng lived in a villa for half a year,
only returning at the end of winter.
One night,
as his wife was just lying down,
she heard the sound of someone walking.
She looked,
and the coal fire in the stove
was blazing very brightly.
She saw an old woman,
around eighty or ninety years old,
with wrinkled skin and a stooped back,
and hair so sparse it could be counted.
She said to the young lady:
"Would you like to eat bótuō?"
The young lady was afraid
and dared not answer.
Thereupon, the old woman poked the fire with iron chopsticks,
and placed a pot on it.
She then poured in water.
Soon, the water boiled.
The old woman lifted her clothes and opened a pouch at her waist,
took out dozens of bótuō,
and threw them into the boiling water.
Each made a distinct sound.
She said to herself:
"Wait for me to find chopsticks."
Then she went out the door.
The young lady, taking advantage of the old woman's departure,
quickly got up, grabbed the pot, and emptied it behind the mat,
then covered herself with the quilt and lay down.
A short while later,
the old woman arrived,
and pressed her, asking where the pot and its contents were.
The young lady was greatly afraid and screamed.
All the family members woke up,
and only then did the old woman leave.
They lifted the mat and shone a light to look,
and saw dozens of tǔbiēchóng
piled up there.
According to the manuscript edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Jīn Yǒngnián from Lìjīn,
eighty-two years old, had no son.
His wife was also seventy-eight years old,
and they themselves had given up all hope.
Suddenly, he dreamt a deity informed him, saying:
"You originally should have no heir.
However, considering that you traded fairly,
I grant you a son."
He woke up and told his wife.
His wife said:
"This is truly a baseless fantasy!
Both of us are about to die;
how can we have a son?"
Not long after,
his wife's belly began to move;
after ten months,
she unexpectedly gave birth to a son.
According to the manuscript edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Ān Yòuyú
was a "bágòng" from Shǎn.
From birth,
he was a generous and righteous person,
who loved to release captive animals.
Whenever he saw hunters capture birds,
he would not hesitate to pay a high price
to buy and release them.
On one occasion, there was a funeral at his maternal uncle's family,
so he went to help carry the coffin.
Returning home in the evening,
he passed through Huà Yuè
and became lost, wandering into a mountain valley.
His heart was greatly afraid.
Just beyond an arrow's shot,
he suddenly saw a light.
He hurried towards it.
Within a few paces,
he suddenly saw an old man,
stooped and dragging a staff,
walking quickly along a winding path.
Ān stopped,
just about to ask a question,
when the old man first asked who he was.
Ān explained that he was lost;
and added that the light must indicate a mountain village,
where he intended to seek shelter.
The old man said:
"This is not a peaceful place.
Luckily, I've come.
You can follow me.
My humble cottage can offer you a place to rest your head."
Ān was overjoyed
and followed him for about a lý.
He saw a small village.
The old man knocked on a wattle gate.
An old woman came out
and opened the gate, saying,
"Is the young master here?"
The old man replied,
"Yes."
Once inside,
their dwelling was indeed cramped and narrow.
The old man lit a lamp and urged Ān to sit,
then immediately ordered a meal to be prepared with whatever was available.
He also said to the old woman:
"This is no stranger;
he is my benefactor.
You can't walk well,
so call Huā Gūzi to pour the wine."
Soon, a young woman entered with the food and drink,
standing by the old man's side,
casting sidelong glances with her lovely eyes.
Ān looked at her;
her beautiful face and youthful age
were almost like a celestial fairy.
The old man turned to her and told her to warm the wine.
In the west corner of the room was a charcoal stove.
The girl immediately entered the room to poke the fire.
Ān asked:
"Who is this gentleman?"
He replied:
"My surname is Zhāng.
For seventy years, I have only had this daughter.
In a farmer's home, there are few servants,
and since you are not an outsider,
I dared to bring out my wife and daughter to meet you.
I hope you won't laugh."
Ān asked:
"Where is her husband's family?"
He replied:
"Not yet married."
Ān praised her beauty,
unable to stop speaking.
The old man was being modest,
when suddenly they heard the young woman cry out in alarm.
The old man rushed in
to find the wine boiling and the fire flaring up.
The old man quickly stopped it,
scolding:
"Old girl,
don't you know how fierce it is?"
Turning his head,
he saw a small figurine of Zǐ Gū made of a "shǔ" heart placed by the stove, not yet finished.
He scolded again:
"Your hair is all fluffy,
yet you're still like a baby!"
He held it out to Ān and said:
"She's so engrossed in this craft,
causing the wine to boil over.
With a gentleman like you praising her,
isn't she terribly ashamed!"
Ān carefully examined it;
the eyebrows, eyes, robes, and attire
were crafted with great skill.
He praised it, saying:
"Though it's close to child's play,
it also shows a clever mind."
As they drank for some time,
the girl frequently came to pour wine,
smiling sweetly
without any shyness.
Ān gazed at her, his heart stirred.
Suddenly, he heard the old woman call,
and the old man left.
Ān, seeing no one else,
said to the girl:
"Seeing your immortal face
has made me lose my soul.
I wish to arrange a marriage proposal,
but I fear it might not succeed.
What should I do?"
The girl held the pot to the fire,
silent as if she hadn't heard;
he asked repeatedly, but she didn't answer.
Ān gradually moved into the room.
The girl rose,
and said sternly:
"Mad fellow, entering the inner room,
what do you intend to do!"
The young man knelt down and pleaded with her.
The girl tried to run out the door.
Ān suddenly stood up to block her,
trying to get close to her.
The girl cried out sharply, her voice trembling.
The old man suddenly rushed in and asked.
Ān released her and went out,
feeling extremely ashamed and afraid.
The girl calmly said to her father:
"The wine was boiling again.
If not for the young gentleman coming,
the pot would have melted."
Hearing the girl's words,
Ān's heart finally settled,
and he esteemed her even more.
His soul was in turmoil,
losing what he had been holding onto.
Thereupon, feigning drunkenness, he left his seat,
and the girl also left.
The old man arranged bedding,
closed the door, and then went out.
Ān could not sleep.
Before dawn,
he called to bid farewell.
Upon reaching home,
he immediately asked a good friend to visit the cottage to propose marriage.
He returned after a full day,
having failed to find her dwelling.
Ān then ordered servants and horses
and went searching himself.
When he arrived, it was a sheer cliff face;
there was no village at all.
He inquired in nearby areas,
but that surname was extremely rare.
Disappointed, he returned,
forgetting even to eat or sleep.
From this, he contracted a delusional illness: if forced to eat soup or porridge,
he would swell and want to vomit.
In his delirium,
he would constantly call for Huā Gūzi.
His family didn't understand,
but they circled him all night,
his condition being critically precarious.
One night,
the watchers, overcome by fatigue, all fell asleep.
In his dazed state,
the young man felt someone touch and rub him.
He slightly opened his eyes
to see Huā Gūzi standing by the bed.
Unconsciously, his spirit became clear and awake.
He looked intently at the young woman and quietly shed tears.
The girl tilted her head and smiled, saying:
"Why have you come to this state, you foolish boy?"
She then got onto the bed,
sat on Ān's lap,
and pressed his temples with both hands.
Ān felt a strange, musky fragrance
penetrate his nostrils and seep into his bones.
After pressing for several minutes,
he suddenly felt sweat cover his forehead,
gradually spreading to his limbs.
She whispered:
"There are many people in the room,
so it's not convenient for me to stay.
I will visit again in three days."
Then she took out several steamed buns from her embroidered sleeve and placed them at the head of the bed,
quietly leaving afterwards.
Towards midnight,
after sweating, Ān felt hungry.
He fumbled for a bun and ate it.
He didn't know what filling it contained,
but it was incredibly delicious.
He finished all three.
He then covered the remaining buns with his clothes
and fell into a deep, confused sleep,
waking up at dawn,
as if a heavy burden had been lifted.
Three days later,
the buns were finished,
and his spirits were doubly refreshed.
He then went to Sǎnjia Rén's house.
He also worried that the girl might come but couldn't enter because the door was locked,
so he stealthily went out to the study courtyard
and completely removed the door bolts and keys.
Not long after,
the girl indeed arrived,
smiling, she said:
"You silly boy!
Aren't you going to thank the shamaness?"
Ān was overjoyed,
embracing her in tender intimacy,
their love and affection were profound.
After a while, she said:
"I ventured here, risking defilement,
precisely
to repay your great kindness.
In truth, we cannot be together forever as husband and wife,
so please make other plans soon."
Ān remained silent for a long time,
then asked:
"We've never met before,
how do I have any past connection with your family?
I truly don't recall."
The girl didn't speak,
only saying:
"You should think about it yourself."
The scholar earnestly pleaded for their everlasting union.
The girl said:
"Repeatedly coming here at night
is certainly not possible;
living together as husband and wife permanently
is also impossible."
Hearing this, Ān
was dejected and sad.
The girl said:
"If you absolutely wish for us to be together,
please come to my house tomorrow night."
Ān then suppressed his sadness and became joyful,
asking:
"The journey is long,
how can you, with your delicate steps,
manage to come here?"
She said:
"I haven't gone back yet.
The old deaf woman at the east end is my aunt,
and because of you,
I've stayed until now.
My family might suspect something strange."
Ān slept with her,
only feeling that her breath and skin
were fragrant everywhere.
He asked:
"What perfume have you used,
that it permeates your skin and bones?"
The girl said:
"I have been like this since birth,
it's not from perfume or adornment."
Ān found it even more remarkable.
The girl rose early to bid farewell.
Ān worried about getting lost,
so the girl promised to wait for him on the road.
Ān hurried there at dusk.
The girl was indeed waiting,
and they went together to her former residence.
The old man and woman welcomed them joyfully.
The food and drink were not exquisite,
just a mix of wild greens and coarse vegetables.
Afterwards, they invited the guest, Ān, to rest.
The girl did not pay him any attention,
which made him somewhat suspicious.
As the night deepened,
the girl finally arrived,
saying:
"My parents kept chattering and wouldn't sleep,
causing you to wait so long."
They spent the entire night in close intimacy,
and she said to Ān:
"This night's meeting
is a farewell for a hundred years."
Ān was shocked and asked her why.
She replied:
"My father considers our small village too secluded,
so he plans a distant relocation.
Our good time together
ends this very night."
Ān couldn't bear to let go,
looking down and up in profound sorrow.
Amidst their reluctance to part,
the night gradually broke into dawn.
Suddenly, the old man burst in,
scolding:
"You hussy, you've disgraced my virtuous family,
making me so ashamed I want to die!"
The girl's face lost color,
and she hastily fled.
The old man also left,
muttering as he went.
Ān was startled, timid, and fearful,
unable to compose himself,
so he stealthily fled home.
For several days, he wandered,
his state of mind almost unbearable.
He then thought of going there at night,
climbing over the wall to see what was happening.
Since the old man had mentioned having a thought,
even if the matter were exposed,
there shouldn't be a major reprimand.
So he took advantage of the night to slip away,
wandering through the mountains,
bewildered and not knowing where he was.
He was greatly afraid.
Just as he was looking for his way back,
he saw a hidden dwelling in the valley;
overjoyed, he approached it,
but the gates were tall and sturdy,
appearing to belong to a prominent family,
and the inner gate had not yet been opened.
Ān asked a gatekeeper for the residence of the Zhāng family.
A person in green clothes came out,
and asked:
"Who is asking for the Zhāng family in the dark of night?"
Ān said:
"They are close relatives of mine,
and I have accidentally lost my way to their house."
The green-clad person said:
"Men do not ask for Zhāng.
This is her aunt's house,
Huā Gū is here now,
I can convey your message."
Not long after entering,
he came out and invited Ān in.
As soon as he stepped onto the veranda,
Huā Gū hurried out to greet him,
and said to the green-clad person:
"Ān Láng has traveled tirelessly through the night,
he must be exhausted,
please prepare a bed for him."
A short while later,
she led him by the hand into the bed curtain.
Ān asked:
"Why is there no one else at your mountain house?"
The girl said:
"My aunt is out,
leaving me to look after the place.
It's fortunate to meet you,
isn't this predestined?"
However, as they embraced,
he felt a strong, rank smell,
and his heart grew suspicious.
The girl embraced Ān's neck,
and suddenly licked his nostrils with her tongue,
piercing his brain like a needle.
Ān was utterly terrified,
desperately wanting to escape,
but his body was as if bound by a huge rope.
A short while later,
he became numb and unconscious.
Ān did not return.
The family members traced his impoverished footsteps.
Someone said they had met him in the evening on a mountain path.
His family went into the mountains,
and found him dead and naked at the foot of a perilous cliff.
Astonished and unable to determine the cause,
they carried him home.
As the crowd gathered and wept,
a young woman came to mourn.
She wailed loudly as she entered from outside the gate.
She stroked the corpse, pressed its nose,
and shed tears all over it,
crying out:
“Heaven,
heaven!
How could you be so foolish and ignorant!”
Her mournful cries became hoarse,
and after a while, she stopped.
She told the family:
“Wait seven days,
do not shroud him.”
Everyone didn't know who she was,
and were about to ask;
but the woman was haughty and did not observe propriety.
She left directly, tears in her eyes,
and did not look back when they tried to detain her.
They followed her,
but she vanished in the blink of an eye.
The crowd suspected she was a spirit,
and carefully followed her instructions.
At night, she came again,
crying as before.
On the seventh night,
Ān suddenly revived,
tossing and turning with moans.
All the family members were shocked.
The woman entered,
and they faced each other, sobbing.
Ān raised his hand,
waving everyone away.
The woman took out a bundle of green grass,
heated about a *shēng* of water,
and gave it to him by the bed.
In a moment, he could speak.
He sighed, saying:
“Only you could kill me again,
and only you could bring me back to life!”
He then recounted what he had encountered.
The woman said:
“This snake spirit impersonated me.
When you were lost before,
the lamplight you saw
was from that creature.”
Ān said:
“How can you raise the dead and restore flesh to white bones?
Are you not an immortal?”
She said:
“I have long wanted to tell you,
but feared causing alarm.
Five years ago,
did you not buy a hunted musk deer on Mount Huà and release it?”
He said:
“Indeed,
I did.”
She said:
“That was my father.
My previous words about your great virtue
were for this reason.
You had already been reborn into the family of Magistrate Wáng in Xīcūn the day before yesterday.
My father and I pleaded our case before King Yánmó,
but King Yánmó was not amenable.
My father wished to break his path and die in your stead.
After seven days of grieving,
he finally succeeded.
Our meeting today
is fortunate.
However, although you are alive,
you will certainly be paralyzed and numb;
if you drink snake blood mixed with wine,
the illness can be cured.”
The student clenched his teeth in hatred,
but worried he had no means to catch it.
The woman said:
“It is not difficult.
But it will reduce many lives,
hindering my ascension for a hundred years.
Its lair is in the old cliff.
You can gather thatch and burn it in the late afternoon,
and prepare strong crossbows outside.
The demon can be caught.”
Having spoken,
she bade farewell, saying:
“I cannot complete this matter,
which is truly grievous.
However, for your sake,
my karma has already been diminished by seven parts.
Please pity and forgive me.
This month, I have felt a slight movement in my womb,
fearing it is a karmic offspring.
A boy or a girl,
after a year, will be entrusted to you.”
She left in tears.
After a night, Ān
felt his lower back completely dead,
scratching and grabbing caused no pain or sensation.
He then told his family what the woman had said.
His family went,
and as she had instructed,
they kindled a fire in the lair.
A giant white snake burst out of the flames.
Several crossbows fired simultaneously,
shooting and killing it.
When the fire died down, they entered the cave,
where hundreds of snakes, large and small,
were all scorched and stinking.
His family returned,
and offered him the snake blood.
Ān took it for three days,
and his legs gradually became able to turn.
After half a year, he finally rose.
Later, walking alone in the valley,
he met an old woman holding a baby wrapped in matting, who handed it to him,
saying:
“My daughter sends her regards to you, my lord.”
Just as he was about to inquire,
she vanished in a flash.
He opened the swaddling clothes and looked;
it was a boy.
He took him home,
and never married again.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“The difference between humans and birds and beasts is slight,
but this is not a definitive statement.
To receive grace and repay it
even unto death,
in this, humans are sometimes shamed by birds and beasts.
As for Huā Gū,
at first she entrusted her wisdom to foolishness,
and finally entrusted her feelings to nonchalance.
Thus, one knows that nonchalance can be the height of wisdom,
and nonchalance can be the depth of emotion.
Immortal,
immortal!”
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wǔ Xiàolián Shí Mǒu
took his money and went to the capital,
intending to seek official appointment.
Upon reaching Dézhōu,
he suddenly fell ill,
spitting blood and unable to rise,
lying long in his boat.
His servant embezzled his money and fled.
Shí was greatly enraged,
his illness worsened,
and his provisions were cut off.
The boatmen planned to abandon him.
Coincidentally, a woman traveling by boat
moored nearby that night.
Hearing of his plight,
she voluntarily offered to carry Shí in her boat.
The boatmen were pleased,
and helped Shí onto the woman’s boat.
Shí looked at her:
the woman was over forty,
dressed splendidly,
and still elegant in demeanor.
He groaned his thanks.
The woman approached and examined him, saying:
“Sir, you have long had the root of consumption,
and now your soul has already wandered to the graveyard.”
Hearing this, Shí
cried out in sorrow.
The woman said:
“I have a pill
that can raise the dead.
If your illness is cured,
do not forget me.”
Shí wept and swore an oath.
The woman then gave Shí the medicine;
after half a day,
he felt slightly better.
The woman served him delicacies by his couch,
more diligently than a husband and wife.
Shí was even more grateful to her.
After more than a month,
his illness was fully cured.
Shí knelt and moved forward,
respecting her like a mother.
The woman said:
“I am alone and without reliance.
If you do not despise me for my faded beauty,
I wish to serve you as your concubine.”
At this time, Shí was over thirty,
and had been a widower for a year.
Hearing this,
he was delighted beyond expectation,
and they became intimately involved.
The woman then brought out her hidden gold,
telling him to go to the capital to seek an appointment,
and they agreed to return together.
Shí Fù, through influential connections,
was selected to be the Commissioner of Military Affairs for his home province.
With his remaining money, he bought a saddle and horse,
and his retinue was magnificent.
He then thought that his wife's age was already advanced,
and she was ultimately not a good match for him.
So, he offered a hundred taels of gold to marry a daughter of the Wáng family as his second wife.
He felt a deep fear in his heart,
dreading that his wife would find out.
Therefore, he avoided the Dēzhōu route,
taking a circuitous path to his post.
More than a year passed,
with no news communicated.
An acquaintance of Shí's,
happened to come to Dēzhōu
and became a neighbor to Shí's wife.
The wife learned of this
and went to inquire about Shí's situation.
The acquaintance told her the truth.
The wife cursed loudly,
and then recounted her story.
The acquaintance also felt it was unfair for her
and comforted her, saying:
"Perhaps the duties at his office are too numerous,
and he hasn't had leisure yet.
Please write a short letter,
and I will send it for you, madam."
The wife did as he said.
The acquaintance respectfully delivered it to Shí,
but Shí paid it no mind.
Another year passed,
and the wife herself went to find Shí.
She stayed at an inn
and asked the usher at the yamen to announce her name.
Shí ordered her to be turned away.
One day,
as he was feasting and drinking,
he heard a noisy commotion and cursing.
He put down his cup and listened intently,
and then his wife had already lifted the curtain and entered.
Shí was greatly startled,
his face ashen.
The wife pointed at him and cursed, saying:
"Heartless wretch!
Are you at ease?
Just think, where did your wealth and nobility come from?
My bond with you is not shallow,
even if you wanted to take a concubine,
what harm would there be in consulting me?"
Shí stumbled and held his breath,
unable to utter another sound.
After a long while,
he knelt down and prostrated himself,
begging for forgiveness with deceptive words.
The wife's anger gradually subsided.
Shí conspired with Wáng shì,
making her treat the wife with the courtesy due to an elder sister.
Wáng shì was naturally reluctant,
but Shí earnestly pleaded with her,
so she agreed.
Wáng bowed,
and the wife returned the bow.
She said:
"Little sister, don't be afraid.
I am not a fierce or jealous person.
The previous affair
was truly something that human nature cannot endure;
even you, little sister, would not wish for such a husband."
Then she recounted the whole story to Wáng.
Wáng was also indignant,
and so they both cursed Shí.
Shí could not defend himself,
only begging to redeem himself,
and thus they settled down peacefully.
Initially,
before the wife entered, Shí had warned the gatekeeper not to let her in.
Now,
he was angry at the gatekeeper,
secretly questioning and blaming him.
The gatekeeper insisted that the locks had not been opened,
and that no one
had been there, refusing to admit fault.
Shí suspected this but dared not question his wife.
Although they spoke and laughed,
it was ultimately not what he preferred.
Fortunately, the wife was gentle and graceful,
and did not contend for his favors at night.
After her three meals,
she would close her door and go to bed early,
never asking where her husband slept at night.
Wáng initially felt insecure;
seeing her behave this way,
she respected her even more.
Every morning she would go to greet her,
as if serving a mother-in-law.
The wife managed her subordinates with leniency and propriety,
yet her perception was almost divine.
One day,
Shí lost his official seal and sash.
The entire yamen was in an uproar,
bustling back and forth,
without any plan.
The wife smiled and said:
"Don't worry,
you can find it by draining the well."
Shí followed her advice,
and indeed found it.
When asked the reason,
she would just smile and not speak.
Implicitly,
she seemed to know the name of the thief,
but she never revealed it.
After living there for a full year,
he observed that her behavior was often unusual.
Shí suspected she was not human,
and often after bedtime, he would have someone eavesdrop on her.
But all he heard was the sound of clothes rustling on the bed all night long,
and he didn't know what she was doing.
The wife and Wáng were extremely fond of each other.
One night,
Shí had gone to the judicial commissioner's office and had not yet returned.
The wife and Wáng drank together,
and without realizing it, became quite drunk.
They lay down on the mat
and the wife transformed into a fox.
Wáng pitied her
and covered her with a brocade quilt.
Soon after,
Shí entered.
Wáng told him about the strange occurrence.
Shí wanted to kill her.
Wáng said:
"Even if she is a fox,
how has she wronged you?"
Shí did not listen,
and urgently searched for his sword.
But the wife had already woken up
and cursed, saying:
"With the behavior of vipers
and the heart of jackals,
you surely cannot live here long!
The medicine I swallowed before,
please return it to me!"
Then she spat on Shí's face.
Shí felt a chilling cold as if drenched in ice water,
and his throat began to itch with a rustling sound.
He vomited it out,
and the pill was as it had been.
The wife picked it up,
and angrily walked straight out.
When they pursued her, she had already vanished.
Shí's old ailment returned in the middle of the night,
with incessant blood-coughing,
and he died half a year later.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Shí Xiàolián
was elegant like a scholar.
Some say he humbled himself and was able to stoop to the common folk,
speaking to people as if fearing to hurt them.
He died young,
and the scholarly community mourned him.
But upon hearing about his betrayal of the fox-wife,
how was he any different from Lǐ Shíláng?"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Chén Shēngbìjiào,
whose courtesy name was Míngyǔn,
was a native of Yān.
His family was poor,
and he served as a secretary to Vice General Jiǎ Suō.
Their boat was moored at Dòngtíng Lake.
Just then, a zhūpólóng (pig-mother-dragon) floated on the surface of the water.
Jiǎ shot it in the back.
A fish was holding onto the dragon's tail and would not let go,
so both were captured.
They were tied to the mast,
barely clinging to life.
The dragon's snout opened and closed,
as if seeking help.
Chén Shēng's heart was moved with pity,
and he asked Jiǎ to release it.
He had some wound medicine with him,
which he playfully applied to its wound,
then released it into the water.
It floated and sank for over a quarter of an hour before disappearing.
More than a year later,
Shēng returned north.
He passed through Dòngtíng again,
when a great storm capsized his boat.
Fortunately, he managed to cling to a bamboo clump,
drifted through the night,
and was stopped when he became entangled in a tree.
As he climbed ashore,
a floating corpse arrived shortly after,
which turned out to be his servant.
He struggled to pull him out,
but he was already dead.
Distressed and helpless,
Shēng sat opposite him to rest.
All he could see were small mountains soaring with emerald,
and slender willows swaying green.
There were very few travelers,
and no one to ask for directions.
From late dawn until after the hour of Chén,
he was disheartened and had nowhere to go.
Suddenly, his servant’s limbs twitched slightly.
Delighted, Shēng felt him.
Before long,
the servant vomited several measures of water,
and fully regained consciousness.
They helped each other spread their clothes on a rock to dry.
It was nearly noon before they were dry enough to wear.
But their stomachs rumbled,
and their hunger was unbearable.
So they hurried over the mountains,
hoping to find a village.
Just as they reached halfway up the mountain,
they heard the sound of a hunting horn.
As they wondered where the sound came from,
two young women came riding on swift horses,
galloping like scattered beans.
Each had a red silk scarf tied around her forehead,
and a pheasant tail feather in her chignon;
they wore small-sleeved purple garments,
and green brocade sashes around their waists;
one carried a slingshot,
and the other had a blue hunting gauntlet on her arm.
When they passed over the ridge,
there were dozens of riders hunting in the thickets,
all of them beautiful,
and dressed identically.
Shēng dared not approach.
A man, running on foot,
who appeared to be a groom,
came over, and Shēng asked him.
He replied:
"This is the hunting ground of the Lord of Xīhú, Shǒushān."
Shēng recounted his journey
and told him of his hunger.
The groom untied his bundled provisions and gave them to Shēng,
instructing him:
"You should leave immediately;
to offend the royal hunt is to die!"
Shēng was afraid.
He hurried down the mountain.
In the dense forest, he vaguely saw a palace,
which he took to be a Buddhist temple (lánruò).
As he approached it,
he saw white walls densely enclosing it,
and a stream flowing across;
a vermilion gate was half-open,
and a stone bridge led to it.
Peeking through the gate,
he saw pavilions and terraces encircling the clouds,
comparable to the Imperial Garden,
and he wondered if it was a nobleman's estate.
He hesitated, then entered.
Horizontal vines obstructed the path,
and fragrant flowers assailed him.
Passing several winding balustrades,
he found another courtyard,
with dozens of weeping willows,
their tops brushing the vermilion eaves.
When a mountain bird sang,
flower petals flew in unison;
a light breeze in the deep courtyard
caused elm coins to fall by themselves.
It was a sight that delighted the eyes and quickened the heart,
almost not of this world.
Passing through a small pavilion,
he saw a swing,
its top reaching the clouds;
but the ropes hung heavily,
with no sign of human presence.
He suspected the place was near women's quarters,
and, feeling timid, dared not go deeper.
Soon, he heard horses galloping at the gate,
and what sounded like women's laughter and talk.
Shēng and his servant hid among the flowers.
Not long after,
the laughter grew closer.
He heard one woman say:
"Today's hunt was not good;
we caught very few birds."
Another woman said:
"If it weren't for the Princess shooting down a wild goose,
our horses and servants would have toiled in vain."
Shortly after,
several women in red dresses
escorted a young woman to sit on the pavilion.
She wore military attire with short sleeves,
and was about fourteen or fifteen years old.
Her hair was styled in many cloud-like chignons,
her waist was slender as if startled by the wind.
Royal pistils and jade-like blossoms
were insufficient metaphors.
The other women offered tea and burned incense,
dazzling like piled brocade.
After a while,
the young woman rose
and descended the steps.
One woman said:
"Princess, your saddle and horse have tired you;
can you still swing?"
The Princess laughed and agreed.
So there were those who supported her shoulders,
those who grasped her arms,
those who hiked up her skirt,
and those who held her shoes,
as they helped her up.
The Princess extended her fair arms,
stepped onto the sharp footboard,
light as a flying swallow,
and kicked up into the clouds.
Soon after, they helped her down.
The group exclaimed:
"Princess is truly an immortal!"
They laughed and departed.
Shēng gazed for a long time,
his spirit soaring.
When the voices had died down,
he came out to the swing,
pacing and lost in thought.
He saw a red scarf by the fence,
knowing it had been left by the beautiful women,
and happily tucked it into his sleeve.
He ascended to the pavilion
and saw writing implements set out on the table.
So he inscribed the scarf, saying:
"What elegant player rivals a half-immortal?
Clearly, a jade maiden reveals her golden lotuses.
Fearing envy among the Guanghán cohort,
she must not trust the waves to carry her to the nine heavens."
After writing,
he recited it and left.
He tried to find the original path again,
but the heavy gate was now locked.
With no way out through the gates,
he explored almost all the pavilions, terraces, and buildings.
A woman hurried in,
and asked in surprise:
"How did you get here?"
Shēng bowed and said:
"I am a lost traveler;
I hope you can save me."
The woman asked:
"Did you pick up a red scarf?"
Shēng replied:
"I did.
However, it is already stained;
what should I do?"
He then took it out.
The woman was greatly alarmed and said:
"You are as good as dead!
This is what the Princess often uses,
and you've defaced it like this.
How can you make amends?"
Shēng's face fell,
and he pleaded for an escape.
The woman said:
"Peeking at the palace rituals,
my crime is already unforgivable.
Considering your cultured demeanor as a scholar,
I wished to protect you with my private intentions;
but now you have brought this disaster upon yourself,
what can be done!"
Thereupon, she went away in a flurry, holding the scarf.
The scholar's heart palpitated, his muscles trembled,
he wished he had wings,
only stretching his neck to await death.
After a long while,
the girl returned,
secretly congratulating him, saying:
"You have a hope of survival!
The Gōngzhǔ looked at the scarf three or four times,
smiling brightly without a trace of anger,
perhaps she will let you go.
You should endure and wait patiently,
do not climb trees or bore through walls,
if discovered, you will not be pardoned."
The sun had already set,
he could not be sure of escaping calamity;
and the flames of hunger burned within him,
he was tormented by worry and wished to die.
Before long,
the girl arrived, carrying a lamp.
A maidservant brought a pot and a box,
offering wine and food to the scholar.
The scholar urgently asked for news,
the girl said:
"Just now, I took the opportunity to say: 'The xiùcai in the garden,
if he can be pardoned, let him go;
otherwise,
he will starve to death.'
The Gōngzhǔ pondered and said: 'Where can I send him so late at night?'
So she ordered food to be given to you.
This is not bad news."
The scholar paced anxiously all night,
restless with danger.
As the morning hour was about to end,
the girl brought him food again.
The scholar pleaded for her to intercede on his behalf,
the girl said:
"The Gōngzhǔ did not say kill,
nor did she say release.
We, as servants,
how dare we bother her with such trivial reports?"
Shortly after, the setting sun shifted westward,
his anxious gaze was intense,
the girl rushed in, panting,
saying:
"It's dire!
The talkative one leaked the matter to the Wángfēi;
the Fēi threw the scarf to the ground,
cursing the 'crazy bumpkin' loudly,
disaster is not far off!"
The scholar was greatly alarmed,
his face turned ash-gray,
he knelt down long to ask for advice.
Suddenly, he heard a clamor of voices,
the girl waved her hand and fled.
Several people holding ropes,
rushed into the dwelling.
One maidservant looked closely and said:
"Who would have thought it was him,
Chén Láng?"
Then she stopped those holding the ropes,
saying:
"Wait, wait,
let me report to the Wángfēi first."
She turned and left quickly.
After a short while she returned,
saying:
"The Wángfēi invites Chén Láng in."
The scholar tremblingly followed her.
Passing through dozens of doorways,
they reached a palace hall,
with green blinds and silver hooks.
Immediately, a beautiful concubine lifted the curtain,
announcing:
"Chén Láng has arrived."
Above sat a beautiful woman, her robes dazzling and elegant.
The scholar prostrated himself, bowing his head to the ground, saying:
"Your humble subject, an orphan from a distant land,
fortunately begs for his life."
The Fēi hurriedly rose and pulled him up herself,
saying:
"Were it not for you, my lord,
I would not be where I am today.
The maids were negligent,
causing such a welcome for an esteemed guest,
how can this crime be atoned for!"
Immediately, a grand banquet was set,
with wine served in carved cups.
The scholar was bewildered and did not understand the reason.
The Fēi said:
"The kindness of giving me a new life,
I regret having no way to repay it.
My daughter receiving your love through the inscribed scarf,
must be a destined connection,
this very evening I will send her to attend to you."
The scholar's thoughts went beyond his expectations,
his spirit was wandering and without a place to rest.
As evening was just falling,
a maidservant came forward and reported,
"The Gōngzhǔ has finished her elaborate makeup."
Thereupon, she led the scholar to the bed-curtain.
Suddenly, the sounds of sheng and guan instruments were boisterous,
the steps were all covered with flower-patterned rugs;
the gate hall and even the outhouse,
everywhere was illuminated with candles.
Dozens of enchanting maids,
supported the Gōngzhǔ as they performed their obeisances.
The fragrance of musk and orchids,
filled the palace hall.
Afterward, they entered the bed-curtain together,
and loved each other deeply.
The scholar said:
"As a transient official,
I have never in my life dared to expect such an attendance.
To have defiled this fragrant place,
and escaped the ax and chopping block,
is fortunate enough;
to be given a marital bond in return,
is truly beyond my hopes."
The Gōngzhǔ said:
"My mother,
Hú Jūn Fēizi,
is the daughter of Yángjiāng Wáng.
Last year, when returning home for a visit,
she accidentally traveled on the lake,
and was struck by a stray arrow.
You graciously rescued her,
and also gave her a small dose of medicine,
our whole family deeply cherishes this,
and it never leaves our hearts.
My lord, do not suspect me of being a different species.
I obtained the secret of immortality from Lóng Jūn,
and wish to share it with you."
The scholar then realized she was a divine being,
and asked:
"How did that maidservant recognize me?"
She said:
"That day on the boat in Dòngtíng,
there was a small fish biting its tail,
that was this maidservant."
He also asked:
"Since I was not to be executed,
why was I not released sooner?"
She smiled and said:
"I truly admired your talent,
but I was not my own master.
The turmoil of the entire night,
others could not have known."
The scholar sighed and said:
"You,
are my Bào Shū.
Who was the one who brought me food?"
She said:
"Ā Niàn,
she is also my confidante."
The scholar said:
"How can I repay such kindness?"
She smiled and said:
"You will attend me for many days,
it is not too late to consider how to repay this great deed later."
He asked:
"Where is the Dàwáng?"
She said:
"He has not yet returned from assisting Guān Shèng in his campaign."
After several days,
the scholar worried that there was no news from home,
his concern was extremely urgent,
so he first sent a servant back with a letter of peace.
His family, having heard that the Dòngtíng boat had capsized,
his wife and children had been in mourning for over a year.
When the servant returned,
they finally knew he was not dead;
but communication was obstructed,
they still feared he was adrift and difficult to return.
Another half year passed,
and the scholar suddenly arrived,
splendidly dressed in fur and riding a fine horse,
his purse filled with precious jade.
From then on, his household possessed immense wealth,
with extravagant sights and sounds,
beyond what even noble families could achieve.
Within seven or eight years,
he had five sons.
Every day he hosted banquets for guests,
the provisions for his palace and meals,
were utterly luxurious.
When asked about his experiences, he spoke of them without the slightest reservation.
I had a childhood friend,
Liáng Zǐjùn, who had been an official in the southern regions for over ten years.
Returning home, he passed through Dòngtíng Lake
and saw a painted pleasure boat,
with carved railings and vermilion windows.
Fine, melancholic music from pipes and strings
gently drifted over the misty waves.
A beautiful woman occasionally pushed open a window to gaze out.
Liáng’s eyes were fixed on the boat’s interior,
where he saw a young man
bareheaded and cross-legged;
beside him were two women, aged sixteen, beautiful and charming,
toying and caressing.
He thought they must be noble officials from Chǔxiāng,
but their retinue was remarkably small.
Staring intently, he realized
it was Chén Míngyǔn.
Unconsciously, he leaned on the railing and shouted with delight.
The man heard the call, ordered the boat stopped,
and came to the bow,
inviting Liáng to cross over.
Liáng saw a table laden with leftover food,
the air still thick with the aroma of wine.
The man immediately ordered it cleared away.
Shortly after,
three to five beautiful maids
brought wine and brewed tea,
along with rare delicacies from mountains and seas,
such as Liáng had never seen before.
Liáng exclaimed in surprise:
“Ten years unseen,
how have you become so rich and noble!”
The man smiled and said:
“Do you underestimate a poor scholar who cannot make his fortune?”
Liáng asked:
“Who were you drinking with just now?”
He replied:
“My humble wife, of course.”
Liáng was again surprised.
He asked:
“Where are you going with your family?”
He answered:
“We are going west.”
Liáng wanted to question him further,
but the man quickly ordered singing to accompany their wine.
As soon as he finished speaking,
a sudden clamor of thunder filled their ears,
and the music from human voices and instruments grew so loud
that conversation and laughter were no longer possible.
Liáng saw beautiful women all around him,
and, emboldened by wine, declared loudly:
“Míngyǔn Gōng,
can you truly make me lose myself in pleasure?”
The man smiled and said:
“You are drunk!
However, I have enough wealth for one beautiful concubine,
which I can present to an old friend.”
He then ordered a maidservant to bring a bright pearl,
saying:
“Buying Lǜzhū is not difficult;
this shows I am not stingy.”
He then quickly bade farewell, saying:
“I am busy with urgent matters,
and cannot linger long with an old friend.”
He escorted Liáng back to his boat,
untied the moorings, and departed directly.
When Liáng returned,
he visited the man’s home,
and found him drinking with guests.
He grew more suspicious.
He then asked:
“Yesterday at Dòngtíng,
how did you return so quickly?”
He replied:
“I wasn’t there.”
Liáng then recounted what he had seen, and everyone present was startled.
The man smiled and said:
“You are mistaken,
how could I have the art of bilocation?”
Everyone found it strange,
but ultimately could not explain the reason.
Eighty-one years later, he died.
When he was being interred,
they were surprised by how light his coffin was;
opening it,
they found it empty.
The Historian of Anomalies says:
“A bamboo basket that does not sink,
verses inscribed on a red tile –
within these things, there are indeed spirits;
but all are connected by a single thought of compassion.
As for mansions, wives, and concubines,
enjoying their service in two places at once,
that
is indeed inexplicable.
In the past, there were those who wished for beautiful wives and concubines,
noble sons and virtuous grandsons,
and also wished for immortality;
they only obtained half of it.
Can it be that among immortals there are also Fényáng
and Jìlún?”
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In front of the Dōngxiāng Shān in Qīngzhōu,
there was a man named Zhōu Shùntíng,
who was extremely filial to his mother.
His mother developed a large carbuncle on her thigh,
the pain unbearable;
she groaned day and night.
Zhōu massaged her skin and administered medicine,
to the point of forgetting to eat or sleep.
Several months passed without a cure,
and Zhōu was distraught, at a loss for what to do.
He dreamt that his father told him:
“Your mother’s illness relies on your filial piety.
However, this sore cannot be healed without applying human fat;
your anxiety is in vain.”
He awoke, finding it strange.
He then got up,
and with a sharp knife, cut a piece of flesh from his ribs: the flesh came off,
and he felt not much pain.
He quickly bandaged his waist with cloth,
and the blood did not flow out.
He then cooked the flesh to render fat,
and applied it to his mother’s afflicted area.
The pain immediately ceased completely.
His mother happily asked:
“What medicine is so miraculously effective?”
Zhōu answered evasively.
His mother’s sore soon healed.
Zhōu always concealed the cut,
so even his wife did not know.
After it healed,
there was a large scar, like a palm print.
His wife questioned him,
and only then learned the truth.
The Historian of Anomalies says:
“Cutting one’s own flesh is an act of self-harm,
which gentlemen do not value.
However, what do ignorant commoners know of self-harm being unfilial?
They simply act on what their heart compels them to do.
That such people exist, and that true filial sons
still abide between heaven and earth, is good.
Those in charge of moral education
have many important duties,
and no time to praise and commend;
thus, the revealing of hidden virtues and subtle truths
relies on these humble writings.”
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
When the lions from Xiānmó were presented as tribute,
wherever they stopped, observers were packed like a wall.
Their appearance was completely different from those depicted in embroidered paintings in the world.
Their fur was black and yellow,
several inches long.
If a chicken was thrown to them,
they would first bat it with their claws and then blow on it;
with one blow,
all its feathers would fall off as if swept away.
This is also a marvel of natural principles.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lǐ Jiǔcháng,
a native of Línxiōng.
He was picnicking in the wild
when he saw a whirlwind approaching, puffing and blowing.
He respectfully poured a libation for it.
Later, for some reason, he moved elsewhere.
By the roadside was a grand mansion,
its halls and pavilions magnificent.
A servant in blue emerged from within
and invited Lǐ.
Lǐ firmly declined.
The servant in blue was very insistent on detaining him.
Lǐ said,
"I've never met you;
surely there's a mistake?"
The servant in blue said,
"No mistake."
Then he stated Lǐ's surname and given name.
Lǐ asked,
"Whose house is this?"
He replied,
"You'll know once you enter."
Entering,
he passed through another gate
and saw a woman with her hands and feet nailed to a door.
On closer inspection,
it was his sister-in-law.
He was greatly shocked.
Lǐ had a sister-in-law
who had developed a severe carbuncle on her arm,
and had been bedridden for over a year.
He wondered how she could have come to be here.
He began to suspect that the invitation had an evil intent,
and, feeling intimidated, he drew back.
The servant in blue urged him on,
so he entered.
Arriving beneath the main hall,
a person was seated above,
dressed in a crown and robes like a king,
with a fierce and majestic demeanor.
Lǐ prostrated himself,
not daring to look up.
The King commanded him to be raised
and comforted him, saying,
"Do not be afraid.
I merely wished to thank you for the disturbance to your picnic in the past;
there is no other reason."
Only then did Lǐ's heart settle,
but he still didn't understand the reason.
The King then said,
"Don't you recall the libation you poured in the fields?"
Lǐ suddenly understood,
knowing him to be a deity,
and bowed his head, saying,
"I just saw my sister-in-law
suffering this severe punishment,
and as one of her flesh and blood,
my heart is truly pained.
I beg Your Majesty to show compassion and pardon her!"
The King said,
"This one is very fierce and jealous;
she deserves this punishment.
Three years ago,
when your brother's concubine gave birth with her intestines prolapsed,
she secretly stabbed her intestines with a needle,
causing her internal organs to be in constant pain until now.
How can this be a human act!"
Lǐ earnestly pleaded for her.
Then the King said,
"I will pardon her for your sake.
When you return, you must persuade the fierce woman to change her ways."
Lǐ thanked him and exited,
and there was no one on the door anymore.
He returned home to see his sister-in-law;
she was lying on the bed,
her wounds bleeding profusely onto the mat.
At that moment, because the concubine had displeased her,
she was in the midst of scolding and cursing.
Lǐ hurriedly advised her, saying,
"Sister-in-law, do not be like this again!
Your terrible suffering today
is all caused by your usual jealousy."
His sister-in-law angrily said,
"If the young master were such a good man,
and if the madam in the inner chambers were as virtuous as Mèng Gūgū,
allowing her husband to sleep at the east house
and stay overnight at the west house
without daring to utter a sound,
then the young master would naturally be a very good master of the house,
and would not need to take his brother's place to subdue this old woman!"
Lǐ smiled faintly and said,
"Sister-in-law, don't be angry.
If I were to tell you the truth,
you might not even have time to cry."
She said,
"I haven't even stolen a thread from the Queen Mother's basket,
nor have I exchanged a glance with an official at the Jade Emperor's incense table.
My heart is frank and open;
what is there for me to cry about, you old hag!"
Lǐ whispered,
"Stabbing someone's intestines with a needle,
what crime is that worthy of?"
His sister-in-law's face suddenly changed color,
and she asked for the reason behind these words.
Lǐ told her the whole story.
His sister-in-law trembled uncontrollably,
tears streaming down her face as she cried mournfully,
"I wouldn't dare anymore!"
Before her tears had dried,
she felt the pain suddenly cease,
and within ten days she recovered.
From then on, she completely changed her former ways
and was praised for her virtue and gentleness.
Later, the concubine gave birth again,
and her intestines prolapsed once more;
the needle was still precisely there.
It was removed,
and the intestinal pain was finally cured.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Some say that there are many fierce and jealous women like this in the world,
and it is regrettable that the net of the underworld has so many leaks.
I say: Not so.
The punishments of the underworld
are not necessarily without those even more severe than being nailed to a door,
but simply that no news of them returns."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A person surnamed Mǎ from Yíshuǐ
married a woman surnamed Wáng.
Their relationship was very harmonious.
Mǎ died young.
Wáng's parents wanted to make her remarry,
but Wáng swore she would not.
Her mother-in-law, pitying her youth,
also advised her to remarry,
but Wáng would not listen.
Her mother said:
"Your resolve is admirable, but you are too young,
and you have no children.
I have often seen those who are steadfast at first,
only to bring shame upon themselves later.
It is certainly better to marry early,
which is the usual course of events."
Wáng was entertaining guests,
so she swore by her death,
and her mother then allowed her to have her way.
The young woman had a sculptor carve an effigy of her husband.
Each meal she would pour out libations and offer sacrifices to it as if he were alive.
One evening,
as she was about to sleep,
she suddenly saw the clay figure stretch and climb down.
Startled and aghast, she looked on,
and it had already grown to the size of a man;
it was truly her husband.
The young woman was afraid
and called for her mother.
