The ghost stopped her, saying:
"Do not do that.
Moved by your deep affection,
I suffer bitterness in the netherworld.
When there is loyalty and chastity in one family,
all the ancestors for several generations are honored.
My father incurred demerits during his life,
and was destined to have no heir,
which led to my untimely death in my prime.
The underworld officials, considering your bitter fidelity,
have therefore allowed me to return
and beget a son with you to continue the ancestral line."
The young woman also shed tears,
and they then made love as if he were still alive.
At cockcrow,
he got out of bed and left.
This continued for over a month,
until she felt a slight movement in her abdomen.
The ghost then wept and said:
"The time limit is up.
From this moment, we part forever!"
Then he vanished.
The young woman initially said nothing;
but when her abdomen gradually grew large,
she could no longer conceal it,
and secretly told her mother.
Her mother suspected it was delusional;
however, seeing that her daughter had no other lovers,
she was greatly perplexed.
After ten months,
she indeed gave birth to a boy.
When she told people about it,
everyone who heard it could not help but secretly laugh;
the young woman also had no way to justify herself.
There was a local community head who had an old grudge with Mǎ,
and he reported it to the district magistrate.
The magistrate detained and questioned the neighbors,
but there was no contradictory testimony.
The magistrate said:
"I've heard that a ghost's child has no shadow;
one with a shadow is a fake."
He held the child in the sunlight,
and the shadow was faint, like light smoke.
He then pricked the child's finger, smeared the blood on the clay figure,
and it instantly sank in without a trace;
he took another figure and smeared it,
and it wiped off immediately.
Because of this, they believed her.
When the child was several years old,
his speech, facial features, and movements
were all exactly like Mǎ's.
Only then did the general doubts resolve.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Chén Huānlè was
a native of Chángzhì in Lù.
He had a beautiful and intelligent daughter.
A Daoist priest, begging for alms,
glanced at her and left.
From then on, he carried his alms bowl daily near the marketplace.
Just then, a blind man came out of Chén's house.
The Daoist priest followed him, walking together,
and asked where he had come from.
The blind man said:
"I just passed by Chén's house to tell fortunes based on birth data."
The Daoist priest said:
"I heard that family has a young woman.
A cousin of mine wishes to seek a marriage alliance with her,
but I do not know her birth details."
The blind man recited them for him,
and the Daoist priest then took his leave.
After several days,
the young woman was embroidering in her room
when she suddenly felt her feet go numb,
which gradually spread to her thighs,
and then to her waist and abdomen;
presently, she fainted and collapsed.
After more than a quarter of an hour,
she slowly managed to stand up,
intending to tell her mother.
When she went out the door,
she saw a vast expanse of black waves,
with a path like a thread;
she was startled and retreated,
as her door, dwelling, and house
were already submerged by black water.
She looked at the path again,
where there were very few travelers,
only the Daoist priest walking slowly ahead.
So she followed him from a distance,
hoping to see someone from her village to speak with.
After walking several *lǐ*,
she suddenly saw a village dwelling.
She looked at it
and realized it was her own house.
Greatly astonished, she exclaimed:
"I have rushed so far,
yet I am still in the village.
Why was I so bewildered just now?"
Joyfully, she entered the house,
but her parents had not yet returned.
She then returned to her own room,
where her unfinished embroidery
was still on the bed.
Feeling extremely exhausted from her journey,
she sat down on the bed to rest.
The Daoist priest suddenly entered,
and the young woman was greatly startled and tried to flee.
The Daoist priest grabbed her and pressed her down.
The young woman tried to scream,
but was mute and could not make a sound.
The Daoist priest quickly used a sharp blade to cut open the young woman's heart.
The young woman felt her soul float out of her body and stand beside it.
She looked around, and her home was completely different,
only a collapsing cliff like an overturned cover.
She watched the Daoist priest dot a wooden figure with her heart's blood,
and then repeatedly pointed and cursed;
the young woman felt the wooden figure merge with her.
The Daoist priest instructed:
"From now on, you must obey my commands.
Do not make any mistakes or delay!"
Then he wore it as an ornament.
The Chén family lost their daughter,
and the whole household was distraught.
They searched until they reached Niútóulǐng,
where they first heard villagers say
that a girl below the ridge had died with her heart cut open.
Chén rushed to verify,
and indeed it was his daughter.
Weeping, he reported it to the zǎi,
who arrested the residents from below the ridge,
tortured them repeatedly,
but found no clues.
He temporarily detained all the suspects,
awaiting further investigation.
A Daoist priest went a few *lǐ* away,
and sat under a willow tree by the roadside.
Suddenly, he said to the girl:
"Today I send you on your first mission:
to scout out the court proceedings in the city's prison.
You must conceal yourself above the warm chamber.
If you see the official using his seal,
you must immediately flee and hide.
Remember this well, do not forget!
You are limited to the time from *chén* to *yǐ*.
If you are one *kè* late,
I will stab a needle into your heart,
causing you intense pain; two *kè* late,
I will stab two needles;
when it comes to three needles,
your soul will be extinguished."
When the girl heard this,
her whole body trembled in fright,
and she floated away.
In an instant, she arrived at the official's yámen,
and as instructed, hid above the chamber.
At that time, the people from below the ridge were kneeling in the hall,
not yet interrogated.
Just as the official seal was about to be affixed to an official document,
the girl had no time to flee,
and the seal was already out of its box.
The girl felt her body become heavy,
as if the paper frame could not bear her weight,
and a loud "pū" sound was heard.
Everyone in the hall looked on in astonishment.
The zǎi ordered it to be lifted again,
and the sound was as before;
on the third lift,
it fell to the ground.
Everyone heard it.
The zǎi rose and prayed:
"If this is a wronged ghost,
you should speak truthfully,
and I will clear your name."
The girl choked back tears and came forward,
recounting in detail how the Daoist priest had killed her and how he had sent her.
The zǎi dispatched yámen runners who galloped away,
and upon reaching the willow tree,
the Daoist priest was indeed there.
They captured him and brought him back,
and he confessed after one interrogation.
The suspects were then released.
The zǎi asked the girl:
"Now that your wrong has been righted, where will you go?"
The girl said:
"I will follow you, my lord."
The zǎi said:
"There is no place for you in my office.
Why not return home for now?"
After a long pause, the girl said:
"The yámen is my home.
I shall enter."
The zǎi asked again,
but the sound had already ceased.
He returned to his residence,
and his wife had given birth to a daughter.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Mǒu Jiǎ from Lù'ān,
whose father was imprisoned and about to die.
He searched through his savings
and found one hundred *jīn*,
intending to go to the prefecture to plead his case.
He set out on a mule,
followed by the black dog he kept.
He shouted at it, driving it away;
but after he had gone some distance,
it followed him again.
He whipped it away, but it would not return.
It followed him for dozens of *lǐ*.
Mǒu dismounted
and went to the roadside for a private moment.
Afterwards,
he threw a stone at the dog,
and the dog finally ran away;
but as Mǒu went on,
the dog suddenly reappeared
and bit the mule's tail and legs.
Mǒu angrily whipped it,
but the dog continued to bark and howl.
Suddenly it leaped forward,
fiercely biting the mule's head,
as if trying to block its path.
Mǒu thought it ominous
and grew even angrier,
turning his mule around to chase it.
Seeing that it was far away,
he turned the reins and galloped swiftly,
arriving at the prefecture as evening fell.
When he reached for his waist pouch,
half of his *jīn* was gone.
Sweat poured down him,
and he lost his composure.
Tossing and turning all night,
he suddenly realized that the dog's barking had a reason.
Waiting for the gate to open, he left the city,
carefully examining the path he had come.
He also reasoned that on the busy north-south thoroughfare,
with people like ants,
there was no way the lost *jīn* would still be there.
He hesitated until he reached the spot where he had dismounted,
and saw the dog lying dead in the grass,
its fur soaked with sweat as if washed.
He lifted it by the ear to look,
and the sealed *jīn* was perfectly intact.
Moved by its loyalty,
he bought a coffin and buried it,
and people called him a great *yìdàjiā*.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Zhái Zhànchí,
who was the Sìlǐ of Ráozhōu,
passed through Póyánghú.
There was a temple on the lake,
and he stopped his carriage to visit.
Inside, there was a statue of Dīng Pǔláng, a loyal minister who died for his country,
and a god surnamed Zhái
was seated at the very end.
Zhái said:
"How can a member of my clan
be seated so low!"
So he changed its seat to a higher position.
Afterwards, he boarded the boat,
when a great wind snapped the sail,
and the mast and rigging tilted,
causing his family to wail in distress.
Suddenly, a small boat
broke through the waves and came;
once it was close to the official boat,
it urgently pulled Zhái onto the small boat,
whereupon all his family members boarded.
Upon closer inspection of the person,
he was identical to the god surnamed Zhái.
Not long after,
the waves subsided,
and when they looked for him, he had disappeared.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Dǐng from Qínyóu,
whose courtesy name was Xiānhú.
He was generous and strong,
with many acquaintances.
At eighteen,
he was not yet married,
but his wife died.
Whenever he traveled far,
he often did not return for a whole year.
His elder brother Nài,
a famous scholar north of the Jiāng River,
was very devoted to his brother.
He advised his brother not to travel
and said he would find a match for him.
The young man did not listen,
ordering his boat to Zhènjiāng to visit a friend named Wén.
His friend was out,
so he rented a room on the upper floor of an inn.
The Jiāng River's waters were clear,
and the entire mountain was visible,
which greatly pleased him.
The next day,
his friend came
and asked him to move, but he refused to leave.
After more than half a month,
one night, he dreamt of a young woman,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
whose appearance was exquisite and beautiful.
She came to his bed and lay with him.
When he awoke, he had had an emission.
He was quite surprised by this,
but also thought it was just a coincidence.
That night,
he dreamt of her again.
This happened for three or four nights.
His heart was greatly astonished,
and he dared not extinguish the candle.
Although he lay down,
he was vigilantly alert.
As soon as he closed his eyes,
the dreamt woman came again;
just as they were intimate,
he suddenly awoke with a start;
he quickly opened his eyes,
and there was the young woman, like an immortal,
still demurely in his arms.
Seeing that Shēng was awake,
she suddenly felt ashamed and shy.
Although Shēng knew she was not human,
he was quite pleased;
without time to ask her name or origin,
he immediately engaged in passion with her.
The woman seemed unable to bear it,
and said:
"You are so wild and violent!
No wonder people don't dare to tell you directly."
Shēng then began to question her.
She replied:
"My name is Wǔ Qiūyuè.
My late father was a renowned scholar,
deeply learned in the principles of the Yìjìng.
He always cherished me;
but he said I would not live long,
and therefore did not allow me to be betrothed to anyone.
Later, at fifteen, I indeed died young,
and was interred in the eastern part of the chamber,
level with the ground,
without any tomb inscription.
Only a stone tablet was erected beside my coffin,
saying: 'The girl Qiūyuè,
buried without a mound.
After thirty years,
she will marry Wáng Dǐng.'
Now thirty years have passed,
and you have just arrived.
My heart rejoiced,
and I urgently wished to present myself;
but my heart was shy and timid,
so I resorted to appearing in your dreams."
Wáng was also pleased,
and again sought to complete the act.
She said:
"I need some Yang energy to seek resurrection,
but I truly cannot endure this wind and rain.
In the future, there will be endless opportunities for intimacy,
why must it be tonight?"
Thereupon, she got up and left.
The next day,
she came again.
They sat opposite each other, laughing and jesting,
as joyful as if they had known each other all their lives.
When the candle was extinguished and they went to bed,
she was no different from a living person;
but once the woman got up,
there was seminal discharge,
staining the mattress.
One night,
the moonlight was clear and bright,
and they walked a short distance in the courtyard.
He asked the woman:
"Are there also cities and towns in the underworld?"
She replied:
"It's the same.
The cities and governmental offices of the underworld
are not here,
but about three or four Lǐ from here.
However, night is taken as day."
He asked:
"Can living people see them?"
She replied:
"They can."
Shēng requested to go and see,
and the woman agreed.
They went under the moonlight.
The woman floated swiftly like the wind,
and Wáng exerted himself to follow.
Suddenly they arrived at a place,
and the woman said:
"It's not far."
Shēng looked around but saw nothing.
The woman applied her saliva to his eyes,
and when he opened them,
his sight was twice as bright as usual.
The night appeared no different from daytime.
He then saw city walls and battlements in the distant haze;
people on the road
were rushing as if to a market.
Presently, two officers
bound three or four people passed by.
The last person strangely resembled his elder brother.
He rushed closer to look,
and it was indeed his brother.
Startled, he asked:
"Brother, how did you come here?"
His brother, seeing Shēng,
shed tears mournfully,
saying:
"I don't know what happened,
but I was forcibly detained."
Wáng angrily said:
"My brother is a cultivated gentleman who upholds propriety;
how could he be imprisoned like this!"
He then pleaded with the two officers,
hoping they would kindly release him.
The officers refused,
and were extremely arrogant and rude.
Shēng became furious,
and wanted to argue with them.
His brother stopped him, saying:
"This is an official command,
and one must obey the law.
However, I lack funds
and they are extorting bribes, which is truly distressing.
When you return,
you should make arrangements."
Shēng grasped his brother's arm,
and cried out, losing his voice.
The officers were angry,
and sharply pulled the rope around his neck,
causing his brother to stumble.
Shēng, seeing this,
was filled with burning indignation,
unable to control himself.
He immediately drew his waist-saber
and instantly cut off one officer's head.
The other officer cried out in alarm,
and Shēng cut him down too.
The woman was greatly alarmed and said:
"Killing government envoys
is an unforgivable crime!
Any delay will bring disaster!
Please quickly find a boat and head north,
return home and do not display mourning banners,
lock your doors and allow no one in or out;
for seven days you will be safe."
Wáng then helped his brother and bought a small boat that night,
urgently crossing north.
Upon returning home, he saw mourners at the gate,
and knew his brother was indeed dead.
He closed and locked the door,
and only then entered.
His brother was already gone;
entering the room,
the deceased had already revived,
and immediately called out:
"I'm starving to death!
Quickly prepare some noodles."
At this time, he had been dead for two days,
and the family members were all astonished.
Shēng then fully recounted what had happened.
Seven days later, they opened the gate
and removed the mourning banners,
and people then learned of his revival.
Relatives and friends gathered to inquire, but they only gave false answers.
He then pondered over Qiūyuè,
his thoughts quite troubled.
So he again headed south,
to the old pavilion,
holding a candle and waiting for a long time,
but the woman never arrived.
He was drowsy and about to sleep
when he saw a woman approach,
who said:
"Miss Qiūyuè sends her regards to the young master: Previously, she was killed by a public servant.
The murderer escaped,
and they seized the young lady,
who is now imprisoned
and subjected to cruel treatment by the oppressive yāyì.
Every day she yearns for the young master,
and hopes he will devise a plan to save her."
Wáng was saddened and enraged,
and followed the woman.
They reached a city district,
entered the western suburb,
and she pointed to a gate, saying:
"The young lady is temporarily lodged here."
Wáng entered
and saw many rooms and buildings,
with many prisoners kept there,
but Qiūyuè was not among them.
He then entered a small door,
and there was lamplight in a tiny room.
Wáng approached the window to peer in,
and saw Qiūyuè sitting on a bed,
covering her face with her sleeve and weeping.
Two yāyì were at her side,
pinching her chin and grabbing her shoes,
teasing her.
The woman cried even more intensely.
One yāyì pulled her neck, saying:
"Since you are a criminal,
do you still maintain your chastity?"
Wáng was furious,
without time to speak,
he drew his sword and went straight in,
killing one yāyì with one stroke each,
slaughtering them like cutting hemp,
and snatched the young lady and left.
Fortunately, no one noticed.
Just as they reached the inn,
he suddenly woke up.
He was still marveling at the ferocity of the illusionary dream,
when he saw Qiūyuè standing there, gazing at him.
The scholar was startled, sat up,
and told her about the dream.
The woman said:
"It is real,
not a dream."
The scholar was shocked, saying,
"What shall we do now!"
The woman sighed:
"This is fate.
I had to wait until the moon waned completely
for my time of rebirth;
but now that it is already like this,
how can I wait urgently.
You must go to the place where I was buried,
carry me back with you,
and call my name frequently every day;
I can revive in three days.
However, before the time is complete,
my bones will be soft and my feet weak,
unable to perform domestic chores for you."
Having said this,
she hastily started to leave.
Then she turned back and said:
"I almost forgot,
what about the pursuit from the underworld?
When I was alive,
my father gave me talismans,
saying that thirty years later,
they could be worn by a couple."
Thereupon, she asked for a brush and quickly wrote two talismans,
saying:
"One you wear yourself,
the other stick to my back."
He escorted her out,
marked her burial place,
and dug about a foot deep,
and immediately saw the coffin,
which was already decayed.
There was a small stele at the side,
just as the woman had said.
He opened the coffin and looked;
the woman's complexion was as if alive.
He carried her into the room,
her clothes disintegrating into dust with the wind.
After sticking the talisman,
he wrapped her tightly in quilts,
and carried her to the riverside;
he hailed a boat,
falsely stating that his sister was gravely ill,
and he was taking her home.
Fortunately, a strong south wind blew,
and by dawn, they had reached the village gate.
He placed the woman down
and then informed his elder brother and sister-in-law.
The whole family was startled and stared,
but no one dared to openly express their bewilderment.
The scholar opened the quilt,
and loudly called Qiūyuè,
sleeping with the corpse embraced every night.
She gradually became warm.
In three days, she revived,
and in seven days, she could walk;
she changed clothes and bowed to her sister-in-law,
as graceful and exquisite as an immortal.
However, beyond ten steps,
she needed someone to help her walk;
otherwise, she would sway with the wind,
frequently on the verge of toppling over.
Those who saw her thought she had this illness,
which only added to her charm.
She often advised the scholar, saying:
"Your sins are too deep,
you should accumulate virtue and recite scriptures to atone for them.
Otherwise,
your life may not be long."
The scholar had always been uninclined towards Buddhism,
but at this point, he became a devout convert.
Later, he also suffered no harm.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"I wish to propose a law: 'Anyone who kills a public servant
shall have their crime reduced by three degrees compared to an ordinary person,
for there is none among these people who cannot be killed.
Therefore, one who can eliminate corrupt yāyì
is a good and upright person;
even if they are somewhat harsh,
it cannot be called tyrannical.
Moreover, there are no fixed laws in the underworld;
if there are evil people,
knives, saws, tripods, and cauldrons
are not considered cruel.
What pleases the human heart
is what the King of the Underworld also approves.
How can one commit a crime that incurs pursuit from the underworld,
and then luckily escape it?'"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dòu Xù of Jiāozhōu,
courtesy name Xiǎohuī.
One day, he was taking an afternoon nap,
when he saw a man in a brown robe standing before his couch,
pacing back and forth, looking around nervously,
as if he had something to say.
Dòu Xù asked him,
and he replied,
"My lord has sent for you."
"Who is this lord?"
He said,
"He is nearby, in the neighboring territory."
Dòu Xù followed him out.
Turning past walls and houses,
he was led to a place
of stacked pavilions and multi-storied buildings,
with myriad rafters connected,
winding as they walked.
He felt that the ten thousand households and thousand gates
were utterly unlike the human world.
He also saw palace ladies and female officials,
a great many coming and going,
all asking the man in the brown robe,
"Has Dòu Láng arrived?"
The man in the brown robe assented.
Soon,
a high official came out,
and greeted Dòu Xù very respectfully.
After entering the hall,
Dòu Xù asked,
"We have never been acquainted,
and I have been remiss in paying my respects.
Now to receive such a gracious welcome,
it causes me considerable doubt and reflection."
The high official said,
"Our humble ruler, seeing your esteemed lineage and hereditary virtue,
is greatly impressed and yearns for your acquaintance,
deeply wishing to meet with you."
Dòu Xù was even more startled,
and asked,
"Who is the King?"
He replied,
"You will know shortly."
Before long,
two female officials arrived,
guiding Dòu Xù with a pair of banners.
Entering through a heavy gate,
he saw a King in the main hall.
Seeing Dòu Xù,
he descended the steps to greet him,
performing the rites of host and guest.
After the rites,
they took their seats.
The feast laid out was magnificent.
Looking up at a plaque in the hall, it read
"Guì Fǔ."
Dòu Xù was constrained and unable to speak.
The King said,
"Although I am unworthy, we are close neighbors,
and our bond is deep.
You should relax and enjoy yourself,
do not harbor doubts or fears."
Dòu Xù assented.
After a few rounds of wine,
music from pipes and singing began below,
but gongs and drums were not sounded;
the music was subtle and delicate.
A little later,
the King suddenly looked left and right and said,
"I have a line;
I trouble you all to provide a matching couplet: 'Cái Rén dēng Guì Fǔ.'"
As everyone was pondering,
Dòu Xù immediately responded,
"Jūn Zǐ ài Lián Huā."
The King was greatly pleased and said,
"How wonderful!
Lián Huā is my princess's pet name.
How could it be so fitting?
Is it not fate from a previous life?
Tell the princess,
she must not fail to come out and meet the gentleman."
After a while,
the sound of jade pendants approached,
and the fragrance of orchids and musk grew strong,
and then the princess arrived.
She was sixteen or seventeen,
of unparalleled beauty.
The King commanded her to perform obeisance to Dòu Xù,
saying,
"This is my little daughter, Lián Huā."
After bowing, she departed.
Dòu Xù, seeing her,
was deeply moved,
and sat still, lost in thought.
The King raised his goblet and urged him to drink,
but Dòu Xù's eyes saw nothing.
The King seemed to subtly perceive his feelings,
and then said,
"My daughter is a suitable match for you,
but I am ashamed that she is not your equal.
What do you say?"
Dòu Xù was dejected, as if infatuated,
and still did not hear.
One sitting nearby nudged him and said,
"Has the King greeted you unseen, or the King spoken unheard by you?"
Dòu Xù was bewildered, as if lost,
and felt ashamed.
He left his seat and said,
"I have received such gracious favor,
that I have become overly drunk,
and my decorum has been disorderly.
I hope you can forgive me.
However, it is already getting late,
so I must take my leave."
The King rose and said,
"Having met you,
my heart is truly content.
Why such haste to speak of departing?
Since you cannot stay,
I dare not force you.
If you find yourself thinking of us,
I shall invite you again."
Then he ordered an inner official to escort him out.
On the way,
the inner official said to Dòu Xù,
"Just now, the King said she was a suitable match,
seeming to wish for a marriage alliance.
Why were you silent and said not a word?"
Dòu Xù stamped his foot in regret,
regretting every step
until he reached home.
Suddenly, he awoke,
and the lingering light of dawn was already fading.
He sat in meditation, reflecting,
and it was all vivid before his eyes.
In the evening, he extinguished the candle in his study,
hoping to find the old dream again,
but the road to Hándān was distant,
and he could only regret and sigh.
One night,
sharing a bed with a friend,
he suddenly saw the former inner official arrive,
conveying the King's summons.
Dòu Xù was delighted
and followed him.
He saw the King prostrate on a couch.
The King pulled him up,
and invited him to sit in a corner,
saying,
"Since we parted, I knew you were troubled by longing.
I presumptuously offer my humble daughter to serve you,
I hope you will not find it objectionable."
Dòu Xù immediately bowed in thanks.
The King ordered scholars and ministers
to accompany them in feasting and drinking.
When the wine was finished,
a palace lady came forward and announced,
"The princess's makeup is complete."
Soon, dozens of palace women
escorted the princess out.
With a red brocade covering her head,
she stepped lightly,
and was led onto a carpet,
where she and Dòu Xù exchanged bows and completed the ceremony.
Afterward, she was sent to the guesthouse.
The bridal chamber was warm and clean,
exquisitely fragrant and luxurious.
Dòu Xù said,
"With you before my eyes,
it truly makes one happy enough to forget death.
But I fear that this encounter today
is but a dream."
The princess covered her mouth and said,
"It is clearly you and I;
how could it be a dream?"
The next morning, as they were getting up,
he playfully helped the princess apply her makeup;
then he measured her waist with a sash,
and her foot with his fingers.
The princess laughed and asked,
"Are you mad?"
He said,
"I have often been misled by dreams,
so I carefully record these details.
If it turns out to be a dream,
it will still be enough to stir fond memories."
Their playful banter ended when
a palace lady rushed in and said,
"A demon has entered the palace gate!
The King has retreated to a side hall.
Calamity is not far off!"
Dòu Xù was greatly alarmed
and rushed to see the King.
The King grasped his hand and wept, saying,
"You, my lord, have not abandoned us,
and we were just planning for everlasting happiness.
How could we have known that evil would descend from heaven,
and that the kingdom's fate would soon be overturned?
What can we do now!"
The student was startled and asked what it was about.
The King took a memorial from the desk,
handed it to the student, and had him open it to read.
The memorial stated:
"Your minister, Hēi Yì (黑翼), Grand Academician of the Hánxiāng Diàn (含香殿),
regarding a most extraordinary and monstrous event,
prays for an early relocation of the capital
to preserve the nation's lifeline: According to reports from the Imperial attendants: Since the sixth day of the fifth month,
a one-thousand-zhàng (丈) giant python arrived,
coiling outside the palace,
swallowing over thirteen thousand eight hundred officials and commoners, both inside and outside the palace;
all palaces in its path have been reduced to ruins,
and so on.
Your minister courageously went to observe,
and indeed saw the demonic python,
its head like a mountain,
its eyes like rivers and seas;
when it raised its head, all pavilions and halls were swallowed whole,
when it stretched its body, all towers and walls were overturned.
Truly an unprecedented calamity of a thousand ages,
a disaster never encountered in ten thousand generations!
The altars of the state and the imperial ancestral temples
are in imminent danger!
I humbly request His Majesty to quickly lead the imperial family
to relocate to a land of peace."
And so forth.
After the student finished reading,
his face was ashen.
Immediately, a palace attendant rushed in to report:
"The monstrous creature has arrived!"
The entire hall erupted in mournful cries,
a scene of utter despair.
The King, in a panic, did not know what to do,
but wept and looked at the student, saying:
"My daughter has already troubled you, sir."
The student gasped for breath and returned.
The princess was embracing her attendants, weeping bitterly,
and seeing the student enter,
she pulled at his sleeve and said:
"My lord, where will you put your concubine?"
The student was heartbroken to the point of collapse,
so he grasped her wrist and thought:
"This humble one is poor and lowly,
ashamed to have no golden house.
I have a few thatched huts;
may we temporarily hide there together?"
The princess, with tears in her eyes, said:
"In such urgency, how can one choose?
Please take me quickly to live there."
The student then helped her out.
Not long after,
they arrived home.
The princess said:
"This is a great, peaceful residence,
much better than the former country.
However, since I have come with you,
where will my parents rely?
Please build another dwelling,
and the entire nation shall follow."
The student found this difficult.
The princess wailed:
"If you cannot help those in urgent need,
what use is a lord like you!"
The student tried to comfort and explain,
but she had already entered the room.
The princess lay on the bed, weeping sorrowfully,
unable to be consoled.
Troubled and without a solution,
he suddenly woke up,
realizing it was a dream.
Yet the sound of weeping by his ear
continued faintly.
Listening carefully,
it was clearly not a human sound,
but two or three bees
flying and buzzing above his pillow.
He shouted that it was a strange occurrence.
His friend questioned him,
so he recounted the dream.
His friend was also amazed by the oddity.
They both got up to look at the bees,
which clung to his clothes and sleeves,
refusing to be brushed away.
His friend advised him to build a nest for them.
The student followed the advice,
supervising the construction.
Just as two walls were erected,
swarms of bees came from outside the wall,
continuous as a rope.
Before the roof was sealed,
they had gathered, filling a dou (斗).
Tracing their origin,
it was the old garden of the neighboring elder.
In the garden, there was a beehive
for over thirty years,
and the colony was quite prosperous.
Someone told the elder about the student's situation.
The elder went to observe,
and the beehive was deserted.
He broke open its wall,
and a snake about a zhàng (丈) long occupied it.
He caught and killed it.
Then he realized that the giant python was this very creature.
The bees entered the student's house,
multiplied even more vigorously,
and there were no other unusual incidents.
Based on the manuscript version of Liáozhāi Zhìyì (聊齋誌異).
Yú Shēng's given name was Jǐng,
his courtesy name was Xiǎosòng.
He was a native of Yìdū.
He studied at Lǐquán Temple.
One night, as he was poring over his books,
a woman suddenly appeared outside his window and praised him, saying:
"Yú Xiànggōng, you study diligently!"
He then thought: From where in these deep mountains could a woman have come?
While he was still pondering in doubt,
the woman had already pushed open the door, smiling as she entered,
saying:
"How diligently you study!"
Yú was startled and rose,
looking at her.
She wore a green dress and a long skirt,
and was incomparably graceful and beautiful.
Yú knew she was not human,
and so pressed her about where she lived.
The woman said:
"Do you think me to be one who can bite and devour?
Why trouble yourself with such exhaustive questions?"
Yú was fond of her,
and so they slept together.
When her silken robe was undone,
her waist was so slender it could scarcely be encircled by a hand.
As soon as the watch drums finished,
she gracefully departed.
From then on, she came every night.
One evening, as they drank together,
her conversation revealed an exquisite understanding of music.
Yú said:
"Your voice is tender and delicate;
if you were to sing a tune,
it would surely captivate the soul."
The woman smiled and said:
"I dare not sing a tune,
lest I captivate your soul."
Yú pressed her persistently.
She said:
"It's not that I'm being stingy,
but I fear others might hear.
If you must have it,
please allow me to offer my poor performance;
but only a faint murmur to convey the meaning will suffice."
Thereupon, she lightly tapped the bed frame with her 'lotus hook' (small foot),
and sang:
"The tallow tree bird on the branch,
tricked me into leaving in the middle of the night.
I do not resent my embroidered shoes getting wet,
I only fear my love has no companion."
Her voice was as faint as a fly's,
barely discernible.
But listening attentively,
it was melodious and fervent,
stirring the ears and shaking the heart.
After the song,
she opened the door and peered out, saying:
"Beware, there might be someone outside the window."
She circled the house, looking around,
but found no one.
Yú Shēng said:
"Why are you so deeply suspicious and fearful?"
She smiled and said:
"The proverb says, 'A ghost who steals life is always afraid of people.'
That describes me."
Soon after, they retired to bed,
but she was uneasy and unhappy,
saying:
"Is our life together
to end here?"
Yú urgently asked her,
and the woman replied:
"My heart is pounding,
my allotted time is ending."
Yú comforted her, saying:
"A pounding heart and blinking eyes
are quite common,
why speak like this so suddenly?"
The woman was slightly cheered,
and they again embraced.
When the water clock ceased,
she donned her clothes and got out of bed.
Just as she was about to open the gate,
she hesitated and returned,
saying:
"I don't know why,
my heart feels timid and afraid.
Please escort me to the door."
Yú indeed rose,
and escorted her outside the gate.
The woman said:
"You wait and watch me;
only when I have climbed over the wall and gone,
should you return."
He said:
"Very well."
He watched the woman turn around the veranda,
and she was silently gone from sight.
Just as he was about to return to bed,
he heard the woman's desperate cries for help.
Yú ran towards the sound,
but saw no trace of her in any direction;
the sound was coming from the eaves.
He raised his head and looked closely,
and saw a spider as large as a bullet,
clutching something,
which was wailing with a hoarse cry.
Yú broke the web and pried the object down,
removing its bonds.
It was a green bee,
fainting and about to die.
He caught it and brought it back to his room,
placing it on his desk.
After a while, it revived,
and began to walk.
Slowly, it climbed onto the inkstone,
deliberately plunged itself into the ink,
then emerged and crawled onto the desk,
and scurried to write
the character "謝" (xiè, thanks).
It then fluttered its wings repeatedly,
and flew out of the window.
From this time on, she was never seen again.
According to the manuscript edition of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Xiè Zhōngtiáo of Lóngmén
was frivolous and without good conduct.
At the age of thirty,
he lost his wife,
leaving behind two sons and one daughter.
They cried day and night,
causing him much distress and entanglement.
He sought to marry a second wife,
but negotiations were difficult and never settled.
He temporarily hired an old woman to care for his children.
One day,
he was strolling along a mountain path,
when suddenly a woman appeared behind him.
He waited and observed her;
she was a beautiful woman,
about twenty years old.
His heart was pleased,
and he jokingly said:
"Madam, walking alone,
are you not afraid?"
The woman walked on without replying.
He said again:
"Madam, with your delicate steps,
this mountain path is particularly difficult."
The woman still did not look at him.
Xiè looked around, saw no one,
approached her side,
and suddenly seized her wrist,
dragging her into a secluded valley,
intending to force himself upon her.
The woman angrily cried out:
"Where is this strong man
who boldly assaults me!"
Xiè pulled her along,
without ceasing.
The woman stumbled,
distressed and at her wits' end,
then said:
"Is this the way to seek a gentle lover?
Is it like this?
Release me,
and I shall come along willingly."
Xiè agreed.
They went together into a secluded gully.
After they had coupled in the wilderness,
they grew fond of each other.
The woman asked his place of residence and surname.
Xiè told her truthfully.
Then he also asked the woman,
the woman said:
"My surname is Lí.
Unfortunately, I became a widow early.
My mother-in-law also passed away,
leaving me all alone,
with no one to depend on.
Therefore, I often visit my maternal home."
Xiè said:
"I am also a widower.
Would you be willing to follow me?"
The woman asked:
"Do you have children, sir?"
Xiè said:
"I shall not deceive you: as for matters of the bedchamber,
I have had quite a few paramours.
It's just that the crying of sons and daughters
is unbearable."
The woman hesitated and said:
"This is a great difficulty!
Looking at the style of your clothes, socks, and shoes,
they are merely ordinary.
I thought I could manage.
But it is difficult to be a stepmother,
and I fear I cannot endure reproaches."
Xiè said:
"Please do not hesitate or obstruct.
If I do not speak of it myself,
how can others interfere?"
The woman also slightly assented.
Then she worried and said:
"Our bodies have already touched;
how can I not follow?
However, there is a fierce uncle
who always regards me as a rare commodity.
I fear he will not consent,
what then shall we do?"
Xiè also became anxious and alarmed,
and suggested they flee.
The woman said:
"I am also utterly grateful to you.
My concern is that if my family spills the secret,
it will be inconvenient for both of us."
Xiè said:
"This is a minor matter.
There is only an old widow in my house;
I will send her away immediately."
The woman rejoiced,
and thus went home with him.
First, she hid in the outer dwelling;
then, after he went in and dismissed the old widow,
he swept the bed to welcome the woman,
and they were exceedingly happy together.
The woman immediately began to work,
and also mended clothes for the children,
working extremely hard.
Having obtained the woman, Xiè
loved her exceptionally,
spending his days behind closed doors with her,
no longer receiving guests.
After more than a month,
he happened to go out on official business,
locking the door behind him as he left.
When he returned,
the central door was tightly shut,
and there was no response when he knocked.
He forced the door open and entered,
but there was no one to be seen.
Just as he reached the bedchamber,
a giant wolf burst out, leaping through the door,
nearly frightening him to death.
He went in to look,
and his children were all gone.
Fresh blood stained the ground,
and only three heads remained.
He turned to chase the wolf,
but it had already disappeared.
Yìshǐshì said:
"The scholar was immoral,
and his retribution was also tragic.
Those who remarry
are all bringing a wolf into the house.
How much more so when seeking a virtuous wife from a wilderness coupling and flight!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zōng Xiāngruò of Húzhōu
was a scholar.
One autumn day, as he patrolled the fields,
he saw intense shaking
where the crops were dense.
Suspicious,
he crossed the paths to investigate,
and found a man and a woman coupling in the wild.
He smiled and was about to return.
Then he saw the man shyly tying his sash
and hastily departing.
The woman also rose.
Upon closer inspection,
she was exquisitely beautiful.
He was pleased with her,
and wished to engage in intimacy,
but was truly ashamed of his own vulgarity.
So he approached slightly, brushing her, and said:
"Was your frolic in the mulberries pleasant?"
The woman smiled but did not speak.
Zōng moved closer and opened her clothes;
her skin was as smooth as lard.
Then he fondled her up and down several times.
The woman smiled and said:
"You old-fashioned scholar!
If you want to do something,
then just do it,
why this frantic probing?"
He asked her surname.
She said:
"A brief encounter like spring breeze,
then we part ways.
Why bother with an inquiry?
Are you going to leave my name to build a chastity archway?"
Zōng said:
"In the wild fields, amidst dew-laden grass,
that is what village swineherds do.
I am not accustomed to it.
Given your beauty,
even a private tryst should show self-respect;
why be so unkempt?"
When the woman heard this,
she greatly approved.
Zōng said:
"My humble studio is not far;
please come and linger awhile."
The woman said:
"I have been out for a long time;
I fear people will be suspicious.
After midnight would be fine."
She asked about Zōng's household and belongings in great detail,
then hurried along a diagonal path
and swiftly departed.
At the first watch,
she indeed arrived at Zōng's study.
They indulged in passionate lovemaking,
showing extreme affection.
This continued for over a month,
and no one knew their secret.
It happened that a Buddhist monk arrived at the village temple,
and upon seeing Zōng, he was startled and said:
"You have an evil aura about you.
What have you encountered?"
He replied:
"None."
Several days later,
Zōng *shào* suddenly fell ill.
Every evening, the woman would bring him delicious fruits to eat,
and diligently inquire after him and caress him,
as if they were a loving couple.
However, after lying down, she would insist on *hé* with Zōng.
Zōng was sick,
and found it quite unbearable.
He suspected she was not human,
but had no way to temporarily separate from her and make her leave.
So he said,
"Earlier, the monk told me I was bewitched by a demon.
Now I am indeed sick,
his words have proven true.
Tomorrow, I will ask him to come,
and then seek talismans and incantations."
The woman's expression changed to one of sorrow.
Zōng grew even more suspicious of her.
The next day,
he sent someone to inform the monk of the situation.
The monk said,
"This is a fox.
Her skill is still shallow,
and it is easy to bind her."
He then wrote two talismans,
and instructed,
"When you return, place a pure altar in front of the bed,
and immediately stick one talisman over the altar's opening.
Wait for the fox to creep in,
then quickly cover it with a basin,
and stick the other talisman on top of the basin.
Throw it into a boiling pot over a raging fire,
and she will die in a moment."
The family members returned,
and did everything as the monk had taught.
Late at night,
the woman finally arrived,
took some kumquats from her sleeve,
and was just about to approach the bed to inquire.
Suddenly, with a whooshing sound from the altar's opening,
the woman was sucked in.
The family members immediately rose,
covered the opening and affixed the talisman,
just about to begin the cooking.
Zōng saw the kumquats scattered all over the ground,
recalled their affection,
and was moved to sorrow.
He hastily ordered her release.
They peeled off the talisman and removed the cover,
and the woman emerged from the altar,
looking quite disheveled and distraught.
She bowed and said,
"My great *dào* was about to be achieved,
and suddenly I was almost reduced to ashes!
You are a benevolent person,
I swear I will repay you."
Then she left.
Several days later,
Zōng became even more critically ill,
as if about to perish.
His family rushed to the market
to buy wood for his coffin.
On the way, they met a woman,
who asked,
"Are you Zōng Xiāngruò's *jìgāng*?"
They replied,
"Yes."
The woman said,
"Master Zōng is my cousin.
I heard he is gravely ill,
and was about to go visit him,
but something came up and I couldn't go.
This packet of miraculous medicine,
please take the trouble to deliver it to him."
The family members received it and returned.
Zōng remembered that he had no sisters among his cousins,
and knew this was the fox repaying him.
He took the medicine,
and indeed recovered greatly,
becoming well again within ten days.
He felt grateful to her,
and prayed to the void,
wishing to see her again.
One night,
he closed his door and drank alone,
when suddenly he heard a snap of fingers tapping on the window.
He unbolted the door and looked out,
and it was the fox woman.
Greatly pleased,
he took her hand, thanked her,
and invited her in to drink together.
The woman said,
"Since we parted, I have been troubled,
thinking how to repay your great kindness.
Now I have found a good match for you;
is this enough to fulfill my responsibility?"
Zōng asked,
"Who is it?"
She said,
"Not someone you know.
Tomorrow at *chén* hour,
cross the South Lake early,
if you see a water chestnut picker,
wearing a light silk cape,
you should quickly row your boat to catch up with her.
If you lose sight of her,
then look by the embankment for a short lotus hidden under the leaves;
pick it and take it home,
burn its stem with a wax flame,
and you will obtain a beautiful wife,
and also prolong your life."
Zōng respectfully accepted her instruction.
Afterwards, she bid farewell,
but Zōng earnestly tried to make her stay.
The woman said,
"Since I suffered that calamity,
I have suddenly realized the great *dào*.
How can I, through the love of the bedchamber,
incur others' enmity?"
She spoke sternly and departed.
Zōng Rú said:
Arriving at Nánhú,
he saw many beautiful women amidst the lotus marsh.
Among them was a girl with hair hanging loose,
clad in a gauze-like silk garment,
peerlessly beautiful.
He hastened his boat to approach her,
but suddenly lost sight of her.
He immediately parted a clump of lotuses,
and indeed found a single branch of red lotus,
its stem less than a foot long.
He plucked it and returned home.
Entering the door, he placed it on a small table,
and scraped some wax beside it,
intending to light a fire.
He turned his head for a moment,
and it had transformed into a beautiful woman.
Zōng was overjoyed and prostrated himself in worship.
The woman said:
"Foolish fellow!
I am a fox demon,
and I will bring misfortune upon you!"
Zōng did not listen.
The woman said:
"Who taught you?"
He replied:
"This humble one can recognize you on his own,
why wait to be taught?"
He seized her arm and pulled her close.
As his hand came down,
she transformed into a grotesque rock,
about a foot high,
exquisitely carved on every side.
So he carried it and placed it on the offering table,
burned incense, bowed again, and prayed to it.
As night fell,
he closed the door and blocked all crevices,
only fearing it would disappear.
At dawn, he looked at it,
and it was no longer a rock.
It was a silk shawl,
from which a fragrant scent wafted from afar.
Spreading it out, he examined the collar and lapels;
some lingering greasiness remained.
Zōng covered himself with it and lay down to sleep.
In the evening, he rose to trim the lamp,
and when he returned,
the girl with loose hair was on the pillow.
Overwhelmed with joy,
fearing she would transform again,
he prayed mournfully before approaching her.
The woman laughed and said:
"Oh, what a nuisance!
I don't know who was gossiping,
leading this wild boy to vex me to death!"
Thereupon, she no longer resisted.
But during their intimacy,
she seemed unable to bear it,
repeatedly begging him to stop.
Zōng did not listen.
The woman said:
"If this continues,
I will transform and leave!"
Zōng was afraid and stopped.
From then on, their affection was very harmonious.
Gold and silk constantly filled their coffers,
the source of which was unknown.
When the woman saw people, she bowed respectfully,
as if unable to speak.
The man also avoided mentioning her strangeness.
After more than ten months of pregnancy,
the day of childbirth was due.
Entering the room,
she instructed Zōng to close the door and forbid visitors.
She then cut open her lower abdomen with a knife,
took out the child,
and ordered Zōng to tear silk to bind it.
After a night, she healed.
Another six or seven years passed,
and she said to Zōng:
"My past karma is fulfilled,
please allow me to take my leave."
Zōng heard this and wept,
saying:
"When you came to me,
I was poor and unable to support myself.
Thanks to you, I have become slightly prosperous.
How can I bear for you to speak of immediate departure?
Moreover, you have no family or clan.
In the future, the child will not know its mother,
which is also a source of regret."
The woman also said wistfully:
"Gatherings must have partings,
this is indeed the norm.
The child has a fortunate appearance,
and you too will reach a great age.
What more could you ask for?
My original surname is Hé.
If you should think of me,
embrace my old belongings and call out: 'Héhuā Sānniángzǐ!'
You will surely see me."
Having spoken, she disrobed,
and said:
"I am leaving."
As he watched in surprise,
she had already flown high above his head.
Zōng leaped up,
urgently pulled at her,
and caught a shoe.
The shoe slipped and fell to the ground,
transforming into a stone swallow;
its color redder than cinnabar,
clear and translucent inside and out,
like rock crystal.
He picked it up and treasured it.
He checked the chest,
and the gauze-like silk garment she wore when she first came was still there.
Whenever he remembered her,
he would embrace it and call out
"Sānniángzǐ!"
and she would appear as if alive,
with a joyous countenance and smiling eyebrows,
exactly as she was in life;
but she would not speak.
[From the Liaozhāi Zhìyì manuscript edition]
A certain resident of Báijiāzhuāng in the west of Yì county
stole a neighbor's duck and cooked it.
That night,
he felt an itch on his skin.
At dawn, he looked at it,
and duck feathers had grown,
which hurt when touched.
Greatly frightened,
he had no cure.
That night, he dreamt of a person who told him:
"Your illness is a heavenly punishment.
You must be cursed by the one who suffered the loss,
then the feathers can fall off."
However, the neighbor, an old man, was always magnanimous,
and in his life, when he lost things,
he never showed anger.
The man cunningly told the old man:
"The duck was stolen by so-and-so.
He is very afraid of being cursed.
Cursing him might also serve as a warning for the future."
The old man smiled and said:
"Who has the spare energy to curse an evil person?"
He ultimately did not curse him.
The man became even more distressed,
and so he honestly told the neighbor.
The old man then cursed him,
and his illness truly improved.
Yǐshǐshì says:
"How terrible
is theft: one theft and duck feathers grow!
How important
is it to guard against curses: one curse and a thief's crime is reduced!
However, there is an art to doing good.
That old neighbor
used cursing to practice his compassion."
[From the Liaozhāi Zhìyì manuscript edition]
Liǔ Xīchuān of Jiāozhōu
was the steward of Fǎ Nèishǐ.
When he was over forty years old,
he had a son,
whom he doted on excessively.
He indulged him,
fearing only to displease him.
When the son grew up,
he became extravagant and beyond restraint,
emptying his father's accumulated wealth.
Not long after,
the son fell ill.
The old man had a fine mule.
The son said:
"The mule is fat and can be eaten.
Kill it and let me eat it,
and my illness can be cured."
Liǔ planned to kill a bad mule instead.
When the son heard this,
he became very angry and cursed,
and his illness worsened.
Liǔ was afraid,
and killed the mule to serve him.
The son was then pleased;
however, he only tasted a small portion,
then discarded it.
The illness did not lessen but worsened,
and soon he died.
Liǔ was so heartbroken he almost died.
Three or four years later,
some villagers went to Dài Mountain for a temple fair with incense offerings.
When they reached halfway up the mountain,
they saw a person riding a mule, speeding towards them.
He looked like Liǔ Zǐ, the nephew of Liǔ.
When he got closer,
it was indeed him.
He dismounted the mule, bowed to everyone,
and they exchanged pleasantries.
The villagers were all startled,
but did not dare to question him about his death.
They just asked:
"What are you doing here?"
He replied:
"Nothing much,
just running about here and there."
Then he asked for the name of the innkeeper.
The crowd told him everything.
Liǔ Zǐ cupped his hands and said:
"I have a small errand just now,
so I don't have time to catch up.
I will come to visit tomorrow."
He then mounted the mule and left.
When the crowd returned to their lodging,
they didn't really expect him to come immediately.
The next morning, they waited for him,
and Zǐ indeed arrived.
He tied his mule to a stable post,
then hurried in, laughing and speaking.
The crowd said:
"Your esteemed father misses you intensely every day,
why don't you go back to visit him?"
Zǐ asked in surprise:
"Who is speaking?"
The crowd replied, "Liǔ."
Zǐ's expression and demeanor both changed,
and after a long while he said:
"Since he misses me,
please go back and tell him: I will wait for him here on the seventh day of the fourth month."
After speaking,
he said goodbye and left.
The crowd returned,
and related the situation to the old man.
The old man cried greatly,
and went as scheduled,
telling the innkeeper his reasons.
The innkeeper stopped him,
saying:
"When I saw the young master earlier,
his demeanor and spirit were cold and detached,
it seems he may not have good intentions.
In my opinion,
it is probably best not to see him."
Liǔ wept but did not believe him.
The innkeeper said:
"I am not trying to stop you,
but spirits and ghosts are unpredictable,
and I fear you may encounter something bad.
If you must see him,
please hide in the chest,
wait for him to come,
observe his words and expression,
and if it is safe to see him, then come out."
Liǔ did as he was told.
Soon after, Zǐ indeed arrived,
asking:
"Has a certain Liǔ come?"
The innkeeper replied:
"No."
Zǐ angrily cursed, saying:
"Old beast!
Why didn't he come then!"
The innkeeper was surprised and said:
"Why do you curse your father?"
He replied:
"What kind of father is he to me!
Initially, I was a guest companion to him out of righteousness,
never imagining he harbored evil intentions,
hiding my blood money,
and stubbornly refusing to return it.
Now I wish to get it and be satisfied,
what father is there to speak of!"
Having spoken,
he exited the door,
saying:
"He got off easy!"
Liǔ was in the chest,
hearing everything distinctly.
Sweat flowed down to his heels,
and he dared not breathe.
The innkeeper called him,
and he came out,
returning home in a panic.
The Chronicler of the Unusual says:
"What joy is there in suddenly gaining much gold?
What is unbearable is having to repay it.
Even after squandering almost everything,
it is still not forgotten in the underworld;
how deep is the resentment and poison in people!"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the third month of the Guǐhài year,
I traveled with Gāo Jìwén to Jìxià,
and we stayed together in an inn.
Jìwén suddenly fell ill.
It so happened that Gāo Zhènměi also arrived at the prefecture with Mr. Niàn Dōng,
so we discussed medicine.
We heard Yuán Lín Gōng say that the Liáng family in Nánguō had a fox immortal,
skilled in
"the art of Cháng Sāng."
So we all went to visit them.
Madam Liáng,
a woman in her forties,
had a languid air about her, with a hint of fox-like charm.
Upon entering her dwelling,
there was a red curtain hanging in the inner room.
Peeking through the curtain,
a Guānyīn statue hung on the wall;
and two or three other scrolls depicted
riders on horses wielding spears,
with many followers.
Under the north wall was a table;
on the table was a small seat,
less than a *chǐ* high,
covered with a small brocade cushion.
It was said that when the immortal arrived,
they would sit here.
Everyone burned incense and bowed in rows.
The woman struck a chime thrice,
muttering indistinct words.
After the prayer,
she respectfully invited the guests to sit on the outer couch.
The woman stood by the curtain,
arranging her hair and resting her chin, conversing with the guests,
fully describing the immortal's spiritual deeds.
After a long time,
the day gradually dimmed.
Fearing that nightfall would make it difficult to return,
the crowd bothered her to pray again.
The woman then struck the chime and prayed once more.
She turned around and stood again,
saying:
"The immortal loves to talk at night the most,
and often cannot be met at other times.
Last night, there was a candidate for the xiùcai examination
who brought food and wine to drink with the immortal;
the immortal also brought out excellent vintage wine to entertain the guests,
and they composed poems and rejoiced.
When they dispersed,
the night watch had almost ended."
Before she finished speaking,
a faint, rapid sound was heard in the room,
like bats flying and chirping.
Just as they were listening intently,
suddenly something like a huge stone fell on the table,
with a very sharp sound.
The woman turned around and said:
"You almost scared me to death!"
Then a sighing sound was heard from the table,
like a strong young man.
The woman used a banana fan to separate the small seat.
A loud voice from the seat said:
"What good fortune!
What good fortune!"
Raising its voice, it offered a seat,
and also seemed to cup its hands in greeting.
After a moment, it asked the guests:
"What instructions do you have?"
Gāo Zhènměi, following Mr. Niàn Dōng's intention,
asked:
"Have you seen the Bodhisattva?"
It replied:
"The South Sea is a familiar path to me,
how could I not have seen her?"
Again:
"Has King Yánluó also been replaced?"
It said:
"It is the same as in the human world."
"What is King Yánluó's surname?"
It said:
"His surname is Cáo."
Then it was asked for medicine for Jìwén.
It said:
"When you return, you should offer tea and water at night.
I will obtain medicine from the Great Bodhisattva and present it to you;
what illness will not be cured?"
Everyone had their own questions,
all of which were clearly answered.
Then they took their leave and returned.
After staying the night,
Jìwén felt a little better.
I and Zhènměi packed our bags to return home,
and thus had no time to visit again.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Gāo Shǎozǎi Niàndōng Xiānshēng said:
"During the Chongzhēn period,
there was a monkey immortal,
named Jìngshān.
He manifested his spirit through an old man from Héjiān,
chatting about poetry and literature with people,
and predicting fortune and misfortune,
tirelessly and eloquently.
When delicacies and nuts were placed on the table,
he would eat and drink messily,
but he could not be seen."
At that time, Xiānshēng's grandfather was critically ill.
Someone sent a letter saying:
"Hóu Jìngshān
is a man of a hundred years,
you must meet him."
So he sent servants and horses to invite the old man.
The old man arrived, and a day passed,
but the immortal still had not come.
They burned incense and offered sacrifices to him.
Suddenly, a loud sigh of praise was heard from the roof, saying:
"What a good family!"
Everyone looked up in surprise.
Soon, the voice spoke again from under the eaves.
The old man rose and said:
"The Great Immortal has arrived!"
The group followed the old man, straightening their headwear, and went out to greet him.
They then heard sounds of bowing and saluting.
After entering the room,
he burst into laughter and talked freely.
At that time, the Shǎozǎi brothers were still students,
having just returned from the imperial examination.
The immortal said:
"The examination papers of the two sirs are also good;
but they are not thoroughly familiar with the classics,
they still need to work harder,
and the path to success will not be far."
The two sirs respectfully inquired about their grandfather's illness.
He said,
"Matters of life and death are great,
their principles are difficult to understand."
Thus, they all knew it was an ill omen.
Not long after,
the Grand Elder passed away.
Previously, there was a monkey trainer
who performed with monkeys in the village.
A monkey broke its chain and escaped,
impossible to catch,
and entered the mountains.
Decades later,
people still saw it.
Its movement was swift and fleeting,
and it would flee upon seeing people.
Later, it gradually entered the village,
stealing fruits and pastries,
but no one could see it.
One day,
it was seen by a villager,
chased into the wilderness,
shot and killed.
But the ghost of the monkey did not know of its own death,
only feeling its body light as a leaf,
traveling a hundred lǐ in a single breath.
So it went to rely on the old man from Héjiān.
It said:
"If you can serve me,
I will make you rich."
Thus, it named itself Jìngshān.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Liú Zōngyù from Yíshuǐ said: His servant, Dù Hé,
happened to be in the garden,
and saw money flowing like water,
about two or three *chǐ* deep and wide.
Dù was surprised and delighted,
scooped it up with both hands,
and then lay down on top of it.
When he got up to look,
the money was all gone;
only what he held in his hands remained.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Guō Shēng,
a man from Dōngshān in the district.
He loved to read in his youth,
but in the mountain village, he had no one to correct him,
so by the age of over twenty,
his characters and calligraphy contained many errors.
Previously,
his family was troubled by a fox,
clothes, food, and utensils
were often lost,
causing them deep distress.
One night, while he was reading,
a scroll placed on the table
was scribbled on by the fox;
even worse,
it was so messy that the lines of text were indistinguishable.
He then selected the cleaner parts and compiled them to read,
only getting sixty or seventy stanzas.
He was very angry but could do nothing.
He also accumulated over twenty essays for his window assignments,
waiting to consult famous scholars.
When he woke up in the morning,
he saw them spread out on the table,
almost completely smeared with thick ink.
He was furious.
It happened that Wáng Shēng,
who came to the mountain for a reason,
had always been on good terms with Guō,
and called on him.
Seeing the defiled books,
he asked about them.
Guō fully explained his troubles,
and also showed the damaged assignments to Wáng.
Wáng carefully examined them,
and the parts that were smeared over
seemed to have profound meaning;
he then looked at the stained scrolls again,
and they seemed redundant and could be deleted.
He exclaimed in surprise:
"The fox seems to have intent.
Not only should you not worry,
you should immediately take it as your teacher."
After several months,
he looked back at his old works,
and suddenly realized that the scribbled parts were indeed accurate.
So he revised two topics,
placed them on the table,
to observe its peculiarity.
By dawn,
they were smeared again.
After more than a year,
it stopped smearing;
instead, it sprinkled large dots of thick ink,
splattering all over the paper.
Guō found this strange,
and showed it to Wáng.
Wáng read it and said:
"The fox is truly your teacher,
these excellent pieces can now be sold!"
That year,
he indeed entered the district school.
Because of this, Guō was grateful to the fox,
and regularly set out chicken and millet
for the fox to eat and drink.
Whenever he bought famous manuscripts from bookstores,
he would not choose them himself,
but would let the fox decide.
Because of this, he ranked high in both examinations,
entering the imperial examination as a sub-candidate.
At that time, the manuscripts of Yè, Miào, and other sirs
were elegant and beautiful,
recited in every household.
Guō had a copied version,
which he cherished immensely.
Suddenly, a bowl of thick ink was overturned onto it,
staining it until almost no words remained;
then he drafted and composed new topics,
feeling satisfied with himself,
and the fox wantonly smeared them all: at this point, he gradually stopped believing in the fox.
Not long after,
Yè Gōng was arrested for his literary style,
and Guō again somewhat acknowledged the fox's foresight.
However, whenever he composed an essay,
after painstaking effort,
it would always be smeared.
He considered himself to have repeatedly excelled,
and his spirits were quite high,
so he increasingly suspected the fox of being erratic.
He then copied the previously heavily dotted and troublesome pieces to test it,
and the fox again smeared them all.
He then laughed and said:
"This is truly absurd!
How can what was right before be wrong now?"
So he no longer prepared meals for the fox,
and locked his reading materials in a chest.
In the morning, he saw the seal intact,
but upon opening it, he saw the cover of the scroll had four strokes drawn on it,
thicker than a finger;
the first chapter had five strokes,
the second chapter also had five strokes,
and after that, there were none.
From then on, the fox was completely silent.
Later, Guō received a fourth-grade once
and a fifth-grade twice,
only then realizing that the omen had been conveyed in the drawings.
The Historian of the Strange said:
"Arrogance incurs loss,
humility brings benefit,
this is the way of Heaven.
Having achieved a little fame,
he immediately thought himself correct,
clung to the leftover habits of Yè and Miào,
and was unwilling to change,
inevitably heading for utter defeat and ruin.
Such is the harm of arrogance!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Jīn Shēngsè
was from Jìnníng.
He married a woman surnamed Mù from the same village.
They had a son,
who was just one year old.
Jīn suddenly fell ill,
convinced he would die,
and told his wife:
“When I die,
you must remarry;
do not remain a widow!”
His wife, hearing this,
made sweet promises and solemn oaths,
vowing to remain faithful until death.
Jīn waved his hand and called his mother, saying:
“When I die,
please take care of Ābǎo,
but do not let her remain a widow.”
His mother wept and agreed.
Soon after, Jīn indeed died.
Mù'ǎo came to offer condolences.
After weeping,
she said to Jīn’s mother:
“Heaven has sent down sorrow and misfortune;
the son-in-law has suddenly met his fate.
My daughter is too young and weak;
what plan can be made for her?”
Amidst her grief,
Jīn’s mother heard Mù'ǎo’s words
and was overcome with indignation.
She replied with great spirit:
“She must remain a widow!”
Mù'ǎo was ashamed and left.
That night, she slept with her daughter
and privately told her:
“Everyone has a husband.
With your good looks and figure,
why would you lack a good match?
If a young woman doesn’t start a family early,
but instead glares and guards this swaddled infant,
isn’t that foolish?
If you must remain a widow,
it’s not appropriate to maintain a pleasant appearance.”
Jīn’s mother passed by
and overheard some of the conversation,
becoming even more incensed.
The next day,
she said to Mù'ǎo:
“The deceased had a dying wish;
he originally didn’t want his wife to remain a widow.
But now, since she is so impatient and cannot wait,
she must remain a widow!”
Mù'ǎo grew angry and left.
That night, the mother dreamed her son came
and tearfully advised her.
She found this unusual.
She sent someone to Mù
to arrange that after the funeral, the wife would be free to remarry.
But when she inquired with geomancers,
the direction of the tomb was unfavorable that year.
The wife, intending to show herself off to find a new husband,
did not forget to apply cosmetics
even while in mourning clothes.
At home, she still wore plain makeup;
but whenever she returned to her parents’ home,
she would be strikingly fresh and beautiful.
Her mother knew this
and was displeased;
but because her daughter-in-law was soon to be another’s wife,
she also endured it.
Thus, the wife became even more brazen.
In the village, there was a scoundrel named Dǒng Guì,
who saw her and took a liking to her.
He bribed Jīn’s neighbor’s old woman
to convey his ardent desires to the wife.
Late at night,
he would go from the old woman’s house, climb over the wall, and reach the wife’s dwelling,
where they would meet.
This continued for over ten days,
and the scandal spread everywhere;
only the mother remained unaware.
At night, the wife’s room only had one small maid,
who was the wife’s confidante.
One evening,
as the two lovers were in a passionate embrace,
they heard the coffin vibrate loudly,
sounding like firecrackers.
The maid, who was on the outer couch,
saw the deceased emerge from behind the curtain
and enter the bedroom, carrying a sword.
Shortly after, they heard the two lovers’ startled cries.
A moment later,
Dǒng ran out naked.
Not long after,
Jīn, dragging his wife by her hair, also came out.
The wife screamed loudly.
Her mother was startled awake
and saw her daughter-in-law running away naked,
just about to open the gate.
When asked, she didn’t answer.
The mother went out to chase and look,
but heard no sound,
and ultimately lost track of where she went.
She entered the wife’s room;
the lamp was still lit.
She saw men’s shoes
and called the maid;
the maid then trembling emerged,
fully recounting the strange events,
and they were both greatly astonished.
Dǒng had fled to a neighbor’s house
and huddled in a corner by the wall.
After some time,
he noticed the sounds of people gradually subsiding,
and then got up.
He was naked,
shivering terribly from the bitter cold,
and planned to borrow clothes from the old woman.
He saw a room in the courtyard
with its double doors ajar,
and so he temporarily entered.
Feeling around in the dark, he touched a woman’s foot on the bed,
realizing it was the neighbor’s daughter-in-law.
He was immediately seized by lust,
and taking advantage of her sleep,
he secretly lay with her.
The woman awoke
and asked,
“You’ve come?”
He replied,
“Yes.”
The woman did not suspect anything
and was intimate with him to the utmost.
Previously,
the neighbor’s son had gone to Běicūn
and instructed his wife to lock the door and wait for his return.
When he returned,
he heard sounds inside the room,
felt suspicious, and listened carefully;
the sounds and manner were utterly lewd.
Greatly enraged,
he grabbed a spear and entered the room.
Dǒng, terrified,
hid under the bed.
The son then killed him.
He also wanted to kill his wife;
but his wife wept and told him it was a mistake,
so he spared her.
However,
he didn’t know who was under the bed.
He called his mother to get up,
and together they lit a fire,
barely able to make out the person.
Looking at him,
he still had a faint breath;
when interrogated about where he came from,
he still confessed.
But with several stab wounds,
blood overflowed ceaselessly,
and in a short while, he was dead.
The old woman was in a panic,
and said to her son:
“You caught them in adultery and killed only him;
what will you do now?”
The son had no choice
and so then killed his wife as well.
That night,
Mù Wēng had just fallen asleep
when he heard a cacophonous noise outside his door.
He went out to peer,
and saw fire blazing on the eaves,
while the arsonist still lingered and had not left.
The elder cried out loudly,
and his household gathered.
Fortunately, the fire had just started,
so it was still easy to extinguish.
He ordered men to take up bows and crossbows,
and pursue the arsonist.
They saw a person as nimble as an ape,
who actually leaped over the wall and left.
Outside the wall was the elder's peach orchard.
The four surrounding walls of the orchard were all high and sturdy.
Several men climbed a ladder to look,
but the tracks were utterly vanished.
Only a lump could be seen faintly moving beneath the wall.
When questioned, it did not respond.
When shot, it went limp.
They opened the gate to investigate,
and found a naked woman lying there,
an arrow piercing her chest and head.
Upon closer inspection,
it was Mù Wēng's daughter, Jīn Fù.
They reported this in shock to the master.
Mù Wēng and his wife were terrified and almost fainted,
unable to comprehend the reason.
The woman's eyes were closed,
her complexion ashen,
and her breath fainter than a silk thread.
They had someone try to pull out the arrow from her head,
but it could not be removed.
They had to step on her neck and then pull it out.
The woman let out a soft groan,
blood gushed out violently,
and her breath immediately ceased.
Mù Wēng was greatly afraid,
and had no plan.
When dawn broke,
he reported the truth to Jīn Mǔ,
kneeling for a long time in mournful supplication.
However, Jīn Mǔ showed no resentment or anger,
but simply told him the reason,
and instructed him to arrange the burial himself.
Jīn Fù had an uncle, Shēng Guāng,
who angrily came to Mù Wēng's door,
and verbally denounced his past wrongs.
Mù Wēng was ashamed and disheartened,
bribing him to leave.
But they still did not know who the woman's secret lover was.
Soon after, a neighbor's son confessed to the adultery,
and after a light reprimand, was released.
However, Jīn Fù's brother, Mǎ Biāo, who was always litigious,
prepared a statement accusing his sister's murderer.
The official detained the neighbor's wife (lần ǒu);
she, in fear,
confessed everything from beginning to end.
Jīn Mǔ was also summoned.
Jīn Mǔ feigned illness,
and sent Shēng Guāng to testify on her behalf,
explaining the whole story.
Thereupon, all previous circumstances came to light,
implicating Mù Wēng and his wife, bringing them out completely.
Everything was thoroughly investigated and the facts were ascertained.
Mù Wēng, for encouraging his daughter's marriage
and being complicit in her promiscuity,
was flogged.
He was made to redeem himself,
and his family property was completely squandered.
The neighbor's wife, who facilitated the adultery,
was beaten to death.
The case was then closed.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Jīn Shì Zǐ, was he divine?
His earnest instructions to his newlywed wife,
how clear they were!
He killed no one,
yet all grievances were redressed.
Can this not be called divine?
The neighbor's wife seduced another's wife,
and in return her own wife committed adultery; Mù Wēng's wife loved her daughter,
but ultimately caused her daughter's death.
Alas!
'If you want to know the cause of future days,
look to the actions of the present,'
retribution is even swifter than in the next life!"
(Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
Péng Hǎogǔ, a scholar from Láizhōu,
was studying at a detached residence,
quite far from home.
He had not returned for the Mid-Autumn Festival,
and felt lonely and without companionship.
He thought there was no one in the village he could talk to.
Only Qiū Shēng was a famous scholar in the district,
but he had a long-standing hidden vice,
which Péng often disdained.
When the moon had risen,
his boredom intensified.
Having no other choice,
he wrote a short note to invite Qiū Shēng.
While they were drinking,
there was a knocking sound.
The study attendant went out to answer the door,
and it was a scholar
who wished to meet the master.
Péng left his seat
and respectfully greeted the guest.
After bowing to each other, they sat in a circle,
and he immediately asked about the guest's clan and residence.
The guest said:
"This humble one is from Guǎnglíng.
I share your surname,
and my courtesy name is Hǎi Qiū.
On this beautiful night,
my inn is especially bleak.
Hearing of your noble elegance,
I therefore presented myself without an introduction."
Observing the man,
he was dressed in clean, neat common clothes,
and his conversation was lively and elegant.
Péng was greatly pleased and said:
"You are of my clan!
What night is this,
to have sent such an excellent guest!?"
He immediately ordered wine to be poured,
treating him as if they were old friends.
He noticed the guest's intention
seemed to greatly disdain Qiū Shēng.
Qiū Shēng looked up and tried to engage him in conversation,
but the guest haughtily refused to respond.
Péng felt ashamed on Qiū Shēng's behalf,
and so he skillfully diverted the topic,
requesting that a folk song be sung first to accompany their drinking.
Thereupon, he looked up, cleared his throat twice,
and sang
"The Song of the Heroic Scholar of Fúfēng."
They all laughed and enjoyed themselves.
The guest said:
"I am not skilled in rhyme,
so I cannot repay your 'Yangchun' [song].
May I ask someone else to do it?"
Péng replied:
"As you instruct."
The guest asked:
"Are there any famous courtesans in Láichéng?"
Péng replied:
"No."
The guest remained silent for a long while,
then said to the study servant:
“I just summoned someone
who is outside the door.
You may guide her in.”
The servant went out,
and indeed saw a woman lingering outside the door.
He led her in;
she was about sixteen years old,
and truly looked like an immortal.
Péng Jīngjué
helped her to sit down.
She wore a willow-yellow shawl,
and her fragrance filled the room.
The guest then greeted her:
“You must have endured quite a journey of a thousand *lǐ*.”
The woman smiled and assented.
Péng was surprised by this
and began to question them.
The guest said:
“Your hometown unfortunately lacks beautiful women,
so I just summoned this one from a boat on Xīhú.”
He said to the woman:
“The ‘Bòxìngláng Qū’
you sang on the boat just now
was excellent.
Please sing it again.”
The woman sang:
“Faithless lover,
leading his horse to wash in the spring pond.
Human voices distant,
horse hooves clattering;
the river sky high,
the mountain moon small.
He turned his head and left, never to return,
white dawn breaking in the courtyard.
I do not resent frequent partings,
but I grieve over too few joyful reunions.
Where do you sleep?
Do not become a willow catkin tossed by the wind.
Even if you don’t become a marquis,
do not go to Línqióng!”
The guest took a jade flute from his stocking
and accompanied her song.
When the song ended, the flute stopped.
Péng was amazed and exclaimed,
saying:
“From Xīhú to here,
it is more than a thousand *lǐ*.
To summon her in an instant,
is this not an immortal?”
The guest said:
“How dare I speak of being an immortal?
I merely view ten thousand *lǐ* as one’s own courtyard.
Tonight, the wind and moon over Xīhú
are even more splendid than before.
One simply must go and see it.
Would you like to come along?”
Péng, keen to witness his extraordinary abilities,
agreed, saying:
“That would be wonderful.”
The guest asked:
“By boat,
or on horseback?”
Péng thought taking a boat would be more leisurely
and replied:
“I prefer a boat.”
The guest said:
“Calling a boat here is quite far;
there should be a ferryman in the Milky Way.”
Then he waved his hand towards the sky and said:
“Boat,
boat!
We wish to go to Xīhú,
we will pay generously.”
Soon after,
a colorful boat,
drifted down from the sky,
enveloped in mist and clouds.
They all boarded.
They saw a person holding a short oar;
at the end of the oar, neatly arranged long feathers,
shaped like a feather fan.
