With one wave of the feathers,
a cool breeze blew gently.
The boat gradually ascended into the clouds,
traveling south,
swift as an arrow.
After a moment,
the boat descended into the water.
They heard only the clamor of strings and pipes,
their sound loud and boisterous.
Stepping out of the boat to look,
the moon was reflected in the misty waves,
and pleasure boats formed a market.
The boatman ceased rowing,
letting it drift by itself.
Upon closer inspection,
it was indeed Xīhú.
From the back of the cabin, the guest
produced exotic dishes and fine wine,
and they happily drank together.
After a short while,
a multi-decked boat gradually approached,
moving alongside them.
Peering through the window,
they saw two or three people inside,
playing chess and laughing loudly.
The guest offered a goblet to the woman and said:
“Drink this to send you on your way.”
While the woman drank,
Péng lingered with affection,
fearing her departure,
and nudged her with his foot.
The woman cast a sidelong glance.
Péng was even more moved
and requested a future meeting.
The woman said:
“If you truly love me,
just ask for Juānniáng by name;
everyone knows her.”
The guest then handed Péng’s silk handkerchief to the woman,
saying:
“I will arrange a three-year engagement for you.”
He then stood up,
held the woman in his palm,
and said:
“Immortal,
immortal!”
Then he pulled open the adjacent window,
took the woman;
the window opening was like a plate,
and the woman lowered her body and slid through like a snake,
not feeling confined at all.
Shortly, they heard from the neighboring boat:
“Juānniáng has awoken.”
The boat then drifted away.
They saw in the distance that the boat had already docked,
and the people in the boat were dispersing.
Their mood for sightseeing immediately vanished.
Péng then spoke to the guest,
wishing to go ashore
and simply take a look around.
Even as we discussed it,
the boat had already docked itself.
Thus, I disembarked and walked,
feeling it was over a *lǐ*.
The guest arrived later,
leading a horse,
and ordered Péng to hold it.
He then left again,
saying:
"I will fetch two more horses."
After a long time, he did not return.
Pedestrians had already become scarce;
looking up, the crescent moon was turning westward,
and the sky was approaching dawn.
Qiū also did not know where to go.
Holding the horse, he was flustered,
without a master for his advance or retreat.
He shook the reins and went to where the boat had docked,
but both the people and the boat were gone.
Recalling his empty purse,
his anxiety doubled.
When it was completely bright,
he saw a small saddlebag on the horse.
He probed it
and found three or four *liǎng* of silver.
He bought food and waited in anxious suspense,
unaware that it was already noon.
He thought it would be better to visit Juānniáng for a while
to gradually inquire about Qiū's fate.
When he inquired about the name Juānniáng,
no one knew her,
and his spirits became even more desolate.
The next day, he departed.
The horse was well-trained
and fortunately not lame or inferior;
he returned after half a month.
When the three of them had boarded the boat and gone upstream,
the *zhāitóng* returned and reported:
"The master has already ascended to immortality."
The whole family wept in sorrow,
believing he would not return.
When Péng returned,
he tied the horse and entered.
His family gathered, surprised and questioning him,
and Péng then fully explained the strange event.
He then thought that if Qiū returned home alone,
Qiū's family might hear of it and question him,
so he warned his family not to spread the news.
In the course of conversation,
he mentioned how the horse came to be.
Everyone, thinking it was left by an immortal,
immediately went to the stable to examine it.
Upon arrival,
the horse had vanished,
but there was Student Qiū,
tied to the manger with a grass halter.
Extremely startled,
they called Péng out to see.
They saw Qiū hanging his head in the stable,
his face ashen and lifeless.
When asked, he did not speak,
only opening and closing his eyes.
Péng felt great pity,
untied him, and helped him onto a couch;
he seemed to have lost his soul.
They poured him hot *tuó* [a kind of beverage],
and he was gradually able to swallow it.
He revived slightly in the middle of the night,
urgently wanting to go to the latrine.
They supported him by the armpits, and he went,
dropping several pieces of horse dung.
After drinking a little more,
he was finally able to speak.
Péng sat by the couch and questioned him in detail.
Qiū said:
"After getting off the boat,
he led me to talk idly.
When we reached an open space,
he playfully patted my neck,
and I became dizzy, confused, and fell.
After lying still for a short while,
I looked at myself and was already a horse.
My mind was clear,
but I simply could not speak.
This is a great humiliation and disgrace,
which I truly cannot tell my wife and children.
I beg you not to reveal it!"
Péng agreed
and ordered a servant to ride the horse and send him home.
Péng had been unable to forget Juānniáng ever since.
Three more years passed.
His brother-in-law was appointed prefect of Yángzhōu,
so he went to visit him.
In the prefecture, there was Young Master Liáng,
who had family ties with Péng,
and he hosted a banquet and invited him to drink.
At the banquet, there were several singing girls,
all coming to pay their respects.
The Young Master asked about Juānniáng,
and a servant reported that she was ill.
The Young Master angrily said:
"That slave girl thinks too highly of herself;
tie her up with a rope and bring her here!"
When Péng heard the name Juānniáng,
he was surprised and asked who she was.
The Young Master said:
"She is this *mā*'s daughter,
the foremost beauty in Guǎnglíng.
Because she has a slight reputation,
she has become arrogant and disrespectful."
Péng suspected it was merely a coincidentally similar name;
however, he was agitated and restless,
desperate to see her.
Soon after,
Juānniáng arrived.
The Young Master, full of anger, reprimanded her.
Péng looked closely
and indeed, it was the one he had seen in mid-autumn.
He said to the Young Master:
"She is an old acquaintance of mine;
I hope you will kindly forgive her."
Juānniáng looked carefully at Péng,
also seeming startled.
The Young Master did not have time to ask further
and immediately ordered the wine to be served.
Péng asked:
"'Bóxìngláng Qǔ' [The Song of the Fickle Lover]
do you still remember it?"
Juānniáng was even more astonished,
gazing at him for a long time
before she finally played the old tune.
Listening to her voice,
it was exactly like that mid-autumn evening.
When the wine party ended,
the Young Master ordered her to attend to the guest for the night.
Péng took her hand and said:
"The three-year promise,
is it finally being fulfilled today?"
Juānniáng said:
"On that day, I followed someone to roam West Lake,
and after only a few sips of wine,
I suddenly felt as if drunk.
In a daze,
I was carried away by someone
and placed in a village.
A servant boy led me in;
there were three guests at the table,
and you were one of them.
Later, I took a boat to West Lake,
and you sent me back through the window lattice,
holding my hand affectionately.
Every time I thought about it,
I considered it a dream;
but the silk handkerchief was clearly there,
and I still treasure it, keeping it carefully stored."
Péng told her the whole story,
and they sighed together.
Juānniáng threw herself into his arms,
sobbing and saying:
"The immortal has already acted as a good matchmaker;
do not abandon me because I am a woman of the 'dusty world,'
and thus forsake this suffering soul."
Péng said:
"The promise made on the boat
has never left my mind for a single day.
If you are willing,
I will empty my purse and sell my horse;
I would not begrudge it."
The next morning,
he informed the Young Master;
he also stated that he leased from the *biéjià* [vice-prefect],
and for a thousand gold, he struck her name from the register,
took her with him to return home,
and occasionally visited a separate estate,
where she could still recognize the place where they had drunk that year.
The Historian of the Strange said:
"If a horse became a man,
it must be because someone became a horse;
if he became a horse,
it is precisely regrettable that he did not become a human.
Lions, elephants, cranes, and *péng* birds
all accept whips and goads,
how can one say this is not the benevolence and love of a divine person?
Even making a three-year promise
is also crossing the sea of suffering."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Yízhōu, the household of Assistant Minister Sòng Jūnchǔ
had always valued geomancy.
Even the women in the inner chambers could read its books
and understand its principles.
When Sòng Gōng passed away,
his two sons each established their own household
to choose a burial site for their father.
Hearing that there were masters of the Qīngwū art,
they spared no expense, traveling a thousand *lǐ*
to contend for their services.
Consequently, the geomancers for both households
numbered over a hundred.
Every day, they rode out in long cavalcades across the countryside,
entering and exiting by separate paths,
like two armies.
After more than a month,
each found a propitious burial spot (a "cow's resting place").
One said it would lead to ennoblement (becoming a *hóu*),
the other said it would lead to becoming a prime minister.
The two brothers would not yield to each other.
Out of indignation, they refused to consult together,
and instead prepared two separate burial grounds (lit. "longevity domains").
Embroidered pavilions and colorful banners
were prepared at both locations.
When the funerary carriage reached the crossroads,
each brother led his retainers to contend,
from dawn until dusk,
unable to resolve the dispute.
All the guests departed.
The pallbearers, having changed shoulders ten times,
were exhausted and could no longer lift it,
so they abandoned the coffin by the roadside.
Thus, the burial was halted.
Workmen were hired to build a hut
to shield it from wind and rain.
The elder brother built a shed nearby,
leaving servants to guard it.
The younger brother also built a shed like his elder brother.
The elder brother built again,
and the younger brother built again: after three years, a village was formed.
Many years accumulated,
and the brothers successively passed away.
Only then did the elder brother's wife (sǎo) and the younger brother's wife (dì) conspire
to forcefully overturn the previous men's "fire and water" disagreements.
They went together in a carriage to the fields
to inspect the two chosen sites.
Both declared them unsatisfactory.
So they jointly prepared gifts and聘贄 (pìnnǐ)
to invite another geomancer to select a site.
Each time a site was found,
a map would certainly be presented to the inner chambers (guītā)
for them to decide its suitability.
Several maps were brought in daily,
all of which they found fault with.
After more than ten days,
a site was finally chosen.
The elder brother's wife (sǎo) viewed the map
and joyfully said,
"This is acceptable."
She showed it to the younger brother's wife (dì).
The younger brother's wife (dì) said,
"This site will first produce a martial *xiàolián*."
Three years after the burial,
Sòng Gōng's eldest grandson indeed gained recognition as a martial candidate from the *xiāngjiàn* (local recommendation).
Yì Shǐshì remarks:
"The Qīngwū art
may indeed have some truth to it;
but to be obsessed and believe in it
is foolish.
Moreover, to contend out of indignation,
and abandon a coffin by the roadside –
if the way of filial piety and fraternal duty is not observed,
how can one hope for good fortune for one's children and grandchildren through geomancy?
As for the women in the inner chambers, such as the *wǎnrú* (gentle and refined),
they are truly elegant and worthy of being passed down."
According to the Líaozhāi Zhìyì manuscript.
Nán Sānfù,
a prominent family from Jìnyáng.
He had a villa
about ten *lǐ* from his residence,
and he would ride there once a day.
One day, he encountered rain.
There was a small village along the way,
and he saw a farmer's house
with a spacious inner courtyard.
So, he sought shelter there.
The villagers nearby naturally held Nán in high regard.
A short while later,
the host came out to invite him in,
bowing very respectfully.
He entered the house,
which was small and humble.
After the guest was seated,
the host began to take up a broom
and diligently swept the floor.
Then, he poured honey to make tea.
When told to sit,
he only then dared to do so.
When asked his name,
he said,
"My given name is Tíngzhāng,
and my surname is Dòu."
Not long after,
he brought out wine and cooked a young chicken,
serving with utmost attentiveness.
There was a young girl (jī nǚ) serving the roasted meat.
She would occasionally stop outside the door,
revealing a little of her half-body.
She was fifteen or sixteen years old,
and exquisitely beautiful.
Nán's heart was stirred.
After the rain stopped, he returned home,
his thoughts intensely focused on her.
The next day,
he prepared grain and silk to go and offer repayment,
using this as an excuse to make progress.
Thereafter, he often visited Dòu's house,
sometimes bringing dishes and wine,
and they would linger together.
The girl gradually became familiar
and no longer avoided him much,
often running ahead of him.
When he glanced at her,
she would lower her hairpins and smile.
Nán became even more infatuated,
not going more than two days without visiting.
One day,
Dòu happened to be out.
Nán sat for a long time,
and the girl came out to attend to the guest.
Nán seized her arm and pressed her.
The girl was ashamed and anxious,
and sternly refused, saying,
"Although I am poor,
I still intend to marry!
How can a noble person be so overbearing?"
At that time, Nán was a widower,
so he bowed and said,
"If I could win your affection,
I would certainly not marry anyone else."
The girl demanded an oath.
Nán swore by the heavens and the sun
to affirm their eternal promise,
and the girl then consented.
From then on,
whenever Dòu was out,
Nán would visit and they would be intimate.
The girl urged him, saying,
"A 'Sangzhong' liaison
cannot last forever.
Now that I am pregnant,
if you would be so kind as to grant me a marriage,
my parents would certainly be honored,
and there would be no disagreement.
You should make plans quickly!"
Nán agreed.
He then thought that a farmer's daughter was hardly a suitable match,
so he merely used her words to put her off.
Soon, a matchmaker came to propose a marriage with a prestigious family.
Initially, he hesitated;
but upon hearing of her beauty and wealth,
his mind was made up.
The girl, being pregnant,
urged him even more insistently.
Nán then completely stopped visiting.
Not long after,
the girl went into labor
and gave birth to a boy.
Her father angrily beat her.
The girl told him the situation,
and also said,
"Nán will marry me."
Dòu then released the girl
and sent someone to ask Nán.
Nán immediately denied it and refused to acknowledge it.
Dòu then abandoned the child
and beat the girl even more.
The girl secretly begged a neighbor woman
to tell Nán of her plight.
Nán also ignored it.
That night, the girl fled.
Seeing that the abandoned child was still alive,
she carried it and ran to Nán.
She knocked on the gate and told the gatekeeper,
"If only your master says one word,
I will not die.
Even if he doesn't care for me,
does he not care for his son?"
The gatekeeper reported everything to Nán,
who instructed him not to let her in.
The girl leaned against the gate, weeping bitterly.
At the fifth watch (five *gēng*), she was no longer heard.
At dawn, when they looked,
the girl was sitting there, stiff with the child in her arms.
Dòu Fèn
sued Nán to the authorities,
exposing all of Nán's unrighteous deeds,
intending to have Nán punished.
Nán, afraid,
bribed officials with a thousand gold pieces and was acquitted.
Nán's mother dreamt that her daughter, with disheveled hair and holding a child, came to her and said:
"You must not agree to the heartless man;
if you do,
I will surely kill him!"
Nán's mother, coveting Nán's wealth,
readily agreed to the marriage.
When the groom came to personally welcome her,
the dowry was rich and abundant,
and the new bride was also beautiful and charming.
However, she was prone to sadness;
all day long, she never showed a happy expression;
in the conjugal bed,
she would often shed tears.
When asked,
she would not speak.
After several days,
the bride's father arrived.
Upon entering the gate, he immediately shed tears.
Nán had no time to ask the reason,
and together they entered the chamber.
Seeing his daughter, he was startled and exclaimed:
"Just now in the back garden,
I saw my daughter hanged on a peach tree;
who is this in the room now?"
When the daughter heard these words,
her complexion drastically changed,
and she collapsed and died.
Upon inspection,
it was Dòu Nǚ.
They rushed to the back garden;
the new bride had indeed hanged herself there.
Extremely alarmed,
they went to inform Dòu.
Dòu went to his daughter's house;
when the coffin was opened, the corpse was gone.
His previous anger had not yet subsided,
and it intensified twofold into grief and rage,
so he sued Nán again to the authorities.
The official, deeming the situation illusory,
deliberated on the punishment but had not yet made a decision.
Nán again offered Dòu a substantial bribe,
pleading for him to drop the case;
the official also accepted his bribe and instructions,
and so the case was dismissed.
However, Nán's family fortunes gradually declined thereafter.
Moreover, with the strange events widely spread,
for several years no one dared to offer their daughter for marriage.
Nán, having no other choice,
hired the daughter of Jìnshì Cáo from over a hundred *lǐ* away.
Before the ceremony could be completed,
there was a rumor circulating among the populace
that the imperial court would select daughters from good families to fill the inner palace.
Because of this, those with daughters
all sent them back to their husbands' families.
One day,
an old woman led a sedan chair to the house,
claiming to be from the Cáo family bringing their daughter.
She helped the daughter into the room
and said to Nán:
"The selection of consorts is urgent;
in our haste, we couldn't follow proper etiquette,
but we've sent the young lady here."
Nán asked:
"Why are there no guests?"
She replied:
"There's a small dowry,
following behind."
The old woman hastily departed.
Nán found the girl to be graceful and charming,
so he joked and laughed with her.
The girl bent her neck and pulled at her sash,
her demeanor strikingly similar to Dòu Nǚ.
Nán felt a sickness in his heart,
but he dared not speak.
The girl got onto the bed,
pulled the quilt over her head, and went to sleep.
Nán took this to be the usual behavior of a new bride,
and didn't pay it much mind.
As evening approached,
the Cáo family people did not arrive,
and he began to suspect something.
He pulled back the quilt to question the girl,
but the girl was already cold and lifeless.
Shocked and bewildered, he didn't know the reason.
He dispatched a messenger to inform the Cáo family,
but the Cáo family had no knowledge of sending their daughter.
This was widely considered a strange event.
At that time, Yáo Xiàolián's daughter had recently been buried,
but the coffin was opened by robbers the next night,
and the corpse was missing.
Hearing of this strange incident,
Yáo went to Nán's place to claim her.
Indeed, it was his daughter.
Opening the quilt to look,
her four limbs were completely bare.
Yáo was enraged
and reported the matter to the authorities.
The official, seeing Nán's repeated misconduct,
detested him
and charged him with grave robbery and discovery of a corpse,
condemning him to death.
Yì Shǐ Shì says:
"To bring initial chaos and finally achieve success
is not virtuous;
how much less so to vow at the beginning and abandon at the end?
Beaten in the chamber,
he tolerated it;
weeping at the gate,
he still tolerated it: how could he be so cruel!
And the retribution he received
was even more tragic than Lǐ Shí-láng!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Liáng Yàn of Xúzhōu
suffered from a runny nose and sneezing,
which continued for a long time.
One day,
as he was lying down,
he felt an extreme itch in his nose,
quickly sat up and sneezed loudly.
Something shot out and landed on the ground,
resembling a tile dog from a rooftop,
about the size of a fingertip.
He sneezed again,
and another one fell.
Four sneezes in all produced four pieces.
They squirmed and moved,
gathering and sniffing each other.
Soon, the stronger one bit the weaker ones and ate them;
after eating one,
its body immediately grew.
In an instant, it swallowed them all,
only one remaining,
larger than a field mouse.
It stretched out its tongue all around
and licked its own mouth.
Liáng was greatly astonished,
and stepped on it,
but the creature climbed up his sock
and gradually reached his thigh.
He grabbed his clothes and shook it off,
but it stuck fast and would not come down.
In a moment it went inside his collar,
scratching at his waist and ribs.
Greatly afraid,
he quickly undressed and threw his clothes to the ground.
He felt for it,
but the creature was already pressed flat against his waist.
He tried to push it but it wouldn't move;
he pinched it and it hurt,
eventually becoming a fleshy growth;
its mouth and eyes were already closed,
like a crouching mouse.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Grand Historian Jiāng Yùxuán said:
"Beneath the Lóngduī,
digging a few feet into the earth,
there is dragon meat filling it.
Anyone can cut and take it,
but do not say the word
'dragon'.
If someone says, 'This is dragon meat,'
then a thunderbolt will strike,
hitting and killing the person."
The Grand Historian himself once ate its meat,
and it was indeed true.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Sòng Guóyīng
was from Dōngpíng.
He was appointed the magistrate of Lùchéng County through the system of teaching appointments.
He was greedy, cruel, and inhumane.
His tax collection methods were particularly harsh.
Those who died under the rod
were strewn across the courtyard.
Xú Báishān from our village happened to pass by
and, witnessing his tyranny,
remarked sarcastically:
"Is the authority of a people's parent
truly to this extent?"
Sòng, full of self-satisfaction, replied,
"Indeed!
I wouldn't dare!
Though the office is small,
in a hundred days of administration,
I have executed fifty-eight people."
Half a year later,
as he was sitting at his desk attending to matters,
he suddenly stared and stood up,
his limbs flailing wildly,
as if struggling with someone.
He muttered to himself:
"My crime deserves death,
my crime deserves death!"
He was helped back into the office
and died shortly after.
Alas!
Fortunately, the netherworld also governs the human realm;
otherwise,
with enough money to bribe one's way up,
then
the reputation for "outstanding service"
would have risen,
and where would the widespread poison end?!
The Historian of Anomalies says:
"The old district of Lù
is where people's souls are resolute,
hence their ghosts are heroic.
Now, when an official holds the seal above,
there are always one or two vulgar sycophants
who flatter and fawn over him.
When his power is flourishing,
they exhaust the remaining fat and anoint him;
they prepare splendid screens for him.
When he is about to fall,
they rally the remaining bodies
to beg for his preservation.
Whether an official is corrupt or upright,
each time he takes office,
these two things inevitably occur.
As long as the prominent figure has not left,
the ignorant masses dare not disobey.
This accumulated habit, passed down through generations,
has become established practice.
It is also a laughingstock for the ghosts of Lùchéng!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Yáng Wànshí
was a *shēngyuán* from Dàmíng.
Throughout his life, he suffered from
"Jìcháng's fear."
His wife, Yǐn Shì,
was remarkably fierce.
If he slightly displeased her,
she would whip and beat him.
Yáng's father was over sixty and a widower.
Yǐn treated him like a slave because of his age.
Yáng and his brother Wànzhèn often secretly fed their father,
not daring to let their wife know.
However, he wore ragged clothes,
and fearing ridicule,
she would not allow him to see guests.
Wànshí was forty and had no son.
He took a concubine, Wáng,
who dared not utter a single word to him day or night.
The brothers were waiting for the provincial examination in the county town.
They saw a young man,
whose appearance and attire were elegant.
They spoke with him and were pleased.
When asked his name,
he replied:
"Jièfǔ,
surname Mǎ."
From then on, their friendship grew close,
and they burned incense to become sworn brothers.
After they parted,
about half a year later,
Mǎ suddenly arrived at Yáng's house with servants.
He found Yáng's father outside the door,
basking in the sun and picking lice.
Mistaking him for a servant,
he announced his name and asked to be introduced to the master.
The old man, clad in rags, left.
Someone informed Mǎ:
"That is his father."
Mǎ was astonished,
and the Yáng brothers, with their caps on, came out to greet him.
They bowed in the hall
and then invited him to pay respects to their father.
Wànshí declined, citing a slight illness.
They sat and chatted, laughing,
unaware that evening was approaching.
Wànshí repeatedly mentioned preparing food,
but it never appeared.
The brothers took turns going in and out,
until a thin servant finally brought a pot of wine.
It was emptied in a moment.
They waited for a long time.
Wànshí frequently stood up to urge and call,
sweat steaming from his forehead and cheeks.
Soon, the thin servant brought out the food,
which was unpolished rice and poorly cooked,
far from delicious.
After eating,
Wànshí quickly departed.
Wànzhōng brought his bedding to accompany the guest to sleep.
Mǎ reproached him, saying:
"Earlier, I admired your lofty righteousness,
and thus we became sworn friends.
To leave your aged father without warmth or proper food,
even passersby would be ashamed of it!"
Wànzhōng wept, saying:
"The feelings in my heart
are ultimately difficult to express.
My family is unlucky,
unhappily encountering a fierce sister-in-law,
so the elders are weak and frail,
and are cruelly treated.
If it weren't for our bond forged in blood,
I would not dare to reveal this shame."
Mǎ was astonished and sighed for some time,
saying:
"I initially intended to leave early tomorrow morning,
but now that I've heard this strange tale,
I must witness it for myself.
Please lend me an empty room
where I can cook for myself."
Wànzhōng followed his instruction
and immediately cleaned a room for Mǎ to settle in.
Late at night, he secretly brought vegetables and rice,
only fearing his wife would know.
Mǎ understood his intention
and firmly refused them.
Moreover, he invited Yáng's father to eat and sleep with him.
He went to the city market himself
and bought cloth
to make him new robes and trousers.
The father and sons were all moved.
Wànzhōng had a son named Xǐ'ér,
who was seven years old
and slept with his grandfather at night.
Mǎ caressed him and said:
"This child's good fortune and longevity will surpass his father's,
but he will experience hardship in his youth."
When the wife heard that the old man was safe and well-fed,
she became enraged,
and immediately cursed,
saying that Mǎ Qiáng had interfered in family matters.
Initially, her harsh words were still confined to the inner chambers,
but she shamefully approached Mǎ's residence,
to show her displeasure.
The Yáng brothers paced back and forth, perspiring,
unable to stop her;
but Mǎ acted as if he heard nothing.
The concubine, Wáng,
was five months pregnant.
The wife only then learned of it
and stripped her clothes and savagely beat her.
Afterward,
she called Wànshí to kneel and receive a woman's headdress,
then brandished a whip and drove him out.
As Mǎ was outside,
he was ashamed and hesitant to approach.
She then pursued and forced him out,
and he finally left.
The wife also followed him out,
clapping her hands and stomping her feet,
while spectators filled the area.
Mǎ pointed at the wife and shouted, saying,
“Go,
go!”
The wife immediately turned and fled,
as if pursued by a ghost.
Her trousers and shoes all came off,
her feet entangled and tripped on the road;
she returned barefoot,
her face deathly pale.
After she had calmed down a little,
a maid brought her stockings and shoes.
After putting them on,
she wailed loudly.
No one in the household dared to ask what happened.
Mǎ dragged Wànshí to remove the woman's headdress.
Wànshí braced himself, holding his breath,
as if afraid it might fall off;
Mǎ Qiáng forcibly took it off him.
He was then restless whether sitting or standing,
still fearing he would be blamed for secretly removing it.
After ascertaining that the wife had finished crying,
he then dared to enter,
walking haltingly forward.
The wife did not utter a single word,
but stood up
and went into her room to sleep.
Wànshí's mind finally relaxed,
and he secretly found it strange with his brother.
Everyone in the family found it unusual,
and gathered to whisper to each other.
The wife overheard a little,
which intensified her shame and anger,
and she beat all the servants and maids.
She called for the concubine,
but the concubine's injuries were too severe for her to get up.
The wife assumed she was faking it,
approached the bed and beat her,
causing a miscarriage with a sudden gush.
Wànshí, in a place where no one could see,
wept sorrowfully to Mǎ.
Mǎ consoled him.
He called a servant to prepare a feast,
and as the watches were announced repeatedly,
he did not let Wànshí return home.
The wife, in her inner chambers,
resented her husband for not returning,
and was greatly incensed;
she heard the sound of a door being pried open,
and hastily called a maid,
only to find the room door already open.
A giant entered,
his shadow obscuring the entire room,
ferocious like a ghost.
Soon after, several more people entered,
each holding a sharp blade.
The wife was terrified and about to scream,
but the giant stabbed her in the neck with a knife, saying:
“Scream and I'll kill you!”
The wife hastily offered gold and silk to buy her life.
The giant said:
“I am an envoy from the Underworld,
I don't want money,
I only want the heart of a shrewish woman!”
The wife became even more frightened,
and prostrated herself, knocking her head on the ground.
The giant then used a sharp blade to mark her heart and counted, saying:
“For such and such a matter,
should you not be killed?”
And immediately made a mark.
All her fierce and unruly deeds
were nearly all recounted,
and the knife marks on her skin
were no less than dozens.
Then he said,
“The concubine's child
is also of your lineage,
how could you bear to beat it to death?
This matter is absolutely unforgivable!”
He then ordered several people to tie her hands behind her back
and dissect the shrewish woman's heart and intestines.
The wife kowtowed and begged for her life,
only saying that she regretted her actions.
Suddenly, the sound of the middle door opening and closing was heard,
and a voice said:
“Yáng Wànshí is coming.
Since she has repented,
let her live a little longer.”
They all dispersed in a flurry.
Soon after,
Wànshí entered,
and saw his wife naked and bound,
her chest covered with innumerable crisscrossing knife marks.
He unbound her and asked what happened,
learning the reason,
he was greatly alarmed,
and secretly suspected Mǎ.
The next day,
he recounted it to Mǎ.
Mǎ was also surprised.
From then on, the wife's domineering attitude gradually subsided,
and for several months she dared not utter a single harsh word.
Mǎ was greatly pleased
and told Wànshí:
“I will tell you the truth,
but please do not reveal it: I used a small trick to frighten her earlier.
Now that you have achieved harmony,
I will take my leave for a while.”
Then he left.
Every evening, the wife
would keep Wànshí as a companion,
welcoming him with laughter and joy.
Wànshí had never known such pleasure in his life,
and experiencing it suddenly,
he felt restless whether sitting or standing.
One night, the wife recalled the appearance of the giants,
and trembled with fear.
Wànshí, wanting to appease his wife,
subtly revealed the deception.
The wife immediately sat up,
and interrogated him relentlessly.
Wànshí realized he had misspoken,
but could not undo it,
so he told her the truth.
The wife immediately cursed him furiously.
Wànshí was terrified
and knelt for a long time under the bed.
The wife ignored him,
and wailed until the third watch.
The wife said:
“If you want my forgiveness,
you must mark your chest with a knife as many times as I was marked,
only then will this hatred be appeased.”
She then got up and grabbed a kitchen knife.
Wànshí was greatly frightened and fled,
the wife pursued him,
dogs barked and chickens scattered,
and everyone in the family woke up.
Wàn Zhōng did not know why,
but simply shielded his brother from left to right with his body.
The wife was still cursing,
when she suddenly saw the old man coming,
and seeing his robes,
her rage intensified twofold;
she immediately went to the old man
and tore at him limb by limb,
slapped his cheeks and pulled out his beard.
Wàn Zhōng saw this and was enraged,
he threw a stone at the wife,
which hit her skull,
and she stumbled and fell, dying.
Wàn Chuí said:
“If I die so that my father and brother can live,
what regret is there!”
Then he threw himself into a well,
and by the time he was rescued, he was dead.
After some time, the wife revived,
and hearing that Wàn Chuí was dead,
her anger also subsided.
After the funeral,
his sister-in-law, missing her child,
vowed not to remarry.
The wife spat and cursed at her, refusing to feed her,
and forced her to leave after a simple ceremony.
The orphaned child
was whipped and beaten morning and night.
After the family had finished eating,
he was only given cold scraps.
After half a year,
the child became emaciated,
barely clinging to life.
One day,
Mǎ 忽然 arrived.
Wànshí instructed his family
not to tell his wife.
Mǎ saw the old man still in rags,
and was greatly shocked;
he also heard that Wànzhōng had passed away,
and stamped his feet in sorrow.
The child heard Mǎ had arrived,
and immediately came to cling to him,
calling out, "Uncle Mǎ!"
Mǎ couldn't recognize him,
but after a careful look, he finally distinguished him,
and exclaimed:
"How emaciated the child has become!"
The old man then timidly and stammeringly explained the situation in full.
Mǎ indignantly said to Wànshí:
"I told you earlier that your brother was not a good person,
and indeed it was no falsehood.
You two only had this one lineage,
to kill it,
what will you do?"
Wànshí said nothing,
but merely bowed his head and wept subserviently.
They talked for several hours.
The wife already knew of it,
but dared not come out herself to drive away the guest,
but called Wànshí in,
and slapped him, telling him to break off with Mǎ.
He came out with tears in his eyes,
the slap marks clearly visible.
Mǎ angrily said:
"If you cannot be firm,
can you not at least make a decision to 'divorce'
her?
To be beaten by your father and have your brother killed,
and yet accept it calmly,
how can you be considered a man?"
Wànshí stretched and yawned,
as if his expression was moved.
Mǎ further incited him, saying:
"If she doesn't leave,
you must assert your authority and force her to leave.
Even if you kill her,
don't be afraid.
I have two or three close friends
who all hold important positions,
they will certainly do their utmost
to ensure you suffer no loss."
Wànshí assented,
and with renewed courage, walked swiftly,
rushing inside.
He happened to meet his wife,
who sharply asked:
"What are you doing?"
Wànshí was flustered and turned pale,
and kneeling on the ground, he said:
"Mǎ Shēng taught me to divorce my wife."
His wife became even more enraged,
and looked for a knife or staff.
Wànshí, terrified, backed away.
Mǎ spat at him, saying:
"You truly cannot be taught!"
Then he opened his satchel,
took out a dao guī medicine,
mixed it with water, and handed it to Wànshí to drink,
saying:
"This is the 'Husband's Rejuvenation Powder'.
The reason it is not used lightly
is that it can harm people,
but now there's no choice,
let's try it for a while."
After drinking it,
a short while later,
Wànshí felt a surge of anger filling his chest,
like a raging flame burning within him,
unbearable for an instant.
He went straight to the women's quarters,
shouting like thunder.
Before his wife could question him,
Wànshí kicked her,
and she fell several feet away with a thud.
He immediately clenched his fists,
and struck her countless times.
His wife's body was almost without a whole patch of skin,
yet she continued to shriek and curse.
Wànshí took out a sword from his waist,
and his wife cursed, saying:
"You pull out a knife,
do you dare to kill me?"
Wànshí said nothing,
but cut a piece of flesh from his thigh,
as large as a palm,
and threw it to the ground;
just as he was about to cut again,
his wife wailed and begged for mercy.
Wànshí did not listen,
and cut again.
The family members, seeing Wànshí's ferocity,
gathered together
and forcefully pulled him out.
Mǎ met them,
and taking his arm, consoled him.
Wànshí's anger had not subsided,
and he repeatedly wanted to rush back in.
Mǎ stopped him.
A short while later,
the medicine's effect gradually faded,
and he became disheartened as if he had lost something.
Mǎ instructed him, saying,
"Brother, don't lose heart.
The reassertion of male authority
depends on this one action.
The reason your wife fears you
is not a matter of a day or night,
its origin has been gradual.
It's like dying yesterday and being reborn today,
you must from now on cleanse the old and renew the new;
if you lose heart again,
then it cannot be done."
He sent Wànshí in to check on her.
His wife trembled and was terrified,
and asked her maid to help her up,
intending to crawl on her knees.
He stopped her,
and she then stopped.
He came out and told Mǎ Shēng,
and father and son congratulated each other.
Mǎ wanted to leave,
but the father and son both tried to make him stay.
Mǎ said:
"I have a journey to Dōnghǎi coming up,
so I just stopped by on my way;
we can meet again when I return."
More than a month later,
his wife recovered,
and waited upon her husband like a guest.
After a long time, feeling he was like a "Guī Lǘ" with no tricks left,
she gradually became familiar,
then subtly mocked,
then cursed;
before long,
her old ways completely returned.
The old man could not bear it,
and fled in the night,
reaching Hénán,
where he joined the ranks of Daoist priests.
Wànshí also dared not look for him.
Over a year later,
Mǎ arrived,
learned of the situation,
and angrily rebuked him.
He immediately called the child,
placed him on a donkey,
and drove straight away.
From then on, the villagers all disdained Wànshí.
When the Xúexìgōng arrived for inspection,
he was dismissed from his official position due to his poor conduct.
Another four or five years later,
he suffered a fire,
and his home and property
were all reduced to ashes;
the fire spread to his neighbors' houses.
The villagers seized him and reported him to the county,
and the fines were burdensome.
Thus, his family property gradually vanished,
until he had no dwelling.
Villages nearby warned each other
not to offer shelter to Wànshí.
The Yǐn family brothers,
angry at the wife's actions,
also firmly rejected him.
When Wànshí was utterly impoverished,
he pawned his concubine to a noble family,
and migrated south with his wife.
When they reached the Hénán border,
their money and provisions were exhausted.
His wife refused to follow him,
and nagged her husband to remarry her.
Just then, there was a widower butcher
who bought her for three hundred cash.
Wànshí, alone,
begged for food in distant villages and nearby towns.
He arrived at a grand mansion,
where the gatekeeper sternly refused him entry.
A short while later,
an official came out,
and Wànshí prostrated himself and pleaded.
The official looked at him carefully for a long time,
briefly asked his name,
and exclaimed:
"It's paternal uncle!
How have you become so poor?"
Wànshí looked closely,
recognized him as Xǐ'ér,
and couldn't help but weep aloud.
Following him inside,
he saw the main hall shining with gold and brilliant colors.
After a moment,
the father helped the boy out.
Facing each other, they choked with sobs.
Wànshí then recounted what he had endured.
Originally,
Mǎ Xié had brought Xǐ'ér here.
After a few days,
she went out to find Yáng Wēng,
so that grandfather and grandson could live together.
She also hired a teacher to educate him.
At fifteen, he entered the district school (yìxiáng),
and the following year, he passed the xiāngjiàn examination,
after which his marriage was completed.
Then Mǎ Xié bade farewell, intending to leave.
The grandfather and grandson wept, begging her to stay.
Mǎ Xié said,
"I am not human;
I am actually a fox immortal.
My Daoist companions have been waiting for me for a long time."
Then she left.
When Xiàolián spoke of this,
he couldn't help but feel a pang of sorrow,
and remembering the past when he and his concubine-aunt had suffered such cruelty,
his grief intensified.
So he used funds from carriages and horses to redeem Wáng Shì, bringing her back.
After more than a year,
she gave birth to a son,
who was then made the legitimate heir.
Yǐn served the butcher for half a year,
still as wild and ill-tempered as before.
Her husband, enraged,
pierced her thigh with a butcher knife,
threaded a coarse rope through it,
and suspended her from a beam.
He then carried out the meat and left.
Her screams were hoarse and extreme,
and only then did the neighbors realize.
They untied her and pulled out the rope;
each pull made her cry out in pain,
shaking the four neighbors.
Because of this, whenever she saw the butcher approaching,
her hair and bones would stand on end.
Later, although the wound on her leg healed,
a broken awn remained in the flesh,
making her permanently unable to walk properly;
yet she still served day and night,
not daring to slacken in the slightest.
The butcher was already tyrannical,
and whenever he returned drunk,
he would beat and curse her mercilessly.
At this point,
she finally realized that what she had done to others in the past
was just like this.
One day,
Madame Yáng and her aunt were burning incense at Pǔtuó Sì.
Farm women from nearby villages also came to pay respects.
Yǐn stood there despondently, not moving forward.
Wáng Shì deliberately asked,
"Who is that?"
A family servant came forward and reported,
"She is Zhāng Tú's wife."
Wáng Shì then told someone to bring her forward,
and she bowed to Dà Fūrén.
Wáng Shì smiled and said,
"This woman, married to a butcher,
surely doesn't lack meat to eat.
Why is she so thin and emaciated?"
Yǐn felt ashamed and resentful, and upon returning, she tried to hang herself,
but the rope was too weak, and she failed to die.
The butcher hated her even more.
After more than a year,
the butcher died.
On the road, she encountered Wànshí.
She gazed at him from afar,
then crawled on her knees,
tears flowing like ropes.
Wànshí was hindered by his servant
and did not exchange a single word with her.
He returned and told his nephew,
intending to arrange a reconciliation ("returning the pearl").
His nephew stubbornly refused.
The woman was scorned by the villagers
and had no place to go for a long time,
so she relied on groups of beggars for food.
Wànshí still occasionally visited Yǐn in the dilapidated temple.
His nephew considered this a blemish
and secretly instructed the beggars to embarrass and humiliate her,
so the visits ceased.
I do not know the full extent of this matter;
the latter part,
after several lines,
was compiled by Bì Gōngquán.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Fear of one's wife
is a common ailment under Heaven.
However, I did not expect that amidst heaven and earth
there would be a Yáng Láng: is this not a mutation?
I once wrote a continuation to the Miàoyīn Jīng,
which I respectfully append here to provoke a laugh: 'I secretly believe that the Way of Heaven produces all things,
heavily relying on the accomplishment of Earth;
a man's ambition is in the four directions,
yet he especially needs assistance from within the home.
Sharing the sweet and enduring the bitter alone,
your labor of ten months of groaning;
moving from wet to dry,
the toil of three years of frowns and smiles.
This consideration of ancestral lineage stirs thoughts,
which is why a jūnzi seeks a spouse;
gazing at the well and millstone brings forth thoughts,
which is why the ancients had the love of fish and water.
However, the banner of yin-teaching is daily established,
and thus the proper order of the masculine principle no longer exists.
Initially, disrespectful noises
might be met with great display but little retaliation;
subsequently, the respect due to a guest
receives a going out but no coming back.
It is merely due to deep affection for children
that heroes are made short of breath.
When a Yèchā sits on the bed,
even a Jīngāng must lower his brows;
when poisonous smoke rises from the bottom of the pot,
even an iron man cannot be strong-necked.
The autumn pounding-block, though handy,
does not pound clothes on a moonlit night;
Mágū's claws can scratch,
lightly trying a lotus-like face.
Receiving a little, fleeing a lot,
as if to replace Mèng Mǔ in casting the shuttle;
the wife sings, the husband follows,
turning to initiate the rites of Zhōu Pó.
Swaggering and leaping about,
stopping to watch the pedestrians filling the road;
clamoring and screeching,
scattering a flock of delicate birds.
Alas!
Crying to Heaven and Earth,
suddenly with dishevelled hair towards the silver bed.
How ugly!
Turning eyes and shaking head,
shamelessly wanting to throw a noose around a jade neck.
At this time:
there are already many shattered gallbladders underground,
and even more startled souls beyond the sky.
Běigōng Yǒu might not necessarily fail to flee,
how could Mèng Shīshě be without fear?
A general, whose spirit is like thunder and lightning,
once entering the inner courtyard,
immediately returns to the land of nothingness;
a great man, whose face is like ice and frost,
by the time he reaches the bedchamber door,
then has an unapproachable demeanor.
Is it truly the aura of cosmetics
that bestows power without authority?
Why then does a filthy body
tremble without cold?
What is still understandable: if a demoness with raised mane comes under the moon,
why not prostrate and take refuge?
What is most unjust: if a hairy-headed Piśāca comes into the human world,
they also demand fragrant flowers and offerings.
Upon hearing the roar of an angry lion,
then both nostrils reach to the sky;
upon hearing the crow of a hen,
then one prostrates completely.
Dēngtúzi, lecherous and oblivious to ugliness,
his 'Huíbōcí' are pitied and become mockery.
If one becomes the son-in-law of Fényáng,
one immediately achieves honor and glory;
there is good reason to flatter one's 'Qīngqīng';
but if one is taken into the Wàihuáng household,
one cannot escape servitude;
bowing down repeatedly, what can one seek?
Those poor wretches, feeling shameless,
let her fell trees and destroy flowers,
only seeking to endure the fierce woman;
even the Qián Shén, who can be said to be powerful,
also gets entangled and transgresses,
unable to rely on Fāng Xiōng.
Is it to bind the heart of the wanderer
only by this treacherous path?
Or to quell the spirit of the霸王 (bàwáng, hegemonic king)
by relying on this Hónggōu (deep chasm/divide)?
Yet, to die in the same grave,
to live under the same quilt,
why is it that one never teaches to chant
'white heads'?
While in the morning, clouds drift,
and in the evening, rain falls,
one always desires to monopolize Wū Shān.
How hateful is
'the clear pond water' (a song title or allusion),
idly tapping on red ivory and jade clappers;
pity your concubine's meager fate,
alone enduring the cold night watch by the water.
Cicada shells on the egret beach,
rejoicing that the black dragon is sleeping;
calf cart with protruding tail,
lamenting that the slow horse does not run.
The person sharing the bed,
after being beaten away, only then is known to be the maternal uncle;
the guest long detained before the bed,
when pulled over, has already turned into a sheep.
What is greatly needed is but a moment,
what flows poisonously is an inexhaustible store.
Buying smiles and tying silk bands (patronizing courtesans),
one creates one's own karma,
even Tài Jiǎ would deem it hard to defy;
bowing one's head and flattening one's ears,
receiving unwarranted punishment,
even Lǐ Yáng would say it's unacceptable.
Bitter winds, piercingly cold,
blow away the spring of the beautiful pavilion;
the ocean of vinegar, vast and boundless,
drowns the moon of Lán Qiáo.
Or perhaps, when a grand gathering suddenly occurs,
and good friends are seated,
a dou of wine is hidden and not served,
and moreover, from the room comes a letter to expel guests;
old friends are estranged and not befriended,
thus one extensively promotes one's own doctrine of cutting off friendships.
Even more, when goose shadows fly apart,
tears are shed in vain under the thorn bush;
when phoenix glue is sought again,
a change arises among the reed flowers.
In ancient times, when drinking at Yángchéng,
in the hall there were only brothers;
Shāngzi, blowing on a pipe,
for over seventy years had no household.
For this, the ancients
had a hidden sorrow.
Alas!
A hundred-year mandarin duck couple
ends up as a bone-attached tumor;
five liǎng of deerskin
might buy the pain of being stripped from the bed.
Even those with beards like halberds are like this;
who are those with gallbladders like dippers
who truly dare not cut off the source of disaster under the horse stall,
and who can excise the root of evil in the silkworm chamber?
The Niángzǐ Jūn unleash their tyranny,
it is difficult to cure jealousy without a method;
the rouge tigers devour all living beings,
fortunately there is a way to cross over from delusion with a bow.
Heavenly fragrance fills the night swallows,
completely clarifying the waves of the boiling cauldron;
flower rain flies in the morning,
extinguishing all fires of the sword wheel.
In the realm of ultimate bliss,
colorful wings perch in pairs;
at the tip of the long tongue,
twin green lotuses bloom.
Uprooting suffering in the land of Yōupó,
establishing a place of practice on the bank of the river of love.
Hee!
May these few chapters of palm-leaf scriptures
be sprinkled as a drop of Yángzhī Shuǐ!'"
According to the manuscript edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Zhāng Jìzì of Yùnchéng,
while lying down but not yet asleep,
suddenly saw light filling the room.
Startled, he looked,
and a ghost holding a brush stood,
resembling Kuí Xīng.
He quickly rose and bowed.
The light also quickly extinguished.
From this, he became conceited,
thinking it was a premonition of becoming Yuánkuí.
Afterwards, he was ultimately unsuccessful and accomplished nothing;
his family also declined,
his closest relatives successively died,
only one living person remained.
That Kuí Xīng,
why did it not bring good fortune but instead disaster?
According to the manuscript edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Shè Dàyǒu,
courtesy name Jūnshí,
was a native of Yángxiàn, Hànzhōng.
As a military scholar, he was attached to Zǔ Shùn's command.
Zǔ treated him generously,
and he was repeatedly promoted,
eventually becoming the Commander-in-Chief of the pseudo-Zhōu dynasty.
Later, realizing that the tide had turned,
he secretly used his troops to attack Zǔ.
Zǔ resisted, injuring his hand,
and was consequently captured.
Shè Dàyǒu then offered his submission to Governor-General Cài.
When he arrived at the capital,
he dreamt he went to the netherworld.
The King of the Underworld was angered by his injustice
and ordered demons to pour boiling water on his feet.
When he awoke,
the pain in his feet was unbearable.
Later, they swelled and festered,
and all his toes fell off.
Malaria was then added to his ailments.
He would often cry out,
"I am truly disloyal!"
Soon after, he died.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Serving a false dynasty is indeed no basis for speaking of loyalty;
however, for a distinguished commoner,
to act out of gratitude,
is something worthy of claiming for oneself as a worthy and heroic person.
This can truly serve as a warning to all ministers in the world who harbor disloyal intentions."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
In the Guǐhài year,
I stayed at Governor Bì's Chuòrán Táng.
The Governor's household had the most flourishing flowers and trees,
and in my leisure, I would often follow the Governor with my staff and shoes,
enjoying free sightseeing.
One day,
after returning from viewing the scenery,
I was extremely tired and wanted to sleep.
I untied my clothes and got into bed.
I dreamt of two maidens, gorgeously dressed,
who approached and said,
"We have something to entrust to you,
and dare to trouble your honorable presence."
I rose in surprise,
and asked,
"Who is calling for me?"
They replied,
"It is Jiàng Fēi."
I was vaguely confused as to what they meant
and quickly followed them.
Soon, I saw a palace,
reaching high into the clouds and Milky Way.
Below it were stone steps,
rising layer upon layer,
about a hundred steps or more,
before reaching the summit.
I saw a vermilion gate wide open,
and two or three other beautiful women
hurrying to announce guests.
Before long,
we arrived outside a hall,
with golden hooks and jade-green screens,
shining brightly into the eyes.
Inside, a woman descended the steps and came out,
her jade pendants clinking,
looking like a noble consort.
Just as I was thinking of bowing,
the concubine spoke first,
"I respectfully trouble you, sir;
I must first offer my thanks."
She called for attendants to lay felt on the ground,
as if about to perform a禮 (lǐ, ritual).
I was greatly alarmed and felt unworthy of such an honor,
so I began by saying,
"I am but a humble and insignificant person from the wilds,
and to receive your gracious summons
is already a great honor beyond measure.
How dare I stand as an equal and resist your courtesy,
thereby increasing my guilt
and diminishing my good fortune!"
The concubine ordered the felt removed and a banquet set,
and we faced each other across the feast.
After several rounds of wine,
I excused myself, saying,
"I get drunk easily from little drink,
and fear I might commit an impropriety.
What are your instructions?
Please alleviate my doubts."
The concubine said nothing,
but simply urged me to drink from a large cup.
I repeatedly asked for her command.
Then she said,
"I
am the Flower Spirit.
My entire family, delicate and frail,
resides here,
and has been repeatedly subjected to brutal destruction
by the maids from the Fēng family.
Now, I wish to make a last desperate stand,
and trouble you, sir, to draft a proclamation for me."
I rose in alarm and replied,
"My learning is shallow and my writing poor,
and I fear I may fail in such an important trust;
but having received your gracious command,
how dare I not exert my utmost humble effort?"
The concubine was pleased,
and immediately bestowed writing materials on the platform.
The beautiful women wiped the table and brushed the seats,
ground ink, and moistened brushes.
Another young girl with braided hair
folded paper into a guide
and placed it under my wrist.
As soon as I wrote a sentence or two,
two or three of them would crowd behind me to peek.
I was usually slow-witted,
but at this time, I felt thoughts gushing forth like a spring.
A short while later,
the draft was finished.
They eagerly took it
and presented it to Concubine Jiàng.
The concubine read it once,
and considered it quite flawless,
then sent me back.
When I woke up and recalled it,
the events were vivid.
However, more than half of the proclamation text was forgotten,
so I completed it based on my memory:
“According to Fēng’s (封氏) account: it is arrogant by nature,
and envious at heart.
It does evil with its talent,
and its jealousy is like one drunk to the bone;
it shoots people in the dark,
and its malice is like spitting sand.
In ancient times, Emperor Yú (虞帝) was charmed by its fox-like allure,
and Yīng (英) and Huáng (皇) were not enough to dispel his sorrow;
instead, he borrowed it to relieve his vexation.
King Chǔ (楚王) was deluded by its bewitchment;
worthy talents could not satisfy him,
but he could rely on it to assert his dominance.
The heroes of Pèi-shàng (沛上),
as clouds flew, thought of fierce warriors; the Son of Heaven of Mào-líng (茂陵),
as autumn grew high, yearned for beautiful women.
From then on, it grew more arrogant daily due to favoritism,
and thus acted wildly without restraint.
It roared through myriad openings,
shattering jade in the royal palace;
it surged at midnight,
stirring cold sounds in the autumn trees.
Suddenly, it goes into the mountains and forests,
borrowing the tiger’s might;
at times, amidst the Yàn-yù (灩澦) rocks,
it creates waves in the river.
Moreover,
curtain hooks frequently move,
emitting clear merchant notes from high pavilions; eaves bells suddenly clang,
breaking the lonely traveler’s serene dream.
It seeks out curtains and couches,
acting like an uninvited guest;
it pushes open doors and enters halls,
becoming a disruptive visitor.
Never having met in its life,
it simply opens doors and comes in;
if not for holding down a skirt with a hand,
it would almost snatch away the consort.
Spitting rainbow threads into the azure sky,
it dares to make a fence by the moon;
turning willow waves across the green plains,
it wrongly claims to send messages through flowers.
For those who return to the fields,
just as their journey home is complete,
it lightly blows their薜荔 (Bìlì) clothes;
for those who ascend high terraces,
just as their joy is profound,
it gently knocks off their茱萸 (Zhūyú) hats.
The reeds swirl up and down,
the lamb's horn of three autumns passes through the void;
the zither’s sound reaches the clouds,
the hundred-foot-long silken thread of mandarin ducks snaps.
Without the Empress Dowager’s summons,
it wishes to make flowers bloom quickly;
before the guests’ hat strings are cut,
it actually blows out the lamp.
Worse still, raising dust and scattering it,
it levels Lǐ Hè’s (李賀) mountain;
calling rain and summoning clouds,
it tears apart the roof of Dù Líng (杜陵).
Fēng Yí (馮夷) rises and beats the drum,
while Shào-nǚ (少女) advances and plays the sheng; as it ripples in,
all grasses bend;
as it roars and charges,
tiles threaten to fly.
Without exerting its power to turn water,
river porpoises sometimes emerge to bow;
suddenly displaying its power to obstruct the heavens,
the geese’s sky-written characters fail to form lines.
Assisting the light sails of Mǎ-dāng (馬當),
it takes credit for that;
pulling the emerald curtains of Yáo-tái (瑤台),
what does it intend?
As for the spiritual sea birds,
they still rely on Lǔ-mén (魯門) for refuge.
As long as travelers are safe,
it wishes to call Yóu Láng (尤郎) home.
In ancient times, there were worthy heroes
who rode it to travel thousands of miles;
in this world, how many noble scholars
can master it to journey?
Riding the wild clouds of Páo-móu (炮牟),
it then acts arrogantly like Yè-láng (夜郎);
relying on the perverse energy of Tān-láng (貪狼),
it wrongly considers Hébó (河伯) as revered.
All sisters suffer its destruction,
all flowers are trampled by it;
a riot of red and startled green,
endlessly fading?
Wicked willows groan,
endlessly rustling.
Rain falls in Jīn-gǔ (金谷),
scattering into cushions for guests;
dew chills Huá-lín (華林),
becoming mud-stained catkins.
Buried fragrance and interred jade,
residual makeup scatters and flies;
vermilion pavilions and carved balustrades,
scattered jade pendants fall in disarray.
Diminishing spring light day and night,
myriad specks are filled with sorrow;
searching for fading red east and west,
the fifth watch is not a mistaken regret.
The graceful girls of Jiāng-hàn (江漢),
idly step on spring gardens in their tiny shoes;
the lonely person in Wáng-lóu (王樓),
whose jeweled bridle whinnies in vain among the fragrant grass.
At this time: those who grieve for spring have a difficult sorrow to bear,
and those who seek beauty sing songs of helplessness.
Then it becomes arrogant and conceited,
issuing groundless, harsh criticisms;
crushing young shoots and shaking down leaves,
moving with ceaseless, stumbling force.
Alas, the green trees still remain,
rustling and falling by the wall;
for a long time, the vermilion has not been erected,
who pities the slender ones shedding tears?
Falling into filth and discarded by fences,
finishing their fragrant souls in a single day;
flourishing in the morning and withering in the evening,
when will they be spared from suffering?
They lament that silken skirts easily open,
their curses are heard in vain at midnight;
they sue the raging tyrant for his abuses,
but the petition has not yet reached the Heavenly Court.
They announce to their fragrant neighbors,
to learn to form an army of beautiful women;
all those of the same kind,
rise up in an army of plants and trees.
Do not say the willow is incompetent,
but only that the fence must have resolve.
Let us see the orioles and swallows,
taking revenge for the usurpation of love;
please join with butterfly friends and bee allies,
to make a common vow.
Orchid oars and cassia rudders,
can be taught to fight at Kūnmíng (昆明);
mulberry canopies and willow pushing,
used to review troops in the imperial garden.
The recluse of Dōng-lí (東籬),
also emerges from his thatched hut;
the Great Tree General,
should harbor righteous indignation.
Quash its arrogance,
to wash away a thousand years of women’s grievances;
annihilate its tyranny,
to dispel ten thousand ages of romantic sorrow!”
According to the handwritten manuscript of Liáo-zhāi Zhì-yì (聊齋誌異)
Héjiān
Jī Shēng's field had wheat piled up like a mound.
His family daily took it for firewood,
hollowing it out.
A fox lived inside,
often meeting the master.
He was an old man.
One day,
he invited the master for a drink,
bowing to escort Shēng into the den.
Shēng found it difficult,
but entered after much persuasion.
Inside, it was a beautiful and splendid house.
He sat down immediately,
and the tea and wine were fragrant and strong.
But the daylight was dim and hazy,
making it impossible to tell if it was mid-evening.
After the banquet, when he came out,
the scenery and objects had all vanished.
The old man went out every night and returned early in the morning,
and no one could trace his whereabouts.
When asked,
he would say that friends had invited him for drinks.
Shēng requested to go with him,
but the old man refused;
after he insisted,
the old man finally agreed.
He pulled Shēng's arm,
and they moved as swiftly as if riding the wind.
In the time it takes to cook millet,
they arrived at a city.
Entering a wine shop,
they saw many guests seated,
drinking together quite noisily.
The old man led Shēng upstairs.
Looking down at the drinkers,
the tables and platters of food
could be counted on one's fingers.
The old man went downstairs,
freely taking wine and fruit from the tables,
and brought them up for Shēng.
No one at the banquet ever stopped him.
After a while,
Shēng saw a man in crimson clothes with kumquats in front of him,
and he ordered the old man to take them.
The old man said:
"This is a righteous person,
you cannot approach him."
Shēng thought to himself: "The fox is associating with me,
he must think I am crooked.
From now on,
I must be upright!"
As soon as he concentrated on this thought,
his body became uncontrollable,
and he fell dizzily from the upstairs.
The drinkers were greatly alarmed,
shouting among themselves that it was an evil spirit.
Shēng looked up,
and it was not upstairs at all,
but rather on the beam.
He reported his situation to the crowd.
The crowd confirmed his story,
gave him money, and sent him away.
When asked where he was,
it was Yútái,
a thousand *lǐ* from Héjiān.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
Liáng Yǒucái,
originally from Jìn,
lived as a sojourner in Jì,
working as a small peddler.
He had no wife, children, or land.
He went with villagers to ascend Dài Mountain.
On Dài Mountain,
in the fourth month,
worshipers were numerous and bustling.
There were also *upāsikā* and monks,
leading groups of dozens or hundreds of men,
kneeling together beneath the divine seat.
They judged the duration by the incense sticks,
calling it
"kneeling incense."
Cái noticed a maiden among the crowd,
seventeen or eighteen years old and beautiful,
and was charmed by her.
He pretended to be an incense pilgrim,
and knelt near the maiden;
he also feigned weakness and fatigue in his knees,
and deliberately supported himself with his hand on the maiden's foot.
The girl turned her head as if in anger,
and moved away on her knees.
Cái also moved closer on his knees;
after a short while,
he leaned on her again.
The maiden noticed,
stood up abruptly,
did not kneel,
and left the gate.
Cái also stood up,
and also went out,
following her footsteps,
but did not know where she went.
Feeling hopeless,
he walked disconsolately.
On the way, he saw the maiden with an old woman,
who seemed to be the maiden's mother.
Cái hurried towards them.
The old woman and the maiden walked and talked.
The old woman said:
"You were able to worship Niángniang,
that's a great thing!
And you have no younger siblings,
but you received Niángniang's invisible protection,
protecting you to find a good husband.
As long as you can be filial and devoted,
he doesn't have to be a noble son or a rich lord."
Cái secretly rejoiced,
and gradually questioned the old woman.
The old woman said her surname was Yún,
and the maiden's name was Cuìxiān,
her daughter.
Their home was forty *lǐ* west of the mountain.
Cái said:
"The mountain road is rough,
Mother walks so slowly,
and young lady is so delicate,
how can you get there quickly?"
She replied:
"It's already late,
we will stay overnight at our uncle's house."
Cái said:
"Just now you spoke of a son-in-law,
not disliking poverty,
not disdaining lowliness.
I am also unmarried,
does this suit your mother's intentions?"
The old woman asked the maiden,
but the maiden did not answer.
The old woman asked repeatedly,
and the maiden said:
"He has little fortune,
and is dissolute and immoral.
His frivolous heart
is easily changeable.
Your daughter cannot be the wife of such a dissolute fellow."
When Cái heard this,
he earnestly expressed his sincerity,
and swore solemnly by the sun.
The old woman was pleased,
and finally agreed.
The maiden was unhappy,
and merely flushed.
Her mother then forced and cajoled her.
Cái was diligent,
emptied his purse,
found two sedan chairs,
and carried the old woman and the maiden.
He walked behind,
as if a servant.
When passing narrow paths,
he always told the sedan chair carriers not to jolt or sway,
showing great care.
Soon they arrived at a village house,
and he was invited to the home of the courageous (勇 *yǒng*) family.
The uncle came out (翁 *wēng*),
the aunt came out (媼 *ǎo*).
Yún's brother and his wife.
She said:
"Cái is my son-in-law.
The day is auspicious,
no need to choose another,
let's get married tonight."
The uncle was also pleased,
and offered wine, dishes, and pastries to Cái.
After this,
beautifully adorned, Cuìxiān came out,
and they cleared the bed, urging them to sleep.
The maiden said:
"I knew you were unrighteous,
but compelled by my mother's command,
I foolishly followed you.
If you are a true man,
you should not have to worry about living together."
Cái meekly assented.
The next morning,
the mother told Cái:
"You should leave first,
I will bring my daughter to follow."
Cái
returned, swept the gate and entrance.
The old woman indeed brought her daughter.
People looked inside the room,
it was empty and had nothing,
then said:
“How can you support yourself like this?
I, an old woman, will return quickly
and help you a little in your hardship.”
Then she left.
The next day,
several men and women,
each carrying food, clothing, and utensils,
filled the room.
They all left without eating,
but left one maid.
Cái
thereby became warm and well-fed, but daily led neighborhood ruffians to drink and gamble,
gradually stealing his wife's hairpins and earrings to support his gambling.
The wife advised him,
but he would not listen;
she became quite annoyed with him,
and strictly guarded her chests and boxes,
as if defending against bandits.
One day,
Cái’s gambling associates knocked on the door to visit him,
and glimpsed the wife,
and were suitably surprised.
They jokingly said to Cái:
“You are greatly rich and noble,
why do you worry about poverty?”
Cái asked why,
and they replied:
“We previously saw your wife,
she is truly an immortal.
She is truly not a suitable match for your family's status.
If sold as a concubine,
you could get a hundred [gold pieces];
if as a courtesan,
you could get a thousand.
With a thousand gold pieces in the house,
do you still lack funds for drinking and gambling?”
Cái did not speak,
but mentally agreed.
Upon returning home,
he would sigh towards his wife,
constantly saying that poverty was unbearable.
His wife ignored him,
so Cái frequently struck the table,
threw down his chopsticks,
cursed the maid,
and put on various displays.
One evening,
his wife bought wine and drank with him.
Suddenly she said:
“Husband, because of poverty,
you worry daily.
I also cannot ward off destitution,
nor share your worries,
how can I not feel ashamed?
But I have no other possessions,
only this maid.
If sold,
she could slightly aid your affairs.”
Cái shook his head and said:
“What is her worth!”
After drinking a little longer,
his wife said:
“To you, husband,
what is there that I do not comply with?
But my strength is exhausted.
To think that if I am this poor,
even if I were to die following you,
it would only be sharing this hundred years of hardship;
how could we ever rise?
It would be better to sell me to a noble family;
it would benefit both of us,
and the price might be higher than for a maid.”
Cái feigned astonishment and said:
“How could it come to this!”
The wife insisted,
her expression solemn.
Cái happily said:
“Let me reconsider.”
So, he used a eunuch,
to sell her into the pleasure quarter.
The eunuch personally went to Cái,
and seeing the wife, was greatly pleased.
Fearing he could not obtain her immediately,
he drew up a contract for eight hundred strings of cash,
and the matter was almost concluded.
The wife said:
“My mother worries about my husband’s poverty every day,
and is always troubled;
now that my mind is made up,
I will temporarily go home to visit;
and since you, husband, are separating from me,
how can you not inform my mother?”
Cái worried his mother-in-law would object.
His wife said:
“I am happy with this myself,
I guarantee there will be no issues.”
Cái agreed.
It was almost midnight
when they reached her mother’s house.
He knocked on the door,
and saw the towering houses were splendid and beautiful,
with maids and servants bustling about.
Cái had lived with his wife,
and each time he asked to visit her mother,
she would stop him;
thus, for over a year as a son-in-law,
he had never once visited his in-laws.
At this, he was greatly astonished,
and because their family was so wealthy,
he feared they would not tolerate her being sold into the pleasure quarter.
The wife led Cái up to the tower.
Her elder sister asked in surprise:
“Why have you two come?”
The wife resentfully said:
“I always said he was unrighteous,
and now it is proven true.”
Then from beneath her clothes, she took out two ingots of gold
and placed them on the table,
saying:
“Fortunately, they were not swindled away by that scoundrel,
and now I return them to mother.”
Her mother asked the reason in surprise,
and the wife said:
“He was going to sell me,
so I hid the gold where it would be useless to him.”
Then she pointed at Cái and cursed him, saying:
“You jackal-rat!
Previously, you carried burdens on your shoulder,
your face covered in dust like a ghost.
When you first approached me,
you reeked of sweaty stench,
your skin-filth almost peeling off,
your hands and feet wrinkled an inch thick,
making people disgusted all night long.
Since I came to your house,
and you sat comfortably eating,
your ghostly skin finally shed.
Mother is present,
am I slandering him?”
Cái lowered his head,
not daring to breathe a sound.
The wife again said:
“I do not consider myself to have a beauty that could overthrow cities,
nor am I fit to serve noblemen;
but for a man like him,
I considered myself still his equal.
What wrong have I done,
that he has not a single thought of marital affection?
Could I not build tall houses and buy fertile land?
But remembering your frivolous nature and beggar-like appearance,
you are certainly not a suitable partner for old age!”
As she spoke,
the maids and old women linked arms,
and quickly surrounded him.
Hearing the wife's accusations,
they all spat and cursed,
saying in unison:
“It would be better to kill him,
why bother talking so much.”
Cái was greatly frightened,
he threw himself on the ground,
only saying he knew his repentance.
The wife then said with great indignation:
“Selling one’s wife and children is already a great evil,
but it is not yet the most extreme;
how could he bear to swindle his bedmate into becoming a prostitute!”
Before she finished speaking,
the crowd glared,
and all used sharp hairpins
and scissor blades to stab his ribs and thighs.
Cái cried out sorrowfully, begging for his life.
The wife stopped them,
saying:
“You may release him for now.
Even if he has no benevolence or righteousness,
I cannot bear to see him tremble in fear.”
Then she led the group downstairs.
As soon as [Cái] sat down and listened for a moment,
all voices fell silent.
He wished to stealthily escape.
Suddenly, he looked up
and saw the Milky Way.
The east was already white,
and the wilderness was vast and indistinct;
the lamp also soon extinguished.
There were no houses at all,
and he was sitting on a sheer cliff face.
He looked down into an abyss,
immeasurably deep.
Terrified,
he feared falling.
As he shifted his body slightly,
with a thudding sound,
the rock he was on collapsed and fell.
A withered branch lay horizontally halfway down the cliff,
which caught him, preventing his fall.
He hugged the withered branch with his belly,
his hands and feet dangling without support.
Looking down, it was a boundless expanse,
he did not know how many zhang deep.
He dared not turn over,
howling in fear until his voice was hoarse.
His whole body swelled,
his eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and bodily strength all exhausted.
As the sun gradually rose,
a woodcutter first spotted him;
he soon brought a rope,
lowered it,
and brought him up onto the cliff,
where he was on the verge of death.
Cái returned to his home.
When he arrived, the door was wide open,
his home was desolate like a ruined temple,
beds, baskets, and various utensils were all gone,
only a rope bed and a broken table
were his old family possessions,
scattered yet remaining.
He lay down dejectedly.
When hungry,
he would beg for food from his neighbor once a day.
Eventually, his swelling festered into leprosy.
The villagers disdained his conduct,
all spitting upon and abandoning him.
Cái had no recourse,
so he sold his house and lived in a cave,
begging for food on the road,
carrying a knife with him.
Someone advised him to exchange the knife for food;
Cái refused,
saying:
"Living in the wilderness, it is to guard against tigers and wolves,
for self-defense."
Later, he met the person who had advised him to sell his wife on the road.
He approached him and spoke sorrowfully,
then suddenly drew his knife, slashed, and killed him,
whereupon he was arrested.
Gōng Lián understood his situation,
and could not bear to torture him severely,
so he was imprisoned,
and soon died of emaciation.
Yìshǐ Shì said:
"To obtain a distant mountain's hibiscus [like wife],
and share four walls with her,
how could one easily exchange this for the kingship of facing south!
If one is not human,
yet complains about encountering evil friends;
therefore, those who are friends must know to be wary.
Whenever narrow-minded youths are enticed into debauchery and gambling,
committing various unrighteous acts,
even if their deeds are not exposed,
though they might resent it, it is not virtuous.
By the time they have no jacket,
their wives have no trousers,
pointed at by a thousand people,
dying without illness,
the thought of poverty and ruin
constantly occupies their mind: the hatred of poverty and ruin
constantly grinds their teeth.
In the quiet night, within a straw cloak,
they toss and turn, unable to sleep.
Only then do they vividly recall the time before their downfall,
vividly recall the time of their impending downfall,
and also vividly recall the reasons for their downfall,
and from that, trace it back to the person who initiated their downfall.
At this point,
the weak rise up,
hugging their rags and cursing;
the strong endure the cold, walk naked,
light a fire and seek a knife,
sharpening it with a grating sound,
not waiting for the end of the night.
Therefore, to guide someone with goodness
is like giving olives;
to entice someone with evil
is like offering tainted meat.
The listener should certainly reflect,
but can the speaker not be afraid!"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Jìsú: Among the common people, when someone is ill,
women in the inner chambers use divine divination.
An old female shaman strikes an iron ringed, single-sided drum,
and the old woman puts on a show,
named
"Tiàoshén."
And this custom is especially prevalent in the capital.
Young wives from respectable families
sometimes perform it themselves.
Meat is placed on the table in the hall,
wine is sprinkled in a basin,
and it is even set on a small table.
Large candles are burned,
making it as bright as day.
The woman ties a short skirt,
bends one leg,
and performs the
"Shāngyáng Dance."
Two people hold her arms,
supporting her on the left and right.
The woman chatters continuously,
like singing,
and also like praying;
the words vary in number,
without rhythm but with a tune.
Several drums in the room beat chaotically like thunder,
booming into people's ears.
The woman's lips open and close,
mingling with the drum sounds,
not very clearly distinguishable.
Soon after, her head droops,
her eyes glance sideways: she stands completely reliant on others,
if unsupported, she would fall.
Then suddenly, she stretches her neck and leaps greatly,
a foot and a cubit off the ground.
The various women in the room
look on in awe and dread, saying:
"Our ancestors have come to eat!"
Then, with a puff,
they blow out the lamps,
making it pitch dark inside and out.
People hold their breath and stand in the dark,
not daring to exchange a word;
words could not even be heard,
due to the chaotic drum sounds.
After about a meal's time,
they hear the woman sharply calling the pet names of her parents-in-law, husband, and sister-in-law;
then they all light candles,
and stoop to ask about good or bad fortune.
Looking into the wine vessel, the jar, and on the table,
all are completely empty again.
They observe her expression,
noting her anger or joy.
They reverently line up to ask her questions,
and she answers like an echo.
If anyone internally criticizes her,
the spirit already knows,
and immediately points to someone, saying, "So-and-so is laughing at me,
most disrespectful,
I will strip your trousers."
The one criticized looks down,
and is clearly already naked,
and then finds her trousers on a tree outside the door.
Manchu women
especially revere this practice.
If there is a slight doubt,
