it must be resolved by it.
At times, they dress elaborately,
ride fake tigers and fake horses,
hold long weapons,
and dance on the couch,
named
"Tiàohǔshén."
The horses and tigers appear enraged,
and the medium's voice is rough and resonant.
Some say it is Guān, Zhāng, Yuántán,
not a single name.
The awesome atmosphere is grim and chilling,
especially capable of striking fear into people.
If a man peeks through the window,
he is immediately poked in the hat by a long weapon through the broken window,
and pulled inside.
The wives and sisters of the family
stand in solemn, respectful rows,
like geese,
without divergent thoughts,
without slackness in their bones.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Shā Huízi (沙回子) acquired the Iron Cloth Shirt Great Strength technique.
He would raise his finger,
and with a powerful chop,
could sever
a bull's neck;
thrusting horizontally,
he could pierce a bull's belly.
Once, at the home of young master Chóu Péngsān (仇彭三),
a wooden beam was suspended in the air.
He sent two strong servants to push it away with all their might,
then it rebounded fiercely.
Shā (沙) received the beam with his bare belly,
and with a resounding thud,
the beam flew far away.
He also demonstrated his power on a rock,
striking it with a wooden pole with great force,
causing no damage at all.
However, he feared blades.
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異))
Zhā Yīhuáng (查伊璜),
a native of Zhè (浙),
was drinking in a deserted temple during the Qīngmíng (清明) Festival.
He saw an ancient bell in front of the hall,
larger than two stone jars;
yet the earth stains and handprints on it,
were smooth as if new.
Suspecting something,
he leaned down to peer beneath it.
There was a bamboo basket holding about eight sheng (升),
but he didn't know what it contained.
He instructed several men to grasp its handles
and lift it with all their might,
but it did not budge an inch.
This astonished him further.
So he sat down to drink and waited for its owner.
Before long,
a beggar came,
carrying his collected dry provisions,
which he piled under the bell.
Then, with one hand he lifted the bell,
and with the other, he scooped the food into the basket. He repeated this four or five times
until it was all in.
After that,
he closed it again
and departed.
After a while, he returned,
reached in to take out food and ate it.
After eating, he reached in again,
as easily as opening a box.
Everyone present was astonished.
Zhā (查) asked:
"You are a strong man, why do you beg?"
He replied:
"I eat too much,
so no one will employ me."
Zhā (查), seeing his strength,
advised him to join the army.
The beggar looked dejected, worrying that he had no connections.
So Zhā (查) took him home and fed him;
he measured his food,
which was roughly five or six times that of an average person.
He gave him new clothes and shoes,
and also fifty *jīn* (金) as travel money.
Over ten years later,
Zhā Yóuzi (查猶子) was an official in Mǐn (閩).
A General Wú Liùyī (吳六一)
suddenly came to pay a call.
During their conversation,
he asked,
"What relation is Yīhuáng (伊璜) to you?"
He replied:
"He is my uncle.
How do you know the General?"
He said:
"He is my teacher.
It has been ten years since we parted,
and I remember him fondly.
Please invite him to honor me with his presence."
He replied casually.
He thought to himself: "My uncle is a renowned scholar,
how could he have a military disciple?"
When Yīhuáng (伊璜) arrived,
he told him about it.
Yīhuáng (伊璜) couldn't recall anything.
Because of the General's earnest inquiries,
he immediately ordered a servant and horse
and presented his calling card at the General's gate.
The General rushed out,
meeting him outside the main gate.
Looking at him, Zhā (查) had no recollection of him at all.
He secretly suspected the General was mistaken,
but the General bowed even more respectfully.
He ushered the guest in,
opening three or four inner doors.
Suddenly, he saw women moving about,
realizing it was a private residence.
He stopped, standing respectfully.
The General bowed to him again.
After a short while, they ascended to the main hall,
where young maids were rolling up curtains
and moving seats.
All were young women.
Once seated,
just as Zhā (查) was about to ask questions,
the General's chin moved slightly,
and a maid brought a court robe.
The General immediately rose to change clothes.
Zhā (查) didn't know why.
After the maids helped him with his sleeves and adjusted his collar,
he first ordered several people to firmly press down on Zhā's (查) seat, preventing him from moving,
then he prostrated himself as if greeting a sovereign or father.
Zhā (查) was greatly astonished,
unable to comprehend the reason.
After the bow,
the General sat down in casual clothes.
He smiled and said:
"Does sir not remember the beggar who lifted the bell?"
Only then did Zhā (查) understand.
Soon, a lavish banquet was set,
and household music played below.
When the wine was almost finished,
the maids lined up to attend.
The General entered the inner chamber,
asked for Zhā's (查) bedding to be prepared,
and then left.
Zhā (查), being drunk, woke late.
The General had already inquired about him three times outside the bedroom door.
Zhā (查) felt uneasy and wished to return home.
The General threw down the bolt and keys,
locking him in.
Zhā (查) saw that the General had no other activities during the day,
only counting maids and servants,
and examining mules, horses, clothes, and utensils.
He supervised their recording in ledgers,
warning against any discrepancies.
Zhā (查), considering it the General's household management,
did not inquire further.
One day,
holding a ledger, the General said to Zhā (查):
"That I, an unworthy person, have achieved what I have today,
is entirely due to your great benevolence.
Not one maid or one item
do I dare keep for myself.
I presume to offer half to you, sir."
Zhā (查) was astonished and refused to accept.
The General would not listen.
He brought out tens of thousands of stored coins,
and also offered half of those.
According to the ledger,
antiques and tables were displayed,
almost filling the hall, inside and out.
Zhā (查) firmly tried to stop him,
but the General ignored him.
After calling out the names of the maids and servants,
he ordered the men to pack the luggage
and the women to gather the utensils,
and also instructed them to serve Zhā (查) respectfully.
A hundred voices responded in awe.
He then personally watched the maids get into carriages,
and the stablemen lead the horses and mules.
The commotion filled the air as they all departed,
then he returned to bid Zhā (查) farewell.
Later, when Zhā (查) was implicated and arrested in a case concerning the compilation of history,
he was ultimately spared,
all thanks to the General's efforts.
The Historian of the Strange (異史氏) comments:
"To bestow generously without seeking recognition,
truly a chivalrous and magnanimous man of old!
And the General's repayment,
so generous and heroic,
is rarely seen throughout the ages.
Such a noble spirit
surely ought not to end up in the gutter.
From this, we know that the meeting of these two virtuous men
was no coincidence."
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異))
The leader of the White Lotus Society, Xú Hóngrú,
obtained a book of heterodox magic,
enabling him to command ghosts and spirits.
When he tried it out on a small scale,
the spectators were all terrified.
Those who flocked to his door were as numerous as migrating birds.
Thereupon, he secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
He then produced a mirror,
claiming it could reflect one's entire life.
He hung it in his courtyard,
and had people gaze into it themselves.
Some appeared with headcloths,
some with gauze caps,
some in embroidered robes and cí chán insignia,
their forms varied and inconsistent.
People grew even more astonished.
Consequently, the news spread far and wide,
and those who came to his door seeking a glimpse
were so many that their sweat formed streams.
Xú then declared:
"All civil and military officials seen in the mirror
are destined by the Tathāgata to be participants in the Lónghuá Assembly.
Each of you must strive diligently,
and must not shrink back."
He then faced the crowd and looked into it himself,
appearing in a royal crown and a dragon robe,
truly like a king.
The crowd looked at each other in astonishment,
and the multitude prostrated themselves in unison.
Xú then raised a banner and wielded a battle-axe,
and all joyfully followed him,
hoping to fulfill what they had seen.
Within a few months,
his followers numbered in the tens of thousands.
The area around Jī [Shān] and Fēng [Shān]
fell before him at the mere rumor of his approach.
Later, a large army advanced to suppress them.
There was a Commander Péng,
a native of Chángshān,
whose skill and bravery were unparalleled.
The rebels sent out two women with垂髮 (垂髮) to fight him.
Both women wielded twin blades,
sharp as frost;
they rode large horses,
which snorted and whinnied furiously.
Swiftly they circled and swayed,
from dawn till dusk,
they could not injure Péng,
nor could Péng gain victory.
After three such days,
Péng felt his strength and energy depleted,
and he died of asthma.
After Hóngrú was executed,
they captured the rebel followers, shackled them, and interrogated them.
Only then did they learn that the blades were wooden swords,
and the mounts were wooden stools.
To use sham soldiers and horses to kill a true general –
that is indeed extraordinary!
According to the manuscript edition of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
A certain scholar from Shùntiān,
was poor.
During a year of famine,
he followed his father to Luò[yáng].
He was dull-witted,
and at seventeen,
could not compose a complete essay.
Yet his appearance was elegant and handsome,
he was good at witty banter,
and skilled at writing letters.
Those who saw him did not know his inner emptiness.
Before long,
his parents successively passed away,
leaving him alone.
He made a living fishing in the bend of the Luò River.
At that time, in the village, the Yán family had an orphaned daughter,
a descendant of scholars.
She was intelligent from a young age.
When her father was alive,
he often taught her to read,
and she would remember it without forgetting after one reading.
At ten-something years old,
she learned to recite her father's poems.
Her father said:
"My family has a female scholar,
alas that she cannot wear an official's cap!"
He loved her dearly,
hoping to choose a noble son-in-law.
After her father died,
her mother maintained this aspiration,
but failed for three years,
and then her mother also died.
Someone advised her to marry a good scholar,
which the girl agreed to but had not yet acted upon.
Just then, a neighbor woman climbed over the wall and came,
and engaged her in conversation.
She wrapped some embroidered thread in paper with writing on it.
The girl opened it and looked,
and it was a letter from that scholar,
sent to the neighbor's son.
She read it repeatedly and liked it.
The neighbor woman, seeing her interest,
whispered:
"This is a dashing young man,
alone like you,
and of a similar age.
If you could be interested,
I'll ask him to facilitate the match."
The girl looked on with longing eyes, but said nothing.
The woman returned home,
and told her husband what she knew.
The neighbor's son was already friends with the scholar,
and when informed, the scholar was overjoyed.
He had a golden crow-shaped hairpin, a family heirloom from his mother,
and entrusted it to the neighbor to deliver.
A date was set for the wedding,
and they were very happy together.
When she saw the scholar's writings,
she laughed and said:
"Your writing and you seem like two different people.
If it's like this,
when can you achieve anything?"
Day and night, she urged the scholar to study,
strict as a teacher or friend.
At dusk,
she would first light a candle and lean over the desk, reciting aloud,
setting an example for her husband.
She would only stop
after three beats of the water clock.
After more than a year of this,
the scholar's examination essays improved considerably;
but he tried the exams twice and failed twice,
his reputation and future withered,
and he couldn't even afford meals.
He felt lonely and despondent,
and cried out in sorrow.
The girl said:
"You are no true man,
to be so defeated!
If I were to change my hairstyle and wear a cap,
I would regard official positions and honors as mere trifles!"
The scholar was already feeling dejected,
and hearing his wife's words,
he flared up in anger and said:
"You women of the inner chambers,
who have never been to the examination halls,
think of fame and wealth as something like drawing water and cooking plain porridge in the kitchen.
If a cap were placed on your head:
I fear you'd be no different from other people!"
The girl laughed and said:
"Don't be angry, my lord.
When the exam date arrives,
I request to change my attire and take your place.
If I fail as miserably as you,
I certainly won't dare to belittle the scholars of the world again."
The scholar also laughed and said:
"You yourself do not know the bitterness of the struggle;
it is truly fitting that you should try it.
But I fear exposure,
and becoming the laughingstock of the neighbors."
The girl said:
"I was just joking.
Your ancestral home in Yān has a vacant cottage,
please let me dress as a man and return with you,
pretending to be your younger brother.
You can claim to have gone out as an infant;
who could tell the difference?"
The scholar agreed.
The woman entered her room,
changed her clothes, and came out,
saying:
"See if I can pass as a man?"
The scholar looked at her,
and she was indeed a dashing young man.
The scholar was delighted,
and bid farewell to all his acquaintances in the village.
His good friends gave him some meager gifts,
he bought a lean horse,
and he and his wife returned home.
Shēng Shū's elder brother was still alive,
and seeing his two younger brothers like flawless jade,
he was very pleased,
caring for them morning and night.
He also saw them toiling diligently from dawn till late,
and his love and respect for them doubled.
He hired a young haircutting boy
to serve their needs.
After dusk,
he would always send him away.
For condolences and celebrations in the village,
the elder brother would personally go and socialize,
while the younger brothers merely drew their curtains and read.
After half a year,
few had seen their faces.
If guests requested an audience,
the elder brother would always decline on their behalf.
When they read their essays,
they were astonished and amazed.
Some would push open the door and press them,
but they would make a quick bow and then disappear.
When guests saw their elegant demeanor,
they all admired them equally.
Because of this, their reputation greatly spread,
and prominent families vied to take them as sons-in-law.
When Shū's elder brother discussed this with them,
they merely smiled broadly.
When pressed again,
they said:
"We are committed to lofty ambitions;
until we pass the imperial examinations,
we will not marry."
When the education commissioner arrived for inspection,
both brothers presented themselves.
The elder brother failed again.
The younger brother, performing as champion in the examination,
ranked fourth in Shùntiān;
the following year, he became a *jìnshì*;
he was appointed magistrate of Tóngchéng,
and was noted for his administrative skills;
soon after, he was promoted to the inspecting censor with authority over documents for Hénán Circuit,
his residence comparable to that of princes and marquises.
Due to feigning illness, he requested to retire,
and was granted permission to return to his hometown.
Guests filled his gate,
but he consistently declined to admit them.
Furthermore, from the time he was a student until he became prominent,
he never spoke of marriage,
and everyone found this strange.
After returning home,
he gradually acquired maids.
Some suspected him of illicit affairs;
but his sister-in-law observed him
and found no impropriety whatsoever.
Not long after,
the Míng dynasty collapsed,
and the world fell into great chaos.
Then he told his sister-in-law:
"To tell you the truth,
I am your younger brother's wife.
Because men are mediocre
and unable to stand on their own,
I, out of defiance, did it myself.
I was deeply afraid that it would become known,
leading the Son of Heaven to summon me for questioning,
and becoming a laughingstock across the land."
His sister-in-law did not believe it,
so he took off his shoe and showed her his foot,
and she was startled;
she looked inside the shoe
and found it filled with ragged cotton.
Thus, she allowed her biological son to assume her title,
and then she again shut her doors and lived in seclusion as a woman.
But she had never been pregnant,
so she provided funds to purchase a concubine.
She said to her son:
"Any man who achieves prominence
buys concubines to serve himself;
I have been an official for ten years,
yet I have remained alone.
What great fortune do you have
to enjoy such beauties?"
He replied:
"Thirty male companions
— I ask you to get them for yourself."
This anecdote was passed around as a joke.
At this time, his parents
had repeatedly received imperial favors.
Officials and gentry came to pay their respects,
honoring her son with the etiquette due to a Censor.
Her son was ashamed to assume his mother's official title,
and only felt comfortable identifying himself as a *zhūshēng*,
never using a carriage or parasol throughout his life.
The historian of the extraordinary says:
"That parents received titles from their daughter-in-law
can be called extraordinary.
However, how could there not be
wives of censors at any time?
But a censor who is a wife is rare indeed.
All men in the world who wear scholars' caps and call themselves husbands
should die of shame!"
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition.
Dù Wēng,
a native of Yíshuǐ.
He happened to be leaving the market,
and sat under a wall
to wait for his companions.
Feeling a little tired,
he suddenly had an old dream,
in which he saw a man holding a summons and taking him away.
He arrived at an administrative office,
which he had never seen before.
A man wearing a *wǎlóng guān*
came out from inside,
who was Zhāng Mǒu of Qīngzhōu,
an old acquaintance of his.
Seeing Dù, he exclaimed in surprise:
"Dù Dàgē, how did you get here?"
Dù said:
"I don't know what it's about,
but there's a summons."
Zhāng suspected it was a mistake
and was about to check it.
He then instructed:
"Stand here carefully,
don't go anywhere else.
Lest you get lost,
it will be hard to save you."
Then he left,
and for a long time did not come out.
Only the man holding the summons came,
admitted his mistake,
and released Dù to return.
Dù took his leave and went on his way.
On the road, he met six or seven young women,
whose appearance was charming and beautiful;
he was delighted and followed them.
He turned off the main road,
took a small path,
and after walking ten-odd steps,
he heard Zhāng shouting loudly from behind:
"Dù Dàgē,
where are you going?"
Dù was infatuated and continued on.
Suddenly, he saw each of the women enter a small cave-like dwelling,
and he recognized it in his heart as the house of the Wáng family, who sold wine.
Unconsciously, he leaned into the doorway,
took a quick look,
and immediately found himself in a pigsty,
lying with several small piglets.
He suddenly realized
that he had transformed into a pig,
and in his ears he still heard Zhāng's shouts.
Greatly frightened,
he urgently butted his head against the wall.
He heard someone say:
"The little piglet has epilepsy."
He looked back,
and had already returned to human form.
He quickly exited the door,
and Zhāng was waiting on the road.
Zhāng scolded:
"I strictly told you not to go anywhere else,
why didn't you listen?
You almost ruined everything!"
Then he took Dù's hand and escorted him to the city gate,
then left.
Dù suddenly awoke,
his body still leaning against the wall.
He went to the Wáng family and inquired,
and indeed, a pig had died by butting its head, they said.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript edition.
At the residence of Bureau Chief Jiāng in Wèinán,
there were many ghosts,
which often troubled people.
Consequently, they moved away.
A servant, Cāngtóu, was left to guard it and died.
Several replacements all died.
So, it was abandoned.
In the village, there was a scholar, Táo Shēng Wàngsān,
who was habitually unconventional,
enjoyed consorting with courtesans,
and would leave once the wine party was over.
When his friends intentionally sent courtesans to him,
he would smile and not refuse them entry;
yet, in reality, he would remain untouched throughout the night.
Once, when he stayed at Bureau Chief Jiāng's house,
a maid ran to him at night,
but the scholar resolutely refused to act improperly.
The Bureau Chief highly regarded him for this.
His family was extremely poor,
and he also suffered
"the sorrow of beating the basin" (the death of his wife).
With only a few thatched huts,
the sweltering heat was unbearable in summer.
So, he asked Bureau Chief Jiāng
to borrow the abandoned residence.
The Bureau Chief refused,
because of its ill repute.
Táo Shēng then wrote "A Sequel to the Treatise on No Ghosts" and presented it to the Bureau Chief,
adding:
"What can ghosts do!"
Given the persistence of his request,
the Bureau Chief assented.
Táo Shēng went and cleaned the main hall.
In the early evening,
he placed books inside;
when he returned after fetching other items,
the books were gone.
He found this strange.
He lay supine on the couch,
breathing quietly to await any change.
After about a meal's time,
he heard footsteps.
Glancing,
he saw two women emerge from the room,
returning the missing books to the table.
One was about twenty,
the other about seventeen or eighteen,
both exceptionally beautiful.
They hesitated and stood at the foot of the couch,
looking at each other and smiling.
Táo Shēng remained still.
The elder one raised a foot and kicked Táo Shēng's abdomen,
while the younger one covered her mouth and stifled a laugh.
Táo Shēng felt his heart stir and almost lost control,
but immediately composed himself with a solemn thought,
and utterly ignored them.
The women came closer, one stroking his beard with her left hand,
the other lightly tapping his cheek with her right,
making a small sound.
The younger one laughed even more.
Táo Shēng suddenly rose,
and shouted:
"How dare you, ghosts!"
The two women were startled, ran, and dispersed.
Táo Shēng feared being tormented during the night
and wanted to move back home,
but was ashamed that his words might not be taken seriously.
So, he lit a lamp and read.
In the darkness, ghostly shadows flickered,
but he paid them no attention.
Around midnight,
he put out the candle and went to bed.
As soon as his eyelids met,
he felt someone poking his nose with a thin object,
causing an intense itch and a big sneeze;
he only heard faint laughter in the dark.
Táo Shēng said nothing,
feigning sleep to wait for them.
Soon, he saw the younger woman picking up a thin twig with a strip of paper,
approaching with the steps of a crane and the crouch of an egret;
Táo Shēng suddenly jumped up and scolded her,
and she darted away.
After he lay down again,
they poked his ear.
He could not bear their disturbance all night.
When the rooster crowed,
there was silence,
and Táo Shēng finally fell into a deep sleep,
seeing and hearing nothing all day.
When the sun set,
they reappeared vaguely.
Táo Shēng then cooked at night,
intending to stay awake until dawn.
The elder one gradually rested her arm on the table,
watching Táo Shēng read;
then she covered his book.
Táo Shēng angrily grabbed her,
but she had already dispersed;
after a short while,
she caressed him again.
Táo Shēng pressed down his book with his hand and read.
The younger one stealthily went behind his head,
crossed her hands, and covered Táo Shēng's eyes,
then vanished,
standing far away and smiling mockingly.
Táo Shēng pointed and cursed:
"Little imp!
If I catch you, I'll kill you all!"
The women, however, were no longer afraid.
So he teased them, saying:
"I don't understand your wanton invitations in the room;
bothering me is useless."
The two women smiled slightly,
turned towards the stove,
split firewood and washed rice,
and cooked for Táo Shēng.
Táo Shēng looked at them and praised them, saying:
"For you two ladies to do this,
is it not better than being silly and mischievous?"
In a moment,
the porridge was cooked,
and they vied to place spoons, chopsticks, and earthen bowls on the table.
Táo Shēng said:
"I am grateful for your service,
how can I repay your kindness?"
The women smiled and said:
"We mixed arsenic and zhen poison into the food."
Táo Shēng said:
"I have no prior grievances with you,
why would you treat me this way?"
After he finished drinking,
they served him again,
competing to wait on him.
Táo Shēng enjoyed it
and grew accustomed to it.
As days passed and they became familiar,
they sat together and talked intimately,
and he learned their names.
The elder one said:
"I am Qiūrōng,
of the Qiáo clan;
she is the junior Xiè of the Ruǎn family."
He then carefully asked about their origins.
Junior Xiè smiled and said:
"Foolish fellow!
You don't even dare to show yourself once,
who wants you to ask about our family background,
as if for marriage?"
Táo Shēng said sternly:
"Facing such beauty,
how can I be heartless?
But the aura of the underworld
is fatal to humans.
If you do not wish to stay with me,
you may leave;
if you wish to stay with me,
then you may remain.
If I am not loved,
why would I defile two beautiful women?
If I am loved,
why would a mad scholar have to die?"
The two women looked at each other, deeply moved.
From then on, they did not torment him as much;
however, occasionally they would reach into his bosom,
or pull down his trousers to the ground,
which he no longer found strange.
One day,
he had not finished copying a book when he went out.
Upon returning, he found Xiǎo Xiè伏案頭 leaning over the desk,
wielding a brush to copy for him.
Seeing Shēng,
she threw down the brush, glaring and smiling.
He looked closely,
and although it was inferior and not proper calligraphy,
the lines were sparse yet neat.
Shēng praised her, saying:
"You are an elegant person!
If you enjoy this,
I will teach you how to do it."
He then embraced her,
holding her wrist to teach her to draw strokes.
Qiū Róng, being an outsider,
her expression suddenly changed,
as if jealous.
Xiǎo Xiè laughed, saying:
"As a child, I once learned calligraphy from my father,
but I haven't practiced for a long time,
so it feels like a dream."
Qiū Róng remained silent.
Shēng understood her feelings,
and pretended not to notice,
then embraced her and handed her a brush,
saying:
"Let me see if you can do this!"
She wrote a few characters and then got up,
saying:
"Aunt Qiū has excellent brushwork!"
Qiū Kè then became happy.
Quán then folded two pieces of paper as templates,
so they could both practice copying;
Shēng lit another lamp to read.
He secretly delighted that each had something to do,
and would not disturb each other.
When they finished copying,
they stood before the table,
listening to Shēng's monthly critique.
Qiū Róng had never understood reading,
her scribbles were unidentifiable,
and when her judgment was made,
she saw herself as inferior to Xiǎo Xiè,
and showed a look of shame.
Shēng praised and comforted her,
and her face brightened.
From then on, the two girls became Shēng's disciples,
sitting to scratch his back,
lying to massage his thighs,
not only not daring to insult him,
but competing to please him.
After a month,
Xiǎo Xiè's calligraphy was surprisingly neat and good,
and Shēng occasionally praised her.
Qiū Róng was greatly ashamed,
her makeup smudged,
tear streaks like threads.
Shēng comforted and consoled her in every possible way,
and only then did she stop.
He then taught her to read,
and she was extraordinarily intelligent,
once instructed,
she never asked again.
She read with Shēng,
often until dawn.
Xiǎo Xiè also brought her younger brother, Sān Láng,
to become Shēng's pupil.
He was fifteen or sixteen years old,
with a handsome and refined appearance.
He paid his tuition with a golden Rú Yì hook;
Shēng ordered him to study a classic with Qiū Róng.
The whole hall was filled with the sound of chanting;
Shēng set up his ghost school there.
The Bù Láng heard of it and was pleased,
giving them their salary on time.
After several months,
Qiū Róng and Sān Láng were both able to write poetry,
often exchanging verses.
Xiǎo Xiè secretly asked him not to teach Qiū Róng,
and Shēng agreed: Qiū Róng secretly asked him not to teach Xiǎo Xiè,
and Shēng also agreed.
One day,
Shēng was about to go for the examination,
the two girls tearfully bid him farewell.
Sān Láng said,
"You can avoid this trip by feigning illness; otherwise,
I fear it will not be auspicious."
Shēng considered feigning illness a disgrace,
and so he went.
Before this,
Shēng was fond of satirizing current affairs with poetry and prose,
which offended the local nobility,
They secretly bribed the Xué Shǐ,
falsely accusing him of misconduct,
and he was imprisoned.
His funds ran out,
who constantly sought to harm him.
believing he had no hope of survival.
Suddenly, a person floated in,
it was Qiū Róng,
who brought food to Shēng.
They faced each other, sobbing,
and she said:
"Sān Láng feared you would be unlucky,
and now it has indeed come true.
Sān Láng came with me,
to appeal to the provincial court."
She said a few words and left,
unseen by others.
The next day,
the Bù Yuàn came out,
Sān Láng blocked his path and pleaded his case,
and was arrested.
Qiū Kè reported this to Shēng in prison,
then turned to investigate,
but did not return for three days.
Shēng was anxious, hungry, and bored,
each day felt like a year.
Suddenly, Xiǎo Xiè arrived,
mournful to the point of collapse,
saying:
"Qiū Róng returned,
passing by the Chéng Huáng temple,
and was forcibly taken by the Black Judge of the West Corridor,
forced to become a concubine.
Qiū Róng refused,
and is now also imprisoned.
I rode a hundred Lǐ,
and am quite exhausted from the journey;
when I reached Běi Guō,
I was pricked in the sole of my foot by an old thornbush,
the pain was bone-deep,
I fear I cannot come again."
She then showed him her foot,
blood stained her beautiful slippers.
She took out three liǎng of gold,
and limped away, disappearing.
The Bù Yuàn investigated Sān Láng,
who was not related to him,
and had baseless made an accusation,
and was about to beat him with a staff,
but he fell to the ground and vanished.
They found this strange.
Upon examining his petition,
the words were moving and sorrowful.
They brought Shēng for a direct interrogation,
asking:
“Who is Sānláng?”
Shēng pretended not to know.
The Bùyuàn realized his injustice
and released him.
After returning home,
not a single person was there all evening.
When the night was late,
Xiǎo Xiè finally arrived,
looking distraught, and said:
“Sānláng was at the Bùyuàn,
seized by the Xièshén and taken to the Míngsī.
The Míngwáng, seeing Sānláng’s righteousness,
ordered him to be reborn into a wealthy and noble family.
Qiūrong has been imprisoned for a long time.
I submitted a petition to the Chénghuáng,
but it was again held back
and not allowed in.
What else can be done?”
Shēng angrily said:
“How dare that black old hag do this!
Tomorrow, I will overturn his statue,
trample it into mud,
and confront the Chénghuáng and blame him.
His subordinate officials are so tyrannical,
he must be in a drunken stupor!”
They grieved and resented together,
not noticing that the four watches were almost over.
Qiūrong suddenly arrived, floating.
The two were surprised and overjoyed,
and immediately asked her.
Qiūrong wept and said:
“I have suffered immensely for you, my lord!
The Pàn (judge) daily threatened me with knives and staffs,
but tonight he suddenly released me,
saying: ‘I have no other intention;
originally, it was out of love.
Since you are unwilling,
I certainly did not defile you.
Please inform Táo Qiūcáo
not to blame me.’”
Shēng felt a little joy upon hearing this
and wished to sleep with her,
saying:
“Today, I would willingly die for you.”
The two women sorrowfully said:
“Having received guidance earlier,
we now understand righteousness and propriety quite well.
How could we bear to kill the one we love?”
They firmly refused.
However, they bowed their heads,
their affection like that of husband and wife.
Because of the difficulties they had endured,
the two women’s jealousy completely vanished.
It so happened that a Dàoshì encountered Shēng on the road
and, looking at him, said:
“You have a ghostly aura.”
Shēng, finding his words unusual,
told him everything.
The Dàoshì said:
“This ghost is very good;
I will not let him down.”
Thereupon, he wrote two talismans and gave them to Shēng,
saying:
“Go home and give them to the two ghosts.
Let their fate decide. If you hear a woman crying outside the gate,
swallow the talisman and rush out;
the one who gets there first will live.”
Shēng bowed, accepted them,
and went home to instruct the two women.
More than a month later,
they indeed heard a woman crying.
The two women scrambled and ran out.
Xiǎo Xiè, in her haste,
forgot to swallow her talisman.
Seeing a funeral carriage pass by,
Qiūrong rushed straight out
and entered the coffin, disappearing;
Xiǎo Xiè could not enter,
wept bitterly, and returned.
Shēng went out to look
and saw that the wealthy Hǎo clan was burying their daughter.
They all saw a woman enter the coffin and leave,
and were all surprised and doubtful.
Shortly after, a sound was heard from within the coffin.
They stopped carrying it and opened it for inspection.
The girl had already completely revived.
She was temporarily lodged outside Shēng’s study,
guarded by attendants.
Suddenly, she opened her eyes and asked for Táo Shēng.
Hǎo Shì questioned her thoroughly,
and she replied:
“I am not your daughter.”
Thereupon, she told them the whole story.
Hǎo Shì did not fully believe her
and wanted to carry her home;
the girl refused,
went straight into Shēng’s study,
lay stiffly down, and would not rise.
Hǎo Shì then recognized Shēng as his son-in-law and left.
Shēng went to see her;
although her face was different,
her radiance and beauty were no less than Qiūrong’s.
He was more pleased than he had hoped
and affectionately recounted his life.
Suddenly, he heard a sobbing ghost crying,
which was Xiǎo Xiè weeping in a dark corner.
His heart was deeply pained for her,
so he immediately moved the lamp over
to comfort her sorrow,
but her sleeves were drenched
with an uncontrollable grief.
She only left near dawn.
At daybreak,
Hǎo Shì sent over toiletries and a trousseau with maids and an old woman,
and they were indeed father-in-law and son-in-law.
In the evening, when he entered the bridal chamber,
Xiǎo Xiè was crying again.
This continued for six or seven nights.
Both husband and wife were moved to pity
and could not consummate their wedding ceremony.
Shēng worried about her sorrow but had no solution.
Qiūrong said:
“The Dàoshì
is an immortal.
Go ask him again;
perhaps he will take pity and save her.”
Shēng agreed.
He traced the Dàoshì’s whereabouts
and prostrated himself, stating his case.
The Dàoshì strongly declared
that he had “no method.”
Shēng pleaded incessantly.
The Dàoshì smiled and said:
“You foolish man are so persistent.
You are fated to have this connection,
so I will exert all my abilities.”
Thereupon, he followed Shēng,
asked for a quiet room,
closed the door, and sat down,
instructing them not to disturb him.
For more than ten days,
he neither drank nor ate.
Secretly observing him,
he appeared to be meditating as if asleep.
One day in the morning,
a young woman lifted the curtain and entered,
with bright eyes and white teeth,
her radiance illuminating those present.
She smiled and said:
“Having traveled all day,
I am extremely exhausted!
Being endlessly entangled by you,
I rushed a hundred *lǐ* away
and finally found a good dwelling.
The Dàorén has already brought her along.
Once I see her,
I will hand her over.”
As dusk gathered,
Xiǎo Xiè arrived.
The woman immediately rose to greet and embrace her,
and they merged into one body,
falling to the ground, stiff.
The Dàoshì came out of the room,
bowed, and left directly.
They bowed and saw him off.
When [the student] returned,
the girl had already revived.
He helped her onto the bed,
her breathing gradually eased,
but she groaned, holding her feet, saying her toes and thighs ached painfully.
It was several days before she could get up.
Later, the student passed the imperial examination and became a successful scholar.
There was a certain Cài Zǐjīng, who was on the same examination roster as him.
Because of some business, he visited the student,
and stayed for several days.
Xiǎo Xiè returned from a neighbor's house.
Cài Zǐjīng saw her,
and quickly stepped forward, following close behind;
Xiǎo Xiè turned sideways and drew back to avoid him,
secretly angered by his frivolousness.
Cài Zǐjīng left the student and said:
"There is one thing that deeply astounds me,
may I tell you about it?"
When pressed,
he replied:
"Three years ago,
my younger sister died young.
After two nights, her body disappeared,
and I have been puzzled ever since.
Just now I saw your wife,
how remarkably similar she is!"
The student laughed and said:
"My humble wife is plain and inferior,
how could she compare to your sister?
However, since we are on the same roster,
our bond is close,
why not let me introduce my wife and children?"
Then he went inside
and had Xiǎo Xiè come out dressed in mourning clothes.
Cài Zǐjīng was greatly astonished and exclaimed:
"It is truly my sister!"
And with that, tears flowed down.
The student then fully recounted the whole story.
Cài Zǐjīng joyfully said:
"My sister is not dead!
I will return quickly
to comfort my revered parents."
So he departed.
After several days,
his entire family arrived.
Thereafter, their comings and goings were like those of Hǎo Yān.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"A peerless beauty,
it is difficult to find even one,
how could one suddenly have two!
Such an event, seen once in a thousand ages,
can only be encountered by one who does not elope with a woman.
Was the Daoist a celestial being?
How divine his art!
If such an art existed,
even an ugly ghost could be married."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain Fàn Shēng
lodged at an inn.
After eating,
he dozed off by candlelight.
Suddenly a maid came,
placed a bundle of clothes on a chair;
then a mirror case and a hairpin box,
lining them up one by one on the table,
and then left.
Presently, a young woman came out from the room.
She opened the box and the case,
and combed and smoothed her hair before the mirror;
after a while, she styled her bun,
then inserted hairpins,
lingering for a long time, admiring her reflection.
The former maid came
and brought a basin for washing.
After washing, she offered a towel,
and when done,
carried away the bathwater.
The woman untied the bundle and took out a skirt and shawl,
which were strikingly new and custom-made,
and put them on.
She buttoned her collar and adjusted the neckline,
dressing meticulously.
Fàn Shēng said nothing,
feeling suspicious and strange in his heart,
thinking she must be an eloping woman
who was dressing carefully to meet a guest.
After the woman finished dressing,
she took out a long sash
and hung it from a beam, tying it there.
He was surprised by this.
The woman calmly stood on her tiny bound feet,
and stretched her neck to receive the noose.
As soon as it touched the sash,
her eyes closed,
her eyebrows bristled,
her tongue protruded about two inches from her mouth,
and her complexion turned ghastly, like a ghost.
Greatly alarmed, Fàn Shēng rushed out,
shouting to inform the innkeeper.
When they checked, she had vanished.
The innkeeper said:
"My daughter-in-law passed away here previously,
could it be her?"
Alas,
how strange!
Even after death, she still performs this act,
what can explain this?
The Historian of the Strange says:
"To be driven to suicide by extreme injustice,
how bitter!
Yet, before, as a human, she did not know [her fate],
and afterwards, as a ghost, she is not aware [of what she does],
the most unbearable part [of the ordeal]
was when she was putting on her clothes and tying the sash.
Therefore, after death, she completely forgot everything else,
but only at this moment and in this situation,
does she still vividly perform it again,
this is what she absolutely cannot forget."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
A certain painter from Wúmén,
whose name is forgotten,
loved to paint Lǚzǔ.
He would always imagine and connect with him spiritually,
hoping for a chance encounter.
This devout wish was constantly in his thoughts,
never absent for a moment.
One day,
he saw a group of beggars drinking outside the city.
Among them, one man was dressed in ragged clothes with exposed elbows,
yet his demeanor was open and vibrant.
His heart suddenly stirred;
he suspected it was Lǚzǔ.
He looked closely,
and his conviction grew stronger.
He immediately grabbed the man's arm and said,
"You are Lǚzǔ!"
The beggar laughed loudly.
The painter insisted he was right
and prostrated himself, refusing to rise.
The beggar said,
"I am indeed Lǚzǔ.
What do you intend to do?"
The painter kowtowed,
only pleading for guidance.
The beggar said,
"That you can recognize me
shows you have a connection.
However, this is not the place to speak.
We shall meet tonight."
Before the painter could ask further,
the beggar vanished in the blink of an eye.
Astonished and awed, he returned home.
That night,
he indeed dreamt that Lǚzǔ came
and said,
"Because your intentions are focused and concentrated,
I specifically came to see you.
However, your character is greedy and parsimonious,
so you cannot become an immortal.
I will let you see someone instead."
He then made a gesture into the air,
and a beautiful woman descended through the air.
Her attire was like that of a noble consort,
her radiance and graceful bearing
illuminated the entire room.
Lǚzǔ said,
"This is Dǒng Niángniáng.
You must remember her carefully."
After a while, he asked again,
"Do you remember?"
He replied,
"I have remembered."
He then said,
"Do not forget."
Soon, the beautiful woman departed,
and Lǚzǔ also left.
He awoke, finding it extraordinary.
He immediately painted what he had seen in the dream,
portraying and preserving it,
though he ultimately did not understand its meaning.
Several years later,
he happened to travel to the capital.
It happened that Consort Dǒng had passed away,
and the emperor, mindful of her virtue,
intended to commission her portrait.
All the painters gathered,
taking verbal descriptions and forming mental images,
but none could achieve a likeness.
The painter suddenly recalled the person from his dream;
"Could this be her?"
He presented his painting.
It was circulated in the palace,
and all said it was a divine likeness.
Consequently, he was offered an official position in the Zhōngshū,
but he declined it.
He was bestowed ten thousand gold pieces.
Thus, his fame greatly increased.
Noble relatives and aristocratic families competed to offer substantial sums,
begging him to paint portraits of their ancestors.
He would paint from memory,
and none failed to be perfectly lifelike.
In a short period,
he accumulated several huge fortunes.
Zhū Gǒngkuí from Láiwú once saw this person.
According to the manuscript version of the Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Qī Ānqī from Jìnán
was usually frivolous
and enjoyed visiting prostitutes.
His wife gently admonished him,
but he did not listen.
His wife, Lín Shì,
was beautiful and virtuous.
When the Northern troops entered the territory,
she was captured.
That night, they camped on the road,
and a soldier intended to molest her.
Lín Shì feigned consent.
Just then, the soldier's sword was hanging by the bed.
She quickly drew the sword and stabbed herself to death;
the soldier picked her up and threw her into the wilderness.
The next day,
they departed.
Someone reported that Lín Shì was dead,
and Qī Ānqī, in great sorrow, went to her.
He saw that
she still had a faint breath.
He carried her home,
and her eyes gradually began to move;
she slightly frowned and moaned.
He forced open her throat
and dripped water into her with a bamboo tube,
which she could swallow.
Qī Ānqī caressed her and said,
"If by any chance you live,
those who harmed you will surely meet a violent end!"
After half a year,
Lín Shì fully recovered;
however, her head was pulled by the neck wound,
so she always looked as if she was glancing to the left.
Qī Ānqī did not consider it ugly,
loving her even more than before.
His visits to pleasure quarters
ceased entirely from then on.
Lín Shì felt her appearance was marred
and intended to procure a concubine for him,
but Qī Ānqī adamantly refused.
After several years,
Lín did not conceive,
and therefore advised Qī to take a maidservant.
Qī said,
“I have sworn an oath to have no other;
surely the gods and spirits hear it?
Even if the family line does not continue,
it is merely my fate.
If it is not meant to be severed,
how can you, my dear, be too old to bear children?”
So Lín feigned illness
and made Qī sleep alone.
She sent the maidservant Hǎitáng
to lie under his bed with a quilt.
After a long time,
she secretly asked the maidservant about his nocturnal activities.
The maidservant said there were none.
Lín did not believe her.
That night,
she instructed the maidservant not to go
and went herself to where the maidservant usually slept.
A short while later,
she heard the sound of sleep coming from the bed.
She quietly got up,
climbed onto the bed, and touched him.
Qī awoke
and asked who it was.
Lín whispered,
“It is I, Hǎitáng.”
Qī, however, refused, saying,
“I have an oath,
and dare not break it.
If it were like previous years,
would I still need you to come to me?”
Lín then got out of bed and left.
From then on, Qī slept alone.
Lín had the maidservant pretend that she had gone to him.
Qī thought that his wife had never in her life been an uninvited guest,
so he was suspicious;
he touched her neck,
and finding no mark,
knew it was the maidservant
and rebuked her again.
The maidservant retreated in shame.
At dawn,
she told Lín what had happened
and urged her to quickly marry off the maidservant.
Lín laughed and said,
“You need not be so stubborn.
If we could get one male child,
that would also be extremely fortunate.”
Qī said,
“If I break my oath,
the spirits’ retribution will follow.
How can I still hope to extend the family line?”
The next day, Lín laughed and said to Qī,
“For farmers,
whether the sprouts will flourish is unknown,
but the usual method of sowing cannot be violated.
The time for nightly plowing and weeding has arrived.”
Qī smiled, understanding her meaning.
That evening,
Lín extinguished the candle and called the maidservant,
making her lie in her own quilt.
Qī went to the bed
and playfully said,
“The tenant farmer has arrived.
I am deeply ashamed that my tools are dull
and have failed this good field.”
The maidservant said nothing.
After a while, when the act was underway,
the maidservant whispered,
“My private parts are a little swollen,
I cannot bear fierce thrusting.”
Qī understood her meaning and was gentle and solicitous.
After the act,
the maidservant pretended to get up to urinate,
and Lín replaced her.
From then on, whenever it was her time of “fallen blossoms,”
she would do this once,
but Qī never knew.
Not long after,
the maidservant’s belly swelled.
Lín often made her sit quietly,
not allowing her to serve in front of Qī.
So she said to Qī,
“I advised you to take a maidservant,
but you did not listen.
Suppose that day, when I feigned illness,
you mistakenly believed me,
and had intercourse and she became pregnant,
what would you do then?”
Qī said,
“Keep the calf and sell the mother.”
Lín then said no more.
Before long,
the maidservant gave birth to a son.
Lín secretly bought a wet nurse
and had the child raised at her mother’s home.
After four or five years,
she again gave birth to a son and a daughter.
The eldest son, named Chángshēng,
was already seven years old
and studying at his maternal grandmother’s house.
Lín would feign a visit home every half month
to go and see them.
As the maidservant grew older,
Qī often urged her to send her away.
Lín always agreed.
One day, the maidservant missed her children,
and Lín, granting her wish,
secretly prepared her hair to be put up
and sent her to her mother’s place.
She said to Qī,
“You always said I wouldn't marry off Hǎitáng;
my mother’s family has a righteous young man,
and she has been married to him.”
Several more years passed,
and the children all grew up.
On the occasion of Qī’s birthday,
Lín prepared a feast in advance
to await guests and friends.
Qī sighed and said,
“Years rush by,
and suddenly half a lifetime is gone.
Fortunately, we are both strong and healthy,
and our family does not suffer from cold or hunger.
What is lacking
is a child at our knees.”
Lín said,
“You are stubborn
and wouldn’t listen to me,
so who is there to blame?
However, to have a son,
two are not difficult,
let alone one!”
Qī brightened his face and said,
“Since you say it’s not difficult,
then bring me two sons tomorrow.”
Lín said,
“Easy!
Easy!”
Early next morning,
she ordered the carriage to her mother’s house,
dressed the children splendidly,
and brought them all back.
Entering the gate,
she made them stand in a line
and call their father to wish him a thousand years.
After bowing and rising,
they looked at each other and giggled.
Qī was astonished and did not understand.
Lín said,
“You asked for two sons,
and I’ve added a daughter.”
Then she fully recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
Qī joyfully said,
“Why didn’t you tell me sooner?”
She replied,
“If I had told you sooner,
I feared you would abandon their mother.
Now that the children are grown,
can they still be abandoned?”
Qī was deeply moved,
and could not stop his tears.
Then he welcomed the maidservant back,
and they grew old together.
In ancient times, there were virtuous women;
one like Lín
can truly be called sagacious!
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Yuè Yújiǔ of Yìdū
had a fox haunting his home.
Cloth and utensils
were often thrown to the neighbors.
He stored fine ramie,
intending to make clothes from it;
he found it bundled as before,
but upon untying it to inspect,
the edges were solid while the middle was hollow,
all having been cut away.
Such incidents
made their lives unbearable.
They cursed and reviled it.
Yuè cautioned them, saying:
"Lest the fox hears."
The fox on the beam said:
"I have already heard it."
From then on, the haunting worsened.
One day,
as the couple lay in bed, not yet risen,
the fox snatched their quilt and clothes away.
They each squatted on the bed,
lamenting and praying towards the empty air.
Suddenly, they saw a beautiful woman enter through the window,
throwing clothes onto the head of the bed.
Looking at them,
they were not particularly long or short;
the clothes were crimson red,
with a white, snowflake-patterned vest worn over them.
Yuè put on the clothes
and bowed, saying:
"If the celestial immortal intends to favor us with your presence,
please do not disturb us further.
May I request you to become our daughter?
How about that?"
The fox said:
"My age is older than yours,
how can you presumptuously elevate yourself?"
He then requested her to be his sister.
She agreed.
So he instructed his family members to all call her Hú Dàgū.
At that time, in the home of Zhāng Bāgōngzǐ in Yánzhèn,
a fox resided upstairs,
often speaking with people.
Yuè asked:
"Do you know her?"
It replied:
"She is our family's Xǐyí,
how could I not know her?"
Yuè said:
"That Xǐyí never disturbs people,
why don't you emulate her?"
The fox did not listen,
and continued to disturb them as before.
Yet it did not heavily haunt others,
but exclusively tormented his daughter-in-law: her shoes, socks, and hairpins
were often abandoned on the road;
whenever they ate,
it would bury dead mice or excrement in the rice porridge bowl.
The daughter-in-law would then throw the bowl and curse the 'smelly fox',
without ever praying for release.
Yuè prayed, saying:
"Our children all call you aunt,
how can you show no respect fitting an elder?"
The fox said:
"Tell your son to divorce that woman,
and I will be your daughter-in-law,
then we will be at peace."
The daughter-in-law cursed, saying:
"Shameless fox, do you want to contend with a human for a husband?"
At that time, the woman was sitting on a clothes chest,
and suddenly saw thick smoke emerge from beneath it,
as hot as a steamer.
Upon opening and inspecting it,
the stored clothes were all burned to ashes;
only one or two items remained,
all of which were the aunt's (Hú Dàgū's) clothing.
It also tried to make Yuè's son divorce his wife,
but the son did not agree.
After several days,
it urged him again,
but he still did not agree.
The fox angrily struck him with a stone,
cracking his forehead,
blood flowing,
nearly killing him.
Yuè was increasingly distressed by this.
Lǐ Chéngyáo of Xīshān,
skilled in talismans and sacred water,
was thus hired with money.
Lǐ wrote talismans on red silk with gold pigment,
completing them after three days.
He then tied a mirror to a stick,
holding it like a handle,
and illuminated the entire house.
He instructed a boy to follow and observe,
and to report immediately
if anything was seen.
Upon reaching one spot,
the boy said:
"Something like a dog is crouching on the wall."
Lǐ immediately made a hand gesture and wrote a talisman there.
Then, performing the Yǔ Step in the courtyard,
he chanted for a while,
and immediately all the dogs and pigs in the house came,
with ears pressed back and tails tucked,
as if listening to commands.
Lǐ waved and said:
"Go!"
And they all scattered and left in a single file.
He chanted again,
and a flock of ducks came,
and he waved them away again.
Afterwards, chickens arrived.
Lǐ pointed to one chicken
and loudly shouted at it.
The other chickens all left,
but this chicken alone remained crouched,
crossing its wings and crowing loudly,
saying:
"I dare not anymore!"
Lǐ said:
"This creature is the Zǐgū made in your home."
The family members all said they had never made one.
Lǐ said:
"Zǐgū is still here now."
Thereupon, they collectively recalled that three years ago,
they had indeed played this game,
and the strange incidents had begun from that very day.
They searched everywhere
and found a straw effigy on the stable beam.
Lǐ took it and threw it into the fire.
Then, a wine jar came out.
After three chants and three shouts,
the chicken rose and went straight away.
A voice was heard from the mouth of the jar, saying:
"Yuè Sì is truly fierce!
In a few years,
I will return."
Yuè begged to have it consigned to fire and water;
Lǐ refused
and took it away.
Some saw dozens of jars hanging on his wall,
all the ones with sealed mouths containing foxes.
It is said that he released them one by one,
to cause hauntings,
thereby earning聘金 (engagement money for services),
considering it a rare commodity.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Mǎn Shēng of Chānghuà
set up a private school in Yúháng.
One day, he casually walked through the market,
passing under a multi-story pavilion facing the street,
when suddenly a lychee shell fell onto his shoulder.
Looking up,
a young woman was leaning on the pavilion,
with a bewitching and exquisite figure,
he couldn't help but gaze at her, mesmerized.
The woman smiled
and went inside.
Upon inquiry,
he learned she was Xìhóu, the daughter of the prostitute Jǐa clan from the brothel.
Her reputation was quite high,
and he felt he couldn't afford her services.
Returning to his study, he pondered deeply,
unable to sleep all night.
The next day,
he went to present his calling card,
and they met,
conversing and laughing very happily,
making his heart even more迷 (enamored).
He used an excuse to borrow money from his colleagues,
collecting a certain amount of gold,
and took it to the woman,
their affection reaching its peak.
He then spontaneously recited a quatrain on the bed to present to her, saying:
"The greasy bronze basin in the deep night,
whispered words by the bed, fragrant with musk and orchid.
Freshly adorned with phoenix makeup tomorrow,
no more wandering clouds dreaming of King Chǔ."
Xìhóu frowned slightly and said:
"Although I am of low status,
I always wish to find a soulmate to serve.
Since you have no wife,
do you think I could manage your household?"
Mǎn Shēng was greatly pleased,
and immediately earnestly
made a firm pledge.
Xìhóu was also happy and said:
"As for composing poetry,
I consider it not difficult,
and often in private,
I wish to try writing a verse,
but I fear it may not be good,
and I would be ridiculed by those who see or hear it.
If I could accompany you,
I would be fortunate to receive your instruction."
She then asked Mǎn Shēng:
“How much family land and property do you have?”
He replied:
“Half a qǐng of poor land,
and a few rafters of a dilapidated house, that is all.”
Xìhóu said:
“After I become your wife,
we should stay together forever,
and you should no longer set up a teaching studio.
Forty mù are sufficient for self-sufficiency,
ten mù can be used to plant mulberries,
from which we can weave five bolts of silk,
more than enough to pay the taxes of the peaceful era.
With the door closed, facing each other,
you read Ānzhī,
and when you are at leisure, poetry and wine can pass the time.
What is there to value in being a marquis of a thousand households!”
The scholar replied:
“What is your approximate value, my dear?”
She said:
“Given the avarice of the old woman,
how can it ever be enough?
No more than two hundred gold pieces will suffice.
It is regrettable that I am young,
and did not know the importance of wealth,
what I earned I immediately gave to my mother,
so what I kept privately is very little.
If you can procure one hundred gold pieces,
anything beyond that is not my concern.”
The scholar said:
“My obscurity,
you know well,
how can I acquire one hundred gold pieces myself?
I have a sworn brother,
who is serving as an official in Húnán,
and has repeatedly invited me to visit.
I, your humble servant, considering the long distance,
have therefore been reluctant to go.
But now, for your sake,
I shall go to seek his help.
I reckon in three or four months,
I can return,
please kindly wait for me patiently.”
Xìhóu assented.
The scholar then abandoned his teaching hall and traveled south.
Upon arrival, the official had already been dismissed from office,
and had erroneously settled in a civilian residence,
his official coffers empty,
unable to provide a gift.
The scholar, crestfallen and unable to return,
resorted to teaching students in the town.
For three years,
he could not return.
By chance, he was instructing a student,
who then drowned himself.
The patron, grieving for his son, sued the teacher,
who was consequently arrested and imprisoned.
Fortunately, other students,
pitying their blameless teacher,
regularly sent food and provisions,
and thus he suffered no hardship.
Since the scholar left,
Xìhóu shut her door and did not receive a single guest.
Her mother interrogated her for the reason,
but could not persuade her,
and so reluctantly allowed it.
There was a wealthy merchant who admired Xìhóu's reputation,
and entrusted a matchmaker to the old woman,
determined to acquire her,
and not stinting on the price.
Xìhóu refused.
The merchant, carrying goods, went to Húnán,
and discreetly investigated the scholar's situation.
At that time, the scholar was about to be released from prison.
The merchant bribed the relevant officials with gold,
to keep him imprisoned longer.
He returned and told the old woman:
“The scholar has died of illness in prison.”
Xìhóu doubted the veracity of the news.
The old woman said:
“Regardless of whether Mǎnshēng is dead,
even if he is not,
rather than following a poor scholar and ending up wearing coarse cloth,
how is that comparable to being splendidly dressed and feasting on fine food?”
Xìhóu said:
“Although Mǎnshēng is poor,
he is of noble character;
to be with a squalid merchant
is truly not my wish.
Moreover, rumor from the road,
how can it be relied upon!”
The merchant then instructed another merchant,
to forge Mǎnshēng's dying letter and send it to Xìhóu,
to extinguish her hopes.
Upon receiving the letter, Xìhóu
mourned and wept day and night.
The old woman said:
“I gave birth to you,
nurturing you with great effort.
You have been an adult for two or three years,
what I have received in return
is very little each day.
Since you are unwilling to be registered as a courtesan,
and also unwilling to marry,
how will you make a living?”
Xìhóu, having no choice,
then married the merchant.
The merchant provided her with clothes, hairpins, and earrings,
in lavish abundance.
After more than a year,
she gave birth to a son.
Not long after,
the scholar, with the help of his students,
was exonerated and released.
Only then did he realize that the merchant had imprisoned him.
However, he recalled having no previous enmity,
and could not figure out the reason.
His students righteously helped him with travel expenses to return.
Having heard that Xìhóu had married,
he felt deeply pained,
and so, with his sorrow,
he entrusted a market woman selling beverages to convey it to Xìhóu.
Xìhóu was greatly saddened,
and then realized that all the previous incidents
were the merchant's cunning schemes.
Taking advantage of the merchant's absence,
she killed the child in her arms,
and, taking all her possessions, fled back to Mǎnshēng;
she took none of the merchant's family clothing or ornaments.
When the merchant returned,
he angrily brought the matter to the authorities.
The official, understanding her situation,
did not pursue the matter.
Alas!
How different was it from the return of Shòutínghóu to Hàn?
Yet, to kill her child and leave,
was also the act of a heartless person in the world!
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
A butcher, returning from selling meat,
found it was already dusk.
Suddenly a wolf appeared,
gazing at the meat in his basket,
seemingly salivating greatly.
It walked as he walked,
following him for several lǐ.
The butcher was afraid,
and showed it his blade,
whereupon it retreated slightly;
but as he walked away, it followed again.
The butcher had no plan.
He silently thought that what the wolf wanted was meat,
it would be better to hang it in a tree and retrieve it early.
So he took out the hook,
stood on tiptoe to hang it among the branches,
and showed an empty basket.
The wolf then stopped.
The butcher immediately went home.
At dawn, he went to retrieve the meat.
From a distance, he saw a huge object hanging in the tree,
resembling a person who had hanged themselves,
and was greatly alarmed.
Hesitantly he approached it,
and it was a dead wolf.
He looked up and carefully examined it,
and saw meat in its mouth,
and the meat hook had pierced the wolf's crotch,
like a fish swallowing bait.
At that time, wolf pelts were expensive,
worth more than ten gold pieces,
and the butcher became somewhat prosperous.
To climb a tree to catch a fish,
and the wolf suffered from it,
is truly laughable!
A butcher returning home late,
the meat in his carrying pole was all gone,
only some leftover bones remained.
On the way, two wolves
followed closely for a long distance.
The butcher was afraid,
and threw a bone to them.
One wolf got the bone and stopped,
the other wolf still followed;
he threw another bone,
the rear wolf stopped but the front wolf came again;
the bones were all gone,
but the two wolves continued to pursue him as before.
The butcher was in great distress,
fearing attack from both front and rear.
He noticed an threshing ground in the wild,
where the owner had piled firewood,
covered to form a mound.
The butcher then ran and leaned against it,
put down his carrying pole and held his knife.
The wolves dared not advance,
staring at him intently.
After a short while,
one wolf went away;
the other sat like a dog in front,
after a long time,
its eyes seemed closed,
appearing very relaxed.
The butcher suddenly leaped up,
and split the wolf's head with his knife,
and with several more strokes killed it.
Just as he was about to leave,
he turned and looked behind the firewood pile,
one wolf had burrowed into it,
intending to tunnel in to attack him from behind.
Its body was already half in,
its Rúannwěi exposed.
The butcher cut its thigh from behind,
and also killed it.
Only then did he realize the front wolf had feigned sleep,
probably to lure the enemy.
Wolves are indeed cunning!
But in an instant both were killed,
what are the tricks and deceptions of beasts,
they only add to the amusement!
One butcher was traveling at dusk,
and was pressed by a wolf.
By the roadside was a portable privy left by a night farmer,
he ran in and hid there.
The wolf clawed its way in through the covering.
The butcher quickly seized its claw,
preventing it from leaving.
But he had no means to kill it.
He only had a small knife less than an inch long,
so he cut open the skin under its claw,
and inflated it using the method of blowing up a pig.
After blowing with all his might for a while,
he felt the wolf was not moving much,
then tied it with a belt.
He went out to look,
and the wolf was swollen like an ox,
its thighs stiff and unable to bend,
its mouth open and unable to close.
So he carried it home.
If not for the butcher,
who could devise such a plan!
All three incidents originated from butchers;
thus, the cruelty of butchers
can also be applied to killing wolves.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chǔ Shāng lived in the capital's lodging house.
The house was connected to the neighboring room,
separated by a wooden partition;
the board had a knot that had fallen out,
the hole was like a teacup.
Suddenly a girl's head peered in,
her Fèngjì neatly done,
extremely beautiful;
then she extended an arm,
pure white as jade.
The crowd was alarmed by her strangeness,
wanting to seize her,
but she had already withdrawn.
A short while later,
she came again,
but her body was not visible through the partition.
They rushed to her,
but she was gone again.
One merchant held a knife and lay in wait by the wall.
Soon the head appeared,
he quickly struck,
and it fell at the touch of his hand,
blood splattered on the dust.
The crowd was startled and reported to the landlord.
The landlord was afraid, and presented her head to the authorities.
When the merchants were arrested and interrogated,
it was very absurd.
They were detained for half a year,
but no confession was obtained,
nor was there anyone who sued for a human life,
so the merchants were released,
and the girl's head was buried.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
I heard from Rén Huáilì of Jǐnán: Liú Gōngliàngcǎi
was the reincarnation of a fox.
Originally,
his great-grandfather lived in Nánshān,
and an old man came to his hut,
calling himself Hú.
When asked where he lived,
he said:
"Just in this mountain.
Few people are in the secluded spots,
only the two of us;
we can spend some mornings and evenings together,
so I came to make your acquaintance."
They then conversed,
his words and meaning were smooth and agreeable,
and he was pleased.
He prepared wine for their enjoyment,
and Hú left after the feast.
The next day he came again,
becoming even more intimate.
Liú said:
"Since you've condescended to befriend me,
our bond is already deep.
But I don't know where your family is,
how can I inquire about your well-being?"
Hú said:
"I dare not conceal it,
I am actually an old fox from the mountains.
I have a predestined connection with you,
which is why I dare to enter your household.
I certainly cannot bring you fortune,
nor dare I bring you calamity,
I hope you believe me and are not alarmed."
Liú also did not doubt,
and they became even closer.
They then discussed their ages,
Hú being the elder brother,
and they visited each other like brothers.
If there were small matters of fortune or misfortune,
he would also inform him.
At that time, Liú lacked an heir,
and the old man suddenly said:
"Sir, do not worry,
I shall be your successor."
Liú was surprised by his strange words.
Hú said:
"My allotted lifespan is over,
the time for my reincarnation has come.
Rather than going elsewhere,
why not be born into the family of an old friend?"
Liú said:
"Your immortal life is ten thousand years,
how can it come to this?"
The old man shook his head and said,
"That is not something you would know."
Then he left.
That night, Liú indeed dreamt that the old man came,
saying:
"I have arrived now."
When he awoke,
his wife had given birth to a son,
who was Liú Gōng.
When Gōng grew up,
he was short,
his speech was quick and harmonious,
exactly like Hú.
From a young age, he had a reputation for talent, and Wáng Chénchéng was a jìnshì.
He was chivalrous,
and eager to help those in need,
because of this, guests from Qín, Chǔ, Yàn, and Zhào
thronged his gate;
vendors selling wine and cakes
formed a market in front of his door.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Mǎ Èrhùn,
lived inside the east gate of Qīngzhōu,
and made a living selling flour.
His family was poor,
he had no wife,
and he and his mother shared a life of hardship.
One day,
while his mother was alone,
a beautiful woman suddenly arrived.
She appeared to be sixteen or seventeen,
dressed in plain cloth, very unadorned,
yet her radiance shone upon people.
The mother was startled and looked at her, then questioned her closely.
The woman smiled and said:
"Because of your worthy son's sincerity and devotion,
I wish to entrust myself to your family."
The old woman was even more astonished and said:
"Young lady, you are a celestial being.
If you say such a thing,
it will shorten the lives of my son and me by several years!"
The woman insisted.
The mother thought she must be a runaway from a noble household,
and refused even more strongly.
The woman then left.
Three days later,
she came again,
lingering and refusing to leave.
When asked her surname and given name,
she said:
"If Mother is willing to accept me,
then I will tell;
otherwise,
there's no need to ask."
The old woman said:
"We are humble and lowly laborers;
to have a wife like this
would be unfitting and inauspicious."
The woman smiled and sat on the edge of the bed,
very affectionately.
The mother politely dismissed her,
saying:
"Young lady, you should leave quickly,
lest you bring harm upon us."
The woman then went out the door,
and the old woman peeked to see her go west.
After a few more days,
Old Woman Lǚ from the west alley came
and said to the mother:
"Your neighbor's daughter, Dǒng Huìfāng,
is an orphan and has no one to rely on.
She wishes to be your worthy son's wife.
Why did you not accept her?"
The mother fully explained her suspicions and worries.
Lǚ said:
"How can there be such a thing?
If there is any impropriety,
the blame will be on this old body."
The mother was overjoyed
and agreed.
After Lǚ left,
the old woman swept the room and spread mats,
preparing to wait for her son to return and go marry her.
As dusk approached,
the woman drifted in by herself.
She entered the room and paid respects to the mother,
bowing and performing all courtesies.
She then said to the mother:
"I have two maidservants,
and without Mother's permission,
they dare not enter."
The old woman said:
"My son and I live in a poor hut,
and we don't understand how to employ maids or servants.
The meager profit we earn daily
is barely enough for ourselves.
Now, with one new daughter-in-law,
delicate and sitting idle,
I still fear we won't have enough to eat;
adding two more maids,
how can we possibly sustain them?"
The woman smiled and said:
"When the maids come,
they will not burden Mother's expenses;
they can all earn their own food."
She asked:
"Where are the maids?"
The woman then called out:
"Qiūyuè! Qiūsōng!"
Before her voice had faded,
suddenly like flying birds falling,
the two maids were already standing before them.
She immediately ordered them to prostrate and kowtow to the mother.
Soon after, Mǎ returned,
and the mother welcomed him and told him the news.
Mǎ was delighted.
He entered the room
and saw emerald beams and carved rafters,
rivalling a palace;
the tables, screens, and curtains within
shone brilliantly, dazzling his eyes.
Extremely astonished,
he dared not enter.
The woman stepped down from the bed, smiling to greet him;
he saw her as if she were an immortal.
He was even more startled
and retreated.
The woman pulled him,
made him sit, and spoke warmly to him.
Mǎ was overjoyed beyond measure,
his body and spirit seeming disjointed.
He immediately got up,
wanting to go out and buy drinks.
The woman said:
"No need."
She then ordered the two maids to prepare a meal.
Qiūyuè took out a leather bag,
held it behind a screen,
and rattled it vigorously.
Then, she reached in with her hand,
and a pot of wine,
a plate of roasted meat,
and all sorts of fragrant delicacies emerged.
After drinking, they went to bed,
which was adorned with flowered carpets and brocade quilts,
exceedingly warm and soft.
When he went out the door at daybreak,
the thatched hut was as it had been.
The mother and son both found it strange.
The mother went to Lǚ's place,
intending to trace the origin of the matter.
Upon entering,
she first thanked her for her kindness in brokering the marriage.
Lǚ was surprised and said:
"I haven't visited in a long time,
how could a neighbor's daughter have entrusted herself to me?"
The old woman was even more perplexed,
and recounted the whole story in detail.
Lǚ was greatly alarmed,
and immediately went with the old woman to see the new bride.
The woman smiled and met them,
explaining the reason for the gathering in great detail.
When Lǚ saw her beauty and grace,
she was stunned for a long time,
unable to discern anything,
and could only assent vaguely.
The woman presented her with a white wooden back-scratcher,
saying:
"I have nothing to repay your kindness with,
so please accept this as a back-scratcher for you, Old Woman."
Lǚ accepted it and returned home,
and upon closer inspection, it had turned into white silver.
From the time Mǎ acquired his wife,
his old business was completely transformed,
and his household became entirely new.
There were countless sable and brocade garments in his chest,
which Mǎ could take and wear;
but when he went out the door of the room,
they turned into plain cloth,
though still light and warm.
It was the same for the clothes the woman wore herself.
After four or five years,
she suddenly said:
"I have been banished to the human world for more than ten years,
and because I had a connection with you,
I temporarily stayed.
Now, it is time to part."
Mǎ desperately tried to make her stay.
The woman said:
"Please choose another good partner
to look after your ancestors' graves.
I will visit once every year."
Suddenly, she vanished.
Mǎ then married a woman from the Qín family.
Three years later,
on the Qīxī festival,
as the couple was conversing,
the woman suddenly entered,
smiling and saying:
“You're so happy with your new partner,
have you forgotten your old friend?”
Mǎ was startled awake,
and sadly sat up with a sigh,
then poured out his heart.
The woman said:
“I was just seeing Zhīnǚ across the river,
and took a moment to look upon you.”
They leaned on each other,
their conversation endless.
Suddenly someone in the sky called
“Huìfāng!”
The woman hastily got up to bid farewell.
Mǎ asked who it was.
She replied:
“I came with my elder sister Shuāngchéng,
she cannot wait much longer.”
Mǎ saw her off.
The woman said:
“You will live to eighty,
and when the time comes,
I will come to collect your bones.”
Having said this,
she vanished.
Now Mǎ is over sixty.
He is merely simple and taciturn,
with no other strengths.
Yìshǐshì said:
“Mǎ Shēng’s name is obscure,
his occupation ignoble,
what did Huìfāng see in him?
From this, one sees that immortals value simplicity and sincerity.
I once said to a friend: 'If it were you and I,
even ghosts and foxes would abandon us;
the only difference that prevents us from being unworthy of immortals
is 'obscurity'
itself.'”
According to a manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lǐ Huìdòu of Yìdū,
while walking in the mountains,
came across several people feasting on the ground.
Seeing Lǐ arrive,
they joyfully rose together,
pulled him to sit,
and vied to offer him drinks.
Looking at their platters of food,
various delicacies were laid out.
After some time,
they drank very merrily;
but the wine tasted thin and astringent.
Suddenly, a person came from afar,
with a long, narrow face,
about two or three feet long;
his tall, slender hat matched it.
The crowd exclaimed in surprise:
“The Mountain God has arrived!”
Immediately they all scattered in all directions.
Lǐ also hid in a pit.
After a while, he got up to look,
and found the food and wine were all gone,
only broken earthenware containing urine,
and a few scorpions on a tile shard.
According to a manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Xú Jìcháng,
a native of Línzī,
lived in Mófáng Zhuāng, east of the city.
He pursued scholarly studies but did not succeed,
then left to become a petty official.
One day, he went to visit in-laws,
passing by the Yǔ family’s burial grounds.
At dusk, he returned drunk,
and as he passed the place,
he saw magnificent pavilions and towers,
and an old man sitting at the door.
Xú, parched from drink,
bowed and asked for water.
The old man rose,
invited the guest in,
and went up to the hall to offer him a drink.
After drinking,
the old man said:
“It’s hard to travel at dusk,
how about staying overnight,
and leaving early in the morning?”
Xú was also tired,
and gladly agreed to the request.
The old man ordered his household to offer wine to the guest,
then said to Xú:
“Old man has a word,
don't mind if it's presumptuous: young sir, your esteemed family is now prominent,
and a marriage alliance could be formed.
I have a young daughter not yet betrothed,
whom I wish to offer as your concubine,
and hope you will kindly accept her.”
Xú was flustered and didn't know how to respond.
The old man immediately sent a messenger to inform his relatives,
and also sent word to have the young lady prepare herself.
Shortly after,
four or five people in tall hats and wide sashes
arrived one after another.
The young lady also came out exquisitely dressed,
her beauty extraordinary.
Then they sat together for a feast.
Xú’s mind was dizzy and confused,
he only wished to sleep quickly.
After a few rounds of wine,
he firmly declined to drink more.
So, a small maidservant led the couple into the bed-curtains,
and they shared affection until they stopped.
Xú asked about her surname and clan.
The woman said:
“My surname is Xiāo,
I am the seventh child.”
He then inquired in detail about her family background.
The woman said:
“Though I am humble and lowly,
marrying a petty official would not disgrace you,
why bother to investigate further?”
Xú was smitten by her beauty,
and showed her utmost intimacy,
no longer having any other doubts.
The woman said:
“This place cannot be our home.
I understand your elder sister-in-law is very kind,
and perhaps will not object,
when you return, clear a room,
and I will arrive myself.”
Xú agreed.
Then, as she put her arm around him,
he suddenly fell asleep.
When he awoke,
his embrace was empty.
The sky was bright,
pine shadows obscured the dawn,
and beneath him was about a foot thick of straw.
He returned home astonished and sighing,
and told his wife.
His wife playfully cleared a room,
set up a bed in it,
closed the door and left,
saying:
“The new bride will arrive tonight.”
They then laughed together.
When evening came,
