his wife playfully pulled Xú to open the door,
saying:
“Has the new person perhaps already arrived in the room?”
Upon entering,
they saw a beautiful woman in splendid attire sitting on the bed.
Seeing the two enter,
she gracefully rose to greet them.
The couple was greatly astonished.
The woman covered her mouth and chuckled,
and bowed respectfully.
His wife then prepared a feast,
to celebrate their union.
The woman rose early to work,
and did not avoid being put to use.
One day she said to Xú:
“My sisters and aunts all wish to come and see our home.”
Xú worried he would have nothing to offer guests on short notice.
The woman said:
“They all know our family is not wealthy,
so they will bring the food and utensils themselves,
you just need our sisters to cook.”
Xú told his wife,
and she agreed.
After breakfast,
indeed, someone brought wine and meat,
set down the load and left.
His wife took on the role of the cook.
After noon,
six or seven young women arrived,
the oldest not over forty,
they sat around and drank together,
their boisterous laughter filling the room.
Xú’s wife secretly peeked from the window,
but only saw her husband and the seventh sister sitting opposite each other,
all other guests were invisible.
When the Big Dipper hung at the corner of the roof,
they joyfully departed.
The woman had not yet returned from seeing off the guests.
His wife entered and looked at the table,
cups and platters were all empty.
She laughed and said:
“Those maidservants must have been afraid of hunger,
so they licked the chopping board clean like dogs.”
After a while,
the woman returned,
sincerely thanked them for their trouble,
took the dishes to wash herself,
and urged them to sleep.
His wife said:
“Guests visiting our home,
and having to provide their own food and drink,
is also a great joke.
Tomorrow, we should invite them separately.”
A few days later,
Xú, following his wife's words,
had the maidservant summon the guests again.
When the guests arrived,
they drank and ate to their heart's content;
only four bowls were left,
untouched by chopsticks or spoons.
The company laughed and said,
"Our hostess considers us unpleasant,
which is why she left these to await the 'mediators'."
Among the company was a young woman,
eighteen or nineteen years old,
wearing plain white slippers and a white skirt.
She was said to be a newly widowed woman,
whom the maidservant called Sixth Sister (Liù Jiě).
Her demeanor was enchanting and alluring,
she laughed easily and was eloquent.
She gradually became close with Xú,
often teasing him with witty remarks.
When they played a drinking game,
Xú acted as the recorder,
prohibiting laughter and jesting.
Liù Jiě frequently broke the rules,
leading to her drinking over ten cups in a row,
becoming flushed and completely drunk.
Her lovely body was languid and delicate,
frail and difficult to support.
Before long,
she disappeared.
Xú lit a candle and searched for her,
finding her soundly asleep inside a dark curtain.
He drew close and kissed her lips,
but she didn't even notice.
He reached his hand into her trousers,
and her private parts were swollen.
His heart was just beginning to stir,
when the company at the table loudly called for Young Master Xú (Xú Láng).
So he quickly adjusted her clothing,
and saw a embroidered handkerchief in her sleeve,
which he secretly took out.
By the middle of the night,
the guests left the banquet,
but Liù Jiě was still not awake.
Seventh Sister (Qī Jiě) entered and shook her,
and only then did she groan loudly and get up.
She tied her skirt and tidied her hair, then left with the others.
Xú, with deep affection,
could not get her out of his mind.
He intended to find a private place to admire the embroidered handkerchief,
but when he searched for it, it was already gone.
He suspected he had dropped it on the way while seeing off the guests,
and holding a lamp, he carefully searched the steps and courtyard,
but it was nowhere to be found.
He felt utterly disheartened.
The maidservant asked him about it,
and Xú replied evasively.
The maidservant smiled and said,
"Don't lie.
Someone has already taken the handkerchief.
You're just wasting your time and effort."
Xú was surprised,
and told her the truth,
also expressing his longing.
The maidservant said,
"You two have no predestined connection from a previous life,
your karma only extends this far."
He asked her the reason,
and she said:
"She was a singing girl (qǔ zhōng nǚ) in her previous life;
you were a scholar,
saw her and were pleased with her,
but your parents hindered you,
so your ambition could not be fulfilled,
and you fell ill and became critically ill.
You sent someone to tell her, 'I am already dying.
If only you would come,
and I could touch your skin once,
I would die without regret!'
She was moved by this sentiment,
and agreed to your request.
But due to pressing commitments,
she did not go immediately;
she arrived the next morning,
but the patient had already passed away: this was the one touch (yī wěn) destiny you had with her in a past life.
Anything beyond this is not to be hoped for."
Later, a banquet was set up to invite the maidservants again,
but only Liù Jiě did not come.
Xú suspected the maidservant was jealous.
He felt quite resentful.
One day, the maidservant said to Xú,
"Because of Liù Jiě, you are wrongly blaming me.
She truly refuses to come,
so how can you blame me?
Our eight years of good relationship
are about to end,
so please allow me to make a strong effort for you,
to resolve your previous confusion.
Even if she doesn't come,
who can stop me from going?
I will visit her at her door,
and perhaps human determination can overcome fate;
who knows?"
Xú was delighted
and agreed.
The maidservant took his hand,
and they floated as if treading on air,
arriving at her house in an instant.
The spacious hall with yellow bricks,
and the winding doorways
were no different from when he first saw them.
Her parents-in-law both came out
and said,
"Our humble daughter has long enjoyed your kindness.
As old people, we are frail and indolent in our declining years,
and have been negligent in our greetings;
we hope you won't mind?"
Immediately, a banquet was spread.
The maidservant then asked about her younger sisters.
The mother said,
"They have all returned home,
only Sixth Sister (Liù Jiě) is still here."
She immediately called a maidservant to fetch Mistress Liù (Liù Niángzi),
but she did not come out for a long time.
The maidservant went in
and dragged her out.
She bowed her head and remained silent,
not like her previous cheerful self.
After a while,
she gently excused herself and left.
The maidservant said to Liù Jiě,
"Sister, you hold yourself too highly,
making others resent me!"
Liù Jiě gave a slight laugh and said,
"How can a frivolous man be suitable for closeness!"
The maidservant picked up two half-empty cups,
forced them to exchange drinks,
saying,
"Your lips have already touched,
why put on an act?"
After a while,
Seventh Sister (Qī Jiě) left,
leaving only the two of them in the room.
Xú suddenly got up and pressed close to her,
Liù Jiě struggled and resisted.
Xú pulled her clothes, knelt down, and pleaded with her,
and her expression gradually softened.
They held hands and entered the room.
Just as they were loosening their robes and sashes,
they suddenly heard shouts and roars shaking the ground,
and firelight shot through the door.
Liù Jiě was greatly startled,
pushed Xú up and said,
"Calamity has suddenly arrived,
what shall we do!"
Xú was flustered and didn't know what to do,
and the young woman had already fled without a trace.
Xú sat down dejectedly for a moment,
and all the houses disappeared.
Over ten hunters,
with falcons and blades, arrived,
and were surprised as they asked,
"Who is hiding here tonight?"
Xú claimed he was lost,
and then gave his name.
One person said,
"We were just chasing a fox;
did you see it?"
He replied,
"No, I didn't."
Upon closer inspection of the area,
it was the funeral hall of the Yú family.
He returned home feeling greatly disheartened,
still hoping that Seventh Sister (Qī Jiě) would come again.
He consulted morning magpie omens and evening lamp-wicks,
but there was still no news.
Account told by Dǒng Yùxuán.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The teacher Xué shī Liú Fānghuī
was from Jīngdū.
He had a younger sister who was betrothed to Dài shēng,
and her wedding day was approaching.
When the northern troops invaded,
her father and elder brother feared that her youth and frailty would be a burden,
so they planned to disguise her and send her to the Dài family.
Before her preparations were complete,
chaotic soldiers burst in,
and father and son scattered.
The girl was captured by a niúlù.
She followed him for several days,
but he did not molest her in the least.
At night, he made her sleep on a separate bed,
and provided her with food and drink with great hospitality.
Later, another young man was captured and brought in;
his age was similar to the girl's,
and his demeanor was refined and elegant.
The niúlù said to him:
"I have no son.
I intend to have you succeed my line.
What do you say?"
The young man assented respectfully.
Then, pointing to the girl, he said:
"If you agree,
then she shall be your wife."
The young man was delighted,
and expressed his willingness to obey.
The niúlù then allowed them to share a bed,
and they were very happy and harmonious.
Afterward, on the pillow, they each stated their surnames and given names,
and it turned out that the young man was Dài shēng himself.
A certain official from Shǎnxī,
serving in a salt administration post,
did not bring his family with him.
During the upheaval of Jiāng Xī's rebellion,
his hometown fell into the hands of bandits,
and communication was cut off.
After the rebellion was quelled,
he sent someone to inquire,
but a hundred *lǐ* were desolate, without a single wisp of smoke,
and there was nowhere to ask for news.
Coincidentally, when he returned to the capital to report,
an old yamen runner had lost his wife
and was too poor to remarry.
The official bestowed upon him several pieces of gold to buy a wife.
At that time, the grand army was returning victorious,
and countless women were taken captive;
they were marked with tags and displayed in the marketplace,
like selling cattle and horses.
So, carrying the gold, the runner went to choose.
Believing the gold to be little,
he dared not ask for a young and beautiful woman.
Among them, an old woman was very neat and clean,
so he redeemed her and brought her home.
The old woman sat on the bed and, looking closely, said:
"Are you not a certain yamen runner?"
He asked how she knew,
and she replied:
"You served my son;
how can you not recognize me?"
The runner was greatly astonished
and quickly reported to the official.
The official looked at her,
and indeed, she was his mother.
Consequently, they wept bitterly
and he compensated the runner doubly.
Since the yamen runner had a lot of gold,
he disdained to consider the old woman.
He saw a woman of over thirty years of age,
whose demeanor was extraordinary and refined,
so he redeemed her.
As they walked,
the woman looked back as she went,
saying:
"Are you not a certain yamen runner?"
Again, he asked in surprise,
and she replied:
"You served my husband;
how could you not recognize me?"
The runner was even more astonished,
and led her to see the official.
The official looked at her,
and she was truly his wife.
He again sobbed uncontrollably.
In a single day, his mother and wife were reunited;
his joy was boundless.
So he gave a hundred pieces of gold to the yamen runner
to marry a beautiful woman.
It must be that the official possessed great virtue,
hence the spirits and gods responded to him.
Alas, the one who recounted this forgot his name;
perhaps someone in Qínzhōng can tell it.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The calamity of the *yán kūn* (barbarians),
where jade and stone were indistinguishable,
was indeed a battle.
For an official's family like this,
it is by gathering that they are transmitted.
After Dǒng Énbái,
there was only one grandson,
who now cannot even offer sacrifices to his ancestors;
this is also the fault of court officials,
what sorrow!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In the mountains of Sìshuǐ,
there used to be a Chan monastery.
With no villages for miles around,
human footsteps were rare.
A Daoist priest resided there.
Some said there were many large snakes inside,
which kept travelers even further away.
A young man entered the mountains to hawk.
As he went deeper,
he found no place to stay.
Distantly, he saw a Buddhist temple,
and hastened to it.
The Daoist priest was surprised and said:
"Layman, how did you come here?
Fortunately, you were not seen by my children!"
He immediately told him to sit
and prepared gruel.
Before he had finished eating,
a giant snake entered,
more than ten arm-spans thick,
raising its head towards the guest,
its angry eyes flashing like lightning.
The guest was greatly terrified.
The Daoist priest struck its forehead with his palm
and scolded:
"Go!"
The snake then lowered its head and entered the east room.
It coiled for a long time
before its body was entirely inside;
it lay coiled within,
completely filling the room.
The guest was greatly terrified
and trembled.
The Daoist priest said:
"These are what I usually keep and raise.
With me here,
there is no harm;
what I worry about
is if you encounter them alone."
Just as the guest sat down,
another snake entered,
slightly smaller than the previous one,
about five or six arm-spans thick.
Seeing the guest, it stopped abruptly,
blinking and flicking its tongue as before.
The Daoist priest again shouted at it,
and it also entered the room.
There was no sleeping space in the room;
half of it coiled around the beams,
and the earth on the wall fell with a sound.
The guest was even more frightened
and did not sleep all night.
He rose early, wishing to return,
and the Daoist priest escorted him.
Stepping out of the house door,
he saw, on the wall and below the steps,
creatures as big as jars and bowls,
some moving, some lying still.
Seeing a living person,
all showed signs of wanting to devour.
The guest was afraid,
and walked close to the Daoist priest's side,
letting him escort him out of the valley entrance,
before returning.
In my hometown, there was a guest from
Zhōngzhōu who lodged at Shéfó Sì.
The temple monks prepared dinner,
and the meat soup was delicious.
All the pieces were round,
like chicken necks.
He was puzzled
and asked the temple monks:
"How many chickens did you kill to get so many necks?"
The monk said:
"These are snake segments."
The guest was greatly startled,
some even went outside and vomited.
When he went to sleep,
he felt something wriggling on his chest;
he touched it,
and it was a snake.
He immediately rose with a startled cry.
The monk rose and said:
"This is common,
why be surprised by it!"
Then he shone a light on the wall,
and it was full of snakes, large and small,
the bed and everything above and below it were covered in them.
The next day,
the monk led him into the Buddhist hall.
Beneath the Buddha's seat was a giant well,
and in the well were snakes,
as thick as giant urns,
peering their heads out from the well's edge but not emerging.
When they lit a fire and looked down,
there were hundreds of thousands of snake offspring and descendants,
living as a clan within it.
The monk said,
"Once, snakes came out and caused harm,
the Buddha sat upon them to suppress them,
and their troubles began to cease."
So it was said.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Mínzhǔ Cóngjiǎn of Háozhōu,
his mother was sitting in her room
when a light rain made it dim and gloomy.
She saw Léigōng holding a hammer,
flapping his wings and entering.
Greatly frightened,
she quickly poured the contents of a chamber pot onto him.
Léigōng was splattered with filth,
as if struck by a knife or axe,
and turned around to flee quickly;
he exerted all his strength to spread his wings and soar,
but could not leave.
He tumbled in the courtyard,
howling like an ox.
The clouds in the sky gradually lowered,
gradually level with the eaves.
In the clouds, there was a rustling sound like horse neighs,
responding to Léigōng.
After a short while,
the rain poured down violently,
washing away all the foul dirt from his body,
then he made a clap of thunder and departed.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Hú Dàchéng,
a native of Chǔ.
His mother had always devoutly worshipped Buddha.
Chéng studied with a private tutor,
and the path went past Guānyīn Cí.
His mother instructed him to always enter and bow.
One day, he arrived at the shrine,
where a young girl was pulling a child, playing within it.
Her hair was just long enough to cover her neck,
and her demeanor was charming.
At that time, Chéng was fourteen,
and his heart was fond of her.
He asked her name,
the girl smiled and said:
"I am Língjiǎo, the daughter of the painter Jiāo from west of this shrine.
What do you wish to ask?"
Chéng asked again:
"Do you have a fiancé?"
The girl, blushing, said:
"No."
Chéng said:
"I will be your husband,
is that good?"
The girl, ashamed, said:
"I cannot decide for myself."
But her eyes were clear and bright,
looking up and down at Chéng,
her expression seemed to indicate she was happily inclined.
Chéng then left.
The girl chased after him and called out from a distance:
"Cuī Ěrchéng,
is a good friend of my father,
use him as a matchmaker,
and there will be no disharmony."
Chéng said:
"Agreed."
Because he thought her intelligent and affectionate,
he admired her even more.
Returning home,
he honestly revealed his wish to his mother.
His mother had only this one son,
and was always afraid of displeasing him,
so she immediately asked Cuī to act as matchmaker.
Jiāo demanded an exorbitant bride price,
and the matter was about to fall through.
Cuī strongly praised Chéng's pure lineage and talent,
and Jiāo finally consented.
Chéng had an uncle,
who was old and childless,
and held a teaching position in Húběi.
His wife died in his official residence,
and his mother sent Chéng to attend her funeral.
After several months, when he was about to return,
his uncle also fell ill
and died.
Having lingered for a long time,
it happened that a great bandit occupied Húnán,
and news from home was cut off.
Chéng hid among the common people,
lonely and fearful, a mere shadow.
One day,
there was an old woman aged forty-eight or nine,
wandering around the village,
not leaving even as the sun set.
She said of herself:
"Having lost my way due to the chaos,
I am going to sell myself."
Someone asked her price,
she said:
"I disdain to be a servant,
nor do I wish to be a wife,
but if there is someone who will treat me as a mother,
then I will follow them,
without haggling over the price."
All who heard her laughed.
Chéng went to see her,
and her face somewhat resembled his mother's in one or two aspects,
which touched his heart and made him greatly sad.
He thought to himself that he was alone and had no one to sew for him,
so he invited her home,
and treated her with the respect due to a child for their mother.
The old woman was happy,
and immediately cooked meals and wove repeatedly for him,
toiling diligently as a mother would.
If something displeased her, she would scold him;
but if he suffered from any illness or pain,
she would care for him more tenderly than his own birth mother.
Suddenly, she said:
"This place is peaceful,
fortunately, there's nothing to worry about.
However, my son has grown up,
and even though he is on a journey,
the great human relations cannot be neglected.
In two or three days,
I will arrange a marriage for you."
Chéng wept and said:
"I already have a wife,
but we are separated by north and south."
The old woman said:
"In times of great chaos,
human affairs are turned upside down,
how can you wait steadfastly?"
Chéng wept again and said:
"Regardless of the unbreakable vow of marriage,
who would entrust a delicate daughter to a wanderer like me?"
The old woman did not answer,
but busied herself preparing curtains, bed hangings, quilts, and pillows,
very thoroughly.
He also didn't know where she came from.
One day,
as dusk fell,
Jǐng Chéng said:
"Tend to the lamp, don't fall asleep.
I'm going to see if the new bride has arrived yet."
Then he went out the door.
After the third watch of the night had completely passed,
Wēn did not return,
and he felt greatly suspicious.
Presently, he heard a commotion outside the gate,
and when he went out to look,
he saw a girl sitting in the courtyard,
with disheveled hair, sobbing.
Startled, he asked:
"Who are you?"
She also did not speak.
After a long while,
she finally said:
"Being married to come here
is certainly not a blessing,
but rather brings only death!"
Chéng was greatly alarmed,
not knowing the reason why.
The girl said:
"I was betrothed at a young age to Hú Dàchéng;
unexpectedly, Hú went north,
and all communication ceased.
My parents forced me to marry into your family.
My body can be brought,
but my will cannot be taken away!"
Chéng heard this and wept, saying:
"I am Hú Mǒu.
Are you Língjiǎo?"
The girl stopped her tears and was astonished,
disbelieving him.
They went together into the room,
and by the lamp, he looked at her closely,
saying:
"Could this be a dream?"
Thereupon, their sorrow turned to joy,
and they recounted their sufferings apart.
Before this, after the chaos,
a hundred *lǐ* of Húnán
were swept clean of inhabitants.
Jiāo carried his family and fled to the east of Chángshā,
and was also betrothed to Zhōu Shēng.
Amidst the chaos, the ceremony could not be completed,
and they had arranged for her to be sent to his family that very evening.
The girl wept and refused to wash or comb her hair,
but her family forcibly placed her in a carriage.
Along the way,
the girl stumbled and fell out of the carriage.
Then four people arrived bearing a sedan chair,
saying they were from the Zhōu family to welcome the bride.
They helped her into the sedan chair,
and it traveled swiftly as if flying,
stopping only when it reached this place.
An old woman pulled her inside,
saying:
"This is your husband's family;
just go in, don't cry.
Your mother-in-law
will arrive soon."
Then she left.
Chéng questioned her and learned the situation,
only then realizing that the old woman was a spirit.
Husband and wife burned incense and prayed together,
wishing for mother and son to be reunited.
The mother, since the military had imposed martial law,
had fled with other women into ravines and valleys.
One night,
there was a clamor that bandits had arrived,
and they all scattered in panic to hide.
A young boy offered a horse to the mother.
In her haste, the mother did not have time to ask questions;
she grasped its shoulder and mounted it.
It was light and swift, running like the wind,
and in an instant, they reached a lake.
The horse galloped across the water,
its hooves creating no ripples.
Before long,
he helped her dismount,
and pointing to a household, said:
"You can live here."
The mother was about to open her mouth to thank him;
she looked back at the horse,
which had transformed into a golden-furred *hǒu*,
more than a *zhàng* tall,
and the boy leaped onto it and departed.
The mother knocked on the door with her hand,
and it opened wide.
Someone came out to ask,
and she found his voice strangely familiar.
She looked,
and it was Chéng.
Mother and son embraced and wept.
The wife also woke up in surprise,
and the whole family was filled with joy and comfort.
They suspected the old woman was Guānyīn Dàshì herself.
From then on, they became even more devout in reciting the Guānyīn *jīngzhòu*.
Thus, they settled in Húběi
and managed fields and houses there.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Mǎ Yǒng,
a native of Qí,
was a greedy
and dissolute person,
whose family was constantly impoverished.
The villagers playfully called him
"Hungry Ghost."
When he was over thirty,
he grew increasingly emaciated,
his clothes a tattered quilt.
With both hands crossed over his shoulders,
he snatched food in the marketplace.
Everyone shunned him,
not even considering him human.
In the district lived an old man named Zhū Sǒu,
who in his youth had lived with his wife in the market of Wǔdū,
engaging in an unsavory occupation.
In his later years, he returned to his hometown,
where he was greatly criticized by scholars;
however, Zhū Jié's conduct was good,
and people gradually began to treat him with respect.
One day,
he happened upon Mǎ snatching food without paying,
and being tormented by the shopkeepers.
Taking pity on him,
he paid the price on his behalf.
He brought him home,
gave him several hundred (cash),
and bade him use it as capital.
Mǎ left,
unwilling to seek employment,
and sat around eating.
Before long,
his funds were again depleted,
and he reverted to his old ways.
But he constantly feared encountering Zhū,
so he left for Línyì.
At dusk, he lodged in the academy.
The winter night was bitterly cold,
and he would pluck the pendants from the crowns of the sages and cuddle up against their boards.
The academy official learned of this
and was furious, wanting to punish him.
Mǎ pleaded for leniency,
offering to generate wealth for the official.
The official was pleased
and let him go.
Mǎ sought out a certain student whose family was wealthy,
demanded money at his door,
and deliberately provoked his anger;
then he cut himself with a knife,
falsely accusing the student and reporting it to the academy.
The academy official extorted a heavy bribe
before he would refrain from expelling the student.
The students were collectively indignant at this,
and publicly denounced him to the county magistrate.
The magistrate, being incorruptible, ascertained the truth,
gave Mǎ forty strokes,
and put him in a cangue around his neck.
He died three days later.
That night,
Zhū Sǒu dreamt of a horse, wearing official robes and a cap, entering and
saying:
"I owe you a great kindness,
and now I come to repay it."
When he awoke,
his concubine gave birth to a son.
Sǒu knew it was the horse,
and named him Mǎ'ér.
He was not bright as a child,
but Sǒu was pleased that he could read.
In his twenties,
he diligently managed the household,
and was able to enter the county school.
Later, while taking an examination at an inn,
he lay on the bed during the day
and saw the wall papered entirely with old examination papers.
He looked at them
and saw
the four-line inscription
on "The Nature of Dogs."
He thought it was truly difficult,
read it, and memorized it.
Upon entering the examination hall,
it happened to be that very topic.
He wrote it down,
received an excellent grade,
and was granted government stipend.
In his sixties,
he was appointed as an instructor in Línwǔ.
He served for several years,
but had not a single friend based on principles or righteousness.
Only when blue flies (money) came out of one's sleeve
would he offer a cormorant-like smile;
otherwise, his eyelashes would seem an inch long,
and he would look sternly as if he didn't recognize you.
Occasionally, when the magistrate handled minor disputes among students,
and sentenced them to light punishment,
he would inflict cruel tortures as if dealing with bandits.
If there was someone who sued a scholar,
a wealthy person would immediately come knocking at his door.
With so many such behaviors,
the students could no longer tolerate him.
By then he was nearly seventy,
swollen, deaf, and withered,
and constantly sought out black beard dye from people.
A certain eccentric scholar
tricked him by grinding up madder root.
At dawn, when everyone looked at him together,
he resembled the statue of a spirit general in a temple.
He became furious,
and apprehended the scholar;
but the scholar had already fled during the night.
This anger built up inside him,
and he died a few months later.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Wén Rénshēng,
a Hénán man.
Having been ill for days,
he saw a *xiùcai* enter,
crouching under his bed,
humble and utterly polite.
After a while, the *xiùcai* invited Wén Rénshēng to take a short walk,
held his arm and spoke at length,
chatting volubly as they walked.
Several *li* away, he still did not say goodbye.
Wén Rénshēng stopped,
cupped his hands and bade farewell.
The *xiùcai* said:
"Please take a few more steps;
I have something to ask of you."
Wén Rénshēng asked him what it was.
He replied:
"We all belong to the jurisdiction of the Department of Examination Irregularities (Kǎobì Sī).
The head of the department is named King Xūdù (King Empty Belly).
When one first sees him,
the rule is to have a piece of thigh flesh cut off.
I implore you to speak a good word for me."
Wén Rénshēng, startled, asked:
"What crime warrants such a fate?"
He said:
"No crime is necessary;
this is an old rule.
If one is rich in bribes,
it can be redeemed.
However, I am poor."
Wén Rénshēng said:
"I have never known the Ghost King;
how can I be of help?"
He said:
"Your maternal grandfather is his elder relative,
so he should listen to you."
As they spoke,
they had already entered the city.
They reached a government office,
whose buildings were not very grand or spacious,
except for one hall that was tall and wide.
Below the hall, two stone tablets stood east and west,
with green inscriptions as large as large baskets.
One read
"Filial piety, brotherly love, loyalty, trustworthiness,"
and the other read
"Propriety, righteousness, integrity, shame."
They ascended the steps,
and saw a plaque above the hall,
with "Kǎobì Sī"
written in large characters.
Between the railings,
a pair of couplets carved with green characters on a board read:
"Daily schools, daily orders, daily treasuries –
two words of virtue and conduct, secretly transforming;
Upper scholars, middle scholars, lower scholars –
one hall of ritual and music, students of the ghost gate."
Before they had finished their tour,
the official had already emerged,
with curly hair and a turtle-like back,
looking like a man of several hundred years;
his nostrils flared towards the sky,
and his lips protruded outwards,
not covering his teeth.
He was followed by a registrar,
with a tiger's head and a human body.
Another dozen or so people stood in attendance,
half of them fierce and malevolent like mountain spirits.
The *xiùcai* said:
"This is the Ghost King."
Wén Rénshēng was utterly terrified
and wanted to retreat.
The Ghost King had already seen him,
descended the steps and bowed, inviting Wén Rénshēng up,
and immediately asked about his well-being.
Wén Rénshēng merely nodded.
He then asked:
"What brings you here?"
Wén Rénshēng fully explained the *xiùcai*'s intention.
The Ghost King's expression changed and he said:
"This is a standing rule,
which even my father's command I dare not obey!"
His demeanor was solemn and forbidding,
as if no word could enter.
Wén Rénshēng dared not speak,
and abruptly rose to bid farewell.
The Ghost King walked sideways, accompanying him,
and only returned when they reached the gate.
Wén Rénshēng did not return home,
but secretly slipped back in to observe the situation.
When he reached the foot of the hall,
the *xiùcai*, along with several companions,
was already bound and their fingers pointed out,
firmly in stocks and ropes.
A fierce man approached with a knife,
bared the *xiùcai*'s thigh,
and cut off a piece of flesh,
about the width of three fingers pressed together.
The *xiùcai* howled loudly, on the verge of choking.
Wén Rénshēng, being a youth of righteousness,
could not contain his indignation,
and shouted:
"How utterly cruel!
What kind of world is this?!"
The Ghost King, startled, rose,
temporarily ordered the cutting to stop,
and hurried to greet Wén Rénshēng.
Wén Rénshēng, still indignant, went out,
and told everyone in the market,
intending to appeal to the Heavenly Emperor.
Someone laughed and said:
"How naive!
The azure sky is vast;
where will you find the Heavenly Emperor to complain of injustice?
These fellows are only close to King Yama;
calling him might get a response."
So, they showed him the way.
He hurried there,
and indeed saw a majestic palace,
where King Yama was seated.
He prostrated himself at the steps and cried out his grievance.
The King summoned and questioned him,
then immediately ordered the ghosts to bind, shackle, and take away the mallet.
A short while later,
the Ghost King and the *xiùcai* both arrived.
After confirming the facts,
King Yama was enraged and said:
"You, having toiled in your previous life,
were temporarily entrusted with this position,
awaiting rebirth into a noble family;
yet now you dare to act like this!
Let your good tendons be removed,
and your wicked bones be increased,
and be punished to never prosper in life, generation after generation!"
The ghost then whipped him,
and he fell to the ground,
losing a tooth.
With a knife, they cut his fingertip,
drew out a tendon,
which was bright white like silk.
The Ghost King cried out in pain,
his voice like a pig being slaughtered.
Soon, the tendons from his feet were also completely extracted,
and two ghosts escorted him away.
The scholar bowed and left.
The xiùcai followed behind him,
expressing profound gratitude.
He escorted him through the market,
where they saw a house with a red curtain hanging down.
Inside the curtain, a woman revealed half her face,
her beauty and makeup exceptional.
The scholar asked,
"Whose house is that?"
The xiùcai replied,
"This is a curved lane."
After they had passed,
the scholar lingered, unable to leave.
He firmly stopped the xiùcai.
The xiùcai said,
"You came for my sake,
and now you want to leave alone;
how can my heart bear it?"
The scholar firmly refused,
and so the xiùcai left.
The scholar watched the xiùcai go far away,
then hurried into the curtain.
The woman received him,
joy evident on her face.
They entered the room and sat close together,
exchanging names.
The woman said of herself,
"My surname is Liǔ,
and my given name is Qiūhuá."
An old woman came out,
and prepared dishes and wine for them.
When the wine was finished,
they entered the bed curtains,
and their love was exceedingly intense,
earnestly agreeing to marriage.
At dawn,
the old woman entered and said,
"Our firewood and water have run out.
We need to spend your money, young master;
what shall we do!"
The scholar remembered that his waist pouch was empty,
and was silently filled with shame and panic.
After a long time,
he said,
"I truly did not bring a single coin.
I should sign a promissory note,
and I will repay you immediately upon my return home."
The old woman's expression changed, and she said,
"Have you ever heard of a 'night ferry-woman' asking for overdue payments?"
Qiūhuá frowned,
and said not a word.
The scholar temporarily took off his clothes as collateral.
The old woman held back a laugh and said,
"This isn't even enough to pay for the wine!"
Grumbling discontentedly,
she and the girl both went inside.
The scholar felt ashamed.
After some time,
he still hoped the girl would come out to say goodbye,
and reaffirm their previous vows;
but for a long time there was no sound.
He secretly went in to peek,
and saw the old woman and Qiūhuá,
from their shoulders up, transformed into ox-headed demons,
their eyes gleaming as they stood facing each other.
Greatly terrified,
he rushed out;
wanting to return home,
he found a hundred branching paths,
and did not know which way to go.
He asked the market people,
but none knew the name of his village.
He wandered between the shops and market stalls,
for two days and two nights,
filled with bitter sorrow,
his stomach rumbling with hunger.
He could not decide whether to advance or retreat.
Suddenly, the xiùcai passed by.
Seeing him,
he exclaimed in surprise,
"Why haven't you returned home yet,
and so dishevelled like this?"
The scholar was too embarrassed to answer.
The xiùcai said,
"Aha!
Could it be that you've been bewitched by a flower yakṣī?"
He then went forward with an air of indignation,
saying,
"Qiūhuá and her mother,
why don't you reveal yourselves!"
After a short while,
he came back with the clothes and handed them to the scholar, saying,
"That immoral maid was rude;
I have already scolded her."
He escorted the scholar home,
then bade farewell and left.
The scholar collapsed and remained unconscious for three days before recovering,
recounting the events clearly.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Xú Gōngxīng of Yízhōu declared that he became Yánluó Wáng at night.
In the same prefecture,
Mǎ shēng also claimed the same.
Xú Gōng heard of this,
visited Mǎ's home,
and asked Mǎ,
"What matters did you deal with in the underworld last night?"
Mǎ replied,
"Nothing else,
just sending Zuǒ Luóshí to ascend to heaven.
Lotus flowers fell from the sky,
as large as houses."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lǐ Xiàolián Zhìjūn (李孝廉質君) of Chángshān (長山) went to Qīngzhōu (青州).
On the way, he met six or seven people.
Their accents resembled those from Yān (燕).
Upon closer inspection, both their cheeks
had scars,
as large as coins.
He found this strange,
and asked what disease they all shared.
The travelers replied: "Last year, we were guests in Yúnnán (雲南).
At dusk, we lost our way,
and entered a large mountain range.
With deep ravines and towering cliffs,
it was impossible to get out.
So we tied up our horses, unloaded our gear,
and rested near a tree.
Late at night,
tigers, leopards, owls, and nightjars
began to howl in succession.
All the travelers huddled together, knees clasped to their chests,
unable to sleep.
Suddenly, we saw a giant man approaching,
about ten feet tall.
The travelers huddled on the ground,
not daring to breathe.
The giant man arrived,
grabbed a horse with his hand and ate it.
Six or seven horses were devoured in an instant.
Then he broke a long branch from a tree,
seized a person's head, and threaded it through their cheek,
like stringing fish.
After threading,
he carried it a few steps,
and the branch creaked and snapped.
The giant man seemed afraid they would fall,
so he bent both ends of the branch,
pressed them down with a huge rock, and left.
When the travelers felt he was far away,
they took out their knives and cut themselves free from the branch,
enduring the pain and fleeing quickly.
They saw the giant man leading another person, even larger, coming together.
Frightened, the travelers
hid in the dense bushes.
They saw that the newcomer was even bigger.
He came to the tree,
patrolled back and forth,
as if searching for something he couldn't find.
Then he made a 'chough-chough' sound,
like a giant bird's cry.
He seemed very angry,
presumably angry at the giant man for feeding him.
So he slapped the giant man's cheek with his palm.
The giant man hunched over and accepted it obediently,
not daring to dispute in the slightest.
Soon after, both left.
The travelers then cautiously came out.
They fled wildly for a long time
and eventually saw lamplight on a distant ridge.
They all rushed towards it.
When they arrived, they found a man living in a stone chamber.
The travelers entered, bowed in a circle,
and told him of their suffering.
The man pulled them to sit,
and said:
"These creatures are truly hateful,
but even I cannot subdue them.
Wait until my younger sister returns;
we can plan with her."
Not long after,
a woman carrying two tigers entered from outside
and asked the travelers where they came from.
All the travelers prostrated themselves and told her the story.
The woman said:
"I've known for a long time that those two are troublemakers,
but I didn't expect them to be so vicious and stubborn!
I will eliminate them immediately."
She took a bronze hammer out of the stone chamber,
weighing three or four hundred hú (斛),
and left the door, disappearing.
The man cooked tiger meat to feed the travelers.
Before the meat was cooked,
the woman had already returned,
saying:
"They saw me and tried to escape.
I pursued them for dozens of *lǐ* (里),
cut off one of their fingers, and returned."
Then she threw the finger to the ground;
it was larger than a shin bone.
Everyone was extremely astonished
and asked her name,
but she did not answer.
A little while later,
the meat was cooked,
but the travelers, in pain from their wounds, could not eat.
The woman sprinkled medicinal powder all over them,
and the pain immediately stopped.
At dawn,
the woman escorted the travelers to the tree,
where all their luggage was still present.
Each carrying their gear, they walked for more than ten *lǐ* (里),
passing by the spot where the fight had occurred the previous night.
The woman pointed it out;
there was still about a basin's worth of residual blood in a stone hollow.
After exiting the mountain,
the woman finally bid them farewell and returned.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
Xiàng Gǎo,
courtesy name Chūdàn,
was from Tàiyuán.
He and his step-brother Shèng
were deeply devoted to each other.
Shèng was intimately involved with a courtesan
named Bōsī,
and they had made a vow with a blood oath.
However, because her mother demanded an exorbitant price,
their intended union could not be realized.
It so happened that Bōsī's mother wished for her to marry a good man
and hoped to send Bōsī away first.
There was a young master, Zhuāng Gōngzǐ,
who had always been fond of Bōsī,
and he offered to redeem her to be his concubine.
Bōsī said to her mother:
"Since you wish to escape this life of 'water and fire' together,
this is like escaping hell to ascend to heaven.
If I were to become a concubine,
how different would that be?
If you are willing to follow my will,
marrying Master Xiàng would be acceptable."
Her mother agreed
and conveyed this intention to Shèng.
At that time, Shèng was a widower and unmarried.
Delighted,
he exhausted his resources to hire Bōsī and bring her home.
When Zhuāng heard of this,
he was furious at having his beloved snatched away.
He happened to encounter Shèng on the road
and severely cursed him.
Shèng refused to submit.
Thereupon, Zhuāng incited his followers to beat him with sticks,
and they left only when Shèng was on the verge of death.
Gǎo heard of it and rushed to see him,
but his brother was already dead.
He was overwhelmed with grief and indignation.
He formally lodged a complaint with the prefecture.
Zhuāng extensively bribed officials,
preventing justice from being served.
Gǎo's suppressed anger festered within him,
with no way to appeal.
He thought only of ambushing and assassinating Zhuāng along a main road.
Daily, he carried a sharp blade,
hiding in the thickets along a mountain path.
After a long time,
his plan gradually leaked out.
Zhuāng learned of his intention
and took very strict precautions when going out.
He heard that there was a person named Jiāo Tóng in Fénzhōu,
who was brave and skilled in archery,
and he hired him as a bodyguard with a large sum of money.
Gǎo had no effective strategy,
yet he continued to lie in wait daily.
One day,
as he was lying in ambush,
a heavy rain suddenly began.
He was drenched from head to foot,
suffering greatly from the cold and shivering.
Soon after, a fierce wind raged from all directions,
followed by hail.
Suddenly, he could no longer feel his body's pain or itching.
There was an old mountain god's temple on the ridge,
and he forced himself to run towards it.
Upon entering the temple,
he found the Daoist priest he knew inside.
Previously,
the Daoist priest had often begged in the village,
and Gǎo would always feed him.
Because of this, the Daoist priest knew Gǎo.
Seeing Gǎo's clothes wet,
he handed him a cloth robe,
saying:
"Change into this for now."
Gǎo changed,
enduring the cold while squatting like a dog.
He looked at himself
and saw that hair and hide had suddenly grown,
and his body had transformed into a tiger.
The Daoist priest had already disappeared.
He was startled and hateful in his heart,
but then thought that if he could get his enemy and eat his flesh,
it would also be a good plan.
He descended the mountain and lay in ambush at the usual spot.
He saw his own corpse lying in the bushes,
and only then realized that his former body was dead.
Still fearing it would be eaten by crows and eagles,
he constantly guarded it.
The next day,
Zhuāng finally passed by this spot.
The tiger sprang out violently,
knocked Zhuāng off his horse,
bit open his head,
and swallowed it.
Jiāo Tóng turned his horse and shot,
hitting the tiger in the belly,
and it fell dead.
Gǎo was in a state of confusion and pain,
as if waking from a dream.
After another night,
he was finally able to walk
and returned home dejectedly.
His family, who had been alarmed and suspicious because he hadn't returned for several nights,
rejoiced and comforted him when they saw him.
Gǎo merely lay there,
unable to speak clearly.
A short while later,
when they heard the news of Zhuāng's death,
they rushed to his bedside to congratulate him.
Gǎo then said:
"I was that tiger."
And he recounted his strange experience.
From this, the story spread.
Zhuāngzǐ was deeply pained by his father's tragic death.
Hearing this, he detested Gǎo
and sued him.
The officials, considering it a fantastic story without evidence,
dismissed the case.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"When a valiant man's ambition for revenge is fulfilled,
he rarely returns alive;
this has been a source of lament throughout the ages.
To borrow another's killing to save one's own life—
how divine is the art of the immortals!
However, there are many things in the world that are infuriating.
If those with grievances were always to remain human,
how regrettable it would be not to let them temporarily become tigers!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Dǒng Shàngshū Kěwèi of Qīngzhōu
maintained a strict household.
No male or female, inside or outside,
dared to utter a word.
One day,
a maid and a servant were laughing and teasing each other outside the central gate.
The young master saw them
and angrily scolded them;
they each ran away.
That night,
the young master slept in his study with a boy servant.
It was the height of summer,
and the room door was wide open.
In the deep of night,
the boy servant heard a very loud sound from the bed
and woke up startled.
In the moonlight,
he saw the aforementioned servant carrying something out the door.
Because it was a household member,
he didn't think much of it
and went back to sleep.
Suddenly, he heard a booming sound of boots,
and a tall man with a red face and long beard,
resembling the image of Shòutíng Hóu,
was holding a human head.
The boy servant was terrified
and crawled under the bed.
He heard creaking and rustling sounds from the bed,
like clothes being shaken or a belly being rubbed,
which only stopped after some time.
The sound of boots rang out again,
and then he left.
The boy servant slowly peeked his head out
and saw the light of dawn through the window lattice.
He touched the bed with his hand
and felt it sticky and wet.
Smelling it, he found it to be bloody.
who was just waking up.
When told, he lit a lamp,
and blood covered the pillow and mat.
He was greatly alarmed,
not knowing the reason.
Suddenly, an official runner knocked on the door.
The young master went out to see him.
The runner was astonished
and just spoke of a strange matter.
They all went to him
and he reported:
“Just now, in front of the yamen, a man with a bewildered expression
shouted loudly, ‘I have killed my master!’
The crowd saw bloodstains on his clothes
and seized him to report to the official.
It was ascertained that he was the young master’s household servant.
He said he had already killed the young master
and buried his head beside the Guānmiào.
When we went to verify,
the excavated earth was still fresh,
but there was no head at all.”
The young master was shocked and puzzled.
He hastened to the public court
and saw that the man was the very one who had previously molested the maid.
He then recounted the strangeness of the matter.
The official was greatly perplexed,
gave the man a severe beating, and released him.
The young master did not wish to make an enemy of a lowly person,
so he married off his former maid to him
and bade them leave.
After several days,
their neighbors
heard a loud, crashing sound like something breaking apart in the servant’s room at night.
They quickly got up and called out to them,
but there was no answer.
They broke down the door to look
and saw the husband and wife and their bed
all neatly cut into two halves.
Both the wood and flesh had削痕 (shāoxén) [marks as if pared or scraped],
as if cut by a single blade.
The divine manifestations of Guān Gōng are numerous,
but none are as extraordinary as this.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Zhāng Tàihuá of Tàiyán
was a wealthy official.
His family was troubled by a fox,
but all attempts to subdue it were ineffective.
He reported the situation to the Zhōuyǐn (Prefect),
but the Zhōuyǐn also could not help.
At that time, in a village to the east of the prefecture, there was also a fox living in a villager’s house,
whom everyone saw as a white-haired old man.
The old man exchanged condolences and inquiries with the residents,
just like an ordinary person.
He called himself the second-born,
and everyone called him
Hú Èryé.
Coincidentally, a scholar was visiting the Yǐn
and mentioned this strange matter.
The Yǐn, on behalf of the official,
sent someone to ask the old man.
At that time, there was a native of the eastern village who served as a petty official (lì).
The lì inquired about it
and it was indeed true,
so he went with him.
They immediately set up a banquet at the lì’s house to invite Hú.
Hú arrived,
bowed, yielded, and toasted,
no different from an ordinary person.
The lì explained his request,
and Hú said:
“I already know all about it,
but I cannot help you.
My friend, Zhōu Sān,
resides temporarily in the Yuèmiào,
and he should be able to subdue it.
I will ask him on your behalf.”
The lì was delighted
and offered his thanks.
Before parting, Hú made an agreement with the lì
that they would set up a banquet to the east of the Yuèmiào the next day.
The lì accepted the instruction.
Hú indeed led Zhōu there.
Zhōu had a curly beard and an iron-like face,
and wore a kùzhé (short jacket and trousers).
After several rounds of drink,
he said to the lì:
“Just now, my younger brother Hú conveyed your wishes,
and I have fully understood the matter.
However, this sort of creature is truly numerous in its followers,
and cannot be persuaded by good words,
so it will be difficult to avoid using force.
Please allow me to temporarily lodge at your house,
I dare not refuse such a minor task.”
The lì thought: to get rid of one fox,
only to gain another fox,
is to replace violence with violence.
He hesitated and dared not agree immediately.
Zhōu knew this already
and said:
“Do not be afraid.
I am not like the others,
and moreover, I have a happy affinity with you,
please do not doubt.”
The lì assented.
Zhōu further instructed:
“Tomorrow, you and your family should all sit inside the room with the doors closed,
and please do not make any noise.”
The lì returned home
and followed all the instructions.
Soon, he heard sounds of attacking, stabbing, and fighting in the courtyard,
which only ceased after some time.
He opened the door and went out to look.
Bloodstains dotted the entire steps.
In the courtyard there were several small fox heads,
as large as bowls.
When he looked at the room where the fox had been removed,
Zhōu was sitting upright within,
cupped his hands and smiled, saying:
“Having received your important trust,
the demonic creatures have already been wiped out.”
From then on, he resided in their common house,
and they interacted as host and guest.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
There are many types of pigeons.
Jìn has Kūn Xīng,
Lǔ has Hè Xiù,
Qián has Yè Dié,
Liáng has Fān Tiào,
Yuè has Zhū Jiān: all are exotic mountain breeds.
There are also Būtóu, Diǎnzǐ, Dàbái, Hēishí, Fūfù Què, Huāgǒuyǎn, and so on.
Their names are too many to count on one’s fingers;
only enthusiasts can distinguish them.
The young master Zhāng Dòngliàng of Zōupíng
had a particular fondness for them.
He sought them out according to manuals,
determined to collect all their species.
When he raised them,
it was like caring for infants;
if they were cold, he treated them with fěncǎo (powdered herbs),
if hot, he gave them salt granules.
Pigeons are prone to deep sleep,
so deep that
some die from paralysis.
Zhāng was in Guǎnglín
and bought a pigeon for ten gold pieces.
Its body was smallest,
and it was good at running.
When placed on the ground,
it would circle endlessly,
never stopping until it died,
so it constantly needed someone to hold it.
At night, placing it among the flock would startle the other pigeons,
which could prevent the disease of leg paralysis.
This is called
“Night Roamer.”
Among pigeon breeders in Qí and Lǔ,
none were as good as the young master;
the young master also prided himself on his pigeons.
One night,
sitting in his study,
suddenly a young man in white clothes knocked on the door and entered.
Zhāng did not recognize him at all.
When asked,
he replied:
“I am a wanderer,
what does my name matter?
I have heard from afar that you keep pigeons most abundantly.
This is also something I have loved all my life.
I wish to have a look.”
Zhāng then brought out all his pigeons,
all five colors were present,
resplendent like clouds and brocade.
The young man smiled and said:
“What people say is indeed true;
you, young master, can be said to be skilled in pigeon rearing.
I also carry one or two with me,
would you perhaps like to see them?”
Zhāng was pleased,
and followed the young man.
The moonlight was dim and hazy,
the wilderness vast and desolate,
and a secret fear arose in his heart.
The young man pointed ahead:
“Please make an effort,
the dwelling is not far.”
After a few more steps,
they saw a Daoist temple,
with only two pillars.
The young man grasped his hand and entered;
it was dark without any lamps or fires.
The young man stood in the courtyard,
and made a cooing sound like a pigeon with his mouth.
Suddenly, two pigeons appeared: their form was like ordinary pigeons,
but their feathers were pure white;
they flew as high as the rafters,
cooing and fighting,
and with every flutter,
they would perform a somersault.
The young man waved his arm at them,
and they flew away, wings linked.
He then pursed his mouth and made a strange sound,
and two more pigeons emerged: the larger one was like a duck,
the smaller one just the size of a fist;
they gathered on the steps,
mimicking a crane dance.
The larger one stretched its neck and stood,
spreading its wings like a screen,
turning and cooing and leaping,
as if inviting the other;
the smaller one flew up and down, cooing,
sometimes landing on its head,
its wings fluttering like a swallow settling on a cattail leaf,
its sound fine and broken,
like a pellet drum;
the larger one stretched its neck and dared not move,
its cooing grew more urgent,
its sound changing like a stone chime,
the two harmonizing,
interspersed in perfect rhythm.
Soon after, the smaller one flew up,
and the larger one again tumbled and called out to it.
Zhāng greatly admired them without end,
feeling ashamed as if looking at the ocean.
Thereupon, he bowed to the young man,
begging for a share of his beloved pigeons;
the young man would not allow it.
He then insisted again.
The young man then shooed the pigeons away,
and again made the previous sound,
calling two white pigeons,
which he held in his hand,
saying:
“If you do not dislike them,
take these to fulfill my obligation.”
Zhāng received them and played with them: in the clear moonlight, they appeared amber-colored,
their two eyes transparent,
as if without obstruction,
the black pupils within rounder than peppercorns;
when he opened their wings,
the flesh on their flanks was crystalline,
their internal organs visible.
Zhāng found this very strange,
but his desire was still not satisfied,
and he continued to ask for more with cunning.
The young man said:
“There are still two kinds not yet presented,
now I dare not ask you to observe them again.”
Just as they were debating,
Zhāng’s family entered with a lit hemp torch, looking for their master.
When he looked back at the young man,
he had transformed into a white pigeon,
as large as a chicken,
and soared into the sky.
Also, the courtyard before his eyes had all vanished,
it was but a small grave,
with two withered cypress trees.
He and his family, holding the pigeons,
returned home in awe and wonder.
He tried to make them fly;
they were tamed and extraordinary as before,
though not the most exceptional,
they were truly rare in the human world.
Thus, he cherished them immensely.
After two years,
they bred three males and three females.
Even when relatives and friends sought them,
he would not give them away.
My father had an old acquaintance, a certain Gōng,
who was a high official.
One day,
he saw Zǐ,
and asked:
"How many pigeons do you keep?"
Zǐ could only murmur a reply and withdraw.
He suspected that Gōng liked pigeons,
and thought about how to reciprocate, but giving them up was truly difficult.
Yet he also considered that an elder's request
should not be denied repeatedly.
And he dared not respond with common pigeons,
so he selected two white pigeons,
sent them in a cage,
believing it was no less than a gift of a thousand pieces of gold.
Another day, he saw Gōng,
who had a somewhat self-satisfied air;
but he offered not a single word of thanks.
Unable to bear it,
he asked:
"Were the birds good?"
He replied:
"They were quite plump and tasty."
Zhāng was startled and said:
"You cooked them?"
He said:
"Yes."
Zhāng was greatly alarmed and said:
"These were no ordinary pigeons;
they were what people call 'Dádá'
ones!"
Gōng thought back and said:
"The taste wasn't particularly different either."
Zhāng sighed in regret and returned.
That night,
he dreamed that a young man in white clothes arrived,
and reproached him, saying:
"I trusted you to cherish them,
and so entrusted my offspring to you.
Why did you cast pearls before swine
and let them be destroyed in the cooking pot!
Now I will lead my children away."
Having spoken,
he transformed into a pigeon,
and all the white pigeons Zhāng kept followed him,
flying and cooing as they went directly away.
At dawn, he looked,
and indeed they were all gone.
He felt great regret,
and so gave away all the pigeons he kept
to his close friends,
and they were all gone within a few days.
Yìshǐ Shì said:
"Things always gather where they are appreciated.
Therefore, when Yè Gōng liked dragons,
a real dragon entered his house;
how much more so for a scholar with good friends,
or a virtuous ruler with worthy ministers?
But as for this thing called 'money',
many more people like it,
yet very few accumulate it.
This also shows that gods and spirits are angered by greed,
but not by foolishness."
Previously, a friend sent some vermilion crucian carp to Sūn Gōngzǐ Yǔnián.
His household had no intelligent servant,
so he sent an old domestic worker.
Upon reaching the gate,
the worker poured out the water and the fish,
asking for a bowl to present them.
By the time he reached his master,
the fish were already shriveled and dead.
Gōngzǐ smiled and said nothing,
rewarded the worker with wine,
and then cooked the fish to serve him.
When he returned,
the master asked:
"Was Gōngzǐ pleased with the fish?"
He replied:
"Extremely pleased."
He asked:
"How do you know?"
He said:
"Gōngzǐ smiled happily upon seeing the fish,
immediately ordered wine to be given,
and even cooked several fish to reward this humble person."
The master was greatly alarmed,
thinking that the gift he had sent
was not at all inferior,
so why would it be cooked and given to a subordinate?
He then reproached him, saying:
"It must be your stupidity, stubbornness, and lack of manners,
which angered Gōngzǐ."
The worker raised his hand and forcefully argued:
"Although I am crude and clumsy,
it's not as if an uncouth person entered Gōngzǐ's door;
I was extremely careful,
still fearing that the 'night bucket' might be improper,
so I respectfully asked for a bowl,
and arranged them one by one before presenting them.
How was anything not thoroughly considered?"
The master cursed and dismissed him.
A certain monk at Língyǐn Sì
was famous for his tea;
his pots and mortars were all exquisite.
However, the tea he kept was of several grades,
and he always brewed and offered it according to the guest's status;
the highest grade
was never served except to noble guests and connoisseurs.
One day,
a corrupt official arrived.
The monk served him with extreme deference,
brought out good tea,
and personally brewed and offered it,
hoping to receive praise.
The corrupt official remained silent.
The monk was very perplexed,
and again brewed and offered the very highest grade.
The drinking was almost finished,
but there was no word of praise.
The monk, impatient,
bowed and said:
"How is the tea?"
The official held up his cup, made a slight bow, and said:
"Very hot."
These two incidents
can be laughed at together with Zhāng Gōngzǐ's gift of pigeons.
According to a manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio.
The Prince of Lù in Huáiqìng
was of depraved character.
He often traveled among the common people,
and whenever he spied a good woman,
he would seize her.
The wife of Wáng Shēng
was seen by the Prince,
who sent palanquins and horses directly to her home.
The woman cried and refused,
but was forcibly carried out.
Wáng fled,
hiding himself at Niè Zhèng's tomb,
hoping his wife would pass by
so he could bid her a distant farewell.
Soon after,
his wife arrived,
saw her husband,
and cried loudly, falling to the ground.
Wáng was moved to pity,
and inadvertently cried out.
His followers recognized him as Wáng Shēng,
seized him,
and were about to flog him.
Suddenly, a man emerged from the tomb,
holding a white blade in his hand,
with a fierce and mighty presence.
He sternly said:
"I am Niè Zhèng!
How can a respectable woman be forcibly taken!
Considering that you lot are not acting of your own free will,
I will pardon you for now.
Tell the unprincipled Prince: if he does not change his ways,
before long I will pluck out his head!"
The crowd was greatly terrified,
abandoned their carriage, and fled.
The man also entered the tomb and disappeared.
The couple kowtowed at the tomb and returned,
still fearing the Prince's order would come again.
After more than ten days,
there was still no news,
and their hearts finally settled.
From then on, the Prince's tyrannical power reportedly diminished somewhat.
Yìshǐ Shì said:
"When I read 'Biographies of Assassins',
I alone am convinced by Zhǐ Shēnjǐnglǐ: his eagerness to repay his benefactor
has the righteousness of Yù;
his public assassination of a high official
has the bravery of Zhū;
his self-mutilation of his face
without implicating his bones
has the wisdom of Cáo.
As for Jīng Kē,
his strength was insufficient to plot against the unprincipled Qín,
and so he made a futile boast and departed,
bringing about his own destruction;
lightly borrowing Fán Jiāngjūn's head,
when could it ever be returned?
This is a regret for all ages,
and something Niè Zhèng would scorn.
I heard from unofficial histories: his grave was dug up by the ghosts of Yáng and Zuǒ.
If that is true,
then alive he failed to achieve renown,
and dead he still lost his righteousness.
How does he compare in worthiness to Niè, who harbored righteous indignation and punished depravity?
Alas!
Niè's worthiness
is all the more evident from this."
According to a manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio.
Lěng Shēng from Píngchéng
was extremely dull when young.
At over twenty years of age,
he still couldn't master a single classic.
Suddenly, a fox came
and lived intimately with him.
Every now and then, people heard them talking all night.
When his brothers questioned him,
he wouldn't reveal anything.
After many days like this,
he suddenly developed a peculiar illness: whenever he got a topic for an essay,
he would close his door and sit silently.
A short while later,
he would burst into loud laughter.
Peeking in,
they would see his hand constantly writing,
and an essay would be finished.
Once he drafted it,
his literary thoughts were also exquisite and subtle.
That year, he passed the entrance exam for the county school,
and the next year, he received his stipend.
Every time he was in the examination hall, he would laugh so loudly
that it echoed through the hall walls.
Because of this,
the name "Xiào Shēng"
became widely known.
Fortunately, the provincial education commissioner [xuéshǐ] had retired
and didn't hear of it.
Later, a certain education commissioner, who was strict and serious,
sat solemnly in the hall all day.
Suddenly hearing laughter,
he angrily seized Lěng Shēng,
intending to punish him severely.
The arresting official explained his madness on his behalf.
The commissioner's anger subsided slightly,
and he released him,
but struck his name off the register.
From then on, Lěng Shēng feigned madness and indulged in wine.
He authored
"Diān Cǎo"
in four volumes,
which is exceptionally brilliant and worth reciting.
The Historian [Yìshǐ Shì] says:
"Closing the door and laughing,
how is that different from a Buddhist's moment of sudden enlightenment?
Writing an essay with a loud laugh
is also a delightful thing.
Why should he be expelled for it?
Such an official in charge,
is he not utterly ignorant?"
Lěng Shēng's teacher, Sūn Jǐngxià,
was visiting a friend.
When he reached his window,
he heard no one speaking,
only the sound of laughter, "chī rán,"
repeated several times in a short while.
He thought Lěng Shēng was playing with someone.
When he looked,
Lěng Shēng was sitting there alone.
He found it strange.
Lěng Shēng then laughed loudly and said,
"I had nothing to do just now,
so I was silently rehearsing a funny story."
Gōng Shēng from the same district [yì],
kept a donkey at home,
which was stubborn and ill-tempered.
Whenever he encountered a pedestrian on the road,
he would bow and say apologetically,
"I'm busy right now,
and don't have time to dismount,
please don't blame me!"
Before he had finished speaking,
the donkey would have already bucked and collapsed onto the road,
and this trick never failed.
Gōng Shēng was greatly ashamed and resentful,
so he conspired with his wife,
making her pretend to be a passerby.
He then rode the donkey around the courtyard,
bowed to his wife,
and uttered the words he used when meeting a guest.
The donkey indeed collapsed.
He then fiercely pricked it with a sharp awl.
Just then, a friend came to visit,
and was about to knock on the gate,
when he heard Gōng Shēng say from inside,
"I don't have time to dismount,
please don't blame me!"
A moment later,
he said it again.
Feeling very strange,
he knocked on the door and asked for the reason.
Gōng Shēng told him the truth,
and they both burst into laughter.
These two anecdotes
can be appended to Lěng Shēng's laughter to be passed down.
According to the "Liáozhāi Zhìyì" Xùexuězhāi manuscript.
A certain scholar bought a new residence [dì],
and was constantly troubled by a fox.
All his clothes [fúwù],
were largely ruined by it,
and it often put dust into his soup and cakes [tāngbǐng].
One day,
a friend visited.
The scholar happened to be out [chū],
and didn't return until evening.
His wife prepared a meal for the guest,
and later ate the leftover food with her maid.
The scholar was always unrestrained [bùjī]
and fond of keeping aphrodisiacs [mèiyào].
No one knows when,
the fox put the medicine into the porridge.
The wife ate it [shí zhī],
and felt the scent of musk and brain-musk [nǎoshè qì].
She asked the maid,
and the maid said she didn't know.
After eating,
she felt a surging desire,
which she could not endure for a moment.
She forced herself to suppress it,
but her dryness and thirst became more urgent.
She considered that there was no one in the house she could turn to [bēnzhe],
except for the guest.
So she went and knocked on his study door.
The guest asked who it was.
She told him the truth.
He asked what she wanted to do,
but she didn't answer.
The guest excused himself, saying,
"I have a righteous friendship with your husband,
and would not dare to behave like a beast."
The wife still lingered.
The guest shouted and cursed, saying,
"Brother Mǒu's [Mǒu] literary talent and character [wénzhāng pǐnxíng]
will be completely ruined by you!"
He spat through the window at her.
The wife was greatly ashamed [dà cán],
and then retreated.
She then thought to herself: Why am I acting like this?
Suddenly recalling the fragrance in the bowl,
could it be an aphrodisiac?
She checked the medicine in the package,
and indeed, it was scattered all over the table,
and in the pots and bowls.
She knew that cold water could alleviate it,
so she drank some.
In a short while,
her mind became clear.
Her shame made her unable to show her face.
After tossing and turning for a long time,
the night watch had already dwindled.
She feared even more that it would be hard to face people at dawn.
So she untied her belt and hanged herself.
The maid discovered her and saved her,
but her breathing had already almost stopped.
It was after Chen hour [chén] (7-9 AM)
that she finally had a faint breath.
The guest had already fled during the night.
The scholar returned only after lunch [bǔ hòu],
saw his wife lying down,
and asked her,
but she didn't speak,
only shed silent tears.
The maid reported the situation.
He was greatly shocked [dà jīng],
and questioned her intensely.
His wife sent the maid away,
and then finally told him the truth.
The scholar sighed, saying,
"This is the retribution for my own lewdness;
how can I blame you, my dear?
Fortunately, I have a good friend;
otherwise,
how could I remain a proper person!"
From then on, he thoroughly reformed his past conduct,
and the fox also completely ceased its activities.
The Historian [Yìshǐ Shì] says:
"Those at home warn each other not to keep arsenic [pīzhèn],
but there are never any who warn each other not to keep aphrodisiacs.
This is like people using weapons against others but being intimate in bed.
Who knows that their poison is even worse than arsenic?
Yet, keeping them is merely to charm one's wife!
This even incurs the jealousy of ghosts and spirits.
Moreover, human indulgence in lust,
is there anything worse than keeping such medicine?"
A certain scholar,
returning from the county seat,
as dusk had fallen,
brought back lotus seeds, water chestnuts, and lotus roots.
Entering his room,
he placed them all on a table.
He also had a rattan-like counterfeit item,
which he immersed in a jar of water.
His neighbors, learning of his recent return,
brought wine and entered the hall.
In a hurry, the scholar placed the jar under the bed and went out,
telling his wife to prepare food and drink,
and had a light drink with his guests.
After the drinking,
he went inside,
and urgently lit a candle under the bed;
the water in the jar was already empty.
He asked his wife,
who said:
"Just now I brought it out with the water chestnuts and lotus roots to serve the guests.
Why are you still looking for it?"
The scholar recalled seeing black strips mixed in the dishes,
and no one at the table knew what they were.
He then burst out laughing and said:
"You foolish woman!
What kind of thing is this,
that it could be served to guests?"
His wife also said, doubtfully:
"I was still complaining that you didn't tell me how to cook it;
its appearance was ugly,
and I didn't know its name,
so I just haphazardly chopped it up."
The scholar then told her,
and they both burst into laughter.
Now that certain scholar is esteemed,
but those close to him still joke about it.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì (聊齋誌異):
Yìshān Shānshì (矣山山市),
is one of the sights of the county.
For several years, it has not been seen even once.
Sūn Gōngzǐ Yǔnián (孫公子禹年),
was drinking upstairs with his companions when
he suddenly saw a solitary pagoda rising from the mountaintop,
soaring high into the blue sky.
They looked at each other in surprise and doubt,
thinking there was no such Buddhist monastery nearby.
Soon after,
they saw dozens of palaces,
with green tiles and flying eaves, and realized it was a Shānshì.
Before long,
high walls with battlements,
stretched for six or seven *lǐ*,
and it truly became a city.
Within it were what seemed to be towers, what seemed to be halls, and what seemed to be marketplaces,
all clearly visible,
numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Suddenly a strong wind rose,
and the dust filled the air diffusely,
the city then only vaguely visible.
After a while, the wind subsided and the sky cleared;
everything was gone;
only a single precarious tower
reached directly into the sky.
All five windowpanes were wide open;
in one row there were five bright spots,
which was the sky outside the tower.
Counting the layers: the higher the tower,
the fewer the bright spots;
counting up to the eighth floor,
they were barely like specks of stars;
and above that,
they were dim and indistinct,
and its number of layers could not be counted.
People on the tower moved busily back and forth,
some leaning, some standing,
in various postures.
After some time,
the tower gradually lowered,
its top becoming visible;
then it gradually became like an ordinary tower;
then gradually like a tall house;
and suddenly like a fist or a bean,
then it could no longer be seen.
It is also said that early travelers
saw human dwellings and market stalls on the mountain,
no different from the world,
hence it is also called
"Ghost Market"
they say.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋) manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì (聊齋誌異):
Gāo Fān (高蕃) from Línjiāng (臨江),
was intelligent from a young age,
and had a handsome and refined appearance.
At fourteen, he entered the district school.
Many families vied to offer their daughters to him;
the scholar was extremely particular in his choices,
repeatedly thwarting his father's wishes.
His father, Zhònghóng (仲鴻),
was sixty years old,
and had only this son,
whom he doted on,
unable to upset him even slightly.
In the east village, there was a Fán Wēng (樊翁),
who taught children in the marketplace,
and moved his family to rent the scholar's house.
The elder had a daughter,
whose childhood name was Jiāngchéng (江城),
the same age as the scholar,
both around eight or nine years old at the time.
The two youngsters were innocent playmates,
playing together daily.
Later, the elder moved away,
and for four or five years,
nothing more was heard of them.
One day,
the scholar, in a narrow alley,
saw a girl,
whose beauty was extraordinary.
She was accompanied by a small maidservant,
only six or seven years old.
He dared not gaze directly,
but only stole a sidelong glance.
The girl paused her gaze,
as if she wanted to speak.
Looking closely,
it was Jiāngchéng.
He was greatly surprised and delighted.
Neither spoke,
standing still and staring at each other.
After some time, they parted,
both reluctant.
The scholar intentionally dropped a red handkerchief on the ground and left.
The small maidservant picked it up,
and happily gave it to the girl.
The girl put it into her sleeve,
exchanged it for her own handkerchief,
and falsely told the maidservant:
"Scholar Gāo (高) is not a stranger;
you must not conceal his lost item,
you should return it to him."
The small maidservant indeed chased after him and handed it to the scholar.
The scholar was greatly pleased to receive the handkerchief.
Returning home, he saw his mother,
and asked her to discuss marriage.
His mother said:
"Her family has not even half a room,
wandering north and south,
how can she be a suitable match?"
The scholar said:
"I desire her myself,
so I will certainly have no regrets."
His mother could not decide,
and consulted Zhònghóng;
Hóng firmly disagreed.
The student heard this and was disconsolate,
unable to swallow a single grain.
His mother was greatly worried,
and said to Gāo:
"Though the Fán family is poor,
they are not like unscrupulous rascals.
I will go visit their home;
if their daughter is suitable,
there should be no harm."
Gāo said:
"Agreed."
His mother, pretending to burn incense at the Hēidì Cí,
went there.
She saw the girl with bright eyes and beautiful teeth,
indeed charming,
and her heart was greatly pleased.
So she presented her with generous gifts of gold and silk,
and frankly stated her intention.
Fán Ǎo humbly declined but later accepted the betrothal.
Upon returning, she recounted the situation,
and the student finally broke into a smile.
After more than a year,
an auspicious day was chosen to bring the girl home,
and the couple was very happy together.
However, the girl was prone to anger,
turning her eyes away as if not recognizing him;
her words were sharp and mocking,
constantly grating on his ears.
Out of love,
the student endured it all.
His parents heard of this,
and were displeased,
secretly reproaching their son.
When the girl overheard,
she became furious,
and her abusive language increased.
The student gradually retorted her harsh words,
and the girl grew even angrier,
beating him and driving him out of the house,
closing the door.
The student lingered outside the door,
not daring to knock,
and slept under the eaves with his knees hugged.
From then on, the girl treated him like an enemy.
At first,
kneeling for a long time could still resolve things;
gradually, kneeling became ineffective,
and the husband suffered even more.
His parents mildly reproached her,
but the girl was indescribably defiant.
His parents became indignant
and forced her to return to her parents' home.
Fán, feeling ashamed and fearful,
asked mutual friends to intercede with Zhònghóng;
Zhònghóng did not agree.
More than a year later,
the student met his father-in-law outside;
his father-in-law invited him to his home,
apologizing profusely.
The dressed-up daughter came out to meet him,
and as the couple looked at each other,
they couldn't help but feel a pang of sorrow.
Fán then bought wine to entertain his son-in-law,
urging him to drink with great warmth.
As night fell,
he insisted that he stay overnight,
swept a separate bed,
and made the couple sleep together.
At dawn, he bid farewell to return,
not daring to tell his parents about the situation,
covering it up.
From then on, every three to five days,
he would occasionally stay at his in-laws' house for the night,
but his parents were unaware.
One day, Fán himself went to see Zhònghóng.
At first, he was not seen,
but eventually he was admitted.
Fán knelt and pleaded,
but Gāo did not agree,
deferring to his son.
Fán said:
"The son-in-law stayed at my house last night,
and I heard no dissenting words."
Gāo was surprised and asked:
"When did he stay?"
Fán told him everything.
Gāo humbly apologized, saying:
"I truly did not know.
If he loves her,
why should I be an enemy?"
After Fán left,
Gāo called his son and scolded him.
The student merely bowed his head,
not daring to breathe.
While they were speaking,
Fán had already brought the daughter back.
Gāo said:
"I cannot bear the fault for my children,
it's better for each to establish their own household,
please bother yourself with the agreement to divide the kitchen."
Fán tried to persuade him,
but he wouldn't listen.
So, they lived in a separate courtyard,
and a maid was sent to serve them.
After more than a month,
they were quite at peace,
and the parents were secretly relieved.
Before long,
the girl gradually became more unrestrained,
and there were often claw marks on the student's face;
his parents knew it clearly,
but endured it and did not question.
One day,
the student, unable to bear the beating,
ran to his father's place for refuge,
looking distraught like a bird attacked by a hawk.
Just as his parents were asking in surprise,
