the girl had already entered, pursuing him with a horizontal stick,
and even caught him by his father's side and beat him.
His parents cried out in tears,
but she paid no heed,
beating him dozens of times
before finally leaving in a huff.
Gāo drove his son away, saying:
"I only sought to avoid the clamor,
which is why I separated you;
if you enjoy this,
how can you escape?"
The student, being driven out,
leaned about with nowhere to go.
His mother, fearing he would be crushed and die,
made him live alone and provided him with food.
She also summoned Fán,
to make him teach his daughter.
Fán entered the room,
and tried to reason with her in every way,
but the girl still would not listen,
instead responding with harsh words.
Fán left in a huff;
vowing to cut ties.
Not long after,
Fán Wēng became ill from anger,
and he and his wife successively died.
The girl hated them,
and did not even attend their funerals,
only yelling abuses through the wall daily,
deliberately making his parents hear.
Gāo pretended to be completely unaware.
The student, living alone,
was as if removed from fire and boiling water,
but only felt desolate.
Secretly, he bribed the matchmaker Lǐ Shì with gold,
bringing a courtesan into his study,
their comings and goings always at night.
After a long time,
the girl vaguely heard about it,
and went to the study to scold him.
The student vehemently denied the accusation,
swearing by heaven and sun,
and the girl finally returned home.
From then on,
she daily watched for the student's lapses.
When Lǐ Ǎo came out of the study,
she happened to meet her,
and immediately called out to her;
the old woman's expression changed,
making the girl even more suspicious,
and she said to the old woman:
"Tell me clearly what you've done,
and perhaps you can be pardoned;
if there are any secrets,
you'll be completely ruined!"
The old woman trembled and said:
"For the past half month,
only the go-between Lǐ Yúnniáng has passed by twice.
Just now, the young master said
he saw Táo Jiāfù on Yùsì Shān,
admired her small feet,
and instructed this servant to invite her.
Although she is not chaste,
she isn't necessarily a 'night-visiting lady' right away,
so whether it will happen is still uncertain."
The girl, believing her words to be sincere,
provisionally granted her leniency.
The old woman wanted to leave,
but was strongly detained again.
When it was already dark,
she reprimanded her, saying:
"You can first go and extinguish her candle,
then say that the Táojiā have arrived."
The old woman did as she was told.
The young woman immediately hurried away.
Shēng was overjoyed,
pulled her arm and urged her to sit,
fully expressing his hunger and thirst,
but the young woman remained silent.
Shēng groped for her feet in the dark,
and said:
"I saw an immortal guest on the mountain,
and I am singularly fond of these ears."
The young woman still said nothing.
Shēng said:
"My long-cherished wish
is now finally fulfilled,
how can you face me and not recognize me?"
He personally hastened to light a fire to illuminate,
and it was then Jiāngchéng.
He was greatly frightened and turned pale,
dropping the candle to the ground,
and knelt down trembling,
as if a blade were at his neck.
The young woman pinched his ear and led him back,
pricking both his thighs almost everywhere with a needle,
then made him lie down on the bed.
When he woke, she scolded him.
Shēng thenceforth feared her like tigers and wolves;
even if she occasionally showed him some kindness,
in bed,
he was still so intimidated he could not act like a man.
The young woman slapped his cheek and yelled at him to leave,
further disdaining and treating him as less than human.
Shēng spent his days in a fragrant boudoir,
like a prisoner in a jail,
revering the jailer.
The young woman had two elder sisters,
both married to scholars.
The eldest sister, Píngshàn,
was slow of speech,
and often did not get along with the young woman.
The second sister married into the Gě clan,
and was cunning and articulate.
She admired herself and struck poses,
her appearance not matching Jiāngchéng,
but her ferocity and jealousy were equal.
When the sisters met, they had no other words,
but each boasted of her domestic authority.
Because of this, the two were best friends.
When Shēng visited relatives or friends,
the young woman would get angry;
only when he went to Gě's place
did she know and not forbid it.
One day,
he drank at Gě's place.
When he was drunk,
Gě mocked him, saying:
"Why are you so afraid of her?"
Shēng laughed and said:
"There are many things in the world that are hard to understand: my fear
is fear of her beauty;
but there is someone whose beauty is not equal to my wife's,
yet he is more afraid than I am.
Is this not even more perplexing?"
Gě was greatly ashamed
and could not reply.
A maidservant overheard this
and told the second sister.
The second sister was furious,
grabbed a stick and rushed out.
Shēng, seeing her ferocity,
shuffled his feet wanting to run.
The stick was raised
and already hit his waist and back;
three blows and he stumbled three times, unable to get up.
He was accidentally hit on the skull,
and blood flowed like wine.
The second sister left,
and Shēng limped home.
His wife asked him in surprise.
At first, fearing it was due to offending his sister-in-law,
he dared not tell her immediately;
after repeated questioning,
he finally recounted everything.
The young woman bandaged Shēng's head with a cloth
and angrily said:
"What a household! What need is there for others to beat and chastise my husband!"
She changed into short sleeves,
tucked a wooden pestle into her bosom,
and, taking a maidservant,
headed directly out.
Upon arriving at Gě's house,
the second sister greeted her with smiles and conversation.
The young woman said nothing,
struck her with the pestle,
making her fall;
her trousers ripped, and she was in pain.
Her teeth fell out and her lips were cut,
and she involuntarily urinated and defecated.
The young woman returned,
and the second sister, in shame and anger,
sent her husband to complain to Gāo.
Shēng rushed out
and tried his best to comfort him warmly.
Gě whispered:
"My coming here
is something I had to do.
That fierce woman is heartless;
luckily, I used your hand to punish and discipline her.
What grudge do the two of us have?"
The young woman had already heard this,
and rushed out,
pointing and scolding:
"Filthy rogue!
Your wife suffers,
yet you secretly make friends with outsiders!
Should such a man
not be beaten to death?!"
She furiously called for a stick.
Gě was greatly embarrassed
and bolted out the door.
From then on, Shēng had no place at all to visit.
His schoolmate Wáng Zǐyǎ visited him
and, after some persuasion, stayed for a drink.
During the drinking,
they joked about women,
quite indecently.
The young woman happened to be peeking at the guest,
listened, and understood everything,
secretly adding croton beans to the soup and serving it.
Before long,
he vomited and had diarrhea uncontrollably,
barely clinging to life.
The young woman sent a maidservant to ask him:
"Do you dare to be rude again?"
Only then did he realize the source of his illness,
and groaned in agony.
Then mung bean soup was already prepared and waiting.
Drinking it stopped the symptoms.
From then on, his friends warned each other
not to drink at his house.
Wáng owned a liquor shop,
where there were many red plum blossoms.
He set up a feast and invited his associates.
Shēng, under the pretext of a literary society,
sought permission and went.
At dusk,
having become quite drunk,
Shēng said:
“There happens to be a famous courtesan from Nánchāng
living here temporarily,
we can call her to drink with us.”
Everyone was greatly pleased.
Only the scholar left his seat
and offered an excuse.
The group pulled him back, saying,
“Although the ears and eyes in the inner chambers are sharp,
they don't reach this far.”
Thereupon, they swore to keep silent.
The scholar then resumed his seat.
After a short while,
the courtesan indeed came out.
She was seventeen or eighteen years old,
with jade pendants tinkling,
and her cloud-like hair neatly combed.
When asked her surname,
she said:
“My surname is Xiè,
and my given name is Fānglán.”
Her speech and manner
were exceedingly elegant and refined,
enchanting everyone present.
Yet Fānglán’s attention was drawn to the scholar,
and she repeatedly conveyed her feelings with her eyes.
Noticed by the others,
they deliberately pulled the two to sit shoulder-to-shoulder.
Fānglán secretly took the scholar's hand
and wrote the character
“宿” (sù)
on his palm with her finger.
At this moment,
the scholar wished to leave but could not bear to,
and wished to stay but dared not;
his heart was like tangled silk,
beyond words.
As they leaned their heads together for a whispered conversation,
her drunken state became even wilder,
and the “rouge tiger” on the bed
was also forgotten.
A short while later,
they heard the water clock had already chimed,
and the wine guests in the establishment were becoming fewer;
only a handsome young man in a distant seat
was drinking alone by candlelight,
with a young page holding a towel attending him.
Everyone secretly admired his refined elegance.
Before long,
the young man stopped drinking
and went out the door.
The page returned,
and said to the scholar:
“My master wishes to say a word to you.”
Everyone else was bewildered,
but the scholar’s expression changed dramatically,
he did not have time to say goodbye,
and hastily left.
It turned out that the young man was Jiāngchéng,
and the page was her family’s maid.
The scholar followed her home
and endured a beating.
From then on, his confinement became stricter,
and all visits for condolences or congratulations were forbidden.
When Wénzōng went to school,
the scholar was demoted to an apprentice due to a mistake in his lecture.
One day,
he spoke with the maid;
the wife suspected an affair,
and struck the maid’s head with a wine jar.
Afterwards, she tied up both the scholar and the maid,
and used embroidery scissors to cut flesh from their stomachs and swapped it,
then released them and made them tie themselves up.
More than a month later,
the wounds supposedly fused together.
The wife often stepped on cakes with her bare feet in the dirt,
and then commanded the scholar to pick them up and eat them.
Such incidents were numerous.
Because his mother missed her son,
she occasionally went to his house,
and seeing her son emaciated,
she returned home and cried bitterly, wishing to die.
That night, she dreamt of an old man who told her
He said,
"You need not worry or be troubled.
This is a long-lived rat nurtured by the monk Yuán Jìngyè of Jiāngchéng in a previous life.
In your previous life, the young master was a scholar,
who happened to travel to that place
and accidentally killed it.
Now, the evil deed is being repaid;
it cannot be reversed by human power.
Every morning,
sincerely recite the Guānyīn mantra a hundred times,
and it will surely be effective."
He awoke and recounted it to Zhònghóng,
who found it extraordinary.
The couple followed the instructions,
sincerely reciting for over two months.
The daughter's uncontrollable behavior remained unchanged,
and she became even more wild and unrestrained.
When she heard gongs and drums outside the gate,
she would immediately grasp her hair and rush out,
foolishly looking around.
Thousands of people would point and stare,
but she remained completely unconcerned.
Her parents-in-law were both ashamed of her,
yet could not restrain her.
Suddenly, an old monk proclaimed Buddhist teachings outside the gate,
with spectators packed like a wall.
The monk blew into the leather of a drum, making it sound like an ox lowing.
The daughter rushed out,
seeing no space among the crowd,
she ordered her maid to move a portable bed,
and climbed onto it, standing on tiptoe.
All eyes were fixed on her,
but the daughter seemed oblivious.
After a while,
the monk was about to finish his performance.
He asked for a bowl of clear water,
held it towards the daughter, and declared:
"Do not be angry,
do not be angry!
The past life was not false,
this life is not true.
Hmph!
Little rat, shrink your head and leave,
lest the cat find you."
After declaring this,
he sucked up water and spat it onto the daughter's face,
her makeup running messily,
staining her collar and sleeves.
Everyone was greatly alarmed,
expecting the daughter to burst into a rage,
but she said nothing.
She wiped her face and returned home on her own.
The monk also left.
The daughter entered her room and sat in a daze,
uttering sounds as if in mourning,
not eating all day.
She hastily swept the bed and went to sleep.
In the middle of the night,
she suddenly called Shēng awake.
Shēng suspected she might need to relieve herself,
and brought forward a urinal.
The daughter pushed it away,
secretly took Shēng's arm,
and pulled him into the quilt.
Shēng obeyed,
his body trembling with surprise,
as if receiving an imperial decree.
The daughter said with emotion,
"For a husband to be like this,
how can one be considered human!"
Then she caressed Shēng's body with her hand,
and whenever she reached a scar from a knife or staff,
she would whimper and sob,
and repeatedly pinch herself with her fingernails,
wishing she would die instantly.
Seeing her condition,
Shēng felt truly unbearable,
and comforted her very sincerely.
The daughter said,
"I believe that monk must be an incarnation of a Bodhisattva.
With one sprinkle of clear water,
it felt as if my inner organs were replaced.
Now recalling my past actions,
it all feels like a lifetime ago.
Was I not human then?
Having a husband and wife but unable to enjoy conjugal bliss,
having parents-in-law but unable to serve them,
what kind of heart was that truly!
Tomorrow, we can move back home
and live with my parents again,
so that I can easily pay my respects morning and evening."
They talked softly through the night,
as if catching up after ten years of separation.
At dawn, she immediately got up,
folded clothes and put away utensils.
The maid carried the basket,
and she herself carried the bedding bundle,
urging Shēng to go and knock on the door.
Her mother came out, surprised, and asked.
She told her of her intentions.
Her mother was still hesitant and looked troubled,
but the daughter had already entered with her maid.
Her mother followed her in.
The daughter prostrated herself on the ground, weeping mournfully,
only begging to be spared death.
Her mother perceived her sincerity,
and also wept, saying,
"How could I have become like this so quickly?"
Shēng recounted the previous events in detail,
and only then did she realize that the previous dream had come true.
Joyfully,
she called servants to clear out the old dwelling.
From then on, the daughter pleased her parents with her obedience,
surpassing even a filial son.
When she saw people,
she was shy like a new bride.
If someone playfully mentioned past events,
her cheeks would flush red.
Moreover, she was diligent and frugal,
and also good at accumulating wealth: after three years, the old couple no longer managed the household finances,
and their wealth was said to be immense.
Shēng passed the provincial examination that year.
She often said to Shēng,
"I still remember the day I first saw Fānglán."
Shēng, not having suffered abuse,
felt his wish was already sufficiently fulfilled,
and dared not entertain any wild thoughts,
only responding with agreement.
It happened that he had to go to the capital for the imperial examination,
and only returned after several months.
Entering the room,
he saw Fānglán was running towards Jiāngchéng.
He was surprised and asked about it,
and learned that his wife had bought her freedom for several hundred taels of silver.
This matter was recounted in great detail by Wáng Zǐyǎ of Zhèzhōng.
The Historian of the Strange said:
"The karmic results of human life,
eating and drinking, must be repaid.
And among karmic retributions, those concerning marriage
are like a festering sore attached to the bone,
their poison is especially cruel.
I often see that among women in the world, ten percent are virtuous wives,
and ninety percent are fierce wives,
which also shows that few people in the world are able to cultivate good karma.
The vow power of Guānzìzài is vast and great;
why not sprinkle the water from the bowl over the great trichiliocosm?"
According to the "Cast Snow Studio Manuscript" of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Sūnshēng,
married a daughter of the former Xīn clan.
When she first entered the household,
she wore narrow trousers,
and had many sashes,
which tightly bound her whole body.
She refused to share a bed with men.
At her bedside, she always kept a sharp tube-like instrument for self-defense.
Sūnshēng was repeatedly pricked and stabbed,
and consequently, slept on a separate bed.
After more than a month,
he still dared not "ask for the tripod" (i.e., attempt intimacy).
Even when they met in broad daylight,
the woman never offered a smile or a word.
A certain classmate of Sūnshēng's knew of this
and privately said to Sūnshēng:
"Can your wife drink?"
He replied:
"She drinks little."
The classmate joked:
"I have a method of adjustment,
which is good and workable."
Sūnshēng asked:
"What method?"
He said:
"Put a narcotic drug into wine,
give it to her to drink,
and then you can do whatever you wish."
Sūnshēng laughed,
but secretly thought the plan was good.
He inquired with a doctor,
and respectfully brewed Aconitum root in wine,
placing it on the table.
At night,
Sūnshēng poured and filtered the wine.
He drank several goblets alone and then went to bed.
After three such evenings,
his wife still did not drink.
One night,
Sūnshēng lay down for a while,
observing his wife still sitting quietly.
Sūnshēng deliberately made snoring sounds;
his wife then got out of bed,
and warmed the wine over the stove.
Sūnshēng secretly rejoiced.
"Then she drank a full cup;
she poured another,
finished about half of it,
put the rest back into the pot,
smoothed the bed, and went to sleep.
For a long time, there was no sound,
but the lamp was still brightly lit and had not gone out.
Suspecting she was still awake,
he shouted loudly:
"The tin wick holder is melting!"
His wife did not respond.
He called again, and still no response.
He got up and went to look,
finding her dead drunk like mud.
He opened her quilt and quietly slipped in,
layer by layer undoing her bindings.
His wife was indeed aware of it,
but could not move,
nor could she speak,
allowing him to take liberties.
When she awoke,
she detested it,
and hung herself with a rope.
Sūnshēng heard gasping sounds in his dream,
got up and rushed to look,
finding her tongue protruding about two inches.
Greatly alarmed,
he cut the rope,
supported her onto the bed,
and after some time, she revived.
From then on, Sūnshēng deeply hated her,
and husband and wife avoided each other,
bowing their heads when they met.
Four or five years passed,
without exchanging a single word.
Sometimes, when his wife was in the room,
laughing and playing with others;
upon seeing her husband approach,
her expression would immediately change,
becoming as stern as frost and snow.
Sūnshēng often stayed in the study,
not returning home for a year;
even if forced to return,
he would face the wall for a while,
and silently go to bed.
His parents were very worried about this.
One day,
an old nun came to their house,
saw the wife,
and praised her profusely.
The mother did not speak,
but only sighed deeply.
The nun questioned the reason,
and she explained the situation in detail.
The nun said:
"This is an easy matter."
The mother happily said,
"If you can change my daughter-in-law's mind,
I will not be stingy with the reward."
The nun observed that no one else was in the room,
and whispered:
"Buy a scroll of erotic paintings,
and three days later,
I will make her dislike it for you."
The nun left,
and the mother immediately bought one and waited.
Three days later,
the nun indeed came,
and instructed:
"This must be very discreet,
do not let the husband and wife know."
Then she cut out the figures from the painting,
and also three needles.
A pinch of mugwort,
all wrapped securely in plain paper,
with several worm-like drawings on the outside.
She instructed the mother to trick the wife out,
secretly take her pillow,
open its seam and put them inside;
then sew it back up,
and return it to its original place.
The nun then left.
In the evening,
the mother urged her son to return home to sleep.
The old maid went to eavesdrop.
As the second watch was about to end,
she heard the wife call Sūnshēng by his pet name,
but Sūnshēng did not answer.
A moment later,
the wife spoke again,
and Sūnshēng grumbled with annoyance.
At dawn,
the mother entered their room,
saw the husband and wife facing away from each other,
and knew the nun's trick was false.
She called her son to a private place,
and told him all about it.
Sūnshēng, hearing his wife's name,
immediately became angry,
grinding his teeth.
His mother scolded him angrily,
and left without looking back.
The next day,
the nun came,
and was told that it had no effect.
The nun was greatly puzzled.
The old maid then recounted what she had heard.
The nun smiled and said:
"Previously I said the wife disliked the husband,
hence her strong aversion.
Now the wife's feelings have changed,
but the husband's have not.
Please allow me to use a two-part method,
which will surely work."
The mother agreed,
and took her son's pillow as before, sealed the items within,
and again called him to return to sleep.
After the first watch,
she still heard turning and tossing sounds from both beds,
occasionally coughing,
both seemingly unable to sleep.
After a long time,
she heard the two talking softly on one bed,
but it was indistinct and incomprehensible.
As dawn approached,
she still heard laughter,
continuous giggling.
The old maid told the mother,
and the mother rejoiced.
When the nun came,
she was handsomely rewarded.
From then on, Sūnshēng and his wife lived in harmony.
They had one son and two daughters,
and for over ten years, there was never a single quarrel.
When others privately asked for the reason,
he smiled and said:
"Before, I saw her reflection and grew angry; afterwards, I heard her voice and was happy.
I myself don't understand what was in my heart."
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"To shift hatred to love,
the magic is truly divine.
However, what can make people happy,
can also make people angry;
the divinity of the sorcerer,
is precisely what makes the sorcerer formidable.
The ancient sage said: 'The six types of old women should not enter the home.'
How insightful!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Féng Shēng of Líntáo,
was descended from a noble family, but had fallen on hard times.
He owed money to a fisherman,
and, being in debt to him,
could not repay it.
Whenever he caught a turtle, he would offer it to the fisherman.
One day,
he offered a giant turtle,
which had a white spot on its forehead.
Féng Shēng, seeing its unusual appearance,
released it.
Later, returning home from his son-in-law's house,
he reached the side of the Hénghé river as dusk was falling.
He saw a drunk man,
accompanied by two or three young attendants,
staggering towards him.
From a distance, the drunk man saw Féng Shēng
and asked,
"Who are you?"
Féng Shēng casually replied,
"A traveler."
The drunk man angrily said,
"Have you no name,
to speak nonsensically of being a traveler?"
Féng Shēng was in a hurry,
so he ignored him and did not answer,
passing directly by him.
The drunk man grew even angrier,
grabbed Féng Shēng's sleeve, preventing him from moving,
and his alcoholic breath reeked.
Féng Shēng was even more annoyed,
but struggled in vain to break free.
He asked,
"What is your name?"
The drunk man stammered in reply,
"I am the former Jìnyǐn of Nándū.
What will you do about it?"
Féng Shēng said,
"If there are such Jìnyǐn in the world,
they would disgrace the world!
Fortunately, you are a former Jìnyǐn;
if you were the current Jìnyǐn,
would there be no travelers on the road?"
The drunk man became furious,
and it seemed he was about to use force.
Féng Shēng declared loudly,
"I, Féng Mǒu, am not one to be beaten!"
When the drunk man heard this,
his anger turned to joy,
and he stumbled forward and bowed, saying,
"You are my benefactor;
please forgive my rudeness!"
He rose and called his attendants,
telling them to return first and prepare a feast.
Féng Shēng tried to decline, but could not.
They walked hand in hand for several *lǐ*,
and saw a small village.
Upon entering,
they found the corridors and houses magnificent,
like those of a noble family.
As the drunk man sobered slightly,
Féng Shēng finally asked his name.
He said,
"Do not be alarmed when I tell you;
I am the Bādàwáng of Táoshuǐ.
Just now, Qīngtóng of Xīshān invited me to a drink,
and I unwittingly became overly drunk,
offending your esteemed presence.
I am truly ashamed and startled."
Féng Shēng knew he was a *yāo*,
but because of his sincere and warm words,
he no longer felt afraid.
Soon after, a lavish banquet was spread,
and they were urged to sit and drink merrily.
The Bādàwáng was very boisterous,
raising several cups in succession.
Féng Shēng, fearing he would get drunk again
and cause more trouble,
pretended to be drunk and asked to sleep.
The Bādàwáng understood his intention,
and laughed, saying,
"Are you perhaps afraid of my wildness?
Please do not be afraid.
People say that a drunk person's bad behavior,
which they claim not to remember the next morning,
is merely deceiving others.
The misconduct of a drunkard
is deliberately committed nine times out of ten.
Although I am not ranked among my peers,
I would never dare to behave so unscrupulously
towards an elder.
Why do you reject me so?"
Féng Shēng then sat down again,
and with a serious expression, admonished him, saying,
"Since you know this yourself,
why do you not change your ways?"
The Bādàwáng replied,
"When I was a Jìnyǐn,
my indulgence in drink was even worse than today.
After incurring the Emperor's wrath,
I was banished to this island.
For more than ten years, I have striven to return to my former path.
Now I am old and nearing death,
so debilitated that I cannot fly horizontally,
and my old habits have resurfaced.
I myself do not understand it.
Nevertheless, I respectfully heed your command."
While they chatted,
a distant bell chimed.
The Bādàwáng rose,
grasped Féng Shēng's arm, and said,
"We will not be together for long.
I have something kept aside
to repay your great kindness.
This cannot be worn for long;
once your wish is granted,
you must return it."
From his mouth, he spat out a small person,
only about an inch tall.
Then, he pinched Féng Shēng's arm with his claw,
causing painful skin lacerations;
he quickly pressed the small person onto the spot,
and upon releasing his hand, it had already entered the flesh.
The claw marks remained,
but the area slowly swelled up,
resembling a phlegm-nodule.
Féng Shēng, surprised, asked about it,
but he laughed and did not answer.
He only said,
"You should go now."
He escorted Féng Shēng out,
and the Bādàwáng returned.
Looking back, the village was completely gone,
only a giant turtle
clumsily entering the water and disappearing.
Féng Shēng was stunned for a long time.
He realized that what he had received
must be a turtle's treasure.
From then on, his eyes became extremely keen;
wherever there were jewels,
he could see them even beneath the Yellow Springs;
and even objects he had never known,
he could name them instantly.
In his bedroom,
he dug up several hundred strings of cash,
which fully supplied his expenses.
Later, when someone wanted to sell an old house,
Féng Shēng saw countless hidden strings of cash inside it,
so he bought and resided in it with a large sum of money.
From then on, he was as rich as kings and nobles.
He collected fire-agate and other precious stones.
He acquired a mirror,
with a phoenix knob on its back,
surrounded by images of water, clouds, and the Xiāngfēi;
its light shone for more than a *lǐ*,
and one could count every hair of one's beard and eyebrows.
If a beautiful woman gazed into it,
her reflection would remain within it,
and could not be removed by polishing: if she changed her makeup and looked again,
or if another beautiful woman looked,
the previous reflection would disappear.
At that time, the Third Princess of the Sù Fǔ was exceptionally beautiful.
He greatly admired her reputation.
It happened that the princess was traveling to Kōngdóng,
so he went and lay hidden in the mountains,
waiting for her to alight from her carriage.
He captured her image and returned,
setting it up on his desk.
He examined it closely,
and saw the beautiful woman within,
holding a handkerchief and smiling faintly,
her mouth about to speak and her gaze about to stir.
Delighted, he hid it.
After more than a year,
it was revealed by his wife,
and the Sù Fǔ heard of it.
The Prince was enraged,
and had him arrested.
They confiscated the mirror/image,
intending to execute him.
The scholar heavily bribed an influential courtier,
and had him speak to the Prince, saying:
“If Your Highness grants a pardon,
the greatest treasures in the world
will not be difficult to obtain.
Otherwise,
he will simply die,
which would truly bring no benefit to Your Highness.”
The Prince intended to confiscate his family’s property and exile him.
The Third Princess said:
“He has already spied on me;
even ten deaths would not be enough to erase this stain.
It would be better to marry him.”
The Prince would not permit it.
The Princess shut her door and refused to eat.
The Princess Consort was greatly distressed,
and strongly pleaded with the Prince.
The Prince then released the imprisoned scholar,
ordering the courtier to subtly convey his intention to the scholar.
The scholar declined, saying:
“An old wife who has shared hardship should not be dismissed.
I would rather die than accept such a command.
If Your Highness would allow me to speak of a redemption,
I could offer my entire family fortune.”
The Prince was enraged,
and had him arrested again.
The Princess Consort summoned the scholar’s wife into the palace,
intending to poison her.
When they met,
the wife presented the Princess Consort with a coral mirror stand,
her words and demeanor gentle and compassionate.
The Princess Consort was pleased with her,
and had her meet the Princess.
The Princess was also pleased with her,
and they became sworn sisters,
then had her convey a message to the scholar.
The scholar told his wife:
“The daughter of a prince or marquis
cannot be categorized as principal or secondary based on precedence.”
The wife did not listen,
but returned home to prepare the betrothal gifts and send them to the Prince’s residence.
The procession of gifts and musicians numbered nearly a thousand people.
Among the precious stones and jade,
there were some whose names the Prince’s household did not even know.
The Prince was greatly pleased,
released the scholar,
and married the Princess to him.
The Princess still carried the mirror/image when she returned.
One night, the scholar slept alone,
and dreamed that Bādàwáng grandly entered and said:
“The object that was presented (to you)
should be returned.
If it is worn for too long,
it will deplete one’s vital essence and blood,
and shorten one’s lifespan.”
The scholar agreed,
and immediately invited him to a feast.
Bādàwáng declined, saying:
“Since I started hearing (the advice of) medicine,
I have abstained from intoxicants,
and it has been three years already.”
Then he bit the scholar’s arm,
causing extreme pain, and he awoke.
He looked,
and the lump had disappeared.
After this, he was like a normal person again.
The Historian of the Strange (Yìshǐshì) comments:
“When sober, he is still a human;
but when drunk, he is like a soft-shelled turtle.
This is largely true of drinkers.
Yet, though the turtle may be accustomed to daily drunken frenzy,
it dares not forget kindness,
nor be disrespectful to elders.
Is the turtle not far superior to humans?
As for Mr. Jǐ, when sober, he is not as good as a human,
and when drunk, he is not as good as a soft-shelled turtle.
The ancients had the ‘turtle’s mirror’ (guījiàn);
perhaps it was intended as a ‘soft-shelled turtle’s mirror’ (biējiàn).
Thus, I compose the "Rhapsody on Drinkers" (Jiǔrén Fù).
The Rhapsody says:
『There is an object,
which delights the spirit and pleases the palate;
drink it, and one becomes tipsy and elated,
its name is
“Jiǔ”.
Its names are manifold,
its功 (gōng) has been long-standing: to feast honored guests,
to hasten fathers-in-law and uncles,
to draw knees together in joy,
to join goblets and become a pair;
some consider it
“the hook for fishing poems”,
others deem it
“the broom for sweeping away sorrow”.
Therefore, when Qūshēng (Qūshēng) frequently arrives,
he is a sworn friend of the literati;
in the depths of the realm of intoxication,
he is a refuge for the sorrowful.
When the terrace of dregs and hills is completed,
the achievement of Chíyí (Chíyí) is imperishable;
the official of Qí (Qí) was thus able to drink a shí (shí),
and scholars likewise claimed five dòu (dòu).
Thus, jiǔ (jiǔ) is indeed transmitted by people,
and people are sometimes disgraced by jiǔ (jiǔ).
As for Mèng Jiā (Mèng Jiā) who lost his cap,
Bó Lún (Bó Lún) who carried a spade,
Shān Gōng (Shān Gōng) who overturned his wine vessel,
and Péng Zé (Péng Zé) who strained it with a kudzu scarf.
Sleeping soundly beside beauties,
some might perceive him as unburdened;
when a scholar’s head nods into ink,
he himself feels inspired.
There were gentlemen who lay at the bottom of boats,
and ministers adorned with jade who were tied by the wine trough.
Even those who imitate a turtle and play with the world,
it is still not harmful to creatures nor inhumane.
As for rainy nights and snowy evenings,
moonlit dawns and flower-filled mornings,
when the wind settles and dust is short,
guests are old and courtesans new,
slippers and shoes intermingle,
the fragrance of orchids and musk settles,
finely slicing and lightly dabbing,
singing softly and sipping gently;
suddenly, when a clear melody is played,
it becomes silent as if no one were there.
Elegant jokes make flowers bloom from teeth,
lofty chants strike jade and tap gold.
Completely absorbed and greatly intoxicated,
their souls are pure and dreams real.
If so,
even getting drunk once a day,
should not incur the wrath of the doctrines of ritual.
Then there are those who are noisy and unharmonious,
with vulgar words spoken freely;
sitting and rising with loud clamor,
forming rows of nagging.
Squabbling over every drop,
threatening to draw knives;
stretching necks and knitting brows,
raising cups as if they contained zhen (zhèn) poison;
overturning and shattering goblets,
knocking over lamps and extinguishing embers.
Green wine and grapes,
scattered wastefully without regret;
sick leaves and wild flowers,
forbidden by the rules of drinking.
Such a state of mind,
it is better not to drink.
Then there are those whose wine is only an inch from their throat,
yet they do not drink it;
muttering and whispering,
still criticizing the host for being stingy,
they sit idly without speaking,
and are incapable of drinking further: such a lack of character in a wine guest,
is the worst.
Even more, when the mad medicine descends,
the guest's temper becomes coarse;
they glare with stony eyes,
and bristle their beard and whiskers;
they bare both arms,
and stomp their feet.
Dust billows across their face,
vomit splatters their robe;
they bark like a sow,
their hair disheveled like a slave.
When they curse the earth and call to heaven,
it is like Lǐ Láng (Lǐ Láng) retching his internal organs,
when they throw themselves down and stamp their feet,
it is like Sū Xiàng (Sū Xiàng) being torn apart by an ox cart.
Those who have "lotuses blooming from their tongues" [eloquent speakers]
cannot fully describe their state;
those who take shadows before the lamp [artists]
cannot depict them.
Before their parents, they cause offense,
their weak wives and children are difficult to support.
Some, who are good friends of their father,
are inexplicably cursed by Guàn Fū (Guàn Fū).
Even gentle admonitions,
only increase their bewilderment and confusion.
This is called
“jiǔ xiōng (jiǔ xiōng)” [wine fiend],
beyond salvation.
There is only one method,
that can sober them up.
What is this method?
It only requires a stick.
Grasping their hands and feet,
like slaughtering a pig.
Just restrict it to their buttocks,
do not harm their head;
beat them until a hundred strokes or more,
and they will suddenly and completely awaken.』
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (Zhùxuězhāi) manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì (Liáozhāi Zhìyì).
A certain person from the district,
was frivolous and dissolute.
He happened to travel outside the village,
and saw a young woman riding a horse.
He said to his companions,
“I can make her smile.”
The others did not believe him,
and made a bet for a banquet.
The man immediately ran off,
came out in front of the horse,
and shouted repeatedly,
“I want to die!”
He then pulled out a thin piece of wood from the top of a wall beam,
about a foot long,
untied his belt and hung it over the wood,
then craned his neck as if to hang himself.
The woman indeed passed by and smiled at him,
and the others also laughed brightly.
After the woman had gone far,
the man still did not move,
which made the others laugh even more.
Upon closer inspection,
his tongue was out and eyes closed,
and his breath had truly ceased.
To hang oneself on a dry beam,
is it not indeed strange?
This can serve as a warning to the shallow and frivolous.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi (Zhùxuězhāi) manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì (Liáozhāi Zhìyì).
Luó Zǔ (Luó Zǔ),
was from Jìmò (Jìmò).
He was poor in his youth.
When it was the turn of his clan to provide a man for border defense,
they sent Luó (Luó).
Luó (Luó) lived on the border for several years
and had a son.
The駐防守備 (zhùfáng shǒubèi) treated him very kindly.
When the守備 (shǒubèi) was promoted to參將 (cānjīang) in Shǎnxī (Shǎnxī),
he wanted to take Luó (Luó) with him.
Luó (Luó) therefore entrusted his wife and son to his friend Lǐ (Lǐ),
and then went west.
From then on, he could not return for three years.
It so happened that the參將 (cānjīang) wanted to send a letter to the northern frontier,
so Luó (Luó) presented himself,
requesting to visit his wife and son along the way.
The參將 (cānjīang) agreed.
Luó returned home.
His wife was unharmed,
which greatly relieved him.
However, there was a man's discarded sandal under the bed,
which made him suspicious.
Shortly after, he went to thank Lǐ Shēn.
Lǐ offered wine with great hospitality;
his wife also spoke of Lǐ's kindness and righteousness,
and Luó was overcome with gratitude.
The next day, he said to his wife:
"I am going to deliver a message from my master,
and will not be able to return by evening,
so do not wait for me."
He went out the door, mounted his horse, and left.
He hid himself nearby,
and returned after the second watch.
He heard his wife talking in bed with Lǐ,
and was furious,
bursting in.
The two were terrified,
and knelt begging for their lives.
Luó drew his blade,
but then sheathed it again, saying:
"I initially took you for a human,
but now that you are like this,
killing you would only defile my sword!
I make you a pact: take my wife,
and fill my name in the registers as well;
my horses, weapons, and tools are still here.
I am gone."
Thereupon he left.
The villagers collectively reported it to the officials.
The officials flogged Lǐ,
who told the truth.
However, there was no evidence to corroborate the story,
nothing could be substantiated or relied upon.
They searched far and wide for Luó,
but he had completely disappeared without a trace.
The officials suspected that murder had been committed due to adultery,
and further shackled Lǐ and his wife;
more than a year later,
they both died in chains and cangues.
Then their son was sent by post-station to Jìmò.
Later, a woodcutter from Shíxiá Yíng went into the mountains
and saw a Daoist priest sitting in a cave,
who never sought food.
Everyone thought this unusual,
and subsequently provided him with food.
Some recognized him;
it was indeed Luó.
Offerings and gifts filled the cave,
but Luó never ate,
appearing to be disgusted by the world's clamor,
which is why visitors gradually became fewer.
After several years,
thickets of wormwood grew into a forest outside the cave.
Someone secretly spied on him,
and saw that he had not moved an inch from his sitting place.
After an even longer time,
they saw him wandering on the mountain,
but when they approached, he had vanished;
they went to look into the cave,
and saw that the dust on his clothes was as it had been before.
This made them even more curious.
After several more days, they went again,
and saw a jade pillar hanging down,
he had passed away in meditation long ago.
The local people built a temple for him;
every third month,
incense and paper offerings lined the road.
When his son went,
everyone called him "Little Luó Zǔ,"
and all the incense tax went to him. Now his descendants
still go once a year
to collect the tax money.
Liú Zōngyù from Yíshuǐ told me this in great detail.
I smiled and said:
"Nowadays, all the devotees
do not seek to become sages,
but only hope to become Buddhas or Patriarchs.
Please tell them all: if you want to become a Buddha instantly,
you must lay down your knife."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
There was a man surnamed Liú from this county,
who was a tiger in a cap.
Later, he moved from Zībó to Yí,
but his bad habits remained,
and the villagers all feared and detested him.
He had several *mǔ* of land,
adjoining that of Míao.
Míao was diligent,
and had planted many peach trees along the edge of his field.
When the peaches first bore fruit,
Míao's children went to pick them;
Liú angrily drove them away,
claiming the trees as his own.
The children cried and told their father.
While the father was still surprised and perplexed,
Liú was already at the door shouting insults,
and furthermore threatened to sue.
Míao smiled and tried to placate him.
Liú's anger was not appeased,
and he left indignantly.
At that time, Lǐ Cuìshí, from the same county, was working as a pawnshop owner in Yí.
Liú went into the city with his complaint,
and happened to meet him.
Being from the same hometown, they were acquainted,
and Lǐ asked:
"What are you doing?"
Liú told him.
Lǐ smiled and said:
"Your reputation is well known to all;
I have always known Míao to be very kind and honest,
how could he dare to occupy and cheat?
Perhaps you are misrepresenting it!"
Thereupon he tore up Liú's complaint paper,
pulled him into the shop,
and intended to mediate.
Liú was filled with bitter resentment and could not let it go.
He secretly took a brush from the shop,
rewrote the complaint,
hid it in his bosom,
resolved to definitely file it.
Before long,
Míao arrived,
explaining the situation in detail,
and then pleaded with Lǐ to resolve the matter,
saying:
"I am a farmer,
and have not seen an official in half my life.
If only the lawsuit can be dropped,
how dare I insist on owning a few peach trees?"
Lǐ called Liú out,
and told him of Míao's intention to yield.
Liú again pointed to heaven and drew on the ground,
cursing incessantly;
Míao, however, maintained a gentle expression and humble words,
not daring to dispute even a little.
After it was over,
four or five days later,
he saw someone from the village
who reported that Liú had died,
which greatly astonished Lǐ.
On another day, while going elsewhere,
he saw someone approaching with a staff,
who was unmistakably Liú.
When he arrived,
he inquired solicitously,
and also invited him to visit.
Lǐ hesitantly asked,
“A few days ago, I suddenly heard the bad news.
How could it have been so false?”
Liú did not answer,
but pulled him into the village,
and when they reached his house,
wine and juice were laid out.
Then he said,
“The report of a few days ago
was not false.
A while ago, when I left the door, I saw two men approaching,
who seized me and brought me before an official.
When I asked what the matter was,
they only said they didn't know.
I thought to myself that I had been going in and out of yámén for decades,
and was not afraid of seeing officials,
nor was I terrified.
I followed them,
and when we reached a public hall,
I saw the person sitting facing south with an angry expression, who said, ‘Are you Mǒu?
Your sins are full,
and you do not repent;
furthermore, you take others’ property
and claim it as your own.
Such arrogance and violence
deserves to be put into a cauldron!’
One person checked a ledger and said, ‘This man has one good deed,
and should not die.’
The person facing south read the ledger,
and his expression somewhat softened.
He then said, ‘Temporarily send him away.’
Dozens of people shouted in unison to expel me.
I said, ‘For what reason did you summon me here?
And for what reason are you sending me away?
I beg for clear instructions.’
The officer brought down the ledger
and pointed out an entry to show me.
It was written: In the thirteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
three hundred qián were used
to save a couple and allow them to reunite.
The officer said, ‘But for this,
your life would have ended today,
and you would have fallen into the animal realm.’
Extremely frightened,
I then followed the two men out.
The two men demanded a bribe.
I angrily said, ‘Don't you know that Liú Mǒu has been going in and out of public offices for twenty years,
and specialized in extorting money from people?
How can you ask a tiger for meat?’
The two men then said no more.
They escorted me to the village
and cupped their hands, saying, ‘We didn't even get a sip of water during this mission.’
Once the two men had left,
I entered the door and immediately revived,
though I had been breathless for a full day already.”
Lǐ heard this and found it extraordinary,
and thus questioned him about the details of his good deed.
Initially,
in the thirteenth year of Chóngzhēn,
the year was extremely harsh,
and people ate each other.
Liú was then in Zī,
serving as a chief jailer.
He happened to see a man and a woman crying very sadly,
and asked them why.
They replied,
“We have been married for just over a year,
and this year's famine
makes it impossible for both of us to survive,
hence our sorrow.”
A short while later,
he saw them again in front of an oil shop,
seemingly arguing.
He approached and questioned them.
The shop owner, whose surname was Mǎ, then said,
“This couple is starving to death,
and daily ask me for sesame paste to survive.
Now they want to sell their wife to me.
My household has already bought more than ten people!
What's the big deal?
If it's cheap, sell her;
otherwise, just leave it.
It's ridiculous how they cling to people!”
The man then said,
“Now grain is like pearls,
and I reckon that without three hundred [qián],
it won't be enough to cover the expenses of fleeing the famine.
We originally wanted both of us to live,
but if I sell my wife and still can't escape death,
what's the point?
I don't dare to speak straightforwardly,
but only ask you to perform a hidden good deed.”
Liú pitied them,
and then asked Mǎ how much he would offer.
Mǎ said,
“Today, a female mouth
is only worth about a hundred [qián].”
Liú asked him not to reduce the amount,
and also offered to contribute half the price.
Mǎ insisted it was not possible.
Liú, feeling a bit indignant,
then said to the man,
“He is petty and not worth mentioning.
I will give you the full amount.
If you can escape the famine
and also keep the couple together,
wouldn't that be even better?”
Thereupon, he opened his purse and gave them the money.
The couple wept, bowed, and departed.
When Liú recounted this story,
Lǐ greatly praised and admired him.
From then on, Liú's behavior completely changed,
and he is still healthy at seventy.
Last year,
Lǐ went to Zhōu Cūn,
where he met Liú arguing with someone,
and the crowd surrounding them could not resolve it.
Lǐ smiled and called out,
“Are you trying to sue for a peach tree again?”
Liú suddenly changed his expression,
mumbled, bowed his hands, and retreated.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“Lǐ Cuìshí's brothers
are all called wealthy men.
However, Cuìshí is also pure and careful.
He loves to do good deeds,
and never boasted of his wealth,
but was a humble, sincere, and honest gentleman.
Observing his mediation of disputes and encouragement of good deeds,
his life can be known.
The ancients said: ‘The rich are not benevolent.’
I do not know if Cuìshí was benevolent before he became rich,
or if he became rich first and then benevolent.”
— According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chái Tíngbīn,
a Tàipíng man.
His wife, Jīn-shì,
was reticent
and extraordinarily jealous.
Chái bought a concubine for a hundred *jīn*,
but Jīn-shì treated her violently,
and she died within a year.
Chái, indignant, moved out,
sleeping alone for several months,
never setting foot in the women's quarters.
One day,
on Chái's birthday,
Jīn-shì humbly and solemnly offered
her husband birthday wishes.
Chái could not bear to refuse,
and they began to speak and laugh together.
Jīn-shì set a banquet in her inner chambers
and invited Chái.
Chái declined, citing drunkenness.
Jīn-shì, elegantly made up, went to Chái's quarters
and said,
"I have exhausted my sincerity all day,
and if you are truly drunk,
please have one more cup before you leave."
Chái then entered,
and they poured wine and conversed.
His wife calmly said,
"The other day, I mistakenly killed the maidservant,
and now I deeply regret it.
Why should we be enemies and harbor resentment,
thus losing the affection of our wedded union?
Later, please take in twelve golden hairpins,
and I will not find fault with you."
Chái was even more pleased;
when the candle burned down to the wick,
he stayed overnight.
From then on, they loved and respected each other as before.
Jīn-shì then called for a matchmaker
and instructed her to find a beautiful concubine;
however, she secretly told the matchmaker to delay and not report back,
while she herself then intentionally urged her on.
This went on for over a year.
Chái could not wait,
and asked all his relatives and friends to procure one for him,
and obtained Lín-shì's adopted daughter.
Upon seeing her, Jīn-shì's
joy was evident on her face.
She shared food and drink with her,
and allowed her to take
any rouge, powder, flowers, or bracelets she wished.
However, Lín-shì was originally from Yān,
and was not skilled in women's needlework;
apart from embroidered shoes,
she needed help to make other things.
Jīn-shì said,
"I am always diligent and frugal,
not like a princely household
that buys people to look at like paintings."
Thereupon, she gave her beautiful brocade
and made her learn how to make garments,
as a strict teacher instructs a pupil.
At first, it was scolding and cursing;
later, it was whipping and flogging.
Chái felt the pain deeply in his heart,
but could do nothing.
Yet, Jīn-shì's affection and love for Lín-shì
was even greater than before;
she often styled her hair and clothes herself,
and applied her makeup.
However, if the heel of a shoe had even a slight crease,
she would strike her bound feet with an iron rod;
if her hair was slightly messy,
she would slap her cheeks. Lín-shì could not endure the abuse
and hanged herself.
Chái was heartbroken and horrified,
and harbored considerable resentment.
His wife angrily said,
"I taught your lady on your behalf,
what sin have I committed?"
Chái then realized her deceit,
and they turned hostile again,
forever severing their marital harmony.
He secretly repaired a room in another property,
intending to buy a beautiful woman and live separately with her.
Half a year passed quickly,
but he still hadn't found the right person.
One day, he happened to attend a friend's funeral,
where he saw a sixteen-year-old girl,
whose radiance filled his eyes.
He paused, captivated.
The girl was surprised by his wild stare,
and her almond-shaped eyes turned askance.
He inquired of others
and learned she was from the Shào clan.
Mister Shào was a poor scholar,
who had only this daughter.
She had been intelligent since childhood,
and he taught her to read;
she could understand anything after one glance.
She especially loved to read *Nèi Jīng* and *Bīng Jiàn* books.
Her father doted on her,
and whenever there was a proposal of marriage,
he would let her choose for herself.
But she found fault with both the rich and the poor,
so at seventeen, she was still unmarried.
Chái learned these details
and knew she was beyond his reach,
yet his heart lingered on her.
He also hoped that since her family was poor,
they might be swayed by money.
He consulted several old women,
but none dared to act as matchmakers.
He consequently became disheartened
and gave up all hope.
Suddenly, an old peddler named Jiǎ Ǎo
passed by Chái's house selling pearls.
Chái told her of his desire,
bribing her with a large sum of gold,
saying,
"I only ask for one sincere attempt to convey my intentions.
Whether it succeeds or not,
you will not be blamed.
If by some chance it can be achieved,
a thousand pieces of gold are no object."
The old woman, tempted by the prospect of gain,
agreed.
Upon arriving at their door,
she deliberately engaged Shào Qī in idle chatter.
Seeing the girl,
she exclaimed in admiration,
"What a beautiful young lady!
If she were in the Zhāo Yáng Court,
the Zhào sisters would be nothing to speak of!"
She then asked,
"Who is the son-in-law?"
Shào Qī replied,
"Not yet."
The old woman said,
"For a girl like this,
why worry about not having princes or marquises as noble guests?"
Shào Qī sighed, saying,
"We dare not hope for princely families;
we only wish for a descendant of scholars who values integrity,
that would be good enough.
Our little mischievous one
is so picky in her selection,
hardly one in ten is suitable;
I don't understand what her intentions are."
The old woman said,
"Madam, you needn't worry and complain.
Such a beautiful person,
who knows what blessings she accumulated in a previous life
to be able to enjoy such good fortune.
Yesterday, there was a great joke: Young Master Chái said that near a certain family's tomb,
he saw her beauty
and wished to offer a thousand pieces of gold as a betrothal gift.
Isn't this like a hungry kite aspiring to be a swan?
I scolded him away immediately!"
Shào Qī smiled slightly but did not answer.
The old woman said,
"Even for a scholar's family,
it's hard to compare;
if it were someone else,
losing an inch and gaining a yard,
it should be acceptable."
Shào Qī smiled again but remained silent.
The old woman clapped her hands and said,
"Indeed,
then my plan would also go awry.
For days, Madam has shown me kindness,
inviting me in and offering me tea and wine;
if I were to receive a thousand pieces of gold,
have carriages and horses,
and enter grand mansions,
when I next came to your door,
the gatekeepers would scold me and drive me away!"
Shào Qī pondered for a long time,
then rose and left
to speak with her husband.
After a while,
she called her daughter.
After another while,
the three came out together.
Shào Qī smiled and said,
"This maid is peculiar;
she refuses so many good matches,
but hearing it's to be a humble concubine, she agrees.
I just fear it will be a laughingstock among scholars!"
The old woman said,
"If she enters the household
and gives birth to a young master,
how would the First Madam react then!"
Having said this,
she informed them of the plan for a separate residence.
Shào Yì was delighted,
and called his daughter, saying,
"Try to speak with Granny Jiǎ.
This is your own decision;
do not regret it later
and resent your parents."
The girl bashfully said,
"If my parents can enjoy generous provisions,
then their old age will be cared for.
Besides, I consider my own fate to be thin;
if I were to get a good husband,
my lifespan would surely be shortened.
Enduring less suffering may not be a misfortune.
I previously saw that Young Master Chái also has an auspicious appearance,
and his descendants are sure to prosper."
The old woman was overjoyed
and rushed to report back.
Chái was delighted beyond expectation.
He immediately prepared a thousand pieces of gold,
arranged for carriages and horses,
and married the girl at a separate estate.
No one in his household dared to speak of it.
The girl said to Chái,
"Your plan
is like a swallow building its nest on a tent,
not considering tomorrow.
Stopping mouths and guarding against gossip,
hoping to keep it a secret,
how can that be achieved?
I ask that we return home early;
it will be a quicker revelation and a smaller disaster."
Chái feared she would be mistreated.
The girl said,
"There is no one in the world who cannot be influenced.
If I commit no fault,
how can anger arise?"
Chái said,
"Not so.
This is an extraordinary fierceness
that cannot be moved by reason or sentiment."
The girl said,
"As a humble concubine,
it is my lot to suffer hardship.
Otherwise,
living day to day,
how can it last?"
Chái thought she was right,
but he still hesitated and dared not make a decision.
One day,
Chái was away on business.
The girl, dressed in blue, came out
and ordered a grey-headed servant to bridle an old mare.
An old maidservant followed her, carrying a bundle.
She went directly to the principal wife's residence
and prostrated herself on the ground, making her case.
The wife was initially angry;
but then she considered that her voluntary surrender was pardonable.
Seeing her humble demeanor and simple attire,
her anger somewhat subsided.
She then ordered a maidservant to bring out a brocade robe and dress her,
saying,
"That unfaithful man spreads evil among everyone,
causing me to suffer unjust gossip.
In truth, it is all the husband's unrighteousness,
and the maids' misconduct
that provokes him.
You try to consider: abandoning a wife and establishing a separate household,
is this still a human being?"
The girl said,
"Upon close observation, he seems to regret it somewhat,
but he just won't humble himself.
The proverb says: 'The great do not submit to the small.'
By etiquette: a wife to her husband
is like a son to his father,
or a concubine to the principal wife.
If Madam is willing to grant him a gentle word and expression,
then accumulated grievances can all be cast aside."
The wife said,
"Since he doesn't come himself,
what do I have to do with it?"
She then ordered the maidservants to prepare a room for her.
Though her heart was not pleased,
she temporarily settled her.
Chái learned of the daughter's return,
and was greatly startled and uneasy.
He secretly thought that a lamb had entered a tiger's den,
and that the situation was already insufferable chaos.
He rushed back,
and seeing that the house was quiet,
his heart finally settled.
The daughter met him at the door and advised,
"Now go to the principal wife's place."
Chái showed a difficult expression.
The daughter cried,
and Chái reluctantly agreed.
The daughter went to see the wife and said:
"Your husband has just returned,
and is ashamed to see you, Madam.
I beg you, Madam, to go and give him a little smile."
The wife refused to go.
The daughter said:
"I have already said: the relationship of a husband to his wife
is like that of a principal wife to a concubine.
Mèng Guāng offered the tray with deference,
but people did not consider it sycophantic.
Why?
It is simply because that is her proper place."
The wife then followed her,
and seeing Chái, said:
"You have three burrows like a cunning rabbit,
why have you returned?"
Chái bowed his head and did not respond.
The daughter nudged him with her elbow,
and Chái then forced a smile.
The wife's expression softened slightly,
and she was about to leave.
The daughter pushed Chái to accompany her,
and also instructed the cook to prepare a drink.
From then on, the husband and wife were reconciled again.
The daughter rose early, put on green clothes, and went to wait upon them in the morning.
After they had washed,
she offered the towel,
performing the duties of a servant with great deference.
Chái entered her room,
but she strongly declined him,
and only after more than ten evenings did she consent to lie with him once.
The wife also inwardly esteemed her for this;
however, she felt ashamed of her own inferiority.
Accumulated shame turned into jealousy.
But the daughter served diligently,
with no flaws to exploit.
Occasionally, when the wife gave a mild scolding or reprimand,
the daughter would only humbly accept it.
One night,
the couple had a minor argument,
and by the morning's dressing, the wife was still seething with anger.
The daughter held up a mirror,
and the mirror fell,
breaking.
The wife became even more enraged,
gripping her hair and splitting her eyes (with anger).
The daughter, frightened,
knelt for a long time begging for forgiveness,
but the anger did not subside.
She was whipped dozens of times.
Chái could not bear it,
and rushed in full of indignation,
dragging the daughter out.
The wife loudly pursued and struck them.
Chái, in a rage,
snatched the whip and hit back,
tearing her facial skin,
before she finally retreated.
From then on, the husband and wife were like enemies.
Chái forbade the daughter from going (to the wife).
The daughter did not listen.
Rising early,
she knelt outside the curtain, waiting.
The wife pounded the bed and cursed angrily,
shouting at her to leave,
and not letting her approach.
Day and night she gnashed her teeth,
intending to wait until [Shái] 柴 was out before venting her anger on the concubine.
[Shái] 柴 knew of this,
and cut off all social interactions,
keeping his door shut, not attending to condolences or celebrations.
His wife could do nothing,
but daily beat the maids and old women to express her hatred,
which all the servants found unbearable.
Since husband and wife had fallen out,
the concubine also dared not attend him at night,
so [Shái] 柴 slept alone.
When his wife heard of this,
her mind was somewhat eased.
There was a head maid who was usually clever and shrewd;
once, she happened to speak with [Shái] 柴.
His wife suspected an affair,
and severely tortured her.
The maid would then, when no one was around,
clutch her head and curse resentfully.
One evening,
when it was the maid's turn to be on duty,
the concubine instructed [Shái] 柴,
forbidding him to go to her,
saying:
"The maid has a murderous look on her face;
she is unpredictable."
[Shái] 柴 followed her words,
summoned the maid,
and deceptively asked:
"What are you doing?"
The maid was startled and frightened,
unable to utter a word.
[Shái] 柴 became even more suspicious,
and searched her clothes,
finding a sharp blade.
The maid said nothing,
but prostrated herself, begging for death.
[Shái] 柴 wanted to beat her,
but the concubine stopped him, saying:
"I fear if Madam hears of this,
this maid will certainly have no chance of survival.
Her crime is indeed unforgivable,
but it is better to sell her.
This way, her life is spared,
and I also gain righteousness."
[Shái] 柴 agreed.
It so happened that there was someone wanting to buy a concubine,
so they quickly sold her.
His wife, because it was done without her consultation,
blamed [Shái] 柴,
and further transferred her anger to the concubine,
cursing and scolding her even more viciously.
[Shái] 柴 was enraged,
and looked at the concubine, saying:
"This is all your own doing.
If you had killed her earlier,
how could there be today's trouble!"
Having said this, he left.
His wife found his words strange,
and questioned everyone around her,
but no one knew anything;
she asked the concubine,
but the concubine also did not speak.
Her heart grew even more vexed and angry,
and she grabbed her skirt, cursing wildly.
[Shái] 柴 then returned,
and told her the truth.
His wife was greatly surprised,
and spoke kindly to the concubine;
but in her heart, she hated her even more for not speaking sooner.
[Shái] 柴 thought that all grudges were resolved,
and no longer took precautions.
When he happened to be away on a distant trip,
his wife summoned the concubine and rebuked her, saying:
"The crime of attempting to kill one's master is unforgivable;
how could you let her go?"
The concubine was flustered and could not express herself.
His wife heated a red-hot iron and branded the concubine's face,
intending to disfigure her.
All the maids and old women felt it was unfair for her.
Each time she cried out in pain,
the whole household wept,
wishing to die in her place.
His wife then stopped branding,
and pricked her ribs over twenty times with a needle,
before finally waving her away.
[Shái] 柴 returned,
saw the facial wound,
and was greatly enraged,
wanting to go and confront his wife.
The concubine grabbed his lapel, saying:
"I knowingly stepped into a pit of fire.
When I married you,
did I consider your family a paradise?
I only considered my own ill fate,
and merely sought to vent the anger of fate.
If I calmly endure,
there will still be a time when it ends;
if I provoke her again,
it would be like digging up a pit that has already been filled."
Then she applied medicine to the wound,
which healed in a few days.
Suddenly, she picked up a mirror and said joyfully:
"You should congratulate me today, sir,
for her branding has broken my ill-fated lines!"
Morning and evening, she served the legitimate wife,
just as before.
When [Jīn] 金 saw everyone crying earlier,
she realized she was like a lonely tyrant,
and a slight feeling of shame and regret began to sprout within her.
She often called the concubine to do things together,
and her words and demeanor were peaceful and kind.
After more than a month,
she suddenly fell ill with an inversion,
losing her appetite.
[Shái] 柴 hated her for not dying,
and barely inquired about her.
After several days,
her abdomen swelled like a drum,
and she became increasingly weak day and night.
The concubine attended her, not having time to sleep or eat,
and [Jīn] 金 became even more grateful to her.
The concubine explained her medical principles;
[Jīn] 金 felt that her past actions had been too cruel,
and suspected it was karmic retribution,
so she thanked the concubine.
[Jīn] 金 was strict and orderly in managing the household,
and all maids and servants were disciplined;
but after her illness,
they all became slack and idle.
[Shái] 柴 personally managed things,
toiling very hard,
yet the household's rice and salt
were depleted without being consumed.
Because of this, he was moved to consider his wife's domestic duties,
and hired a doctor to treat her.
[Jīn] 金 often told people she had
"Qi-gǔ" (氣蠱, qi stagnation resulting in a distended abdomen),
which is why when doctors took her pulse,
they all diagnosed her with qi stagnation.
She changed several doctors,
but none were effective,
and she was also on the verge of death.
Once again, when they were about to prepare medicine,
the concubine stepped forward and said:
"This kind of medicine,
a hundred packets would be useless,
only making it worse."
[Jīn] 金 did not believe her.
The concubine secretly replaced it with a different prescription.
After taking the medicine,
within the time it takes to eat a meal, she had three bowel movements,
and her illness seemed to disappear.
She then laughed even more at the concubine's "presumptuous" words,
groaning and calling her:
"Lady [Huàtuó] 華陀,
how is it now?"
The concubine and all the maids laughed.
[Jīn] 金 asked why,
and was then told the truth.
She wept and said:
"I have daily received your care and support without knowing it!
From now on,
please take charge of the household,
and I will follow your lead."
Not long after,
the illness was cured.
Chái Zhěng hosted a celebratory banquet.
The young woman held a pot, serving by the side.
Jīn herself rose, snatched the pot,
pulled her, linking arms,
showing affection far beyond the ordinary.
Late into the night,
the young woman made an excuse to leave the seat.
Jīn sent two maids to pull her back,
forcing her to share the bed.
From then on,
they consulted on every matter,
ate every meal together;
even sisters were not so harmonious.
Before long,
the young woman gave birth to a son.
After childbirth, she was often ill,
and Jīn personally attended to her,
as if serving an elderly mother.
Later, Jīn suffered from heart pain.
When the pain flared up,
her face would turn completely green,
and she only wished to die.
The young woman urgently took out several silver needles.
By the time she arrived,
Jīn's breathing was almost gone.
She pressed on the acupoints and pricked them,
and with a sudden sound, the pain stopped.
After more than ten days, it recurred;
she pricked again.
After six or seven days, it flared up again.
Although it was immediately effective,
and the suffering was not severe,
her heart was always anxious,
fearing its recurrence.
One night, she dreamed she went to a place
that looked like a temple,
where the ghosts and spirits in the hall were all stirring.
A spirit asked:
"Are you the Jīn氏?
Your sins are numerous,
and your lifespan should be over.
Considering your repentance,
I have only sent down this calamity
to show a slight reprimand.
Previously, you killed two concubines;
this is the karmic retribution for that.
What crime did the Shào氏 commit,
to be treated with such cruelty and poison?
The punishment of whipping
has already been repaid by Chái Shēng on your behalf,
which can be considered even.
As for the one branding you owe,
and twenty-two needles,
you have only partially paid for it in three instances;
do you expect the root of the illness to be eradicated?
Tomorrow it will act up again!"
She awoke in great fear,
still hoping it was a deceptive dream.
After eating, she indeed fell ill,
and the pain was doubly severe.
When the young woman arrived,
she pricked her,
and the pain immediately subsided.
She wondered aloud:
"My skill only goes so far;
why isn't the root of the illness removed?
Please cauterize it again.
This cannot be cured without thorough cauterization,
but I fear madam cannot endure it."
Jīn remembered the words in her dream,
and therefore showed no difficulty.
However, while groaning and enduring,
she secretly thought that she still owed nineteen needles,
and wondered what kind of complications might arise.
It would be better to suffer it all at once,
to avoid future pain.
When the moxa cone was exhausted,
she asked the young woman to needle her again.
The young woman smiled and said:
"How can needles be applied so casually?"
Jīn said:
"You don't need to consider the acupoints,
just give me nineteen pricks."
The young woman smiled and refused.
Jīn pleaded more earnestly,
getting up and kneeling on the bed.
The young woman ultimately couldn't bear it.
Jīn then truthfully recounted her dream.
The young woman then roughly identified the meridians,
and pricked her according to the number.
From then on, she recovered,
and indeed did not fall ill again.
She greatly repented,
and treated her subordinates without harshness.
Her son's name was Rìjùn,
and he was extraordinarily talented and intelligent.
The young woman often said:
"This child has the bearing of a scholar of the Hànlín Academy."
At the age of eight, he was regarded as a child prodigy,
and at fifteen, he was appointed to the Hànlín Academy after passing the imperial examination.
At this time, Chái's couple were forty,
and the concubine was only thirty-two or thirty-three.
When he returned to his hometown with carriages and horses,
the local community honored him.
Since old Shào sold his daughter,
his family had suddenly become wealthy,
but the gentry were ashamed to associate with him.
By this time,
people finally began to interact with them.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The cunning and jealousy of women
are their innate nature.
And concubines,
moreover, flaunt their beauty and plot schemes,
thereby increasing the main wife's anger.
Alas!
This is the origin of disaster.
If one accepts one's fate with peace,
and adheres to one's lot,
unswayed in resolve despite a hundred setbacks,
how could a drawn blade harm such a person?
Yet it took saving her from death twice
for a glimmer of remorse and understanding to emerge.
Alas!
Is she even human?
To repay in full,
without added interest,
is also the Creator's forgiveness.
But to use benevolent skills to bring about evil retribution,
is that not perverse?
I often see ignorant couples suffering from chronic illness all day,
then summoning ignorant shamans,
allowing them to prick their skin and burn their flesh without daring to groan.
My heart often wondered why,
but now I understand."
There was a man from Mǐn who took a concubine.
In the evening, he went to his wife's room,
not daring to leave immediately,
and pretended to untie his shoes as if getting into bed.
His wife said:
"Go!
Don't put on an act!"
The husband still lingered.
His wife said sternly:
"I am not like those jealous wives in other families;
why do you need to be like this?"
The husband then left.
The wife slept alone,
tossing and turning, unable to sleep.
So she got up
and went to hide outside the door to secretly listen.
She only heard the concubine's voice indistinctly,
not very clearly.
Only
"lángbà"
— these two words
— could be vaguely distinguished.
Lángbà
is what people in Mǐn call father.
The wife listened for more than an hour,
then fainted from phlegm-swoon and fell,
her head hitting the door with a sound.
The husband was startled awake,
opened the door,
and the body fell in.
He called the concubine to light a lamp for him,
and it was his wife.
He quickly helped her up and tried to revive her.
Her eyes barely opened,
and she immediately moaned:
"Whose lángbà did you call out to!"
The jealousy is laughable.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Gǒng Dào rén,
had no given name,
nor was it known where he was from.
He once sought an audience with Lǔ Wáng,
but the gatekeeper would not announce him.
A high-ranking eunuch came out,
and Gǒng Dào rén bowed and entreated him.
The eunuch, seeing his rustic appearance,
drove him away;
soon after, he returned.
The eunuch was enraged,
and drove him away while also beating him.
When they reached an secluded spot,
Gǒng Dào rén laughingly produced two hundred taels of gold
and asked the attendant who had driven him away to tell the eunuch:
"Tell him I no longer wish to see the king;
I merely heard that the flowers, trees, pavilions, and terraces in the royal gardens
are among the finest human landscapes.
If he could guide me on a tour,
my life's wish would be fulfilled."
He also bribed the attendant with white gold.
The man was delighted
and reported back.
The eunuch was also pleased,
and led Gǒng Dào rén through the rear gate,
touring all the scenic spots.
They then ascended to the top of a tower.
As the eunuch leaned against the window,
Gǒng Dào rén gave him a push.
The eunuch only felt himself falling out of the tower,
with a thin hemp rope tied around his waist,
suspending him in mid-air.
Looking down,
the great height made him dizzy,
and the rope faintly made snapping sounds.
Extremely terrified,
he screamed loudly.
Soon after,
several guards arrived,
greatly astonished.
Seeing that he was extremely far from the ground,
they ascended the tower to look together,
and found that the end of the rope was tied to a tree root.
They wanted to untie and rescue him,
but the rope was too thin to bear the force.
They searched everywhere for Gǒng Dào rén,
but he had vanished.
Helpless,
they reported it to Lǔ Wáng.
The king went to see,
and was greatly astonished.
He ordered a bed of straw and cotton to be laid beneath the tower,
intending to cut the rope once it was ready.
As soon as it was finished,
the rope snapped cleanly by itself,
and the eunuch was barely a cubit from the ground.
They all burst into laughter.
The king ordered an inquiry into the whereabouts of the Dàoist.
He heard that he was lodging at the home of Shàng Xiùcái,
and went to inquire,
but he had gone out and not returned.
Later,
they met on the road,
and Gǒng Dào rén was then introduced to the king.
The king granted him a banquet seat,
and immediately requested him to perform a trick.
The Dàoist said:
"I am a man of the wilderness,
with no other ordinary skills.
Since I have received such kindness and favor,
I dare to present female musicians to celebrate Your Majesty's birthday."
Thereupon, he reached into his sleeve and produced a beautiful woman,
placed her on the ground,
and she bowed respectfully to the king.
The Dàoist commanded her to perform
"Yáo Chí Yàn"
as a play,
wishing the king ten thousand years of life.
The woman sang a few introductory lines.
The Dàoist then produced another person,
who introduced herself
as "Wáng Mǔ".
A short while later,
Dǒng Shuāngchéng, Xǔ Fēiqióng,
and all the other celestial maidens,
appeared one after another.
Finally, Zhī Nǚ came to pay her respects,
and presented a robe of heavenly fabric,
whose golden colors were dazzling,
illuminating the entire room.
The king suspected it was fake,
and requested to examine it.
The Dàoist quickly said:
"No!"
The king did not listen
and ultimately examined it;
indeed, it was a seamless garment,
impossible for human hands to create.
The Dàoist unhappily said:
"I sincerely served Your Majesty,
and borrowed this temporarily from the celestial weaver maiden.
Now, being stained by the mundane atmosphere,
how can I return it to its original owner?"
The king then thought that the singing old women must be celestial maidens,
and wished to keep one or two of them.
Upon closer inspection,
they were all palace musicians.
He then suspected that this music
was not what they usually played,
and when he asked them,
they were indeed completely unaware.
The Dàoist placed them in a brazier and burned them,
then put them into his sleeve,
and when he searched again,
they were gone.
The king then held the Dàoist in high esteem,
and had him stay within the palace.
The Dàoist said:
"The nature of a man of the wilderness
views palaces as cages,
and cannot compare to the freedom at the home of a Xiùcái."
Every night at midnight,
he would return to his lodging;
sometimes, when strongly pressed to stay,
he would spend the night.
He would often, during banquets,
play tricks by making flowers and trees of all four seasons appear.
The king asked:
"I've heard that immortals cannot forget their earthly desires;
is that true?"
He replied:
"Perhaps some immortals are like that;
I am not an immortal,
so my heart is like withered wood."
One night,
when he stayed at the palace,
the king sent a young courtesan to test him.
Upon entering his room,
she called him several times, but he did not respond; when she lit a candle,
he was sitting motionless on the couch.
When she shook him,
his eyes flashed once and then closed again.
When she shook him again,
a snoring sound began.
When she pushed him,
he fell over with her hand still on him,
sleeping soundly like thunder.
When she flicked his forehead,
it sounded like an iron pot.
She returned and reported this to the king.
The king had him pricked with a needle,
but the needle would not penetrate.
When pushed,
he was too heavy to be moved.
More than ten people lifted and threw him off the bed,
like a thousand-pound stone falling to the ground.
At dawn, when they peeped in,
he was still sleeping on the ground.
Upon waking, he laughed and said:
"What a terrible sleep!
I fell off the bed without realizing it!"
Thereafter, the palace women often pressed him as a game when he was sitting or lying down: at first, he was still soft,
but with further contact, he became like iron or stone.
The Dàoshì left the Xiùcai's house,
and was constantly not returning in the middle of the night.
The household would still lock their doors,
but by dawn, when the doors were opened,
the Dàoshì was already lying in his room.
Initially,
the Xiùcai and the courtesan Huì Gē were on good terms,
having pledged to marry.
