Huì was graceful and a skilled singer,
her string music captivating all at the time.
When Prince Lǔ heard of her fame,
he summoned her to serve him,
thus severing their affection.
The Xiùcai constantly thought of her, but had no way to communicate.
One evening,
he asked the Dàoshì:
"Have you seen Huì Gē?"
He replied:
"I have seen all the courtesans,
but I don't know who among them is your Huì Gē."
The Xiùcai described her appearance,
and told her age,
whereupon the Dàoshì remembered her.
The Xiùcai begged him to relay a message.
The Dàoshì smiled and said:
"I am an outsider to this world,
I cannot act as your messenger."
The Xiùcai pleaded persistently.
The Dàoshì extended his sleeve and said:
"If you must see her,
please enter this."
The Xiùcai peered into it,
and it was as large as a house inside.
He bent down and entered,
finding it bright and clear throughout,
as spacious as a hall;
with tables, beds, and couches,
nothing was absent.
Dwelling within,
he felt no distress or discomfort whatsoever.
The Dàoshì entered the prince's residence,
and played chess with the Prince.
When he saw Huì Gē arrive,
he deliberately brushed away dust with his robe sleeve,
and Huì Gē was already taken into his sleeve,
while others did not see it.
As the Xiùcai sat alone, lost in thought,
suddenly a beautiful woman fell from the eaves,
and when he looked,
it was Huì Gē.
Both were pleasantly surprised,
and their intimate affection reached its peak.
The Xiùcai said:
"This extraordinary encounter today
must not be left unrecorded.
Please let me write it with you."
He wrote on the wall:
"The noble household is like a sea, long without a trace."
Huì continued, saying:
"Who knew that Xiāo Láng would be met again today?"
The Xiùcai said:
"The universe within the sleeve is truly vast."
Huì said:
"It embraces all separated lovers and longing wives."
No sooner had the writing finished,
than five people suddenly entered,
wearing octagonal crowns
and pale red clothes.
Recognizing them,
they were all strangers.
Silently,
they seized Huì Gē and left.
The Xiùcai was shocked and frightened,
not knowing why.
When the Dàoshì returned,
he called him out
and asked about the situation,
but the Xiùcai was evasive and did not tell everything.
The Dàoshì smiled slightly,
took off his upper garment, turned up his sleeve, and showed it to him.
The Xiùcai examined it closely,
and faintly saw traces of characters,
finely written like nits;
these were indeed the lines they had inscribed.
Ten-odd days later,
he requested another visit.
In total, he entered three times.
Huì Gē said to the Xiùcai:
"There is movement in my belly,
which greatly worries me.
I constantly bind my waist tightly with silk cloth.
There are many eyes and ears in the residence;
if one day I were to give birth,
where could a baby's cry be accommodated?
Please consult with Gǒng Xiān,
and when you see me holding my waist with three fingers,
please come to my rescue."
The Xiùcai agreed.
Upon returning, he saw the Dàoshì,
and prostrated himself, not rising.
The Dàoshì pulled him up and said:
"What you speak of,
I already understand perfectly.
But please do not worry.
Your family line depends on this single thread,
how could I not exert my utmost meager efforts?
But from now on, you need not enter again.
What I am repaying you for
was never for personal affection."
Several months later,
the Dàoshì came in from outside,
smiling, and said:
"I have brought the young master!
Quickly bring the swaddling clothes!"
The Xiùcai's wife was most virtuous,
nearly thirty years old,
had several pregnancies but only one surviving son;
she had just given birth to a daughter,
who died a month later.
Hearing the Xiùcai's words,
she came out in surprised joy.
The Dàoshì took an infant from his sleeve,
soundly sleeping as if in slumber,
its umbilical cord still uncut.
The Xiùcai's wife took and embraced it,
and it then began to cry "guā guā."
The Dàoshì removed his garment and said:
"Birth blood spattered on clothes
is most taboo for Dàoshì.
Today, for your sake,
a twenty-year-old garment,
I cast it aside at once."
The Xiùcai helped him change clothes.
The Dàoshì instructed:
"Do not discard the old garment.
Burn some paper money,
and it can treat difficult births
and expel dead fetuses."
The Xiùcai followed his words.
After dwelling there for a long time,
he suddenly told Shàng,
"The old cassock I have stored away,
I should keep a small portion for my own use;
don't forget it after I die."
Shàng thought his words were ominous.
The Dàoshì left without speaking.
He went in to see the Wáng and said,
"Your servant wishes to die!"
The Wáng was startled and asked him about it.
He said,
"This is a fixed destiny;
what more is there to say?"
The Wáng did not believe him and
insisted on keeping him.
They played a game of chess;
then he suddenly got up.
The Wáng again stopped him.
He requested to go to the outer house,
and the Wáng agreed.
The Dàoshì hurried to lie down,
and when they checked, he was already dead.
The Wáng prepared a coffin
and buried him with due ceremony.
Shàng wept with utmost grief at the funeral,
only then realizing that the earlier words were a premonition.
The remaining cassock was used to aid childbirth,
responding as if by echo,
and those seeking help came in continuous streams to his door.
At first, he would give them a piece from the soiled sleeve;
later, he cut pieces from the collar and lapel,
and none failed to be effective.
When he heard the Dàoshì's instruction,
he suspected his wife would surely have a birth calamity,
so he cut a piece of blood-stained cloth the size of a palm
and treasured it.
It happened that the Rǔ Wáng's beloved concubine was in labor;
after three days, the child had not yet been delivered,
and the physicians had exhausted their skills.
Someone informed him about Shàng's abilities,
and he was immediately summoned.
With a single dose, she gave birth.
The Wáng was greatly pleased
and generously bestowed white gold and colored silks upon him.
Shàng declined to accept any of it.
The Wáng asked what he desired.
He said,
"Your servant dares not speak."
When pressed again,
he kowtowed and said,
"If you would extend your heavenly favor,
just granting me the old courtesan Huì Gē would be enough."
The Wáng summoned her,
and asked her age.
She said,
"Your concubine entered the palace at eighteen,
and it has been fourteen years since then."
The Wáng, seeing her advanced age,
ordered all the courtesans to be called,
allowing Shàng to choose for himself.
Shàng liked none of them.
The Wáng laughed and said,
"How foolish, scholar!
Was the marriage arranged ten years ago?"
Shàng replied truthfully.
Thereupon, the Wáng lavishly prepared a carriage and horses,
and even used the colored silks Shàng had declined as Huì Gē's dowry,
sending her off.
The son Huì had given birth to
was named Xiù Shēng — Xiù meaning 'sleeve' — and by this time he was eleven years old.
Every day, Shàng remembered the immortal's kindness,
and during Qīngmíng, he would visit his tomb.
There was a traveler who had long resided in Chuānzhōng,
who met the Dàorén on the road.
The Dàorén produced a scroll and said,
"This is something from the palace.
I was in a hurry when I left,
and didn't have time to return it to the wall.
Please deliver it for me."
When the traveler returned,
he heard that the Dàorén had died,
and dared not deliver it to the Wáng.
Shàng presented it on his behalf.
The Wáng unrolled and examined it,
and indeed, it was the scroll borrowed by the Dàoshì.
He doubted it,
so he opened his tomb,
and it was merely an empty coffin.
Later, Shàng's son died young,
and relied on Xiù Shēng to continue the line,
further proving Gǒng's foresight.
The Yìshǐ Shì says:
"A universe in a sleeve"
is merely an ancient parable;
how could it truly exist?
Yet how marvelous it is!
Within it are heaven and earth, sun and moon,
where one can marry and have children,
and yet be free from the hardships of taxes
and the annoyances of human affairs.
Then the fleas and lice in the sleeve
are no different from the chickens and dogs of Táoyuán.
If the traveler were to live there permanently,
growing old in that land would be quite acceptable.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Jǔ, there was a man named Shāng.
His elder brother was rich, and his younger brother was poor;
they lived next door to each other.
During the Kāngxī era,
there was a great famine,
and the younger brother struggled to feed himself day and night.
One day,
at noon,
he still had not lit the stove.
He paced back and forth, clutching his stomach,
with no means to cope.
His wife told him to go and ask his brother.
Shāng said,
"It's useless.
If my brother pitied my poverty,
he would have already done something about it long ago."
His wife insisted,
so Shāng sent his son instead.
A short while later,
the son returned empty-handed.
Shāng said,
"What did I tell you?"
His wife questioned the son in detail about what his uncle had said.
The son replied,
"Uncle hesitated and looked at Auntie;
Auntie told me: 'Brothers have separated their households,
and each has their own food to prepare;
who can still look after others?'"
The couple was silent.
For a while, they managed to survive
by exchanging leftover bowls and broken beds for a little chaff and husks.
In the village, three or four scoundrels,
spying the elder Shāng's (商) ample wealth,
climbed over the wall at night and entered.
The couple awoke with a start,
and made their washbasin clatter while shouting.
Their neighbors all detested them,
and offered no help.
Having no other choice,
they urgently called out to the two Shāng brothers.
The Shāng brothers heard their sister-in-law's cries
and wanted to rush to her rescue.
Their wife stopped them,
and loudly called out to their sister-in-law, saying,
"Brothers live separately,
each suffers his own misfortune;
who can still look after one another now!"
Soon,
the bandits broke down the door,
seized the elder Shāng and his wife,
and branded them with hot irons,
their cries becoming utterly tragic.
The two Shāng brothers said:
"He is indeed heartless,
but how can we sit by and watch our brother die without helping him!"
They led their son over the wall,
shouting loudly and urgently.
The two Shāng brothers and their son were naturally brave and strong,
and feared by others.
Fearing that they might alert other aid,
the bandits then left.
They looked at their brother and sister-in-law,
whose two thighs were scorched.
They helped them onto the bed,
called together their maids and servants,
and then returned home.
Although the elder Shāng was injured,
no gold or silk was lost,
so he said to his wife:
"What we have remaining now
is all due to our brothers' gift;
we should divide it among them."
His wife said:
"If you had good brothers,
you wouldn't have suffered this hardship!"
The Shāng brother then said no more.
The two Shāng families ceased eating,
believing their brother would surely give them some reward;
after a long time,
they heard nothing.
The wife could not wait,
and sent her son with a sack to borrow from them,
returning with a peck of millet.
The wife was angry that it was so little,
and wanted to return it;
the two Shāng brothers stopped her.
More than two months passed,
and their poverty and hunger became increasingly unbearable.
The two Shāng brothers said:
"Now we have no way to make a living;
it's better to sell our house to our brother.
Our brother might fear that we will move elsewhere,
and might not accept the deed but instead pity us,
which is unknown;
even if that's not the case,
if we get more than ten pieces of gold,
we can still survive."
His wife agreed,
and sent her son with the deed to the elder Shāng.
The elder Shāng told his wife,
and also said:
"Even if my brothers are unfeeling,
they are my limbs.
If they leave, I will be isolated;
it's better to return their deed and provide for them."
His wife said:
"Not so.
Their saying they will leave
is a way to coerce me;
if it really happens,
then we would just fall into their trap.
Are there no people in the world without brothers,
who then all die?
If I raise the thorny walls high,
it will be enough to protect myself.
It's better to accept their deed,
let them go wherever they please,
and I can also enlarge my house."
The plan settled,
they made the two Shāng brothers sign the end of the deed,
paid them the price, and they left.
The two Shāng brothers then moved to a neighboring village.
The unruly individuals in the town,
hearing that the two Shāng brothers had left,
attacked them again.
They seized the elder Shāng once more,
flogging and beating him with various instruments,
tormenting him terribly,
so that all his money and valuables
were used to ransom his life.
Before the bandits left,
they opened the granary and called out to the poor people in the village,
allowing them to take whatever they wanted,
and in an instant everything was gone.
The next day,
the two Shāng brothers first heard about it,
and when they rushed to see,
their brother was already unconscious and unable to speak;
he opened his eyes and saw his brothers,
but could only clutch the bedsheets.
A short while later, he died.
The two Shāng brothers angrily complained to the county magistrate (yì zǎi).
The bandit leader escaped,
and could not be apprehended.
The more than ten people who stole the millet
were all poor villagers,
and the prefect (zhōu shǒu) could do nothing about it.
The elder Shāng left behind a young son,
only five years old.
Since the family was poor,
he often went to his uncle's place to work for himself,
not returning for several days;
when sent home,
he would not stop crying.
The two Shāng brothers' wife was quite unkind to him.
The two Shāng brothers said:
"His father was unrighteous,
but what sin has his son committed?"
Therefore, they bought several steamed buns
and delivered them themselves.
After several days,
they again avoided their wife and children,
secretly carrying a peck of millet to their sister-in-law,
to feed the child.
This became their regular practice.
After several more years,
the elder Shāng's mother sold her fields and house,
getting enough money to support herself,
and the two Shāng brothers no longer visited.
The following year, there was a great famine,
with dead bodies lining the roads as far as the eye could see.
The two Shāng brothers' family responsibilities increased,
and they could not look after others.
Their nephew, at fifteen,
was frail and unable to work,
so they made him carry a basket and sell Hu (胡) pancakes with his brothers.
One night,
he dreamt his brother came,
his face sorrowful, and said:
"I was misled by my wife's words,
and thus lost the righteousness of brotherhood.
My brothers, not dwelling on past grudges,
fills me with sweat and shame.
The old house that was sold
is still empty now;
you should rent it.
Under the thorny bush behind the house,
there is a cellar of gold hidden.
Dig it up,
and you can become a little prosperous.
Let the 'ugly' son (referring to his own son) accompany you;
as for the 'long-tongued woman' (referring to his wife), I greatly resent her,
do not mind her."
When he woke up,
he found it extraordinary.
He bribed the landlord with a large sum,
and was finally able to move in.
Indeed, he dug up five hundred pieces of gold.
From then on, he abandoned his humble occupation,
and had his brothers set up shops in the marketplace.
The nephew was quite intelligent,
and his calculations were never wrong;
he was also honest and sincere,
and would report every single item, no matter how small.
He would always report
all transactions. The two Shāng brothers grew to love him even more.
One day,
he tearfully asked for millet for his mother.
The Shāng brothers' wife did not want to give it;
but the two Shāng brothers, considering his filial piety,
gave her a monthly allowance of grain.
After several years, their family grew even wealthier.
The elder Shāng's wife fell ill and died,
and the two Shāng brothers also grew old,
so they divided their nephew's inheritance,
giving him half of their family assets.
Yìshǐshì said:
"I heard that the elder merchant did not take or give away even a trifle lightly,
and was also pure, upright, and self-respecting.
However, he listened to his wife's words,
was confused and said nothing,
treated his own flesh and blood with indifference,
and ultimately died of stinginess.
Alas!
What's so strange about that!
The younger merchant started with greed
and ended up as a rich commoner.
What was his forte as a person?
He just didn't strictly follow domestic teachings.
Alas!
One line of conduct differed,
and thus their character became distinct."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
A certain xiùcai from Yíshuǐ,
was studying in the mountains.
At night, two beautiful women entered,
smiling silently,
each sweeping the couch with her long sleeve,
and sat down together,
their clothes soft and noiseless.
After a short while,
one beautiful woman rose
and unfurled a white silk handkerchief on the table;
on it were three or four lines of cursive script,
though he never distinguished what words they were.
The other beautiful woman placed a silver ingot,
about three or four liǎng in weight;
the xiùcai picked it up and put it in his sleeve.
The beautiful woman took her handkerchief,
clasped hands, smiled, and exited,
saying:
"Intolerably vulgar!"
The xiùcai felt for the silver,
but it was gone.
With beauties sitting there,
offering their fragrant favor,
he disregarded it;
but the silver he took—
that's the look of a beggar,
how can it be tolerated!
The fox's child, Kě'ér,
her elegant demeanor can be imagined.
A friend spoke of this,
and also thought of intolerable things,
which are appended here: [Facing a] vulgar guest.
A commoner writing in literary language.
The airs of the rich and noble.
A xiùcai pretending to be a renowned scholar.
Bystanders' fawning expressions.
Shameless, unending lying.
Bowing and sitting, excessively yielding precedence.
Forcing others to read or listen to bad poetry or prose.
A miser crying poverty.
A drunkard's twisted talk.
Speaking in the Mǎnzhōu accent.
Speaking with an oppressive, forced tone.
Vulgar, malicious jokes.
Being so foolish as to grab dishes and fruit at a banquet.
A hypocrite like Xú Wēi putting on airs.
Crooked officials discussing poetry and prose.
Frequently mentioning noble relatives in conversation.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Fēng Yúntíng,
a man from Tàiháng.
He once visited the prefecture and
slept during the day in his lodging.
At that time, he was young and had lost his wife,
and in his solitude,
he was rather pensive.
As he gazed intently,
he saw a woman's shadow on the wall,
dimly like a painting.
He thought it must be a product of his imagination.
But it remained motionless for a long time,
and did not disappear.
He found it strange.
He rose and looked, and it became even more real;
approaching it again,
it was clearly a young girl,
her face drawn, her tongue extended,
a noose around her graceful neck.
Before his surprise and gaze subsided,
it slowly descended.
He knew it was a ghost of someone hanged,
but emboldened by daylight,
he was not greatly afraid.
He said:
"If, my lady, you have some grave injustice,
this humble one can exert his utmost effort."
The shadow actually descended,
saying:
"As someone who passed through like duckweed on water,
how dare I hastily burden a gentleman with such a weighty matter.
But my withered bones in the underworld,
my tongue cannot retract,
the noose cannot be removed.
I beg you to cut down the roof beam and burn it;
your kindness will be as vast as mountains."
He assented,
and it vanished.
He called the landlord,
and asked about what he had seen.
The landlord said:
"This was Měi's old house ten years ago.
One night, a thief entered the room,
was caught by Měi,
and sent to the diǎnshǐ.
The diǎnshǐ took five hundred in silver from the thief
and falsely accused Měi's daughter of having an affair with him,
intending to arrest her for examination.
The daughter, hearing this, hanged herself.
Afterwards, Měi and his wife successively died,
and the house reverted to me.
Guests often see strange things,
but I have no means to pacify it."
Fēng told the landlord the ghost's words.
The cost of demolishing the house and replacing the beams
was not small,
so the landlord found it difficult;
Fēng then helped him with the work.
Once it was completed, he moved back in.
Měi Nǚ arrived that night,
expressing her thanks,
her joy overflowing,
her姿態嫣然.
Fēng was delighted with her
and wished to seek pleasure with her.
She blushed and said with shame:
"The chilly yin energy
is not only unbeneficial to you;
if such a thing were to happen,
then the defilement of my life
could not be washed away even by the Xījiāng River.
Our meeting has its time,
but today is not yet it."
He asked:
"When?"
She only smiled and did not speak.
Fēng asked:
"Will you drink?"
She replied:
"I do not drink."
Fēng said:
"To gaze at a beautiful woman with dull eyes,
what taste is there in that?"
The woman said:
"Among the tricks I know in life,
I am only skilled at Dǎmǎ.
But with only two people, it is lonely,
and it's late at night, so there's no board.
Now that the long night has no diversion,
let's play the game of 'intertwined lines' for a while."
Fēng agreed.
They sat knee to knee, pointing their fingers,
changing positions for a long time.
Fēng was confused and didn't know what to do;
the woman would verbally guide him and point with her chin,
becoming more and more fantastical,
inexhaustible in her skill.
Fēng smiled and said:
"This is a unique skill for a boudoir."
The woman said:
"I realized this myself;
with just two lines,
one can form patterns,
people just don't notice it."
As the night deepened, he grew quite weary,
and she urged him to sleep,
saying:
"I am a yin person and do not sleep;
please rest yourself.
I know a little of the art of massage,
and wish to use my skill
to accompany your sweet dreams."
Fēng accepted her offer.
The woman stacked her palms and lightly massaged him,
from head to heel, covering him completely;
wherever her hands passed,
his bones felt as if drunk.
Then she held his fingers and rubbed them delicately,
like touching with a wad of cotton,
his body felt indescribably comfortable and relaxed:
when she rubbed his waist, his mouth and moon (a typo, likely 骨-bone or perhaps 舌-tongue, or a classical expression for body parts) were all languid;
when she reached his thighs,
he had already fallen into a deep sleep.
When he awoke,
the sun was already high,
and he felt his joints light and harmonious,
quite different from previous days.
His heart grew even more fond of her,
and he walked around the room calling her,
but there was no response.
As evening approached,
the woman finally arrived.
Fēng said:
“Where do you reside,
that I have to call you until my voice is hoarse?”
She said:
“Ghosts have no fixed abode;
they are primarily underground.”
He asked:
“Are there crevices underground large enough to accommodate a body?”
She said:
“Ghosts do not perceive the ground,
just as fish do not perceive water.”
Fēng grasped her wrist and said:
“If I could bring you back to life,
I would break my family and buy it for you.”
The woman laughed and said:
“There’s no need to break your family.”
Their dalliance lasted until midnight,
when Fēng pressed her hard.
The woman said:
“Please do not pester me.
There is a Zhè-jiang courtesan who loves you,
newly residing next door to the north,
and quite charming.
Tomorrow evening,
I’ll invite her to come with me
to serve as my substitute;
how about that?”
Fēng agreed.
The next evening,
she indeed arrived with a young woman,
around thirty years of age,
with eyes that darted about,
subtly hinting at flirtation.
The three sat intimately and played card games.
When the game ended,
the woman rose and said:
“The joyous gathering is just getting started,
but I must leave.”
Fēng tried to hold her back,
but she had already vanished gracefully.
The two ascended the couch,
and enjoyed themselves immensely.
When he inquired about her family background,
she spoke evasively and incompletely,
only saying:
“If my lord truly loves your concubine,
you should flick the north wall with your finger,
and softly call ‘Hú-lú-zi’
and I will come.
If I do not respond after three calls,
you’ll know I am busy,
and should not call again.”
At dawn,
she entered a crevice in the north wall and departed.
The next day,
the woman came.
Fēng asked about Ài-qīng.
The woman said:
“She was invited by Gāo Gōng-zi to attend him while he drank,
which is why she could not come.”
Consequently, they trimmed the candle and conversed.
Whenever the woman wished to say something,
her lips would open but then stop;
when he pressed her firmly,
she ultimately refused to speak,
only sighing.
Fēng forced her to play,
and she departed at the fourth watch.
From then on, the two women came frequently,
their laughter resounding through the night until dawn,
which caused it to be known throughout the city and community.
A certain Diǎn-shǐ,
also from a prominent family in Zhè-jiang,
had dismissed his principal wife due to a private servant.
He subsequently married a woman from the Gù clan,
whom he loved deeply;
but she died after a month,
and he grieved greatly for her.
Hearing that Fēng had spirit-ghosts,
he wished to inquire about their karmic ties in the underworld,
and so he rode his horse to visit Fēng.
Fēng initially refused to agree,
but the man earnestly persisted,
so Fēng set up a banquet and they sat,
and he promised to summon the ghost-courtesan.
As dusk fell,
he knocked on the wall and called,
and before three calls were finished,
Ài-qīng entered.
Upon looking up and seeing the guest,
her expression changed and she tried to flee,
but Fēng blocked her with his body.
The man scrutinized her,
became enraged,
and threw a large bowl at her,
whereupon she instantly vanished.
Fēng was greatly astonished,
not understanding the reason,
and was about to question him.
Suddenly, an old woman emerged from the dark room,
cursing loudly:
“You greedy thief!
You ruined the money tree of my family!
You must repay thirty strings of cash!”
She struck Mǒu with her staff,
hitting his skull.
Mǒu clutched his head and wailed:
“This Gù Shì
was my wife.
She died young,
and I am still deeply sorrowful;
I didn't expect her to be an unchaste ghost.
What has this to do with the old woman?”
The old woman angrily said:
“You are originally a good-for-nothing scoundrel from Zhèjiāng,
who, having bought an ox-horn belt,
now has his nose bone turned upside down!
What sense of right and wrong do you, an official, have?
With three hundred coins in your sleeve,
you act like a venerable elder!
Gods are angered and people resentful;
your death is imminent.
Don't you know that your parents interceded for you in the netherworld,
wishing to send their beloved daughter-in-law to a brothel
to repay your greedy debts?”
Having spoken,
she struck him again.
Mǒu writhed and moaned pitifully.
Just as [Fēng] was astonished and at a loss how to intervene,
he suddenly saw Méi Nǚ emerge from her room,
eyes wide and tongue sticking out,
her complexion transformed.
She approached and stabbed her ear with a long hairpin.
Fēng was extremely startled
and shielded the guest with his body.
The woman’s indignation was boundless.
Fēng advised:
“Even if Mǒu is guilty,
should he die in my lodging,
the blame would fall on this humble student.
Please spare him out of consideration for the dwelling.”
The woman then dragged the old woman away, saying:
“Let him breathe a little longer
for the sake of my dear Fēng Láng.”
Mǒu fled in a panic, like a scurrying rat.
Upon reaching the yámen,
he suffered from a brain illness
and died in the middle of the night.
The next night,
the woman came out and smiled, saying:
“How satisfying!
The evil qi has been expelled!”
He asked:
“What was the enmity?”
The woman said:
“I told you before: accepting bribes and falsely accusing someone of illicit relations.
I have harbored this grudge for a long time,
and often wanted to ask you
to clear my name.
I was ashamed of my lack of even a speck of virtue,
so I would stop whenever I was about to speak.
Just now I heard a quarrel,
and secretly listened in,
not expecting him to be my enemy.”
Fēng was surprised and said:
“Was this the one who falsely accused you?”
She replied:
“That Diǎnshǐ has been here
for eighteen years;
my unjust death was sixteen years ago.”
He asked:
“Who was the old woman?”
She replied:
“An old prostitute.”
He then asked about his beloved,
and she said:
“She is just sick.”
Then, with a sudden crack like a whip, she said:
“I once said that our reunion had a date,
and now it is truly not far off.
You once wished to break your family to redeem me,
do you still remember?”
Fēng said:
“Today, I still have that same heart.”
The woman said:
“To tell you the truth: on the day I died,
I was reborn into the family of Zhǎn Xiàolián in Yán'ān.
It is only because my great grievance has not been redressed
that I have lingered thus.
Please use a new silk cloth to make a ghost bag,
so that I can attach myself to you as you go,
and then seek a marriage proposal from the Zhǎn family;
I believe it will surely be granted.”
Fēng worried that the disparity in status
might prevent success.
The woman said:
“Just go, have no worries.”
Fēng followed her words.
The woman instructed:
“On the way, be sure not to call my name;
wait until the night of the wedding ceremony,
hang the bag over the new bride’s head,
and urgently cry: ‘Do not forget! Do not forget!’”
Fēng agreed to it.
As soon as he opened the bag,
the woman leaped in.
He carried it to Yán'ān
and inquired there.
Indeed, there was a Zhǎn Xiàolián,
who had a daughter,
extremely beautiful in appearance;
but she was afflicted with idiocy,
and often stuck her tongue out beyond her lips,
like a panting dog.
She was sixteen years old,
but no one asked for her hand in marriage.
Her parents were distressed with worry.
Fēng arrived at their door, presented his calling card,
and fully declared his family's standing.
After he left,
he engaged a matchmaker.
Zhǎn was pleased
and took Fēng as a live-in son-in-law.
The daughter was utterly idiotic,
unaware of proper etiquette,
and had to be led and supported by two maids to her room.
Once the maids had left,
the daughter unbuttoned her top, revealing her breasts,
and grinned foolishly at Fēng.
Fēng covered the bag and called to her.
The daughter paused, scrutinizing him,
as if deep in thought.
Fēng smiled and said:
“Do you not recognize this humble student?”
He lifted the bag and showed it to her.
The daughter then understood,
quickly covered her top,
and they laughed together in joyous intimacy.
The next morning,
Fēng went to pay his respects to his father-in-law.
Zhǎn consoled him, saying:
“My foolish daughter is ignorant.
Since you have deigned to favor her,
if you are willing,
there is no lack of intelligent maids in my household,
and I would not begrudge giving one to you.”
Fēng vehemently argued that she was not idiotic.
Zhǎn was skeptical.
Soon after,
the daughter arrived,
her demeanor and actions all excellent,
causing great astonishment.
The daughter merely covered her mouth and smiled.
Zhǎn questioned her in detail,
but the daughter was shy and hesitant to speak;
Fēng briefly recounted the general situation for her.
Zhǎn was greatly delighted,
and loved her more than ever.
He had his son, Dàchéng, study with his son-in-law,
and provided abundantly for them.
After more than a year,
Dàchéng gradually grew to dislike him,
and thus the brothers-in-law could not get along;
the servants also found fault with his shortcomings.
Zhǎn, swayed by these insidious slanders,
became somewhat lax in his treatment.
The daughter sensed this
and said to Fēng:
“My parents’ house is not a place to stay long;
all those who stay long
become common and mediocre.
Before a major rift occurs,
we should return quickly.”
Fēng agreed,
and told Zhǎn.
Zhǎn wanted to keep his daughter,
but she refused.
Her father and brothers were all angry
and did not provide a carriage or horses.
The daughter used her own dowry funds to buy horses and return.
Later, Zhǎn invited her to return for a visit,
but the daughter firmly declined to stay.
Later, Fēng was recommended as Xiàolián,
and only then did relations become cordial.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“Are lower-ranking officials generally more greedy?
Is that the normal state of affairs?
Three hundred [coins] for false accusation of illicit relations,
and the last vestiges of moral character are completely lost.
To snatch a good match
and send her to a brothel,
ultimately leading to a violent death.
Alas!
How dreadful!”
In the *jiǎzǐ* year of the Kāngxī
era (1684), the district magistrate of Bèiqiū
was most greedy and deceitful, and the people all resented him.
Suddenly, his wife was lured away by a cunning man and eloped with him.
Someone put up a wanted poster on his behalf which read:
"A certain official, due to his own carelessness,
has lost one wife.
She carries nothing else on her person,
only seven *chǐ* of red silk,
wrapping one *yuánbǎo*,
with upturned edges and fine patterns,
and no damage whatsoever."
This was also a small, witty report.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A scholar from Dōngyuè, by the surname Guō,
was returning from a friend's house in the evening,
when he got lost in the mountains
and burrowed into the thickets.
After a longer while,
he heard laughter and talking from the mountaintop,
and hurried towards it.
He saw more than ten people
drinking on the ground.
Seeing Guō,
they jovially said:
"We're just missing one guest at our gathering,
excellent!
Excellent!"
Once Guō sat down,
he saw that half of the guests wore scholar's caps,
so he asked them to show him the way.
One person laughed and said:
"You are truly a pedantic old fogey!
How can you not appreciate this bright moon,
and instead ask for the road?"
Then a wine goblet flew towards him.
Guō drank it,
its fragrance filled his nostrils,
and one draught emptied it.
Another person held a pot and poured for him.
Guō was an able drinker,
and furthermore, he had been running and was parched,
so he drank ten goblets in one go.
Everyone greatly praised him, saying:
"What a hero!
Truly our friend!"
Guō was uninhibited and liked to joke,
and could imitate the sounds of birds
without any failing to be strikingly similar.
He left his seat to relieve himself,
and secretly made the sound of a swallow.
The group wondered, saying:
"How can there be a swallow at midnight?"
He then imitated a cuckoo,
and the group grew even more suspicious.
Guō sat down,
but only smiled and said nothing.
While they were discussing in confusion,
Guō suddenly mimicked a parrot, saying:
"Scholar Guō is drunk,
let's send him home!"
The group listened in surprise,
then it became silent again.
A little later,
he did it again.
Soon after, they realized it was Guō,
and then burst into laughter.
They all pursed their lips and tried to learn,
but not one could.
One person said:
"It's a pity Qīngniángzǐ hasn't arrived yet."
Another person said:
"We will gather here again on Mid-Autumn Festival,
Mr. Guō must not fail to come."
Guō respectfully agreed.
One person stood up and said:
"Our guest has extraordinary skills;
we too will offer a shoulder-stepping trick,
what do you say?"
Thereupon, they all rose up with a clamor.
The first person stood tall and erect;
then another person swiftly climbed onto his shoulders,
and also stood erect;
they piled up to four people,
so high that it was impossible to climb further;
those who followed
climbed on shoulders and stepped on arms,
like ascending a ladder: more than ten people
were all up in an instant,
looking as if they could reach the sky.
While he was looking on in astonishment,
they collapsed straight to the ground,
transforming into a long, thin path.
Guō stood frozen in terror for a long time,
then followed the path and found his way home.
The next day,
he suffered severe abdominal pain;
his urine was green,
like copper rust,
and could stain objects,
but had no urinary odor,
and this lasted for three days.
He went to inspect the former spot,
and found bones from food scattered about,
with dense bushes all around,
and no path at all.
When Mid-Autumn Festival arrived,
Guō wanted to keep the appointment,
but his friends advised him against it.
If he dared to go again to meet Qīngniángzǐ,
there would surely be more strangeness.
Alas, his resolve wavered!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Daoist priest,
traveling during the day, came to a wild temple
as evening fell.
Seeing the monk's cell locked,
he borrowed a meditation cushion
and sat cross-legged under the corridor.
When night was quiet,
he heard the sound of a door opening and closing.
Soon, he saw a monk approach,
covered in blood,
yet he seemed not to see the Daoist priest,
and the Daoist priest also seemed not to see him.
The monk went straight into the hall,
climbed onto the Buddha's seat,
embraced the Buddha's head and laughed,
then left after a long while.
When dawn came,
he looked at the room;
the door was locked as before.
Finding it strange,
he entered the village and recounted what he had seen.
The villagers went to the temple,
unlocked the door and inspected it,
and found the monk killed on the ground,
with mats and baskets in the room overturned,
knowing it was a robbery.
They suspected the ghost's laughter had a reason;
they all examined the Buddha's head,
and saw a faint mark on the back of its head.
When they chiseled it open,
they found more than thirty pieces of gold hidden inside.
They then used it to bury him.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"There's a proverb: 'Wealth is tied to life.'
Is it not true!
For a person to be frugal and accumulate wealth
for someone they don't know who they are,
is already foolish;
how much more so for a monk who doesn't know who they are and has no one!
He refused to enjoy it in life,
and even after death, he still looked back and laughed at it—
such is the lamentable state of a miser.
The Buddha says: 'Not one coin can be taken with you,
only your karma follows your body.'
This refers to that monk, does it not!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Gān Yù,
courtesy name Bìrén,
was a native of Lúlíng.
His parents died early.
He was left with a younger brother, Jué,
courtesy name Shuāngbì,
who was only five years old.
Gān Yù raised him as his own.
Yù was kind and affectionate,
nursing his brother as if he were his son.
Later, as Jué gradually grew up,
he became strikingly handsome
and also intelligent and skilled in writing.
Yù loved him even more,
often saying:
"My brother is outstanding;
he must not be without a worthy match."
However, he was overly selective in his choices,
so no marriage was settled.
It happened that he was studying in a Buddhist temple on Kuāng Shān.
One night, just as he lay down to sleep,
he heard female voices outside his window.
Peering out,
he saw three or four young women sitting on the ground,
with several maids setting out wine.
All of them were exceptionally beautiful.
One woman said:
"Lady Qín,
why hasn't Āyīng come?"
The one sitting below replied:
"She came from Hángǔ yesterday,
and was injured in her right arm by a villain.
She cannot join us in our outing,
and is quite resentful about it."
Another woman said:
"Last night I had a terrible dream;
I'm still sweating and trembling from it."
The one sitting below waved her hand and said:
"Don't speak of it,
don't speak of it!
Tonight is a joyful gathering for us sisters,
talking about it would be frightening and unpleasant."
The woman laughed and said:
"How timid you are, girl!
What if a tiger or wolf carried you away?
If you wish not to speak,
then you must sing a song
to toast us ladies with wine."
The woman sang softly:
"On the quiet steps, peach blossoms open in succession,
yesterday's outing to pick herbs shouldn't have been wrong.
I've told my neighbor friend to wait a little longer and not rush me,
I'll be there as soon as I put on my phoenix-head slippers."
When she finished singing,
everyone present admired and praised her.
Amidst their laughter and chatter,
suddenly a towering, imposing man entered from outside.
His hawk-like eyes gleamed,
and his appearance was fierce and ugly.
The women cried out:
"The monster is here!"
In a panic, they dispersed with a clamor,
almost like birds scattering.
Only the singer, graceful and unwilling to retreat,
was seized and cried out mournfully,
struggling to resist.
The man roared in anger,
biting off her fingers and severing them,
then immediately chewing and eating them.
The young woman fell to the ground as if dead.
Yù, pitying her, could no longer bear it.
He quickly drew his sword, opened the door, and came out.
He swung it,
striking the monster's thigh;
its thigh fell off,
and it fled in pain.
He helped the woman into the room;
her face was like dust,
blood stained her collar and sleeves;
examining her hand,
her right thumb was indeed severed.
He tore cloth to bandage it.
The woman began to moan:
"How can I repay your life-saving kindness?"
From the moment Yù first peeked,
his heart had already secretly planned for his brother.
He therefore told her his intention.
The woman said:
"A person afflicted by a wolf
cannot wield a broom.
You should plan separately for your worthy brother."
When asked her surname,
she replied:
"Qín."
Yù then spread a quilt,
allowing her to rest temporarily;
he himself wrapped his bedding and went elsewhere.
At dawn, when he looked,
the bed was already empty,
thinking she had returned home.
But when he inquired in nearby villages,
there were very few people with this surname;
he entrusted friends and relatives with a wide search,
but there was no definite news.
He returned and told his brother,
regretting it as if he had lost something precious.
One day, Jué was casually strolling in the countryside
when he met a sixteen-year-old girl.
Her appearance was exquisite.
She looked at him and smiled,
as if she was about to speak.
Then, she looked around with her beautiful eyes and asked:
"Are you the second young master of the Gān family?"
He said:
"Yes."
She said:
"Your esteemed father once had a marriage agreement with me,
why today do you wish to break the former pledge
and arrange another marriage with the Qín family?"
Jué said:
"I was young when I lost my parents,
and have never heard of any such old arrangements.
Please state your family and clan,
I will ask my brother when I return."
The woman said:
"There's no need for a detailed explanation;
just a single word,
and I will come myself."
Jué declined, citing that he had not yet obtained his brother's permission.
The woman laughed and said:
"You foolish young man!
Are you so afraid of your older brother?
My surname is Lù,
and I live in Wàng Cūn, Dōng Shān.
In three days,
I shall await your good news."
Then she bid farewell and left.
Jué returned
and told his brother and sister-in-law.
His brother said:
"This is utterly mistaken!
When father died,
I was over twenty years old.
If there had been such an agreement,
how could I not have heard of it?"
Moreover, because she was alone in the wilderness
and spoke with a man,
he despised her even more.
Then he asked about her appearance.
Jué's face and neck turned red,
and he said not a word.
His sister-in-law smiled and said:
"It must be a beautiful woman."
Yù said:
"How can a boy distinguish beauty from ugliness?
Even if she is beautiful,
she must be inferior to Qín;
if the Qín marriage doesn't work out,
it's not too late to consider her."
Jué silently withdrew.
Several days later,
Yù was on the road
when he saw a woman walking ahead, shedding tears.
He lowered his whip and held his reins, glancing slightly at her;
there was scarcely her equal in the human world.
He sent his servant to ask her,
and she replied:
"I was formerly betrothed to the second young master of the Gān family;
because my family was poor and moved far away,
all news and contact ceased.
Only recently have I returned,
and I heard again that the young master's family has been fickle,
breaking the former pledge.
I am going to ask Uncle Gān Bìrén
how he intends to treat me?"
Yù was surprised and delighted, saying:
"Gān Bìrén,
that is me.
I truly did not know of our ancestors' former agreement.
My home is not far,
please come back with me to discuss it immediately."
He then dismounted, handed over the reins,
and walked alongside her to return home.
The woman said of herself:
"My given name is Āyīng,
I have no brothers or sisters in my family,
only my older cousin, Lady Qín, lives with me."
Only then did he realize that the beautiful woman was indeed that person.
Yù wanted to tell his family,
but the woman firmly stopped him.
He was secretly pleased that his brother had found a good wife,
but feared that her frivolity might invite criticism.
After some time,
the woman was exceptionally dignified,
and also charming and eloquent.
She served his mother like a daughter,
and his sister-in-law also greatly admired her.
It was the Mid-Autumn Festival.
The couple was enjoying an intimate banquet
when his sister-in-law summoned him.
Jué felt dispirited.
The woman sent the messenger ahead,
promising to follow;
but she sat upright, laughing and talking for a long time,
showing no intention of leaving.
Jué feared his sister-in-law would have to wait long,
so he repeatedly urged her.
The woman merely smiled,
and ultimately did not go.
At dawn the next day,
after her morning toilette was just completed,
his sister-in-law came herself to inquire:
"Last night, when we were together,
why were you so sullen?"
The woman gave a slight smile.
Jué noticed something amiss;
their accounts did not match.
His sister-in-law was greatly alarmed:
"If she is not a demon,
how can she possess the art of splitting her body?"
Yù was also frightened,
and said to her from behind the curtain:
"Our family has accumulated virtue for generations;
we have never had any grievances or enemies.
If you are indeed a demon,
please leave quickly,
and fortunately do not kill my brother!"
The woman said blushingly:
"I am not human to begin with.
It is only because of Ēwēng's (阿翁) old pact
that Qínjiā Zǐ (秦家姊) persuaded me to come.
I have often wanted to leave;
the reason I lingered
is that my brother and sister-in-law have treated me well.
Now that I am suspected,
please allow me to bid farewell here."
In a blink, she transformed into a parrot
and flew away gracefully.
Initially,
when Gān Wēng (甘翁) was alive,
he kept a very intelligent parrot,
which he often fed himself.
At that time, Jué was four or five years old,
and asked:
"Why are you feeding the bird?"
His father playfully said:
"I will make it your wife."
Sometimes, when the parrot was short of food,
it would call out to Jué, saying:
"If you don't bring food,
your wife will starve to death!"
The family members also all made a game of this.
Later, its lock broke and it escaped.
Only then did they realize that the old pact referred to this.
However, even though Jué knew she was not human,
he could not stop thinking about her;
his sister-in-law's concern was even more profound,
weeping day and night.
Yù regretted it, but there was nothing she could do.
Two years later, they arranged for his brother to marry a woman from the Jiāng (姜) family,
but he never felt content.
A cousin, who was the Sì Lǐ (司李) in Yuè (粵),
Yù went to visit him,
and did not return for a long time.
It happened that local bandits caused chaos,
and nearby villages
were half-reduced to ruins.
Jué was terrified,
and led his family to take refuge in a mountain valley.
On the mountain, men and women were quite mixed,
and no one knew who was who.
Suddenly, he heard a woman's soft voice,
remarkably like Yīng's (英).
His sister-in-law urged Jué to go closer and verify,
and it was indeed Yīng.
Jué was overjoyed,
grabbing her arm and not letting go.
The woman then said to her companions:
"Sister, you go ahead;
I will wait for my sister-in-law to come."
When she arrived,
his sister-in-law saw her and choked with emotion.
The woman comforted and advised her repeatedly,
and also said:
"This is not a peaceful place."
So she persuaded them to return.
Everyone feared the bandits would arrive,
but the woman insisted:
"It's fine."
So they all went back together.
The woman gathered earth to block the door,
instructing them to stay put and not go out,
said a few words,
then turned to leave.
His sister-in-law quickly grasped her wrist,
and also made two maids seize her left and right feet,
so the woman had no choice
but to stay.
However, she did not really return to her private room;
Jué pleaded with her three or four times
before she finally went there.
His sister-in-law often said that the new wife could not satisfy her brother-in-law.
So the woman rose early to do Jiāng's (姜) makeup;
after combing her hair,
she meticulously applied powder and yellow pigment.
When people looked at her,
her beauty increased severalfold;
after three such days,
she had truly become a beauty.
His sister-in-law was astonished,
and then said:
"Moreover, I have no sons.
I wish to buy a concubine,
but for now, I have no leisure.
I wonder if these maids can be painted and adorned?"
The woman said:
"No one is impossible to transform,
but those with good natural quality are easier to work with."
Thereupon, she examined all the maids.
Only one, who was dark and ugly,
had the auspicious appearance for bearing sons.
So she called her to be washed and cleaned,
and afterward, applied a thick powder mixed with herbal paste to her.
After three days of this,
her complexion gradually turned yellow;
after twenty-eight days (four sevens),
the oils and ointments had permeated her skin,
making her quite presentable.
Daily, she would close her doors and practice smiling,
not concerning herself with war or fire.
One night,
clamor arose from all directions,
and the whole family did not know what was happening.
Soon, they heard people and horses stirring outside the gate,
then scattering and departing.
When dawn broke,
they realized the village had been mostly burned and plundered;
the bandits had let their groups search exhaustively,
and all who had hidden in caves or on banks
were killed or abducted.
Thereupon, they held the woman in even greater esteem,
regarding her as divine.
The woman suddenly said to the sister-in-law:
"I came here
solely because I could not forget your kindness,
merely to relieve your worries during this time of chaos.
When Ābó arrives,
for me to be here
is, as the proverb says,
neither a plum nor a peach,
making one a laughingstock.
I shall take my leave now,
and will seize an opportunity to visit you again."
The sister-in-law asked:
"Are the travelers safe?"
She replied:
"There is great danger nearby.
This has nothing to do with others;
Qínjiā Zǐ has received excessive kindness,
and will surely repay it,
so there should be no harm."
The sister-in-law urged her to stay the night,
but she left before dawn.
Yù returned from Dōngyuè,
heard about the chaos,
and hastened his journey.
On the way, he encountered bandits;
master and servant abandoned their horses,
each securing gold around their waist,
and hid themselves in a thicket.
A Qín Jíliǎo flew and perched on the thicket,
spreading its wings to cover them.
He looked at its feet,
and it was missing a toe;
he found this strange.
Soon, groups of bandits converged from all directions,
searching almost every part of the wilderness,
as if looking for them.
The two dared not breathe.
When the bandits dispersed,
the bird finally flew away.
Upon returning home,
they each recounted what they had seen,
and only then realized that the Qín Jíliǎo was the beautiful one they had saved.
Later, Yù often went out and did not return;
Yīng would surely arrive in the evening;
Jue planned for Yù to return and leave early.
Jue sometimes met at the sister-in-law's place,
and occasionally invited her,
but she would agree and then not come.
One evening,
Yù went out,
and Jue, believing Yīng would surely come,
lay in wait.
Not long after,
Yīng indeed arrived.
He suddenly rose,
intercepted her, and took her back to his room.
The woman said:
"My romantic fate with you is exhausted.
Forcibly uniting us,
I fear, will incur the displeasure of the Creator.
If we leave some things unsaid,
meeting occasionally,
how would that be?"
Jue did not listen,
and finally had intimacy with her.
At dawn,
she went to the sister-in-law,
who found it strange.
The woman smiled and said:
"I was robbed by strong bandits midway,
I've made you worry."
With a few words, she hurried out.
Not long after,
a giant civet cat carrying a parrot passed by the bedroom door.
The sister-in-law was utterly shocked,
firmly suspecting it was Yīng.
She was bathing at the time,
stopped washing, cried out urgently,
and everyone rose and attacked,
finally getting the parrot.
Its left wing was stained with blood,
and it was barely clinging to life.
She held it on her lap,
stroking it for a long time,
until it gradually revived.
It used its beak to preen its wing.
A moment later,
it flew around the main hall,
crying out:
"Sǎosǎo,
farewell!
I resent Jue!"
It flapped its wings and then left,
never to return.
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Liú Gōng of Shǎnxī,
served as the magistrate of Xīnghuà.
A Daoist priest came to present a potted plant;
when he looked at it,
it was a small orange tree,
finely trimmed to the size of a finger.
He rejected it.
Liú had a young daughter,
then six or seven years old,
who was celebrating her first birthday.
The Daoist priest said:
"This is not sufficient for an adult's elegant enjoyment,
it is merely to wish the young lady good fortune and longevity."
So he accepted it.
The daughter, upon seeing it,
was exceedingly delighted.
She placed it in her private quarters,
protecting it day and night for fear of damage.
When Liú's term of office expired,
the orange tree was already as thick as a handful.
It bore fruit for the first time that year.
When packing for the journey,
considering the orange tree a heavy burden,
he planned to discard it.
The daughter embraced the tree and cried plaintively.
Her family deceived her, saying:
"It's just for a moment,
and it will return later."
The daughter believed it,
and her tears stopped.
Fearing that a strong person might carry it away,
she watched her family transplant it to the steps below,
then they departed.
When the daughter returned home,
she was betrothed to a man named Zhuāng.
Zhuāng passed the imperial examination in the bǐngxū year,
and was appointed magistrate of Xīnghuà.
The lady was greatly pleased.
She secretly thought that after more than ten years,
the orange tree would no longer exist,
but when she arrived,
the orange tree was already ten arm-spans in circumference,
with countless fruits hanging in clusters.
When she asked the old servants,
they all said:
"After Liú Gōng left,
the orange tree was very lush but did not bear fruit;
this is its first time bearing fruit."
She found it even stranger.
Zhuāng served for three years,
and it bore fruit profusely without cease;
in the fourth year,
it withered, losing all its splendor.
The lady said:
"Your term of office here will not be long."
By autumn,
he was indeed relieved of his post.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Did the orange tree share a past karmic connection with the lady?
How coincidental their encounter!
Its bearing fruit seems like gratitude,
and its loss of splendor seems like sadness at separation.
If things are like this,
how much more so for humans?"
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
On a winter night in the Yǐwèi year of Shùnzhì,
red characters like fire appeared in the sky.
The text read:
"Bái Tiáo dài Jìng fǒu fù yì cháo yě chí."
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Niú Chéngzhāng
was a cloth merchant from Jiāngxī.
He married a woman surnamed Zhèng,
and they had one son and one daughter.
Niú died of illness at the age of thirty-three.
His son, named Zhōng,
was then only twelve;
his daughter was eight or nine years old.
The mother could not remain chaste;
she pocketed their assets,
remarried, and left.
She abandoned the two orphans,
who found it difficult to survive.
An aunt of Niú,
already sixty years old,
poor, widowed, and homeless,
came to live with them.
After several years,
the old woman died,
and the family declined even further.
As Zhōng gradually grew up,
he wished to continue his father's business but lacked capital.
His sister married a man named Máo,
who was a wealthy merchant.
The daughter, out of pity for her brother, borrowed several tens of gold coins from her husband and gave them to him.
The brother followed someone to Jīnlíng,
but on the way, he encountered bandits,
lost all his money and belongings,
and drifted, unable to return home.
He happened to go into a pawnshop
and saw that the proprietor remarkably resembled his father;
he went out and secretly investigated him,
and both his surname and given name matched.
He was surprised and bewildered, not understanding the reason.
He spent days lingering nearby,
trying to discern his intentions,
but the man barely paid him any attention.
After three such days,
observing his speech, laughter, and gestures,
it was truly his father without a doubt.
Yet he still dared not acknowledge him;
instead, he introduced himself to the shop assistants,
requesting, on account of their shared hometown,
to be taken on as a servant.
After the contract was drawn up,
the master looked at his hometown and surname,
seeming somewhat moved,
and asked where he came from.
Zhōng tearfully recounted his father's name.
The master was dejected, as if having lost something.
After a long while,
he asked:
“Is your mother well?”
Zhōng again dared not say his father was dead,
and subtly replied:
“My father went on a business trip six years ago and never returned.
My mother remarried and left.
Fortunately, my aunt raised us;
otherwise,
we would have been buried in a ditch long ago.”
The master said sadly:
“I am your father.”
Then they clasped hands and wept with sorrow.
He then led him in to meet his stepmother.
The stepmother, Jī,
was over thirty years old,
had no children,
and was delighted to have Zhōng.
She arranged a feast in the inner chamber.
Niú, however, remained tearful and unhappy,
immediately wishing to return to his old home.
His wife worried about the lack of staff in the shop,
so she stopped him.
Niú then directed his son to manage the shop affairs;
after three months,
he entrusted all the ledgers to his son
and packed his bags to return west.
After their departure,
Zhōng truthfully told his mother that his father had died.
Jī was greatly astonished,
saying:
“He has been a peddler here,
and those I befriended before
stayed on as regular merchants;
I have been married to him for six years.
Why do you say he is dead?”
Zhōng then recounted the details.
They both felt doubt and confusion,
not understanding how this could be.
A day and a night passed,
and Niú had already returned,
bringing with him a woman
whose hair was like tangled weeds.
Zhōng looked at her
and saw that it was his birth mother.
Niú grabbed her ear and cursed fiercely:
“Why did you abandon my children!”
The woman cowered, daring not to move slightly.
Niú bit her neck.
The woman cried to Zhōng:
“Son, save me!
Son, save me!”
Zhōng felt great pity
and stood between them to protect her.
Niú was still enraged,
but the woman had already disappeared.
Everyone was greatly astonished,
shouting about a ghost.
They then looked at Niú,
whose complexion had terribly changed;
he shed his clothes onto the ground
and turned into a black mist,
which also quickly vanished.
The mother and son were shocked and sighed,
gathering his clothes and hat and burying them.
Zhōng inherited his father's business
and became wealthy with ten thousand pieces of gold.
Later, when he returned home to inquire,
his remarried mother had died on that very day,
and her entire family had seen Niú Chéngzhāng, it was said.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Huò Héng,
courtesy name Kuāngjiǔ,
was from Jìn.
His father served as a county magistrate [xiànwèi]
but died young.
He was the youngest of the remaining children,
exceptionally intelligent and wise.
At eleven,
he was admitted to the government school as a child prodigy.
However, his mother was overly protective,
forbidding him from leaving the courtyard,
so at thirteen, he still couldn't distinguish between uncles, cousins, nephews, and maternal uncles.
In the same village lived a Grand Councilor [Píngshì] Wǔ,
who was devoted to the Dao [dào],
entered the mountains, and never returned.
He had a daughter, Qīng'é,
aged fourteen,
whose beauty was extraordinary.
As a child, she secretly read her father's books
and admired Hè Xiānggū.
After her father went into seclusion,
she resolved not to marry.
Her mother could do nothing about it.
One day,
Huò Héng caught a glimpse of her outside his gate.
Though a child and ignorant,
he felt extreme love for her
but could not express it;
he went directly to his mother,
asking her to arrange a betrothal.
His mother knew it was impossible,
so she made difficulties.
Huò Héng became depressed and uneasy.
His mother, fearing to upset her son,
then entrusted a passerby to convey her intentions to Wǔ,
but it indeed did not succeed.
Huò Héng pondered while walking and sat thinking,
with no plan in mind.
It happened that there was a Daoist priest at the gate,
holding a small pickaxe in his hand,
about a foot long.
The scholar borrowed it for a look,
and asked:
"What is this for?"
He replied:
"This is a tool for digging herbs;
though it is small,
it can penetrate solid rock."
The scholar was not entirely convinced.
The Daoist priest immediately used it to chop at a stone on the wall,
and it crumbled like rotten wood with a touch.
The scholar was greatly amazed by this,
and played with it, unable to put it down.
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
"If Young Master likes it,
I shall present it to you."
The scholar was overjoyed,
and offered money in return,
but he refused it and left.
Bringing it home,
he tried it on bricks and stones,
finding absolutely no impediment.
He suddenly thought that by tunneling through the wall, he could see the beauty,
and did not realize that it was unlawful.
When evening arrived,
he climbed over the wall and went out,
straight to the residence of the Wǔ [武] family;
he tunneled through two layers of walls,
before finally reaching the central courtyard.
He saw that in a small side room,
there was still lamplight,
so he crouched down and peeped,
and saw Qīng'é [青娥] removing her evening attire.
A short while later,
the candle went out,
and there was complete silence.
He dug through the wall and entered;
the girl was already fast asleep.
He gently removed his shoes,
and quietly got onto the bed;
then, fearing the young lady might wake up in surprise,
and he would surely be reprimanded and driven out,
he stealthily hid by the side of the embroidered quilt,
barely smelling her fragrance,
his heart’s desire secretly fulfilled.
However, having been active in the middle of the night,
he was quite exhausted,
and after a moment of closing his eyes,
he unconsciously fell asleep.
The girl awoke,
and heard a gentle snore;
she opened her eyes,
and saw light streaming in through a hole.
Greatly alarmed,
she secretly shook her maid awake,
pulled back the bolt and gently went out,
tapped on the window to call the female servants,
and together they lit a fire and armed themselves with sticks to go back.
They saw a young scholar,
with hair tied in two knots, deeply asleep on the embroidered bed;
upon closer inspection,
they recognized him as Scholar Huò [霍].
They pushed him, and he finally awoke,
and suddenly rose,
his eyes shining like shooting stars,
seemingly not greatly afraid,
but blushingly he said not a word.
The crowd pointed at him as a thief,
and were about to scold him.
He then shed tears and said:
"I am not a thief;
it is truly because I love the young lady,
and wished to be near her fragrance."
The crowd then doubted that tunneling through several walls
was possible for a young boy.
The scholar brought out the pickaxe and explained its extraordinary nature.
They all tried it,
and were utterly astonished,
marveling that it was divinely bestowed.
They were about to report it to the madam.
The girl bowed her head in deep thought,
her intention seemingly disapproving.
The crowd perceived her meaning,
and therefore said:
"This young man’s reputation and family background
would not bring disgrace.
It would be better to let him go,
and have him seek a matchmaker again.
Tomorrow morning,
we can pretend it was a thief when we inform the madam,
how about that?"
The girl did not answer.
So the crowd urged the scholar to leave.
The scholar had forgotten his pickaxe.
They all laughed and said:
"Silly child!
Still can't forget your weapon?"
The scholar glanced at the bedside,
and there was a phoenix hairpin;
he secretly slipped it into his sleeve.
This was seen by a maid,
who immediately reported it.
The girl neither spoke nor showed anger.
An old woman patted his neck and said:
"Don't say he's silly;
his little scheme is quite clever."
Then they dragged him,
and he exited through the hole again.
Upon returning,
he dared not tell his mother the truth,
but only instructed her to send a matchmaker again.
His mother could not bear to outright refuse,
but only entrusted various matchmakers
to urgently find another good marriage.
Qīng'é [青娥] knew this,
and felt anxious in her heart,
secretly sending a trusted confidante to hint to the old woman.
The old woman was persuaded,
and entrusted a matchmaker to go.
It happened that a little maid leaked the previous incident,
and Madame Wǔ [武] disgraced him,
overwhelmed with anger and indignation.
When the matchmaker arrived,
it further fueled her rage,
she drew lines on the ground with a stick,
cursing the scholar and his mother.
The matchmaker fled in fear,
and fully recounted the situation.
The scholar’s mother also angrily said:
"What my unworthy son did,
I know nothing about.
Why would she treat me with such disrespect?
At the time of their encounter,
why didn't they kill both the dissolute boy and the immoral girl?"
From then on, whenever she saw her relatives,
she would immediately complain.
The girl heard this,
and was ashamed to death.
Madame Wǔ [武] greatly regretted it,
but could not stop her from speaking.
The girl secretly sent someone to gently convey to the scholar's mother,
and also vowed her fidelity,
her words were sorrowful and sincere.
The mother was moved by this,
and no longer spoke of it;
and the matchmakers discussing the marriage,
also ceased their efforts.
At that time, Ōu Gōng [歐公] from Qín Zhōng [秦中] was the magistrate of this county.
He saw the scholar’s writings,
and deeply admired him,
often summoning him to his private residence,
treating him with extreme favor and kindness.
One day,
he asked the scholar:
"Are you married?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
When asked in detail,
he answered:
"I had an old agreement with the daughter of the late Censor Wǔ [武];
later, due to a minor misunderstanding,
it was suspended."
He asked:
"Do you still wish for it?"
The scholar blushed and said nothing.
The Duke smiled and said:
"I shall arrange it for you."
He immediately entrusted the County Lieutenant and the Education Officer
to offer betrothal gifts to the Wǔ [武] family.
The Madam was pleased,
and the marriage was then settled.
After a year,
he married her and brought her home.
When the girl entered the door,
she threw the pickaxe to the ground and said:
"This is a thief's tool,
you may take it away!"
The scholar laughed and said:
"Do not forget the matchmaker."
He treasured and wore it, always keeping it close to him.
The woman was gentle, kind, and quiet.
Three times a day, she paid respects to her mother.
For the rest, she merely closed her door and sat silently,
not paying much attention to household chores.
If her mother happened to go stay elsewhere due to visiting,
then she would manage everything,
and nothing was not orderly.
After more than a year,
she gave birth to a son, Mèngxiān.
She entrusted everything to the wet nurse and nanny,
seemingly not caring much for him.
Another four or five years passed,
when she suddenly said to the student:
"Our bond of joyful love
has lasted eight years now.
To part long and meet short now,
what can be done!"
The student was startled and questioned her,
but she immediately fell silent.
She dressed elaborately, bowed to her mother,
turned, and entered her room.
When he pursued and questioned her,
she was already lying on the bed, looking up, and had stopped breathing.
Mother and son mourned deeply,
purchased good timber, and buried her.
The mother was already frail and aged.
She frequently held her grandson and thought of her daughter,
which felt like her lungs and liver were torn apart.
Because of this, she fell ill,
and then became so weak that she could not rise.
She rejected food and drink,
but only longed for fish soup.
There was none nearby,
and it could only be purchased a hundred *lǐ* away.
At that time, all the servants and riders had been dispatched;
the student was by nature purely filial,
and could not wait.
He took money and went alone,
without stopping his steps day or night.
When he returned to the mountains,
the sun had already set and it was dark.
Both his feet were swollen and his stride was impaired,
unable to walk even a *zhǐ*.
Later, an old man arrived
and asked,
"Are your feet not blistered?"
The student assented.
The old man then pulled him to sit by the roadside,
struck a stone to make fire,
wrapped some powdered medicine in paper,
and fumigated the student's feet with it.
When he tried to walk,
not only did the pain stop,
but he also became more robust.
He was extremely grateful and offered his thanks.
The old man asked,
"Why are you in such a hurry?"
He replied that his mother was ill,
and then recounted the entire reason.
The old man asked,
"Why do you not marry again?"
He replied,
"I have not found a good one."
The old man pointed far to a mountain village and said,
"There is a beautiful woman here.
If you can come with me,
I will be the matchmaker for you."
The student declined, saying his mother was ill and waiting for fish,
and he currently had no leisure.
The old man then cupped his hands in a salutation,
agreed to meet another day in the village,
saying to just ask for Lǎo Wáng,
and then he left.
The student returned,
cooked the fish, and offered it to his mother.
His mother ate a little,
but after several days, she passed away.
He then ordered servants and horses to go search for the old man.
Upon reaching the familiar place,
the location of the village was lost.
After wandering for a long time,
the evening sun gradually set;
the mountains and valleys were very intricate,
and it was impossible to see far.
So I climbed a hilltop with my servant
to look for the village;
but the mountain path was rugged,
too difficult to ride again,
so we trudged upwards,
as dusk enveloped the mist.
Pacing back and forth, looking in all directions,
there was no village to be seen.
Just as I was about to descend the mountain,
the way back was already lost.
My heart burned with anxiety.
Amidst my frantic search,
I plunged down a sheer cliff.
Fortunately, a few feet below was a narrow, desolate platform,
where I fell and lay,
just wide enough for my body,
with darkness so deep below that I couldn't see the bottom.
Terrified,
I dared not move even slightly.
Again fortunately, small trees grew along the cliff edge,
enclosing my body like a railing.
After a while,
I saw a small cave entrance near my feet;
my heart secretly rejoiced,
and with my back against the rock,
I crawled in like a grub.
My mind felt slightly more at ease,
hoping that I could call for help when day broke.
A short while later,
a light like a star point appeared in the deep interior.
Gradually approaching it,
after about three or four *lǐ*,
I suddenly saw a corridor and dwelling,
without any oil lamps,
yet as bright as day.
A beautiful woman came out from the room,
and looking at her,
it was indeed Qīng'é.
Seeing the scholar,
she exclaimed in surprise:
"How could you have come, my lord?"
The scholar had no time to explain,
and embraced her, sobbing mournfully.
The woman advised him to stop.
When she asked about his mother and son,
the scholar recounted all his hardships,
and the woman also looked sorrowful.
The scholar said:
"You died over a year ago;
is this not the underworld?"
The woman replied:
"No,
this is an immortal's abode.
I did not die that time;
what was buried
was merely a bamboo staff.
Your coming now
means you have a share in immortal destiny."
She then led him to meet her father,
who was a long-bearded man
sitting in the main hall;
the scholar bowed to him.
The woman announced:
"Huò Láng has arrived."
The old man rose in surprise,
shook his hand, and briefly inquired about his well-being.
He said:
"It is excellent that my son-in-law has come;
it is destined that you stay here."
The scholar declined, citing his mother's expectation,
and that he could not stay long.
The old man said:
"I know that too.
But what harm is there in delaying for three or four days?"
Then he offered him food and wine,
and immediately ordered a maidservant to set up a bed in the west hall,
laying out a brocade mattress.
After the scholar had retired,
he invited the woman to share the bed with him.
The woman refused, saying:
"What kind of place is this,
that would allow such intimacy?"
The scholar grasped her arm and would not let go.
Outside the window, the maidservants' laughter was heard,
and the woman became even more ashamed.
While they were still struggling and refusing,
the old man entered,
and scolded:
"Your vulgar bones defile my immortal cave!
You should leave immediately!"
The scholar had always been hot-headed,
and, unable to bear the shame,
he flushed and said:
"The affections between a man and a woman
are unavoidable for humans;
why should an elder spy on me?
I can leave without difficulty,
but you must let the woman come with me."
The old man had nothing to say,
beckoned the woman to follow him,
and opened the back door to see them off;
he tricked the scholar into leaving the door,
then the father and daughter closed the door and left.
Turning around, there were only sheer cliffs and peaks,
without the slightest crevice,
and he was all alone,
with nowhere to go.
He looked at the high, slanting moon in the sky,
and the stars were already sparse.
Despondent for a long time,
he felt sorrow, then hatred,
and faced the wall, crying out,
but there was no response.
Filled with extreme rage,
he took out a pickaxe from his waist,
and started chiseling at the stone, pushing forward,
chiseling and cursing.
In an instant, the cave extended three or four *chǐ*,
and faintly, human voices were heard saying:
"What a demonic obstacle!"
The scholar exerted more force, chiseling even faster.
Suddenly, two doors opened at the bottom of the cave,
and Qīng'é was pushed out, saying:
"You can go,
you can go!"
The wall immediately closed again.
The woman complained:
"Since you love me as your wife,
how can you treat your father-in-law like this?
Who is this old Daoist priest
who gave you such a fierce tool,
to entangle people and almost kill them?"
Having regained the woman,
the scholar's wish was fulfilled,
and he no longer argued;
he only worried that the road was dangerous and difficult to return by.
The woman broke two branches,
each straddled one,
and immediately they became like horses,
traveling swiftly,
and in a moment they arrived home.
At that time, the scholar had been missing for seven days.
Initially,
when Shēng and his servant lost each other,
he couldn't find her.
He returned home and told his mother.
His mother sent people to search the valleys thoroughly,
but there was no trace.
Just as she was anxiously distressed,
she heard her son had returned on his own,
and joyfully welcomed him.
When she raised her head and saw the woman,
she was nearly frightened to death.
Shēng briefly recounted the story,
and his mother was even more relieved and comforted.
The woman, finding her circumstances strange and unusual,
feared alarming others,
and asked to move immediately.
His mother agreed.
They had another property in a different prefecture,
and they set a date to move there,
unknown to anyone.
They lived together for eighteen years,
and had a daughter,
who married into the Lǐ family of the same district.
Later, his mother's life ended.
The woman said to Shēng:
"In the thatched field of our home,
there is a pheasant incubating eight eggs;
that spot is suitable for burial.
You and your son should carry the coffin back for interment.
Your son is already grown,
so he should stay and guard the tomb immediately;
there is no need to return."
Shēng followed her words and
returned by himself after the burial.
More than a month later,
Mèngxiān went to visit them,
but his parents were both gone.
When he asked an old servant,
he said:
"They went to the burial and haven't returned yet."
He knew in his heart it was unusual,
and could only sigh deeply.
Mèngxiān's literary reputation was very high,
but he struggled in the imperial examinations,
failing for forty years.
Later, as a '拔貢' (bágòng, a selected candidate), he entered the northern examination hall.
He met a fellow examinee,
who was about seventeen or eighteen years old,
with outstanding and elegant demeanor,
and he liked him.
Looking at his paper,
it was registered to Huò Zhòngxiān, a '順天廩生' (Shùntiān Lǐnshēng, an imperial student from Shùntiān prefecture).
He stared in great astonishment,
and then introduced his own name.
Zhòngxiān was also surprised,
and asked about his native place,
which Mèngxiān fully told him.
Zhòngxiān happily said:
"When I was heading to the capital,
my father instructed me that if I met anyone with the surname Huò from Shānyòu in the examination hall,
they were of our clan,
and I should treat them kindly.
Now it has indeed come true.
But why are our names so similar?"
Mèngxiān then inquired about his great-grandparents and parents' names,
and then exclaimed in surprise:
"They are my parents!"
Zhòngxiān doubted this due to the disparity in their ages.
Mèngxiān said:
"My parents are both immortals;
how can one trust their age based on their appearance?"
He then recounted the past events,
and Zhòngxiān finally believed him.
After the examination, without resting,
they ordered a carriage and returned together.
As soon as they arrived at the door,
the family members came to inform them
that that night the whereabouts of their '太翁' (tàiwēng, father) and '夫人' (fūrén, mother) were unknown.
Both were greatly shocked.
Zhòngxiān went in and asked his wife,
who said:
"Last night we were still drinking together,
and mother said: 'You husband and wife are young and inexperienced.
When Eldest Brother comes tomorrow,
I will have no worries.'
Early this morning, when I entered the room,
it was utterly empty."
The brothers heard this
and stomped their feet in sorrow.
Zhòngxiān still wanted to go search;
Mèngxiān thought it useless,
so they stopped.
In that year, Zhòng received the '鄉薦' (xiāngjiàn, recommendation from the provincial examination).
Because his ancestral tomb was in Jìnzhōng,
he returned with his elder brother.
They still hoped their parents were in the human world
and inquired wherever they went,
but ultimately found no trace.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Sleeping in a hole under the bed,
his intention was foolish;
carving the wall and scolding the old man,
his action was wild.
The immortals who brought them together
only wished to repay his filial piety with longevity.
However, since they mingled in the human world
