and intimately bore children,
would it not have been acceptable to live there until the end?
Why then,
after thirty years, did they repeatedly abandon their sons?
How peculiar!
It is truly strange!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
The Zhèng brothers of Yìdū
were both scholars.
The elder Zhèng gained fame early,
and his parents always doted on him,
and consequently also on his son and his wife.
The younger Zhèng was unaccomplished
and not much favored by his parents,
who thus disliked his second wife,
to the point of not treating her with proper courtesy.
The contrast between their warmth and coldness caused considerable resentment.
The second wife often said to the younger Zhèng,
"You are also a man;
why can't you bring honor to your wife?"
She then refused to sleep with him.
Thus, the younger Zhèng felt indignant,
applied himself diligently to study and thought,
and also achieved fame.
His parents gradually showed him more care and attention,
but he was still overshadowed by his elder brother.
The second wife's hopes for her husband were extremely high.
In that year of the grand examination,
on New Year's Eve, she secretly used '鏡聽' (jìng tīng, mirror divination) to divine.
Two people had just gotten up,
pushing each other playfully,
saying:
"You too, go relax!"
The wife returned,
unable to decipher the fortune or misfortune,
and put it aside.
After the examination,
both brothers returned.
At that time, the summer heat was still intense,
and both wives were cooking in the kitchen to send food to those working in the fields,
suffering greatly from the heat.
Suddenly, a messenger on horseback arrived at the door,
announcing the success of the elder Zhèng.
The mother entered the kitchen and called to the elder wife, saying:
"My eldest son has passed the examination!
You can go relax."
The second wife felt resentful and sorrowful,
crying while still cooking.
Soon after, another messenger announced the success of the younger Zhèng.
The second wife forcefully threw down her rolling pin and stood up,
saying:
"I too, go relax!"
At this moment, stirred by her innermost feelings,
she unconsciously blurted it out;
only afterward, when she thought about it,
did she realize the validity of the mirror divination.
Yìshǐshì said:
"When one is poor, parents do not treat one as their child;
there is reason for this!
Within the household,
it is certainly not a place for indignation;
however, the younger Zhèng's wife, by spurring her husband,
is quite different from those who merely complain and are good-for-nothing.
To throw down the rolling pin and rise,
that is truly a moment of great satisfaction throughout history!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chén Huáfēng,
a Měngshān man.
Due to the oppressive heat of summer,
he lay down under a wild tree.
Suddenly, a man rushed over,
wearing a neck-wrap,
quickly approached the shade of the tree,
scooped up a stone to sit on,
fanned himself incessantly,
and sweat streamed down like a torrent.
Chén sat up,
and smilingly said:
"If you remove your neck-wrap,
you can be cool without fanning."
The guest said:
"Taking it off is easy,
but putting it back on is difficult."
Then they engaged in conversation,
which was quite profound and cultured.
After a while, he said:
"At this moment, I have no other thoughts
than to have some fine vintage wine chilled with ice,
a stream of cold fragrance
passing down the twelve-storied pagoda,
and half of the summer heat would dissipate."
Chén smiled and said:
"This wish is easy to fulfill;
I will grant it for you."
Thereupon, he clasped hands and said:
"My humble dwelling is near,
please come with me."
The guest smiled and followed him.
Upon reaching home,
Chén took out stored wine from a stone cave,
its coldness made one's teeth chatter.
The guest was greatly pleased,
and drank ten goblets in one go.
As dusk was setting in,
it suddenly rained;
so, Chén lit lamps in the room,
and the guest then removed his neck-wrap,
and they chatted freely.
In the course of their conversation,
Chén saw light leaking intermittently from the back of the guest's head,
and he became suspicious.
Before long,
the guest was drunk,
and fell asleep on the couch.
Chén moved the lamp and secretly peeked at him,
seeing a huge hole behind his ear,
the size of a bowl;
several membranes were partitioned like a lattice;
outside the lattice, soft leather hung down,
and the inside seemed empty.
He was extremely startled,
secretly drew out his hair ornament,
pushed aside the membrane to peer in,
and saw a creature resembling a small ox,
which flew out at his touch,
broke through the window and left.
He was even more startled,
and dared not poke again.
Just as he was about to turn away,
the guest had already woken up.
Startled, he said:
"You have spied my secret,
and released the Niúhuáng.
What shall I do now?"
Chén bowed and asked the reason.
The guest said:
"Since it is already like this,
what is there to conceal?
I will tell you the truth: I am the god of livestock plague.
What I just released was the Niúhuáng,
I fear that within a hundred *lǐ*, no cattle will survive."
Chén's traditional occupation was cattle farming,
hearing this, he was greatly terrified,
and bowed, begging for a method to resolve it.
The guest said:
"I myself cannot escape punishment,
what method can resolve it?
Only *kǔshēn sǎn* (bitter ginseng powder) is most effective;
widely disseminate this formula,
and harbor no selfish thoughts."
Having said this,
he bid farewell and exited the door.
He then scooped up some earth and piled it into a wall niche,
saying:
"Using one *hé* (a measure of volume) of this each time is also effective."
He cupped his hands and was seen no more.
Not long after,
the cattle indeed fell ill,
and a great plague broke out.
Chén wanted to monopolize the profit,
kept the formula secret,
and refused to transmit it;
he only transmitted it to his younger brother.
His brother tried it and found it miraculously effective.
But when Chén himself chopped and fed it to the cattle,
it had no effect at all.
Of his two hundred head of cattle,
almost all dropped dead;
the remaining four or five old cows
also staggered and soon died.
He was vexed at heart,
and powerless.
Suddenly he remembered the earth scooped into the niche,
thinking it might not be effective,
but decided to try it anyway.
Overnight,
all the cattle stood up.
Only then did he realize that the medicine's ineffectiveness
was a divine punishment for his selfishness.
Several years later,
the cows bred profusely,
gradually restoring his former situation.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本 edition)
In Kuàijī, there was a temple of Méigū.
The deity's surname was Mǎ,
her clan resided in Dōngguǎn,
she died young before marriage,
and thus vowed not to remarry,
dying at thirty.
Her clan commemorated her,
calling her Méigū.
In the *bǐngshēn* year,
Jīnshēng from Shàngyú,
passing through here on his way to an examination,
entered the temple and lingered,
becoming quite lost in thought.
That night,
he dreamt that a green-clad figure came,
conveying Méigū's command to summon him.
He followed.
Entering the temple,
Méigū stood waiting under the eaves,
and smilingly said:
"I am honored by your visit,
and truly feel a deep affection.
If you do not despise my humble clumsiness,
I wish to be your concubine."
Jīn merely assented.
Méigū sent him off saying:
"You may go now.
When your seat is arranged,
I will come to meet you."
He woke up angry about it.
That night,
the local residents dreamt that Méigū said:
"Jīnshēng from Shàngyú
is to be my husband,
you should sculpt his image."
When questioned, the villagers' dreams were all the same.
The clan leader feared it would taint her chastity,
and therefore refused.
Not long after,
every family member fell ill.
Greatly frightened,
they carved his likeness to the left.
Once completed,
Jīnshēng told his wife and children:
"Méigū is coming to welcome me."
He dressed formally and died.
His wife was heartbroken and resentful,
went to the temple, pointed at the female statue and cursed it filthily;
she then ascended the seat and slapped its cheek several times,
then left.
Nowadays, the Mǎ clan calls him Jīngūfū.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"To remain chaste though unmarried,
one cannot say she was not virtuous.
To be a ghost for several hundred years,
and then finally change her principles,
how shameless is that?
Generally, chaste souls and ardent spirits
do not necessarily reside in clay idols;
as for those temple statues that have spiritual power,
astounding the world and shocking common custom,
they are all possessed by ghosts or foxes."
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本 edition)
Graduate Cháng Dàzhōng,
a Tàiyuán man.
Was awaiting appointment in the capital.
The night before,
he dreamt that Wénchāng presented a calling card.
He drew a lot,
and got the magistrate of Zǐtóng.
He found it strange,
and later, after his parent's mourning period,
he was re-eligible for appointment,
and dreamt the same dream again.
He silently wondered if he would return to the post of Zǐtóng.
And indeed, he did.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本 edition)
Lǐ mǒu was lying down during the day
when he saw a woman emerge from the wall.
Her hair was disheveled like a basket,
and it hung down to cover her face.
When she reached the bed,
she finally used her hand to part her hair,
revealing her face.
She was plump, dark, and extremely ugly.
Lǐ mǒu was greatly terrified
and wanted to flee.
The woman suddenly climbed onto the bed,
powerfully embraced his head,
and then pressed her lips against his,
passing her saliva with her tongue.
It was as cold as ice,
gradually invading his throat.
He wanted not to swallow, but he couldn't breathe if he didn't.
When he swallowed, it was thick and sticky, blocking his throat.
Just as he took one breath,
his mouth was full again,
and in his urgency, he swallowed again.
This continued for a long time,
until his breathing was so obstructed he could no longer endure it.
He heard someone walking outside the door,
and the woman then released him and left.
After this, his abdomen swelled and he had difficulty breathing,
and he couldn't eat for dozens of days.
Someone taught him to induce vomiting with Shēn Lú Tāng.
He vomited a substance like egg white,
and then he recovered.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Miǎn,
courtesy name Mǐnzhāi,
was a native of Língshān.
He was talented and intelligent,
and repeatedly topped the literary examinations.
His disposition was quite arrogant;
he was skilled at sarcastic criticism
and often humiliated others.
One day, he met a Daoist priest
who looked at him and said:
"Your physiognomy shows extreme nobility,
however, you have been afflicted by 'frivolous transgressions,'
which have almost entirely destroyed it.
With your wisdom,
if you were to turn back and cultivate the Dao,
you could still ascend to the ranks of immortals."
Wáng scoffed and said:
"Fortune is indeed unknowable,
but how can there be immortals in the world?"
The Daoist priest said:
"Why do you hold such low opinions?
I seek nothing else;
I myself am an immortal."
Wáng then laughed even more at his deception.
The Daoist priest said:
"What is so extraordinary about me?
If you can come with me,
you can immediately see dozens of true immortals."
Wáng asked:
"Where are they?"
He replied:
"They are very close by."
Then, he placed his staff between his legs,
and immediately offered one end to Wáng,
telling him to do as he did.
He instructed him to close his eyes,
and shouted:
"Rise!"
Wáng felt the staff was as thick as a five-dou sack,
and it flew swiftly through the air.
He secretly touched it,
and it had scales and teeth.
Terrified,
he dared not move again.
After some time,
the Daoist priest again shouted:
"Stop!"
Then he withdrew the staff,
and they landed in a grand residence,
with multiple stories and extended corridors,
like an emperor's abode.
There was a platform about a *zhàng* tall;
on the platform were eleven bays of halls,
magnificent beyond compare.
The Daoist priest led his guest up,
and immediately ordered a boy servant to set up a banquet and invite guests.
Dozens of banquets were arranged in the hall,
lavishly displayed and dazzling to the eye.
The Daoist priest changed into formal attire to receive them.
A moment later,
various guests arrived from the sky,
riding dragons, or tigers, or luán-fèng,
of various kinds.
Each also carried a musical instrument.
There were women,
there were men,
and some had bare feet.
Among them, one particularly beautiful woman
rode a colorful phoenix;
dressed in palace-style attire,
she had a maidservant carrying a musical instrument for her.
It was about five *chǐ* long,
neither a *qín* nor a *sè*,
its name unknown.
After the wine had been served,
various delicacies were presented,
sweet and fragrant to the taste,
all surpassing ordinary gourmet food.
Wáng sat silently,
his eyes fixed only on the beautiful woman;
he loved her person,
and also wished to hear her music,
secretly fearing she would not play even once.
When the wine party was coming to an end,
an old man initiated the conversation, saying:
"Thanking Zhēn Rén Cuī for his elegant invitation,
today can indeed be called a grand gathering,
and we should all enjoy ourselves fully.
Let those with the same instruments
form groups to play music."
Thereupon, everyone paired up according to their instruments.
The sounds of strings and flutes
resounded through the heavens.
Only the woman riding the phoenix
had no musical partner.
When the collective music ceased,
her maidservant began to open an embroidered pouch,
placing the instrument horizontally on a small table.
The woman then extended her jade wrist,
as if to pluck a *zhēng*.
Its brightness was several times that of a *qín*,
its intensity could open the chest,
its gentleness could sway the soul.
She played for about the time it takes to cook half a meal.
The entire hall was silent,
no one dared to cough.
When she finished,
there was a clang,
like striking a clear chime.
Everyone praised her, saying:
"Fū Rén Yúnhé's skill is superb indeed!"
Then everyone rose to bid farewell,
cranes cried and dragons roared,
and they all dispersed at once.
The Daoist priest set up an ornate bed and brocade quilt,
preparing a sleeping place for [Wáng 王].
When [Wáng] first saw the beautiful woman,
his heart was already stirred;
after hearing the music,
his thoughts were especially restless.
He thought of his own talent and ability,
which should naturally lead him to high official positions,
and after achieving wealth and honor, what could he not obtain?
In an instant, a hundred thoughts
were as tangled as flax.
The Daoist priest seemed to know this,
and said:
"Your previous incarnation was my fellow student,
but later your resolve was not firm,
and so you fell into the dust net.
I do not treat you as a stranger;
I truly wish to pull you out of the defilement;
unexpectedly, your delusion is already deep,
and you are in a dream-like state from which you cannot be awakened.
Now I must send you off.
It is not certain that we will never meet again,
but to become a celestial immortal
will require another two kalpas."
Thereupon, he pointed to a long stone at the foot of the steps,
bade [Wáng] close his eyes and sit,
and strictly enjoined him not to look.
Presently,
he drove the stone with his whip.
The stone flew up,
the sound of wind roared in his ears,
and he knew not how far they traveled.
Suddenly, he thought of the scenery below,
wondering what it was like;
he secretly opened his two eyes a tiny slit,
and saw a vast, boundless ocean,
utterly without end.
Greatly alarmed,
he immediately closed them again,
but his body, along with the stone, had already plunged down,
with a crashing sound,
submerging like a gull.
Fortunately, he had lived near the sea in the past,
and knew a little about swimming.
He heard someone clap their hands and say:
"What a beautiful fall!"
When he was in extreme peril,
a girl pulled him onto a boat,
and moreover said:
"Good fortune,
good fortune,
the scholar has 'become wet'!"
Looking at her,
she appeared about sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a beautiful and radiant complexion.
[Wáng], emerging from the water, shivered with cold,
and asked for fire to warm himself.
The girl said:
"Follow me home,
and I will arrange things for you.
If you are pleased,
do not forget me."
[Wáng] said:
"What kind of words are these!
I am a talented scholar from the central plains,
who has accidentally encountered this predicament;
if I pass this way, I intend to repay you with my life,
how could I merely not forget you!"
The girl propelled the boat with her oar,
as swift as wind and rain,
and soon they approached the shore.
From the cabin, she took a handful of freshly picked lotus flowers,
and led him to go together.
After about half a *lǐ* (里), they entered a village,
and saw a vermilion gate opening to the south.
They went through several layers of doors,
and the girl rushed in first.
A moment later,
a man came out,
about forty years old.
He bowed to [Wáng] and invited him to ascend the steps,
then ordered attendants to bring a cap, robe, socks, and shoes,
and helped [Wáng] change his clothes.
Afterwards,
he inquired about his family and origin.
[Wáng] said:
"I am not deceiving you;
my talent and reputation are somewhat known.
[Cuī Zhēnrén 崔真人] earnestly cherished and longed for me,
inviting me to ascend to the celestial palace.
I believed that fame and fortune were easily within my grasp,
and thus I was unwilling to live in reclusion."
The man rose in respect and said:
"This is called [Xiānrén Dǎo 仙人島] (Immortal Island),
far removed from the human world.
My given name is [Wénruò 文若],
and my surname is [Huán 桓].
My family has lived in this remote place for generations;
how fortunate to be near a renowned personage."
Thereupon, he cordially set out wine.
Then he spoke calmly:
"I have two daughters,
the elder, [Fāngyún 芳雲],
is sixteen years old,
and has not yet found a good match.
I wish to offer her to serve a distinguished personage;
what do you think?"
[Wáng] thought it must be the lotus-picking girl,
and rose from his seat to express his thanks.
[Huán] ordered for two or three respectable elders
to be invited from among his neighbors.
He looked around,
and immediately called for the young lady.
Presently,
a rich, exotic fragrance diffused,
and more than ten beautiful maids,
surrounded [Fāngyún] as she came out,
radiant and charming,
like a lotus flower reflecting the morning sun.
After bowing,
she immediately sat down.
A crowd of maids stood in attendance,
and the lotus-picking girl was also among them.
After several rounds of wine,
a young girl with unbound hair came out from within,
only about ten years old,
but her posture was elegant and graceful,
smiling as she leaned against [Fāngyún]'s elbow,
her autumn-like eyes sparkling.
[Huán] said:
"A girl should not be out of her boudoir;
what are you doing out here?"
Then he turned to the guest and said:
"This is [Lǜyún 綠雲],
my youngest daughter.
She is quite intelligent,
and can recall classics and records."
He then bade her recite poetry for the guest.
Thereupon, she recited three chapters of *Zhúzhī Cí* (竹枝詞),
which were charming and pleasant to listen to.
He then bade her sit by her sister in the corner.
[Huán] then said:
"Young [Wáng]'s talent is extraordinary,
his accumulated compositions must be rich;
may this humble person have the honor of hearing your teachings?"
[Wáng] then grandly recited a recent poem,
looking around with self-assurance.
The middle two lines said:
"My body still retains a beard and eyebrows,
a small drink can dispel my vexations."
The neighboring old man recited them repeatedly.
[Fāngyún] whispered to her sister:
"The first line is [Sūn Xíngzhě 孫行者] leaving the Huǒyún dòng (火雲洞),
the second line is [Zhū Bājiè 豬八戒] crossing the Zǐmǔ Hé (子母河)."
The whole company clapped.
[Huán] asked for another.
[Wáng] spoke of water birds waiting for clouds:
"The pond-head crows *gégē* (格磔), ... ..."
Suddenly he forgot the next line.
Just as he pondered,
[Fāngyún] whispered to her sister,
then covered her mouth and smiled.
[Lǜyún] told her father:
"She is finishing the next line for brother-in-law.
It says: 'The dog's rear makes a *pēngbā* (弸巴) sound.'"
The whole table burst into laughter.
[Wáng] looked ashamed.
[Huán] glared at [Fāngyún],
angrily looking at her.
When [Wáng]'s expression had somewhat settled,
[Huán] again asked for his literary works.
[Wáng] thought that people outside the world must not know about *bāgǔ wén* (八股文) (eight-legged essays),
so he showed off his top-ranking composition,
titled
"Filial indeed is Mǐn Zǐqiān (閔子騫)"
(two lines),
which began:
"The Sage praised the great worthy's filial piety..."
[Lǜyún] looked at her father and said:
“The elder sister said, ‘It would be appropriate to delete
the character “qiē”
Everyone was confused.
Huán feared that her words were rude,
and dared not investigate further.
After Wáng finished reciting,
he then presented a general critique,
which included the line:
“One strike of the jiégǔ
makes myriad flowers fall all at once.”
Fāngyún again covered her mouth and spoke to her sister,
and both laughed so hard they could not straighten up.
Lǜyún then announced,
“The elder sister said!
‘The jiégǔ should be struck four times.’ ”
Everyone was again confused.
Lǜyún opened her mouth, wanting to speak,
but Fāngyún stifled her laughter and chided her, saying,
“How dare a maidservant speak!
You’ll be beaten to death!”
Everyone was greatly bewildered
and started guessing and discussing among themselves.
Lǜyún could not bear it,
and finally said,
“If you remove the character ‘qiē’
(cut),
and say ‘tòng’ (pain),
then it becomes ‘bù tōng’ (impassable/not understood).
Four strikes of the drum,
its sound is like ‘bù tōng yòu bù tōng’ (impassable, and again impassable/not understood, and again not understood).”
Everyone burst into laughter.
Huán angrily scolded her.
Thereupon he rose to pass the wine cup,
apologizing profusely.
Wáng had initially prided himself on his talent and reputation,
and truly thought little of any throughout history;
at this point,
his spirits were dejected,
and he merely sweated profusely.
Huán flattered and comforted him, saying,
“Just now there was a phrase;
I invite someone at the banquet to provide a matching couplet: ‘By Prince Wáng’s side,
not a single spot is unlike jade.’”
Before anyone else could think of a response,
Lǜyún replied immediately,
“On Old Man Mǐn’s head,
add half a ‘xī’ and it becomes a turtle.”
Fāngyún burst out laughing,
and scolded her, pinching her ribs several times.
Lǜyún broke free and ran off,
turning back to say,
“What business is it of yours!
You scold him frequently,
and don’t consider it wrong;
why won’t you allow others even a single phrase?”
Huán scolded her,
and she finally laughed and left.
The neighbor elder bid farewell.
The maids led the couple into the inner chambers;
lamps, candles, screens, and beds
were arranged meticulously.
They also saw in the bridal chamber,
shelves full of ivory slips,
no book was absent.
Slightly posing a question or difficulty,
there was an endless stream of responses.
Wáng, at this point,
only then felt ashamed, like "looking at the ocean."
The woman called
“Míngdāng,”
and the lotus-gatherer responded quickly,
which was how her name first became known.
Having repeatedly suffered reproaches and insults,
he feared he would not be respected in the women’s quarters;
fortunately, although Fāngyún’s words were harsh,
within the bed curtains,
they still loved each other.
Wáng, dwelling at ease with nothing to do,
often resumed chanting poetry.
The woman said,
“I have some good advice;
I wonder if you would be willing to accept it?”
He asked,
“What advice?”
She said,
“From now on, do not write poetry;
it is also a way to hide one’s clumsiness.”
Wáng was greatly ashamed
and consequently stopped writing.
After a long time,
he gradually became intimate with Míngdāng.
He told Fāngyún,
“Míngdāng has the virtue of saving my life,
I wish you would show her a little more kindness.”
Fāngyún immediately agreed.
Whenever they played games in the bedroom,
she invited Míngdāng to join them,
and the affection between the two grew stronger,
sometimes exchanging glances and hand gestures.
Fāngyún subtly noticed,
and reproached them repeatedly;
Wáng merely babbled,
trying hard to clear himself.
One evening,
while drinking together,
Wáng felt lonely
and suggested inviting Míngdāng.
Fāngyún did not allow it.
Wáng said,
“You read all books;
why don’t you remember the lines about ‘dú lè lè’ (enjoying oneself alone)?”
Fāngyún said,
“I said you are ignorant,
and now it’s even more proven.
Don’t you even know punctuation?
‘Dú yào (only want),
nǎi lè yú rén yào (then joy in what others want);
wèn lè (ask about joy),
shú yào hū (who wants it)?
Yuē: bù (Answer: No).’”
She smiled and stopped.
Just then, Fāngyún’s younger sister went to meet a neighbor girl,
and Wáng seized the opportunity,
quickly drew Míngdāng aside,
and they were utterly intimate.
That evening,
he felt a slight pain in his lower abdomen;
after the pain subsided,
his entire front阴 was swollen.
He was greatly frightened
and told Fāngyún.
Yún smiled and said,
“It must be Míngdāng’s repayment of gratitude!”
Wáng dared not conceal it
and confessed the truth.
Fāngyún said,
“This calamity is of your own making;
there is truly no strategy for it.
Since it’s not agonizing,
just let it be.”
It did not heal after several days,
and he was worried and unhappy.
Fāngyún knew his intention
but did not inquire,
only gazed at him,
her autumn eyes full of tears,
clear as the morning star.
Wáng said,
“Your expression is what is called,
‘If the mind is upright,
then the pupils are bright as a water bird (yì).’”
Fāngyún laughed and said,
“Your expression is what is called, ‘If the mind is not upright,
then the water bird (yì) has pupils (móu).’”
Indeed,
the ‘mò’
of ‘méiyǒu’ (not exist)
is commonly read like
‘móu’ (pupil),
hence she teased him with this.
Wáng burst out laughing,
then pleaded for a remedy.
She said,
“You didn’t listen to good advice;
before this, you might not have doubted that I was jealous.
You don’t know that this maidservant
is inherently not to be approached.
In the past, I truly loved you,
but you were like the east wind blowing past a horse’s ear (heedless),
so I abandoned you and had no pity.
If there’s no other choice,
I will treat you.
However, the physician must examine the affected area.”
Thereupon, she reached into his clothes and chanted,
“‘Yellow bird, yellow bird,
do not alight on Chǔ!’”
Wáng could not help but laugh loudly;
after laughing, he recovered.
After several months,
Wáng, seeing that his aged father was troubled,
constantly felt a pang of longing
and expressed his thoughts to his wife.
She said:
"Returning is indeed not difficult,
but there will be no day for our reunion."
Wáng's tears streamed down his cheeks,
sorrowfully pleading with her to return together.
His wife pondered repeatedly,
and only then agreed.
Huán Wēng hosted a farewell banquet.
Lǜyún entered carrying a basket,
saying:
"Sister, you are departing far away,
and I have nothing to give you as a keepsake.
Fearing that when you reach the southern seas,
you will have no home,
I have tirelessly built these palaces for you,
do not despise their makeshift nature."
Fāngyún bowed and accepted them.
Upon closer inspection,
they were pavilions and towers crafted from fine grass,
some as large as a pomelo,
some as small as an orange,
about twenty or more in total.
Every beam, pillar, rafter, and decorative panel
was clearly discernible;
the furnishings, tents, beds, and couches inside
were like sesame seeds.
Wáng looked at them as if they were toys,
but secretly marvelled at their craftsmanship.
Fāngyún said:
"I must be frank with you: we are all earth immortals.
Due to a past affinity,
we have been able to accompany you.
Originally, we did not wish to tread the dusty world,
but merely because you have an aged father,
we could not bear to disobey.
Once your father reaches his natural lifespan,
we must return."
Wáng respectfully assented.
Huán then asked:
"By land?
Or by boat?"
Wáng, considering the treacherous winds and waves,
wished to go by land.
Upon exiting, carriages and horses were already waiting at the gate.
They bid farewell and departed,
their journey swift.
Soon they reached the shore,
Wáng worried there would be no path.
Fāngyún took out a bolt of plain silk,
threw it towards the south,
and it transformed into a long causeway,
more than a *zhàng* wide.
They sped across in an instant,
and the causeway gradually receded.
They arrived at a place
where the tides flowed,
and the view stretched boundless in every direction.
Fāngyún stopped them from proceeding,
alighted from the carriage, took out the grass structures from the basket,
and with several maidservants, Míngdāng,
arranged them according to a method,
and in the blink of an eye, they transformed into a grand mansion.
They dismounted and unpacked,
and it was no different from their dwelling on the island;
the inner chambers had all the tables and couches perfectly arranged.
It was already dusk,
so they stayed for the night.
Early the next morning,
Wáng was ordered to bring his father to be cared for.
Wáng commanded his riders to hasten to his old village,
but upon arrival, his former residence already belonged to another family.
Asking the villagers,
he learned that both his mother and wife had passed away,
and only his aged father remained.
His son, being skilled at gambling,
had lost all their property,
and the grandfather and grandson had nowhere to live,
temporarily renting a home in Xīcūn.
When Wáng first returned,
he still harbored thoughts of fame and official position,
not entirely unconcerned;
but upon hearing this situation,
he was profoundly saddened and grieved,
thinking to himself that even if wealth and rank could be obtained,
how were they different from illusory flowers?
He rode his horse to Xīcūn to see his father,
whose clothes were tattered and worn,
and who was pitiably old and frail.
Upon meeting,
they both cried out loud.
When he inquired about his unworthy son,
he was told that he had gone out gambling and had not returned.
Wáng then carried his father back.
After Fāngyún had completed her morning greetings,
she heated water and invited him to bathe,
presented him with brocade robes,
and housed him in fragrant chambers.
She also remotely summoned old acquaintances for conversations and banquets,
their hospitality exceeding that of noble families.
One day, his son sought them out,
but Wáng rejected him,
not allowing him entry,
but only giving him twenty gold coins,
and having someone relay a message, saying:
"You can use this to buy a wife
and plan for your livelihood.
If you come again,
you will be whipped to death immediately!"
The son wept and left.
After Wáng returned,
he did not socialize much with others;
however, if old friends happened to visit,
he would certainly welcome them and entertain them,
with even greater humility than usual.
Only Huáng Zǐjiè,
who had studied in the same school with him,
and was also an unfortunate scholar of repute,
was kept by Wáng for a very long time,
and with whom he often shared secret conversations,
bestowing upon him lavish gifts.
After three or four years,
Wáng Wēng passed away.
Wáng spent ten thousand coins to select an auspicious burial site
and carried out the funeral rites with full propriety.
By this time, the son had married,
and his wife was strict in managing him,
so the son gambled less often;
he arrived at the funeral,
and only then had the opportunity to greet his paternal aunt and uncle.
Fāngyún, upon seeing her,
acknowledged her ability to manage a household,
and bestowed three hundred gold coins for the cost of acquiring land.
The next day,
Huáng and the son went together to visit,
but the house was completely gone,
its whereabouts unknown.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Where there is beauty,
people will even seek it in hell,
how much more so when the enjoyment is endless?
If earth immortals were allowed to take beautiful women,
I fear the celestial court would be empty of people.
For the frivolous to have their allotted blessings reduced,
is indeed reasonable,
how could immortals not be wary of it?
That wife's words,
how harsh they were indeed!"
According to the Chuìxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The father of a certain governor Xúnfǔ
had previously been the governor-general Zǒngdū of the southern provinces,
and had passed away long ago.
One night, the governor dreamt his father came,
his countenance pale and terrified,
and said:
“In my life, I committed no great transgressions;
it was only a single brigade Zhènshī
that I mistakenly mobilized when it should not have been,
and on their way, they encountered sea pirates,
and the entire army was annihilated.
Now, I am being judged by King Yán,
and the tortures are cruel and severe,
truly terrifying and dreadful.
King Yán is none other than
the experienced officer Jīnglì transporting provisions who will arrive tomorrow,
whose surname is Wèi.
You must plead for me on his behalf;
do not forget!”
He woke up, finding it strange,
but was not deeply convinced.
When he slept again,
he dreamt his father admonished him, saying:
“Your father is suffering a great calamity,
yet you do not engrave it in your heart,
and instead dismiss it as a mere dream?”
The governor was greatly astonished.
The next day,
he paid careful attention during inspection,
and indeed there was an experienced officer Wèi Jīnglì,
who had just arrived with the transport.
He immediately summoned him in,
made two people hold a seat for him,
and only then rose to bow,
like a court audience ceremony.
After bowing,
he knelt for a long time, shedding tears as he explained the situation.
Wèi did not accept the task,
but the governor prostrated himself on the ground and would not rise.
Wèi then said:
“Indeed,
it is possible.
But the laws of the underworld Yīncáo
are not like the ignorant ways of the mortal world Yángshì,
where one can manipulate things.
I fear I may not be able to help.”
The governor’s plea grew even more urgent.
Wèi, having no choice,
agreed.
The governor also requested him to act quickly.
Wèi considered and worried that he would have no quiet place.
The governor offered to clean out the guest quarters Bīnxiè for him,
and he agreed.
Then the governor rose.
He also asked to go and observe and listen,
but Wèi refused.
When he insisted repeatedly,
Wèi instructed:
“If you go, make no sound.
Although the punishments of the underworld Míngxíng are terrible,
they are different from those of the human world.
They are temporarily like death,
but in reality, not death.
If you see anything,
there is no need to be alarmed or surprised.”
That night,
he secretly hid by the side of the guest quarters,
and saw prisoners below the steps,
countless numbers of them, with severed heads and broken arms,
all in disarray.
In the courtyard, there were cauldrons of fire and woks of oil,
with several people stoking the flames beneath.
Suddenly, he saw Wèi emerge, dressed in official robes and hat,
and ascend to the seat.
His demeanor was fierce and awe-inspiring,
completely different from before.
All the ghosts prostrated themselves at once,
crying out their grievances in unison.
Wèi said:
“You were killed by pirates,
so your grievances have their own masters.
How can you falsely accuse your superiors?”
The ghosts clamored, saying:
“We should not have been mobilized according to regulations,
yet we were falsely ordered to come forward,
and thus suffered a cruel fate.
Who is responsible for this injustice?”
Wèi again tried to skillfully explain away,
but the ghosts howled their grievances,
their voices tumultuous.
Wèi then called out to the ghost attendants:
“Take a certain official to the oil cauldron,
and let him be briefly scalded once;
it is also proper according to the law.”
Observing his intent,
it seemed he wished to use this to vent the general anger.
Immediately, ox-headed guards Āpáng
brought the governor’s father,
and with a sharp trident, stabbed him into the oil cauldron.
When the governor saw this,
his heart was profoundly grieved,
and the pain was unbearable.
He involuntarily let out a cry,
and the courtyard became utterly silent,
all forms seemed to vanish in fright.
The governor sighed and exclaimed as he returned.
By morning,
he checked on Wèi,
who had already died in the guest quarters.
Zhāng Yǔdìng of Sōngjiāng recounted this.
Since it was not a good reputation,
the person’s name is withheld.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A mad Daoist monk Diāndàorén,
whose name was unknown,
resided in Měngshān Temple.
His singing and weeping were irregular,
and people could not fathom him.
Some had seen him cooking stones for food.
During the Double Ninth Festival Chóngyáng,
a local dignitary Yìguì came with wine to ascend the mountain,
traveling in a sedan chair with an umbrella.
After the feast, they passed by the temple.
As they just reached the gate,
the Daoist monk, barefoot and in a tattered robe,
held up a yellow umbrella for himself,
and came out making a clearing-the-way sound Jǐngbì,
his intention seemingly to mock.
The dignitary was thus shamed and angered,
and waved his servants to chase and curse him.
The Daoist monk laughed and ran backward.
As the pursuit became urgent,
he abandoned the umbrella,
and they all tore it to shreds.
Piece by piece, it transformed into eagles and falcons,
scattering and flying in groups.
The crowd was then startled.
The umbrella handle turned into a giant python,
its red scales dazzling the eyes.
The crowd clamored, wanting to flee,
but a companion who was with them stopped them, saying:
“This is merely an illusion to deceive the eyes,
how can it devour people!”
Thereupon, he grasped a blade and went straight forward.
The python opened its maw in angry defiance,
and swallowed the guest.
The crowd was terrified,
and rushed away with the dignitary,
stopping three lǐ away.
They sent several people to cautiously go back and investigate.
As they gradually entered the temple,
neither the man nor the python was there.
Just as they were about to return to report,
they heard urgent panting like a donkey from within an old locust tree,
and were greatly alarmed.
At first, they dared not approach;
they secretly moved closer,
and saw that the tree was rotten and hollow,
with a hole like a plate.
They tried to climb and peer in,
and saw that the man who fought the python was stuck head-down inside it,
but the hole was only wide enough for two hands,
with no way to get him out.
They urgently chopped the tree with knives.
By the time the tree opened, the man was already dead.
After some time, he revived slightly,
and returned, finding it strange.
The Daoist monk was nowhere to be found.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Zhāng Chā traveled in the mountains,
and the oppressive atmosphere permeated his bones and marrow.
How laughable is the immortal's game of absorption!
In my hometown, Yīn Shēng Wénpíng,
the brother-in-law of Bì Sīnóng,
was a man who mocked the world and was unconventional.
There was a Zhōu Shēng from Zhāngqiū
who rose from humble beginnings,
and whenever he went out, he would travel by sedan chair.
He also had an old connection with Sīnóng.
When the Grand Madam's birthday came,
Yīn expected him to come,
so he waited for him on the road beforehand,
wearing pigskin boots,
in official attire, holding a memorial tablet.
When Zhōu arrived,
he bowed by the roadside,
and announced: 'Zīchuān student
receives Zhāngqiū student!'
Zhōu was ashamed,
alighted from his carriage,
exchanged a few words, and departed.
A short while later,
they gathered together in Sīnóng's hall.
The hall was full of officials in their caps and robes;
observing Yīn's attire,
everyone secretly laughed,
but Yīn remained aloof and composed.
Eventually, when the banquet ended and they went out the door,
each ordered his carriage and horses.
Yīn also shouted loudly: 'Where is Master Yīn's "solitary dragon carriage"?'
Two strong servants
placed a flat staff horizontally in front,
and he leaped onto it.
He bowed and expressed thanks loudly,
then sped away.
Yīn was also a lesser immortal."
According to the Xiějiànzhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chéng Xiàosī
was a man from Jiànnán.
In his youth, he was intelligent and skilled in writing.
Both his parents died early,
and his family was utterly poor,
without means for clothing or food.
He sought employment as a scribe for Hú Yíntái.
Master Hú tested his writing skills
and was greatly pleased with him,
saying:
"This man will not remain poor for long;
he is worthy of being a husband."
Yíntái had three sons and four daughters,
all of whom had been betrothed in infancy to prominent families.
Only his youngest daughter, Sìniáng,
was born out of wedlock
and her mother had died early;
she was of marriageable age but still unwed.
So, Chéng was married into the family.
Some ridiculed this,
believing it to be a confused decree from an old man,
but Master Hú paid them no heed.
He was provided with a residence for a live-in student,
and his provisions were abundant.
The young masters of the family disdained to eat with him,
and the maids and servants all mocked him.
Chéng silently ignored their criticisms,
and studied very diligently.
When others criticized him from the side,
Chéng did not stop reading.
Then the others made a din with gongs and cymbals beside him,
so Chéng took his scrolls and left,
reading in the women's chambers.
Initially,
when Sìniáng was not yet betrothed,
there was a divine shaman who knew people's nobility and lowliness.
He examined everyone,
but offered no flattering words.
However, when Sìniáng came,
he said:
"This is truly a noble person!"
After Chéng married into the family,
her younger sisters all called her
"noble person"
to mock her,
but Sìniáng was dignified and quiet,
as if she heard nothing.
Gradually, even the maids and old women
began to call her that.
Sìniáng had a maid named Guì'ér,
who felt quite indignant.
She declared loudly:
"How do you know our young master
won't become a high official?"
The second elder sister heard this and sneered, saying:
"If Master Chéng becomes a high official,
I will pluck out my eyeballs!"
Guì'ér angrily replied:
"By that time,
I fear you won't be willing to part with your eyeballs!"
The second elder sister's maid, Chūnxiāng, said:
"If the second mistress goes back on her word,
I will substitute my two eyes for hers."
Guì'ér was even more enraged,
and clapped her hands, vowing:
"I'll make sure both pairs are blind!"
The second elder sister, incensed by her offensive words,
slapped her immediately.
Guì'ér cried out loudly.
When the mistress heard about it,
she didn't express approval or disapproval,
but merely smiled faintly.
Guì'ér noisily complained to Sìniáng.
Sìniáng was spinning thread at the time,
and neither grew angry nor spoke,
but continued spinning calmly.
It happened that Master Hú's first birthday celebration took place,
and all the sons-in-law arrived,
with birthday gifts filling the courtyard.
The eldest daughter-in-law mocked Sìniáng, saying:
"What kind of celebratory gift does your family have?"
The second daughter-in-law said:
"Two shoulders carrying a mouth!"
Sìniáng remained composed,
showing no trace of shame.
People saw that she acted foolishly in everything,
and treated her even more familiarly.
Only Master Hú's beloved concubine, Lǐ Shì,
who was the mother of the third elder sister,
always treated Sìniáng with respect,
and often looked out for her.
She often said to the third sister:
"Sìniáng is intelligent on the inside but simple on the outside;
her cleverness is profound but not revealed.
All the maids are within her grasp,
yet they don't realize it themselves.
Moreover, Master Chéng studies diligently day and night;
how can he remain subservient for long?
You must not imitate their behavior,
but treat her well,
so you can have a good relationship in the future."
Thus, whenever the third sister returned home to visit,
she always made an effort to be friendly with Sìniáng.
In that year,
Chéng, with Master Hú's influence,
was admitted to the county school.
The following year,
the provincial education commissioner held examinations for scholars,
but Master Hú happened to pass away.
Chéng mourned with filial piety as if he were a son,
and was unable to take the examination.
After leaving the mourning hut,
Sìniáng gave him money,
enabling him to join the list of talented individuals.
She instructed him, saying:
"In the past, when you lived here for a long time,
you were not driven away
only because the old master was present.
Now, it is absolutely impossible!
If you can make a name for yourself,
perhaps there will still be a home when you return."
Upon their departure,
Lǐ Shì and the third sister gave generous gifts.
Chéng entered the examination hall,
dedicated his will and focused his thoughts
to ensure success.
Not long after,
the results were posted,
and he was unexpectedly rejected.
His hopes dashed and his spirit dejected,
it was difficult for him to return home.
Fortunately, his travel funds were somewhat ample,
so he took his scrolls and went to the capital.
At that time, many of his wife's relatives held official positions in the capital,
and fearing their ridicule,
he changed his old name,
falsely claiming a different hometown,
and sought to conceal himself at the residence of a high official.
Lǐ Lántái of Dōnghǎi saw him and appreciated his talent,
taking him into his retinue,
providing him with funds for study,
and helping him apply for the Shùntiān provincial examination.
He succeeded in consecutive battles,
and was appointed a Shùjíshì.
Only then did he reveal the true circumstances.
Master Lǐ loaned him a thousand gold pieces,
and first sent his steward to Jiànnán
to arrange a residence for him.
At that time, Hú Dàláng, due to his father's death and financial emptiness,
was selling his fertile estate,
so Chéng purchased it.
Once completed,
he then borrowed carriages and horses
and went to welcome Sìniáng.
Formerly,
after Chéng Zhuó (程擢) had passed the imperial examination,
there was a postal messenger,
and the whole household disliked hearing of it;
furthermore, upon verifying that his name did not match,
they shouted him away.
Just then, Sānláng (三郎) completed his wedding,
and relatives and in-laws came to the hall to offer wedding gifts.
Sisters and aunts were all present,
but Sìniáng (四娘) was not invited by her elder brothers and sisters-in-law.
Suddenly, a person rushed in,
presenting a letter from Chéng (程) to Sìniáng (四娘).
The brothers opened and read it,
and looked at each other, losing color.
All the guests at the banquet
then requested to see Sìniáng (四娘).
The sisters were anxious,
only fearing that Sìniáng (四娘) would harbor resentment and not come.
Before long,
she gracefully arrived.
Some offered congratulations,
some pulled her to sit,
some exchanged pleasantries—
the room was filled with clamor.
Ears listened,
listening to Sìniáng (四娘);
eyes watched,
watching Sìniáng (四娘);
mouths spoke,
speaking of Sìniáng (四娘)—yet Sìniáng (四娘) remained composed as before.
When the crowd saw that she showed neither shortcomings nor excesses,
they gradually settled down,
and then eagerly raised their cups to toast Sìniáng (四娘).
While they were feasting and laughing,
a frantic wailing was heard outside the door,
and everyone asked about it in surprise.
Soon, Chūnxiāng (春香) rushed in,
her face stained with blood.
They all questioned her,
but she wept and could not answer.
Èrniáng (二娘) scolded her,
and she then tearfully said:
“Guì’ér (桂兒) forcibly demanded my eyes;
if I hadn't broken free,
they would have almost been gouged out!”
Èrniáng (二娘) was greatly shamed,
and sweat and powder streamed down her face.
Sìniáng (四娘) was indifferent.
The whole table was silent, not a single word was spoken,
and everyone then bade farewell.
Sìniáng (四娘), in full attire,
alone bowed to Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人) and her third sister,
then left the door, boarded a carriage, and departed.
Only then did the crowd realize that the buyer of the villa
was none other than Chéng (程).
When Sìniáng (四娘) first arrived at the villa,
many of her belongings were lacking.
Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人) and the various gentlemen each sent her maids, servants, and implements as gifts,
but Sìniáng (四娘) accepted none of them;
only a maid given by Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人)
did she accept.
Not long after,
Chéng (程) took leave to return home and visit his ancestral graves,
his carriages and entourage like clouds.
He went to his wife's family home,
paid respects at Gōng (公)'s coffin,
then called on Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人).
The gentlemen, having already competed in their attire and caps,
had already ascended their carriages.
After Hú Gōng (胡公) died,
the various young masters daily competed for wealth,
neglecting his coffin.
Several years later,
the spirit chamber leaked and was damaged,
gradually turning what was once a grand house into a mound.
Chéng (程) was saddened by this sight,
and without consulting the various gentlemen,
he set a date for the burial,
performing everything with utmost propriety.
On the day of the burial,
officials and gentry followed in an endless stream,
and the people in the village all praised and admired him.
For over ten years, Chéng (程) held positions of clean renown and prominence;
whenever his fellow villagers were in distress or urgent need,
he always exerted his utmost effort.
Èrláng (二郎) was arrested for a homicide case,
and the巡方 (xúnfāng) censor,
who was a fellow clansman of Chéng (程),
was very strict in his conduct.
Dàláng (大郎) asked his father-in-law, Wáng Guānchá (王觀察), to write a letter to him,
but received no reply at all,
and became even more frightened.
He wanted to go and ask his sister for help,
but felt he had no face,
so he carried a letter written by Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人) and went.
Upon reaching the capital,
he dared not enter immediately,
but waited until Chéng (程) had gone to court
before calling on him.
He hoped Sìniáng (四娘) would remember their sibling bond
and forget their past grievances.
After the gatekeeper announced him,
an old maidservant came out,
led him into the hall,
and provided wine and food,
though rather simply.
After eating,
Sìniáng (四娘) came out,
her face warm and misty,
and asked:
“Elder Brother's affairs are so busy;
how do you have time to trouble yourself to come from such a distant place?”
Dàláng (大郎) prostrated himself,
weeping as he recounted why he had come.
Sìniáng (四娘) helped him up and smiled, saying,
“Elder Brother is a good man;
what is this great matter,
that you should be so distraught?
I, a mere woman,
have I ever been seen weeping to others?”
Dàláng (大郎) then produced Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人)'s letter.
Sìniáng (四娘) said:
“The wives of my elder brothers
are all like goddesses;
each should seek help from their own fathers and brothers,
and that would be sufficient.
Why come all this way?”
Dàláng (大郎) was speechless,
only looking at her imploringly.
Sìniáng (四娘) sternly said:
“I thought you traveled all this way to visit your sister,
but instead you come to seek a noble person's help for a major lawsuit!”
She flung her sleeve and walked straight in.
Dàláng (大郎) left feeling ashamed and resentful.
Upon returning home and describing everything in detail,
everyone, old and young, cursed and blamed her;
Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人) also called her heartless.
A few days later,
Èrláng (二郎) was released and returned home,
and everyone was overjoyed,
then laughed at Sìniáng (四娘) for having provoked resentment and criticism in vain.
Soon after, Sìniáng (四娘) sent an envoy to call on Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人).
When admitted,
the servant presented gold and silk,
saying:
“My mistress was very busy with Second Uncle's matter,
and had no time to reply in writing.
She sends this small gift,
to serve as a substitute for a letter.”
Only then did everyone realize that Èrláng (二郎)'s return
was due to Chéng (程)'s efforts.
Later, when Sānniáng (三娘)'s family gradually became poor,
Chéng (程) offered assistance that exceeded the usual standard.
Furthermore, because Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人) had no sons,
he took her in to care for her as if she were his own mother.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異) from Zhùxuězhāi (鑄雪齋).
Huáng Shēng (黃生)
was the son of an old family.
His talent and sentiments were quite ample,
and his early ambition soared high.
Outside the village, at a Buddhist temple,
there was a certain resident monk
with whom he had long shared a deep connection.
Later, the monk went on a pilgrimage,
and returned after more than ten years.
Seeing Huáng (黃),
he sighed, saying:
“I thought you had long achieved prominence,
yet you are still in plain white cloth?
Perhaps your fortune is inherently thin.
Please allow me to bribe the master of the underworld for you.
Can you afford ten thousand cash?”
Huáng (黃) replied:
“No, I cannot.”
The monk said:
“Please try your best to raise half of it,
and I will gradually lend you the rest.
Let us set a three-day deadline.”
Huáng (黃) agreed,
and exhausted his efforts to pawn his possessions for the required amount.

"Could it be that the underworld also has a system of 'donations for degrees'?
To obtain a degree for ten thousand [coins]

However, who contributed the one thousand?
It is still expensive.
If one does not pass the 'illuminated classics' examination,

According to a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio of
A certain prominent person often engaged in unethical deeds.
His wife repeatedly admonished him with warnings of retribution,
but he would not listen or believe her.
Just then, there was a geomancer,
who could discern a person's allotted lifespan and wealth,
who came to him.
The geomancer looked at him carefully and said:
"You have twenty more *shí* of rice and forty *shí* of flour to eat,
then your heavenly allotment will end."
He returned and told his wife.
He calculated that a single person only eats two *shí* of flour in an entire year,
so he still had over twenty years of heavenly allotment,
how could good deeds possibly cut it short?
He continued his wicked ways as before.
More than a year later,
he suddenly fell ill with
"hollow stomach" disease,
eating a great deal but quickly becoming hungry again,
eating more than ten times in a day and night.
Before a full year had passed,
he died.
According to a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio of
Zhōu Shēng
Shùntiān.
He was good friends with
Liǔ
and was skilled in the arts of
He once said to
"You have no destined share of fame and success;
however, with ten thousand *chuí* of capital,
it might still be possible to achieve something through human effort.
But your wife has an unfortunate countenance,
I fear she cannot assist you in achieving your endeavors."
Not long after,
his wife indeed died.
His household was desolate,
and he could not cope.
So he went to
to consult about marriage.
He entered the guest room,
and sat for a long time,
but
He called him repeatedly,
and only then did he come out,
saying:
"I have been searching for a suitable match for you all day,
and now I have finally found one.
I was just inside performing a small ritual,
asking the Old Man Under the Moon to tie the red string."
Zhōu
asked about it.
He replied:
"Just now, a person carrying a bag went out,
did you meet him?"
He said:
"I met him.
He was ragged like a beggar."
He said:
"That is your father-in-law;
you should treat him with respect."
Zhōu
"We are close friends,
so we should discuss private matters,
why do you tease me so much!
Even if I am in decline,
I am still a descendant of an official family;
how could I marry down to a market peddler?"
Liǔ
"Not so.
Even a yak has a tail,
what harm is there?"
Zhōu
"Have you seen his daughter?"
He replied:
"Not yet.
I have no acquaintance with him,
I only learned his name by asking around."
Zhōu
"If you don't even know the yak,
how can you know its offspring?"
Liǔ
"I believe it based on calculations.
That man is unfortunate and lowly,
but he will have a daughter destined for great blessings.
However, a forced union will certainly bring great misfortune,
I will perform another ritual to avert it."
After
he was unwilling to believe his words,
and searched in various places,
but never found a successful match.
One day,
Liǔ Shēng suddenly arrived
and said,
"There is a guest
for whom I have already prepared an invitation."
When asked,
"For whom?"
He replied,
"Do not ask yet;
you should quickly prepare millet."
Zhōu did not understand the reason,
but he prepared the meal as commanded.
Soon, the guest arrived.
He was a soldier surnamed Fù.
Zhōu did not feel agreeable internally,
but outwardly he conversed with him;
while Liǔ Shēng was extremely deferential in his attendance.
A short while later,
after the wine and dishes had been laid out,
and various coarse provisions were served,
Liǔ stood up and addressed the guest:
"My lord has admired you for a long time,
often asking me to visit on his behalf,
and only last night did we finally meet.
Hearing also that you are soon to go on a distant campaign,
he immediately invited you.
One might say he is a host in a hurry!"
During the meal,
Fù worried that his horse was sick
and could not be ridden.
Liǔ also bowed his head and pondered a solution for him.
After the guest left,
Liǔ said to Zhōu,
"A thousand gold pieces could not buy such a friend,
why do you regard him so indifferently?"
He borrowed a horse to ride home,
and, feigning Zhōu's name,
went to Fù's door to present it.
When Zhōu found out,
he was somewhat displeased,
but there was nothing he could do.
A year passed,
and he was about to go to Jiāngxī
to work as a clerk in the Judicial Commissioner's yámen.
He went to Liǔ to have his fortune told.
Liǔ said,
"Great auspiciousness!"
Zhōu smiled and said,
"I have no other intention
than to acquire a little,
and then I should buy a good wife.
I rather hope your prediction is not accurate
— is this possible?"
Liǔ replied,
"It will all be as you wish."
When he arrived in Jiāngxi,
he encountered a major bandit rebellion,
and for three years he could not return home.
Later, when things had somewhat settled,
he chose a day and set out on his journey.
Midway, he was robbed by local bandits.
Seven or eight fellow travelers
were all robbed of their money and valuables
and then released;
only Zhōu was captured and taken to their lair.
The bandit chief questioned him about his family background
and then said,
"I have a daughter
whom I wish to offer to you as a wife;
you should not refuse immediately."
Zhōu did not answer.
The bandit became angry
and immediately ordered him to be beheaded.
Zhōu, afraid,
thought it would be better to temporarily agree to his request
and then subtly abandon her.
So he said,
"The reason this junior student hesitated
is that I am weak and cannot follow a military career,
lest I become an even greater burden to my father-in-law.
If husband and wife could go together,
no greater kindness could be shown."
The bandit said,
"I am precisely worried that my daughter burdens people;
why can this not be agreed to?"
He led him inside,
and his daughter, adorned, came out to meet him.
She appeared eighteen or nineteen years old,
and was truly a heavenly beauty.
That evening, they joined in marriage,
far exceeding his expectations.
Upon closer inquiry into her surname and given name,
he learned that her father
was the very man who had carried the moneybag that year.
He then recounted Liǔ's words
and sighed with emotion.
After three or four days,
as they were about to depart,
a large army suddenly descended,
and the entire family was captured and bound.
Three military officers were supervising;
they had already beheaded his father-in-law,
and it was Zhōu's turn next.
Zhōu resigned himself to his fate, believing he had no chance of survival.
One officer scrutinized him and said,
"Is this not a certain Zhōu?"
It turned out that the soldier Fù had been awarded the title of Vice General for his military achievements.
He said to his colleagues,
"This is a renowned scholar from a distinguished family in my hometown;
how could he be a bandit?"
He untied him
and asked where he came from.
Zhōu cunningly said,
"I had just married a wife from the Jiāngxī Judicial Commissioner's yámen and was returning home,
unexpectedly falling into a bandit's lair on the way.
Fortunately, I was saved,
and for this grace, I am doubly grateful to Heaven!
However, my wife is separated from me,
so I request your mighty power
to grant us both safe passage."
Fù ordered all the captives to be lined up
and told her to identify herself,
and she was found.
He specifically gave them wine and food,
and provided them with money for travel,
saying,
"I received the kindness of your unharnessing your horse for me back then,
and I have not forgotten it for a moment.
However, amidst the chaos of war,
I have not had the chance to repay the favor.
Please accept two horses and fifty taels of gold
to assist your return north."
He also dispatched two riders with a token arrow to escort them.
On the way,
the woman said to Zhōu,
"My foolish father did not listen to faithful advice,
and my mother died because of it.
I have known this day would come for a long time.
The reason I have clung to life until now
is that when I was young, a fortune-teller predicted something for me,
and I hoped one day to be able to retrieve my parents' bones.
The enormous sum of gold I have hidden
can be used to redeem my father's bones;
the remainder, when taken home,
will still be sufficient to plan for our livelihood."
She instructed the riders to wait by the road,
and the two of them went to the old site.
The huts had already been burned to ashes.
From the ashes, she took out a dagger and dug about a foot deep,
and indeed found the gold.
They loaded it all into their pouches
and then returned.
They bribed the riders with a hundred taels of gold
to bury her father's body;
they then led Zhōu to bow at her mother's grave
before proceeding.
Upon reaching the Zhílì border,
they generously rewarded the riders and they departed.
Zhōu had been gone for so long
that his family thought he had died.
They recklessly embezzled and squandered
all the grain, silk, and utensils,
leaving nothing.
Hearing of their master's return,
they were terrified
and all fled in a panic;
only an old woman, a maidservant, and an old slave remained.
Having escaped death and found life,
Zhōu did not pursue the matter further.
When he inquired about Liǔ,
he found that no one knew where he had gone.
The woman managed the household better than a man.
She selected honest and reliable individuals and provided them with capital,
distributing the interest evenly.
Whenever the various merchants settled accounts under the eaves,
the woman would listen from behind a curtain;
if a single bead was mistakenly placed on the abacus,
she would immediately point out the error.
No one, inside or outside, dared to deceive her.
Within a few years,
her business partners numbered over a hundred,
and her family's wealth amounted to tens of millions.
Then she sent people to move her parents' bones
and buried them with great honors.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"If the Old Man of the Moon can be bribed,
no wonder matchmakers are no different from brokers!
But how could a bandit have such a daughter?
'A hillock does not produce pines and cypresses'
— this is but my humble opinion.
If even women and girls are misunderstood,
how much more so when judging the world's scholars!"
Based on the Chaste Snow Studio manuscript of Liaozhai Zhiyi
Zhū Shēng,
a native of Yánggǔ.
In his youth, he was frivolous
and enjoyed jesting.
Having lost his wife,
he went to seek a matchmaker.
He met his neighbor's wife
and gazed at her beauty.
He playfully said to the matchmaker:
"Just now I saw your neighbor,
who is truly young and beautiful.
Please seek a phoenix for me;
she would do."
The matchmaker also jokingly replied:
"Please kill her husband,
and I will scheme it for you."
Zhū laughed and said:
"Agreed."
More than a month later,
the neighbor went out to collect a debt
and was killed in the wild.
The county magistrate detained the neighborhood head
and, by torture, tried to ascertain the facts,
but could find no clue.
Only the matchmaker recounted their joking words,
and with this, Zhū was suspected.
He was arrested,
but denied it vehemently.
Now, the magistrate also suspected an affair with the neighbor's wife,
and beat and tortured her,
applying all sorts of cruel punishments.
The woman could not endure it
and falsely confessed.
When Zhū was interrogated again,
Zhū said:
"She is delicate and cannot bear harsh torture;
what she said is all false.
Since he died an unjust death,
and now she is further given the name of unchastity,
even if ghosts and gods are ignorant,
how can my heart bear it?
I shall confess it truthfully: desiring to kill her husband and marry his wife
was all my doing;
the wife knew nothing of it."
He was asked:
"What evidence do you have?"
He replied,
"The bloody clothes can prove it."
When men were sent to search his house,
they could not find it.
He was tortured again,
and revived twice after dying.
Zhū then said,
"My mother cannot bear to produce the evidence and cause my death.
Wait, I will fetch it myself."
So, he was escorted home and said to his mother:
"If you give me the clothes,
I will die;
if you don't give them,
I will also die:
since it's death either way, it's better to be quick than to delay."
His mother wept,
entered her room for a time,
and brought out the clothes, handing them over.
The magistrate examined the evidence, found it conclusive,
and proposed beheading.
It was appealed and re-examined twice,
with no change in testimony.
More than a year passed,
and the day for the verdict was approaching.
The magistrate was contemplating the prisoners
when suddenly a man walked straight up to the public hall,
glared at the magistrate, and cursed loudly, saying:
"So muddled and confused!
How are you fit to govern the people!"
Dozens of yamen runners
were about to seize him.
The man waved his arm,
and they stubbornly all fell over.
The magistrate was terrified
and wanted to flee.
The man declared loudly:
"I am General Zhōu before Guāndì!
If this muddled official dares to move,
I shall slay him immediately!"
The magistrate trembled with fear and listened.
The man said:
"The killer is Gōng Biāo,
what does Zhū Mǒu have to do with it?"
Having spoken,
he fell to the ground,
his breath seemingly gone.
A moment later, he awoke,
his face drained of color.
When asked who he was,
it was Gōng Biāo.
When flogged,
he confessed all his crimes.
It turned out that Gōng had always been unscrupulous.
Knowing that a certain person was returning after collecting a debt,
he imagined that the person must be rich,
but after killing him,
he found nothing.
Hearing that Zhū was falsely accused and confessed,
he secretly rejoiced.
On that day, he entered the public yamen
without knowing it himself.
The magistrate asked where Zhū's bloody clothes came from,
and Zhū also did not know.
His mother was summoned and interrogated,
and it turned out to be from a cut arm.
The knife mark on her left arm was examined,
and it had not yet healed.
The magistrate was also astonished.
Later, because of this, he was impeached, dismissed from office,
fined, detained, and died.
More than a year later,
the neighbor's mother wanted to marry off her daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law was moved by Zhū's righteousness
and married him.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Lawsuits are the foremost duty of officials.
Accumulating secret virtues
or destroying heavenly principles
all depend on this;
one must not be incautious.
Hasty, defiling, and violent actions
are certainly contrary to cosmic harmony;
stagnation and procrastination
also harm the lives of the people.
When one person files a lawsuit,
several farmers miss their farming season;
when one case is concluded,
ten families are ruined: how can this be a trivial matter!
I once said that for officials,
not indiscriminately accepting lawsuits
is a great virtue.
Moreover, unless the circumstances are very serious,
there is no need to detain people;
if there are no difficult or doubtful matters,
why hesitate?
Even if it's ignorant villagers
or boastful mountain folk,
who accidentally get into a dispute over geese and ducks
and thus become angry over a 'sparrow's corner,'
this merely requires a word from the official
to settle it.
There is no need to summon everyone;
only the two parties are needed.
Administer a caning or flogging immediately,
and cut off all entanglements.
Is this not what is meant by a discerning magistrate?
I often see how those who hear lawsuits today behave:
once a summons is issued,
they seem to forget it.
The summoner, not having received enough money,
will not allow the 'notice of summons' to be seen;
the executioner, not having received a full bribe,
will not put up the 'notice of hearing.'
Obscured and procrastinated,
it often drags on for months and years.
Before even appearing before the senior official's court,
the people's flesh and bones are almost entirely wasted!
Yet, those who appear dignified and superior to the people
rest contentedly on their beds,
as if nothing is happening.
How can they know that in the fiery prison,
countless wronged souls
stretch their necks and gasp for breath, hoping for rescue!
Of course, the malicious obstinacy of cunning commoners
is not worth pitying;
but for good commoners who are implicated,
how can it be endured?
Moreover, in cases of innocent involvement,
there are often fewer cunning commoners and more good commoners;
and the suffering of good commoners
is often double that of cunning commoners.
Why is this?
Cunning commoners are difficult to abuse,
while good commoners are easy to deceive.
The beatings and curses of the yamen runners,
the demands of the clerks and assistants,
are all directed at those who seem good, inflicting violence upon them.
Once inside the yamen,
it is like stepping into boiling water or fire.
To conclude a case one day earlier
is to secure one day earlier of peaceful life.
What great matter is there
that those who sit languidly in the hall like dead men,
fearing that the ravines will not be quickly filled, intentionally drag it out for years,
though not cruel or violent,
their crime is in fact equally grave.
I have often seen that in a single lawsuit,
those who are urgently and indispensably needed
are no more than three or four people;
the rest are innocent people,
falsely accused.
Some have incurred ill will over a petty grudge in the past,
others have brought trouble upon themselves by possessing something valuable;
thus, those who initiate lawsuits use all their might to pursue the main case,
and use their remaining malice to exact petty revenge.
To add a name to the end of a document
becomes a festering sore stuck to the bone;
to suffer countless torments in the yamen
becomes a pain that cuts to the quick.
When others kneel, they kneel,
like crows gathering; when others leave, they leave,
like monkeys tied up.
Yet, in the end, the officials don't question them,
the clerks don't interrogate them.
In fact, they are of no use at all,
only serving to bankrupt families,
fill the greedy pockets of corrupt yamen servants,
sell sons and pawn wives,
and vent the private anger of petty individuals.
I sincerely wish that officials,
whenever a petition is submitted,
would conduct a brief inquiry:
those who should be dismissed, dismiss them;
those who should be weeded out, weed them out.
It is merely a matter of dipping a brush and moving a wrist,
yet it can preserve so many lives and families,
and nurture so much vital energy.
If those in government never give this a thought,
why must instruments of torture and execution be able to kill people!"
Based on the Shuǐxuězāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Jiàoyù Zhǎn xiānshēng
was a free and easy man of note.
However, he was a mad drunkard,
who disregarded propriety.
Whenever he returned home drunk,
he would gallop his horse onto the palace steps.
On the steps were many ancient cypresses.
One day,
as he spurred his horse onward,
he hit a tree, splitting his head.
He said to himself,
"Zǐlù is angry at my impoliteness,
and has smashed my head!"
He died that same night.
A certain Mr. Yǐ from the county,
who peddled his wares in his village,
slept at an old temple at night.
As the watch changed and people were few,
he suddenly saw four or five people bringing wine and drinking.
Zhǎn was also among them.
After a few rounds of wine,
someone used a character to pose a riddle:
"The character tián (田) has no ventilation,
the character shí (十) is in its center;
push the character shí (十) up,
and the character gǔ (古) wins a bell."
One person said:
"The character huí (回) has no ventilation,
the character kǒu (口) is in its center;
push the character kǒu (口) up,
and the character lǚ (呂) wins a bell."
Another person said:
"The character líng (囹) has no ventilation,
the character lìng (令) is in its center;
push the character lìng (令) up,
and the character hán (含) wins a bell."
Yet another person said:
"The character kùn (困) has no ventilation,
the character mù (木) is in its center;
push the character mù (木) up,
and the character xìng (杏) wins a bell."
Finally, it was Zhǎn's turn,
but he pondered and could not find an answer.
The group laughed and said,
"Since you cannot command,
you must obey."
A goblet was flown over.
Zhǎn immediately said,
"I've got it: the character yuē (曰) has no ventilation,
the character yī (一) is in its center; ..."
The group laughed again and said,
"What do you push it up into?"
Zhǎn drained the goblet and said,
"Push the character yī (一) up,
and it's a mouth (口) with a big bell!"
They all burst into laughter,
and soon after left.
That person (Mr. Yǐ) did not know Zhǎn was dead,
and secretly suspected he had resigned from office and returned home.
When he returned and inquired,
he learned that Zhǎn had been dead for a long time.
Only then did he realize that those he had met were ghosts.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Liú Zhòngkān of Luòchéng
was dull in his youth but immersed in classics.
He always secluded himself to study assiduously,
not associating with the world.
One day,
as he was reading,
he suddenly smelled a peculiar fragrance filling the room;
after a while,
the sound of jade pendants was very frequent.
Startled, he looked,
and a beautiful woman entered,
her hairpins and earrings shining brightly;
her attendants were all dressed in palace attire.
Liú was alarmed and prostrated himself on the ground.
The beautiful woman helped him up and said,
"Why were you so proud before and so respectful now?"
Liú became even more alarmed and said,
"Which celestial immortal is this?
I have never had the honor of meeting you.
When did I ever insult you before?"
The beautiful woman smiled and said,
"How long has it been since we parted,
and you are already so muddled!
The one sitting upright grinding a brick,
was that not you?"
Then she spread out an embroidered mat,
set out jade nectar,
pulled him to sit and drink opposite her,
and discussed ancient and modern affairs with him,
showing extraordinary erudition.
Liú was bewildered and did not know how to respond.
The beautiful woman said,
"I only went to the Yáochí for one banquet;
you, after experiencing this life,
have completely lost your intelligence!"
Then she ordered her attendant
to serve him crystal paste warmed with soup.
After Liú drank it,
he suddenly felt his mind become clear.
Later, as dusk fell,
all the attendants left,
she extinguished the candle, untied her robes,
and they indulged in complete intimacy.
Before dawn,
the concubines had already reassembled.
The beautiful woman rose,
her makeup and appearance as before,
her hair neat and tidy,
without needing to arrange it again.
Liú earnestly pressed her for her name,
and she replied,
"Telling my dear sir is not a problem,
but I fear it will only increase your doubt.
I am
Zhēn shì;
you are
the reincarnation of Gōngwàn.
On that day, because of me, you suffered punishment,
which I truly could not bear.
Today's meeting
is also merely to repay your foolish love."
He asked,
"Where is Wèi Wén?"
She said,
"Pī
is merely an incompetent son of a treacherous father.
I merely associated with the wealthy and powerful for a few years of amusement,
and once it was over, I no longer gave it a thought.
In the past, because of Āmàn,
he was long detained in the underworld,
and I have not heard of him yet.
On the contrary, Chén Sī serves as an imperial archivist,
and I see him from time to time."
Soon, a dragon carriage was seen stopping in the courtyard.
She then gave Liú a jade cream box as a gift,
bade him farewell, boarded the carriage,
and it was propelled away by clouds.
Liú 劉's literary skill made great progress thereafter.
However, remembering the beautiful woman,
his thoughts became fixated as if in a trance.
After several months,
he gradually became emaciated and frail.
His mother did not know the reason,
and worried about him.
An old nanny in the household
suddenly said to Liú 劉:
"Young master, are you perhaps in love?"
Liú 劉, seeing his hidden feelings were touched upon,
told her.
The nanny said:
"Young master, try writing a short letter,
I can deliver it for you."
Liú 劉 was overjoyed and said:
"You possess extraordinary skill!
I have been pondering this matter for days.
If you can truly do it,
I will not forget your kindness."
So he folded a letter,
gave it to the nanny, and she left.
She returned at midnight and said:
"Fortunately, nothing went wrong.
When I first arrived at the gate,
the gatekeepers took me for a demon
and wanted to tie me up.
I then produced your letter,
and they let me pass.
A moment later, they called someone,
and the Fūrén 夫人 also sighed mournfully,
saying she could not meet again.
She was about to write a reply.
I said: 'The young master is weak and ill,
and not a single word can cure him.'
The Fūrén 夫人 pondered for a long time,
then put down her brush and said: 'Please first inform Liú Láng 劉郎
that I will immediately send a fine wife to him.'
As she was about to leave,
she again instructed: 'What I just said
is a plan for a hundred years;
just do not reveal it,
and it can last forever.'"
Liú 劉 was delighted
and waited for her.
The next day,
indeed, an old woman led a young lady
to his mother's residence.
Her beauty was peerless,
and she introduced herself as Chén 陳;
the young lady was her daughter,
named Sīxiāng 司香,
and she wished to be his wife.
His mother loved her
and discussed the betrothal;
no bride-price was requested,
and they simply waited for the ceremony to be completed before leaving.
Only Liú 劉 knew in his heart that something was extraordinary,
and secretly asked the young lady:
"What is your relation to the Fūrén 夫人?"
She replied:
"Your humble servant was a former courtesan of Tóngquè 銅雀."
Liú 劉 suspected she was a ghost.
The young lady said:
"No.
Both your humble servant and the Fūrén 夫人 were once listed in the immortal register,
but were coincidentally banished to the human world due to transgressions.
The Fūrén 夫人 has already returned to her former position;
my term of banishment has not yet expired.
The Fūrén 夫人 pleaded with the Heavenly Bureau
to temporarily assign me to service;
my departure and stay are entirely up to the Fūrén 夫人,
hence I am able to attend to your bed for a long time."
One day,
a blind old woman led a yellow dog, begging for food at their house,
beating clappers and singing folk songs.
The young lady came out to peek;
before she could stand steadily,
the dog broke its leash and bit the young lady.
The young lady fled in fright,
her silk jacket torn.
Liú 劉 urgently struck the dog with his staff.
The dog was still enraged,
bit off a strip of fabric,
and in an instant, shredded it like hemp
and swallowed it.
