The blind old woman grabbed the dog by the scruff
and tied it up to leave.
Liú 劉 went inside to check on the young lady,
whose face was still pale with fright,
and said:
"You are an immortal,
why are you afraid of a dog?"
The young lady said:
"You yourself do not know: the dog is an incarnation of Lǎo Mán 老瞞.
He is angry that I did not uphold the precept of 'sharing fragrance'."
Liú 劉 wanted to buy the dog and beat it to death.
The young lady forbade it,
saying:
"This is a punishment from the Supreme Emperor;
how can you arbitrarily kill it?"
After two years,
all who saw her were astonished by her beauty,
but upon inquiring about her origin,
it was very vague and elusive,
so everyone began to suspect her of being a demon.
His mother questioned Liú 劉,
and Liú 劉 also subtly mentioned her extraordinary nature.
His mother was greatly alarmed
and warned him to break off with her.
Liú 劉 did not listen.
His mother secretly sought out a sorcerer
to perform a ritual in the courtyard.
As he was just drawing lines on the ground to form an altar,
the young lady said sadly:
"I had hoped for a lifelong union;
now that the old mother suspects me,
our bond of righteousness is severed.
For me to leave
is also not difficult,
but I fear it cannot be banished by incantations alone!"
Then she gathered firewood, piled it up, set it alight,
and threw it down the steps.
In an instant, smoke enveloped the houses,
making it impossible to see those directly opposite.
Suddenly, there was a sound like thunder.
A moment later, the smoke dissipated,
and the sorcerer was seen dead, bleeding from all seven orifices.
Entering the room,
the young lady had already vanished.
He called the nanny to ask,
but the nanny also did not know where she had gone.
Liú 劉 then told his mother.
The nanny was actually a fox spirit.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Beginning with Yuán 袁,
ending with Cáo 曹,
and then turning attention to Gōngwò 公斡,
immortals should not be like this.
However, to be fair:
why should there be chaste women for a usurper like the treacherous Mán 瞞?
When the dog saw its former courtesan,
it should have greatly awakened to the folly of 'sharing fragrance and selling shoes',
yet it was still jealous?
Alas!
The treacherous hero has no time to grieve for himself,
and later generations already grieve for him!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi 鑄雪齋 manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* 聊齋誌異.
Wēn Rúchūn 溫如春 was a prominent family in Qín 秦.
From a young age, he was extremely fond of the qín 琴;
even when traveling, he never for a moment parted with it.
While traveling as a guest in Jìn 晉,
he passed an ancient temple,
tied his horse outside the gate,
and briefly rested.
Upon entering, he saw a Daoist priest in a coarse robe
sitting cross-legged in the corridor,
his bamboo staff leaning against the wall,
and a qín 琴 in a floral cloth bag.
Wēn 溫, seeing something he liked,
asked:
"Are you also skilled in this?"
The Daoist priest said:
"I am not skilled;
I wish to learn from someone who is."
Thereupon, he took the qín 琴 from the bag and handed it to Wēn 溫.
Looking at it,
the grain and texture were exquisite and wonderful.
With just a light pluck,
the sound was exceptionally clear and soaring.
Delighted, Wēn 溫 played a short tune.
The Daoist priest smiled slightly,
as if not entirely approving.
So Wēn 溫 then exerted all his skill.
The Daoist priest chuckled and said:
"It's good,
it's good!
But it's not enough to be my teacher."
Wēn 溫, thinking his words boastful,
then earnestly asked him to play.
The Daoist priest took the qín 琴 and placed it on his lap;
as he merely plucked it,
one felt a gentle breeze approaching;
a moment later,
birds gathered in flocks,
filling the trees in the courtyard.
Wēn 溫 was extremely astonished
and bowed, requesting to become his disciple.
The Daoist priest repeated his playing three times.
Wēn 溫 listened with his ears and heart,
gradually grasping its rhythm.
The Daoist priest then had him try playing,
and pointed out some minor details,
saying:
"This has no equal in the mortal world."
From then on, Wēn 溫 dedicated himself to practicing with meticulous care,
and thus became renowned for his peerless skill.
Later, on his return journey,
dozens of *lǐ* from home,
night had fallen,
and a violent rain made it impossible to find shelter.
There was a small village by the roadside,
so he hastened towards it.
Without time to choose carefully,
he saw a gate
and hurried in.
He entered the hall,
but it was utterly silent and empty.
Presently, a young woman came out,
seventeen or eighteen years old,
her appearance like a divine immortal.
She looked up and saw the guest,
then, startled, ran inside.
Wēn Shí was not yet married,
and his affections were deeply stirred.
Presently, an old woman came out and asked the guest,
and Wēn stated his name
and requested lodging.
The old woman said,
"Lodging is certainly no problem,
but we are short of beds;
if you don't mind bending your body,
you can make do with straw."
A short while later,
she brought a candle
and spread grass on the ground,
her intentions very considerate.
He asked her surname,
and she replied,
"The surname Zhào."
He further asked,
"Who is the young woman?"
She said,
"This is Huànniáng,
my old body's niece."
Wēn said,
"Without presuming on my humble and rustic self,
I wish to seek a connection [marriage],
how would that be?"
The old woman frowned and said,
"This I dare not agree to."
Wēn questioned her reason,
but she only said it was difficult to speak of,
so he sadly gave up.
After the old woman left,
Wēn saw that the straw spread on the ground was rotten and damp,
unfit for sleeping on.
So he sat upright and played his *qín*,
to pass the long night.
When the rain stopped,
he braved the night and returned.
In the district, there was Gé Gōng, a minister of the imperial retinue,
who enjoyed the company of literati.
Wēn coincidentally visited him
and was asked to play the *qín*.
Behind the curtain, vaguely, there were female family members peeping and listening.
Suddenly, the wind blew and the curtain opened,
revealing a woman of marriageable age,
exquisitely beautiful, unmatched in her generation.
It happened that Gé had a daughter,
whose pet name was Liánggōng,
skilled in poetry and prose,
and renowned for her beauty.
Wēn's heart was stirred.
He returned and spoke with his mother,
and a matchmaker was sent;
but Gé, seeing Wēn's declining status,
did not consent.
However, after hearing the *qín*, the daughter
secretly admired him
and always hoped to hear his elegant music again;
but Wēn, with the marriage unsuccessful,
his spirits low and will thwarted, ceased visiting the Gé household.
One day,
the daughter was in the garden
and picked up an old folded note,
on which was written a poem titled "Xī Yú Chūn" (Lamenting Lingering Spring), which read:
"Because of hatred, one becomes infatuated,
then turns to yearning,
daily overthrown by passion.
Crabapples, as if drunk,
willows, pained by spring,
share the same sentiment.
How many new sorrows and old sorrows,
though swept away, rise again,
just like green grass.
Since separation,
I am only in a state of helplessness,
passing the dawn and dusk.
Today, my brows are furrowed like spring mountains,
my autumn eyes gaze through,
saying I've resolved to abandon!
The fragrant quilt envies dreams,
the jade clepsydra startles the soul,
how can one sleep well?
Don't say the long night is like a year,
even a year,
is less than a watch: past the third watch is already three years,
who among us does not grow old!"
The daughter recited it several times,
her heart delighted and fond of it.
She took it back with her,
took out a brocade note,
and carefully wrote a letter,
placing it on the desk;
after some time, she looked for it
but could not find it,
secretly thinking the wind had blown it away.
It happened that Gé passed by her boudoir gate
and picked it up;
he thought Liánggōng had written it,
disliked its dissolute words,
burnt it but could not bear to speak of it,
wishing to marry her off quickly.
A young master, Liú Fāngpà of Lín Yì,
came to inquire about a marriage proposal;
Gé thought well of him,
but still wished to see the person.
The young master arrived in ceremonial attire,
his appearance refined and handsome.
Gé was greatly pleased
and entertained him generously.
After saying goodbye,
a embroidered slipper [female shoe] was left under the seat.
Gé immediately disliked his frivolousness
and called the matchmaker to explain the reason.
The young master urgently tried to defend against the false accusation;
Gé would not listen,
and ultimately broke off the engagement.
Previously,
Gé had a green chrysanthemum variety,
which he grudged sharing,
and Liánggōng planted it in her boudoir.
In Wēn's courtyard, suddenly one or two chrysanthemum plants turned green;
those who heard of it
often came to his house to admire them;
Wēn also treasured them.
Early in the morning, he hurried to look
and found a note by the edge of the flowerbed with the poem "Xī Yú Chūn" written on it.
He read it repeatedly,
not knowing where it came from.
He
took the character "者" (*zhě*)
to be his own name,
which confused him even more.
He then meticulously added red and yellow marks to it on his desk,
with inappropriate comments.
It happened that Gé heard Wēn's chrysanthemums had turned green,
was surprised,
and personally visited his study.
He saw the poem and took it to read.
Wēn, because of its inappropriate comments,
snatched it and crumpled it up.
Gé had only read one or two lines,
which was indeed the one he had picked up outside the boudoir.
He was greatly suspicious,
and also guessed that the green chrysanthemum seeds
had been given by Liánggōng.
He returned and told his wife,
and made her press Liánggōng for answers.
Liánggōng wept as if she wished to die,
but there was no verifiable evidence,
nothing to substantiate the claim.
The wife, fearing that her reputation would be further exposed,
concluded it would be better to give the daughter to Wēn.
Gé agreed to this
and sent word to Wēn from afar.
Wēn was overjoyed.
On that day,
he invited guests for a green chrysanthemum feast,
burning incense and playing the *qín*,
and the good night only ended later.
After returning to his bedchamber,
his study boy heard the *qín* playing by itself,
at first thinking it was a prank by a servant;
when he realized it was not a person,
he then informed Wēn.
Wēn personally went to see,
and indeed it was not false.
The sound was rough and halting,
as if trying to imitate him but unable to.
He lit a fire and burst in,
but saw nothing.
Wēn took his *qín* away,
and then it was silent all night.
He thus thought it was a fox,
and knew it wished to learn from him,
so he played a tune for it every evening,
and set up the strings for it to play as if it were his teacher,
listening stealthily every night.
By the sixth or seventh night,
it actually composed a tune,
elegant enough to listen to.
Wēn ēn then personally welcomed his bride.
Each recounted their previous words,
and only then did they understand the reason for their union,
though they still didn't know the origin of the events.
Liáng Gōng heard the unusual sound of the zither,
went to listen,
and said:
"This is no fox.
The tune is mournful and sorrowful,
with a ghostly sound."
Wēn ēn did not fully believe him.
Liáng Gōng then said that his family had an ancient mirror
that could reflect demons and goblins.
Yì yì said,
send someone to fetch it,
and wait for the zither music to begin;
grasp the mirror and quickly enter;
light it up,
and indeed there was a woman there,
huddled in a corner of the room in a panic,
unable to hide again.
Upon close inspection,
it was the ghost of Zhào Shì's daughter.
They were greatly astonished and
questioned her thoroughly.
She wept and said:
"To act as a go-between
is not without virtue,
why are you pressing me so hard?"
Wēn ēn asked to put away the mirror,
and pledged that she should not flee;
she agreed.
Then he put the mirror in its bag.
The woman sat down at a distance and said:
"I am the daughter of the Tàishǒu,
and have been dead for a hundred years.
In my youth, I loved the qín and zhēng;
I was quite proficient with the zhēng,
but this skill was not truly passed down,
and I regretted it even in the afterlife.
When you honored me with your presence,
I was able to listen to your elegant performance,
and my heart was drawn to it;
I also regretted that as a different being, I could not attend to your needs,
so secretly I helped you find a good match,
to repay your kindness.
The women's shoes of Liú Gōngzǐ's daughter,
and the rustic lyrics of 'Xī Yú Chūn',
were all made by me.
One cannot say that the payment to the teacher was not arduous."
The couple bowed and thanked her.
Huànniáng said:
"Your skill,
I believe I have grasped more than half of it;
but I have not yet fully comprehended its spirit and essence.
Please play it again for me."
Wēn ēn complied with her request,
and again detailed his method.
Huànniáng was greatly pleased and said:
"I have now fully understood it!"
Then she rose, wished to take her leave, and departed.
Liáng Gōng was originally skilled in the zhēng,
and hearing her excellence,
wished to listen.
Huànniáng did not refuse;
her tunes and scores
were not of this mortal world.
Liáng Gōng beat time,
then asked to become her disciple.
The woman ordered a brush to draw eighteen chapters of scores,
then rose to bid farewell again.
The couple tried hard to detain her.
Huànniáng sadly said:
"Your harmony on the qín and sè,
you are each other's true connoisseurs;
a person of ill fate like me cannot have such blessings.
If there is destiny,
we can reunite in another life."
Then she handed a scroll to Wēn ēn and said:
"This is my small portrait.
If you do not forget your matchmaker,
you should hang it in your bedroom,
and when you are happy, burn a stick of incense,
and play a tune opposite it,
then I will receive it."
She went out the door and disappeared.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì,
Liú Zǐgù of Hǎizhōu,
at the age of fifteen,
went to Gài to visit his maternal uncle.
He saw a girl in a general store,
of unparalleled beauty,
and fell in love with her.
He secretly went to her shop,
claiming to buy a fan.
The girl then called her father.
When the father came out,
Liú's enthusiasm waned,
so he haggled over the price and left.
From a distance, he saw her father go elsewhere,
and went to the shop again.
The girl was about to look for her father when
Liú stopped her, saying:
"No need,
just tell me the price,
I am not stingy with money."
The girl spoke as she was told,
and Gù ɡù raised the price.
Liú could not bear to argue,
took out the money and left.
The next day he went again,
and did the same.
After walking a few paces,
the girl called out, chasing him:
"Come back!
What I said earlier was false,
the price was excessively high."
Then she returned half the money.
Liú was even more touched by her sincerity,
and whenever he found an opportunity, he went there,
thus becoming increasingly familiar.
The girl asked:
"Where does the young master reside?"
He answered truthfully.
When he in turn questioned her,
she said:
"My surname is Yáo."
Before leaving,
the items he bought,
the girl wrapped perfectly with paper,
and then sealed it with her tongue.
Liú carried it home, not daring to move it again,
fearing to disturb her tongue marks.
After half a month,
he was spied upon by a servant,
who secretly urged his uncle to force him to return home.
He felt restless and unhappy.
He secretly placed the purchased scented handkerchiefs, cosmetics, and other items
in a basket,
and when no one was around,
he would close the door and examine them once,
contemplating as he touched each item.
The following year,
he returned to Gài,
and as soon as he had unpacked,
he immediately hurried to the girl's place;
when he arrived, the shop was closed,
and he returned disappointed.
He still thought she might have just gone out and not yet returned,
so early the next morning he went again,
but the sign was still the same.
He asked the neighbors,
and only then learned that Yáo was originally from Guǎngníng,
and because trade was not very profitable,
they had temporarily returned home;
and he didn't know when they would return.
His spirit was lost and depressed.
After staying for several days,
he returned home disconsolately.
His mother tried to arrange a marriage for him,
but he repeatedly obstructed it,
making his mother both puzzled and angry.
The servant privately told his mother about the past events,
and his mother became even more vigilant and watchful,
thus cutting off his route to Gài.
Liú suddenly ate and slept less.
His mother was worried and at her wit's end,
thinking it would be better to follow his wishes.
So she set a date to prepare his luggage,
sent him to Gài,
and had him relay a message to his uncle to act as a matchmaker.
His uncle immediately obeyed and went to Yáo.
After some time, he returned,
and told Liú:
"The matter is not harmonious!
Ā Xiù is already engaged to someone from Guǎngníng."
Liú hung his head in despair,
his heart turned to ashes and he lost all hope.
Upon returning,
he held his casket and sobbed,
but then he paced and looked around,
hoping there might be someone similar in the world.
A matchmaker came,
extolling a daughter of the Huáng clan of Fùzhōu.
Liú feared it was inaccurate,
so he ordered his carriage to Fù.
Entering the west gate,
he saw a house facing north.
Its two doors were half-open,
and inside was a young woman,
strangely resembling Āxiù.
He looked at her again,
and as she walked and looked around, she entered.
It was truly unmistakable.
Liú was greatly moved.
He then rented a dwelling from her eastern neighbor
and through careful inquiry learned it belonged to the Lǐ clan.
Doubts arose repeatedly!
How could there possibly be someone so strikingly similar in the world?
He stayed for several days,
unable to find any way to make a connection.
He merely stared intently at her door,
hoping the young woman might come out again.
One day,
as the sun was setting,
the young woman indeed came out.
Suddenly seeing Liú,
she immediately turned and walked away,
pointing her finger behind her.
Then she brought her palm to her forehead
and entered.
Liú was overjoyed,
but he couldn't understand.
After pondering for a while,
he strolled to the back of the house
and saw a vast, desolate garden.
To the west was a low wall,
roughly shoulder-high.
Suddenly, he understood.
He then crouched hidden in the dewy grass.
After a long time,
someone revealed their head from over the wall,
and whispered:
"Are you here?"
Liú assented and stood up.
Looking closely,
it was truly Āxiù.
He was greatly distressed,
and tears fell like a rope.
The young woman leaned over the wall,
wiping his tears with a scarf,
and comforting him deeply.
Liú said:
"A hundred plans failed;
I thought my life was over,
who would have expected a night like this again?
But how did you come to be here, my dear?"
She said:
"The Lǐ clan
are my maternal relatives."
Liú asked to climb over the wall.
The young woman said:
"You go back first,
send your attendants to sleep elsewhere,
and I will come myself."
Liú did as she said
and sat waiting for her.
A short while later,
the young woman quietly entered.
Her makeup was not particularly dazzling,
and her robes and trousers were as before.
Liú pulled her to sit,
and recounted his hardships.
Then he asked:
"You were already betrothed,
why have you not married yet?"
The young woman said:
"Those who say I received an engagement gift are
mistaken.
My father, because of the great distance,
was unwilling to have me marry into your noble family.
This was probably an artful deception
from my maternal uncle to dash your hopes."
After they lay on the bed,
they indulged in countless intimate moments,
the joy of their loving reunion
was inexpressible.
At the fourth watch, she suddenly rose
and crossed the wall to leave.
From then on, Liú no longer paid attention to the Huáng clan.
He forgot to return from his travels,
not going back for a month.
One night,
his servant got up to feed the horse
and saw the lamp in the room was still lit.
Peeking in,
he saw Āxiù,
and was greatly alarmed,
but dared not question his master.
At dawn,
he visited the market
before returning to question Liú, saying:
"Who was the person
you were with last night?"
Liú initially concealed it.
The servant said:
“This residence is exceedingly desolate,
a den of foxes and ghosts.
Young Master, you should take care of yourself.
As for that young lady of the Yáo family,
why has she come here?”
Liú Shǐ, looking embarrassed, said:
“The western neighbor is her maternal uncle;
what is there to be suspicious or hindered about?”
The servant said:
“I have investigated thoroughly: the eastern neighbor only has a lonely old woman,
and the western household has a child still young.
There are no other close relatives.
What you encountered must be a ghost or goblin;
otherwise,
how could her clothes, after several years,
still not have been changed?
Furthermore, her complexion is excessively pale,
her cheeks somewhat thin,
and when she smiles, there are no dimples.
She is not as beautiful as Āxiù.”
Liú pondered repeatedly,
then, greatly alarmed, said:
“So what should we do now?”
The servant planned to wait for her arrival,
then, wielding a weapon, enter and attack her together.
By evening,
the woman arrived,
and said to Liú:
“I know you have doubts,
but I have no other intentions;
it is merely to fulfill an old destiny.”
Before she finished speaking,
the servant pushed open the door and entered.
The woman scolded him, saying:
“Discard your weapon!
Quickly bring wine;
I must bid farewell to your master.”
The servant immediately dropped his weapon,
as if it were snatched from him.
Liú became even more frightened,
and forced himself to prepare wine and food.
The woman talked and laughed as usual,
then raised her hand to Liú and said:
“Your intentions,
I was just about to exert myself slightly for them,
why then did you hide soldiers?
Although I am not Āxiù,
I believe I am not inferior in fairness.
Do you view me the same as before?”
Liú’s hair stood on end,
and he remained silent.
The woman listened to three drips of the water clock,
took a sip from her cup,
stood up and said:
“I shall go now.
After the wedding candles,
I will compete with the new bride to see who is superior.”
She turned and vanished.
Liú believed the fox’s words,
and it turned out to be exactly so.
He resented his maternal uncle for deceiving him,
and did not leave his home.
He stayed near the Yáo family,
used a matchmaker to communicate,
and tempted them with heavy bribes.
Yáo’s wife then said:
“The young man is seeking a son-in-law in Guǎngníng.
Your father-in-law went there for this reason;
whether it will succeed is unknown.
You must wait for the day of his return to calculate.”
When Liú heard this,
he wandered aimlessly, unable to control himself.
He could only stand firm and await her return.
More than ten days passed,
when suddenly he heard news of military unrest.
He still suspected it was a false rumor;
after a long time,
the news became more urgent,
so he hastily packed and set off.
He encountered chaos on the way;
master and servant were separated,
and he was plundered by scouts.
Because Liú was weak and scholarly,
they were lax in guarding him.
He stole a horse and fled.
Upon reaching the borders of Hǎizhōu,
he saw a woman,
with disheveled hair and dirty ears.
Her shoes were worn out, making her stumble and trip,
a pitiable sight.
Liú rode past her,
when the woman suddenly cried out:
“Is the person on horseback not Liú Láng?”
Liú stopped his whip and looked closely,
and it was Āxiù.
and said:
“Are you truly Āxiù?”
He still suspected her to be a fox,
“Why do you say that?”
Liú recounted what he had encountered.
The woman said:
“I am truly Āxiù.
My father brought me back from Guǎngníng,
we encountered soldiers and were captured.
I was given a horse, but fell repeatedly.
Suddenly, a woman
grabbed my wrist and urged me to flee.
We scurried wildly through the army,
with no clean escape.
The woman walked as fast as a flying falcon;
I struggled to keep up,
and after a hundred steps, I repeatedly lost my footing.
After a while,
I heard the shouts and roars gradually fade into the distance,
then she released my hand and said: ‘Farewell!
The path ahead is clear;
you can walk slowly.
The one who loves you will arrive soon;
you should return home together with him.’ ”
Liú knew she was the fox,
and was grateful.
He then explained the reason for his stay in Gài.
The woman said her maternal uncle had arranged a marriage for her with the Fāng family,
but before the betrothal gifts were presented, the rebellion began.
Liú then realized his maternal uncle’s words were not fabricated.
He carried the woman on his horse,
riding together back home.
Upon entering the door, his old mother was safe and sound,
and he was overjoyed.
The stableman
also explained everything.
His mother was also pleased;
she washed and bathed the woman,
and when her makeup was complete,
her face glowed with radiance.
His mother clapped her hands and said:
“No wonder my foolish son was haunted by her in his dreams!”
Then she arranged bedding,
and had her sleep with her.
She also sent someone to Gài,
and delivered a letter to the Yáo family.
Within a few days,
Mr. and Mrs. Yáo both arrived,
chose an auspicious day, completed the ceremony, and then left.
Liú took out the hidden chest,
its seal and marks intact.
Inside was a box of powder.
Opening it,
it had turned into red earth.
Liú found this strange.
The woman covered her mouth and said:
"The theft of several years
is only now discovered.
That day, you saw your husband let your concubine wrap it up,
without further examining its authenticity,
so I just played this trick on you."
As they were laughing and joking,
a person lifted the curtain and entered, saying:
"So happy,
should you not thank Jiǎnxiū?"
Liú looked at her,
and it was another Āxiù.
He quickly called his mother.
His mother and family all gathered,
but none could distinguish them.
Liú turned his gaze and was also confused;
he stared for a while,
then bowed and thanked her.
The woman asked for a mirror to look at herself,
then blushingly hurried out,
and when sought, she was already gone.
The couple, moved by her righteousness,
set up a tablet in their room and worshipped her.
One evening,
Liú returned drunk,
it was dark and deserted.
He was just about to light a lamp himself
when Āxiù arrived.
Liú pulled her and asked:
"Where have you been?"
She smiled and said:
"Your drunken smell is suffocating,
making one unbearable!
With such questioning,
who would flee like one caught in Sāngzhōng?"
Liú smiled and cupped her cheek.
The woman said:
"Husband, who do you think is better, your concubine or the fox sister?"
Liú said:
"You surpass her.
However, those who judge by appearance cannot tell the difference."
Soon after, they closed the door and became intimate.
Suddenly there was a knock at the door.
The woman got up and smiled, saying:
"You too are one who judges by appearance."
Liú didn't understand,
he hurried to open the door,
and Āxiù entered,
greatly astonished.
He then realized that the one he had been speaking with
was a fox.
In the darkness, he heard laughter again.
The couple looked up at the sky and prayed,
beseeching her to appear.
The fox said:
"I do not wish to see Āxiù."
He asked:
"Why not transform into another appearance?"
She said:
"I cannot."
He asked:
"Why can you not?"
She said:
"Āxiù
is my younger sister.
In a previous life, she unfortunately died young.
When she was alive,
she accompanied me and our mother to the Celestial Palace,
saw the Xīwángmǔ,
and secretly admired her,
so upon returning, she devoted herself to imitating her.
My sister was more intelligent than me;
in one month she was spiritually alike;
I took three months to achieve it,
but still never surpassed my sister.
Now that a lifetime has passed,
I thought I had surpassed her,
but unexpectedly, I am still the same as before.
I am moved by the sincerity of you two,
hence I occasionally visit;
now I must leave."
Then she spoke no more.
From then on, she would come every three to five days,
resolving all doubts and difficulties.
When Āxiù returned to her parents' home,
she would often stay for several days,
and the family members all feared and avoided her.
Whenever something was lost,
she would sit elegantly adorned,
with a tortoiseshell hairpin several inches long,
and solemnly declare to the family:
"The stolen item
shall be sent to such-and-such a place tonight;
otherwise,
a severe headache will ensue,
and regret will be too late!"
At dawn,
it was indeed found at the said place.
After three years,
she never came again.
Occasionally, if gold or silk was lost,
Āxiù would imitate her attire,
to frighten the family,
and it often worked.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A hunter,
lying in ambush in the mountains at night,
saw a small person,
about two feet tall,
walking alone at the bottom of a ravine.
A short while later,
another person came,
also of similar height.
They met and asked each other where they were going.
The first one said:
"I am going to visit Yáng Bāyǎn.
I saw his complexion was dark and gloomy,
likely to suffer many misfortunes."
The second person said:
"I am also here for this reason;
your words are not mistaken."
The hunter knew they were not human,
and shouted loudly in a stern voice;
the two instantly vanished.
That night, he caught a fox,
which had a scar above its left eye,
as big as a coin.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Wáng Tàicháng,
a man from Yuè.
When he was a child,
he was sleeping on the bed during the day.
Suddenly it became dark and gloomy,
and a violent thunderclap erupted.
A creature larger than a cat
came and hid under his body,
rolling about and not leaving.
After some time, the sky cleared,
and the creature immediately ran out.
He looked at it;
it was not a cat.
He was scared at first,
and called his brother from the next room.
His brother heard him,
and joyfully said:
"My brother will surely become very noble;
this is a fox that came to escape the thunderbolt calamity."
Later, he indeed passed the imperial examination at a young age,
and entered government service as a censor after being a county magistrate.
He had a son
named Yuánfēng,
who was extremely foolish;
at sixteen, he could not distinguish between male and female,
and consequently, no one in the village would marry him.
Wáng worried about this.
Just then, a woman led a young girl to their door,
and offered her as a wife.
Looking at the girl,
she smiled charmingly,
truly a celestial beauty.
Joyfully, he asked her name.
She introduced herself:
"My surname is Yú.
My daughter is Xiǎocuì,
she is sixteen years old."
They discussed the betrothal gift.
She said:
"She has been unable to eat her fill of husks with me;
if she can suddenly live in a grand mansion,
command maids and servants,
and enjoy rich food,
if her wishes are fulfilled,
my desire will be comforted.
Am I selling vegetables
that I should ask for a price?"
Madam was greatly pleased,
and treated her generously.
The woman then instructed her daughter to bow to Wáng and Madam,
and admonished her:
"These are your father-in-law and mother-in-law;
you should serve them with diligence.
I am very busy;
I will leave for now,
and will return in three to five days."
Wáng ordered servants and horses to escort her.
The woman said:
"The village is not far;
no need for such trouble."
Then she left the door.
Xiǎocuì showed no sadness or longing,
and immediately took out embroidery patterns from her trousseau.
Madam also loved and enjoyed her company.
Several days passed,
but the woman did not return.
When Wáng Gōng asked the girl about her dwelling,
the girl was also too simple-minded to describe her route.
So, Wáng Gōng prepared a separate courtyard
and arranged for the couple to be wed.
When relatives heard that Shídé had taken a simple-minded boy's wife as his own,
they all ridiculed and mocked him;
but upon seeing the girl, they were all astonished,
and their collective murmuring ceased.
The girl was also very intelligent,
able to discern her parents-in-law's joys and angers.
Wáng Gōng and his wife
cherished and doted on her more than usual,
yet they were constantly apprehensive,
fearing she might despise their foolish son;
but the girl was exceedingly cheerful
and showed no aversion.
She was simply playful.
She would cut cloth into a round shape,
and kick it around for fun.
Wearing small leather boots,
she would kick it dozens of paces away,
making Gōngzǐ run to retrieve it;
Gōngzǐ and the maids constantly sweated one after another.
One day,
Wáng Gōng happened to pass by,
and the round object came flying
straight at his face.
The girl and the maids quickly hid,
but Gōngzǐ was still eagerly chasing it.
Wáng Gōng was angry
and threw a stone at him,
whereupon he finally crouched down and cried.
Wáng Gōng told Fūrén;
Fūrén went to reprimand the girl,
who bowed her head, smiled,
and tapped the bed with her hand.
After Fūrén left,
she was as playfully mischievous as before,
smearing Gōngzǐ with cosmetics
to make his face look like a flowered ghost.
When Fūrén saw this,
she was furious
and called the girl to scold her.
The girl leaned on the table, playing with her belt,
unaFraid
and silent.
Fūrén had no choice
but to cane her son.
When Yuánfēng cried out loudly,
the girl's expression finally changed,
and she knelt to beg for forgiveness.
Fūrén's anger immediately subsided,
and she put down the cane and left.
The girl smiled, pulled Gōngzǐ into the room,
brushed the dust from his clothes,
wiped his tears,
rubbed the cane marks on his palms,
and fed him dates and chestnuts.
Only then did Gōngzǐ stop crying and become cheerful.
The girl closed the courtyard gates,
and again dressed Gōngzǐ up as Bawang,
or as a desert nomad;
then she put on glamorous clothes,
cinched her waist,
and gracefully performed a tent dance;
or she would insert pheasant feathers into her topknot,
play the pípa,
making a 'dīng dīng lǚ lǚ' sound,
filling the room with laughter,
and this became their daily routine.
Wáng Gōng, due to his son's foolishness,
could not bear to overly blame his daughter-in-law;
even if he faintly heard of her antics,
he would act as if he ignored it.
In the same alley, there was Wáng Jǐjiàn,
living a dozen or so households away,
but they had always been on good terms privately.
It was the time of the triennial Grand Review of Officials,
and Wáng Jǐjiàn was jealous that Wáng Gōng held the seal of the Hénán Circuit,
and sought to harm him.
Wáng Gōng knew of his scheme
and worried, unable to devise a plan.
One evening,
he went to bed early.
The girl donned official robes and a hat,
dressed up as a minister,
cut plain silk threads to make a false beard,
and also dressed two maids in green clothes as attendants.
She secretly mounted a stable horse and rode out,
jokingly saying:
"I will pay my respects to Wáng Xiānshēng."
She galloped to Wáng Jǐjiàn's gate. Then she whipped and chastised her followers,
and loudly declared:
"I am visiting Wáng Shìyù,
not Wáng Jǐjiàn!"
Then she turned her reins and returned.
By the time she reached her family gate,
the gatekeeper mistook her for real
and rushed to inform Wáng Gōng.
Wáng Gōng hastily rose to welcome her,
only to realize it was his daughter-in-law's prank.
He was furious
and said to Fūrén:
"People are already seeking out my flaws,
and she actually takes a domestic scandal
and proclaims it at someone's door.
Further misfortune is not far off!"
Fūrén was angry,
rushed to the girl's room,
and scolded her severely.
The girl merely smiled foolishly
and did not say a single word.
To beat her,
they couldn't bear it;
to expel her,
she had no home: the couple felt regret and resentment,
unable to sleep all night.
At that time, the Grand Minister, Mǒu Gōng, was extremely influential;
his official attire and retinue
were indistinguishable from the girl's disguise,
and Wáng Jǐjiàn also mistook it for real.
He repeatedly spied on Wáng Gōng's gate,
and when no one emerged in the middle of the night,
he suspected the Grand Minister and Wáng Gōng had a secret plot.
The next day during the morning court,
he saw Wáng Gōng and asked:
"Last night,
did Xiànggōng visit your home?"
Wáng Gōng suspected he was being ridiculed
and stammered 'yes, yes' with embarrassment,
not giving a clear answer.
Wáng Jǐjiàn became even more suspicious,
so his scheme ceased,
and from then on, he deepened his friendly relations with Wáng Gōng.
Wáng Gōng discovered his true feelings,
secretly rejoiced,
and privately instructed Fūrén
to persuade the girl to change her ways;
the girl smiled in response.
A year later,
the prime minister was dismissed.
It so happened that someone intended to send a private letter to Gōng [gōng],
but mistakenly sent it to the Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn].
The Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn] was overjoyed,
and first entrusted a good friend of Gōng [gōng] to go and borrow ten thousand pieces of gold,
but Gōng [gōng] refused.
The Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn] then personally went to Gōng [gōng]'s residence.
Gōng [gōng] looked for his headscarf and gown,
but could not find either;
the Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn] waited for a long time,
angry at Gōng [gōng]'s disrespect,
and was about to leave in a huff.
Suddenly, he saw Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] in court robes and a ceremonial cap, and a woman pushing him out from inside the gate.
He was greatly astonished;
after a moment, he smiled and caressed him,
then removed his robes and cap and departed.
Gōng [gōng] rushed out,
but the guest had already gone far.
When he heard the reason,
his face turned ashen with shock,
and he cried loudly,
"This is a disaster!
It will surely bring ruin to our clan very soon!"
He and his wife took staffs and went.
The woman already knew,
and shut the door, letting them curse and scold.
Gōng [gōng] was furious,
and chopped at her door with an axe.
The woman, inside, smiled and said to him:
"Elder, there's no need to be angry.
With your new daughter-in-law here,
whether it's knives, saws, axes, or halberds,
your daughter-in-law will take it herself,
and will certainly not let harm befall her parents-in-law.
If you do this,
are you trying to kill your daughter-in-law to silence her?"
Gōng [gōng] then stopped.
When the Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn] returned,
he indeed submitted a memorial exposing the King's impropriety,
using the court robes and cap as evidence.
The Emperor was surprised and investigated,
and found that the ceremonial cap was made by Liáng Xiá Xīn [liáng xiá xīn],
and the robe was a tattered cloth yellow wrapper.
The Emperor was angry at his slander.
He then summoned Yuán Fēng [yuán fēng],
and seeing his idiotic appearance,
smiled and said:
"Can this person be an Emperor?"
Then he handed him over to the judicial authorities.
The Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn] again accused Gōng [gōng]'s family of having an evil person.
The judicial authorities strictly questioned the servants,
who all said there was nothing unusual,
only a crazy wife and a foolish son,
who spent their days in playful laughter;
the neighbors also had no different account.
The case was then settled,
and the Gěi Jiàn [gěi jiàn] was banished to the army in Yún Nán [yún nán].
The King, from this, regarded the woman as extraordinary.
Also, as her mother had not visited for a long time,
he suspected she was not human.
He sent his wife to inquire,
but the woman only smiled and did not speak.
When pressed further,
she covered her mouth and said:
"Your son is the Jade Emperor's daughter,
doesn't Mother know?"
Before long,
Gōng [gōng] was appointed to a high official position in the capital.
He was over fifty,
and always worried about not having a grandson.
The woman lived there for three years.
Every night she slept in a different bed from Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ],
as if they had never been intimate.
His wife moved her bed away,
and instructed Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] to sleep with his wife.
After several days,
Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] told his mother:
"The borrowed bed is gone,
and she stubbornly won't return it!
Xiǎo Cuì [xiǎo cuì] puts her leg on my abdomen every night,
so I can't breathe;
and she's used to pinching my inner thigh."
The maids and old women all laughed brightly.
His wife scolded him and made him leave.
One day,
the woman was bathing in the room,
Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] saw her,
and wanted to join her;
the woman smiled and stopped him,
telling him to wait a moment.
When she came out,
she then poured hot water into a jar,
undid his robes and trousers,
and with the help of a maid, helped him get in.
Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] felt suffocated,
and cried loudly, wanting to get out.
The woman did not listen,
and covered him with a quilt.
After a short while,
there was no sound.
She opened it to look,
and he was already dead.
The woman smiled calmly, not surprised,
pulled him onto the bed,
wiped his body clean and dry,
and covered him with an extra quilt.
His wife heard of it,
cried and rushed in,
cursing:
"Mad maid, why did you kill my son!"
The woman smiled broadly and said:
"Such a foolish child,
it's better not to have him."
His wife became even more furious,
and bumped her head against the woman;
the maids scrambled to pull her away and dissuade her.
While they were in a clamor,
a maid announced:
"Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] is groaning!"
She stopped her tears and caressed him,
and indeed, he was breathing softly,
and profusely sweating,
drenching the bedding.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
the sweat stopped,
he suddenly opened his eyes and looked around,
looking at all his family members,
as if he didn't recognize them,
and said:
"Now I recall the past,
it's all like a dream,
why is that?"
His wife was greatly surprised by his sensible words,
and was very astonished.
She brought him to meet his father,
who tested him repeatedly,
and indeed he was no longer foolish.
They were overjoyed,
as if they had found a rare treasure.
By evening,
they returned to the original bed,
and placed an extra quilt and pillow to observe them.
Gōngzǐ [gōng zǐ] entered the room,
and sent all the maids away.
In the morning, they secretly looked,
and found the bed empty.
From then on, the foolishness and madness never recurred,
and their marriage was harmonious and beautiful,
like body and shadow.
Jīn Héshang,
a native of Zhūchéng.
His father was a scoundrel,
who sold his son for a few hundred cash to the Wǔliánshān Temple.
The boy was dull-witted
and unable to pursue monastic studies.
He herded pigs and went to market,
like a hired servant.
Later, his master died,
and he acquired some leftover money.
He wrapped it up and left the temple,
becoming a peddler.
He was skilled at calculating profits
from buying and selling.
In a few years, he became suddenly rich,
buying fields and houses in Shuǐpō Lǐ.
His disciples were numerous,
with thousands of dependents eating daily.
Hundreds of acres of fertile land surrounded the village.
Dozens of residences were built in the village,
all belonging to monks,
with no other inhabitants;
if there were any,
they were poor and jobless,
bringing their wives and children,
renting houses and tilling fields.
Within each gate,
surrounding connected houses,
were rows of these people living there.
The monks' quarters were in the middle: in front was a main hall,
with ornate beams and pillars,
painted in gold and green,
dazzling to the eye;
on the platform were tables and screens,
shining brightly;
behind that was the inner chamber,
with red curtains and embroidered hangings,
filled with the overpowering scent of orchid and musk;
the bed was made of mother-of-pearl and carved sandalwood,
on the bed were brocade cushions and mats,
folded to a thickness of a foot;
on the walls were famous paintings of beauties, landscapes, and other subjects,
leaving almost no gaps.
With one long shout,
dozens of people outside the gate responded like thunder.
Those with fine headbands and leather boots
gathered like crows and stood like pigeons;
when given orders, they all covered their mouths to speak,
and cocked their ears to listen.
When guests arrived unexpectedly,
more than ten banquets could be prepared in an instant,
with rich delicacies steaming and fragrant,
piled disorderly like mist.
However, they dared not openly keep singing girls;
but ten or so cunning boys,
all clever and charming,
with black gauze wrapped around their heads,
sang erotic songs,
which were quite pleasant to hear.
Whenever Jīn went out,
dozens of riders preceded and followed him,
with bows and arrows clattering at their waists.
His servants all called him
"Yé";
even the local people,
some called him
"Zǔ,"
or
"Bó, Shú,"
not using
"Shī,"
nor
"Shàngrén,"
nor
his monastic title.
When his disciples went out,
they were slightly less imposing than Jīn,
but with flying manes and cloud-like reins,
they were also comparable to noble young masters.
Jīn also formed extensive connections,
even breathing could communicate over a thousand miles,
using this to manipulate the influence of regional officials;
if someone accidentally offended him,
they would immediately tremble with fear.
Yet, his character was
vulgar and unrefined,
with no elegant bones from head to toe.
In his life, he never chanted a single scripture,
nor held a single mantra,
his footsteps never entered a monastery,
nor did his room ever contain a drum for chanting;
these things,
his disciples never saw,
nor even heard of.
All the women who rented houses,
were as glamorous as those in the capital,
their cosmetics, gold, and powder,
all provided by the monks;
the monks were not stingy about it,
so there were hundreds of people in the village who did not farm but lived like farmers.
Sometimes, wicked tenants would smash a monk's head and bury it under the bed,
but they were not thoroughly investigated,
merely driven away;
such was their ingrained custom.
Jīn also bought a boy of a different surname,
secretly adopting him as his son.
He invited a Confucian scholar
to teach him the art of writing official documents for examinations.
The boy was intelligent and good at writing,
so he was made a student of the county school;
soon after, he was promoted by special grace to become a National University student;
not long after,
he went to the northern examination hall,
and obtained the provincial recommendation.
From then on, Jīn's name was known as
"Tàigōng."
Those who previously called him
"Yé"
now called him
"Tài,"
and those who sat on mats
now held their hands down and performed the rites of children and grandchildren.
Not long after,
Tàigōng Sēng passed away.
The Xiàolián wore sackcloth and lay on a straw mat and clods of earth,
facing north and proclaiming himself "orphan";
all the disciples placed their staffs on the beds;
and behind the spirit screen, soft sobbing was heard,
only from the Xiàolián's wife.
Officials and their wives, all in elaborate attire, came,
lifting the screen to offer condolences,
with carriages and horses blocking the roads.
On the day of the funeral,
pavilions and scaffolds extended like clouds,
and banners and pennants overshadowed the sun.
Funerary figures,
adorned with gold and silk;
dozens of carriages, covers, and ceremonial guards;
a thousand horses,
a hundred beautiful women,
all lifelike.
Fāngzhōu and Fāngxiàng figures,
giant effigies made of paper shells,
with black headbands and golden clasps;
hollow inside with a wooden frame horizontally placed,
live people were put inside to carry them.
Machines were set to make them move,
whiskers and eyebrows flying;
eyes flashing,
as if about to roar.
Spectators were astonished,
and some small children, seeing them from afar,
would cry and run away.
The underworld mansion was as grand and magnificent as a palace,
with connected buildings, towers, and corridors spanning dozens of acres,
a thousand gates and ten thousand doors,
those who entered would get lost and could not get out.
Many sacrificial objects and effigies
were hard to name.
Those attending the funeral rubbed shoulders,
from high-ranking officials.
All bowed,
rising and prostrating like court rituals;
down to tribute students, students of the National Academy, clerks, and historians,
they would put their hands on the ground to kowtow,
not daring to trouble the young master,
or the various "Shīshú."
At that time,
the entire populace looked on,
men and women sweating profusely on the road;
those carrying wives and infants,
calling for brothers and seeking sisters, their voices tumultuous.
Mixed with the din of drums and music,
and the clamor of a hundred entertainments,
human voices could not be heard at all.
From the shoulders down, spectators were completely hidden,
only countless bobbing heads could be seen.
A pregnant woman experienced labor pains,
her female companions spread their skirts to form a tent,
guarding her;
only the crying of the infant was heard,
with no time to ask if it was male or female,
a strip of cloth was torn to bind it to her chest,
some helped her up,
some dragged her,
limping away.
What a spectacle!
After the funeral,
Jīn's inherited assets
were divided into two equal parts: one for his son,
and one for his disciples.
The Xiàolián received half,
and resided in the south of the residence;
the north, west, and east,
all belonged to the Buddhist faction.
However, they all addressed each other as brothers,
sharing each other's joys and sorrows, it was said.
Yìshǐshì said:
"This is one sect!
It has no connection to the two schools of Chan,
nor any transmission from the Six Patriarchs.
It can be said to have opened up its own unique Dharma gate.
I have also heard: When the five aggregates are all empty,
and the six sense-objects do not defile,
this is called 'Héshàng' (monk, literally 'harmony exalted').
When one speaks the Dharma from the mouth,
and practices Chan meditation on the cushion,
this is called 'Héyàng' (harmony in manner).
When shoes are fragrant in the land of Chǔ,
and hats are heavy in the skies of Wú,
this is called 'Hézhuàng' (harmony clashing).
When drums and gongs clang noisily,
and sheng and pipes play raucously,
this is called 'Héchàng' (harmony singing).
When one is as lowly as a dog seeking connections,
and as busy as a fly engaging in debauchery and gambling,
this is called
'Hézhàng' (harmony of obstacles/screen).
Now, is
this 'Shàng'?
Or?
'Yàng'?
Or?
'Chàng'?
Or?
'Tóng' (child)?
Or?
Is it the 'Zhàng' of hell?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Xúgōng was the magistrate of Qídōng.
In his yamen, there was a multi-storied building
used for storing food and bait.
Often, things would steal and eat the food,
leaving a mess on the ground.
His household members were repeatedly scolded and blamed,
so they lay in wait to observe.
They saw a spider,
as large as a bushel basket.
Terrified, they ran to tell the magistrate.
Considering it unusual,
the magistrate daily sent his maids to put out bait for it.
The spider became increasingly tame;
when hungry, it would come out and approach people,
and leave after it was full.
More than a year passed.
One day, as the magistrate was reviewing official documents,
the spider suddenly came and lay on his desk.
Suspecting it was hungry,
he was about to call for a servant to fetch bait;
then he saw two snakes lying beside the spider,
thin as chopsticks.
The spider's claws curled and its abdomen contracted,
as if overwhelmed with fear.
In a flash,
the snakes grew enormously,
thicker than an egg.
The magistrate was greatly alarmed
and tried to flee.
A tremendous thunderclap erupted,
and his entire family was struck dead.
After a while,
the magistrate revived;
his wife and seven maidservants and attendants had been struck dead.
The magistrate was ill for over a month
and then passed away.
The magistrate was an upright and honest man who loved his people.
On the day his coffin was dispatched,
the people collected money to send him off,
and cries of sorrow filled the fields.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Dragons playing with spiders –
I always thought these were just rumors from the streets and alleys.
Are they truly real?
I heard that lightning strikes
are reserved for wicked people.
Why did such an upright and good official
suffer this cruel calamity?
Is the Heavenly Duke's confusion
not too frequent! "
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A certain merchant from Tiānjīn,
intending to trade in a distant region,
borrowed several hundreds of currency from a rich man.
He was noticed by a thief,
who, in the evening,
hid in his room in advance, awaiting his return.
However, the merchant, considering that day auspicious,
departed immediately with the borrowed money.
only hearing the merchant's wife tossing and turning on the bed,
seemingly unable to sleep.
Presently, a small door on the wall opened,
and the entire room became bright.
From within the door emerged a woman,
The thief had been hiding for a long time,
holding a long strip of cloth.
She approached the bed and offered it to the wife,
who pushed it away with her hand.
The woman insisted on giving it to her;
the wife then accepted the strip,
got up, hung it on the beam,
stretched her neck, and hanged herself.
The woman then left,
and the wall door also closed.
The thief was greatly astonished,
unlocked the door, and fled.
When dawn broke,
the family saw the wife dead
and reported it to the authorities.
The official arrested a neighbor and tortured him,
forcing a confession and sentencing him to prison.
He was to be executed in a few days.
The thief, indignant at the injustice,
confessed to the yamen
and recounted what he had seen that night.
The investigation confirmed the truth of his account,
and the neighbor was consequently acquitted.
When asked, the local villagers
said that the former owner of the house had once had a young wife who had died,
whose age and appearance
matched exactly what the thief had described.
Thus, it was known that it was her ghost.
It is popularly believed that those who die violently always seek a substitute.
Is this true?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Shàoshēng of Jìnghǎi
was poor.

When his mother's first birthday (after a specific event, possibly a death or other significant milestone, or simply her first celebration in a long time, though "初度" literally means "first crossing/degree", often used for birthday) arrived,
he prepared sacrificial animals and wine and offered them in the courtyard.
After bowing and rising,
all the food on the table was gone.
Greatly alarmed,
he told his mother what had happened.
His mother suspected that he was too poor to prepare a proper birthday feast,
and thus made up this story.
Shào remained silent, unable to explain himself.
Before long,
the Education Commissioner arrived for an inspection.
Suffering from a lack of funds,
he reluctantly borrowed money and went.
On the way, he met a person
waiting by the roadside,
who invited him most earnestly.
He followed him,
and saw magnificent halls, pavilions, and towers
extending across the streets.
Upon entering,
a king sat on the main hall.
Shào prostrated himself in homage.
The king, with a serene countenance, ordered him to be seated,
and immediately bestowed a feast and drinks upon him,
then said:
"Previously, I passed by your esteemed residence,
and my servants were hungry and thirsty on the road,
and so we partook of your generous feast."
Shào was astonished and did not understand.
The king said:
"I am Wùguānwáng.
Do you not remember the day your honored mother made offerings?"
When the banquet concluded,
he produced a packet of silver,
saying:
"This is merely a small repayment for the disturbance of your pig's trotter."
Shào received it and went out.
Then, the palaces and figures
all vanished at once;
only several large trees
stood desolate by the roadside.
He looked at the gift
and found it to be real silver,
weighing five liǎng.
After the examination,
he had only spent half of it,
and still brought the rest home to present to his mother.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Shānxī Yáng Yī
was skilled in acupuncture and moxibustion;
he could also command ghosts.
As soon as he left his house,
those who led his mule and wielded the whip
were all spectral beings.
Once, returning home from elsewhere at night,
he walked with a friend.
On the way, they saw two men approaching,
tall and exceptionally grand.
His friend was greatly alarmed.
Yáng then asked:
"Who are you?"
They replied:
"Zhǎngjiǎo Wáng
and Dàtóu Lǐ,
we respectfully welcome our master."
Yáng said:
"Go ahead and clear the way for me."
The two turned on their heels and walked,
stopping to wait whenever Yáng walked slowly,
like servants.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Xìliǔniáng
was the daughter of a scholar from Zhōngdū.
Some, finding her waist slender and lovely,
playfully called her
"Xìliǔ."
Liǔ was intelligent from a young age,
understood writing,
and enjoyed reading books on physiognomy.
However, she was quiet and reserved throughout her life,
never speaking ill or well of others;
but whenever someone asked for her hand in marriage,
she would insist on personally seeing the suitor.
She met many people,
but none were suitable,
and she was already nineteen.
Her parents angrily said to her:
"Is it possible that there are no good matches in the world?
Are you going to grow old as a maiden?"
The daughter said:
"I truly wish to triumph over fate through my choice;
however, after a long time without success,
it must also be my destiny.
From now on,
I will only obey my parents' command."
At that time, there was a scholar named Gāo Shēng,
a renowned gentleman from a prominent family,
who, having heard of Xìliǔ,
offered betrothal gifts.
After the wedding,
the couple lived happily.
Gāo Shēng had an orphaned child from a previous marriage,
whose pet name was Chángfú,
then five years old.
The daughter nurtured and cared for him thoroughly.
Whenever the daughter returned to her parents' home,
Fú would cry and follow her,
and could not be stopped even by scolding.
A year later,
the daughter gave birth to a son,
named Chánghù.
Gāo Shēng asked for the meaning of the name,
to which she replied:
"Nothing else,
I just hope he will always remain at my side."
The daughter was rather unskilled in needlework
and often paid it no attention;
but when it came to the fields in the southeast,
the amount of tax,
she would consult the records and inquire,
fearing any lack of detail.
After a long time,
she said to Gāo Shēng:
"Please leave household matters to me and don't worry about them.
I will manage them myself.
I wonder if I am capable of running the household?"
Gāo Shēng did as she said.
After half a year, there were no neglected affairs in the household,
and Gāo Shēng also admired her.
One day,
Gāo Shēng went to a neighboring village to drink wine,
and just then, tax collectors seeking arrears
banged on the door and swore;
he sent a servant to appease them,
but they would not leave.
So, he quickly sent a boy to summon Gāo Shēng home.
After the officials had left,
Gāo Shēng smiled and said:
"Xìliǔ,
only now do I realize that a wise woman should not be matched with a foolish man?"
When the daughter heard this,
she bowed her head and wept.
Gāo Shēng was surprised, pulled her close, and consoled her,
but the daughter remained unhappy.
Gāo Shēng could not bear to burden her with household management
and still wished to take charge himself,
but the daughter would not agree.
From dawn to dusk,
her management became even more diligent.
Every year, a year in advance,
she would save up the taxes for the coming year,
thus, throughout the year, no tax collector ever came to their door to demand payment;
she also used this method to budget for food and clothing,
whereby expenses became even more manageable.
Thereupon, Gāo Shēng was greatly pleased,
and once playfully said to her:
"How slender Xìliǔ is: slender brows, slender waist, slender steps,
and what's more, her mind is even more slender!"
The daughter replied:
"Gāo Láng is truly lofty: lofty character,
lofty ambition,
lofty scholarship,
I only wish your lifespan be even loftier."
There was a person in the village selling fine timber,
and the daughter spared no expense to acquire it;
when the price was insufficient,
she borrowed from relatives in various ways.
Gāo Shēng, seeing it as an unurgent item,
firmly tried to stop her,
but she ultimately did not listen.
After storing it for over a year,
a wealthy family suffering a bereavement
bought it back from her for double the price.
Gāo Shēng then, seeing the profit, discussed with the daughter,
but the daughter disagreed.
When he asked her reason,
she did not speak;
when he asked again,
tears welled up in her eyes.
He found this strange,
yet could not bear to contradict her further,
so he dropped the matter.
Another year passed,
when Shēng was twenty-five years old,
Nǚ (細娘) forbade him from traveling far.
When he returned a little late,
servants and escorts
followed each other on the road.
Thereupon, his acquaintances all joked and slandered him.
One day,
Shēng went to a friend's house for drinks.
Feeling unwell, he returned.
Midway, he fell from his horse
and died.
It was then the height of summer,
and fortunately, his clothes and shrouds had all been prepared long ago.
Only then did the villagers come to admire Xìniáng's (細娘) wisdom.
Fú (福) was ten years old
when he began to learn to write.
After his father died,
he was spoiled and lazy, refusing to study,
and would often run off to play with the shepherd boys.
Reprimands did not change him;
they were followed by flogging,
but he remained as stubborn as ever.
His mother had no choice,
so she called him and instructed him, saying:
"Since you don't wish to study,
how can I force you?
But a poor family has no idle people,
so change your clothes
and work alongside the servants.
Otherwise,
I will flog you without regret!"
Thereupon, she dressed him in tattered rags
and made him herd pigs.
When he returned, he had to fetch his own pottery
and eat gruel with the servants.
After a few days,
he suffered greatly.
He knelt crying in the courtyard,
wishing to resume his studies.
His mother turned her back to the wall,
pretending not to hear.
Having no alternative,
he took the whip, sobbing, and went out.
As late autumn drew to a close,
he had no clothes on the rack,
no shoes on his feet.
Drenched by cold rain,
he huddled like a beggar.
Villagers who saw him pitied him,
and those taking a second wife
all cited Xìniáng (細娘) as a warning,
voicing many complaints.
The Nǚ (女) also heard it gradually,
but paid no attention.
Fú (福) could not endure the hardship,
abandoned the pigs, and ran away.
The Nǚ (女) also let him go,
not bothering to inquire further.
After several months,
having no place to beg for food,
he returned, emaciated.
He dared not enter directly,
but tearfully begged a neighbor old woman to inform his mother.
The Nǚ (女) said:
"If he can endure a hundred strokes,
he may come to see me.
Otherwise,
he should leave quickly again."
Upon hearing this, Fú (福)
rushed in,
crying bitterly and begging to be flogged.
His mother asked:
"Do you now know to repent?"
He said:
"I repent."
She said:
"Since you repent,
there is no need for flogging.
You can contentedly herd pigs.
If you transgress again, you will not be forgiven!"
Fú (福) cried loudly, saying:
"I wish to receive a hundred strokes,
please let me study again."
The Nǚ (女) did not agree.
Only after the neighbor old woman urged her
did she finally relent.
She washed his hair and gave him clothes,
and arranged for him to study with his younger brother Hù (怙).
He worked diligently and thought sharply,
greatly different from before,
and after three years, he passed the preliminary examination.
Censor Yáng Gōng (楊公)
saw his writing and appreciated him,
giving him a monthly allowance
to help with his lamp oil.
Hù (怙) was the dullest;
after several years of studying, he could not remember names.
His mother made him abandon his books and farm.
Hù (怙) was idle and disliked hard labor.
His mother angrily said:
"The four classes each have their principal occupation.
Since you can neither read
nor farm,
will you not die in a ditch?"
She immediately flogged him.
From then on, she made him lead the servants in farming.
If he rose late one morning,
he would be scolded and cursed.
However, for clothing and food,
his mother always gave the best to his elder brother.
Although Hù (怙) dared not speak,
he secretly felt indignant.
After the farm work was done,
his mother invested money to let him learn hawking.
He indulged in lust and gambling;
money that came into his hands was soon squandered,
and he cunningly attributed it to bandits and bad luck
to deceive his mother.
His mother found out
and flogged him nearly to death.
Fú (福) knelt long and pleaded mournfully,
offering himself as a substitute,
and only then did her anger subside.
From then on, whenever he left the house,
his mother would investigate him.
Hù's (怙) conduct became somewhat restrained,
but it was not what his heart desired.
One day,
he asked his mother
to travel to Luò (洛) with other merchants.
He actually intended to use the distant journey
to satisfy his desires,
and his heart was apprehensive,
fearing his request would not be granted.
His mother heard it
and showed no doubt or hesitation.
She immediately took out thirty taels of碎金 (suìjīn, broken gold)
to prepare his outfit.
A little later, she gave him a gold ingot,
saying:
"This is an heirloom from your grandfather's official purse;
you must not spend it.
Let it merely serve as a weight for your luggage,
to be used only in an emergency.
Moreover, as you are just beginning to travel,
I don't expect great profits.
Just avoiding losses with these thirty gold pieces will be enough."
She instructed him again before he left.
Hù (怙) agreed and left,
feeling joyful and self-satisfied.
Upon arriving in Luò (洛),
he dismissed his travel companions
and stayed at the house of the famous courtesan Lǐ Jī (李姬).
After more than ten nights,
his gold was gradually depleted.
Believing he had a large sum of gold in his pouch,
he initially did not realize that the empty compartment was a concern.
But when he took it out and listened to it,
it was fake gold.
Greatly shocked,
he turned pale.
Lǐ Āo (李媼) saw his condition
and spoke coldly to the guest.
Hù (怙) was uneasy in his heart,
but with an empty purse and nowhere to go,
he still hoped Lǐ Jī (李姬) would remember their old affection
and not immediately cut him off.
Suddenly, two men entered holding ropes
and swiftly seized him by the neck.
Terrified, he didn't know what to do.
When he mournfully asked the reason,
it turned out Lǐ Jī (李姬) had already secretly taken the fake gold and reported it to the public court.
At the official's office,
he couldn't explain the broken pieces of gold,
and was shackled and flogged nearly to death.
Imprisoned,
and without funds for bribes,
he was greatly abused by the jailers,
begging for food from other prisoners,
barely surviving.
Originally,
when Hù (怙) was leaving, his mother said to Fú (福):
“Remember, twenty days from now,
I will send you to Luòyáng.
My affairs are many,
I fear I might forget it.”
Fú did not know what was meant,
and felt a gloom approaching sorrow,
but dared not ask again and withdrew.
After twenty days, he inquired.
She sighed and said:
“Your brother’s current profligacy
is like your former negligence in studies.
If I had not risked a bad name,
how would you have what you have today?
Everyone calls me cruel,
but tears soak my pillow and mat,
and no one knows it!”
Thereupon she wept.
Fú stood respectfully attending,
not daring to question further.
When she had finished weeping,
she then said:
“Your brother’s wild heart is not dead,
so I gave him counterfeit gold to frustrate him.
By now, he should be in shackles.
The Censor-in-chief treats you generously;
you go and seek his help,
you can save him from a fatal disaster,
and make him feel shame and regret.”
Fú departed immediately.
By the time he arrived in Luòyáng,
his brother had already been arrested for three days.
When he saw him in prison,
Hù’s face was emaciated and ghost-like;
seeing his brother, tears flowed uncontrollably.
Fú also wept.
At that time, Fú was favored and esteemed by the Censor-in-chief,
so his name was known far and wide.
The magistrate, knowing he was Hù’s brother,
promptly released him.
When Hù arrived home,
still fearing his mother’s anger,
he kneeled and crawled forward.
His mother looked at him and said:
“Has your wish been fulfilled?”
Hù shed tears and dared not make a sound again.
Fú also knelt with him,
and then his mother scolded them to stand up.
From then on, he deeply regretted his actions.
Regarding all household affairs,
he managed them diligently;
even if he occasionally indulged in pleasure,
his mother would not scold or question him.
For several months,
she did not speak to him about business.
He wanted to ask on his own but dared not,
so he conveyed his intention to his brother.
His mother heard and was pleased,
and pooling resources and borrowing, she gave it to him.
Within half a year, the profit doubled.
That year,
Fú passed the provincial examination in autumn,
and three years later, passed the imperial examination;
his brother, through trade, had accumulated vast wealth.
A guest from the local county who had traveled to Luòyáng,
secretly saw Tàifūrén.
She was forty years old,
yet appeared like someone in her early thirties,
and her clothes and makeup were simple and plain,
like those of an ordinary family.
Yìshǐshì says:
“When the ‘Black-Heart Talisman’ came out,
the ‘White-Flower Incident’ occurred,
ancients and moderns are like badgers from the same mound,
truly lamentable!
Some, to avoid such slander,
often overcorrect,
to the extent of idly watching their children indulge without a single question.
How does that compare to those who are cruelly treated?
Only when one beats one’s own child daily
do people not consider it cruel;
but if applied to a stepchild,
criticism follows.
Indeed, Xìliǔ was not uniquely harsh towards her stepson;
however, if her own children had been worthy,
how could she have expressed such a heart to clear her name before the world?
Yet she did not avoid suspicion,
nor shirk criticism,
and ultimately made her two sons one rich and one noble,
distinguished in the world.
This, regardless of women’s quarters,
must also be the mark of a true man!”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Cuī Shēng of Línqīng,
his family was often poor.
The courtyard walls were not repaired.
Every morning he rose,
and invariably saw a horse lying among the dewy grass,
black with white markings;
only its tail hair was disheveled,
as if scorched off by fire.
He chased it away,
but at night it returned again,
he knew not whence it came.
Cuī had a good friend
who held office in Jìn,
and wished to go and join him,
but suffered from lack of a sturdy mount.
So he seized the horse, saddled it, and rode off,
instructing his family:
“Should anyone come looking for a horse,
they should be told to go to Jìn to inform me.”
Once on the road,
the horse galloped swiftly,
covering a hundred *lǐ* in an instant.
At night it did not eat much fodder,
he thought it was ill.
The next day he reined it in tightly
not allowing it to gallop,
but the horse neighed, snorted foam,
and was as strong and spirited as yesterday.
He let it go again,
and by noon he had reached Jìn.
When he rode into the marketplace at that time,
all who watched could not but praise it.
The Prince of Jìn heard of it
and offered a high price to buy it.
Cuī feared it would be sought by its owner,
and dared not sell it.
After living there for half a year
with no news,
he then sold it for eight hundred gold pieces at the Prince of Jìn’s residence,
and bought a strong mule to return home.
Later, the Prince, for an urgent matter,
dispatched a military escort to ride to Línqīng.
The horse bolted,
and was pursued to Cuī’s eastern neighbor,
entered the gate,
and disappeared.
They demanded it from the owner.
The owner’s surname was Zēng,
and he truly had not seen it.
Upon entering the room,
they saw a painting by Zǐ'áng of a horse hanging on the wall,
inside which was a horse whose coat color was almost identical,
and whose tail had been singed by incense,
only then did they realize the horse
was a painting-spirit.
The military escort found it difficult to report back on their mission,
so they sued Zēng.
At this time, Cuī had obtained the horse’s price,
and his accumulated wealth exceeded ten thousand.
He voluntarily offered to lend the amount to Zēng,
and sent the military escort away.
Zēng was very grateful to him,
not knowing that Cuī was the same seller from that year.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A retainer of a certain Yùshǐ,
happened to be standing in the marketplace.
A man, splendidly dressed and adorned,
approached him and struck up a conversation.
He gradually inquired about his master's surname, given name, and official rank,
and the retainer told him all.
The man introduced himself, saying:
"My surname is Wáng,
and I am a chamberlain for the family of a noble princess."
Their conversation gradually became cordial,
whereupon he said:
"The official career path is perilous.
Those who are prominent all attach themselves to the houses of powerful relatives.
To whom has your esteemed master entrusted himself?"
The retainer replied:
"To no one."
Wáng said:
"This is what is called 'being stingy with small expenses and forgetting about great calamities'."
The retainer asked:
"To whom can one entrust oneself that would be suitable?"
Wáng said:
"The Gōngzhǔ treats people with courtesy,
and is able to protect and assist others.
A certain Shìláng advanced through my recommendation.
If you are not unwilling to offer a thousand pieces of gold as a gift,
seeing the Gōngzhǔ should also not be difficult."
The retainer was pleased,
and asked about his residence.
Wáng then pointed to his own gate and said:
"Do you not know that we live in the same alley?"
The retainer returned and reported to the Shìyù.
The Shìyù was delighted,
and immediately prepared a grand feast,
sending his retainer to invite Wáng.
Wáng came gladly.
During the banquet, he spoke very intimately about the Gōngzhǔ's temperament and daily trivial matters,
and furthermore said:
"Were it not for the friendship of being in the same alley,
even if I were given a hundred pieces of gold as a reward,
I would not be willing to serve like an ox or horse."
The Yùshǐ admired him even more.
Before parting,
they made an agreement.
Wáng said:
"You merely prepare the gift,
and I will speak of it when the opportunity arises.
You should receive a reply soon, morning or evening."
Some days later, he finally arrived.
Riding a splendid horse, he looked very dignified.
He said to his attendant:
"You should quickly prepare for the journey.
The princess's affairs are extremely troublesome;
visitors come one after another,
from morning till evening,
without a single break.
Now we have found a brief interval,
so we should go quickly.
If we miss it, there will be no definite time to see her again."
The attendant then took out gold and heavy silks,
and followed him.
After winding for more than ten *lǐ*,
they finally reached the princess's residence.
They dismounted and waited respectfully.
The attendant first presented the tribute.
After a long time,
he came out,
declaring:
"The princess summons Steward Mǒu."
Immediately, several people relayed the call.
The attendant bowed and entered,
seeing a beautiful woman seated on the high dais,
her appearance like a celestial being,
her attire resplendent;
the serving maids were all dressed in brocade,
arranged in rows.
The attendant prostrated himself, observing all rites.
A command was relayed to grant him a seat beneath the eaves,
and tea was served in a golden bowl.
The princess briefly expressed a gentle message,
and the attendant reverently withdrew.
From within, a satin boot and a sable hat were bestowed upon him.
Upon returning,
he was deeply grateful to the attendant,
and went to present his calling card to express thanks,
but the gate was closed and there was no one.
He suspected the attendant had not yet returned from serving the princess.
For three days he visited three times,
but never saw him again.
He sent someone to inquire at the gate of the noble princess,
but the tall doors were locked and barred.
He asked the residents,
who all said,
"There has never been a noble princess here.
Previously, a few people rented a house to live in,
but they left three days ago."
The messenger returned with the report,
and the master and servant were simply disheartened.
Vice General Mǒu,
carrying funds, entered the capital,
intending to secure an official post,
but struggled to find a way.
One day,
a man dressed in furs and riding a horse called on him,
introducing himself:
"My maternal cousin is a close attendant to the Son of Heaven."
After tea,
he asked for a private word, saying:
"Currently, there is a general's vacancy in a certain place.
If you are not reluctant to spend a large sum,
I will ask my maternal cousin to speak highly of you before the Sacred Lord.
This position can be secured,
and even those with great power cannot take it away."
Mǒu doubted his sincerity.
The man said:
"There's no need to hesitate about this.
I merely wish to take a small commission from my maternal cousin,
and I expect nothing from the General.
Once the amount is agreed upon,
a bond will be signed as proof.
Only after you are summoned,
will I ask for actual payment;
if it doesn't work,
your money will still be with you,
who can snatch it from your pocket?"
Mǒu was then pleased,
and agreed.
The next day,
the man came again to take Mǒu with him,
to see his maternal cousin,
who, he said,
"is surnamed Tián."
His residence was as grand as a marquis's.
Mǒu paid his respects,
but Tián was very arrogant and rather impolite.
The man held the bond towards Mǒu and said:
"I just discussed it with my maternal cousin,
and less than ten thousand *jīn* will not suffice.
Please sign the bottom immediately."
Mǒu complied.
Tián said,
"People's hearts are unpredictable,
I worry about reversals after the fact."
The man smiled and said:
"Elder brother, you worry too much.
Since we can give it to him,
can we not also take it away?
Moreover, among the court's generals and ministers,
there are those who wish to associate with us but cannot.
The General's future is still long,
he shouldn't be so foolish as to lose his mind."
Mǒu also swore strongly and left.
The man saw him off,
saying:
"In three days, I will bring you good news."
Two days later,
as the sun was setting,
several people rushed in shouting,
saying:
"The Holy One is waiting!"
Mǒu was greatly startled,
and hastily rushed to court.
He saw the Son of Heaven seated in the main hall,
with his formidable guards standing around.
Mǒu had performed his bows.
The emperor ordered him a seat,
and asked about his welfare with great warmth,
then looked around and said:
"I heard that Mǒu's military prowess is extraordinary.
Now that I see him,
he truly possesses the talent of a general!"
Then he said:
"A certain strategic location,
I now entrust to you, Your Lordship.
Do not disappoint My expectations.
A marquisate will be granted soon."
Mǒu bowed in thanks and exited.
Immediately, the man in furs and on horseback from the previous day followed him to his lodging,
exchanged the money according to the bond, and left.
Thereupon, Mǒu rested easy, awaiting his sash of office,
boasting daily of his honor to relatives and friends.
After several days,
he inquired about it,
and found that the previous vacancy had already been filled by someone else.
Greatly enraged,
he furiously argued in the hall of the Ministry of War,
saying:
"I was personally appointed by the Emperor,
