how could it be given to someone else?"
The Minister of War found this strange.
When Mǒu recounted the imperial favor and reception,
it seemed half like a dream.
The Minister of War became angry,
and had him arrested and sent to the Imperial Prosecutor.
Only then did he confess the name of the person who introduced him,
but there was no such person in the court.
He then spent another ten thousand *jīn*,
and only then was he stripped of his office and released.
How strange!
Though military officers are often simple-minded,
can even the court gate be faked?
I suspect some illusionary art was involved,
which is what is meant by
"a great bandit does not wield a spear or bow."
1025Lǐ Shēng of Jiāxiáng,
was skilled in playing the *qín*.
Once, while visiting the eastern suburbs,
he saw workmen digging up an ancient *qín*,
and he acquired it for a low price.
When wiped, it emitted an unusual glow;
when strings were attached and played,
its sound was exceptionally clear and powerful.
Overjoyed,
as if he had obtained a priceless jade *bi*,
he stored it in a brocade bag,
and hid it in a secret room,
not showing it even to close relatives.
The county assistant, Chéng Shì,
who had recently arrived in office,
sent his calling card to visit Lǐ.
Lǐ usually had few associates,
but because Chéng had initiated contact,
he returned the visit.
After several days,
Chéng invited him again for a drink,
and Lǐ went only after being strongly urged.
Chéng was a man of unparalleled elegance and refinement,
with a free and easy manner in conversation,
and Lǐ was delighted.
The next day,
Lǐ sent a card to return the courtesy,
and their joyful camaraderie grew even closer.
From then on, on moonlit evenings and flower-filled mornings,
they were always together.
More than a year later,
he happened to see a *qín* wrapped in a brocade bag placed on a desk in the county assistant's office.
Lǐ then took it out to examine it.
Chéng asked:
"Do you also understand this?"
Lǐ replied:
"Throughout my life, I have loved it most."
Chéng said in surprise:
"We have been close friends for more than a day,
why have I never heard your superb skill?"
He stirred the incense burner and lit some agarwood,
then requested a short performance.
Lǐ Jìngrú taught.
Chéng said:
"A great master!
I wish to offer my humble skill,
do not laugh at this small sorcerer."
Thereupon, he played
"Yùfēng Qǔ"
(Song of Riding the Wind).
Its sound was clear and distinct,
with an intention of being peerless and transcending the mundane.
Lǐ was even more impressed,
wishing to serve him as his teacher.
From then on, the two became friends through the qín,
their affection growing deeper.
After more than a year,
Chéng had taught him all his techniques.
However, whenever Chéng visited Lǐ,
Lǐ would provide an ordinary qín for him,
unwilling to reveal his own treasured instrument.
One evening,
slightly tipsy,
Chéng said:
"I have recently learned a new piece,
would you also like to hear it?"
He then played
"Xiāng Fēi"
(Xiāng Consorts),
its melancholy like weeping.
Lǐ praised it profusely.
Chéng said:
"My only regret is not having a good qín;
if I had one,
the melody would be even more exquisite."
Lǐ happily said:
"I possess a qín
that is quite exceptional.
Now that I have met a Zhōng Qī,
how can I continue to keep it secret?"
Thereupon, he opened a box, took it out of its bag, and presented it.
Chéng dusted it with his robe sleeve,
leaned on the table, and played again.
The soft and strong notes responded to the rhythm,
the skill reaching a divine level.
Lǐ tapped his foot incessantly.
Chéng said:
"My humble skill
does not do this fine qín justice.
If my wife were to play it once,
there would surely be a note or two worth hearing."
Lǐ exclaimed in surprise:
"Does your wife also excel at it?"
Chéng smiled and said:
"This very piece was taught to me by my humble wife."
Lǐ said:
"It's a pity she is in the inner chambers,
this young man cannot hear it."
Chéng said:
"We are good friends,
and should not be constrained by formalities.
Tomorrow,
please bring your qín,
and I will have her play it for you from behind the curtain."
Lǐ was delighted.
The next day,
he carried the qín and went.
Chéng immediately prepared a feast and they drank joyfully.
A short while later,
he took the qín inside,
then came out and sat down.
Soon, a beautifully dressed figure could be faintly seen behind the curtain,
and after a moment,
fragrance wafted outside the door.
After another short while,
the sound of strings began softly.
Listening to it,
he did not know what piece it was;
but only felt it stirred his heart and charmed his bones,
making his soul soar.
When the music ended, he immediately peeked behind the curtain,
and it was indeed more than twenty peerlessly beautiful women.
Chéng urged him to drink a large cup to the dregs,
and inside, the strings were changed to play
"Xiánqíng zhī Fù"
(Rhapsody of Leisurely Sentiments).
Lǐ's mind and spirit became even more bewildered.
Having drunk excessively and become very drunk,
he rose from his seat to take his leave,
and asked for his qín.
Chéng said:
"After drinking, you might stumble.
Come again tomorrow,
and I will have my wife demonstrate her full skill."
Lǐ returned home.
The next day, he went to visit him,
but the residence was silent,
with only an old servant answering the door.
When asked,
he said:
"They left with their family before dawn,
I don't know what they are doing,
but they said they would be back in about three days."
He waited as scheduled,
but by dusk,
there was no news.
The servants were all suspicious,
reported it to the magistrate,
who broke open the door to peek into the room;
the room was completely empty,
only the table and bed remained.
This was reported to the superior authorities,
but no one could figure out why.
Lǐ, having lost his qín,
neglected his eating and sleeping,
and traveled thousands of lǐ to inquire about Chéng's family.
Chéng was originally from Chǔ.
Three years ago,
he donated money to be appointed as magistrate of Jiāxiáng.
When his name was held,
and his residence inquired about,
there was no such person in Chǔ.
Someone said:
"There was a Daoist named Chéng Dàoshì
who was skilled at playing the qín;
it was also rumored that he had the art of turning stone into gold.
Three years ago,
he suddenly left and was never seen again."
They suspected it was the same person.
Upon closer examination of his age
and appearance,
they matched perfectly.
Thus, it was known that the Daoist's official appointment
was all for the qín.
They had been friends for over a year,
and he never mentioned music;
then he gradually brought out the qín,
gradually displayed his skill,
and then gradually seduced with beautiful women;
after immersing himself for three years,
he obtained the qín and left.
The Daoist's obsession
was even greater than that of scholar Lǐ.
There are many kinds of deceptions in the world,
but a Daoist like him
is among the most refined of swindlers.
Based on a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuě Zhāi of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì".
When Wáng Jìnshì Dǒushēng of Chángshān was a magistrate,
whenever he heard a lawsuit,
he would, according to the severity of the crime,
order the payment of butterflies as redemption;
hundreds and thousands would be released in the hall,
like scattered brocade fluttering in the wind,
and Wáng would slap the table and laugh heartily.
One night,
he dreamed of a woman,
beautifully dressed,
who entered calmly,
and said:
"Because of your harsh rule,
many of my sisters have perished.
You should first suffer a minor romantic punishment."
Having spoken,
she transformed into a butterfly
and flew away, circling.
The next day,
as he was drinking alone in his office,
he was suddenly informed that the imperial inspector had arrived.
He rushed out in a panic,
having playfully adorned his cap with white flowers in his private chambers,
which he forgot to remove.
The imperial inspector saw it,
considered it disrespectful,
and he was severely reprimanded before returning.
From then on, the order to punish with butterflies ceased.
Based on a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuě Zhāi of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì".
Yáng Fǔ, the Commander-in-Chief of Fújiàn,
had a catamite
whose belly began to vibrate.
When ten months were complete,
he dreamed that a divine being cut open his two flanks and took them out.
Upon waking,
two boys were crying, one on each side.
He got up and looked at his flanks,
and the incision marks were clearly visible.
He named the children Tiānshě and Dìshě.
Based on a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuě Zhāi of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì".
Zhōng Qìngyú
was a renowned scholar from Liáodōng.
He went to Jǐnán to take the provincial examination.
He heard that there was a Daoist at the princely estate who could predict people's fortunes and misfortunes,
and his heart yearned to meet him.
After the second session of the examination,
he went to Báotū Quán
and happened to encounter him.
The Daoist was over sixty years old,
with a beard long enough to pass his chest,
a venerable Daoist indeed.
Those who gathered to ask about calamities and signs were as numerous as a wall,
and the Daoist imparted subtle words to all of them.
Amidst the crowd, he saw Zhōng,
happily took his hand,
and said:
"Your character and virtue
are admirable!"
He invited Zhōng to ascend the pavilion,
dismissed others,
and then asked:
"Do you wish to know your future destiny?"
Zhōng replied:
"Yes."
The Daoist said:
"Your fate is extremely thin,
yet you can hope for success in this year's provincial examination.
But after your glorious return,
I fear you may not see your esteemed mother again."
Zhōng, being extremely filial,
wept upon hearing this,
and intended to forgo the examination and return home.
The Daoist said:
"If you pass this point,
even a single success will be unattainable."
Zhōng said:
"If my mother dies and I do not see her,
and moreover, I cannot be a human again,
what good is it to be a high official or prime minister?"
The Daoist said:
"I have had a predestined affinity with you in a previous life,
and today I must exert my full effort."
He then gave Zhōng a pill and said:
"You can send someone to take it day and night;
taking it can prolong life by seven days.
Depart after the examination is finished,
and mother and son can still meet."
Zhōng hid it,
rushed out hastily,
his mind in a daze.
He calculated that since there was a limit to his mother's life,
returning one day earlier
would mean one more day of care.
He took his servant and rented a donkey,
immediately heading east.
After riding for about a *lǐ*,
the donkey suddenly turned back and ran.
When he dismounted, it was unruly;
when he tried to control it, it stumbled.
Zhōng was at a loss,
sweating profusely like rain.
His servant urged him to stop,
but Zhōng did not listen.
He rented another donkey,
and it behaved similarly.
The sun had already touched the mountains,
and he knew not what to do.
His servant again advised:
"The examination will be over tomorrow;
why dispute this one morning or evening?
Please go on ahead, master;
it is a good plan."
Having no choice,
Zhōng agreed.
The next day,
he hastily finished the examination,
departed immediately,
without even taking a breath,
and sped home.
His mother was critically ill,
but after taking the red pill,
she gradually recovered.
Zhōng went to see her
and wept by her bed.
His mother shook her head to stop him,
held his hand, and joyfully said:
"I just dreamt that I was in the underworld,
and saw the King with a benevolent expression.
He said that after examining your life,
you have committed no great sins;
now, considering your son's pure filial piety,
he grants you a lifespan of one *jì* (twelve years)."
Zhōng was also delighted.
After several days,
she was indeed healthy as before.
Not long after,
he heard of his success in the examination,
and bidding his mother farewell, he went to Jǐnán.
He then bribed a eunuch
to convey his regards to the Daoist.
The Daoist happily came out,
and Zhōng immediately prostrated himself.
The Daoist said:
"Since you have achieved high success,
and your esteemed mother has also gained a longer lifespan,
all this is due to your great virtue;
what power did this Daoist have in it!"
Zhōng was again surprised by his foresight,
and thus bowed to ask about his entire life.
The Daoist said:
"You will not attain great nobility,
but it is enough to live to a ripe old age.
In your previous life, you and I were monks,
and you threw a stone at a dog,
accidentally killing a frog,
which has now been reborn as a donkey.
According to your predetermined fate,
you were to suffer a violent death;
but now your filial virtue has moved the spirits,
and a star of resolution has entered your destiny,
so you will surely be unharmed.
However, your wife was unchaste in her previous life,
and her fate dictates that she should be widowed early.
Since your virtue has prolonged your life,
she is not a suitable partner for you.
I fear that after a year, your 'Jade Terrace' will fall."
Zhōng felt sorrowful for a long time,
and asked where his future wife was.
The Daoist said:
"She is in Zhōngzhōu,
and is now fourteen years old."
Before parting, he cautioned:
"If you encounter danger,
you should flee to the southeast."
Over a year later,
his wife indeed fell ill and died.
Zhōng's maternal uncle was the magistrate of Xījiāng,
and his mother sent him to visit,
so he could pass through Zhōngzhōu on the way,
thus fulfilling the prophecy about his next wife.
He happened upon a village
where performers were acting by the river,
with many men and women gathered.
Just as he was about to adjust his reins and ride past,
an unbridled male donkey
followed him,
causing his mule to stumble.
Zhōng turned his head
and struck the donkey's ear with his whip;
the donkey was startled
and ran wildly.
At that time, Prince Wáng's son, who was six or seven years old,
was being held by his wet nurse and sitting on the embankment;
the donkey charged past,
and none of the retinue could react in time,
pushing the child into the river.
Everyone cried out loudly,
wanting to seize Zhōng.
Zhōng spurred his mule to gallop away,
suddenly remembering the Daoist's words,
and strenuously fled southeast.
After about thirty *lǐ*,
he entered a mountain village.
There was an old man at the gate,
so Zhōng dismounted and bowed to him.
The old man invited him in,
and said
his surname was Fāng.
He then asked where Zhōng came from.
Zhōng prostrated himself on the ground
and recounted the entire situation.
The old man said:
"No matter.
Please stay here for now;
I will make the pursuers leave."
That evening, he received news
and only then learned that it was the Prince's son.
The old man was greatly alarmed and said:
"I can help with other families,
but this is truly a situation where I wish to help but cannot!"
Zhōng pleaded ceaselessly.
The old man pondered and said:
"It cannot be done.
Please stay one more night;
let's see how urgent the situation is,
and then perhaps we can reconsider."
Zhōng was distraught with fear
and did not sleep all night.
The next day, he listened for news,
and learned that official documents had already been issued to investigate,
and anyone harboring him would be executed in the market.
The old man had a troubled expression,
and entered without speaking.
Zhōng was suspicious and afraid,
unable to compose himself.
In the middle of the night, the old man came,
sat down, and immediately asked:
"How old is your wife?"
Shēng replied that he was a widower.
The old man joyfully said:
"My plan has succeeded!"
When asked,
he replied:
"My elder sister's husband, Mùdào,
has hung up his staff on Nánshān;
my sister has also passed away.
She left behind an orphaned daughter,
who has been raised by servants,
and she is quite intelligent.
How about presenting her to serve you?"
Shēng was delighted that it matched the words of the Dàoshi,
and also hoped that having relatives nearby
would allow him to get their full assistance.
He said:
"This humble one is truly fortunate.
However, being a criminal from a distant land,
I deeply fear causing trouble for you, venerable sir."
The old man said:
"This is a plan for your sake.
My sister's husband's Dàoshù is quite divine,
but he has long been detached from worldly affairs.
After the wedding,
you can discuss it with your niece yourselves,
and there will surely be a solution."
Shēng was overjoyed,
and became the son-in-law.
The daughter was sixteen years old,
and her beauty was unparalleled.
Shēng often sighed when he faced her.
The girl said:
"If I am plain,
why do you so suddenly show aversion?"
Shēng apologized and said:
"My lady is like an immortal; it is my good fortune to be paired with you.
However, there is a calamity,
and I fear it will lead to separation."
He then told her the truth.
The girl resentfully said:
"My maternal uncle is truly inhumane!
This is a calamity reaching to the heavens,
for which no plan can be made,
yet he did not speak clearly,
but instead trapped me in this pit!"
Shēng knelt down for a long time and said:
"It is this humble one who desperately begged my maternal uncle,
and my maternal uncle, out of compassion, was at his wit's end concerning the method,
knowing that you can bring the dead back to life and put flesh on white bones.
I am truly not worthy to be called a good match,
but my family would fortunately not be disgraced or forgotten.
If I can be reborn,
there will surely be a day for fragrant offerings."
The girl sighed and said:
"Things have come to this;
what more can be said?
However, my father has cut off his hair and entered the monastery,
so his affection for his children has already ceased.
If there is no other way,
let us go together to plead with him;
I fear we will incur no small burden of humiliation."
So, they did not sleep all night,
making thick knee pads from felt and cotton,
each concealing them under their clothes;
then they called a palanquin
and entered Nánshān for over ten Lǐ.
The mountain path was winding and extremely perilous,
so they could no longer ride.
They got out of the palanquin,
and the girl found each step very difficult.
Shēng held her arm and supported her,
and only with great effort did they manage to ascend.
Not far,
they saw the mountain gate,
and sat down to rest for a while.
The girl was panting heavily and profusely sweating,
and her makeup was running down.
When Shēng saw this,
he could not bear it,
and said:
"For my sake,
I have made you suffer this hardship!"
The girl calmly said:
"I fear this is not yet hardship!"
When their fatigue somewhat subsided,
they went together into the Lánruò,
bowed to the Buddha and proceeded.
Turning and winding, they entered the meditation hall,
and saw an old monk sitting cross-legged,
his eyes seemingly closed,
with a young attendant holding a whisk serving him.
In the abbot's room,
it was swept clean and bright;
but in front of where he sat, sand and gravel were spread everywhere,
as dense as stars.
The girl did not dare to choose,
and knelt on it;
Shēng also followed behind her.
The monk opened his eyes, glanced once,
and then closed them again.
The girl bowed and said:
"It has been a long time since I paid my respects.
Now your daughter is married,
so I have come with my husband."
After a long time,
the monk opened his eyes and looked, saying:
"Little girl, you are a great burden!"
Then he said nothing more.
The couple knelt for a long time,
their muscles and strength completely exhausted,
the sand and stones pressing into their bones,
the pain unbearable.
After another period,
he finally said:
"Have you brought the mule yet?"
The girl replied:
"No."
He said:
"The couple may leave now,
but quickly bring it here."
The two bowed and rose,
and left in disarray.
Upon returning,
they followed the command,
not understanding its meaning,
but merely submitting to it.
A few days later,
it was reported that the criminal had been apprehended
and executed.
The couple celebrated.
Soon after,
the mountain dispatched an attendant,
who delivered a broken staff to Shēng, saying:
"The one who died in his place
is this gentleman."
He then instructed them to bury and offer sacrifices to it,
to resolve the injustice to the bamboo and wood.
Shēng examined it,
and there was a bloodstain on the broken end.
So, he offered prayers and buried it.
The couple dared not stay long,
and traveled back to Liáoyáng overnight.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Niè Péngyún
of Tài'ān, and his wife,
were deeply harmonious.
His wife fell ill and died.
Niè was overcome with grief,
feeling disoriented and lost.
One evening, as he sat alone,
his wife suddenly pushed open the door and entered.
Niè, startled, asked:
"Where do you come from?"
She smiled and said:
"I am already a ghost.
Moved by your sorrowful remembrance,
I appealed to the lord of the underworld,
to be granted a brief ghostly rendezvous."
Niè was delighted,
and took her to bed;
everything was as usual.
From then on, they met occasionally,
for over a year.
Niè no longer spoke of remarrying.
His uncles and brothers feared the extinction of their lineage,
and privately consulted with the clan,
urging Niè to take another wife.
Niè agreed,
and became engaged to a respectable family.
However, fearing his wife's displeasure,
he kept it a secret.
Before long,
the wedding day approached.
The ghost knew his intentions,
and reproached him, saying:
"I, because of your righteousness,
risked the condemnation of the underworld;
but now you break your vow before its completion.
Is this how a devoted lover acts?"
Niè explained the intentions of his clan members.
The ghost remained displeased,
bid farewell, and departed.
Although Niè pitied her,
he considered it a practical decision.
On the evening of the wedding,
when the couple was asleep,
the ghost suddenly arrived,
and struck the new bride in bed,
cursing loudly:
"How dare you occupy my bed!"
The new bride rose,
and began to resist her.
Niè squatted nervously,
not daring to take sides.
After a while,
the rooster crowed,
and the ghost departed.
The new bride suspected that Niè's former wife had not died,
believing she had been tricked,
and grabbed a rope, intending to hang herself.
Niè then recounted the story,
and the new bride finally understood it was a ghost.
She returned every evening.
The new bride, afraid, avoided her.
The ghost also no longer slept with Niè,
but merely pinched his skin and flesh with her fingers;
then, she would sit opposite him, staring angrily at him by candlelight,
silently.
This continued for several nights.
Niè was distressed by it.
There was a skilled sorcerer in a nearby village,
who carved stakes from peach wood,
and drove them into the four corners of the tomb;
only then did the haunting cease.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Huáng Jìngnán, when he was of humble status,
traveled to the capital with two Xiàolián,
and encountered bandits on the way.
The Xiàolián were afraid,
and knelt down to offer their valuables.
Huáng was furious,
having no weapon at hand,
he immediately gripped the mule's legs with both hands,
lifted it, and threw it.
The bandits were caught off guard;
horses fell, and men tumbled.
Huáng punched them until their arms broke,
plundered them, and returned.
The Xiàolián admired his bravery,
and used their funds to persuade him to join the army.
Later, he repeatedly achieved extraordinary feats,
and thus earned the title of a high-ranking official.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain Zhōngtáng,
who was a former Ming dynasty chancellor.
He had surrendered to the rebel leader,
and public opinion condemned him.
In his old age, he retired to the countryside.
After his ancestral hall was completed,
several people slept there overnight.
At dawn,
they saw a plaque in the hall that read:
"Elder Statesman of Three Dynasties."
And a couplet that read:
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven;
Filial piety, brotherhood, loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity."
They did not know when it had been hung.
They found it strange,
and did not understand its meaning.
Someone speculated, saying:
"The first line implies the missing 'eight' (八, bā),
and the second implies 'shamelessness' (無恥, wúchǐ)."
Hóng Jīnglüè went on a southern expedition,
and returned victoriously.
Upon reaching Jīnlíng,
he performed a ritual for the fallen generals and soldiers.
An old former student came to visit him.
After bowing,
he presented a piece of writing.
Hóng had long been weary of literary matters,
and declined, citing his failing sight.
The man said:
"Just trouble yourself to listen,
and allow me to recite it to reach your esteemed ears."
Thereupon, he pulled a document from his sleeve,
and read aloud with a clear voice;
it was none other than the late Míng Emperor Sīzōng's imperial memorial for Hóng Liáoyáng, who died in the line of duty.
After reading,
he wept bitterly and departed.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì, with additions from the Shāndōng Shěng Bówùguǎn manuscript.
Mr. Zhāng,
a poor man from Yí.
On his way, he met a Taoist priest
skilled in physiognomy,
who examined him and said:
"You will become rich through your craft."
Zhāng asked:
"Which path should I follow?"
The priest looked at him again,
and said:
"Medicine would be suitable."
Zhāng replied:
"I only know 'zhī' (之) and 'wú' (無)
(a few basic characters),
how can I do that?"
The Taoist laughed and said:
"How naive!
Why must a famous doctor know many characters?
Just go and do it."
After returning home,
he was poor and jobless,
so he collected folk remedies,
and set up a stall on the ground in the marketplace,
displaying fish teeth and honeycomb,
seeking a small profit through persuasion,
but people didn't find him remarkable.
It happened that the Prefect of Qīngzhōu suffered from a cough,
and sent dispatches to his subordinates to summon doctors.
Yí was indeed a remote mountainous area,
with few medical practitioners;
and the magistrate, fearing he would not be able to fulfill his responsibility,
again ordered the villagers to nominate someone themselves.
Thereupon, they all nominated Zhāng.
The magistrate immediately summoned him.
Zhāng himself was suffering from phlegm and asthma,
and could not even cure himself.
Upon hearing the order, he was terrified,
and firmly refused.
The magistrate did not listen,
and eventually sent him by post.
On the way through deep mountains,
he became extremely thirsty,
and his cough worsened.
He looked for water,
but water in the mountains was as precious as jade liquid;
he begged everywhere,
but no one would give him any.
He saw a woman rinsing wild vegetables;
there were many vegetables and little water,
and the liquid in her pot was thick and turbid like saliva.
Zhāng, desperate and unable to bear it,
begged for the remaining sediment to drink.
Shortly after,
his thirst was quenched,
and his cough also stopped suddenly;
he secretly thought: this must be a good remedy.
When [Zhāng] arrived at the commandery,
the physicians and artisans of various towns
had already begun administering treatment,
but without any cure or relief.
Zhāng entered,
sought out a secret place,
and pretended to issue a list of medicines,
circulating it both inside and outside [the residence].
Then he sent people to collect various weeds and wild plants from among the common folk,
which were processed according to the method.
He then presented the juice to the Grand Protector.
After one dose,
the illness was largely cured.
The Grand Protector was greatly pleased,
bestowed generous gifts,
and honored him with a golden plaque.
From this, his fame greatly spread,
his gate was constantly like a market,
and everyone he treated was unfailingly effective.
There was a person suffering from a cold-induced disease,
who described his symptoms and requested a prescription.
Zhāng, being drunk at the time,
mistakenly gave him a malaria medicine.
When he sobered up and realized his mistake,
he dared not tell anyone.
Three days later,
a person arrived at his gate with a lavish ceremony to express gratitude.
When asked,
it turned out to be the person with the cold-induced disease,
who had recovered after severe vomiting and purging.
There were many such cases.
Due to this, Zhāng was called a "commoner millionaire,"
and he increasingly valued his own reputation and worth,
so that those who sought his services would only come with ample funds and a comfortable carriage.
Old man Hán from Yìdū,
was a renowned physician.
When he was not yet famous,
he peddled medicine in all directions.
One evening, having nowhere to stay,
he sought lodging at a certain family's home.
It happened that their son was gravely ill with a cold-induced disease and near death.
Consequently, they requested him to administer treatment.
Hán thought that if he didn't treat, he would have nowhere else to go,
but to treat him, he truly had no skill.
He paced back and forth,
rubbing his body with his hands,
and the sweaty grime formed into flakes,
which he could roll into pellets.
He suddenly thought of using this to deceive them,
believing it would cause no harm.
If the boy wasn't cured by dawn,
at least he would have earned a comfortable night's rest and food.
So, he gave it to the boy.
In the middle of the night,
the master of the house pounded on the door very urgently.
Thinking that his son had died,
and fearing that he would be disgraced or abused,
Hán woke up in a fright,
climbed over the wall and swiftly fled.
The master of the house chased him for several li,
and Hán had nowhere to escape,
so he finally stopped.
Only then did he learn that the patient had sweated profusely and recovered.
He was pulled back,
and generously feasted;
upon his departure,
he was given rich gifts.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, Shāndōng Shěng Bówùguǎn edition.
A certain villager,
happened to be sitting under a tree,
and found a louse.
He wrapped it in a small piece of paper,
stuffed it into a tree hollow, and left.
Two or three years later,
he passed by the same spot again,
suddenly remembered it,
and saw the paper-wrapped object still intact in the hollow.
He opened it to examine it,
and the louse was as thin as bran.
He placed it in his palm to scrutinize it.
After a short while,
his palm began to itch strangely,
and the louse's abdomen had gradually become full.
He put it down and returned home.
A hard lump rose at the itching spot,
which swelled and was painful for several days,
and then he died.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, Shāndōng Shěng Bówùguǎn edition.
Old Man Bái,
was a native of Zhílì.
His eldest son, Jiǎ,
had gone to serve as an official in the southern regions,
and for two years there had been no news.
Just then, a relative named Dīng came to visit,
and the old man entertained him.
Dīng was known to be able to travel to the underworld.
During their conversation,
the old man frequently asked about matters of the underworld,
and Dīng's replies were somewhat fantastical;
the old man didn't fully believe him,
but merely smiled faintly.
A few days after Dīng left,
as the old man was lying down,
he saw Dīng arrive again,
inviting him to travel together.
He followed him,
and they entered a city gate.
After a while,
Dīng pointed to a gate and said:
"This is your nephew's place."
At that time, the old man had a sister's son who was a magistrate in Jìn,
so he exclaimed in surprise:
"How could he be here?"
Dīng said:
"If you don't believe it,
enter and you will know."
The old man entered,
and indeed saw his nephew,
wearing a cicada-crown and badger-embroidered robes, sitting in the hall,
with rows of colorful banners,
and no one could approach him.
Dīng pulled him out and said:
"Young Master [Jiǎ]'s official residence is not far from here;
would you also like to see him?"
The old man assented.
After a short while,
they arrived at a mansion,
and Dīng said:
"Enter."
Peering through the gate,
he saw a giant wolf blocking the path,
and was greatly frightened,
not daring to advance.
Dīng again said:
"Enter."
Again, they entered another gate,
and saw that in the hall and below the hall,
those sitting and those lying down
were all wolves.
Looking again at the courtyard,
there were mountains of white bones,
which frightened him even more.
Dīng then shielded the old man with his body as they advanced.
Young Master Jiǎ
was just coming out from inside,
and was very happy to see his father and Dīng.
After sitting for a while,
he called a servant to prepare dishes of vegetables.
Suddenly, a giant wolf
carried a dead person in its mouth.
The old man trembled and rose,
saying:
"What is this for?"
Jiǎ said:
"Just to fill the kitchen."
The old man quickly stopped him.
His heart was restless and uneasy,
and he wanted to leave,
but the pack of wolves blocked the way.
As he was undecided whether to advance or retreat,
he suddenly saw the wolves howling and scattering,
some scurrying under the bed,
others lying low beneath the table.
He was astonished and didn't understand the reason.
Presently, two fierce golden-armored warriors with glaring eyes entered,
and produced a black rope to tie up Jiǎ.
Jiǎ fell to the ground and transformed into a tiger,
with jagged teeth.
One person drew a sharp sword,
intending to decapitate him.
The other person said:
"Not yet,
not yet,
this matter is for April of next year;
it is better to just knock out his teeth for now."
Then they took out a large hammer and hammered his teeth,
which fell out and dropped to the ground.
The tiger roared loudly,
its sound shaking the mountains and valleys.
The old man was greatly frightened,
and suddenly awoke,
realizing it was a dream.
He found it extraordinary,
and sent someone to summon Dīng,
but Dīng declined to come.
Wēng Zhì remembered his dream,
and sent his second son to visit Jiǎ,
enclosing a letter to warn him strictly.
When he arrived,
he saw that his elder brother's front teeth were all missing: startled, he asked about it,
and learned that they had been broken when he fell from his horse while drunk.
When he checked the time,
it was the day of his father's dream.
He was even more surprised.
He brought out his father's 1051 letter.
Jiǎ read it and his expression changed,
then he said,
"This is just a coincidence with a fantastic dream,
what's so strange about it?"
At that time, he was bribing those in power,
and had obtained a top recommendation,
so he did not take the ominous dream to heart.
His younger brother stayed for several days,
and saw his house filled with corrupt clerks and servants,
and those who offered bribes and sought favors came unceasingly even in the middle of the night.
He tearfully advised him to stop.
Jiǎ said,
"Brother, you live in a humble dwelling every day,
so you don't understand the intricacies of officialdom.
The power to promote and demote
lies with the superiors, not with the common people.
If the superiors are pleased,
then one is a good official;
if one loves the common people,
what method can make the superiors pleased?"
The younger brother knew he could not persuade him to stop, so he returned
and told his father.
Wēng wept bitterly when he heard this.
Unable to do anything,
he could only donate his family's wealth to help the poor,
and prayed to the gods daily,
only asking that the retribution for his wayward son
not implicate his wife and children.
The following year,
Jiǎ was reported to have been recommended to serve in the Ministry of Personnel,
and congratulators filled his gate;
Wēng merely sighed,
lay on his pillow feigning illness and did not go out.
Before long,
he heard that his son had encountered bandits on his way home,
and both master and servant had lost their lives.
Wēng then rose
and said to people,
"The wrath of ghosts and gods
only reached his person;
that they protected my family cannot be said to be not generous."
So he burned incense and offered thanks.
Those who consoled Wēng
all thought it was a false rumor on the road,
but Wēng deeply believed it without doubt,
and set a date to prepare a burial site for him.
But Jiǎ had not actually died.
Earlier,
in April,
Jiǎ was relieved of his post,
and as soon as he left the district,
he immediately encountered bandits.
Jiǎ offered all his belongings to them.
The bandits said,
"We came
to vent the grievances of the people of this district,
not just for this!"
Then they cut off his head.
They also asked his family,
"Who is the chief clerk, Dàchéng?"
The clerk was originally Jiǎ's confidant,
and one who helped him commit atrocities.
The family all pointed him out.
The bandits also killed him.
There were also four corrupt servants,
who were Jiǎ's agents for extortion,
and he was planning to take them to the capital.
— After searching and beheading all of them,
they then divided the money into their bags
and rode away swiftly.
Jiǎ's spirit lay by the roadside,
and saw an official pass by,
who asked,
"Who killed them?"
The vanguard said,
"It is the Magistrate Bái of such-and-such a county."
The official said,
"This is Bái Mǒu's son;
it is not right to let the old man see this cruel tragedy after his time,
his head should be reattached."
Immediately, a person picked up the head and placed it on the torso,
saying,
"A wicked person should not be made upright;
placing his jaw on his shoulder will do."
Then they left.
After a while, he revived.
His wife and children went to retrieve his body,
saw that he still had some breath,
and carried him away;
they slowly poured water for him,
and he was able to drink.
But they stayed at an inn,
too poor to return home.
After about half a year,
Wēng finally received definite news,
and sent his second son to bring him home.
Although Jiǎ was revived,
his eyes could see his own back,
and he no longer counted among normal people.
Wēng's sister's son had a good reputation in government,
and that year he was selected to be a Censor,
all of which matched the dream.
Yìshǐ Shǐ said:
"I secretly lament that officials who are tigers and clerks who are wolves
are everywhere in the world.
Even if the official is not a tiger,
the clerk will become a wolf,
let alone those who are more ferocious than tigers!
People suffer because they cannot see behind themselves;
to revive him and make him see behind himself,
how subtle is the teaching of ghosts and gods!"
Lǐ Jìnshì Kuāngjiǔ of Zōupíng,
was quite honest and clear-headed in office.
There was often a rich commoner who was framed by others,
and a clerk intimidated him, saying,
"The official wants two hundred gold from you,
you should prepare it quickly;
otherwise,
you'll be ruined!"
The rich commoner was afraid,
and agreed to prepare half the amount.
The clerk waved his hand, refusing.
The rich commoner pleaded bitterly,
and the clerk said,
"I will do my utmost,
but I'm afraid he won't agree.
Wait until the hearing,
you will personally see me plead for you,
whether he agrees or not
will also make my sincerity clear."
A short while later,
the lord presided over this matter.
The clerk knew that Lǐ abstained from tobacco,
and approached him to ask,
"Do you smoke?"
Lǐ shook his head.
The clerk immediately went down and said,
"I just mentioned the amount,
the official shook his head, not allowing it,
did you see that?"
The rich commoner believed him,
was frightened,
and promised the full amount.
The clerk knew that Lǐ loved tea,
and approached him to ask,
"Do you drink tea?"
Lǐ nodded.
The clerk pretended to brew tea,
went down and said,
"It's done!
He just nodded,
did you see that?"
Afterwards, the case was concluded,
and the rich commoner was indeed acquitted.
The clerk immediately collected his bribes,
and also demanded a thank-you fee.
Alas!
The official considered himself honest,
yet accusations of his greed were heard on the roads,
this is again one who indulged wolves without realizing it.
There are many more such cases in the world,
and they can serve as a mirror for those in official positions.
Moreover, the magistrate of the district, Yáng Gōng,
had a stiff and unyielding nature.
Whoever incurred his wrath was sure to die.
He especially loathed the yamen runners and servants,
never forgiving even minor offenses.
Whenever he sat sternly in the hall,
the clerks and their ilk
dared not even cough.
If these subordinates occasionally reported something,
he would invariably turn it against them.
It so happened that a district resident committed a grave crime,
fearing death.
A yamen runner demanded a heavy bribe
to intercede for him.
The resident did not believe him,
and moreover said,
"If you can do it,
why should I begrudge the reward?"
So they made a sworn agreement.
Shortly after,
the Duke interrogated the case.
The resident refused to confess.
The yamen runner, at his side, chided him, saying,
"If you don't quickly confess the truth,
His Honor will shackle and bind you to death!"
The Duke angrily said,
"How do you know I will necessarily shackle and bind him?
I suppose your bribe has not arrived yet."
Thereupon, he punished the yamen runner
and released the resident.
The resident then rewarded the yamen runner with a hundred pieces of gold.
It must be understood that the deceptions of wolves are manifold;
a slight lapse in vigilance
and one will be taken advantage of.
It is not merely about them baring their fangs and claws to devour people in the countryside.
Such individuals ruin our hidden virtues,
and can even lead to the loss of our family and lives.
I wonder what is in the hearts of those in official positions,
that they insist on feeding innocents to the barbarians!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
A merchant was sailing in the Southern Sea.
At the third watch,
the boat became as bright as dawn.
He rose to look
and saw a gigantic creature,
half of its body out of the water,
appearing like a mountain;
its eyes were like two rising suns,
radiating light in all directions,
illuminating the entire earth.
Terrified, he asked the boatmen,
but none knew what it was.
Together they prostrated themselves and gazed at it.
After a while,
it gradually shrank back into the water,
and darkness returned.
Later, upon reaching Mǐnzhōng,
everyone spoke of how a certain night became bright and then dark again,
which was widely regarded as an anomaly.
Calculating the time,
it was indeed the night they saw the strange creature on the boat.
According to the twenty-four-volume manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
On the sixth day of the seventh month of the Dīnghài year,
there was a heavy snowfall in Sūzhōu.
The common people were terrified
and collectively prayed at the temple of the Great King.
The Great King suddenly possessed someone and spoke, saying,
"Nowadays, those called 'Lǎoyé'
all have a 'dà' (great) character added;
do you think my deity is too minor
to warrant a 'dà' character?"
The crowd was startled
and unanimously shouted
"Dà Lǎoyé!"
The snow immediately stopped.
From this perspective,
even spirits enjoy flattery.
No wonder those who govern subordinates get so many carriages!
Yìshǐshǐ commented:
"As the ways of the world change,
the lower ranks become more obsequious,
and the upper ranks become more arrogant.
Even within the forty-odd years of Kāngxī's reign,
the changes in address
are truly laughable.
Calling a jǔrén 'yé'
began only twenty years ago;
calling a jìnshì 'lǎoyé'
began only thirty years ago;
calling a sī or yuàn 'dà lǎoyé'
began only twenty-five years ago.
In the past, when a district magistrate called on a provincial governor,
it was merely 'lǎo dàrén' and nothing more;
nowadays, this address has long been abandoned.
Even if there are gentlemen,
they too have become accustomed to flattery and practice sycophancy,
none daring to voice a different opinion.
As for wives of gentry calling themselves 'tàitài,'
that has only been for a few years.
In the past, only the mothers of gentry
had this title;
for a wife to receive this title,
only Jiáo Lín in the history of licentiousness did,
I have not seen it elsewhere.
In the Táng dynasty,
the emperor wanted to appoint Zhāng Yuè as a Grand Academician (Dà Xuéshì).
Zhāng Yuè declined, saying, 'Academicians have never had the 'dà' title,
your minister dares not accept it.'
As for today's 'dà,'
who made it great?
Initially it was due to the flattery of petty men,
and thereby gained the favor of the arrogant nobles,
who accepted it without doubt,
and thus it spread throughout the world.
I secretly speculate that after a few more years,
those called 'yé' will certainly advance to 'lǎo,'
and those called 'lǎoyé' will certainly advance to 'dà.'
But I wonder what honorific will be invented beyond 'dà'?
It is beyond imagination!"
On the third day of the sixth month of the Dīnghài year,
there was over a foot of heavy snow in Guīdé Fǔ, Hénán,
and all the crops froze to death.
Alas, they did not know the art of flattering the Great King!
What a tragedy!
According to the twenty-four-volume manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
In the town of Mùdú, Sūzhōu,
a common girl was sitting in her courtyard at night,
when suddenly a star fell and struck her head,
and she collapsed to the ground and died.
Her parents were old and childless,
with only this daughter,
and cried out for urgent help.
After a while, she revived
and laughed, saying,
"I am now a man!"
Upon examination,
it was indeed true.
Her family did not consider it a monstrosity,
but secretly rejoiced at having gained a son.
This happened around the Dīnghài year.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
In a certain temple in Tiānjīn,
storks nested on the owl-tail ridges.
Above the ceiling of the main hall,
a large snake, as big as a basin, was hidden.
Whenever the stork chicks were about to fledge,
it would emerge and swallow them all.
The storks would cry mournfully for several days before leaving.
This went on for three years.
People expected them surely not to return,
but the next year the nest was as before.
When the chicks were almost fully grown,
they flew straight away,
returning only after three days.
They entered the nest, crying "a-a,"
and fed their young as before.
The snake again wriggled its way up.
Just as it neared the nest,
the two storks were startled,
flying up with mournful, urgent cries,
straight into the clear sky.
Suddenly, a rushing sound like "pēng pēng" was heard,
and in an instant,
heaven and earth seemed to darken.
Everyone was astonished and looked,
seeing a colossal bird whose wings obscured the sun and sky,
descending swiftly from the air,
rapid as wind and rain.
With its claws, it struck the snake,
and the snake's head immediately fell off.
It then destroyed several feet of the temple's corner
and flew away, flapping its wings.
The storks followed behind it,
as if to see it off.
The nest having collapsed,
both chicks fell,
one alive and one dead.
The monk took the living one and placed it on the bell tower.
A short while later,
the storks returned,
and continued to feed it until its wings were fully grown, and then it left.
Yìshǐshǐ commented:
"That they returned the next year
means they had not expected the calamity to repeat;
that the nest remained for three years
implies the plan for revenge was already decided;
not returning for three days
shows they went to weep at Qín Tíng,
which is understandable.
The great bird must have been a sword immortal of the avian tribe.
It came like a whirlwind,
struck once and left.
How much more could a 'Mìaoshǒu Kōngkōng' add to this?"
In Jǐnán there was an army recruit.
He saw a stork fly by
and shot it.
It fell at the sound of the bowstring.
It held a fish in its beak,
intending to feed its young.
Someone advised him to pull out the arrow and release it,
but the recruit did not listen.
A short while later,
it flew away with the arrow.
Afterwards, it was seen flying around the city outskirts
for over two years,
the arrow still piercing it as before.
One day,
the recruit was sitting under the main gate,
when the stork flew by
and the arrow fell to the ground.
The recruit picked it up and looked at it, saying,
"The arrow is perfectly fine, isn't it?"
His ear happened to itch,
so he used the arrow to scratch it.
Suddenly, a strong wind slammed the gate shut.
The gate snapped shut,
hitting the arrow, which pierced his brain, and he died.
According to a copy from the Zhùxuězhāi studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A fowler from Tiānjīn caught a wild swan.
Its male companion followed it to the fowler's house,
crying sadly and circling in the air,
only leaving at dusk.
The next day,
when the fowler went out early,
the swan was already there,
flying and crying, following him;
then it landed at his feet.
The fowler was about to catch both.
He saw it stretch its neck, bobbing up and down,
and spit out half a bar of gold.
The fowler understood its intention,
and said,
"It intends to redeem its mate."
So he released the female.
The two swans lingered,
as if expressing sorrow and joy,
then flew away together.
The fowler weighed the gold
and found it to be a little over two liǎng and six qián.
Alas!
What do birds know,
yet they are so deeply attached!
No sorrow is greater than separation in life.
Is it the same for all creatures?
According to a copy from the Zhùxuězhāi studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Yuè there was a hunter
whose hunting arrows were like a mountain.
He happened to lie down to rest,
and unwittingly fell into a deep sleep.
An elephant came and picked him up with its trunk and carried him away.
He assumed he would surely be harmed.
Before long,
he was released and placed under a tree.
The elephant bowed its head once and trumpeted,
and a group of elephants came rushing,
circling around from all sides,
as if seeking something.
The first elephant knelt under the tree,
looking up at the tree and down at the man,
seemingly wanting him to climb.
The hunter understood,
and immediately stepped onto the elephant's back,
climbing up the tree.
Although he reached the treetop,
he still didn't know what its intention was.
A short while later,
a suānní (lion-like beast) came,
and all the elephants knelt down.
The suānní chose a plump one,
intending to fight and devour it.
The elephants trembled,
none daring to flee,
only looking up at the tree,
as if pleading for mercy and rescue.
The hunter understood,
and so aimed a crossbow at the suānní
and shot it. The suānní immediately dropped dead.
The elephants looked up at the sky,
as if bowing and dancing.
The hunter then came down,
and the elephants again knelt,
pulling his clothes with their trunks,
as if wanting him to ride.
The hunter then mounted it,
and the elephant began to walk.
Upon reaching a certain spot,
it dug the ground with its hooves,
uncovering countless shed tusks.
The hunter dismounted,
bundled them up and placed them on the elephant's back.
The elephant then carried them out of the mountain
before returning.
According to a copy from the Zhùxuězhāi studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A woodcutter went to the market
and returned carrying a staff.
Suddenly he felt as if there was a heavy weight at the top of his staff.
He looked back
and saw a headless man hanging from it.
Greatly startled,
he dropped the staff and struck wildly at it,
whereupon it was no longer seen.
Frightened, he ran
to a village.
It was already dusk,
and several people were lighting fires and illuminating the ground,
seemingly looking for something.
He approached and asked,
and learned that the group had just been sitting together
when a human head suddenly fell from the sky,
with disheveled beard and hair,
but then vanished in an instant.
The woodcutter also recounted what he had seen,
and putting the two together, it formed a complete person.
They ultimately did not understand where it came from.
Later, someone was carrying a basket
when he suddenly saw a human head inside.
People were surprised and questioned him,
only then did he become greatly alarmed,
tilting it onto the ground,
where it rolled and disappeared.
According to a copy from the Zhùxuězhāi studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dīng Shēng from Zhūchéng,
was the grandson of Yěhè Gōng.
A young scholar of renown,
he died of a lingering illness,
but revived the next night,
saying,
"I have attained enlightenment."
At that time, there was a monk skilled in profound Buddhist philosophy.
Dīng Shēng sent someone to invite him,
and had him lecture on the *Léngyán Sūtrà* by his couch.
Every section Dīng Shēng heard,
he declared incorrect,
and then said,
"If my illness can be cured,
realizing the Dao will not be difficult.
Only a certain Mr. Mǒu can cure my ailment,
he should be earnestly invited."
It happened that there was a Mr. Mǒu in the district
who was skilled in medicine but did not practice professionally.
Only after three invitations did he arrive,
prescribed a formula and administered medicine,
and the illness was cured.
After Mr. Mǒu returned home,
a woman entered from outside,
saying,
"I am a maidservant from the mansion of Dǒng Shàngshū.
Monk Zǐhuā and I have an old grudge.
Now I have my revenge,
and you wish to save him again?
If you go again,
calamity will befall you."
After speaking,
she vanished.
Mr. Mǒu was frightened,
and declined Dīng Shēng's request.
Dīng Shēng's illness recurred,
and he insisted on Mr. Mǒu's help,
so Mr. Mǒu told him the truth.
Dīng Shēng sighed, saying,
"This karma is from a previous life;
death is my fate."
Soon after, he died.
Later, people searched,
and indeed found a Monk Zǐhuā,
a high monk,
whom the wife of Dǒng Shàngshū of Qīngzhōu had often supported in her home;
but no one knew how their grudge had formed.
According to a copy from the Zhùxuězhāi studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zhōu Yāoyí, a gòngshēng from Huáishàng,
was fifty years old,
and had only one son,
named Kèchāng,
whom he doted on.
By the age of thirteen or fourteen,
his appearance became even more refined;
but he disliked studying,
often skipping school
to play with other children,
and would often not return home all day.
Zhōu Yāoyí also allowed him to do so.
One day,
when evening came, he did not return.
They began to search for him,
but utterly found nothing.
The couple wailed
and almost did not wish to live.
More than a year later,
Zhōu Chāng suddenly returned on his own.
He said,
"I was led astray by a Dàoshì and taken away,
but fortunately, I was not harmed.
When he went out,
I managed to escape and return."
Zhōu was overjoyed
and did not inquire further.
When he taught him to read,
his intelligence and understanding were double what they had been before.
After another year,
his literary talent greatly advanced.
When he took the examination at the prefectural school,
he became famous.
Prominent families vied to arrange marriages,
but Zhōu Chāng was quite unwilling.
The daughter of Jìnshì Zhào was beautiful,
and Zhōu insisted on marrying her to him.
After she entered the household,
the couple joked and laughed very happily;
yet Zhōu Chāng always slept alone,
as if he had no private affections.
A year later,
he succeeded in the autumn examination.
Zhōu was even more pleased.
However, as he grew older,
he daily hoped for a grandchild,
and so he often subtly hinted to Zhōu Chāng.
Zhōu Chāng was indifferent, as if he didn't understand.
His mother could not bear it
and often murmured about it morning and evening.
Zhōu Chāng's expression changed,
and he stepped out, saying,
"I have long wanted to leave and run away,
the reason I have not immediately abandoned you
is merely the affection of a child for his parents.
I truly cannot explore the marriage bed
to fulfill your hopes.
Please allow me to leave again;
the one who will comply with your wishes will return again."
They tried to pull him back,
but he had already vanished,
his clothes and hat like an empty cicada shell.
They were greatly astonished,
suspecting that Zhōu Chāng had already died,
and that this must have been his ghost.
They could only sigh in sorrow.
The next day,
Zhōu Chāng suddenly arrived on horseback, causing the whole family to be alarmed and bewildered.
When they questioned him closely,
he also said: He was abducted by villains and sold to the home of a wealthy merchant;
the merchant had no son,
and so adopted him.
After adopting Zhōu Chāng,
the merchant suddenly had a son.
Zhōu Chāng longed for home,
so the merchant sent him back.
When asked about his studies,
he was as dull and slow-witted as before.
Thus, this one was the true Zhōu Chāng;
the one who entered the government school and succeeded in the provincial examination
was a ghost impersonating him.
Nevertheless, they secretly rejoiced that the matter had not been exposed,
and so allowed him to assume the title of Xiàolián.
When he entered the room,
his wife was very familiar with him;
but Zhōu Chāng looked ashamed,
like a newlywed.
Just one year later,
he had a son.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zōng Zǐměi from Tàiyuán
traveled and studied with his father,
residing in Guǎnglíng.
His father had long been acquainted with an old woman, Lín Mǔ, who lived by the Hóngqiáo.
One day,
the father and son passed by Hóngqiáo,
met her,
and she earnestly invited them to her home
to brew tea and chat.
There was a girl nearby,
of extraordinary beauty.
The old man frequently praised her.
The old woman looked at Zōng and said,
"Dàláng is gentle and elegant like a maiden,
he has an auspicious appearance.
If you do not disdain her,
I will offer her to serve you with broom and dustpan,
how about that?"
The old man smiled,
urged his son to leave his seat,
and made him bow to the old woman, saying,
"Your words are worth a thousand pieces of gold!"
Before this,
the old woman lived alone,
when the girl suddenly arrived on her own,
telling of her loneliness and suffering.
When asked her childhood name,
it was Cháng'é.
The old woman loved her and kept her,
actually intending to hold onto a rare commodity.
At that time, Zōng was fourteen.
When the girl took off, he secretly rejoiced,
thinking the old man must have fixed the marriage;
but when the old man returned, he seemed to have forgotten.
His heart burned,
and he secretly told his mother.
The old man laughed, saying,
"I was just joking with that greedy old woman earlier.
She doesn't know how much gold she intends to sell her for;
how can this be easily spoken of!"
A year later,
both the old man and the old woman passed away.
Zǐměi could not forget Cháng'é,
and as his mourning period was nearing its end,
he asked someone to convey his intentions to Lín Mǔ.
The old woman initially did not agree.
Zōng angrily said,
"I have never lightly bowed my head in my life,
why does the old woman regard me as worthless?
If you renege on the previous agreement,
you must return her!"
The old woman then said,
"Perhaps there was a playful agreement with your father,
that is possible.
But there was no formal word,
so I completely forgot.
Now that you say so,
am I keeping her to marry a king of heaven?
I dress her up every day,
truly hoping to exchange her for a thousand pieces of gold;
if you offer half of that,
would that be acceptable?"
Zōng considered it difficult to manage
and so let the matter drop.
Just then, a widowed old woman rented a house in the western neighborhood,
who had a daughter by her deceased husband,
whose childhood name was Diāndāng.
He happened to catch a glimpse of her,
and she was no less refined and beautiful than Cháng'é.
He admired her
and often offered gifts as a way to advance;
after a long time, they gradually became familiar,
often exchanging flirtatious glances,
but there was no opportunity to speak.
One evening,
she climbed over the wall to beg for fire.
Zōng happily pulled her in,
and they became intimate.
He proposed marriage,
but she refused, saying her brother, who was a peddler, had not yet returned.
From then on, they took advantage of opportunities to visit each other,
their movements careful and discreet.
One day,
he happened to pass by Hóngqiáo,
and saw Cháng'é just inside the door,
so he quickly walked past.
Cháng'é saw him
and beckoned with her hand,
Zōng stopped;
the girl beckoned again,
so he entered.
The girl reproached Zōng for breaking his promise,
and Zōng explained his reasons.
The girl went into the room,
took a piece of gold and gave it to him,
Zōng did not accept it,
and refused, saying,
"I decided to be forever separated from you,
and so made another agreement.
If I accept the gold and act on your behalf,
that would be betraying someone else;
if I accept the gold and do not act on your behalf,
that would be betraying you: I truly dare not betray anyone."
The woman said after a long while,
"What you promised,
I know quite well.
That matter will certainly not succeed;
even if it does,
I will not resent your faithlessness.
Go quickly,
the old woman is about to arrive."
Zōng, in a hurry, was unable to control himself,
accepted it and returned.
The next night,
he told Diāndāng about it.
Diāndāng deeply approved of his words,
but advised Zōng to devote himself to Cháng'é.
Zōng said nothing;
when she expressed her willingness to marry,
Zōng was then pleased.
He immediately dispatched a matchmaker to offer a betrothal gift to Línshū,
who readily accepted,
and gave Cháng'é to Zōng.
After she entered the door,
she fully recounted Diāndāng's words.
Cháng'é smiled,
and feigned encouragement.
Zōng was delighted,
eager to make everything clear to Diāndāng,
but Diāndāng's traces had long disappeared.
Cháng'é knew it was for her sake,
so she temporarily returned home to her parents,
thereby giving him an opportunity,
and instructed Zōng to secretly take her pouch.
Soon after, Diāndāng indeed arrived,
and discussed the plan,
but only said not to rush.
When she loosened her belt and smiled,
there was a purple lotus pouch under her armpit,
which he was about to pluck.
Diāndāng's expression changed,
and she stood up saying:
"You are of one heart with another,
but with me!
Faithless man!
Let us part from this moment."
Zōng tried to persuade and reconcile her with a forced smile,
but she did not listen,
and eventually left.
One day,
he passed by her door to investigate,
and already another Wú guest had moved in;
Diāndāng and her mother had moved away long ago,
their shadows vanished and traces gone,
making it impossible to inquire.
Since Zōng married Cháng'é,
his family became suddenly rich,
with connected pavilions and long corridors,
stretching across the streets.
Cháng'é was good at jesting.
Once, seeing a scroll of beautiful paintings,
Zōng said:
"I consider
that there is no one else like you in the world,
but I have never seen Fēiyàn or Yángfēi."
The woman smiled and said:
"If you wish to see them,
what difficulty is there in that?"
She then took the scroll and examined it carefully,
then went into a room,
applied makeup before the mirror,
imitated Fēiyàn's dance in the wind,
and also learned Yángfēi's tipsy demeanor.
Short or tall, plump or slender,
she changed at will;
her charm and attitude,
were uncannily true to the scroll.
As she was posing,
a maid came from outside,
unable to recognize her,
and asked her colleague in surprise;
then looked closely again,
and only then laughed with realization.
Zōng exclaimed with joy:
"I have obtained a beauty,
and all the beauties of a thousand ages
are now in my bedchamber!"
One night,
while he was sound asleep,
several people pried open the door and entered,
their torchlight illuminating the walls.
The woman suddenly rose,
crying out in alarm:
"Thieves have entered!"
Zōng had just awakened
and was about to cry out.
One person held a bare blade to his neck,
making him too terrified to breathe.
Another seized Cháng'é and carried her on his back,
then noisily departed.
Zōng then began to wail,
and all the household servants gathered.
The precious items and curiosities in the room
were all accounted for; nothing was missing.
Zōng was greatly saddened,
completely losing his wits and his purpose,
with no will left for life.
He reported it to the officials for pursuit and arrest,
but there was no news whatsoever.
Three or four years passed quickly,
and he was utterly dejected.
So he took leave to go to Dōu as a candidate for the examinations.
After staying for half a year,
making divinations, inquiries, and investigations,
he left no stone unturned.
One day, passing through Yáo Xiàng,
he encountered a woman,
with a dirty face and tattered clothes,
looking like a beggar.
He stopped and looked at her,
and it was none other than Diāndāng.
He exclaimed in shock:
"How have you become so emaciated?"
She replied:
"After we parted, I moved south,
and my old mother passed away.
I was seized by evil people and sold into slavery under a banner,
enduring flogging, humiliation, cold, and hunger—
things I cannot bear to speak of."
Zōng wept and asked:
"Can you be redeemed?"
She said:
"It's difficult;
the expenses are numerous and troublesome,
and I cannot manage it."
Zōng said:
"To tell you the truth, in recent years I have become somewhat wealthy,
but unfortunately, my funds are limited here as a traveler.
I will empty my luggage and sell my horse;
I dare not refuse.
If the required amount is too extravagant,
I will return home to arrange for it."
The woman agreed to meet him outside the West Gate tomorrow,
beneath the clustered willows;
she instructed him to come alone,
without any attendants.
Zōng said:
"Understood."
The next day,
he went early,
and the woman was already there,
dressed in bright, fresh clothes,
entirely different from her previous state.
He asked her in surprise,
and she smiled and said:
"I was merely testing your heart.
Fortunately, your intention of 'gifting the wadded gown' still remains.
Please come to my humble abode;
I shall surely reward you appropriately."
After walking several paces north,
they reached her house.
She then brought out food and wine,
and they talked and feasted together.
Zōng proposed that she return with him.
The woman said:
"I have too many worldly encumbrances
and cannot accompany you.
I have, however, heard some news of Cháng'é."
Zōng eagerly asked where she was.
The woman said:
"Her whereabouts are elusive;
I also do not know them intimately.
There is an old nun in Xī Shān,
a one-eyed elder;
if you ask her,
you will know for yourself."
Zōng then stayed overnight at her house.
At dawn, she showed him the path.
Zōng arrived at the place,
where there was an ancient temple,
with all its surrounding walls in ruins.
Within a bamboo grove, there was a half-collapsed thatched hut,
where an old nun was mending her patched robe.
Seeing a guest arrive,
she showed no courtesy.
Zōng bowed to her,
and the nun then raised her head and offered a greeting.
He then stated his name
and explained what he sought.
The nun said:
"I am an eighty-year-old blind woman,
cut off from the world;
how could I know the whereabouts of a beautiful lady?"
Zōng insisted on his request.
Then she said:
"I truly do not know.
I have two or three relatives
coming to visit tomorrow evening;
perhaps some of the young women among them know,
it's hard to say.
You can come tomorrow evening."
Zōng then left.
The next day, when he arrived again,
the nun was out,
and the dilapidated door was open.
After waiting for a long time,
the water clock had already announced the late hour,
and the bright moon hung high.
As he paced back and forth, at a loss,
he distantly saw two or three young women enter from outside,
and Cháng'é was among them.
Zōng was overjoyed,
suddenly stood up,
and eagerly grasped her sleeve.
Cháng'é said:
"Oh, impulsive young master!
You've scared me to death!
How hateful of Diāndāng to be so talkative
and let desire entangle people!"
Zōng pulled her to sit,
held her hand, and spoke intimately,
recounting his hardships,
unable to help feeling sorrowful.
The woman said:
"To tell you the truth, I am actually Cháng'é, banished,
floating and sinking in the mortal world,
and my term is now complete.
My abduction by bandits was
meant to cut off your hopes.
The nun is also a guardian of Wáng Mǔ's mansion;
when I was first banished,
she kindly took care of me,
so I often visit her in my spare time.
If you release me,
I will send Diāndāng to you in my stead."
Zōng did not listen,
lowering his head and shedding tears.
The woman looked into the distance and said:
"My sisters are coming!"
As Zōng looked around,
Cháng'é had already vanished.
Zōng cried loudly, losing his voice,
wishing not to live again,
and so he untied his belt and hanged himself.
In a trance, he felt his soul had left his body,
wandering aimlessly and forlornly.
Suddenly, he saw Cháng'é come,
seize and lift him,
his feet off the ground.
She entered the temple,
took the corpse from the tree, pushed and squeezed it,
and called out:
"Foolish fellow,
foolish fellow!
Cháng'é is here!"
Suddenly, he awoke as if from a dream.
After a moment of calm,
the woman angrily said:
"Diāndāng, that lowly maid!
She harmed me and killed my husband;
I cannot forgive her!"
She descended the mountain, hired a palanquin, and returned home.
After instructing her family to pack,
she turned and went out the West Gate,
to visit and thank Diāndāng.
Upon arrival, the house was completely different,
and she returned in astonishment and regret.
Secretly, she was glad Cháng'é did not know.
Upon entering the door,
Cháng'é greeted her with a smile and said:
"Did you see Diāndāng?"
Zōng was stunned and unable to answer.
The woman said:
"You betrayed Cháng'é;
how could you get Diāndāng?
Please sit and wait for her;
she will come herself."
Not long after,
Diāndāng indeed arrived,
frantically prostrating herself beneath the couch.
Cháng'é snapped her fingers at her
and said:
“The imp is in deep trouble!”
Diāndāng 叩 (kòutóu) kowtowed,
only begging for a reprieve from death.
Cháng’é said,
“You've pushed yourself into a pit,
and now you want to escape to the heavens?
Guǎnghán’s eleventh aunt will be marrying in a few days;
you need to embroider a hundred pillows and a hundred pairs of shoes.
You can come with me
and we'll work together.”
Diāndāng respectfully replied,
“I only ask to be assigned work,
and to deliver it on time.”
The lady did not consent,
and said to Zōng,
“If you speak on his behalf,
I will let him go immediately.”
Diāndāng looked at Zōng,
and Zōng smiled without speaking.
Diāndāng glared at him in anger.
Then he begged to return and inform his family,
which was granted,
and he left.
Zōng asked about his background,
and then learned that he was a fox from Xīshān.
He bought a sedan chair and waited for him.
The next day,
he indeed came,
and they returned together.
However, when Cháng’é came again,
she always maintained a serious demeanor and did not engage in lighthearted joking.
Zōng strongly urged playful intimacy,
but only secretly taught Diāndāng to do it.
Diāndāng was extremely clever
and skilled at charming.
Cháng’é enjoyed sleeping alone,
and often declined to stay the night.
One night,
after the third watch,
sounds of incessant giggling
could still be heard from Diāndāng’s room.
She sent a maid to eavesdrop.
When the maid returned,
she did not report it,
but simply asked the mistress to go herself.
Peeking through the window,
she saw Diāndāng elaborately made up to resemble herself,
while Zōng embraced him,
calling him Cháng’é.
The lady scoffed and withdrew.
Not long after,
Diāndāng suddenly felt a sharp pain in his heart,
hastily put on his clothes,
dragged Zōng to Cháng’é’s dwelling,
and prostrated himself upon entering.
Cháng’é said,
“Am I a healer, a sorceress who wards off evil?
You merely want to hold your chest and imitate Xīzǐ.”
Diāndāng bowed his head,
only saying he knew his fault.
The lady said,
“You are cured.”
Then he got up,
chuckled, and left.
Diāndāng privately said to Zōng,
“I can make Madam learn from Guānyīn.”
Zōng did not believe it,
and playfully made a wager with him.
Whenever Cháng’é sat cross-legged,
her eyes half-closed as if meditating,
Diāndāng quietly placed a willow branch in a jade vase
on the table;
then he let down his hair, clasped his hands,
stood attendant by her side,
his cherry lips slightly parted,
his melon-seed teeth faintly visible,
his gaze unwavering.
Zōng laughed at this.
Cháng’é opened her eyes and asked about it.
Diāndāng said,
“I am imitating Lóngnǚ attending Guānyīn.”
Cháng’é laughed and scolded him,
punishing him by making him imitate a child bowing.
Diāndāng tied up his hair,
then bowed in all four directions,
rolling on the ground,
displaying various postures,
bending left and right,
so that his socks could touch his ears.
Cháng’é was amused,
sat down and kicked him.
Diāndāng looked up,
bit a phoenix hook in his mouth,
lightly touching it with his teeth.
While Cháng’é was laughing playfully,
she suddenly felt a thread of seductive charm
rise from her toes,
reaching directly into her heart,
her mind becoming stirred and lustful,
as if she could not control herself.
So she quickly composed herself
and scolded,
“You fox-slave deserves to die!
Do you not choose whom you bewitch?”
Diāndāng was frightened,
released his mouth, and fell to the ground.
Cháng’é again harshly rebuked him,
but the others did not understand.
Cháng’é said to Zōng,
“Diāndāng's fox nature has not changed;
just now I was almost fooled by him.
If one does not have deep karmic roots from previous lives,
how easy it is to fall!”
From then on, whenever she saw Diāndāng,
she always treated him with strict control.
Diāndāng felt ashamed and fearful,
and told Zōng,
“I cherish every limb and body part of Madam;
there is nothing I do not love.
My love is so extreme
that I unconsciously become exceedingly charming.
To say I have ill intentions,
not only do I not dare,
but I also cannot bear to.”
Zōng then related this to Cháng’é,
and Cháng’é treated him as before.
However, because of the boundless playful intimacy,
she repeatedly warned Zōng,
but Zōng did not listen;
consequently, all the maids and women, young and old,
competed in playful intimacy.
One day,
two people supported a maid,
imitating Yáng Fēi.
The two exchanged knowing glances,
tricking the maid into relaxing her body as if drunk,
then suddenly released their hands;
the maid fell violently down the steps,
with a sound like a collapsing wall.
Everyone cried out in alarm;
upon approaching to examine her,
the concubine had already 'died' at Mǎwéi.
The crowd was frightened
and urgently informed the master.
Cháng’é exclaimed in shock,
“Disaster has struck!
What did I tell you?”
She went to examine her,
but she could not be saved.
She sent someone to inform her father.
The father, a certain Jiǎ,
who was usually unruly,
rushed over, wailing,
carried the corpse into the main hall,
and shouted curses of all kinds.
Zōng closed the door, anxious and afraid,
not knowing what to do.
Cháng’é herself came out to rebuke him,
saying,
“Even if a master abuses a maid to death,
the law has no compensation for it;
moreover, she died suddenly and by chance,
how do you know she won't revive?”
Jiǎ shouted,
“Her four limbs are already cold,
how can there be life?”
Cháng’é said,
“Stop making a fuss.
Even if she doesn't live,
there is still a dwelling (for her).”
Then she entered the hall and touched the corpse,
and the maid had already revived,
and stood up with her touch.
Cháng’é turned around and angrily said,
“The maid is fortunate not to have died,
how dare this scoundrel be so rude!
He can be bound with rope and sent to the authorities!”
Jiǎ was speechless,
and knelt down begging for mercy.
Cháng’é said,
“Since you know your fault,
I will temporarily refrain from prosecuting you.
But lowly people are unreliable
and fickle;
keeping your daughter will ultimately lead to trouble,
so you should take her away immediately.
The original price was in the thousands;
arrange it quickly.”
She sent people to escort him out,
instructing them to ask a few village elders
to sign as witnesses to the deed.
After this,
she summoned the maid to her presence,
and made Jiǎ question her himself:
"Are you well?"
He replied:
"I am well."
Then he paid her and left.
Later,
she summoned all the maids,
sternly rebuked and beat them all over.
She also called Diāndāng,
and severely forbade such behavior.
She said to Zōng:
"Now I understand that for those in superior positions,
even a smile or a frown cannot be taken lightly.
The origin of this jest began with your concubine,
yet its harmful consequences became uncontrollable.
All sorrow belongs to Yīn,
and joy belongs to Yáng;
when Yáng reaches its extreme, Yīn is born;
this is the fixed number of cycles.
The maids' misfortune
was a gradual warning from the ghosts and spirits.
If one remains confused and unawakened,
then ruin will befall them."
Zōng listened respectfully.
Diāndāng tearfully begged to be relieved.
Cháng'é then pinched her ear;
after a quarter of an hour, she released her hand,
Diāndāng felt relieved and calm for a moment,
suddenly as if waking from a dream,
she threw herself to the ground,
overjoyed and wanting to dance.
From then on, the Fúzhōu pavilion was serene and solemn,
and no one dared to make noise.
When the maid returned to her home,
she died violently without illness.
As Jiǎ could not repay the ransom,
he sought the village's
elders to plead for mercy and forgiveness,
which was granted.
Moreover, out of consideration for her service,
he provided her with timber before she left.
Zōng often worried about not having sons.
Cháng'é's belly suddenly heard a baby crying,
so she used a blade to cut open her left flank and extracted it,
and it was indeed a boy;
not long after,
she became pregnant again,
and again cut open her right flank to extract a girl.
The boy closely resembled his father,
and the girl closely resembled her mother,
and both were married into distinguished families.
According to a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
Jú Lèrú,
a native of Qīngzhōu.
His wife died,
and he abandoned his home and left.
Several years later,
he arrived in Daoist robes carrying a meditation mat.
After staying for a night, he wished to leave,
but his relatives strongly insisted on keeping his clothes and staff.
Jú pretended to take a stroll outside the village,
and the clothes and utensils in his room
all slowly flew out
and followed him away.
According to a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
Chén Xiàolián from Shùntiān,
when he was sixteen or seventeen *suì*,
once studied with a tutor in a Buddhist temple,
and his fellow students were very numerous.
Among them was a student named Chǔ,
who claimed to be from Shāndōng,
and diligently applied himself to study and discussion,
none of them taking a break;
moreover, he lodged in the study hall,
and was never seen returning home.
Chén was most friendly with him,
and so questioned him,
he replied:
"My family is poor,
it is not easy to prepare tuition fees,
so I cannot spare even an inch of time,
and by adding the middle of the night,
my two days
can count as three days for others."
Chén was moved by his words,
and wanted to bring his mat to sleep with him.
Chǔ stopped him, saying:
"No,
no!
I see that your learning, Sir,
is not from my teacher.
There is a Mr. Lǚ at Fùchéngmén,
although he is old,
he can be your teacher,
please move there with me."
For in the capital, many who set up schools charged by the month,
at the end of the month, once the tuition was paid,
they were free to stay or leave.
So the two students went together to Mr. Lǚ.
Lǚ,
an old scholar from Yuè,
was down and out and could not return home,
so he taught young children,
which was not his true ambition.
He was very happy to get the two students;
and Chǔ was also very intelligent,
grasping things at a glance,
so he especially valued him.
The two became very close friends,
sharing a desk by day,
and a bed by night.
When the month ended,
Chǔ suddenly went home on leave.
For more than ten days, he did not return.
Everyone suspected something.
One day,
Chén, having gone to Tiānníngsì for a battle,
met Chǔ in the corridor.
He was splitting jute fiber and quenching sulfur,
making fire-starting materials.
Seeing Chén,
he was embarrassed and ill at ease.
Chén asked:
"Why did you suddenly stop studying?"
Chǔ clasped his hand and asked for a private word,
saying sadly:
"I am poor and have nothing to give to the teacher.
