I must sell goods for half a month
before I can study for one month."
Chén was moved with emotion for a long time,
then said:
"Just go and study;
I will do my utmost to help."
He ordered his attendant to collect Chǔ's belongings
and return together to the school.
He warned Chǔ not to reveal this,
but to make an excuse to tell the teacher.
Chén's father was originally a shopkeeper
who became wealthy by dealing in goods.
Chén often secretly took his father's gold
to give to the teacher on Chǔ's behalf.
When his father questioned him about the missing gold,
Chén told him the truth.
His father thought he was foolish,
and thus made him stop his studies.
Chǔ was greatly ashamed
and wanted to leave the teacher.
Lǚ knew the reason,
and reproached him, saying:
"Since you are poor,
why did you not tell us earlier?"
He then returned all the gold to Chén's father,
kept Chǔ studying as before,
and shared meals with him,
as if he were family.
Although Chén did not return to the school,
he often invited Chǔ to a tavern for a drink.
Chǔ firmly refused to go to avoid suspicion;
but Chén's insistence grew stronger,
often waiting below his window.
Chǔ could not bear to refuse,
and so they began to interact frequently.
More than two years passed,
Chén's father died,
and Chén again sought to be taught.
Lǚ was touched by his sincerity
and accepted him;
but having ceased studying for so long,
his progress was far behind Chǔ's.
After half a year,
Lǚ's eldest son came from Yuè
begging for food and searching for his father.
The students collected money to help with his travel expenses,
but Chǔ only shed tears and was reluctant to part.
As Lǚ was about to depart,
he instructed Chén to take Chǔ as his teacher.
Chén followed this instruction
and housed Chǔ in his home.
Not long after,
Chén entered the county school,
and
took the examination
as a "left-behind talent."
Chén worried he could not finish the essay,
so Chǔ offered to substitute for him.
When the time came,
Chǔ arrived with a man
who said he was his cousin, Liú Tiānrúo,
and instructed Chén to go with him for a while.
As Chén was leaving,
Chǔ suddenly pulled him from behind.
Chén was about to stumble,
but Liú quickly pulled him along and left.
After looking around once,
they went together to stay at Liú's house.
There were no women in the house,
so the guest was housed in the inner quarters.
After staying for several days,
it was suddenly Mid-Autumn Festival.
Liú said:
"Today, Lǐ Huángqīn's garden
has many visitors.
We should go there to relieve our accumulated gloom,
and then I will conveniently send you home."
He sent someone to carry a tea set and wine utensils to go.
They only saw the waterside pavilion and plum pavilion
too noisy to enter.
Passing through the water gate,
under an old willow,
lay a painted boat.
They boarded the boat together.
After several rounds of wine,
it felt too quiet.
Liú looked at a servant boy and said:
"The Plum Blossom Pavilion recently had a new courtesan.
I wonder if she is at home?"
The boy left and returned shortly
with the courtesan.
It was none other than Lǐ Èyún, from the brothel.
Lǐ was a famous courtesan in the capital,
skilled in poetry and good at singing.
Chén had once drunk at her house with friends,
so he recognized her.
They met and exchanged brief greetings.
The courtesan looked sorrowful and worried.
Liú ordered her to sing,
and she sang "Hāolǐ."
Chén was displeased,
saying:
"Even if the host and guest are not to your liking,
why sing a song for the dead to the living?"
The courtesan stood up and apologized,
forcing a smile,
then sang a beautiful love song.
Chén was pleased
and grasped her wrist, saying:
"I read your former 'Huànxīshā' several times,
and now you have forgotten it."
The courtesan recited:
"Tearful eyes brim before the dressing table,
drawing aside the curtain, suddenly seeing a young aunt arrive,
head bowed, turning to look at her bound feet.
Forcing herself to unbind her brows and smile,
frequently wiping her fragrant cheeks with red sleeves,
carefully, still fearing she might be guessed."
Chén repeated it several times.
After a while, they docked the boat,
passed through a long corridor,
and saw many poems inscribed on the wall.
He immediately asked for a brush to write a lyric on it.
As dusk approached,
Liú said:
"The people from the examination hall will be coming out soon."
So he sent Chén home.
Upon entering the door,
Liú immediately departed.
Chén saw the room was dark and empty.
After a short delay,
Chǔ had already entered the door;
upon closer inspection,
it was not Chǔ.
Just as he was wondering,
the guest suddenly came close to him and collapsed.
The family members said:
"The young master is exhausted!"
They all helped to lift him.
He then realized that the one who collapsed was no other
than himself.
After he rose,
he saw Chǔ standing beside him,
feeling as if in a dream.
He sent the others away and questioned him.
Chǔ said:
"Don't be alarmed by what I tell you: I am actually a ghost.
I was long due for reincarnation,
but I have lingered here
because I cannot forget your great kindness.
Therefore, I attached myself to your body
to take the examination on your behalf;
once the three sessions are complete,
this wish will be fulfilled."
Chén again asked him to attend the spring examination.
Chǔ said:
"Your ancestors were of meager fortune.
Their miserly bones
are not worthy of imperial commendation and gifts."
Chén asked:
"Where will you go?"
He replied:
"Teacher Lǚ and I have a father-son relationship,
and I constantly worry about him.
My cousin is a clerk in the Underworld Office,
and if he requests the Lord of the Underworld on my behalf,
there might be a way."
Then he bid farewell and left.
Chén was surprised by this.
At dawn,
he visited Lǐ Jī,
intending to ask about the boating incident,
but Jī had been dead for several days.
He also went to Huángqīn Yuán,
and saw the inscribed verses still there,
but the faint ink was indistinct,
as if about to fade away.
Only then did he realize that the inscribing person was a soul,
and the author was a ghost.
In the evening,
Chǔ arrived joyfully,
saying:
"My plan has fortunately succeeded;
I respectfully bid you farewell."
Thereupon he stretched out his two palms,
and bade Chén write the character "褚" (Chǔ) on them to mark the occasion.
Chén was about to prepare wine for a farewell,
but Chǔ shook his head and said:
"No need.
If you do not forget our old friendship,
after the results are announced,
do not fear the long journey."
Chén waved his tears as he saw him off.
He saw a person waiting by the door;
as Chǔ was lingering,
that person pressed their hand on Chǔ's neck,
and Chǔ flattened with the hand,
gathered Chǔ into a bag,
and carried him away.
After several days,
Chén indeed passed the examination.
Thereupon he prepared his luggage and went to Yuè.
Lǚ's wife had been barren for decades,
and after more than fifty years of age,
suddenly gave birth to a son,
whose two hands were firmly clasped and could not be opened.
When Chén arrived,
he asked to see the child,
and immediately said that there must be the character
"褚" (Chǔ) in its palm.
Lǚ did not fully believe him.
When the child saw Chén,
its ten fingers opened by themselves,
and looking, it was indeed so.
Amazed, Lǚ asked for the reason,
and Chén told him everything.
They were both delighted and astonished.
Chén generously gave them gifts,
and then returned.
Later, Lǚ, as a tribute student, came to the imperial examination and stayed in the capital (Dū),
lodging with Chén;
by then the child was thirteen years old,
and had already entered the local school (pàn).
The Yìshǐshì says:
"Old Lǚ taught his disciples,
but did not know how to teach his own son.
Alas!
To do good for others,
yet to lower oneself,
what a difference!
Chǔ-shēng,
unable to repay his teacher in person,
first repaid his friend with his soul.
His will and his deeds
can illuminate the sun and moon,
how could one marvel at him merely because he was a ghost!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
in the regions of Xī and Yì,
seven out of ten people were bandits,
and officials dared not arrest them.
Later, they surrendered and were placated,
and the county magistrate designated them
"bandit households" (dàohù).
Whenever there was a dispute with law-abiding citizens,
the magistrate would deliberately favor them,
presumably fearing that they might rebel again.
Later, litigants would often falsely claim to be bandit households,
while their adversaries would vehemently expose their falsehood;
whenever both parties presented their cases,
the right and wrong would be set aside without distinction,
and instead, they would first argue back and forth about the authenticity of being a bandit,
causing great trouble to each other,
and bothering the authorities to check the registers.
It so happened that there were many foxes in the yamen,
and the magistrate's daughter was bewitched by one.
A sorcerer was hired,
who used talismans to trap a fox in a bottle,
intending to burn it with fire.
The fox inside the bottle cried out loudly:
"I am a bandit household (dàohù)!"
All who heard could not help but chuckle.
The Yìshǐshì says:
"Nowadays, if there are those who rob people with open fire,
officials do not consider them bandits but rather ruffians;
those who climb over walls to commit adultery
often do not admit to being adulterers but rather to being bandits: the state of affairs has changed again.
If today there were a fox in the yamen,
it would surely cry out loudly: 'I am a bandit,
no doubt about it.'"
In Zhāngqiū, the corvée labor for grain transport
and the collection of melting fees (huǒhào),
often imposed on common people several times more than on gentry,
so those with land competed to seek patronage.
Although this caused no harm to the national revenue,
it actually harmed the magistrate's own coffers.
The county magistrate, Zhōng,
submitted a request to rectify the abuses,
which was granted.
Initially, he ordered people to confess voluntarily;
subsequently, opportunistic commoners used this to leverage the gentry,
falsely claiming and cunningly associating all properties sold decades ago
with the gentry,
and litigating against the original owners.
The magistrate completely favored these commoners,
so many good but weak people lost their property.
Lǐ-shēng was also sued by a certain Jiǎ,
and they both went for interrogation.
Jiǎ called him
"xiùcai" (scholar);
Lǐ argued back vehemently,
refusing to accept the title of xiùcai.
The clamor did not cease.
The magistrate questioned his attendants,
and they all indicated that he was indeed a xiùcai.
The magistrate then asked:
"Why do you not acknowledge it?"
Lǐ said:
"Let the xiùcai title be put aside for now;
after the land dispute is settled,
it will not be too late to become one again."
Alas!
As for the name of bandit,
people competed to claim it;
as for the name of xiùcai,
people competed to decline it: how strange the changes are!
Someone submitted an anonymous petition saying:
"The petitioner Yuán Rǎng,
regarding the matter of resisting the law and appropriating property: Being old and unable to perform corvée duties,
I had fifty *mǔ* of land outside the city,
which, in the first year of Yǐnggōng,
was temporarily registered under the name of the wicked gentry Yán Yuān.
Now that the regulations are strict,
it is reasonable to confess voluntarily.
Unexpectedly, the wicked Yán Yuān held it for a long time and did not return it,
usurping it as his own.
I went to reason with him,
but was beaten by his master leading seventy-two evil followers,
with vicious staffs raining down,
severely injuring my shins and thighs;
furthermore, I was locked up in a dark alley,
given a meager basket of food and a gourd of drink daily,
imprisoned and nearly starved to death.
With mutual village witnesses and land deeds,
I humbly request a thorough investigation and removal from office,
so that my blood-earned property may be returned to its owner.
Respectfully submitted."
This could follow Liǔ Zhí's accusation of Yí and Qí!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì. Appendix supplemented according to the twenty-four-volume manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the west of the district, there was a certain Yǐ,
who used to be a "Gentleman of the Beams" (burglar).
His wife was deeply afraid of this,
and repeatedly urged him to stop. Yǐ then completely reformed himself.
After two or three years,
his poor wife could no longer endure the poverty,
and thought of becoming a Fēng Fù just once and then stopping.
So, feigning a trading trip,
she went to a skilled diviner
to decide their direction.
The diviner said:
"Southeast is auspicious;
it benefits a 'small person'
but not a 'gentleman'."
The omen secretly matched her thoughts,
and she was secretly pleased.
So, she traveled south,
arriving between Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng.
She spent days wandering through villages and towns,
for several months.
One day, she chanced upon a temple,
and saw two or three small stones piled in a corner of the wall.
She knew in her heart that this was unusual,
so she also threw one stone onto the pile.
She then went straight behind the shrine to lie down.
As dusk fell,
people gathered and talked in the temple;
there seemed to be more than ten people.
Suddenly, one person counted the stones,
and was surprised by their number.
They then searched together,
and found Yǐ behind the shrine.
They asked:
"Are you the one who threw the stone?"
Yǐ assented.
They questioned him about his hometown and name,
and Yǐ gave a false reply.
They then gave him weapons
and led him away with them.
They arrived at a grand mansion,
took out a rope ladder,
and competed to climb over the wall and enter.
Since Yǐ had traveled a long distance
and was unfamiliar with the route,
he was ordered to lie in wait outside the wall,
to oversee the passing of goods and guard the bags.
A short while later,
a wrapped bundle was thrown down;
then a little later,
a basket was lowered by rope.
Yǐ lifted the basket and knew it contained something.
He then broke the basket,
reached in with his hand, and took things out.
He put all the heavy objects
into one bag,
and carried it away at a swift run,
eventually taking the road home.
From this, he built towers and pavilions, bought good land,
and paid grain to become a government student (or official).
The district inscribed his gate with the words
"Good Scholar."
Later, a major case came to light,
and all the bandits were caught;
only Yǐ,
who had no name on their register,
could not be traced,
and thus escaped.
After the matter had long subsided,
Yǐ would sometimes recount it when drunk.
There was a notorious bandit in the county, Mǒu,
who returned with significant wealth
and slept soundly.
Two or three small thieves
climbed over the wall and entered,
seized him,
and demanded gold.
Mǒu refused to give it;
beating and branding were applied,
and all his possessions were taken
before they left.
Mǒu said to others:
"I never knew the pain of branding and torture was like this!"
Consequently, he deeply hated thieves,
and volunteered to become a cavalry constable,
capturing almost all the bandits in the district.
When he caught the bandit who had stolen his bag,
he applied to him what had been applied to himself.
According to a handwritten copy of Volume 24 of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zhū Dàxīng was from
Zhāngdé.
His family was wealthy but exceedingly parsimonious;
unless it was for a child's marriage,
there would be no guests at his table,
and no meat in his kitchen.
However, he was frivolous and loved women;
wherever there was beauty,
he would not begrudge lavish expenses.
Every night,
he would climb over the wall, cross the village,
and sleep with loose women.
One night,
he encountered a young woman walking alone,
knew she was a widow,
coerced her,
and brought her back with him.
By candlelight,
she was exceptionally beautiful.
She said of herself:
"My surname is Huò."
He questioned her in detail and thoroughly.
The woman was displeased,
saying:
"Since you have already taken me in,
why must you question me further?
If you are afraid I will be a burden,
it is better that I leave early."
Zhū dared not ask again
and kept her to sleep with.
However, the woman could not eat coarse food and disliked seeing meat stew;
she required bird's nest, chicken heart, and fish maw to make soup
before she could be satisfied.
Zhū had no choice
but to exert himself to provide for her.
She was also often ill,
requiring a bowl of ginseng soup daily.
Zhū initially refused.
The woman groaned as if at death's door;
having no alternative,
he gave it to her,
and her illness vanished as if by magic.
This then became routine.
The woman's clothes had to be embroidered silk;
after a few days,
she would tire of their oldness.
After more than a month of this,
the expenses were immeasurable,
and Zhū gradually stopped supplying them.
The woman wept and refused to eat,
asking to leave.
Zhū was afraid
and again made concessions to humor her.
Whenever she was bored,
she would order a troupe of actors for entertainment every ten or so days.
During the performance,
Zhū would set up a stool outside the curtain,
holding his child and watching;
the woman, however, showed no joy,
and often scolded him.
Zhū did not argue much either.
After two years,
the family gradually declined.
He gently spoke to the woman,
asking for a slight reduction;
the woman agreed,
and all expenses were cut by half.
After a long time,
it was still not enough.
The woman, however, accepted the declining household fare
and gradually no longer insisted on luxuries.
Zhū was secretly pleased.
Suddenly one night,
she opened the back door and ran away.
Zhū was disheartened as if he had lost something,
and searched everywhere for her,
only to find she was in the Hē family's house in the neighboring village.
Hé Dàxìng,
a scion of an influential clan,
was extravagant, dissolute, and fond of entertaining guests.
His lights would burn until dawn.
Suddenly, a beautiful woman
entered his boudoir in the middle of the night.
When questioned,
she turned out to be the runaway concubine of Zhū family.
Hé had always
looked down on Zhū's character;
moreover, he was charmed by the woman's beauty,
so he accepted her.
After several days of intimacy,
he became even more infatuated with her,
indulging her every extravagant desire,
serving her just as Zhū had.
When Zhū received the news,
he demanded her return,
but Hé paid no heed.
Zhū filed a complaint with the authorities.
The officials, deeming her name and origin unclear,
did not process the case.
Zhū sold property to offer bribes,
and only then was the detention and complaint approved.
The woman said to Hé:
"When I was in the Zhū family,
I was not originally taken through a betrothal ceremony or matchmaker.
Why should we fear him?"
Hé was pleased,
and intended to proceed with the lawsuit.
Guò Shēng, a guest present, advised him:
"Harboring a fugitive
already violates state law;
moreover, this woman, since entering your home,
has been spending without limits.
Even a family with a thousand gold coins
could not sustain this!"
Hé was greatly enlightened,
abandoned the lawsuit,
and returned the woman.
After a day or two,
the woman ran away again.
There was a certain Huáng Shēng,
who was formerly a poor scholar
and unmarried.
The woman knocked on his door and entered,
telling him where she came from.
Huáng, seeing such a beautiful woman suddenly appear,
was startled and did not know what to do.
Huáng had always been law-abiding,
so he firmly refused her.
The woman left.
During their conversation,
she was charmingly sweet and utterly captivating.
Huáng's heart was moved,
and he kept her,
but worried she could not endure poverty.
The woman rose early,
personally handled the household chores,
working more diligently than in her previous homes.
Huáng was a refined and uninhibited person,
skilled in inner charm,
and thus regretted meeting her so late;
he only feared that word would get out,
and their joy would not last long.
However, since the lawsuit, Zhū's family
had become even poorer;
and he also surmised that the woman could not settle down,
so he eventually dropped the investigation.
The woman had followed Huáng for several years,
and their affection was profound.
One day,
she suddenly wished to visit her parents,
and asked Huáng to escort her.
Huáng said:
“You previously said you had no home;
how is it that your words are now contradictory?”
She replied:
“Those were empty words.
I am from Zhènjiāng.
Formerly, I followed a profligate man,
and drifted across rivers and lakes,
until I arrived here.
My family is quite wealthy.
If you exhaust your resources and go,
you will certainly not suffer any loss.”
Huáng followed her advice,
hired a palanquin, and went with her.
Upon reaching the borders of Yángzhōu,
they moored their boat by the river.
The woman happened to be leaning by the window,
when a rich merchant's son passed by.
Struck by her beauty,
he turned his boat around and followed them,
but Huáng did not know this.
The woman suddenly said:
“Your family is exceedingly poor.
Now I have a method to cure your poverty;
I wonder if you can follow it?”
Huáng questioned her.
The woman said:
“I have been with you for several years,
but have been unable to bear you children,
which is also an unfinished matter.
Although I am homely,
fortunately I am not yet old.
If there is someone who can give a thousand gold pieces as a gift,
I will then sell myself off.
Then you will have a wife,
land, and a house, all ready.
How is this plan?”
Huáng turned pale,
not knowing why.
The woman smiled and said:
“Don't be anxious.
There are indeed many beautiful women in the world.
Who would be willing to buy me for a thousand gold pieces?
Just speak of it playfully outside
to observe whether such a person exists or not.
To sell or not to sell
is entirely up to you.”
Huáng refused.
The woman spoke to the boatman’s wife herself.
The wife looked at Huáng,
and Huáng vaguely assented.
Not long after the wife left,
she returned and said:
“A merchant’s son on the neighboring boat
is willing to offer eight hundred.”
Huáng deliberately shook his head to make it difficult.
Before long,
she came back again,
saying the offer was as requested,
and immediately invited him to cross boats to complete the exchange.
Huáng subtly smiled.
The woman said:
“Tell him to wait for a moment;
I will instruct Huáng Láng,
and he will leave immediately.”
The woman said to Huáng:
“I have served you with a body worth a thousand pieces of gold every day.
Do you just now realize this?”
Huáng asked:
“With what words should I dismiss him?”
The woman said:
“Please immediately draw up the deed,
whether to leave or not is entirely up to me.”
Huáng disagreed.
The woman pressed him,
and Huáng, having no choice, went there.
The payment was exchanged immediately.
Huáng ordered the money to be sealed and marked,
saying:
“Because of poverty,
it indeed came to this.
This separation,
if my wife does not agree,
I will return the original gold to redeem you.”
As the gold was being carried to the boat,
the woman had already boarded the merchant's boat from the stern with the boatman’s wife,
looking back from afar to bid farewell,
without any trace of sorrowful attachment.
Huáng’s soul was shocked out of his body,
unable to speak.
Presently, the merchant’s boat untied its纜 and
departed with the swiftness of an arrow.
Huáng cried out loudly,
wanting to pursue and stop it.
The boatman refused
and steered the boat southward.
In an instant, they reached Zhènjiāng,
and the money was transported ashore.
The boatman quickly untied his boat and left.
Huáng sat dejectedly, guarding his luggage,
having nowhere to go.
He gazed at the surging river water,
which felt like a myriad of pickaxes tearing at his body.
While he was secretly weeping,
he suddenly heard a delicate voice calling
“Huáng Láng!”
Astonished, he looked back,
and the woman was already ahead.
Overjoyed,
he carried his luggage and followed her,
asking:
“How did you manage to come so quickly?”
The woman smiled and said:
“If I had delayed a few more moments,
you would have become suspicious.”
Huáng then suspected her to be extraordinary
and insisted on questioning her about the situation.
The woman smiled and said,
“Throughout my life, I break those who are stingy,
and deceive those who are evil.
If I had truly consulted you,
you would certainly not have agreed.
How else could I have obtained a thousand pieces of gold?
Your moneybag is full,
and the pearls of Hépǔ have returned.
You should be fortunate enough.
Why ask further?”
Then she hired a porter to carry the moneybag,
and they went together.
Inside the water gate,
a south-facing residence
was entered directly.
Soon, an old man and woman, men and women,
came out in a flurry to welcome them,
all saying:
“Huáng Láng has arrived!”
Huáng entered to pay respects to the elders.
Two young men bowed, sat, and conversed with him;
these were the woman's elder brother Dàláng and third brother Sānláng.
At the banquet, there were not many dishes,
but four jade plates
already filled the table.
Chicken, crab, goose, and fish
were all neatly cut into cylinders.
The young men poured wine in large bowls, their conversation bold and unrestrained.
After a while, they were led to a separate courtyard,
for the husband and wife to stay together.
The quilts and pillows were soft and smooth,
and the bed was made of processed leather instead of palm fiber and rattan.
Every day, a maid brought three warm meals,
and the woman sometimes did not go out for the entire day.
Huáng, living alone, felt bored and miserable,
and repeatedly spoke of returning.
The woman firmly stopped him.
One day,
she said to Huáng:
“Now I will make a plan for you: please buy a person
for the sake of an heir.
However, buying a maid or concubine is expensive;
we should pretend I have an elder brother
and let my father discuss a marriage with him.
It won't be difficult to obtain a good family's daughter.”
Huáng disagreed.
The woman did not listen.
There was a newly widowed daughter of a scholar, Zhāng Gòngshì.
A betrothal gift of one hundred strings of cash was proposed,
and the woman insisted on marrying her.
The new bride's given name was Āměi,
and she was quite gentle and exquisite.
The woman’s sister-in-law called her;
Huáng felt uneasy and uncomfortable,
but the woman was quite composed.
Another day,
she said to Huáng:
“I will go with my elder sister to Nánhǎi
to visit my aunt.
I should return in about a month.
Please, husband and wife, live peacefully.”
Then she left.
The couple lived alone in one courtyard.
Food and drink were provided on time,
and they were very generously supplied.
However, since entering the door,
no one had ever come again to their room.
Every morning,
Āměi would visit Wēn,
say a word or two, and then withdraw.
The sisters-in-law nearby
would only exchange a smile.
Even after lingering and sitting for a long time,
they did not engage in friendly conversation.
Huáng saw Wēng,
and it was the same.
Occasionally, when the young masters were gathered, talking,
Huáng would arrive,
and they would all fall silent.
Huáng was perplexed and had no one to confide in.
Āměi noticed this,
and questioned him, saying:
"Since you are like brothers to the young masters,
why have you been like a stranger for the past month?"
Huáng was flustered and couldn't answer,
stuttering:
"I have been abroad for ten years,
and have only just returned."
Měi then meticulously inquired about the Wēng-Gū's prominent family background,
and the co-wives' neighborhood residence.
Huáng was greatly embarrassed,
unable to conceal it any longer,
and the whole truth was revealed.
The woman wept, saying:
"Although my family is poor,
we do not have those who demean concubines.
No wonder all the Wǎnrúo despise me and do not count me among them!"
Huáng was terrified, not knowing what to plan,
and could only kneel for a long time, listening to the woman's command.
Měi wiped her tears and pulled him up,
then asked him what he intended to do.
Huáng said:
"How dare I make other plans?
My only course is to leave by myself."
The woman said:
"Having married and then returned,
how could my feelings bear it?
Although she was the first to follow you,
that was private;
although I arrived later,
that was public.
It would be better to wait for her to return,
and then ask her, since she initiated this plan,
what she intends to do with me?"
After several months,
the woman still did not return.
One night,
they heard boisterous drinking from the guest house.
Huáng secretly went to peek,
and saw two guests in military attire seated at the head: one wrapped in leopard skin,
stern as a celestial deity;
the one facing east
wore a helmet made of tiger-head leather,
the tiger's mouth clasping his forehead,
with nose and ears all present.
He returned in astonishment,
and told Āměi,
but they still couldn't fathom who the Huò father and son were.
The couple was filled with suspicion and fear,
and planned to rent lodging elsewhere,
but also feared arousing their suspicion.
Huáng said:
"I'll tell you the truth, my dear: even if the Nánhǎi person returns,
the evidence is already settled,
and I cannot make a home here.
Now I want to take you away,
but I fear your esteemed elders will have other objections.
It would be better to part for now;
I will return within two years.
If you can wait,
then wait;
if you wish to go elsewhere,
that is also your own decision."
Āměi wanted to tell her parents and follow him,
but Huáng refused.
Āměi wept,
demanded a solemn oath,
and then parted and returned home.
Huáng then bid farewell to Wēng-Gū.
At that time, all the young masters were out,
and Wēng urged him to stay and wait for their return,
but Huáng did not listen and left.
He boarded the boat disconsolately,
his spirit lost.
Upon reaching Guāzhōu,
he suddenly looked back and saw a sail approaching,
speeding like flight;
as it drew closer,
the one sitting at the bow with a sword at his side
was Huò Dàláng.
He called out from afar:
"You wished to abandon your wife and return,
why did you not consult me again?
If you leave your wife,
who can wait for two or three years?"
As he spoke,
their boat was already close.
Āměi emerged from the other boat,
Dàláng helped her board Huáng's boat,
then jumped back and left directly.
Before this,
when Āměi had returned,
she was just about to weep and tell her parents,
when Dàláng suddenly brought a palanquin to their door,
threatened them with his sword,
and forced the woman to leave swiftly.
The whole family held their breath in fear,
not daring to stop or question.
The woman described the situation.
Huáng did not understand the meaning,
but was very happy to have Měi,
so he set sail and departed.
Upon reaching home,
he invested in business,
and became quite wealthy.
Āměi often worried about her parents,
and wanted Huáng to go visit them;
but also feared that with the Huò woman having come,
there would again be discrepancies between the principal wife and concubine.
Not long after,
Zhāng Wēng visited,
and seeing the house well-maintained,
he felt quite relieved,
and said to the woman:
"After you left,
I immediately went to the Huò family to inquire,
and saw that the gate was already locked,
and the landlord also did not know about it.
For half a year, there was no news.
Your mother wept day and night,
saying you had been deceived and taken away by a scoundrel,
and she didn't know where you were wandering.
Now, fortunately, you are safe?"
Huáng truthfully told him the situation,
and thus they suspected them to be spirits.
Later, Āměi gave birth to a son,
named Xiāncì.
When he was over ten years old,
his mother sent him to Zhènjiāng.
Upon reaching the borders of Yángzhōu,
he rested at an inn,
and all his attendants went out.
A woman came,
led the boy into another room,
drew the curtain,
held him on her lap,
and smilingly asked his name;
the boy told her.
She asked:
"What is the meaning of your name?"
He replied:
"I don't know."
The woman said:
"Go home and ask your father; you will know then."
She then tied his hair into a bun,
and took a flower from her own bun to use as a hairpin for him;
she put a golden bracelet on his wrist.
She also put some gold into his sleeve,
saying:
"Take this to buy books to read."
The boy asked who she was,
and she said:
"Does the child not know that he has another mother?
Go tell your father: Zhū Dàxīng died without a coffin;
he should help him,
do not forget."
The old servant returned to the room,
having lost his young master;
he looked for him in the other room,
heard him talking to someone,
and peeking,
saw it was his former mistress.
He coughed lightly outside the curtain,
intending to speak.
The woman pushed the boy onto the bed,
and had vanished in a flash.
He asked the innkeeper,
but no one knew anything.
After several days,
he returned from Zhènjiāng,
told Huáng,
and also showed him the gifts.
Huáng sighed with endless emotion.
When he inquired about Zhū,
he had indeed died just three days prior,
his body exposed and not yet buried,
so Huáng generously helped with the burial.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Is this woman a celestial being?
Changing her owner three times does not count as chaste.
However, for the stingy, she broke their miserliness;
for the lecherous, she hastened their depravity.
The woman was not heartless.
Yet, once broken, there is no need for her pity.
As for the bones of greed, lechery, vileness, and stinginess,
why pity them in a ditch?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Wáng Yùpíngzi from Píngyáng,
going to take the examination in the northern capital,
rented lodgings at Bàoguósì.
In the temple, there was a student from Yúháng already staying there.
Wáng, living next door to him,
presented his calling card.
The student did not reply.
Meeting him morning and evening,
he was often rude.
Wáng was angered by his arrogance and impudence, and their acquaintance ceased.
One day,
a young man was strolling in the temple,
wearing white clothes, a skirt, and a hat,
looking majestic from a distance.
When Wáng approached and conversed with him,
his words were witty and marvelous.
Wáng admired and respected him in his heart.
When asked about his native place and clan,
he said:
"My surname is Zhū from Dēngzhōu."
Wáng then ordered his servant to set up seats,
and they chatted happily face to face.
The Yúháng student happened to pass by.
They both rose to offer him a seat.
The student actually took the principal seat,
without any modesty. Suddenly, he asked Zhū:
"Are you also entering the examination hall?"
Zhū replied,
"No.
With the talent of a worn-out horse,
I have long had no ambition to gallop high."
He then asked:
"Which province are you from?"
Zhū told him.
The student said:
"To not pursue advancement truly shows your high intelligence.
There isn't a single person of learning in the provinces to the east and west of the mountains."
Zhū said:
"Northerners are indeed less learned,
but those who are not learned are not necessarily me;
Southerners are indeed more learned,
but those who are learned are not necessarily you."
Having spoken,
he clapped his hands.
Wáng joined in,
and the room burst into laughter.
The student, ashamed and angry,
raised his eyebrows and rolled up his sleeves, saying loudly:
"Dare you be given a topic right now
to compare literary works?"
Zhū looked away and sneered, saying:
"What is there to dare not do!"
Then he went to his lodging,
took out a classic, and handed it to Wáng.
Wáng casually flipped through it,
pointed, and said:
"'The children of the noble families are being sent on a mission.'"
The student rose,
asking for writing brushes and paper.
Zhū pulled him back, saying:
"You can recite it aloud.
My opening is already formed: 'In a place where guests come and go,
one sees a completely ignorant person.'"
Wáng burst out laughing, holding his belly.
The student angrily said:
"Completely unable to write, merely resorting to insults,
how can you be a person!"
Wáng tried his best to mediate,
requesting another good topic.
He flipped again and said:
"'There were three benevolent men in Yīn.'"
Zhū immediately responded:
"The three men did not follow the same path,
yet their ultimate aim was one.
What was that one thing?
It was benevolence.
A junzǐ is merely benevolent,
why must they be the same?"
The student then stopped writing,
rose, and said:
"This person has a little talent."
Then he left.
Wáng consequently respected Zhū even more.
He invited him to his lodging,
and they talked cordially for a long time.
Wáng brought out all his compositions for Zhū to review.
Zhū read through them extremely quickly;
in less than a quarter of an hour, he had finished a hundred pieces,
saying:
"You are also deeply immersed in this path.
However, when you put pen to paper,
you do not have the thought of 'must achieve a result,'
but still harbor a hope of 'luckily achieving,'
which alone places you in a lower category."
Then he took the reviewed pieces one by one
and "explained them.
Wáng was greatly delighted,
treating him as a teacher;
he had the cook prepare shuǐjiǎo with cane sugar.
Zhū ate them and found them sweet,
saying:
"I have never tasted this flavor in my life;
please have them made again another day."
From then on, they got along very happily.
Zhū would arrive every three to five days,
and Wáng would always prepare shuǐjiǎo for him.
The Yúháng student occasionally met him,
and though he did not converse much,
his arrogant air significantly diminished.
One day,
he showed his examination writings to Zhū.
Zhū saw that his friends' praises were already effusive,
glanced at it once,
pushed it onto the table,
and said nothing.
The student suspected he hadn't read it,
and asked him again.
Zhū replied that he had finished reading it.
The student then suspected he didn't understand.
Zhū said:
"What's difficult to understand?
It's just not good!"
The student said,
"With one glance, there are so many red and yellow marks,
how can it be not good?"
Zhū then recited his essay,
as if he had read it before.
He recited and criticized it simultaneously.
The student cowered and sweated,
leaving without a word.
After a while,
Zhū left;
the student entered,
insisting that Wáng write something.
Wáng refused.
The student forcibly searched and found it,
seeing many circles and dots in the text,
he laughed and said:
"This is very much like shuǐjiǎo!"
Wáng was naturally simple and earnest,
and only looked sheepish.
The next day,
Zhū arrived,
and Wáng told him everything.
Zhū angrily said:
"I thought 'Southerners would never rebel again.'
How dare those vulgar Chǔ people be so!
I must surely have a way to retaliate!"
Wáng earnestly presented the warning against frivolity to persuade him,
and Zhū was deeply grateful and impressed.
After the examination,
he showed his essay to Sòng,
who was quite appreciative.
He happened to be walking through the palace halls
when he saw a blind monk sitting in the corridor,
setting out medicines and practicing healing.
Lái exclaimed,
"This is a remarkable man!
He is most skilled at understanding literature,
we must ask for his instruction."
Thereupon, he ordered Guī-Qín to fetch the essays.
He met Yúháng-Shēng
and they came together.
Wáng addressed the monk as "master" and consulted him.
The monk, thinking he was asking for medical advice,
immediately inquired about his symptoms.
Wáng explained his intention to seek instruction.
The monk laughed, saying,
"Who has been so talkative?
How can I comment on literature without eyes?"
Wáng requested that his ears serve as his eyes.
The monk said,
"Three essays, over two thousand characters—
who has the patience to listen to them all?
It's better to burn them;
I can perceive them with my nose."
Wáng complied.
Each time an essay was burned,
the monk would sniff and nod, saying,
"You are initially imitating the great masters.
Though not yet truly authentic,
it is quite close.
I have received it with my spleen."
He asked,
"Is it passable?"
He replied,
"It is passable."
Yúháng-Shēng was not yet fully convinced,
so he first burned an essay by an ancient great master to test him.
The monk sniffed again and said,
"Marvelous!
I have received this essay with my heart;
without Guī or Hú, who could achieve this?"
Shēng was greatly astonished.
Then he burned his own essay.
The monk said,
"I just received a piece of art,
not yet a full view of the leopard.
Why has a different person suddenly come?"
Shēng gave the excuse,
"This is a friend's work,
only this one piece;
this is my own work."
The monk sniffed the remaining ashes,
coughed several times,
and said,
"Do not throw any more in!
It is stuck and cannot go down;
I forced myself to receive it with my diaphragm.
If you burn another,
it will make me sick."
Shēng retreated in shame.
A few days later, the results were posted,
and Shēng indeed passed the examination;
Wáng failed.
Shēng and Wáng went to tell the monk.
The monk sighed, saying,
"Although I am blind in my eyes,
I am not blind in my nose.
The people behind the curtain are blind even in their noses!"
Soon after, Yúháng-Shēng arrived,
full of pride,
saying,
"Blind monk,
do you also eat people's dumplings?
How about it now?"
The monk said,
"What I commented on was literature;
I did not intend to discuss your fate.
You try to find the essays of the examination officials,
take one piece from each and burn it,
and I will know who your teacher is."
Shēng and Wáng searched for them all,
finding only eight or nine people.
Shēng said,
"If there is any mistake,
what will be the punishment?"
The monk indignantly said,
"Pluck out my blind eyes!"
Shēng burned them.
For each essay,
he said it was not right.
When it came to the sixth piece,
the monk suddenly exclaimed indignantly,
"Pluck out my blind eyes!"
Shēng burned them.
For each essay,
he said it was not right.
When it came to the sixth piece,
he suddenly vomited violently towards the wall,
expelling gas like thunder.
Everyone agreed it was true.
The monk wiped his eyes and said to Shēng,
"This is truly your teacher!
I didn't know at first and sniffed it suddenly.
It pricked my nose,
and stung my stomach.
My chest could not contain it,
so it went straight out from my lower parts!"
Shēng was furious,
and left,
saying,
"You will see tomorrow,
don't regret it,
don't regret it!"
Two or three days later,
he still didn't come.
They looked,
and he had already moved away.
Then they realized he was indeed a certain official's protégé.
Zhū consoled Wáng, saying,
"All of us scholars
should not blame others,
but should overcome ourselves: not blaming others makes virtue more expansive,
being able to overcome oneself makes learning more advanced.
Failing this time
is indeed due to unfortunate circumstances;
but frankly speaking,
your essay is not yet at its peak.
If you use this to spur yourself on,
there will naturally be silent judges in the world."
Wáng stood up respectfully.
He also heard that the provincial examination would be held again next year,
so he did not return home,
but stayed to receive instruction.
Sòng said,
"In the capital, firewood is as expensive as cassia and rice as pearls.
Don't worry about living expenses.
Behind my house there is a cellar with money,
you can use it."
He immediately showed him the spot.
Wáng thanked him, saying,
"In ancient times, Dòu and Fàn were poor but incorruptible.
If I am fortunate enough to support myself,
how dare I defile myself?"
One day, Wáng was drunk and fell asleep.
His servants and attendants secretly opened the cellar.
Wáng suddenly awoke and
heard a sound from behind the house.
He secretly went out and found gold piled on the ground.
Their intentions were exposed,
and they were all intimidated.
While he was rebuking them,
he saw some golden goblets,
many of them inscribed.
Upon closer inspection,
they all bore his grandfather's given name.
It turned out that Wáng's grandfather had once been a Nánbù Láng
and had stayed in this residence.
He died of a sudden illness,
and the gold was his inheritance.
Wáng was delighted,
weighing over eight hundred taels of gold.
The next day, he told Sòng
and showed him the goblets,
wanting to divide it with him,
but Sòng firmly refused.
He took a hundred taels of gold to give to the substitute monk,
but the monk had already left.
Several months passed,
and his diligent study intensified.
When the examination came,
Sòng said,
"If you don't succeed in this battle,
then it truly is fate!"
Soon after, he was dismissed for an infraction.
Wáng still said nothing;
Sòng cried loudly,
unable to stop.
Wáng, in turn, comforted and soothed him.
Sòng said:
"I am resented by the Creator,
and have been in distress all my life.
Now I have even implicated a good friend.
It is fate!
It is fate!"
Wáng said:
"All things indeed have their fixed number,
but if a gentleman like you has no will to strive,
it is not fate."
Sòng wiped away his tears and said:
"I have long wanted to speak,
fearing I would startle you.
I am not a living person,
but a wandering soul.
In my youth, I had a reputation for talent,
but I did not achieve my ambition in the examinations.
Feigning madness, I went to the capital,
hoping that someone who understood me
would pass down my writings.
In the year of Jiǎshēn,
I tragically died,
and have been drifting ever since.
Fortunately, we became close,
so I tried my best to
'attack with stones from other hills.'
My lifelong unfulfilled wish
was truly to borrow a good friend to achieve it once.
Now that the misfortune of writing is like this,
who can remain indifferent?!"
Wáng was also moved to tears,
and asked:
"Why are you delayed?"
He replied:
"Last year, the Heavenly Emperor commanded
Xuānshèng and Yánluó Wáng to investigate the '劫鬼 (jiéguǐ)' [souls who died in calamities],
the superior ones to be appointed to various offices,
and the rest to be immediately reincarnated.
My humble name has already been recorded,
but what I haven't yet submitted to [the underworld office]
is that I wished to witness a moment of success.
Now, please, let us part!"
Wáng asked:
"What position are you being considered for?"
He replied:
"There is a vacancy for a Sīwénláng in the Zǐtóng Prefecture,
but for now a deaf and ignorant person is temporarily in charge,
which is why the literary fate is in disarray.
If by some chance I am lucky enough to obtain this post,
I will make the sacred teachings flourish."
The next day,
Sòng arrived joyfully,
and said:
"My wish has been fulfilled!
Xuānshèng commanded me to write a 'Xìngdàolùn' [Treatise on Nature and the Way].
He looked at it with pleasure,
and said I was fit to be a Sīwén.
Yánluó checked the ledger,
and wanted to reject me
due to '口孽 (kǒuniè)' [sins of the mouth],
but Xuānshèng argued for me,
and so I got the position.
I prostrated myself and thanked him,
and he called me closer to the table,
and instructed me, saying: 'Now, out of pity for your talent,
I have promoted you to an important position;
you must cleanse your heart and diligently perform your duties,
and not repeat your former mistakes.'
From this, one can see that the underworld values virtue even more than literature.
You must still be lacking in cultivation,
but accumulate good deeds without slackening, and that will be sufficient."
Wáng asked:
"If that's the case,
where is Yúháng's virtue?"
He replied:
"I don't know.
But the rewards and punishments of the underworld
are all perfectly just.
Even the blind monk from the other day
was also a ghost;
he was a famous scholar from a previous dynasty.
Because he discarded too much paper with writing on it during his lifetime,
he was punished by becoming blind.
He himself wanted to heal people's suffering
to atone for his past sins,
hence he wandered in the marketplaces."
Wáng ordered wine to be set out.
Sòng said:
"No need.
The disturbance of the whole year
ends at this moment.
Just prepare some '水角 (shuǐjiǎo)' [water dumplings] for me, and that will be enough."
Wáng was sad and did not eat,
and sat watching Sòng eat by himself.
In a moment,
he had already finished three servings,
and, holding his stomach, said:
"This meal can sustain me for three days.
I eat it to commemorate your virtue.
What I ate earlier
is all behind the house,
and has already turned into mushrooms.
Keep them as medicine;
they can benefit your children's intelligence."
Wáng asked about their next meeting,
and he said:
"Since I have an official responsibility,
I should avoid further association."
He then asked:
"If I make an offering and pray
in the Zǐtóng temple,
can it reach you?"
He replied:
"All that is useless.
The Nine Heavens are very far.
Just keep yourself pure and act diligently,
and the local earth deities will report it,
then I will certainly know of it."
Having spoken,
he bid farewell and disappeared.
Wáng looked behind the house,
and indeed purple mushrooms had grown.
He picked them and stored them.
Nearby, a new mound of earth had risen,
and the '水角 (shuǐjiǎo)' were distinctly there.
Wáng returned,
and diligently disciplined himself even more.
One night,
he dreamt that Sòng arrived in a grand carriage,
and said:
"You once, in a moment of anger,
accidentally killed a maid,
and your official salary was removed;
now, your diligent conduct has atoned for it.
However, your fate is too thin to hold an official position."
That year,
he passed the provincial examination;
the next year,
he passed the metropolitan examination again.
Subsequently, he no longer served as an official.
He had two sons,
one of whom was extremely dull.
He fed him the mushrooms,
and the son became greatly intelligent.
Later, he went to Jīnlíng for a reason,
and met Xú Háng in an inn,
where they spoke at length about their separation,
and Xú Háng greatly humbled himself,
but his temples were already streaked with grey.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Mù Shēng,
a native of Chángshā.
His family was poor,
and in winter, he had no padded clothes.
One evening, as he sat alone,
a woman entered.
Her clothes were dazzling, but her complexion was dark and ugly.
She smiled and said:
"Are you not cold?"
Mù Shēng was startled and asked her,
and she replied:
"I am a fox immortal.
I pity your loneliness,
so I have come to warm your cold bed with you."
Mù Shēng feared her fox nature,
and was disgusted by her ugliness,
and cried out loudly.
The woman placed a silver ingot on the table,
and said:
"If we get along well,
I will give you this as a gift."
Mù Shēng was pleased and agreed.
There were no mattress or bedding on the bed,
so the woman replaced them with her robe.
As dawn approached,
she got up and instructed him, saying:
"With the gift,
you can quickly buy soft cloth to make bedding;
for the rest, make padded clothes for warmth,
that will be enough.
If we can have a lasting good relationship,
you need not worry about poverty."
Then she left.
Mù Shēng told his wife,
and his wife was also happy,
and immediately bought cloth to sew for him.
The woman arrived that night,
and seeing the new bedding,
she said happily:
"Your wife is very diligent!"
She left gold to reward her.
From then on, there was no empty evening.
Each time she left,
she would leave something behind.
More than a year later,
his house was clean and tidy,
and everyone, inside and out, wore fine silk and brocade,
becoming a wealthy commoner.
The woman’s bribes and gifts gradually decreased,
which made Shēng dislike her.
He hired a Daoist priest
who drew talismans on his door.
The woman bit off the talismans and discarded them,
then entered and pointed at Shēng, saying:
“To be so ungrateful and heartless,
you have reached an extreme!
However, what can this do to me?
If you despise me,
I will leave on my own.
But since our affection is broken,
what I have given you
must be repaid!”
She left in a rage.
Shēng was terrified
and told the Daoist priest.
The priest set up an altar;
before his arrangements were complete,
he suddenly tumbled to the ground,
blood flowing over his cheeks.
When they looked,
one ear had been cut off.
Everyone was greatly frightened
and scattered.
The Daoist priest also covered his ear and fled.
Stones were thrown in the room as if from a basin,
and doors, windows, cauldrons, and steamers
were all shattered.
Shēng cowered under the bed,
trembling and sweating profusely.
Suddenly, he saw the woman enter, holding an object,
which had a cat’s head and a small dog’s tail.
She placed it in front of the bed
and incited it, saying:
“Hehe,
you can chew the feet of this treacherous man.”
The creature immediately gnawed at his shoes,
its teeth sharper than a blade.
Shēng was greatly afraid
and tried to curl up and hide,
but his limbs could not move.
The creature gnawed at his toes,
making a crisp, clear sound.
Shēng was in extreme pain
and cried out in lament.
The woman said:
“Bring out all your gold and pearls,
do not hide anything.”
Shēng agreed.
The woman said:
“Hēhē!”
The creature then stopped.
Shēng could not get up,
but only told her where they were.
The woman went to search for herself.
Besides the pearls, jade, and clothes,
she only found a little over two hundred taels of gold.
The woman found it insufficient
and again said:
“Xīxī!”
The creature chewed again.
Shēng cried out in agony, begging for mercy.
The woman set a limit of ten days
to repay six hundred taels of gold.
Shēng agreed, and the woman then left with the creature.
After a long time,
his family members gradually gathered,
pulled Shēng out from under the bed.
His feet were covered in blood,
and he had lost two toes.
Looking at the room,
all his valuables were gone,
only the tattered quilt from that year remained.
They used it to cover Shēng,
who was now lying down.
Fearing she would return in ten days,
he sold his maidservant and clothes
to make up the amount.
When the date arrived,
the woman indeed came.
He quickly paid her,
and she left without a word.
From then on, the contact ceased.
Shēng’s foot wounds
took half a year of medicine to heal,
and his family was as poor as before.
The fox then approached a man named Yú Zǐ in a nearby village.
Yú worked as a farmer,
and his family was not wealthy.
Within three years,
he had joined the ranks of the gentry by donating grain,
his splendid houses extended continuously,
and the luxurious clothes he wore
were half from Shēng’s former possessions.
Shēng saw this
but dared not ask.
One day, he happened to go to the countryside
and met the woman on the road.
He knelt down by the roadside.
The woman said nothing,
but wrapped five or six taels of gold in a plain cloth
and threw it to him from a distance,
then turned and left directly.
Later, Yú Shì died prematurely,
but the woman still occasionally visited his home,
and the gold and silk in the house would disappear.
Yú Zǐ saw her coming
and bowed to her,
praying from afar:
“My father has passed away,
and we children are all like your own.
Even if you don’t care for us,
how can you bear to let us sit in poverty?”
The woman left
and never returned.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“When an evil creature arrives,
killing it is brave;
but having received its kindness,
even a ghost cannot be betrayed.
To kill Zhào Mèng after gaining power,
this would be condemned by the wise and heroic.
If something is not what a person truly desires in their heart,
then even ten thousand *zhōng* of grain cannot move them.
Looking at her joy upon seeing gold,
is it also where her interest lies,
causing her to ruin her body and disgrace her conduct without hesitation?
Alas for the greedy,
who ultimately suffer ruin and defeat!”
According to the Chuìxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Sūn Gōngzǐ of Luòyáng,
named Qí,
married the daughter of Jiǎng Tàishǒu,
and they were very much in love.
At twenty, she died prematurely,
and he was overcome with grief.
He left home
to live in a separate estate in the mountains.
It happened to be a rainy day,
and he was napping in the daytime.
No one was in the room.
Suddenly, he saw a woman’s feet appear
from under the curtain of the inner room.
He was puzzled and asked about it.
A young woman,
around eighteen or nineteen years old,
entered through the curtain.
Her clothes were plain and clean,
but she was slightly dark-skinned and had many freckles,
resembling a girl from a poor family.
He supposed she must be someone renting a house in the village,
and scolded her, saying:
“You should inform the family of what you need;
how can you just enter casually!”
The woman smiled faintly and said:
"This concubine is not from this village.
My ancestral home is Shāndōng,
my surname is Lǚ.
My father was a scholar.
My pet name is Wúbìng.
I followed my father on his travels,
and left my parents early.
I admire the公子's noble family and reputation as a scholar,
and I wish to be a literary maid like Kāngchéng's."
Sūn smiled and said:
"Your intention is very good.
However, my servants live in crowded conditions,
which would truly be inconvenient.
When I return home,
I will arrange for a carriage and formally betroth you."
The woman hesitantly said:
"Considering my humble and inferior qualities,
how dare I aspire to be an equal match?
I merely wish to serve at your desk,
and I will not even make the mistake of holding books upside down."
Sūn said:
"Taking a maid also requires an auspicious day."
He then pointed to the shelf,
and told her to fetch the fourth volume of the almanac.
—This was to test her.
The woman flipped through and found it.
She first perused it herself,
and then presented it,
smiling and saying:
"Today, Héquí is not in the room."
Sūn's heart was slightly moved,
and he kept her hidden in his room.
The woman, having nothing to do in her leisure,
dusted his desk, tidied his books,
burned incense, and wiped the censers,
making the entire room bright and clean.
Sūn was pleased with her.
By evening,
he sent his servants to sleep elsewhere.
The woman lowered her eyebrows and eyelashes,
serving him with utmost diligence.
When he ordered her to sleep,
she finally took the candle and left.
In the middle of the night, Sūn awoke,
and it seemed as if someone was sleeping by his bed;
he reached out his hand to feel,
and knew it was the woman,
so he grabbed and shook her.
The woman started up in surprise,
and stood by the bed.
Sūn said:
"Why don't you sleep elsewhere?
Is the bedside your sleeping place?"
The woman said:
"This concubine is easily frightened."
Sūn pitied her,
and spread a pillow inside the bed.
Suddenly, he smelled her breath,
which was as pure as a lotus bud,
and he found it unusual;
he called her to share the pillow,
and found his heart stirred;
gradually, they shared the same quilt,
and he was greatly pleased with her.
He thought that hiding her was not a good plan,
and also feared that taking her home would invite gossip.
Sūn had a maternal aunt,
who lived just over ten doors away.
He planned to have her temporarily stay at his aunt's house,
and then bring her back later.
The woman agreed,
and immediately said:
"Auntie,
this concubine knows her well,
there's no need to notify her in advance,
please let me go now."
Sūn saw her off,
and she climbed over the wall and left.
Sūn's maternal aunt was
a lonely old woman.
She opened her door at dawn,
and the woman slipped in.
The old woman questioned her,
and she replied:
"Your nephew sent me to ask about you, Auntie.
The公子 wishes to return home,
but the road is long and he lacks a mount,
so he asked his servant to temporarily stay here."
The old woman believed her.
So she stayed there.
When Sūn returned,
he falsely claimed that his aunt's family had a maid
they wished to give him,
and sent someone to carry her back,
keeping her by his side whether sitting or sleeping.
Over time, he grew even fonder of her,
and took her as a concubine.
When noble families proposed marriages,
he always refused them,
seemingly intent on spending his life with her.
The woman knew this,
and strongly urged him to marry;
so he married into the Xǔ family,
but still doted on Wúbìng.
Madame Xǔ was very virtuous,
and hardly ever disputed over Sūn's time;
Wúbìng served Madame Xǔ with even greater respect: thus, the principal wife and concubine got along well.
Madame Xǔ gave birth to a son, Ājiān,
whom Wúbìng loved and embraced as if he were her own child.
When the child was just three years old,
he would leave his wet nurse
to sleep with Wúbìng,
and Madame Xǔ could not call him away.
Before long,
Madame Xǔ fell ill and died.
Before her death,
she instructed Sūn, saying:
"Wúbìng loves our child the most,
so you may let her be the child's mother;
you may even enthrone her as the principal wife."
After the burial,
Sūn intended to act on her words,
and informed his clan members,
who all deemed it impermissible;
the woman also firmly refused,
so he stopped.
In the district, there was a daughter of Wáng Tiānguān,
newly widowed,
who came to seek marriage.
Sūn Yǎ did not wish to marry her,
but Wáng again pressed the matter.
The matchmaker spoke of her beauty,
and the clan admired her influence,
so they all urged him on.
Sūn was confused,
and married her.
Her looks were indeed dazzling;
but her arrogance was excessive.
Clothing and utensils
were often disliked and scorned,
and she would readily destroy them.
Out of love and respect, Sūn
could not bear to cross her in anything.
Within a few months of entering the household,
she monopolized his favor and the main chamber,
while Wúbìng was called to her presence even without illness,
and both laughter and tears were considered offenses.
At times, her anger would turn to her husband,
and they frequently quarreled and fought.
Sūn suffered greatly from this,
and often slept alone.
The wife again grew angry.
Sūn could no longer endure it,
so he made an excuse to go to the capital,
fleeing the difficulty posed by his wife.
The wife blamed Wúbìng for his distant travels.
Wúbìng bowed and held her breath,
trying to please her,
but the wife was never pleased.
At night, she made Wúbìng sleep directly under the bed,
and her son followed her.
Whenever Wúbìng was called to perform a task,
the son would cry.
The wife grew annoyed and cursed him.
Wúbìng quickly called the wet nurse to hold him,
but he wouldn't go;
when forced,
he cried even more.
The wife rose in anger,
and cruelly whipped him countless times,
before he finally went with the wet nurse.
Because of this, the child became ill and convulsed,
refusing to eat.
The wife forbade Wúbìng from seeing him.
The child cried all day,
and the wife scolded the wet nurse,
telling her to throw him on the ground.
The child, his breath exhausted and voice hoarse,
called out begging for a drink;
the wife warned them not to give him any.
As evening approached,
Wúbìng, seeing the wife was absent,
secretly gave the child a drink.
When the child saw her,
he threw away the water and clutched her clothes,
crying inconsolably.
When the wife heard this,
she emerged with a furious temper.
The child, hearing her voice, stopped crying,
and with a single jump, suddenly died.
Wúbìng wept bitterly.
The wife angrily said:
“You base maid, what an ugly display!
Are you trying to threaten me with the child's death?!
Never mind the infants of the Sūn family;
even if I kill the heir of the Wáng mansion,
the daughter of Wáng Tiānguān can still bear it!”
Wúbìng then suppressed her sobs and tears,
and asked for funeral arrangements.
The wife refused,
and immediately ordered the body to be discarded.
When the wife left,
Wúbìng secretly stroked the child;
his four limbs were still warm.
She whispered to the wet nurse:
“You must quickly take him away,
wait for a while in the wilderness,
and I will follow.
If he is dead,
we will discard him together;
if he is alive,
we will raise him together.”
The wet nurse said:
“Yes.”
Wúbìng entered the room,
took out her hairpins and earrings,
and caught up with them.
They both looked at the child,
who had already revived.
The two were overjoyed,
and planned to head to another property,
to rely on her aunt.
The wet nurse worried that her small steps would be a hindrance,
so Wúbìng ran ahead to wait for her,
swift as a whirlwind.
The wet nurse had to run with all her might to catch up.
After about two *gēng* (hours),
the child's condition became critical,
and they could not go on.
So they detoured into a village,
arrived at the house of an old farmer,
waited at the door until dawn,
knocked on the door to borrow a room,
took out her hairpins and earrings to exchange for money,
and summoned both shamans and doctors,
but the child's illness ultimately did not improve.
The woman covered her face and wept, saying:
“Wet nurse, please take good care of the child;
I am going to find his father.”
The wet nurse was still astonished by her delusion,
when the woman had already vanished.
The wet nurse was filled with endless shock and bewilderment.
On that day,
Sūn was in the capital,
resting on his bed,
when the woman quietly entered.
Sūn was startled and rose, saying:
“Have I already dreamt this while just falling asleep?!”
The woman grasped his hand and choked back sobs,
stamping her foot but unable to utter a sound.
After a long, long time,
she finally cried out and said:
“Your concubine has endured a thousand hardships,
and with our child escaped to Yáng—”
Before she finished the sentence,
she burst into loud sobs,
fell to the ground, and vanished.
Sūn was utterly horrified,
still doubting if it was a dream;
he called his attendants to look at her together,
and her clothes and shoes were clearly there,
which was extremely strange and incomprehensible.
Immediately, he packed his bags,
and galloped back like a shooting star.
When [Sūn] heard that his son had died and his concubine had fled,
he clasped his chest in great sorrow.
He spoke harshly to his wife,
but the wife retorted.
[Sūn] was enraged
and drew a white blade;
maidservants and old women rushed to intervene,
preventing him from getting close.
He threw it from afar.
The spine of the knife struck her forehead;
her forehead split, and blood flowed.
She rushed out, hair disheveled and howling,
intending to run and report it to her family.
[Sūn] caught her and brought her back,
whipping her countless times with a staff.
Her clothes were all in tatters,
and she was so injured and in pain that she could not turn over.
[Sūn] ordered her to be carried into a room and guarded,
intending to release her only after she had recovered.
The wife’s brothers heard of this
and, enraged,
led many horsemen to their gate.
[Sūn] also gathered his strong servants, armed them, and resisted them.
They cursed and shouted at each other,
and only dispersed at the end of the day.
Wáng was not satisfied
and brought a lawsuit.
[Sūn] defended himself by going to the city
and personally presenting himself for examination,
recounting the wife’s wicked behavior.
The magistrate (zǎi) could not make him yield,
so he sent [the wife] to Guǎngwén for punishment to please Wáng.
Guǎngwén Zhū Xiānshēng
was from a prominent family
and was upright and unyielding.
Upon carefully investigating the matter,
he angrily said,
“Does the high official (tángshàng gōng) take me for a contemptible instructor (jiàoguān) of the empire,
one who extorts money that violates heavenly principles and harms righteousness,
to suck people’s sores and hemorrhoids?!
Such a beggarly appearance
is something I cannot tolerate!”
In the end, he did not accept the order.
[Sūn] openly returned home.
Wáng had no choice
but to hint to friends
to mediate the situation,
wanting [Sūn] to personally apologize to her family.
[Sūn] refused,
and after ten back-and-forths, no decision could be reached.
The wife’s wounds gradually healed.
[Sūn] wanted to send her out,
but he also feared that the Wáng clan would not accept her,
so he procrastinated and kept her there.
With his concubine gone and his son dead,
[Sūn] was heartbroken day and night.
He longed to find the wet nurse
to inquire about the situation.
He then recalled Wúbìng’s words,
“fled to the Yángs.”
There was a Yángjiātǔn (Yáng Family Hamlet) near the village,
and he suspected she was there.
He went to inquire,
but no one knew anything.
Someone said there was Yánggǔ (Yang Valley) fifty lǐ away.
He sent riders to investigate,
and indeed found her there;
his son was gradually recovering.
They were all delighted to see each other
and carried him back home.
When the child saw his father,
he cried out loudly.
[Sūn] also shed tears.
When the wife heard that the child was still alive,
she rushed out full of fury,
intending to scold him.
As the child was crying,
he opened his eyes and saw the wife,
then fearfully threw himself into his father’s arms,
as if seeking to hide.
When [Sūn] held and looked at him,
his breath had already stopped.
He urgently called out to him,
and after a moment, he revived.
[Sūn] resentfully said,
“I don’t know what kind of cruelty [she inflicted]
to bring my son to this state!”
So he immediately drew up a divorce letter
and sent his wife back.
Wáng indeed did not accept her,
and again carried her back to [Sūn].
[Sūn] had no choice;
father and son lived separately in one courtyard,
not communicating with the wife.
The wet nurse then fully described Wúbìng’s condition,
and [Sūn] finally realized she was a ghost.
Moved by her righteousness,
he buried her clothes and shoes
and inscribed a tablet saying,
“Tomb of Lǚ Wúbìng, the Ghost Wife.”
Not long after,
the wife gave birth to a boy,
who died with his hands clasped around his neck.
[Sūn] grew even more enraged
and again sent the wife away.
Wáng again sent her back.
[Sūn] then prepared a detailed complaint
and presented it to the higher authorities,
but they all, due to the heavenly official (tiānguān),
set it aside and did not deal with it.
Later, when the tiānguān died,
[Sūn] continued to complain,
and she was finally ordered to be divorced completely (dàguī).
From then on, [Sūn] never remarried,
but took a maidservant.
Once the wife had returned,
her notorious reputation spread widely,
and for three or four years, no one came to propose marriage.
The wife suddenly regretted it,
but it was already too late to turn back.
An old maidservant from the [Sūn] family
happened to visit her home.
The wife treated her kindly
and wept before her;
sensing her feelings,
she seemed to be missing her former husband.
The old woman returned and told [Sūn],
who laughed and dismissed it.
After another year or so,
the wife’s mother also died,
leaving her an orphan with no one to depend on.
Her younger sisters-in-law (dìsì) were quite annoyed and jealous of her;
the wife felt even more displaced
and wept daily.
A poor scholar who had lost his wife
discussed sending her off with a generous dowry,
but the wife refused.
She would secretly ask passersby to convey her feelings to [Sūn],
tearfully expressing her regret,
but [Sūn] would not listen.
One day,
the wife, with a maidservant,
secretly rode a donkey
and actually rushed to [Sūn].
As [Sūn] was coming out from inside,
she knelt down to greet him at the foot of the steps,
crying uncontrollably.
[Sūn] wanted to leave her,
but the wife tugged at his clothes and knelt again.
[Sūn] firmly declined, saying,
“If we are to reunite,
and there are never any disputes, then so be it.
But should anything happen again,
and your brothers are like wolves and tigers,
how could I ever again seek to divorce you?!”
The wife said,
“I have secretly run here,
and there is no way I can return.
Either keep me,
or I will die!
Moreover, I have been with you since I was twenty-one,
and was expelled at twenty-three.
Even if I truly had ten parts of wickedness,
could there be no single part of affection?”
Then she took off a bracelet,
and bound her two feet with it,
covering them with her sleeve,
and said,
“Do you not remember this oath made before the incense and fire
then?”
[Sūn] then felt his eyes well up with tears,
and had someone help her into the room.
But he still suspected that the Wáng clan was deceitful
and wanted a word from her brothers as proof.
The wife said:
"I eloped privately,
how can I face my brothers again?
If you don't believe me,
I have a cutting tool hidden here.
Please let me cut off a finger to prove myself."
Thereupon, she took out a sharp blade from her waist,
stretched out her left hand by the bedside, and cut off a finger.
Blood gushed out like a spring.
Sūn was greatly alarmed,
and immediately bandaged her.
The woman's complexion changed greatly with pain,
yet she did not groan.
She smiled and said:
"My dream of Huángliáng has awakened today.
I merely borrow this small room to live as a renunciant.
Why must there be suspicion between us?"
Sūn then made his son and the concubine live in a separate residence,
and he himself went back and forth between the two places morning and evening.
He also sought good medicine daily to treat the finger wound,
and it healed in over a month.
From then on, the woman did not eat meat or drink alcohol,
but simply closed her door and chanted Buddhist scriptures.
After residing there for a long time,
she saw the household management becoming neglected,
and said to Sūn:
"When I came here,
I originally intended not to inquire about other matters;
but now seeing such expenditures,
I fear that your descendants may starve.
Since there's no alternative,
I will brazenly manage it once more."
Thereupon, she gathered the maidservants,
and held them accountable for their weaving performance daily.
The family, seeing that she had thrown herself at them,
treated her lightly,
secretly scoffing and slandering her,
but the woman acted as if she heard nothing.
Afterwards, when assessing their work,
she mercilessly whipped the lazy ones,
and the household finally began to fear her.
She also drew a curtain and supervised the chief accountant,
managing everything meticulously.
Sūn was then greatly pleased,
and made his son and concubine both pay their respects to her every morning.
Ājiān was already nine years old,
and the woman gave him special care and affection.
When he went to school in the morning,
she often saved sweets for him to await his return;
the boy also gradually grew fond of her.
One day,
the boy threw a stone at a sparrow,
and the woman happened to pass by,
hitting her head and causing her to fall,
remaining speechless for over a quarter of an hour.
Sūn was furious,
and flogged the boy.
The woman revived,
and strenuously stopped him,
even happily saying:
"In the past, I abused my son,
and my heart was always troubled by it.
Today, fortunately, one karmic debt has been resolved."
Sūn favored and loved her even more,
and the woman often refused him,
making him sleep with the concubine.
After several years,
she bore children repeatedly, but they all died young,
saying:
"This is the retribution for having killed a child in the past."
When Ājiān got married,
she then entrusted external affairs to her son,
and internal affairs to her daughter-in-law.
One day she said:
"I will die on a certain day."
Sūn did not believe her.
The woman arranged her burial provisions herself,
and on that day,
she changed her clothes, entered the coffin, and died.
Her complexion was lifelike,
and an unusual fragrance filled the room;
only after she was interred
did the fragrance gradually dissipate.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"What the heart loves
is originally not dependent on beauty or ugliness.
As for Máozhí and Xīshī,
how do we know they weren't considered beautiful by those who loved themselves?
However, if not for encountering fierce jealousy,
her virtuousness would not have become manifest,
almost making people laugh at her alongside those who relish scabs.
As for the person from Jǐnpíng,
her innate roots were originally deep,
hence she suddenly enlightened,
immediately attaining Bodhi.
If it were in the path of hell,
all would be rich and noble people who had not experienced hardship."
According to "Liáozhāi Zhìyì" (The Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio) Chuìxuězhāi manuscript
Xià Shāng,
a native of Héjiān.
His father, Dōnglíng,
was enormously wealthy and extravagant,
whenever he ate steamed buns,
he would often discard their corners,
leaving them scattered everywhere.
People, because of his stoutness,
called him
"Diūkǎo Tàiwèi."
In his later years,
his family became extremely poor,
unable to afford meals daily;
his two arms became thin,
hanging down like empty bags,
and people then called him
"Mùzhuāng Sēng"
— meaning he carried a hanging bag.
Before his death,
he said to Shāng:
"In my life, I have wantonly wasted nature's gifts,
incurring the wrath of Heaven above,
leading to death from hunger and cold.
You must cherish blessings and act diligently,
to cover your father's transgressions."
Shāng scrupulously obeyed his dying wishes,
being sincere and unswerving,
cultivating the land himself to make a living.
The villagers all loved and respected him.
A certain rich elder pitied his poverty,
lent him capital,
and made him learn to be a peddler,
but he always lost money.
Ashamed of being unable to repay,
he asked to be hired as a laborer.
The elder refused.
Shāng felt uneasy and distraught,
sold all his fields and dwelling,
and went to repay the elder.
The elder questioned him and understood the situation,
felt even more sorry for him,
and insisted on buying back his former property for him;
he also lent him a large sum of money again,
instructing him to trade.
Shāng declined, saying:
"I cannot even repay ten taels of gold,
how can I incur the debt of being a donkey or horse in the next life?"
The elder then invited another merchant to go with him.
They returned after a few months,
barely breaking even;
the elder did not collect interest,
and made him go again.
After more than a year,
the goods and capital filled a cart,
and on their way back, they reached the river,
where they encountered a hurricane,
the boat almost capsized,
and half their goods were lost.
Calculating what was left upon returning,
it was barely enough to repay the master.
He then said to the merchant:
"Whom Heaven impoverishes,
who can save?
This is all because of me, harming you!"
Thereupon, he checked the ledger, handed it to the merchant,
and withdrew himself.
The elder urged him again,
but he absolutely refused,
and continued farming as before.
He often sighed to himself:
"People on this earth,
all have a certain number of years to enjoy,
why then am I so desolate?"
There was an itinerant shamaness
who divined with coins,
knowing everyone's fate entirely.
He respectfully went to her.
The shamaness
was an old woman.
Her dwelling was spotlessly clean,
with a divine altar set up in the middle,
and the scent of incense constantly permeated it.
After the merchant finished his prostrations,
the shamaness immediately demanded payment.
The merchant gave her a hundred coins,
which the shamaness put entirely into a wooden tube.
Holding it, she knelt below the altar,
shaking it to make a rattling sound like praying.
After a moment, she rose,
poured the coins into her hand,
and then arranged them in order on the table.
Her method was to treat a character as 'no' (否),
and a blank space (幕) as 'yes' (亨).
All the numbers up to fifty-eight were characters,
but after that, they were all blank spaces.
She then asked,
"How old are you now?"
He replied,
"Twenty-eight sui."
The shamaness shook her head and said,
"Too early!
Too early!
Your current fortune, sir, is your ancestors' fortune,
not your own.
At fifty-eight sui,
you will finally enter your own fortune,
and then there will be no more difficulties."
He asked,
"What do you mean by ancestors' fortune?"
She said,
"If ancestors had good deeds,
and their blessings are not exhausted,
then their descendants enjoy them;
if ancestors had bad deeds,
and their misfortunes are not exhausted,
then their descendants also suffer them."
The merchant counted on his fingers and said,
"In another thirty years,
I will be old and feeble,
about to enter my coffin."
The shamaness said,
"Before fifty-eight,
there will be five years of 'leap' fortune (回閏),
during which you can manage to make some plans;
