however, you will merely avoid hunger and cold.
In your fifty-eighth year,
a huge sum of gold will come to you spontaneously,
without needing to strive for it.
Sir, you have lived a faultless life,
and in future generations, you will enjoy endless blessings."
He left the shamaness and returned,
half doubting, half believing.
However, he remained content with his poverty and self-disciplined,
not daring to seek anything beyond his means.
Later, when he reached fifty-three sui,
he paid close attention to verify it.
At that time, it was spring planting,
but he was sick with malaria and unable to plow.
After he recovered,
there was a great drought,
and all the early crops withered.
It only rained near autumn.
Having no other seeds in his household,
he planted all his several *mǔ* of fields with grain.
Soon after, there was another drought,
and half of the buckwheat and beans died,
but only the grain was unharmed;
later, it rained and the grain burst forth,
yielding double the harvest.
The following spring there was a great famine,
but he was able to avoid starvation.
The merchant, believing the shamaness because of this,
borrowed capital from an elder (翁),
making small profits as a moneylender (子母);
he always made a small gain.
Someone advised him to become a big merchant,
but he refused.
When he was fifty-seven sui,
he happened to be repairing his wall
and dug up an iron cauldron.
When he opened it,
white vapor, like cotton, rose out.
Frightened, he dared not open it fully.
After a while,
the vapor dissipated,
and the jar was filled with white silver.
The couple together carried it out
and weighed it: one thousand three hundred and twenty-five *liǎng*.
They secretly discussed how the shamaness's prediction was slightly off.
A neighbor's wife entered the merchant's house,
saw it secretly,
and went home to tell her husband.
The husband was jealous
and secretly reported it to the district magistrate (邑宰).
The magistrate, who was most greedy,
detained the merchant and demanded the gold.
His wife wanted to hide half of it,
but the merchant said,
"This is not what we should have.
Keeping it will invite disaster."
He presented it all.
The magistrate received the gold,
and fearing he might have hidden some,
he pursued the storage containers,
filled them with gold,
until they were full,
and then released the merchant.
Not long after,
the magistrate was transferred to be the Assistant Prefect (同知) of Nánchāng.
A year later,
the merchant went to Nánchāng for trade (懋遷),
and the magistrate had already died.
His wife and children were about to return home,
and were selling their bulky goods.
There were several baskets of tung oil.
The merchant, seeing their low price,
bought them to take home.
Upon arriving home,
the containers had leaks.
As he poured the oil into other containers,
he found two ingots of white silver inside;
he found this to be the case throughout.
When converted,
it was exactly the same amount as the silver he had dug up previously.
The merchant thus became instantly rich,
and further assisted the poor,
being generous and unsparing.
His wife advised him to accumulate for his descendants,
but the merchant said,
"This is precisely how I bequeath to my descendants."
The impoverished neighbor became a beggar,
wishing to ask for something,
but feeling ashamed in his heart.
The merchant heard this and told him,
"The former incident
was because my destined time had not yet arrived,
so the spirits used your hand to ruin it.
How can I blame you?"
Thereupon, he provided generously for him.
The neighbor was moved to tears.
Later, the merchant lived to eighty years old,
and his descendants inherited his wealth,
thriving for several generations without decline.
Yì Shǐ Shì (異史氏) says:
"Excessive extravagance,
even kings and nobles cannot escape it,
let alone commoners!
Living to squander Heaven's bounty
and dying with no rice in the mouth—
how lamentable!
Fortunately, though the bird's death cries are sorrowful,
the son can 'handle the consequences' (幹蠱),
after seventy years of poverty and ruin,
he eventually revived.
Otherwise,
the father's evil deeds would burden the son,
and the son would in turn burden the grandson,
continuing until they became beggars passed down endlessly.
What sort of old shamaness
could reveal Heaven's secrets?
Alas!
How strange!"
According to "Liáozhāi Zhìyì", volume 24, manuscript edition.
When the Míng dynasty collapsed,
war and beacon fires erupted.
Mr. Liú Zhīshēng of Yúlíng
gathered tens of thousands of people,
intending to cross the river south.
Suddenly, a corpulent man approached the stockade gate,
with his clothes open, exposing his belly,
and requested to see the military leader.
The先生 invited him in and spoke with him,
and was greatly pleased.
When asked his name,
he called himself Cǎiwēi Wēng.
Liú kept him to participate in strategy councils,
and presented him with a sword.
The Wēng said:
"I have my own sharp weapons;
I don't need spears and halberds."
When asked:
"Where are your weapons?"
The Wēng then rolled up his clothes and exposed his belly,
whose navel was large enough to hold a chicken's egg.
He held his breath and puffed it up,
and suddenly, with a tearing sound, the skin of his navel split open,
and the hilt of a sword protruded.
He grasped it and drew it out,
and a white blade shone like frost.
Liú was greatly astonished
and asked:
"Is this all?"
He smiled and pointed at his belly, saying:
"This is an armory;
what is there that I don't have?"
He commanded to fetch a bow and arrows,
and again, in the same manner as before,
he produced a carved bow.
With a brief holding of his breath,
an arrow flew out,
and its output was inexhaustible.
Afterward, the sword was reinserted into his navel,
and it all disappeared.
Liú regarded him as divine,
and shared his sleeping quarters with him,
treating him with utmost respect.
At that time, although the camp's orders were strict,
the rabble
would frequently go out to pillage.
The Wēng said:
"Soldiers value discipline.
Now, commanding tens of thousands of men,
yet being unable to instill awe in their hearts,
this is the path to defeat and destruction."
Liú was pleased by this,
and so he investigated the troops.
Those who plundered women and property
were decapitated and displayed to the public.
The army gradually became orderly,
but it could not be completely stopped.
The Wēng would occasionally ride out on horseback,
roaming among the troops,
and among the fierce generals and arrogant soldiers,
their heads would frequently fall to the ground by themselves,
without anyone knowing why.
Because of this, they all began to suspect the Wēng.
His previous strict disciplinary measures
had already made the soldiers fear and dislike him;
by this point, their resentment and animosity grew.
The various division leaders slandered Liú, saying:
"Cǎiwēi Wēng
uses demonic arts.
Since ancient times, famous generals
were only known for their wisdom,
not for their magic.
Those like Fúyún and Báiquè
ultimately met destruction.
Now, innocent officers and soldiers
frequently lose their heads by themselves,
and people's hearts are filled with fear.
For the general to associate with him
is also a dangerous path;
it is better to eliminate him."
Liú followed their advice
and plotted to execute him while he slept.
He sent someone to spy on the Wēng.
The Wēng was lying with his belly exposed,
snoring like thunder.
The crowd was greatly pleased,
surrounding his dwelling with soldiers.
Two men entered with knives
and cut off his head.
As they raised their knives,
the head had already reattached,
and his breathing was as before.
They were greatly astonished.
They then hacked at his belly.
The belly split open without blood,
and inside, spears and halberds were densely packed,
all revealing their points.
The crowd was even more terrified
and dared not approach.
They remotely poked him with lances,
but iron crossbows fired loudly,
shooting several people.
The crowd dispersed in fright
and reported to Liú.
Liú rushed to him,
but he had already vanished.
Based on a handwritten copy of Volume 24 of Líaozhāi Zhìyì.
Cuī Měng,
courtesy name Wùměng,
was the son of a prominent family from Jiànchāng.
He was resolute and unyielding by nature.
As a child in school,
if other children committed even a minor offense,
he would immediately clench his fists and beat them.
His teacher frequently warned him, but he did not reform.
His given name and courtesy name
were both bestowed by his teacher.
By the age of sixteen or seventeen,
he was extraordinarily strong and skilled,
and could even hold a long pole and leap onto a tall house.
He delighted in righting wrongs,
and because of this, the villagers all respected him,
with those seeking redress filling his steps and rooms.
Cuī suppressed the strong and supported the weak,
not shying away from animosity or suspicion.
If someone slightly opposed him,
stones and sticks would rain down,
leaving their limbs mutilated.
Whenever he was in a great rage,
no one dared to move.
He was, however, filial to his mother.
When his mother arrived, his rage would subside.
His mother's reprimands and condemnations were thorough,
and Cuī would meekly obey,
but forget once he left the house.
A neighbor had a shrewish wife
who daily abused her mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law was starving and on the verge of death.
Her son secretly fed her.
When the wife found out,
she cursed her in countless ways,
her voice audible in all four courtyards.
Cuī became angry,
climbed over the wall,
and cut off her nose, ears, lips, and tongue,
killing her instantly.
His mother was greatly alarmed when she heard,
and called the neighbor's son, comforting him with utmost care,
and marrying him to a young maidservant.
The matter then subsided.
His mother was so angry that she wept and refused to eat.
Cuī was afraid,
knelt and begged to be beaten,
and also confessed his regret.
His mother wept and ignored him.
Cuī's wife, Zhōu,
also knelt beside him.
His mother then beat her son,
and also pricked his arm with a needle,
making a cross pattern,
which she painted red
to ensure it would not fade.
Cuī endured it all.
Only then did his mother eat.
My mother enjoyed feeding Buddhist monks and Daoist priests,
often satisfying them with ample food.
Once, a Daoist priest was at the gate.
Cuī passed by,
and the Daoist priest looked at him and said:
"Young master has too much fierce and unruly energy,
I fear it will be difficult for him to secure a good end.
A family that accumulates good deeds
should not have this."
Cuī had recently been admonished by his mother,
and hearing this,
he rose with respect and said:
"I also know this myself;
but as soon as I see injustice,
I painfully cannot control myself.
If I make an effort to change,
might I perhaps avoid it?"
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
"For now, do not ask whether it can be avoided or not;
please first ask yourself whether you can change or not.
You must earnestly suppress yourself;
if there is even one chance in ten thousand,
I will tell you the art of escaping death."
Cuī had never in his life believed in witchcraft or exorcism,
so he smiled and said nothing.
The Daoist priest said:
"I certainly know you don't believe.
But what I say
is not like what shamans and sorcerers say;
acting on it is also a great virtue;
even if it does not prove effective,
it will also do no harm."
Cuī asked for his instruction,
and the Daoist priest then said:
"Just now, there was a young man outside the gate;
you should form a close bond with him.
Even if you commit a capital crime,
he will be able to save your life."
He called Cuī out,
and pointed out the person.
He was the son of the Zhào family,
named Sēnggē.
Zhào,
a native of Nánchāng,
had, due to a lean year and famine,
taken up temporary residence in Jiànchāng.
Cuī, from this, formed a deep bond with him,
and invited Zhào to lodge in his home,
providing generous provisions.
Sēnggē, at twelve years old,
ascended the hall to bow to Cuī's mother,
and they agreed to be brothers.
A year later, at spring plowing,
Zhào took his family and left.
Communication then ceased.
After Cuī's mother's neighbor died,
her admonitions to her son became even more earnest;
if anyone came to complain,
she would always reject them.
One day,
Cuī's maternal uncle died,
and he accompanied his mother to the funeral.
On the road, they encountered several people
tying up a man,
cursing and urging him forward,
and beating him.
Spectators blocked the road,
and their carriage could not advance.
Cuī asked about it,
and those who recognized Cuī eagerly crowded around to tell him.
Before this,
there was a son of a powerful gentry, named Mǒu Jiǎ,
who was tyrannical throughout the village.
He coveted Lǐ Shēn's wife, who was attractive,
and wanted to seize her,
but found no means to do so.
So he ordered his servants to lure her into gambling,
lending her money and charging high interest,
demanding that she sign over her wife on the bond.
When the money ran out, he would give more.
Overnight,
she accumulated a debt of several thousand;
after half a year,
the principal and interest amounted to over thirty thousand.
Shēn could not repay,
so Mǒu Jiǎ forcibly used many people to seize his wife.
Shēn cried outside his gate.
Mǒu Jiǎ became angry,
pulled him and tied him to a tree,
whipped, flogged, and stabbed him,
forcing him to write
"a statement of no regret."
and his anger rose like a mountain.
He whipped his horse forward,
intending to use force.
His mother lifted the curtain and called out:
"Alas!
Cuī heard this,
Cuī then stopped.
After the funeral, they returned,
and he neither spoke nor ate.
He sat motionless, staring straight ahead,
as if he harbored anger.
His wife questioned him,
but he did not answer.
At night,
he lay on the bed with his clothes on,
tossing and turning until dawn.
The next night was the same;
suddenly, he opened the door and went out,
then immediately returned and lay down.
This happened three or four times.
His wife dared not question him,
only holding her breath to listen.
After a long delay, he finally returned,
closed the door, and slept soundly.
That night,
someone killed Mǒu Jiǎ in his bed,
cutting open his belly and spilling his intestines;
Shēn's wife was also found naked and dead beneath the bed.
The official suspected Shēn,
arrested and interrogated him.
He was cruelly tortured,
his ankle bones exposed,
but he had no confession.
After more than a year,
unable to bear the torture,
he falsely confessed
and was sentenced to death.
Coincidentally, Cuī's mother died.
After the burial,
he told his wife:
"The one who killed Mǒu Jiǎ
was actually me.
Only because I had an elderly mother
did I not dare to reveal it.
Now that the great matter is concluded,
how can I let someone else suffer for my crime?
I will go to the authorities and die!"
His wife was shocked and tried to stop him,
but he tore off his sleeve and left,
surrendering himself at the yámen.
The official was astonished,
chained him and sent him to prison,
and released Shēn.
Shēn refused,
insisting on confessing himself.
The official could not decide,
and arrested both.
All relatives and friends reproached Shēn.
Shēn said:
"What the young master did
was what I wanted to do but could not.
He did it on my behalf,
how can I bear to stand by and watch him die?
Even if we say the young master did not go out tonight, it is fine."
He stuck to his story,
firmly arguing with Cuī.
After a long time,
the yámen officials all knew the truth,
and forcibly released Shēn,
holding Cuī responsible for the crime,
who was on the verge of execution.
At that time, the minister for judicial relief, Zhào Bùláng,
came to inspect the prisoners.
When he reached Cuī's name,
he dismissed everyone and called him.
Cuī entered,
and looking up at the dais,
it was Sēnggē.
With both sorrow and joy, Cuī told him the full story.
Zhào paced for a long time,
then still ordered Cuī to be returned to prison,
instructing the jailers to treat him well.
Soon after, because of his self-surrender, his sentence was reduced,
and he was conscripted into the army in Yúnnán.
Shēn served him and left,
but before a year was out,
Cuī returned due to a pardon: all thanks to Zhào's efforts.
After returning,
Shēn Zhōng never left,
acting on behalf of Cuī Měng to manage his livelihood.
Cuī Měng offered him money,
but he refused.
Because of his skill in pole fighting and martial arts,
Cuī Měng cared for him deeply.
Cuī Měng treated him generously,
buying him a wife and giving him land.
From then on, Cuī Měng drastically changed his previous conduct,
and whenever he touched the刺痕 (cìhén) on his arm,
tears would stream down his face.
When neighbors in his hometown had problems,
Shēn Zhōng would often fabricate orders to mediate and resolve them,
without consulting Cuī Měng.
There was a guānshēng (監生) named Wáng,
whose family was extremely wealthy.
Rascals and unscrupulous people from all directions
came and went through his doors.
Many of the affluent people in the district
were extorted and plundered;
if they relocated,
Wáng would send robbers to kill them on the road.
His son was also lewd and violent.
Wáng had a widowed aunt,
and both father and son defiled her.
Wáng's wife, by the surname of Chóu,
repeatedly tried to stop Wáng,
so Wáng strangled her to death.
Chóu's brothers reported this to the authorities,
but Wáng bribed officials,
resulting in the accusers being charged with making false accusations.
The brothers, full of unredressed grievance and indignation,
went to Cuī Měng to seek justice.
Shēn Zhōng turned them away.
After several days,
a guest arrived.
As there were no servants available,
Cuī Měng asked Shēn Zhōng to prepare tea.
Shēn Zhōng silently went out
and told someone:
"I am merely a fierce friend to Cuī Měng.
To follow him for ten thousand *lǐ* (里)
cannot be said to be insincere;
yet I receive no provisions
and am treated like a hired servant.
This I cannot tolerate!"
So he angrily left.
Someone reported this to Cuī Měng.
Cuī Měng was surprised by his change of heart,
but did not find it particularly strange.
Suddenly, Shēn Zhōng sued Cuī Měng in court,
claiming that Cuī Měng had not paid him wages for three years.
Cuī Měng was greatly astonished,
and personally went to court to confront him,
where Shēn Zhōng angrily argued against him.
The official deemed Shēn Zhōng's claim unjust
and ordered him to be expelled.
Several more days passed.
Suddenly, Shēn Zhōng entered Wáng's house at night,
killing the father, son, aunt, and wife.
He stuck a paper on the wall,
writing his own name on it;
but when they pursued him,
he had vanished without a trace.
The Wáng family suspected Cuī Měng of instigating it,
but the official did not believe them.
Cuī Měng then realized that the previous lawsuit
was probably to distance him from the crime of murder.
The pursuit extended to nearby prefectures and districts,
and was very urgent.
However, when the Chuǎng (闖) rebels committed treason,
the matter was dropped.
After the Míng (明) dynasty was overthrown and replaced,
Shēn Zhōng returned with his family,
and remained on good terms with Cuī Měng as before.
At that time, local bandits gathered.
Wáng's nephew, Dé Rén,
assembled the ruffians his uncle had recruited,
occupied a mountain as a bandit,
and burned and plundered villages.
One night,
they came with their entire force,
under the guise of seeking revenge.
Cuī Měng happened to be out. Shēn Zhōng only became aware when the door was broken open,
so he climbed over a wall and hid in the darkness.
The bandits searched for Cuī Měng.
When they could not find him,
they abducted Cuī Měng's wife
and took away his valuables.
When Shēn Zhōng returned,
there was only one servant.
He was extremely furious,
so he cut dozens of ropes,
giving the shorter ones to the servant,
and keeping the longer ones himself.
He instructed the servant to go past the bandit lair,
climb halfway up the mountain,
set the ropes on fire,
scatter them among the thorns,
and then return without looking back.
The servant agreed and left.
Shēn Zhōng observed that all the bandits had red sashes around their waists
and red silk tied to their hats,
so he imitated their attire.
There was an old mare that had just given birth to a foal,
which the bandits had abandoned outside the gate.
Shēn Zhōng tied the foal, mounted the horse,
placed a bit in its mouth,
and rode straight to the bandit's stronghold.
The bandits occupied a large village.
Shēn Zhōng tethered his horse outside the village
and climbed over the wall to enter.
He saw the bandits in a chaotic throng,
still grasping their spears.
Shēn Zhōng secretly asked some bandits
and learned that Cuī Měng's wife was with a certain Wáng.
Soon, he heard an order being relayed,
telling everyone to rest,
and they responded with a roar.
Suddenly, someone reported a fire on the eastern mountain,
and all the bandits looked towards it;
at first, there were only one or two points of light,
but then they became numerous like stars.
Shēn Zhōng, out of breath, urgently shouted that there was an alarm on the eastern mountain.
Wáng was greatly alarmed,
dressed himself, and led his men out.
Shēn Zhōng seized the opportunity to slip out from their right,
then turned back and re-entered the camp.
He saw two bandits guarding a tent
and tricked them, saying:
"General Wáng left his saber."
The two bandits eagerly searched for it.
Shēn Zhōng chopped them from behind;
one bandit fell;
the other turned to look,
and Shēn Zhōng cut him down too.
He then carried Cuī Měng's wife and climbed over the wall to escape.
He untied the horse and handed her the reins,
saying:
"Madam, you don't know the way,
just let the horse run."
The mare, longing for her foal, galloped away,
and Shēn Zhōng followed.
Upon reaching a narrow pass,
Shēn Zhōng ignited the ropes,
hanging them everywhere,
and then returned home.
The next day,
Cuī Huán
considered it a great humiliation.
His body and spirit were restless,
and he wanted to ride alone to quell the bandits.
Shēn advised him against it.
He gathered the villagers to deliberate,
but the crowd was timid and none dared to respond.
He explained repeatedly,
and obtained more than twenty brave men.
However, they were still short of weapons.
By chance, they caught two spies at a relative's house of Dé Rén.
Cuī wanted to kill them,
but Shēn disagreed.
He ordered the twenty men to each hold a white staff,
and arrayed them before him.
Then he cut off the spies' ears and released them.
The crowd complained, saying:
"With soldiers like these,
we ought to fear the bandits knowing,
yet you deliberately show them.
If they come with a full troop,
the entire village will not be safe!"
Shēn said:
"I precisely want them to come."
He executed those who harbored thieves.
He sent people out in all directions
to borrow bows, arrows, and firearms,
and also went to the district to borrow two large cannons.
At dusk,
he led the brave men to the narrow pass,
placing the cannons to block its main route.
He had two men hide fire and lie in ambush,
instructing them to fire only when they saw the bandits.
Then he went to the eastern entrance of the valley,
felling trees and placing them on the cliff.
After this, he and Cuī each led more than ten men,
and lay in ambush on either bank.
As the first watch was almost over,
they heard horses neighing in the distance.
The bandits indeed arrived in great numbers,
a continuous stream.
After they had all entered the valley,
the trees were pushed down,
blocking their return path.
Immediately, the cannons fired,
and the clamor of shouts and cries
shook the mountain valley.
The bandits retreated abruptly,
trampling each other.
When they reached the eastern entrance,
they could not get out,
and gathered with no space left.
Firearms and arrows attacked from both banks,
with the force of wind and rain.
Those with severed heads and broken limbs
lay piled in the ditch.
Over twenty men were left,
kneeling and begging for their lives.
They were then tied up and sent back.
Riding on their victory, they advanced directly to the bandits' lair.
Those guarding the lair fled upon hearing the news.
They searched for their supplies and returned.
Cuī was greatly pleased,
and asked about his strategy for setting fires.
Shēn said:
"Setting fires to the east
was to fear them pursuing to the west;
making them short
was to make them extinguish quickly,
fearing they would detect there was no one there;
and then setting them at the mouth of the valley,
where the mouth is very narrow,
and one man can block it,
so if they pursued,
they would surely be afraid upon seeing the fires—all were temporary, risky, inferior strategies."
They captured a bandit and interrogated him.
Indeed, he had pursued into the valley,
and retreated in fright upon seeing the fires.
All twenty-odd bandits
had their noses cut off and feet amputated before being released.
From this, his prestige greatly increased.
Those from near and far seeking refuge followed him like a market crowd,
and he obtained over three hundred local militia.
Strong bandits from all areas dared not offend,
and the region relied on him for peace.
The Historian of Anomalies says:
"A swift ox must be able to break the cart,
this describes Cuī!
His aspirations were grand and generous,
rarely matched.
However, to wish for no injustice in the world,
is this not an intention that exceeds common sense?
Lǐ Shēn,
a mere commoner,
was able to achieve this fine deed.
Climbing poles and flying in,
he cut down beasts in deep boudoirs;
blocking paths and attacking from both sides,
he swept away evil demons in narrow valleys.
If he were allowed to carry a five-zhang banner
and serve the nation,
why would he not face south and rule as king!"
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Fàn Xiǎoshān, a resident of Qīngzhōu,
whose trade was selling brushes,
had not returned from his travels.
In the fourth month,
his wife, Hè Shì, lived alone
and was killed by a thief at night.
That night, there was a light rain,
and a poem-fan was left in the mud.
It was one given by Wáng Shèng to Wú Fēiqīng.
Shèng,
it was unknown who he was;
Wú,
a wealthy man from Yìdū,
was from the same village as Fàn,
and had a reputation for being somewhat frivolous.
Thus, the villagers all believed it.
The prefecture and county arrested and interrogated him.
He steadfastly denied it,
suffered cruel shackling,
and was falsely convicted.
His case was remanded back and forth,
passing through more than ten officials,
without any dissenting opinion.
Wú also resigned himself to death,
instructing his wife to use all their possessions
to aid the lonely.
To those who recited a thousand Buddhist chants at his gate,
he gave padded trousers;
to those who recited ten thousand, padded jackets. Thus, beggars were like a market,
and the sound of Buddhist chants was heard for over ten *lǐ*.
As a result, his family quickly became poor,
only selling land and property daily to provide for expenses.
He secretly bribed the jailer to buy poison.
One night, he dreamed of a divine being who told him:
"You must not die.
Formerly 'danger outside,'
now 'good fortune inside'
has arrived."
He slept again,
and the dream repeated,
so he did not die.
Not long after,
Mr. Zhōu Yuánliàng was appointed to oversee this circuit.
When reviewing prisoners, he came to Wú,
and seemed to be in thought.
He then asked:
"What concrete evidence is there
that Wú Mǒu committed murder?"
Fàn responded with the fan.
Mr. looked closely at the fan
and then asked:
"Who is Wáng Shèng?"
Both said they did not know.
He then carefully reviewed the legal documents once more,
and immediately ordered Wú's death shackles removed,
moving him from the prison to the granary.
Fàn strenuously objected.
Mr. angrily said:
"Do you just want to wrongly kill one person and be done with it?
Or will you be satisfied only when you get an enemy?"
The crowd suspected Mr. of favoritism towards Wú,
and no one dared to speak.
Mr. marked a red slip
and immediately ordered the arrest of the owner of a certain shop in Nánguō.
The owner was terrified,
not knowing why.
When he arrived, Mr. asked:
"On the shop wall, there is a poem by Lǐ Xiù from Dōngguǎn.
When was it inscribed?"
He replied:
"Last year, when the Provincial Education Commissioner came,
two or three Xiùcaì from Rìzhào
got drunk and left an inscription,
but I don't know where they live."
So he dispatched a runner to Rìzhào
and arrested Lǐ Xiù.
A few days later,
Lǐ Xiù arrived.
Mr. angrily said:
"Since you are a Xiùcaì,
how could you plot murder?"
Lǐ Xiù kowtowed, bewildered,
and said:
"None!"
The *xiānshēng* threw down the fan,
ordering him to look at it himself,
and said:
"It is clearly your work;
why do you deceitfully pin it on Wáng Shèng?"
Xiù scrutinized it,
and said:
"The poem is truly my work,
but the handwriting is certainly not mine."
He said:
"Since the poem is known to be yours,
it must be your friend's.
Who wrote it?"
Xiù said:
"The traces resemble those of Wáng Zuǒ from Yízhōu."
So, a runner was dispatched to detain Wáng Zuǒ.
When Zuǒ arrived,
he was interrogated in the same manner as Xiù.
Zuǒ confessed:
"This was Zhāng Chéng, an iron merchant from Yìdū, who asked me to write it.
He said Shèng was his cousin."
The *xiānshēng* said:
"The thief is here!"
He had Shèng arrested,
and with one interrogation, Shèng confessed.
Previously,
Shèng had coveted Hè Měi,
and wished to proposition her,
fearing it would not succeed.
He thought that if he used Wú's name,
everyone would surely believe it.
Therefore, he counterfeited Wú's fan,
held it, and went.
If it succeeded, he would claim it as his own;
if it failed, he would blame Wú.
He did not actually intend to kill her.
He climbed over the wall and entered,
assaulting the woman.
The woman, living alone,
always guarded herself with a blade.
Upon realizing what was happening,
she grabbed Shèng's clothes,
and rose with the knife.
Shèng was frightened,
and snatched her knife.
The woman pulled hard,
preventing him from escaping,
and also cried out.
Shèng became more desperate,
and so he killed her,
abandoned the fan, and left.
A three-year miscarriage of justice
was cleared in a single day,
and everyone praised the divine wisdom.
Wú finally realized that
"lǐbiān jí" (inside auspicious)
was
the character "zhōu" (周).
However, he still could not understand the reason.
Later, a local gentry member took the opportunity to ask him about it.
He smiled and said:
"This is very easy to know.
If you examine the fan carefully,
Hè was killed in early April.
That night was overcast and rainy,
and the weather was still cold.
A fan is not an urgent item.
How could someone, in a moment of hurried desperation,
carry this to add to their burden?
His intention to shift blame is obvious.
Earlier, I took shelter from the rain in the southern suburb,
and saw a poem inscribed on a wall,
which was similar in style
to the one on the fan.
Thus, I made a bold guess about Lǐ *Shēng*,
and indeed, through this, found the true culprit."
Those who heard him were filled with admiration.
The Historian of Anomalies says:
"For those who delve deeply into worldly affairs,
when there is nothing, it has its use.
Poetry and prose are instruments for glorifying the nation,
yet the *xiānshēng* used them to appraise scholars of the realm,
earning him the praise of Sūn Yáng.
Is this not delving deeply into it?
And yet, the art of appraising scholars
was applied to judging cases.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
'To know the subtle beginnings is divine.'
The *xiānshēng* possessed this."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Beyond the passes, in the mountains, there are many deer.
The local people wear deer heads,
lie hidden in the grass,
and make sounds by rolling leaves.
Deer then gather in herds.
However, males are few and females are many.
A male deer will mate with many females,
hundreds or thousands,
and once finished, it dies.
The females sniff it,
know it is dead,
and scatter into the valley,
bringing back unusual grasses which they place beside its mouth to fumigate it.
In an instant, it revives.
They quickly clang metal and fire guns,
and the herd of deer scatters in fright.
Thus, they obtained the grass
which can bring back the dead.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a boatman in Tiānjīn.
One night, he dreamed of a person who taught him, saying:
"Tomorrow, there will be someone carrying bamboo suitcases who wants to rent a boat.
Demand a thousand pieces of gold from him;
otherwise,
do not ferry him across."
The boatman awoke,
not believing it.
When he fell asleep again,
he dreamed again,
and the person wrote
three characters on the wall,
and instructed him:
"If he is reluctant to pay the price,
immediately write these characters to show him."
The boatman found this strange.
But he did not recognize the characters,
nor did he understand their meaning.
The next day,
he paid close attention to travelers.
As the sun moved west,
sure enough, a man came driving a mule laden with suitcases,
asking for a boat.
The boatman demanded the price as in his dream.
The man laughed at him.
After much back and forth,
the boatman took his hand,
and wrote the previous characters with his finger.
The man was greatly astonished,
and immediately vanished.
They searched his load,
and found tens of thousands of small coffins,
each only about a finger long,
each containing only a drop of blood.
The boatman showed the three characters far and wide,
but no one understood them.
Not long after,
Wú's rebellion plot was exposed,
and his partisans were all executed,
their corpses almost matching the number of coffins.
This was told by Xú Báishān.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Téng, there was a man named Yáng Mǒu,
who, as a member of the White Lotus Society (Bái Lián Jiào Dǎng),
acquired heterodox magical arts.
After Xú Hóngrú's execution,
Yáng Mǒu fortunately escaped detection,
and then used his arts to gain wealth.
His household's fields, gardens, and mansions
were quite considerable, testifying to his riches.
One day, he went to the house of a certain gentleman (shēn) in Sīshàng,
where he performed illusory magic as entertainment.
When the women came out to peek,
Yáng Mǒu cast his gaze upon the gentleman's beautiful daughter.
Upon returning home, he planned to abduct her.
His concubine, Zhū Shì,
who was also graceful,
was adorned with splendid makeup
and disguised as an immortal maiden (xiān jī).
He also gave her a wooden bird
and instructed her on how to use it.
Then he pushed her down from the top of a tower.
Zhū Shì felt her body become as light as a leaf,
and she floated ethereally, soaring through the clouds.
Before long,
she arrived at a certain place,
where the clouds stopped moving forward,
and she knew she had arrived.
That night,
the moon shone bright and clear,
and she could see very distinctly when looking down.
She took the wooden bird and threw it,
and the bird flapped its wings and flew away,
straight into the lady's chamber.
When the lady saw the colorful bird flying in,
she called her maid to catch it,
but the bird had already flown out through the curtain.
The lady chased it,
and the bird fell to the ground, flapping its wings;
as she approached it closely,
it fluttered into her skirt. In an instant,
it carried the lady upwards,
soaring straight into the sky.
The maid cried out loudly.
Zhū Shì, in the clouds, said:
"People of the lower realm, do not be alarmed!
I am Hénge from the Moon Palace (Yuè Fǔ Hénge).
She is the ninth daughter of the Queen Mother of the West (Wáng Mǔ),
who was temporarily banished to the mortal world.
The Queen Mother yearns for her daily,
and has temporarily called her up for a reunion;
she will be sent back soon."
Thereupon, the two flew on, side by side.
Just as they reached the border of Sīshuǐ,
there happened to be someone setting off firecrackers,
one of which accidentally struck the bird's wing;
the bird, startled, fell,
pulling Zhū Shì down with it,
and they landed in the home of a scholar.
The scholar, Xíng Zǐyǐ,
was extremely poor but upright in character.
Once, a neighbor's wife came to him at night,
but he refused to admit her.
The woman, holding a grudge,
slandered him to her husband,
falsely accusing him of seduction.
Her husband, being a ruffian,
came to Xíng Zǐyǐ's door morning and evening to insult him.
Due to this, Xíng Zǐyǐ sold his property
and rented a home in another village.
There was a physiognomist named Gù Mǒu,
who was skilled at predicting people's fortunes and lifespans.
Xíng Zǐyǐ went to his door to consult him.
Gù Mǒu looked at him and smiled, saying:
"Your fortune (gōng) is sufficient for a thousand measures of grain (qiān zhōng),
why do you come to me wearing rags?
Do you think I have no eyes?"
Xíng Zǐyǐ sneered at his extravagance.
Gù Mǒu scrutinized him further and said:
"That's right.
Though you are currently destitute,
a trove of gold is not far off."
Xíng Zǐyǐ again dismissed it as fantasy.
Gù Mǒu said:
"Not only will you become suddenly rich,
but you will also acquire a beautiful woman."
Xíng Zǐyǐ still refused to believe it.
Gù Mǒu pushed him out,
saying:
"Just go, just go.
You can thank me after it's verified."
That night,
Xíng Zǐyǐ was sitting alone under the moon,
when suddenly two women descended from the sky.
He looked at them;
they were both beautiful maidens.
He suspected them to be demons and
questioned them,
but they initially refused to speak.
When Xíng Zǐyǐ threatened to call the villagers,
Zhū Shì, in fear,
began to confess her story,
and also urged him not to reveal it,
offering to stay with him forever.
Xíng Zǐyǐ thought that a lady from a prominent family should not be equated with a demon's wife,
so he sent someone to inform her family.
Her parents, ever since their daughter flew away,
had been weeping and distraught;
when they suddenly received the letter,
they were overjoyed beyond expectation
and immediately ordered carriages and horses to depart at top speed.
They rewarded Xíng Zǐyǐ with a hundred taels of gold
and took their daughter home.
Xíng Zǐyǐ, having gained a beautiful wife,
and previously worried about his empty house,
was greatly comforted by the gold.
He went to thank Gù Mǒu.
Gù Mǒu again scrutinized him and said:
"Not yet, not yet.
Your prosperous fortune (tài yùn) has already begun,
what is a hundred taels of gold to speak of!"
Thus, he refused the thanks.
Previously,
the gentleman (shēn) had returned home
and requested the authorities to arrest Yáng Mǒu.
Yáng Mǒu had already fled,
and his whereabouts were unknown,
so his property was confiscated,
and a warrant was issued to apprehend Zhū Shì.
Zhū Shì, in fear,
clung to Xíng Zǐyǐ and wept.
Xíng Zǐyǐ was also at his wits' end.
He then bribed the warrant bearer,
rented a carriage, and took Zhū Shì to the gentleman (shēn),
pleading mournfully for their release.
The gentleman (shēn) was moved by his righteousness
and exerted all his efforts to arrange
their redemption;
he kept the couple in a separate guest house,
treating them with the affection of close relatives.
The gentleman's daughter had been engaged to a man named Liú since childhood.
Liú,
who held a prominent official position (xiǎn zhì),
heard that the daughter had stayed overnight at Xíng Zǐyǐ's house,
and considered it a disgrace.
He returned the marriage contract,
breaking off the engagement with the daughter.
The gentleman (shēn) was about to arrange a marriage into another family;
but his daughter told her parents
that she vowed to marry Xíng Zǐyǐ.
Xíng Zǐyǐ was delighted upon hearing this;
Zhū Shì was also happy
and voluntarily offered to become his concubine.
The gentleman (shēn) worried that Xíng Zǐyǐ had no home.
At that time, Yáng Mǒu's former residence was being sold by the authorities,
so the gentleman (shēn) bought it on Xíng Zǐyǐ's behalf.
The couple then returned home,
took out the previous gold,
roughly furnished the house with implements,
and hired maids and servants.
Within ten days, all the gold was spent.
They only hoped for the daughter's arrival,
expecting to receive more financial assistance from her.
One evening,
Zhū Shì said to Xíng Zǐyǐ:
"That wicked husband Yáng Mǒu
once buried a thousand taels of gold under the tower,
and only I know about it.
I just looked at the spot;
the bricks and stones are still intact,
so the hidden treasure might be unharmed."
They went and dug it up together,
and indeed found the gold.
Because of this, they believed in the divine accuracy of Gù Mǒu's predictions
and rewarded him handsomely.
Later, when the daughter married (yú guī),
her dowry was abundant,
and within a few years,
Xíng Zǐyǐ became the wealthiest in the entire prefecture.
The Historian of the Strange (Yì Shǐ Shì) remarks:
"The White Lotus Society (Bái Lián) was annihilated, yet Yáng Mǒu alone did not die,
and was even further enriched,
making one almost suspect that the vast net of heaven (huī huī zhě) is loose and leaky.
Who knew that Heaven preserved him
precisely for Xíng Zǐyǐ's sake?
Otherwise,
even if Xíng Zǐyǐ's misfortune turned to prosperity (fǒu jí ér tài),
how could he have suddenly acquired mansions and accumulated vast wealth?
He rejected one beauty (yī sè),
and Heaven rewarded him with two.
Alas!
The Creator (Zào Wù) speaks no words,
yet his intent is knowable."
According to the Jiàn Xuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì.
Lǐ Shēng
of Shānghé
was fond of the Dao.
A li or so outside the village,
there was a Buddhist temple.
He built three cells there
and sat cross-legged in them.
Wandering monks and mendicants,
when they came to stay,
would always chat with him,
and he would provide for them tirelessly.
One day,
during a severe snowstorm and bitter cold,
an old monk carrying a bag borrowed a couch.
His words were profound and subtle.
When he was about to leave after two nights,
Lǐ Shēng insisted on keeping him,
and he stayed for several more days.
Just then, Lǐ Shēng had to go home for another reason.
The monk urged him to return early,
intending to bid him farewell.
Lǐ Shēng went at cockcrow,
but knocked on the door and received no answer.
He climbed over the wall and entered.
He saw a lamp flickering in the air,
suspecting something was afoot,
so he stealthily peeked.
The monk was packing his luggage.
A lean donkey was suspended on the lamp stand.
Upon closer inspection,
it did not resemble a real donkey,
but rather something for burial.
However, its ears and tail moved occasionally,
and it snorted faintly.
Soon, the packing was finished,
the door was opened, and the donkey was led out.
Lǐ Shēng secretly followed.
Outside the door was a large pond.
The monk tied the donkey to a tree by the pond,
stripped naked and entered the water,
washing himself thoroughly.
Then he dressed, led the donkey in,
and also washed it.
Afterward, he loaded the luggage, mounted,
and rode off at extreme speed.
Lǐ Shēng then called out to him.
The monk merely bowed remotely in thanks.
His words were inaudible,
and he was already far away.
Wáng Méiwū said:
Lǐ Shēng was his friend.
He had once visited his home
and saw a plaque in the hall inscribed
"Hall of Awaiting Death."
He was also a man of understanding.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Zhào Gōng,
a native of Wǔlíng, Húguǎng,
was an official of the Gōngjiān,
who retired and returned home.
A young man waited at his gate,
seeking to be his scribe.
Zhào Gōng summoned him in,
seeing that the man was elegant and refined.
When asked his name,
he introduced himself as Lù Yāguān.
He did not ask for wages.
Zhào Gōng kept him,
and he was more intelligent than ordinary servants.
For official documents and memorials,
he would draft replies as he pleased,
all of them skillful and marvelous.
When Zhào Gōng entertained guests,
Lù Yāguān would assist him,
and his suggestions were always superior.
Zhào Gōng increasingly favored and cherished him.
The other servants, seeing that he had earned their master's favor,
jokingly asked him to host a banquet.
Yāguān agreed
and asked:
"How many subordinates are there?"
At that time, the steward of the separate estate had about thirty-odd people.
Everyone told him the number to make it difficult for him.
Yāguān said:
"This is very easy,
but there are many guests,
and I cannot prepare for it in a hurry.
A restaurant will do."
So he invited all his companions
to a shop facing the street.
Everyone sat down.
As the wine was just being served,
someone holding a pot stood up and said:
"Gentlemen, don't drink yet.
May I ask who is hosting today?
They should first put down money as a guarantee
before we can drink freely.
Otherwise,
if it costs several thousands,
and everyone disperses noisily,
from whom shall we seek compensation?"
Everyone looked at Yāguān.
Yāguān smiled and said:
"You don't think I have no money, do you?
I certainly have money."
Then he stood up
and pinched wet flour from a basin into a fist-sized ball,
then broke off pieces and placed them on the table.
As he threw them,
they immediately transformed into mice,
scurrying across the entire table.
Yāguān randomly caught one,
tore it open,
and with a squeak, its belly burst,
revealing a small piece of gold.
He caught another,
and it was the same.
In a moment, all the mice were gone,
and the table was full of broken gold.
Then he announced to the crowd:
"Is this not enough for drinks?"
Everyone was surprised,
and then they all drank to their hearts' content.
When it was finished,
the bill was over three liǎng.
The crowd weighed the gold,
and it precisely matched the amount.
Some asked for a piece to take home,
and reported the marvel to their master.
Their master ordered them to retrieve the gold,
but when searched, it was already gone.
When they questioned the shop owner,
all the money paid had turned into caltrops.
The servant reported this to Zhào Gōng,
who questioned him.
Yāguān said:
"My companions pressed me for food and drink,
and my purse was empty.
I learned a little trick when I was young,
so I just tried it out."
The crowd again demanded compensation.
Yāguān said:
"In the wheat chaff of a certain village,
if you winnow it again,
you can get two dàn of wheat,
which is more than enough to pay for the wine."
So he pulled one person to go with him.
The steward of that village was about to go home,
so he went along with them.
When they arrived, several hù of clean wheat
were already piled in the threshing ground.
Because of this, everyone marveled at Yāguān even more.
One day,
Zhào Gōng went to a friend's banquet,
where there was a very lush potted orchid in the hall,
which he admired.
Upon returning, he still praised it.
Yāguān said:
"If you truly love this orchid,
it's not difficult to obtain."
Zhào Gōng still doubted him.
Early the next morning, when he arrived at his study,
he suddenly smelled a rich fragrance,
and there was a pot of orchids,
with the same number of arrow-like leaves,
exactly as he had seen.
He then suspected it was stolen
and questioned him.
Yāguān said:
"My family has no fewer than thousands of these,
why would I need to steal?"
Zhào Gōng did not believe him.
Just then, the friend arrived,
saw the orchid, and exclaimed:
"How strikingly similar to my family's!"
“I just bought it,
and don’t know where it came from.
But when you leave the gate,
will you see if the orchids are still there?”
Mǒu said:
“I’ve never actually been to the study,
so whether they are there or not is indeed unknowable.
But how did it come to this?”
Zhào looked at the jailor,
who said:
“This is not difficult to distinguish.
The official pot is broken
and has mended spots;
this pot has none.”
After verification, he finally believed.
That night, he told his master:
“You mentioned that Mǒu’s family has quite a lot of flowers.
Now, I would like to trouble your honorable self
to go and see them by moonlight.
But no one else can come,
only Āyā is harmless.”
—Yā,
was a pageboy of Gōngjiān.
So he agreed to the request.
When Gōng went out,
four people were already carrying a sedan chair,
waiting prostrate by the roadside.
Zhào rode in it,
as fast as a galloping horse.
In a moment, they entered the mountains,
hearing only an exotic fragrance penetrating to the bone.
They arrived at a cave dwelling,
where they saw the characters for “dwelling” shining brightly,
strikingly different from the human world;
everywhere were arranged flowers and rocks,
in exquisite pots with beautiful plants,
radiating light and spreading fragrance.
Just of orchids alone,
there were about several dozen pots,
all flourishing.
After viewing,
he returned as previously ordered.
The jailor had followed Zhào for over ten years.
Later, Zhào died without illness,
and he and Āyā left together,
their whereabouts unknown.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāizhìyì*,
Jiǎng Tàishǐ Chāo
recorded that in his previous life, he was a monk from Éméi,
who frequently dreamt of washing his feet by the pond in front of his former hermitage.
He was deeply devoted to Buddhist scriptures,
focused solely on the Tiāntái school.
Although he ascended to officialdom early,
he often harbored thoughts of withdrawing from the world.
He took leave to return to Jiāngnán,
and upon reaching Qínyóu,
he did not wish to return home.
His son cried and pleaded with him,
but he did not listen.
He then entered Shǔ,
residing at Jīnshāsì in Chéngdū;
after a long time,
he went to Éméi again,
residing at Fúhǔsì,
where he manifested illness and passed away.
He personally wrote a gāthā, which said:
“Carefree apes and cranes befriend themselves,
the old monk aimlessly fell into the dust of karma.
Vainly seeking to avoid the heat in a cauldron of boiling oil,
how can one turn over in the great ocean?
Fame and merit are puppets on a stage,
wife and children are people in a procession of skeletons.
Only for my ruler and parents have I not repaid,
life after life I always pray for the ability to be benevolent.”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāizhìyì*,
Shào Jìnshì,
named Shìméi,
was from Jìníng.
Initially appointed as a professor in Dēngzhōu,
two old *xiùcai* presented their calling cards.
Upon seeing their names,
he felt a strong sense of familiarity;
he pondered for a long time,
and suddenly realized his former life.
He then asked his study attendant:
“Does Mǒu Shēng live in Mǒu Cūn?”
He also described their appearance,
which matched perfectly.
Soon, the two *xiùcai* arrived,
holding hands and conversing intimately,
as joyful as if they had known each other all their lives.
During the conversation,
they asked about Gāo Dōnghǎi’s situation.
The two *xiùcai* said:
“He died in prison more than twenty years ago,
and one son is still alive.
He was a humble commoner in this village,
how do you know him?”
Shào smiled and said:
“I am an old relative.”
Before this,
Gāo Dōnghǎi was a unruly person;
however, his nature was bold and straightforward,
valuing righteousness over wealth.
There was a man who, unable to pay rent, sold his daughter,
and Gāo Dōnghǎi emptied his purse to redeem her.
He had an affair with an old woman,
who was accused of being a hidden thief.
The authorities were pursuing her urgently,
so she took refuge in Gāo’s house.
The officials found out,
arrested Gāo,
and severely flogged him.
He never confessed,
and eventually died in prison.
The day he died
was the day Shào was born.
Later, Shào went to Mǒu Cūn,
consoled his wife and children,
and everyone far and near knew of this extraordinary event.
This was told by Gāo Shàozǎi,
who was Gāo Gōngzǐ Jìliáng’s contemporary in the examinations.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāizhìyì*.
A scholar from Jiāngnán, Gù Shēng,
was a guest in Jìxià.
His eyes suddenly swelled,
and he groaned day and night,
without any medicine or doctor.
After more than ten days,
the pain slightly subsided.
Whenever he closed his eyes,
he would see a grand mansion: it had four or five courtyards,
and all the doors were wide open.
In the deepest part, people were coming and going,
but from a distance, he couldn't make them out clearly.
One day,
as he focused his mind intently on it,
he suddenly felt his body enter the mansion.
He passed through three sets of doors,
and there was no one around.
There were north and south halls,
with red felt covering the ground inside.
He peered in briefly
and saw a room full of infants,
some sitting, some lying, some crawling on their knees,
countless in number.
While he was astonished and wondering,
a person came out from behind the house.
Seeing him, he said,
"The young prince said there was a distant guest at the door,
and so it is."
Then he invited him in.
Gù did not dare to enter, but
when pressured, he entered,
and asked,
"What place is this?"
He replied,
"This is the residence of the Crown Prince of the Ninth Prince (Jiǔwáng Shìzǐ).
The Crown Prince has just recovered from malaria,
and today relatives and friends are celebrating.
Sir, you are fortunate."
Before he finished speaking,
someone rushed in,
urging them to hurry.
Soon they arrived at a place with
carved pavilions and vermillion railings.
A hall faced north,
with nine bays.
Ascending the steps,
the guests were already seated.
He saw a young man seated facing north,
knowing he was the prince,
and immediately bowed down in the hall.
Everyone in the hall rose.
The prince pulled Gù to sit facing east.
After wine was served,
drums and music suddenly erupted,
and the courtesans ascended the hall
to perform
"Huáfēng Zhù."
Just as it passed the third movement,
the innkeeper and his servant called for lunch,
repeatedly shouting by the bed.
His ears heard it very clearly,
and fearing the prince would know,
he excused himself to change clothes and left.
He looked up, and the sun was setting.
He saw his servant standing by the bed,
and then realized he had not left the inn.
He wished to return quickly,
so he sent the servant to close the door and leave.
As soon as he closed his eyes,
he saw the palace still there.
He quickly followed the old path and entered.
Passing by the place where the infants were before,
there were no infants,
but dozens of old women with disheveled hair and hunched backs
were sitting and lying there.
Seeing Gù,
they spoke in harsh voices, saying,
"Whose unruly child
comes here to spy!"
Gù was startled and afraid,
dared not argue,
and hurried to the back courtyard,
ascended the hall, and sat down.
He saw that the prince's chin had grown a beard over a foot long.
Seeing Gù,
he smiled and asked,
"Where did you go?
The play has passed the seventh movement."
Then he showed him a large wine goblet as punishment.
After a while, the music ended,
and another performance was presented.
Gù ordered
"Péngzǔ Qǔfù."
The courtesan immediately served wine with a coconut dipper,
which could hold about five dòu.
Gù left his seat and politely said,
"This humble subject has an eye ailment,
and dares not get too drunk."
The prince said,
"You are suffering from an eye ailment.
There is an imperial physician (tàiyī) here;
he should examine you."
A guest on the east side
immediately left his seat and came over,
opened Gù's eyelids with two fingers,
and dabbed white ointment like fat with a jade hairpin,
instructing him to close his eyes and sleep for a while.
The prince ordered a maidservant to lead him into an inner room
and told him to lie down.
After lying down for a short time,
he felt the bed and curtains were fragrant and soft,
and consequently fell into a deep sleep.
Not long after,
he suddenly heard a loud, clanging sound of gongs,
and was startled awake again.
He suspected the play was not over.
Opening his eyes,
he saw that it was a dog in the inn licking an oil pan,
but his eye ailment was as if gone.
He closed his eyes again,
and saw nothing more.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chén Xījiǔ
was a native of Pī.
His father, Zǐyán,
was a famous scholar in the county.
A wealthy man named Zhōu Mǒu,
admiring his reputation,
arranged a marriage.
Chén repeatedly failed the examinations,
and his family fortunes declined.
He went to study in Qín,
and there was no news for several years.
Zhōu secretly began to regret the arrangement.
He married his younger daughter to Wáng Xiàolián as his second wife;
Wáng's betrothal gifts were lavish,
and his servants and horses were splendid.
Because of this, he increasingly despised Xījiǔ's poverty
and was determined to break off the marriage.
He asked his daughter,
but she refused.
Enraged,
he dressed her in poor clothes and sent her back to Xījiǔ.
They had no fire for cooking,
and Zhōu completely disregarded them.
One day,
he sent a maidservant with a lunch box (kē) to feed his daughter.
Upon entering, the maid said to the mother,
"My master sent me to see if the young mistress (xiǎogūgu) has starved to death."
The daughter, fearing her mother would be ashamed,
forced a smile to confuse her words.
Then she took out the food from the lunch box
and placed it before her mother.
The maid stopped her, saying,
"There's no need for that!
Since the young mistress entered this family,
has she ever exchanged a cup of warm or cold water?
These are our family's things,
and I expect the old mistress (lǎolao) wouldn't have the face to eat them either."
The mother was greatly enraged,
her expression and voice changing.
The maid was not submissive
and hurled insults.
Amidst the commotion,
Xījiǔ entered from outside.
Upon hearing what had happened, he was furious.
He grabbed her hair, slapped her cheeks,
and flogged her out the door.
The next day,
Zhōu came to take his daughter back,
but she refused to go.
The next day, he came again,
with more people.
They chattered noisily,
as if preparing for a fight.
The mother strongly urged her daughter to go.
The daughter secretly bowed to her mother
and got into the carriage and left.
After a few days,
Zhōu again sent someone to press for a divorce letter.
The mother forced Xījiǔ to give it.
She only hoped for Zǐyán's return
to make other arrangements.
Someone from the Zhōu family came from Xī'ān
and reported that Zǐyán had died.
Chén's mother, overcome with grief and indignation, fell ill and died.
Xījiǔ, in his deep sorrow and distress,
still hoped for his wife's return.
After a long time, with no sign of her,
his grief and indignation intensified.
He sold a few *mǔ* of meager land
to purchase burial necessities.
After the burial,
he begged for food and went to Qín,
to seek his father's bones.
Arriving in Xī'ān,
he inquired everywhere among the residents.
Someone said that several years ago, a scholar died in an inn,
and was buried in the eastern suburbs.
Now that the family was gone,
Xījiǔ had no plan.
He could only beg in the market in the morning,
and sleep in a wild temple at night,
hoping someone would know.
One evening, as he passed by the mass burial ground,
several people blocked his way,
demanding money for food.
Xījiǔ said:
"I am a stranger from another land,
begging for food in the city.
Where do I have money for food for these people?"
They all grew angry,
dragged him to the ground,
and stuffed his mouth with tattered rags from a buried child.
His strength failed, his voice became hoarse,
and he gradually approached death.
Suddenly, they all cried out in alarm:
"Where has the official arrived from?"
They let go and fell silent.
Soon, a carriage and horses arrived,
and someone immediately asked:
"Who is that person lying down?"
Immediately, several people lifted him to the carriage.
The person in the carriage said:
"This is my son.
How dare these evil ghosts do such a thing!
Bind them all,
do not let any escape."
Xījiǔ felt someone remove the gag,
and after a little while,
he looked closely,
and it was indeed his father.
He cried out loudly:
"Your son has suffered greatly for your bones.
Are you truly still among the living?"
His father said:
"I am not human;
I am the Superintendent of Tàiháng.
I came here also for my son."
Xījiǔ cried even more sorrowfully,
and his father comforted him.
Xījiǔ sobbed as he recounted his in-laws divorcing him.
His father said:
"Do not worry,
your new wife is also with your mother now.
Your mother misses you greatly;
you should go visit for a while."
Then, he rode with him in the same carriage,
galloping like wind and rain.
After a short time,
they arrived at an official residence.
He dismounted and entered through multiple gates,
and there was his mother.
Xījiǔ was so pained he nearly fainted,
but his father stopped him.
Xījiǔ listened obediently, choking back tears.
Seeing his wife beside his mother,
he asked his mother:
"My wife is here;
is she also in the underworld?"
His mother said:
"No,
your father brought her here.
When you return home,
she will be sent back."
Xījiǔ said:
"I will serve my parents;
I do not wish to return."
His mother said:
"You traveled with great hardship
for your father's bones.
If you do not return,
what was your original intention?
Moreover, your filial piety has reached the Heavenly Emperor,
who has bestowed upon you ten thousand *jīn* of gold.
You and your wife have a long future to enjoy;
why speak of not returning?"
Xījiǔ wept silently.
His father repeatedly urged him to go,
and Xījiǔ cried uncontrollably.
His father angrily said:
"Are you not going?"
Xījiǔ, frightened,
stopped crying,
and then inquired about the burial place.
His father pulled him along, saying:
"Go, my son,
and I will tell you: a hundred *bù* or so from the mass burial ground,
where there is a mother and son white elm, that is it."
He pulled him along very urgently,
so much so that he had no time to bid his mother farewell.
Outside the gate, there were strong servants
holding horses ready for him.
After mounting quickly,
his father instructed:
"At the place where you slept yesterday,
there is a small amount of money and an axe.
Quickly prepare your belongings and return home,
then demand your wife from your in-laws.
Do not rest
until you get your wife back."
Xījiǔ assented and departed.
The horse galloped exceptionally fast,
and he arrived in Xī'ān at cockcrow.
The servant helped him dismount;
just as he was about to bow and thank his parents,
the people and horses had already vanished.
He went to his former lodging place,
leaned against the wall, and dozed off,
waiting for daybreak.
There was a fist-sized stone at his sitting place, bothering his leg;
at dawn, he looked at it,
and it was white silver.
He bought a coffin and hired a cart,
found the spot under the twin elms,
and retrieved his father's bones to return home.
After the joint burial was completed,
his house was utterly bare.
Fortunately, the villagers pitied his filial piety
and shared food with him.
When he was about to go demand his wife,
he realized he could not use force by himself,
so he went with his clan cousin Shíjiǔ.
Upon reaching the gate,
the doorkeeper denied them entry.
Shíjiǔ, who was always a scoundrel,
began to behave outrageously and insultingly.
The Zhōu family sent someone to persuade Xījiǔ to return home,
promising to send their daughter immediately.
Xījiǔ returned.
Initially,
when the daughter returned,
Zhōu berated the son-in-law and his mother.
The daughter said nothing,
but only wept silently facing the wall.
When Chén mǔ died,
she was not even informed.
When the letter of divorce was received,
it was thrown at the daughter, saying:
"The Chén family has cast you out!"
The daughter replied:
"I have never been fierce or rebellious,
why am I being cast out?"
She wanted to return to question the reason,
but was again confined.
Later, Xījiǔ went to Xī'ān,
and so a fabricated death notice was created,
to sever the daughter's hopes.
Once this news spread,
Dù Zhōnghàn came to propose marriage,
and it was ultimately agreed to.
When the day for the groom's personal reception was set,
the daughter first learned of it,
and then wept and refused to eat,
covering her face with a quilt,
her breath as faint as a spider's silk.
Zhōu was at a loss,
when suddenly he heard Xījiǔ had arrived.
His speech was disrespectful,
expecting the daughter would surely die,
so he surprisingly sent Xījiǔ back,
intending to wait for the daughter's death to vent his anger.
When Xījiǔ returned,
the people delivering the daughter had already arrived;
still fearing Xījiǔ would see her illness and not take her in,
as soon as she entered the gate,
they abandoned her and left.
Neighbors worried on their behalf,
and conspired to send her back;
Xījiǔ did not listen,
but helped her onto the couch,
but her breath had already ceased.
Only then did he become greatly frightened.
While in a panic,
Zhōu Zǐ led several men armed with weapons and entered,
destroying all the doors and windows.
Xījiǔ fled and hid,
and they searched for him relentlessly.
The villagers all felt indignant;
Shíjiǔ gathered more than ten people to bravely rush to the rescue.
Zhōu Zǐ and his brothers were all injured,
and then scurried away like rats.
Zhōu became even angrier,
and sued them to the officials,
arresting Xījiǔ, Shíjiǔ, and others.
Xījiǔ was about to go,
and entrusted his wife's corpse to a neighboring old woman.
Suddenly he heard a faint breath from the couch,
and looking closer,
her beautiful eyes were faintly moving;
a short while later,
she could already turn over.
Greatly delighted,
he went to the official to state his case.
The magistrate was angry at Zhōu for making a false accusation.
Zhōu was afraid,
and bribed him with a heavy sum,
only then was he spared.
When Xījiǔ returned,
husband and wife met,
with a mix of sadness and joy.
Before this,
the daughter had abstained from food and lay dying,
vowing to herself that she would surely die.
Suddenly someone picked her up and said:
"I am a member of the Chén family,
come with me quickly,
husband and wife can meet;
otherwise,
it will be too late!"
Unconsciously, her body was already out the door,
and two people helped her onto a shoulder palanquin.
In a moment, they arrived at an official's residence,
where she saw her parents-in-law both present,
and asked:
"What place is this?"
Her mother said:
"There's no need to ask,
we will send you home when appropriate."
One day,
she saw Xījiǔ arrive,
and was very happy.
But after one glance, he suddenly left,
and her heart was quite puzzled and strange.
Her father-in-law did not know what was happening,
and constantly did not return for several days.
Last night he suddenly returned,
saying:
"I was in Wǔyí,
and returned two days late. It was difficult to protect my child.
You should quickly send the child home."
Then he sent the daughter with a palanquin and horses.
Suddenly seeing her family's door,
it was as if she awoke from a dream.
The daughter and Xījiǔ recounted the past events together,
mutually astonished and delighted.
From then on, husband and wife lived together,
but had no means to support themselves day and night.
Xījiǔ set up a children's school in the village,
and also diligently worked hard,
often privately remarking:
"My father said heaven grants gold,
but now the four walls are empty,
how can teaching lead to success?"
One day,
returning from the school,
he met two men,
who asked him:
"Are you Chén Mǒu?"
Xījiǔ said:
"Yes."
The two men immediately produced iron chains and bound him.
Xījiǔ did not understand the reason.
A short while later,
the villagers all gathered,
and questioned him together,
only then did they realize he was being taken by the county bandits.
Everyone pitied his injustice,
and pooled money to bribe the escorts,
so he suffered no hardship on the way.
Upon reaching the county and seeing the Grand Administrator,
he recounted his family history.
The Grand Administrator was astonished and said:
"This is the son of a renowned scholar,
gentle and refined,
how could he be a thief!"
He ordered to release him from his shackles,
and severely punished the thief with a cangue,
only then did he confess that Zhōu Mǒu had bribed and instructed him.
Xījiǔ further complained about the reason for the father-in-law and son-in-law's falling out,
and the Grand Administrator was even angrier,
immediately ordering their arrest.
He then invited Xījiǔ to his office,
and discussed their family's long-standing friendship,
for the Grand Administrator was the son of the former Pī Magistrate, Hán Gōng,
who was indeed the person Zǐyán had studied under and sought advice from.
He presented a hundred taels of silver for his study expenses;
and also two mules for travel,
so he could frequently come to the county,
to be tutored in literature and art.
He then propagated his filial piety to various superior officials,
from the Governor-General downwards,
all sent gifts.
Xījiǔ returned riding the mules,
and husband and wife were greatly comforted.
One day,
his wife's mother arrived weeping,
and saw her daughter prostrate on the ground unable to rise.
The daughter, startled, asked her,
and only then learned that Zhōu had been shackled and was in prison.
The daughter cried sadly, blaming herself,
only wishing to die.
Xījiǔ had no choice,
but went to the county to plead on his behalf.
The Grand Administrator released him allowing him to redeem himself,
punishing him with a hundred *shí* of grain,
and inscribed it as a gift to the filial son, Chén Xījiǔ.
Upon his release,
he took out grain from the granary,
mixed with husks and chaff, and transported it.
Xījiǔ said to his wife:
"Your father-in-law measured a gentleman with the heart of a petty man.
How did he know I would accept it,
and so meticulously mix in husks and chaff?"
Thus, he smiled and refused it.
Xījiǔ's household, though somewhat well-off,
had dilapidated and shabby walls.
One night,
a band of thieves broke in.
The servants awoke
and shouted loudly,
stopping the theft of only two mules, after which the thieves fled.
More than half a year later,
Xījiǔ was reading at night
when he heard a knocking sound at the door.
He inquired, but there was silence.
He called a servant to get up and look,
and the door was ajar.
Two mules leaped in,
the very ones that had been stolen earlier.
They ran straight under a willow tree,
huffing and puffing, covered in sweat.
When illuminated by a candle,
each was seen to be carrying a leather bag.
He untied and looked inside;
they were full of silver ingots.
He was greatly astonished,
not knowing where they had come from.
Later, he heard that on that night, a great bandit gang had robbed Zhōu,
departing fully loaded.
They were pursued closely by the defense troops,
so they abandoned their bundles and fled.
The mules recognized their former master
and ran straight home.
Zhōu returned from prison,
his wounds from torture still severe.
Then he was robbed by bandits,
fell seriously ill, and died.
His daughter dreamed at night that her father, imprisoned, came to her,
saying:
"What I did in my life,
I regret, but it's too late.
Now I suffer karmic punishment in the underworld.
No one but your father-in-law can release me.
Plead with your husband for me
and deliver a letter to him."
She awoke weeping.
When questioned,
she recounted everything.
Xījiǔ had long wanted to visit Tàiháng,
so he departed that very day.
Upon arrival,
he prepared sacrificial animals and dairy offerings, making prayers.
He then slept outdoors at that spot,
hoping to see something.
Nothing unusual happened all night,
so he returned.
After Zhōu's death,
his mother and daughter became even poorer,
relying on the second son-in-law for support.
Wáng Xiàolián, a scholar, was appointed county magistrate
but was disgraced by corruption.
His entire family moved to Shěnyáng,
with nowhere to return.
Xījiǔ often cared for them at this time.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"There is no greater good than filial piety;
even ghosts and spirits are moved by it,
which is certainly reasonable.
If someone is a person of high virtue,
even if they remain poor throughout their life,
they will still be valued.
How much more certain is their future prosperity?
Some entrust their precious daughters
to a decrepit old man
and proudly declare: 'So-and-so high official
is my son-in-law.'
Alas!
The young and innocent girl remains the same,
but her 'golden tortoise' son-in-law returns in a coffin,
which is already tragic enough.
How much more so if the young wife is made to follow the army?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
The daughter of a certain elder from Línzī
was the wife of Student Lǐ from the Imperial Academy.
Before she was married,
a diviner predicted her destiny,
concluding that she would certainly suffer official punishment.
The elder was angry,
then laughed and said:
"Such wild talk!
Aside from the fact that a daughter from a prominent family would never go to court,
how could a mere Imperial Academy student not protect his wife?"
After she was married,
she was extremely fierce,
beating and scolding her husband as a matter of course.
Lǐ could not endure her abuse
and angrily reported it to the yamen.
The county magistrate, Shào Gōng, approved his petition
and immediately dispatched a runner to summon her.
When the elder heard of it,
he was greatly alarmed.
He led his sons and younger brothers to the court
and tearfully begged for the case to be dropped.
He was not granted it.
Lǐ also regretted it
and asked for it to be dismissed.
The magistrate angrily said:
"How can the yamen's proceedings be started and stopped entirely at your will? She must be arrested and interrogated!"
Once she arrived,
he briefly questioned her a word or two,
then said:
"What a fierce woman!"
He ordered thirty strokes with the rod,
stripping the flesh from her buttocks.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Was the magistrate perhaps pained by family matters?
Why such violent anger!
However, if a county has a worthy magistrate,
then there will be no fierce women in the villages.
This is recorded
to supplement what is lacking
in the 'Biographies of Upright Officials'."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Táo Shèngyú from Běipíng
was a renowned scholar.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
he went to the provincial examinations
and lodged in the outskirts of the city.
One day, he happened to step out of his door
and saw a person carrying a satchel, wandering about,
as if having not yet found lodging.
He questioned him briefly,
and the man set down his burden on the road.
They conversed,
and his words and opinions showed the style of a renowned scholar.
Táo was greatly pleased with him
and invited him to live together.
The guest happily
carried his bag in,
and they resided together.
The guest introduced himself:
“Shùntiān rén
Yú
Qù'è.”
Táo *chāi cháng*,
xiōng zhī.
Yú xìng bù xǐ yóuzhǔ,
cháng dú zuò yī shì,
ér àntóu wú shūjuàn.
Táo bù yǔ tán,
zé mò wò éryǐ.
Táo yí zhī,
sōu qí nángqiè,
zé bǐyàn zhīwài,
gèng wú chángwù.
Guài ér wèn zhī,
xiào yuē:
“Wúbèi dú shū,
qǐ lín kě shǐ jué jǐng yé?”
Yī rì,
jiù Táo jiè shū qù,
bì hù chāo shèn jí,
zhōngrì wǔshí yú zhǐ,
yì bù jiàn qí zhédié chéng juàn.
Qiè kuī zhī,
zé měi yī gǎo tuō,
zé shāo huī tūn zhī.
Yù yì guài yān.
Jí qí gù,
yuē:
“Wǒ yǐ cǐ dài dú ěr.”
Biàn sòng suǒ chāo shū,
qǐngkè shù piān,
yī zì wú é.
Táo yuè,
yù chuán qí shù;
Yú yǐwéi bù kě.
Táo yí qí lìn,
cí shè qiàoràng.
Yú yuē:
“Xiōng chéng bù liàng wǒ zhī shēn yǐ.
Yù bù yán,
zé cǐ xīn wú yǐ zì pōu;
zòu yán zhī,
yòu kǒng jīng wèi yìguài.
Nàihé?”
Táo gù wèi:
“Bùfáng.”
Yú yuē:
“Wǒ fēi rén,
shí guǐ ěr.
Jīn míngzhōng yǐ kēmù shòuguān,
qīyuè shísìrì fèng zhào kǎo liánguān,
shíwǔrì shìzǐ rùwéi,
yuè jǐn bǎng fàng yǐ.”
Táo wèn:
“Kǎo liánguān wèihé?”
Yuē:
“Cǐ Shàngdì shènzhòng zhī yì,
wúlùn niǎolì biēguān,
jiē kǎo zhī.
Néngwén zhě yǐ nèilián yòng,
bùtōng zhě bùdé yǔ yān.
Gài yīn zhī yǒu zhū shén,
yóu yáng zhī yǒu shǒulìng yě.
Dézhì zhū gōng, mù bù dǔ féndiǎn,
búguò shàonián chí qiāoménzhuān,
lièqǔ gōngmíng,
mén jì kāi,
zé qì qù;
zài sī bùshū shíshù nián,
jí wénxuéshì,
xiōngzhōng shàng yǒu zì yé!
Yángshì suǒyǐ lòuliè xìngjìn,
ér yīngxióng shīzhì zhě,
wéi shǎo cǐ yī kǎo ěr.”
Táo shēnrán zhī,
yóushì yì jiā jìngwèi.
One day,
Yú came from outside,
with a worried expression,
sighing:
"I was born humble and poor,
and thought that after death I could be free;
I didn't expect adversity to go ahead
and accompany me underground."
Táo asked the reason,
and Yú said:
"Wén has already been ordered to be enfeoffed as a king in the Duōluó Guó,
and the examination for the curtain official has thus been canceled.
For decades, having exhausted my spirit and ghosts
and mixed into literary circles,
how can we have any hope?"
Táo asked:
"Who are these people?"
Yú said:
"If I tell you,
you won't know them either.
If I briefly mention one or two,
you can generally understand: Yuèzhèng Shīkuàng and Sīkù Hèjiào are they.
I think to myself that fate cannot be relied upon,
and writing cannot be depended on,
so it's better to quit."
Having spoken, he was sullen,
and was about to prepare to leave.
Táo restrained and comforted him,
and then he stopped.
On the evening of Zhōngyuán,
Yú said to Táo:
"I am going into the examination hall.
Please, at dawn,
hold an incense stick in the east wilderness,
call out 'Qù'è' three times,
and I will arrive."
Then he went out.
Táo bought wine and cooked fresh food to await him.
When the east was already white,
he respectfully did as instructed.
Soon after,
Yú came with a young man.
Táo asked for his name,
and Yú said:
"This is Fāng Zǐjìn,
my good friend,
whom I just met in the examination hall.
Hearing of your great reputation,
he deeply wishes to meet you."
They went together to the lodging,
and held candles as a courtesy.
The young man was tall and straight like jade,
and his demeanor was humble and gentle.
Táo liked him very much,
and immediately asked:
"Zǐjìn's excellent works must be very satisfying."
Yú said:
"It's laughable to mention!
Of the seven regulations in the examination hall,
more than half were completed;
after carefully examining the name of the chief examiner,
he packed his belongings and left directly.
What a remarkable person!"
Táo fanned the stove and offered wine,
and then asked:
"What were the topics in the examination hall?
Did Qù'è pass with flying colors?"
Yú said:
"One on calligraphy and one on classical treatises,
which anyone can do.
The policy question was: 'From ancient times, there have been many wicked people,
but the worldly customs have reached such a point today
that illicit affairs and ugly behaviors
are increasingly indescribable,
not only because the eighteen hells cannot contain them all,
but also because the eighteen hells cannot even accommodate them.
What method can truly address this?
Some suggest appropriately adding one or two hells,
but this greatly loses the Sàngdì's benevolent heart.
Whether it is appropriate to add them or not,
or if there is another way to cleanse their source,
all you scholars should speak fully and hide nothing.'
Duō-dì's policy essay, though not excellent,
was quite forthright.
The memorial was: 'Proposed that the demons be annihilated,
and that ministers be granted dragon horses and heavenly robes with distinctions.'
Next were 'Poems for the Imperial Examination on Yáotái'
and 'Rhapsody on the Peach Blossoms of Xīchí'.
These three,
I believe, were unrivaled in the examination hall!"
Having spoken, he clapped his hands.
Fāng smiled and said:
"This moment of joy,
allow brother to be unrivalled;
after a few days,
if he doesn't cry bitterly, then he's a man."
At dawn,
Fāng wanted to take his leave.
Táo asked him to stay and share the lodging,
but Fāng refused,
only agreeing to come in the evening.
Three days later,
he did not come again.
Táo sent Yú to look for him.
Yú said:
"No need.
Zǐjìn's earnestness
is not without reason."
When the sun had set in the west,
Fāng indeed came.
He took out a scroll and handed it to Táo,
saying:
"I broke my promise for three days,
so I have respectfully copied over a hundred of my old works,
seeking your comments."
Táo took it and read it with great joy,
praising every sentence,
briefly quoting one or two pieces,
and then put them away in a box.
They talked until late at night,
and Fāng then stayed,
sharing a bed with Yú.
From then on, this became a habit.
Fāng came every evening,
