and Táo was happy every time Fāng came.
One evening,
Fāng rushed in,
and said to Táo:
"The underworld's results have been posted,
and Yú-Wǔ-xiōng has failed!"
Yú was lying down,
and hearing this, he started up in shock,
bursting into tears.
The two men tried their best to comfort him,
and his tears finally stopped.
However, they sat facing each other in silence,
which was truly unbearable.
Fāng said:
"I just heard that the Grand Inspector Zhāng Huán Hóu
will arrive soon, which might be a fabrication by disheartened individuals;
otherwise,
there are still reversals in the literary examinations."
Yú heard this
and his face lit up with joy.
Táo inquired about the reason,
and Yú said:
"Huán Hóu Yìdé [Zhāng Fēi]
inspects the underworld once every thirty years,
and the human world once every thirty-five years.
All the injustices in both realms
await this elder to eradicate them."
Then he rose
and pulled Fāng to leave with him.
They returned two nights later.
Fāng joyfully said to Táo:
"Are you not going to congratulate our fifth brother?
Huán Hóu arrived the night before last
and tore up the earth roster.
Of the names on the roster,
only one-third remained.
He read through the remaining scrolls
and was very pleased to find our fifth brother.
He recommended him as the Inspector of the Seas for Jiāonán.
His carriage and horses should arrive morning or evening."
Táo was greatly pleased,
set out wine, and offered congratulations.
After a few rounds of wine,
Yú asked Táo:
"Does your family have a spare room?"
Táo asked:
"What for?"
Yú said:
"Zǐjìn is an orphan with no hometown,
and I also cannot bear to suddenly abandon my brother.
My intention is to borrow lodging and live together."
Táo happily said:
"If so,
it would be a great fortune.
Even if there aren't many rooms,
what harm is there in sharing a bed?
However, there is my strict father,
whom I must inform beforehand."
Yú said:
"I know your esteemed father is kind and reliable.
Your examination is approaching.
If Zǐjìn cannot wait,
how about he returns first?"
Táo asked him to stay and accompany him at the inn,
awaiting their return together.
The next day,
as dusk fell,
a carriage and horses arrived at the gate
to escort Yú to his post.
Yú rose,
shook hands, and said:
"From now on, we part ways.
I have one thing I want to tell you,
but I fear it might hinder your ambition to advance."
Táo asked:
"What is it?"
Yú said:
"Your fate is difficult and impeded,
you were born at the wrong time.
For this examination, your chances are one in ten;
in the next examination, Huán Hóu will descend to the world,
and public justice will begin to manifest,
then it will be three in ten;
only in the third examination can you truly hope."
Hearing this, Táo
wanted to give up.
Yú said:
"No,
these are all destined by heaven.
Even if you clearly know it's impossible,
the ordained hardships
must still be endured to the end."
He then looked at Fāng and said:
"Don't delay.
This morning, the year, month, day, and hour are all auspicious.
I will send you home with my carriage and canopy.
My servants will ride their horses and depart on their own."
Fāng joyfully bowed in farewell.
Táo's heart was confused,
he didn't know what to instruct,
but he waved his tears as he saw them off.
He saw the carriage and horses go their separate ways,
and in an instant, they all dispersed.
Only then did he regret that Zǐjìn had headed north
without sending a single word,
but it was already too late.
After the three examination sessions were over,
Táo was not very satisfied,
and hurried home.
Entering the gate, he asked about Zǐjìn,
but no one in the family knew anything.
He then related the story to his father.
His father joyfully said:
"If so,
then the guest arrived long ago."
Earlier, Old Táo was sleeping during the day,
and dreamt that a carriage and canopy stopped at his gate.
A handsome young man emerged from the carriage
and entered the hall to bow.
Surprised, Old Táo asked where he came from,
and the young man replied:
"My elder brother promised to lend me a room,
but as he entered the examination hall, he couldn't come with me.
I arrived first."
Having spoken,
he asked to enter and bow to his mother.
As Old Táo was modestly declining,
the old family woman entered and said:
"Madam has given birth to a young master!"
Old Táo awoke with a start,
greatly amazed.
On that day, what Táo said
perfectly matched his dream,
and he then knew that the child was indeed Zǐjìn reborn.
Father and son were both delighted,
and named the child Xiǎojìn.
When the child was first born,
he would cry loudly at night,
which distressed his mother.
Táo said:
"If he is Zǐjìn,
when I see him,
his crying should stop."
Custom prohibited a visitor from offending [the newborn],
so Táo was not allowed to see him.
But the mother found the crying unbearable,
so she called Táo in.
Táo soothed him, saying:
"Zǐjìn, don't be like that!
I'm here!"
The child was crying intensely,
but hearing the voice, he immediately stopped,
staring fixedly without blinking,
as if scrutinizing.
Táo stroked his head and left.
From then on, he never cried again.
A few months later,
Táo dared not see him: once seen,
the child would bend over and demand to be held;
if Táo walked away,
the crying would become uncontrollable.
Táo also doted on him affectionately.
At four years old, he left his mother
and always slept with his brother;
if his brother went out,
he would pretend to sleep while waiting for his return.
His brother taught him
the "Máo Shī" on the pillow,
and his recitations were a murmur,
forty-odd lines by the end of the night.
Táo gave him Zǐjìn's unfinished writings,
which he happily read,
committing them to memory as soon as they passed his lips;
but when tested with other texts,
he could not.
At eight or nine years old,
his features were bright and clear,
exactly like Zǐjìn.
Táo entered the examination hall twice,
but did not pass either time.
In the Dīngyǒu year,
a scandal broke out in the literary examinations,
many examination officials were punished and dismissed,
and the path to official selection was thoroughly rectified,
which was the power of Zhāng Xúnhuán.
Táo passed as a "vice-car" (an alternate) in the next examination,
and soon became a gòngshì.
He then gave up his ambitions for an official career
and lived in seclusion, teaching his younger brother.
He once told people:
"With this joy I have,
I would not trade it for the Imperial Academy."
The Recorder of Strange Tales says:
"Every time I visit the temple of Master Zhāng,
I gaze upon his whiskers and eyebrows,
and there is a vivid, awe-inspiring vitality.
Moreover, his life's obscure actions were like thunder,
and wherever his spear and horse reached,
everything was greatly satisfying,
exceeding expectations.
The world considers the general fond of martial arts,
and thus places him among Jiàng and Guàn;
who knew that the affairs of the Wénchāng were complicated,
and that many 'Hóu' were truly needed!
Alas!
Thirty-five years,
how late he arrives!"
From the hand-copied edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì from Zhùxuězhāi.
Liú Xuéshī said:
“In Jìníng there was a mad scholar,
who was good at drinking.
His family had no property to speak of,
but whenever he got money, he would buy wine.
He never took his poverty to heart.
It happened that a new cìshǐ took office,
who was unmatched in drinking.
Hearing the scholar's name,
he invited him to drink and was pleased with him,
often chatting and feasting together.
The scholar presumed upon their familiarity,
and whenever there was a minor dispute where someone sought justice,
he would accept a small bribe to intercede for them;
the cìshǐ always granted his requests.
The scholar became accustomed to this,
and the cìshǐ grew tired of it.
One day, during an early court session,
the scholar presented his card and entered the hall.
The cìshǐ smiled upon reading it.
The scholar sternly said: ‘If you grant my request,
then grant it;
if you don't grant my request,
then deny it.
Why do you smile?
I've heard: a scholar can be killed but not disgraced.
Though I cannot repay you in other ways,
how could I not repay a mere smile?’
Having spoken,
he laughed loudly,
his voice shaking the hall walls.
The cìshǐ angrily said:
‘How dare you be so rude!
Have you not heard of the yĭn that destroys families?!’
The scholar swung his arm and walked out,
shouting: ‘A raw student has no family to destroy!’
The cìshǐ grew even angrier and
arrested him.
Upon inquiring about his home,
it was found he had no land or property at all,
only that he and his wife lived on the city wall.
The cìshǐ heard this and released him,
but expelled him, no longer allowing him to reside on the city wall.
His friends pitied his madness
and bought him a few feet of land,
purchasing a small room for him.
When he moved in,
he sighed: ‘From now on, I fear the yĭn!’”
The Historian of the Strange said:
“A gentleman who upholds the law and observes propriety
dares not oppress people in the marketplace.
What can those in power do to me?
However, the reason one can still be harmed by an enemy
is simply because one has a family;
if one has absolutely no family to destroy,
then the angry person has nothing more to inflict.
Alas!
Is this what is meant by ‘the poor and lowly are arrogant’?
Yet, a gentleman, though poor,
does not easily impose on others.
To be burdened by the demands of food and drink,
chattering in the public hall,
is indeed a low character.
Nevertheless,
his madness is unmatched.”
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A man from Chéngrén transformed into a rat and other creatures,
and went out of the academy to seek food.
A guest staying at an inn
often saw groups of rats entering the rice jar;
when he drove them away, they would flee.
The guest waited for them to enter,
then suddenly covered the jar,
and poured water into it.
In a short while, they all died.
The host's entire family died suddenly,
only one son remained.
He sued the official,
who pardoned and released the guest.
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liú Chìshuǐ,
a native of Pínglè,
was intelligent and outstanding in his youth.
At fifteen, he entered the prefectural treasury.
His parents died early,
so he became dissolute and ruined himself.
His family was not wealthy,
but he was by nature fond of adornment,
and his bedding and couch were all exquisite.
One evening,
he was invited out for a drink
and forgot to extinguish the lamp before leaving.
After a few rounds of wine,
he suddenly remembered
and hurried back.
He heard faint whispers in his room
and peeped stealthily,
seeing a young man embracing a beautiful woman, sleeping on his couch.
His house was next to a dilapidated residence of a noble family,
where strange occurrences were common,
so he knew they were foxes,
but he was not afraid.
He entered and shouted,
"How can one snore on my couch!"
The two, flustered,
grabbed their clothes and fled naked.
They left behind a pair of purple damask trousers,
with a needle case tied to the belt.
Liú Chìshuǐ was greatly pleased.
Fearing it would be stolen,
he hid it in his bedding and embraced it.
Presently, a dishevelled maid entered through a crack in the door
and demanded it from Liú Chìshuǐ.
Liú Chìshuǐ laughed and demanded compensation.
The maid offered to leave him wine,
but he did not agree;
she offered him gold,
but he still did not agree.
The maid laughed and left.
She soon returned and said,
"My elder sister says: if you return it,
she will repay you with a beautiful partner."
Liú Chìshuǐ asked,
"Who is she?"
She replied,
"Our family name is Pí.
My elder sister's pet name is Bāxiān.
The one sleeping with her is Hú Láng.
My second sister is Shuǐxiān,
who married Dīng Guānrén of Fùchuān.
My third sister is Fèngxiān,
even more beautiful than both sisters,
and there is no one who would not be pleased with her."
Liú Chìshuǐ feared losing the opportunity,
so he asked her to sit and wait for the good news.
The maid left and returned again, saying,
"My elder sister sends a message to the gentleman: How can a good deed be accomplished suddenly?
I just spoke with him,
but was met with harsh reproaches.
Just wait for a while;
our family does not make empty promises."
Liú Chìshuǐ gave her the trousers.
Several days passed,
but there was no news.
In the late afternoon,
he returned from outside,
closed his door, and had just sat down,
when suddenly both doors opened themselves,
and two people carried a young woman in a quilt,
holding the four corners,
saying,
"The new bride has arrived!"
They laughed, placed her on the couch, and left.
He looked closely at her:
she was deeply asleep and not yet awake,
the scent of wine still pleasant,
her flushed face and drunken state
were utterly captivating.
He was overjoyed.
He held her feet to remove her socks
and embraced her body to loosen her clothes.
But the woman had slightly woken,
opened her eyes and saw Liú Chìshuǐ.
Her limbs could not move on their own,
but she merely said resentfully,
"Bāxiān, that immoral maid, sold me out!"
Liú Chìshuǐ amorously embraced her.
The woman disliked his cold skin,
and smiled faintly, saying,
"What night is this,
that I should meet such a cold person!"
Liú Chìshuǐ said,
"Oh you, oh you,
what can one do with such a cold person!"
Then they made love joyfully.
Afterward, she said,
"That shameless maid
defiled someone's bed,
and exchanged a concubine for trousers!
I must get a small revenge!"
From then on, she came every night,
and their intimacy was very deep.
She took out a gold bracelet from her sleeve,
saying,
"This belongs to Bāxiān."
A few more days later,
she brought a pair of embroidered shoes,
inlaid with pearls and embroidered with gold,
of exceptionally exquisite craftsmanship,
and instructed Liú Chìshuǐ to display them widely.
Liú Chìshuǐ showed them off to relatives and friends,
and those who wished to see them had to pay for wine as a loan.
Thus, he dealt in this rare commodity.
One night, the woman came
and bid farewell.
He asked, puzzled,
and she replied,
"My sister hates me because of the shoes
and wants to move the family far away,
to cut off our good relationship."
Liú Chìshuǐ was alarmed
and offered to return them.
The woman said,
"No need.
She is using this to coerce me;
if I return them,
I will fall into her trap."
Liú Chìshuǐ asked,
"Why don't you stay alone?"
She said,
"My parents are moving far away.
The entire family, more than ten people,
are all entrusting Hú Láng with their affairs.
If I don't go with them,
I fear long-tongued women will spread rumours."
From then on, she never came again.
More than two years passed,
and his yearning was extremely strong.
One day, while on the road,
he encountered a young lady riding a dappled horse,
with an old servant leading it.
They brushed shoulders as they passed;
she then lifted her veil and glanced back,
her beauty stunning.
A moment later,
a young man arrived.
He asked:
"Who was that woman?
She seemed quite beautiful."
Liú immediately praised her,
and the young man cupped his hands and smiled, saying:
"You praise her too highly!
This is my wife."
Liú, embarrassed and apologetic, excused himself.
The young man said:
"No matter.
But among the three Gé of Nányáng,
you have the most distinguished one;
mine is hardly worth mentioning!"
Liú doubted his words.
The young man said:
"Do you not recognize the one who secretly slept on your couch?"
Liú then realized it was Hú.
They recounted their relationship as brothers-in-law,
teasing and laughing with great joy.
The young man said:
"Our father-in-law has just returned.
We are going to pay our respects.
Would you like to come along?"
Liú was delighted
and followed him into Yíngshān.
On the mountain, there was an old residence where villagers had taken refuge from unrest.
The lady dismounted and entered.
A short while later,
the servant came out and looked,
saying:
"Liú guānrén has also arrived."
They entered the gate to pay their respects to the elder couple.
Another young man was already there,
his boots and robes dazzlingly beautiful.
The elder said:
"This is our son-in-law Dīng from Fùchuān."
They all bowed and took their seats.
After a short time,
wine and roasted meat were lavishly served,
and their conversation and laughter were very congenial.
The elder said:
"Today, all three sons-in-law are here;
it can be called a wonderful gathering.
And since there are no outsiders,
we can call the children to come
and have a family reunion feast."
Soon,
the sisters all came out.
The elder ordered seats to be arranged,
each by her husband.
Bāxiān, upon seeing Liú,
only covered her mouth and smiled;
Fèngxiān frequently teased him;
Shuǐxiān's appearance was slightly inferior,
but she was calm and gentle,
and while everyone else chatted,
she merely held her wine and smiled.
Then, shoes and slippers were intermingled,
and the fragrance of orchid and musk filled the air.
They drank with great merriment.
Liú saw that all the musical instruments were ready at the bedside,
so he took a jade flute
and offered to play a tune for the elder's longevity.
The elder was pleased,
and ordered those who were skilled to each perform an art,
whereupon the entire company eagerly vied for instruments;
only Dīng and Fèngxiān did not take any.
Bāxiān said:
"It's understandable for Dīng Láng not to,
but why do you always refuse?"
She then threw the clappers into Fèngxiān's arms.
A burst of lively music followed.
The elder exclaimed with joy:
"The joy of our family is boundless!
The children can all sing and dance;
why not each display their talents?"
Bāxiān stood up,
grabbed Shuǐxiān, and said:
"Fèngxiān's voice has always been like jade and gold,
we dare not trouble her;
we two can sing 'Luò Fēi'
a song."
As soon as they finished singing and dancing,
a maid brought in fruits on a golden tray,
the names of which were unknown to anyone.
The elder said:
"These were brought from Zhēnlà,
they are called 'Tiánpóluó'."
He then scooped out several and sent them to Dīng.
Fèngxiān was displeased and said:
"Does a son-in-law distinguish between rich and poor in his affections?"
The elder smiled faintly and said nothing.
Bāxiān said:
"Our father considers Dīng Láng from a different county,
so he is a guest.
If we talk about seniority,
is Fèng Mèimei the only one with a 'fist-sized sour son-in-law'?"
Fèngxiān remained unhappy,
removed her elaborate makeup,
handed the drumstick to a maid,
and sang
"Pòyáo"
an aria,
with tears streaming down her face and voice.
After she finished,
she flung her sleeves and left directly,
and the entire company became unhappy because of her.
Bāxiān said:
"That girl's arrogant nature is still the same."
Then she went after her,
but did not know where she had gone.
Liú felt ashamed
and also excused himself to return home.
Halfway there,
he saw Fèngxiān sitting by the roadside.
She called him to sit beside her
and said:
"You are a man,
can you not speak up for your bedfellow?
A golden house lies within books,
I hope you will do well."
She lifted her foot and said:
"I left in a hurry,
and a thorn has broken my old shoe.
Is the gift I gave you
with you?"
Liú took it out.
The woman took it and exchanged it for her own.
Liú begged for her worn-out one.
She smiled broadly and said:
"You are truly shameless!
How often do you see someone wanting to keep
their own intimate bedding?
If you love me,
I can give you one item."
She then produced a mirror and handed it to him, saying:
"If you wish to see me,
you must seek me in books;
otherwise,
there will be no date for us to meet."
After speaking,
she vanished.
Liú returned home disheartened.
He looked into the mirror,
and Féngxiān 背立 (bèi lì) was there within it,
like a person seen from a hundred paces away.
Recalling her instructions,
he dismissed his visitors and lowered the curtains.
One day,
he saw the person in the mirror suddenly turn to face him,
her figure graceful and on the verge of a smile,
which made him love her even more deeply.
When no one was around,
he would always face the mirror with her.
After more than a month,
his sharp resolve gradually waned,
and he often forgot to return from his outings.
Upon returning, he saw her reflection in the mirror,
looking sorrowful, as if on the verge of tears.
The next day, he looked again,
and she was standing with her back to him as before. He then realized it was due to his neglected studies.
So, he shut himself indoors to study,
day and night without cease.
After more than a month,
her reflection turned outward again.
From then on, he used this as a test:
whenever he was negligent in his duties,
her expression would be sad;
after several days of hard work,
her expression would be smiling.
Thus, he hung it up morning and evening,
as if facing a teacher or guardian.
After two such years,
he succeeded in the imperial examination in one attempt.
Joyfully, he said:
“Now I can face my Féngxiān!”
He picked up the mirror and looked into it,
seeing her brows beautifully drawn and long,
her white teeth slightly revealed,
her joyous expression captivating,
as if right before his eyes.
He loved her immensely,
and gazed without stopping.
Suddenly, the person in the mirror smiled and said:
“‘My lover in the reflection,
my beloved in the painting,’
this is what is meant by it today.”
Startled and overjoyed, he looked around,
and Féngxiān (Féngxiān) was already seated beside him.
He grasped her hand and asked after his father-in-law (Wēng) and mother-in-law’s (Ǎo) health,
to which she replied:
“After I left you,
I never returned home,
but hid in a cave,
merely to share your hardships.”
Liú (Liú) went to a banquet in the prefecture,
and the girl asked to go with him.
They rode together,
and people opposite them did not notice them.
After a while, when they were about to return,
she secretly plotted with Liú,
to pretend they were being married in the prefecture.
Once the girl returned,
she began to appear before guests and manage the household.
Everyone was astonished by her beauty,
but did not know she was a fox.
Liú (Liú) was a student of the magistrate (lìng) of Fùchuān (Fùchuān),
and went to visit him.
He met Dīng (Dīng),
who earnestly invited him to his home,
treating him with great courtesy and generosity.
Dīng said:
“My parents-in-law (yuè fù mǔ) have recently moved elsewhere again.
My wife (nèi rén) has gone to visit her parents (guī níng),
and will return soon.
I should send a letter to her place
and also go to congratulate them.”
Liú (Liú) initially suspected Dīng (Dīng) was also a fox,
but upon careful inquiry into his family and clan,
he learned he was the son of a wealthy merchant from Fùchuān (Fùchuān).
Initially,
Dīng (Dīng), returning home late from his separate property,
met Shuǐxiān (Shuǐxiān) walking alone.
Seeing her beauty,
he glanced at her slightly.
The girl asked to join his carriage for the ride.
Dīng (Dīng) was pleased,
and took her to his study,
where they slept together.
She was able to enter through a window crack,
and only then did he realize she was a fox.
The girl said:
“My lord, do not doubt me.
Because you are sincere and honest,
I am willing to entrust myself to you.”
Dīng (Dīng) favored her,
and never married again.
When Liú (Liú) returned,
he rented a spacious mansion from a noble family,
prepared guest rooms and private chambers,
swept and cleaned them till they shone,
but was troubled by the lack of furnishings.
The next night, when he looked,
the decorations and furnishings were resplendent.
After a few days,
indeed, more than thirty people arrived in succession, bearing banners, colorful wines, and gifts,
their carriages and horses bustling,
filling the steps and alleys.
Liú (Liú) bowed to his father-in-law (Wēng) and Dīng (Dīng) and Hú (Hú), inviting them into the guest hall.
Féngxiān (Féngxiān) welcomed her mother-in-law (Yù) and two aunts (yí) into the inner chambers.
Bāxiān (Bāxiān) said:
“My maidservant is now noble,
and no longer blames her matchmaker.
Are the bracelet and shoes still there?”
The girl searched and handed them over,
saying:
“The shoes are still the same,
but they have been seen by a thousand people.”
Bāxiān (Bāxiān) struck her back with a shoe,
saying:
“I punish you for being entrusted to Lord Liú (Liú Láng).”
Then she threw them into the fire,
and prayed:
“New times are like blossoming flowers,
old times like fading flowers;
treasured, never worn,
Cháng’é (Cháng’é) comes to borrow them.”
Shuǐxiān (Shuǐxiān) also prayed on her behalf:
“Once encased tender bamboo shoots,
worn, they drew praise from thousands;
if Cháng’é (Cháng’é) were to see them,
she would pity their excessive slenderness.”
Féngxiān (Féngxiān) stirred the fire and said:
“Night after night ascending to the azure sky,
one morning leaving my beloved;
a slender shadow remains,
for all the world to see.”
Then she mixed the ashes with her fingers in a tray,
piling them into more than ten portions.
Seeing Liú (Liú) approach,
she entrusted them to him as a gift.
He saw embroidered shoes filling the tray,
all of the old style.
Bāxiān (Bāxiān) rushed out,
pushing the tray to the ground.
There were still one or two pairs left on the ground,
so she bent down and blew on them,
and their traces finally vanished.
The next day,
Dīng (Dīng), due to the long distance,
and his wife returned first.
Bāxiān (Bāxiān) was so engrossed in playing with her sister,
that her father (Wēng) and Hú (Hú) repeatedly urged her.
She only came out at noon,
and left with the others.
When they first arrived,
their retinue was excessively grand,
and spectators were like a market crowd.
Two bandits spied the beautiful women,
and lost their souls,
thus plotting to rob them on the road.
They scouted their departure from the village,
and followed them.
They were no more than a foot apart,
but the horses galloped extremely fast,
and they could not catch up.
When they reached a place
where two cliffs flanked the path,
the carriage moved a little slower.
They caught up,
held their knives, and roared,
and the crowd all fled.
They dismounted and lifted the curtain,
and an old woman was seated within.
They were just wondering if they had mistakenly robbed someone’s mother;
as soon as they looked away,
one bandit’s right arm was injured,
and he was instantly bound.
Upon closer inspection,
the cliffs were not cliffs,
but the city gate of Pínglè (Pínglè);
and inside the carriage was Lǐ Jìnshì’s (Lǐ Jìnshì) mother,
returning from her village.
The other bandit arrived later,
and was also tied up after his horse’s leg was cut.
The gate guards apprehended and sent them to the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu),
who interrogated them, and they confessed.
At that time, there was a major bandit who had not been caught,
and when questioned,
it was indeed he.
The following spring,
Liú (Liú) passed the imperial examination.
Féngxiān (Féngxiān), fearing it would bring misfortune,
declined all congratulations from her maternal relatives.
Liú (Liú) also never married anyone else.
When he became an official,
he took a concubine
and had two sons.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Alas!
The states of warmth and cold,
between immortals and mortals, are indeed not different!
'If one does not strive in youth,
one will only grieve in old age.'
It's a pity there's no competitive beauty
to reflect sorrow and joy in a mirror.
I wish that immortals as numerous as the sands of the Ganges
would all send their lovely daughters to marry into the human world;
then, in the ocean of poverty,
there would be fewer suffering beings."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Dǒng Shēng,
a native of Xúzhōu,
was fond of sword-fighting,
and always proud and self-assured.
He chanced to meet a traveler on the road,
who rode a lame donkey alongside him.
He spoke with him,
and found his conversation bold and unrestrained.
When asked his name,
he said:
"My surname is Tóng, from Liáoyáng."
He asked:
"Where are you going?"
He replied:
"I left home twenty years ago,
and have just returned from overseas."
Dǒng said:
"You have traveled the four seas,
and met many people;
have you ever seen any extraordinary individuals?"
Tóng said with a smile:
"What kind of extraordinary individuals?"
Dǒng then described his own passion,
regretting that he had not received the transmission of an extraordinary individual.
Tóng said:
"Extraordinary individuals are everywhere;
but only loyal ministers and filial sons
can receive their arts."
Dǒng again resolutely boasted of himself;
he then drew his sword,
flicked it, and sang;
he also cut down a small tree by the roadside
to show off its sharpness.
Tóng smiled as he stroked his beard,
and then asked to borrow it for a look.
Dǒng handed it to him.
After examining it,
he said:
"This is cast from armor iron,
and has been steamed by sweat,
making it the lowest quality.
Although I have not learned swordsmanship,
I have a sword
that is quite usable."
Thereupon, from beneath his clothes, he produced a short blade about a foot long,
and used it to pare Dǒng's sword.
It peeled like a melon or gourd,
and snapped diagonally at his touch,
like a horse's hoof.
Dǒng was extremely startled,
and also asked to handle it.
He stroked and wiped it repeatedly before returning it.
He invited Tóng to his home,
and insisted he stay for a night or two.
When asked about sword techniques,
he humbly claimed not to know.
Dǒng talked grandly, leaning on his knees,
while Tóng merely listened respectfully.
When the night grew deep,
he suddenly heard a commotion in the adjacent courtyard.
The adjacent courtyard was where his father lived,
and he was alarmed and suspicious.
He listened intently by the wall,
only hearing someone angrily say:
"Tell your son to come out quickly to be punished,
and we will spare you!"
A moment later,
it seemed as if they were being looted,
and the incessant moaning was indeed his father's.
Dǒng seized a spear, intending to go.
Tóng stopped him, saying:
"Going there now might mean no survival;
it's better to consider a foolproof plan."
Dǒng, flustered, asked for advice.
Tóng said:
"The bandits are calling for you by name;
they will surely not be satisfied otherwise.
You have no other close relatives,
so you should entrust your wife with your affairs after death;
I will open the door
to warn your servants."
Dǒng agreed,
and went in to tell his wife.
His wife clutched his clothes and wept.
Dǒng's brave resolve instantly vanished,
and so they both ascended to an upper floor,
searching for bows and arrows
to prepare for the bandits' attack.
Before their panic subsided,
they heard Tóng laughing on the eaves of the building, saying:
"The bandits have fortunately left."
When they lit a candle,
he was already gone.
After a moment, they went out
and saw his father, who had been drinking at a neighbor's,
returning with a lantern;
only a pile of burnt rush fragments remained in the courtyard.
Then they knew Tóng was an extraordinary individual.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Loyalty and filial piety
are the very nature of humanity;
in ancient times, when ministers and sons could not die for their lord or father,
did they initially not have moments of brave resolve to seize a spear and go?
It was all just a change of mind that led them astray.
In the past, Xiè Jìn and Fāng Xiàorú pledged to die together,
but ultimately he broke his word;
how do we know that after making the vow and returning home,
he did not hear his bedside companion weeping?"
There was a certain quick-witted yamen runner in the district,
who would not return home for several days at a time.
His wife then had an affair with a local scoundrel.
One day he returned
and happened to see the young man coming out of the room.
He was greatly suspicious
and pressed his wife with questions.
His wife denied it.
Later, he found the young man's forgotten item by the bedside,
and his wife was too embarrassed to speak,
only kneeling and begging for mercy.
The runner was furious,
threw a rope at her,
and forced her to hang herself.
His wife asked to dress up before dying,
which he allowed.
His wife then entered the room to arrange her makeup;
the runner poured himself a drink and waited for her,
shouting and urging her frequently.
Soon, his wife emerged in splendid attire,
and with tears in her eyes, bowed, saying:
"Are you truly so heartless as to make your slave die?"
The runner indignantly scorned her.
His wife turned and ran back into the room,
just as she was about to tie the rope,
the runner threw down his cup and shouted:
"Hah!
Come back!
A green turban
might not be able to crush a person to death!"
And so they were husband and wife as before.
This is also like those great gentlemen,
a laugh.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
A certain man from Yíshuǐ,
during the late Míng dynasty, served as a soldier in Liáoyáng.
When Liáochéng fell,
he was killed by the mutinous soldiers;
although his head was severed,
he was not quite dead.
At night,
a person came holding a ledger,
checking off the ghosts.
When he reached the man,
he said he should not have died,
and ordered his attendants to reattach his head and send him back.
So they collectively took his head and placed it on his neck,
and the group helped him.
With a rustling sound of wind,
they traveled for some time,
then set him down and left.
He looked at the ground,
and it was his hometown.
When the Yí magistrate heard of this,
he suspected him of desertion.
He detained and questioned him,
and although he understood the situation, he was quite disbelieving;
he also examined his neck and found no trace of a severed wound,
and intended to punish him.
The man said:
"My words are unbelievable,
but please just keep me in prison.
A severed head can be faked,
but a fallen city cannot be faked.
If Liáochéng had not fallen,
then it would not be too late to receive punishment."
The magistrate agreed to his request.
A few days later,
news from Liáo arrived,
and the time and date were exactly as he had said,
so he was released.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Zhāng Gòngshì of Ānqiū,
was ill in bed,
lying on his back at the head of the bed.
Suddenly, he saw a small figure emerge from his mind,
barely half a chi tall;
wearing scholarly robes and a scholar's cap,
resembling an actor.
It sang a Kūnshān tune,
with a clear and distinct sound,
and in its spoken dialogue, it introduced its name as Guàn,
which was the same as his own;
the end of each section it sang
recounted events from his own life.
After the four acts were finished,
it recited a poem and disappeared.
Zhāng still remembered the gist of it
and recounted it to others.
According to a manuscript of chapter 24 of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Xú Shēng of Héjiān,
was teaching in ēn.
At the beginning of Làyuè, he returned home,
and on the way, encountered an old man,
who looked closely and said:
"Mr. Xú, your teaching term is over.
Where will you teach next year?"
Xú replied:
"Still the same place."
The old man said:
"My name is Shī Jìngyè.
I have a nephew who is seeking a good teacher,
and I happened to entrust someone to go to Dōngtuǎn to hire Lǚ Zǐlián,
but he has already accepted a聘禮 at Jìmén.
If you would consider taking the position,
the tuition fee will be double that of ēn."
Xú declined, citing his existing agreement.
The old man said:
"You are indeed a trustworthy gentleman.
However, the New Year is still far off,
I respectfully offer you one liǎng of gold as a hiring gift,
for you to teach temporarily,
and we can discuss next year separately, what do you think?"
Xú agreed.
The old man dismounted and presented a letter of invitation,
and also said:
"My village is not far now.
My house is quite cramped,
and it's difficult to feed livestock,
please send your servant and horse away now: it's also good to walk."
Xú complied,
entrusting his luggage to the old man's horse.
After walking about three or four lǐ,
as dusk fell,
they finally reached his residence,
with bronze nail heads and beast-head door knockers,
appearing quite like an aristocratic family's home.
He called his nephew out to pay respects,
a boy of thirteen or fourteen.
The old man said:
"My sister's husband, Jiǎng Nánchuān,
was formerly a Zhǐhuīshǐ.
He left only this child,
who is not at all dull,
but merely spoiled.
If he receives a month of good guidance from you,
it will be worth ten years."
Soon after,
a banquet was set,
prepared with extreme richness and beauty;
and the serving of wine and food
was all done by maids and old women.
One maid, holding a kettle, stood attending,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
with an exceptionally charming demeanor,
which secretly moved Xú's heart.
When the feast concluded,
the old man ordered his sleeping arrangements to be made,
then bid farewell and left.
Before dawn,
the boy came out for lessons.
As Xú was just getting up,
a maid came to present a towel and attend to his washing,
it was the same person who had held the kettle.
She served his three meals a day,
and in the evening,
also came to sweep the bed.
Xú asked:
"Why are there no male servants?"
The maid smiled without speaking,
laid out the quilt, and left directly.
The next evening, she returned.
When Xú spoke playfully to her,
the maid smiled and did not resist,
and thus they became intimate.
She then told him:
"Our family has no men,
so external affairs are entrusted to Uncle Shī.
My name is Àinú.
My mistress deeply respects you,
and fearing that other maids might not be clean,
she sent me.
For today, you must keep it secret,
lest it be discovered,
and we both lose face."
One night,
they slept together and forgot the dawn,
and were discovered by the young master,
which made Xú feel ashamed and uneasy.
In the evening,
the maid came and said:
"Fortunately, my mistress values you,
otherwise, it would have been ruined!
When the young master came to report,
my mistress quickly covered his mouth,
as if afraid you would hear.
She merely warned me not to stay long in the study."
Having said that,
she left.
Xú was very grateful to her.
However, the young master was not good at studying,
and when Xú rebuked him,
the mistress would always intercede for him.
At first, she still sent the maid to convey messages;
gradually, she came out herself,
speaking to the teacher through the door,
often shedding tears.
She would always ask about the young master's daily lessons every evening.
Xú grew quite impatient,
and said with a stern expression:
"Since you indulge your son's laziness,
yet also demand diligence from him,
I am not accustomed to being this kind of teacher!
I request to resign."
The mistress sent the maid to apologize,
and Xú then stayed.
Since entering the residence,
whenever he wanted to go out and enjoy the scenery,
he was always locked in.
One day,
feeling depressed while drunk,
he called the maid and asked why.
The maid said:
"Nothing else,
just fearing it would interfere with his studies.
If you must go out,
please do so at night."
Xú angrily said:
"Am I to be imprisoned until death just because I accepted a few pieces of gold?
Where do you expect me to sneak off to at night?
I have long been ashamed of eating plain food,
and the reward is still in my purse!"
So he took out the gold and placed it on the table,
preparing his belongings to leave.
The mistress came out,
gazing silently,
only covering her sleeves and sobbing,
sending the maid to return the gold,
opening the lock, and seeing him off.
Xú felt the doorway was cramped;
after walking a few steps,
sunlight shone in,
and he found himself emerging from within a tomb,
with a desolate view all around,
it was an ancient tomb.
He was greatly shocked.
However, moved by their righteousness,
he sold the gold they had given him,
built a mound and planted trees there before leaving.
The year passed,
and he again passed through that place.
He bowed in worship and proceeded.
In the distance, he saw Shī Sǒu,
who smiled and offered greetings,
inviting him with great earnestness.
He knew in his heart that Shī Sǒu was a ghost,
but wished to inquire after Fūrén's well-being.
So, they went together into the village
and bought wine to drink together.
Before he knew it, dusk fell.
The old man rose to pay for the wine
and then said:
"My humble abode is not far.
My younger sister has also just returned home.
I hope you will grace us with your presence
to dispel ill omens for this old man."
After walking a few paces out of the village,
they reached another hamlet.
He knocked on the door and entered,
where a candle was lit for the guest.
Presently,
Jiǎng Fūrén came out from the inner chambers.
Only then did he truly observe her:
she was a beautiful woman of about forty.
She bowed and thanked him, saying:
"Our clan is in decline,
and our household is desolate.
Sir, your kindness extends even to withered bones;
truly, there is no way we can repay it."
Having spoken,
tears flowed.
Soon after, she called for Àinú,
and said to Xú:
"This maidservant
is one whom I cherish.
Now I present her to you,
to comfort you in your loneliness while away from home.
Whatever your needs,
she is somewhat able to understand your wishes."
Xú assented.
A short while later,
both the brother and sister left,
and the maidservant remained to attend to him in bed.
At the first crow of the rooster,
the old man came to urge him to pack and send him off;
Fūrén also came out,
instructing the maidservant to serve the gentleman well.
She then said to Xú:
"From now on, you must be especially discreet.
Our encounter has been strange and unusual,
and I fear that busybodies may spread rumors."
Xú agreed and bid farewell,
riding together with the maidservant.
When they reached the inn,
they stayed in a single room,
cohabiting.
If a guest arrived,
the maidservant would not avoid them,
but people also could not see her.
Occasionally, if he desired something,
the moment the thought arose,
the maidservant would already have brought it.
She was also skilled in witchcraft;
with a rub, illnesses would immediately be cured.
When Qīngmíng arrived,
he went to the burial ground,
and the maidservant excused herself and descended.
Xú instructed her to thank Fūrén on his behalf.
She replied:
"Yes."
And then disappeared.
A few days later, he returned,
just intending to visit the tomb,
when he saw the maidservant, splendidly adorned, sitting under a tree.
So, he set off with her.
All year long, they went back and forth,
this being their usual routine.
He wanted to take her home with him,
but she firmly refused.
At year's end,
he bid farewell to the inn and returned home,
agreeing on a future meeting.
The maidservant escorted him to their previous resting place,
pointed to a pile of stones and said:
"This is Jiāng's tomb.
Before Fūrén was married,
she served her;
when she died young, she was buried here.
If you pass by again,
offer a stick of incense to mourn her,
and you will surely meet again."
He left and returned home,
feeling quite distressed by longing.
He reverently went to offer sacrifices,
but there was no response whatsoever.
So, he bought a coffin and dug up the grave,
intending to bring the bones home for reburial,
to express his affection and admiration.
He opened the burial chamber and entered,
and saw her complexion as if alive.
Although her skin had not decayed,
her clothes were ruined like ash;
the jade ornaments and golden bracelets on her head
were all like new.
He also looked at her waist,
wrapped around which were several ingots of gold;
he took them and put them in his bosom.
He then removed his robe and covered the corpse,
carried it into the coffin,
hired a cart, and brought it home;
he placed it in a separate residence,
adorned it with embroidered robes,
and slept alone beside it,
hoping for a spiritual response.
Suddenly, Àinú entered from outside,
and laughed, saying:
"Is the grave-robbing thief here?!"
Xú was both surprised and delighted, and asked her how she was.
The maidservant said:
"I followed Fūrén to Dōngchāng,
and when I returned after three days,
the house was already empty.
I have often been invited,
but the reason I refused to follow you
was that I had received great kindness from Fūrén,
and could not bear to leave her.
Now that you have 'robbed' me and brought me here,
if you quickly bury me,
you will see great virtue."
Xú asked:
"There are those who revive after a hundred years;
now your fragrant body is as it was,
why not imitate them?"
She sighed and said:
"This has a fixed destiny.
The legendary wonders of the world
are half illusory.
If one truly wished to make me move and walk again,
what difficulty would there be?
But I cannot be like a living person,
so there is no need."
Then he opened the coffin,
and the corpse immediately rose,
standing gracefully and lovely.
He touched her chest,
and it was cold as ice and snow.
She then prepared to enter the coffin and lie down again,
but Xú strongly stopped her.
The maidservant said:
"I was overly favored by Fūrén.
My master came from a foreign land,
obtaining tens of thousands of gold,
which I secretly took,
and he did not inquire much about it.
Later, when she was near death,
and had no relatives,
she hid it to be buried with herself.
Fūrén grieved my untimely death,
and also put precious ornaments in the coffin.
The reason my body has not decayed
is merely due to the residual vital energy of the gold and treasures.
If I were in the human world,
how could I last long?
If you truly wish for this,
you must absolutely not force me to eat or drink;
if the vital energy disperses,
then my wandering spirit will also vanish."
Xú then built a private study
and slept and lived with her.
Her laughter and speech were just like that of an ordinary person;
but she did not eat or breathe,
and did not see living people.
After more than a year,
Xú, slightly tipsy,
forcibly poured the remaining dregs of wine down her throat;
she immediately fell to the ground,
blood and water overflowing from her mouth,
and within a day, the corpse had changed.
Grieving and regretting, it was too late,
so he gave her a grand burial.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Fūrén's teaching of her son
was no different from that in the human world;
and how generously she treated the master!
Is she not virtuous!
I say that an alluring corpse is inferior to an elegant ghost,
yet it was due to the vulgar recklessness of a pedant
that a spiritual being could not enjoy its long years.
What a pity!"
Zhāngqiū's Zhū shēng,
Qin gānggěng,
set up a school at a certain gòngshì's house.
Whenever he punished a student,
the mistress would invariably send a maid to beg for an exemption,
but he would not listen.
One day,
she personally went outside his window,
and tried to intercede with Zhū.
Zhū grew angry,
grabbed his ruler, and stormed out, cursing loudly.
The woman, frightened, fled;
Zhū chased her,
and struck her buttocks and thighs from behind,
making a resonant thwack.
It made people die of laughter!
A certain man from Chángshān,
whenever he hired a teacher,
would calculate the annual payment
based on the entire year's income and expenses,
determining how much was earned daily;
he would also keep a detailed record
of the days the teacher left and returned to the study.
At year's end,
they would collectively tally and subtract based on the days.
Mǎ shēng was hired at his house.
When he first saw the man approach with an abacus,
he was greatly astonished by this old custom;
but then he secretly devised a plan,
turning his annoyance into delight,
allowing the man to recount without the slightest dispute.
The elder was very pleased,
and firmly booked him for the following year.
Mǎ declined, citing a reason.
He then recommended a rather eccentric student to take his place.
Upon taking up residence,
the new teacher would frequently scold and curse.
The elder had no choice
but to endure it all.
At the end of the year,
he brought the abacus.
The teacher, filled with extreme indignation,
nevertheless allowed him to calculate.
The elder also counted the travel days
as entirely belonging to the teacher,
but the teacher refused,
sliding the beads back to the elder's side.
Unable to resolve the dispute,
they brandished weapons at each other,
and both ended up with broken heads and mangled faces, going to the public court.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain commoner from Qīngzhōu,
over fifty years old,
married a young wife.
His two sons, fearing he might have more children,
while their father was drunk,
secretly cut off his testicles and applied medicinal powder.
The father, upon realizing it,
pretended to be sick and said nothing.
After a long time,
the wound gradually healed.
Suddenly, he entered the room,
the stitches burst open,
and blood flowed ceaselessly,
soon after, he died.
His wife knew the reason
and sued the officials.
The officials interrogated his sons with instruments of torture,
and they confessed.
The official exclaimed:
"I am now the 'Magistrate of Dānfù'
And executed them both.
In the county, there was a Wáng shēng,
who divorced his wife after a little over a month.
The wife's father sued him.
At that time, the Zī county magistrate, Xīn Gōng,
asked Wáng:
"Why did you send your wife away?"
He replied:
"It's not to be spoken of."
When pressed,
he said:
"Because she cannot bear children."
The magistrate said:
"Nonsense!
A newlywed of a little over a month,
how can you know she won't bear children?"
After much blushing and hesitation,
he reported:
"Her yīn is very crooked."
The magistrate laughed and said:
"Then it is the crookedness that causes harm,
and that is why the family is not harmonious."
This can be passed down alongside
"Magistrate of Dānfù"
A laugh.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Sūn Bìzhèn was crossing the river,
when he encountered a great storm with snow.
The boat swayed violently,
and everyone on board was terrified.
Suddenly, they saw a golden-armored deity standing in the clouds,
holding a golden tablet with characters, which he lowered and showed;
everyone looked up at it together,
and it read
"Sūn Bìzhèn"
in three characters,
very clearly.
The crowd said to Sūn:
"You must have offended Heaven and incurred its wrath.
Please take your own boat,
and don't implicate us."
Sūn had not yet spoken,
but the crowd, without waiting for his consent,
seeing a small boat nearby,
pushed him onto it.
Once Sūn had boarded the boat,
he looked back,
and the former boat had capsized.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the county, there was a villager,
who was always a scoundrel.
One day,
he rose in the morning,
and two men seized him and took him away.
Upon reaching the market,
they saw a butcher with half a pig hanging on a frame.
The two men then pushed and shoved him with all their might,
and he felt his body merge with the meat.
The two men then departed directly.
A short while later,
the butcher sold the meat.
As he wielded his knife and cut,
the villager felt a pang of pain with each cut,
piercing to his very bones.
Later, a neighboring elder came to buy meat,
haggling bitterly over the price,
adding fat and extra meat.
Each piece was cut into fragments,
and his suffering was even more agonizing.
When all the meat was sold,
he then found his way home;
by the time he returned,
the sun had already reached chén (7-9 AM).
His family thought he had risen late,
so he recounted in detail what he had suffered.
They called a neighbor to ask,
and indeed, the neighbor had just returned from buying meat,
stating the number of pieces and pounds,
precisely matching.
In the span of a single morning,
he had already endured a lingchi once—
was it not strange indeed!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Guǎngdōng, the cliffs of the Línjiāng mountains are rugged and steep,
and often contain gold ingots embedded in the rocks.
Below the cliffs, waves surge,
making it impossible for boats to moor.
If one paddles close to pick them,
they are firmly unmovable;
but if the person is destined to obtain one,
it falls off with a single pluck,
and upon turning one's head, it has already regenerated.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wáng Zhòngchāo said:
"Between Dòngtíng and Jūnshān, there is a stone cave,
high enough for a boat,
dark and unfathomably deep,
with lake water flowing in and out of it.
I once held a torch and paddled a boat into it.
I saw that both walls were black stone,
their color like lacquer,
soft to the touch;
when I took out a knife and cut it,
it was like cutting firm bean curd.
I made an inkstone out of it at will.
After exiting,
it became harder and more solid than other stones upon exposure to wind.
I tested it with ink,
and it was excellent.
Many boatmen and travelers come and go,
and though there are good stones,
they do not know to use them.
This also relies on curious individuals to appreciate and name them."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wǔyí Shān has sheer cliffs a thousand *rèn* high.
People often pick up fragrant eaglewood and jade pieces from below.
The Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) heard of this,
and supervised hundreds of people in building a cloud ladder,
intending to reach the top to investigate its wonders.
It took three years to complete.
The Grand Administrator ascended it.
As he was about to reach the peak,
he saw a huge foot extend downwards.
One big toe was thicker than a clothes-pounding pestle.
A loud voice said,
"Don't go down,
you will fall!"
Greatly astonished,
he quickly descended.
As soon as he reached the ground,
the wooden scaffolding decayed and broke,
collapsing completely.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本)
During the Wànlì reign,
there were rats in the palace,
as large as cats,
causing severe harm.
Excellent cats were sought from among the populace to catch and control them,
but they were always spied upon and eaten.
Coincidentally, an exotic "lion cat" (shīmāo) was offered as tribute,
its fur white as snow.
It was carried and thrown into the rat-infested room,
its door closed,
and secretly observed.
The cat squatted for a long time.
A rat tentatively emerged from its hole,
saw the cat,
and furiously rushed at it.
The cat avoided it by leaping onto a small table.
The rat also climbed up,
then the cat jumped down.
This back and forth continued,
no less than a hundred times.
Everyone thought the cat was cowardly,
believing it to be useless.
Soon, the rat's leaps and bounds became slower,
its large belly seemed to be panting,
and it squatted on the ground to rest for a moment.
The cat then quickly descended,
grabbed the fur on its head with its claws,
bit its head,
and they struggled, rolling back and forth.
The cat made a "wūwū" sound,
and the rat a "jiūjiū" sound.
They opened the door and quickly looked,
and the rat's head was already chewed to pieces.
Only then did they realize that the cat's avoidance
was not cowardice,
but waiting for its moment.
When the other came out, it retreated;
when the other retreated, it returned.
It used this intelligence.
Alas!
What difference is there between a common man clutching his sword
and a rat?
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本)
A certain merchant (jiǎrén),
upon reaching the Zhílì region,
suddenly encountered a heavy hailstorm.
He hid among the crops.
He heard a voice from the sky say,
"This is Zhāng Bùliàng's (張不量) field;
do not harm his crops."
The merchant privately thought that since the Zhāng (張) family was referred to as
"Bùliáng" (不良 - bad character),
why was their crop instead protected?
When the hail stopped,
he entered the village
and inquired about the person,
and also asked about the meaning of the name.
It turned out that Zhāng (張) was a long-established wealthy family,
having accumulated a great deal of grain.
Every spring, poor people would borrow from him,
and at repayment time, he did not scrutinize the amount,
but accepted it all,
never insisting on taking the full amount.
Therefore, he was named
"Bùliàng" (不量 - not measuring/calculating),
not "bùliáng" (不良 - bad character).
Everyone rushed to the fields,
and saw that the stalks and ears were broken like flax,
but Zhāng's (張) fields alone were unharmed.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本)
Two shepherd boys went into the mountains to a wolf's den.
In the den were two small wolves.
They planned to catch them separately.
Each climbed a tree,
dozens of paces apart.
A short while later,
the large wolf arrived,
entered the den and found its pups missing,
looking extremely distraught.
A boy in a tree twisted a small wolf's paw and ear, intentionally making it howl.
The large wolf heard the sound, looked up,
and furiously ran to the foot of the tree,
howling and clawing.
The other boy then, from his tree, made the other small wolf cry out urgently.
The wolf stopped howling, looked around,
and finally saw it.
It then left this tree and rushed to the other,
running and howling as before.
The first tree howled again,
and it turned and ran there again.
Its mouth never stopped howling,
its feet never stopped moving.
After dozens of back-and-forths,
its running gradually slowed,
and its voice gradually weakened.
Soon, it lay stiff and breathless,
not moving for a long time.
The boys looked down at it;
its breath had already ceased.
Nowadays, if a powerful and arrogant man
glares and clutches his sword,
as if about to fight and devour;
and the one he is angry at simply avoids him;
and the powerful man, exhausted and hoarse,
finds no opponent,
would he not feel triumphant and mighty?
They do not realize that this display of beastly power
was deliberately provoked by humans for amusement.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本)
A certain rich man (fùwēng)
lent capital to many merchants.
One day, he went out,
and a young man followed behind his horse.
When asked,
he also wished to borrow capital.
The rich man assented.
When they arrived home,
there happened to be several tens of coins on a small table.
The young man immediately stacked the coins with his hands,
piling them up and down.
The rich man dismissed him with thanks,
and ultimately did not give him capital.
Someone asked why.
The rich man said,
"This person must be good at gambling,
not an upright person.
His accustomed skill
unconsciously manifested in his hands and feet."
Upon investigation, it was indeed so.
According to *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (鑄雪齋抄本)
When Wáng Jì (王霽) of Xīnchéng (新城), the Grand Minister of War (Dà Sīmǎ), was guarding the northern frontier,
he often had artisans cast a large pole-arm (gǎndāo),
over a foot wide and weighing a hundred *gōu*.
Whenever he inspected the border,
he would have four men carry it.
Wherever his retinue stopped,
it would be placed on the ground.
Thus, northern people who tried to move it by force could not budge it.
The Grand Minister secretly had a wooden sword (dāo) made of paulownia wood in the same style,
with identical width and size.
He covered it with silver foil
and would sometimes wield it on horseback.
All the tribes who saw it
were without exception greatly shocked.
He also buried thin reeds as a boundary outside the frontier,
extending for more than ten *lǐ* horizontally and diagonally.
It looked like a fence.
He publicly declared,
"This is my Great Wall."
When the northern troops arrived,
they pulled it all out and burned it.
The Grand Minister then re-established it.
After it had been burned three times,
he placed cannons and booby traps beneath it.
When the northern troops burned the reeds,
the gunpowder and stones all discharged,
causing many casualties.
After they fled,
the Grand Minister set up the reeds as before.
The northern troops, seeing it from afar, all retreated,
and thus submitted as if to a deity.
Later, the Grand Minister requested to retire due to old age,
but the frontier was again alerted.
He was summoned to resume his post.
The Grand Minister was then eighty-three years old,
and, overcoming illness, he resigned before the emperor.
The emperor comforted him, saying,
"I only ask that you govern while resting."
Thereupon, the Grand Minister returned to the frontier.
Wherever he stayed,
he would lie down behind a curtain.
The northern people heard that the Grand Minister had arrived,
but all disbelieved it.
So, they pretended to negotiate for peace,
intending to verify the truth.
When the curtain was opened,
they saw the Grand Minister merely lying down.
They all bowed down towards the couch,
and retreated, speechless.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
The assistant prefect (tóngzhī) of Yángzhōu,
dreamt one night that the God of Mount Tài summoned him,
his words and expression full of anger.
Looking up, he saw a person attending by the god's side,
who briefly spoke in his favor.
He awoke disliking the dream.
Early in the morning, he went to the Mount Tài temple
and silently offered prayers and expiations.
After coming out,
he saw a person at a pharmacy,
who exactly resembled the one he had seen in his dream.
He questioned him
and learned he was a doctor.
Upon returning home,
he fell gravely ill.
He specifically sent someone to hire the doctor.
When the doctor arrived, he prescribed a remedy.
He took it that evening,
and died in the middle of the night.
Some say: King Yánluó and the Son of Heaven of Mount Dōngyuè
send forth 108,000 male and female attendants daily,
distributing them across the world to act as shamans and doctors,
named
"Soul-Snatching Envoys"
One must not be careless when using medicine!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Wáng Mùzhēn of Méngyīn
came from a prominent local family.
He happened to be traveling in Jiāngzhè
when he saw an old woman weeping by the roadside.
He questioned her.
She said:
"My late husband left only one son,
who is now condemned to death.
Who can save him?"
Wáng, who was always generous,
noted her son's name
and took gold from his purse to intercede on his behalf,
eventually getting him acquitted.
When the man was released,
he heard that Wáng had saved him,
but was utterly bewildered as to why.
He sought out Wáng at Lǚqiū
and expressed his gratitude and inquired.
Wáng said:
"Nothing special,
I just pitied your old mother."
The man was greatly surprised and said:
"My mother died a long time ago."
Wáng also found this strange.
By dusk,
the old woman came to express her thanks.
Wáng admonished her for the deception.
The old woman said:
"To tell you the truth: I am an old fox from Dōngshān.
Twenty years ago,
I had a night of intimacy with your son's father,
so I could not bear for his ghost to be hungry."
Wáng rose in awe and respect,
and when he wanted to question her further,
she had already vanished.
Before this,
Wáng's wife was virtuous and devoutly Buddhist,
abstaining from meat and wine;
she kept a clean room,
hung an image of Guānyīn,
and, being childless,
prayed and burned incense there daily.
The deity was also extremely efficacious,
often appearing in dreams
to advise people on what to seek and avoid.
For this reason, all household matters were decided based on these omens.
Later, she fell gravely ill,
critically so,
and had her bed moved into that room;
she also arranged a separate brocade cushion in the inner room and locked its door,
as if waiting for someone.
Wáng thought she was deluded,
but given the severity of her illness and her muddled state,
he could not bear to upset her.
She lay ill for two years,
disliking noise,
and often sent people away to sleep alone.
He secretly listened and
it sounded as if she was talking to someone;
when he opened the door to look,
it was silent again.
During her illness, she had no other worries,
except for their fourteen-year-old daughter,
whom she urged daily to prepare her dowry and get married.
After the wedding,
she called Wáng to her bedside,
held his hand and said:
"This is our farewell!
When I first fell ill,
the Bodhisattva told me I was destined for a swift death: my only lingering concern
was that our daughter was not yet married,
so she bestowed a little medicine
to prolong my life until then.
Last year,
the Bodhisattva was returning to Nánhǎi
and left her attending maiden, Xiǎoméi,
to serve me.
Now I am about to die,
and this unfortunate woman has no children.
Bǎo'ér,
whom I dearly love,
I fear he might marry a fierce and angry woman,
and now his mother is lost.
Xiǎoméi is beautiful and graceful,
and also gentle and virtuous,
so you can take her as your secondary wife."
Indeed, Wáng had a concubine
who bore him a son
named Bǎo'ér.
Wáng considered her words absurd
and said:
"You have always revered the gods;
to utter such words now,
is it not sacrilegious?"
She replied:
"Xiǎoméi has served me for over a year,
we have forgotten our physical forms [in our intimacy],
and I have already gently asked her."
He asked:
"Where is Xiǎoméi?"
She said:
"Is she not in the room?"
Just as he was about to question her further,
she closed her eyes and passed away.
Wáng night kept watch over the spirit canopy.
He heard faint sobbing from inside the room,
and was greatly startled,
suspecting it to be a ghost.
He called all the maidservants and concubines to open the lock and look,
and there was a beautiful woman of sixteen,
in mourning clothes, in the room.
Everyone thought she was a spirit,
and together they prostrated themselves before her.
The woman wiped away her tears and helped them up.
Wáng stared intently at her,
but she merely lowered her head.
Wáng said,
"If the words of the deceased Kōng were not false,
please ascend to the main hall at once,
to receive the morning salutations of your children;
if that is not possible,
I too dare not entertain such presumptuous thoughts,
lest I incur sin."
The woman came out gracefully,
and indeed ascended the northern hall.
Wáng had a maidservant arrange a seat for her facing south.
Wáng bowed first,
and the woman returned the bow;
then, from oldest to youngest, and lowest to highest in status,
they prostrated themselves in turn,
and the woman sat with a solemn expression, receiving their obeisance;
only when a concubine arrived,
did she pull her up.
Since Fūrén fell ill,
the maidservants were wanton and the slaves pilfered,
and the household had long been in decline.
After everyone had paid their respects,
they stood reverently in rows.
The woman said,
"I am grateful for Fūrén's great kindness,
detaining me in the human world,
and entrusting me with this great matter.
You all should cleanse your hearts,
and exert yourselves for your master.
All previous faults and transgressions
will not be held against you;
otherwise,
do not say that the room is empty!"
Everyone looked at the seat,
it was truly like a hanging image of Guānyīn,
at times swayed by a gentle breeze.
Hearing her words, they were astonished and intimidated,
and chorused their assent.
The woman then managed the funeral arrangements,
everything orderly.
From then on, none, great or small, dared to be remiss.
The woman managed the household, inside and out, all day long.
When Wáng had something to do,
he would also report it before acting;
yet, though they saw each other several times a night,
they never exchanged a single private word.
After the burial,
Wáng wanted to fulfill their previous agreement,
but dared not say it directly,
so he instructed a concubine to subtly hint at it.
The woman said,
"I have received Fūrén's earnest instructions,
and duty does not allow me to refuse;
but the great ceremony of marriage
must not be done hastily.
My elder, Huáng Xiānshēng,
is of high status and great virtue;
if he can be asked to preside over our Qin-Jin alliance,
then I will obey his command."
At that time, Huáng Tàipú of Yíshuǐ,
had retired from office and was living in leisure.
He was a close family friend to Wáng,
and their relationship was very good.
Wáng immediately visited him in person
and told him the truth.
Huáng was surprised by this,
and immediately came with him.
When the woman heard,
she immediately came out and bowed respectfully.
Upon seeing her, Huáng
was astonished, thinking she was a celestial being,
and humbly declined to accept her禮;
afterwards, he provided generous dowry assistance,
and left after the ceremony was complete.
The woman presented pillows and slippers as gifts,
as if serving her parents-in-law.
From this, their relationship became even closer.
After the wedding night,
Wáng, still thinking she was a spirit,
mixed reverence with intimacy,
and at times questioned the Búsà's daily life.
The woman smiled and said,
"You are too foolish!
How can an upright spirit marry into the mortal world?"
Wáng then pressed her about her origins.
The woman said,
"There's no need to investigate thoroughly. Since you already consider me a spirit,
and offer sacrifices morning and evening,
there will naturally be no misfortune or calamity."
The woman was usually lenient with her subordinates, never speaking of anything but laughter;
yet, when maidservants or concubines were playing mischievously,
if she saw them from a distance,
they would immediately fall silent.
The woman smiled and advised them,
"Do you still take me for a spirit?
What kind of spirit am I?
I am actually Fūrén's maternal cousin,
we were close when young;
when my sister fell ill and missed me,
she secretly sent Wáng Mǔ of Náncūn to invite me here.
It's just that being so close to my sister's husband,
there was an impropriety between men and women,
so I pretended to be a spirit and stayed in the inner room.
In reality, I am no spirit."
The multitude still did not believe her.
But serving by her side daily,
they saw that her every action
was no different from an ordinary person's,
and the rumors gradually subsided.
However, even stubborn slaves and dull maids,
whom Wáng's usual floggings could not reform,
would happily obey the woman's single word.
They all said,
"We don't even realize it ourselves.
It's not that we fear her;
but just seeing her appearance,
our hearts soften naturally,
so we cannot bear to displease her."
Because of this, all neglected matters were addressed.
In a few years,
their fields stretched for miles and their granaries held ten thousand *shí* of grain.
After several more years,
the concubine bore a daughter.
The daughter gave birth to a son—when the son was born,
he had a red mark on his left arm,
and was therefore nicknamed Xiǎohóng.
When he was a month old, the woman sent a maidservant to invite Huáng to a grand banquet.
Huáng sent generous congratulatory gifts,
but declined, citing his old age,
unable to travel far;
the woman sent two strong men to insist,
and Huáng finally came.
She carried the child out,
bared his left arm,
to show the meaning of his naming.
She also repeatedly asked about his fortune.
Huáng smiled and said,
"This is 'joy red',
you can add a character and name him Xǐhóng."
The woman was greatly pleased,
and came out again to prostrate herself.
That day,
drums and music filled the courtyard,
and noble relatives were as numerous as in a market.
Huáng stayed for three days before leaving.
Suddenly, carriages and horses arrived outside the gate,
to escort the woman home for a visit to her parents.
For more than ten years,
there had been no contact.
Everyone discussed it,
but the woman acted as if she hadn't heard.
After finishing her makeup,
she held the child in her arms,
and asked Wáng to accompany her.
Wáng agreed.
After traveling twenty or thirty *lǐ*,
there were no pedestrians.
The woman stopped her carriage,
called Wáng to dismount,
and, dismissing the others, spoke to him,
saying:
"Wáng Láng, Wáng Láng,
our meeting was short, our parting long,
would you say this is not regrettable?"
Wáng, surprised, asked the reason,
and the woman said,
"Who do you think I am?"
He replied:
"I don't know."
The woman said,
"Did you save a man condemned to death in Jiāngnán?"
She replied,
"Yes."
She said,
"Yes."
"The one crying by the roadside was my mother.
Moved by your righteousness and wishing to repay you,
and knowing that your wife was devoutly Buddhist,
I attached myself as a divine being,
intending to repay you with myself.
Now, fortunately, this swaddled child has been born,
and this wish has been fulfilled.
I see that a dark fate is approaching you.
If this child stays at home,
I fear he cannot be raised.
Therefore, I am borrowing the excuse of returning home to my parents
to save the child from danger.
Remember this: when there is a death in your family,
at the first crow of the morning cock,
go to the willow embankment of Xīhé.
If you see someone carrying a sunflower lantern,
block their path and beg earnestly,
and you can avoid disaster."
Wáng said,
"Understood."
Then he asked about her return date.
The woman said,
"It cannot be set in advance.
You must remember my words firmly;
our next meeting is not far off either."
At parting, they clasped hands,
and tears streamed down their faces with sorrow.
Soon, she got into her carriage,
swift as the wind.
Wáng watched until she was out of sight,
then returned.
Six or seven years passed,
with no news whatsoever.
Suddenly, a plague spread through the four villages,
and many died.
A maid fell ill and died after three days.
Wáng remembered the earlier instructions
and was quite concerned.
That day, he drank with guests
and fell into a deep, drunken sleep.
When he awoke,
he heard the cock crow,
hastily got up and went to the embankment head,
saw the lantern light twinkling,
but it had just passed.
He chased it urgently,
but it was only about a hundred paces away,
and the more he chased, the further it got,
gradually becoming invisible.
He returned in regret and anger.
A few days later, he fell seriously ill
and soon died.
Many of the Wáng clan were unscrupulous,
jointly bullying his orphaned wife and child.
Fields, crops, and trees
were openly cut down and taken,
and the family's fortunes declined daily.
A year later,
Bǎo'ér also died young,
leaving the family with no one to lead it.
The clan members became even more overbearing,
carving up their land and property.
The stables were emptied of oxen and horses.
They also wanted to divide up the mansion.
Because the concubine lived there,
several people came,
forcibly seized and sold it.
The concubine clung to her young daughter,
and mother and child wept together,
moving the neighbors to pity.
Just when they were in dire straits,
suddenly they heard someone in a sedan chair outside the gate.
Everyone peered out,
and saw the woman leading the young boy out of a carriage.
People gathered around like a market crowd,
and she asked,
"Who are these people?"
The concubine cried and explained the situation.
The woman's expression changed dramatically,
and she immediately called her former servants,
closed the gate, and locked it.
The crowd wanted to resist,
but their limbs seemed to wither.
The woman ordered them to be bound one by one,
tied to the corridor pillars,
and given thin porridge three times a day.
She then sent an old servant to go and inform Huáng Gōng,
and then entered the room to mourn her husband.
After weeping,
she said to the concubine,
"This is fate.
I had planned to come last month,
but was delayed by my mother's illness,
so it has come to this.
I never expected that in the blink of an eye, it would become a ruin!"
She asked about the old maids and servants,
and learned that they had all been plundered by the clan members,
which made her sigh even more.
The next day,
when the maids and servants heard the woman had arrived,
they all returned on their own,
and everyone shed tears upon seeing each other.
The clan members who had been seized
all clamored that the child was not Mùzhēn's offspring,
but the woman did not dispute it.
Soon after, Huáng Gōng arrived,
and the woman led the child out to greet him.
Huáng clasped the child's arm,
then pulled back his left sleeve,
saw the red mark clearly there,
and then bared it to the crowd
to prove its authenticity.
He then carefully investigated the lost property,
recorded the names in a ledger,
and personally went to the district magistrate.
The magistrate arrested the unruly individuals,
each receiving forty strokes,
and was imprisoned while strict investigation continued.
In a few days,
the land, horses, and cattle
were all returned to their former owner.
When Huáng was about to leave,
the woman led the child to bow and said,
"I am not a person of this world,
as you, Uncle, know.
I now entrust this child to you, Uncle."
Huáng said,
"As long as this old man still draws breath,
I will do everything to arrange for him."
After Huáng left,
the woman finished checking everything,
entrusted the child to the concubine,
and then prepared a meal to offer sacrifices to her husband.
She did not return for half a day.
When they looked,
the cups and food were still laid out,
but she had vanished.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Those who do not cut off others' lineage,
others will not cut off their lineage.
This is a person, but truly one who has died prematurely.
When one has good friends at the table,
carriages and furs can be shared.
But when the autumn weeds grow thick,
and wives and children are bullied,
then the person in the carriage looks on and leaves.
To remember a deceased friend and not bear to forget them,
to be grateful and think of how to repay—
who else could it be but
a fox!
If you had much wealth,
I would manage it for you."
According to the Zhùxuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain person from Jìníng
chanced upon
a traveling monk
lousing himself in the sun
outside a wild temple.
His staff hung with a gourd, he looked like a seller of medicine.
So, jestingly, he said,
"Monk, do you also sell bedroom pills?"
The monk replied,
"I do.
The weak can become strong,
the small can become huge.
It takes effect instantly,
no need to wait overnight."
The man was delighted
and asked for some.
The monk untied his monastic robe,
took out a pill,
the size of a millet grain,
and told him to swallow it.
After about half the time it takes to cook a meal,
his lower part suddenly grew.
After more than an hour, it stopped by itself,
having increased by one-third of its original size.
Still not satisfied,
he watched the monk go relieve himself,
then secretly untied his robe,
and took two or three pills, swallowing them all at once.
Immediately, he felt his skin tearing,
his sinews being pulled,
his neck shrinking, his waist bulging,
while his yin organ grew incessantly.
Greatly frightened,
he had no solution.
The monk returned,
saw his condition,
and exclaimed in surprise,
"You must have stolen my medicine!"
He quickly gave him a pill,
and only then did the growth cease.
He untied his clothes to look at himself,
and found it was almost one-third the size of his two thighs.
Shrinking his neck, he shuffled back home.
His parents could not recognize him.
From then on, he was a disabled person,
lying on the street every day,
seen by many.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Yú Chénglóng, the Censor-in-Chief,
was inspecting his department when he arrived at Gāoyóu.
It so happened that a wealthy gentry family was about to marry off their daughter;
the dowry was very rich.
That night, it was taken away by "arrow-piercing" (a method of burglary) and swept clean.
The Prefect was helpless.
The Duke ordered all gates to be closed,
leaving only one gate for people to enter and exit,
with the local magistrate guarding it,
strictly searching all baggage.
He also issued a proclamation,
ordering all households in the city to return to their residences,
to await inspection and search the next day,
to ensure the whereabouts of the stolen goods were found.
Then he secretly instructed the local magistrate: if anyone enters and exits the city gate more than once,
arrest them.
After noon, two people were caught.
Other than their clothes,
they carried no luggage.
The Duke said,
"These are indeed the thieves."
The two argued deceitfully without end.
The Duke ordered them to remove their clothes and search them,
and found two sets of women's clothing worn inside their robes,
all items from the dowry.
Apparently, fearing a big search the next day,
they were eager to move the goods,
but there were too many to carry,
so they secretly wore them and repeatedly went in and out.
Another time, when the Duke was a magistrate,
