he traveled to a neighboring district.
Early in the morning,
passing outside the city wall,
he saw two people carrying a sick person on a bed,
covered by a large quilt.
Hair was exposed on the pillow,
and a phoenix hairpin was stuck in the hair,
as the person lay sideways on the bed.
Three or four strong men followed beside them,
taking turns holding the quilt down with their hands,
pressing it against the body,
as if afraid of the wind getting in.
A moment later,
they rested their shoulders by the roadside,
and then made two other people take turns carrying the bed.
When Duke Yú passed by,
he sent a subordinate back to inquire,
who said it was their sister, critically ill,
being sent back to her husband's family.
The Duke traveled two or three lǐ further,
then sent the subordinate back again
to see which village they entered.
The subordinate followed them
to a village house,
where two men welcomed them in.
He returned and reported to the Duke.
The Duke said to the district magistrate,
"Are there no bandits or robbers in the city?"
The magistrate replied,
"There are none."
At that time, the official regulations were strict,
and superiors and subordinates alike concealed robberies.
Therefore, even if people were robbed and killed by bandits,
they would endure it and dare not speak.
The Duke went to his lodging
and instructed his household staff to investigate thoroughly.
Indeed, a wealthy family had been robbed by strong bandits,
and their members tortured and burned to death.
The Duke summoned the son
and questioned him about the situation.
The son stubbornly refused to admit it.
The Duke said,
"I have already arrested the great bandits here on your behalf;
there is no other reason."
The son then bowed his head and wept sorrowfully,
begging for vengeance for the deceased.
The Duke knocked on the door and met the district magistrate,
sending strong constables out of the city at the fourth watch (about 1-3 AM),
directly to the village house,
where they arrested eight people,
who confessed after one interrogation.
When questioned about who the "sick woman" was,
the bandits confessed:
"That night, we were all in a gambling den,
so we conspired with a prostitute,
placed the gold on the bed,
and had her lie on it until we reached our hideout, where we divided it."
Everyone admired the Duke's divine insight.
Someone asked how he was able to know.
The Duke said,
"This is very easy to explain,
but people simply don't pay attention.
How could a young woman on a bed
allow people to put their hands under the quilt,
and also switch shoulders while being carried?
The burden felt very heavy;
when hands were used to protect it,
I knew there must be something inside.
If a sick woman were indeed unconscious and being brought back,
there would surely be women leaning by the door to welcome her;
seeing only men,
and not asking a single question in surprise,
is how I definitively knew they were bandits."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
During the Wànlì era,
the Magistrate of Lìchéng dreamed that the City God demanded people for service.
He printed the names of eight yamen runners on a dish
and burned it in the temple.
By night,
all eight men died.
To the east of the temple was a wine shop,
whose owner was acquainted with one of the yamen runners.
That night, the runner came to buy wine,
and the owner asked,
"Who are you entertaining?"
He replied,
"Many colleagues are here,
I'm just buying a pot of wine to briefly mention their names."
At dawn,
when the owner saw other yamen runners,
he first learned that the man had died.
He entered the temple and opened the door,
and there was the bottle,
still filled with wine as before.
He returned to look at the money he was given,
and it was all paper ash.
The magistrate ordered eight statues to be made and placed in the temple.
Whenever yamen runners received an assignment,
they would first pay respects to the statues before departing.
Otherwise,
they would certainly suffer retribution.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Shàoxīng, there was an old widow who spun thread at night.
Suddenly, a young woman pushed open the door and entered,
smiling and saying:
“Old mother, are you not tired?”
The widow looked at her;
she was eighteen or nineteen years old,
her appearance graceful and beautiful,
her robes splendid.
The old woman was startled and asked,
“Where do you come from?”
The woman said:
“I pity your solitary life,
so I came to keep you company.”
The old woman suspected she was a runaway from a noble household
and pressed her with questions.
The woman said:
“Old mother, do not fear.
I am an orphan,
just like you, old mother.
I admire your purity,
so I came to be with you.
Isn’t it good for both of us to avoid loneliness?”
The old woman again suspected she was a fox spirit
and remained silent, hesitating.
The woman then ascended the bed and began to spin on her behalf,
saying:
“Old mother, don’t worry.
This kind of work,
I am excellent at it.
I will certainly not burden you for food and clothing.”
The old woman saw her gentleness and loveliness,
and so she was at ease.
Deep in the night,
she said to the old woman:
“The quilt and pillow I brought
are still outside the door.
When you go out,
please fetch them.”
The old woman went out
and indeed found a bundle of clothes.
The woman untied it on the old bed.
No one knew what kind of silk and embroidery it was;
it was incomparably fragrant and smooth.
The old woman also laid out her cotton quilt
and shared the bed with the woman.
As soon as her silk collar was unfastened,
a strange fragrance filled the room.
After she had fallen asleep,
the old woman thought to herself:
“Meeting such a beautiful person,
it’s a pity I am not a man.”
The woman by her pillow smiled and said:
“Old mother, at seventy, are you still having such wild thoughts?”
The old woman said:
“No.”
The woman said:
“Since you’re not having wild thoughts,
why do you wish to be a man?”
The old woman increasingly realized she was a fox spirit
and was greatly afraid.
The woman again smiled and said:
“What kind of heart desires to be a man,
and yet fears me?”
The old woman became even more terrified;
her legs trembled, shaking the bed.
The woman said:
“Alas!
To have such courage,
and still wish to be a man!
To tell you the truth: I am a true immortal,
but I will not harm you.
However, you must be careful with your words,
and your food and clothing will be sufficient.”
The old woman rose early
and bowed beneath the bed.
The woman extended her arm and pulled her up.
Her arm was as smooth as fat,
emitting a hot, overflowing fragrance;
as soon as her skin touched a person,
one felt a relaxed lightness.
The old woman’s heart stirred,
and she again indulged in distant thoughts.
The woman scoffed and said:
“Old woman, your trembling has just stopped,
and where has your mind gone again!
If you were a husband,
you would die for love.”
The old woman said:
“If I were a husband,
how could I not die tonight!”
From then on, their hearts were in perfect harmony,
and they worked together daily.
The thread she spun
was even, fine, and lustrous;
when woven into cloth,
it was crystal clear like brocade,
its price three times that of ordinary cloth.
When the old woman went out,
she would bar her door;
if anyone visited the old woman,
the young woman would answer from another room.
They lived together for half a year,
and no one knew.
Later, the old woman gradually leaked the secret to her relatives,
and all the women in the neighborhood entrusted the old woman to seek a meeting.
The woman admonished:
“Your words are not careful;
I will not be able to stay much longer.”
The old woman regretted her slip of the tongue
and deeply blamed herself;
but those seeking a meeting grew daily in number,
even to the point of some using influence to coerce the old woman.
The old woman tearfully pleaded her case,
and the woman said:
“If they are just female companions,
seeing them is no harm;
but I fear there might be frivolous young men
who will make advances.”
The old woman again pleaded earnestly,
and only then did she allow it.
The next day,
old women and young girls
followed each other like a continuous fragrant smoke on the road.
The woman was annoyed by their bother;
regardless of their status,
she did not speak with any of them;
she merely sat silently,
listening to their morning salutations.
Young men in the village heard of her beauty
and were captivated,
but the old woman refused all of them.
There was a certain Fèi Shēng,
a famous scholar in the county,
who spent his entire fortune
to tempt the old woman with a large sum of money.
The old woman agreed
and made arrangements for him.
The woman already knew of it
and reproached her, saying,
“Are you selling me?”
The old woman prostrated herself on the ground.
The woman said:
“You are greedy for his bribe,
and I am moved by his foolishness;
we can meet once.
However, our destined relationship is over.”
The old woman again prostrated herself and kowtowed.
The woman agreed to meet the next day.
Fèi Shēng heard of it
and was delighted.
He prepared incense and candles and went,
making a deep bow upon entering the door.
The woman spoke with him from behind a curtain,
asking:
“You broke your fortune to see me;
what will you instruct me with?”
Fèi Shēng said:
"Indeed, I dare not seek anything else.
Merely hearing tales of Wáng Qiáng and Xīzǐ
is enough for renown to spread;
if I am not cast aside for my dullness,
and am allowed to broaden my horizons,
my humble wish will be fulfilled.
As for fortune or misfortune, if they are predetermined,
that is not what I wish to hear."
Suddenly, within the fabric curtain,
a radiant light shone forth,
with emerald brows and vermillion lips
all clearly visible,
as if there were no screen or curtain separating them.
Shēng, dazzled and his spirit captivated,
unconsciously bowed low.
After bowing and rising,
the thick curtain was drawn,
and he could hear a voice but no longer see.
Amidst his disappointment,
he secretly regretted not having seen her lower body;
suddenly, beneath the curtain, a pair of embroidered shoes peeked out,
so slender they were less than a finger's width.
Shēng bowed again.
A voice from within the curtain said:
"Sir, please return home!
My body is delicate!"
The old woman led Shēng to another room,
and brewed tea for him.
Shēng inscribed a poem, "Nánxiāngzǐ," on the wall, saying:
"Vaguely before the painted curtain,
three inches of jade shoots, walking on waves, stirred the dust;
where they touched the ground, lotus petals clearly fell,
slender,
and even more pitiful with their doubled pedestals.
Flowers adorned the curved phoenix-head shoes,
held in hand, they must surely be soft as silk floss;
I only wish to transform into a butterfly,
by her skirt,
to breathe in the lingering fragrance, even death would be sweet."
After inscribing it, he left.
The maiden read the inscription and was displeased,
saying to the old woman:
"I said our predestined affinity was over,
and now it's not a baseless claim."
The old woman prostrated herself and begged for forgiveness.
The maiden said:
"The fault is not entirely yours.
I accidentally fell into a snare of emotion,
showing my physical form to a person,
and thus was defiled by lewd verses.
This is all self-inflicted;
what blame is there on you?
If I do not move quickly,
I fear I will become trapped in this den of passion,
and find it difficult to escape in future reincarnations."
Thereupon, she packed up her belongings and departed.
The old woman tried to hold her back,
but in a flash, she was gone.
According to a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
Hóngmáo Guó [Holland]
had long been permitted to trade with China.
The border commander, seeing their numbers,
did not allow them to land.
The Hóngmáo people pleaded:
"Grant us a felt mat's worth of land, that is all."
The commander thought a felt mat could not hold many,
and permitted it.
The people placed the felt on the shore,
which barely held two men;
they stretched it,
and it held four or five men;
as they stretched and more landed,
in an instant, the felt grew to about an acre,
and there were already hundreds of men.
Short blades were drawn simultaneously,
unexpectedly,
and they plundered for several *lǐ* before departing.
According to a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
A certain resident of Láiyáng was sleeping one day,
when he saw a man and a woman enter, hand in hand.
The woman was jaundiced and swollen,
her waist so thick she seemed about to fall backwards,
her expression sorrowful and bitter.
The man urged her, saying:
"Come,
come!"
Mǒu thought they were engaged in an illicit affair,
and so he pretended to sleep to spy on their actions.
Once inside,
they seemed not to notice anyone on the bed.
The man again urged:
"Hurry!"
The woman then bared her chest,
exposing her belly,
which was as big as a drum.
The man pulled out a butcher's knife,
and forcefully stabbed it in,
slicing straight down from below the heart to the navel,
making a gurgling sound.
Mǒu was terrified,
daring not to breathe.
But the woman endured with knitted brows,
not uttering a single groan.
The man held the knife in his mouth,
reached his hand into her belly,
and began pulling out her intestines;
as he pulled them out,
in an instant, his arm was full.
Then he used the knife to cut them,
lifted them, and placed them on a small table;
then he continued to pull out more,
when the table was full,
he hung them on a chair;
when the chair was also full,
he piled them into dozens of heaps,
like a fisherman lifting a net,
and threw them towards Mǒu's head.
Mǒu felt a wave of hot stench,
his face, eyes, and throat were completely covered without a gap.
Mǒu could no longer endure it,
he pushed the intestines away with his hand,
letting out a great cry and rushing off.
The intestines fell before the bed,
his feet were seized,
and he collapsed unconscious.
His family rushed to look,
only to see him wrapped in pig entrails;
but upon closer inspection,
there was nothing there at all,
everyone thought their eyes were playing tricks on them,
and were not alarmed.
Only when Mǒu recounted what he had seen
did they all find it strange.
Yet there were no traces in the room,
only a bloody stench that lingered for several days.
According to a manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
Zhāng Hóngjiàn,
a native of Yǒngpíng.
At eighteen,
he was a renowned scholar in the prefecture.
At that time, Zhào Mǒu, the magistrate of Lúlóng, was corrupt and tyrannical,
and the people suffered greatly.
A scholar named Fàn Shēng was beaten to death,
and his fellow students, enraged by his injustice,
intended to appeal to the provincial authorities
and asked Zhāng to draft the petition for them,
inviting him to join their cause.
Zhāng agreed.
His wife, Fāng Shì,
who was beautiful and virtuous,
heard of his plan and
advised him:
"Generally, when scholars undertake something,
they can succeed together,
but cannot fail together: if they succeed, everyone claims the credit,
but if they fail, they will fall apart like scattered tiles,
unable to remain united.
In today's world of power and influence,
right and wrong are difficult to determine by reason;
you are also alone;
if something goes wrong,
who will help you in your distress?"
Zhāng heeded her words,
regretting his decision,
and so he politely declined the students,
only drafting the petition for them before leaving.
After an initial review,
nothing was approved or denied.
Zhào offered a large sum of money to a high-ranking official,
and the students were arrested for forming a faction,
with orders also issued to apprehend the petition writer.
Zhāng Jù
fled.
When he reached the border of Fèngxiáng,
his travel funds were exhausted.
As night fell,
he wandered hesitantly in the wilderness,
with nowhere to go.
Suddenly, he spotted a small village
and hurried towards it.
An old woman was just opening her door.
Seeing the young man,
she asked what he wanted.
Zhāng told her the truth.
The old woman said:
"Food and a bed
are trivial matters;
but there are no men in my house,
so it's not convenient to keep a guest."
Zhāng said:
"I wouldn't dare to ask for too much;
but if I could just find shelter inside your gate,
to escape tigers and wolves, that would be enough."
The old woman then had someone
close the door,
gave him a straw mat,
and instructed him:
"I pity you for having nowhere to go,
and have privately allowed you to stay.
You should leave early before dawn,
lest my young mistress hear of it
and blame me."
The old woman left,
and Zhāng leaned against the wall, pretending to sleep.
Suddenly, a lantern light flickered,
and he saw the old woman leading out a young lady.
Zhāng quickly hid in a dark place,
secretly peeking.
She was a beautiful woman of about twenty.
When she reached the door
and saw the straw mat,
she questioned the old woman.
The old woman told her the truth.
The lady angrily said:
"With our household being so weak and vulnerable,
how can you accommodate a ruffian!"
She then asked:
"Where is this person staying?"
Zhāng, afraid,
came out and prostrated himself below the steps.
The lady carefully questioned him about his family and clan,
and her expression softened a little.
She said,
"Fortunately, he is a refined scholar,
so it won't hurt to keep him.
However, this old servant didn't even inform me;
such carelessness,
how can this be how one treats a gentleman?"
She ordered the old woman to lead the guest into the house.
A moment later,
wine and drinks were served,
and the provisions were exquisite and clean.
Afterward, a brocade cushion was laid on the bed.
Zhāng was very grateful to her,
and privately inquired about her surname.
The old woman said:
"Our family name is Shī.
Both the venerable master and mistress have passed away,
leaving only three daughters.
The one you just saw
is the eldest daughter, Shùnhuá."
The old woman left.
Zhāng saw a copy of the *Nánhuá Jīng* commentary on the small table.
He picked it up and, resting on the pillow,
lay on the bed, flipping through it.
Suddenly, Shùnhuá pushed open the door and entered.
Zhāng put down the scroll
and fumbled for his cap and shoes.
The lady immediately sat down on the bed, pressing on it, and said:
"No need,
no need!"
She then sat closer to the bed
and said boldly:
"I see you as a charming and talented scholar,
and wish to entrust my household to you, thus incurring the suspicion of improper intimacy.
Will you not reject me?"
Zhāng was flustered and didn't know how to respond,
only saying:
"I wouldn't steal you,
but I already have a wife
at home."
The lady laughed and said:
"This also shows your sincerity and integrity,
so it doesn't matter.
Since you don't dislike me,
tomorrow we should bother a matchmaker."
Having spoken,
she wanted to leave.
Zhāng reached out and held her back,
and the lady stayed.
She rose before dawn
and gave Zhāng gold, saying:
"Take this as money for sightseeing;
towards evening,
you should come back late,
lest others spy on us."
Zhāng followed her words,
leaving early and returning late,
making this his routine for half a year.
One day,
he returned quite early.
When he reached the place,
the village cottages were all gone,
and he was utterly amazed.
As he was pacing about,
he heard the old woman say, "
Why have you come so early!"
In a blink of an eye,
the courtyard was as it had been,
and he was already inside the room.
He found this even stranger.
Shùnhuá came out from within,
and laughing, said,
"Are you suspicious of me?
I will tell you the truth: I
am a fox immortal,
and I have a predestined affinity with you.
If you are truly alarmed,
please let us part immediately."
Zhāng, enchanted by her beauty,
also settled his mind.
That night, he said to the woman,
"Since you are an immortal,
you must be able to travel a thousand *lǐ* in a single breath.
I have been away from home for three years,
and the thought of my wife and children never leaves my mind.
Can you take me home for a visit?"
The woman seemed displeased,
and said,
"Regarding the love between husband and wife,
I believe my affection for you is sincere;
your thinking of her while with me,
is a delusion for those who are intimately entwined."
Zhāng apologized, saying,
"How can you say such a thing?
The proverb says, 'A
day as husband and wife,
a hundred days of kindness and righteousness.'
When I think of you upon my return in the future,
it will be just like my thinking of her today.
If I were to forget the old when I get the new, what value would you see in me?"
The woman then smiled and said,
"I have a narrow mind: for
me, I wish you would not forget me;
for others,
I wish you would forget them.
However, if you wish to return temporarily,
what difficulty is there in that? For you, it's just a short measure."
Thereupon, she took his sleeve and went out the door.
Seeing the road dark,
Zhāng hesitated and did not advance.
The woman pulled him along,
and in a short time,
said,
"We have arrived.
You go home,
and I will leave."
Zhāng stopped and carefully looked,
and indeed saw his own door.
He scaled the garden wall and entered,
seeing the lamp in the room still flickering.
He approached and tapped the door with two fingers.
Someone inside asked who it was,
and Zhāng fully explained his arrival.
The person inside lit a candle and opened the gate.
It was truly Fāng-shì,
and they were both surprised and overjoyed,
holding hands as they entered the curtained bed.
Seeing their son sleeping on the bed,
he said with emotion,
"When I left, our son was only an inch to the knee;
now he is grown so tall!"
Husband and wife embraced,
as if in a dream.
Zhāng recounted his experiences.
When he inquired about the legal case,
he then learned that some scholars had died of starvation,
and some had been exiled far away.
He was even more impressed by his wife's foresight.
As he relaxed into her embrace,
he said,
"You have such a beautiful partner,
I suppose you no longer think of the one who weeps alone in her bed!"
Zhāng said,
"If I didn't think of you,
why would I be here?
Although she and I are said to have affection,
we are ultimately not of the same kind;
it is only her kindness and righteousness that are hard to forget."
Fāng-shì said,
"Who do you take me for?"
Zhāng looked closely,
and it was not Fāng-shì,
but Shùnhuá.
He reached out to touch the child,
and it was only a bamboo wife.
He was greatly ashamed and speechless.
The woman said,
"Your heart is known!
It is fitting that we part ways from this point,
yet fortunately you have not forgotten kindness and righteousness,
which is somewhat redemptive."
After two or three days,
she suddenly said,
"I think this foolish infatuation has
ultimately no meaning.
You complain daily that I don't see you off;
now, I happen to want to go to the capital,
and we can go together along the way."
She then took the bamboo wife from the bedside and they both straddled it,
telling him to close both eyes.
He felt that they were not far from the ground,
and the wind whistled.
After a while,
they landed.
The woman said,
"From here, we part."
Just as he was about to give instructions,
the woman had already vanished.
He stood there lost for a moment,
then heard village dogs barking.
In the dim light, he saw trees and houses,
all familiar sights of his hometown.
He followed the path home.
He scaled the wall and knocked on the door,
just as before.
Fāng-shì was startled awake,
disbelieving her husband had returned;
after questioning and confirming,
she finally lit a lamp and came out, sobbing.
Upon seeing each other,
her tears could not be suppressed.
Zhāng still suspected Shùnhuá's illusion;
he also saw a child sleeping on the bed,
just like last night.
So he laughed and said,
"Did Zhúfūrén take someone away again?"
Fāng shì did not give up,
and said with a change of expression:
"I have waited for you as if for years;
the tear stains on my pillow are still there.
Now that we are finally reunited,
you show no sorrowful love,
how can you be so heartless!"
Zhāng perceived her true feelings,
then held her arm and sighed,
explaining everything in detail.
He asked about the outcome of the lawsuit,
and it was just as Shùnhuá had said.
Fāng xiāng was filled with emotion,
when she heard footsteps outside the door,
she asked but received no reply.
It happened that there was a scoundrel, Jiǎ, from the neighborhood,
who had long been lusting after Fāng yàn.
That night, returning from another village,
he saw someone climb over the wall from a distance,
thinking it must be someone going to an illicit rendezvous,
and he followed them in.
Jiǎ did not know Zhāng very well,
but just lay in wait and listened.
When Fāng shì urgently asked,
he then said:
"Who is in the room?"
Fāng lied:
"No one."
Jiǎ said:
"I've been eavesdropping for a long time,
and I will respectfully apprehend you."
Fāng had no choice
but to tell him the truth.
Jiǎ said:
"The major case of Zhāng Hóngjiàn has not been settled,
even if you return home,
you should still be bound and sent to the authorities."
Fāng pleaded bitterly with him,
and Jiǎ's words became increasingly disrespectful and pressing.
Zhāng, burning with rage,
grabbed a knife and went straight out,
chopping Jiǎ in the skull.
Jiǎ fell,
still howling;
Zhāng chopped him again repeatedly,
and he died.
Fāng said:
"Things have come to this,
the crime is even more serious.
You must escape quickly,
I will bear the guilt."
Zhāng said:
"A man dies if he dies,
how can I disgrace my wife and implicate my son to save my own life!
You have no worries,
just let this son continue his scholarly pursuits,
then I can close my eyes in peace."
At dawn,
he went to the county to surrender.
Zhào, as an involved party in the Qīn case,
merely gave him a light punishment.
Soon, he was escorted from the prefecture to the capital,
and the shackles were quite painful.
On the way, he met a woman riding on horseback,
with an old woman holding the reins;
it was Shùnhuá.
Zhāng called out to the old woman, wanting to speak,
and tears fell with his voice.
The woman turned her reins,
lifted the veil with her hand,
and exclaimed:
"My cousin,
how have you come to this?"
Zhāng briefly recounted his story.
The woman said:
"According to your usual self, cousin,
you would just turn your head and ignore me;
but I cannot bear to,
my humble dwelling is not far,
I will invite the public servants to come along,
it can also help a little with expenses."
They followed her for two or three lǐ,
and saw a mountain village,
with tall and neat buildings.
The woman dismounted and entered,
ordering the gatekeeper to open the door and invite the guests in.
Soon, wine and roasted meat were plentiful and exquisite,
as if prepared beforehand.
She then sent the gatekeeper out to say,
"There are no men in the house right now,
Official Zhāng, please urge the public servants to drink a few more cups;
much reliance will be placed on them for the journey ahead.
I sent someone to prepare several tens of gold for your expenses,
and to reward the two guests,
but they haven't arrived yet."
The two officers secretly rejoiced,
drank heartily,
and no longer talked about proceeding.
As night gradually fell,
the two officers became thoroughly drunk.
The woman came out,
and pointed at the shackles with her finger.
The shackles immediately came off;
she pulled Zhāng onto one horse with her,
galloping like a dragon.
After a short while,
she urged him to dismount,
saying:
"You stop here.
My sister and I have an appointment at Qīnghǎi,
and I have already delayed for a while for you,
they must have been waiting for a long time."
Zhāng asked:
"When will we meet again?"
The woman did not answer,
and when he asked again,
she pushed him off the horse and left.
At dawn,
he asked about the place,
it was Tàiyuán.
So he went to the prefecture,
rented a house and taught students there.
He used the pseudonym Gōng Zǐqiān.
After living there for ten years,
he found out that the pursuit of fugitives had gradually slackened,
so he cautiously turned eastward again.
When he approached his village gate,
he dared not enter immediately,
waiting until deep night before entering.
Upon reaching the gate,
the walls were high and sturdy,
no longer possible to climb over,
so he could only strike the door with a whip.
After a long while,
his wife finally came out to ask.
Zhāng whispered to her.
Overjoyed,
she let him in,
making a scolding sound,
saying:
"You're short on expenses in the capital,
you should have returned earlier,
why did you have to send someone in the middle of the night?"
Entering the room,
they each recounted their experiences,
only then did she know that the two officers had fled and not returned.
While they were talking,
a young woman frequently came to the curtain,
Zhāng asked who she was,
she said:
"She is my daughter-in-law."
He asked:
"Where is our son?"
She said:
"He went to the prefectural examination and has not returned."
Zhāng shed tears and said:
"After years of wandering,
our son has grown up,
I didn't expect him to be able to continue the family's scholarly tradition;
you must have exhausted all your heart and blood!"
Before he finished speaking,
his daughter-in-law had already warmed wine and cooked rice,
arranged abundantly on the table.
Zhāng was overjoyed beyond expectation.
He stayed for several days,
hiding in the house,
fearing that others would know.
One night,
as Fāng was lying down,
she suddenly heard a clamor of voices,
and violent pounding on the door.
Greatly frightened,
they both got up.
She heard someone say:
"Is there a back door?"
Even more frightened,
she quickly used a door panel as a ladder,
helping Zhāng climb over the wall and escape into the night;
then she went to the door to ask the reason,
it was to report a newly successful official.
Fāng was overjoyed,
deeply regretting Zhāng's escape,
and that he could not be recalled.
That night, Zhāng scrambled through dense vegetation and thorny bushes,
too rushed to choose a path;
by dawn,
he was utterly exhausted.
His initial thought was to go west,
but when he asked passersby,
he found he was far from the main road to the capital.
So he entered a village,
intending to pawn clothes for food.
He saw a grand gate: with a notice pasted on the wall;
looking closer,
he learned it was the Xǔ family,
a new Xiàolián.
A moment later, an old man came out from inside,
Zhāng went up to greet him, bowed, and explained his situation.
Wēng saw the guest's demeanor was elegant,
knowing he was not one who earned his food by deception,
invited him in and treated him well.
As for all his travels,
Zhāng claimed:
"I set up a tent outside the capital gates,
and on the way home, I encountered bandits."
Wēng kept Hǎi, his younger son.
Zhāng briefly inquired about their noble lineage,
and learned that they were retired officials from the capital.
The xiàolián
was his nephew.
After more than a month,
the xiàolián returned with a fellow successful candidate,
saying he was a person surnamed Zhāng from Shuǐpíng,
a youth of eighteen or nineteen.
Zhāng, seeing their family genealogies matched,
secretly suspected he was his son;
however, there were many people with this surname in the district,
so he kept silent for a while.
In the evening, he unpacked his belongings,
took out
"the family register,"
and eagerly read it through.
It was truly his son.
Unconsciously, tears flowed down.
Everyone was surprised and asked him,
and he pointed to the name and said:
"Zhāng Hóngjiàn,
that is me."
He fully recounted his story,
and Zhāng, the xiàolián, embraced his father and wept loudly.
Xǔ, the uncle and nephew, comforted and persuaded them,
and only then did their sorrow turn to joy.
Xǔ immediately sent a letter with gold and silk,
to inform the xiàntái,
and the father and son then returned home together.
When the news was first heard,
they had been daily grieving for Zhāng's absence,
but suddenly, when they learned the xiàolián had returned,
their grief intensified.
A little while later,
father and son entered together,
startling them as if they had fallen from the sky.
After inquiring about the reason,
they finally shared in the sorrow and joy.
Father Jiǎ, seeing his son's prominence,
dared not let his malicious thoughts resurface.
Zhāng treated him even more generously,
and again recounted the circumstances of that year.
Father Jiǎ felt ashamed and grateful,
and so they became good friends.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
During the Wànlì era,
Sūn Píngshì was orphaned young,
his mother observed strict widowhood from the age of nineteen.
Sūn passed the imperial examination,
but his mother had already died.
He often said to people:
"I must obtain an imperial patent of nobility to glorify her resting place,
only then will I not have failed my mother's bitter faithfulness."
Suddenly, he contracted a severe illness,
which was extremely serious.
He had always been good friends with an imperial physician,
so he sent someone to summon him;
the messenger had just left the door,
when his illness worsened greatly.
He stared with wide eyes and said:
"If I cannot achieve fame and honor my parents during my life,
how can I face my old mother underground?!"
Then he died,
his eyes not closing.
Before long,
the imperial physician arrived,
heard the sound of weeping,
and immediately came to offer condolences.
Seeing his condition,
he found it unusual.
The family told him the reason,
and the imperial physician said:
"If you wish to obtain an imperial patent,
it is not difficult.
The empress will give birth any day now,
if he can just live for ten more days or so,
the imperial patent can be obtained."
He immediately ordered moxa to be brought,
and cauterized the corpse at eighteen points.
As the moxa sticks were about to finish,
a groan was already heard from the bed;
they quickly administered medicine,
and he actually came back to life.
The physician instructed:
"Be sure not to eat bear or tiger meat."
Everyone remembered this;
however, as these items were not commonly available,
they didn't pay much attention to it.
After three days, he recovered,
and still attended court for congratulations.
After six or seven days,
the Crown Prince was indeed born,
and the emperor summoned and feasted all the officials.
An imperial envoy brought out rare delicacies,
distributing them to civil and military officials,
white slices with red threads,
sweet and incomparably delicious.
Sūn ate it,
not knowing what it was.
The next day,
he inquired among his colleagues,
who said:
"It was bear fat."
He was greatly shocked and turned pale;
he immediately fell ill,
and died upon reaching home.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain person from the district
bought an ox,
which was quite strong.
At night, he dreamed the ox grew two wings and flew away,
he considered it inauspicious,
and suspected he would suffer a loss.
He led it to the market and sold it at a reduced price.
He wrapped the gold in his sash,
and tied it around his arm.
On his way home, halfway there,
he saw a hawk eating a leftover rabbit,
and it was very tame when approached.
So he tied its head to its leg with his sash,
and held it on his arm.
The hawk repeatedly flapped and struggled,
and when his grip slackened slightly,
it flew away with the sash.
Although this was fate,
if he hadn't mistrusted his dream,
and hadn't been greedy for a free catch,
how could the one that walked have flown away?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wáng Zǐ'ān,
a famous scholar from Dōngchāng,
was confined to the examination hall.
After entering the hall,
his expectations were very keen.
Near the time of the announcement of results,
he drank heavily and got very drunk,
returning to lie down in his inner room.
Suddenly someone reported:
"A messenger has arrived!"
Wáng staggered up and said:
"Reward him ten thousand cash!"
His family, because of his drunkenness,
deceived him to pacify him, saying:
"Just please sleep,
the reward has already been given."
Wáng then fell asleep.
After a short while, someone else said,
"You have passed the *jìnshì* examination!"
Wáng said to himself,
"I haven't even gone to the capital yet,
how could I have passed the examination?"
That person said:
"Have you forgotten?
All three rounds of the examination are over."
Wáng was greatly pleased,
got up and cried out:
"Reward him ten thousand cash!"
His family again deceived him as before.
After another while,
a person urgently entered and said:
"You have passed the palace examination and become a *hànlín*,
the attendants (*chángbān*) are here."
Indeed, he saw two people bowing beneath his bed,
their clothes and caps neat and clean.
Wáng called for wine and food to be bestowed,
his family again gave it to them,
secretly laughing at his drunkenness.
After a long time,
Wáng thought to himself that he must go out and show off to his hometown,
and loudly called his attendants (*chángbān*);
he called dozens of times,
but no one answered.
His family laughed and said:
"Just lie down and wait for a bit,
we'll go look for them."
After a longer while,
the attendants (*chángbān*) indeed returned.
Wáng pounded the bed and stamped his feet,
cursing loudly:
"Where did you dullards go?!"
The attendants (*chángbān*) angrily said,
"You uncouth rogue!
We were just playing a trick on you,
and you're truly scolding us?"
Wáng was enraged,
suddenly got up and pounced on them,
knocking off their cap.
Wáng also stumbled and fell.
His wife entered,
helped him up and said:
"How could you be so drunk?!"
Wáng said:
"The attendants (*chángbān*) are hateful,
I was just punishing them,
what drunkenness is this?"
His wife laughed and said:
"Our family only has one servant,
who cooks for you by day,
and warms your feet by night.
Where are these attendants (*chángbān*),
serving your poor bones?"
His children all laughed.
Wáng's drunkenness also slightly subsided,
suddenly as if waking from a dream,
he then realized the absurdity of what had preceded.
However, he still remembered the attendants' (*chángbān*) cap falling off: he searched behind the door,
and found a tasseled cap as big as a teacup.
Everyone was puzzled.
He laughed to himself, saying:
"In the past, people were ridiculed by ghosts,
but now I have been mocked by a fox spirit."
Yìshǐ Shì said:
"When a *xiùcai* enters the examination hall,
there are seven similarities.
When first entering,
with bare feet carrying a basket,
he resembles a beggar.
When names are called,
officials scold and clerks curse,
he resembles a prisoner.
When returning to his cubicle,
heads poke out of every hole,
and feet are exposed from every room,
like cold bees before autumn.
When leaving the examination ground,
his expression is lost in prayer,
and heaven and earth change color,
like a sick bird let out of its cage.
By the time he awaits the results,
even plants and trees are alarmed;
dreams are also illusory.
Sometimes he imagines success,
and in an instant, towers and pavilions are all built;
sometimes he imagines failure, and in a flash, his bones have already decayed.
At this moment, he cannot sit or stand still,
resembling a gibbon tied up.
Suddenly, a mounted messenger arrives,
reporting that his name is not on the list.
At this time, his expression completely changes,
collapsing as if dead,
resembling a fly that has eaten poison;
even if prodded, it does not feel it.
At first, despairing,
his heart ashes and his will defeated,
he curses the examiners as blind,
and his brush and ink as powerless.
He will surely take everything on his desk and burn it;
if burning is not enough,
he will smash it;
if smashing is not enough,
he will throw it into the muddy stream.
From then on, he will let his hair down and enter the mountains,
facing a stone wall.
If anyone again brings him essays with 'furthermore'
or 'it has been said',
he will certainly take up a spear and drive them away.
Before long,
as days pass,
his anger gradually subsides,
and his skill again gradually itches;
he then resembles a dove whose eggs have been broken,
only able to carry wood to build a new nest,
and hatch again.
In such circumstances,
those involved are distraught and wish to die;
but from the perspective of an outsider,
what could be more ridiculous?
Within Wáng Zǐ'ān's small mind,
in an instant, myriad thoughts arise.
Presumably, ghosts and foxes had been secretly laughing for a long time,
and thus took advantage of his drunkenness to toy with him.
When the man by the bed woke up,
how could he not burst out laughing?
However, the taste of achieving one's ambition lasts but a moment;
the various gentlemen of the literary world
only experience two or three such moments.
Zǐ'ān experienced it all in one morning,
so the fox's kindness is equivalent to that of a recommending teacher."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a man named Diāo,
whose family had no livelihood.
He would often go out to sell the art of physiognomy—though in reality, he had no such art—
returning once every few months,
with gold and silk filling his mansion.
Everyone found it strange.
It so happened that a villager who was a guest outside
saw from afar a person inside a grand gate,
wearing a Huáyáng cap,
speaking with a clear voice,
surrounded by many women.
Upon closer inspection,
it was Diāo.
So he secretly observed what he was doing.
He saw someone asking:
"Among all of us here,
there is a noble lady.
Can you identify her?"
It was because a noble lady was disguised among them,
intending to test his skill.
The villager felt embarrassed for Diāo.
Diāo calmly looked into the air,
pointed sideways,
and said: "What's difficult to distinguish about this?
Just look at the noble person's head;
there will naturally be auspicious clouds circling it."
Everyone's gaze involuntarily gathered on one person,
observing their "auspicious clouds."
Diāo then pointed at that person and said:
"This is truly the noble person!"
Everyone was amazed, thinking he was a divine being.
The villager returned and recounted his cunning wisdom.
Thus, one knows that even a minor art
must possess extraordinary talent;
otherwise, how could one deceive eyes and ears,
earn money,
and grow rich without capital?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
West of the district, in Cíyáo'wù, there was a farmer's wife.
She was as brave and strong as a man,
and often resolved difficulties and disputes for the villagers.
She lived in a different county from her husband.
Her husband's family was in Gāoyuàn,
over a hundred *lǐ* from Zībó.
He would occasionally come,
stay for a night or two, then leave.
The wife went to Yánshān herself
and worked as a vendor of pottery.
If she had any surplus,
she would give it to beggars.
One evening, she was talking with a neighbor woman,
when she suddenly rose and said,
"My belly is a little painful;
I imagine the karmic obstacle wants to leave my body."
Then she left.
At dawn, they went to check on her,
and saw her carrying two huge wine vats on her shoulders,
just about to enter her house.
They followed her to her room,
and found a swaddled infant lying there.
They asked her in shock,
as she had already carried heavy loads for a hundred *lǐ* after childbirth.
She was good friends with the nun of Běi'ān
and had sworn sisterhood with her.
Later, hearing the nun had engaged in immoral acts,
she angrily grabbed a stick,
intending to go and beat her.
The numerous *púsà* advised her to stop, and she did.
One day,
she encountered the nun on the road
and immediately struck her.
She asked,
"What is my crime?"
The nun did not answer.
She rained down punches and kicks
until the nun could no longer cry out,
then released her and left.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"People say 'a man among women,'
still acknowledging she is not a man.
But this woman even forgot she wore a headscarf.
Her straightforward and self-pleasing character
was no different from ancient sword immortals.
Could it be that her husband was also one of those 'mirror grinders'?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain man named Yǐ, a wine seller in Jīnlíng,
whenever he brewed wine,
would pour water into it and add poison.
Even a good drinker,
after no more than a few cups,
would become dead drunk.
Because of this, he gained
the name
"Zhōngshān"
and amassed great wealth.
One morning,
he saw a fox lying drunk beside the trough.
He bound its four limbs,
and was about to find a knife,
when the fox awoke
and pleaded,
"Don't harm me;
I will grant whatever you ask."
So he released it,
and in an instant, it transformed into a human.
At that time, in the alley, the Sūn family's
eldest daughter-in-law was afflicted by a fox spirit,
so he asked about it.
The fox replied,
"That is me."
Yǐ noticed that the wife's younger sister was especially beautiful,
and asked the fox to bring her to him.
The fox found this difficult.
Yǐ insisted.
The fox invited Yǐ to go with it,
entered a cave,
took out a brown robe and gave it to him,
saying,
"This was left by my elder brother;
wearing it, you should be able to go."
After putting it on and returning home,
his family could not see him.
He put on his own clothes and went out,
and then they could see him.
Greatly pleased,
he went with the fox to the Sūn family's house.
He saw a huge talisman pasted on the wall,
drawn writhing like a dragon.
The fox, frightened, said,
"The monk is truly evil;
I shall not go!"
Then it left.
Yǐ cautiously approached it,
and saw that a real dragon was coiled on the wall,
its head raised as if about to fly.
Greatly frightened, he also left.
It turned out that Sūn had sought a foreign monk
to perform an exorcism for him,
and the talisman had been given beforehand, but the monk had not yet arrived.
The next day,
the monk came
and set up an altar to perform the ritual.
The neighbors all came to watch,
and Yǐ was among them.
Suddenly, his expression changed, and he ran desperately,
as if being caught. Outside the gate,
he fell to the ground and transformed into a fox,
its four limbs still clad in human clothes.
They were about to kill it.
His wife and children pleaded for mercy.
The monk ordered it to be led away,
given food and drink daily,
and it died a few months later.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Sūn Wǔlì
had a young servant who slept alone in a room
and was vaguely taken away by someone.
He arrived at a palace
and saw Yánluó enthroned above.
Yánluó looked at him and said,
"Mistake!
This is not the one."
So he was sent back.
After returning,
he was greatly frightened
and moved to another sleeping place.
Then a colleague and servant named Guō Ān,
seeing the bed empty,
lay down in it.
Another servant, Lǐ Lù,
had a long-standing grudge against the young servant
and had harbored a desire for revenge for a long time.
That night, he entered with a knife,
felt around,
thought it was the young servant,
and killed him.
Guō's father reported it to the authorities.
At that time, Chén Qíshàn was the district magistrate,
and he was not at all distressed by this.
Guō cried out,
saying,
"I only had this one son in my half-life;
how can I live now!"
Chén then assigned Lǐ Lù as his son.
Guō, nursing his grievance, withdrew.
This is not strange because the young servant saw ghosts,
but strange because of Chén's judgment in the case.
In the western district of Jìzhī, there was a murderer,
and his wife sued him.
The magistrate was enraged
and immediately had the murderer apprehended.
He slammed the table and cursed,
"A good husband and wife living together,
and you make her a widow!
I will marry you to her,
and make your wife a lonely widow too."
So he ruled that they should be joined.
Such clear-sighted judgments
are all done by those who pass the *jiǎbǎng* examination;
those from other paths cannot do it.
But Chén was also like that;
what path lacks talent!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Xīyázhuāng village, west of the district,
a merchant named Jiǎ was killed on the road.
The next night,
his wife also hanged herself.
Jiǎ's younger brother reported it to the authorities.
At that time, the magistrate of Zībó was Fèi Gōng Yīzhǐ of Zhèjiāng.
He personally went to investigate.
He saw five *qián* of silver wrapped in a cloth bundle
still at his waist,
knowing that it was not for money.
He detained and questioned the neighbors and bailiffs of the two villages,
but found very few clues.
He did not use torture or flogging,
but released them back to their farming.
He only ordered them to observe the area carefully
and report back every ten days.
Over half a year passed,
and the case gradually slackened.
Jiǎ's younger brother resented the magistrate's leniency
and repeatedly bothered him in court.
The magistrate angrily said,
"Since you cannot name anyone,
do you want me to put good citizens in shackles and cangues?"
He shouted at him and drove him out.
Jiǎ's younger brother had no one to appeal to
and angrily buried his brother and sister-in-law.
One day,
due to the collection of the general levy,
several people were apprehended and brought in.
Among them was Zhōu Chéng,
who, fearing punishment,
declared that he had already prepared sufficient money and grain,
and immediately took out a silver pouch from his waist,
presenting it for the magistrate's inspection.
After inspecting it,
the magistrate asked:
"Where is your home?"
He replied:
"In a certain village."
Again the magistrate asked:
"How many *lǐ* is it from Xīyá?"
He replied:
"Five or six *lǐ*."
"The Jiǎ Mǒu who was murdered last year,
what relation was he to you?"
He replied:
"I don't know the man."
The magistrate suddenly said in a rage:
"You killed him,
and still say you don't know him!"
Zhōu strenuously argued,
but was not listened to;
he was severely shackled,
and indeed confessed his crime.
Previously,
Jiǎ's wife, Wáng Shì,
was about to visit her in-laws,
but was ashamed of having no hair ornaments,
so she nagged her husband to borrow some from a neighbor.
Her husband refused;
so the wife borrowed them herself,
and treasured them greatly.
On her way home,
she removed and wrapped them in a pouch,
and put it inside her sleeve;
when she arrived home,
she searched for it and found it gone.
She dared not tell her husband,
and also had no means to repay the neighbor,
so she was so distressed she wanted to die.
On that day,
Zhōu happened to pick it up,
knowing it was lost by Jiǎ's wife.
He watched for Jiǎ to go out,
and at midnight, he scaled the wall,
intending to seize her and demand intercourse.
It was then oppressively hot,
and Wáng Shì was sleeping in the courtyard.
Zhōu stealthily approached and raped her.
Wáng Shì awoke
and cried out loudly.
Zhōu quickly stopped her,
leaving the pouch containing the hairpin.
After the act,
the woman cautioned him:
"Don't come again later,
the man of our house is fierce,
if you trespass, we might both die."
Zhōu angrily said:
"I have brought the cost of several nights in a brothel,
can one time compensate for that?"
The woman comforted him, saying:
"It's not that I don't want to be with you,
but he is often ill,
it would be better to wait patiently for his death."
Zhōu then left,
and thereupon killed Jiǎ.
That night he visited the woman and said:
"That person has already been killed,
just as we agreed."
When the woman heard this, she cried bitterly.
Zhōu, frightened, fled,
and by dawn, the woman was dead.
The magistrate, through investigation, uncovered the truth,
and punished Zhōu for his crime.
Everyone admired his sagacity,
but did not know how he was able to discern the truth.
The magistrate said:
"No case is difficult to discern,
the key lies in being attentive everywhere.
When the corpse was first examined,
a silver pouch with a *wàn* character embroidered on it was seen;
Zhōu's pouch was also like this,
meaning they were made by the same hand.
And when he was questioned,
he also claimed no acquaintance,
his words and demeanor being shifty and evasive,
thus I was certain he was the true murderer."
The Historian of the Strange says:
"When it comes to judging cases in this world,
people either dismiss them casually,
or they imprison dozens of people and make a mess of it.
On the dais, there are musicians playing,
the clamor heard until noon.
Then they frown and say: 'I am toiling over the people's affairs.'
When the cloud gong strikes thrice,
then beautiful sounds and sights are advanced,
and difficult testimony
is no longer considered;
they merely wait for court to convene
to harm the mulberry tree to cook the old turtle.
Alas!
How can the people's true feelings be ascertained!
I always say:
'The wise are not necessarily benevolent,
but the benevolent must be wise;
for when one exerts oneself diligently, stratagems will emerge.'
The words 'be attentive everywhere'
can be taught
to all who govern the people in the world."
The village man, Hú Chéng,
lived in the same village as Féng Ān.
They had been neighbors for generations.
Hú's father and son were strong and assertive,
while Féng, though trying to be agreeable and friendly,
Hú always suspected him.
One day,
they were drinking together and became slightly tipsy,
confiding in each other quite frankly.
Hú boasted:
"Don't worry about poverty;
it's not hard to acquire a fortune of a hundred pieces of gold."
Féng, knowing Hú's family was not wealthy,
scoffed at him.
Hú, with a stern expression, said:
"I'll tell you the truth: yesterday on the road I met a wealthy merchant
who was carrying a large amount of treasure.
I pushed him into a dry well in Nánshān."
Féng laughed at him again.
At that time, Hú's brother-in-law, Zhèng Lún,
had entrusted Hú with several hundred pieces of gold
to arrange the purchase of land.
Hú then took it all out to show off to Féng.
Féng believed him.
After they parted,
Féng secretly reported the situation to the magistrate of the district, Yì.
The magistrate, Gōng, detained Hú for questioning.
Hú told the truth,
and inquiries about Zhèng and the land owner confirmed his statements.
So they all went to inspect the dry well.
A laborer was lowered down,
and indeed there was a headless corpse in it.
Hú was greatly alarmed,
unable to offer any defense,
but merely claimed he was wronged.
The magistrate, Gōng, grew angry,
striking him dozens of times with a cane,
saying:
"There is concrete evidence,
yet you still cry injustice!"
He ordered Hú to be imprisoned with the implements used for condemned criminals.
He commanded that the corpse not be removed,
but instead announced it to all the villages,
instructing the owner of the corpse to file a complaint.
The next day,
a woman came with a complaint,
identifying herself as the wife of the deceased,
saying:
"My husband, Hé Jiǎ,
took several hundred pieces of gold to conduct trade
and was killed by Hú."
The magistrate, Gōng, said:
"There is a dead person in the well,
but it may not necessarily be your husband."
The woman insisted very firmly.
The magistrate then ordered the corpse to be taken out of the well.
Upon examination,
it was indeed as she said.
The woman dared not approach,
standing back and wailing.
The magistrate, Gōng, said:
"The true culprit has been found,
but the body is not complete.
You may return home for now;
once the head of the deceased is found,
I will summon you to claim compensation."
He then called Hú out from prison
and rebuked him:
"If you don't bring the head tomorrow,
your legs will be broken with chains!"
Hú was escorted away for the entire day and then returned.
When questioned,
he only wailed and cried.
The magistrate then placed the torture instruments before him as if to inflict punishment,
but then did not punish him,
saying,
"I suppose you were busy and hurried carrying the corpse that night,
and don't know where the head fell.
Why didn't you search carefully?"
Hú pleaded for permission to search immediately.
The magistrate, Gōng, then asked the woman:
"How many children do you have?"
She replied:
"None."
He asked:
"What relatives does Hé Jiǎ have?"
"Only one paternal grand-uncle."
The magistrate said with emotion:
"Losing a husband so young,
and so solitary,
how will she manage to live!"
The woman then cried,
kowtowing and begging for pity.
The magistrate, Gōng, said:
"The crime of murder has been established,
but once the body is complete,
this case will be closed.
After the case is closed,
you can remarry quickly.
You are a young woman;
do not frequent the public office again."
The woman was moved to tears,
kowtowing and leaving.
The magistrate, Gōng, immediately posted a notice to the villagers,
asking them to help find the head.
The next morning,
Wáng Wǔ, a villager,
reported that he had found it.
After careful questioning and verification,
he was rewarded with a thousand coins.
Hé Jiǎ's grand-uncle was summoned
and told:
"The major case has been concluded;
however, a human life is a grave matter,
and it cannot be finalized without years of process.
Since your nephew has no heirs,
and the young widow will also struggle to survive,
she should be allowed to marry someone else early.
After this, there will be no other duties,
but if the higher authorities question or reject the case,
you only need to respond."
Hé Jiǎ's grand-uncle refused,
and two strokes of the cane were given.
He argued again,
and another stroke was given.
Hé Jiǎ's grand-uncle was afraid
and agreed, then left.
The woman heard this
and went to thank the magistrate for his kindness.
The magistrate comforted and advised her earnestly.
He also secretly announced:
"Anyone wishing to marry the woman
should declare it in court."
Soon after,
someone submitted a marriage proposal;
it was none other than Wáng Wǔ, who had reported finding the head.
The magistrate called the woman up
and asked:
"Do you know the true culprit of the murder?"
She replied:
"Hú Chéng."
The magistrate said:
"No.
You and Wáng Wǔ are the true culprits."
The two were greatly shocked
and vehemently protested their innocence.
The magistrate said:
"I have long known the truth,
and the reason I delayed revealing it
was out of fear of a possible injustice.
Before the body was taken out of the well,
how could you be so certain it was your husband?
Clearly, you already knew of his death.
Furthermore, Hé Jiǎ died still wearing tattered clothes;
where did the several hundred pieces of gold come from?"
He then said to Wáng Wǔ:
"How did you know so well
the location of the head!
The reason you were so urgent
was that you intended to get married quickly."
Both of their faces turned ashen with terror,
unable to utter a single word.
They were both shackled,
and indeed they confessed the truth.
It turned out that Wáng Wǔ and the woman had been having an affair for a long time
and had conspired to murder her husband,
which happened to coincide with Hú Chéng's boast.
Hú was then released.
Féng was severely flogged for false accusation
and exiled for three years.
When the case was concluded,
not a single person had been unjustly punished.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Zhōucūn, there was a merchant, Jiǎ Mǒu,
who traded in Wúhú
and acquired great wealth.
He hired a boat to return home.
He saw a butcher on the embankment tying up a dog,
and he redeemed it at double the price,
keeping and feeding it on the boat.
The boatmen were inveterate pirates.
They spied on the guest's luggage,
steered the boat into the dense reeds,
and brandished knives, intending to kill.
Jiǎ pleaded for a complete corpse,
so the bandits wrapped him in a felt blanket and cast him into the river.
The dog saw this,
howled mournfully, and plunged into the water,
holding the wrapped bundle in its mouth,
floating and sinking with it.
Drifting for an unknown number of *lǐ*,
they reached a shallow sandbar and stopped.
The dog swam out
to a place where there were people,
barking sadly and whining.
Someone thought it strange,
followed it,
and saw the felt bundle in the water.
They pulled it out and cut its ropes.
The guest was not yet dead
and then recounted his experience.
He again pleaded with the boatmen
to take him back to Wúhú,
planning to wait for the pirate boat to return.
When he boarded the boat, he realized the dog was missing,
and his heart was deeply saddened.
Three or four days after reaching the pass,
merchant boats were as numerous as a forest,
but the pirate boat was nowhere to be seen.
Just then, a fellow merchant from his hometown was about to take him along for the return journey.
Suddenly, the dog appeared,
howling loudly at the guest,
and when called, it ran away.
The guest got off the boat and followed it.
The dog ran onto another boat,
bit a man's shins and thighs,
and would not let go even when beaten.
The guest approached and shouted at it,
realizing that the person it was biting was precisely the former bandit.
His clothes and boat had both been changed,
so he had failed to recognize him.
They tied him up and searched him,
finding that the wrapped gold was still there.
Alas!
A mere dog, yet it repaid kindness thus.
Those in the world who lack heart and conscience,
should they not also be ashamed before this dog?
Based on a copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
Dàhóng Mr. Yáng Lián,
when he was obscure, was a famous scholar in Chǔ,
considering himself extraordinary.
After the imperial examinations,
he heard the announcement of those who had passed with distinction.
He was eating at the time,
and with food still in his mouth, he went out to ask:
"Is there a Yáng Mǒu?"
The reply was:
"No."
He became dejected and lost control,
swallowing the food, which lodged in his diaphragm,
and it formed a tumor,
causing great difficulty in swallowing and obstruction.
Everyone advised him to enroll among the talented who had missed out.
He worried about lacking funds,
so everyone pooled ten pieces of gold to send him on his way,
and he reluctantly set out.
That night, he dreamt a person told him:
"There is someone ahead who can cure your illness;
you should earnestly seek him out."
Before leaving,
the person gave him a poem
which contained
the lines: "By the river, under the willows, thrice play the flute,
Cast it into the river's heart, lament not."
The next day, on his journey,
he indeed saw a Daoist sitting under a willow,
so he immediately went to inquire.
The Daoist smiled and said:
"You are mistaken.
How can I cure illnesses?
I can play the flute thrice for you, however."
Thereupon, he took out a flute and played it.
Remembering his dream,
Yáng Lián bowed and pleaded even more earnestly,
also emptying his purse and offering it.
The Daoist took the gold
and threw it into the river.
Yáng Lián, knowing how difficult it was to obtain,
was astonished and regretted it, speechless.
The Daoist said:
"Are you still unable to let go?
It's all by the river;
please retrieve it yourself."
Yáng Lián went to look, and indeed it was there.
He was even more amazed,
calling him an immortal.
The Daoist casually pointed and said:
"I am not an immortal;
the immortal is coming from that direction."
He tricked Yáng Lián into looking back,
then forcefully patted his neck and said:
"How vulgar!"
Yáng Lián, receiving the pat,
opened his mouth and made a sound,
and something heaved out from his throat,
falling to the ground with a thud.
He bent down and broke it open,
and rice wrapped in red threads was still inside.
His illness vanished as if it had never been there.
He looked back, and the Daoist had already disappeared.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Yáng Lián was born as mountains and rivers,
and upon death became sun and stars.
Why must one live forever to be immortal?
Some might consider that because he could not escape worldliness,
he did not become a celestial immortal,
and thus they lament and pity him.
I say that it is better for the world to have one more sage
than for heaven to have one more immortal.
Those who understand will surely not dispute the error of my words."
Based on a copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* from Zhùxuězhāi.
On Zhāyá Shān in Zhāngqiū,
there is a stone cave like a well,
several *chǐ* deep.
On the north wall, there is a cave entrance,
visible if one stoops and stretches one's neck.
Recently, several people from a nearby village,
on the Double Ninth Festival,
gathered to drink there,
and together planned for someone to explore it.
Three people took lamps
and were lowered down.
The cave was high and spacious, like a grand house;
after a few paces,
it gradually narrowed,
then suddenly the bottom appeared.
At the bottom was a crevice,
passable by crawling like a snake.
When illuminated by a torch,
it was pitch-dark and unfathomably deep.
Two people, hungry, retreated;
one person snatched the torch, scoffed at them,
squeezed his body through and advanced.
Fortunately, the narrow passage was only as thick as a wall,
then it suddenly became high and wide again,
allowing him to stand
and walk.
The rocks on the ceiling were uneven, precariously towering, seeming about to fall but not falling.
The two walls were rugged and uneven,
resembling temple mountain sculptures,
all forming shapes of birds, beasts, humans, and ghosts: birds as if flying,
beasts as if running,
humans as if sitting or standing,
ghosts and *wǎngliǎng* appearing enraged;
strange and bizarre,
mostly ugly with few beautiful ones.
A chill gripped his heart, filling him with dread.
He was pleased the path was level,
without any slopes.
After wandering a few hundred paces,
a stone chamber opened in the west wall.
To the left of the door was a monstrous stone ghost,
standing with a human face,
glaring eyes,
a wide-open mouth,
and fierce teeth and tongue;
its left hand was clenched into a fist,
touching its waist;
its right hand had five fingers spread,
as if to pounce on someone.
He was greatly terrified,
his hair stood on end.
From a distance, he saw burnt ash inside the door,
knowing someone had been there before,
which somewhat emboldened him,
and he forced himself to enter.
He saw bowls and cups arranged on the ground,
soiled with mud;
however, they were all recent objects,
not ancient pottery.
Beside them were four tin pots.
He coveted them,
untied his belt, and fastened them around his neck and waist.
Immediately, he looked around again.
A corpse lay in the western corner,
with two festering wounds spreading horizontally to its thighs.
Extremely horrified.
He gradually examined it.
Its feet wore pointed shoes,
with plum blossom carvings still visible on the soles,
so he knew it was a young woman.
He didn't know where she was from,
nor in what year she died.
Her clothes were dark and decayed,
impossible to distinguish blue from red;
her hair was bushy, like a basketful,
tangled strands stuck to the skull;
there were two eyes and two nostrils;
two rows of sharp and white teeth,
which he presumed were the mouth.
Imagining there should be gold and pearl ornaments on her head,
he brought the torch near the skull.
It seemed as if breath blew on the lamp;
the lamp flickered unstably,
its flame a reddish-yellow,
and her clothes stirred.
Again greatly frightened,
his hands trembled,
and the lamp suddenly went out.
He remembered the way and ran frantically,
not daring to feel for the walls with his hands,
fearing he might touch something belonging to the ghost.
His head hit a rock,
he fell,
then immediately got up again;
a cold wetness soaked his jaw and cheeks,
and he knew it was blood.
He felt no pain,
nor did he dare to groan;
panting, he ran to the crevice.
Just as he was about to crawl through,
it seemed as if someone grabbed his hair and held him,
and he fainted and lost consciousness.
The others sat by the well for a long time, waiting.
Suspecting something,
they lowered two more people.
Peering into the crevice,
they saw his hair caught on a rock,
and his blood-soaked body was already stiff.
The two turned pale,
dared not enter,
and sat lamenting with worry.
Soon, two more people were sent down from above the well;
among them was a brave one
who advanced courageously
and dragged him out.
He was placed on the mountain,
and only woke up half a day later.
He recounted his story in fragments,
regretting that he had not explored the very bottom;
if he had,
there would surely be even more beautiful sights.
Later, the *Zhānglìng* heard of it.
He sealed the crevice with mud,
making it impossible to enter again.
Between the 26th and 27th years of Kāngxī,
a cliff collapsed south of Yǎngmǔ Yù,
revealing a cave entrance;
looking at it,
the stalactites were numerous like dense bamboo shoots.
However, it was deep and dangerous,
and no one dared to enter.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest arrived,
claiming to be a disciple of Zhōnglí,
saying:
"My master sent me to arrive first
and clean out the cave dwelling."
The local residents provided him with oil and fire.
The Daoist priest took them and descended,
but fell onto a stalagmite,
which pierced his abdomen, and he died.
Reporting this,
the magistrate ordered the cave sealed.
There must be wonderful sights within,
but alas, the Daoist priest underwent *shījiě*,
and there was no further news.
According to the Zhùxuě Zhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Liú Hóngxùn of Chángshān, a *Zhōngtáng*,
went on an embassy to Cháoxiān with a certain Wǔ.
He heard that Ānqī Dǎo was where immortals resided,
and wanted to order a boat to visit.
An official named Jīn in that country said it was not permissible,
and ordered them to wait for Xiǎo Zhāng.
For Ānqī did not communicate with the mortal world,
and only his disciple, Xiǎo Zhāng,
would visit once or twice a year.
Those who wished to go to the island
must first declare their intentions.
If it was deemed permissible,
they could reach it with a single sail;
otherwise, a hurricane would capsize their boat.
One or two days later,
the king summoned them for an audience.
Entering the court,
they saw a man wearing a sword,
with a palm-fiber hat,
seated on the dais;
he was about thirty years old,
with a refined and clean appearance.
When asked,
he was indeed Xiǎo Zhāng.
Liú then expressed his longing to visit,
and Xiǎo Zhāng agreed.
But he said:
"The Vice-Envoy cannot go."
He then went out
and surveyed all the attendants;
only two could accompany them on the trip.
So he ordered a boat to guide Liú and the others there.
The water journey's distance was unknown,
but it felt like riding on clouds and mist.
In a moment, they arrived at their destination.
It was then a time of severe cold,
but upon arrival,
the climate was warm and mild,
with mountain flowers covering the cliffs and valleys.
They were led into a grotto,
where they saw three old men sitting cross-legged.
The ones to the east and west, seeing the guests enter,
were indifferent, as if unaware;
only the one in the middle rose to greet the guests,
and they exchanged courtesies.
After sitting,
tea was called for.
A young attendant carried a tray away.
On the stone wall outside the grotto was an iron awl,
its sharp tip embedded in the stone.
The attendant pulled out the awl,
and water immediately gushed out,
which he caught with a cup;
when full,
he plugged it again.
Soon after, the tray was brought back,
the tea's color a pale jade green.
Upon tasting it,
its coolness was teeth-chattering.
Liú Wèihán feared the cold and did not drink.
Yú looked at the attendant and motioned to him with his chin.
The attendant took the cup away,
sipping the remainder;
then he pulled the awl from the same spot as before,
letting water flow out and returning.
The tea was then fragrant and potent, steaming,
as if freshly out of a cauldron.
Liú Wèihán secretly found this strange.
He asked about fortune and misfortune,
to which they smiled and said:
"People outside the world do not know the years and months;
how can they understand human affairs?"
He asked about the art of retaining youth,
to which they replied:
"This is not something that wealthy and noble people can achieve."
Liú Wèihán took his leave,
and Xiǎo Zhāng still escorted him back.
Upon reaching Cháoxiǎn,
he thoroughly recounted these strange happenings.
The king sighed and said:
"It's a pity you didn't drink the cold one.
That was the Jade Elixir of the Primordial,
one cup of which can extend life by a hundred years."
When Liú Wèihán was about to return,
the king presented him with an object,
heavily wrapped in paper and silk,
and instructed him not to open it near the sea.
After leaving the sea,
he eagerly took it out and unwrapped it.
After removing hundreds of layers,
he finally saw a mirror;
upon examining it,
the Shark Palace and Dragon Clan
were clearly visible within.
While he was gazing intently,
he suddenly saw a tidal wave higher than buildings,
surging and already close.
Greatly alarmed,
he galloped furiously;
the tide pursued him.
It was as swift as wind and rain.
In great fear,
he threw the mirror at it,
and the tide immediately receded.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lǐ Jìlín was appointed as the magistrate of Yuánjiāng.
Upon first taking office,
he saw cats and dogs filling the hall,
which surprised him.
His subordinates said:
"These are the local people of the village,
admiring your prestige."
A short while later,
people and animals were half gone;
in a moment,
they all returned to human form,
and scattered and left.
One day,
he went out to visit a guest,
his sedan chair on the road.
Suddenly, one of the sedan chair bearers urgently cried out:
"This humble one has been harmed!"
He immediately asked another servant to take over the carrying,
and prostrated himself, begging for leave.
Lǐ Jìlín angrily reprimanded him,
but the servant did not listen,
and ran away quickly.
He sent someone to follow him.
The servant ran into the market,
found an old man,
and immediately asked him to examine him.
The old man looked at him and said:
"Indeed, you have been harmed."
He then felt his skin and flesh with his hand,
pushing forcefully from top to bottom;
when he pushed down to the calf,
he saw a swelling beneath the skin.
He broke it open with a sharp knife,
took out a stone pellet,
and said:
"You are cured."
The servant then ran back.
Later, it was heard that among their customs, there were those whose bodies lay in their rooms,
but whose hands would fly out,
enter other people's houses,
and steal valuables.
If caught by the owner,
and restrained from leaving,
then that person's arm would become useless.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Ān Dàyè,
a Lúlóng person.
Born able to speak,
his mother gave him dog's blood to drink,
and only then did he stop.
When he grew up,
he was elegant and handsome,
with no equal when he looked at his reflection;
he was intelligent and could read.
Prominent families competed to marry him.
His mother dreamt, saying:
"My son will marry a princess."
She believed it.
When he reached fifteen or sixteen,
there was still no verification,
and she gradually began to regret it herself.
One day,
Ān was sitting alone
when he suddenly smelled a strange fragrance.
Shortly after, a beautiful maid rushed in,
saying:
"The Princess has arrived."
She immediately laid a long felt mat on the ground,
extending from outside the door directly to the front of the couch.
While he was still in startled disbelief,
a young lady entered, leaning on the maid's shoulder;
her attire and radiant beauty
illuminated all four walls.
The maid immediately placed an embroidered cushion on the couch
and helped the young lady to sit.
Ān, flustered and not knowing what to do,
bowed and asked:
"What immortal from where
has deigned to grace me with their jade footsteps?"
The young lady smiled,
covering her mouth with her robe sleeve.
The maid said:
"This is Yúnluó Gōngzhǔ from the Holy Empress's household.
The Holy Empress is fond of the young master
and wishes to bestow the Princess upon him in marriage,
which is why she sent her to inspect the residence herself."
Ān was pleasantly surprised,
not knowing what to say;
the lady also lowered her head: they faced each other in silence.
Ān was particularly fond of Go,
and a board was always placed beside his seat.
A maid dusted it with a red cloth,
moved it onto the table,
and said:
"Our mistress plays this daily,
we wonder who will win, her or 'Lord Powder'?"
Ān moved his seat closer to the table,
and the mistress smiled, allowing it.
After just over thirty moves,
the maid intentionally messed up the board,
saying:
"The Imperial Son-in-Law has lost!"
She gathered the Go pieces into a box,
saying:
"The Imperial Son-in-Law must be a master in the mortal world;
our mistress can only concede six stones."
Then she placed six black stones on the board,
and the mistress also agreed.
When the mistress was seated,
she always made a maid lie beneath her seat,
taking her feet on her back: if she placed her left foot on the ground,
another maid would lie down on the right.
Furthermore, two young maids attended her closely: whenever Ān was deep in thought,
they would bend an elbow and rest it on her shoulder.
Before the game concluded,
a young maid laughed and said:
"The Imperial Son-in-Law loses by one stone."
She then added:
"The mistress is weary,
it is appropriate to retire for now."
The lady then leaned over and whispered into the maid's ear.
The maid left,
and returned shortly,
placing a thousand pieces of gold on the couch,
and told the scholar:
"The mistress just said the residence is cramped and narrow,
so please accept this small sum for renovations;
we will meet again once it is completed."
Another maid said:
"This month is afflicted by heavenly punishment,
and is not suitable for construction;
after this month will be auspicious."
The lady rose;
the scholar tried to stop her,
closing the door.
A maid produced an item
that looked like a leather fan,
and inflated it on the ground;
clouds and mist billowed forth,
and in a moment, they enveloped everything,
making it too dark to see anything,
and when they searched, she was already gone.
His mother knew about this,
and suspected it to be a phantom.
But the scholar's spirit soared with dreams and fantasies,
unable to let go.
Eager for the completion,
he had no time for taboos;
he set a date and pressed for its completion,
and the corridors and buildings became brand new.
Previously,
a scholar from Luánzhōu, Yuán Dàyòng,
resided in a neighboring ward
and left his calling card at the door.
The scholar, by nature not given to much socializing,
feigned absence,
and then, when he saw Yuán Dàyòng leave, reported that he was out.
Over a month later,
they happened to meet outside the gate.
He was a young man of about twenty,
wearing a single garment of court silk,
with a silk sash and black shoes,
and appeared very refined and elegant.
They chatted for a while,
and Yuán Dàyòng was quite warm and careful.
The scholar was pleased,
bowed, and invited him in.
They played chess,
with alternating wins and losses.
Afterward, wine was served, and they lingered,
laughing and talking with great joy.
The next day,
Yuán Dàyòng invited the scholar to his residence.
Sumptuous dishes were served one after another,
and he was treated with great generosity.
A young boy of about twelve or thirteen
clapped a clapper and sang clear songs,
and also jumped and played tricks.
The scholar became very drunk
and unable to walk,
so Yuán Dàyòng ordered the boy to carry him.
The scholar, seeing the boy's slender build,
feared he would not be able to bear the weight.
Yuán Dàyòng insisted.
The boy, with ample strength to spare,
carried him home.
The scholar was surprised by this.
The next day,
he rewarded the boy with gold,
which was only accepted after a second refusal.
From then on, their friendship became close and intimate,
visiting each other every three or four days.
Yuán Dàyòng was a quiet person
but generous and fond of giving.
When there was someone in the market who was in debt and selling his daughter,
he would open his purse and redeem her,
without a hint of reluctance.
The scholar respected him even more for this.
After several days,
Yuán Dàyòng called on the scholar to say goodbye,
