presenting him with more than ten items, including ivory chopsticks and nánzhū beads,
and five hundred taels of silver
to assist in his construction project.
The scholar returned the gold but accepted the other items,
and in return presented him with a bolt of silk.
Over a month later,
a returning official from Lètíng
had a full and abundant purse.
Thieves broke in at night,
seized the master,
tortured him with hot iron tongs,
and plundered everything.
The family recognized Yuán Dàyòng,
and a warrant was issued for his arrest.
Tú Shì from the neighboring courtyard,
who had long been at odds with the scholar's family,
secretly harbored suspicion and jealousy because of the scholar's extensive construction work.
It happened that a young servant stole the ivory chopsticks
and sold them to Tú Shì's family.
Upon learning that they were a gift from Yuán Dàyòng,
they reported it to the Dàyǐn.
The Dàyǐn surrounded the residence with soldiers.
As the scholar and his servants were out,
they seized his mother and took her away.
The mother, old and frail and suffering from fright,
barely clung to life,
and for two or three days could not eat or drink.
The Dàyǐn released her.
When the scholar heard of his mother's condition,
he rushed home,
but his mother's illness was already critical,
and she passed away the next night.
Immediately after the burial was completed,
he was seized by arresting officers
and taken away.
The Dàyǐn, seeing that he was a young, gentle scholar,
secretly suspected he was being falsely accused,
so he tried to intimidate him.
The scholar truthfully recounted the origin of his acquaintance.
The Dàyǐn asked,
"How did you suddenly become rich?"
The scholar replied,
"My mother had hidden money,
and because I wanted to personally fetch my bride,
I was preparing the bridal chamber."
The Dàyǐn believed him,
drew up a report, and sent him to the commandery.
The neighbors, knowing he would be cleared,
bribed the jailers with a large sum of money
to kill him on the way.
Passing through a deep mountain,
he was dragged to a steep cliff
and was about to be pushed down.
With his life in danger and facing an urgent crisis,
suddenly a tiger emerged from the thickets,
bit both officers to death,
and carried the scholar away.
It arrived at a place
with towering pavilions and overlapping chambers.
The tiger entered
and set him down.
He saw Yúnluó扶 (Pú) Bì come out,
who sadly consoled him,
saying,
"I wish to keep you,
but your mother's burial is yet to be decided.
You may take this document and present yourself at the commandery;
I guarantee no harm will come to you."
She then took the sash from his chest
and tied more than ten knots in it,
advising him,
"When you see the official,
take this knot and untie it;
this can avert disaster."
The scholar followed her instructions
and presented himself at the commandery.
The Grand Administrator was pleased by his honesty and trustworthiness,
and upon examining the document, knew he was innocent,
so he cleared his name and ordered him to return.
Midway on his journey,
he met Yuán Dàyòng,
who dismounted, grasped his hand,
and fully explained the situation.
Yuán Dàyòng became angry,
his face changing color,
and he said not a word.
The scholar said,
"With your distinguished demeanor,
why would you debase yourself?"
Yuán Dàyòng replied,
"Those I kill are all unrighteous people,
and what I take is all ill-gotten wealth.
Otherwise,
even if something is left on the road,
I do not pick it up.
Your advice to me is certainly good,
but how can people like your neighbors
be allowed to remain in the world!"
Having spoken,
he mounted his horse and rode off.
The scholar returned home,
buried his mother,
and then kept to his house, declining visitors.
Suddenly, one day,
thieves broke into the neighbor's house.
More than ten members of the family, father and sons,
were all killed,
leaving only one maidservant.
They swept away the valuables
and distributed them among the servants.
Before leaving,
holding a lamp, he said to the maidservant,
"You recognize me.
I am the killer.
It has nothing to do with anyone else."
He did not open the gate at all,
but flew over the eaves and scaled the walls to depart.
The next day,
the matter was reported to the officials.
Suspecting the scholar knew something,
they again seized him.
The Yìzǎi's words and demeanor were very stern.
The scholar, on entering the hall, grasped his sash,
explaining and untying it simultaneously.
The Yìzǎi could not question him further
and released him again.
After returning,
he became even more withdrawn and reclusive,
studying without going out,
with only a lame old woman cooking for him.
Once the mourning period was over,
he swept the steps and courtyard daily,
awaiting good news.
One day,
a strange fragrance filled the courtyard.
He went up to the pavilion to look,
and the furnishings inside and out were completely renewed.
He quietly lifted the painted curtain,
and there sat the Princess in full makeup.
He quickly bowed to her.
The woman took his hand and said,
"You did not believe in destiny,
which led to the disaster of construction,
and then, due to the sorrow of mourning,
delayed our marriage by three years. This is a case where haste led to delay;
most things in the world are like this."
The scholar was about to provide funds for the preparations.
The woman said,
"No need for that."
A maidservant searched a chest,
There was hot savory soup, fresh as if just out of the cauldron,
and the wine was also fragrant and potent. After drinking for a while,
the sun had already set.
The maidservants upon whom [Shēng]'s feet rested
gradually all vanished.
The woman's limbs were delicate and languid;
her legs and thighs bent and stretched
as if without support.
Shēng familiarly embraced her.
The woman said,
"Please release your hands for a moment, sir.
Now there are two paths;
please choose one."
Shēng clasped her neck and asked the reason.
She said,
"If we become companions in chess and wine,
we can be together for thirty years.
If we make love in the bedchamber,
we can be in harmony for only six years.
Which will you choose, sir?"
Shēng replied,
"We can discuss that again after six years."
The woman then fell silent,
and they became intimate.
The woman said,
"I knew, of course, that you could not escape the ways of the mundane world;
this, too, is fate."
Thereupon, she had Shēng acquire maidservants and old women,
who lived separately in the South Courtyard,
cooking, spinning, and weaving
to make a living.
In the North Courtyard, there was no smoke or fire at all,
only chessboards and wine utensils.
The door was usually closed;
when Shēng pushed it, it would open by itself,
but others could not enter.
However, the people in the South Courtyard worked diligently,
and the woman always knew about it.
She often made Shēng go and admonish them,
and they all obeyed.
The woman had no superfluous words,
no loud laughter;
when speaking with someone,
she merely lowered her head and smiled faintly.
Whenever they sat shoulder to shoulder,
she liked to lean against him.
When Shēng lifted her onto his lap,
she was as light as holding a baby.
Shēng said,
"You are so light,
you could dance on my palm."
She replied,
"What is difficult about that?
But it is a maidservant's act,
which I disdain.
Fēiyàn (飛燕) was originally Jiǔjiě (九姊)'s maidservant,
who repeatedly incurred guilt with her frivolity,
and was angrily banished to the mortal world.
Moreover, she did not maintain a woman's chastity;
she is now imprisoned."
The chamber upstairs was fully covered with brocade mattresses;
in winter, it was never cold,
and in summer, it was never hot.
In severe winter, the woman always wore light silk gauze;
Shēng made her new clothes,
and forced her to wear them.
After a while, she took them off and said,
"These vulgar, dirty things
almost crushed my bones and made me ill!"
One day,
as he held her on his lap,
he suddenly felt her weight double that of before,
and found it strange.
She smiled and pointed to her belly, saying,
"There is a mundane seed in here now."
A few days later,
she frowned and refused food,
saying,
"Recently, I have been suffering from morning sickness,
and I rather crave the taste of cooked food."
Shēng then prepared delicious food for her.
From then on, her diet was no different from ordinary people.
One day, she said,
"My constitution is fragile
and not suitable for childbirth.
The maidservant Fán Yīng (樊英) is quite strong;
she can take my place."
Thereupon, she took off her undergarments, dressed Fán Yīng (樊英) in them,
and locked her in the room.
A short while later,
they heard a child crying.
Opening the door to look,
it was a boy.
She joyfully said,
"This child has an auspicious appearance;
he will be a great man!"
She therefore named him Dàqì (大器).
Wrapping him in swaddling clothes, she placed him in Shēng's arms,
and had him entrusted to a wet nurse
to be raised in the South Courtyard.
After her delivery,
the woman's waist was as slender as before,
and she no longer ate cooked food.
Suddenly, she bid Shēng farewell,
wishing to return home for a short visit.
When asked about her return date,
she answered with
"three days."
The sound of drums and pipes arose as before,
and then she disappeared.
She did not return by the appointed time;
after more than a year,
all news of her vanished,
and [Shēng] had already given up hope.
Shēng locked the door and hung the curtains,
and subsequently passed the provincial examination.
He never consented to marry;
every night, he slept alone in the North Courtyard,
bathing in her lingering fragrance.
One night,
as he tossed and turned in bed,
he suddenly saw lamplight shining through the window,
the door also opened by itself,
and a group of maidservants entered, escorting the princess.
Shēng rejoiced,
stood up, and asked about the offense of breaking the appointment.
The woman said,
"I did not miss the deadline;
it has only been two and a half days in heaven."
Shēng proudly boasted,
telling her about his success in the autumn examination,
thinking the princess would surely be pleased.
The woman sadly said,
"What use are these fleeting achievements!
They are not worth honor or disgrace,
they only reduce one's lifespan.
After not seeing you for three days,
you have sunk another layer deeper into the mundane entanglement."
Shēng thereafter no longer pursued advancement.
After several months,
she again wished to return home for a visit.
The lord was deeply reluctant.
The woman said,
"This time, I will surely return early;
there is no need for anxious waiting.
Moreover, the meetings and partings in life
all have a fixed number;
if one controls them, they will be long,
but if one indulges in them, they will be short."
After she left,
she returned in just over a month.
From then on, she would leave once every year or half a year,
often returning after several months.
Shēng grew accustomed to it,
and was no longer surprised.
She then gave birth to another son.
The woman held him and said,
"He is a jackal!"
She immediately ordered him to be abandoned.
Shēng could not bear to and stopped her,
naming him Kěqì (可棄).
Just when he was a year old,
she urgently sought a marriage match for him.
Many matchmakers came one after another,
and when asked about their birth dates,
all said they were incompatible.
She said,
"I wanted to build a deep enclosure for the wolf cub,
but I could not find one.
The current decline and ruin over six or seven years
is also fate."
She instructed Shēng, saying,
"Remember that four years from now,
the Hóu (侯) family will have a daughter
with a small wart on her left rib;
she is this child's wife.
Marry her,
and do not be concerned about her family background."
She then ordered it to be written down and recorded.
Later, she again returned home for a visit, and never came back.
Shēng often relayed his mother's instructions to his relatives and friends.
Indeed, there was a daughter of the Hóu氏,
who had warts.
Hóu was of low status and behaved badly,
and everyone scorned her.
But Shēng still arranged their marriage.
Dàqì passed the imperial examination at seventeen,
and married a woman of the Yún氏.
Both husband and wife were filial and kind.
Their father dearly loved him.
Kěqì gradually grew up,
but disliked studying.
He would always secretly gamble with ruffians,
and constantly stole things to pay off gambling debts.
His father was angry,
and whipped him,
but he never changed.
They warned each other to be on guard,
and not let him get anything.
So he went out at night,
and committed a minor act of burglary (literally, "piercing an arrow").
He was discovered by the owner,
tied up, and sent to the county magistrate.
The magistrate verified his name and surname,
and sent him home with a calling card.
His father and elder brother tied him up together,
and whipped and tortured him so severely,
he was nearly dead.
His brother pleaded for him to be spared,
and only then was he released.
His father, full of resentment and anger, fell ill,
and his appetite sharply decreased.
He then drew up a will for the division of property between his two sons,
and all the buildings, pavilions, and fertile fields
were given to Dàqì.
Kěqì was resentful and furious,
and at night, he took a knife and entered the room
to kill his brother,
but mistakenly struck his sister-in-law.
Before this,
the master had left behind some soft leather,
which was extremely light and pliable.
Yún picked it up and made it into a nightgown.
When Kěqì chopped at it,
sparks flew everywhere.
Greatly frightened, he ran out.
His father knew,
and his illness worsened.
He died a few months later.
Kěqì heard of his father's death,
and only then returned.
His brother treated him well,
but Kěqì became even more unrestrained.
After more than a year,
the land and property he had been allotted were almost entirely gone.
He went to the prefecture to sue his brother.
The official recognized him upon investigation,
and expelled him.
The fraternal bond was thus severed.
Another year passed,
Kěqì was twenty-three,
and the Hóu girl was fifteen.
His brother remembered his mother's words,
and wished to quickly arrange their marriage.
He summoned her to their home,
and cleared out a fine house for her to live in.
When he welcomed the bride into the house,
he registered and handed over
all the good land left by his father,
saying:
"Several *qǐng* of meager property,
I diligently guarded for you for fear of death.
Now I hand it all over to you.
My brother has no principles,
and if even a blade of grass is given to him,
it will all be wasted.
From now on, success or failure
depends on the new bride: if you can make him change his ways,
you will not worry about cold and hunger;
otherwise,
your brother also cannot fill a bottomless pit."
Although Hóu was from a minor family,
she was inherently intelligent and beautiful.
Kěqì deeply respected and loved her,
and dared not disobey anything she said.
Whenever he went out,
she limited him with a fixed time (literally, "hanging a clepsydra");
if he was late,
she would scold him harshly and withhold food and drink.
Because of this, Kěqì somewhat restrained himself.
After more than a year,
they had a son.
The wife said:
"After this, I will not ask anything of anyone.
With several *qǐng* of fertile land,
what trouble will mother and son have in being warm and well-fed?
Without a husband,
it is also fine."
At that time, Kěqì stole grain to go gambling.
His wife knew of it,
and stood at the door with a drawn bow to prevent him.
He was greatly frightened,
and fled.
He spied on his wife,
and after hesitating, also entered.
The wife grasped a knife and stood up.
Kěqì ran back,
the wife chased and chopped at him,
cutting his robe and injuring his buttocks,
blood stained his socks and shoes.
Extremely indignant,
he went to complain to his brother.
His brother did not treat him courteously,
so he left feeling wronged and ashamed.
He stayed overnight and returned again,
kneeling and crying to his sister-in-law,
begging her to intercede with his wife for him.
His wife resolutely refused to admit him.
Kěqì was angry,
and intended to go kill his wife.
His brother said nothing.
Kěqì angrily stood up,
grabbed a spear, and went straight out.
His sister-in-law was startled,
and wanted to stop him.
His brother signaled her with his eyes to restrain her.
After he left,
he then said:
"He is indeed putting on this act,
but in reality, he dares not return."
He sent someone to spy on him,
and he had already entered his own home.
His brother's expression then changed,
and he was about to rush over,
but Kěqì had already rushed in, gasping for breath.
It turned out that when Kěqì arrived home,
his wife was playing with their child.
Seeing him,
she threw the child onto the bed,
and found a kitchen knife.
Kěqì was frightened,
dragged his spear, and ran back.
His wife chased him out the door and only then returned.
His brother had already understood the situation,
so he questioned him.
Kěqì did not speak,
but only cried in the corner,
his eyes completely swollen.
His brother pitied him,
and personally led him away.
His wife then let him in.
After his brother left,
she punished him by making him kneel for a long time,
demanding a solemn oath from him,
and only then gave him food in an earthenware bowl.
From then on, he changed his ways and became good.
His wife managed the finances and calculated carefully,
making them prosperous day by day.
Kěqì only enjoyed the fruits of her labor.
Later, at seventy years old,
with children and grandchildren all around him,
his wife would still occasionally hold his white beard,
and make him crawl on his knees.
Yìshǐshì said:
"A fierce wife and a jealous woman,
those who encounter them are like a carbuncle attached to the bone,
which only ceases upon death.
Is it not poisonous!
However, arsenic and aconite
are the most potent poisons in the world.
If used correctly,
they can cause a dramatic recovery from severe illness,
which ginseng and poria cannot achieve.
But without a celestial being who can see into the inner organs,
how could one dare to give such poisonous medicine to one's descendants!"
Lǐ Xiàolián
Shànqiān from Zhāngqiū was
a free-spirited and unconventional youth, skilled in all kinds of music and lyrics.
Both his elder brothers had passed the imperial examinations with distinction,
but Xiàolián became even more unrestrained.
He married a woman surnamed Xiè,
who gradually began to control him.
He then ran away,
and for three years he did not return,
despite being sought everywhere without success.
Later, he was found in a brothel in Línqīng.
When his family entered,
they saw him sitting facing south,
with a dozen young courtesans attending him on his left and right;
these were apparently all students of music and art who had become his disciples.
When he was about to leave,
he collected a pile of clothes and stacked cylinders,
all gifts from the courtesans.
After he returned,
his wife confined him to a single room,
with books piled high on the desk.
She tied a long rope to the leg of his bed,
passed its end out through the window lattice,
threaded a large bell onto it,
and attached it in the kitchen.
Whenever he needed anything,
he would pull the rope;
when the rope moved and the bell rang,
she would respond.
His wife personally set up a pawnshop,
hanging a curtain, receiving items, and appraising their value;
she held tallies in her left hand
and a writing brush in her right;
an old servant merely ran errands: in this way, she accumulated wealth and became rich.
She was always ashamed that she was not as noble as her sisters-in-law.
For three years he was kept in strict confinement,
but Xiàolián was quick-witted.
She happily exclaimed:
"Three eggs, two hatched!
I thought you were a rotten egg,
but is it still so now?"
Also,
Gěng Sōng, a *jìnshì* by birth,
was also from Zhāngqiū.
His wife would often light a lamp for him while he studied: she would spin without stopping,
and he dared not rest from reading.
If friends or old acquaintances visited him,
she would secretly listen: if they discussed literature, she would brew tea and cook millet;
but if they indulged in jesting and mockery,
she would angrily drive the guests away.
Whenever he scored an "average" grade in a test,
he dared not enter her room;
only if he scored "excellent"
would she greet him with a smile.
Any money earned from teaching,
he would present entirely to her,
not daring to hide a single cent.
Therefore, when his employers gave him gifts,
she would always openly examine the smallest amounts.
People sometimes laughed at her,
but did not know how difficult it was for her to settle accounts.
Later, his father-in-law invited him to tutor his younger brother-in-law.
That year, his brother-in-law passed the *tóngshēng* examination,
and his father-in-law offered ten *jīn* as a ceremonial fee.
Gěng received the offering box but returned the gold.
His wife, knowing of this, said:
"Although he is a close relative,
what do you call 'plowing with your tongue'?"
She chased after him, brought him back, and made him accept it.
Gěng dared not argue,
but felt a lingering sense of indebtedness,
and thought of secretly compensating for it.
Thus, each year he would short the amount of his tutoring fees
when reporting to his wife.
After more than two years,
he had accumulated a certain sum.
Suddenly, he dreamt that a person told him:
"Climb to a high place tomorrow,
and the amount of gold will be complete."
The next day,
he tried going for a walk and looking out,
and indeed found some lost gold,
which exactly made up the deficit,
so he could repay his father-in-law.
Later, when he became a *jìnshì*,
his wife still scolded him.
Gěng said:
"Now that I am an official,
how can you still be like this?"
His wife said:
"The proverb says:
'As the water rises, the boat also rises.'
Even if you become a prime minister,
would that make you truly great?"
Based on the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript, missing text supplemented from the Zhùxuězhāi copy.
There was a Daoist priest in the region of Zhōngzhōu,
who begged for food in the countryside.
After eating,
he heard an oriole sing;
he then told the host to be careful with fire.
When asked why,
he replied:
"The bird said: 'A great fire is hard to save,
dreadful!'"
The crowd laughed at him,
and indeed took no precautions.
The next day,
a fire did break out,
spreading and burning several houses,
which made them finally realize his divine power.
Curious people chased after him,
calling him an immortal.
The Daoist priest said:
"I merely understand bird language,
how am I an immortal!"
Just then, a magpie-robin was chirping on a tree,
and the crowd asked what it was saying.
He replied:
"The sparrow says: 'Born on the sixth,
born on the sixth;
died on the fourteenth, died on the sixteenth.'
This family must have given birth to twins.
Today is the tenth,
so in five or six days,
they will both die."
Upon inquiry,
it was indeed found that two children had been born;
before long,
they both died,
and the dates all matched.
yìlìng heard of his strangeness,
summoned him,
and invited him as a guest.
At that time, a flock of ducks passed by,
and the yìlìng questioned him about them.
He replied:
"In your bright lord's inner chambers,
there must be contention.
The ducks are saying: 'Stop, stop!
Favor him more!
Favor him more!'"
The yìlìng was greatly convinced,
for his wife and concubines had just been arguing,
and the yìlìng had just been driven out by their clamor.
He then kept him to live in the yáshǔ,
treating him with great respect.
At times, he would interpret bird speech,
often with uncanny accuracy.
But the dàoshì was simple and rustic,
and spoke without any inhibitions.
The yìlìng was extremely greedy;
all the provisions and supplies
were converted into money for his own gain.
One day,
as he was sitting,
a flock of ducks came again,
and the yìlìng questioned him once more.
He answered:
"What is said today
is not the same as before;
it is merely an account for your bright lord."
He asked:
"What account?"
He said:
"They are saying: 'One hundred and eight candles,
one thousand and eight cinnabar.'"
The yìlìng was ashamed,
suspecting he was being mocked.
The dàoshì asked to leave,
but the yìlìng would not permit it.
After several days,
while feasting guests,
he suddenly heard a dùyǔ.
A guest asked about it,
and he replied:
"The bird is saying: 'Lose your office and depart.'"
Everyone was stunned and turned pale.
The yìlìng was furious,
and immediately expelled him.
Not long after,
the yìlìng indeed suffered a defeat due to corruption.
Alas!
This immortal was warning him,
but those whose minds are consumed by danger and avarice
do not comprehend it.
In Qí province, people call cicadas
"shāoshuō,"
and the green ones are called
"dūliǎo."
There was a father and son in the district,
both from Qīng province and Shè province respectively,
who were about to take the annual examination.
Suddenly, a cicada landed on the father's lapel.
The father joyfully said:
"A 'shāoshuō'
is an auspicious sign."
A servant boy looked at it and
said:
"What 'shāoshuō'?
It's just a 'dūliǎo'."
The father and son were displeased.
Soon after, they were indeed both dismissed.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Guō Shēng
was a man from Jīngdū.
He was over twenty years old,
with a handsome and refined appearance.
One day,
at dusk,
an old woman presented him with a jar of wine.
He found it strange that there was no reason for it.
The old woman smiled and said,
"No need to ask.
Just drink it,
and good things will naturally follow."
Then she left directly.
He uncovered the jar and lightly sniffed it;
a strong fragrance diffused all around,
so he drank it.
Suddenly, he became greatly drunk,
completely unconscious.
When he awoke,
he was lying in bed with someone else, their pillows side by side.
He touched them;
their skin was smooth as fat,
emitting the scent of musk and orchid.
It was a woman.
He asked her,
but she did not answer.
So he made love to her.
After making love,
he felt the wall with his hand;
the walls were all stone,
with a damp, earthy smell,
much like a tomb.
Greatly alarmed,
he suspected he was bewitched by a ghost,
so he asked the woman,
"What kind of spirit are you, my lady?"
The woman said,
"I am not a spirit,
but an immortal.
This is a cave dwelling.
We have a destined connection,
so do not be surprised,
just endure staying here.
If you go through another door,
there is a place with a sliver of light,
where you can relieve yourself."
Soon after, the woman rose,
closed the door, and left.
After a long time,
he felt hungry. Then a young maidservant came,
bringing him flatbread and duck stew,
and told him to feel for it and eat.
It was pitch dark, and he could not tell day from night.
Before long,
the woman came to sleep,
and only then did he know it was night.
Guō said,
"By day, there is no sun;
by night, no lamps;
when eating roasted meat, I don't know where my mouth is.
If it's always like this,
then how does Hēng'é differ from a rākṣasa,
and how is heaven different from hell!"
The woman smiled and said,
"Because you are a mortal,
you talk a lot and like to gossip,
so I do not wish to show you my form.
Moreover, when fumbling in the dark,
beauty and ugliness should still be distinguishable,
so why bother with lamps and candles!"
After staying for several days,
he felt exceptionally melancholic and requested repeatedly to return home for a while.
The woman said,
"Tomorrow night, I will take you on a tour of the Heavenly Palace,
and then we shall part."
The next day,
a young maid suddenly entered with a lantern,
saying,
"My lady has been waiting for you for a long time."
He followed her out.
Amidst the starlight,
he saw countless pavilions and towers.
After passing through several winding painted corridors,
they finally reached a place
where a pearl curtain hung in the hall,
and giant candles burned as brightly as day.
Entering,
he saw a beautiful woman in splendid attire seated facing south,
appearing to be about twenty years old;
her brocade robe was dazzling;
the bright pearls on her head
quivered and hung down on all four sides;
short candles were placed all over the floor,
illuminating the area beneath her skirt: truly a celestial being.
Guō was bewildered and lost his composure,
unconsciously bending his knees.
The woman ordered a maid to help him to a seat.
A moment later,
eight delicacies were arranged.
The woman offered him wine and said,
"Drink this to send you on your way."
Guō bowed and said,
"That I did not recognize the immortal when we first met
truly fills me with shame and regret;
if you would allow me to redeem myself,
I wish to be taken as your faithful servant for life."
The woman glanced at her maid with a smile,
then ordered her to move their seats to the bedroom.
In the room, there were embroidered curtains with tassels,
and the quilts and mattresses were fragrant and soft.
She made Guō sit on the couch.
As they drank,
the woman repeatedly said,
"You have been away from home for a long time;
a temporary return would do no harm."
When the last measure of wine was finished,
Guō did not speak of parting.
The woman called a maid to bring a candle and escort him.
Guō did not speak,
feigning drunkenness and sleeping on the couch,
and he could not be moved.
The woman ordered the maids to lift and undress him.
One maid pointed at his private parts and said,
"This man has a gentle and elegant appearance,
but why is this thing so uncouth!"
They placed him on the bed
and left with loud laughter.
The woman also went to sleep,
and Guō then turned over.
The woman asked,
"Are you drunk?"
He said,
"How could this junior be drunk!
Upon first seeing an immortal,
my mind was simply in a daze."
The woman said,
"This is the Heavenly Palace.
Before dawn,
you should leave early.
If you dislike the gloom in the cave,
it would be better to part early."
Guō said,
"Suppose someone obtains a famous flower at night,
smells its fragrance, and feels its stem,
but suffers from the lack of lamps and candles—
how can such a situation be endured?"
The woman smiled
and agreed to provide lamps and candles.
At the fourth watch,
she called a maid with a candle,
embraced his clothes, and escorted him out.
Entering the cave,
he saw exquisite crimson and white decorations,
and the bedding was a thick mat of palm fiber about a foot deep.
Guō repeatedly pulled the quilt around himself,
but the maid lingered and did not leave.
Guō gazed at her intently;
her charm was captivating,
and he jokingly asked,
"Was it you who said I was uncouth?"
The maid laughed
and kicked his pillow with her foot, saying,
"You should be stiff!
Don't talk so much anymore."
He noticed the tips of her shoes were inlaid with pearls as large as broad beans.
He grabbed and pulled her,
and the maid fell into his arms.
They then became intimate,
and she groaned in unbearable pleasure.
Guō asked,
"How old are you?"
She replied,
"Seventeen."
He asked,
"Does a virgin also know about love?"
She said,
"I am not a virgin,
but it has been three years since I was last intimate."
Guō pressed her for the immortal's surname,
her official position, and her honorable conduct.
The maid said,
"Don't ask!
Even if it's not heaven,
it's different from the human world.
If you insist on knowing the exact details,
I'm afraid you'll have nowhere to die!"
Guō then dared not ask again.
The next night,
the woman indeed came with a candle,
and they slept and ate together,
making this their routine.
One night,
the woman said,
"We had hoped for eternal harmony;
unexpectedly, human affections are fickle and disheartening.
I am now going to cleanse the Heavenly Palace,
and can no longer accommodate you.
Please take this last wine as our farewell."
Guō wept,
begging for rouge and powder as a token of affection.
The woman refused,
presenting him with a catty of gold and a hundred pearls.
After the three cups were finished,
he suddenly became dizzy and intoxicated.
When he awoke,
he felt his four limbs as if bound,
tightly entangled,
unable to stretch his thighs,
unable to lift his head.
Struggling to turn over,
he fell dizzily from the bed.
He reached out to feel,
finding himself wrapped in a brocade quilt,
tied with fine cords.
He sat up, lost in thought,
and vaguely saw the bed lattice,
only then realizing he was in his own study.
He had been away from home for three months by then,
and his family believed him dead.
Guō initially dared not speak openly,
fearing divine retribution,
but felt inwardly suspicious and strange about it.
He secretly confided in a close acquaintance,
but no one could fathom the reason.
The quilt was placed at the head of the bed,
its fragrance filling the room;
upon opening and inspecting it,
it was found to be made of lake cotton mixed with fragrant shavings,
which he then treasured.
Later, a certain high-ranking official heard of it and questioned him,
saying with a smile:
"This is an old trick of Empress Jiǎ (Jiǎ Hòu).
How could an immortal be like this?
Nevertheless,
this matter should also be kept strictly confidential,
if you reveal it,
your clan will be annihilated!"
A shaman who frequently visited noble families
described the shape of her pavilion,
saying it strikingly resembled the home of Yán Dōnglóu.
Guō heard this,
and was greatly frightened,
taking his family and fleeing.
Not long after,
Yán was executed,
and he finally returned.
The Historian of the Unusual (Yìshǐ Shì) remarks:
"Lofty pavilions, dreamlike and indistinct,
fragrance filling embroidered curtains;
young maidservants mincing,
their shoes adorned with bright pearls: were it not for the licentious indulgence of powerful villains,
and the arrogant extravagance of the influential,
how could such things exist?
Yet, with one throw of the dice of debauchery,
the golden house transforms into Chángmén;
before the spittoon is dry,
the field of love is overgrown with lush weeds.
An empty bed wounds the heart,
dim candles consume the soul.
Frowning before the jade terrace,
gazing intently within the precious tent.
Thus, on Zāoqīu tái,
a path leads to a heavenly palace;
in Wēnróu Xiāng,
people mistake mortals for immortals.
The humble curtains and partitions of commoners are certainly not shameful,
but those who let their vast fields lie fallow,
should also take heed!"
From the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Píngyuán, there was a man named Qiáo Shēng.
He had a daughter, Hēi Chǒu, who had a cleft
nose and a limp
foot. She was twenty-five or twenty-six years old,
but no one came to ask for her hand in marriage.
In the same town, there was a man named Mù Shēng,
over forty,
whose wife had died.
Being poor, he couldn't afford to remarry,
so he eventually married her.
Three years later,
they had a son.
Not long after,
Mù Shēng died,
and their family became even poorer.
In great distress,
Hēi Chǒu would beg her mother for help.
Her mother became quite impatient with her.
The daughter also resented it and refused to return,
only supporting herself by spinning and weaving.
There was a man named Mèng Shēng whose wife had died,
leaving behind a son named Wū Tóu,
who was just one year old.
Lacking someone to nurse him,
Mèng Shēng was eager to find a new wife.
However, though matchmakers spoke to him several times,
none met his approval.
Suddenly, he saw Hēi Chǒu
and was greatly pleased with her.
He secretly sent someone to discreetly sound her out.
Hēi Chǒu declined,
saying:
"Being so hungry and cold,
would I not wish to be warm and well-fed by following an official's son?
However, I am disabled and ugly, unlike others.
The only thing I can be confident in
is my virtue.
Moreover, I have already served two husbands;
what would an official's son gain by taking me?"
Mèng Shēng esteemed her even more,
and his admiration grew fervent.
He sent a matchmaker with gold and additional gifts to persuade her mother.
The mother was pleased
and personally went to her daughter's place,
insistently urging her.
But the daughter's resolve could not be shaken.
Her mother was ashamed
and offered to marry her younger daughter to Mèng Shēng.
All the family members were happy,
but Mèng Shēng was particularly unwilling.
Not long after,
Mèng Shēng suddenly fell ill and died.
Hēi Chǒu went to mourn him, crying with utmost sorrow.
Mèng Shēng had no close relatives.
After his death,
the ruffians in the village completely plundered his property,
taking all the furniture until nothing was left.
They were even planning to divide his land and assets among themselves.
His household servants also stealthily stole things and left.
Only an old woman held the child and wept inside the curtained bed.
Hēi Chǒu asked and learned the situation,
feeling great injustice.
Hearing that Lín Shēng was a good friend of Mèng Shēng,
she went to his door and said:
"Husband and wife,
and friends,
are great human relationships.
Because of my unusual ugliness,
I am scorned by the world.
Only Mèng Shēng could truly appreciate me.
Though I firmly refused him before,
I had already promised him my heart.
Now that he is dead and his child is young,
I ought to repay my kindred spirit.
However, it is easy to preserve an orphan,
but difficult to resist insult.
If there are no brothers or parents,
and one simply sits by and watches his child die and his family be destroyed without offering any help,
then the five human relationships might as well do without friends.
I do not ask much of you, Master Lín;
just send a note to the district magistrate.
As for raising the orphan,
I would not dare to decline."
Lín Shēng said,
"Understood."
Hēi Chǒu then left and returned home.
Lín Shēng was about to do as she instructed;
the ruffians were enraged,
and actually planned to take revenge with weapons.
Lín Shēng was greatly frightened,
closed his door, and dared not proceed.
Hēi Chǒu waited for several days,
hearing no news.
When she inquired,
Mèng Shēng's land and assets were already completely gone.
Hēi Chǒu was furious.
She personally went to the official's office.
The official questioned what relation she was to Mèng Shēng.
Hēi Chǒu said:
"Your Excellency governs a district;
what you rely on is reason.
If my words are false,
even the closest relative cannot escape punishment.
If they are not false,
then even a stranger on the road should be heard."
The official was angered by her blunt words
and scolded her, driving her out.
Hēi Chǒu, unable to air her grievances,
wept and pleaded at the doors of the gentry.
A certain gentleman heard of it and was moved by her righteousness.
He presented her case to the magistrate on her behalf.
The magistrate investigated,
and it was indeed true.
He thoroughly punished all the ruffians
and had everything they had taken returned.
Some suggested that Hēi Chǒu stay in Mèng Shēng's residence
to raise the orphan.
Hēi Chǒu refused.
She boarded up his gate,
made the old woman carry Wū Tóu,
and took them with her to her own home,
settling them separately.
Whenever Wū Tóu needed daily provisions,
she would open the door with the old woman, take out grain,
and arrange for it.
She herself did not take a single coin,
but supported her own son in poverty,
just as before.
After several years,
Wū Tóu gradually grew up.
She hired a teacher to educate him.
As for her own son, she made him learn manual labor.
The old woman advised her to let both boys study.
Hēi Chǒu said:
"Wū Tóu's expenses
are his own.
If I use another's wealth to educate my own son,
how can my conscience be clear?"
After a few more years,
she had accumulated several hundred *shi* of grain for Wū Tóu.
Then she arranged a marriage for him with a prominent family,
prepared his residence,
and sent her own son home.
Wū Tóu insisted that she live with him.
Hēi Chǒu then agreed,
but continued to spin and weave as before.
Wū Tóu and his wife took away her tools.
Hēi Chǒu said:
"If my son and I just sit and eat,
how can my heart be at ease?"
So she managed their affairs from morning till night,
making her own son patrol the fields,
as if he were a laborer.
If Wū Tóu or his wife made a slight mistake,
she would rebuke them without leniency.
If they were slightly unyielding,
she would angrily threaten to leave.
The couple would kneel and apologize,
and only then would she stop.
Not long after,
Wū Tóu passed the imperial examination for county students,
and Hēi Chǒu again asked to return home.
Wū Tóu refused.
He donated the betrothal gifts
to arrange his stepbrother's wedding.
Hēi Chǒu then sent her son home.
Wū Tóu could not persuade her to stay.
Secretly, he had someone buy a hundred *mu* of permanent land in a nearby village before sending her off.
Later, Hēi Chǒu fell ill and asked to return home.
Wū Tóu did not allow it.
As her illness worsened,
she instructed him,
"You must bury me back home!"
Wū Tóu agreed.
After she died,
he secretly gave gold to Mù Zǐ,
to have her buried with Mèng Shēng.
When the day came,
the coffin was so heavy
that thirty men could not lift it.
Mù Zǐ suddenly collapsed,
bleeding from his seven orifices.
He said to himself:
"Worthless son,
how could you sell your mother!"
Wū Tóu was frightened,
bowed, and prayed,
and only then did Mù Zǐ recover.
So they stopped for a few more days,
repaired Mù Shēng's tomb,
and only then buried her together with Mù Shēng.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"To feel so deeply grateful to a kindred spirit
as to devote one's life to him
is the act of a heroic man.
What did this woman know,
to be so remarkably great?
If she had met Jiǔ Fāng Gāo,
he would have simply seen her as a mare."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
In the Eastern Sea, there is a clam.
When hungry, it floats to the shore,
its two shells opening wide.
A small crab emerges from within,
tied to it with a red thread.
It ventures several feet from the shell,
and having eaten its fill,
it returns,
and the shells close.
If one secretly cuts the thread,
both creatures die.
This is indeed a marvel of nature.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Lián Shēng,
a native of Zhāngdé.
From a young age, he was devoted to study;
however, he became an orphan early,
and his family was extremely poor.
One day, he went out,
and returned at dusk, halfway through his journey.
Entering a village,
a Wēn came and said to him:
"Lián Gōngzǐ, where are you going?
Is it not getting late?"
Shēng was just then feeling lost and afraid,
and had no time to ask who this person was,
so he immediately asked for a place to stay.
Wēn led him away,
into a grand mansion.
Two maidservants with lamps
guided a woman out,
aged over forty,
The old woman greeted her, saying:
"Lián Gōngzǐ has arrived."
Shēng hurried to bow.
The woman happily said:
"Gōngzǐ is so distinguished,
why should he only be a rich man's son-in-law!"
Then a banquet was laid out,
the woman sat to the side,
and urged him to drink very earnestly,
but she herself never drank when raising her cup,
nor did she ever eat when raising her chopsticks.
Shēng was perplexed,
and repeatedly inquired about her family background.
She smiled and said:
"After you finish three more cups, I will tell you."
Shēng complied with her instruction.
The woman said:
"My late husband's surname was Liú,
he was a merchant in Jiāngyòu,
and tragically died in an accident.
This widow lives alone in a desolate place,
and is becoming increasingly neglected day by day.
Though I have two grandsons,
they are either utterly useless
or simply incompetent.
Although Gōngzǐ has a different surname,
you are like kin from a past life;
moreover, your nature is truly pure and earnest,
hence I have boldly come to meet you.
There are no other troubles,
I have a small hidden store of several taels of gold,
and I wish to ask Gōngzǐ to take them to travel the rivers and lakes for trade.
Dividing the profits
is better than decaying and dying by the desk with a glow-worm.
Shēng declined, saying that as a young bookworm,
he feared he could not handle such a weighty trust.
The woman said:
"The strategy for studying
comes before making a living.
Gōngzǐ is intelligent,
how can anything be impossible for you?"
She sent a maid to bring out the capital,
exchanging it for over eight hundred taels.
Shēng, alarmed, firmly declined.
The woman said:
"I also know that Gōngzǐ is not accustomed to trade,
but just try it,
and nothing will go amiss."
Shēng worried that such a large sum could not be managed by one person,
and considered partnering with other merchants.
The woman said:
"No need.
Just find an honest, simple, and experienced servant
to work for Gōngzǐ, and that will be enough."
Then she moved her slender finger to divine,
saying:
"A person surnamed Wǔ will be auspicious."
She ordered a servant to lead a horse with the gold in saddlebags to send Shēng off,
saying:
"When the year ends, wash your cups,
awaiting the cleaning of precious ornaments."
Then she looked at the servant and said:
"This horse is well-trained
and suitable for riding,
I will give it to Gōngzǐ,
you need not bring it back."
Shēng returned,
it was only the fourth watch of the night,
and the servant tied up the horse and left by himself.
The next day,
he searched extensively for a servant,
and indeed found one named Wǔ,
and hired him with a generous payment.
Old Wǔ was a seasoned traveler
and a simple, honest, and unpretentious man,
so Shēng entrusted all the funds to him.
They traveled to Jīngxiāng,
and only returned at the end of the year,
having tripled their profit.
Shēng felt that Wǔ's efforts were considerable,
so beyond the usual,
he gave him an extra reward,
planning to spend it together,
without letting the mistress know.
As soon as they arrived home,
the woman had already sent someone to greet them,
so they went with him.
They saw a lavish banquet already set in the hall;
the woman came out,
and offered extreme comfort and welcome.
After Shēng handed over the funds,
he immediately presented the account books;
the woman put them aside without looking.
Soon after, they took their seats,
with singing and dancing;
Wǔ was also given a banquet in an outer room,
and only returned after getting completely drunk.
Because of the lack of a home for insects,
he stayed to guard the New Year.
The next day,
Shēng again asked to check the accounts.
The woman smiled and said:
"No need for that in the future,
I have kept accounts for a long time."
Then she brought out a ledger and showed it to Shēng,
everything was recorded in great detail,
and even the payments to servants
were listed on it.
Shēng said in astonishment:
"Madam is truly a divine person!"
Several days passed,
and the lodging and food were abundant,
treating him like a son or nephew.
One day,
a banquet was set up in the hall,
one facing east,
one facing south;
outside the hall, a feast faced west.
He said to the student:
“Tomorrow, the Wealth Star will shine,
and it is suitable for you to travel far.
Today, on behalf of your patron, a rough farewell feast has been prepared,
to boost your spirits for the journey.”
A little later,
Wǔ also was called and arrived,
and was given a seat outside the hall.
At once, drums and gongs clanged noisily.
A female entertainer presented a song list,
and the student requested
“Táo Zhū.”
The woman smiled and said:
“This is a good omen;
you will surely acquire Xī Shī as a helper in your household.”
After the feast,
she again gave all the gold to the student,
saying:
“This journey cannot be measured by years and months;
do not return unless you have gained a vast fortune.
What I and the young master rely on
is fortune and fate,
and what we trust in is our innermost feelings.
Do not bother to calculate;
I will know of the profits accumulated in distant lands
myself.”
The student assented repeatedly and withdrew.
He traveled to the area along the Huái River,
and established himself as a salt merchant.
After more than a year,
his profits again multiplied several times.
However, the student was fond of reading;
even while managing accounts, he did not forget his books,
and all his companions were literati.
Once his gains were abundant,
he secretly thought of stopping when satisfied,
and gradually entrusted responsibilities to Wǔ.
Xuē Shēng from Táoyuán was his best friend.
He happened to visit him,
but the entire Xuē family had gone to another property.
As it was late evening and he had nowhere else to go,
the gatekeeper invited the student in,
swept a bed, and prepared a meal.
Upon inquiring about the master’s daily life,
he learned that at that time, there was a widespread rumor that the imperial court wished to select girls from good families
to reward the border garrisons,
causing unrest among the populace.
It was said that if there were young men without wives,
and no matchmakers involved,
girls were simply sent to their homes,
to the extent that some obtained two wives in one night.
Xuē, too, had recently married into a prominent family,
and still feared that the noise of carriages and horses
would be heard by the magistrate,
so he had temporarily moved to the countryside.
As the first watch was nearing its end,
and he was about to sweep the bed and lie down,
suddenly he heard several people pushing open the door and entering.
The gatekeeper did not know what they were saying,
but only heard one person say:
“Since the master is not at home,
who is holding the candle?”
The gatekeeper replied:
“It is Lián Gōngzǐ,
a distant guest.”
Soon, the questioner had entered.
His robe and hat were clean and bright.
He merely raised a hand
and immediately inquired about his clan and native place.
The student informed him.
The man rejoiced and said:
“We are from the same native place.
Whose family is your wife from?”
He replied:
“I have none.”
The man was even more delighted,
hurried out,
and urgently called a young man who was with him
to respectfully perform a礼 with the student.
Suddenly, he said:
“I must tell Gōngzǐ truthfully: my surname is Mù.
Tonight, I came here
to send my younger sister to Xuē Guānrén,
but now I know it is useless.
At this moment of being caught between a rock and a hard place,
I happened to meet Gōngzǐ;
is this not fate!”
Since the student did not yet fully know the person,
he hesitated and dared not respond.
Mù, however, did not listen to his words,
and urgently called those who were escorting the girl.
A little later,
two old women helped the young lady in,
and she sat on the student’s bed.
He glanced at her:
she was fifteen or sixteen years old,
peerlessly beautiful.
The student was delighted,
and then straightened his headwear and expressed his gratitude to Mù;
he also instructed the gatekeeper to go and buy wine,
and showed him full hospitality.
Mù said:
“My ancestors were from Zhāngdé;
my mother’s family was also a prominent clan,
but is now in decline.
I heard my maternal grandfather left two grandsons,
but I don’t know what their family situation is like.”
The student asked:
“Who are they?”
He said:
“My maternal grandfather was Liú,
courtesy name Huīruò.
I heard he was thirty lǐ north of the prefecture.”
The student said:
“I am from the southeast of the prefectural city,
quite far from the northern village;
and I am also very young,
without many acquaintances.
This surname is very common in the prefecture,
and I only know of a Liú Jīngqīng north of the prefecture,
also a literatus,
but I am unsure if it is he,
though he is poor.”
Mù said:
"My ancestors' tombs are still in Zhāngjùn.
I have often wished to carry their two coffins back to our hometown for burial,
but as I haven't yet managed to secure the travel funds,
I have kept delaying it.
Now that my younger sister is accompanying me,
my resolution to return is even stronger."
Shēng heard this
and eagerly took on the responsibility himself.
The two Mùs were both delighted.
After a few rounds of wine,
Shēng bid them farewell.
Shēng dismissed his servant and moved the lamp;
the love between the zither and se [referring to Shēng and his wife]
was inexpressible.
The next day,
Xuē already knew of this,
and hurried into the city
to arrange a separate residence for Shēng.
Shēng went to Huái,
and after completing the handover,
left Wǔ to manage the shop;
he gathered funds and returned to Táoyuán,
where he and the two Mùs exhumed the bones of their parents-in-law.
The children from both families
were all taken back with them.
After settling them in upon entering the gate,
he took the gold in his pouch to the madam.
The former servant was already waiting on the road.
As he followed,
the madam met them,
her face beaming, saying:
"Táo Zhūgōng has brought Xīzǐ!
The other day he was a guest,
today he is my nephew-in-law."
She set out wine to welcome them,
and grew even more fond of him.
Shēng was impressed by her foresight,
and asked:
"How close are Madam and my mother-in-law?"
The madam said:
"Do not ask;
you will know in time."
Then she piled the gold on the table,
dividing it into five portions;
she took two portions for herself,
saying:
"I have no use for it;
I'll just leave it for my eldest grandson."
Shēng felt it was too much
and declined to accept it.
She said mournfully:
"My family is in decline;
the tall trees in our residence
have been cut down for firewood by others;
my grandson lives quite far from here,
and our household is desolate.
I trouble you, young master, to manage this."
Shēng agreed,
but only accepted half of the gold.
The madam insisted on him taking it.
She saw Shēng out,
waving and returning with tears.
While Shēng was puzzled and surprised,
he looked back at the residence,
which had become a ruin and a graveyard.
Only then did he realize that the madam was his wife's maternal grandmother.
Upon his return,
he redeemed a qǐng of tomb land,
and planted it grandly and beautifully.
Liú had two grandsons;
the elder was Jīngqīng;
the younger was Yùqīng,
who was dissolute and a gambler,
both were poor.
The brothers visited Shēng to express their gratitude,
and Shēng generously gave them all substantial gifts.
From then on, their comings and goings were very frequent.
Shēng largely explained the reasons for his business,
and Yùqīng secretly thought there was much gold in the house.
That night, he gathered several gamblers
and dug up the tomb to search it,
opening the coffin and exposing the bones,
but ultimately found nothing,
and dispersed in disappointment.
Shēng knew the tomb had been disturbed,
and told Jīngqīng.
Jīngqīng went with Shēng to verify it,
entered the burial chamber,
and saw the piles on the table;
the gold previously divided was all there.
Jīngqīng wanted to take it with Shēng.
Shēng said:
"The madam originally left this here for you, my brother."
Jīngqīng then bagged it and carried it home,
informing the county magistrate,
who launched a very strict investigation.
Later, a person was caught selling a jade hairpin from the tomb,
and was apprehended.
His accomplices were thoroughly interrogated,
and it was then discovered that Yùqīng was the ringleader.
The magistrate was about to sentence him to the severest punishment;
Jīngqīng pleaded on his behalf,
and he barely escaped death.
Both families worked together to repair and rebuild the tomb,
making it stronger and more beautiful than before.
From then on, the Lián and Liú families both became wealthy,
only Yùqīng remained as he was.
Shēng and Jīngqīng often gave him financial aid,
but it was never enough to support his gambling.
One night,
robbers broke into Shēng's house,
demanding gold.
Shēng's hidden gold,
which was all in lots of fifteen hundred,
was shown to them.
The robbers took two lots,
and there was only a ghost horse in the stable,
which they used to transport it away.
They made Shēng take it to the wilderness,
then released him.
The villagers, seeing the robbers' torch not far off,
shouted and pursued them;
the bandits were alarmed and fled.
When they reached the spot,
the gold was left by the roadside,
and the horse had collapsed into ashes.
Only then did they realize the horse was also a ghost.
That night, only a golden bracelet was lost.
Previously,
the robbers had seized Shēng's wife,
and, charmed by her beauty,
were about to assault her,
when a masked robber
forcefully stopped them,
his voice similar to Yùqīng's.
The robbers released Shēng's wife,
but only took her wrist bracelet and left.
Shēng was suspicious of Yùqīng because of this,
but secretly felt grateful to him.
Later, the robber pawned the bracelet for gambling,
and was caught by the constables,
who interrogated his accomplices,
and indeed Yùqīng was among them.
The magistrate was furious,
and subjected him to the severest tortures.
His brother and Shēng plotted
to bribe their way out for him,
but before their plan was complete, Yùqīng had already died.
Shēng still occasionally looked after his wife and children.
Later, Shēng passed the imperial examinations,
and his family remained wealthy for several generations.
Alas!
The strokes of the character 'tān' (貪, greed)
are very similar in form
to 'pín' (貧, poverty).
Those like Yùqīng
can serve as a warning.
According to the manuscript of 'Liáozhāi Zhìyì'
from the household of Grand Historian Lǐ in Língxiàn,
he often saw ancient vases, tripods, and curiosities
moved and arranged on the edge of the table,
in a precarious position about to fall.
He suspected his servants were responsible,
and would angrily rebuke them.
The servants protested their innocence,
but also did not know the reason,
so he strictly locked the study door,
but in the morning it was the same again.
He knew it was something strange,
and secretly spied on it.
One night,
the room was filled with light,
and he was surprised, thinking it was a thief.
Two servants peered closely,
and saw a fox lying on a calf,
light emanating from its two eyes,
sparkling and radiating in all directions.
Fearing it would escape,
they quickly rushed in to catch it.
The fox bit his wrist flesh trying to get free,
but the servant held it more firmly,
so they tied it up together.
When they lifted and looked,
all four of its legs had no bones,
and they swayed limply like dangling ribbons.
The Grand Historian, remembering its spiritual nature,
could not bear to kill it;
he covered it with a willow basket.
The fox could not get out,
and ran off with the basket on its head.
He then counted its misdeeds and released it,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
According to the manuscript of 'Liáozhāi Zhìyì'
An old man, a wine merchant in Jǐnán,
sent his younger son, Xiǎo'èr, to Qíhé to collect overdue payments.
He left the West Gate.
He saw his elder brother, Ādà.
At that time, Ādà had been dead for a long time.
Xiǎo'èr was startled and asked,
"Brother, how did you come here?"
He replied,
"The underworld has a suspicious case
that requires your testimony."
Xiǎo'èr's expression changed, and he complained bitterly.
Ādà pointed to a person behind him who looked like a jailer,
saying,
"The official escort is here;
how can I be free?"
He simply gestured with his hand to call him,
and Xiǎo'èr unknowingly followed him.
They ran wildly all night,
reaching the foot of Tài Shān.
Suddenly, he saw a government office.
Just as he was about to enter,
he saw a crowd of people coming out.
The jailer bowed and asked,
"How did the matter turn out?"
One person said,
"There's no need to go back in;
it's concluded."
The jailer then released him to return home.
Ādà worried that his brother had no money for the journey.
The jailer thought for a long time,
then led Xiǎo'èr away,
walking twenty or thirty *lǐ*.
They entered a village
and arrived at a house's eaves.
He instructed,
"If someone comes out,
ask them to see you off;
if they refuse,
then say Wáng Huòláng told you to."
Then he left.
Xiǎo'èr lay stiffly, as if in a trance.
When dawn broke,
the master of the house came out,
saw a person dead outside his gate,
and was greatly alarmed.
After watching for a moment,
Xiǎo'èr faintly revived.
He was helped inside and given food.
Only then did he speak of his home.
He immediately asked for funds to return.
The master of the house found it difficult.
Xiǎo'èr spoke as the jailer had instructed.
The master of the house was utterly astonished
and quickly rented a horse to send him home.
He offered payment,
but the master would not accept it.
When asked why,
he also did not say.
He then departed.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Yù Shìyù of Jiāozhōu
was sent as an envoy to Liúqiú.
While his boat was sailing in the sea,
a giant dragon suddenly fell from the clouds,
splashing water several *zhàng* high.
The dragon was half-floating, half-submerged,
raising its head,
resting its chin on the boat.
Its eyes were half-closed,
and it appeared listless and dejected.
Everyone on the boat was greatly frightened,
stopping their oars and daring not to move slightly.
A boatman said,
"This is a weary dragon from heaven that was performing rain duties."
They hung a royal edict above,
burned incense, and collectively prayed to it.
After a while,
it slowly departed.
Just as the boat set off,
another dragon fell,
in the same manner as before.
This happened three or four times that day.
The next day,
the boatmen ordered more white rice to be prepared,
warning,
"We are not far from Qīngshuǐ Tán.
If you see anything,
just scatter rice into the water
and remain silent, without commotion."
Soon, they reached a place where
the water was crystal clear to the bottom.
Below were many dragons,
five-colored,
some as big as basins, some as big as urns.
Every single one was lying prostrate.
There were some that were twisting and turning,
their scales, manes, claws, and teeth
distinctly visible.
Everyone was utterly terrified,
holding their breath and closing their eyes,
not daring to peek,
and unable to move.
Only the boatmen held rice and scattered it themselves.
After a long time,
when the sea waves turned deep black,
did someone begin to groan.
They then asked the reason for throwing the rice,
and the boatman replied,
"Dragons fear maggots
because they might enter their scales.
White rice resembles maggots,
so when dragons see it, they immediately lie prostrate,
and the boat can pass over them
without harm."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Jiǎ Zǐlóng, a scholar from Cháng'ān,
happened to pass a nearby alley
and saw a guest with a refined demeanor.
When asked, it was Zhēn Shēng,
who rented lodging in Xiányáng.
Jiǎ Zǐlóng admired him.
The next day,
he went to present his calling card,
but Zhēn Shēng happened to be out.
He visited three times in total,
but never met him.
So he secretly sent someone to check if Zhēn Shēng was home before going over,
but Zhēn Shēng still hid and would not come out.
Jiǎ Zǐlóng searched for him, and only then did he appear.
They sat close and talked heartily,
becoming great friends.
Jiǎ Zǐlóng stayed in an inn
and sent his servant to buy wine.
Zhēn Shēng was also a good drinker and
was adept at refined jokes,
making the occasion very enjoyable.
When the wine was almost finished,
Zhēn Shēng searched his box and took out a drinking vessel.
It was a jade goblet without a bottom.
He poured a cup of wine into it,
and it was already full to the brim.
He used a small ladle to scoop it into a pot,
and not the slightest amount was reduced.
Jiǎ Zǐlóng found this extraordinary
and firmly asked for his technique.
Zhēn Shēng said,
"The reason I did not want to meet you
is not because you have any other faults,
but simply because your greedy heart is not yet calm.
This is a hidden technique of the immortals;
how can I impart it to you?"
Jiǎ Zǐlóng said,
"Unfair!
How am I greedy?
Any occasional luxurious thoughts
are merely due to poverty."
They smiled and dispersed.
From then on, they visited each other without interruption,
forgetting all formality.
Whenever Jiǎ Zǐlóng was in distress or lacked funds,
Zhēn Shēng would take out a black stone,
blow a charm upon it,
and rub it against a tile shard,
which immediately turned into white silver.
He would then give it to Jiǎ Zǐlóng;
it was just enough for his needs,
never more than required.
Jiǎ Zǐlóng often asked for more,
and Zhēn Shēng would say,
"I told you that you were greedy;
how about that,
how about that!"
Jiǎ Zǐlóng thought that openly asking would certainly not work,
so he planned to steal the stone
when Zhēn Shēng was drunk and asleep, and thus obtain it.
One day,
after drinking, Zhēn Shēng lay down.
Jiǎ Zǐlóng quietly got up
and searched under his clothes.
Zhēn Shēng awoke and
said,
"You truly have lost your heart;
this cannot continue!"
So he bade farewell
and moved away.
More than a year later,
Jiǎ was traveling by the river,
and saw a stone, pure and bright,
remarkably like a real living thing.
He picked it up,
and treasured it like a precious gem.
A few days passed,
when Zhēn suddenly arrived,
looking as if he had lost something.
Jiǎ asked him sympathetically.
Zhēn said,
"What you saw before
was the immortal's alchemical stone.
Previously, I traveled with Bàozhēnzǐ:
he pitied my uprightness
and gave this to me.
After getting drunk, I lost it,
and a hidden divination indicated it should be with you.
If you would return it to me,
I would not dare forget your kindness."
Jiǎ smiled and said,
"I, your humble servant, would not deceive a friend.
It is indeed as your divination indicated.
But who knows Guǎn Zhòng's poverty
better than Bào Shú?
What will you do then?"
Zhēn offered a gift of a hundred gold coins.
Jiǎ said,
"A hundred gold coins is not a small sum,
but if you teach me the secret incantation,
and let me try it once,
I will have no regrets."
Zhēn feared his untrustworthiness.
Jiǎ said,
"You are an immortal yourself,
how could you not know that I, Jiǎ Mǒu, would rather lose faith in friends?"
Zhēn taught him the incantation.
Jiǎ looked at a huge stone on the terrace,
intending to try it.
Zhēn grabbed his arm at that moment,
not allowing him to proceed.
Jiǎ then bent down and scooped half a peck of grain, placing it on an anvil, saying:
"If it is like this,
is it not too much?"
Zhēn then allowed it.
Jiǎ did not rub the grain, but rubbed the anvil;
Zhēn's expression changed, wanting to argue,
but the anvil had already transformed into solid gold.
He returned the stone to Zhēn.
Zhēn sighed and said,
"Since it has come to this,
what more can be said?
However, presumptuously bestowing blessings and prosperity upon people
will certainly incur heavenly punishment.
If you would absolve me of my crime,
by distributing one hundred coffins and one hundred padded garments,
would you agree to this?"
Jiǎ said,
"The reason I wanted money
was originally not to hoard it.
Do you still consider me a greedy hoarder of wealth?"
Zhēn departed joyfully.
Jiǎ obtained the gold,
and both distributed and traded it;
in less than three years,
the required distributions were fulfilled.
Zhēn suddenly arrived,
clasped his hand and said,
"You are a man of integrity and righteousness!
After we parted, the God of Fortune reported me to the Emperor,
and my immortal status was revoked;
thanks to your extensive generosity,
I have now happily expiated my sins through merit and virtue.
I hope you will strive on,
and not cease."
Jiǎ asked Zhēn,
"What heavenly department do you belong to?"
He replied,
"I am merely a fox who has attained the Dao.
My origins are extremely humble,
and I cannot bear the burden of karma,
so throughout my life I have cherished myself,
not daring to act rashly in the slightest."
Jiǎ set out wine for him,
and they drank happily as before.
When Jiǎ reached over ninety years old,
the fox still occasionally visited his home.
A certain Mǒu from Chángshān,
sold an antidote that was truly miraculous;
even if one was on the verge of death,
administering it unfailingly brought them back to life.
However, he kept the formula secret,
not even passing it on to close relatives or friends.
One day,
he was arrested due to implication in a case.
His wife's younger brother brought him food in prison,
secretly placing the antidote within it.
He waited until Mǒu had eaten,
and only then informed him.
Jiǎ did not believe it.
A short while later,
his abdomen began to churn and move,
and he became greatly alarmed,
cursing,
"You beast, hurry!
Although there is medicine at home,
I fear the journey is too far to wait;
quickly find *xuèlì* (fig vine) in the city, pulverize it,
and bring a cup of clear water,
and bring it quickly!"
His wife's younger brother followed his instructions.
By the time he found it,
Mǒu was already vomiting and purging, on the verge of death;
he quickly administered it,
and Mǒu recovered instantly.
His formula was thus passed down from then on.
This is also like the fox keeping its stone a secret.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript
A certain cloth merchant,
upon reaching the border of Qīngzhōu,
happened to enter a ruined temple,
and seeing its scattered courtyards,
sighed and lamented incessantly.
A monk stood nearby and said,
"If there is now a good patron
who would temporarily rebuild the mountain gate,
it would also be a glory to the Buddha's face."
The merchant resolutely took on the responsibility.
The monk was pleased,
and invited him into the abbot's quarters,
treating him with great hospitality.
Later, he brought up the inner and outer halls and pavilions,
and also requested their renovation;
the merchant declined, saying he was unable.
The monk forcefully insisted,
his words and expression becoming fierce and angry.
The merchant was afraid,
and requested to empty his purse immediately,
so he poured out his belongings
and gave everything to the monk.
As he was about to leave,
the monk stopped him and said,
"It is not my wish for you to exhaust your resources,
do you perhaps resent me?
It is better to end it now."
He then drew a knife and faced him.
The merchant begged earnestly,
but the monk would not listen;
he asked to hang himself,
and the monk granted it.
He was forced into a dark room and hastened.
Just then, a general defending the coast passed outside the temple,
and from a distance, through a broken wall, saw a red-clad woman enter the monk's quarters,
which made him suspicious.
He dismounted and entered the temple,
searching everywhere,
but could not find her.
Upon reaching the dark room,
whose double doors were tightly bolted,
the monk refused to open them,
claiming it was a haunted place.
The general was enraged,
cut open the lock, and entered,
where he saw the merchant hanging from a beam.
He rescued him,
and in a moment he revived,
and the situation was interrogated and understood.
He also questioned, with shackles, the whereabouts of the woman,
but in reality, there was none;
it was a manifestation of divine beings.
The monk was killed,
and the merchant's belongings were returned to him.
The merchant further solicited funds to repair the temple,
and from then on, the temple's incense offerings flourished greatly.
Zhào Xiàolián Fēngyuán narrated this in great detail.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript
Hán Gōngfǔ of Yǔchéng himself said:
"I was walking along the road with Páng Èrzhēng from our town,
when suddenly I turned my head and he was gone,
only his empty donkey following along.
But I heard urgent cries for help,
and listening closely, realized they were coming from inside his travel sack.
Upon closer inspection, the inside of the sack was bulging,
and although it was lopsided,
it had not fallen off.
I wanted to get him out,
but the mouth of the sack was very tightly sewn;
I used a knife to cut the threads,
and only then saw Páng Èr lying inside.
After he came out,
I asked how he got in,
but he was also utterly unaware.
It seems there was a fox haunting his family,
and many such incidents occurred."
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript
Chángshān Prince Gōngzǐ Ruìtíng,
could divine using a planchette.
The spirit of the planchette called itself Hé Xiān,
a disciple of Chúnyáng,
or some said it was Lǚ Zǔ's crane-riding cloud.
Each time it descended,
it would discuss literature and compose poetry with people.
Grand Historian Lǐ Zhìjūn served it as a teacher,
marking essays with red and yellow,
its reasoning clear and precise;
the Grand Historian's success in grasping literary principles
largely relied on Hé Xiān's power,
and because of this, many scholars of literature became its adherents.
However, in resolving difficult matters for people,
it mostly relied on reason,
and did not speak much of good or bad fortune.
In the Xīnwèi year (1691),
Zhū Wénzōng came to Jǐnán for the provincial examination.
After the examination,
his friends discussed and decided the grades.
Hé Xiān asked for the examination papers
and evaluated all of them.
Among those present, there was someone who was good friends with Lǐ Biàn of Lèlíng.
Lǐ was indeed a diligent and deep-thinking scholar,
and everyone had high hopes for him,
so his essay was presented,
and a request was made on his behalf.
The planchette wrote:
"First class."
A little later,
it wrote again:
"Just now, when evaluating student Lǐ,
I judged based on the essay.
However, this student's fortune is very obscure,
and he is likely to commit a disciplinary offense [i.e., suffer caning].
How strange!
His literary quality and his fate do not match.
Could it be that Wénzōng does not judge by literary merit?
Gentlemen, wait a moment,
I will go and investigate."
A short while later,
it wrote again:
"I just went to the office of the Education Commissioner,
and saw Commissioner Wénzōng busy with official duties,
his anxieties were clearly not about literature.
Everything was handed over to six or seven private secretaries,
who were all mediocre students.
Even those designated as 'exemplary students'
were among them,
with no foundation in their previous lives,
mostly wandering souls from the realm of hungry ghosts,
begging for food in all directions.
They had been in the dark prison for eight hundred years,
damaging the essence of their eyesight,
like someone who has been in a cave for a long time,
and upon sudden emergence, finds the world a different color,
without clear vision.
Among them, one or two were transformed from human bodies,
dividing into groups to review the papers,
but I fear they may not be suitable to match [the essays with their true worth]."
Everyone asked about a method to remedy the situation,
and it wrote:
"The method is very practical,
and known to everyone,
why ask?"
Everyone understood its meaning,
and informed Lǐ.
Lǐ was scared,
and took his essay to Sun Rénshǐ Zǐwèi,
also telling him about the omen.
The Grand Historian praised his essay,
and then dispelled his doubts.
Lǐ, considering the Grand Historian a national master,
felt more emboldened,
and no longer took the planchette's words to heart.
Later, when the results were released,
he was indeed in the fourth class.
The Grand Historian was greatly astonished,
and took his essay to review it again,
finding no flaws whatsoever.
He commented,
"Shímén Gōngzǔ [Zhū Wénzōng],
has always had a literary reputation,
he would certainly not be so careless as to make such an error.
This must be the work of a drunken fellow in the secretariat,
who doesn't even recognize punctuation."
At this, everyone admired Hé Xiān even more,
and burned incense to thank it.
The planchette wrote:
"Student Lǐ, do not let this temporary setback
cause you shame or dismay.
You should write more examination papers,
and expose them widely,
then you can achieve an excellent grade next year."
Lǐ followed its instruction.
After some time, this became well-known in the office,
and a special plaque was hung to console him.
The following year, he indeed achieved an excellent grade,
such was its miraculous efficacy.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"There are many such guests in the private secretariat;
no wonder in the 'Ugly Woman Alley' in the capital,
there is no empty bed by evening.
Alas!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
(Beginning missing) Niú passed his father's room,
and the old man was lying in bed, still awake.
From this, he knew it was a fox,
and angrily said:
"A fox is tolerable,
but why ruin my morality!
Guān Shèng is revered as 'Demon Subduer,'
where is he now,
to allow such creatures to run rampant!"
Therefore, he wrote a memorial to the Jade Emperor,
subtly complaining about Guān Dì's dereliction of duty.
After a long time,
(Guān Dì suddenly heard a loud cry from the air,
it was Guān Dì.
He angrily scolded:
"How dare you, scholar, be so disrespectful!
Am I specifically in charge of expelling foxes for your family?
If your complaint is not accepted,
how can I avoid blame?"
He then ordered Niú to be given twenty strokes with a staff,
his thigh flesh almost tore off.
A moment later,
a black-faced general bound a fox and led it away,
and the haunting then ceased.
Three years later,
the daughter of the Jǐnán Colonel was bewitched by a fox,
and a hundred methods could not dispel it.
The fox told the girl:
"The only one I have ever feared in my life
is a man named Niú."
The Colonel did not know where this Niú was,
and could not find him.
It happened that the Education Commissioner was inspecting,
and Niú went to take the examination.
While in the provincial capital, he was accidentally insulted by a camp soldier,
and in anger, he lodged a complaint at the Colonel's gate.
The Colonel, hearing his name,
was overcome with surprise and joy,
and bowed very respectfully.
He immediately seized the soldier,
and beat him according to the law.
After this,
he then honestly told Niú the situation.
Niú had no choice but
to present a complaint to Guān Dì on her behalf.
In a moment,
a golden-armored god descended into their house.
The fox was still in the room,
its countenance suddenly changed,
assuming the shape of a dog,
howling and scurrying around the house.
Soon after, it ran out
and threw itself down the steps.
The god said:
"The Emperor previously spared it,
but if it offends again,
it will not be pardoned!"
He seized and tied it to the neck of his horse and departed.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Mǐ Shēng was a native of Mǐn,
but the recorder has forgotten his name, courtesy name, and commandery or district.
He happened to enter the commandery
and, in a drunken state, passed through the marketplace
when he heard the sound of flutes and drums like thunder from within a tall gate.
He asked the residents about it,
who said it was a birthday celebration,
yet the gate and courtyard were remarkably quiet and deserted.
Listening to the rich sounds of pipes and songs,
he, in his drunkenness, deeply loved and enjoyed the music.
Without even asking whose family it was,
he immediately bought a congratulatory gift from a street vendor
and presented his calling card.
Someone, seeing his simple attire,
then asked:
"How are you related to this old gentleman?"
He replied:
"Not at all."
Someone else said:
"This sojourner is staying here as a temporary resident.
I don't know what official rank he holds,
but he is very noble and arrogant.
Since you are not a relative,
what do you seek?"
Shēng heard this and regretted it,
but the card had already been sent in.
Soon after,
two young men came out to welcome guests,
their splendid clothes dazzling the eyes.
They were both elegant and refined,
and bowed to Shēng, inviting him in.
He saw an old man sitting facing south,
with several tables arranged to the east and west.
There were six or seven guests,
all appearing to be noble descendants.
When they saw Shēng arrive,
they all rose to greet him,
and the old man also rose with the aid of his staff.
Shēng stood for a long time,
waiting to exchange courtesies,
but the old man did not leave his seat.
The two young men addressed him, saying:
"Our father is old and infirm,
and rising to bow is truly difficult.
My brothers and I offer our apologies on behalf of this esteemed guest for troubling yourself."
Shēng modestly declined and desisted.
Then an additional table was set at the head,
next to the old man's seat.
Before long,
female musicians began to perform below.
Behind the seats, a glass screen was placed
to separate the inner family members.
The drums and wind instruments played loudly,
and the guests could no longer converse.
