As the banquet was nearing its end,
the two young men rose,
each offering guests a massive cup,
each cup capable of holding three dǒu.
Shēng showed a look of difficulty,
but seeing the other guests accept,
he also accepted.
In a moment, he looked around in all directions,
and the host and guests had all drained their cups.
Shēng had no choice
but to force himself to drain it too.
The young men poured again;
Shēng felt extremely weary
and rose to excuse himself.
The young men forcibly pulled at his clothes.
Shēng, heavily drunk, fell to the ground,
but then felt someone sprinkle cold water on his face,
and he seemed to awaken suddenly.
He rose and looked,
and the guests had all dispersed.
Only one young man held his arm to escort him,
and then they parted ways and he returned home.
Later, when he passed by that gate again,
they had already moved away.
After returning from the commandery,
he happened to pass through the market.
A person came out from a shop
and invited him to drink.
He looked but did not recognize the person.
He tentatively followed him in,
and found that his fellow villager, Bāo Zhuāng, was already seated.
He asked about the person,
who was a man named Zhū,
a mirror-polisher in the market.
He asked:
"How do you know each other?"
Zhū said:
"The one who celebrated his birthday the other day,
do you know him?"
Shēng said:
"No, I don't."
Zhū said:
"I often go in and out of his gate, I'm very familiar with him.
The old man,
whose surname is Fù,
I don't know what province he is from or what official rank he holds.
When you paid your respects on his birthday,
I was right there below the steps,
that's how I know you."
As dusk fell,
the drinking party dispersed.
Bāo Zhuāng died on the road that night.
Bāo's father did not recognize Zhū,
and seized upon the name to sue Shēng.
Upon examination, Bāo Zhuāng's body was found to have severe injuries.
Shēng was sentenced to death for murder
and endured various instruments of restraint and torture.
However, as Zhū had not been apprehended
and there was no corroborating evidence for the crime,
the case was held in abeyance.
Over a year later,
an imperial censor on circuit
learned of his wrongful conviction
and had him released.
His family's fields and property were all lost.
Stripped of his scholar's attire,
he hoped to appeal and reclaim them,
so he took his money bag and went to the prefecture.
As dusk approached,
his steps were quite weary,
so he rested by the roadside.
He saw a small carriage coming from afar,
with two attendants in green robes accompanying it.
After it passed,
it suddenly ordered the carriage to stop.
No one knew what was said inside the carriage,
but soon an attendant in green asked the scholar,
"Are you not named Mǐ?"
The scholar, startled, stood up and assented.
The attendant asked,
"Why are you so poor?"
The scholar told him the reason.
He then asked,
"Where are you going?"
The scholar told him again.
The attendant in green left,
spoke to someone in the carriage;
then soon returned,
inviting the scholar to the front of the carriage.
From within the carriage, a delicate hand lifted the curtain,
and he was subtly glanced at;
it was a peerless beauty.
She said to the scholar,
"You have unfortunately suffered an undeserved calamity;
I sigh deeply upon hearing of it.
Today, the office of the Commissioner of Education
is not a place one can enter or exit empty-handed.
I have nothing to offer you along the way...
So, she plucked a pearl flower from her hair bun
and handed it to the scholar, saying,
"This item can be sold for a hundred gold pieces;
please keep it sealed away carefully."
The scholar bowed down,
wishing to ask about her official rank,
but the carriage drove off very quickly,
and it was already far away;
he did not know who she was.
Holding the flower, he pondered;
it was adorned with bright pearls,
not an ordinary object.
He treasured it and continued on his way.
Upon reaching the prefecture,
he submitted his petition,
but was greatly extorted by those above and below.
He took out the flower and displayed it,
but could not bear to part with it,
so he returned home.
Returning home, he had no house,
so he stayed with his elder brother and sister-in-law.
Fortunately, his brother was virtuous
and managed his affairs for him,
so he did not abandon his studies despite his poverty.
After a year,
he went to the prefecture to take the boy's examination,
but mistakenly entered deep mountains.
It was the Qīngmíng Festival,
and there were many visitors.
Several women on horseback arrived,
and one of the young women
was the very person from the carriage that year.
Seeing the scholar halt his horse,
she asked where he was going.
The scholar replied fully.
The woman exclaimed,
"Have your scholar's robes not yet been restored?"
The scholar sadly took out the pearl flower from under his clothes,
saying,
"I could not bear to part with this,
so I am still a 'boy' (meaning, not yet achieved official status)."
The young woman's cheeks flushed red,
and she then instructed a servant to wait by the roadside.
She rode away slowly.
After a long while,
a maid came galloping on a horse,
handed a wrapped item to the scholar,
and said,
"My lady said: Today, the gate of the Commissioner of Education is like a marketplace; she gives two hundred *bái jīn* [silver]
as funds for your advancement."
The scholar declined, saying,
"My lady has bestowed much kindness upon me!
I believe it will not be difficult for me to pass the examination myself,
and I dare not accept such heavy gold.
But if you would tell me your name
and allow me to paint a small portrait of you,
which I will offer incense to,
that would be enough."
The maid paid him no heed,
threw the item on the ground, and left.
From then on, the scholar's expenses were quite ample,
yet he ultimately disdained to seek connections through bribery.
Later, he ranked first in the county examination.
He gave the gold to his elder brother;
his brother was good at managing wealth,
and within three years, their former property was entirely recovered.
Coincidentally, the Provincial Governor of Mǐnzhōng was a former student of the scholar's grandfather,
and showed them great favor and sympathy,
so the brothers became known as a wealthy family.
However, the scholar had always been upright and outspoken,
and although he was connected to a high-ranking official's family,
he never sought anything from them.
One day,
a guest arrived at their gate in furs and on horseback,
but no one recognized him.
He went out to look,
and it was Fù Gōngzǐ.
They bowed and entered,
each speaking of their long separation.
He prepared a meal to entertain the guest,
but the guest declined, citing his busy schedule,
though he did not insist on leaving.
After a while, the dishes and wine were laid out.
Fù Gōngzǐ rose and asked a question;
they went inside together,
and he prostrated himself on the ground.
Shēng asked in surprise what was the matter.
Fù Gōngzǐ said mournfully:
"My father has just suffered a great misfortune.
He wishes to seek help from the Fǔtái,
and only you, elder brother, can do it."
Shēng declined, saying:
"Though he is a friend from a long-standing family acquaintance,
to ask a favor for private matters
is something I have never done in my life."
Fù Gōngzǐ prostrated himself and wept bitterly.
Shēng sternly said:
"You and I, young sir,
are merely acquaintances from one shared drink.
How can you compel me to compromise my integrity!"
Fù Gōngzǐ was greatly ashamed,
rose, and took his leave.
The next day,
as he sat alone,
a man in green clothes entered.
Looking at him,
it was the one who had given him gold in the mountains.
Shēng was just getting up in surprise,
when the green-clothed man said:
"Have you forgotten the pearl hairpin?"
Shēng said:
"Yes, yes,
I dare not forget it."
The man said:
"Yesterday's Fù Gōngzǐ
is the lady's own brother."
Hearing this, Shēng
secretly rejoiced
and feigned to say:
"This is hard to believe.
If I could personally see the lady and hear a word from her,
then I would even tread into a boiling cauldron;
otherwise,
I dare not obey the command."
The green-clothed man went out
and galloped away on horseback.
Half a watch later, he returned,
knocked on the door, and entered, saying:
"The lady has come."
Not long after he spoke,
the young woman entered with a mournful expression,
turned to the wall and wept,
without saying a word.
Shēng bowed and said:
"Without you, young sir,
I would not be where I am today.
Just give me a task,
and how would I dare not obey!"
The woman said:
"Those who ask for help are often proud,
and those who are asked are often afraid.
Rushing here in the middle of the night,
how can you, Shēng, explain this suffering,
except out of fear of others?
What more can be said!"
Shēng comforted her, saying:
"The reason I did not immediately agree
was because I feared it would be difficult to meet again after this one time.
To make you endure dew night and day,
I know my fault!"
Thereupon, he pulled her sleeve,
and surreptitiously scratched her.
The woman said angrily:
"You are truly a depraved person!
You do not remember the past kindness,
but wish to take advantage of someone's distress.
I was wrong!
I was wrong!"
She furiously went out
and boarded the carriage, wanting to leave.
Shēng chased out to apologize,
kneeling for a long time to block her.
The green-clothed man also intervened for him.
The woman's anger slightly subsided,
and from the carriage, she said to Shēng:
"To tell you the truth: I am not human,
but a goddess.
My father is the Dū Lǐ Sī of Nányuè,
and he accidentally offended the Dìguān,
which will be reported to the emperor;
without the official seal and credentials of the local Dū Rén official,
it cannot be resolved.
If you do not forget our old friendship,
please use a piece of yellow paper
to request it for me."
Having spoken,
the carriage departed.
Shēng returned,
filled with trepidation.
So he pretended to expel evil spirits,
speaking to the Xúnfǔ.
The Xúnfǔ considered the matter to be close to witchcraft
and refused.
Shēng bribed his confidant with much gold,
who agreed,
but had not yet found an opportune moment.
Upon returning,
the green-clothed man was waiting at the door.
Shēng told him everything,
and he silently left,
his intention seeming to resent Shēng's disloyalty.
Shēng chased after him, sending him off, saying:
"Go tell the lady,
if the matter does not succeed,
I will sacrifice my life for it!"
After returning,
he tossed and turned all night,
not knowing what plan to make.
It happened that a favorite concubine in the yamen desired a pearl.
Shēng then presented the pearl hairpin to her.
The concubine was greatly pleased,
and secretly used the seal to embed it for him.
He carried it home,
just as the green-clothed man arrived.
He smiled and said:
"Fortunately, I did not fail the mission.
But the pearl, which I could not bear to sell even when I was poor and begging for years,
has now been abandoned by its owner!"
Then he explained the situation.
And he added:
"I don't care about the gold I threw away.
Tell the lady: the pearl hairpin must be repaid."
After several days,
Fù Gōngzǐ came to the hall to express his gratitude,
offering one hundred taels of gold.
The scholar said with a stern expression:
"The reason I did what I did
was solely due to the selfless kindness of your younger sister to me;
otherwise,
even ten thousand taels of gold would not be enough to exchange for my reputation and integrity!"
When he tried to insist again,
the scholar's voice and expression became even sterner.
The young master left feeling ashamed,
saying:
"This matter is far from settled!"
The next day,
a maid in green, acting on the young lady's orders,
presented one hundred pearls,
saying:
"Are these enough to compensate for the pearl flower?"
The scholar said:
"What I valued in the flower
was not its preciousness.
Had she given me ten thousand *yì* of treasures that day,
I would have simply sold them to become a rich old man;
but to treasure it and endure poverty,
what purpose would that serve?
Madam, you are a divine being;
how dare this humble scholar desire anything else?
To have the fortune to repay even a ten-thousandth of your immense kindness,
I would die without regret!"
The maid in green placed the pearls on the table,
and the scholar bowed respectfully before declining them.
After several more days,
Gōngzǐ came again.
The scholar ordered food and wine to be prepared.
Gōngzǐ sent his attendants into the kitchen,
and personally cooked and prepared the meal himself.
They drank freely opposite each other,
as joyful as a family.
A guest offered some bitter glutinous rice wine,
and Gōngzǐ drank it, finding it delicious.
He drained one hundred cups,
his cheeks slightly flushed,
then said to the scholar:
"You are a man of integrity and resolve.
We foolish brothers did not know you earlier;
we are greatly ashamed compared to a woman.
Our father is grateful for your great virtue,
and has no means to repay you.
He wishes to marry his younger sister to you,
but fears you might object due to the difference between the living and the dead."
The scholar was overcome with joy and fear,
unable to respond.
Gōngzǐ bowed and left,
saying:
"Tomorrow night, the ninth day of the seventh month,
when the new moon hooks the star Chén,
the Weaver Girl's young daughter will marry below.
It is an auspicious day,
you may prepare a green bridal chamber."
The next evening,
the young lady was indeed brought over,
everything just as with an ordinary person.
Three days later,
from her elder brother and sister-in-law to all the maids and servants,
everyone received gifts and rewards.
She was also most virtuous,
serving her sister-in-law as if she were her mother-in-law.
After several years without children,
she advised him to take a concubine,
but the scholar refused.
Just then, her brother was trading in Jiānghuái,
and bought a young concubine to bring back.
The concubine,
whose surname was Gù and
whose courtesy name was Bóshì,
was also clear and graceful in appearance.
Both husband and wife were pleased.
When Bóshì saw a pearl flower pinned in the house,
it greatly resembled the old item from that year;
she took it down to examine it,
and indeed it was.
Surprised, the scholar questioned her,
and she replied:
"Once, a beloved concubine of a巡撫 Xúnfǔ died,
and her maid stole it and sold it in the market.
My late father found its price reasonable
and bought it.
My concubine loved it.
My late father had no sons,
and only had this concubine,
so she got everything she asked for.
Later, after my father died and the family declined,
my concubine was fostered in the household of Gù Wēn.
Gù,
who was my concubine's aunt,
saw the pearl and
repeatedly wanted to sell it.
My concubine threw herself into a well to seek death,
which is why it still exists today."
The couple sighed, saying:
"An item from ten years ago
returning to its former owner—
is this not fate?"
The young lady then produced another pearl flower,
saying:
"This item has been without a match for a long time!"
Thereupon she bestowed both upon her,
and personally pinned them in her hairbun.
After Bóshì retired,
she asked the young lady's family history in great detail,
but the family members all avoided speaking of it.
She secretly said to the scholar:
"I perceive that the young lady
is not a human being;
there is a divine aura in her brows and eyes.
Yesterday, when I pinned the flowers, I had a close look,
and her beauty emanates from her skin,
unlike ordinary people whose beauty is merely an arrangement of black and white."
The scholar laughed at her words.
Bóshì said:
"You must not speak of it,
but I will secretly test her.
If she is divine,
then whatever I need,
I will burn incense in a private place to ask for it,
and she will surely know."
The young lady's embroidered socks were exquisitely crafted,
and Bóshì loved them,
but dared not speak of it.
So she immediately burned incense in her chamber and prayed.
The young lady rose early,
and suddenly searched her chest,
took out a pair of socks,
and sent a maid to give them to Bóshì.
The scholar saw this and smiled.
The young lady asked why,
and he told her the truth.
The young lady said:
"Clever maid!"
Because of her wisdom,
she loved her even more;
however, Bóshì became even more respectful.
At dawn,
she would always bathe in fragrant water to pay her respects.
Later, Bóshì gave birth to two sons in one delivery,
and the two men shared the task of naming them.
When the scholar was eighty years old,
the young lady's appearance was still like that of a maiden.
When the scholar fell ill,
the young lady hired craftsmen to make his coffin,
ordering it to be twice as wide and large as usual.
After his death,
the young lady did not cry;
the sons and daughters had gone elsewhere,
and the young lady had already died inside the coffin.
Therefore, they were buried together.
To this day, it is handed down as
"The Great Coffin Tomb."
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The young lady was divine,
but how could Bóshì know this?
By what method did she achieve this?
Thus, one knows that human intelligence
can sometimes be more spiritual than the divine itself!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Yàn Zhòng
was from Yán'ān, Shǎnxī.
He lived with his elder brother, Bó,
and their fraternal affection was profound and sincere.
Bó died at the age of thirty,
leaving no heir;
his wife also died subsequently.
Zhòng mourned him deeply,
and often thought that if he were to have two sons,
he would give one to his brother as an heir.
He had just had a son
when Zhòng’s wife also died.
Zhòng feared that a second wife would not care for his son,
so he intended to buy a concubine.
There was someone in a neighboring village selling a maidservant.
Zhòng went to inspect her,
but she was not at all to his liking.
Feeling bored and dejected,
he was detained by a friend for drinks and returned home completely intoxicated.
On the way, he met Liáng Shēng, an old classmate,
who grasped his hand warmly
and invited him to his house.
In his drunken state, Zhòng forgot that Liáng Shēng had already died,
and went with him.
Entering his door,
it was not his old residence.
Zhòng felt suspicious and asked about it.
Liáng Shēng replied:
“We just moved here.”
They went in, and Liáng Shēng tried to get wine,
but his homebrew was exhausted.
He instructed Zhòng to sit and wait,
then took a bottle to go buy some.
Zhòng went out and stood at the door to wait for him.
He saw a woman leading a donkey past,
with a young boy following her,
who appeared to be eight or nine years old.
His face and demeanor
were remarkably similar to his elder brother’s.
His heart was stirred,
and he quickly followed them,
then asked:
“What is the boy’s surname?”
She replied:
“The surname is Yàn.”
Zhòng was even more surprised,
and asked again:
“What is your father’s name?”
The boy replied:
“I don’t know.”
As they spoke,
they had already reached her door.
The woman dismounted the donkey and entered.
Zhòng seized the boy and said:
“Is your father home?”
The boy nodded and went in.
After a moment,
an old woman came out to peer,
who was indeed his sister-in-law.
She was surprised to see her brother-in-law.
Zhòng was deeply grieved,
and followed her inside.
He saw that the house was also neat and tidy.
He then asked:
“Where is my brother?”
She said:
“He hasn’t returned from collecting debts.”
He asked:
“Who was the person on the donkey?”
She said:
“That is your brother’s concubine, Gān Shì.
She has borne two sons.
The eldest, Ā Dà,
has gone to the market and not yet returned;
the one you saw was Ā Xiǎo.”
After sitting for a long time,
the wine gradually wore off,
and he began to realize that everyone he had seen was a ghost.
But because of the depth of his fraternal affection,
he was not afraid.
His sister-in-law warmed wine and prepared a meal.
Zhòng was anxious to see his brother,
and urged Ā Xiǎo to look for him.
After a long while,
Ā Xiǎo returned crying, saying:
“The Lǐ family hasn’t repaid their debt
and instead argued with father.”
When Zhòng heard this,
he ran off with Ā Xiǎo,
and saw two men wrestling his brother to the ground.
Zhòng was furious,
and charged straight in with his fists,
knocking down all who opposed him.
He quickly helped his brother up,
and the enemies had all fled.
He pursued and caught one man,
and beat him countless times
before he finally stood up.
He took his brother’s hand
and stamped his foot, weeping bitterly;
his brother also wept.
When they returned,
the whole family comforted and asked about them,
then prepared food and drink,
and the brothers celebrated together.
Not long after,
a young man entered,
about sixteen or seventeen years old.
Bó called him Ā Dà,
and told him to bow to his uncle.
Zhòng pulled him up,
and wept to his brother, saying:
“Big brother, you have two sons in the underworld,
yet your grave is not swept;
and I, your brother, have few sons and am a widower,
what should we do?”
Bó was also mournful.
His sister-in-law said to Bó:
“Sending Ā Xiǎo to go with his uncle
would also be good.”
When Ā Xiǎo heard this,
he immediately clung to his uncle,
unwilling to leave.
Zhòng stroked him,
feeling even more sorrowful.
He asked:
“Are you happy to come along?”
He replied:
“I am happy to come along.”
Zhòng thought that although a ghost is not human,
it would still be better for his comfort than having no one.
So he brightened his expression.
Bó said:
“Let him go,
but do not spoil him.
You should feed him blood and meat,
and expose him to the sun,
until after noon.
A child of six or seven,
if he experiences spring and summer,
his flesh and bones will regenerate,
and he can marry and have children;
but I fear he may not live long.”
As they spoke,
a young girl peeked and listened outside the door,
her manner gentle and graceful.
Zhòng suspected she was his brother’s daughter,
and asked his brother about her.
His brother said:
“This is Xiāng Qún,
my concubine’s younger sister.
She is an orphan with no home,
and has been fostered here for ten years.”
He asked:
“Has she been betrothed yet?”
Bó said:
“Not yet.
Recently, there was a matchmaker proposing the Tián family from the East Village.”
The girl whispered from outside the window:
“I will not marry the cowherd boy from the Tián family.”
Zhòng was quite moved by this,
but did not yet speak his mind.
Soon after, Bó rose
and set up a bed in the study,
telling his brother to stay the night.
Zhòngyǎ did not wish to stay,
but his heart was smitten with Xiāngqún.
He decided to find a way to sound out his elder brother's intentions,
so he bade his brother farewell and went to his couch.
It was early spring,
and the weather was still cold.
The study, having been unheated by a fire overnight,
felt chillingly desolate.
He sat by the candle, feeling cold,
and thought of having a small drink.
Suddenly, Āxiǎo pushed open the door and entered,
placing a cup of soup and a measure of wine on the table.
Zhòng was extremely pleased,
and asked:
"Whose doing is this?"
She replied:
"Aunt Xiāng."
When the wine was almost finished,
she covered the basin fire with ash,
and threw it under the bed.
Zhòng asked:
"Are your parents asleep?"
She said:
"They've been asleep for a long time."
"Where do you sleep?"
She said:
"I share a couch with Aunt Xiāng."
Āxiǎo waited until her uncle was asleep,
then closed the door and left.
Zhòng thought of Xiāngqún's kindness and understanding,
and admired her even more;
also, because she could care for Āxiǎo,
his desire to have her grew stronger.
He tossed and turned on his bed,
unable to sleep all night.
Rising early,
he told his elder brother:
"Your younger brother is alone and without a companion;
please, elder brother, keep an eye out for me."
Bó said:
"Our family is not one of poverty;
there will naturally be someone suitable to look for.
Even if there were a beauty from the underworld,
I fear she would bring no benefit to my brother."
Zhòng said:
"The ancients also had ghost wives,
what harm is there?"
Bó seemed to understand,
and then said:
"Xiāngqún is also good,
but only if she can draw blood non-stop by being pricked with a large needle in her pulse point,
can she become a wife for a living person.
How can we be so hasty?"
Zhòng said:
"To have Xiāngqún care for Āxiǎo would also be good."
Bó merely shook his head.
Zhòng pleaded relentlessly,
and his sister-in-law said:
"Let's try to catch Xiāngqún and forcefully prick her to test it;
if it doesn't work, then so be it."
So she took a needle and went outside.
She met Xiāngqún,
and quickly seized her wrist,
finding the bloodstain still wet.
It turned out that when she heard Bó's words,
she had already tested herself.
The sister-in-law released her hand and smiled,
then turned to tell Bó:
"She has been feigning her intentions for a long time now;
must we still worry on her behalf?"
The concubine heard this and became angry.
She rushed towards Xiāngqún,
poked her cheek with a finger, and cursed:
"Shameless hussy!
Do you want to run off with your uncle?
I will certainly not let you have your way!"
Xiāngqún was ashamed and indignant,
weeping and wishing to die,
causing the whole household to be in an uproar.
Zhòng was greatly ashamed,
bade farewell to his elder brother and sister-in-law,
and led Āxiǎo out.
His elder brother said:
"Brother, go for now;
do not let Āxiǎo come back again,
lest it harm her vital energy."
Zhòng assented.
Upon returning home,
he falsely increased Āxiǎo's age,
and claimed her to be the posthumous child of a maid his elder brother had sold.
People, seeing her striking resemblance,
also believed her to be Bó's offspring.
Zhòng taught her to read,
always sending her to hold a scroll and recite it in the sunlight.
At first she found it difficult,
but over time she grew accustomed to it.
In mid-June,
the table and desk were scorching to the touch,
yet the child played and read,
showing no sign of complaint.
The child was very intelligent,
finishing half a scroll daily,
and at night she would lie foot-to-foot with her uncle,
constantly reciting from memory.
Her uncle was greatly comforted.
Also, because he never forgot Xiāngqún,
he no longer entertained
thoughts of
"Yàn Lóu".
One day,
two matchmakers came to discuss a marriage for Āxiǎo.
There was no one to manage the household,
and his heart was very anxious.
Suddenly, Gān Sǎo came in from outside and said,
"Uncle, don't be offended,
I have brought Xiāngqún.
It's because the maid doesn't know shame,
that I deliberately humiliated her.
You are such an outstanding man,
and yet she doesn't follow you,
whom else would she be pleased to follow?"
He saw Xiāngqún standing behind her,
and his heart was greatly pleased.
He seated his sister-in-law respectfully;
explained that he had guests in the hall,
and then hurried out.
A short while later, he re-entered,
and Gān Shì had already left.
Xiāngqún removed her makeup and went to the kitchen,
the sounds of knife and chopping board filling the air.
Soon after, a spread of dishes was presented,
cooked perfectly.
After the guests left,
Zhòng entered,
and saw Xiāngqún sitting in the room, elegantly made up.
So they exchanged bows and were married.
That evening,
the woman still wanted to sleep with Āxiǎo.
Zhòng said:
"I want to warm her with my yang energy;
she cannot be separated."
He therefore placed the woman in a separate room,
and only in the evening would they share a cup of wine and enjoy each other's company.
Xiāngqún cared for his former child as if she were her own,
and Zhòng thought her even more virtuous.
One night,
as the couple conversed intimately,
Zhòng playfully asked:
"Are there beauties in the netherworld?"
The woman thought for a long time,
and then replied:
"I haven't seen any.
Only a neighboring girl, Wēi Língxiān,
is considered beautiful by all;
but her appearance is still like a human's,
she just knows how to adorn herself well.
I spent the longest time with her,
and secretly despised her flirtatiousness.
If you wish to see her,
I can bring her instantly.
However, people like her
should not be provoked."
Zhòng eagerly wanted to see her.
The woman picked up a brush as if to write a letter,
but then threw down the brush and said:
"No,
no!"
He urged her repeatedly,
four times,
and then she said:
"Don't be led astray."
Zhòng assented.
Then he tore paper and made several drawings like talismans,
and burned them outside the door.
A short while later,
the curtain moved and the hooks jingled,
and giggling sounds were heard.
The woman rose and led him in.
Her high topknot was like a cloud;
she was almost like a figure in a painting.
She helped him sit on the bed,
and they poured wine and spoke of their separation.
When she first saw Zhòng,
she still covered her mouth with her red sleeve,
and did not speak very freely;
after a few cups,
she became playful and unrestrained,
gradually stretching a foot to press down on Zhòng's clothes.
Zhòng's heart was in a daze,
he didn't know where his soul had gone.
At that moment, only Xiāngqún was in the way;
Xiāngqún, moreover, deliberately guarded against her,
not leaving his side for a moment.
Wēilíngxiān suddenly rose,
pulled back the curtain and went out;
Xiāngqún followed her,
and urged Zhòng to follow as well.
Wēilíngxiān grasped Zhòng's hand,
and hurried into another room.
Xiāngqún was very resentful,
but there was nothing she could do.
She returned to her room in anger,
and just listened to what they were doing.
Afterwards, when Zhòng entered,
Xiāngqún scolded him, saying:
"You don't listen to my words.
Later, I fear you won't be able to get rid of her."
Zhòng suspected she was jealous,
and dispersed unhappily.
The next evening,
Wēilíngxiān came without being summoned.
Xiāngqún greatly disliked seeing her,
and haughtily offered no greeting;
the fairy, nevertheless, went away with Zhòng.
This continued for several evenings.
When the woman (Xiāngqún) saw her come,
she would revile and insult her,
but still could not get rid of her.
More than a month later,
Zhòng fell ill and could not get up.
He then greatly regretted it,
and called Xiāngqún to sleep with him,
hoping to avoid her (Wēilíngxiān).
If the guard slackened slightly day or night,
the human and the ghost were already on the "sunny terrace".
Xiāngqún wielded a staff to drive her away,
the ghost angrily contended with her,
Xiāngqún was weak,
and her hands and feet were all injured by her.
Zhòng gradually became gravely ill.
Xiāngqún wept, saying:
"How can I face my elder sister now!"
A few more days passed,
and Zhòng died peacefully.
At first, he saw two attendants holding official documents enter.
He unconsciously followed them.
When they reached the road, he realized he had no money for the journey.
He invited the attendants to take a detour to his elder brother's place.
His elder brother saw him,
was shocked and turned pale,
and asked:
"What have you been doing recently, younger brother?"
Zhòng replied:
"Nothing much,
just a ghost illness."
He told him the truth.
His elder brother said:
"That's right."
Then he took out a packet of silver,
and said to the attendants:
"Please accept this with a smile.
My younger brother's crime does not warrant death,
please release him to return.
I will send my humble son to go with you,
and perhaps there will be no disharmony."
He then called Ādà to drink with the attendants.
He turned back and entered the house,
telling everyone the story.
Then he ordered Gān-shì to call Wēilíngxiān from next door.
She arrived shortly,
and seeing Zhòng, tried to flee.
The elder brother seized her, dragged her back, and cursed, saying:
"You lewd wench!
Living, you were a dissolute woman;
dead, you are a despicable ghost.
You have long been disdained by the common folk;
and now you're plaguing my younger brother!"
He immediately slapped her,
her cloud-like hair flew wildly,
and her demonic charm instantly diminished.
After a while,
an old woman came,
prostrating herself on the ground and pleading sorrowfully.
The elder brother again chastised the old woman for allowing her daughter to engage in promiscuity,
scolding and reviling her for a long time,
before finally allowing her and the girl to leave together.
The elder brother then sent Zhòng out.
In a flash, they had already reached his home,
and went straight to the bedroom.
He suddenly awoke as if from a dream,
and only then realized he had just been dead.
The elder brother scolded Xiāngqún, saying:
"Your elder sister and I,
thought you were virtuous and capable,
and so we let you accompany my younger brother;
but instead you wish to hasten my younger brother's death!
If it weren't for the impropriety of our relationship (as in-laws),
I would surely whip you!"
Xiāngqún was ashamed, fearful, and sobbed,
bowing down to thank the elder brother.
The elder brother looked at Āxiǎo and said happily:
"My child is actually a living person again!"
Xiāngqún wanted to go out and prepare millet,
but the elder brother declined, saying,
"My younger brother's matter is not yet settled,
I don't have time."
Āxiǎo was thirteen years old.
He gradually came to miss his father: seeing his father leave,
he shed tears and followed him.
His father said:
"Following your uncle is the most enjoyable thing.
I'm just leaving and will return."
He turned and departed,
and from then on, there was no more news from him.
Later, Āxiǎo married,
and had a son,
who also died at the age of thirty.
Zhòng raised his orphan,
as if he were his nephew from birth.
When Zhòng was eighty years old,
his son was already over twenty,
so he divided the family.
Xiāngqún had no children.
One day,
she said to Zhòng:
"May I go ahead and drive away the foxes in the underworld?"
She put on heavy makeup, lay on the bed, and died.
Zhòng also did not grieve.
Half a year later, he also died.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"How many people in the world have such fraternal love as Zhòng's elder brother!
How many indeed!
It is fitting that he did not die and his years were extended.
The Yang line was broken, but the Yin line succeeded.
This was all due to the sincere heart of the elder brother who could not bear his death;
among humans, there is no such principle,
but how could heaven not have such a destiny?
Giving birth to a son in the underworld,
those who wish to continue the ancestral line,
I imagine are not few: but I fear that virtuous elder brothers and younger brothers who inherit from those without heirs
would not be willing to take them in and care for them!"
According to the manuscript version of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain person from Húnán,
could recall three past lives.
In one life, he was a Lìngyǐn,
serving as an examiner for the imperial examinations.
A renowned scholar, Xīng Gàn Táng, was dismissed,
and died in anger and frustration,
then went to the underworld to file a complaint.
Once this petition was submitted,
tens of thousands of others who had died from the same grievance
nominated Xīng as their leader,
gathering in crowds.
The certain person was arrested,
and brought to confront Xīng.
King Yánluó then asked:
"Since you, Mǒu, were judging the essays,
how could you reject excellent scholars and promote mediocre ones?"
Mǒu defended himself, saying:
"There was a chief examiner above me;
I merely followed his instructions."
Yánluó immediately issued a summons
to apprehend the chief examiner.
After some time,
he was brought in.
Yánluó then recounted Mǒu's words.
The chief examiner said:
"I merely oversaw the overall process;
though there might have been excellent essays,
if the section examiners did not recommend them,
how could I have seen them?"
Yánluó said:
"You cannot shirk responsibility from each other;
your dereliction of duty is the same,
and you both deserve to be flogged."
Just as the punishment was about to be administered,
Xīng was not satisfied,
and let out a piercing cry;
all the ghosts on the two platforms
joined in with a myriad of voices.
Yánluó asked the reason,
and Xīng defiantly said:
"Flogging is too light a punishment;
they must have their eyes gouged out,
as retribution for not recognizing good writing."
Yánluó was unwilling,
but the crowd's shouting grew more intense.
Yánluó said:
"They did not dislike good writing;
it's just that their vision was narrow."
The crowd then requested to have their hearts cut open.
Yánluó, having no choice,
ordered his attendants to strip off their robes,
and with a white blade, to carve open their chests.
Both men bled and screamed.
Only then did the crowd feel greatly satisfied,
and they all said:
"We, who have been suppressed in the underworld,
have never been able to vent our anger like this;
now that we have Mr. Xīng,
all our resentments have dissipated."
They then dispersed noisily.
After Mǒu's chest was carved open,
he was sent to Shǎnxī to be born as the son of a commoner.
When he was a little over twenty years old,
there was a great uprising of local bandits,
and he was caught among the rebels.
A military patrol was sent to suppress the bandits,
and captured many,
with Mǒu among them.
He still inwardly believed he was not a bandit,
hoping to be identified and released.
When he saw the official in the hall,
who was also a little over twenty years old,
he looked closely
and realized it was Xīng.
Startled, he exclaimed:
"My time has come!"
Soon, all the captives were released,
but Mǒu was the last to arrive,
and was given no chance to explain;
he was simply executed.
Mǒu went to the underworld to file a complaint against Xīng.
Yánluó did not immediately apprehend Xīng,
waiting for his allocated lifespan to end.
Thirty years later,
Xīng finally arrived,
and they confronted each other.
Xīng was punished for wantonly taking human lives
and condemned to be reborn as an animal.
Considering Mǒu's actions,
he had once beaten his parents,
so his crime was equally severe.
Fearing retribution in his next life, Mǒu
requested to be a large animal.
Yánluó sentenced Mǒu to be a large dog,
and Xīng to be a small dog.
Mǒu was born in a market stall in the northern part of Shùntiān Fǔ.
One day,
as he lay in the street,
a traveler came from the south,
carrying a golden-haired dog,
as large as a civet.
Mǒu looked at it
and realized it was Xīng.
He resented its small size
and bit it.
The small dog bit Mǒu's throat,
hanging there like a bell;
the large dog struggled, yelped, and fled.
The market people tried to separate them but could not,
and soon both died.
They both arrived at the underworld,
and engaged in mutual dispute.
Yánluó said:
"When will this cycle of vengeance ever end?
Let me resolve it for you two."
He then ruled that Xīng would be Mǒu's son-in-law in the next life.
Mǒu was born in Qìngyún,
and passed the provincial examination at twenty-eight.
He had a daughter,
who was refined, quiet, and beautiful,
and prominent families vied to propose marriage.
Mǒu refused them all.
One day, he happened to pass through a neighboring prefecture
and encountered the education commissioner dismissing students.
The top-ranked student had the surname Lǐ—
it was actually Xīng.
Mǒu then invited him to his inn
and treated him with great generosity.
When he inquired about Lǐ's family,
he found that Lǐ had no wife,
so they arranged a marriage.
Everyone said Mǒu was appreciative of talent,
but they did not know there was a past cause.
After Lǐ married his daughter and took her away,
they were very happy together.
However, the son-in-law, relying on his talent, often insulted his father-in-law,
and would often not visit his gate for years.
The father-in-law endured it.
Later, the son-in-law struggled and faced setbacks in middle age,
unable to succeed.
The father-in-law devised countless schemes to help him,
and only then did he achieve his ambitions in the examinations.
From then on, they were as harmonious as father and son.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"One dismissal led to three lives of unresolved conflict;
such was the extreme depth of their resentment!
Yánluó's mediation was indeed good;
however, with thousands of people on the platforms,
if things are so tumultuous,
are not all beloved sons-in-law in this world
also those who wailed and cried out in the underworld?"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Shí Tàipú,
a native of Tàishān,
was fond of the art of exorcism.
A Daoist priest met him
and, appreciating his intelligence,
accepted him as a disciple.
The priest opened his scroll box
and took out two volumes—the upper volume for expelling fox spirits,
the lower volume for expelling ghosts.
He then gave Shí the lower volume,
saying:
"Devoutly follow this book,
and you will have fine clothes, food, and beautiful women."
When asked his name,
he replied:
"I am Wáng Chìchéng from the Yuándì Guàn in Bìanchéng Běicūn."
He stayed for several days,
imparting all his secrets.
Shí thereby became skilled in talismans and incantations,
and those who offered gifts came in continuous streams to his door.
One day,
an old man came,
calling himself Wēng (Wēng 翁) by surname.
He displayed wealth of silks and coins,
saying that his daughter, Hóngtíng (Hóngtíng 紅亭), was critically ill with a ghost ailment,
and earnestly requested Shí (Shí 石) to visit her in person.
Shí (Shí 石), hearing of the critical illness,
refused to accept any gifts,
and simply went with him.
After more than ten *lǐ* (lǐ 里),
they entered a mountain village
and arrived at his house.
The corridors and chambers were splendid.
Entering the room,
he saw a young girl lying within a gauze canopy.
A maid used a hook to hang the canopy.
Looking at her,
she appeared to be about fourteen or fifteen years old,
her limbs barely clinging to the bed,
her face already withered.
As he approached her,
she suddenly opened her eyes and said,
"The good physician has arrived."
The whole family rejoiced,
saying that she had not spoken for several days.
Shí (Shí 石) then went out
and inquired about the symptoms.
The old man said,
"During the daytime, a young man comes
and sleeps with her.
When we try to catch him, he disappears.
After a short while, he returns.
We suspect it is a ghost."
Shí (Shí 石) said,
"If it is a ghost,
it is not difficult to exorcise.
But I fear it might be a fox spirit,
in which case I would not dare to meddle."
The old man said,
"Certainly not, certainly not."
Shí (Shí 石) gave him a talisman
and stayed at their house that night.
In the middle of the night,
a young man entered,
his attire neat and proper.
Shí (Shí 石) suspected he was a family member of the host
and rose to question him.
He said,
"I am a ghost.
Wēng's (Wēng 翁) family are all foxes.
I happened to be charmed by his daughter Hóngtíng (Hóngtíng 紅亭),
so I merely stayed here.
A ghost is troubled by a fox,
and the *yīnzì* (yīnzì 陰騭) (divine retribution for hidden good deeds) is not harmed.
Why must you sever human bonds to protect them?
The girl's elder sister, Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭),
is exceptionally beautiful and radiant.
I respectfully leave her untouched,
awaiting a worthy sage.
If she agrees to a marriage proposal,
only then can you treat her;
at that time, I will depart on my own."
Shí (Shí 石) agreed.
That night,
the young man did not return,
and the girl suddenly awoke.
At dawn,
the old man was delighted
and informed Shí (Shí 石),
inviting Shí (Shí 石) to come in and examine her.
Shí (Shí 石) burned the old talisman
and then sat down to take her pulse.
He saw a young woman behind the embroidered curtain,
beautiful like a celestial being.
He knew in his heart it was Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭).
After the diagnosis,
he asked for water to sprinkle on the curtain.
The young woman quickly handed him a bowl of water,
and in the midst of her elegant steps,
his heart was stirred and his spirit captivated.
At this moment, Shí (Shí 石)
was utterly distracted from the ghost.
He went out and bade farewell to the old man,
claiming he needed to prepare medicine and left,
not returning for several days.
The ghost became even more rampant.
Aside from Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭),
the sons' wives, maids, and young women
were all seduced and corrupted.
Again, they sent servants and horses to summon Shí (Shí 石),
but Shí (Shí 石) feigned illness and did not go.
The next day,
the old man came in person.
Shí (Shí 石) deliberately feigned a leg injury,
leaning on a cane as he came out.
After the old man bowed and
asked why,
he said,
"This is the hardship of a widower!
The other night, a maid climbed onto my bed,
stumbled and fell,
and scalded both my feet in a basin of hot water."
The old man asked,
"Why have you not remarried for so long?"
Shí (Shí 石) said,
"I regret not finding a respectable family like yours, Wēng (Wēng 翁)."
The old man left in silence.
Shí (Shí 石) hurried to see him off, saying,
"When my illness is cured, I will come myself.
There's no need for your esteemed presence again."
Several more days passed,
and the old man came again.
Shí (Shí 石) met him with a limp.
The old man offered a few words of comfort
and then said,
"I just spoke with my wife,
and if you can drive away the ghost
and bring peace to our entire household,
our younger daughter Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭),
who is seventeen years old,
we are willing to send her to serve you, sir."
Shí (Shí 石) was delighted
and kowtowed to the ground.
Then he said to the old man,
"Since your intention is so noble,
how can my ailing body dare to cherish itself anymore?"
He immediately set out,
and they rode together.
After inspecting all those who were afflicted,
Shí (Shí 石) feared they would break their promise
and asked to make an oath with the old woman.
The old woman quickly came out and said,
"Sir, why do you doubt us?"
She immediately took a golden hairpin that Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭) wore
and gave it to Shí (Shí 石) as a token.
Shí (Shí 石) bowed to it respectfully.
Then he gathered all the family members
and performed exorcisms for them all.
Only Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭) hid so deeply that no trace of her could be found.
So, he wrote a talisman to be worn
and had someone deliver it to her.
That night was utterly quiet,
all ghost shadows vanished.
Only Hóngtíng (Hóngtíng 紅亭) was still moaning.
He gave her consecrated water,
and her ailment disappeared as if it had never been.
Shí (Shí 石) wanted to take his leave,
but the old man earnestly pleaded with him to stay.
By evening,
dishes and fruits were lavishly laid out,
and they toasted each other with great warmth.
After the second watch,
the host finally bid the guest farewell.
As Shí (Shí 石) was just settling into bed,
he heard an urgent knocking at the door.
He rose to look,
and it was Chángtíng (Chángtíng 長亭) hurrying in,
her voice agitated,
saying,
"My family intends to attack you with knives;
you must escape quickly!"
Having said that,
she immediately turned and left.
Shí (Shí 石) was terrified and pale.
He quickly scaled the wall to investigate.
He saw a firelight in the distance,
and rushed towards it,
only to find it was villagers on a night hunt.
He was relieved.
After the hunt was over,
he returned with them.
His heart was filled with resentment and anger,
with nowhere to vent it.
He thought of going to Biàn (Biàn 汴) to find Chìchéng (Chìchéng 赤城),
but his aged father at home
had been ill and disabled for a long time.
He pondered day and night,
unable to decide whether to go or stay.
One day,
a pair of carriages arrived at the gate,
and it was the old couple accompanying Chángtíng [長亭] back.
They said to Shí [石]:
"When you returned that night,
why did you not come again?"
Shí [石] saw Chángtíng [長亭],
and all resentment vanished,
so he also concealed it and did not speak.
The old woman urged the two to perform obeisance in the courtyard.
Shí [石] was about to set a feast,
but they declined, saying:
"We are not idle folk;
we cannot sit and enjoy delicacies.
Our old man at home is confused and muddle-headed.
Should anything be unclear,
it would be a great fortune if you, sir, could think of this old woman for Chángtíng [長亭]'s sake."
They then boarded their carriages and left.
It seems the old woman was unaware of the plot to kill her son-in-law;
it was not until they pursued him in vain and returned
that she learned of it.
She was quite displeased,
and daily quarreled with the old man.
Chángtíng [長亭] also wept and refused to eat.
The old woman strongly insisted on sending her daughter back;
it was not the old man's intention.
When Chángtíng [長亭] entered the house,
Shí [石] questioned her,
and only then understood the reason.
After two or three months,
Chángtíng [長亭]'s family sent for her to visit her parents.
Shí [石] anticipated she would not return,
and forbade her to go.
From that moment, the woman shed tears.
More than a year later,
she bore a son,
named Huì'ér [慧兒],
and a wet nurse was hired to feed him.
However, the child cried often
and always returned to his mother at night.
One day,
Chángtíng [長亭]'s family again sent a carriage,
saying that the old woman missed her daughter greatly.
Chángtíng [長亭] became even more sorrowful,
and Shí [石] could not bear to keep her any longer.
She wanted to take her son with her,
but Shí [石] would not allow it.
Chángtíng [長亭] then went home by herself.
At their parting,
they set a one-month deadline,
but after half a year there was no news.
He sent someone to investigate,
only to find the previously rented house long empty.
Another two years passed,
and all hope was lost;
yet the child cried all night,
and Shí [石]'s heart was torn.
Soon after, Shí [石]'s father fell ill and died,
doubling his grief;
he consequently became debilitated by illness,
lying gravely ill on the mourning mat,
unable to receive condolences from friends.
While he was in a state of confusion,
he suddenly heard a woman crying as she entered.
He looked,
and it was Chángtíng [長亭] in mourning attire.
Shí [石] was greatly grieved,
and fainted from a single cry of sorrow.
The maidservants cried out in alarm,
and the woman stopped weeping.
She caressed him for a long time,
until he gradually revived.
He doubted if he was still alive,
thinking they were reunited in the underworld.
The woman said:
"No.
Your concubine was unfilial,
unable to win the heart of my strict father.
My three-year stay away from home
was truly a betrayal.
It happened that my family members, traveling from the east of the sea, passed through here
and received the sad news of your father.
I obeyed my strict father's command and severed all ties of affection for my child,
not daring to follow a disordered command and lose the propriety due between father-in-law and daughter-in-law.
When I came,
my mother knew, but my father did not."
As she spoke,
the child threw himself into her embrace.
After speaking,
she finally caressed him,
and weeping, said:
"I have a father,
but my child has no mother!"
The child also wailed loudly,
and the entire room wept silently.
The woman rose,
managed the household affairs,
and ensured that offerings for the coffin were prepared cleanly and abundantly.
Shí [石] was greatly comforted.
But having been ill for a long time,
he could not get up quickly.
The woman then asked Shí [石]'s elder maternal cousin to courteously entertain the mourners.
After the mourning period concluded,
Shí [石] was finally able to get up with a staff,
and together they arranged for the rituals and burial.
After the burial,
the woman wished to take her leave and return home,
to accept the censure for defying her father.
Her husband and son pleaded with cries,
and she reluctantly stayed.
Not long after,
someone came to report her mother's illness.
She then said to Shí [石]:
"I came for your father;
will you not let me go for my mother?"
Shí [石] consented.
The woman had the wet nurse take the child elsewhere,
and departed from the gate, weeping and sniffling.
After she left,
she did not return for several years.
Shí [石] and his son gradually forgot about her.
One day,
at dawn, when he opened the door,
Chángtíng [長亭] floated in.
As Shí [石] was asking in surprise,
the woman sat sadly on the couch,
sighing:
"Having grown up in the women's quarters,
I considered even one *lǐ* [里] as far;
now I have traveled a thousand *lǐ* [里] in a day and a night—
it is perilous indeed!"
When he questioned her closely,
the woman wanted to speak but stopped again.
He kept asking,
and she cried, saying:
"If I tell you now,
what is sorrowful to me,
may be delightful to you.
In recent years, I resided alone in the region of Jìn [晉],
renting a residence from the scholar-gentry Zhào [趙].
The host and guest were on very good terms,
and he married Hóngtíng [紅亭] to his son.
His son frequently squandered money,
and the family was quite unsettled.
My sister returned to tell our father;
our father kept her,
not allowing her to return for half a year.
The son became furious and resentful,
and somehow hired a wicked person
who sent deities to lock up
and bind my old father and take him away.
The entire household was greatly alarmed,
and scattered in an instant."
When Shí [石] heard this,
he could not help but laugh.
The woman angrily said:
"Though he was unkind,
he is my father.
You and I have been husband and wife for several years,
only having mutual affection and no mutual blame.
Today, a person is dead, a family ruined,
and a hundred mouths are scattered.
Even if you do not grieve for my father,
will you not pity me?
To hear this and dance with joy,
without even a word of comfort,
how unjust!"
She flicked her sleeve and left.
Shí [石] pursued her to apologize,
but she was already gone.
He regretted it mournfully,
resigned to the complete break.
After two or three days,
the old woman and her daughter both came.
Shí [石] was delighted and greeted them.
Mother and daughter both knelt down.
Alarmed, he questioned them,
and mother and daughter both wept.
The woman said:
"I left in a fit of pique,
and now I cannot maintain my resolve.
To seek help from others again,
what face do I have left?"
Shí [石] said:
“Your father-in-law is indeed not human;
your mother’s kindness,
and your affection,
I will not forget.
However, hearing of misfortune and rejoicing
is also human nature.
Why could you not bear it for a moment?”
The woman said:
“A moment ago, on the way, I met my mother,
and only then did I learn that the one who imprisoned my father
was indeed your master.”
Shí said:
“If that is truly the case,
it is also very easy.
However, if your father does not return,
then you and your father will be separated;
I fear that if your father returns,
then you will weep for your husband and your son will be saddened.”
The old woman swore to clear herself,
and the woman also vowed to repay him.
Shí then immediately prepared his journey to Biàn,
and inquired until he reached Yuán Dì Guàn,
where Chì Chéng had not long returned.
He entered and paid his respects,
then asked:
“Whence have you come?”
Shí saw an old fox under the kitchen stove,
its front leg pierced and tied.
He smiled and said:
“Your disciple has come
for this old demon.”
Chì Chéng questioned him,
and he replied:
“This is my father-in-law.”
He then told the whole story.
The Daoist priest considered him cunning and deceitful,
and was unwilling to release him lightly.
After repeated pleading,
he finally agreed.
Shí then fully recounted the fox’s deceptions.
When the fox heard this,
it squeezed its body into the stove,
appearing ashamed.
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
“Its sense of shame and hatred
is not entirely lost yet.”
Shí got up,
pulled it out,
and cut the rope with a knife to draw it out.
The fox was in extreme pain,
gnashing its teeth.
Shí did not pull it out quickly,
but rather pushed and pulled it,
smilingly asking:
“You are in pain,
should I not pull it out?”
The fox’s eyes flashed,
appearing to have a look of gratitude.
Once released,
it wagged its tail and left the temple.
Shí took his leave to return home.
Three days prior,
someone had already reported news of the old man.
The old woman had left first,
leaving her daughter to wait for Shí.
When Shí arrived,
the woman met him and prostrated herself.
Shí helped her up, saying:
“If you do not forget our conjugal affection,
there is no need for gratitude.”
The woman said:
“Now we have moved back to our old residence,
the village houses are close,
so communication will not be difficult.
I wish to return home to visit my parents;
I can return in three days.
Do you believe me?”
He said:
“Our son was born without a mother,
he should not die prematurely.
I live in widowed solitude every day,
and have grown accustomed to it.
Now I am not like Zhào Gōngzǐ,
but rather repay kindness.
What I have done for you is complete.
If you do not return,
it will be unrighteous of you.
Though the distance is short,
I will not inquire about you again.
Why would I not believe you?”
The woman left the next day,
and returned on the second day.
He asked:
“Why so fast?”
She replied:
“My father, because you had teased him in Biàn,
has not been able to forget it,
and talked about it incessantly;
I did not wish to hear it again,
so I came back early.”
From then on, their domestic comings and goings were uninterrupted,
but the father-in-law and son-in-law still did not communicate for condolences or congratulations.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
“The fox’s emotions are fickle,
and its trickery is excessive.
The matter of breaking off the engagement,
two daughters with the same approach,
its cunning is evident.
However, to insist on marrying her,
is to have initiated the regret from the very beginning.
Moreover, since the son-in-law loved his daughter and saved her father,
he should have simply set aside past grievances and transformed him with benevolence;
instead, he again made sport of him in a moment of crisis,
how can it be surprising that he would never forget it!
In this world, there are those like ice and jade who cannot get along,
similar to this.”
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì*
Xí Fāngpíng,
a native of Dōng'ān.
His father’s name was Lián,
his nature was dull and clumsy.
Because he had a grievance with a wealthy family named Yáng in the village,
Yáng died first;
several years later,
Lián was critically ill,
and said to people:
“Yáng Mǒu has now bribed the underworld envoy to flog me.”
Soon after, his body became red and swollen,
he cried out and then died.
Xí was grief-stricken and did not eat,
saying:
“My father was simple and honest,
now he is being bullied by a powerful ghost.
I shall go to the underworld
to redress his grievances.”
From then on, he spoke no more,
sometimes sitting, sometimes standing,
appearing foolish,
for his soul had already left his body.
Xí felt himself leaving the door,
not knowing where he was going.
He only saw people on the road
and asked about cities.
After a short while,
he entered a city.
His father had already been taken to prison.
Arriving at the prison gate,
he saw his father lying under the eaves from a distance,
appearing very distraught.
He looked up and saw his son,
and tears streamed down his face,
then he said:
The jailer led him out the north gate,
pointed out the way home,
turned, and departed.
Xí thought that the darkness of the underworld was even worse than that of the human world,
but there was no way to reach the Emperor's ear.
It was said in the world that Guànkǒu Èrláng was a relative of the Emperor,
and that his spirit was intelligent and just;
a plea to him would surely bring a miraculous response.
He secretly rejoiced that the two jailers had left,
and then turned south.
While he was running,
two men caught up to him,
saying:
"The King suspected you would not return,
and now it is indeed so."
They seized him and dragged him back to see the King of the Underworld.
He secretly thought that the King of the Underworld would be even angrier,
and that his misfortune would surely be even worse;
but the King showed no stern expression at all,
and said to Xí:
"Your devotion is sincere.
But your father's wrong
I have already redressed for you.
He has now been reborn into a wealthy family;
what use is your crying out?
Now I will send you home,
and grant you an inheritance of a thousand pieces of gold and a lifespan of one hundred years.
Will your wishes be fulfilled then?"
Then he recorded it in the registry,
affixed a large seal,
and made him witness it with his own eyes.
Xí thanked him and went down.
The ghosts went out with him,
and when they reached the road,
they drove him and cursed him, saying:
"You cunning rogue!
Constantly changing your mind,
making us run ourselves to death!
If you offend again,
we will seize you and put you into a great mill,
and grind you finely!"
Xí opened his eyes and rebuked them, saying:
"What are you ghostlings doing?
My nature can endure knives and saws,
but not floggings and scourges.
Please let me return to see the King.
If the King now allows me to go home by myself,
why bother sending me off?"
Then he ran back.
The two ghosts were frightened,
and spoke gently, persuading him to return.
Xí deliberately walked slowly and haltingly,
taking a few steps,
then resting by the roadside.
The ghosts contained their anger and dared not speak again.
After about half a day,
they arrived at a village.
One gate was ajar.
The ghosts led him to sit together;
Xí then sat on the threshold.
The two ghosts, taking advantage of his unpreparedness,
pushed him through the gate.
When he recovered from his shock and looked at himself,
his body had already been born as an infant.
He cried indignantly and refused to nurse,
and died on the third day.
His soul, swaying and wavering, did not forget Guànkǒu.
After running for several tens of *lǐ*,
he suddenly saw feather canopies approaching,
and banners and halberds arrayed across the road.
He crossed the road to avoid them,
but because he intruded upon the imperial retinue,
he was seized by the vanguard horsemen
and bound and sent before the carriage.
He looked up and saw a young man in the carriage,
of magnificent bearing.
He asked Xí:
"Who are you?"
Xí's injustice and anger had nowhere to be expressed,
and he thought this must be a great official,
who might be able to wield power and influence.
So he tearfully recounted his bitter pain.
The person in the carriage ordered his bonds to be released
and made him follow the carriage.
Soon they arrived at a place where
over ten officials
were waiting to greet them by the roadside.
The person in the carriage exchanged greetings with each of them.
Afterward, he pointed to Xí and said to an official:
"This person is from the lower realm,
and is just about to lodge a complaint.
You should immediately resolve it for him."
Xí inquired of the attendants
and then realized that the person in the carriage was none other than the Níně Wáng, a prince of the Emperor,
and the official he had addressed was Èrláng.
Xí looked at Èrláng:
he was tall and bearded,
unlike what was commonly depicted in the world.
After the Níně Wáng departed,
Xí followed Èrláng to an official's office.
There, his father, along with the person surnamed Yáng and the yá lì, were all present.
A moment later,
prisoners were brought out from a cage cart:
they were the King of the Underworld, the Jùn Sī, and the Chénghuáng.
They confronted each other in the hall;
everything Xí had said was not false.
The three officials trembled,
looking like cowering mice.
Èrláng took up his brush and immediately pronounced judgment;
after a moment,
the judgment was passed down,
ordering all those involved in the case to look at it.
The judgment read:
"My brother has been residing a thousand *lǐ* away,
without even a servant to answer the door.
You, brother and sister, are frail.
How will you make a living?
I think it would be better for you to come with me.
There is a small dwelling where we can live together.
How about it?"
Xúnjiǔ was overjoyed,
and promised to do so after the examinations.
After the examination,
Xúnjiǔ invited the young master to go with him,
saying:
"The Mid-Autumn moon is as bright as day,
and my younger sister, Sùqiū,
has prepared a simple meal with wine.
Please do not disappoint her."
He then pulled him inside.
Sùqiū came out,
exchanged a brief greeting,
and then returned to the inner room,
lowering the curtain to arrange the dishes.
A short while later,
she came out herself to roast the meat.
The young master rose and said:
"Sister has been toiling,
how can I bear it!"
Sùqiū smiled and went back in.
Presently,
she lifted the curtain and came out.
There was a maid in green clothes holding a pot,
and an old woman carrying a tray with cooked fish.
The young master exclaimed in surprise:
"Where did these people come from?
Why didn't they attend to things earlier,
and trouble sister instead?"
Xúnjiǔ smiled faintly and said:
"Sùqiū is playing tricks again."
All they heard was a giggling sound from behind the curtain,
and the young master did not understand why.
Later, when the feast ended,
and the maid and old woman cleared the dishes,
the young master happened to cough
and accidentally dropped some spittle onto the maid's clothes.
The maid fell down with the spittle,
shattering a bowl and spilling the roasted meat.
Upon looking at the maid,
it was a small figure cut from silk,
barely four *cùn* tall.
Xúnjiǔ laughed heartily,
and Qínqiū came out laughing,
picked it up, and left.
Soon after, the maid reappeared,
running around as before.
The young master was greatly astonished.
Xúnjiǔ said:
"This is merely a small trick my sister played when she was young,
divining with Zǐgū."
The young master then asked:
"Both you and your sister have grown up,
why are you not yet married?"
He replied:
"Our ancestors passed away,
and we still have no fixed abode,
hence the delay."
Thereupon, they settled on a date for their departure,
sold the house,
and he took his sister and the young master to the west.
Upon their return,
he provided them with a dwelling;
he also sent a maid to serve them.
The young master's wife,
who was the niece of Hàn Shìláng,
especially doted on Sùqiū,
sharing meals with her.
The young master and Xúnjiǔ also did the same.
And Xúnjiǔ was also exceptionally intelligent,
reading ten lines at a glance,
and when he attempted an essay,
the old masters could not surpass him.
The young master urged him to take the prefectural examination.
Xúnjiǔ said:
"My only reason for pursuing this career
is merely to share your burdens, my lord.
I deem my fortune to be thin,
unfit for official advancement;
moreover, once one enters this path,
one cannot but be anxious about gains and losses,
therefore I shall not pursue it."
After three years,
the young master again failed the examination.
Xúnjiǔ greatly wrung his hands,
and indignantly said:
"A name on the list,
why is it so difficult!
I originally did not wish to be swayed by success or failure,
thus preferring to remain obscure.
Now, seeing that elder brother cannot achieve his aspirations,
I feel a burning passion inside,
and though a nineteen-year-old old student,
I must gallop like a colt."
The young master was delighted,
and sent him to the examination hall on the day of the test.
He came first in the district, prefecture, and circuit examinations.
He then redoubled his efforts with the young master, studying diligently.
The following year, at the *kēshì* (provincial examination),
he was again champion of both the prefecture and district.
Xúnjiǔ's name became very famous,
and people from far and near vied to propose marriage to him,
but Xúnjiǔ rejected them all.
The young master strongly urged him,
and he only agreed to consider it after the examinations.
Not long after,
the examination ended,
and admirers vied to copy his essays,
circulating and praising them.
Xúnjiǔ himself also felt that he was unwilling to be second to anyone.
When the results were announced,
both brothers failed.
At that time, they were drinking together,
and the young master still forced a laugh;
Xúnjiǔ turned pale,
his wine cup dropped,
and he collapsed beneath the table.
They helped him onto the couch,
but he was already critically ill.
He urgently called his sister to him,
opened his eyes and said to the young master:
"Though our affection is like that of siblings,
we are not truly of the same clan.
I feel that I have already entered the register of ghosts.
Having received kindness with nothing to repay,
Sùqiū has grown up,
and since she has been loved and cared for by your wife,
it would be acceptable to make her your concubine."
The young master sternly said:
"This is truly a nonsensical command from my brother!
Would you take me for someone who has the head of a man but the cry of a beast!"
Xúnjiǔ wept.
The young master immediately bought good funeral wood with a large sum of money.
Xúnjiǔ ordered it to be carried in,
and with great effort, despite his illness, he entered
and instructed his sister, saying:
"After I die,
close the coffin immediately,
and allow no one to open it and look."
The young master still wished to speak,
but his eyes had already closed.
The young master grieved,
as if he had lost a limb.
However, he secretly suspected the unusual nature of his instruction.
After Qínqiū had gone out,
he opened it and looked.
The robe and clothing in the coffin were like a shed skin;
when he lifted them,
there was a silverfish, a *chǐ* long,
lying stiff inside.
While he was astonished,
Sùqiū urged him to come,
and sadly said:
"Why is there any estrangement between us, brothers?
The reason for this
is not to avoid you, my brother;
but I fear that if this spreads and becomes known,
I too will not be able to remain here long."
The young master said:
"Propriety arises from human feelings,
and where feelings exist,
what difference does a different clan make?
Do you not know my heart, sister?
Even within my household, no word will be leaked,
please do not worry."
Thereupon, he quickly chose an auspicious date,
and gave him a grand burial.
After several days,
Gōngzǐ sat alone in his study at night.
Sùqiū, accompanied by an old woman,
suddenly entered.
Gōngzǐ, startled, asked,
"Is younger sister truly unharmed?"
She smiled and said,
"The python transformation was just a small trick of your younger sister.
That night, I snuck into the house of a xiùcai,
and stayed with his mother.
He himself said he knows you,
and is now outside the gate.
Please invite him in."
Gōngzǐ rushed out,
and by candlelight,
saw it was none other than
Zhōu Shēng,
a renowned scholar from Wǎnpíng,
with whom Gōngzǐ had long been on good terms.
They clasped hands and entered the study,
where their conversation was most cordial.
After a long discussion,
Gōngzǐ finally learned the whole story.
Initially,
Sùqiū arrived at Zhōu Shēng’s gate at dawn.
His mother took her in,
and questioned her.
Upon learning she was Gōngzǐ’s sister,
she immediately wanted to send a message.
Sùqiū stopped her,
and stayed with the mother.
Intelligent and understanding,
she pleased the mother.
As the son had no wife,
the mother secretly took a liking to Sùqiū,
and hinted at it.
Sùqiū declined, citing that she had not yet received her brother's command.
Zhōu Shēng, too, valuing his friendship with Gōngzǐ,
was unwilling to form a match without a matchmaker,
but frequently made inquiries.
When it was known that the lawsuit had been settled,
Sùqiū told the mother she wished to return.
The mother dispatched Zhōu Shēng to escort her with an old woman,
and instructed the old woman to act as a matchmaker.
Gōngzǐ, having known Sùqiū had stayed at Zhōu Shēng's house for a long time,
secretly had an idea but hadn't spoken it;
upon hearing the old woman's words,
he was greatly pleased,
and immediately agreed to the match with Zhōu Shēng face-to-face.
Earlier,
Sùqiū had returned that night
intending to announce her return after Gōngzǐ had received the gold.
Gōngzǐ refused,
saying:
"I was angry and had no outlet,
so I sought gold to ruin them.
Now that I see my sister again,
how can ten thousand pieces of gold compare!"
He immediately sent word to both families,
and dropped the lawsuit.
He also considered that Zhōu Shēng’s family was not very wealthy,
the journey was long,
and a personal escort would be difficult.
Therefore, he moved Zhōu Shēng's mother to his side,
and lodged her in Xún Jiǔ's old residence;
Zhōu Shēng also prepared betrothal gifts, drums, and music,
and the wedding ceremony was performed.
One day,
Gōngzǐ's wife teased Sùqiū,
"Now that you have a new husband,
do you still recall the affections of the pillow and mat from years past?"
Sùqiū smiled,
then looked at her maid and said,
"Do you recall?"
Gōngzǐ's wife did not understand,
and pressed her with questions.
It turned out that for three years in bed,
she had always used the maid as a substitute.
Each night,
she would use a brush to draw two eyebrows on the maid,
send her away,
then sit alone by candlelight,
and the husband never discerned it.
Gōngzǐ's wife was even more astonished,
and asked for her technique,
but Sùqiū only smiled and said nothing.
The following year was the grand imperial examination,
and Zhōu Shēng intended to go with Gōngzǐ.
Sùqiū said,
"There's no need."
Gōngzǐ insisted on taking him along.
In that examination,
Gōngzǐ passed,
while Zhōu Shēng failed and returned home,
secretly entertaining thoughts of retirement.
A year later,
his mother passed away,
and he no longer spoke of pursuing advancement.
One day,
Sùqiū told Gōngzǐ's wife,
"You once asked me about my technique,
but I was unwilling to startle people with it.
Now, a long departure is imminent,
the day is set.
Please allow me to secretly impart it to you;
it can also help you avoid the ravages of war."
Gōngzǐ's wife was startled and asked her.
She replied,
"In three years,
this place will be uninhabited.
I am too frail to endure such terror,
and will hide by the seashore.
Elder Brother is destined for wealth and honor,
so I cannot accompany him,
hence this farewell."
She then taught all her techniques to Gōngzǐ's wife.
A few days later,
she informed Gōngzǐ.
He tried to make her stay,
even shedding tears,
and asked,
"Where are you going?"
But she also said nothing.
At cockcrow, she rose early,
took a white-bearded servant,
mounted two guards, and departed.
Gōngzǐ secretly sent someone to follow and escort her.
Upon reaching the border of Jiāocài,
dust and mist obscured the sky.
When it cleared,
they had already lost sight of where she went.
Three years later,
Chǎngkòu rebels attacked,
and the villages became ruins.
Hán Fūrén cut silk and placed it inside her gate.
When the rebels arrived,
they saw clouds surrounding a Wéituó statue more than ten feet high,
and were frightened away,
thus preserving her safety.
Later, a merchant from the village went to the seaside
and met an old man who resembled the old servant,
but whose beard and hair were completely black,
so he suddenly couldn't recognize him.
The old man stopped and smiled,
"Is my young master still well?
Please tell him for me: Aunt Qiū is also very peaceful and happy."
When asked where he lived,
he replied,
"Far, far away!"
He then hastily departed.
When Gōngzǐ heard of this,
he sent people to search everywhere she might be,
but no trace was found.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The scholar [literally, 'Master Guan City,' referring to a brush, here symbolizing a scholar] has no meat-eating appearance [i.e., lacks official ambition],
this has been true for a long time.
His initial intention was very clear,
but then he did not hold firm to it.
How could he know that the muddle-headed chief examiner
valued fate, not literature?
One strike, and he missed,
then silently died.
The foolishness of the bookworm,
how truly pitiful!
Alas for the soaring phoenix,
it is better to lie low like the hen."
Based on the missing text from the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, supplemented by the text from the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript.
Jiǎ Fèngwéi,
a native of Píngliáng,
was celebrated for his talent and literary reputation in his time,
yet always failed in the examinations.
One day,
on the road, he met a scholar
who introduced himself with the surname Láng.
His demeanor was refined,
and his words subtle but insightful.
Jiǎ therefore invited him back home
and presented his examination essays for correction.
After Láng read them,
he did not praise them much,
saying:
“Your essays,
for a minor examination, are more than sufficient to take first place,
but for the imperial examination hall, they are insufficient even to be at the bottom of the list.”
Jiǎ asked:
“What then?”
Láng replied:
“In the affairs of the world,
reaching high makes things difficult,
but stooping to accommodate makes things very easy.
Why should I, an unworthy person, need to tell you this!”
Then he pointed to one or two individuals and one or two essays as standards,
which were largely those Jiǎ despised and disdained to mention.
Hearing this, Jiǎ laughed and said:
“When scholars establish their words,
it is precious for them to be immortal.
Even if the taste ranks among the eight delicacies,
it should be such that the world does not consider it extravagant.
To hunt for fame and fortune in this manner,
even if one ascends to high office,
is still ignoble.”
Láng said:
“Not so.
Although an essay may be beautiful,
if it is ignoble, it will not be transmitted.
If you wish to hug your scrolls until the end, then so be it;
otherwise,
the officials behind the screen [of the examination hall]
all advanced themselves with such material,
and I fear they cannot, upon reading your essays,
suddenly change their eyes and hearts.”
Jiǎ remained silent.
Láng rose, laughed, and said:
“Such youthful vigor!”
Then he took his leave.
That autumn, Jiǎ entered the examination again and failed,
feeling vexed and unfulfilled.
He quite thought of Láng’s words,
so he took what had been indicated before and forced himself to read it.
Before finishing the essay,
he felt drowsy and dizzy,
his heart bewildered and beyond his control.
Three more years passed,
and as the imperial examination hall approached,
Láng suddenly arrived,
and they met with great joy.
Láng presented seven proposed topics
and had Jiǎ compose essays on them.
The next day,
he asked for the essays and read them,
not considering them acceptable,
and ordered him to write them again;
after they were written,
he criticized them again.
Jiǎ, jesting, took phrases from his discarded drafts,
collected their superfluous, overly effusive, and unmentionable sentences,
strung them into an essay,
and waited for Láng to come and show it to him.
Láng was delighted and said:
“You’ve got it!”
He then made him memorize it thoroughly,
insisting he not forget it.
Jiǎ laughed and said:
“To be honest, these words do not come from my heart,
they will vanish in an instant;
even if subjected to torture,
I won’t be able to recall them.”
Láng sat at the desk
and strongly made him recite it once;
then he had him bare his back,
wrote a talisman with a brush, and left,
saying:
“This alone is enough;
you can put all your other books aside.”
When Jiǎ examined the talisman,
washing could not remove it;
it had penetrated deep into his skin.
When he arrived at the examination hall,
not a single one of the seven topics was missed.
Recalling his previous compositions,
he remembered nothing clearly,
only the essay he had strung together playfully
was clear in his mind.
However, holding the brush, he still felt ashamed;
he wanted to make minor alterations,
but no matter how hard he thought and deliberated,
he couldn’t change a single word.
The sun had already set in the west,
so he copied it directly and came out.
Láng had been waiting for him for a long time
and asked:
“Why are you so late?”
Jiǎ told him the truth
and immediately asked to wipe off the talisman;
he looked at it,
and it had already faded away.
Recalling the essay from the hall,
it now felt like something from another life.
He found it extremely strange
and asked:
“Why don’t you make plans for yourself?”
Láng laughed and said:
“It is precisely because I don’t entertain such thoughts
that I am able not to read such essays.”
Then he agreed to visit his lodging the next day.
Jiǎ assented.
After Láng left,
Jiǎ took his essay draft and read it himself.
It was far from his original intention,
and he felt displeased and discontented,
so he did not visit Láng again
