and returned home dejected.
Not long after,
the results were posted,
and he actually passed as the top scholar in the classics.
He then reviewed his old draft again.
Each time he read, he broke a sweat;
after finishing,
his heavy clothes were completely soaked.
He said to himself:
“With this essay published,
how can I face the scholars of the world!”
Just as he was feeling ashamed and restless,
Láng suddenly arrived
and said:
“Since you sought success and achieved it,
why are you so unhappy?”
Jiǎ said:
“I was just thinking to myself
that putting dog excrement in a golden basin and jade bowl
truly makes me ashamed to face my peers.
I will soon go into hiding in the mountains and hills,
and forever cut myself off from the world.”
Láng said:
“This is also very noble,
but I fear you cannot do it.
If you can truly do it,
I will introduce you to someone,
and you can attain immortality;
even a thousand years of fame
would not be worth clinging to,
let alone transient wealth and honor!”
Jiǎ was pleased
and kept Láng to stay the night with him,
saying:
“Allow me to consider it.”
At dawn,
he said to Láng:
“My mind is made up!”
Without telling his wife and children,
he departed freely and without a trace.
Gradually he entered deep mountains,
and arrived at a cave dwelling.
Inside, there was a world of its own.
An old man (sǒu) sat in the hall.
A young man (láng) had him pay respects,
and called him Master (shī).
The old man said:
"Why have you come so early?"
The young man said:
"This person's devotion to the Dao (dàoniàn) is already firm.
I hope you will take him in."
The old man said:
"Since you have come,
you must cast this body aside and beyond your concerns
to succeed."
Jiǎ merely assented and obeyed.
The young man led him to a courtyard,
arranged his sleeping quarters,
and gave him some food,
before leaving.
The room was also clean and tidy;
but the door had no leaves,
the window no lattices,
and inside there was only one table and one couch.
Jiǎ removed his shoes and climbed onto the couch.
The moonlight shone through;
he felt a faint hunger,
took the food and ate it.
It was sweet and easily satiating.
He secretly thought the young man would return.
He sat for a long time in silence,
without a sound,
but felt a clear fragrance filling the room,
his internal organs empty and clear,
and his veins and arteries all enumerable.
Suddenly, he heard a very harsh sound,
like a cat scratching.
He peered through the window,
and there was a tiger crouching beneath the wall.
At first sight,
he was very alarmed;
but remembering his Master's words,
he immediately composed himself and sat still.
The tiger seemed to know there was someone there,
and soon came near the couch,
panting,
sniffing his feet and legs all over.
A moment later,
he heard a howl in the courtyard,
like a chicken being tied up,
and the tiger immediately rushed out.
He sat for a little while longer,
when a beautiful woman entered,
her perfume (lánshè) assailing him.
She quietly ascended the couch,
and whispered in his ear:
"I have come."
With that one word,
the fragrance of her lip rouge diffused.
Jiǎ feigned sleep and did not stir at all.
She then whispered again:
"Are you asleep?"
Her voice was quite like his wife's,
and his heart stirred slightly.
He thought again:
"This is all a Master's (shī) illusory technique to test me."
He feigned sleep as before.
The beautiful woman laughed and said:
"The little mouse (shǔzi) has moved!"
Previously,
he and his wife shared a room with a maid,
and for their intimacy, they were afraid the maid would hear.
They privately agreed on a riddle:
"If the little mouse moves,
then we will enjoy each other."
Suddenly hearing these words,
he could not help but be greatly moved.
He opened his eyes and gazed intently.
It was truly his wife.
He asked:
"How were you able to come?"
She replied:
"Young Master (Láng Shēng) feared you would be lonely and wish to return home,
so he sent an old woman (yù) to guide me here."
While speaking,
because Jiǎ had left without telling her,
as they nestled together,
she showed quite a bit of resentment.
Jiǎ comforted her for a long time
before they began to laugh and enjoy themselves.
After they finished,
night was already turning to dawn.
He heard the old man (sǒu) scolding loudly,
gradually approaching the courtyard.
His wife quickly got up,
with no place to hide herself,
so she climbed over the low wall and left.
A moment later,
the young man (láng) entered with the old man (sǒu).
The old man (sǒu) caned the young man (láng) in front of Jiǎ,
and then ordered the guest to be expelled.
The young man (láng) also led Jiǎ out through the low wall,
saying:
"I expected too much of you,
and could not avoid being impetuous;
I did not anticipate that your emotional ties were not yet severed,
causing me to be beaten and punished repeatedly.
For now, depart,
and we shall meet again another day."
He pointed out the way home,
cupped his hands, and they parted.
Jiǎ俯視故村，
故在目中。
意妻弱步 ，
必滯途間。
疾趨里餘，
已至家門，
但見房垣零落，
舊景全非，
村中老幼，
竟無一相識者，
心始駭異。
忽念劉、阮返自天台 ，
情景真似。
不敢入門，
於對戶憩坐。
良久，
有老翁曳杖出。
賈揖之，
問：
「賈某蒙何所？ 」
翁指其第曰：
「此即是也。
得無慾問奇事耶？
僕悉知之。
相傳此公聞捷即遁 ；
遁時，
其子才七八歲，
後至十四五歲，
母忽大睡不醒。
子在時，
寒暑為之易衣；
迨歿 ，
兩孫窮踧 ，
房舍拆毀，
惟以木架苫覆蔽之 。
月前，
夫人忽醒，
屈指百餘年矣。
遠近聞其異，
皆來訪視，
近日稍稀矣。 」
Jiǎ豁然頓悟，
曰：
「翁不知賈奉雉即某是也。 」
翁大駭，
走報其家。
時長孫已死；
次孫 Xiáng至，
五十餘矣。
以賈年少，
疑有詐偽。
少間，
夫人出，
始識之。
雙涕霪霪 ，
呼與俱去。
苦無屋宇，
暫入孫捨。
大小男婦，
奔入盈側，
皆其曾、玄 ，
率陋劣少文。
長孫婦 Wú氏，
沽酒具藜藿；
又使少子 Gǎo及婦，
與已共室，
除捨捨祖翁姑。
賈入捨，
煙埃兒溺，
雜氣熏人。
居數曰；
懊惋殊不可耐。
兩孫家分供餐飲，
調飪尤乖 。
裡中以賈新歸，
日日招飲；
而夫人恆不得一飽。
Wú氏故士人女，
頗嫻閨訓 ，
承順不衰。
Xiáng家給奉漸疏，
或呼爾與之 。
賈怒，
攜夫人去，
設帳東裡。
每謂夫人曰：
「吾甚悔此一返，
而已無及矣。
不得已，
復理舊業，
若心無愧恥，
富貴不難致也。 」
居年餘，
Wú氏猶時饋餉，
而 Xiáng父子絕跡矣。
是歲，
試入邑癢 。
邑令重其文，
厚贈之，
由此家稍裕。
Xiáng稍稍來近就之。
賈喚入，
計曩所耗費，
出金儈之，
斥絕令去。
遂買新第，
移 Wú氏共居之。
Wú二子，
長者留守舊業；
次呆頗慧，
使與門人輩共筆硯 。
賈自山中歸，
心思益明澈，
遂連捷登進士第 。
又數年，
以侍御出巡兩浙 ，
聲名赫奕 ，
歌舞樓台，
一時稱盛。
賈為人鯁峭 ，
不避權貴，
朝中大僚，
思中傷之。
賈屢疏恬退 ，
未蒙俞旨 ，
未幾而禍作矣。
先是，
Xiáng六子皆無賴，
賈雖擯斥不齒 ，
然皆竊餘勢以作威福，
橫占田宅，
鄉人共患之。
有某乙娶新婦，
Xiáng次子篡娶為妾 。
乙故狙詐，
鄉人斂金助訟，
以此聞於都。
當道交章攻賈 。
賈殊無以自剖，
被收經年。
樣及次子皆瘐死。
賈奉旨充遼陽軍 。
時 Gǎo入泮已久，
為人頗仁厚，
有賢聲。
夫人生一子，
年十六，
遂以屬 Gǎo，
夫妻攜一僕一媼而去。
賈曰：
「十餘年富貴，
曾不如一夢之久。
今始知榮華之場，
皆地獄境界，
悔比劉晨、阮肇，
多造一重孽案耳 。 」
數日抵海岸，
遙見巨舟來，
鼓樂殷作 ，
虞候皆如天神 。
既近，
舟中一人出，
笑請侍御過舟少憩。
賈見驚喜，
踴身而過，
押隸不敢禁 。
夫人急欲相從，
而相去已遠，
遂憤投海中。
漂泊數步，
見一人垂練於水，
引救而去。
隸命篙師盪舟 ，
且追且號，
但聞鼓聲如雷，
與轟濤相間，
瞬間遂杏。
僕識其人，
蓋郎生也。
異史氏曰：
「世傳陳大士在闈中 ，
書藝既成：吟誦數四，
嘆曰： 『亦復誰人識得！ 』
遂棄去更作 ，
以故闈墨不及諸稿 。
賈生羞而遁去，
此處有仙骨焉 。
乃再返人世，
遂以口腹自貶 ，
貧賤之中人甚矣哉： ！ 」
據《聊齋誌異》手稿本
In Dōngchāng, the Biàn
family, who were cattle doctors,
had a daughter whose given name was Yānzhī.
She was talented, beautiful, and intelligent.
Her father doted on her,
wishing to marry her into a prominent family,
but the aristocratic families disdained their humble origins
and were unwilling to form an alliance.
For this reason, she remained unmarried by the time she was of age.
The wife of the Gōng family next door, surnamed Wáng,
was frivolous and fond of joking.
She was Yānzhī's confidante in the women's quarters.
One day,
as Wáng was seeing Yānzhī to the door,
they saw a young man passing by.
He was dressed in white robes and a cap,
and his demeanor was very handsome.
Yānzhī's heart seemed to stir,
and her beautiful eyes lingered on him.
The young man bowed his head and hurried away.
After he had gone far,
Yānzhī still gazed fixedly.
Wáng perceived her feelings
and teased her, saying,
"With your talent and beauty,
if you could be matched with such a man,
you would surely have no regrets."
Yānzhī's cheeks flushed red,
and she remained silent, full of emotion.
Wáng asked,
"Do you know this young man?"
Yānzhī said,
"No, I don't."
Wáng said,
"This is Ōu Xiùcai Qiūzhǔn from South Lane,
the son of the late Xiàolián.
I used to live in the same neighborhood as him,
so I know him.
There's no man in the world as gentle as him.
He's wearing white today
because he's still in mourning for his wife.
If you are interested,
I should send word to him to send a matchmaker."
Yānzhī said nothing,
and Wáng laughed and left.
Several days passed with no news.
Yānzhī suspected that Wáng had not yet had time to go,
or she feared that a family of officials would not condescend to marry into their humble background.
She paced around anxiously,
her thoughts plaguing her severely,
and she gradually stopped eating and drinking,
falling critically ill.
Wáng happened to come to visit
and pressed her for the cause of her illness.
Yānzhī replied,
"I don't know myself.
But after you left that day,
I suddenly felt unwell.
I'm barely clinging to life;
I could pass away at any moment."
Wáng whispered,
"My husband
is out peddling and hasn't returned yet,
so there's no one to convey the message to young Ōu.
Is your delicate body unwell
because of this?"
Yānzhī's face turned crimson for a long time.
Wáng teased her, saying,
"If it is truly for this reason,
and your illness has reached this point,
what more scruples can you have?
First, let him come for a tryst tonight;
he wouldn't refuse, would he?"
Yānzhī sighed, saying,
"Things have come to this;
I can no longer feel shame.
If he doesn't disdain my humble origins,
then let him send a matchmaker quickly,
and my illness will surely improve.
But if it's a private arrangement,
that is absolutely impossible!"
Wáng nodded,
then left.
When Wáng was young, she had an affair with a neighboring student named Sù Jiè.
After she married,
Sù would look for her whenever he learned her husband was out,
resuming their old intimacy.
That night, Sù happened to come over,
and Wáng recounted Yānzhī's words as a joke,
playfully entrusting him to convey the message to young Ōu.
Sù had long known of Yānzhī's beauty,
and hearing this, he secretly rejoiced,
thinking it a lucky opportunity he could exploit.
He intended to discuss it with his wife,
but feared her jealousy.
So he feigned an innocent curiosity
and inquired about the details of Yānzhī's chamber.
The next night,
he scaled the wall and entered,
going directly to Yānzhī's room.
He tapped on the window with his finger.
A voice inside asked,
"Who is it?"
He replied,
"Young Ōu."
Yānzhī said,
"The reason I think of you
is for a lifelong union,
not for a single night.
If you truly love me,
you should quickly send a matchmaker.
If you speak of a secret union,
I dare not comply."
Sù reluctantly agreed,
pleading earnestly for just one clasp of her slender wrist as a token.
Yānzhī couldn't bear to refuse completely
and, with difficulty due to her illness, opened the door.
Sù rushed in
and immediately embraced her, seeking intimacy.
Yānzhī was too weak to resist
and collapsed to the ground,
her breathing faltering.
Sù hastily dragged her.
Yānzhī said,
"What wicked young man are you?
You cannot be young Ōu. If you were young Ōu,
he is gentle and kind;
knowing the cause of my illness,
he would pity and care for me.
Why are you so violently aggressive?
If you continue like this,
I shall surely die,
and your character will be disgraced,
benefiting neither of us!"
Sù feared his disguise would be exposed
and dared not force her further.
He only requested a future meeting.
Yānzhī set her wedding day as the time.
Sù thought this too far off
and asked again.
Yānzhī, weary of the entanglement,
agreed to meet after her recovery.
Sù asked for a keepsake,
but Yānzhī refused.
Sù grabbed her foot, untied her embroidered shoe, and left.
Yānzhī called him back,
saying,
"My body is already promised to you;
what more can I begrudge?
But I fear that 'drawing a tiger and ending up with a dog'
will lead to scandal and disgrace.
Now that my intimate item is in your hand,
I expect it cannot be returned.
If you betray me,
there is only death for me!"
After Sù left,
he went to Wáng's residence.
Once in bed,
he couldn't forget the shoe;
he secretly felt within his clothes
but found it was utterly gone.
He hurriedly lit a lamp
and searched desperately through his clothes.
He questioned Wáng,
but she did not respond.
He suspected his wife had hidden it,
and she deliberately laughed to make him suspect.
Sù couldn't hide it
and told her the truth of the situation.
After speaking,
he searched all around outside the door with the lamp,
but still could not find it.
He returned to bed in vexation and regret,
still thinking that since it was late at night and no one was around,
the lost item must still be on the path.
He looked for it early the next morning, but it was also nowhere to be found.
Previously,
in the alley lived Máo Dà,
a loafer without a profession.
He had once tried to flirt with Wáng Shì without success.
Knowing that Sù and Qìa often met,
he thought of ambushing and capturing her to threaten her.
That night,
he passed by her door,
pushed it, and found it unlatched,
so he crept in.
Just as he reached outside the window,
he stepped on something
soft like silk floss.
He picked it up and examined it,
and it was a woman's embroidered slipper wrapped inside.
He hid and listened,
hearing Sù recounting her story in detail.
Overjoyed,
he withdrew with a suppressed gasp.
After several nights,
he climbed over the wall into the girl's house.
Unfamiliar with the doors,
he mistakenly went to the father's room.
The father peered through the window
and saw a man.
Observing his voice and movements,
he knew he had come for his daughter.
His heart filled with anger,
he grabbed a knife and rushed out.
Máo Dà was terrified and
ran back.
Just as he was about to climb the wall,
Biàn's pursuit was already close.
With no escape in his haste,
he turned around and snatched the knife.
The mother got up and cried out loudly,
Máo could not get away,
and consequently killed her.
The girl, having somewhat recovered,
rose upon hearing the commotion.
They lit a candle together,
and the father's skull was cracked, unable to speak,
and in a moment, he was dead.
Under the wall, they found an embroidered slipper.
The mother looked at it,
it was a woman's item.
Pressing the girl,
the girl cried and told the truth,
but, unwilling to implicate Wáng Shì because of the pregnancy,
she only said that È Shēng had come on his own.
At dawn,
they brought the case to the county.
The county magistrate arrested È.
È was a cautious and reserved person.
At nineteen,
he was shy around guests like a child.
When he was apprehended,
he was utterly terrified,
and when brought before the court, he didn't know what to say,
only trembled.
The magistrate increasingly believed his guilt was genuine,
and arbitrarily put him in shackles.
Unable to bear the pain,
he falsely confessed.
After being transferred to the prefecture,
he was beaten and flogged as in the county.
È's grievances filled him,
and he wished to confront the girl face to face.
But when they spoke,
the girl always cursed and insulted him,
so he became tongue-tied and could not defend himself,
and was therefore sentenced to death.
The case was reviewed repeatedly,
and after passing through several officials, there was no change in the verdict.
Later, the case was entrusted to Jǐnán Prefecture for re-examination.
At that time, Gōng Nándài of Wú was the prefect of Jǐnán.
Upon seeing È Shēng,
he doubted that he was the type to commit murder.
Secretly, he sent someone to question him gently and privately,
to allow him to fully state his case.
From this, Gōng became even more convinced of È Shēng's innocence.
After several days of deliberation,
he began to interrogate him.
First, he asked Yānzhī:
"After the agreement,
was there anyone who knew about it?"
She replied:
"No."
"When you met È Shēng,
was anyone else present?"
She also replied:
"No."
Then he called È Shēng up
and spoke to him kindly to comfort him.
È Shēng said:
"I once passed by her door,
but only saw the old neighbor Wáng Shì and a young girl coming out.
I immediately avoided them,
and after that, I didn't say a word at the well."
Wú Gōng sternly asked the girl:
"You just said there was no one else present,
how can there be a neighbor then?"
He intended to torture her.
The girl, frightened, said:
"Although Wáng Shì was there,
she had no actual involvement with him."
Gōng stopped the questioning and ordered Wáng Shì to be apprehended.
She arrived within a few days,
and was forbidden to communicate with the girl.
She was immediately brought to trial,
and Wáng was asked:
“Who killed the person?”
Wáng replied:
“I don’t know.”
Gōng feigned surprise, saying:
“Yānzhī stated that
you know everything about the killing of a certain Biàn,
how can you conceal it?”
The woman cried out, saying:
“What an injustice!
That wanton maidservant herself longed for a man.
Although I did make a jesting remark about matchmaking,
it was merely a joke.
She herself brought her adulterous lover into the courtyard,
how could I know about it?!”
Gōng carefully interrogated her,
and she then recounted the details of their playful exchange before and after.
Gōng called the maidservant up,
and angrily said:
“You said she was unaware,
how is it now that you yourself admit to arranging the match?”
The maidservant, weeping, said:
“I myself am unworthy,
which caused my father’s tragic death.
The lawsuit’s conclusion is unknown as to what year it will be,
and to also implicate others,
I truly cannot bear it.”
Gōng asked Wáng Shì:
“After the jest,
to whom did you speak about it?”
Wáng replied:
“To no one.”
Gōng angrily said:
“Husband and wife in bed,
there should be nothing left unsaid,
how can you say ‘to no one’?”
Wáng replied:
“My husband has been away for a long time and has not returned.”
Gōng said:
“Even so,
those who play tricks on others
all laugh at the foolishness of others
to show off their own cleverness.
If you don’t even tell a single person,
whom will you deceive?”
He ordered her ten fingers to be manacled.
The woman, having no choice,
truthfully confessed:
“I once spoke of it with Sù.”
Gōng then released the shackles and detained Sù.
When Sù arrived,
he himself confessed:
“I don’t know.”
Gōng said:
“One who frequents prostitutes is certainly no good person!”
He severely tortured him.
Sù confessed:
“It is true that I seduced the maidservant.
After losing my shoe,
I did not dare to go again,
I truly know nothing about the murder.”
Gōng angrily said:
“What can one not achieve by climbing over a wall!”
He tortured him again.
Sù could not endure the torment,
so he confessed.
The confession was finalized and reported upwards,
and everyone praised Gōng Wú’s sagacity.
The case was as firm as a mountain,
and Sù thus awaited his autumn execution with bated breath.
However, although Sù was dissolute and lacking in conduct,
he was a famous scholar in Dōngguó.
He heard that Xuéshǐ Shī Gōng Yúshān was known as the most virtuous and capable,
and also possessed the virtue of cherishing talent and pitying scholars.
Therefore, he submitted a poem appealing his unjust treatment,
its words full of sorrow.
Gōng reviewed his confession,
contemplating it repeatedly,
then slammed the table and said:
“This scholar has been wronged!”
He then requested the Yuàn and Sī,
to transfer the case for a retrial.
He asked the scholar Sù,
“Where did you lose your shoe?”
He replied,
“I forgot.
But when I knocked on the woman’s door,
it was still in my sleeve.”
He then questioned Wáng Shì again:
“Besides Sù Jiè,
how many adulterous lovers have you had?”
She replied:
“None.”
Gōng said:
“How can a licentious person only have one private lover?”
She replied:
"My body and Sù Jiè
were intimate in our youth,
so I was unable to refuse him;
later, it's not that there weren't those who propositioned me,
but I truly dared not comply."
Thereupon, he was made to point out the person to confirm it.
She confessed:
"Máo Dà from the same village
propositioned me repeatedly, and I repeatedly refused him."
Gōng said:
"Why are you suddenly so chaste and pure?"
He ordered her to be flogged.
The woman kowtowed until her head bled,
strenuously arguing she had not,
so he released her.
He then questioned:
"Your husband is away on a long journey,
surely there aren't those who come under false pretenses?"
She replied:
"There are.
Mǒu Jiǎ and Mǒu Yǐ
both came to my humble home once or twice
under the guise of borrowing or giving gifts."
Indeed, Jiǎ and Yǐ were both idlers from the alley,
who had designs on the woman but had not yet acted on them.
Gōng registered all their names
and apprehended them as well.
Once they were assembled,
Gōng went to the Chénghuáng Miào,
and made them all drink before the altar.
He then said:
"I recently dreamt that a divine being told me
that the murderer is among you four or five people.
Now, before the gods,
you must not speak falsely.
If you are willing to confess,
you may still be pardoned or deferred;
if you hide the truth,
when it is discovered, there will be no pardon!"
They all said in unison that they had not committed murder.
Gōng placed the cangue and stocks on the ground,
intending to apply them to all;
with their hair tied up and bodies bared,
they cried out their grievances in unison.
Gōng ordered them released,
saying,
"Since the officials cannot make you confess,
the ghosts and gods must point him out."
He had men use felt rugs to completely block the temple windows,
leaving no gap;
he bared the backs of the prisoners,
drove them into the darkness,
then gave them basins of water –
ordering them to wash themselves thoroughly;
he tied them against the walls,
instructing them
"to face the wall and not move.
The murderer
will have his back inscribed by a god."
A short while later,
he called them out for inspection,
and pointed at Máo saying:
"This truly is the murderer!"
Gōng had previously had someone paint the wall with ash,
and then blackened his hands with soot: the murderer, fearing the god would come to write,
thus pressed his back against the wall, resulting in ash marks;
when leaving,
he covered his back with his hands,
which then bore soot marks.
Gōng had already suspected Máo,
and this now solidified his belief.
He subjected him to severe torture,
and he confessed everything.
The judgment read:
"Sù Jiè: Treading the basin, he became entangled in the path of murder,
earning the name of a licentious man like Dēng Túzǐ.
Merely because two youths were innocent,
their wild passion became like the affection for a domestic fowl;
because of one word leaked,
it led to the desire to achieve more after gaining something (like 'looking to Shǔ after gaining Lǒng').
Taking Zhòngzǐ over the garden wall,
was like a bird falling;
encountering Liú Láng at the cave entrance,
he actually lured the gate open.
Feeling the kerchief and startling the dragon,
what kind of rodent's hide is this?
Climbing flowers and breaking trees,
what does it mean for a scholar to have no conduct!
Fortunately, hearing the plaintive cry of the sick swallow,
still cherished the jade;
pitying the withered weak willow,
not like a frenzied oriole.
Releasing the small breeze from the net,
still had the intention of a cultured man;
but robbing the fragrant oath from beneath the sock,
how could this not be the utmost villainy!
Butterflies crossed the wall,
ears were behind the window;
lotus petals shed,
falling to the ground without a trace.
What is false among the false is born,
who believes the injustice beyond injustice?
Heaven sends down calamity,
cruel instruments bringing him near death;
he brought about his own evil deeds,
almost losing his head permanently.
He climbed walls and drilled through gaps,
indeed he had a common butcher's heart beneath his scholar's cap;
but to frame another,
it is truly difficult to dissipate his aggrieved spirit.
It is proper to slightly lighten the beating,
to alleviate the suffering he has already endured;
for now, grant him the blue uniform (of a minor official),
opening a path for his self-renewal.
As for Máo Dà,
he is cunning, dissolute,
a vicious ruffian of the marketplace.
Struck by a neighbor girl,
his lustful heart did not die;
lying in wait for the wild boy to enter the alley,
a wicked scheme suddenly arose.
Opening the door to welcome the wind,
he rejoiced to follow in Zhāng Shēng's footsteps;
seeking water but finding wine,
he foolishly hoped to steal Hán Chuàn's fragrance.
Unexpectedly, his spirit was seized by heaven,
his soul captured by ghosts.
Recklessly riding a wooden raft,
he went straight into the palace of the moon;
directly sailing a fishing boat,
mistakenly taking the path to Peach Blossom Spring.
This caused the fire of passion to extinguish,
and waves to rise in the sea of desire.
The knife lay directly before him,
he cast a rat without other considerations;
where could the desperate bandit go,
a cornered rabbit bites back.
Crossing the wall into a private home,
he only expected Zhāng to wear the cap and Lǐ to borrow;
snatching weapons and leaving embroidered shoes,
he thus allowed the fish to escape the net and the swan to depart.
From the path of romance, such a demon was born;
in the land of tenderness, how could such a monster exist!
Immediately behead him,
to satisfy the people's hearts.
Yānzhī: Though not yet married,
her age has reached the pinning of the hair.
As a fairy from the moon palace,
she should naturally have a husband like jade: from the old troupe of 'Rainbow Garments,'
why worry about no gold stored in the house?
Yet, feeling the 'Guan Ju' and yearning for a good mate,
she eventually wandered into the dream of spring;
resenting the falling plums and longing for a good gentleman,
her soul thus left her beautiful body.
Because of one thread intertwined,
it caused all demons to arrive.
Contending for the beauty of women,
fearing the loss of 'Yānzhī';
stirring up the chaotic flight of mandarin ducks,
both entrusting 'Qiūzǔn'.
Her lotus feet (bound feet) removed,
it's hard to preserve a single petal of fragrance;
the iron bar struck,
almost shattering the priceless jade.
Red beans embedded in the dice,
the bones of lovesickness became steps to calamity;
felling a tall tree with an axe,
the hateful talent truly became the root of disaster!
Modestly self-controlled,
fortunately the white jade was flawless;
struggling bitterly in fetters,
glad the brocade quilt could cover her.
Praising her refusal at the door,
still the chaste lover;
fulfilling her heart's desire to throw fruit,
also an elegant affair of romance.
I implore the county magistrate,
to act as your matchmaker."
Once the case was concluded,
it was widely circulated and praised far and near.
Only after Wú Gōng's judgment
did the woman realize È Shēng's innocence.
When they met below the hall,
she was shy and tearful,
seemingly with words of deep regret,
but unable to speak them.
Shēng was moved by her lingering affection,
and his admiration was exceedingly strong;
yet he also considered her humble origins,
and that she had appeared daily in the public court,
seen and pointed at by thousands,
fearing that marrying her would make him an object of ridicule.
Day and night, these thoughts intertwined,
leaving him unable to decide for himself.
Once the judgment document was issued,
his mind finally found peace.
The county magistrate acted as matchmaker,
sending drummers and musicians for the engagement.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"How profound!
It is truly imperative to be cautious when adjudicating lawsuits!
Even if one is able to discern that Lǐ took the place of the wronged party,
who would then consider that Táo, too, suffered an injustice?
However, although matters may be obscure,
there must be a reason behind them,
and it is certainly not something that can be attained
without careful deliberation and thorough investigation.
Alas!
Everyone admires a wise person for their sharp judgment in criminal cases,
but they do not realize the painstaking efforts of a skilled craftsman.
Those in the world who hold positions of authority,
pass the days playing chess,
and return home from court wrapped in quilts,
unwilling to exert even a moment's thought
for the hardships of the common people.
When the drums beat and the yamen opens,
they sit imposingly in the hall,
silencing the clamoring petitioners with shackles,
so it is no wonder that under the overturned basin there are many hidden injustices!"
Yúshān Xiānshēng,
was my teacher.
When he first recognized me,
I was still a child.
I secretly observed him encouraging and promoting scholars,
earnestly, as if afraid of not doing enough.
If there was even a minor injustice or grievance,
he would certainly protect and care for them thoroughly,
never daring to wield authority in the schools
to curry favor with the powerful.
He was truly a guardian of the Sage's teachings,
not merely a master of his generation who judged essays fairly without wronging any scholar.
And his love for talent was like his very life,
which is particularly beyond what later imperial examiners, who merely went through the motions, could achieve.
There was once a famous scholar who entered the examination hall
and wrote an essay
titled "Bǎozàng Xīng"
(The Treasure Emerges),
mistakenly recording
"underwater."
[He] only realized this after finishing the transcription,
believing there was no reason why he wouldn't be rejected.
He composed a poem saying:
"The treasure lies in the mountains,
mistakenly thought to be by the water's edge.
On the mountaintop, a crystal palace is built,
corals grow on the peaks,
pearls form on the treetops;
this time, a boatman is dashed to death in the cliffs!
I implore Heaven: leave a little remnant,
so friends may see."
When the先生 read the essay to this point, he responded, saying:
"The treasure boasts of mountains,
suddenly appearing by the water's edge.
The woodcutter idly tells tales of the fisherman.
Although the topic is amiss,
the writing is excellent,
how could it be placed beneath others?
I have often seen him
fear danger when ascending heights;
but have I ever seen him
drown when he knows how to swim?"
This is also a glimpse of his refined taste and an instance of his compassion for talent.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Xīshān,
was a native of Gāomì.
He made a living as a merchant,
often staying between Méng and Yí.
One day,
he was delayed by rain on the road,
and by the time he reached his usual lodging,
it was already late at night.
He knocked on many inn doors,
but no one answered,
so he lingered below.
Suddenly, two doors swung open,
an old man emerged,
and immediately invited the guest in.
Xīshān gladly followed him.
He tethered his mule and entered the hall,
but there were no tables or couches in the hall.
The old man said:
"I pity you for having no place to go,
so I have taken you in.
I am not actually a vendor of food or drink.
My household has few hands,
only my old wife and my weak daughter,
who are fast asleep.
Although there is leftover food,
I regret that there is little to cook,
so please do not mind eating it cold."
Having said this,
he went in.
A moment later,
he brought a small footed bed and placed it on the ground,
urging the guest to sit;
then he brought a short-legged table.
He moved back and forth,
bustling with great effort.
Xīshān rose and sat uneasily,
pulling him to rest for a moment.
Soon after,
a young woman came out to serve wine,
and the old man looked at her and said:
"My Āxiān is up."
Looking at her,
she was sixteen or seventeen years old,
graceful and delicate,
with a charming demeanor.
Xīshān had a younger brother who was not yet married,
and secretly felt a liking for her.
He then asked the old man about his family's official rank and esteemed lineage,
to which he replied:
"My humble name is Gǔ Shīxū.
My surname is Gǔ.
My sons and grandsons all died young,
leaving only this daughter.
I just couldn't bear to disturb her deep sleep,
I suppose my old wife has woken her up."
He asked:
"Who is the groom's family?"
He replied,
"She is not yet betrothed."
Xīshān was secretly pleased.
Presently, various dishes were served,
seemingly what was already on hand.
After eating,
he respectfully said:
"As a stranger who met you by chance,
I have received your gracious kindness,
which I will never forget as long as I live.
Because of your great virtue,
I dare to abruptly present my humble and clumsy proposal: I have a young brother, Sānláng,
who is seventeen years old.
He studies diligently
and is quite intelligent.
I wish to seek a connection,
do you not despise my humble origins?"
The old man joyfully said:
"I, the old man, am also a sojourner here.
If I can entrust her to you,
I will rent a house,
move my family there,
and thus be free from worry."
Xīshān agreed to everything,
and then stood up to express his gratitude.
The old man kindly settled him and left.
When the rooster crowed,
the old man had already come out,
calling the guest to wash.
After packing his belongings,
he offered payment for the meal.
The old man firmly declined, saying:
"You stayed for a meal,
there is absolutely no reason for me to accept money;
moreover, we are about to become relatives through marriage!"
After parting,
the guest spent more than a month,
then returned.
When he was more than a li from the village,
he met an old woman leading a young woman,
both dressed entirely in white mourning clothes.
As they approached,
he suspected it was Āxiān.
The young woman also frequently turned to look,
then tugged the old woman's sleeve,
whispering something in her ear that was unclear.
The old woman then stopped,
and said to Xīshān:
"What is your surname, sir?"
Shān merely nodded.
The old woman said sadly:
"Unfortunately, my old husband was crushed by a collapsed wall.
I am now going to visit his grave.
My home is empty and without anyone.
Please wait a moment by the roadside;
I will return shortly."
Then she entered the woods and left.
After some time, she finally returned.
The road was already dim.
So, she went with the monk.
As she spoke of her loneliness and weakness,
she could not help but weep sadly.
Shān also felt sorrowful.
The old woman said:
"The people here are very unkind.
A lonely and beautiful woman finds it difficult to get by.
Since Āqiān is to be your family's wife,
if she passes through here, it might delay things.
It's better for us to return together tonight."
Shān agreed.
Upon arriving home,
the old woman lit a lamp and served the guest.
She then said to Shān:
"I expected you would arrive,
but all the stored grain has been taken away by evil spirits.
There are still more than twenty dàn remaining,
but they are too far to transport.
Four or five lǐ north from here,
the first gate in the village,
belongs to one Tán Èrquán,
who is my buyer.
Sir, do not be afraid of the trouble.
First, take one sack with your honorable vehicle,
knock on his door and tell him,
just say that an old woman from the southern village has several dàn of grain
taken by evil spirits for road expenses,
and request him to drive his donkey to transport them."
She then gave the sack of grain to Shān.
Shān rode his donkey and left.
He knocked on the door,
and a corpulent man came out.
Shān told him the situation,
then emptied the sack and returned first.
Soon, two men arrived with five mules.
The old woman led Shān to where the grain was,
which was in a cellar.
Shān went down to measure and level.
The mother poured, and the daughter collected.
In a moment, the loads were full.
They were paid and left.
After four trips, the grain was finally exhausted.
Afterwards, they gave gold to the old woman.
The old woman kept one person and two animals,
then prepared for the journey and headed east.
After traveling twenty lǐ,
the sky began to lighten.
They arrived at a market.
They rented a horse at the market entrance,
and the servants then returned.
Upon returning,
Shān told his parents the situation.
They were very happy to meet.
They immediately housed the old woman in a separate residence
and chose an auspicious day for Sānláng's wedding.
The old woman prepared the dowry very thoroughly.
Āqiān was a woman of few words and seldom angry.
If someone spoke to her,
she would only smile.
Day and night, she spun and wove,
never stopping.
Because of this, everyone, high and low, loved and admired her.
She instructed Sānláng, saying:
"Tell your eldest uncle: when you pass through the western road again,
do not speak of my mother and daughter."
After three or four years,
the Xī family became increasingly wealthy,
and Sānláng entered the government school.
One day,
Shān was staying overnight with an old neighbor of his former village
and happened to mention the time he had nowhere to go years ago,
and stayed with the old man and woman.
The host said:
"Sir, you are mistaken.
The eastern neighbor is the separate residence of Ābó.
Three years ago,
the residents there frequently witnessed strange occurrences,
so it has been empty and abandoned for a long time.
How could there have been an old man and woman staying there?"
Shān was very surprised,
but did not fully believe it.
The host further said:
"This house has been empty for ten years,
and no one dared to enter it.
One day,
the back wall of the residence collapsed.
Bó went to inspect it,
and found a giant rat, as big as a cat, crushed by a stone,
its tail still wagging outside.
He hurried home,
called everyone to go together,
but it was already gone.
Everyone suspected it was a monster.
More than ten days later,
they went to inspect again,
but there was no trace or sound.
Another year later,
someone finally moved in."
Shān was even more intrigued.
He returned home and secretly discussed it,
suspecting that the new wife was not human,
and secretly worried for Sānláng.
However, Sānláng loved her devotedly as always.
After a long time,
the family members began to dispute and suspect each other.
The woman subtly noticed this.
One night, she said to Sānláng:
"I have been with you for several years,
and have never been lacking in wifely virtue.
Now I am not considered a human being.
Please grant me a divorce letter,
and let you choose a good match yourself."
With that, tears fell.
Sānláng said:
"My sincere heart
should have been known to you long ago.
Since you entered our home,
the family has become increasingly prosperous.
Everyone attributes our good fortune to you.
How can there be any different opinions?"
The woman said:
"You have no second thoughts,
how could I not know?
But the multitude of voices is confusing.
I fear I cannot avoid being discarded like an autumn fan."
Sānláng repeatedly comforted and appeased her,
and then she stopped.
Shān, however, remained uneasy.
He daily sought a cat good at catching rats
to observe her reaction.
Although the woman was not afraid,
she was nevertheless displeased and anxious.
One evening,
she said that the old woman was slightly ill,
and excused herself from Sānláng to visit and attend to her.
At dawn,
Sānláng went to inquire,
but the room was already empty.
Extremely alarmed,
he sent people to track her along all roads,
but there was no news.
His heart was anxious and troubled;
he neglected sleep and food.
His father and brothers, however, considered it a blessing,
comforted him,
and prepared to arrange another marriage for him.
But Sānláng was very unhappy.
He waited for more than a year,
but all news had ceased.
His father and brothers frequently reproached and blamed him.
Having no choice,
he bought a concubine with a large sum of money.
However, his thoughts of Āqiān did not diminish.
Several more years passed,
and the Xī family gradually became poorer.
Because of this, he came to remember Āqiān.
His younger paternal cousin, Lán,
went to Jiāo for some reason,
and took a detour to stay at the home of his maternal relative, Lù Shēng.
At night, he heard a neighbor crying very sadly,
but did not immediately inquire.
Upon returning,
he heard it again,
and then asked the host.
The host replied:
“Several years ago,
there was a widowed mother and an orphaned daughter
who rented a dwelling here.
About a month ago,
the old woman died,
leaving the daughter to live alone.
She has no relatives whatsoever,
which is why she grieves.”
He asked,
“What is her surname?”
He replied,
“Her surname is Gǔ.
She always kept her door closed and did not interact with the local community,
so we do not know her family history.”
Lán exclaimed in surprise,
“She is my sister-in-law!”
Thereupon, he went and knocked on the door.
Someone came out, wiping away tears,
and from behind the screen, she responded,
“Who is this visitor?
There are no men in my household.”
Lán peeked through a crack and observed her from a distance.
Indeed, it was his sister-in-law.
He then said,
“Sister-in-law, open the gate.
I am your husband’s younger brother, Āsuí.”
When the woman heard this,
she unbarred the gate and let him in.
She recounted her solitary suffering,
her spirits filled with sorrow and grief.
Lán said,
“Your third elder brother misses you terribly.
Even if there were differences between husband and wife,
why did you flee so far away to this place?”
He immediately wanted to hire a carriage to take her home.
The woman said mournfully,
“Because I was scorned by others,
I went into seclusion with my mother.
Now, if I return and depend on others again,
who will not look at me with disdain?
If I am to return,
I must live separately from my eldest brother.
Otherwise,
I will take poison and seek death!”
After Lán returned,
he told the third elder brother.
The third elder brother rushed there that very night.
When husband and wife met,
both shed tears.
The next day,
he informed the landlord.
The landlord, Xiè Jiānshēng,
had noticed the woman's beauty
and secretly wished to take her as a concubine.
For several years, he had not collected the rent,
frequently hinting at his intentions to the old woman.
The old woman rejected him.
After the old woman died,
he secretly hoped to succeed in his scheme,
but the third elder brother suddenly arrived.
He calculated the total rent due to make things difficult for them.
The third elder brother's family was not well off,
and hearing the large sum of money,
he looked quite troubled.
The woman said,
“Don’t worry.”
She led the third elder brother to inspect the granary.
There were about thirty *shí* of grain,
more than enough to pay the rent.
The third elder brother was pleased and
told Xiè,
but Xiè would not accept the grain.
He insisted on cash.
The woman sighed and said,
“This is all due to my own evil karma!”
She then explained the situation to the third elder brother.
The third elder brother was furious
and planned to take the matter to the magistrate.
Lù Shì stopped him,
distributed the grain among the villagers,
collected funds to pay Xiè,
and sent the two home by carriage.
The third elder brother truthfully informed his parents
and lived separately from his elder brother.
Āxiān took out private funds
to build granaries daily,
yet there was no grain at home.
Everyone found this peculiar.
A year later, upon inspection,
the granaries were full.
Within a few years,
the family became very wealthy,
while the mountainous region remained poor.
The woman moved her parents-in-law to live with and support them.
She frequently gave gold and grain to her elder brother-in-law,
making it a regular practice.
The third elder brother happily said,
“You can truly be said to not harbor old grievances.”
The woman said,
“He is merely a beloved younger brother.
Moreover, if not for him,
how would I have come to know my third elder brother?”
After this, there were no other significant strange occurrences.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Ruìyún,
a famous courtesan from Hángzhōu,
was unparalleled in beauty and artistry.
At the age of fourteen,
her mother, Cài Ǎo,
was about to make her available to guests.
Ruìyún told her,
“This is the beginning of your servant’s lifelong journey,
so it cannot be done hastily.
The price will be set by mother,
but the guest will be chosen by your servant.”
The old woman said,
“Agreed.”
So, the price was set at fifteen gold coins,
and she began to receive guests daily.
Those who sought an audience had to bring a gift.
If the gift was generous,
she would entertain them with chess and
reciprocate with a painting.
If it was meager,
she would merely offer a cup of tea.
Ruìyún’s fame had long been widespread,
and from then on, wealthy merchants and noble gentlemen
thronged her door daily. Xú Háng Hèshēng,
whose talent and reputation were long established,
was only of moderate means.
He had always admired Ruìyún,
but dared not hope for a romantic relationship.
Nevertheless, he offered a small gift,
hoping to catch a glimpse of her beauty.
He secretly feared that having met so many people,
she would not take a humble scholar like him seriously.
However, when they met and conversed,
her reception was exceptionally warm.
They sat and talked for a long time,
her eyes and brows filled with affection.
She composed a poem and presented it to Hèshēng, saying:
“Why does the seeker of nectar
knock at Blue Bridge at dawn?
If you wish to find the jade pestle,
it is indeed only found among mortals.”
Hèshēng was overjoyed to receive it.
He wanted to say more,
but a young maid suddenly announced,
“A guest has arrived.”
Hèshēng hastily departed.
After returning home,
he repeatedly recited and pondered the poem, his dreams and soul troubled.
After one or two days,
unable to control his feelings,
he prepared another gift and went again.
Ruìyún received him very happily.
She moved her seat closer to Hèshēng
and quietly said,
“Can you arrange for us to spend one night together?”
Hèshēng said,
“As an impoverished and humble scholar,
I only have my deep affection to offer a kindred spirit.
The small gift I brought
has already exhausted my meager means.
To be close to your beautiful presence
is already enough for my heart’s desire.
As for physical intimacy,
how dare I even dream of such a thing?”
When Ruìyún heard this,
she became sad and unhappy; they then sat in silence.
Hèshēng stayed for a long time without leaving,
and the old woman frequently called Ruìyún to urge him to leave.
Hèshēng then returned home.
His heart was deeply troubled;
he thought of exhausting his family's wealth to gain one night of joy.
But to spend everything and then part ways,
how could such a situation be endured?
As he pondered this,
all his passionate thoughts vanished.
From then on, communication ceased.
Ruìyún (瑞雲) had been choosing a husband for several months,
but could not find a suitable one.
The old woman (媼) was quite vexed,
and was about to force a choice,
but had not yet acted.
One day,
a xiùcái (秀才) came to present his card.
They sat and conversed for a short while,
then he stood up
and pressed a finger to the girl’s forehead, saying:
“What a pity,
what a pity!”
Then he left.
Ruìyún (瑞雲) returned after seeing the guest off,
and together they saw a black fingerprint on her forehead, like ink.
Washing it only made it more distinct.
After several days,
the ink mark gradually widened;
after more than a year,
it covered her cheekbones and nose.
Those who saw her invariably laughed,
and the traces of carriages and horses ceased.
The old woman (媼) dismissed her decorations,
making her associate with the maidservants.
Ruìyún (瑞雲) was also weak and delicate,
unable to endure hard labor,
and grew more emaciated day by day.
Hè (賀) heard of this and visited her,
seeing her with disheveled hair in the kitchen,
her ugly appearance resembling a ghost.
When she saw the scholar (生), she started
and turned to the wall to hide herself.
Hè (賀) pitied her,
and immediately spoke to the old woman (媼),
wishing to redeem her as his wife.
The old woman (媼) agreed.
Hè (賀) sold his land and emptied his purse,
bought her, and returned home.
Upon entering the door,
she tugged at his clothes and wiped away tears,
not daring to claim herself as his equal,
but wishing to serve as a concubine,
awaiting another.
Hè (賀) said,
“What is valued in life is a confidant: if you could still know me in your prime,
how could I forget you because of your decline!”
Thus, he did not marry again.
Those who heard of it all mocked and laughed at him,
but his affection only deepened.
After more than a year,
he happened to go to Sū (蘇),
where he shared a host with Hè (和) Shēng (生).
Suddenly, Hè (和) Shēng (生) asked:
“How is the famous courtesan Ruìyún (瑞雲) of Hángzhōu (杭州) doing recently?”
Hè (賀) replied that she had married,
and he asked again:
“To whom?”
He said:
“The man is generally like me.”
Hè (和) Shēng (生) said:
“If he can be like you,
she can be said to have found a good husband.
I wonder what the price was?”
Hè (賀) said:
“Because she had a strange illness,
she was sold for a cheap price.
Otherwise,
how could someone like me
buy a beauty from a brothel!”
Hè (和) Shēng (生) asked again:
“Is the man really like you?”
Hè (賀), finding his question unusual,
therefore retorted.
Hè (和) Shēng (生) smiled and said:
“I will not deceive you: I once saw her beautiful appearance,
and greatly regretted that such a peerless beauty
was left to wander unfortunate.
Therefore, I used a small trick to obscure her radiance and protect her pure essence,
saving her for a true connoisseur who appreciates talent.”
Hè (賀) eagerly asked:
“If you can mark it,
can you also wash it away?”
Hè (和) Shēng (生) smiled and said:
“Why not?
But the person must sincerely ask.”
Hè (賀) stood up and bowed, saying:
“The husband of Ruìyún (瑞雲)
is none other than I.”
Hè (和) Shēng (生) happily said:
“Only truly talented people in the world are capable of deep affection,
not changing their minds due to beauty or ugliness.
Please allow me to return with you,
and I will present you with a beautiful woman.”
So they returned together.
Upon arrival,
Hè (賀) was about to order wine.
Hè (和) Shēng (生) stopped him, saying:
“Let me first perform my method;
we should first make the one who prepares things happy.”
He immediately ordered a washing basin to be filled with water,
pointed his finger at it and wrote,
saying:
“Wash it, and it will heal.
However, the person must personally come out to thank the physician.”
Hè (賀) laughed, took it, and left,
standing by as Ruìyún (瑞雲) washed her own face.
As she washed, it became bright and clean,
resplendent as she was in her prime.
Husband and wife both felt grateful to him,
and together went out to express their thanks,
but the guest was already gone,
searched for everywhere but not found.
Could he have been an immortal?
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異).
Qiú Zhòng (仇仲),
a man from Jìn (晉),
his prefecture and county are forgotten.
During a great rebellion,
he was captured by bandits.
His two sons, Fú (福) and Lù (祿), were both young;
his second wife, Shào (邵) Shì (氏),
raised the two orphans,
and their inherited property fortunately allowed them to live comfortably.
However, there were repeated years of famine,
and powerful individuals again oppressed them,
to the point where their livelihood was not secure.
Zhòng (仲)'s uncle, Lián (廉), coveted her for marriage,
repeatedly urging her to remarry,
but Shào (邵) Shì (氏) remained steadfast in her vow.
Lián (廉) secretly made a bond with a prominent family,
intending to forcibly take her;
the arrangements were already made,
but others did not know of it.
A local man, Wèi Míng (魏名),
had long been cunning and mischievous,
and had a long-standing feud with Zhòng (仲)'s family,
always looking to harm them.
Because Shào (邵) was a widow,
he fabricated rumors to ruin and disgrace her.
The prominent family heard of it,
disapproved of her supposed impropriety, and stopped.
After a long time,
Lián (廉)'s secret plot and the external rumors
gradually reached Shào (邵)'s ears.
Grief accumulated in her heart,
and she shed tears day and night.
Her four limbs gradually became numb,
and she was confined to her bed.
Fú (福) was just sixteen,
and because there was no one to do sewing,
he urgently married Bì Yān (畢煙).
The wife,
daughter of the xiùcái (秀才) Jiāng Qǐzhān (姜屺瞻),
was quite賢能 (xiánnéng) (virtuous and capable),
and everything depended on her management.
Because of this, their financial situation gradually improved,
and Lù (祿) was still sent to study under a teacher.
Wèi was jealous of him,
but outwardly pretended to be friendly with him.
He frequently invited Fú to drink,
and Fú came to rely on him as a bosom friend.
Wèi took the opportunity to say:
“Your esteemed mother is sick and infirm,
unable to manage the family's livelihood and production;
your younger brother is idle,
doing absolutely no work.
Why do you and your wife toil like horses and oxen!
Moreover, when your brother buys a wife,
it will greatly deplete your money.
For your sake,
it would be better to divide the family early,
then poverty will be your brother's and wealth will be yours.”
Fú returned,
and discussed it with his wife;
his wife admonished him.
However, Wèi gradually influenced him with subtle words day by day,
and Fú was deluded.
He straightforwardly told his mother his own idea.
His mother was angry,
and scolded him.
Fú became even more resentful,
and began to regard the gold and grain as belonging to others, discarding them.
Wèi seized the opportunity to lure him into gambling,
and the granary gradually became empty.
His wife knew but dared not speak.
When the food supply was exhausted,
and his mother questioned her in alarm,
she finally told the truth.
His mother was furious,
but there was nothing she could do,
so she divided the family.
Fortunately, Jiāng-nǚ was virtuous;
morning and evening she cooked for her mother,
serving her just as she had on ordinary days.
After Fú had divided the family,
he became even more reckless,
indulging greatly in lewdness and gambling.
Within a few months,
all his fields and houses were used to pay off gambling debts,
but his mother and wife were unaware of it.
When Fú's resources were exhausted,
and he had no plan,
he tried to mortgage his wife for funds,
but unfortunately, there were no takers.
The local man Zhào Yánluó,
a notorious bandit who had previously escaped the net of justice,
tyrannized the whole village.
He naturally did not fear Fú's empty words,
and generously lent him money.
Fú took it away,
but in a few days it was empty again.
He hesitated,
intending to break the bond and agreement.
Zhào glared at him.
Fú was frightened,
and tricked his wife into going to Zhào.
Wèi heard of this and secretly rejoiced,
rushing to tell Jiāng,
actually intending to ruin his rival.
Jiāng was angry,
and a lawsuit began.
Fú was extremely frightened,
and fled.
When Jiāng-nǚ arrived at Zhào's house,
she first learned that she had been sold by her husband.
She wept bitterly,
only wishing to die.
Zhào initially tried to comfort and persuade her,
but she would not listen;
afterward, he threatened her,
but she cursed him even more;
he became furious,
and whipped her,
but she still refused to submit.
Thereupon, she pulled out her hairpin and stabbed her own throat.
They rushed to save her,
but it had already pierced her esophagus,
and blood gushed out.
Zhào hastily bound her neck with silk,
still hoping to slowly break her will.
The next day,
the summons for arrest had arrived,
but Zhào acted as if it was nothing.
The official examined the woman's severe injury,
and ordered her to be flogged.
The yamen runners looked at each other, none daring to apply the punishment.
The official had long heard of Zhào's tyranny,
and this incident further confirmed it.
He became greatly enraged,
called out his family members,
and instantly killed him.
Jiāng then carried the woman home.
Ever since Jiāng's lawsuit,
Shào shì first learned of Fú's unworthy behavior.
She let out a cry that almost killed her,
and was gravely ill, seemingly near death.
Lù was fifteen years old at the time,
and was forlorn, without a good master to turn to.
Prior to this,
Zhòng had a daughter from his previous wife, Dàniáng,
who was married into a distant prefecture.
She had a strong and fierce character.
Every time she returned home to visit her parents,
if the gifts and offerings did not satisfy her,
she would immediately argue with her parents,
often leaving in anger.
Zhòng therefore resented and disliked her.
Also, because the journey was far,
several years had passed without her visiting or inquiring after them.
When Shào shì was on the verge of death,
Wèi intended to invite Dàniáng to come, but also wished to stir up trouble.
It happened that there was a peddler
who lived in the same village as Dàniáng.
Wèi entrusted him with a message for Dàniáng,
and also enticed her with the prospect of profiting from the family estate.
A few days later,
Dàniáng indeed arrived with her young son.
Upon entering the house,
she saw her young brother attending to their ailing mother.
The scene was desolate and grim,
and she couldn't help but feel sorrowful.
She then asked her brother, Fú,
and Lù told her everything.
When Dàniáng heard this,
her throat was choked with indignation.
She said:
"The family has no adults to take charge,
so we've been left for others to trample upon to this extent!
How could those villains
have defrauded us of our family's land and property?!"
She then went into the kitchen,
lit a fire and cooked porridge,
first serving it to her mother,
and then calling her brother and son to eat.
After they had eaten,
she angrily left
and went to the county seat to file a complaint,
suing the gamblers.
The gamblers were afraid
and collected money to bribe Dàniáng.
Dàniáng accepted the rest of the money,
but still sued them.
The county magistrate detained Jiǎ, Yǐ, and others,
and each was flogged,
but the land and property were completely ignored.
Dàniáng's indignation did not cease.
She took her son and went to the prefecture.
The prefect especially detested gamblers.
Dàniáng forcefully recounted their孤苦孤苦 pitiful and lonely situation,
and the details of how the villains had conspired to deceive them,
her words filled with passion and righteousness.
The prefect was moved by her,
and ruled that the county magistrate should recover the land and return it to its owner;
he also punished Chóu Fú
to warn others who were unworthy.
Upon her return,
the county magistrate, obeying the order, initiated the process of assessment and recovery,
and thus all the former property was returned.
Dàniáng had been a widow for a long time by then,
so she sent her young son back
and instructed her cousin to diligently pursue his studies and work,
and not to return again.
From then on, Dàniáng remained at her mother's home,
caring for her mother and teaching her brother,
keeping the household affairs, both internal and external, in order.
Her mother was greatly comforted,
her illness gradually recovered,
and all household matters were entrusted to Dàniáng.
If the local strongmen
showed any slight disrespect or bullying,
she would immediately grasp a blade and confront them at their doors,
arguing logically and righteously,
and none failed to submit.
After more than a year,
the family's land and property increased daily.
She often bought medicinal herbs and rare delicacies
and sent them as gifts to Jiāng nǚ.
Seeing that Lù was gradually growing up,
she frequently urged matchmakers to find a suitable spouse for him.
Wèi told people:
"The family's assets
all belong to Dàniáng.
I'm afraid they can never be recovered in the future."
People all believed this,
and therefore no one was willing to discuss marriage with him.
There was a young master, Fàn Gōngzǐ Zǐwén,
whose family's famous garden
was the best in Jìn.
Famous flowers lined the path in the garden,
leading directly to the inner chambers.
If someone, unaware, mistakenly entered it
and chanced upon the young master's private banquet,
he would angrily seize them as a thief
and beat them almost to death.
It happened to be Qīngmíng Festival,
and Lù returned from school.
Wèi led him to go sightseeing,
and they arrived at the garden.
Wèi had an old acquaintance among the gardeners,
who let them in,
and they walked around the pavilions and terraces.
Presently, they came to a place
where a stream surged,
with a painted bridge and vermilion railing
leading to a lacquered gate.
Looking into the gate from afar,
the dense flowers were like brocade;
this was indeed the young master's inner study.
Wèi deceived him, saying:
"Please go in first,
I just need to relieve myself."
Lù believed him,
followed the bridge and entered the gate,
reaching a courtyard,
where he heard the sound of women laughing.
Just as he paused,
a maid came out,
saw him,
and immediately turned back.
Lù was startled and fled.
Soon after,
the young master came out,
shouting at his servants to tie a rope and chase him.
Lù was in great distress
and threw himself into the stream.
The young master's anger turned to laughter,
and he ordered his servants to pull him out.
Seeing his elegant appearance and clothes,
he ordered him to change his clothes and shoes,
and led him into a hall,
inquiring about his surname and given name.
His expression was gentle and his words warm,
showing great friendliness.
Soon, he hurried inside;
presently he came out,
smiling and taking Lù's hand,
crossed the bridge,
and gradually reached the place from before.
Lù did not understand his intention,
and hesitated, not daring to enter.
The young master forcefully pulled him in,
and he saw faint glimpses of beautiful women peeking from behind the flower hedge.
Once seated,
the maids served wine.
Lù declined, saying:
"Being an ignorant child,
I mistakenly trespassed into the women's quarters.
To receive forgiveness
is already beyond my expectations.
I only ask to be released to return home early;
my gratitude for this favor is immense."
The young master did not listen.
A short while later,
dishes and roasted meats were served in abundance.
Lù again rose,
declining, saying he was drunk and full.
The young master pressed him to sit,
and said with a smile:
"I have a tune name,
if you can provide a matching couplet for it,
then I will let you go."
Lù humbly agreed and asked to be enlightened.
The young master said:
"The tune name is 'Húnbùsì' [Completely Unlike]."
Lù pondered for a long time,
and replied:
"Yínchéng 'Méinàihé' [No Alternative to Silver]."
The young master burst out laughing, saying:
"Truly a Shí Chóng!"
Lù was utterly perplexed.
It turned out that the young master had a daughter named Huìniáng,
who was beautiful and educated,
and was daily seeking a good match.
One night, she dreamt that someone told her:
"Shí Chóng
is your husband."
She asked:
"Where is he?"
He replied:
"Tomorrow, he will fall into the water."
She told her parents early in the morning,
and they both found it extraordinary.
Lù happened to match the dream's omen,
which is why he was invited into the inner residence
to be observed by the madam and the other women.
The young master was delighted upon hearing the couplet,
and then said:
"This tune name was devised by my little daughter.
She has repeatedly tried to find a match for it but failed.
Now that a matching couplet has been provided,
also has a heavenly affinity.
I wish to offer my daughter to serve you;
my humble abode does not lack mansions,
so there is no need for a formal welcome by the groom. ”
Lù was dismayed and humbly declined,
citing his mother's illness as a reason for not being able to become an adopted son-in-law.
The young master then told him to go back and discuss it,
and immediately dispatched a groom to carry his wet clothes,
sending him off with a horse.
When he returned and told his mother,
his mother was alarmed, deeming it inauspicious.
Only then did they realize the treacherous nature of the Wèi clan;
however, since misfortune had turned into good fortune,
they did not seek revenge,
but merely warned their son to keep his distance.
A few days later,
the young master again sent someone to convey his regards to the mother,
but the mother still dared not respond.
Dàniáng responded on her behalf,
and immediately engaged two matchmakers to arrange the betrothal gifts.
Not long after,
Lù married into the young master's family as an adopted son-in-law.
After more than a year, he passed the imperial examinations,
and his talent and reputation were widely acclaimed.
As his wife's younger brother grew up,
his respect for Lù somewhat diminished;
Lù became angry,
and took his wife home,
where his mother was already able to walk with a cane.
For several years, thanks to Dàniáng's management,
their mansions were quite well-maintained.
When the new bride returned,
servants were like clouds,
indeed, having the demeanor of a great family.
As the Wèi clan was again rejected,
their jealousy deepened,
regretting that there was no flaw to exploit,
so they induced a runaway under their banner to falsely accuse Lù of harboring assets.
The law during the early days of the dynasty was very strict,
so Lù was exiled beyond the pass according to the decree.
Fàn Gōngzǐ bribed and sought connections from all levels,
barely managing to exempt Huìniáng from the exile;
their lands were all confiscated by the government.
Fortunately, Dàniáng held the document of property division,
bravely appealed the case,
and added fertile land of about a thousand qǐng,
all registered under Fú's name,
allowing the mother and daughter to live in peace.
Lù, believing he would not return,
wrote a divorce letter and sent it to his wife's family,
and departed alone.
After traveling for several days,
he reached the north of the capital,
and ate at an inn.
There was a beggar outside the door,
whose appearance greatly resembled his elder brother;
upon closer inquiry,
it was indeed his elder brother.
Lù then recounted his own story,
and the brothers wept bitterly.
Lù took off his outer garment,
divided some gold,
and urged him to return home.
Fú received it tearfully and parted ways.
Lù arrived outside the pass,
and became a servant under a general's tent.
Because Lù was gentle and weak,
he was assigned to manage the records,
residing with the other servants.
The servants inquired about his family background,
and Lù told them everything.
One of them exclaimed,
“That is my son!”
It turned out that Qiú Zhòngchū had been herding horses for a bandit family,
and later, when the bandits surrendered,
Zhòng was sold under a banner,
and at that time, he followed his master to garrison outside the pass.
Upon Lù's detailed narration,
they finally realized they were truly father and son,
and embraced each other, weeping in sorrow,
filling the room with poignant grief.
After a while, he indignantly said,
“What kind of runaway from the east
dared to swindle my son!”
Then he tearfully reported to the general.
The general immediately appointed Lù as a secretary;
sent a letter to the prince,
and entrusted Zhòng to go to the capital.
Zhòng waited for the imperial carriage to depart,
and first presented his petition of injustice.
The prince subtly intervened on his behalf,
and thus he was exonerated,
with the local official ordered to redeem the property and return it to Qiú.
When Zhòng returned,
father and son were both happy.
Lù meticulously inquired about the family members,
planning for their redemption.
Only then did he learn that since Zhòng joined the banner,
he had remarried twice but had no offspring,
and was currently a widower.
Lù then prepared to return.
Initially,
Fú, after parting ways with his younger brother,
prostrated himself and surrendered.
Dàniáng, with his mother seated in the hall,
held a cane and questioned him:
“If you are willing to accept a beating,
then you may stay for now;
otherwise,
since your land and property are all gone,
and there is no place for you to eat,
please leave again. ”
Fú knelt on the ground, weeping,
willing to accept the punishment.
Dàniáng threw down the cane and said:
“A man who sells his wife
is not worth punishing.
But the old case has not been cleared,
so just report him to the chief official if he commits another crime. ”
He then sent someone to inform Jiāng.
Jiāngnǚ cursed,
“Who am I to the Qiú family, that you should tell me!”
Dàniáng frequently recounted Fú’s wrongdoings and ridiculed him.
Fú was ashamed and dared not breathe.
After half a year,
although Dàniáng provided for everything meticulously,
Fú was treated like a servant.
Fú toiled without complaint,
and if entrusted with money, he was never lax.
Dàniáng observed that he had no other intentions,
so she reported to her mother,
asking for Jiāngnǚ to return.
Her mother thought it was impossible to persuade her back.
Dàniáng said:
"Not so.
If she were willing to serve two masters,
why would she willingly suffer such torment?
It must be that she cannot help but feel this resentment."
She then led her brother and personally went to offer an apology (literally, "carry thorns on her back").
Her parents-in-law humbly declined with great earnestness,
but Dàniáng scolded them, making them kneel for a long time,
and then requested to see Jiāngnǚ.
She asked repeatedly,
but Jiāngnǚ firmly avoided coming out;
Dàniáng searched for her and dragged her out.
The woman then pointed at Fú, spat, and cursed him,
Fú was so ashamed and perspiring that he didn't know where to hide himself.
Jiāngmǔ finally pulled him up.
Dàniáng then asked about her return date,
the woman said:
"Previously, I received much kindness from my elder sister;
now, receiving your esteemed command,
how dare I have any other words?
But I am only afraid that I cannot guarantee he will not sell me again!
Furthermore, our bond of kindness and duty is already severed,
what face do I have to live with that black-hearted scoundrel?
Please arrange a separate room;
I will go and serve my old mother,
which is better than having my feet bound and pared (referring to suffering hardship)."
Dàniáng spoke on Fú’s behalf about his repentance,
made an agreement for the next day, and then departed.
The next morning,
she fetched her home in a carriage.
Her mother met her at the gate and knelt to bow to her.
The woman prostrated herself on the ground and wept loudly.
Dàniáng persuaded her to stop,
arranged a feast to celebrate,
ordered Fú to sit by the table,
then held a goblet and said:
"The reason I strenuously contended
was not for my own benefit.
Now that my brother has repented,
and the virtuous wife has returned,
I ask to hand over the household registers;
I came alone,
and I shall leave alone."
The couple both rose from their seats, their expressions changing,
and bowed repeatedly, weeping sorrowfully.
Only then did Dàniáng stop.
Not long after,
the order for the reversal of the unjust judgment arrived,
and within a few days,
all the land and properties were returned to their former owner.
Wèi was greatly astonished,
not knowing how it happened,
regretting that he had no means to act again.
Coincidentally, there was a fire (literally, "calamity of Huílù") at his western neighbor's house.
Wèi pretended to help fight the fire and went there,
secretly using woven straw to ignite Lù’s residence.
The wind also picked up violently,
spreading the fire and burning almost everything;
only two or three rooms of Fú’s dwelling remained,
and the whole family gathered there.
Not long after,
Lù arrived,
and they met with both sorrow and joy.
Initially,
Fàn Gōngzǐ received the divorce letter,
and discussed it with Huìniáng.
Huìniáng wept bitterly,
tore it up, and threw it on the ground.
Her father followed her will,
no longer forcing her.
When Lù returned,
hearing that she was still unmarried,
he was as happy as if he had returned to his in-laws’ house.
Gōngzǐ knew about his disaster
and wanted to keep him;
but Lù refused,
so he resigned and departed.
Dàniáng fortunately had hidden gold,
and brought it out to repair the damaged walls.
Fú carried a shovel to build,
and dug up a hoard of money.
That night, he and his brother unearthed it together;
a stone pool a *zhang* wide
was full of statues of the Immovable Wisdom King (Bùdòng Zūn).
From then on, they hired many workers for extensive construction,
and magnificent buildings rose up in clusters,
their splendor comparable to those of noble families.
Lù was grateful for the general's righteousness,
and prepared a thousand pieces of gold to redeem his father.
Fú requested to go,
so he dispatched a team of strong servants to assist him.
Lù then welcomed Yìniáng back.
Not long after,
his father and elder brother returned together,
and the whole family was filled with joy.
Dàniáng stayed at her maternal home,
forbidding her children from visiting her,
fearing people would gossip about her personal affairs.
After her father returned,
she firmly declined to stay, wishing to leave.
Her brothers could not bear it.
Her father then divided the family property into three parts: the sons received two,
and the daughter received one.
Dàniáng firmly declined.
Both brothers wept, saying:
"If not for our elder sister,
how could we be where we are today!"
Only then did Dàniáng settle down.
She sent someone to summon her children and moved her family to live together with them.
Someone asked Dàniáng:
"Stepmother's children,
why are you so concerned for them?"
Dàniáng said:
"Only birds and beasts know they have a mother but not a father;
how can humans imitate them?"
Fú and Lù both shed tears upon hearing this,
and instructed the laborers to build her residence
to be equal to their own.
Wèi reflected that for more than ten years,
his attempts to harm them had only resulted in blessing them,
and he felt deeply ashamed and regretful.
He also admired their wealth,
and wished to establish friendly relations with them.
So, he used Màozhòng as an intermediary,
prepared gifts, and went.
Fú wanted to refuse them;
but Zhòng could not bear to reject him,
so he accepted the chicken and wine.
The chicken, with its feet bound by cloth,
escaped into the stove;
the stove fire ignited the cloth,
and it flew to perch on the stack of firewood.
The servants did not notice it.
Soon after, the firewood caught fire, causing a disaster to the house,
and the whole family was terrified.
Fortunately, there were many helping hands,
and the fire was extinguished at once,
but everything in the kitchen was gone.
Both brothers said that the gifts were inauspicious.
Later, at their father's birthday,
Wèi again sent a sheep as a gift.
They could not refuse it,
so they tied the sheep to a tree in the courtyard.
That night, a servant boy was beaten by a servant,
and in anger, he ran to the tree,
untied the sheep's rope, and hanged himself.
The brothers sighed, saying:
"His blessings are not as good as his curses!"
From then on, even though Wèi was assiduous,
they dared not accept an inch of his thread,
preferring to heavily repay him instead.
Later, Wèi grew old,
became poor and a beggar.
Chóu provided him with cloth and millet every week, repaying his kindness.
The Chronicler of Anomalies says:
"Alas!
The Creator’s distinctions are not determined by humans!
The more one tries to harm them, the more one blesses them;
for those who are cunning and deceitful, this saying is indeed profound.
Yet, to receive their love and respect,
and instead incur misfortune,
is it not even stranger?
From this, one can know that the water from the Robber's Spring,
even a single scoop, is defiled."
(According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
Outside Xǔchéng, there was a river that surged
deep and dark near the cliffs.
During the height of summer,
a person went in to bathe
and was suddenly as if struck by a knife or an axe;
his corpse, severed, floated to the surface.
Afterward, another person met the same fate.
People were alarmed and surprised.
The Yìzǎi heard of it
and dispatched many men to dam the upstream
and drain the water.
Beneath the cliff, they saw a deep cave
with a rotating wheel inside.
On the wheel were arranged sharp blades like frost.
They removed the wheel and entered the cave.
There was a small stele,
the characters all in Hàn zhuàn script.
Upon closer inspection,
it was Cáo Mèngdé’s tomb.
They broke open the coffin and scattered the bones,
taking all the gold and treasures buried with him.
Yìshǐshì said,
“A later worthy’s poem states: ‘If all seventy-two suspected tombs are dug up,
there must be one where your corpse is buried.’
Who knew it was actually outside the seventy-two tombs?
How deceitful Mán was!
Yet, after more than a thousand years, his decaying bones could not be preserved;
what good did his trickery do?
Alas,
Mán’s cleverness
was precisely Mán’s foolishness!”
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* manuscript.
Dài Shēng from Ānqìng,
when young, had a poor character
and was undisciplined.
One day,
he was returning drunk from elsewhere
and on the way met his deceased maternal cousin Jì Shēng.
Drunk and muddled,
he had forgotten his death
and asked,
“Where have you been?”
Jì said,
“I am already a being from another world;
have you forgotten?”
Only then did Dài realize,
but even drunk, he was not afraid
and asked,
“What do you do in the underworld?”
He replied,
“Recently, I have been serving as a registrar under the Palace of the Zhǎnlún Wáng.”
Dài asked,
“Surely you must know about the fortunes and misfortunes of the human world?”
Jì said,
“This is my duty,
how could I not know?
However, it is too much trouble,
and if it’s not particularly important,
I cannot remember everything.
Three days ago, I happened to check the register
and still saw your name.”
Dài urgently asked what it said,
and Jì replied,
“I dare not deceive you,
your name is in the Dark Prison.”
Dài was greatly frightened,
and his drunkenness also cleared.
He desperately pleaded for rescue.
Jì said,
“This is not something I can help with;
only good deeds can put an end to it.
However, your register of evil deeds is full;
without great good deeds, it cannot be reversed.
What great power does a poor scholar have?
Even if you start performing good deeds today,
it will take more than a year to make a difference.
It’s already too late.
But if you correct your conduct from now on,
then there might be a time when you can leave hell.”
Dài wept upon hearing this,
prostrating himself and begging.
When he looked up,
Jì had already vanished.
He returned home dejected.
From then on, he changed his ways and dared not make any mistakes.
Formerly,
Dài illicitly interacted with his neighbor’s wife.
The neighbors, upon hearing of it, were unwilling to expose him,
but Ēn (a person) covered and seized him.
Dài thereupon reformed his behavior,
permanently severing ties with the woman.
The neighbors, watching him, found no opportunity (to catch him in wrongdoing)
and felt resentful.
One day,
they met in the fields.
Feigning conversation,
they enticed him to peek into a dry well
and consequently pushed him in.
The well was several *zhàng* deep,
and they calculated he must be dead.
However, Dài revived in the middle of the night,
sat in the well, and cried out loudly,
but no one knew.
The neighbors, fearing he might still be alive,
came to listen the following morning.
Hearing his voice,
they immediately threw stones.
Dài moved and hid in a cavity in the well wall,
not daring to make a sound again.
The neighbors, knowing he was not dead,
dug earth and filled the well,
almost to the top.
Inside the cavity, it was pitch black,
truly no different from hell.
The empty cavity offered no food,
and he calculated there was no way to survive.
He crawled forward little by little,
then found water three paces away in every direction,
nowhere else to go,
so he returned to his original sitting place.
At first, he felt hungry in his belly;
after a long time, he completely forgot it.
He then thought that there were no good deeds to be performed beneath the heavy springs,
only to continuously chant the Buddha's name.
Soon, he saw phosphorescent lights floating,
faintly glowing and filling the cavity.
He thereupon prayed to them:
"I hear that green phosphorescence is all wronged ghosts.
Although I am temporarily alive,
it is truly difficult for me to return;
if we can converse together,
it would also alleviate my loneliness."
He then saw all the lights gradually float towards him across the water;
within each phosphorescence was a person,
about half the height of a human body.
He questioned where they came from.
They replied:
"This is an ancient coal well.
The owner was mining coal,
which disturbed an ancient tomb,
and the water from the subterranean sea, summoned by Lóngfēi Xiànggōng,
drowned forty-three people.
We are all ghosts."
He asked:
"Who is this *xiànggōng*?"
They said:
"We do not know.
But the *xiànggōng* is a man of letters,
