now a retainer for the Chénghuáng.
He also pities us for being innocent,
and every three to five days he bestows water gruel.
We think our bones are soaked in cold water,
with no day for transcendence.
If you should ever return to the human world,
please retrieve our remaining bones and bury them in a communal grave.
Then the benefit to those beneath the springs would be great."
Dài said:
"If there is even one chance in ten thousand,
how difficult could this be?
But deeply in the nine earths,
how can I hope to see the light of day again!"
He then taught the ghosts to recite the Buddha's name,
twisting lumps of earth to substitute for prayer beads,
and recorded their counts.
He did not know whether it was dawn or dusk;
when tired, he slept;
when awake, he simply sat.
Suddenly, he saw a caged lamp in the depths.
The ghosts joyfully exclaimed:
"Lóngfēi Xiànggōng is bestowing food!"
They invited Dài to go with them.
Dài worried about the water hindering him,
but the ghosts forcibly pulled and supported him as they went,
floating as if walking on air.
After a winding half-mile or so,
they reached a place.
The ghosts released him, allowing him to walk by himself;
his steps went increasingly upward,
as if ascending steps several *rèn* high.
When the steps ended,
he saw a house and a corridor.
In the main hall, a bright candle burned,
as thick as an arm.
Dài had not seen firelight for a long time
and, overjoyed, hurried forward.
An old man sat above,
dressed in scholar's robes and cap.
Dài stopped, not daring to advance.
The old man had already seen him
and asked in surprise:
"From where does a living person come?"
Dài came forward,
prostrated himself on the ground, and explained his situation.
The old man said:
"I am his (the ancestor's) descendant."
He then ordered him to rise
and granted him a seat.
He identified himself:
"My name is Dài Qián,
courtesy name Lóngfēi.
Because my unworthy descendant Táng
associated with bandits,
and dug a well near my tomb,
making me uneasy in my night chamber,
I therefore flooded it with seawater.
What has become of his descendants now?"
There were five branches of Dài's immediate clan,
and Táng was the eldest.
Initially,
a prominent family in the district bribed Táng
to mine coal beside their ancestral burial ground.
The other younger brothers feared their strength
and dared not contend.
Soon after,
subterranean water suddenly surged,
and all the coal miners died in the well.
The families of the deceased
collectively raised a major lawsuit,
and Táng and the prominent family both became impoverished because of this;
Táng's descendants reached a point of having no place to stand.
Dài was a descendant of Táng's younger brother.
He had heard his ancestors recount the event,
and so he told the old man.
The old man said:
"Such unworthiness,
how could their descendants prosper!
Since you have come here,
you must not neglect your studies."
Thereupon, he provided him with wine and food,
then placed scrolls on the table,
all *chéng* and *hóng* style examination essays,
compelling him to study them.
He also set essay topics
and assigned texts,
like a teacher instructing a student.
The candle in the hall always burned brightly,
neither trimmed nor extinguished.
When tired, he slept;
he could not distinguish morning from evening.
When the old man was out,
a young servant attended to his needs.
Time passed, feeling like several years,
yet fortunately, there was no hardship.
But there were no other books to read,
only a hundred *chéng* and *hóng* style essays,
each having been read over four thousand times.
One day, the old man said:
"Your karmic retribution is fulfilled;
you should return to the human world.
My tomb is next to the coal pit,
and the Yin wind is bone-chilling.
After you achieve your aspirations,
you should move me to Dōngyuán."
Dài respectfully agreed.
The old man then summoned the multitude of ghosts
and sent them back to the old sitting place.
The ghosts bowed repeatedly, giving further instructions. Dài still did not know how he could get out.
Earlier,
a man named Dài was lost from his home.
After all searches had failed,
his mother reported it to the authorities.
Many people were arrested and interrogated,
but there was still no trace of him.
Three or four years passed,
the official left his post,
and the search also slackened.
Dài’s wife was unhappy at home,
so she was sent away to be remarried.
Then some villagers were cleaning out an old well,
and entering the cavity, they saw Dài.
They touched him, and he was not dead.
Greatly alarmed,
they reported it to his family.
After he had been home for a day,
he was finally able to explain the whole story.
When Dài had fallen into the well,
a neighbor had beaten his wife to death.
The neighbor was then sued by the wife's father,
and after more than a year of appeals and investigations,
he returned home with only skin and bones left.
Hearing that Dài had revived,
he fled in great fear.
The clansmen discussed pursuing and prosecuting him,
but Dài would not allow it.
He further stated that he had brought it upon himself in the past,
and that this was a divine retribution,
so what did it have to do with the neighbor?
The neighbor, sensing that Dài had no ulterior motive,
then hesitantly returned.
Once the well water had dried up,
Dài hired someone to enter the cavity and collect the bones,
arranging for each to be properly prepared.
He bought coffins and arranged a burial site,
burying them in a communal mound.
He also consulted the family genealogy and found the name Qián,
with the courtesy name Lóngfēi.
He first prepared offerings and sacrificed at his tomb.
The education commissioner heard of his unusual experience,
and also appreciated his writing.
In that year, he entered the examination hall with excellent grades,
and consequently passed the provincial examination.
Upon his return,
he constructed a burial site on the eastern plain and reinterred Lóngfēi with a lavish burial.
He visited the grave in spring and autumn,
never failing year after year.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“In my hometown, there were coal miners
whose mine was flooded,
and more than ten people drowned in it.
The water was drained to find the bodies,
and it took over two months for it to dry out,
but none of the more than ten people were dead.
When the great flood came,
they all swam to higher ground,
and thus did not drown.
When they were hauled up,
they only expired upon exposure to the air,
and gradually revived after a day and a night.
This showed that when people are underground,
like hibernating snakes or birds,
they cannot die quickly.
However, none have reached several years.
If it were not for extreme good fortune,
who could still be alive
after three years in a hell underground?!”
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Ān Shēng, courtesy name Dàchéng,
was from Chóngqìng.
His father, Xiàolián,
died young.
His younger brother was Èrchéng,
still a child.
Shēng married a woman from the Chén family,
whose childhood name was Shānhú,
and who was gentle and virtuous.
However, Shēng’s mother, Shěn,
was fierce, unreasonable, and unkind.
She treated Shānhú cruelly,
but Shānhú showed no resentment.
Every morning,
she would dress beautifully and go to pay her respects.
Once, when Shēng was ill,
his mother accused Shānhú of being seductive,
and scolded her severely.
Shānhú withdrew,
removed her makeup, and then returned.
Her mother became even angrier,
and hit her own forehead in frustration.
Shēng was always filial,
so he whipped his wife,
and only then did his mother's anger slightly subside.
From then on, she disliked his wife even more.
Although his wife served her with utmost care,
she never spoke a single word to her.
Shēng knew his mother was angry,
so he also lodged elsewhere,
indicating that he had severed ties with his wife.
After a long time,
his mother remained unhappy,
cursing at anything she came across,
with all her anger directed at Shānhú.
Shēng said:
“A wife is married to serve her parents-in-law.
If things are like this now,
why have a wife?”
So he divorced Shānhú,
and sent an old maid to escort her back to her family.
Just as they exited the village gate,
Shānhú wept, saying:
“As a woman, I could not be a good wife.
How can I face my parents if I return?
It would be better to die!”
She pulled out scissors from her sleeve and stabbed herself in the throat.
They quickly saved her,
blood spilled and stained her collar,
and she was helped back to Shēng’s paternal aunt’s house.
The aunt, Wáng,
was a widow without a partner,
so Shānhú stayed there.
When the old maid returned,
Shēng instructed her to hide the situation,
but secretly feared his mother would find out.
A few days later,
he learned that Shānhú’s wound was gradually healing.
He went to Wáng’s door,
and told her not to keep Shānhú.
Wáng called Shēng in;
he did not enter,
but haughtily demanded Shānhú’s expulsion.
Soon after,
Wáng led Shānhú out to see Shēng,
and immediately asked:
“What crime has Shānhú committed?”
Shēng blamed her for not being able to serve his mother.
Shānhú remained silent, not uttering a single word,
only bowing her head and weeping silently,
her tears were all red,
completely staining her white blouse.
Shēng felt sorrowful and could not finish his words, so he withdrew.
A few more days passed,
and his mother had already heard about it.
Angrily, she went to Wáng’s,
and scolded her with harsh words.
Wáng, being arrogant, did not back down,
but instead enumerated her faults,
and said:
“The wife has already been divorced.
To whom does she still belong in the Ān family?
I am keeping the Chén family’s daughter,
not the Ān family’s wife.
Why do you bother interfering with other families’ affairs?”
His mother was extremely angry but ran out of words.
Seeing Wáng’s aggressive demeanor,
she returned ashamed, dejected, and crying bitterly.
Shānhú felt uneasy and
considered going elsewhere.
Earlier,
Shēng had a maternal aunt, Yú,
who was Shěn’s elder sister.
She was over sixty years old,
her son had died,
leaving only a young grandson and a widowed daughter-in-law.
She had also always treated Shānhú kindly.
So, Shānhú bade farewell to Wáng
and went to stay with Aunt Yú.
Aunt Yú inquired about the situation and
spoke at length about her sister’s foolish violence,
immediately wanting to send Shānhú back.
Shānhú strongly stated that it was impossible,
and also urged her not to mention it.
Thus, she lived with Aunt Yú,
as if they were mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.
Shānhú had two elder brothers,
who heard about it and pitied her.
They wanted to bring her home and marry her off.
Shānhú stubbornly refused,
only spinning and weaving with Aunt Yú to support herself.
Shēng's biological mother
tried many ways to arrange a marriage for Shēng,
but his fierce reputation spread,
and no one far or near would be his partner.
After three or four years,
Èrchéng gradually grew older,
and so was married off first.
Èrchéng's wife, Zāng Gū,
was arrogant, fierce, and ill-mannered,
even more so than her mother-in-law.
If her mother-in-law showed anger in her expression,
then Zāng Gū would show anger in her voice.
Èrchéng, being timid,
dared not side with either.
Thus, the mother-in-law's authority greatly diminished;
no one dared provoke her,
and she had to curry favor with Zāng Gū by trying to get her to smile,
yet still could not win Zāng Gū's favor.
Zāng Gū treated her mother-in-law like a maidservant.
Shēng dared not speak,
but instead personally took over his mother's chores,
including washing dishes and sweeping.
Mother and son would often be in a place where no one could see them,
weeping together.
Before long,
the mother fell ill from accumulated distress,
bedridden and weak,
requiring Shēng for all her needs, including urination, defecation, and turning over.
Shēng could not sleep day or night,
and both his eyes were bloodshot.
When he called his younger brother to take his place,
as soon as he entered the door,
Zāng Gū would immediately call him away.
Shēng then ran to tell Yú Ǎo,
hoping Yú Ǎo would come to visit.
Upon entering the door,
he wept and recounted his woes.
Before he finished his story,
Shānhú came out from behind the curtain.
Shēng was greatly ashamed,
stopped speaking, and wanted to leave,
but Shānhú blocked the door with both hands.
Shēng was extremely embarrassed;
he squeezed out from under her elbow and returned home,
not daring to tell his mother either.
Before long,
Yú Ǎo arrived,
and the mother happily welcomed her.
From then on, Yú Ǎo's family sent someone daily,
and they always brought delicious food to Yú Ǎo.
Yú Ǎo sent a message to her widowed daughter-in-law:
"I am not hungry here;
do not do this again in the future."
But the offerings from home
never ceased.
Yú Ǎo refused to taste the food,
saving it to give to the sick mother.
The mother's illness also gradually improved.
Yú Ǎo's young grandson also brought fine pastries, on his mother's orders, to inquire about the illness.
Shěn sighed, saying,
"What a virtuous woman!
What kind of person is my sister?"
Yú Ǎo said,
"How do you regard my former daughter-in-law?"
Shěn replied,
"Alas!
She was certainly not as bad as Jǐ Shì!
But how could she compare to your nephew's wife?"
Yú Ǎo said,
"While she was here, you did not know hardship;
when you were angry,
she felt no resentment: in what way was she inferior?"
Shěn then burst into tears,
and confessed her regret,
saying,
"Has Shānhú married yet?"
Yú Ǎo replied,
"I don't know,
I will inquire about it."
A few more days passed,
and the illness was quite cured.
Yú Ǎo wished to depart.
Shěn wept, saying,
"I fear that if you leave,
I will die again!"
Yú Ǎo then conferred with Shēng
to arrange for Èrchéng to live separately.
Èrchéng told Zāng Gū.
Zāng Gū was displeased,
and her words attacked her elder brother,
and also extended to Yú Ǎo.
Shēng offered to give all his good fields to Èrchéng,
and Zāng Gū then became happy.
After the property division document was drawn up,
Yú Ǎo finally left.
The next day,
she came with a carriage to pick up Shěn.
When Shěn arrived at her house,
she first asked to see her nephew's wife,
and immediately spoke of her nephew's wife's virtues.
Yú Ǎo said,
"A young woman may have a hundred good qualities,
but how could she have no flaws at all?
I can tolerate her, of course.
But even if you had a wife like my daughter-in-law,
I fear you might not be able to enjoy her."
Shěn exclaimed,
"Alas, how unjust!
Do you think I am made of wood and stone, or a deer or a pig?
I have a mouth and a nose;
how could I touch fragrance or stench and not know it?"
Yú Ǎo said,
"If you were divorced like Shānhú,
what would you say about not thinking of your child?"
Shěn replied,
"I would curse her."
Yú Ǎo said,
"If you truly reflect and find nothing to curse yourself for,
then why would you curse her?"
She said:
“Faults are sometimes present in people,
it is only because he cannot be virtuous
that one knows his abuse.”
The old woman said:
“When those who should resent do not resent,
then those who show kindness can be known;
when those who should leave do not leave,
then those who provide comfort can be known.
The one who previously offered gifts and served
was certainly not your wife,
but my daughter-in-law.”
Shěn Jīng was shocked and said:
“How so?”
She said:
“Shānhú has been here for a long time.
What was provided previously
was all earned by her night weaving.”
When Shěn heard this,
tears streamed down her face in several lines,
and she said:
“How can I face my wife!”
The old woman then called Shānhú.
Shānhú came out, her eyes brimming with tears,
and prostrated herself on the ground.
The mother, ashamed and pained, beat herself,
but the old woman strongly persuaded her to stop,
and thus mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were as before.
More than ten days later, they returned together.
At home, a few *mǔ* of meager fields
were not enough for self-sufficiency.
They relied solely on *shēng* to earn a living through writing.
His wife earned a living through needlework and weeding.
The two Chéng were considered to be well-off,
but the elder brother did not seek their help,
nor did the younger brother care for them.
Zāng Gū disdained the elder sister-in-law for having left;
the elder sister-in-law also detested her ferocity
and held her in contempt.
The brothers lived in separate courtyards.
Zāng Gū often committed abuses,
but the whole family covered their ears.
Zāng Gū, having no one to abuse,
abused her husband and maidservant.
One day, the maidservant hanged herself.
The maidservant’s father sued Zāng Gū.
Èr Chéng represented his wife in the lawsuit,
suffered greatly from beatings and accusations,
and Zāng Gū was still detained.
*Shēng* went to great lengths to arrange for her release,
but ultimately failed.
Zāng Gū’s ten fingers were shackled,
and all the flesh was stripped off.
The officials were corrupt and tyrannical,
and their demands were extravagant.
Èr Chéng mortgaged his fields and borrowed funds,
which were paid in full,
and only then was she released.
However, the creditors’ demands for repayment became more urgent day by day,
and left with no choice,
they sold all their good fields to Rèn Wēng in the village.
Wēng offered half the fields as a concession to Dà Chéng,
and wanted *shēng* to sign the deed.
*Shēng* went,
and Wēng suddenly said to himself:
“I am Ān Xiàolián.
Who is this Rèn Mǒu,
who dares to buy my property!”
Then he looked at *shēng* and said:
“In the underworld, I am touched by your and your wife’s filial piety,
so I was allowed to return temporarily for a meeting.”
*Shēng* shed tears and said:
“Father, if you have a spirit,
please quickly save my brother!”
He said:
“He is rebellious towards a fierce woman,
he is not worth pitying!
Go home and quickly prepare gold,
to redeem my ancestral property.”
*Shēng* said:
“Mother and son barely survive,
how can we have so much gold?”
He said:
“There is hidden gold under the Crape Myrtle tree,
which you can take and use.”
He wanted to ask more,
but Wēng was already silent;
a short while later, he awoke,
completely unaware of what had happened.
*Shēng* returned and told his mother,
who also did not fully believe him.
Zāng Gū had already led people to dig for the cellar,
digging four or five *chǐ* deep,
but only saw bricks and stones,
and no gold as mentioned,
so they left disappointed.
*Shēng* heard that they were digging for treasure,
and warned his mother and wife not to go and see.
Later, knowing that they had found nothing,
his mother secretly went to peek,
saw bricks and stones mixed in the earth,
and then returned.
Shānhú arrived afterward,
and saw that the earth was all white silver;
she called *shēng* to come and verify it,
and it was indeed true.
*Shēng*, considering it an inheritance from his ancestors,
could not bear to keep it privately,
so he called Èr Chéng to divide it equally.
The amount happened to be two shares of what was dug up,
and each put it in a bag and returned.
Èr Chéng and Zāng Gū together verified it.
Upon opening the bags, they found them full of rubble,
which greatly astonished them.
They suspected that Èr Chéng had been tricked by his elder brother,
so they sent Èr Chéng to secretly observe his brother.
The brother was arranging gold on a small table,
celebrating with his mother.
Thus, he truthfully told his brother,
and his brother was also astonished,
but felt very sorry for him,
and offered all the gold to him.
Èr Chéng was then happy,
and went to pay off the debts.
He was very grateful to his brother.
Zāng Gū said:
“This further confirms that my brother is deceitful.
If he wasn’t ashamed in his heart,
who would give away what was already divided?”
Èr Wēi was half-doubting, half-believing.
The next day,
the creditor sent a servant,
saying that all the repaid money was counterfeit,
and intended to seize them and report to the official.
Both husband and wife turned pale.
Zāng Gū said:
“What did I tell you!
I insisted that my brother couldn’t be so virtuous,
he is trying to kill you!”
Èr Chéng was afraid,
and went to beg the creditor, but the creditor was angry and would not release them.
Èr Chéng then deeded the fields to the creditor,
allowing him to sell them himself,
and only then did he get the original gold back and return.
Upon closer inspection,
he saw two broken ingots of gold,
only wrapped with a *jiǔyè* of real gold,
the inside was entirely copper.
Zāng Gū then conspired with Èr Chéng: to keep the broken ones,
and return the rest to his brother to observe him.
And she taught him to say:
“I have repeatedly received your kindness,
which I truly cannot bear,
so I will keep a small amount,
to show the meaning of reciprocity.
The remaining property
is still the same as yours, brother,
it is unnecessary to have many fields.
I have already abandoned them;
whether to redeem them or not is up to you, brother.”
*Shēng* did not know their intention,
and firmly declined.
Èr Chéng refused very decisively,
so *shēng* accepted.
It weighed five *liǎng* less,
so he ordered Shānhú to pawn her window ornaments to make up the number,
and took them to the creditor.
The creditor suspected it was old gold,
and clamped it with scissors to test it.
The texture and color were all correct,
without the slightest discrepancy,
so he collected the gold
and exchanged the deed with *shēng*.
After Èr Chéng returned the gold,
he expected there would be some discrepancy;
but when he heard that the old property had been redeemed,
he was greatly surprised.
Zāng Gū suspected that when they dug it up,
his brother had first hidden the real gold.
Angrily, she went to her brother’s place,
reproaching and scolding him fiercely,
and *shēng* then realized the reason for returning the gold.
Shānhú countered with a smile and said:
“The property is indeed still there,
why be angry?”
She made *shēng* take out the deed and give it to them.
One night, Èr Chéng dreamed that his father scolded him, saying:
“You are unfilial and unbrotherly,
your time in the underworld is imminent.
Not an inch of land is yours,
what will you do with your reliance and possession!”
He awoke and told Zāng Gū,
wanting to return the fields to his brother.
Zāng Gū scoffed at his foolishness.
At this time, Èr Chéng had two sons,
the elder seven years old,
the younger three years old.
Soon after,
the elder son died of smallpox.
Zāng Gū finally became afraid,
She made the two boys return the deeds to her brother.
She spoke of it repeatedly,
but the scholar would not accept them.
Not long after,
her second son also died.
Zānggū grew even more frightened,
and personally placed the deeds at her sister-in-law's place.
As spring was almost over,
the fields were overgrown and unplowed.
The scholar, having no choice,
sowed and tended to them.
Zānggū changed her ways from then on,
regularly visiting and inquiring after her mother-in-law like a filial child.
Her reverence for her sister-in-law also reached its peak.
Less than half a year later, her mother-in-law fell ill and died.
Zānggū wept for her in profound grief,
to the point of not being able to swallow a spoonful of drink.
She said to people:
"My mother-in-law died early,
preventing me from serving her.
This is Heaven not allowing me to redeem myself!"
She gave birth to ten children, all of whom died silently.
So, she took her brother-in-law's son as her own.
The couple both lived to a ripe old age.
The scholar had three sons, two of whom became *jìnshì*.
People said this was the reward for filial piety and brotherly love.
The Chronicler of Strange Tales says:
"If one does not encounter the evil of the overbearing,
one does not know the loyalty of the tranquil and upright.
A family and a nation share the same sentiment.
The rebellious wife transformed, and the mother-in-law died—
this is because an entire household's filial piety
had no virtue to conquer it.
Zānggū, having overcome herself,
said that Heaven would not allow her to redeem herself.
If not one who has realized the Way, who could utter such words?
Yet, though she ought to have been forced to die,
she lived to a ripe old age.
Heaven had indeed forgiven her.
Life springs from hardship—
there is a reason for this!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In the south, there are Wǔtōng,
just as in the north there are foxes.
However, while northern fox spirits
can still be driven away by a hundred stratagems,
regarding the Wǔtōng of Jiāngzhè,
if a common family has a beautiful wife,
she is invariably defiled and possessed.
Parents and siblings
dare not utter a sound.
Their harm is especially severe.
There was a Zhào Hóng,
a pawnshop merchant from Wú.
His wife, Yánshì,
was quite elegant.
One night,
a stern-looking man entered from outside.
He held his sword, looking around,
and all the maids and old women fled.
Yánshì wanted to leave,
but the man stood in her way,
saying:
"Do not fear me.
I am Sìláng, the Wǔtōng god.
I love you,
and will not bring you harm."
He then held her waist as if lifting a baby,
placed her on the bed,
her skirt and sash came undone by themselves,
and then he dallied with her.
He was so huge and mighty that it was unbearable;
in her daze, she groaned in pain, almost expiring.
Sìláng also felt pity,
and did not fully exert his member.
After a while, he got off the bed,
saying:
"I will return in five days."
Then he left.
Hóng had set up his pawnshop outside the gate.
That night, a maid ran to tell him.
Hóng knew it was Wǔtōng,
and dared not ask.
At dawn, he looked at his wife;
she was too exhausted to get up.
He felt deeply ashamed of this in his heart,
and warned his family not to spread it.
It was three or four days before the wife began to recover,
but she feared their return.
The maids and sisters dared not sleep in the inner chambers,
all avoiding them for the outer rooms;
only the wife, with a candle, sat full of sorrow, awaiting him.
Soon after,
Sìláng entered with two companions,
both refined young men.
A servant boy laid out dishes and wine,
and they drank together with the wife.
The wife, shy and withdrawn, kept her head down;
even when pressed, she would not drink.
Her heart was fluttering with fear,
worried that they might take turns defiling her,
in which case her life would surely be over.
The three men exchanged toasts,
some calling "Elder Brother,"
others "Third Brother."
They drank until midnight,
when the two guests in the seats of honor rose,
saying:
"Today, Sìláng invited us with a beautiful woman.
We should invite Èrláng and Wǔláng to contribute to a celebratory feast."
Then they took their leave.
Sìláng pulled the wife into the bed curtains.
The wife pleaded for exemption;
Sìláng forced himself upon her.
Blood flowed profusely,
she fainted and lost consciousness.
Only then did Sìláng leave.
The wife lay prostrate on the bed,
overwhelmed with shame and indignation,
wanting to kill herself.
But when she tried to hang herself, the rope would break on its own;
she tried repeatedly, but it was always the same.
She suffered, unable to die.
Fortunately, Sìláng did not come often,
promising to return only when the wife had recovered.
For two or three months,
the entire family had no peace.
There was a Wànshēng from Kuàijī,
Zhào's cousin,
who was fierce and a skilled archer.
One day, he visited Zhào.
It was already evening.
As Zhào's guest quarters were used by his family,
he led his guest to stay in the inner courtyard.
Wànshēng could not sleep for a long time.
He heard someone walking in the courtyard.
He peeked through the window,
and saw a man enter the wife's room.
Suspicious,
he grabbed a knife and secretly watched.
He saw the man sitting shoulder to shoulder with Yánshì,
and dishes were laid out on a table.
Furious anger flared within him.
He rushed in.
The man sprang up in alarm.
He frantically searched for his sword;
but the knife had already struck his skull.
His skull split, and he fell.
Looking at him,
it was a small horse,
as big as a donkey.
He asked the wife in astonishment.
The wife told him everything,
adding:
"The gods will arrive soon!
What shall we do?"
Wànshēng waved his hand,
signaling her to be silent.
He extinguished the candle, took his bow and arrows,
and hid in the darkness.
Not long after,
four or five people fell from the sky.
Wànshēng quickly fired an arrow,
and the leader dropped dead.
Three people roared in rage,
drawing their swords to search for the shooter.
Wànshēng held his blade, leaning behind the door,
remaining perfectly still.
One person entered,
and was also cut down by the neck.
Wànshēng still leaned behind the door.
After a long silence,
he came out,
knocked on the gate, and told Zhào.
Zhào was greatly alarmed.
Together, they lit candles,
and found a horse and two pigs dead in the room.
The whole family rejoiced.
Still fearing revenge from the remaining entities,
they kept Wànshēng at home,
roasting the pigs and cooking the horse to offer him.
The taste was delicious,
different from ordinary delicacies.
The name of Wànshēng
thus became widely known.
After staying for more than a month,
the strange occurrences completely ceased.
So, he bade farewell, intending to leave.
A certain lumber merchant was desperate to keep him.
Previously,
a certain Mǒu had an unmarried daughter.
Suddenly, Wǔtōng descended in broad daylight.
He was a handsome man of over twenty,
who said he would take her as his wife.
He offered a hundred taels of gold
and left after setting an auspicious date.
As the date approached,
the whole family was terrified.
Hearing of Wàn Shēng’s reputation,
they earnestly invited him to their home.
Fearing Wàn Shēng would refuse,
they concealed the truth from him.
After the elaborate banquet,
the daughter, adorned, came out to greet the guest.
She was sixteen or seventeen,
a beautiful girl.
Wàn Shēng was astonished and didn't understand the reason,
leaving his seat and bowing.
Mǒu pressed him to sit and then told him the truth.
Wàn Shēng was surprised at first hearing it,
but being naturally proud and spirited,
he did not decline.
On the appointed day,
Mǒu still hung colorful silks at his gate
and made Wàn Shēng sit in the room.
As the sun began to set, Wǔtōng had not arrived.
He secretly thought the "groom" had already been executed.
Shortly after,
he saw something like a bird suddenly falling from the eaves,
which turned out to be a young man in splendid attire entering.
Seeing Wàn Shēng,
he turned and fled.
Wàn Shēng chased him out,
only to see a black qi about to fly away.
He leaped and swung his sword at it,
severing one of its feet.
It howled loudly and departed.
Looking down,
he saw a giant claw as big as a hand,
but he didn't know what creature it belonged to.
Following its blood trail,
it led into the river.
Mǒu was overjoyed,
and grateful to Wàn Shēng for eliminating the demon.
That very evening, using the prepared bedding,
he had him perform the ritual of the bridal cup with his daughter.
From then on, all who had previously suffered from Wǔtōng
came to invite Wàn Shēng to stay a night at their homes.
After more than a year,
he finally took his wife and left.
From that time on, there was only one Wǔtōng in Wúzhōng,
who dared not openly cause harm.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"Wǔtōng and Qīngwā
have deluded the populace for too long,
leading to widespread licentiousness,
with no one daring to criticize
or utter a word.
Wàn Shēng is truly a forthright man of the world!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Jīn Shēng,
courtesy name Yùsūn,
was a native of Sūzhōu.
He set up a school in Huái,
residing in the garden of a gentry member.
There were not many buildings in the garden,
and the flowers and trees were dense and overgrown.
As night deepened,
the servants and boys all dispersed,
leaving him a lone figure wandering,
his mood quite despondent.
One night,
as the third watch was almost over, someone suddenly tapped on the door with a finger.
He hastily asked who it was,
to which the reply was,
"begging for fire,"
the voice resembling that of a student.
He opened the door and let her in;
it was a beautiful woman of sixteen,
with a maidservant following behind her.
Shēng suspected she was a demon,
and scrutinized her very closely.
The woman said:
"I pity you as a refined scholar,
so lonely and pitiable.
I am not afraid of much exposure,
and wish to spend this good night with you.
If I were to tell you the reason,
I would not dare to come, and you would not dare to admit me."
Shēng again thought she was a runaway girl from a neighbor's house,
and fearing for his reputation,
respectfully declined.
The woman cast a sidelong glance,
and Shēng felt his soul and spirit completely entranced.
Suddenly, he was uncontrollably disoriented.
The maidservant, realizing this,
immediately said,
"Xiágū,
I shall go now."
The woman nodded.
After a moment, she scolded,
"Go if you must,
but why say 'Yúnnà' or 'Xiá'!"
After the maidservant left,
the woman smiled and said,
"Just now there was no one in the room,
so I came with my maid.
Being so ignorant,
she let you hear my given name."
Shēng said,
"Since you are so meticulous,
I fear there might be trouble."
The woman replied,
"You will know in due time.
I guarantee I will not ruin your conduct,
so do not worry."
She went to the bed and loosened her attire.
He saw on her arm a wristlet
with gold strung with fire-polished jade,
holding twin bright pearls.
When the candle was extinguished,
their light illuminated the entire room.
Shēng was even more astonished,
but still could not guess her origin.
As soon as the deed was done,
the maidservant came and knocked on the window.
The woman rose,
illuminating the path with her clasp.
She entered the dense trees and left.
From then on, she came every night.
Once, when she left,
Shēng stealthily followed her from a distance;
the woman seemed to sense it,
and quickly obscured her light.
The trees were thick and luxuriant,
and it was too dark to see his hand, so he returned.
One day,
Shēng went north of the river.
The strap of his bamboo hat was broken,
and the wind threatened to blow it off,
so he constantly held it with his hand while on horseback.
Upon reaching the river,
he sat in a small boat.
A gust of wind blew his hat off,
and it drifted away with the waves.
He was quite dismayed.
After crossing,
he saw a strong wind lifting his hat,
spinning in the air.
Gradually it descended,
and he caught it with his hand;
the strap was already mended.
He was surprised.
Returning to his study,
he recounted the incident to the woman; she did not speak,
but only smiled faintly.
Shēng suspected the woman had done it,
and said,
"If you are indeed a divine being,
you should tell me plainly,
to dispel my worries and doubts."
The woman said,
"In this solitude,
to have such a foolishly devoted person like me to relieve your boredom,
I consider myself not bad.
Even if I could do this,
it would only be out of love.
If you insist on questioning me,
do you wish to break off our relationship?"
Shēng dared not speak again.
Formerly,
Shēng had a niece whom he raised.
After she was married,
she was plagued by the Wǔtōng.
Shēng was worried about this but had not told anyone.
As he and the girl had been intimate for a long time,
he poured out his heart to her without reservation.
The girl said,
"Such things
my father can exorcise.
But how dare I disclose a lover's private affairs to my stern father?"
Shēng desperately pleaded for a solution.
The girl pondered and said,
"This is also easy to remove,
but I must go in person.
Those beings are all my family's slaves.
If I were to touch their skin with a finger,
this disgrace would not be outshone even by the Xījiāng."
Shēng pleaded endlessly.
The girl said,
"I will arrange it immediately."
She arrived the next evening,
and announced,
"I have sent a maid south for you.
The maid is weak,
I fear she may not be able to completely eliminate them."
The next night, as Shēng was about to sleep,
the maid came knocking at the door.
Shēng hastily let her in.
The girl asked,
"How was it?"
She replied,
"I was unable to capture it with force,
so I castrated it."
Shēng asked, smiling, about the details.
She said,
"At first, I thought it was the young master's home;
but when I arrived,
I realized it was not.
By the time I reached the son-in-law's house,
the lamps were already lit.
I went in and saw the young mistress sitting under the lamp,
leaning on a table as if asleep.
I collected her soul and covered it in a jar.
A short while later,
the entity arrived,
entered the room, and quickly retreated,
saying, 'How can a living person be staying here!'
It carefully inspected but found nothing else,
so it re-entered.
I pretended to be unconscious.
It opened her dress and entered,
then exclaimed in surprise, 'How can there be a soldier's aura!'
I originally did not want to defile my fingers with such a filthy thing,
but fearing delay would cause trouble,
I quickly seized and castrated it.
The creature shrieked in surprise
and fled.
Then I got up and uncovered the jar,
the young mistress seemed to wake up,
and the maid left."
Shēng was delighted and thanked her,
and the girl left with the maid.
For more than half a month afterward,
she did not return,
and Shēng had given up hope.
At the end of the year,
he was closing his study and preparing to return home,
when the girl suddenly arrived.
Shēng happily went to meet her,
saying,
"You have abandoned me for so long,
I thought you must have committed some offense somewhere;
fortunately, it is not a complete severance?"
The girl said,
"A year's affection,
yet to part without a single word
would indeed be incomplete.
I heard you were packing up your scrolls,
so I secretly came to bid you farewell."
Shēng invited her to return with him.
The girl sighed, saying,
"It's difficult to explain!
Now that we are about to part,
I cannot bear to hide my feelings: I am actually the daughter of Jīnlóng Dàwáng.
Because we had a karmic connection from a previous life,
I came to be with you.
I should not have sent my maid to Jiāngnán,
causing rumors to spread throughout the jiānghú,
saying that I had castrated the Wǔtōng for you.
My father heard about it
and considered it a great disgrace.
In his rage, he wanted to put me to death.
Fortunately, the maid took responsibility for herself,
and his anger subsided somewhat;
he flogged the maid a hundred times.
For my every step,
I am accompanied by a wet nurse.
I seized a moment to come here,
but I cannot fully express my feelings,
what can I do!"
Having spoken,
she wished to depart.
Shēng held her back and wept.
The girl said,
"Do not be like this,
we can reunite in thirty years."
Shēng said,
"I am thirty years old now,
in another thirty years,
I will be a white-haired old man.
How can I bear to see you again?"
The girl said,
"Not so,
there are no old men in the Lónggōng.
Moreover, a person's lifespan
does not depend on their appearance.
If you merely wish to retain your youth,
that is also very easy."
Then she wrote a prescription at the beginning of a scroll and left.
Shēng returned home,
and his niece finally spoke of her strange experience,
saying,
"That night was like a dream.
I felt someone seize me and stuff me into a jar;
when I woke up,
blood stained the bedclothes,
and the strange creature was gone."
Shēng said,
"I prayed to Hébó earlier."
All doubts then resolved.
Later, when Shēng was over sixty,
his appearance still resembled that of a thirty-year-old.
One day,
as he was crossing a river,
he saw a lotus leaf floating far upstream,
as large as a mat.
A beautiful woman sat upon it.
On closer inspection,
it was the divine maiden.
He leaped to follow her,
but the person and the lotus leaf both shrank,
gradually becoming coin-sized and then disappearing.
This incident and the one involving Zhào Hóngyī
both happened in the late Míng dynasty,
it is unknown which occurred first or last.
If it was after Wàn Shēng used his power,
then only half of a Wǔtōng would have remained in Wúxià,
which explains why it was not enough to cause harm.
According to the handwritten manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Beside the Jīng Hé,
there was a scholar’s son named Shēn Shì.
His family was impoverished and destitute;
all day long, they constantly lacked fire for cooking.
Husband and wife faced each other,
having no means to make a living.
The wife said:
"There is no alternative.
Perhaps you should become a thief!"
Shēn replied:
"As a scholar's son,
I cannot glorify my ancestors,
but instead disgrace my family and shame my forebears.
To live as a thief
is worse than to die in obscurity!"
The wife angrily said:
"Do you wish to live but abhor disgrace?
In this world, for those who do not farm but seek to make a living,
there are only two paths. Since you cannot steal,
I might as well become a prostitute!"
Shēn became enraged,
and he and his wife exchanged insulting words.
The wife, full of anger, went to sleep.
Shēn thought: As a man, I cannot even provide two meals,
to the point where my wife contemplates prostitution.
Indeed, it would be better to die!
He stealthily got up
and threw a noose among the courtyard trees.
Just then, he saw his father arrive,
who exclaimed in surprise:
"Foolish child,
why resort to this!"
He cut the rope
and instructed:
"Theft can be done,
but you must choose a place deeply hidden among tall crops to lie in wait.
This venture can make you rich;
there's no need to do it again."
The wife heard a falling sound
and woke up with a start.
She called her husband, but received no reply.
She lit a fire to search for him
and saw the noose on the tree snapped,
with Shēn lying dead beneath it.
She was greatly alarmed.
She caressed and pressed him,
and after a while, he revived,
and she helped him lie on the bed.
The wife's anger subsided somewhat.
At dawn,
she pretended her husband was ill,
begged from neighbors, and obtained thin gruel to feed Shēn.
After Shēn had sipped it,
he went out and departed.
By noon,
he returned, carrying a sack of rice.
When his wife asked where it came from,
he said:
"All my father's friends are from prominent families.
I used to be ashamed of 'wagging my tail' (begging),
so I disdained to ask them for help.
The ancients said: 'One who has not met with misfortune can be free from doing anything improper.'
But now I am about to become a thief,
what do I care!
You can quickly cook;
I will follow your words
and go commit robbery."
The wife suspected he hadn't forgotten the previous anger,
and she suppressed it.
So, she washed the rice and made gruel.
After Shēn had eaten his fill,
he quickly found a sturdy piece of wood,
hewed it into a club,
and holding it, intended to go out.
The wife observed that his intention seemed genuine,
so she pulled him back and stopped him.
Shēn said:
"You taught me to do it.
If the matter fails and implicates us both,
you must not regret it!"
He broke free and left.
At dusk,
he reached a nearby village,
and hid about a *lǐ* away from the village.
Suddenly, there was a heavy rain,
drenching him from head to toe.
He looked from afar at dense trees,
intending to seek shelter there.
But a flash of lightning revealed
he was already near the village wall.
In the distance, there seemed to be a person walking, and fearing he might be seen, he noticed dense crops below the wall,
so he quickly rushed in
and crouched to hide among them.
Before long,
a man came,
of very strong and robust build,
and also entered the crops.
Shēn was afraid
and dared not make the slightest movement.
Fortunately, the man moved away diagonally.
Shēn subtly peered
and saw him enter inside the wall.
He silently recalled that inside the wall was the mansion of the wealthy Kàng Shì.
This must be a "gentleman on the beam" (burglar),
and when he emerges with his loot,
there should be a share for him.
He also thought: This person is strong and robust;
if he takes skillfully and refuses to share,
it will surely come to blows.
He estimated he was no match for him in strength,
so it would be better to take advantage of his unpreparedness and knock him down.
Having made up his mind,
he lay in wait attentively.
It was almost cockcrow
before the figure finally climbed over the wall and emerged.
Before its feet touched the ground,
Shēn suddenly sprang up
and struck its waist and spine with his club.
It stumbled and fell with a thud.
It was a giant turtle,
with a beak gaping like a basin.
Greatly startled,
he struck it again and again,
and it died.
Before this,
Old Kàng had a daughter,
exceptionally intelligent and beautiful,
whom both parents loved dearly.
One night,
a man entered her room,
intimately pressed her for pleasure.
When she tried to cry out,
her tongue was already in her mouth,
she fainted and lost consciousness,
allowing him to do as he pleased before leaving.
Ashamed to tell anyone,
she only gathered many maids,
and strictly barred the doors.
After everyone had gone to bed at night,
they would again not know how the door opened. Upon entering the room, everyone would be in a trance,
and the maids would be violated one after another.
Thereupon, they told each other, greatly alarmed,
and informed Old Kàng.
Old Kàng instructed his family to arm themselves and surround the embroidered chambers,
while those inside sat with candles.
Around midnight,
people inside and outside all fell into a trance simultaneously.
Suddenly, as if waking from a dream,
they saw the daughter lying naked,
appearing dazed.
After a long time, she finally woke up.
Old Kàng was very angry
but helpless.
After several months,
the daughter became emaciated and quite frail.
He often told people:
"Whoever can drive away this entity
will be rewarded with three hundred taels of gold."
Shēn had also heard all about this in ordinary times.
That night, upon obtaining the turtle,
he realized that the one harassing Old Kàng's daughter
must be this creature.
So, he knocked on the door to claim the reward.
Old Kàng was delighted,
invited him to the place of honor,
and had someone carry the turtle to the courtyard
and butcher it.
He kept Shēn overnight,
and indeed, the strange occurrences ceased.
So, he gave him the promised amount of gold.
Shēn returned home, carrying the gold.
Shēn's 妻 (qī) had been
anxiously waiting for him, as he had not returned the previous night.
Seeing Shēn (Shēn) enter,
she eagerly questioned him.
Shēn (Shēn) did not speak,
but placed the whole bundle on the couch.
His wife opened and looked at it,
nearly fainting from fright,
and said:
“Are you really a thief? ”
Shēn (Shēn) said:
“You forced me to do this,
and now you speak like this! ”
His wife wept and said:
“Before, I was just teasing you.
Now you have committed a crime punishable by beheading,
and I cannot bear the burden of a thief.
Please let me die first! ”
Then she ran away.
Shēn (Shēn) chased after her,
smilingly pulled her back,
and told her the whole truth.
His wife then rejoiced.
From then on, they planned their livelihood,
and became known as "plainly wealthy."
Yìshǐshì (Yìshǐshì) said:
“People do not suffer from poverty,
but from lack of virtue.
Those whose conduct is upright,
even if they starve, will not die;
even if they are not pitied by others,
they will have the protection of ghosts.
As for the poor people of this world,
where there is profit, they forget righteousness;
where there is food, they forget shame.
People dare not entrust even a single coin to them,
so how can they expect to be forgiven by ghosts and gods? ”
There was a certain poor man named Yǐ (Yǐ) in the district.
As the twelfth lunar month was drawing to a close,
he had no complete clothes on his body.
He thought to himself: How can I see out the year?
He dared not speak to his wife,
but secretly grasped a white cudgel,
went out and lay hidden in a grave,
hoping that someone traveling alone would pass by,
so he could rob them of their possessions.
His anticipation was very bitter,
and there was no one in sight;
the pine wind, however, pierced his bones,
and he could not bear it any longer.
His intention was almost spent,
when he suddenly saw a hunched figure approaching.
He secretly rejoiced in his heart,
and quickly emerged with his cudgel.
It was an old woman carrying a sack by the roadside,
who sorrowfully said:
“I truly have nothing extra on me.
My family is out of food,
I just begged five shēng (shēng) of rice from my son-in-law's family. ”
Yǐ (Yǐ) snatched the rice,
and then wanted to strip her of her padded jacket.
The old woman pleaded bitterly.
Yǐ (Yǐ) pitied her old age,
released her,
and carried the rice home.
His wife questioned him about its origin,
and he deceitfully replied
“gambling debt.”
Secretly, he thought this strategy was quite good.
The next night, he went again.
Not long after,
he saw a person carrying a cudgel approaching,
who also entered the grave,
squatting and looking around,
seeming to be of the same ilk.
Yǐ (Yǐ) then cautiously emerged from behind the tomb.
The person was startled and asked:
“Who is it? ”
He replied:
“A traveler. ”
The other asked:
“Why are you not moving? ”
He said:
“Waiting for you. ”
The person laughed.
Each understood the other's meaning,
and they both spoke of the hardships of hunger and cold.
As the night deepened,
they caught nothing.
Yǐ (Yǐ) wanted to return,
but the person said:
“Although you are engaged in this line of work,
you are still a novice.
In the front village, there is a family marrying off a daughter;
they will be busy until midnight,
and the whole family will surely be exhausted.
Follow me,
and we can divide what we get. ”
Yǐ (Yǐ) rejoiced
and followed him.
They reached a gate,
and through the wall, they heard the sound of baking cakes,
knowing they were not yet asleep.
They lay in wait.
Before long,
a person opened the gate, carrying a pole, and went out to draw water.
The two took the opportunity to slip in.
They saw a lamp shining in the north chamber,
while other rooms were dark.
They heard an old woman say:
“Sister,
please check the east chamber.
Your trousseau is all in the chest.
Did you forget to lock it? ”
They heard the young woman make a soft, sleepy sound.
The two secretly rejoiced,
and stealthily hurried to the east chamber.
In the dark, they groped and found the sleeping chest.
They opened the lid and felt inside;
it was so deep that they couldn't reach the bottom.
The person said to Yǐ (Yǐ):
“Get in! ”
Yǐ (Yǐ) indeed got in,
found a bundle,
and passed it out.
The person asked:
“Is that all? ”
He said:
“That's all. ”
The other then added:
“Search again. ”
Then he closed the chest,
locked it, and left.
Yǐ (Yǐ) was inside,
distressed and without a plan.
Not long after,
a lamp was brought in,
first illuminating the chest.
They heard the old woman say:
“Who has already locked it? ”
Then the mother and daughter went to bed and put out the candle.
Yǐ (Yǐ) was in a great hurry,
and made a sound like a mouse gnawing on something.
The daughter said:
“There's a mouse in the chest! ”
The old woman said:
“Don't let it ruin your clothes.
I am utterly exhausted;
you should check it yourself. ”
The daughter got up, shaking her clothes,
unlocked and opened the chest.
Yǐ (Yǐ) darted out,
and the daughter screamed and fell.
Yǐ (Yǐ) pulled open the gate and ran off,
though he got nothing,
he secretly rejoiced at having escaped.
The theft at the wedding family's house
spread far and wide.
Some suspected Yǐ (Yǐ).
Yǐ (Yǐ) was afraid,
fled a hundred lǐ (lǐ) to the east,
and worked as a hired hand for an innkeeper.
After more than a year,
the rumors gradually subsided,
and he finally brought his wife to live with him,
no longer practicing with the white cudgel.
This is his self-narration,
which resembles the story of the Shēn (Shēn) family,
hence it is appended.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Hóng Dàyè
was a man from the capital.
His wife, née Zhū,
was quite beautiful and charming,
and they loved each other deeply.
Later, Hóng took a maid named Bǎodài as his concubine.
Her looks were far inferior to Zhū’s,
but Hóng doted on her.
Zhū was displeased
and often quarreled with him over this.
Although Hóng dared not openly spend the night in the concubine’s room,
he doted on Bǎodài even more
and neglected Zhū.
Later, they moved their residence
and became neighbors with a silk merchant named Dí.
Dí’s wife, Héngniáng,
first called on Zhū.
Héngniáng was about thirty,
of only average looks,
but her words were light and charming, and Zhū liked her.
The next day,
Zhū returned her visit
and saw that Dí’s house also had a junior wife,
who was around twenty years old
and very pretty.
They had been neighbors for almost half a year,
and Zhū had never heard a single quarrel from them;
yet Dí exclusively doted on Héngniáng,
the junior wife being merely an empty position.
One day, Zhū saw Héngniáng and asked her,
“I used to think that a husband’s love for his concubine
was because she was a concubine,
and I often wished to change my wife’s title to concubine.
Now I know that is not the case.
What is your secret, madam?
If you can teach me,
I am willing to become your disciple.”
Héngniáng said,
“Alas!
You alienate yourself,
yet you blame your husband?
To nag him morning and night
is like driving sparrows into a thicket,
only making them flee further!
When he returns, give him more freedom.
Even if he comes to you himself,
do not let him in.
After a month,
I will devise a further plan for you.”
Zhū followed her advice: she adorned Bǎodài even more,
and made her sleep with her husband.
She also
made Bǎodài share
every meal with him.
When Hóng occasionally approached Zhū,
Zhū resisted him even more strongly,
so everyone praised Madame Zhū’s virtue.
After more than a month of this,
Zhū went to see Héngniáng.
Héngniáng happily said,
“You’ve got it!
Go home and ruin your makeup,
don’t wear fancy clothes,
don’t use powder or rouge,
with a dirty face and worn-out shoes,
mingle with the family and do chores.
After a month,
you can come again.”
Zhū obeyed: she wore patched clothes,
deliberately looked untidy,
and concerned herself with nothing but spinning and weaving.
Hóng pitied her
and asked Bǎodài to share her labor;
Zhū refused
and would scold Bǎodài away.
After a month of this,
she went to see Héngniáng again.
Héngniáng said,
“You, my child, are truly teachable!
The day after tomorrow is the Shàngsì Festival,
and I want to invite you to stroll in the spring garden.
You must shed all your worn-out clothes,
and put on new robes, trousers, socks, and shoes,
looking completely fresh.
Come to me early.”
Zhū said,
“Yes.”
On that day,
she carefully applied powder and yellow pigment while looking in the mirror,
exactly as Héngniáng had instructed.
When her makeup was done,
she went to Héngniáng.
Héngniáng happily said,
“Excellent!”
She then helped Zhū arrange her phoenix-like topknot,
which was so bright it reflected shadows.
Her robe sleeves did not conform to the current style,
so Héngniáng unstitched them
and remade them.
Saying her shoe style was clumsy,
she took out her own shoes from a chest
and together they finished them,
then
told Zhū to change into them immediately.
Before parting,
she offered Zhū wine
and instructed her:
“When you return and see your husband,
close your door early and go to bed.
When he comes knocking,
do not let him in.
After he calls three times,
you may let him in once,
but be stingy with kisses
and touches.
Be reserved in all things.
In half a month,
come again.”
Zhū returned,
displaying her new makeup to Hóng.
Hóng gazed at her up and down,
smiling with an unusual joy.
Zhū spoke little of her outing,
then propped her chin and adopted an alluring posture.
Before dusk,
she rose, went to her room,
closed the door, and went to bed.
Soon after,
Hóng indeed came knocking,
but Zhū lay firmly in bed and did not get up,
so Hóng eventually left.
The next evening was the same.
The day after,
Hóng expressed his displeasure.
Zhū said,
“I am accustomed to sleeping alone and cannot bear to be disturbed again.”
When the sun was already setting,
Hóng entered her boudoir and sat waiting for her.
After extinguishing the candle and getting into bed,
he treated her like a new bride,
and they enjoyed great intimacy.
He made an appointment for the next night,
but Zhū refused;
instead, she made a long-term agreement with Hóng,
setting the rate at three days
between their intimacies.
About half a month later,
Zhū returned to Héngniáng.
Héngniáng closed her door and said to her,
"From now on, you can have sole possession of your husband's chamber.
However, although you are beautiful,
you lack charm.
With your looks,
a little charm could win you favor even over Xīshī,
let alone lesser women!"
Thereupon, she had her try a sidelong glance,
and said,
"No!
The fault is in the outer corner of the eye."
She had her try a smile,
and again said,
"No!
The fault is in the left cheek."
Then, Héngniáng sent a charming glance with her beautiful eyes,
and smiled broadly, subtly revealing her beautiful teeth,
and made Zhū imitate her.
After dozens of attempts,
Zhū finally managed to vaguely capture the resemblance.
Héngniáng said, "
You may return now.
Practice with a mirror until you are proficient;
there is nothing more to teach.
As for matters in the bedroom,
you should act spontaneously,
and cater to his preferences.
This cannot be conveyed through words."
Zhū returned,
and followed all of Héngniáng's instructions.
Hóng was extremely pleased,
completely enchanted in both body and spirit,
fearing only rejection.
As dusk approached,
they would flirt and tease each other,
never leaving the boudoir by even a single step,
making it a daily routine.
He ultimately could not bring himself to send her away.
Zhū treated Bǎodài even better,
and whenever there was a feast in their chambers,
she would invite Bǎodài to sit on the bed with them.
However, Hóng viewed Bǎodài as increasingly ugly,
would not finish the meal with her,
and would send her away.
Zhū lured Madame Bǎodài to her room,
locked it,
and Hóng had no one to lie with all night.
Consequently, Bǎodài resented Hóng,
and would complain and slander him to others.
Hóng became even more disgusted and angry with her,
and gradually resorted to whipping and beating her.
Bǎodài, in her resentment,
neglected herself,
wearing worn and dirty shoes,
her hair like tangled weeds,
no longer looking like a proper person.
One day, Héngniáng said to Zhū,
"How do you find my methods?"
Zhū replied,
"The method is truly marvelous;
however, your disciple can follow it,
but still cannot understand its principles.
What is the reason for indulgence?"
Héngniáng said,
"Have you not heard: human nature tires of the old and delights in the new,
values what is difficult to obtain and takes lightly what is easy?
A husband's love for his concubine
is not necessarily because of her beauty;
it is because he relishes what he has just acquired,
and treasures what he has had to strive for.
If you indulge him and satiate him,
then even rare delicacies become common,
let alone humble fare!"
"And what about discrediting her and then flaunting her again?"
Zhū asked.
Héngniáng replied,
"If she is ignored and unnoticed,
she appears to have been absent for a long time;
when he suddenly sees her in splendid attire,
it is as if she is newly arrived. It is like a poor person who suddenly gets fine meat;
he will then find plain rice tasteless.
And if you do not make it easy for him to be with her,
then she becomes old and you become new,
she becomes easy and you become difficult.
This is the method by which you transform a wife into a concubine."
Zhū was greatly pleased,
and thereafter became Héngniáng's intimate friend in the boudoir.
After several years,
Héngniáng suddenly said to Zhū,
"Our affection for each other is like that of one body,
so it is only right that I do not deceive you.
I wanted to tell you before, but I was afraid you would doubt me.
Since we are about to part,
I dare to tell you the truth: I am a fox spirit.
As a child, I suffered the calamity of a stepmother,
and was sold as a concubine in the capital.
My husband treated me well,
so I could not bear to leave him abruptly,
and lingered until now.
Tomorrow, my old father will 'shed his corpse' and ascend,
and I will go to visit him.
I will not return."
Zhū clasped her hand and sighed mournfully.
Early the next morning, when Zhū went to check,
the entire household was alarmed and terrified;
Héngniáng had vanished.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"Those who buy pearls value the casket more than the pearl itself. The human inclination to tire of the old and desire the new, to value the difficult and scorn the easy,
is a delusion that cannot be broken through the ages;
and thus, the art of turning hatred into love
is able to operate within it.
In ancient times, obsequious ministers serving their lords
would prevent others from seeing them,
and prevent them from reading books.
Thus, one knows that securing one's position and maintaining favor
all have their secret transmissions."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Cháng Dàyòng,
a native of Luò,
had a particular fondness for peonies.
He heard that the peonies of Cáozhōu were the finest in Qí and Lǔ,
and his heart yearned for them.
It so happened that he had other business in Cáo,
so he took lodging in the garden of a gentry member.
It was then the second month,
and the peonies had not yet blossomed.
He merely wandered in the garden,
his eyes fixed on the budding shoots,
hoping to see them burst forth together.
He composed a hundred poems expressing his thoughts on peonies.
Before long,
the flowers gradually began to bud,
but his travel funds were running low.
He soon pawned his spring clothes,
lingering and forgetting to return.
One day,
early in the morning, he went to the flower beds,
where he saw a young lady and an old nanny.
Suspecting they were family members of a noble household,
he quickly turned back.
In the evening, he went again,
and saw them again.
He calmly avoided them and left.
He secretly observed them:
the young lady's palace attire was dazzlingly beautiful.
In his dazed state,
a thought suddenly struck him: this must be an immortal.
How could such a woman exist in the world?
He quickly turned back and searched for her.
Suddenly, passing the rockery,
he happened to encounter the nanny.
The young lady was sitting on a rock.
They looked at each other, startled.
The nanny shielded the girl with her body,
and scolded,
"Mad student, what are you doing!"
The student knelt down and said,
"My lady must be a divine immortal!"
The nanny chided him,
"Such wild talk!
You should be arrested and sent to the magistrate!"
The student was greatly frightened.
The young lady smiled faintly and said,
"Leave him!"
She left, passing over the mountain.
The student returned,
unable to move a step.
He thought the young lady would go and tell her father and elder brothers,
and that humiliation would surely follow. He lay down in his empty study,
regretting his rashness.
He secretly hoped that the young lady had no angry expression,
and perhaps would not dwell on it.
Regret and fear intertwined,
and he fell ill overnight.
By the hour of Chén (7-9 AM),
he was relieved that no accusers had come,
and his heart gradually settled.
But recalling her voice and appearance,
his fear turned into longing.
After three such days,
he was emaciated and felt on the verge of death.
Holding a candle late at night,
his servant already fast asleep,
the nanny entered,
holding a bowl, and offered it, saying:
“My lady Gě Jīn (葛巾) has
personally prepared a cup of zhèn tāng (鴆湯)
for you. Drink it quickly!”
The student heard this and was alarmed.
After a moment, he said,
“My lady and I
have never had any grievances or ill will.
How could you want to grant me death?
Since it has been personally prepared by you,
rather than suffer from lovesickness,
it is better to take the poison and die!”
So, he took it and drank it all.
The old woman smiled,
took the bowl, and left.
The student felt the aroma of the medicine was cool,
seemingly not poisonous.
Soon, he felt his chest and diaphragm broaden,
his head clear and refreshed,
and he fell into a deep sleep.
When he awoke,
the red sun filled the window.
He tried to get up,
his illness was as if it had vanished,
and his heart believed even more that she was an immortal.
Unable to make contact,
he would, when no one was around,
reverently bow and silently pray
in the places where he imagined she stood or sat.
One day,
as he was walking,
he suddenly met the young lady face-to-face
deep within a grove of trees.
Fortunately, there was no one else around,
so he was overjoyed
and prostrated himself.
The young lady approached and pulled him up.
He suddenly smelled an exotic fragrance all over her body,
and immediately took her jade-like wrist in his hand to help her rise.
Her fingers felt soft and smooth,
making his bones and joints feel as if they were melting.
Just as he was about to speak,
the old woman suddenly arrived.
The young lady told him to hide behind a rock,
then pointed south and said,
“Tonight, use the flower ladder to scale the wall;
the one with the four red windows
is my dwelling.”
She then hurried away.
The student was crestfallen,
his soul scattered,
unable to know where she had gone.
That night,
he moved a ladder to climb the south wall.
To his delight, a ladder was already there at the foot of the wall,
so he joyfully descended.
Indeed, there were red windows,
and inside the room, he heard the sound of chess pieces being played.
He stood there, not daring to advance further,
and for now, climbed back over the wall and returned.
After a short while,
he went back again,
and the sound of the pieces was still frequent.
He gradually approached and peeped inside,
seeing the young lady facing a beauty in plain white,
with the old servant also seated,
and a maid attending them.
He returned again.
He went back and forth three times in total,
and the three water-clocks had already chimed.
The student lay hidden on the ladder,
and heard the old woman come out saying,
“The ladder,
who put it here?”
She called the maid to help move it away.
The student climbed the wall,
but there was no way down,
so he returned in frustration and anger.
The next evening, he went again,
and the ladder was already set up.
Fortunately, it was quiet and deserted.
He entered,
and saw the young lady sitting idly,
as if in thought.
Seeing him, she rose in surprise,
standing shyly to one side.
The student bowed and said,
“I always thought my fortune was thin,
fearing I had no share with a celestial being;
yet such a night as this has come!”
Then he intimately embraced her.
Her slender waist was a mere armful; her breath was like orchids.
She pushed him away, saying,
“Why are you so hasty?”
The student said,
“Good things often encounter obstacles;
any delay invites the envy of ghosts.”
Before he could finish speaking,
he heard distant voices.
The young lady urgently said,
“My sister Yù Bǎn (玉版) is coming!
You must hide under the bed for now.”
The student obeyed.
Soon after,
a woman entered,
and laughed, saying,
“A defeated general,
can he still speak of fighting?
I have already brewed tea,
and dare to invite you for a night of pleasure.”
The young lady declined, citing her weariness.
Yù Bǎn (玉版) insisted,
but the young lady remained firmly seated.
Yù Bǎn (玉版) said,
“Such lingering attachment,
could it be that there’s a man hidden in the room?”
She forcibly pulled her out the door and left.
The student crawled out on his knees,
feeling utterly frustrated.
He then searched the pillows and mats,
hoping to find some keepsake,
but there was no perfumed box in the room,
only a crystal ruyi (如意) at the head of the bed,
tied with a purple scarf,
fragrant and lovely.
He took it,
climbed over the wall, and returned home.
Adjusting his collar and sleeves,
her body's fragrance still lingered,
intensifying his yearning.
However, due to the fear of being discovered under the bed,
he now feared punishment,
and, after much deliberation, dared not go again.
He simply cherished the ruyi (如意),
hoping she would come looking for it.
The next evening,
the young lady indeed came,
and smiled, saying,
“I always thought you were a gentleman,
but I didn’t realize you were a thief.”
The student said,
“Indeed so.
The reason I occasionally acted unbecomingly
was simply to fulfill my desires.”
Then he pulled her into his embrace,
and untied her skirt for her.
Her jade-like skin was suddenly revealed,
a warm fragrance permeated all around.
As they embraced,
he felt her breath and sweat,
every scent was fragrant.
He then said,
“I always believed you were an immortal,
and now I know my belief was not in vain.
To receive your kind attention
means our fate extends through three lives.
But I fear that like Dù Lánxiāng's (杜蘭香) marriage to a mortal,
it will ultimately end in sorrowful separation.”
The young lady smiled and said,
“Your worries are excessive.
I am merely a Qīannǚ (倩女) with a detached soul,
merely moved by emotion.
This matter must be kept secret and handled carefully,
lest wagging tongues
fabricate truths and falsehoods.
You cannot grow wings,
and I cannot ride the wind.”
then separation and disaster will be even more tragically different.”
The student agreed,
but ultimately suspected she was an immortal,
and pressed her for her surname.
The woman said,
“Since you take your concubine for an immortal,
why should an immortal convey her name?”
He asked,
“Who is the old woman?”
She replied,
“This is Sāng Mǔ.
When your concubine was young, she received her protection and care,
so she is not treated the same as other maidservants.”
She then rose,
wanting to leave,
and said,
“There are many eyes and ears where your concubine lives,
I cannot stay long.
I will return by stepping through the cracks.”
As they parted,
she asked for the *rúyì*,
and said,
“This is not your concubine’s item,
but was left by Yùbǎn.”
He asked,
“Who is Yùbǎn?”
She replied,
“She is your concubine’s younger paternal cousin.”
She gave him a hook and then left.
After she left,
many pillows were dyed with a strange fragrance.
From then on, she came every two or three nights.
The student was captivated by her,
and no longer thought of returning home.
But his purse was empty,
and he wanted to sell his horse.
The woman knew of this
and said,
“Because of your concubine,
you have emptied your purse and pawned your clothes;
my feelings cannot bear it.
Moreover, if you lose your means of travel,
how will you return a thousand *lǐ* away?
Your concubine has private savings,
which can help with your travel expenses.”
The student declined, saying,
“Your affection and kindness,
pledged with all my heart and body,
are beyond repayment; yet to be greedy and base,
and to deplete your wealth,
how could I be a proper person!”
The woman insisted,
saying,
“Just lend it to you for now.”
Thereupon she grasped the student’s arm,
led him to a mulberry tree,
pointed to a stone,
and said,
“Turn it!”
The student complied.
She then pulled out a hairpin from her head,
pricked the earth dozens of times,
and again said,
“Scratch it.”
The student again complied.
Then the mouth of an urn was already visible.
The woman reached in
and took out nearly fifty *liǎng* of white silver;
the student grasped her arm to stop her,
but she did not listen,
and took out ten more ingots.
The student forced half of them back before she covered it.
One evening,
she said to the student,
“Recently there have been some rumors,
which cannot be allowed to grow.
This must be planned for in advance.”
The student was alarmed and said,
“What shall we do then!
Your humble servant has always been rather cautious and reserved,
but now, for your sake,
like a widow who has lost her virtue,
I can no longer control myself.
I will only obey your command;
even swords, saws, axes, and halberds,
I would not have time to regard!”
The woman planned to flee together,
ordering the student to return first,
and arranging to meet in Luò.
The student readily agreed and returned to his hometown,
intending to go home first and then meet her;
by the time he arrived,
the young lady’s carriage had already reached his gate.
She entered the hall and greeted his family,
and the four neighbors were astonished and offered congratulations,
but no one knew that she had secretly fled.
The student secretly felt imperiled;
the woman, however, was quite unconcerned,
and said to the student,
“Regardless of whether a thousand *lǐ* away is beyond the reach of surveillance,
even if it were known,
your concubine is from a prominent family,
and Zhuō Wángsūn would not know what to do about Chángqīng.”
The student’s younger brother, Dàqì,
was sixteen years old.
The woman looked at him and said,
“He has good roots
and a future even brighter than yours.”
The wedding date was set,
when his wife suddenly died.
The woman said,
“My younger sister, Yùbǎn,
you have indeed seen her before;
her appearance is quite good,
and her age is also similar.
As a couple, you would be a perfect match.”
The student heard this and laughed,
playfully asking her to act as matchmaker.
The woman said,
“If you truly wish to achieve it,
it is not difficult.”
He happily asked,
“What is the method?”
She said,
“My sister and I are very close.
Two horses driving a light carriage,
and one old woman going back and forth, is all it takes.”
The student feared that their previous affair would be exposed,
and dared not follow her plan.
The woman insisted,
“No harm will come.”
Thereupon she ordered a carriage
and sent Sāng Mǔ away.
A few days later,
she arrived at Cáo.
As they approached the village gate,
the old woman alighted from the carriage,
made the driver stop and wait by the road,
and entered the village by night.
After a long while,
she came with a young woman,
who got into the carriage and they immediately set off.
They lodged in the carriage at dusk,
and resumed their journey at the fifth watch.
The young lady calculated the days,
and had Dàqì dress splendidly and meet them about fifty *lǐ* away,
where they met.
They returned by carriage,
with drums and trumpets and flowered candles,
rising to bow and complete the rites.
From this, both brothers obtained beautiful wives,
and their family grew wealthier day by day.
One day,
several dozens of mounted bandits
suddenly burst into their mansion.
The student knew there was trouble
and led his entire family upstairs.
The bandits entered
and surrounded the building.
The student looked down and asked,
“Do we have any enemies?”
They replied,
“No enemies.
But we have two requests: firstly, we hear that your two wives are unequaled in the world;
please grant us a glimpse of them;
secondly, for fifty-eight people,
each requests five hundred gold coins.”
They piled firewood beneath the building;
planning to set it on fire to threaten them.
The student agreed to their request for gold;
the bandits were not satisfied,
wanting to burn the building,
and the family was greatly frightened.
The woman wanted to go downstairs with Yùbǎn,
but was stopped from listening.
Dressed in dazzling makeup, they descended;
three steps from the bottom,
she said to the bandits,
“My sisters and I are all immortal maidens,
temporarily treading the mortal world.
Why should we fear bandits and thieves!
We wish to grant you ten thousand gold coins,
but fear you would not dare to accept it.”
The crowd of bandits all bowed in unison,
their assenting murmurs
“Not letting go.”
The sisters wanted to withdraw,
but one bandit said,
“This is a trick!”
The woman heard this,
turned around and stood still,
saying,
“What do you intend to do?
Plan it quickly,
it’s not too late yet.”
The bandits looked at each other,
silently, not saying a word.
The sisters calmly went upstairs and left.
The bandits looked up but saw no trace,
and then dispersed with a clamor.
Two years later,
the sisters each gave birth to a son.
Then, they gradually began to say:
"Our surname is Wèi,
and our mother was enfeoffed as the Cáo State Madam."
Shēng became suspicious, thinking there was no aristocratic family surnamed Wèi in Cáo,
and moreover, if a daughter of a great family had gone missing,
how could
no one have inquired about it?
He didn't dare to press for answers,
but his heart was secretly puzzled.
So he made an excuse to visit Cáo again.
Upon entering the territory, he inquired,
but among the prominent families, there was no one named Wèi.
He then stayed again at the home of his former host.
Suddenly, he saw a poem on the wall dedicated to the Cáo State Madam,
which somewhat startled him.
He questioned the host about it.
The host laughed
and immediately invited him to see the Cáo Madam.
When they arrived, it was a single peony plant,
as tall as the eaves.
When asked why it was given that name,
the host said that its flowers were the finest in Cáo,
so people jokingly gave it that title.
When asked
"What kind is it?",
he replied:
"It is a purple one from the Gě family."
Shēng was even more startled,
and then suspected the girls were flower spirits.
When he returned,
he dared not speak plainly,
but only recited the poem dedicated to the Madam to observe them.
The girls frowned and changed color,
then quickly went out and called Yùbǎn to bring the children.
They said to Shēng:
"Three years ago,
we were moved by your affection
and so presented ourselves to repay you.
Now that you harbor suspicions,
how can we remain together?"
With that, they and Yùbǎn each threw their children remotely.
The children fell to the ground and vanished.
As Shēng stared in astonishment,
the two girls had already disappeared.
He was filled with endless regret.
Several days later,
two peony plants grew where the children had fallen.
They grew a foot tall overnight
and bloomed that same year,
one purple and one white.
Their blossoms were as large as plates.
Compared to ordinary Gě peonies,
the Yùbǎn petals were especially numerous and delicate.
After several years,
they grew into dense thickets.
When transplanted elsewhere,
they changed into different varieties,
and no one could identify their names.
From then on, the splendor of peonies
in Luòxià was unparalleled.
Now, Liǎoyì Shǐshì says:
"With single-minded affection,
one can commune with spirits.
Even the contrary cannot be said to be heartless.
The magistrate was lonely,
taking a flower as his wife.
And if it could truly speak,
why bother exhausting its origins?
It's a pity Cháng Shēng was not enlightened!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The Military Governor Zhōu Yǒudé
rebuilt the old princely mansion into the departmental yáshǔ.
At that time, workers were being gathered,
and the master carpenter Féng Mínghuán was staying overnight inside.
As he was about to go to sleep one night,
he suddenly saw the latticed window half-open,
the moonlight bright as day.
Looking into the distance on the low wall,
stood a red rooster.
As he watched,
the rooster had already flown down to the ground.
Shortly after, a young girl
appeared halfway, peering in.
Féng suspected it was a secret liaison of a colleague.
He listened quietly,
but everyone was sound asleep.
His heart pounded,
secretly hoping she had come to him by mistake.
A moment later,
the girl indeed climbed through the window
and went straight into his arms.
Féng was delighted and
said not a word.
After their tryst,
the girl also left.
From then on, she came every night.
At first, she concealed herself,
but later she told him clearly.
The girl said:
"I did not come by mistake;
I respectfully gave myself to you."
Their affection grew deeper day by day.
After the work was completed,
Féng wanted to return home.
The girl was already waiting in the wilderness.
Féng's village
was not very far from the county,
so the girl went with him.
Upon entering his room,
his family members could not see her,
and Féng then realized she was not human.
After several months,
his spirit gradually diminished,
and his fear grew.
He invited a master to ward off and expel her,
but it had no effect.
One night,
the girl came, beautifully adorned,
and said to Féng:
"All worldly destinies have a fixed number: what is meant to come cannot be pushed away;
