what is meant to go cannot be held back.
Now, I bid you farewell."
Then she left.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Mǎ Zicái
was a native of Shùntiān.
His family had long loved chrysanthemums,
but Zicái was especially fond of them.
When he heard of a good variety,
he would certainly buy it,
not deterred by a thousand *lǐ*.
One day,
a guest from Jīnlíng stayed at his house.
He said that his cousin had one or two varieties
that were not found in the North.
Mǎ was moved with joy
and immediately prepared his luggage,
following the guest to Jīnlíng.
The guest made many efforts to seek them out for him,
and he obtained two shoots,
which he wrapped and cherished like treasures.
On his way back,
he met a young man,
riding a limping donkey and followed by an oil-green carriage,
whose demeanor was elegant and unrestrained.
They gradually approached and spoke.
The young man introduced himself,
saying his surname was Táo.
His conversation was refined and scholarly.
He then asked Mǎ where he had come from,
and Mǎ told him truthfully.
The young man said:
"No variety is inherently bad;
it is the cultivation and care that matters."
Then he discussed the art of cultivating chrysanthemums with him.
Mǎ was greatly pleased
and asked:
"Where are you going?"
He replied:
"My sister dislikes Jīnlíng
and wishes to settle in Héshuò."
Mǎ joyfully said:
"Although I am certainly poor,
my humble hut can offer a bed.
If you don't mind its desolation,
there's no need to go elsewhere."
Táo went to the front of the carriage
and reported to his sister.
The person in the carriage drew back the curtain and spoke;
she was an unparalleled beauty of about twenty.
She looked at her brother and said:
"A house need not be grand,
but the courtyard should be spacious."
Mǎ agreed on her behalf,
and so they all returned together.
To the south was an uncultivated garden,
with only a small house of three or four rafters.
Táo was pleased,
and lived there.
Daily he passed by the northern courtyard,
where Mǎ cultivated chrysanthemums.
When the chrysanthemums withered,
he pulled up the roots and replanted them,
and none failed to live.
However, his family was poor,
and Táo daily ate and drank with Mǎ,
but noticed that Mǎ's family seemed not to light a fire.
Mǎ's wife, Lǚ,
also loved Táo's elder sister,
and from time to time sent her a peck or a pint as sustenance.
Táo's elder sister's pet name was Huáng Yīng,
and she was skilled at conversation.
She often visited Lǚ's place
to spin and weave together.
One day, Táo said to Mǎ: "
Your family is certainly not well-off.
I daily burden my intimate friend with my appetite,
how can this be constant?
As for the present plan,
selling chrysanthemums would also be enough to make a living."
Mǎ was always principled.
Hearing Táo's words,
he greatly scorned him,
saying:
"I considered you a refined and noble scholar,
who could contentedly endure poverty.
Now to make such an argument
is to turn the eastern hedge into a marketplace,
which disgraces the yellow flowers."
Táo laughed and said:
"To live by one's own labor is not greedy,
and to sell flowers for a living is not vulgar.
One should certainly not seek wealth greedily,
but one also need not deliberately pursue poverty."
Mǎ said nothing.
Táo rose and left.
From then on,
Táo picked up all the discarded branches and inferior varieties that Mǎ had thrown away.
From this point, he no longer ate or slept at Mǎ's place,
and only came once when invited.
Before long,
when the chrysanthemums were about to bloom,
he heard that Táo's gate was as noisy as a market.
Surprised,
he went over and peeked,
and saw market people buying flowers,
heavily loaded and carrying them on their shoulders,
forming a continuous line on the road.
All their flowers were unusual varieties,
which he had never seen before.
He resented Táo's greed in his heart,
and wanted to break off relations;
but then he also resented Táo's privately hoarding the finest specimens,
so he knocked on the door,
intending to confront and blame him.
Táo came out,
grasped his hand, and pulled him in.
He saw that half an acre of the uncultivated garden was all chrysanthemum beds,
and there was no idle space outside the few rafters.
Those that had been dug up
were replaced by branches broken off and inserted;
the buds in the beds
were all excellent and wonderful: and upon closer inspection,
they were all the ones he had previously uprooted and discarded.
Táo went into the house,
brought out wine and food,
and set up a table beside the bed,
saying:
"I am poor and cannot maintain my pure precepts,
but luckily, I have obtained some small funds in recent days,
quite enough to get drunk."
A little later,
a voice from the room called
"Sān Láng,"
and Táo answered and left.
Presently, fine dishes were served,
the cooking exquisitely done.
Mǎ then asked:
"Why is your esteemed elder sister not yet married?"
He replied:
"The time is not yet ripe."
Mǎ asked:
"When is the time?"
He said:
"Forty-three months."
Mǎ further pressed:
"What does that mean?"
Táo only smiled and did not speak.
They dispersed only after having thoroughly enjoyed themselves.
The next day,
Mǎ visited him again,
and the newly inserted cuttings were already a foot tall.
He was greatly astonished,
and eagerly sought Táo's method.
Táo said:
"This is indeed not something that can be taught in words;
moreover, since you do not make a living,
what use is this to you?"
After a few more days,
the gate and courtyard were somewhat quiet.
Táo then wrapped the chrysanthemums in straw mats,
loaded several carts, and departed.
Over a year later,
when spring was halfway through,
he finally returned with exotic flowers from the south,
set up a flower shop in the capital,
sold them all within ten days,
and returned to cultivate chrysanthemums.
He asked those who had bought flowers the previous year.
They had kept the roots,
but the next year they all changed and became inferior,
so they bought from Táo again.
Táo thus became richer day by day: in one year he expanded his dwelling,
in two years he built a summer house.
His constructions followed his desires,
no longer consulting the master of the house.
Gradually, the old chrysanthemum beds
were all turned into verandas and houses.
He then bought a plot of land outside the wall,
built a surrounding wall,
and planted chrysanthemums entirely.
In autumn,
he carried the flowers away,
and did not return until the end of spring.
Meanwhile, Mǎ's wife fell ill and died.
He thought of Huáng Yīng,
and subtly sent someone to convey his intention to her.
Huáng Yīng smiled slightly.
Her expression seemed to consent,
only waiting specifically for Táo to return.
More than a year passed,
but Táo did not arrive.
Huáng Yīng instructed her servants to plant chrysanthemums,
just like Táo.
She earned more money and partnered with merchants,
managing twenty qǐng of fertile land outside the village,
and her splendid mansion grew even grander.
Suddenly, a guest came from Dōng Yuè,
delivering a letter from Táo Shēng.
When opened,
it instructed his sister to marry Mǎ.
He checked the date the letter was sent,
which was the very day his wife died;
recalling the drinking in the garden,
it had been exactly forty-three months.
He found it extremely peculiar.
He showed the letter to Yīng,
and asked
"where should the betrothal gifts be sent?"
Yīng declined to accept the betrothal gifts.
Mǎ also thought his old residence was humble,
and wanted her to move into the southern mansion,
as if he were marrying into her family.
Mǎ refused,
and chose a day to perform the personal welcoming ceremony.
After Huáng Yīng married Mǎ,
she opened a door in the partition wall connecting to the southern mansion,
and daily went over to supervise her servants.
Mǎ was ashamed of being enriched by his wife,
and constantly instructed Huáng Yīng to keep separate accounts for the north and south,
to prevent confusion.
But for anything needed in the household,
Huáng Yīng would always take it from the southern mansion.
In less than half a year,
everything in the house was Táo's family's property.
Mǎ immediately sent people to return each item,
and warned her not to take them again.
Before ten days passed,
they were mixed again.
After several such changes,
Mǎ could not bear the annoyance.
Huáng Yīng smiled and said:
"Is Chén Zhòngzǐ not weary?"
Mǎ was ashamed,
and no longer checked,
leaving everything to Huáng Yīng.
She gathered workers and prepared materials,
undertaking large construction projects,
which Mǎ could not forbid.
After several months,
buildings extended continuously,
and the two mansions eventually merged into one,
with no boundary distinct.
However, obeying Mǎ's instruction,
she closed the gate and no longer engaged in the chrysanthemum business,
yet their lifestyle exceeded that of established gentry families.
Mǎ felt uneasy,
and said:
"My thirty years of untainted virtue
have been ruined by you.
Now I live and breathe in this world
merely dependent on my wife's family for sustenance,
truly without a shred of masculine spirit.
Everyone wishes for wealth,
I only wish to be poor!"
Huáng Yīng said:
"I am not greedy or lowly;
but if he does not accumulate a little wealth,
then people a thousand years from now
will say that Táo Yuānmíng had a lowly, poor destiny,
and could not achieve success for a hundred generations.
Thus, I merely acted to save my Táo Péngzé from ridicule.
However, for the poor to wish for wealth
is difficult;
for the rich to seek poverty,
of course, is also very easy.
You may spend the gold by the bed as you wish,
I will not begrudge it."
Mǎ said:
"To donate someone else's gold
is also quite ugly."
Yīng said:
"You do not wish for wealth,
and I also cannot be poor.
If that is the case,
let us divide your residence: the pure will be pure,
the turbid will be turbid,
what harm is there?"
So, she built a thatched cottage in the garden
and selected a beautiful maidservant to attend to Mǎ.
Mǎ was content with it.
However, after a few days,
he longed for Huáng Yīng bitterly.
He summoned her,
but she refused to come;
having no choice,
he returned to her.
He would come every other night,
making it a habit.
Huáng Yīng laughed and said:
"Eating at the East for two nights,
a man of integrity should not be like this."
Wū also laughed to himself,
having no reply,
and so they resumed living together as before.
It so happened that Mǎ had business in Jīnlíng,
and it was the autumn of chrysanthemums.
He passed a flower shop early,
and saw that the pots in the shop were arranged in great abundance,
with beautiful and excellent varieties.
His heart was stirred,
suspecting them to be Táo's creations.
After a short while,
the owner came out,
and it was indeed Táo.
Overjoyed,
he fully expressed their long separation,
and then stayed the night there,
inviting him to return with him.
Táo said:
"Jīnlíng
is my native land,
and I am about to marry here.
I have accumulated a small amount of capital,
please trouble my elder sister to keep it.
I will temporarily leave at the end of the year."
Mǎ did not listen,
and pressed him harder to come.
He also said:
"My home is fortunately abundant,
you can merely enjoy it,
without needing to trade again."
Sitting in the shop,
he had his servants negotiate the prices,
making them cheap,
and sold everything within a few days.
Urging him to pack his bags,
he hired a boat and went north.
Upon entering the gate,
his elder sister had already tidied up the house,
and the beds, mattresses, and quilts were all laid out,
as if she had known beforehand that her brother would return.
After Táo returned,
he unpacked and assigned tasks,
greatly renovating the pavilions and gardens.
He only played chess and drank wine with Mǎ daily,
and no longer entertained any other guests.
They sought a marriage for him,
but he declined, unwilling.
His sister sent two maidservants to attend to his sleeping quarters.
After living there for three or four years,
he had a daughter.
Táo was usually a heavy drinker,
but was never seen utterly drunk.
He had a friend, Zēng Shēng,
whose capacity was also unmatched.
When Zēng happened to visit Mǎ,
Mǎ had him compete in drinking with Táo.
The two drank freely and joyfully,
regretting they had not met sooner.
From dawn until the fourth watch,
it was calculated that each had consumed a hundred pots.
Zēng was utterly drunk, like mud,
and fell into a deep sleep in his seat.
Táo rose to return to his quarters,
stepped out the door onto the chrysanthemum bed,
and toppled over like Mount Yù.
He cast off his clothes by his side,
and immediately transformed into a chrysanthemum on the spot,
as tall as a person;
there were over ten flowers,
all of the 'Prince's Fist' variety.
Mǎ was utterly terrified
and told Huáng Yīng.
Yīng rushed over,
pulled it up and placed it on the ground,
saying:
"How can you be so drunk!"
She covered it with clothes,
asked Mǎ to leave with her,
and warned him not to look.
When morning came, they went there,
and Táo was lying by the chrysanthemum bed.
Mǎ then realized that both the elder sister and younger brother were chrysanthemum spirits,
and respected and loved them even more.
After Táo revealed his true form,
he drank even more unrestrainedly,
constantly writing invitations to Zēng.
Thus, they became bosom friends.
On the occasion of the Flower Festival,
Zēng came to visit,
bringing a jar of medicated white wine carried by two servants,
agreeing to finish it together.
When the jar was almost empty,
the two were still not very drunk.
Mǎ secretly added another jug of wine;
the two then finished that as well.
Zēng was already exhausted from drunkenness,
and his servants carried him away.
Táo lay on the ground,
and again transformed into a chrysanthemum.
Mǎ was used to the sight and was not surprised.
He gently pulled it up,
and guarded its side to observe its changes.
After a long time,
the leaves became increasingly withered.
Greatly frightened,
he finally told Huáng Yīng.
Yīng heard and exclaimed in shock:
"You've killed my brother!"
She rushed to look,
and the roots and stem were already withered.
Overwhelmed with pain,
she snipped its stem,
buried it in a pot,
carried it into her boudoir,
and watered it daily.
Mǎ was consumed by regret and grief,
and greatly resented Zēng.
A few days later,
he heard that Zēng had already died from drunkenness.
The flower in the pot gradually sprouted,
and in September, it bloomed.
With short stems and pink blossoms,
it smelled of wine,
and was named
"Drunken Táo".
It thrived when watered with wine.
Later, the daughter grew up
and married into a prominent family.
Huáng Yīng lived to old age,
without any other unusual occurrences.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"A man of green mountains and white clouds
thus died from drunkenness.
The world universally pities him,
yet he himself might not necessarily have been unhappy about it.
To plant this species in one's courtyard
is like seeing a good friend,
like facing a beautiful woman;
one cannot but seek it out."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Láng Yùzhù from Péngchéng
had ancestors who served as officials, reaching the rank of Tàishǒu.
They were incorruptible in office,
and did not use their salaries to build up their estate,
but instead accumulated books until they filled the house.
When it came to Yùzhù,
he was especially obsessed: his family was miserably poor,
and they sold everything they owned,
except for his father's collection of books,
not a single scroll of which he could bear to part with.
When his father was alive,
he had written the "Quànxué Piān"
and pasted it on the right side of his seat.
Láng recited it daily;
he even covered it with plain gauze,
for fear it would wear out.
It was not for seeking official position,
but because he truly believed that there was real "golden millet" in books.
He studied day and night,
regardless of cold or heat.
When he was over twenty years old,
he did not seek a spouse,
hoping that a beautiful woman from the scrolls would arrive on her own.
When he saw guests or relatives, he would not inquire about their well-being,
but after a few words,
he would begin to recite loudly,
and the guests would soon leave of their own accord.
Whenever the Wénzōng came to administer examinations,
he would always be selected first,
but he struggled to pass the actual exams.
One day,
as he was reading,
a strong wind suddenly blew a scroll away.
He chased after it in a hurry,
and his foot sank into the ground;
when he probed it,
there was decayed grass in the hole;
when he dug it up,
it turned out to be ancient stored chestnuts,
already rotten and turned into dirt.
Although they were inedible,
it strengthened his belief
that the saying of "a thousand *zhōng*"
was not false,
and he read with even greater effort.
One day,
climbing a tall shelf with a ladder,
he found a gilded palanquin, a *chǐ* in diameter, among the chaotic scrolls.
He was overjoyed,
thinking it was
the proof of a "golden house."
He took it out to show people,
but it was gilded and not real gold.
He secretly resented the ancients for having deceived him.
Not long after,
a colleague of his father's,
an Guānchá of the circuit,
who was fond of Buddhism, arrived.
Someone persuaded Láng to offer the palanquin as a Buddhist shrine.
The Guānchá was greatly pleased,
and gave him three hundred gold pieces and two horses.
Láng was delighted,
thinking that the golden house and the carriages and horses had all come true,
and consequently studied even harder.
However, he was already thirty years old.
Someone advised him to marry,
saying:
"'In books, there is naturally a face like jade,'
so why should I worry about not having a beautiful wife?"
He read for another two or three years,
but still to no avail,
and people began to ridicule him.
At that time, there was a rumor among the people that the Weaver Girl from heaven had secretly eloped.
Someone joked to Láng:
"The heavenly *Sūn* secretly ran away,
presumably for you."
Láng knew they were joking
and did not bother to refute it.
One evening,
he was reading the *Hàn Shū* up to the eighth scroll,
when the scroll was about halfway through,
he saw a cutout paper beauty hidden within it.
He exclaimed in surprise:
"The 'face like jade in books,'
could this be its fulfillment?"
He felt a sudden pang of loss.
But upon closer inspection of the beauty,
her eyebrows and eyes were lifelike;
on her back, faintly, were fine characters that read:
"Zhīnǚ."
He was greatly astonished.
He placed her on the scroll daily,
admiring and playing with her repeatedly,
to the point of forgetting to eat and sleep.
One day,
as he was gazing at her,
the beauty suddenly bent her waist and stood up,
sitting on the scroll and smiling.
Láng was utterly shocked,
and prostrated himself under the desk.
When he rose,
she was already a *chǐ* tall.
He was even more astonished,
and kowtowed again.
She then gracefully descended to the table,
a truly peerless beauty.
He bowed and asked:
"What spirit are you?"
The beauty smiled and said:
"My surname is Yán,
and my courtesy name is Rúyù,
you have known me for a long time.
You have gazed upon me with favor daily,
and if I do not come just once,
I fear that in a thousand years there will be no one left who truly believes in the ancients."
Láng was delighted,
and they subsequently lived together.
However, their intimacy in bed was extreme,
but he did not know she was a human.
Whenever he read,
he would always make the woman sit by his side.
The woman advised him not to read,
but he did not listen.
The woman said:
"The reason you cannot achieve success
is solely because of reading.
Just look at those on the spring examination rosters;
how many are like you in their reading?
If you don't listen,
I will leave."
Láng obeyed her for a moment.
A little while later,
he forgot her instruction,
and resumed his chanting.
After an hour,
he looked for the woman,
but she was nowhere to be found.
His mind was distraught,
he implored and prayed to her,
but there was no trace of her.
Suddenly, he remembered where the woman was hidden,
and took out the *Hàn Shū* to examine it closely,
until he reached her hiding place,
and indeed found her.
He called out to her but she did not move,
so he prostrated himself and prayed sorrowfully.
The woman then descended and said:
"If you do not listen again,
we will be separated forever!"
She then had him prepare chessboards and dice-game sets,
and played games with him daily.
But Láng's heart was not in it at all.
When he saw the woman was not present,
he would secretly take out scrolls and browse them.
Fearing the woman would notice,
he secretly took the eighth scroll of the *Hàn Shū*,
and mixed it with other scrolls to mislead her.
One day,
he was absorbed in reading,
when the woman arrived,
but he did not notice her at all;
suddenly he saw her,
and quickly covered the scroll,
but the woman was already gone.
He was greatly frightened,
and frantically searched through all the scrolls,
but she was nowhere to be found;
then,
he found her again in the eighth scroll of the *Hàn Shū*,
the page numbers matching perfectly.
Thereupon, he bowed down and prayed again,
swearing never to read again.
The woman then descended
and played *yì* with him,
saying:
"If you do not become skilled in three days,
I will leave again."
By the third day,
he suddenly won a game against the woman by two pieces.
The woman was then pleased,
and taught him how to play stringed instruments,
limiting him to mastering one tune in five days.
Láng focused his hands and eyes,
having no time for anything else;
after a long time,
his fingers moved with the rhythm,
and he unconsciously became joyful.
The woman then drank and gambled with him daily,
and Láng consequently enjoyed himself and forgot about reading.
The woman also allowed him to go out,
and make friends,
thereby establishing his reputation as an unconventional and unrestrained individual.
The woman said:
"You can now go out and try your luck."
The **láng** one night said to his wife:
"Normally, when a man and woman live together, they have children;
now I have lived with you for a long time,
why has it not been so?"
The woman smiled and said:
"You read books all day,
and I always said it was useless.
Now, even the chapter on 'husband and wife'
you have not yet fully comprehended:
the two words 'pillow and mat' contain a lot of work."
The **láng** was surprised and asked:
"What work?"
The woman smiled but did not speak.
After a short while,
she secretly invited him to her.
The **láng**, in extreme delight, said:
"I did not expect the joy of husband and wife
to contain something that cannot be expressed in words."
Thereupon, he would tell everyone he met,
and there was no one who did not cover their mouths.
The woman knew and reproached him.
The **láng** said:
"Those who bore holes and climb over walls
are the ones whose deeds cannot be told to others;
the joy of human relations,
which everyone experiences,
why should it be taboo?"
After eight or nine months,
the woman indeed bore a son,
and they bought an old woman to nurse and raise him.
One day,
she said to the **láng**:
"I have been with you for two years,
and have already borne a son;
it is time for us to part.
To stay longer, I fear, would bring disaster upon you,
and then regret would be too late."
The **láng** heard her words,
and tears fell;
he prostrated himself and could not rise, saying:
"Do you not think of our crying baby?"
The woman also looked sad,
and after a long time, said:
"If you insist on me staying,
you must take all the books on the shelf and scatter them."
The **láng** said:
"These are your native place,
and my very life;
how can you say such a thing!"
The woman did not force the issue,
saying:
"I also know that there is a limit,
and I had no choice but to warn you in advance."
Before this,
relatives or acquaintances who caught sight of the woman
were all greatly astonished,
and yet had not heard with which family she had contracted marriage;
they collectively questioned him.
The **láng** could not fabricate a story,
but simply remained silent.
People became even more suspicious,
and rumors spread almost everywhere,
reaching the **yìzǎi Shǐ Gōng**.
**Shǐ** was
a native of **Mǐn**,
a **jìnshì** in his youth.
Upon hearing the rumors, he was greatly moved,
and secretly desired to see her beautiful face,
and therefore arrested the **láng** and the woman.
When the woman learned of this,
she vanished without a trace.
The **zǎi** was enraged,
arrested the **láng**,
stripped him of his **yījīn**,
and applied all manner of shackles and instruments,
determined to find out where the woman had gone.
The **láng** was near death,
but uttered not a word.
They tortured his maid,
who vaguely described her appearance.
The **zǎi** believed her to be a demon,
and ordered his carriage to personally visit their home.
He saw books filling the house,
too many to search through,
so he burned them;
the smoke in the courtyard gathered and did not disperse,
darkening like a haze.
Once the **láng** was released,
he traveled far to seek a letter from his father's disciple,
and managed to clear his name and be reinstated.
That year, he passed the autumn examination,
and the following year became a **jìnshì**.
However, the resentment in his heart cut to the bone.
He made a memorial tablet for **Yán Rúyù**.
Morning and evening, he prayed, saying:
"If you have a spirit,
you must bless my appointment to **Mǐn**."
Later, he indeed became an Imperial Censor (**zhízhǐ**) touring **Mǐn**.
After three months,
he investigated **Shǐ**'s misdeeds,
and confiscated his property.
At that time, a cousin was the judicial officer (**sīlǐ**),
who coerced him into accepting a favorite concubine,
claiming to buy a maid and leave her at the yamen.
Once the case was closed,
the **láng** immediately acted,
took the concubine, and returned home.
The Historian of Anomalies (**Yì Shǐ Shì**) remarks,
"Among all things under heaven,
accumulation attracts jealousy,
and beauty breeds demons:
the woman's demon,
the books' demon.
The matter is almost grotesque,
and punishing it might not be wrong;
but the tyranny of **Zǔlóng**,
was it not too cruel!
His selfish intentions
deserve even more the報 of resentment and malice.
Alas!
What is so strange about it!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
**Xǔ Shèng**,
a man from **Yǎn**.
He accompanied his elder brother **Chéng** to trade in **Mǐn**,
and his goods were not yet stored.
A guest said that the Great Sage's divine power was manifest,
and suggested they pray at the temple.
**Shèng** did not know which deity the Great Sage was,
and went with his brother.
When they arrived, the halls and pavilions stretched out in a continuous expanse,
reaching the utmost in grandeur and beauty.
Entering the hall to gaze upon him,
the deity had a monkey's head and a human body;
he was none other than **Qítiān Dàshèng Sūn Wùkōng**. All the guests stood up reverently,
none daring to show any disrespectful expression.
**Shèng** was always straightforward and upright,
and secretly laughed at the ignorance of common folk.
While the crowd burned offerings, kowtowed, and prayed,
**Shèng** secretly left.
Once he returned,
his elder brother reproached him for his disrespect.
Shèng said:
“Sūn Wùkōng is merely a fable by Qiū Wēng,
why take it so seriously?
If he truly has divine power,
be it blades, spears, or thunder,
I will gladly receive it myself!”
The masters of Nìxuán, hearing him call out Dàshèng’s name,
all waved their hands, their faces drained of color,
as if afraid Dàshèng might hear.
Shèng, seeing their reaction,
argued even more boisterously;
those listening covered their ears and fled.
That night,
Shèng indeed fell ill,
suffering from a severe headache.
Some advised him to go to the temple to apologize,
but Shèng refused to listen.
Not long after,
his headache slightly improved,
but his thigh began to ache,
and a large carbuncle formed on it overnight,
causing his entire leg to swell,
making him unable to sleep or eat.
His elder brother prayed on his behalf,
but it had no effect.
Someone said: “Divine punishment requires self-prayer.”
Shèng, in the end, did not believe it.
After more than a month,
the sore gradually healed,
but another carbuncle appeared,
its pain doubly severe.
A doctor came
and used a knife to cut away the rotten flesh;
blood filled a bowl: fearing people would exaggerate his suffering,
he endured it without groaning.
After another month,
he finally recovered.
But then his elder brother fell gravely ill.
Shèng said:
“What do you make of this!
Even those who revere the gods suffer likewise,
which is sufficient proof that my illness
was not caused by Wùkōng.”
His elder brother, hearing his words,
became even angrier,
saying that the god had shifted his wrath,
and blamed his younger brother for not praying on his behalf.
Shèng said:
“Brothers are like hands and feet.
Previously, my limbs were rotting, yet I did not pray; should I now, because of a limb’s illness,
abandon my principles?”
He only hired doctors and prepared medicine
but did not follow his brother’s plea for prayer.
After taking the medicine,
his elder brother died suddenly.
Shèng’s heart was filled with intense grief,
and after buying a coffin and enshrouding his brother,
he went to the temple, pointed at the god, and reproached it, saying:
“My brother fell ill,
saying that you shifted your wrath,
preventing me from clearing my name.
If you are truly divine,
you should bring the dead back to life.
I will then face north and call myself your disciple,
daring not to speak otherwise;
if not,
I will apply the method of the Sānqīng that you used
and return it to your own person,
also to dispel my brother’s confusion in the underworld.”
That night,
he dreamt that a person beckoned him away,
into Dàshèng’s temple.
He looked up and saw Dàshèng with an angry expression,
reproaching him:
“Because of your misbehavior,
I used a bodhisattva’s knife to pierce your shin and thigh;
yet you do not repent,
but instead utter vexatious words.
You ought to be sent to the Tongue-Plucking Hell,
but considering your lifelong stubbornness,
I shall temporarily spare you.
Your brother’s illness
was due to you using an incompetent doctor who cut short his lifespan;
what fault is it of others?
If I don’t exert some divine power now,
it will only encourage more arrogant individuals to use it as an excuse.”
Then he ordered a green-clad attendant to seek instructions from Yánluó.
The green-clad attendant reported:
“After three days,
his name has already been reported to the heavenly court for premature death,
so it might be difficult to help.”
The god took a tablet,
ordered a brush,
wrote something (unknown what words),
and sent the green-clad attendant away with it.
After a long while, he returned.
Chéng came with him,
both kneeling in the hall.
The god asked:
“Why the delay?”
The green-clad attendant reported:
“Yánmó dared not act on his own,
and also carried Dàshèng’s decree to consult with Dǒusù,
which is why I am late.”
Shèng hastened forward to prostrate himself and thank the divine grace.
The god said:
“You may quickly leave with your brother.
If you can turn towards goodness,
it will be for your benefit.”
The brothers, filled with both sorrow and joy,
went home together.
He awoke, finding it extraordinary.
He quickly rose,
opened the coffin to look,
and his brother had indeed revived,
and came out,
extremely grateful for Dàshèng’s power.
Shèng from then on was truly convinced,
and his devotion became twice that of ordinary people.
However, the brothers’ capital
had already been half depleted during their illnesses;
and his elder brother was not yet fully recovered,
so they faced each other in prolonged sorrow.
One day,
while casually strolling in the outskirts of the city,
a brown-clad person suddenly addressed him, saying:
“What troubles you?”
Shèng, having been suffering with no one to confide in,
therefore recounted his misfortunes in full.
The brown-clad person said:
“There is a beautiful place;
if you briefly go to see it,
it will also be enough to alleviate your worries.”
He asked:
"Where to?"
He merely said,
"Not far."
Shèng followed him.
After going about half a *lǐ* outside the city wall,
the man in brown clothes said,
"I have a small art;
we can arrive in an instant."
He then ordered Shèng to embrace his waist with both hands,
gave a slight nod,
and Shèng immediately felt clouds forming beneath his feet,
ascending and leaping upwards,
not knowing how many hundreds of *yóuxún*.
Shèng was greatly alarmed,
closing his eyes and not daring to open them even a little.
After a moment,
the man said,
"We have arrived."
Suddenly, Shèng saw a world of *liúlí*,
radiating an unusual light and color.
He asked in surprise,
"Where is this?"
The man replied,
"This is the Celestial Palace."
They walked at will,
going higher and higher.
From afar, Shèng saw an old man,
and the brown-clothed man said joyfully,
"To meet this elder just now
is your good fortune!"
He raised his hands and bowed to the elder.
The elder invited them to his dwelling,
brewed tea, and offered it to his guests;
there were only two cups,
which was far less than Shèng.
The brown-clothed man said,
"This is my disciple,
who travels a thousand *lǐ* for trade,
respectfully visiting the immortal residence
to request a small gift."
The elder ordered a boy to bring out something like white stones,
shaped like sparrow eggs,
clear and translucent like ice,
and let Shèng take them himself.
Shèng thought he could use them as gaming pieces if he took them home,
so he took six of them.
The man in brown clothes thought this was too modest,
took six more for him,
gave them to Shèng, and wrapped them up together.
He instructed him to put them in his waist-pouch
and, bowing his hands, said,
"That's enough."
They bid farewell to the elder and left,
and again the man in brown told Shèng to cling to him and descend.
In an instant, they reached the ground.
Shèng prostrated himself and asked for the immortal's name.
The man smiled and said,
"That was precisely the *Jīndǒu Yún* (somersault cloud) I spoke of earlier."
Shèng was enlightened,
realizing he was the Great Sage,
and again requested protection and blessings.
The man said,
"The wealth you obtained earlier
has granted you twelve-fold profit;
what more do you need to seek?"
Shèng bowed to him again,
and when he stood up, the man had already vanished.
After returning home,
he joyfully told his brother.
They untied the pouch to look together,
and the stones were still in his waist-pouch.
Afterwards, when he transported goods and returned,
his profits were five times over.
From then on, whenever he traveled to Mǐn,
he would always pray to the Great Sage.
Other people's prayers
were sometimes not very effective;
but whatever Shèng sought was always answered.
The Grand Historian (Yìshǐ Shì) remarks:
"In the past, a scholar passed by a temple,
drew a *pípá* on the wall, and left;
by the time he returned,
its efficacy was greatly manifested,
and incense offerings were continuously made to it.
It is true that for things in the world, there need not necessarily be a real person;
if people believe it to be efficacious,
then it becomes efficacious.
Why is this?
It is because where people's hearts gather,
things may find their sustenance.
As for Shèng's straightforwardness,
he certainly deserved the protection of the gods: how could it be truly about a needle embroidered in the ear, or hairs that can transform,
or somersaults underfoot allowing one to ascend to the azure sky?!
To ultimately be deluded by evil
also shows the shallowness of his understanding."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
the custom is to worship the Frog God most devoutly.
In the shrine, there are hundreds of thousands of frogs,
some as large as cages.
If one incurs the god's wrath,
strange omens will immediately appear in the home: frogs will crawl on tables and beds,
or even cling to slippery walls without falling,
their manifestations vary,
indicating that the family will face misfortune.
People then become greatly afraid,
slaughtering animals and offering prayers to avert the calamity.
If the god is pleased, the trouble ceases.
In Chǔ, there was a man named Xuē Kūnshēng,
who was intelligent in childhood
and handsome in appearance.
When he was six or seven years old,
a servant in green clothes came to his house,
claiming to be a divine messenger,
conveying the god's message,
wishing to marry his daughter to Kūnshēng.
Old Xuē was simple and unsophisticated by nature
and truly disliked the idea,
declining on the grounds that his son was too young.
Although he explicitly refused,
he still dared not arrange a marriage with another family.
Several years later,
Kūnshēng gradually grew up,
and a marriage proposal was sent to the Jiāng family.
The god informed the Jiāng family, saying,
"Xuē Kūnshēng
is my son-in-law;
how dare you approach my forbidden delicacy!"
The Jiāng family was frightened
and returned the engagement gifts.
Old Xuē was worried about this,
so he prepared sacrifices and went to pray,
stating that he dared not be a match for a god.
After the prayer,
he saw giant maggots floating in all the food and wine,
wriggling and stirring;
he poured it all out,
apologized, and returned home.
He became even more afraid,
and for the time being, he conceded to the god's will.
One day,
Kūnshēng was on the road
when a messenger came to greet him and convey a divine command,
urgently inviting him to move his feet.
Having no choice,
he went with the messenger.
They entered a vermilion gate,
where the pavilions were splendid and beautiful.
An old man sat in the hall,
appearing to be seventy or eighty years old.
Kūnshēng prostrated himself.
The old man ordered him to be helped up
and granted him a seat by the table.
After a short while,
female servants gathered,
filling the sides.
The old man looked around and said,
"Go in and say that Master Xuē has arrived."
Several maids ran off.
After some time,
an old woman led a young lady out,
aged sixteen or seventeen,
of peerless beauty.
The old man pointed and said,
"This is my youngest daughter, Shíniáng.
She believes she would be a good match for you;
however, your honored father rejected her on the grounds that we are of different species.
This is a matter of a hundred years;
parents only govern half of it:
the decision rests with you."
Kūnshēng gazed at Shíniáng,
his heart filled with admiration for her,
and he remained silent.
The old woman said,
"I already know that the young master's intention is good.
Please return first,
and we will immediately send Shíniáng there."
Kūnshēng said,
"Yes."
He hurried home to tell his father.
Old Xuē was in a rush and did not know what to do,
so he gave Kūnshēng a message
to go back and convey his apologies,
but Kūnshēng refused to go.
While he was being scolded and reprimanded,
a palanquin was already at the door,
with groups of green-clad servants,
and Shíniáng entered.
She went up to the hall to bow to her father-in-law and mother-in-law,
who were both pleased to see her.
That very evening, they performed the wedding ritual,
and their harmony was like *qín* and *sè*.
From then on, the divine old man and divine old woman
frequently visited their home.
When observing their clothes,
red signified joy,
and white signified wealth;
it was always fulfilled,
which is why the family prospered day by day.
Since he married the divine woman,
the gates, halls, fences, and privies were all covered with frogs.
No one dared to insult or kick them.
Only Kūnshēng, being young and willful,
would stomp them to death when happy,
and trample them when angry,
without much care or affection.
Although Shíniáng was humble and gentle,
she was prone to anger,
and was quite displeased with Kūnshēng's actions;
yet Kūnshēng did not restrain himself on account of Shíniáng.
Shíniáng's words became aggressive towards Kūnshēng,
and Kūnshēng angrily said,
"Could it be that your family's father and mother can bring disaster upon people?
What does a man fear about frogs?!"
Shíniáng greatly avoided the word
"frog,"
and hearing it caused her much distress.
She said,
"Since I entered your home, I have increased your family's land and grain,
and raised the value of your goods,
which is no small amount.
Now that old and young are all warm and well-fed,
are you like an owl growing wings,
wanting to peck out your mother's eyes?!"
Kūnshēng became even more indignant and said,
"I only resent the added filth,
unfit to pass down to descendants.
It would be better to separate early."
So he drove Shíniáng away.
When the elders heard of it,
Shíniáng had already left.
They scolded Kūnshēng,
and told him to hurry and pursue her to bring her back.
Kūnshēng, full of pride, would not yield.
By night,
both mother and son fell ill,
dizzy and unable to eat.
The elder feared,
and carrying thorns, went to the temple,
his plea sincere and earnest.
After three days,
their illness gradually recovered.
Shíniáng also arrived of her own accord,
and the couple's relationship was as good as before.
Shíniáng would spend the day meticulously dressed,
not doing needlework;
Kūnshēng's clothes and shoes
were entirely entrusted to his mother.
One day, his mother angrily said,
"My son is already married,
yet I, the old woman, am still burdened!
Other families' wives serve their mothers-in-law,
but in our family, the mother-in-law serves the wife!"
Shíniáng happened to hear this,
and indignantly entered the hall, saying,
"A daughter-in-law serves food in the morning,
and asks about rest in the evening.
As for serving one's mother-in-law,
what is the proper way?
My shortcoming is
that I cannot be stingy with servant wages,
and must do the hard work myself."
The mother was speechless,
ashamed and tearfully crying to herself.
Kūnshēng entered,
saw his mother's tear stains,
and upon questioning, learned the reason.
He angrily rebuked Shíniáng.
Shíniáng insisted on arguing and would not yield.
Kūnshēng said,
"A wife who cannot bring joy
is better off not having!
Even if I provoke the old frog's anger,
it's nothing more than dying by accident!"
Again he sent Shíniáng away.
Shíniáng was also angry,
and left the door immediately.
The next day,
a disaster befell their dwelling,
spreading fire to several houses,
and everything — tables, beds, and mats —
was reduced to ashes.
Kūnshēng was furious,
and went to the temple to rebuke them, saying,
"You raise a daughter who cannot serve her parents-in-law,
without any family instruction,
and yet you protect her shortcomings!
The divine are supremely just,
is there anyone who teaches people to fear their wives?!
Moreover, the clashing of bowls and plates
was all my doing [3O],
unrelated to my parents.
Let knives, saws, axes, and halberds
be inflicted upon my body;
if not,
I will also burn your dwelling,
as a small act of retribution."
Having spoken,
he carried firewood below the main hall,
and lit a fire, intending to ignite it.
The local residents gathered and pleaded with him,
and only then did he return, resentful.
His parents heard of it,
and were greatly frightened, losing color.
By night,
the deity appeared in a dream to a nearby village,
instructing them to build a house for their son-in-law's family.
By dawn,
they gathered materials and assembled workers,
collectively building for Kūnshēng,
and would not stop when he declined;
hundreds of people lined the road daily,
and in a few days,
the residence was completely new,
with beds, curtains, and all furnishings provided.
As soon as the renovation was complete,
Shíniáng had already arrived,
entered the hall to apologize,
her words gentle and soft.
She turned and smiled at Kūnshēng,
and the whole family's resentment turned to joy.
From then on, Shíniáng's temperament became even more harmonious,
and for two years,
there was no disagreement.
Shíniáng (十娘) hated snakes most.
Kūnshēng (昆生) playfully enclosed a small snake
in a box and had the servant open it.
Shíniáng's (十娘) face changed color
and she scolded Kūnshēng (昆生).
Kūnshēng (昆生) in turn changed from laughter to anger,
and they were equally hostile.
Shíniáng (十娘) said:
"This time, I won't wait to be driven out;
I ask to end things here."
Thereupon she left the house.
Xuēwēng (薛翁) was greatly alarmed,
beat Kūnshēng (昆生) with a stick,
and begged the deity for forgiveness.
Fortunately, no misfortune befell them,
but there was also no sound or sign.
More than a year passed,
and Kūnshēng (昆生) missed Shíniáng (十娘),
feeling quite remorseful.
He secretly went to the deity's shrine to plead for Shíniáng (十娘),
but there was no response.
Not long after,
he heard that the deity had betrothed Shíniáng (十娘) to a man named Yuán (袁氏).
He was deeply disappointed
and consequently also sought marriage with another family;
but after looking at several families,
none were like Shíniáng (十娘),
and thus he missed Shíniáng (十娘) even more.
He went to inquire about the Yuán (袁氏) family,
only to find that they had already whitewashed the walls and cleaned the courtyard,
awaiting the fish-carriage.
He felt so ashamed and indignant that he could not control himself,
neglected food and became ill.
His parents were worried and anxious,
not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, in a dazed state of indignation, someone stroked him and said:
"Great man, you frequently wish to break off,
and now you're acting like this again!"
He opened his eyes,
and it was Shíniáng (十娘).
Overjoyed,
he leaped up and said:
"How did you come here?"
Shíniáng (十娘) said:
"With the courtesy accorded to a frivolous person,
I should just follow my father's command
and remarry and leave.
Indeed, I had long received the betrothal gifts from the Yuán (袁) family,
but I thought about it a thousand times, ten thousand times, and couldn't bear it.
The auspicious day was already this evening,
and father also had no face to retract the betrothal,
so I personally took them and placed them back.
Just as I stepped out the door,
father rushed out to send me off, saying:
'Foolish maid!
If you don't listen to my words,
and later suffer ill-treatment from the Xuē (薛) family,
even if you die, don't come back!' "
Kūnshēng (昆生) was moved by her righteousness
and shed tears for her.
The family members were all happy,
and rushed to tell Wēng (翁) and Aǒ (媼).
When Aǒ (媼) heard it,
without waiting to go to the main hall,
she rushed into her son's chamber
and held his hand, weeping.
From then on, Kūnshēng (昆生) also became mature
and did not play mischievous pranks,
and thus their affection grew deeper.
Shíniáng (十娘) said:
"I used to think you were frivolous
and that we might not be able to grow old together,
so I didn't want to leave troublesome descendants in the human world;
now that I have no other choice,
I will bear children."
Not long after,
the divine Wēng (翁) and divine Aǒ (媼), dressed in vermilion robes,
descended upon their home.
The next day,
Shíniáng (十娘) went into labor
and gave birth to two sons at once,
and from then on, their comings and goings were unimpeded.
If residents occasionally incurred the deity's wrath,
they would first seek Kūnshēng (昆生);
then he would send women dressed in elaborate attire into the inner chambers
to pay respects to Shíniáng (十娘),
and if Shíniáng (十娘) smiled, the problem would be resolved.
The descendants of the Xuē (薛) family were very numerous,
and people called their family
"the family of Xuē Wāzǐ (薛蛙子)."
Those nearby dared not call them that,
but those from afar did.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* (聊齋誌異),
the Frog Deity
often spoke through shamans.
The shamans could discern the deity's anger or joy: they would tell the faithful
"The deity is pleased"
and blessings would arrive;
"The deity is angry"
, and wives and children would sit sighing in sorrow,
some even forsaking meals.
Is this how popular custom is?
Or is the deity truly efficacious,
not entirely without basis?
There was a wealthy merchant, Zhōu (周) by name,
who was stingy by nature.
When the residents were collecting money to repair the temple of Guānshèng (關聖),
the rich and poor alike contributed greatly,
but Zhōu (周) alone would not spare a single hair.
After a long time,
the construction was not completed,
and the organizers had no plan.
At that time, the crowd was offering sacrifices to the Frog Deity,
and the shaman suddenly said:
"General Zhōu (周將軍) has urgently commanded this humble deity to oversee the fundraising,
bring forth the account books."
The crowd complied.
The shaman said:
"Those who have already donated
will not be forced again;
those who have not donated,
note down your contribution according to your ability."
The crowd obediently listened,
and each noted their contribution.
The shaman looked and said,
"Is Zhōu Mǒu (周某) here?"
Zhōu (周) was just hiding among the back rows,
fearing the deity would know,
and hearing this, his face lost color.
He stammered forward.
The shaman pointed to the register and said:
"Note down one hundred *jīn* (金)."
Zhōu (周) was even more embarrassed.
The shaman angrily said:
"You paid two hundred for illicit debts,
how much more for a good deed!"
It turned out that Zhōu (周) had a private affair with a woman,
and was caught by her husband,
and redeemed her with two hundred *jīn* (金),
hence the shaman exposed him.
Zhōu (周) was even more ashamed and frightened,
and had no choice but
to note it down as commanded.
After he returned home,
he told his wife.
His wife said:
"This is just a trick of the shaman."
The shaman repeatedly asked for it,
but he never gave it.
One day,
while he was taking a nap,
he suddenly heard a sound outside the door like a cow panting.
He looked,
and it was a giant frog.
The doorway barely allowed its body to pass,
its steps were slow and difficult,
blocking both doors as it entered.
Once inside,
it turned and lay down,
resting its chin on the threshold.
The whole family was startled.
Zhōu (周) said:
"This must be asking for the donation money."
He burned incense and prayed,
vowing to pay thirty first,
and the rest would be sent in succession.
The frog did not move;
he offered to pay fifty,
and its body suddenly shrank by about a foot;
he added twenty more,
and it shrank further to the size of a *dǒu* (斗);
he offered to pay the full amount,
and it shrank to the size of a fist,
leisurely exited,
and left through a crack in the wall.
Zhōu (周) urgently took fifty *jīn* (金) to the supervisor's office,
and everyone found it strange,
but Zhōu (周) did not explain the reason.
After several days,
the sorcerer again said,
“Zhōu Mǒu owes fifty (taels of) gold.
Why not press him for payment?”
Zhōu heard this,
and, fearing,
again sent ten taels of gold,
intending to conclude the matter with this.
One day,
as the couple was eating,
the frog arrived again,
in its previous state,
its eyes bulging.
After a short while,
it climbed onto their bed.
The bed shook and seemed about to collapse;
it moreover howled as it lay on the pillow to sleep,
its belly swollen like a sleeping ox,
filling all four corners.
Zhōu, in fear,
immediately offered the full hundred (taels) to it.
When examined,
it still did not move an inch.
Within half a day,
small frogs gathered profusely,
and the next day they became even more numerous.
They burrowed into storerooms and climbed onto couches;
there was no place they did not reach.
Those larger than bowls
climbed onto the stove to gulp down flies,
rotting in the cooking pot,
making the food so filthy as to be inedible.
By the third day,
the courtyard was teeming,
with no space left.
The whole family was bewildered and terrified,
not knowing what course of action to take.
Having no alternative,
they sought advice from the sorcerer.
The sorcerer said,
“This must be because the amount is too little.”
Thereupon, he prayed for it,
adding twenty taels of gold,
and its head began to lift.
He added more,
and one leg rose.
Only when it reached a hundred taels of gold
did all four legs rise completely,
and it got off the bed and exited the door.
It stumbled a few steps,
then turned back and lay down inside the door.
Zhōu, in fear,
asked the sorcerer.
The sorcerer divined his intention,
wishing Zhōu to immediately open his purse.
Zhōu had no choice but
to pay the sorcerer the full amount.
Only then did the frog depart.
A few steps away,
its body suddenly shrank,
mingling among the multitude of frogs,
making it indistinguishable.
They, too, gradually dispersed in confusion.
Once the shrine was completed,
and the consecration ceremony held,
there were further needs.
The sorcerer suddenly pointed at the principal organizers and said,
“So-and-so should contribute a certain amount.”
There were fifteen people in total,
leaving only two out.
The crowd prayed, saying,
“We, along with so-and-so,
have already donated.”
The sorcerer said,
“I do not consider poverty or wealth in terms of what you have or do not have,
but rather the amount you have illicitly gained.
Such money
must not be used for self-enrichment,
lest you suffer unexpected calamities and misfortunes.
Considering your diligent efforts as organizers,
I am therefore resolving this for you.
Except for so-and-so, who is honest and without compromise,
even my own sorcerer,
I will not spare him in the slightest;
I will have him contribute first,
to set an example for all.”
He immediately rushed to his house,
searching through chests and boxes.
His wife asked him,
but he did not answer,
instead emptying all his stored money and bringing it out.
He told the crowd,
“So-and-so privately misappropriated eight taels of silver;
now he is compelled to empty his purse.”
When weighed with the crowd,
it measured just over six taels,
and he had someone record the deficit.
The crowd was stunned,
not daring to dispute,
and all paid the full amount.
The sorcerer, after this, was utterly unaware of it.
When someone informed him,
he was greatly ashamed,
and pawned his clothes to make up the deficit.
Only two individuals were short of their amount.
After the event was concluded,
one person was ill for over a month,
and the other treated a swollen foot.
The cost of their medicine
exceeded the amount they owed.
People considered this the retribution for their misappropriation.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“If the old frog acts as a fundraiser,
there is no one who cannot be persuaded to do good.
Is it not much better than those who prick with needles and drag with ropes?
And the earth also exposed the theft of the custodian,
and averted their disaster.
Thus, its manifest fierceness
was precisely its act of compassion.”
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Rèn Jiànzhī,
a native of Yútái,
dealt in felt and furs for a living.
He exhausted his capital to go to Shǎnxī.
On the way, he met a man
who introduced himself as
“Shēn Zhútíng,
a traveler from Yùrén.”
Their conversation was congenial,
and they swore to be brothers,
traveling together.
Upon reaching Shǎnxī,
Rèn fell ill and could not recover.
Shēn treated him kindly.
After more than ten days,
his illness worsened considerably.
He said to Shēn,
“My family has no permanent property.
The food and clothing for eight mouths
all depend on me alone enduring hardships.
Now, unfortunately,
I am dying in a foreign land.
You
are my closest kin.
Two thousand *lǐ* away,
who else is there?
My pouch contains over two hundred taels of gold.
You may take half of it for yourself,
and prepare a simple burial for me with a small portion of it.
The remainder can serve as travel expenses.
The other half, please send to my wife and children,
so that they may transport my coffin back.
If you are willing to carry my remains back to my hometown,
then do not consider the travel costs.”
He then leaned on his pillow to write a letter, which he entrusted to Shēn,
and died that evening.
Shēn used five or six taels of gold to buy cheap materials
and buried him.
The innkeeper urged him to move the coffin.
Shēn pretended to look for a temple or monastery,
but instead fled and never returned.
It was over a year before Rèn’s family received definite news.
Rèn Xiù, then seventeen years old,
was studying under a teacher.
He consequently abandoned his studies,
wishing to go and find his father’s coffin.
His mother pitied his youth.
Xiù pleaded and wept, wishing to die.
So she pawned their assets to arrange for his trip,
and had an old servant assist him.
They returned after half a year.
After the burial,
the family was utterly impoverished.
Fortunately, Xiù was intelligent.
After the mourning period,
he entered the *pàn* of Yútái.
However, he was frivolous and loved gambling.
His mother’s teachings and warnings were strict,
but he never changed.
One day,
the Literary Chancellor arrived for an examination,
and he was ranked in the fourth class.
His mother wept in anger and refused to eat.
Xiù felt ashamed and afraid,
and was at a loss before his mother.
Thereupon, he secluded himself for over a year,
and subsequently received an excellent ranking and stipend.
His mother urged him to set up a private school,
but people ultimately regarded him as dissolute and unrestrained,
and all scorned him.
My maternal granduncle Zhāng Mǒu was a merchant in the capital.
He urged Xiù to go to the capital,
offering to take him along
without him having to spend his own money.
Xiù was pleased
and followed him.
Upon reaching Línqīng,
they moored their boat outside the customs gate.
At that time, salt boats were gathered there,
their sails and masts like a forest.
After lying down,
Xiù heard the sound of water and people,
which was so noisy he couldn't sleep.
When the watch had quieted down,
he suddenly heard the clear and crisp sound of dice from a neighboring boat,
which entered his ears and lingered in his mind,
and he couldn't help but feel his old habit returning.
He secretly listened to the other passengers,
who were all fast asleep.
He had a thousand cash ready in his purse,
and longed to cross over to the boat for a game.
He quietly got up and untied his purse,
hesitating with the money in hand.
Recalling his mother's instruction,
he immediately tied it up again.
After he lay down,
his heart pounded,
and he struggled to sleep.
He got up again,
and untied it again; he did this three times.
His urge erupted,
and he could no longer bear it,
so he took the money and went directly.
Arriving at the neighboring boat,
he saw two people gambling face-to-face,
with a rich pile of money at stake.
He placed his money on the table
and immediately asked to join the game.
The two men were pleased
and immediately began throwing dice with him.
Xiù won big.
When one player ran out of money,
he used a large sum of gold to mortgage to the boat owner,
gradually betting more than ten strings of cash in a single stake.
As the gambling was in full swing,
another person came aboard the boat,
staring intently for a long time.
He also emptied his purse, offering a hundred gold pieces as collateral to the owner,
and joined the game to gamble together.
Zhāng woke up in the middle of the night,
realized Xiù was not on the boat,
heard the sound of dice,
and knew what was happening.
So he went to the neighboring boat,
intending to dissuade him.
Upon arrival,
he saw a mountain of winnings piled beside Xiù’s lap,
so he said nothing more,
but took several thousand cash and returned.
He called all the other passengers to get up
and move the money,
still leaving more than ten thousand.
Before long,
the three players were all defeated,
and all the money on the boat was gone.
The players wanted to gamble with gold,
but Xiù wanted to stop while he was ahead.
So he feigned that he would not gamble with anything other than cash to make it difficult for them.
Zhāng was at his side,
also urging him to return.
The three players became agitated and impatient.
The boat owner, profiting from his commission,
lent money from other boats,
obtaining over a hundred thousand cash.
With the money, the players
gambled even more extravagantly;
before long,
it all went to Xiù again.
Dawn had broken,
and the customs gate was opened.
They moved the winnings together and returned.
The three players also left.
The owner looked at the more than two hundred gold pieces that had been pledged,
which had all turned into foil ash.
Greatly shocked,
he immediately went to Xiù’s boat,
explained what had happened,
and demanded compensation from Xiù.
When he asked for his name and hometown,
he learned that he was the son of Jiànzhī,
and shrinking his neck in shame and sweat, he retreated.
Upon inquiring from the boatmen,
he learned that the owner was none other than Shēn Zhútíng.
When Xiù was in Shǎn,
he had also heard of his name.
Now the ghost had exacted its revenge,
so he no longer pursued the matter of the previous refusal.
Xiù then invested his winnings with Zhāng in a joint venture and headed north,
earning a profit of five times the principal within a year.
He then, following the precedent, entered the Imperial Academy.
He further profited from usury,
and within ten years,
he became immensely wealthy in his region.
From the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
between Wú and Yuè, there was a game of dragon boat racing.
Wood was carved into dragons,
their scales painted,
and adorned with gold and blue-green;
on top were carved rafters and vermilion railings;
sails and banners were all made of brocade.
At the stern of the boat was a dragon tail,
over a zhàng tall,
from which wooden planks were suspended by cloth ropes.
Children sat on these planks,
tumbling and rolling,
performing various ingenious acts;
below them was the river,
perilous, as if they might fall.
Therefore, when hiring such children,
their parents were first lured with gold,
and they were trained in advance,
so that if they fell into the water and died,
there would be no regret.
In Wúmén, however, beautiful courtesans were carried,
which was somewhat different.
In Zhènjiāng, there was a boy of the Jiǎng family named Āduān,
only seven years old,
quick and extraordinarily skilled,
whom no one could surpass.
His reputation grew even more,
and he was still employed at sixteen.
When he reached the foot of Jīnshān,
he fell into the water and died.
Old Lady Jiǎng, who had only this one son,
could only wail in sorrow.
Āduān did not know he was dead;
two people led him away,
and he saw a different world in the water;
looking back,
he saw swirling waves all around,
standing tall like walls.
Soon he entered a palace,
where he saw a person seated with a helmet.
The two people said,
"This is the Dragon Lair Lord (Lóngwō Jūn)."
They immediately made him prostrate himself.
The Dragon Lair Lord's expression was gentle and serene,
and he said,
"Āduān's skill can be admitted to the Willow Branch Division (Liǔtiáo Bù)."
He was then led to a place
with a spacious hall surrounded by four sides.
He hurried up the east corridor,
where several young boys came out to greet him,
mostly thirteen or fourteen years old.
Then an old woman came,
whom everyone called Aunt Jiě (Jiě Mǔ).
She sat them down and had them display their skills.
After that,
she taught them the "Flying Thunder of Qiántáng" dance (Qiántáng Fēitíng zhī Wǔ)
and the "Harmonious Wind of Dòngtíng" music (Dòngtíng Héfēng zhī Yuè).
They only heard the crashing of drums and gongs,
resounding through all the courtyards;
then all the courtyards fell silent.
Aunt Jiě feared that Āduān would not immediately become proficient,
and she alone tutored him in detail;
but Āduān, after one try,
had already mastered it perfectly.
Aunt Jiě happily said,
"With this child,
he will not yield to Wǎnxiá!"
The next day,
the Dragon Lair Lord reviewed the divisions,
and all divisions gathered.
First, he reviewed the Yaksha Division (Yèchā Bù): they wore鬼面魚服 (guǐmiàn yúfú) [demon masks and fish costumes];
they struck large gongs,
about four chi in circumference;
the drums were so large that four people could embrace one,
their sound like giant thunder,
so loud that other noises could not be heard.
When they danced,
giant waves surged,
flowing horizontally through the air,
occasionally a speck of starlight would fall,
and vanish upon reaching the ground.
The Dragon Lair Lord quickly stopped them
and ordered the Oriole Division (Rǔyīng Bù) to advance: all were beautiful girls of sixteen,
playing delicate sheng music;
at once, a gentle breeze wafted,
the sound of waves completely quieted,
and the water gradually solidified into a crystal world,
transparent both above and below.
After the review,
they all retreated to stand below the west steps.
Next, he reviewed the Swallow Division (Yànzi Bù): all were children with braided hair,
among them a girl,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
who shook her sleeves and tilted her hairpins,
performing a scattered flower dance;
she fluttered and soared,
and from between her collars, sleeves, stockings, and shoes,
came forth five-colored flowers,
which scattered down with the wind,
drifting and covering the courtyard.
After the dance,
her division also went down to the west steps.
Āduān glanced sideways,
and was deeply fond of her.
He asked his division mates,
and it was Wǎnxiá.
Not long after,
the Willow Branch Division was called.
The Dragon Lair Lord specifically tested Āduān.
Āduān performed his previous dance,
joy and anger following the melody,
his bows and lifts in perfect rhythm.
The Dragon Lair Lord praised his clever understanding,
and bestowed upon him a five-colored jacket and trousers,
and a gold hair tie made of fish whiskers,
inlaid with a luminous pearl.
Āduān bowed to receive the gifts and stepped down,
also hurrying to the west steps,
each standing in their assigned place.
From among the crowd, Āduān gazed intently at Wǎnxiá,
and Wǎnxiá also gazed intently at him.
A short while later,
Āduān cautiously stepped out of his division and went north,
while Wǎnxiá also gradually stepped out of her division and went south;
they were a few paces apart,
but the rules were strict, and they dared not break formation,
they merely looked at each other with their minds wandering.
Then the Butterfly Division (Jiádié Bù) was reviewed: boys and girls all danced in pairs,
their heights, ages, and yellow-and-white costumes
were all matched.
After all divisions had been reviewed,
they exited in single file.
The Willow Branch Division was behind the Swallow Division.
Āduān rushed out to the front of his division,
while Wǎnxiá had slowly fallen behind.
She turned her head and saw Āduān,
and deliberately dropped a coral hairpin,
which Āduān quickly tucked into his sleeve.
Upon returning,
he became ill from brooding,
losing his appetite and sleep entirely.
Aunt Jiě would regularly bring him delicacies,
visiting him three or four times a day,
massaging him with deep affection,
but his illness did not abate in the least.
Aunt Jiě was worried,
and at a loss for what to do,
she said,
"The Wújiāng King's (Wújiāng Wáng) birthday celebration is approaching,
what shall we do?"
At dusk,
a young boy came,
sat on his bed, and spoke with him,
claiming to belong to the Butterfly Division.
He calmly asked,
"Are you ill because of Wǎnxiá?"
Āduān was startled and asked,
"How do you know?"
The boy smiled and said,
"Wǎnxiá is also like you."
Āduān sadly sat up,
and immediately sought a plan.
The boy asked,
"Can you still walk?"
He replied,
"I can still manage with effort."
The boy pulled him out,
opened a door to the south;
then turned west,
and opened another double door.
He saw dozens of亩 of lotus flowers,
all growing on flat ground;
the leaves were as large as mats,
the flowers as large as canopies,
and fallen petals piled up a chi deep beneath the stalks.
The boy led him into them
and said,
"Sit here for now."
Then he left.
A short while later,
a beautiful woman parted the lotus flowers and entered,
it was Wǎnxiá.
They met with surprise and joy,
each expressing their longing,
and briefly recounting their lives.
Then they used a stone to press down a lotus leaf to one side,
making it a suitable screen;
they also evenly spread lotus petals as a mat,
and joyfully slept together intimately.
Afterward,
they made a future appointment,
to meet daily when the evening sun appeared,
and then parted.
Āduān returned,
and his illness also quickly healed.
From then on, the two met daily in the lotus patch.
After several days,
Suí Lóngwō Jūn went to Sòng Wújiāng Wáng to offer congratulations.
After the congratulations were offered,
all the troupes returned,
leaving only Wǎnxiá and one person from the Rǔyīng troupe in the palace to teach dance.
Several months passed,
but there was no further news,
and Duān was utterly distraught, as if he had lost something precious.
Only Jiě Mǔ frequently visited the Wújiāng residence;
Duān entrusted her to convey to Wǎnxiá that he considered her an adopted sister,
and asked her to bring Wǎnxiá away,
hoping to see her.
Jiě Mǔ stayed at the gate of Wújiāng for several days,
but the palace security was so strict
that Wǎnxiá was unfortunately unable to leave,
and Jiě Mǔ returned disappointedly.
After more than a month,
Duān's longing became unbearable.
One day,
Jiě Mǔ entered,
and sorrowfully commiserated, saying:
“Alas!
Wǎnxiá has thrown herself into the river!”
Duān was greatly alarmed,
and tears streamed down his face uncontrollably.
He then destroyed his cap and tore his clothes,
hid his gold and pearls, and went out,
intending to join her in death.
But he saw the river water was like a wall,
and even with all his might, he could not penetrate it with his head.
He thought of returning,
but feared being questioned about his cap and clothes,
which would only increase his guilt.
Feeling utterly desperate,
sweat drenched him from head to heel.
Suddenly, he noticed a large tree beneath the wall,
so he climbed it like a monkey,
gradually reaching the tip of a branch;
then he leaped down with great force,
luckily not touching the water,
and found himself floating on the surface.
Unexpectedly,
he seemed to glimpse the human world,
and so he drifted away, swimming.
After a while,
he reached the shore,
sat for a moment by the riverbank,
and suddenly thought of his elderly mother.
So he took a boat and departed.
Upon arriving in his hometown,
he looked around at the houses,
which seemed as distant as if from another world.
As he slowly approached his home,
he suddenly heard a woman in the window say:
“Your son has come.”
The voice was very much like Wǎnxiá's.
Soon,
she came out with his mother,
and it was indeed Wǎnxiá.
At this moment, their joy surpassed their sorrow;
while the old woman was bewildered by a mix of sorrow, doubt, surprise, and joy,
displaying all sorts of emotions.
Initially,
when Wǎnxiá was in Wújiāng,
she felt a tremor in her abdomen.
The laws of the dragon palace were strict,
and she feared that she would give birth any day
and be severely punished;
moreover, she could not see Ā Duān.
She only wished for death,
so she secretly threw herself into the river.
Her body floated up,
bobbing in the waves.
A passenger boat rescued her,
and asked her place of residence.
Wǎnxiá, formerly a famous courtesan in Wú,
knew that her body would not be found if she drowned.
She thought to herself that she could not return to the Yǎnyuàn,
so she said:
“The Jiǎng family in Zhènjiāng,
that is my husband's family.”
The passenger then helped her hire a small boat
and sent her to their home.
Jiǎng Āo doubted that she was correct,
but the woman said she was not mistaken,
and then explained her situation in detail to the old woman.
The old woman, finding her style and charm exquisite,
was quite pleased with her;
but she worried that the girl was too young,
and would surely not be willing to remain a widow forever.
However, the girl was filial and cautious,
and seeing the family was poor,
she immediately took off her precious ornaments and sold them for tens of thousands.
The old woman observed that her intentions were sincere,
and was very happy.
However, she had no son,
and feared that if the girl were to give birth one day,
she would not be believed by relatives and neighbors,
so she discussed it with the girl.
The girl said:
“Mother, as long as you get a true grandson,
why must you seek human recognition?”
The old woman then felt at ease.
Just then, Duān arrived,
and the girl was overjoyed beyond measure.
The old woman also doubted that her son was dead;
she secretly excavated her son's grave,
and found his bones fully intact.
She then used this to question Duān.
Duān finally realized the truth with a shock;
however, he feared that Wǎnxiá would dislike him for not being human,
and instructed his mother not to speak of it again.
His mother agreed.
So she told their fellow villagers
that what they had found that day was not her son's body,
but she still worried that he would not be able to father children.
Before long,
Wǎnxiá indeed gave birth to a boy.
When they held him, he was no different from an ordinary child,
and then they were pleased.
After a long time,
the girl gradually realized that Ā Duān was not human,
and then said:
“Why did you not say so earlier!
When ghosts wear dragon palace clothes,
their seven-seven souls and spirits become firm and condensed,
making them indistinguishable from living people.
If we could get dragon horn glue from the palace,
it could connect bones and joints and regenerate flesh and skin.
It's a pity we didn't acquire it earlier.”
Duān sold his pearls,
and a foreign merchant offered a million in capital,
making the family extremely wealthy from then on.
On the occasion of his mother's birthday: husband and wife sang and danced to offer a toast,
and the news spread to the King's residence.
The King wanted to forcefully take Wǎnxiá.
Duān was afraid,
and went to see the King, explaining:
“Both my wife and I are ghosts.”
When it was verified that they cast no shadows, the King believed them,
and thus did not take her.
He merely sent palace maids to a separate courtyard to learn her skills.
The girl disfigured her face with tortoise urine
before seeing them.
She taught for three months,
but they ultimately could not master all her skills and left.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Zhílì there was a man named Mù,
whose childhood name was Shàn-gōng.
He was the son of the merchant Mù Xiǎo-huán.
He was intelligent, clever, and loved to read.
When he was sixteen,
his father, considering scholarship too circuitous a path,
sent him to learn trade.
He accompanied his father to Chǔ.
Whenever there was nothing to do on the boat,
he would chant and recite.
Upon reaching Wǔchāng,
his father left him to stay in an inn,
to guard their stored goods.
When Mù-shēng's father went out,
he would hold a scroll and chant poems,
his voice clear and resonant.
He often saw a flickering shadow outside the window,
as if someone were secretly listening,
but he did not find it strange.
One evening,
his father went to a banquet,
and did not return for a long time.
Mù-shēng chanted even more intensely.
Someone lingered outside the window,
clearly visible in the moonlight.
Finding it strange,
he quickly went out to peek,
and saw a stunningly beautiful girl of fifteen or sixteen.
Seeing Mù-shēng,
she quickly fled.
Two or three days later,
they loaded their goods and headed north,
mooring by the lake at dusk.
His father happened to be out,
when an old woman entered and said,
"Young master, you have killed my daughter!"
Mù-shēng was startled and asked her,
to which she replied,
"My surname is Bái.
I have a daughter, Qiū-liàn,
who is quite learned.
She said that in the county city,
she heard your clear chanting,
and since then has been infatuated,
even to the point of losing sleep and appetite.
She wishes to be married to you,
and you must not refuse again."
Mù-shēng truly liked her in his heart,
but he was only concerned about his father's cautious nature,
so he told her the truth.
The old woman did not believe him,
and insisted on an oath.
Mù-shēng refused.
The old woman angrily said,
"In this world, for a marriage,
some seek to offer a wild goose but cannot.
Now I, an old woman, propose it myself,
and am instead not admitted;
what could be more shameful!
Please do not think of crossing north anymore!"
Then she left.
A short while later,
his father returned.
Mù-shēng chose his words carefully to tell him,
secretly hoping he would accept.
But his father, considering the long distance,
and also looking down on a girl's youthful infatuation,
laughed and dismissed it.
At the place where they moored,
the water was so deep it submerged the oars;
but suddenly that night, a sandbar rose up,
and the boat became stuck and couldn't move.
Every year on the lake, passing boats would inevitably be detained to guard the sandbar;
when the peach blossom floods arrived the following year,
and other goods had not yet arrived,
the goods on the boat would be worth a hundred times their original price.
For this reason, his father was not overly worried or surprised.
He only planned that for his next trip south,
he would still need to raise capital.
So, he left his son and returned alone.
Mù-shēng secretly rejoiced,
regretting that he hadn't asked the old woman where she lived.
When dusk fell,
the old woman arrived with a maid, supporting the young lady,
and laid her on the couch, saying to Mù-shēng,
"The person is so ill;
don't act as if nothing is happening!"
Then she left.
Mù-shēng was initially startled by what he heard; he moved the lamp to look at the girl,
and saw her charming sickened state,
her beautiful eyes naturally flowing.
He briefly inquired,
and she smiled sweetly.
Mù-shēng pressed her for a word.
She said,
" 'Wasted for my lord, yet ashamed before my lord,'
this can be recited for your concubine."
Mù-shēng was overjoyed,
and wanted to approach her,
but pitied her weakness.
He reached into her embrace,
and they playfully touched.
The girl unconsciously expressed joyful teasing,
then said,
"If you recite Wáng Jiàn's 'Luó-yī Yè-yè'
poem three times for your concubine,
my illness will surely heal."
Mù-shēng followed her words.
After only two repetitions,
the girl pulled up her clothes and sat up, saying,
"I am healed!"
When he read it again,
her delicate trembles harmonized with his.
Mù-shēng's spirits soared even higher,
and so he extinguished the candle and they slept together.
Before dawn, the girl was already up,
saying,
"My old mother will be arriving soon."
Not long after,
the old woman indeed arrived.
Seeing her daughter beautifully dressed and happily sitting,
she was uncontrollably pleased;
she invited her daughter to leave,
but the girl lowered her head and said nothing.
The old woman then left by herself,
saying,
"You enjoy playing with the young master;
that's up to you."
Then Mù-shēng began to inquire about her dwelling place.
The girl said,
"Between your concubine and you, it's merely a casual encounter;
marriage is not yet certain,
so why must you know my family home?"
However, the two loved each other deeply,
and their vows were very firm.
One night, the girl got up early and lit a lamp,
then suddenly opened a scroll, shedding tears sorrowfully.
Mù-shēng quickly got up and asked her.
The girl said,
"My father-in-law will soon arrive.
As for our matter,
your concubine just divined with this scroll,
opening it to Lǐ Yì's 'Jiāngnán Qǔ',
and the meaning of the words is inauspicious."
Mù-shēng comforted her,
saying,
"The first line, 'Married to a merchant from Qūtáng,'
is already a great omen of good fortune;
how could it be inauspicious!"
The girl then became a little happier,
stood up and bid farewell, saying,
"Please let us part for a moment;
at dawn, thousands will point and stare."
Mù-shēng grasped her arm and choked up,
asking,
"If this good thing is to succeed,
where can I send a message?"
She said,
"Your concubine often sends people to scout;
whether it succeeds or not, I will surely hear."
Mù-shēng was about to go down to the boat to see her off,
but the girl strongly declined and left.
Not long after,
Mù-shēng's father indeed arrived.
Mù-shēng gradually confessed his feelings.
