His father suspected him of hiring a courtesan,
and angrily reprimanded him severely.
He carefully checked the valuables on the boat,
and finding no losses,
his scolding ceased.
One evening,
when his father was not on the boat,
the girl suddenly arrived.
They met and embraced,
uncertain of a plan.
The girl said,
"There is a limit to ups and downs;
let us consider the present.
Let me stay with you for two months,
then we will discuss what to do."
Before parting,
they agreed to meet by his chanting.
From then on, whenever his father went out,
Mù-shēng would chant loudly,
and the girl would arrive by herself.
Four months passed,
and the price of goods fell out of season.
The merchants had no strategy,
so they collected funds and prayed at the temple of the lake god.
After Duānwǔ,
heavy rains came,
and the boat finally became passable.
Three or four years later,
a son was born.
One day,
she wept, longing to return home.
So the old man (Wēng) took his son and his daughter-in-law to Chǔ.
When they reached the lake,
they did not know where the old woman (ǎo) was.
The girl knocked on the boat's side, calling for her mother,
her spirit and form utterly lost.
She urged the scholar (shēng) to inquire along the lake.
There happened to be someone fishing for sturgeon,
who caught a white *jì*.
The scholar (shēng) looked closely at it;
it was a giant creature,
its form entirely like a human,
with breasts and genitalia fully present.
He found it strange
and returned to tell the girl.
The girl was greatly alarmed
and said she had long wished to release living creatures,
instructing the scholar (shēng) to redeem and release it.
The scholar (shēng) went to negotiate with the fisherman;
the fisherman demanded an exorbitant price.
The girl said:
"When you were at your home,
you planned to raise not less than tens of thousands of gold;
why be so stingy with a mere trifle?
If you absolutely refuse to comply, I will throw myself into the lake and die forever!"
The scholar (shēng) was afraid
and dared not tell his father.
He stole gold and redeemed and released it.
When he returned,
he did not see the girl.
He searched but could not find her.
At dawn, she finally appeared.
He asked:
"Where have you been?"
She replied:
"I just went to my mother's place."
He asked:
"Where is your mother?"
She blushingly said:
"Now I must tell you the truth: what I just redeemed
was my mother.
Previously, in Dòngtíng,
Lord Lóng ordered her to oversee travelers.
Recently, the palace wanted to select concubines,
and I was praised by those who spread rumors.
So Lord Lóng ordered my mother
to be imprisoned and searched for me.
My mother truthfully reported this.
Lord Lóng did not listen
and banished my mother to the southern shore,
where she was on the verge of starvation,
hence she suffered the previous misfortune.
Now, though the misfortune is averted,
the punishment is not yet lifted.
If you love your concubine,
pray on my behalf to the True Monarch (Zhēnjūn) to have it removed.
If you despise me for being of a different species,
please throw the child back to you.
I will leave on my own.
The provisions in the Dragon Palace (Lónggōng)
might not be a hundred times less than in your home."
The scholar (shēng) was greatly surprised,
fearing that the True Monarch (Zhēnjūn) could not be seen.
The girl said:
"Tomorrow, at the appointed hour,
the True Monarch (Zhēnjūn) will arrive.
When you see a Daoist pacing, immediately bow to him,
and follow him even if he enters the water.
The True Monarch (Zhēnjūn) likes scholars,
so he will surely take pity and grant your request."
Then she took out a piece of fish-belly silk (yúfǔlíng).
She said:
"If he asks what you seek,
just present this
and ask him to write a 'miǎn'
character."
The scholar (shēng) waited as she instructed.
Indeed, a Daoist hobbled over,
and the scholar (shēng) prostrated himself in reverence.
The Daoist walked quickly,
and the scholar (shēng) followed behind him.
The Daoist threw his staff into the water
and leaped onto it.
The scholar (shēng) actually followed him and climbed on.
Then it was not a staff,
but a boat.
He bowed again.
The Daoist asked:
"What do you seek?"
The scholar (shēng) took out the silk (luó) and requested writing.
The Daoist unfolded it and looked, saying:
"This is *báihàiyì*!
How did you come by it?"
The scholar (chánggōng) dared not conceal anything,
detailing the whole story.
The Daoist smiled and said:
"This creature is truly elegant!
How could the old dragon be so debauched?"
Then he took out a brush and hastily wrote
the character "miǎn" (免),
like a talisman,
and ordered the boat back.
Then he saw the Daoist treading on his staff, floating away,
and in an instant, he had vanished.
Returning to the boat,
the girl was happy,
but she warned him not to reveal it to his parents.
Two or three years after returning,
the old man (Wēng) traveled south
and did not return for several months.
The lake water was completely gone,
and she waited long, but it did not come.
The girl then fell ill,
gasping day and night,
and instructed:
"If I die,
do not bury me.
At the *mǎo*, *wǔ*, and *yǒu* hours,
recite Dù Fǔ's poem 'Dreaming of Lǐ Bái' once.
My death will then be imperishable.
When the water arrives,
pour it into a basin,
close the door, loosen my clothes,
and carry me in to immerse me.
I should then live."
She gasped for several days
and then suddenly died.
Half a month later,
Mù Wēng arrived.
The scholar (shēng) quickly followed her instructions,
immersing her for about an hour,
and she gradually revived.
From then on, she constantly thought of returning south.
Later, after the old man (Wēng) died,
the scholar (shēng) followed her wish
and settled in Chǔ.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain Governor Hú Nán,
dispatched a subordinate official (zhōuzuǒ) to escort sixty boxes of military provisions to the capital.
On the way, they were caught in the rain,
and as night fell, they fell behind schedule.
Having nowhere to stay,
they saw an ancient temple in the distance
and went there to rest.
At dawn,
they looked at the provisions they were escorting,
and they were entirely gone.
Everyone was shocked and puzzled,
and no one could be blamed.
They returned to report to the Governor (fǔgōng),
who considered it a fabrication
and was about to punish them by law.
However, when the various clerks were questioned,
they all gave consistent accounts.
The Governor (gōng) ordered them to return to the original place
to investigate the matter.
Arriving in front of the temple,
he saw a blind man,
whose appearance was strikingly unusual.
He had posted a sign that said:
"Can attend to matters with utmost care."
Therefore, he sought divination.
The blind man said:
"This is for one who has lost silver."
The zhōuzǔo said:
"Exactly."
Then he recounted his previous distress.
The blind man then requested a shoulder litter,
saying,
"Just follow me,
and you will know for yourself."
So they did as he said,
and all the palace servants followed him.
The blind man said:
"East."
They went east.
The blind man said:
"North."
They went north.
After five days,
they entered a deep mountain,
and suddenly beheld a city,
where residents gathered densely.
Entering the city,
they moved for a while,
then the blind man said:
"Stop."
Thereupon, he got down from the litter,
and pointed south with his hand:
"You will see a tall gate facing west;
you can knock on the gate and ask yourself."
He cupped his hands and left.
The zhōuzǔo followed his instruction,
and indeed saw a tall gate,
and gradually entered it.
A person came out,
dressed in Hancì clothing,
but did not state his name.
The zhōuzǔo recounted where he had come from.
The person said:
"Please stay for a few days;
I will arrange for you to meet the person in charge."
Then he led him away,
and made him stay alone in a dwelling,
providing him with food and drink.
In his leisure time, he strolled,
and reached the back of the residence,
where he saw a garden pavilion,
and entered it.
Old pines shaded the sun,
and fine grass was like a felt rug.
After turning through several corridors and pavilions,
there was another high pavilion;
he ascended the steps and entered,
seeing several human skins hanging on the wall,
all five sense organs complete,
emitting a strong, fishy smell.
He felt his hair stand on end and shivered,
and quickly retreated to his dwelling.
He resigned himself to being skinned and kept in a foreign land,
having no hope of survival,
and therefore thought that whether he advanced or retreated, death was certain,
so he might as well let it be.
The next day,
the man in official attire summoned him,
saying:
"Today you can see him."
The zhōuzǔo assented.
The man in official attire rode a swift, angry horse,
and the zhōuzǔo ran on foot after him.
Soon,
they arrived at a yúanmén,
which resembled a zhìfǔ's yáshǔ,
with men in black robes arranged on both sides,
the scale solemn and awe-inspiring.
The man in official attire dismounted,
and led him in.
There was another heavy gate.
He saw a king,
with a pearl crown and embroidered ribbons,
sitting facing south.
The zhōuzǔo hurried forward,
and prostrated himself.
The king asked:
"Are you the official from Húnán whose term has ended?"
The zhōuzǔo affirmed.
The king said:
"All the silver is here.
This is a trivial matter;
if your fǔjūn generously grants it to you,
it is not impossible."
The zhōuzǔo tearfully pleaded:
"The deadline has passed,
and I will surely be executed upon my return.
How can I report and prove this?"
The king said:
"This is not difficult."
Then he handed him a large letter, saying:
"Return with this,
and you will be safe."
He also dispatched strong men to escort him.
The zhōuzǔo held his breath,
not daring to argue,
and received the letter and returned.
The mountains, rivers, and roads
were completely different from those he had traveled on his way there.
Once out of the mountains,
the escorts departed.
A few days later,
he arrived in Chángshā,
and respectfully reported to the fǔgōng.
The gōng thought it was utterly baseless,
and angrily would not allow him to explain,
ordering his attendants to quickly fetch silk ropes.
The zhōuzǔo untied the letter from his waist;
the gōng opened it and had not finished reading,
when his face turned ashen.
He ordered his bonds to be released,
and simply said:
"The silver is also a small matter;
you may leave for now."
Thereupon, he immediately issued an urgent dispatch to his subordinate officials,
to devise a way to make up the deficit and send it.
A few days later,
the gōng fell ill,
and soon died.
Prior to this,
the gōng was sleeping with his beloved concubine;
when he awoke,
all of the concubine's hair was gone.
The entire yáshǔ was astonished and puzzled,
unable to fathom the reason.
Indeed, the hair in the letter was hers.
Outside, there was a letter which said:
"You rose from a humble background to become a shǒulìng,
and your position is extremely high among men.
Your bribery and greed
are too numerous to count.
The previous six hundred thousand silver taels
have already been verified and stored in the treasury.
You should open your corrupt purse
and supplement the original amount.
The official whose term has ended is innocent,
and must not be censured.
The previous taking of the concubine's hair
was a slight warning.
If you again fail to obey the command,
your head will be taken tomorrow morning or evening.
The concubine's hair is returned
as clear proof."
After the gōng died,
his family members first circulated this letter.
Later, his subordinates sent people to look for the place where he had stayed,
but found only towering cliffs and impassable ravines,
with no paths whatsoever.
Yìshǐshì says:
"The red thread and golden box used to punish greed
were truly strange and delightful.
However, the immortals of Táoyuán
do not engage in robbery;
even among gatherings of swordsmen,
how could there be cities and yáshǔ?
Alas!
What kind of deity was this?
If its location were known,
I fear there would be no end to those in the world seeking redress."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Mǒu Jiǎ privately coveted his servant's wife,
and therefore killed the servant and took his wife,
fathering two sons and one daughter.
Nineteen years passed,
when a great bandit broke into the city,
and looted it bare.
A young bandit,
holding a knife, entered Jiǎ's house.
Jiǎ looked at him,
and he bore a striking resemblance to the deceased servant.
He sighed, saying:
"I am done for now!"
He emptied his purse to ransom his life.
But the bandit ignored him,
and did not say a word,
but only searched for people and killed,
killing twenty-seven members of the family before leaving.
Jiǎ's head was not completely severed;
after the bandit left, he briefly revived,
and was still able to speak.
Three days later, he died.
Alas!
Retribution is unfailing,
how terrifying it is!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Zhāng Wòzhòng
served in Qúzhōu and said:
"In Qúzhōu, when the night is quiet,
no one dares to walk alone.
There is a ghost on the Zhōnglóu.
It has a horn on its head,
and its appearance is fierce and hideous.
It descends immediately upon hearing footsteps.
People are startled and flee,
and the ghost also then leaves.
However, whoever sees it invariably falls ill,
and many die.
Also, in the city, there is a pond.
At night, a bolt of white cloth emerges,
lying across the ground like a piece of white silk.
If a passerby picks it up,
they are immediately dragged into the water.
There are also duck ghosts.
When night falls and is quiet,
and there is absolutely nothing by the pond,
if one hears a duck's sound,
people immediately fall ill."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Hé Jiǒngqīng
was from Píngyīn.
When he first served as a magistrate in Qínzhōng,
a oil vendor committed a minor offense.
His words were blunt,
and Hé became angry,
beating him to death with a staff.
Later, he rose to the position of Quánsī,
and his family fortune was abundant.
He built a multi-story building.
On the day the main beam was raised,
relatives and guests raised cups to congratulate him.
Suddenly, he saw the oil vendor enter,
secretly startled and suspicious.
Soon after, it was reported that his concubine had given birth to a son.
He said sadly,
"The building work is not yet complete,
but the one who will dismantle it has already arrived!"
People thought he was joking,
but they did not know that he had actually seen something.
Later, the son, once grown,
was extremely mischievous
and squandered his family's wealth.
He was hired as a servant for others.
Every time he earned a few coins,
he would buy sesame oil to eat.
The Historian of the Strange said:
"I often see the continuous mansions and towers of wealthy families.
After their death,
when I pass by again, they are already ruins.
This must be because the 'dismantler of buildings' has been born into their family.
Living above others,
how can one not be vigilant early on!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
During the Míng dynasty, General Péng Hóng
led a campaign against bandits into Shǔ.
Upon reaching deep mountains,
there was a large Chan monastery.
It was said that it had been without monks for a hundred years.
When he inquired of the local scholars,
they said,
"There are demons in the temple;
whoever enters invariably dies."
Péng feared hidden bandits,
so he led his soldiers, clearing the overgrown grass, and entered.
In the front hall,
a black eagle flew out and through the gate. The middle hall was unremarkable.
Advancing further,
they reached the Buddha pavilion.
They looked around but saw nothing,
but all who entered suffered an uncontrollable headache.
Péng entered himself,
and it was the same.
A moment later,
a large scorpion, the size of a pípa,
crawled down from the planks.
The entire army fled in panic.
Péng then set fire to the monastery.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Zhēn Yùshēng
was a native of Chǔ Yílíng,
the son of a xiàolián.
He was skilled in writing,
with a handsome appearance,
and became renowned in his early twenties.
When he was a child,
a physiognomist said:
"Later, he will marry a female Daoist priestess."
His parents both laughed at this.
However, when they discussed marriage for him,
it was difficult to find a suitable match, whether high or low in status.
Yùshēng's birth mother, Madame Zāng,
had ancestors who lived in Huánggāng.
Yùshēng therefore went to visit his maternal grandmother.
He heard people of the time say:
"Among the 'Four Clouds' of Huángzhōu,
the youngest is peerless."
This was because there was a Lǚzǔ'ān in the prefecture,
where all the female Daoist priestesses were beautiful,
hence the saying.
The abbey was only a little over ten lì from the Zāng family village,
so Yùshēng secretly went there.
He knocked on its gate,
and indeed, there were three or four female Daoist priestesses.
They humbly and joyfully welcomed him,
and their demeanor was all refined and pure.
Among them, the youngest one
was truly unrivaled in the world.
His heart was drawn to her, and his eyes lingered on her.
The girl rested her chin on her hand,
but looked elsewhere.
The Daoist priestesses searched for cups to brew tea.
Yùshēng seized the opportunity to ask her name and surname.
She replied:
"Yúnqī,
surname Chén."
Yùshēng jested:
"How wonderful!
I happen to be surnamed Pān."
Chén blushed, her cheeks reddening,
lowered her head without speaking,
stood up, and left.
A moment later,
tea was brewed,
and fine fruits were served.
Each gave their names and surnames: one was
Bái Yúnshēn,
about thirty years old;
another was
Shèng Yúnmián,
around twenty years old;
another was
Liáng Yúndòng,
approximately twenty-four or twenty-five,
who was actually their junior.
But Yúnqī did not appear.
Yùshēng felt quite disheartened,
so he asked about her.
Bái said:
"That maid fears strangers."
Yùshēng then stood up to leave,
but Bái strongly urged him to stay,
and he did not remain but left.
Bái said:
"If you want to see Yúnqī,
you can come again tomorrow."
Yùshēng returned,
his thoughts of her exceedingly keen.
The next day,
he visited again.
All the Daoist priestesses were there,
but only Yúnqī was absent, so he did not immediately ask.
The Daoist priestesses prepared a meal and urged him to stay,
but Yùshēng strongly declined,
though they did not listen.
Bái broke off a cake and offered chopsticks,
earnestly encouraging him to eat.
He then asked:
"Where is Yúnqī?"
They replied:
"She will come on her own."
After a long time,
as evening was approaching,
Yùshēng wanted to leave.
Bái grabbed his wrist to detain him,
saying:
"Stay here for now.
I will bring the maid for you to see."
Yùshēng then stayed.
Soon,
they lit lamps and prepared wine,
and Yúnmián also left.
After several rounds of wine,
Yùshēng claimed to be drunk.
Bái said:
"Drink three more goblets,
and Yúnqī will come out."
Yùshēng indeed drank as many.
Liáng also used this to press him to drink,
and Yùshēng again finished them,
then overturned his cup and announced his departure.
Bái looked at Liáng and said:
"Our faces are thin [i.e., we are too shy],
we cannot persuade him to drink more.
You go and drag that maid Chén here,
and tell her that Master Pān has been waiting for the wonderful Miàocháng for a long time."
Liáng went,
and returned a short while later,
fully stating:
"Yúnqī will not come."
Yùshēng wanted to leave,
but it was already deep night,
so he feigned drunkenness and lay down on his back.
The two of them took turns stripping him naked,
and alternately engaged in lewd acts with him.
He could not endure their harassment all night.
When dawn broke,
he left without sleeping.
For several days, he dared not return,
but his heart could not forget Yúnqī.
However, he did not immediately approach to investigate.
One day,
at dusk,
Bái left the gate
and departed with a young man.
Yùshēng rejoiced,
not fearing Liáng much, and eagerly knocked on the gate.
Yúnmián came out to answer the door.
When he asked,
Liáng had also gone elsewhere.
He then asked about Yúnqī.
Shèng led him away,
and then entered another courtyard,
calling out:
"Yúnqī!
A guest has arrived."
He only saw the room door clang shut.
Shèng smiled and said:
"The door is closed."
Yùshēng stood outside the window,
as if he was about to speak,
then Shèng left.
Yúnqī spoke from behind the window:
"Everyone uses me as bait
to lure you.
If you come frequently, your life will be in danger.
I cannot permanently uphold my pure rules,
nor dare I completely abandon modesty and integrity.
I only wish to serve someone like Master Pān."
Yùshēng then promised her a lifetime commitment.
Yúnqī said:
"My master raised me,
and it was not easy.
If you truly love me,
you must redeem me with twenty [taels of silver].
I will wait for you for three years.
If you hope for a ' mulberry field' liaison [i.e., illicit affair],
that is impossible."
Yùshēng agreed.
Just as he was about to reveal his true situation,
Shèng returned,
and he left with her,
then bid farewell and went home.
His heart was filled with melancholy and longing.
He thought of giving in to the circumstances
and having another intimate encounter with her charming form,
when coincidentally, a family servant reported his father's illness,
so he returned immediately, traveling day and night.
Not long after,
the xiàolián died.
Fūrén’s family training was extremely strict,
and he dared not let his inner thoughts be known.
He merely cut down on his gold and silver,
accumulating it daily.
When there were proposals for marriage,
he always used the excuse that the mourning period had not ended.
His mother did not listen.
He gently pleaded, saying:
“Previously in Huánggāng,
my maternal grandmother wished to arrange a marriage with the Chén family,
which was truly my heartfelt desire.
Now, having suffered a great loss,
news has been cut off.
For a long time, I haven’t gone to Huáng to inquire;
I wish to go there soon.
If it doesn’t work out,
I will follow my mother’s command.”
Fūrén agreed.
So, he took what he had accumulated and left.
Upon arriving in Huáng,
he went to the nunnery.
The courtyards were desolate,
vastly different from before.
Gradually entering,
he saw only an old nun cooking by the stove.
He approached and asked.
The nun said:
“Two years ago, the old Daoist priestess died,
and the ‘Sìyún’
scattered.”
He asked:
“Where did they go?”
She said:
“Yúnshēn and Yúndòng
went with some unruly youths;
I heard Yúnqī is temporarily residing north of the prefecture;
I don’t know anything about Yúnmián.”
Hearing this,
he sighed with sorrow.
He ordered his carriage and immediately went north of the prefecture.
Whenever he encountered a Daoist temple, he inquired,
but found no trace.
He returned disheartened and regretful,
and falsely told his mother:
“My maternal uncle said that Elder Chén has gone to Yuèzhōu.
When he returns,
he will send a messenger.”
More than half a year passed,
and Fūrén returned to her parents’ home.
She asked her mother about the matter,
and her mother was quite bewildered.
Fūrén was angry that her son had lied;
the old woman suspected her nephew and brother-in-law were conspiring,
but she hadn't mentioned it.
Fortunately, her maternal uncle was away on a distant journey,
so there was no way to verify his falsehood.
Fūrén had vowed to offer incense at Liánfēng,
and stayed overnight at the foot of the mountain for fasting.
After she had laid down,
the innkeeper knocked on her door,
sending a female Daoist priestess to share her room.
She introduced herself, saying:
“I am Chén Yúnqī.”
Hearing that Fūrén’s family was from Yílíng,
she moved her seat to the couch
and recounted her hardships,
her words filled with sorrow and pity.
Finally, she said:
“I have a maternal cousin, Pān Shēng,
who shares the same lineage as Fūrén.
I would trouble you to ask your sons and nephews to pass on a message,
just tell him that I am temporarily staying at Hèqīguān with my Daoist uncle Wáng Dàochéng,
suffering hardship day and night,
each day like a year.
This morning, I came for a visit;
I fear that after this,
he might not know about it.”
Fūrén tried to ascertain the name,
but then she didn't know it,
only saying:
“Since he is at the academy,
the xiùcai must all have heard of him.”
Before dawn, they parted,
and she earnestly re-emphasized her request.
After Fūrén returned,
she spoke of it to her son.
The son knelt for a long time and said:
“I will tell Mother the truth: the so-called Pān Shēng
is none other than your son.”
When Fūrén learned the truth,
she angrily said:
“Worthless child!
Engaging in promiscuity in temples,
taking a Daoist priestess as a wife,
how will you face your relatives and guests!”
The son hung his head,
not daring to utter a word.
Coincidentally, the son entered the prefecture for an examination.
He secretly ordered a boat to visit Wáng Dàochéng.
Upon arrival,
Yúnqī had left for a trip half a month earlier and had not returned.
After he returned,
he fell ill with melancholy.
Just then, Zāng'ǎo died.
Fūrén went to attend the funeral.
After the burial, she lost her way
and arrived at the Jīng family home.
When she inquired,
she found it was her clan sister.
She was cordially invited in.
She saw a young girl in the hall,
about eighteen or nineteen years old,
whose beauty and grace were exquisite,
unlike anything she had ever seen.
Fūrén always hoped to find a good daughter-in-law
to prevent her son from being resentful.
Her heart was stirred,
so she agreed to meet her.
Her sister said:
“This is the daughter of the Wáng family,
a niece of the Jīng family.
She has lost both parents
and is temporarily staying here.”
She asked:
“To whose family is she betrothed?”
She replied:
“To no one.”
She took her hand and conversed with her.
Her manner was charming and gentle,
which greatly pleased the mother.
She stayed overnight for her
and privately expressed her intention to her sister.
Her sister said:
“That would be excellent.
But this person holds herself in high regard;
otherwise,
why would she have delayed marriage until now?
Allow me to discuss it with her.”
Fūrén invited her to share her bed,
and they talked and laughed very happily;
she willingly called Fūrén “mother.”
Fūrén was delighted
and asked her to return to Jīngzhōu with her;
the girl was even more pleased.
The next day,
they returned by boat.
Upon their arrival,
the son was still ill in bed.
His mother comforted him in his severe illness,
and privately had a maid tell him:
“Fūrén has brought a beautiful woman for the young master.”
The son did not believe it.
He leaned against the window to peek,
and she was even more strikingly beautiful than Yúnqī.
He then thought: the three-year agreement has passed;
she left for a trip and did not return,
so her beautiful face must already have a master.
To obtain such a beauty
greatly comforted his heart.
Thus, his expression brightened,
and his illness soon recovered.
His mother then arranged for the two to meet and greet each other.
When the son came out,
Fūrén asked the girl:
“Do you know my intention in bringing you back with me?”
The girl smiled faintly and said:
“I already know.
But my initial intention for returning with you,
mother, you do not know.
I was rashly betrothed in my youth to the Pān family of Yílíng.
News has been completely cut off,
so he must have found another good match.
If so,
then I will be your daughter-in-law;
if not,
then I will forever be your daughter,
and the day to repay you will come.”
Fūrén said:
"Since there is an existing agreement,
I will not insist.
But formerly on Mount Wǔzǔ,
a female Daoist priestess asked about the Pān family.
Now again the Pān family.
I certainly know that the aristocratic families of Yílíng do not have this surname."
The woman was surprised and said,
"Is the one who sleeps at the foot of Liánfēng Peak my mother?
The one who inquired about Pān
is me."
The mother then suddenly understood,
and smilingly said,
"If so,
then Pān Shēng is certainly here."
The woman asked,
"Where is he?"
The madam ordered a maid to lead her to ask Shēng.
Shēng was surprised and said,
"Are you Yúnqī?"
The woman asked,
"How do you know?"
Shēng told her the situation,
and then she realized she had been playing a trick with Pān Láng.
When the woman knew it was Shēng,
she was too embarrassed to continue talking,
and quickly returned to tell her mother.
The mother asked why her surname was Wáng again.
She replied,
"My original surname is Wáng.
The Daoist master took a liking to me,
and so adopted me as his daughter,
taking his surname."
The madam was also pleased,
and chose an auspicious day to arrange their marriage.
Before this,
the woman and Yúnmián both stayed with Wáng Dáochéng.
Dáochéng's dwelling was cramped,
so Yúnmián went to Hànkǒu.
The woman was delicate and foolish, unable to endure hardship,
and was also too ashamed to practice the Daoist profession.
Dáochéng was rather displeased with her.
Coincidentally, Jīng Shì went to Huánggāng,
and the woman met her and wept,
so she went with her.
Jīng Shì made her change into women's clothes,
intending to arrange a marriage with an aristocratic family,
and therefore concealed the fact that she had once been a Daoist adherent.
However, when suitors inquired,
the woman was always unwilling,
and her uncle and aunt both did not understand her intentions,
feeling annoyed and suspicious of her.
On this day,
returning with the madam,
she found her refuge,
as if relieved of a heavy burden.
After the wedding ceremony,
each recounted their past experiences,
crying with extreme joy.
The woman was filial and respectful,
and the madam doted on her greatly;
but she played the zither and enjoyed chess,
not knowing how to manage household affairs or earn a living,
which made the madam quite worried.
More than a month passed,
and the mother sent two people to Jīng Shì,
who stayed for several days and then returned.
As they were boating on the river,
a boat suddenly passed,
with a female Daoist priestess inside.
Upon approaching,
it was Yúnmián.
Yúnmián had a unique friendship with the woman.
The woman was delighted,
and invited her to share the boat,
where they faced each other, filled with bitterness and sorrow.
She asked,
"Where are you going?"
Shèng said,
"I have been deeply worried for a long time.
I traveled far to Hèqī Guān,
only to hear that you were staying with Uncle Jīng.
So I was going to Huánggāng,
just to visit.
I never knew that my beloved had already found her partner.
Now I see you like an immortal,
while I am left drifting,
not knowing when it will end!"
She then sighed.
The woman devised a plan: she instructed her to change into women's clothes,
pretend to be her elder sister,
accompany the madam,
and slowly choose a good match.
Shèng agreed.
Upon their return,
the woman first informed the madam,
then Shèng entered.
Her demeanor was that of an aristocratic lady;
in her conversation and laughter,
she showed great worldly wisdom.
Since the mother was a widow,
she suffered from loneliness.
She was very happy to have Shèng,
and was only afraid that she would leave.
Shèng woke up early to labor on behalf of the mother,
not treating herself as a guest.
The mother was even more pleased,
secretly thinking of accepting the woman's 'sister',
to cover up her identity as a female Daoist priestess,
but had not dared to speak of it.
One day,
she forgot something she had not done,
and anxiously inquired about it,
only to find that Shèng had already prepared it long ago.
She then said to the woman,
"A person in a painting cannot manage a household;
what good is she?
If my daughter-in-law were like her elder sister,
I would have no worries."
Little did she know that the woman had been considering this for a long time,
only fearing her mother's caution.
Hearing her mother's words,
she smiled and replied,
"Since mother loves her so much,
your daughter-in-law wishes to emulate Yīng and Huáng,
what do you think?"
The mother did not speak,
but also smiled wryly.
The woman withdrew,
and told Shēng,
"The old mother has agreed."
Then she tidied another room,
and said,
"When we shared a pillow in the temple,
you said: 'As long as we find someone who knows how to cherish and love,
the two of us shall serve him together.'
Do you still remember?"
Shèng's eyes shimmered without her realizing it,
and she said,
"What I meant by cherishing and loving
is not something else: for example, day after day of managing things,
yet no one knows the sweetness or bitterness of it;
in the past few days,
with just a little bit of minor effort,
the old mother immediately shows concern and care,
and then the warmth and coldness in my heart are suddenly vastly different.
If I am not given an eviction order,
and can long accompany the old mother,
my wish will be fulfilled,
and I do not expect the fulfillment of our past words."
The woman told her mother.
The mother had her younger sister burn incense,
and each swore no regrets,
then allowed Shēng to perform the marriage rites with her.
As they were about to sleep,
she told Shēng,
"I am a twenty-three-year-old old virgin."
Shēng still did not believe her.
Soon, when blood stained the mattress,
he was astonished.
Shèng said,
"The reason I am happy to have a good husband
is not that I cannot endure solitude;
it is truly that as a woman of the inner chambers,
to be treated and respond like a courtesan
is what I cannot bear.
Using this one time,
to be registered in your family,
I shall serve the old mother for you,
and manage the household affairs.
As for the pleasures of the bedchamber,
please discuss them with others."
Three days later,
she bundled her bedding and followed the mother,
refusing to leave even when sent away.
The woman went to her mother's room early,
occupied her bed,
and having no other choice,
Shèng then went with Shēng.
From then on, they alternated every two or three days,
which became their custom.
Fūrén used to be skilled at弈,
but since becoming a widow,
she had no leisure for it.
Since acquiring Shèng,
who managed affairs meticulously,
Fūrén had nothing to do during the day.
She would then play弈 with her daughter.
They would light lamps, pour fresh tea,
and listen to the two women play the qín,
not dispersing until midnight.
She often said to people:
"Even when my son-in-law was alive,
we could not have enjoyed such happiness."
Shèng managed the accounts,
and regularly reported the records to Fūrén.
Fūrén, suspicious, asked:
"My children often say you were orphaned young;
who taught you to write and play棋? "
Her daughter smiled and told her the truth.
Fūrén also smiled and said:
"I initially did not want to marry my son to a Daoist,
but now I have ended up with two!"
Suddenly remembering the divination from her childhood,
she finally believed that fate is inescapable.
Shēng failed the examinations twice more.
Fūrén said:
"Although our family is not wealthy,
we have three hundred *mǔ* of thin fields.
Fortunately, with Yúnmián's management,
we are increasingly well-off.
My son, just stay by my side,
and let the two women and me enjoy ourselves together;
I do not wish for you to seek wealth and status."
Shēng followed her advice.
Later, Yúnmián had one son and one daughter;
Yúnqī had one daughter and three sons.
Fūrén died at over eighty years of age.
All the grandchildren passed the prefectural examination;
the eldest grandson,
Yúnmián's child,
had already passed the provincial examination.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A certain Yóujī Guān
had many wives and concubines.
He most avoided his childhood nickname;
he called "year" as "day," "birth" as "hard,"
and "horse" as "big donkey."
He also avoided "defeat" as "victory,"
and "peace" as "release."
Although in letters and correspondence
he did not strictly avoid them,
if his family members spoke of them,
he would become angry.
One day,
a clerk managing correspondence was reporting an affair
and inadvertently committed the taboo.
Greatly enraged,
Yóujī Guān struck him with an inkstone,
killing him instantly.
Three days later,
he lay drunk,
and saw the clerk enter with a calling card,
asking:
"What is it?"
The clerk replied:
"'Mǎ Zǐ'ān'
has come to pay respects."
Suddenly realizing it was a ghost,
Yóujī Guān quickly rose,
drew his sword, and swung it.
The clerk smiled faintly,
threw the calling card onto the table,
and vanished.
He picked up the card and looked at it;
it read:
"Suì family member Yìng Dàlǘzǐ Fàng Shèng."
Such an arrogant and unreasonable man,
to be mocked by a ghost,
how ridiculous!
A monk from Niúshǒushān
named himself Tiěhàn,
and also Tiěshǐ.
He had forty poems;
all who saw them collapsed with laughter.
He carved two seals for himself: one named
"Húnzhàng Hángzǐ" (Blockhead Peddler),
and the other named
"Lǎoshí Pōpí" (Honest Rogue).
Yù Sīzhí of Xiùshuǐ imitated his poems
and named them
"Niúshān Forty Farts."
The inscription read:
"Released by Húnzhàng Hángzǐ, Lǎoshí Pōpí."
There's no need to read his poems;
the title alone is enough to provoke laughter.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
At the home of Xuéshǐ Zhū Yùsān,
under the threshold, there was a centipede
several *chǐ* long.
It would emerge whenever there was wind and rain,
coiling on the ground like a white silken ribbon.
It is said that centipedes resemble millipedes,
cannot be seen during the day,
but emerge at night,
gathering wherever there is a smell of blood.
Some say millipedes have no eyes but are very greedy.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A certain Jiàoguān
was very deaf,
but was friends with a fox;
he could even hear the fox whisper in his ear.
Whenever he met a superior,
he would bring the fox with him,
and people did not know he was hard of hearing.
After five or six years,
the fox bade farewell and left,
advising:
"You are like a puppet;
if not manipulated,
all five senses will be useless.
Rather than inviting trouble with your deafness,
it's better to retire early."
Jiàoguān was attached to his salary
and could not follow the advice;
his responses were often inappropriate.
The Xuéshǐ wanted to dismiss him,
but Jiàoguān sought intercession from powerful figures
to delay it.
One day, he was on duty at the examination hall.
After the roll call,
the Xuéshǐ retired to sit informally with the other Jiàoguān.
Each Jiàoguān took out a register from their boots
and presented it with a request for influence.
After a while, the Xuéshǐ smiled and asked:
"Why is it that your academy alone has nothing to present?"
Jiàoguān was bewildered and did not understand.
Someone sitting nearby poked him
and put his hand into his boot,
showing him what to do.
Jiàoguān was selling fake artifacts on consignment for a relative,
which he always hid in his boots
to sell wherever he went.
Because of the Xuéshǐ's smiling words,
he suspected he was being asked for this item,
so he bowed and stood up to answer:
"The eight-money ones are the best,
but your humble servant dare not present them."
The entire assembly suppressed their laughter.
The Xuéshǐ shouted at him to leave,
and he was subsequently dismissed from office.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Píngyuán alone had nothing,
which was also a pillar in the midstream.
If a Xuéshǐ asks for things to be presented,
then it is proper to offer this.
To be dismissed for this,
how unjust!"
Zhū Gōngzǐ Zǐqīng's Ěrlù states:
"Lǐng Chí, a Mingjīng from Dōnglái,
was the Sīxùn of Yíshuǐ.
He was eccentric and foolish.
Whenever his colleagues gathered,
he would remain silent;
but after sitting for a while,
he would unknowingly start moving all his facial features,
laughing and crying simultaneously,
as if there were no one else present.
If he heard someone laugh,
he would immediately stop.
He lived frugally and self-deprecatingly,
accumulating over a hundred *liǎng* of gold,
which he buried in his study,
without even his wife and children knowing.
One day,
sitting alone,
his hands and feet suddenly moved,
and after a moment he said: 'Having done evil and made enemies,
suffered hunger and endured starvation,
what was so easily accumulated
is now in the study.
If anyone were to know,
what would happen?'
This happened repeatedly.
A gate attendant nearby
did not notice anything unusual.
The next day,
Chí went out, and the gate attendant entered,
dug up the gold, and took it away.
After two or three days,
Chí felt uneasy;
he dug up the spot to check,
only to find it empty.
He stamped his feet and beat his chest,
sighing with regret, wishing he could die."
Among teaching positions, one could truly say there are a thousand types and a hundred forms.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Lǐ Zǒngzhèn of Jiāozhōu
bought two black slaves.
They were as black as lacquer.
Their soles were rough and thick;
they could walk on an upright blade
back and forth
without sustaining any injury.
Zǒngzhèn married one to a maid.
She bore a white son.
His subordinates and servants joked about it,
saying he was not the father.
The black slave also suspected it,
and so he killed his son.
When he examined the bones, they were all black.
Only then did he regret it.
The duke often made the two slaves dance facing each other,
and their expressions were also worth watching.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Dòngtíng Hú,
water deities often borrow boats.
When an empty boat is encountered,
the rope suddenly unties itself,
and it drifts away.
One only hears music playing in the air,
while the boatman crouches in a corner,
listening with closed eyes,
not daring to look up,
letting it go wherever it pleases.
After the journey,
it returns to its original mooring.
There was a scholar named Liǔ Shēng,
who, having failed the imperial examination, was returning home.
He lay drunk on a boat when
the sound of sheng music suddenly began.
The boatmen shook Liǔ Shēng but could not wake him,
so they hastily hid under the bow.
Soon, someone pushed Liǔ Shēng.
Liǔ Shēng was very drunk,
so he fell to the ground with the push,
sleeping as before.
He was then left alone.
A short while later,
drums and wind instruments clamored.
Liǔ Shēng slightly woke up
and smelled the strong fragrance of orchids and musk.
He squinted
and saw the boat full of beautiful women.
He knew it was unusual
and pretended to be asleep.
A short while later,
someone called out, "Zhīchéng!"
Immediately, a maid came
and stood close to his cheek.
She wore emerald socks and purple shoes,
and was as slender as a finger.
He liked her in his heart
and secretly bit her sock with his teeth.
A short while later,
the woman moved,
pulling and dragging, making her stumble.
The lord asked her about it,
and she explained the reason.
The one in charge was angry
and ordered her immediate execution.
Immediately, warriors entered,
seized and bound him, and lifted him up.
He saw a person facing south,
wearing a crown like a king.
He walked and spoke,
saying:
"I hear Dòngtíng Jūn is of the Liǔ clan,
and I am also of the Liǔ clan.
In the past, Dòngtíng failed the imperial examination;
now, I also failed the imperial examination.
Dòngtíng met the Dragon Maiden and became an immortal;
now, I, by flirting with a concubine while drunk, am to die. What a vast disparity between fortune and misfortune!"
When the king heard this,
he called him back
and asked:
"Are you the scholar who failed the examination?"
Liǔ Shēng affirmed.
Then the king handed him a brush and paper,
ordering him to compose a poem
on "wind-swept hair and mist-like temples" (fēng huán wù bìn).
Liǔ Shēng was indeed a famous scholar from Xiāngyáng,
but his contemplation was rather slow,
and he held the brush for a long time.
The king rebuked him, saying:
"How can a famous scholar be like this?"
Liǔ Shēng put down the brush and explained:
"In the past, the Sāndū Fù took ten years to complete.
From this, one knows that writing values craftsmanship, not speed."
The king listened with a smile.
From dawn to noon,
the draft was finally completed.
The king read it
and was greatly pleased, saying:
"Truly a famous scholar!"
Then he bestowed wine upon him.
In an instant,
exotic dishes arrived in abundance.
Just as they were about to feast,
an official presented a ledger and announced:
"The drowning registry is complete."
He asked:
"How many people?"
He said:
"One hundred and twenty-eight people."
He asked:
"Who have been designated for the task?"
He replied:
"Máo and Nán, the two lieutenants."
Liǔ Shēng rose to take his leave.
The king presented him with ten catties of gold
and also a crystal bracelet (jiè fāng) that fit in a hand,
saying:
"There is a small tribulation in the lake;
holding this will spare you."
Suddenly, feathered and adorned cavalry
stood in rows on the water.
The king descended from the boat and ascended his carriage,
and then was no longer seen.
For a long time, it was silent.
The boatmen then emerged from under the bow
and rowed the boat north across the lake,
but the headwind prevented them from advancing.
Suddenly, an iron cat was seen floating out of the water.
The boatmen exclaimed in fright,
"General Máo has appeared!"
Merchants on all boats prostrated themselves.
Soon after,
a log stood upright in the lake,
shaking violently.
They were even more afraid, saying:
"General Nán has appeared again!"
A short while later,
great waves surged,
obscuring the sky and sun above.
Looking around at the boats on the lake,
all were capsized at once.
Liǔ Shēng, holding the bracelet, sat precariously in his boat.
The ten-thousand-zhang torrent
vanished upon reaching his boat,
and so he was saved.
After he returned,
he often recounted his unusual experience to people,
saying:
"Though I couldn't fully discern the faces of the maids on the boat,
the tiny bound feet (shuāng gōu) beneath their skirts
were unlike anything in the human world."
Later, he went to Wǔchāng for a reason.
There was an old woman named Cuī Āo selling her daughter,
whom no one had bought for a thousand pieces of gold.
She kept a crystal bracelet (jiè fāng)
and said that whoever could match it
would marry her daughter.
Liǔ Shēng found this strange,
so he brought his bracelet and went there.
The old woman joyfully welcomed him,
called her daughter out to meet him.
She was fifteen or sixteen years old,
charming and graceful,
beyond compare.
She made a brief bow
and then turned and entered the curtain.
At first sight, Liǔ Shēng's soul was stirred,
and he said:
"This junior also possesses an item.
I wonder if it might match what the old woman's family keeps?"
Then each took out their item to compare.
Their lengths matched perfectly, not off by a single hair's breadth.
The old woman was delighted
and asked for his lodging.
She asked Liǔ Shēng to immediately return home and send a carriage,
and kept the bracelet as a token.
Liǔ Shēng was unwilling to leave it,
so the old woman smiled and said:
“Master, you are too cautious!
How could this old woman run away just for a small amount of money? ”
Shēng had no choice but to
let her stay.
He went out and quickly hired a sedan chair to return,
but the old woman’s room was already empty.
He was greatly alarmed.
He asked all the residents,
but no one knew anything.
The sun was already setting in the west,
his spirits were low and distressed,
and he returned dejectedly.
Midway,
he encountered a passing sedan chair,
and suddenly the curtain was pulled aside, saying:
“Why is Liǔ Láng so late? ”
He looked,
and it was Cuī Ǎo.
Joyfully, he asked:
“Where are you going? ”
The old woman smiled and said:
“You must suspect this old woman of swindling you.
After we parted,
a convenient sedan chair happened to be available,
and I thought that since you, Master, are also staying temporarily,
making arrangements would be very difficult,
so I simply sent the girl back to the boat. ”
Shēng invited her to turn the carriage back,
but the old woman absolutely refused.
Shēng was flustered and couldn't be sure,
so he rushed to the boat,
and indeed the girl and a maid were there,
seeing Shēng enter,
they greeted him with a smile.
Shēng saw her emerald socks and purple shoes,
and the maid’s attire on the boat,
which were no different at all.
He felt it was strange in his heart,
and he paced and stared intently.
The girl smiled and said:
“Are you staring so intently, as if you’ve never seen such a sight in your life? ”
Shēng leaned closer to observe her,
and saw the teeth marks distinctly behind her socks,
and was surprised, saying:
“Are you Zhīchéng? ”
The girl covered her mouth and smiled slightly.
Shēng bowed deeply, saying:
“If you are truly a divine being,
please tell me straightforwardly earlier,
to remove my vexations and doubts. ”
The girl said:
“I will tell you honestly: the one you met in the previous boat
was none other than Dòngtíng Jūn.
He admired your great talent;
and wanted to give me to you;
but because I was overly beloved by the queen,
he returned to consult with her.
My coming
is by the queen’s command. ”
Shēng was delighted,
washed his hands, burned incense,
and bowed towards the lake,
then returned.
Later, when he went to Wǔchāng,
the girl asked to go with him,
planning to conveniently visit her parents.
Once they arrived at Dòngtíng,
the girl pulled out her hairpin and threw it into the water,
and suddenly a small boat appeared from the middle of the lake,
the girl leaped onto it,
like a flying bird alighting,
and in an instant, it had already passed.
Shēng sat at the prow of the boat,
gazing intently at the spot where she disappeared.
From afar, a large boat arrived,
and as it drew near, a window opened,
suddenly like a colorful bird flying by,
it was Zhīchéng arriving.
A person from inside the window threw out many golden pearls and precious objects,
all gifts from the queen.
From then on,
they would meet once or twice a year as a regular occurrence.
Therefore, Shēng’s family was rich in jewels,
and every item brought out
was not common in noble families.
It is said that in the Táng Dynasty, Liǔ Yì met the Dragon Princess,
and Dòngtíng Jūn took him as his son-in-law.
Later, he abdicated his throne to Yì.
Also, because Yì's appearance was refined,
he could not intimidate the water monsters,
so he was given a ghost mask,
to wear during the day and remove at night;
after a long time, he gradually got used to it and forgot to remove it,
thus it merged with his face and became one.
Yì looked in the mirror and felt ashamed.
Therefore, when travelers sail on the lake,
if they point at something with their finger,
they are suspected of pointing at him;
if they cover their forehead with their hand,
they are suspected of peeking at him: winds and waves immediately rise,
and many boats capsize.
Therefore, upon first boarding a boat,
boatmen must warn them of this.
Otherwise, one must offer sacrifices of livestock and food,
and only then can they cross.
Xǔ Zhēnjūn once came to the lake,
but was blocked by waves and could not proceed.
Zhēnjūn was angry,
seized Yì and imprisoned him in the prefectural jail.
The jailers checking the prisoners
always found one extra person,
and could not fathom the reason.
One night,
Yì appeared in a dream to the prefect,
pleading for rescue.
The prefect, knowing that the living and the dead have different paths, declined.
Yì said:
“Zhēnjūn will arrive in this area on a certain day,
if you just plead for me,
it will surely be successful. ”
Soon after, Zhēnjūn indeed arrived,
and because he pleaded on Yì’s behalf,
Yì was released.
Thereafter, the lake’s restrictions gradually subsided.
According to the Zhùxuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Yú Kè,
a native of Húnán,
his prefecture and county are forgotten.
His family was poor,
and after failing the examination and returning home,
his money and supplies were exhausted.
Ashamed to beg,
he was very hungry,
and temporarily rested in Wú Wáng Miào,
bowing and praying before the divine seat.
He went out and lay under the corridor,
when suddenly a person led him away,
he saw the King,
knelt and reported, saying:
“The black-clothed troop is still short one soldier,
he can fill the vacancy. ”
The King said:
“Good.
Immediately give him black clothes.
As soon as he put them on,
he transformed into a bird,
flapping his wings and flying out.
He saw a flock of crow friends gathered,
and they went together,
scattering and settling on the sails and masts.
Travelers on the boats
eagerly threw things upwards.
The flock caught and ate them in the air.
He also imitated them,
and in a short while, his belly was full.
He soared and perched among the trees,
feeling quite content.
After two or three days,
Wú Wáng pitied him for being without a mate,
and paired him with a female,
calling her
Zhúqīng.
They were very much in love and happy.
Whenever Yú went to get food,
he was always tame and harmless.
Zhúqīng constantly advised him,
but he ultimately could not listen.
One day,
some Mǎn soldiers passed by,
and shot him in the chest with a bullet.
Fortunately, Zhúqīng carried him away,
so he was not captured.
The flock of crows was angry,
flapped their wings and fanned the waves,
the waves surged up,
and all the boats capsized.
Zhúqīng still threw bait to feed Yú.
Yú was severely wounded,
and died at the end of the day.
Suddenly, as if waking from a dream,
he found himself lying in the temple.
Earlier,
the residents saw Yú lying dead,
not knowing who he was,
touched him and found him not yet cold,
so they periodically sent people to investigate.
At this point,
they learned the reason after questioning,
collected money and sent him home.
Previously,
the maid married into the Luán clan. After five or six months,
she gave birth to a son, Huái.
Luán Fǔ treated him the same as his other sons.
At eighteen, he joined the household.
Later, Yì died.
His brothers divided the property,
excluding Huái and treating him unequally compared to Yì's sons.
Huái questioned his mother
and only then learned the truth.
He said:
"Since I belong to two families,
each with its own ancestral roots,
why must I remain here to inherit others' hundred *mǔ* of land?!"
So he dispatched a rider to Duàn.
But Duàn had already died.
The account was concrete and detailed,
surely trustworthy.
Lián Fāng, who had been furious and pained,
was greatly pleased upon hearing this.
She directly declared:
"I, too, now have a son!
All the cattle, horses, and various goods that were borrowed
can now be properly returned;
otherwise,
there will be a lawsuit!"
Yì's nephews looked at each other, their faces losing color,
and gradually withdrew.
Huái then brought his wife
to mourn his father.
The Duàn family was displeased
and conspired to drive Huái out.
Huái knew of this
and said:
"The Luán family doesn't consider me Yì's son,
and the Duàn family no longer considers me a Duàn.
Where then shall I go?!"
In his anger, he wanted to lodge a complaint with the authorities.
However, relatives on both sides mediated,
and the conspiracy was also put to rest.
But Lián, because of the cattle and horses,
would not give up.
Huái persuaded her to drop it.
Lián said:
"I am not doing this for the cattle and horses;
a jumble of emotions fills my chest.
Your father died of indignation.
The reason I swallowed my anger and endured
was because I had no son.
Now I have one;
what is there to fear?!
You do not know the details of the previous events;
let me personally bring the complaint to the court."
Huái firmly tried to stop her
but she wouldn't listen.
She prepared the petition and submitted it to the Magistrate.
The Magistrate detained the Duàn family members,
and examined the situation.
Lián spoke with righteous indignation and pathos,
her words flowing like a spring.
The Magistrate was moved,
punished the Duàn family,
and ordered the return of the property to the owner.
Upon their return,
Lián summoned her brothers' sons
and, identifying those who had not participated in the conspiracy,
distributed all the recovered property to them.
Lián, being over seventy years old,
and nearing death,
called her daughter and granddaughter-in-law
and instructed them:
"Remember this: if you have no children by thirty,
you must pawn or sell your hairpins and earrings
to find a concubine for your husband.
The suffering of childlessness
is truly unbearable!"
Yì Shǐ Shì said:
"Although Lián Shì was jealous,
she was able to make a swift change,
and it was fitting that Heaven restored her spirit by granting her an heir.
Observing her generous and impassioned nature,
ah!
She was indeed a remarkable woman!"
Jiǎng Jià from Jǐnán,
whose wife was Máo Shì,
was childless and jealous.
Her sister-in-law often admonished her,
but she would not listen,
saying:
"I'd rather let the lineage die out
than allow one who casts eyes and raises eyebrows to anger me!"
As she approached forty,
she became quite concerned about an heir.
She wanted to adopt her elder brother's son.
Both her brother and sister-in-law agreed,
but then intentionally procrastinated.
Whenever the child came to his uncle's house,
the couple would tempt him with sweets and treats
and ask:
"Would you like to come live with us?"
The child would always agree.
His elder brother privately instructed the child
saying: "If they ask again,
answer that you don't want to.
If they ask why you don't want to,
answer: 'Wait until you die;
why worry that the land and property won't be mine?'"
One day,
Jiǎng Jià went out for a distant trade,
and the child came again.
Máo asked him again,
and the child immediately replied with his father's words.
Máo was greatly enraged and said:
"So, with my wife and child at home,
are you calculating my property every day?
Your calculations are all wrong!"
She chased the child out
and immediately summoned a matchmaker
to buy a concubine for her husband.
At that time, there was a maid for sale,
whose price was high.
Even after spending all their assets, they could not meet the price,
making it seem difficult to succeed.
Her brother, fearing delay and a change of heart,
secretly gave gold to the matchmaker,
falsely claiming it was a loan from her, to complete the transaction.
Máo was greatly pleased
and thus bought the maid and brought her home.
Máo told her husband the situation.
Her husband was angry
and severed ties with his brother.
After more than a year,
the concubine gave birth to a son.
The couple was overjoyed.
Máo said:
"The matchmaker doesn't know who loaned the money,
and has not inquired about it for over a year.
This kindness cannot be forgotten.
Now that a son has been born,
we must repay her for the price!"
Jiǎng Jià then took a bag of gold to the matchmaker.
The matchmaker smiled and said:
"I should be greatly thanking you, honorable sir.
This old woman is dirt poor;
who would dare lend me gold?"
She then told him the truth.
Jiǎng Jià understood and was moved.
He returned and told his wife,
and they were both deeply touched.
They then prepared a feast and invited his brother and sister-in-law.
The couple both knelt
and offered the gold to his brother,
but the brother would not accept it.
They dispersed in joy.
Later, Jiǎng Jià had three sons.
According to the "Liaozhai Zhiyi" Manuscript from Zhùxuě Zhāi
Yī Gǔn,
a native of Jiǔjiāng.
At night, a woman came,
and they slept together.
He knew in his heart she was a fox-spirit,
but loved her beauty,
and secretly told no one.
His parents also did not know.
After a long time, his body became emaciated.
His parents questioned him relentlessly,
and he finally told them the truth.
His parents were greatly worried,
and had someone else take turns sleeping with him,
but could not stop it in the end.
When the father himself slept in the same bed,
the fox-spirit did not come;
when another person was substituted,
she would come again.
Yī Gǔn asked the fox-spirit,
the fox-spirit said:
“How can worldly talismans and incantations
control me?
However, I fear moral principles;
how could I commit lewd acts with a father-in-law!”
When the father heard this,
he stayed with his son even more persistently,
and the fox-spirit then ceased coming.
Later, when rebellious bandits rampaged violently,
all the villagers fled,
and his family became separated.
Yī Gǔn rushed into Kūnlún Shān,
looking around to find it desolate.
As night fell,
he became very afraid.
Suddenly, he saw a woman coming.
Looking closely,
it was the fox-spirit.
In the midst of the chaos,
they were delighted and comforted to see each other.
The woman said:
“The sun has already set,
you should stay here for now.
I will find a good spot,
and temporarily construct a room,
to avoid tigers and wolves.”
Then she walked a few paces north,
and squatted down in the bushes,
it was unclear what she was doing.
A short while later she returned,
pulled Yī Gǔn and went south;
after about ten-plus paces,
she dragged him back again.
Suddenly, they saw a thousand large trees,
surrounding a high pavilion,
with copper walls and iron pillars,
its roof resembling gold foil;
on closer inspection,
the walls were shoulder-high,
with no doors around,
and the walls were densely lined with holes and pits.
The woman stepped on them with her foot and crossed over,
Yī Gǔn also followed her.
Once inside,
he suspected that a golden house could not be made by human hands,
and asked where it came from.
The woman smiled and said:
“You, sir, can live in it,
tomorrow I will gift it to you.
The gold and iron each number in the tens of millions,
half a lifetime of eating and spending would not exhaust it.”
Soon after, she bade farewell.
Yī Gǔn earnestly kept her,
so she stayed.
She said:
“Having been scorned by others,
I had resigned myself to eternal separation;
now I cannot remain steadfast again.”
When he awoke,
the fox-spirit had already left at some unknown time.
At dawn,
he climbed over the wall and went out.
Looking back at where he had slept,
there was no pavilion or house,
only four needles stuck into a ruined pit,
with a box of rouge covering it;
the large trees
were merely clumps of thorns and old brambles.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wherever large armies go,
the harm they inflict is worse than that of bandits: for bandits, people can still hate them,
but soldiers are those whom people dare not hate.
The slight difference they have from bandits
is merely that they dare not casually kill people.
In the Jiǎyín year (1674),
when the Sān Fān revolted,
the southern expeditionary forces
pastured their horses in Yǎngjùn,
leaving chickens, dogs, and houses empty,
and all women were defiled.
At that time, there was continuous heavy rain,
and the fields filled with water, forming lakes.
The people had nowhere to hide,
so they took rafts into the thickets of sorghum.
The soldiers knew this,
and, naked and on horseback,
entered the water to search for and defile them;
few escaped.
Only Mrs. Zhāng did not submit,
publicly staying at home.
She had a kitchen shed,
and at night, with her husband, dug a pit several feet deep,
and piled hay in it;
they covered it with a thin plank,
and placed a mat on top,
as if it were a sleeping place.
She cooked by the stove.
When soldiers arrived,
she would go out the door to attend to them.
Two Mongol soldiers forcibly desired to defile her.
The woman said:
“How can such things
be done in front of people!”
One of them smiled slightly,
and beckoned her out.
The woman led him into the room,
pointed to the mat, and told him to go on it first.
The thin plank broke,
and the soldier fell into the pit.
The woman then took another mat and thin plank and covered the pit,
deliberately standing by the pit's edge,
to lure the next one.
A short while later,
the other one re-entered.
He heard shouts from within the pit,
but did not know where.
The woman, smiling, beckoned him with her hand and said:
“It's here.”
The soldier stepped on the mat,
and also fell.
The woman then threw more firewood in,
and tossed fire into it.
The fire blazed fiercely,
and the house burned.
The woman then cried for help.
When the fire was extinguished,
the charred bodies emitted a foul smell.
People asked her about it,
the woman said:
“I feared the two pigs might be harmed by the soldiers,
so I put them in the pit.”
After this, she moved a few *lǐ* from the village,
to a treeless spot by the main road,
and sat in the blazing sun with her needlework.
The village was far from the county seat,
and soldiers usually came on horseback,
arriving in numbers in an instant.
They laughed and joked,
and though she mostly did not understand,
it was generally words of teasing and flirtation.
However, she was not far from the road,
with nothing to conceal herself,
yet they always left,
and for several days she was unharmed.
One day,
a soldier arrived,
very shameless,
and attempted to defile the woman right there in the blazing sun.
The woman smiled faintly and did not resist much.
Secretly, she pricked his horse with a needle.
The horse immediately snorted and whinnied,
so the soldier pulled on the horse's haunch to restrain it,
and then embraced the woman.
The woman pulled out a large awl and fiercely stabbed the horse's neck.
The horse, in pain, bolted in fright.
The rein, tied to its haunch, could not be freed,
and it dragged the soldier for dozens of *lǐ*.
His comrades finally caught it.
His head and body were nowhere to be seen,
but a leg, slowly pulled up,
was indeed still there.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“With six clever schemes,
she preserved her honor from fierce soldiers.
How virtuous the woman was,
intelligent and yet chaste!”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A person from the seashore said:
“One day,
a tall mountain suddenly emerged from the sea.
The inhabitants were greatly alarmed.
A xiùcai lodged in a fishing boat,
bought wine, and drank alone.
Late at night,
a young man,
dressed and capped like a scholar,
introduced himself as ‘Yú Zǐyóu.’
His speech was elegant and refined.
The xiùcai was pleased,
and they drank joyfully together.
They drank until midnight,
then the young man left his seat to bid farewell.
The xiùcai said, ‘Where is your home,
that you wander alone in the vast night?
You suffer too much.’
He replied,
‘I am not a local resident.
As the Qīngmíng Festival is approaching,
I will accompany the Great King to visit his tomb.
My family has gone ahead;
the Great King is resting for a while,
and will depart at the hour of chén tomorrow.
You should return home
and prepare early.’
The xiùcai did not know who the Great King was.
He saw him off to the bow of the boat,
where he leaped into the water,
splashed away,
and then the xiùcai realized he was a fish demon.
The next day,
he saw the mountain peak floating,
and it vanished in an instant.
He then realized the mountain was a giant fish,
which was what he referred to as the Great King.”
It is popularly said that before the Qīngmíng Festival,
giant fish in the sea take their children to pay respects at their tomb.
Could this be true?
In the early years of Kāngxī,
a giant fish emerged from the tide in Láijùn,
crying out for several days,
its sound like that of an ox.
After it died,
those carrying loads and cutting meat
followed one after another in a line.
The fish was as large as an acre,
complete with fins and tail;
but it had no eyeballs.
Its eye sockets were as deep as wells,
filled with water,
and anyone cutting meat who accidentally fell in
would drown.
Some said,
“When a giant fish is banished from the sea,
its eyes are removed,
because the eyes are luminous pearls.”
So it is said.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
A gentry official in Yángzhōu wanted to buy a concubine.
He interviewed several families in a row,
but none suited him.
Only an old woman who was staying with others was selling her daughter.
The girl was fourteen or fifteen,
beautiful and charming,
and skilled in various arts.
He was greatly pleased,
and bought her for a high price.
That night,
when he went to bed,
her skin was smooth as fat.
When he happily touched her private parts,
it was a man.
Extremely alarmed,
he immediately interrogated him thoroughly.
It turned out he had bought a handsome young boy,
carefully dressed him up,
and set up a scheme to deceive people.
At dawn,
he sent his servants to look for the old woman,
but she had already fled without a trace.
He was deeply chagrined,
unsure whether to advance or retreat.
Just then, a peer from Zhèzhōng came to visit,
and he told him the story.
The peer immediately asked to see the boy,
and was greatly pleased upon seeing him.
He bought him for the original price and left.
Yìshǐshì said:
“If one meets a kindred spirit,
even Nánwēi would not be exchanged for them.
Why should ignorant old women
create such a deception!”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Wāng Kěshòu from Huángméi County in Húguǎng
could recall three past lives: in one life he was a xiùcai,
studying in a Buddhist temple.
The monks had a mare that gave birth to a mule colt,
which he coveted and took.
Later, when he died,
the King of the Underworld checked the register,
and, angry at his greed and tyranny,
punished him by making him a mule to repay the temple monks.
After he was born,
the monks cherished him,
and he wanted to die but could not.
When he grew a little older,
he often thought of throwing himself into a ravine,
but also feared that he would betray the kindness of his upbringing
and his karmic punishment would worsen,
so he resigned himself to it.
After several years,
his karmic debt was fulfilled, and he died naturally.
He was born into a farmer's family: he could speak at birth,
which his parents found strange,
so they killed him.
He was then born into the family of Xiùcai Wāng.
The xiùcai was nearly fifty,
and extremely happy to have a son.
Wāng was intelligent from birth;
but he remembered his previous death due to speaking early,
so he dared not speak.
By three or four years old,
everyone thought he was mute.
One day,
his father was writing an essay.
A friend happened to visit,
and he put down his brush to greet the guest.
Wāng entered and saw his father's work,
and, feeling an irresistible urge to write,
completed it for him.
His father returned and saw it,
asking:
“Who came here?”
The family said:
“No one.”
His father was greatly suspicious.
The next day,
he deliberately placed a writing topic on the desk and then left;
after a short while, he returned,
creeping in stealthily.
He saw his son bent over the desk,
several lines already written.
Suddenly seeing his father arrive,
he involuntarily cried out,
and knelt, begging to be spared death.
His father was delighted,
and holding his hand, said:
“Our family has only you.
Since you can write,
it is a blessing for our family,
why hide it?”
From then on, he taught him even more.
He became a jinshì in his youth,
and his official position rose to Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
A farmer from Chǔzhōng, returning from the market,
rested briefly on the road.
A fortune-teller arrived later,
stopped, and talked with him.
Suddenly he looked at the farmer and said:
“Your complexion is ominous;
within three days you will suffer financial loss
and official punishment.”
The farmer said,
“I have paid all my government taxes,
and have never engaged in disputes in my life,
so how could punishment come?”
The fortune-teller said:
“I do not know either.
But your complexion is thus,
so you must be cautious!”
The farmer was not entirely convinced,
bowed in farewell, and returned home.
The next day,
he was herding a calf in the field.
An express horse passed by.
The calf saw it,
mistook it for a tiger,
and charged forward to butt it.
The horse died,
and the attendant seized the farmer and took him to the yamen.
The official lightly punished him,
making him pay for the horse.
Indeed, water buffaloes will fight tigers when they see them,
so cattle traders sleeping outdoors
often use their cattle for self-protection;
when they see a horse passing by,
they quickly drive their cattle away,
fearing they might accidentally butt it.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Lǐ Xìn,
was a gambler.
One day, as he lay resting during the day,
he suddenly saw his old gambling friends Wáng Dà and Féng Jiǔ arrive,
inviting him to play a game.
Lǐ Xìn, forgetting that they were ghosts,
happily followed them.
After they went out,
Wáng Dà went to invite Zhōu Zǐmíng from the village,
while Féng Jiǔ led Lǐ Xìn ahead,
and they entered the East Temple.
A short while later,
Zhōu Zǐmíng indeed arrived with Wáng Dà.
Féng Jiǔ took out some cards,
and proposed they play *liáolíng*.
Lǐ Xìn said,
"We are in a hurry and I have no gambling money.
It's a pity to disappoint such a generous invitation.
What shall we do?"
Zhōu Zǐmíng also agreed.
Wáng Dà said,
"Huáng Bā Guānrén from Yànzǐ Gǔ lends money at interest.
Let's go borrow from him;
he will surely agree."
So the four of them went together.
In a flash,
they arrived at a large village.
First-class residences lined the walls of the village.
Wáng Dà pointed to a door,
saying,
"This is Young Master Huáng's house."
An old servant came out from inside,
and Wáng Dà told him their intention.
The servant immediately went in to report.
He soon came out,
conveying the Young Master's order,
to invite Wáng Dà and Lǐ Xìn to meet him.
They went in and saw the Young Master,
who was eighteen or nineteen years old,
with a pleasant smile and demeanor.
He then handed a large string of cash to Lǐ Xìn,
saying,
"I know you are honest and upright,
so there's no harm in lending to you.
I cannot vouch for Zhōu Zǐmíng."
Wáng Dà pleaded on Zhōu Zǐmíng's behalf with much persuasion.
The Young Master asked Lǐ Xìn to sign as guarantor,
but Lǐ Xìn refused.
Wáng Dà egged him on from the side,
so Lǐ Xìn finally agreed.
He also received a thousand coins and left.
He then gave it to Zhōu Zǐmíng,
and also related the Young Master's words,
to make sure he would repay.
Coming out of the valley,
they saw a woman approaching.
She was Zhào Shì's wife from the village,
who was known for her contentious and abusive nature.
Féng Jiǔ said,
"There's no one here.
This shrew should be given a minor haunting."
So they seized her and dragged her back into the valley.
The woman screamed loudly,
and Féng Jiǔ scooped up dirt and stuffed it into her mouth.
Zhōu Zǐmíng praised, saying,
"For a woman like this,
she only deserves to have a stake driven into her yin!"
Féng Jiǔ then pulled up his trousers
and forcibly inserted a long stone into her.
The woman seemed to die.
Then the group dispersed,
returning to the temple,
and gambled together.
From noon until midnight,
Lǐ Xìn won greatly,
and Féng Jiǔ and Zhōu Zǐmíng's funds were all gone.
Lǐ Xìn then gave the substantial winnings, including interest, entirely to Wáng Dà;
he had him repay Young Master Huáng on his behalf;
Wáng Dà then distributed some to Zhōu Zǐmíng and Féng Jiǔ,
and the game resumed.
Not long after,
they heard a commotion of human voices, and one person rushed in saying,
"Old Master Chénghuáng is personally apprehending gamblers;
he's here now!"
Everyone paled.
Lǐ Xìn abandoned his money and escaped by climbing over the wall.
The others, preoccupied with their money,
were all bound.
After he got out,
he indeed saw a divine figure sitting on a horse,
with more than twenty gamblers tethered behind the horse.
Before dawn,
they had already reached the county city, and entered through the opened gates.
They arrived at the衙署yámén (magistrate's office),
where the Chénghuáng sat facing south.
He called for the culprits to come forward,
and identified names from a register.
After calling out the names,
he ordered everyone
to have their index fingers chopped off with a sharp axe,
and then to have both eyes smeared with black ink and red pigment,
and to be paraded around the market three times.
The guards demanded bribes before removing the ink and pigment,
and everyone bribed them.
Only Zhōu Zǐmíng refused,
claiming his purse was empty;
the guards offered to escort him home and be paid then,
but he still refused.
The guards pointed at him and said,
"You are truly an 'iron bean',
which cannot burst even when fried!"
Then they saluted and left.
Zhōu Zǐmíng exited the city,
wet his sleeve with saliva,
and wiped as he walked.
When he reached the river and looked at his reflection,
the ink and pigment had not come off;
he scooped water to wash it,
but it was firmly stuck and could not be removed.
He returned home filled with regret.
Yuè Zhòng,
from Xī'ān.
His father died early,
and Zhòng was born posthumously.
His mother was fond of Buddhism
and abstained from meat and wine.
When Zhòng grew up,
he was addicted to drinking and good eating.
He secretly complained about his mother
and often tried to persuade her with rich and sweet foods.
His mother rebuked him.
Later, his mother fell ill,
on her deathbed,
she yearned for meat.
Zhòng was in a hurry and could not find any meat,
so he cut a piece from his left thigh and offered it to her.
Her illness slightly improved,
but she regretted breaking her precepts,
refused to eat, and died.
Zhòng's grief intensified,
and he used a sharp blade to cut his right thigh until the bone was visible.
His family members collectively rescued him,
bandaged the wound, and applied medicine,
and he soon recovered.
He thought of his mother's strict observance,
and also of her foolishness,
so he burned the Buddhist statues he had offered
and set up a memorial tablet to worship his mother.
After getting drunk,
he would often cry bitterly before it.
He did not marry until he was twenty,
still a virgin.
Three days after his marriage,
he told people:
"The cohabitation of men and women,
it is the most filthy thing in the world,
I truly find no joy in it!"
Thereupon he left his wife.
His wife's father, Gù Wénjiàn,
asked relatives to seek her return,
pleading three or four times,
but Zhòng resolutely refused.
Half a year later,
Gù allowed his daughter to marry someone else. Zhòng remained a widower for twenty years.
His behavior became increasingly unrestrained: he drank with slaves and actors; when villagers begged,
he generously gave;
if someone said they were marrying off a daughter but had no cooking pot,
he would take his own pot from the stove and give it to them.
After that, he would borrow a pot from his neighbor to cook.
Those without morals knew his nature
and cheated and swindled him day and night.
Sometimes they would gamble away all their money. They would sigh and weep before him,
saying they were being urgently pursued
and were about to sell their children.
Zhòng would find the tax money as required,
emptying his purse to give it to them;
when the rent collector came to his door,
he would pawn things to get the money himself.
Because of this,
his family became increasingly poor.
Before this, Zhòng was wealthy,
and his kinsmen vied to serve him,
allowing him to take whatever he wanted,
no one dared to dispute it;
but when Zhòng became poor,
visits and inquiries became extremely rare.
Zhòng was broad-minded
and did not mind.
On his mother's death anniversary,
Zhòng happened to be ill
and could not visit the grave.
He wanted to send his kinsmen to offer sacrifices on his behalf;
but all the kinsmen excused themselves with various reasons.
Zhòng then poured libations in his room,
wailing in pain before the tablet;
the sorrow of having no heir
greatly burdened his heart,
and his illness consequently worsened.
In his delirium,
he felt someone caressing him;
he slightly opened his eyes,
and it was his mother.
He asked in surprise:
"Whence do you come?"
His mother said:
"Because there was no one in the family to visit the grave,
I came to receive offerings,
and also to check on your illness."
He asked:
"Where has mother been dwelling?"
His mother said:
"Nánhǎi."
After the caress,
he felt a coolness throughout his body.
He opened his eyes and looked around,
there was no one to be seen,
and his illness was cured.
After getting up,
he thought of going to Nánhǎi.
It happened that there were people in a neighboring village forming an incense society,
so he sold ten *mǔ* of land
