and, taking his money, asked to go with them.
The society members disliked his impurity
and collectively rejected him.
So he followed along, waiting for their departure.
On the way, he was not careful about eating beef and drinking wine,
which made the group dislike him even more.
Taking advantage of his drunken sleep,
they left without telling him.
Zhòng then traveled alone.
When he arrived in Mǐn,
he met a friend who invited him for a drink,
and the famous courtesan Qiónghuá was present.
When the subject of his trip to Nánhǎi came up,
Qiónghuá wished to accompany him.
Zhòng was delighted
and immediately waited for her to prepare,
then they set off together;
although they shared lodging and meals,
there was absolutely nothing private between them.
When they arrived at Nánhǎi,
the people from the society saw him arrive with a courtesan,
and they mocked him even more,
despising him and refusing to worship with him.
Zhòng and Qiónghuá understood their intention,
so they waited for the others to worship first, and then they would worship.
When the crowd worshipped,
they were disappointed that there was no manifestation.
When the two of them worshipped,
as soon as they prostrated themselves,
suddenly lotuses appeared all over the sea,
each flower adorned with pearl garlands;
Qiónghuá saw it as a Bodhisattva.
Zhòng saw his mother on every flower.
He immediately cried out and ran towards his mother,
leaping in to follow her.
The crowd saw ten thousand lotus flowers
all transform into radiant colors,
covering the sea like brocade.
A moment later,
the clouds were still and the waves clear,
everything disappeared,
but Zhòng was still on the seashore.
He himself did not understand how he got out,
and his clothes and shoes were not at all wet.
He wept loudly facing the sea,
his voice shaking the islands.
Qiónghuá pulled and persuaded him,
then respectfully descended to a Buddhist temple,
and ordered a boat to cross northward.
On the way, a wealthy family invited Qiónghuá away,
and Zhòng rested alone at an inn.
There was a boy, only eight or nine years old,
begging for food in the eatery,
whose appearance was not like that of a beggar.
When questioned closely,
he said he had been driven out by his stepmother.
Zhòng felt pity for him.
The boy clung to him,
earnestly pleading for rescue,
so Zhòng took him along home.
When asked his name,
he said:
"My name is Ā Xīn,
my surname is Yōng,
and my mother's surname was Gù.
I once heard my mother say: six months after marrying into the Yōng family,
she gave birth to me.
My original surname was Yuè."
Zhòng was greatly astonished.
He doubted himself, thinking he had lived a celibate life,
and should not have a son.
So he asked where the Yuè family lived,
and the boy replied:
"I don't know.
But when my mother died,
she gave me a letter,
instructing me not to lose it."
Zhòng eagerly asked for the letter.
He looked at it,
and it was indeed the divorce paper from the Gù family that year.
He exclaimed in surprise:
"You truly are my son!"
Upon careful verification of the year and month, it was indeed accurate.
He was quite comforted in his heart's desire,
however, his family finances were daily declining.
After two years,
his land was gradually sold off,
and he eventually could not even keep servants.
One day,
the father and son were cooking for themselves
when suddenly a beautiful woman entered.
Upon seeing her,
it was Qiónghuá.
He asked in surprise,
"Whence do you come?"
She smiled and said,
"Since we were meant to be a false couple,
why ask again?
The reason I did not immediately follow you before
was simply because an old woman was present;
now she is dead.
Considering that if I do not follow a man,
I will have no one to protect me;
if I follow a man,
I will then have no way to keep myself pure. Weighing both options,
nothing is better than following you.
Therefore, I did not fear a journey of a thousand li."
Then she untied her baggage and helped the son cook.
Zhòngliáng was pleased.
By night,
the father and son slept together as before,
and a separate room was prepared for Qiónghuá.
The son treated her as his mother,
and Qiónghuá also took good care of the son.
When relatives and friends heard of this,
they all sent gifts to Zhòngliáng,
and both of them happily accepted them.
When guests arrived,
Qiónghuá would prepare all the food and drink,
and Zhòngliáng did not ask about her origin.
Qiónghuá gradually redeemed their former property with gold and pearls,
acquired many maids, servants, oxen, and horses,
and daily grew more prosperous.
Zhòngliáng often said to Qiónghuá,
"When I am drunk,
you should hide
and not let me see you."
Qiónghuá smiled and agreed.
One day,
he became very drunk and
urgently called for Qiónghuá.
Qiónghuá appeared in glamorous makeup.
Zhòngliáng gazed at her for a long time,
then was greatly pleased,
dancing wildly as if insane,
saying,
"I understand now!"
He instantly became sober.
He felt the world was bright,
and the humble dwelling where he lived
was completely transformed into a magnificent jade palace.
This transformation lasted for some time before it ceased.
From then on, he no longer drank in the market,
but only drank daily with Qiónghuá.
Qiónghuá ate vegetarian food
and served him tea.
One day,
feeling slightly sore,
he ordered Qiónghuá to massage his thigh.
He saw a red mark on his thigh
that had transformed into two red lotuses,
faintly appearing at the flesh's edge.
He was surprised.
Zhòngliáng smiled and said,
"When you see these flowers bloom,
our twenty-year false marriage will end."
Qiónghuá believed him.
After they arranged the marriage for Āxīn,
Qiónghuá gradually entrusted the household to the new daughter-in-law
and lived in a separate courtyard with Zhòngliáng.
The son and daughter-in-law paid their respects every three days
and did not report anything unless it was a difficult matter.
They employed two maids: one to warm wine,
and one to brew tea, nothing more.
One day,
Qiónghuá went to her son's place.
The son and daughter-in-law consulted with her for a long time,
then went together to see the father.
Upon entering,
they saw the father sitting barefoot on the couch.
Hearing their voices,
he opened his eyes, smiled, and said,
"It's excellent that mother and son have come!"
Then he closed his eyes again.
Qiónghuá exclaimed in great surprise,
"What are you trying to do?"
She looked at his thigh,
and the lotus flowers were in full bloom.
She tested him,
and his breath had already ceased.
Immediately, she used both hands to press the flowers together,
and prayed, saying,
"Your concubine followed you for a thousand li,
which was not easy at all.
For your sake, I taught your son and instructed your daughter-in-law,
and also made a small contribution.
Even if it's just two or three years,
why not wait a little longer?"
After a moment,
Zhòngliáng suddenly opened his eyes, smiled, and said,
"You have your own affairs;
why must you drag someone else along as a companion?
If it cannot be otherwise,
I will stay for your sake."
Qiónghuá released her hands,
and the flowers had rejoined.
From then on, they conversed and laughed as before.
After more than three years,
Qiónghuá was nearly forty,
yet still looked like a twenty-year-old.
Suddenly she said to Zhòngliáng,
"When ordinary people die,
being handled by others, head here and feet there,
is not at all clean."
So she ordered a craftsman to make a double coffin.
Āxīn asked in alarm,
and she replied,
"It is not for you to know."
After the work was completed,
she bathed and dressed,
then told her son and daughter-in-law,
"I am about to die."
Āxīn wept and said,
"For several years, we have relied on mother's management
to avoid cold and hunger.
Mother has not yet enjoyed a moment of peace and comfort,
why then abandon your son and leave?"
She said,
"The father sows blessings, and the son enjoys them.
The servants, oxen, and horses are all the result of debts repaid to your father.
I have no merit.
I was originally a celestial maiden who scattered flowers,
but occasionally harbored a mortal thought,
and was therefore banished to the human world for over thirty years.
Now my time limit is up."
Then she ascended into the wooden coffin herself.
When they called her again,
her eyes were already closed.
Āxīn cried and reported to his father,
but his father, at some unknown moment, had also become rigid,
his clothes and cap perfectly in place.
They wailed and grieved desperately.
After putting him into the coffin,
both were placed in the main hall.
For several days they were not interred,
hoping they might return.
Light emerged from his thigh,
illuminating all four walls.
From Qiónghuá's coffin,
fragrant mist emanated,
discernible to nearby houses.
Once the coffin was closed,
the fragrant light gradually diminished.
After the funeral rites,
the various younger male relatives of the Lè clan coveted his possessions
and conspired to drive out Xīn.
They brought a lawsuit against him before the officials.
The officials were unable to resolve the matter,
and proposed to give half of the land and property to the various Lè relatives.
Xīn was not satisfied
and appealed to the prefecture with a written plea.
It remained undecided for a long time.
Initially,
Gù married his daughter to Yōng.
After more than a year,
Yōng became a wanderer in Mǐn,
and all news of him ceased.
Gù, being old and without a son,
suffered from missing his daughter.
He went to his son-in-law's home,
only to find that his daughter had died and his grandson had been driven out.
He reported it to the local magistrate.
Yōng was afraid,
and bribed Gù,
but Gù did not accept.
He insisted on finding his grandson,
but searched everywhere without success.
One day,
Gù happened upon a road
and saw a decorated carriage passing by.
He stepped aside to the left of the road.
A beautiful woman in the carriage called out:
"Are you not Elder Gù?"
Gù assented.
The woman said:
"Your grandson is my son.
He is currently at the Lè family's home;
do not litigate.
Your grandson is now in trouble,
you should go quickly."
Gù wanted to ask for more details,
but the carriage had already gone far.
Gù then accepted the bribe in Xī'ān.
Upon arrival,
the lawsuit was still raging.
Gù presented himself to the official,
stating the date of his daughter's first marriage,
the date of her remarriage,
and the year and month of her son's birth,
all with great detail.
All the Lè relatives were flogged and banished,
and the case was concluded.
When he returned,
he recounted the day he saw the beautiful woman,
which was precisely the day Qiónghuá passed away.
Xīn moved Gù's family,
gave him a house, and presented him with maids.
At over sixty years old, Gù had a son,
and Xīn looked after him.
Yìshǐshì said:
"Abstaining from meat and avoiding the inner chambers is the semblance of a Buddha.
Being untrammeled and innocent is the true nature of a Buddha.
Lè Zhòng, when facing a beautiful woman,
regarded her directly as a pure companion on the path,
and did not view her as a land of tender allure.
Living together for thirty years,
as if with feeling,
as if without feeling,
this is the true face of a Bodhisattva.
How can worldly people fathom this!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Below Láo Shān, in the Qīng Gōng,
the winter camellia was two zhàng high,
its circumference several tens of folds.
The peonies were over a zhàng high,
and when in bloom, they were brilliant like brocade.
Huáng Shēng from Jiāozhōu
stayed there to study.
One day,
he saw a young woman from the window,
dressed in plain white, amidst the flowers.
He wondered how there could be such a person in the monastery.
He hurried out,
but she had already vanished.
From then on, he saw her repeatedly.
So he hid himself in a clump of trees
to wait for her arrival.
Before long,
the young woman came again, accompanied by a woman in red.
Looking from afar,
their beauty was unparalleled.
As they gradually approached,
the woman in red stepped back,
saying:
"There's a living person here!"
Shēng suddenly jumped out.
The two women ran in fright,
their sleeves and skirts fluttering,
a fragrant breeze wafting about.
He chased them past a low wall,
where they had already disappeared in silence.
His longing became even more intense,
so he inscribed a verse beneath a tree, saying:
"Limitless is the bitterness of lovesickness,
I stand before a small jar, filled with emotion.
Fearing she returns to Shāzhàlì,
where shall I find her matchless beauty?"
He returned to his study, lost in thought.
Suddenly, the young woman entered,
and he greeted her with surprise and joy.
The woman smiled and said:
"You were boisterous like a strong bandit,
making people terrified;
I did not know you were a refined scholar,
so there is no harm in us meeting."
Shēng asked about her life,
and she said:
"My pet name is Xiāngyù,
I am registered in Píngkāng Xiàng.
Being confined in the mountains by a Daoist priest
is truly not what I desired."
Shēng asked:
"What is the Daoist priest's name?
I shall cleanse you of this disgrace."
The woman said:
"There's no need;
he hasn't dared to coerce me either.
Using this opportunity to have frequent secret meetings
with a romantic gentleman
is also fine."
He asked:
"Who is the one in red?"
She said:
"Her name is Jiàngxuě,
and she is my sworn sister."
Then they became intimate.
When he awoke,
the dawn light was already red.
The woman hastily rose,
saying:
"We indulged in pleasure and forgot the dawn."
She put on her clothes and changed her shoes,
and also said:
"I will repay you with a poem;
do not laugh: 'The good night easily ends,
the morning light is already on the window.
I wish to be like the swallows on the beam,
dwelling in pairs naturally.'"
Shēng grasped her wrist and said:
"You are beautiful outwardly and wise inwardly,
making one love you to the point of forgetting death.
Even a single day of your absence
is like a separation of a thousand li.
You should come when you have a chance,
do not wait for night."
The woman assented.
From then on, they were always together day and night.
Each time he invited Jiàngxuě to come,
she never did,
which Shēng regretted.
The woman said:
"Jiàngjiě's temperament is quite aloof,
not like my infatuation.
You should persuade her slowly,
there's no need to be too hasty."
One evening,
the girl sadly entered and said,
"Sir, if you cannot even hold Lǒng,
how can you hope for Shǔ?
Now we part forever."
He asked,
"Where are you going?"
She wiped away her tears with her sleeve and
said,
"This is a predetermined fate,
difficult for me to explain to you.
Those beautiful lines from former days
have all become ominous prophecies.
'The fair one now belongs to Shāyùlì,
the righteous warrior is now without Gǔ Yāyá.'
you can recite these for your concubine."
When he questioned her,
she would not speak,
but only sobbed.
She did not sleep the entire night, and
left early the next morning.
Shēng found this strange.
The next day,
a certain Lánshì from Jìmò,
came to the temple to sightsee.
He saw the white peony,
was pleased with it, and
dug it up and carried it away.
Shēng then realized that Xiāngyù was a flower spirit,
and was filled with regret and sorrow.
A few days later,
he heard that the flower Lánshì had transplanted to his home
was withering day by day.
Full of extreme hatred,
he composed fifty poems lamenting the flower,
and daily shed tears at the empty pit.
One day,
as he was returning from mourning,
he vaguely saw a person in red clothes wiping away tears beside the pit.
He calmly approached, and
the girl did not avoid him.
Shēng then took her hand, and
they wept facing each other.
After a while, he invited her into his room, and
the girl followed him.
She sighed,
"My childhood sister,
suddenly separated!
Hearing of your sorrow
only increases my grief.
My tears fall to the Yellow Springs,
perhaps by sincere emotion she might return;
but the spirit of the deceased has already dispersed,
how can she suddenly share laughter and conversation with us two?"
Shēng said,
"This humble one is ill-fated,
harming my beloved;
I probably have no blessing to enjoy two beauties.
Previously, I frequently bothered Xiāngyù,
conveying my humble sentiments,
why do you not visit again?"
The girl said,
"I thought young scholars
were mostly unfaithful;
I did not know you were indeed such a devoted lover.
However, my relationship with you
is based on affection, not lust.
If we were to be intimate day and night,
that is something I cannot do."
Having spoken,
she bade farewell.
Shēng said,
"Xiāngyù's eternal departure
makes me lose my appetite and sleep.
I relied on you to stay a little longer
to comfort this longing,
why are you so decisive in leaving!"
The girl then stopped,
stayed the night, and departed.
For several days, she did not return.
In the cold rain by the secluded window,
he bitterly longed for Xiāngyù,
tossing and turning in bed,
his tears congealing on the pillow.
He picked up his clothes and rose again,
trimming the lamp and resuming the previous rhyme, saying:
"In the mountain courtyard, dusk rain falls,
I sit by the small window, curtains drawn.
My beloved is unseen in my longing,
tears stream down in pairs in the middle of the night."
He recited the poem to himself when it was finished.
Suddenly, someone outside the window said,
"The author should not be without a response."
Listening,
it was Jiàngxuě.
He opened the door and let her in.
The girl looked at the poem and
immediately added after it:
"Where has my companion gone?
A lonely lamp illuminates the late window.
One person in the empty mountains,
her shadow becomes a pair."
Shēng shed tears as he read it,
and resented their infrequent meetings.
The girl said,
"I cannot be as passionate as Xiāngyù,
but I can at least alleviate your loneliness."
Shēng wished to be intimate with her.
She said,
"The joy of meeting
does not necessarily lie in this."
Thus, whenever he was feeling forlorn,
the girl would arrive.
Upon her arrival, they would feast, drink, and exchange poems.
Sometimes she would leave without sleeping,
and Shēng would allow it.
He would say,
"Xiāngyù is my beloved wife,
Jiàngxuě is my good friend."
Every time he wanted to ask,
"Which tree in the courtyard are you?
Please tell me soon,
I will transplant you to my home,
to avoid you being taken by wicked people like Xiāngyù,
leaving me with a hundred years of regret."
The girl said,
"It is difficult to move from one's native soil,
telling you would be of no benefit.
Even a wife cannot stay forever,
let alone a friend!"
Shēng did not listen,
grabbed her arm, and went out.
Every time they came to a peony,
he would ask,
"Is this you?"
The girl did not speak,
but covered her mouth and smiled.
Soon, Shēng returned home for the New Year.
Around the second month,
he suddenly dreamed that Jiàngxuě came,
and sadly said,
"I am in great danger!
If you hurry,
you can still see me;
if you delay, it will be too late."
He awoke, found it strange,
and immediately ordered a servant and horse.
He rushed to the mountain.
A Daoist priest was about to build a house,
and a Camellia,
obstructing his construction,
was about to be chopped down by the foreman.
Shēng quickly stopped him.
At night,
Jiàngxuě came to thank him.
Shēng smiled and said,
"You didn't tell me the truth before,
so you deserved this calamity!
Now I know you;
if you had not come,
I would have used a moxa stick to burn you."
The girl said,
"I knew you were like this,
that's why I dared not tell you before."
After sitting for a while,
Shēng said,
"Now, facing a good friend,
I miss my beautiful wife even more.
I haven't wept for Xiāngyù in a long time,
can you cry with me?"
The two then went
and shed tears at the pit.
After more than an hour,
Jiàngxuě stopped crying and advised him to stop.
A few evenings later,
as Shēng was sitting in silence,
Jiàngxuě smilingly entered and said,
"I bring you good news: the flower spirit has been moved by your deep affection
and has allowed Xiāngyù to return to the temple."
Shēng asked,
"When?"
She replied,
"I don't know,
but it should not be long."
At daybreak, he got out of bed.
Shēng instructed her,
"I came for you,
do not keep me lonely for long."
The girl smiled and agreed.
For two nights, she did not come.
Shēng went to hug the tree,
shaking and caressing it,
calling frequently but receiving no sound.
He then returned,
and by the lamp, rolled up a moxa stick,
intending to burn the tree.
The girl suddenly entered,
snatched the moxa stick and threw it away,
saying:
"You are mischievous,
making people suffer wounds,
I should break up with you!"
Shēng smiled and embraced her.
Before they were seated firmly,
Xiāngyù entered gracefully.
Shēng saw her,
and in a state of agitation,
quickly rose to grasp her.
Xiāngyù held Jiàngxuě with one hand,
and they choked with sobs facing each other.
When they were seated,
Shēng felt an emptiness as he held her,
as if he was holding his own hand.
Startled, he asked her about it.
Xiāngyù, with tears welling up, said:
"In the past, I, your concubine,
was the spirit of a flower,
hence solidified;
now I, your concubine,
am the ghost of a flower,
hence dispersed.
Though we are together now,
do not take it as real;
merely consider it a dream."
Jiàngxuě said:
"Sister's arrival is most welcome!
I am being pestered to death by your family's man."
Then she left.
Xiāngyù smiled gently as before;
but as they nestled together,
it was as if her body was just a shadow.
Shēng was unhappy and dispirited.
Xiāngyù also looked down, regretting her state,
and then said:
"If you sprinkle some *báilǐanxiè*,
mixed with a little sulfur,
and pour a cup of water for your concubine daily,
on this day next year, I will repay your kindness."
Then she departed.
The next day,
he went to observe the former spot,
and indeed, the peony had sprouted.
Shēng then cultivated it daily,
and built a carved railing to protect it.
When Xiāngyù came,
her gratitude increased manifold.
Shēng planned to transplant it to his home,
but the woman disagreed,
saying:
"Your concubine's constitution is delicate,
and cannot endure another transplantation.
Moreover, every living thing has its destined place.
Your concubine originally did not intend to be born at your home;
going against this would shorten my lifespan.
Just cherish and love each other,
and a good reunion will come in due time."
Shēng regretted that Jiàngxuě did not come.
Xiāngyù said:
"If you absolutely wish to compel her to come,
your concubine can bring her."
So she went with Shēng, lamp in hand, to the base of the tree.
She took a stalk of grass,
held it in her palm to measure,
and measured the base of the tree.
From bottom to top,
when it reached four *chǐ* and six *cùn*,
she pressed that spot
and had Shēng scratch it with both his nails.
Suddenly, Jiàngxuě appeared from behind,
laughing and scolding:
"You maidservant, you come to help the tyrant commit evil!"
She pulled and dragged her, and they entered together.
Xiāngyù said:
"Sister, do not be angry!
Please bear with accompanying my lord for a while;
in one year, I will no longer bother you."
From then on, this became their routine.
Shēng observed the flower bud,
which grew fatter and lusher day by day.
By the end of spring,
it was about two *chǐ* tall.
After returning,
he gave gold to the Daoist priest,
instructing him to cultivate it morning and evening.
The next year, in April, he arrived at the palace,
where there was one flower,
still in bud and not yet open;
as he lingered,
the flower swayed, about to unfurl;
a short while later, it had opened.
The flower was as large as a plate,
and a small beauty,
only three or four fingers tall,
sat gracefully within the pistil.
In a flash, she floated down as if to descend,
and it was Xiāngyù.
She smiled and said:
"Your concubine endured wind and rain waiting for you,
why have you come so late!"
Then she entered the room.
Jiàngxuě also arrived,
smiling and saying:
"Daily playing the role of someone else's wife,
today I am fortunate to retire and be a friend."
Then they talked and feasted.
Towards midnight,
Jiàngxuě then departed.
The two slept together,
as intimate and harmonious as before.
Later, Shēng's wife died,
and Shēng then went into the mountains and did not return.
At this time,
the peony was already as thick as an arm.
Shēng often pointed to it and said:
"In the future, I will entrust my soul here,
and be born to your left."
The two women smiled and said:
"Do not forget this, my lord."
Over ten years later,
he suddenly fell ill.
His son came,
and grieved before him.
Shēng smiled and said:
"This is my rebirth date,
not my death date,
why grieve!"
He said to the Daoist priest:
"One day, a red shoot will grow vigorously beneath the peony,
one that blooms with five leaves,
that will be me."
Then he spoke no more.
His son carried him home,
and he died immediately.
The next year,
indeed, a plump shoot emerged,
with leaves matching the number he described.
The Daoist priest considered it extraordinary,
and irrigated it even more.
Three years later,
it was several *chǐ* tall,
and as thick as a large embrace,
but it did not flower.
The old Daoist priest died,
and his disciples, not knowing its value,
cut it down.
The white peony also withered and died;
not long after,
the winter-enduring plant also died.
Yìshǐ Shì says:
"When love is utterly profound,
even ghosts and spirits can be communicated with.
The flower followed as a ghost,
and the man entrusted his soul;
is this not because their bond of affection was deep?
One departed, and two martyred themselves for him;
even if not steadfastly chaste,
they died for love.
If people cannot be chaste,
it is also because their affection is not earnest.
When Kǒng Ní read about the *tángdì* and said, 'He did not think,'
how true it is!"
(According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* Zhùxuězhāi manuscript)
A scholar went to take the imperial examination in Jīnlíng.
Passing through Sùqiān,
he met three xiùcái.
Their discussion was expansive and profound,
so he bought wine and conversed cordially with them.
Each stated his name: one was Jiè Qiūhéng,
one Cháng Fēnglín,
and one Má Xīchí.
They drank freely and very happily,
not noticing that dusk had fallen.
Jiè said:
“We haven't yet performed the formalities of hosts,
yet we have suddenly imposed upon your excellent company.
This is not proper.
My humble abode is not far,
you may lodge there.”
Cháng and Má both rose,
tidied their clothes and called their servants,
and together they left.
Arriving at the mountain north of the town,
they suddenly saw a courtyard,
with a clear stream flowing around its gate.
Once inside,
the dwelling was clean and tidy.
Calling for servants to light lamps,
they also ordered arrangements for the scholar's attendants.
Má said:
“In the past, we made friends through literature.
Now the examination period is approaching,
we must not let this good night pass in vain.
Please propose four topics, we will draw lots,
each taking one,
and only drink after the essays are complete.”
Everyone agreed.
A topic was prepared and proposed,
written and placed on the table,
and whoever picked it up composed their thoughts at the desk.
Before the second watch was over,
all had completed their drafts,
passing them around for each other to read.
The xiùcái read the three works,
and was deeply impressed,
roughly copying them and hiding them in his bosom.
The hosts offered fine wine,
and urged them to drink from large cups,
before they realized it, they were tipsy.
The hosts then led the guest to sleep in a separate courtyard.
The guest, being drunk,
did not take off his shoes,
and lay down fully clothed.
When he awoke,
the red sun was already high,
and looking around, there was no courtyard,
but he and his servant were lying in a mountain valley.
He was greatly alarmed.
He saw a cave nearby,
with water trickling from it.
He wondered if he was lost and bewildered.
Reaching into his bosom,
he found that the three works were all still there.
He asked the local people,
and only then learned it was
“Sānxiān Dòng” (Three Immortals' Cave).
Inside were crabs, snakes,
and toad-like creatures, these three things,
which were most spiritual,
sometimes coming out to wander,
and people often saw them.
When the scholar entered the examination hall,
the three topics were exactly those immortal works,
and because of this, he was selected as the top candidate.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Two yāmén lì from Lìchéng County,
acting on the orders of the county magistrate Hán Chéngxuān,
had gone to work in another prefecture,
and were only returning at the end of the year.
On the way, they met two men,
whose attire also resembled that of government runners,
and they conversed lively while traveling together.
The two men claimed to be prefectural jùnyì.
The lì said:
“Among the kuàizào of Jǐnán,
we know eight or nine out of ten.
We are quite unfamiliar with you two gentlemen.”
The two men said,
“To tell you the truth: we are the ghostly lì of the Chénghuáng.
We are now going to deliver official documents to Dōngyuè.”
The lì asked:
“What is the matter with the official documents?”
They replied:
“A great calamity in Jǐnán;
what is reported
is the number of people to be killed.”
The lì asked, startled, about the number.
They said:
“We are not very sure,
but approximately close to a million.”
The lì asked about the date,
and they replied with
“zhèngshuò” (the New Year's Day)
The two lì looked at each other in alarm,
calculating that they would arrive in the prefecture exactly on New Year's Eve.
They feared they would fall victim to the disaster;
yet delaying might incur reprimand.
The ghosts said:
“Missing the deadline is a small offense,
but entering and encountering the calamity is a great disaster.
You should go somewhere else to avoid it,
and for now, do not return.”
The lì followed their advice.
Not long after,
Northern troops arrived in great numbers,
slaughtered Jǐnán,
and piled up a million corpses.
The two men escaped by fleeing and hiding.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wáng Shí of Gāoyuàn
was carrying salt at Bóxīng.
At night, he was captured by two men.
He thought they were patrolmen from a local salt merchant,
so he abandoned his salt and tried to flee;
but his feet were so weary he couldn't move forward,
and he was consequently tied up.
He pleaded for mercy.
The two men said,
"We are not men from the salt trade,
but ghost emissaries."
Shí was terrified.
He begged to go home just once
to bid farewell to his wife and children.
They refused,
saying,
"You won't necessarily die immediately after going there;
it's merely a temporary service."
Shí asked,
"For what business?"
They replied,
"A new King Yán has arrived in the underworld.
Seeing that the Nàihé (river) is silted up
and the pits and toilets of the eighteen hells are all full,
he is therefore catching three types of people to dredge the river: petty thieves, private coiners, and private salt vendors;
and another type of people to clean the toilets: prostitutes."
Shí followed them,
entered a city,
and arrived at an official yamen,
where he saw King Yán enthroned,
currently checking the registers.
The ghosts reported,
"We have brought Wáng Shí, a private salt peddler."
King Yán looked at him
and angrily said,
"Private salt vendors are those
who deprive the state of taxes above
and harm the livelihood of the people below.
However, those whom the violent officials and wicked merchants of this world label as private salt vendors
are all good people of the realm.
Poor people who invest a pittance
to earn a meager profit,
how can that be considered private?"
He punished the two ghosts by ordering them to purchase four dou of salt from the market,
together with what Shí had been carrying,
and deliver it to his home.
He detained Shí
and gave him a caltrop mace (jílī gǔduǒ),
ordering him to supervise the river work with the other ghosts.
The ghosts led Shí away
to the edge of the Nàihé (river),
where he saw laborers in the river
crowding like ants.
He also saw the river water was turbid and red,
and its stench was unbearable.
Those dredging the river were all naked, holding shovels and baskets,
disappearing and reappearing within it.
Rotten bones and decaying corpses
were carried out in baskets and on their backs;
in deeper parts, they would immerse themselves completely to search.
The lazy ones were immediately struck on the back and thighs with the mace.
His fellow supervisors gave him a fragrant cotton ball as large as a broad bean
to hold in his mouth,
and then he approached the bank.
He saw a merchant from Gāoyuàn
was also among them.
Shí alone treated him harshly: hitting his back when he entered the river,
and striking his thighs when he came ashore.
The merchant was afraid,
and often immersed himself completely in the water,
which was when Shí stopped.
After three days and nights,
half the river workers had died,
and the river work was also completed.
The two former ghosts again escorted him home,
and he suddenly revived.
Before this,
Shí had not returned with his salt.
At dawn,
his wife opened the door
to find two bags of salt placed in the courtyard,
but Shí had been long overdue.
She sent people to search everywhere for him,
and he was found dead on the road.
They carried him home,
and he faintly showed a trace of breath,
though the reason was unknown.
When he awoke,
he finally recounted his story.
The merchant had also died the day before,
and only now revived.
Where he had been struck by the mace,
all had turned into huge carbuncles,
his whole body festered and putrid,
unbearably close.
Shí therefore went to visit him.
Upon seeing Shí,
he still shrank his head into the quilt,
as if he were still in the Nàihé (river).
It was a year
before he finally recovered
and ceased to be a merchant.
The Recorder of Strange Tales says:
"Regarding the matter of salt,
what the court calls 'private'
is that which does not comply with the public regulations;
what officials and merchants call 'private'
is that which does not comply with their private interests.
Recently, in Qí and Lǔ, new regulations have been established:
local merchants set up shops everywhere
and are restricted to their own territories.
Not only are the people of this district
forbidden from going to that district;
even the people of this shop
are forbidden from going to that shop.
Yet, within their shops, they secretly set baits to attract people from other districts;
when they sell to other districts,
they make the price cheap;
but when they sell to local people,
they double the price to inflate it.
And they also set up patrols on the roads
to ensure that people within their territory
cannot escape their inflated prices.
If anyone from within their territory dares to come from another district,
the law shows no mercy.
As they bait each other,
the foolish people who cross boundaries and pretend to be from another shop increase.
Once caught by the patrol,
they are first maimed in their body and limbs with knives and clubs,
and then sent to the authorities;
the officials then shackle them,
and this is called 'private salt.'
Alas!
How unjust!
Evading tens of thousands in taxes is not private,
but carrying a mere dou of salt is deemed private;
selling from one's own territory to another territory is not private,
but buying within one's own territory is deemed private.
How unjust!
The 'Salt Law'
in the statutes is most severe,
yet it specifically does not prohibit
poor and distressed soldiers and civilians
who carry salt on their backs for food.
But now, everything is prohibited,
and it specifically kills these poor and distressed soldiers and civilians!
Moreover, these poor and distressed soldiers and civilians,
whose wives and children are wailing,
uphold the law above and do not steal,
and know shame below and do not become prostitutes;
out of desperation,
they risk ten mothers to save one child.
If every district were full of such people,
then 'doors would not need to be closed at night'
would be possible.
Are they not the good people of the realm?
As for those shop merchants,
not only should they be made to dredge the Nàihé (river),
they should directly be made to clean the hell toilets!
And officials, during the spring and autumn festivals,
receive their fleeting profits,
and then use the three-foot law to help them kill our good people.
Therefore, for the sake of the poor,
it is better to be a thief or a private coiner.
Thieves rob people in broad daylight,
and officials act as if deaf;
coiners' furnaces blaze to the sky,
and officials act as if blind;
even if they are to dredge the river on another day,
it would still not be as if those who carry goods have little to gain,
and official punishment immediately arrives.
Alas!
When there are no benevolent and kind teachers above,
and the laws of wicked merchants are listened to,
changing and becoming more bizarre day by day,
how can it be that unruly people do not increase daily,
and good people do not die daily?"
In each town, traveling merchants,
according to old custom,
annually presented a certain amount of salt revenue
to the local county,
called "salt tax."
When a festival or season arrived,
they prepared generous gifts.
When merchants visited officials on business,
the officials would treat them courteously,
sitting and conversing with them,
perhaps offering tea.
If salt peddlers arrived,
they would be severely punished without delay.
When Zhāng Gōng Shínián was the magistrate of Zī,
a traveling merchant came to see him,
following the old custom,
bowing but not kneeling.
The magistrate angrily said,
"The previous magistrate accepted your bribes,
and thus had no choice but to treat you with great deference.
I buy and eat salt myself,
what kind of merchant
dares to refuse to kneel in the public hall?!"
He rolled up his trousers, about to beat him.
The merchant kowtowed and apologized for his transgression,
and only then was he released.
Later, two peddlers were caught in the market.
One escaped,
the other was seized and brought to the official.
The magistrate asked,
"There were two peddlers,
where did the other one go?"
The peddler replied,
"He escaped."
The magistrate said,
"Are your legs diseased that you cannot run?"
He replied,
"I can run."
The magistrate said,
"Since you were caught,
you must not be able to run.
If you truly can,
stand up and try to run,
to test your ability."
The man ran a few steps and wanted to stop.
The magistrate said,
"Run, don't stop!"
The man ran swiftly,
and indeed ran out of the magistrate's gate and away.
All who saw it laughed.
The magistrate's acts of loving the people were numerous;
this was a lighthearted incident,
yet the townspeople still enjoyed recounting it.
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Xī Chéngliè was
a scholar from Chéngdū.
He had one wife and one concubine.
The concubine was Hén Shì,
whose given name was Zhāokè.
His wife died early,
and he later married Shēn Shì,
who was jealous
and treated Hé cruelly,
and even extended this to Xī;
she bickered constantly all day long,
making their lives unbearable.
Xī grew angry
and fled.
After he left,
Hé gave birth to a son, Dànán.
Xī left and did not return.
Shēn ostracized Hé and did not let her cook with them,
giving her a daily ration of grain.
Dànán gradually grew older,
and the provisions were insufficient.
Hé spun and wove to supplement their food.
Dànán saw the other children in the private school chanting and reciting,
and also wanted to read.
His mother, thinking him too young,
nonetheless sent him to study.
Dànán was intelligent;
he read twice as much as the other children.
The teacher found him remarkable
and was willing not to ask for tuition fees.
Hé then allowed him to follow the teacher,
offering a small token of gratitude.
After two or three years,
he had thoroughly mastered the classics.
One day he returned
and said to his mother,
"There are five or six children in the school,
all asking their fathers for money to buy cakes.
Why am I the only one without?"
His mother said,
"Wait until you are older,
and I will tell you."
Dànán said,
"I am only seven or eight years old now,
when will I be older?"
His mother said,
"When you go to school,
you pass by the Guāndì Miào.
You should bow to him;
he will bless you to grow up quickly."
Dànán believed her,
and would enter and bow every time he passed.
His mother, knowing this,
asked,
"What did you pray for?"
He laughed and said,
"I only prayed that next year I would be sixteen or seventeen years old."
His mother laughed at him.
However, Dànán's studies and physical growth both accelerated: by the age of ten,
he was like someone thirteen or fourteen;
the essays he wrote were already well-formed.
One day,
he said to his mother,
"Since I am now grown,
you should tell me my father's whereabouts.
It is permissible now."
His mother said,
"Not yet,
not yet."
After another year or so,
he was truly a grown man.
His inquiries became more frequent,
so his mother recounted the story.
Dànán was overcome with grief
and wanted to go search for his father.
His mother said,
"My son, you are too young.
We don't know if your father is alive or dead.
How can you search so soon?"
Dànán left without a word,
and by noon had not returned.
His mother went to the school to ask the teacher,
but he had not returned since morning meal.
His mother was greatly alarmed,
spent money to hire servants,
and searched everywhere,
but there was no trace of him.
Dànán left the house,
followed the path and ran,
not knowing where he was going.
He happened to meet a man going to Kuízhōu,
who said his surname was Qián.
Dànán begged for food and followed him.
Qián found him slow,
so he rented a substitute means of transport for him,
exhausting his travel funds.
When they reached Kuí,
they ate together.
Qián secretly put poison in the food,
but Dànán ate it unknowingly.
Qián took him to a large monastery,
pretended he was his own son,
who had accidentally fallen ill and run out of funds,
and sold him to the monks.
The monks saw his handsome and extraordinary appearance,
and competed to buy him.
Qián took the gold and left.
The monks gave him water to drink,
and he slightly regained consciousness.
The elder knew of this and came to examine him,
was struck by his appearance,
and through diligent inquiry,
finally learned the whole story.
He pitied him greatly,
gave him money and told him to leave.
There was a Xiùcai named Jiǎng from Hùzhōu,
who was returning home after failing the imperial examination.
On the way, he learned of Dànán's situation,
praised his filial piety,
and took him along.
When they arrived in Hù,
he stayed at Jiǎng's house.
After more than a month,
Jiǎng made inquiries everywhere.
Someone said that among the Fújiàn merchants, there was one with the surname Shuài.
So Dànán bid farewell to Jiǎng,
and wanted to go to Fújiàn.
Jiǎng gave him clothes and shoes,
and his neighbors and fellow villagers all pooled funds to assist him.
On the way, he met two cloth merchants,
who wanted to go to Fúqīng,
and invited him to join them.
After traveling a few stages,
the merchants eyed his money bag,
led him to an empty place,
bound his hands and feet,
untied and robbed him, and left.
Just then, an elderly man named Chén from Yǒngfú passed by the same place,
untied him,
and took him home.
The elder was wealthy,
and many merchants from various routes
came from his household.
The elder instructed merchants from north and south to inquire about Xī Hào on his behalf.
He kept Dànán to accompany his children in their studies.
Dànán then settled in the elder's house,
and no longer traveled.
However, the further he was from home,
the more his news was cut off.
Hé Zhāoróng lived alone for three or four years.
Shēn Shì reduced her living expenses
and pressured her to marry.
Hé's resolve remained unshaken.
Shēn forcibly sold her to a merchant from Chóngqìng.
The merchant seized her and left.
That night,
she used a knife to disembowel herself.
The merchant dared not press her,
and after her wound healed,
he resold her to a merchant from Yántíng.
Upon arriving in Yántíng,
she stabbed herself in the heart,
exposing her internal organs.
The merchant was greatly frightened,
applied medicine to her,
and when the wound was flat,
she asked to become a nun.
The merchant said,
"I have business partners,
and I myself lack a wife.
I always wanted someone to take charge of sewing.
This is no different from being a nun,
and it can also somewhat repay my value."
Hé agreed.
The merchant carried her and sent her away.
Upon entering the gate,
the master rushed out,
and it was Xī Shēng.
It turned out Xī had already abandoned his scholarly life to become a merchant,
and the merchant, seeing he had no wife,
had gifted her to him.
They met with grief and shock,
each recounting their hardships,
and then learned that their son had gone to search for his father and had not returned.
Xī then instructed his fellow travelers
to inquire about his eldest son.
And so, Zhāoróng became his wife instead of a concubine.
However, having endured great hardship,
she was often ill and in pain,
unable to perform manual labor,
so she advised Xī to take a concubine.
Xī, remembering the previous misfortune,
did not comply with her request.
Hé said,
"If I were one to contend for the marriage bed,
I would have already borne children for someone else years ago.
Could I still be with you today?
Moreover, the pain inflicted upon me by others
is hidden in my heart; how could I bring it upon myself by doing the same to others?"
Xī then instructed his fellow travelers
to buy an old concubine over thirty years of age for him.
After more than half a year,
the traveler indeed bought a concubine and returned.
Upon entering the gate,
it was his wife, Shēn Shì.
They were all amazed and startled.
Previously,
Shēn had lived alone for over a year.
Her elder brother, Bāo, advised her to remarry.
Shēn followed his advice.
However, her land and property were obstructed by her son and nephews
and could not be sold.
She sold all she had,
accumulating several hundred gold pieces,
and brought them back to her brother's home.
There was a merchant from Bǎoníng
who, hearing of her rich dowry,
bribed Bāo with much gold
to persuade him to arrange the marriage.
However, the merchant was old and infirm, unable to be a proper husband.
Shēn resented her brother
and was uneasy in her confinement.
She attempted to hang herself and throw herself into a well,
making her life unbearable.
The merchant was angry,
seized her assets,
and planned to sell her as a concubine.
Those who heard of it all declined, citing her age.
The merchant was going to Kuízhōu,
so he took her with him.
He met Xī at the same market stall,
and finding her suitable,
he sold her and left.
Upon seeing Xī,
she was too sluggish and afraid to utter a single word.
Xī asked the merchant at the same stall,
and vaguely learned the general situation.
Then he said,
"Had you met a healthy man,
then in Bǎoníng,
there would be no chance of seeing him again.
This, too, is fate.
However, today I bought a concubine,
not married a wife.
You may first bow to Zhāoróng
and perform the rituals of principal wife and concubine."
Shēn was ashamed of this.
Xī said,
"How was it when you were the principal wife in the past?"
Hé tried to stop him.
Xī refused,
grabbed a stick, and forced her.
Shēn, having no choice,
bowed to her.
However, she still disdained to serve her,
only working in a separate room.
Hé was entirely gracious to her,
also not bearing to evaluate her diligence or idleness.
Whenever Xī conversed and feasted with Zhāoróng,
he would make Shēn serve at their side.
Hé would substitute her with a maidservant,
not allowing her to come forward.
At that time, Chén Gōng Sìzōng was the magistrate of Yántíng.
Xī had a minor dispute with a local resident,
and the resident sued Xī, alleging he forced his wife to become a concubine.
The magistrate did not accept the case
and scolded him away.
Xī was delighted
and secretly praised the magistrate's virtue with Hé.
As soon as the first watch of the night was over,
a servant shouted and knocked on the door,
reporting,
"The magistrate is now at our house!"
Xī was extremely alarmed,
hastily searched for his clothes and shoes,
only to find the magistrate already at his bedroom door.
He was even more shocked,
not knowing what to do.
Hé examined him,
and quickly exclaimed,
"It is our son!"
Then she wept.
The magistrate then prostrated himself, weeping sorrowfully.
Indeed, the eldest son had adopted the surname Chén Gōng
and had become a magistrate.
Initially,
when the magistrate returned from the capital,
he passed through his old village on his journey
and only then learned that both his mothers had remarried,
and he felt deep sorrow.
His clansmen, knowing the eldest son had become noble,
returned his fields and houses.
The magistrate left servants to build and manage,
hoping his father would return.
Later, when he was appointed to Yántíng,
he again wanted to abandon his office to search for his father.
Chén Wēng painstakingly persuaded him to stop.
There was a diviner,
so he asked him to perform a divination.
The diviner said,
"The younger one resides above the elder;
the junior one becomes the senior;
seeking male, you gain female;
seeking one, you gain two: to be an official is auspicious."
The magistrate then went to his post.
Because he could not find his parents,
he abstained from meat and wine while in office.
On that day,
he received the local resident's complaint,
saw Xī's name,
and suspected it might be him.
He secretly dispatched an aged envoy to investigate thoroughly,
and indeed it was his father.
He left in a clandestine manner that night.
Upon seeing his mother,
he believed even more in the diviner's supernatural ability.
Before leaving,
he instructed them not to spread the news,
gave two hundred pieces of gold,
and told his father to prepare to return home.
When his father arrived home,
the gates and doors were all new,
and he had many servants and horses,
indeed a prominent family.
Shēn, seeing the eldest son's nobility and prosperity,
became even more restrained.
Her brother, Bāo, was indignant,
sued the official,
and contended for his sister's position as principal wife.
The magistrate honestly investigated the matter
and angrily said,
"Greedily prompting her to marry,
she has already had two other husbands.
How can she still have the face to contend for the position of principal wife from years ago?"
He severely flogged Bāo.
From this, the official status was even more settled.
And Shēn called Hé "older sister,"
and Hé also called her "older sister."
Clothes and food,
none were kept for themselves.
Shēn initially feared their revenge;
now she felt even more shame and regret.
Xī also forgot her past misdeeds,
and had everyone inside and outside the household call her "Tàimǔ,"
though she did not receive an official enfeoffment.
Historian Yì Shǐ Shì said:
"Bewildering all sentient beings,
it is unfathomable,
how clever is the Creator!
Why is it that Xi Shēng could not establish himself between his wives and concubines,
being merely a mediocre person?
If not for a filial son and a virtuous mother,
how could there have been such a wondrous union,
allowing him to enjoy wealth and honor for the rest of his life!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the autumn of the Jǐyǐ year,
from Língnán a huge ship drifted in from overseas.
On board were eleven people,
clothed in bird feathers,
with brilliant patterns.
They said of themselves,
"We are people from the country of Lǚsòng.
Our ship was overturned by a storm,
and dozens of people all died;
only eleven of us clung to a huge log,
drifting to a large island where we escaped.
For nearly five years,
we seized birds and insects to eat by day;
by night, we hid in stone caves,
weaving feathers into a sail.
Suddenly another boat drifted to us,
without oars or sail,
having also been shattered by the wind in the sea.
So we attached ourselves to it, intending to return.
Then we were carried by a great wind to Àomén."
The governor reported the matter in a memorial,
and they were sent back to their country.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wéi Gōngzǐ,
from a prominent family in Xiányáng.
He was dissolute and lustful;
if a maid or a servant's wife was attractive,
there was none he did not secretly dally with.
He once carried several thousand pieces of gold,
desiring to see all the famous courtesans under heaven,
and there was no prosperous and splendid region
he did not visit.
If they were not very pleasing,
he would leave after a night or two;
if they pleased him,
he would stay for a hundred days.
His uncle was also a renowned official,
who had retired and returned home.
Angered by his conduct,
he invited a famous teacher,
set up a separate estate,
and made him study with the other young masters, keeping the gate locked.
Gōngzǐ would wait until the teacher was asleep at night,
climb over the wall to go home,
and return at dawn.
One night,
he slipped and broke a bone,
which was how the teacher first found out.
He told Gōng,
who inflicted more corporal punishment,
not giving him medicine until he was unable to get up.
When he recovered,
Gōng made an agreement with him: if he could study twice as much as his younger brothers,
and his writing was good,
he would not be forbidden from going out;
but if he secretly indulged in pleasure,
he would be flogged as before.
However, Gōngzǐ was exceptionally intelligent,
and often surpassed his required studies.
Several years later,
he passed the provincial examination.
He wanted to break the agreement himself,
but Gōng restrained him.
When he went to the capital,
he was accompanied by an old servant,
who was given a diary and a register,
and told to record all his words and actions.
Thus, for several years he committed no transgression.
Later, he became a *jìnshì*,
and Gōng gradually relaxed his restrictions.
Whenever Gōngzǐ might be about to misbehave,
fearing his father would hear,
he would enter a winding alley
and always give his surname as Wèi.
One day,
passing through Xī'ān,
he saw the actor Luó Huìqīng,
sixteen or seventeen years old,
beautiful and refined like a pretty girl,
and was delighted by him.
He stayed the night, dallying intimately,
and gave generous gifts.
Hearing that Luó Huìqīng's new wife was especially graceful and exquisite,
he secretly hinted this to Huìqīng.
Huìqīng showed no difficulty,
and indeed brought his wife that night,
with all three sharing one bed.
They stayed for several days,
and their affection reached its peak.
He planned to take them both home with him.
He asked about Huìqīng's family,
who replied:
"My mother died early,
my father is still alive.
I am not originally surnamed Luó.
My mother served in the Wéi family in Xiányáng when she was young,
then was sold to the Luó family,
and gave birth to me four months later.
If I could go with Gōngzǐ,
I might also find out news of her."
Gōngzǐ was startled and asked his mother's surname,
to which he replied:
"Lǚ."
The young man was extremely alarmed,
sweat drenching his body,
for Luó Huìqīng's mother was his own household maid.
He said nothing.
By then, it was already morning,
so he gave him generous gifts,
advised him to change his profession.
He falsely claimed he was going elsewhere,
promising to send for him upon his return,
and then left.
Later, when he was in Sūzhōu,
there was an entertainer, Shěn Wéiniáng,
elegant and peerlessly beautiful.
He loved to stay and dally with her.
He jokingly said:
"Is your pet name taken from 'A tune of spring breeze, Dù Wéiniáng'
She replied:
"No.
My mother was a famous courtesan at seventeen,
and a young master from Xiányáng with the same surname as you
stayed for three months,
pledging marriage.
After Gōngzǐ left,
eight months later she gave birth to me,
and so I was named Wéi,
which is truly my surname.
When Gōngzǐ departed,
he gave her a pair of golden mandarin ducks,
which we still have.
He left and there was no news,
and my mother died of resentment because of this.
When I was three,
I was adopted by Granny Shěn,
and thus took her surname."
Hearing this, Gōngzǐ
was filled with such shame and remorse that he could not bear it.
After a silent moment,
a plan suddenly formed.
He abruptly got up and lit a lamp,
called Wéiniáng to drink,
and secretly placed poison in her cup.
As soon as Wéiniáng swallowed it,
she collapsed in agony, groaning and screaming.
Everyone gathered to look,
and she was already dead.
He called the actors,
gave them the body,
and heavily bribed them.
However, Wéiniáng's associates were all powerful families,
and hearing of this, they were all indignant.
They bribed and incited the actors,
who sued him to the authorities.
The young man, in fear,
emptied his purse to smooth things over,
and was finally dismissed from office for his rashness.
Returning home,
he was only thirty-eight,
and somewhat regretted his past actions.
But his five or six wives and concubines
were all childless.
He wanted to adopt a successor for Gōng;
Gōng, believing there was misconduct within the household,
feared his grandson would pick up bad habits.
Although he allowed adoption,
he insisted on waiting until he was old before handing him over.
Gōngzǐ, resentful, wanted to invite Huìqīng,
but his family all considered it unacceptable,
so he stopped.
Several more years passed,
when he suddenly fell ill,
often beating his chest and saying:
"One who defiles maids and sleeps with courtesans
is not human!"
Gōng heard this and sighed:
"He is probably going to die!"
So he sent the son of his second son
to his house,
to attend to him daily.
He indeed died after more than a month.
Historian Yì Shǐshì said:
"Stealing maids and keeping private prostitutes
—their consequences are indeed unfathomable.
However, to have one's own flesh and blood
call another man father
is already shameful enough.
Yet ghosts and spirits further mock them,
inducing them to consume their own bodily fluids.
If they still do not examine their own hearts,
or sever their own heads,
but merely sweat and resort to poison,
are they not humans in form but beasts in cry!
Nevertheless,
the children born to a licentious young master,
even if they live in the world of courtesans,
are all still adept in their fields."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Xíng Yúnfēi,
a native of Shùntiān.
He loved stones,
and when he saw a beautiful stone,
he would not begrudge a high price.
One day, while fishing in the river,
something snagged his net.
He pulled it up from the depths,
and it was a stone, a *chǐ* in diameter,
exquisitely carved on all four sides,
with layered peaks and beautiful ridges.
He was overjoyed,
as if he had found a rare treasure.
When he returned,
he carved a purple sandalwood base for it
and placed it on his desk.
Whenever it was about to rain,
clouds would form in every hole,
looking from afar like newly stuffed cotton.
A certain powerful dignitary
came to his door, asking to see it.
Upon seeing it,
he handed it to a strong servant
and rode away immediately.
Xíng Yúnfēi was helpless,
only stamping his feet in sorrow and indignation.
The servant carried the stone to the riverbank
and rested on a bridge.
Suddenly, he lost his grip, and it fell into the river.
The dignitary was furious
and whipped the servant.
He then offered gold to hire skilled swimmers,
who tried every means to drag it out,
but it was nowhere to be seen.
So, he posted a reward and left.
From then on, stone-seekers filled the river daily,
but none succeeded.
Later, Xíng Yúnfēi went to the spot where the stone had fallen,
and peered into the flowing water with deep sadness.
He saw that the river water was clear,
and the stone was indeed at the bottom.
Xíng Yúnfēi was greatly delighted.
He took off his clothes and entered the water,
embracing it and bringing it out.
He carried it home,
not daring to display it in the hall,
but carefully prepared his inner chamber to enshrine it.
One day,
an old man knocked on the door and requested to enter.
Xíng Yúnfēi claimed the stone had been lost for a long time.
The old man smiled and said:
"Is it not in the guest chamber?"
Xíng Yúnfēi then invited him in
to prove that it was not there.
Upon entering,
the stone was indeed displayed on the table.
He was too astonished to speak.
The old man stroked the stone and said:
"This is an old family possession of mine,
lost for a long time.
So, it is truly here now.
Since I have seen it,
please return it to me immediately."
Xíng Yúnfēi was greatly embarrassed
and began to dispute ownership of the stone with him.
The old man smiled and said:
"If it is your family's item,
what proof do you have?"
Xíng Yúnfēi could not answer.
The old man said:
"I, however, know it well.
It has ninety-two holes,
and in the holes are five characters that say: 'Qīngxū Tiānshí Gòng.'
Xíng Yúnfēi examined it carefully,
and indeed there were tiny characters in the holes,
as small as millet grains,
discernible only by straining his eyesight;
he also counted the holes,
and they were exactly as he said.
Xíng Yúnfēi had no reply,
but insisted on not giving it up.
The old man smiled and said:
"Whose property it is,
how can it be decided by you alone!"
He cupped his hands and left.
Xíng Yúnfēi escorted him outside the door;
when he returned,
the stone was already gone.
Xíng Yúnfēi urgently chased after the old man,
who was walking slowly and not far off.
He ran to pull his sleeve and pleaded with him.
The old man said:
"How strange!
A stone a *chǐ* in size,
how could it be held in a hand or hidden in a sleeve?"
Xíng Yúnfēi knew he was a spirit,
and forcibly dragged him back,
kneeling for a long time to implore him.
The old man then said:
"Is the stone truly yours, or is it mine?"
He replied:
"It truly belongs to you,
but I only ask you to part with it out of affection."
The old man said:
"In that case,
the stone is indeed here."
Entering the room,
the stone was already in its original place.
The old man said:
"The treasures of the world
should go to those who cherish them.
This stone
can choose its own master;
I am also pleased with this.
However, it was eager to reveal itself,
and its appearance was too early,
so the demonic tribulation has not yet been removed.
I was actually going to take it away
and present it to you
after three years.
If you wish to keep it now,
you must reduce your lifespan by three years,
only then can you have it from beginning to end.
Do you wish for this?"
He said:
"I wish for it."
The old man then pinched a hole with two fingers;
the hole became soft like mud
and closed under his hand.
After closing three holes,
he said:
"The number of holes on the stone
is your lifespan."
He bid farewell and was about to leave.
Xíng Yúnfēi earnestly tried to keep him,
but his refusal was very firm;
when asked his name,
he also did not say,
and then departed.
More than a year later,
Xíng Yúnfēi went out on business.
At night, a thief entered his room.
Nothing else was lost,
only the stone was stolen and taken away.
When Xíng Yúnfēi returned,
he grieved as if he would die.
He investigated and sought to buy it back,
but there was no trace of it.
Several years passed.
One day, he happened to enter Bàoguó Sì
and saw a stone seller.
It was his old possession,
and he immediately recognized and claimed it.
The seller disagreed,
so they carried the stone to the magistrate.
The magistrate asked:
"What proof do you have?"
The stone seller could state the number of holes.
Xíng Yúnfēi asked him other things,
but he was clueless.
Xíng Yúnfēi then mentioned the five characters in the holes and the three finger marks,
and his case was proven.
The magistrate intended to flog the stone seller,
but the seller stated that he had bought it in the market for twenty gold coins,
so he was released.
Xíng Yúnfēi returned with the stone,
wrapped it in brocade,
and hid it in a cabinet,
occasionally taking it out.
First, he would burn exotic incense,
and then take it out.
Xiào returned,
but never showed gratitude to Yǒuzǐ.
Not long after,
Yǒu-yú's mother, Fūrén Zhāng, passed away,
but Xiào and the others did not observe mourning for her,
feasting and drinking as usual.
Rén and Yì grew even more indignant.
Yǒu-yú said:
"This is their disrespect,
how does it harm me?"
When it came to the burial,
they held the tomb gates shut,
not allowing the coffins to be joined.
Yǒu-yú then buried his mother in a tunnel leading to the tomb.
Not long after,
Xiào's wife died,
and Yǒu-yú invited Rén and Yì to come with him to offer condolences.
The two said:
"'Qī'
is not even to be discussed,
what 'gōng'
is there?"
He urged them again,
but they scattered with a clamor.
Yǒu-yú then went by himself,
weeping sorrowfully at the mourning place.
From beyond the wall, he heard Rén and Yì playing drums and flutes.
Xiào was enraged,
and rallied his younger brothers to go beat them.
Yǒu-yú, carrying a dry staff, was the first to follow.
Upon entering their house,
Rén sensed them and fled first.
Yì was just climbing over the wall when
Yǒu-yú struck him from behind, knocking him down.
Xiào and the others rained down punches and staffs,
beating him relentlessly.
Yǒu-yú stepped in front to block them.
Xiào was furious,
and rebuked Yǒu-yú.
Yǒu-yú said:
"He is blamed
because of his disrespect,
but his crime certainly does not warrant death.
I do not condone my younger brothers' wickedness,
nor do I aid my elder brothers' violence.
If your anger is not appeased,
I will take his place."
Xiào then turned his staff and lashed Yǒu-yú.
Zhōng and Xìn also helped beat their elder brother.
The sound shook the neighborhood,
and a crowd gathered to intervene,
whereupon they dispersed.
Yǒu-yú immediately leaned on his staff and went to his elder brother to apologize.
Xiào chased him away,
not allowing him to stay at the mourning place.
Meanwhile, Yì was severely wounded
and could not eat or drink.
Rén, on his behalf, prepared a lawsuit for the official,
accusing them of not observing mourning for their stepmother.
The official issued a warrant to detain Xiào, Zhōng, and Xìn,
and ordered Yǒu-yú to state his case.
Yǒu-yú, due to his facial injuries,
could not go to the yámen,
but instead submitted a written statement,
piteously begging for the matter to be dropped.
The magistrate then closed the case.
Yì also soon recovered.
From then on, their enmity deepened.
Rén and Yì were both young and weak,
and were often beaten.
The resentful Yǒuzǐ said:
"Everyone has brothers,
I alone have none!"
Yǒu-yú said:
"These two phrases
should be said by me,
what are you two younger brothers saying!"
He then earnestly tried to persuade them,
but they ultimately did not listen.
Yǒu-yú then locked his door,
and took his wife and children to stay elsewhere,
more than fifty lǐ from home,
hoping they would not hear from each other.
While Yǒu-yú was at home, though he did not assist his younger brothers,
Xiào and the others still had some scruples;
once he left,
if any of the elder brothers were even slightly amiss,
they would shout and curse at their gate,
and insult their mother's taboo name.
Rén and Yì judged that they could not resist,
so they just shut their doors and plotted to assassinate them when the opportunity arose,
carrying knives when they went out.
One day,
Chéng, the eldest brother who had been abducted by bandits,
suddenly returned with his wife.
Since the family had been divided for a long time,
the brothers gathered to discuss for three days,
but there was no place where he could be settled.
Rén and Yì secretly rejoiced,
invited him to live with them and supported him.
They went to tell Yǒu-yú.
Yǒu-yú was pleased,
returned,
and together they offered fields and a dwelling to Chéng.
The elder brothers were angry at them for showing favor,
and came to their door to embarrass and humiliate them.
But Chéng had been among bandits for a long time,
accustomed to ferocity,
and he angrily said:
"When I returned,
no one else would even give me a house;
fortunately, my three younger brothers thought of our bond,
yet you blame them.
Are you trying to drive me away?"
He threw a stone at Xiào,
who fell.
Rén and Yì each came out with a staff,
grabbed Zhōng and Xìn,
and beat them countless times.
Chéng then sued the magistrate.
The magistrate again sent someone to consult Yǒu-yú.
Yǒu-yú went to the magistrate,
bowed his head and said nothing,
but merely shed tears.
The magistrate asked him,
and he said:
"I only seek a fair judgment."
The magistrate then ruled that Xiào and the others should each yield their land and property to Chéng,
making the seven parts equally proportionate.
From then on, Rén, Yì, and Chéng showed increased love and respect for each other.
When the matter of burying their mother was brought up,
they wept together.
Chéng lamented:
"Such inhumanity,
truly like beasts!"
He then wanted to open the grave
and rebury her.
Rén rushed to tell Yǒu-yú.
Yǒu-yú hastily returned to admonish him to stop.
Chéng did not listen,
set a date to exhume the tomb,
and performed a vegetarian feast at the burial mound.
He cut a tree with a knife,
and said to his younger brothers:
"Those who do not follow me in mourning attire
will be like this tree!"
They all assented,
and so the whole family cried at the mourning place,
completing the rites with full solemnity.
From then on, the brothers lived in peace.
But Chéng's nature was fierce and unyielding,
and he would often strike and beat his younger brothers,
especially Xiào.
He only held Yǒu-yú in high regard.
Even in a great rage,
when Yǒu-yú arrived,
a single word would resolve it.
Whenever Xiào did something,
Chéng would often be displeased with him,
so Xiào did not spend a day without going to Yǒu-yú's place,
secretly complaining and cursing to Yǒu-yú.
Yǒu-yú gently remonstrated,
but he would ultimately not accept it.
Yǒu-yú could not bear the disturbance,
and again moved his residence to Sānbó,
even further from home,
and their communication gradually dwindled.
Two more years passed,
and all the younger brothers feared Chéng,
and over time also became accustomed to him.
Meanwhile, Xiào was forty-six years old
and had five sons: the eldest, Jìyè,
the third, Jìdé,
born of his principal wife;
the second, Jìgōng,
the fourth, Jìjī,
born of concubines;
and Jìzǔ, born of a maid.
All were grown.
They emulated their father's former behavior,
each forming their own faction,
contending daily,
and Xiào could not stop them.
Only Zǔ had no brothers
and was the youngest,
so all his elder brothers could scold and harshly treat him.
His maternal relatives lived near Sānbó.
When he went to visit his maternal relatives,
he took a detour to visit his uncle.
Upon entering,
he saw his uncle's two elder brothers and one younger brother
studying diligently with string instruments and chanting,
and he was delighted,
staying for a long time without mentioning going home.
His uncle urged him,
and he tearfully begged to stay.
His uncle said:
"Your parents don't even know,
how could I begrudge you a bowl of food and a ladle of drink?"
So he returned.
A certain young master from
Jiāpíng was of elegant demeanor and exquisite beauty.
At seventeen or eighteen years old,
he went to the prefecture to take the tóngzǐ test.
He happened to pass by the door of Xǔ Chāng's house,
and saw a beautiful woman of sixteen in it,
so he fixed his gaze upon her.
The woman smiled and nodded,
and the young master approached to speak with her.
The woman asked:
"Where do you reside?"
He told her everything.
She asked:
"Is there anyone in your residence?"
He replied:
"No."
The woman said:
"I will visit you in the evening;
do not let anyone know."
The young master returned home,
and when dusk fell,
he dismissed his servants.
The woman indeed arrived,
and introduced herself:
"My given name is Wēnjī."
She also said:
"I admire your refinement, young master,
and have therefore come against my āo's wishes.
My humble intention
is to serve you for the rest of my life."
The young master was also pleased.
From then on, she would visit every two or three nights.
One evening,
she came in the rain,
and upon entering, she took off her wet clothes,
and hung them on the clothes rack;
she also took off the small boots on her feet,
and asked the young master to remove the mud for her.
She then got into bed and covered herself with the quilt.
The young master looked at her boots,
which were made of new five-colored brocade,
almost completely stained with mud.
He felt it a pity.
The woman said:
"I would not dare to bother you with such a humble item,
but wish for you to know how deeply I am infatuated."
Listening to the ceaseless rain outside the window,
she then chanted:
"The desolate wind and cold rain fill the river city."
She asked the young master to continue it.
The young master declined, saying he was not skilled.
The woman said:
"How can a gentleman such as you
be ignorant of elegance!
You have dampened my refined interest!"
She then urged him to practice,
and the young master assented.
As their comings and goings became frequent,
the servants all became aware.
The young master's brother-in-law, Sòng Shì,
who was also from a prominent family,
heard of it,
and secretly asked the young master for a glimpse of Wēnjī.
The young master spoke of it to her,
but the woman absolutely refused.
Sòng Shì then hid himself in the servants' quarters,
and waited for the woman to arrive.
He lay in wait by the window to peek at her,
and was so captivated he felt like going mad.
He hastily pushed open the door,
but the woman rose,
and climbed over the wall to leave.
Sòng Shì's yearning for her was very intense,
so he presented a gift to Xǔ Āo,
and specifically asked for her.
The āo said:
"There was indeed a Wēnjī,
but she has been dead for a long time."
Sòng Shì retreated in astonishment,
and informed the young master.
Only then did the young master realize she was a ghost.
That night,
he used Sòng Shì's words to try to dismiss the woman.
The woman said:
"Indeed.
You wish to have a beautiful woman,
and I also wish to have a handsome husband.
It is enough for each to fulfill their desires;
what does it matter if one is human and the other a ghost?"
The young master thought her words reasonable.
After the examination, he returned home,
and the woman also followed him.
Others could not see her,
only the young master could.
Upon arriving home,
he housed her in his study.
The young master stayed alone in his study and did not return home,
which made his parents suspicious.
When the woman returned for a visit,
he implicitly told his mother,
who was greatly alarmed,
and warned the young master to break off the relationship.
The young master could not obey.
His parents were deeply worried,
and tried every method to drive her away, but to no avail.
One day,
the young master had an instruction note for his servants
placed on his desk.
It contained many errors:
"椒 (jiāo)"
was mistakenly written as
"姜 (jiāng)"
was mistaken as
"江 (jiāng)",
and "可恨 (kěhèn)"
was mistaken as
"可浪 (kělàng)".
The woman saw it,
and wrote on its back:
"What is so 'kělàng' (disgraceful)?
'Huā Shū shēng Jiāng' (Flowers and beans grow in the river).
With such a husband,
it is better to be a prostitute!"
She then scolded the young master, saying:
"I initially thought you were a cultivated scholar from a prominent family,
and therefore shamefully recommended myself.
I never expected you to be merely a superficial appearance!
To judge people by their looks,
wouldn't that make me the laughingstock of the world!"
Having spoken, she vanished.
Although the young master was ashamed and resentful,
he still did not understand what she had written,
and folded the note to show his servants.
Those who heard of it spread it as a humorous anecdote.
The Historian of Anomalies (Yì Shǐ Shì) remarks:
"Wēnjī is lovely!
How could a graceful young master
be so harsh about what is contained within her!
It even led her to regret not being a prostitute;
truly, wives and concubines should be ashamed to hold their positions!
Yet, after all efforts failed to drive her away,
upon seeing the note, she departed indignantly.
Thus, 'Huā Shū shēng Jiāng'
is no different from Dù Fǔ's 'Zǐ Zhāng dúlóu'!"
The Ěr Lù (Record of Ears) says:
"A person selling beverages by the roadside
had a sign that read:
'Offering 'gōng' (respect)
to form connections.'
Mistaking 'chá' (tea) for 'gōng' (respect) is also laughable.
There was a young man from an old family,
who, having become poor,
put up a sign on his door that read:
'Selling ancient 'yín qì' (lewd instruments).'
Mistaking 'yáo' (jade) for 'yín' (lewd) in 'yáo qì' (jade artifacts), he wrote,
'Those who want 'yí yín' (suitable lewdness) or 'dìng yín' (fixed lewdness),
both large and small, are available.
Come inside to view the items and discuss prices.'
Such descendants of the Cuī and Lú clans are numerous,
why only blame
'Huā Shū shēng Jiāng'!"
According to the Zhùxuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáo Zhāi Zhì Yì.
Yīn Yuánlǐ,
a native of Yúnnán,
was skilled in the art of acupuncture and moxibustion.
When he encountered banditry and chaos,
he fled deep into the mountains.
As the day had already turned to dusk,
and the villages were still far away,
he feared encountering tigers and wolves.
He saw two people ahead on the path,
and quickly hastened to catch up with them.
When he reached them,
the two asked the guest where he had come from.
Yīn then introduced himself and his family background.
The two cupped their hands in respect and said:
"This is the excellent physician Mr. Yīn,
whose reputation we have long admired!"
Yīn then questioned them in turn,
and the two men said their surname was Bān,
one being Bān Zhuǎ,
and the other Bān Yá.
Then they said:
"Sir,
we are also escaping calamity,
and fortunately, a stone chamber offers a place to stay.
May we venture to trouble your esteemed footsteps?
We also have a request."
Yīn gladly followed them,
and soon arrived at a place
where the chamber was beside a rocky gorge.
They burned firewood as a substitute for candles,
and only then did Yīn see that the two Bāns had fierce and imposing appearances,
seeming not to be good people.
Having nowhere else to go,
he simply submitted to their lead.
He also heard groaning on a couch,
and upon careful examination,
it was an old woman lying stiff,
seemingly suffering from something.
He asked:
"What is the ailment?"
Yá said:
"It is for this reason
that we respectfully sought your presence, Sir."
Then he bundled fire to illuminate the couch,
and invited the guest to look closely.
He saw two large tumors below her nose and at the corners of her mouth,
both as big as bowls.
They also said:
"The pain is unbearable to touch,
and it obstructs eating and drinking."
Yīn said:
"It's easy."
He took out moxa wool,
and performed dozens of moxibustion applications,
saying:
"It will heal overnight."
The two Bāns were delighted,
and roasted deer to feed the guest;
there was no wine or rice,
only one kind of meat.
Zhuǎ said:
"We were caught unawares by your arrival,
please do not take our humble offerings amiss."
Yīn ate his fill and slept,
using a stone as a pillow.
Although the two Bāns were simple and unadorned,
their roughness and wildness were frightening,
so Yīn tossed and turned, not daring to sleep soundly.
Before dawn,
he called the old woman,
and asked about her illness.
The old woman had just woken up,
and when she felt herself,
the tumors had burst into wounds.
Yīn urged the two Bāns to get up,
brought a fire close to illuminate,
applied medicinal powder,
and said:
"It is healed."
He cupped his hands and took his leave.
Bān also gave him a roasted deer elbow.
For three years thereafter, there was no news.
Yīn happened to enter the mountains for some reason,
and encountered two wolves blocking the path,
preventing him from proceeding.
As the sun set,
more wolves arrived in a pack,
making him besieged front and back.
A wolf pounced on him,
and he fell;
several wolves fought to bite him,
his clothes were all torn.
