He resigned himself to certain death.
Suddenly, two tigers appeared swiftly,
and all the wolves scattered.
The tigers roared furiously,
and the wolves, terrified, all prostrated themselves.
The tigers killed them all,
and then departed.
Yīn, disheveled and in distress, continued his journey,
fearing he had nowhere to stay.
He met an old woman coming,
who, seeing his state,
said,
"Mr. Yīn has suffered greatly!"
Yīn sadly recounted his situation,
and asked how she knew him.
The old woman said:
"I am the patient whose tumors you moxibusted in the stone chamber."
Yīn then suddenly understood,
and asked to stay the night.
The old woman led him away,
into a courtyard
where lanterns were already lit,
and said:
"I have been waiting for you, Sir, for a long time."
Then she brought out robes and trousers,
to replace his worn-out ones.
She arranged refreshments and served wine,
urging him to drink with earnest sincerity.
The old woman also poured for herself from a clay bowl,
her conversation and drinking both unrestrained,
unlike a woman.
Yīn asked:
"Those two young men the other day,
what relation are they to you, old woman?
Why are they not to be seen?"
The old woman said:
"My two sons were sent to meet you, Sir,
but they have not yet returned,
they must have lost their way."
Yīn was touched by her kindness,
and drank heartily,
unaware that he had become deeply intoxicated,
and fell into a deep sleep in his seat.
When he awoke,
it was already dawn,
and looking around, there was no dwelling at all;
he was sitting alone on a rock.
He heard breathing like an ox from below the rock,
and upon closer inspection,
it was a tiger still asleep and not yet awake.
On its forehead were two scars,
both as big as a fist.
He was extremely alarmed,
fearing only that it would wake up,
and quietly slipped away and fled.
Only then did he realize that the two tigers were the two Bāns.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
A cart driver was carrying a child up a slope,
when he was exerting himself to the utmost,
a wolf came and bit his buttocks.
He wanted to let go,
but his cargo would crush him,
so he endured the pain and pushed it.
When he reached the top,
the wolf had already gnawed off a piece of flesh and left.
To secretly taste a morsel
at a moment when he was powerless to resist
was also cunning and laughable.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì:
Mǐ Bùyún of Zhāngqiū
was skilled in divination using a planchette.
Whenever he gathered with cultured friends,
he would summon immortals to compose poems in harmony.
One day,
a friend saw a faint cloud in the sky,
and got a line of poetry,
asking for an opposing couplet,
saying:
"White jade of sheep fat, a sky."
The planchette wrote:
"Ask old Dǒng from south of the city."
Everyone doubted its veracity.
Later, for some reason, he happened to go to the south of the city,
and arrived at a place
where the earth was like cinnabar,
which he found strange.
He saw an old man tending pigs nearby,
and so he asked him.
The old man said:
"This is 'pig blood red mud ground'."
Suddenly, he recalled the planchette's words,
and was greatly astonished.
He asked his surname,
and he replied:
"I am old Dǒng."
The opposing couplet was not extraordinary,
but to know beforehand about old Dǒng from south of the city—
this truly was divine!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Gōng Shēng,
a native of Mínzhōu,
went to Xī'ān for the imperial examinations.
Resting at an inn,
he bought wine and drank alone.
A burly man entered
and sat down to chat with him.
Gōng Shēng offered him a cup of wine,
and the guest did not refuse.
He introduced himself as Miáo,
speaking roughly and boisterously.
Gōng Shēng, finding him uncultured,
treated him with disdain.
When the wine was finished,
he did not buy more.
Miáo Shēng said:
"Scholars' drinking
makes one terribly bored!"
He rose and went to the counter to buy more,
returning with a large wine jar.
Gōng Shēng declined to drink,
but Miáo grabbed his arm, urging him to toast,
making his arm ache as if it would break.
Gōng Shēng had no choice
but to drink several more cups.
Miáo then drank from a large bowl,
laughing and saying:
"I'm not good at urging guests.
You may come and go as you please."
Gōng Shēng immediately packed his bags and set off.
After a few *lǐ*,
his horse fell ill and lay down on the road.
He sat by the roadside, waiting.
His baggage was heavy and cumbersome,
and he had no plan.
Miáo arrived shortly after.
Upon learning the reason,
he told Gōng Shēng's servant to take the baggage,
then hoisted the horse onto his shoulders by supporting its belly,
and walked for over twenty *lǐ*
until they reached an inn,
where he released the horse into a stable.
After some time,
Gōng Shēng and his servant arrived.
Gōng Shēng was amazed, thinking him a spirit.
He treated him with great hospitality,
buying wine and food
to share with him.
Miáo said:
"I'm a hearty eater;
you can't satisfy me.
But a good drink is fine."
He emptied a jar of wine
and then rose to bid farewell, saying:
"It will take some time for you to cure your horse.
I cannot wait.
I must go."
And so, he left.
Later, after Gōng Shēng's examinations were over,
three or four friends invited him to ascend Huàshān.
They spread out a mat on the ground for a banquet.
As they were feasting and laughing together,
Miáo suddenly arrived,
carrying a huge wine jar in his left hand
and a pork shoulder in his right.
He threw them to the ground and said:
"I heard you gentlemen were climbing the mountain,
so I came along."
Everyone rose to greet him,
and they sat together in mixed company,
drinking heartily and making merry.
The group wished to compose linked verses.
Miáo protested, saying:
"Heavy drinking is a delight,
why bother with melancholy thoughts?"
The others did not listen
and imposed the
"Jīngǔ penalty."
Miáo said:
"Those who do poorly
shall be dealt with by military law!"
Everyone laughed, saying:
"The crime doesn't warrant that."
Miáo replied:
"If you don't punish them,
even I, a mere warrior, can do it."
Jìn Shēng, who sat at the head, said:
"The vast panorama makes the eyes feel empty."
Miáo then blurted out:
"Spittoons shatter, sword light glows red."
The person at the lower seat pondered for a long time,
so Miáo poured himself a drink from the jar.
After a while,
the verses were composed in turn,
gradually becoming vulgar.
Miáo shouted:
"This is enough!
If you want to spare me,
don't compose any more!"
The others did not listen.
Miáo could bear it no longer.
He suddenly let out a dragon's roar,
and the valleys echoed.
He then stood up and performed a lion dance, bowing and straightening.
Their poetic inspiration was disrupted,
so the company ceased their versifying
and resumed drinking, passing cups around.
By then, they were half-drunk.
The guests then recited poems composed amidst the revelry,
praising each other repeatedly.
Miáo did not wish to listen.
He pulled Gōng Shēng into a finger-guessing game.
They played many rounds, with wins and losses,
but the other guests continued their recitations and praises without end.
Miáo said in a stern voice:
"I have heard enough of this.
Such writings are only fit to be read to old women by the bedside,
and this incessant chatter in a large gathering is truly annoying!"
The others looked ashamed,
but they were even more annoyed by his rudeness,
so they recited their poems even louder.
Miáo became furious.
He crouched down and let out a great roar,
instantly transforming into a tiger,
which pounced on and killed the other guests,
then roared and departed.
The only ones left were
Gōng Shēng and Jìn Shēng.
Jìn Shēng was the top recommendee in that examination.
Three years later,
passing through Huàyīn again,
Jìn Shēng suddenly saw Yóu Shēng,
who was also one of those devoured on the mountain.
Terrified, Jìn Shēng tried to flee,
but Yóu Shēng grabbed his bridle, preventing him from moving.
Jìn Shēng dismounted
and asked him what he was doing.
Yóu Shēng replied:
"I am now Miáo's *chāng* (tiger's familiar),
and this servitude is truly苦苦苦bitter.
I must kill another scholar
to be replaced.
In three days,
a scholar wearing scholarly attire
will be devoured by the tiger.
However, it must be below Cānglóng Lǐng
for him to be my replacement.
On that day,
please invite many literati here.
This will be a plan for your old friend."
Jìn Shēng dared not argue
and respectfully agreed before parting.
Upon reaching his lodgings,
he deliberated all night,
unsure how to devise a plan.
He decided to break his promise
and accept the ghost's retribution.
Coincidentally, his cousin Jiǎng Shēng arrived.
Jìn Shēng recounted the strange events to him.
Jiǎng Shēng was a lesser scholar,
and Yóu Shēng's examination ranking was above his in their district.
He secretly harbored jealousy.
Hearing Jìn Shēng's words,
he secretly plotted to entrap Yóu Shēng.
He wrote a note inviting Yóu Shēng
to climb the mountain with him.
He himself wore white clothes and stayed behind,
though Yóu Shēng did not understand his intention.
Halfway up the ridge,
food and wine were laid out,
and Jìn Shēng showed utmost courtesy.
At that moment, the Prefectural Governor, who was a family friend of Jiǎng Shēng,
was also ascending the ridge.
Hearing that Jiǎng Shēng was below,
he sent someone to summon him.
Jiǎng Shēng dared not go in white clothes,
so he exchanged caps and robes with Yóu Shēng.
Before the exchange was complete,
the tiger suddenly arrived,
seized Jiǎng Shēng, and carried him away.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Those who are self-satisfied and garrulous,
grabbing sleeves and forcing people to listen;
the listeners yawn repeatedly,
wanting to sleep or flee,
while the reciters stamp their feet and wave their hands,
completely unaware.
Even close friends should nudge or step on them from the side,
lest there be an impatient Miáo Shēng in the audience.
However, the jealous one changed clothes and died,
from which we know that Miáo also had no particular intention;
thus, the one who caused the aversion and anger was Miáo — not Miáo."
(Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*)
A merchant from Nánshāng who sold scorpions,
every year would travel to Línqú
and purchase a great many.
The local people would take wooden tongs and go into the mountains,
searching holes, overturning rocks, and capturing them.
One year,
the merchant came again
and stayed at an inn.
Suddenly, he felt his heart stir,
and his hair stood on end in horror.
He quickly told the innkeeper,
“I have taken many lives,
and now I have incurred the wrath of the scorpion spirits;
they are going to kill me!
Please save me quickly!”
The innkeeper looked at a large urn in the room,
then told him to squat down
and covered him with the urn.
After a while,
a person rushed in,
with yellow hair and a hideous appearance.
He asked the innkeeper,
“Where is the southern merchant?”
The innkeeper replied,
“He went out.”
The person entered the room, looked around,
and sniffed three times with his nose,
then left.
The innkeeper said,
“Fortunately, you are safe.”
When he lifted the urn to look at the guest,
the guest had already turned into bloody water.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dù Xiǎoléi,
a man from the western mountains of Yìdū.
His mother was blind in both eyes.
Dù served her with great filial piety,
and though his family was poor,
she never lacked delicious food.
One day,
he was going out,
so he bought meat and gave it to his wife,
telling her to make *bótuō*.
His wife was extremely perverse;
while cutting the meat, she mixed scarab beetles into it.
His mother noticed the foul smell and found it inedible,
so she hid it to wait for her son.
When Dù returned,
he asked,
“Was the *bótuō* good?”
His mother shook her head
and showed it to her son.
Dù tore it open and saw the scarab beetles,
and was extremely angry.
He went into the room,
intending to beat his wife,
but then feared his mother would hear.
He lay on the bed, deep in thought.
His wife asked him,
but he did not speak.
His wife, feeling disheartened,
wandered by the bed.
After a long time,
there was a sound of panting.
Dù shouted,
“Not sleeping?
Are you waiting for a beating?!”
Then he felt it was quiet.
He got up and lit a candle,
only to see a pig.
Upon closer inspection,
its two feet were still human-like,
and he then realized it was his wife transformed.
The county magistrate heard of it,
arrested it,
and had it paraded through the four gates
to warn everyone.
Tán Wēichén once saw it himself.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Máo Dàfú from Tàiháng,
was a surgeon.
One day,
returning after practicing his art,
he encountered a wolf on the road,
which spat out a wrapped object
and squatted on the left side of the road.
Máo picked it up and looked,
and it was a cloth wrapping several gold ornaments.
While he was still wondering at this strangeness,
the wolf came forward, frolicked,
and slightly pulled his robe,
then left.
Máo continued walking,
and it pulled him again.
Noticing its intentions were not hostile,
he followed it.
Before long,
they reached a cave,
where he saw a sick wolf lying down.
He saw a large sore on its head,
ulcerated and full of maggots.
Máo understood its meaning,
cleaned it thoroughly,
applied medicine as prescribed,
and then left.
As it was already late,
the wolf escorted him for a distance.
After walking three or four *lǐ*,
he met several more wolves,
which roared and approached aggressively.
He was extremely frightened.
The first wolf quickly entered their group,
as if speaking to them,
and all the wolves dispersed.
Máo then returned home.
Previously,
in the county, there was a silver merchant, Níng Tài,
who had been robbed and murdered on the road,
and no one could identify the culprits.
When Máo sold the gold ornaments,
they were recognized by the Níng family,
who seized him and took him to court.
Máo explained where they came from,
but the official did not believe him
and put him in shackles.
Máo was extremely wronged and could not clear himself,
only requesting to be released
and for the wolves to be questioned.
The official sent two constables to escort him into the mountains,
straight to the wolf's den.
It so happened that the wolves had not yet returned,
and by evening they still had not arrived,
so the three returned.
Halfway back,
they met two wolves,
one of which still had the scar.
Máo recognized it,
bowed to it and prayed,
“Before, I received your gift,
and now I am being wrongfully accused because of it.
If you do not clear my name,
I will die from flogging when I return!”
When the wolf saw Máo in shackles,
it angrily rushed at the constables.
The constables drew their swords.
The wolf propped its snout on the ground and howled loudly;
after two or three howls,
a hundred wolves gathered from the mountains
and surrounded the constables.
The constables were in a dire predicament.
The wolves aggressively came forward and gnawed at the shackles and ropes.
The constables understood their intent,
untied Máo,
and then the wolves all left.
When they returned and recounted the situation,
the official was surprised,
but did not immediately release Máo.
Several days later,
the official was traveling,
and a wolf carried a worn-out shoe and left it on the road.
When the official passed by,
the wolf again carried the shoe, ran ahead, and placed it on the road.
The official ordered the shoe to be collected,
and the wolf then left.
When the official returned,
he secretly sent someone to inquire about the shoe's owner.
It was reported that a woodcutter in a certain village
had been chased by two wolves,
who carried off his shoes.
The woodcutter was detained and asked to identify it;
indeed, it was his shoe.
Thus, it was suspected that the woodcutter must have been the one who killed Níng,
and when interrogated, it turned out to be true.
It was the woodcutter who killed Níng,
took his large sum of gold,
and hid the ornaments under his clothes.
He had not yet had time to put them away when they were carried off by the wolves.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Once, a midwife was returning home
when she met a wolf blocking the road,
pulling her clothes as if to summon her.
So she followed,
and saw a female wolf giving birth with difficulty.
The old woman helped by pressing and assisting,
and after the birth, she was allowed to return.
The next day,
the wolf carried deer meat and placed it at her home to repay her.
From this, one can know that such incidents have often occurred.
The magistrate of Chángshān, Yáng,
was extraordinarily greedy.
During the Yǐhài year of the Kāngxī reign (1695),
troops were deployed to Xīsài,
requisitioning mules and horses from the common people to transport grain.
Yáng used this as a pretext to confiscate,
emptying the local area of its livestock.
Zhōucūn was a gathering place for merchants,
and those who came to the market had a constant stream of carts and horses.
Yáng led his able-bodied men to seize them all,
no fewer than several hundred head.
Merchants from all directions
had nowhere to complain.
At that time, the other magistrates were all in the provincial capital on official business.
Coincidentally, Magistrate Dǒng of Yìdū, Magistrate Fàn of Láiwú, and Magistrate Sūn of Xīnchéng
had gathered in a guesthouse.
Two merchants from Shānxī
came to the door, crying out their grievances.
They complained that they had four strong mules,
all of which had been plundered.
Being far from home and deprived of their livelihood,
they could not return.
They tearfully begged the gentlemen to intercede for them.
The three gentlemen pitied their situation
and agreed.
So they went together to see Yáng.
Yáng prepared a feast to entertain them.
After the wine had been served,
the group stated their purpose.
Yáng would not listen.
The group pressed their case more urgently.
Yáng raised his cup, urging them to drink to disrupt the conversation,
saying:
"I have a game,
and those who cannot do it will be punished.
There must be one in the heavens, one on earth, and one ancient person.
The attendants on the left and right will ask what object is held,
and what words are spoken,
and you must answer as asked."
Then he initiated, saying:
"In the heavens there is the moon's orb,
on earth there is Kūnlún,
and there is an ancient person, Liú Bólún.
The left asks what object is held,
and the answer is: 'I hold a wine cup.'
The right asks what words are spoken from the mouth,
and the answer is:
'It is said that nothing beyond the wine cup need be mentioned.'"
Magistrate Fàn said:
"In the heavens there is Guǎnghán Palace,
on earth there is Qiánqīng Palace,
and there is an ancient person, Jiāng Tàigōng.
He holds a fishing rod,
and says: 'Those who wish may take the bait.'"
Sūn said:
"In the heavens there is the Tiānhé (Milky Way),
on earth there is the Huánghé (Yellow River),
and there is an ancient person, Xiāo Hé.
He holds a copy of the Great Qīng Code,
and he says: 'Corrupt officials and corrupt clerks!'"
Yáng showed a look of shame,
pondered for a long time,
and said:
"I have another one.
In the heavens there is Língshān,
on earth there is Tàishān,
and there is an ancient person, Hánshān.
He holds a broom,
and says: 'Everyone sweeps the snow from their own doorstep.'"
The others looked at each other with embarrassment.
Suddenly, a young man entered with an arrogant bearing,
his robes splendid and neat.
He raised his hands in a bow.
They all invited him to sit
and poured him wine in a large cup.
The young man smiled and said:
"Do not drink the wine yet.
I have heard of your elegant game,
and wish to offer my humble thoughts."
The others invited him.
The young man said:
"In the heavens there is the Jade Emperor,
on earth there is the Emperor,
and there is an ancient person, the Hóngwǔ Zhū Emperor.
He holds a three-foot sword,
and says: 'Corrupt officials will be skinned!'"
Everyone burst into laughter.
Yáng, enraged, cursed and said:
"What arrogant fellow dares to be so rude!"
He ordered his subordinates to seize him.
The young man leaped onto the table,
transformed into an owl,
flew out through the curtain,
and perched among the courtyard trees.
He looked back into the room
and made a laughing sound.
The master of the house struck at it,
but it flew away, laughing as it went.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"During the requisition of horses,
seven out of ten of the great magistrates had strong livestock filling their courtyards,
but as for those who dealt in mules and horses,
assembling them in groups of hundreds and thousands,
it was rarely seen outside of Chángshān.
The wise and sagacious emperor cherished the people's strength,
surely compensating for every item taken.
How could he know that those who carried out his orders would cause such widespread suffering?
When an owl arrives,
people most dislike its laughter,
and children spit at it together,
considering it inauspicious.
But this laugh,
how is it different from the singing of a thousand phoenixes!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of _Liáozhāi Zhìyì_.
The well in Běicūn, Zīyì, dried up.
Villagers Jiǎ and Yǐ climbed down to dredge it.
After digging a little over a foot,
they found a skull.
They accidentally broke it open,
and it contained gold in its mouth.
Happily, they put it into their waist pouches.
They dug again,
and found six or seven more skulls.
They broke them all open,
but found no gold.
Beside them were two porcelain bottles and one bronze vessel.
The vessel was large enough to be embraced,
weighing dozens of pounds,
with a pair of rings on its side,
whose purpose was unknown;
it was mottled and variegated.
The bottles were also ancient,
not of recent make.
As soon as they came out of the well,
Jiǎ and Yǐ both died.
After a while, Yǐ revived
and said:
"I am a Hàn person.
During the chaos of Xīn Máng,
my whole family threw themselves into the well.
I happened to have a little gold,
and put it in my mouth;
it was not an object accumulated by everyone.
Why did you shatter all our skulls?
The situation is truly hateful!"
The crowd collectively prayed with incense and paper,
promising a proper burial,
and Yǐ then recovered;
Jiǎ, however, could not be revived.
Sūn Shēng from Yánzhèn heard of this strange event
and bought the bronze vessel.
Yuán Xiàolián Xuān Sī obtained one of the bottles,
which could detect changes in yin and darkness: when a moist spot appeared,
initially like a grain of millet,
it gradually widened and filled the bottle.
Soon after, rain would come;
when the moisture receded,
the clouds would clear and the sky would brighten.
The other bottle entered Zhāng Xiùcái's house,
and could record the new and full moons: at the new moon, a black spot would rise like a bean,
growing larger with each passing day;
at the full moon, the entire bottle would be filled;
after the full moon,
it would gradually recede,
returning to its original state by the last day of the month.
Because it had been buried in the earth for a long time,
there was a small stone stuck to the mouth of the bottle,
which could not be brushed off or removed.
When they tapped it off,
the stone fell, and the mouth was slightly chipped,
which was a pity.
When flowers were steeped in it,
the fallen flowers would bear fruit,
seemingly no different from those on the tree.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of _Liáozhāi Zhìyì_.
When Hán Yuánshào先生 was a student,
an official suddenly arrived,
and announced that his master wished to engage him as a teacher,
but there was no name card.
When asked about his family's lineage,
the official answered vaguely.
The gifts of silk and other offerings
were exceedingly generous.
先生 agreed,
set a date, and the official departed.
On the appointed day,
a carriage indeed came for him.
When it finally set off,
the roads were all unfamiliar.
Suddenly, he saw palaces and pavilions.
After he alighted,
the atmosphere resembled a prince's mansion.
Once he was settled in his quarters,
wine and roasted meats were lavishly served,
and guests were encouraged to help themselves,
but there was no host.
When the feast was cleared,
the young master came out to bow;
he was fifteen or sixteen years old,
with a remarkably handsome and distinguished appearance.
After the courtesies were exchanged,
he went to another room,
and only then did he come to the teacher's place to receive instruction.
The young master was very intelligent,
grasping every concept as soon as he heard it.
先生, being unaware of the family's background,
felt quite doubtful and uneasy.
There were two pages attending in the馆,
and he privately questioned them,
but they both refused to answer.
He asked:
"Where is the master?"
They replied that he was busy.
先生 sought guidance to catch a glimpse of him,
but the pages refused.
After repeated requests,
they finally led him to a place
where he heard the sounds of flogging and torture.
Looking intently through a crack in the door,
he saw a king seated in the hall,
and below the steps were sword trees and knife mountains,
all things of the underworld.
Greatly alarmed,
just as he was about to step back,
the king inside already knew of it,
and therefore paused his administration,
shouted for the ghosts to retreat,
and urgently called the page.
The page's expression changed, and he said:
"Because of先生,
misfortune has befallen me!"
Trembling, he rushed inside.
The king angrily said:
"How dare you lead someone to peek inside!"
He then severely flogged the page with a huge whip.
Then he summoned先生 in,
saying:
"The reason I did not appear
is because the realms of the living and the dead are different paths.
Now that you know,
it is difficult for us to be together again."
He then gave him a bundle of gold and bade him leave,
saying:
"You are the foremost person in the world,
only your trials are not yet complete."
He sent a servant in green clothes to escort him on horseback.
先生 suspected that he was already dead.
The servant in green clothes said:
"How can that be!
All that先生 ate and used
came from the mortal world,
not things of the underworld."
Upon his return,
he experienced hardship for several years,
then passed the provincial and national examinations,
and the king's words all proved true.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì:
Fēng Yùguì,
was a scholar from Liáochéng.
He was poor and without a livelihood.
During the Wànlì era,
there was a great famine,
and he fled south alone.
When he returned,
he fell ill upon reaching Yí.
He forced himself to walk a few Lǐ,
and reaching a communal burial ground south of the city,
he became even more exhausted,
and so lay down by a tomb.
Suddenly, as if in a dream,
he arrived at a village,
where an old man came out from a door
and invited him in.
The house had two pillars,
and was also rather crude.
Inside the room was a young woman,
sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a bright and elegant appearance.
The old man quickly had her brew a soup of cypress branches,
and served it to the guest in an earthenware vessel.
Then he questioned the student about his hometown and age.
Afterward,
he said:
"My surname is Lǐ from Hóngdū,
a clan from Píngyáng.
I have been living here as a migrant
for thirty-two years now.
Please remember this door and house number.
If my children and grandchildren come looking for me,
I would trouble you to direct them.
This old man would not forget your kindness.
My adopted daughter Wèiniáng
is not at all ugly,
and could be a match for a gentleman.
When the three pig-sons arrive,
I will send them to be the matchmakers."
The student was delighted,
and bowed, saying:
"My age is twenty-two,
and I still lack a good spouse.
Your kind intention and favor
are truly excellent;
but where can I find your family members to tell them?"
The old man said:
"You just stay in the North Village.
Wait for more than a month,
and someone will naturally come.
Just ask that you not mind the trouble."
The scholar feared his words were untrue,
and pressed him, saying:
"Tell me truthfully, old man: my former home was utterly destitute.
I fear that later it may not turn out as hoped,
and being abandoned midway
is something people find hard to bear.
Even if there is no marital connection,
I dare not fail to keep the promise of Jìlù,
so why not speak plainly?"
The old man smiled and said:
"Do you want this old man to swear every day?
I well know you are poor.
This betrothal is not solely for you;
to comfort Niáng's孤 and the helpless,
she has been entrusted to me for a long time.
I cannot bear to see her wander destitute,
so I offer her to you, a gentleman.
Why doubt me!"
He then grabbed the scholar's arm and saw him out,
cupped his hands, closed the door, and left.
The scholar awoke,
finding himself lying by the tomb,
with the sun already near noon.
He slowly rose
and hesitantly entered the village.
The villagers were all shocked to see him,
thinking he had died by the roadside days ago.
He suddenly realized that the old man was the person from the tomb,
who had concealed his identity,
merely seeking lodging.
The villagers feared they might also die
and no one dared to take him in.
There was a xiùcai in the village who shared the same surname as him.
Hearing of this,
he hurried to inquire about his family background,
discovering that the scholar was his uncle by the five-month mourning attire.
Happily, he led him home,
fed and treated him,
and he recovered in a few days.
He then recounted what he had encountered,
and his uncle was also surprised and amazed.
So, they sat and waited to observe what would happen.
Not long after,
a palace attendant indeed arrived at the village,
looking for his father's grave site.
He identified himself as Lǐ Shūxiàng, a Jìnshì from Píngyáng.
Earlier,
his father, Lǐ Hóngdōu,
had gone trading with a certain Mǒu Jiǎ from the same鄉,
and died at Yí,
whereupon Mǒu buried him in a place of scattered graves.
After returning,
Mǒu also died.
At that time, the old man's three sons were all young.
The eldest, Bórén,
passed the Jìnshì examination
and became a magistrate in Huáinán.
He sent people numerous times to search for his father's grave,
but no one knew its location.
The second, Zhòngdào,
was recommended as Xiàolián.
Shūxiàng, the youngest,
also passed the imperial examination.
Thereupon, he personally sought his father's bones,
going to Yí and searching everywhere.
On this day he arrived,
but none of the villagers knew the location.
The scholar then led him to the tomb site
and pointed it out.
Shūxiàng dared not believe it,
so the scholar fully recounted what he had encountered.
Shūxiàng found it extraordinary.
Upon careful examination, the two graves were adjacent.
Someone said that three years ago a eunuch
had buried a young concubine there.
Shūxiàng feared disturbing another family's grave,
so the scholar then showed him where he had slept.
Shūxiàng ordered a coffin to be placed beside it,
and then they began to open the tomb.
When the tomb was opened,
they saw a female corpse,
her clothes and adornments faded and ruined,
but her powder and makeup were as if she were alive.
Shūxiàng realized his mistake,
was extremely shocked,
and didn't know what to do.
But the woman had already risen abruptly,
looked around and said:
"Is Third Brother here?"
Shūxiàng was startled,
and went to ask her,
and it was Wèiniáng.
He then took off his clothes to cover her,
and carried her back to the inn.
He quickly opened the adjacent tomb,
hoping his father would revive.
When it was opened,
his skin and flesh were still intact,
but when touched, they were stiff and dry.
He grieved incessantly.
They dressed and coffined his father's remains,
and offered clear sacrifices for seven days;
the woman also wore mourning clothes as if she were his daughter.
She suddenly told Shūxiàng:
"Earlier, old Áwēng had two ingots of gold.
He once gave one to me as part of my dowry.
Being alone and vulnerable with no place to hide it,
I merely tied it to my waist with silk thread,
but did not take it with me.
Did you find it, brother?"
Shūxiàng did not know,
so he sent the scholar back to search the tomb,
and indeed found it,
exactly as the woman had said.
Shūxiàng then gave the ingot marked with the thread to Wèiniáng.
In his leisure, he then inquired about her family background.
Previously,
the woman's father, Xuē Yínhóu, had no sons,
only Wèiniáng,
whom he loved dearly.
One day,
the woman was returning from her maternal uncle's home in Jīnlíng,
and asked an old woman to ferry her across.
The boatman was a matchmaker from Jīnlíng.
Coincidentally, there was an official
whose term had ended and was going to the capital.
He had sent people to find a beautiful concubine,
but having visited several families,
no one pleased him,
so he was about to take a small boat to Guǎnglíng.
Suddenly he met the woman,
and a treacherous scheme arose in his mind.
He quickly hailed them to board the ferry.
The old woman knew him well,
so she crossed with him.
Midway,
he put poison in the food,
and both the woman and the old woman became disoriented.
He pushed the old woman into the river;
carried the woman back,
and sold her for a large sum to the official.
Upon entering the household,
the legitimate wife first found out
and was furious.
The woman was also bewildered
and did not know how to behave properly,
so she was beaten and imprisoned.
Three days after crossing north,
the woman finally woke up.
A maid told her the whole story,
and the woman wept greatly.
One night,
staying at Yí,
she hanged herself and died,
and was then buried in a scattered grave.
While the woman was in the tomb,
she was harassed by a multitude of ghosts.
Old Lǐ then protected her,
so the woman treated the old man as her father.
The old man said:
"It is your fate not to die,
and I should choose a good husband for you."
After the scholar had seen her and left,
he instead told the woman:
"This scholar's character and integrity are trustworthy.
When your third brother arrives,
I will arrange your marriage."
One day he said:
"You can go back and wait;
your third brother is about to come."
This was the day the tomb was opened.
While in mourning, the woman
recounted this to Shūxiàng.
Shūxiàng sighed for a long time,
then took Wèiniáng as his sister,
allowing her to take the surname Lǐ.
He bought some clothes and makeup,
sent her back to the scholar,
and furthermore said:
"I don't have much money,
so I cannot prepare a dowry for my sister.
“I intend to borrow her to return [home],
to comfort my mother’s heart,
how about that?”
The daughter also was pleased.
Thereupon, the couple followed Shū Xiàng,
transporting the coffin and departing together.
When they arrived home,
the mother questioned them and learned the reason,
loving her even more than her own children,
housing her in a separate courtyard.
During the mourning period,
the daughter’s grief and lamentation surpassed that of her own children and grandchildren.
The mother pitied her even more,
not allowing her to return east,
instructing her sons to buy a house for her.
Coincidentally, there was a Fēng-shì selling a house,
for a price of six hundred jīn.
They were hastily unable to raise the full amount,
so they temporarily accepted the contract,
agreeing on a day for the exchange.
When the day arrived,
Fēng-mǒu arrived early;
coincidentally, the daughter also came from the separate courtyard to visit her mother,
suddenly seeing him,
he looked exactly like the boatman from that year.
Fēng-mǒu was also startled upon seeing her.
The daughter hurried past him.
Her two elder brothers also, due to their mother’s slight illness,
had all gathered at their mother’s place.
The daughter asked:
“Who is that person pacing outside the hall?”
Zhòng Dào said:
“This must be the person who sold the house the other day.”
He immediately rose, wanting to go out.
The daughter stopped him,
telling him of her suspicion,
and asked him to question the man thoroughly.
Zhòng Dào agreed and went out,
but Fēng-mǒu had already left,
and in his place was Xuē Xiānshēng, the tutor from the south of the lane.
He then asked:
“Why are you here?”
He replied:
“Last night, Fēng-mǒu asked me to come early,
to sign as a guarantor for the contract.
I happened to meet him on the way,
he said he had forgotten something,
and would return temporarily and come back soon,
asking me to sit and wait for him.”
After a short while,
Shēng and Shū Xiàng all arrived,
and they began to chat.
Wèi Niáng, due to Fēng-mǒu,
secretly came behind the screen to peek at the guest,
and upon closer inspection,
it was her father.
She rushed out,
embracing him and crying loudly.
The old man, startled, wept and said:
“My child, why are you here!”
Only then did everyone realize that Xuē was Yín Hóu.
Although Zhòng Dào often met him on the street,
he had never known his name.
At this point, everyone rejoiced,
recounting the previous events,
and set up a banquet to celebrate.
They kept him for a night,
and he recounted his own travels.
It turned out that after losing his daughter,
his wife died of grief,
and he, a widower, had no one to rely on,
so he wandered as a scholar until he reached this place.
Shēng agreed that after buying the house,
he would welcome him to live with them.
The old man went to investigate the next day,
but Fēng-mǒu had already fled with his entire family,
so they realized that the person who killed the old woman and sold his daughter
was indeed him.
Fēng-mǒu initially came to Píngyáng
and built a family through trade;
but in recent years, due to gambling,
his wealth gradually diminished,
which is why he sold his residence,
and the money from selling his daughter
was also almost depleted.
Wèi Niáng had found her place,
and did not harbor much hatred towards him,
but merely chose a day to move,
no longer pursuing his whereabouts.
Lǐ Mǔ continuously sent gifts,
supplying all their daily necessities.
Shēng thus made his home in Píngyáng,
but his attempts to pass the imperial examinations were very difficult.
Fortunately, in that year’s examination, he was selected as a Xiàolián.
Wèi Niáng, now wealthy and noble,
often thought of the old woman, believing her to be dead,
and wished to repay her son.
The old woman’s husband’s surname was Yīn,
and her son’s name was Fù,
who was fond of gambling,
and so poor he had no place to stand.
One day,
he quarreled over a stake at a gambling table,
and in an ensuing fight, killed someone,
so he fled to Píngyáng,
seeking refuge with Wèi Niáng from afar.
Shēng then kept him as a retainer.
When he thoroughly questioned him about the name of the person he killed,
it turned out to be Fēng-mǒu, the boatman.
They were shocked and sighed for a long time,
and then informed him of the truth,
only then did he realize that Fēng-mǒu was the enemy who had killed his mother.
He was even more pleased,
and thus served at Shēng’s house.
Xuē Yín Hóu was supported by his son-in-law,
who bought him a wife,
and they had one son and one daughter.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Tián Zǐchéng
of Jiāngníng, crossing Dòngtíng
Lake, his boat capsized and he drowned.
Tián Zǐliáng,
a *jìnshì* during the late Míng
dynasty, was still an infant in arms at the time.
His wife, Lady Dù,
upon hearing the news,
took poison and died.
Zǐliáng was raised and brought up by his adoptive grandmother,
and began his official career in Húběi.
After a year or so,
he received a provincial command to manage military affairs in Húnán.
When he reached Dòngtíng,
he wept bitterly and turned back.
He declared that his abilities were insufficient,
and was demoted to county magistrate's aide (*xiànchéng*),
serving under Hànyáng.
He resigned and did not take the post.
The governor and judicial commissioner
strongly urged him, so he took the position.
He often roamed idly among the rivers and lakes,
not holding himself to the standards of his office.
One evening,
as he moored his boat by the riverbank,
he heard the sound of a *dòngxiāo*,
its melody rising and falling beautifully.
Following the moonlight, he walked for
about half a *lǐ*,
and saw a few thatched huts in an open field,
with glimmering lamplight.
Peeking through a window nearby,
he saw three people drinking together inside.
The one in the seat of honor was a *xiùcai*,
about thirty years old;
below him was an old man;
and the one on the side playing the *xiāo*
was the youngest.
When the music finished,
the old man beat time and praised it as excellent.
The *xiùcai* faced the wall, lost in thought,
as if he hadn't heard.
The old man said:
"Lú Shíxiōng must have composed a fine piece.
Please recite it at length,
so we may all enjoy it."
The *xiùcai* then recited:
"The river is full of cold, desolate wind and moon,
withered grass and fallen flowers have turned to mud.
A thousand *lǐ* of clouds and mountains, I cannot fly over,
my dream-soul returns night after night to the west of the bamboo bridge."
His voice was mournful.
The old man smiled and said:
"Lú Shíxiōng is back to his old ways!"
He then poured him a large goblet
and said:
"This old man cannot compose a reply,
please sing to accompany the wine."
He then sang
the verses of
"Lánlíng Měijiǔ."
After the song,
everyone in the company was delighted.
The young man rose and said:
"I've seen how many times the moon has slanted."
Suddenly, he saw the guest
and clapped his hands, saying:
"Someone is outside the window!
All our wild behavior has been exposed!"
Then he pulled the guest in,
and they all exchanged greetings.
The old man had him sit opposite the young man.
When they offered him wine, it was all cold,
so he declined to drink.
The young man rose
and used a reed torch to warm the pot before serving it.
Zǐliáng also ordered his attendant to fetch money to buy more wine,
but the old man firmly stopped him.
Then, inquiring about his family and clan,
Zǐliáng recounted his life story.
The old man paid his respects, saying:
"You are the parents of our village.
The young gentleman's surname is Jiāng,
a native of this place."
He pointed to the young man and said:
"This is Jiāng Xīshè Yěhóu."
Then he pointed to the *xiùcai*:
"This is Lú Shíxiōng,
a fellow townsman of yours."
From the moment Lú saw Zǐliáng,
he was rather aloof and not very polite.
Zǐliáng then asked:
"Where is your home?
With such refined talent,
it's surprising I haven't heard of you earlier."
He replied:
"I have been a wanderer for a long time.
My relatives often don't recognize each other.
Alas, what a man!"
He spoke with sorrow.
The old man waved his hand, interrupting him:
"When good friends meet,
we don't bother with the rules of drinking.
Such chattering,
it tires one to listen!"
He then raised his cup and drank,
saying:
"Now let us all proceed together;
whoever cannot will be penalized.
Each time we throw three dice,
and 'meeting each other' is the theme,
it must match a classical allusion."
He then threw a one, a two, and a three,
and chanted:
"Three plus one and two make the same points,
the chicken and millet appointment of Fàn Gōng for three years: friends rejoice in meeting."
Next was the young man,
who threw two twos and a four,
saying:
"I am an unlettered man,
I only know common sayings,
don't laugh at me.
Four plus two twos make the same points,
four men gathered in righteousness in the ancient city: brothers rejoice in meeting."
Lú got two ones and a two,
saying:
"Two plus two ones make the same points,
Lǚ Xiàng held an old man in both hands: father and son rejoice in meeting."
Zǐliáng threw,
and it was the same as Lú's,
saying:
"Two plus two ones make the same points,
Máo Róng served Lín Zōng with two bowls: host and guest rejoice in meeting."
When the game finished,
Zǐliáng prepared to leave.
Lú then rose,
saying:
"The sentiments of our hometown,
I haven't had time to express them fully.
Why depart so suddenly?
I have something to ask,
please stay a little longer."
Zǐliáng sat down again,
asking:
"What is it?"
He said:
"I have an old friend, a certain Mr. So-and-so,
who drowned in Dòngtíng Lake.
Is he of the same clan as you?"
Zǐliáng said:
"He is my late father.
How did you know him?"
He replied:
"We were good friends when young.
On the day he drowned,
only I saw him,
and so I collected his bones
and buried them by the riverbank."
Zǐliáng shed tears and prostrated himself,
asking for the location of the tomb.
Lú said:
"Come here tomorrow,
and I will show you.
It's also easy to distinguish;
a few *bù* from here,
just look for a clump of ten old reeds on the grave, that's it."
Zǐliáng, weeping,
bowed in farewell to the group.
Reaching his boat,
he couldn't sleep all night,
pondering Lú's words and sentiments, which seemed to all have a hidden meaning.
At dawn, when he went
to the place, the huts were completely gone,
which startled him even more.
He then followed the directions to search for the tomb
and indeed found it.
A clump of reeds was on it,
and counting them,
the number perfectly matched.
He suddenly realized that the name "Lú Shíxiōng"
was all an allegory,
and that the person he had met
was the ghost of his father.
Upon asking the locals in detail,
he learned that twenty years ago,
there was an old man named Gāo, who was rich and benevolent,
and would rescue the bodies of those who drowned and bury them.
Hence, there were several graves there.
So, he opened the grave and carried his father's bones,
abandoning his official post and returning home.
He told his grandmother,
and she confirmed that the descriptions of their appearances were all accurate.
Jiāng Xīshè Yěhóu
was his maternal cousin,
who was nineteen years old
when he drowned in the river;
later, his father became a wanderer in Jiāngxī.
He also realized that after Lady Dù died,
she was buried to the west of the bamboo bridge,
which was why the speaker remembered it.
But I don't know who Yú is.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*,
Wáng Xī,
courtesy name Guì'ān,
was a scion of a prominent family in Dàmíng.
He happened to be traveling south
and moored his boat on the riverbank.
Next to his boat was a boatman's daughter,
embroidering slippers inside,
her demeanor exceptionally beautiful.
Wáng had been observing her for a long time,
but the girl seemed not to notice.
Wáng recited aloud
"A Luòyáng girl lives opposite,"
deliberately letting the girl hear him.
The girl seemed to understand it was meant for her,
and slightly raised her head, casting a sidelong glance at him,
then lowered her head and resumed embroidering as before.
Wáng's spirits soared further,
and he threw a gold ingot to her,
which fell onto her lapel.
The girl picked it up and discarded it,
and the gold fell to the bank.
Wáng picked it up and returned it,
finding it even stranger,
then threw a gold hair clasp at her,
which fell at her feet;
the girl continued her work without a glance.
Before long,
the boatman returned from elsewhere.
Wáng was afraid he would see the gold and question her,
feeling very anxious;
the girl calmly covered it with a pair of hooks.
The boatman untied the mooring rope
and went straight away.
Wáng was crestfallen and lost,
sitting blankly in thought.
At that time, Wáng had just lost his wife,
and regretted not having immediately arranged a marriage with her.
He then asked the boatmen,
but none of them knew her surname.
He returned to his boat and chased after them urgently,
but didn't know where they had gone.
Having no choice,
he returned to his boat and headed south.
When his business was concluded,
he turned north,
and again searched carefully along the river,
but found no news.
Upon arriving home,
he thought of her constantly, day and night.
More than a year later,
he went south again,
bought a boat on the river,
and made it his home.
Every day he carefully counted the passing boats,
and became familiar with all the sails and oars of those coming and going,
but the former boat was truly gone.
After staying for half a year,
his funds were exhausted, and he returned.
He thought of her constantly, walking or sitting,
unable to put her out of his mind even for a moment.
One night,
he dreamed he arrived at a riverside village,
passed several doors,
and saw a house with a brushwood gate facing south.
Inside the gate, sparse bamboo formed a fence;
he thought it was a garden,
and entered directly.
There was a night-blooming cestrum,
with red filaments covering the tree.
He secretly thought: the poem says,
"A tree of Horse-Tail flower in front of the gate,"
this must be it.
After a few paces,
the reed fence was clean and bright.
He entered again
and saw three bays of northern rooms,
with double doors closed.
To the south was a small chamber,
with red plantains obscuring the window.
He leaned in for a peek,
and found a clothes rack by the door,
with a painted skirt hanging on it.
He knew it was a girl's boudoir,
and retreated in surprise;
but someone inside also noticed,
and rushed out to look at the visitor.
Her light makeup showing,
it was the girl from the boat.
Overjoyed, he exclaimed,
"Is there also a time for us to meet again!"
Just as he was about to approach,
the girl's father happened to return,
and he suddenly awoke with a start,
realizing it was a dream.
The scenery was vivid,
as if right before his eyes.
He kept it a secret,
fearing that telling others
would break this pleasant dream.
Another year or so later,
he traveled to Zhènjiāng again.
In the south of the prefecture lived Xú Tàipú,
who had a long-standing family friendship with him,
and invited him to a banquet.
He let his horse wander,
and accidentally entered a small village.
The scenery along the road
was exactly like what he had experienced in his dream.
Inside a gate,
a Horse-Tail flower tree,
the dream scene was strikingly real.
Extremely startled,
he dropped his whip and entered.
All the objects
were no different from his dream.
Upon entering again,
the rooms
were exactly as in his dream.
Since the dream had come true,
he no longer had any doubts,
and went straight to the southern chamber.
The girl from the boat was indeed inside.
Seeing Wáng from a distance,
she rose in surprise,
shielded herself with the door,
and shouted,
"Whose son is this?"
Wáng Qūnxún hesitated for a moment,
still doubting if it was a dream.
The woman saw him approaching very closely,
and with a bang, she bolted the door.
Wáng said,
"Do you not remember the one who threw the bracelet?"
He fully recounted the bitterness of his lovesickness,
and also spoke of the dream omen.
The woman, from behind the window, carefully inquired about his family background,
and Wáng explained it all.
The woman said,
"Since you belong to a family of officials,
there must be a beautiful woman in your household.
Why would you need me?"
Wáng said,
"It's not because of you;
my marriage was settled long ago."
The woman said,
"If it is as you say,
then I understand your heart.
This feeling of mine is difficult to tell my parents,
yet I have also defied their wishes and turned down several families.
The gold bracelet is still here,
and I presume that the one deeply in love will surely hear the news.
My parents happened to be visiting relatives on my mother's side
and will be arriving soon.
Sir, please withdraw for now.
Send a matchmaker to offer the betrothal gifts,
and there will be no impediment to your wishes.
If you hope to achieve union through impropriety,
then your intentions are mistaken."
Wáng was in a hurry to leave.
The woman called out to Lord Wáng from afar, saying,
"I am Yúnniáng,
my surname is Mèng.
My father's courtesy name is Jiānglí."
Wáng remembered and left.
He ended the banquet early and returned,
to call upon Jiānglí.
Jiāng welcomed him in,
and offered him a seat by the fence.
Wáng stated his family's lineage,
then immediately conveyed his intentions,
and presented a hundred pieces of gold as betrothal gifts.
The old man said,
"My daughter is already betrothed."
Wáng said,
"I have inquired and confirmed it;
she is indeed awaiting betrothal.
Why such a firm refusal?"
The old man said,
"What I just said,
I dare not lie about."
Wáng, losing all spirit,
bowed and returned.
That night, he tossed and turned,
finding no one to act as a matchmaker.
He had previously intended to tell Tàipú about his feelings,
fearing he would be laughed at by the master for marrying a boatman's daughter.
Now, desperate,
with no one to mediate,
at dawn,
he went to Tàipú,
and frankly told him everything.
Tàipú said,
"This old man is related to me;
he is my grandmother's legitimate grandson.
Why didn't you say so earlier?"
Wáng then revealed his hidden feelings.
Tàipú doubted, saying,
"Jiānglí is indeed poor,
but he has never made a living by operating a boat.
Could there be a mistake?"
So he sent his eldest son, Dàláng, to Mèng.
Mèng said,
"Although I am destitute,
I am not one to sell a marriage.
Earlier, that young gentleman offered gold as a match,
presuming I would be swayed by profit,
so I dared not agree to the marriage.
Since it is an order from you, sir,
there can be no mistake.
However, my stubborn daughter is quite spoiled and beloved,
and often rejects good matches.
I must discuss it with her,
to avoid her regretting the marriage later."
Thereupon, he rose,
went inside briefly, and returned,
bowing his hands and saying, "As you command."
They agreed on a date and parted.
Dàláng reported back,
and Wáng then sumptuously prepared the betrothal gifts,
and performed the "Nàcǎi" ceremony at Mèng's house.
He temporarily stayed at Tàipú's residence,
and personally escorted the bride to complete the rites.
Three days later,
he bid farewell to his in-laws and returned north.
While staying in the boat overnight,
he asked Yúnniáng,
"When I met you here before,
I already doubted you were a boatman's daughter.
Where were you going that day on the boat?"
She replied,
"My uncle lives north of the river,
and I just borrowed a small boat to visit him.
My family can barely support itself,
but we don't highly value external possessions.
I laughed at your eyes, which were like peas,
repeatedly trying to tempt people with money.
When I first heard your verses,
I knew you were refined and elegant,
but then I also suspected you were a frivolous young man trying to provoke a loose woman.
If my father had seen the gold bracelet,
you would have died without a place to be buried.
Was I not deeply sympathetic to your talent?"
Wáng smiled and said,
"You are indeed very clever,
but you also fell into my trap!"
The woman asked,
"What trap?"
Wáng stopped and did not speak.
She pressed him again,
and he then said,
"As our home draws near,
this cannot remain a secret forever.
I must truthfully tell you: I already have a wife at home,
the daughter of Minister Wú."
Yúnniáng did not believe it,
so Wáng deliberately embellished his words to make it seem true.
Yúnniáng's expression changed,
and she was silent for a while.
Suddenly, she rose
and ran out.
Wáng quickly pursued her,
but she had already thrown herself into the river.
Wáng cried out loudly,
startling the other boats.
The night was dim and hazy,
with only scattered points of stars across the river.
Wáng grieved all night,
and went downstream along the river,
offering a high price to search for her remains,
but no one found them.
He returned disconsolate,
overwhelmed by sorrow and pain.
He also feared that the old man would come to see his daughter,
and he would have no words to answer him.
His brother-in-law held an official post in Hénán,
so he ordered his carriage and went to him.
More than a year later, he finally returned.
On the way, he encountered rain,
and took shelter in a commoner's house.
He saw that the rooms and corridors were clean,
and an old woman was playing with a child in the hall.
When the child saw Wáng Rén,
he immediately rushed over, wanting to be held.
Wáng was surprised by this.
He also saw that the child was exquisite and lovable,
so he embraced him and placed him on his lap.
The old woman called him,
but he wouldn't go.
A short while later,
the rain cleared,
and Wáng handed the child to the old woman,
then went down the hall to prepare his luggage.
The child cried,
"Daddy is leaving!"
The old woman was ashamed,
and scolded him incessantly,
forcibly holding him and taking him away.
Wáng sat waiting for his luggage to be prepared,
when suddenly a beautiful woman emerged from behind a screen, holding the child,
and it was Yúnniáng.
While he was still greatly astonished,
Yúnniáng cursed,
"Heartless man!
You abandoned this piece of my flesh,
where should I put him?"
Wáng then knew it was his own son.
Sorrow pierced his heart,
and he had no time to ask about her past experiences,
but first, regarding the playful words from before,
he swore by the sun to clear himself.
Yúnniáng then turned her anger into sorrow,
and they wept together.
Before this,
the master of the mansion, Mò Wēng,
who was sixty and childless,
took his wife to worship at Nánhǎi.
On their way back, they anchored by a river,
and Yúnniáng floated downstream with the current,
accidentally bumping into Wēng's boat.
Wēng ordered his attendants to rescue her,
and after a night of treatment and care,
she gradually revived.
Wēng and his wife looked at her,
and seeing she was a good girl,
were very happy,
taking her as their own daughter,
and brought her home.
After a few months,
they wanted to choose a husband for her,
but the girl refused.
More than ten months later,
she gave birth to a son,
named Jìshēng.
Wáng was taking shelter from the rain at their house,
and Jìshēng was just one year old.
Wáng then unpacked his luggage,
entered and bowed to Wēng and his wife,
thus becoming their son-in-law.
After staying for a few days,
he finally brought Měng home.
Upon arrival,
Mèng Wēng was already waiting,
and had been for two months.
When Wēng first arrived,
he saw that the servants' expressions and words were vague,
and his heart was quite suspicious;
after meeting,
they were finally all happy and comforted.
After recounting what had happened,
he then understood why they had been evasive.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Jìshēng,
courtesy name Wángsūn,
was a famous scholar in the prefecture.
His parents, seeing him recognize his father in swaddling clothes,
said he had innate wisdom,
and doted on him.
As he grew, he became even more handsome and refined,
able to write essays at eight or nine,
and entered the prefectural academy at fourteen.
He always chose his own spouse.
His father Guì'ān had a younger sister, Èrniáng,
who married Zhèng Xiùcái, Zǐqiáo,
and gave birth to a daughter, Guīxiù,
whose intelligence and beauty were unparalleled.
When Wángsūn saw her,
his heart was deeply enamored.
Over time,
he neglected both sleep and food.
His parents were greatly worried,
and after much questioning,
he finally told them the truth.
His father sent a matchmaker to Zhèng;
Zhèng's nature was upright and cautious,
and he considered their being cousins an impediment,
so he refused.
Wángsūn became even sicker,
and his mother, having no other plan,
secretly and tactfully approached Èrniáng,
only asking Guīxiù to visit him once.
When Zhèng heard this,
he became even angrier,
and uttered harsh words.
Since the parents had lost all hope,
they could only let it be.
In the commandery, there was a prominent clan, the Zhāng [張] family.
They had five beautiful daughters;
the youngest was named Wǔkě [五可],
who was particularly outstanding among her sisters.
They had not yet chosen a husband for her.
One day,
as she was visiting a grave,
she met Wángsūn [王孫] on the road.
He spied her from his carriage,
and upon returning, he reported it to his mother.
His mother, discerning his intention,
met the matchmaker, Mrs. Yú [于],
and subtly hinted at it.
The matchmaker then went to Wángsūn’s residence.
At that time, Wángsūn was ill,
and when he heard the news, he laughed and said,
“This illness, my old body can cure it.”
Yúnniáng [芸娘] asked for the reason.
The matchmaker relayed the Zhāng [張] family’s intention,
and greatly extolled Wǔkě’s [五可] beauty.
Yúnniáng [芸娘] was pleased,
and sent the matchmaker to attend to Wángsūn.
The matchmaker entered,
and, stroking Wángsūn, told him.
Wángsūn shook his head and said,
“The medicine doesn’t match the ailment,
what can be done!”
The matchmaker laughed and said,
“Just ask if the doctor is good or not: if he is good,
summon a Hè [和] and wait for him to arrive slowly,
that will do: to seize a person and demand it,
to wait for it until death,
is that not foolish?”
Wángsūn sighed and said,
“But among all the doctors in the world,
none are better than Hè [和].”
The matchmaker said,
“Why is your view not broad enough?”
Then, describing Wǔkě’s [五可] face, hair, and skin,
her expression and demeanor,
she described it both orally and with gestures.
Wángsūn again shook his head and said,
“Matchmaker, you understand!
This is beyond my wishes.”
He turned his body towards the wall,
and would not listen anymore.
The matchmaker saw that his resolve was unmoved,
and so she left.
One day,
Wángsūn was in the throes of a serious illness,
when suddenly a maid entered and said,
“The person you have been thinking of has arrived!”
Overjoyed,
he leapt up.
He rushed out of the room,
and the beautiful woman was already in the courtyard.
Upon closer inspection,
she was not a gūixiù [閨秀] (lady of the inner chambers),
but wore a pine-flower-colored finely pleated embroidered skirt,
her small bound feet slightly revealed,
no less than an immortal.
He bowed and asked her name,
and she replied,
“I am
Wǔkě [五可].
You are deeply sentimental,
yet you exclusively favor ladies of the inner chambers,
which makes people feel unfair.”
Wángsūn apologized and said,
“I have never seen your countenance in my life,
so in my eyes there was only one type of gūixiù [閨秀].
Now I know my error!”
Then he swore an oath with her.
As they were clasping hands sincerely,
his mother happened to come and stroke him,
and he suddenly awoke,
realizing it was all a dream.
He recalled her voice, appearance, smile, and expression,
as if they were right before his eyes.
He secretly thought: if Wǔkě [五可] is truly as beautiful as in the dream,
why must I pursue what is so difficult to attain?
Thus, he related the dream to his mother.
His mother was pleased that his obsession had somewhat lessened,
and eagerly wished to arrange a marriage.
Wángsūn feared that the dream might not be accurate,
so he entrusted Mrs. Qín [秦], a neighbor who knew the Zhāng [張] family,
to visit them under a false pretext,
instructing her to secretly observe Wǔkě [五可].
When Mrs. Qín [秦] arrived at their house,
Wǔkě [五可] was ill,
leaning against a pillow, chin in hand,
her graceful demeanor
unparalleled in the world.
She approached and asked,
“What ails you?”
The girl silently fiddled with her sash,
not uttering a word.
Her mother answered for her,
“It’s not an illness.
She’s been quarreling with her parents for days!”
Mrs. Qín [秦] asked for the reason.
She replied,
“Several families have proposed marriage,
but she doesn’t want any of them;
she insists on marrying only someone like Wáng Jiā Jìshēng [王家寄生].
As her mother, I urged her strongly,
so she deliberately hasn’t eaten for several days.”
Mrs. Qín [秦] laughed and said,
“If young mistress marries Wáng Láng [王郎],
you will truly be a perfect match.
If he were to see Fifth Miss,
I fear he would again become emaciated and die!
When I return,
I will immediately send a matchmaker,
how about that?”
Wǔkě [五可] stopped her and said,
“Auntie, don’t do that!
I fear it won’t succeed,
and will only invite more ridicule!”
Mrs. Qín [秦] confidently took responsibility for its success,
and only then did Wǔkě [五可] smile faintly.
Mrs. Qín [秦] returned,
reported back,
and everything was as the matchmaker had said.
Wángsūn meticulously asked about her clothes and shoes,
which also matched his dream,
and he was greatly pleased.
Although his mind was somewhat eased,
he still would not trust hearsay.
After a few days,
he gradually recovered.
He secretly summoned the matchmaker, Mrs. Yú [于],
and discussed how to personally see Wǔkě [五可].
The matchmaker found it difficult,
but provisionally agreed and left.
After a long time,
she did not return.
Just as he was about to inquire,
the matchmaker suddenly arrived joyfully and said,
“The opportunity can thankfully be seized.
Fifth Miss has had a slight illness,
so she has ordered her maids to assist her
in moving to the opposite courtyard.
Young master can go and lie in wait for her;
Fifth Miss walks slowly and with difficulty,
so you can fully observe her delicate movements.”
Wángsūn was delighted.
The next day,
he ordered his carriage early and went,
where the matchmaker was already present.
She immediately ordered his horse to be tied to a village tree,
led him into a room facing the road,
arranged a seat, closed the door, and left.
A short while later,
Wǔkě [五可] indeed emerged, supported by her maids.
Wángsūn watched her intently through a crack in the door.
As the girl passed outside the door,
the matchmaker deliberately pointed to clouds and trees to delay her delicate steps,
allowing Wángsūn to observe every detail.
He was so moved he could not control himself.
Shortly after,
the matchmaker arrived and said,
“Can she replace the gūixiù [閨秀]?”
Wángsūn thanked her and returned,
then finally informed his parents
and sent a matchmaker to propose an alliance.
However, when the matchmaker went,
Wǔkě [五可] had already been promised to another.
Wángsūn was crestfallen,
filled with regret and despair to the point of wanting to die,
and immediately fell ill again.
His parents were extremely worried,
blaming him for his own mistake.
Wángsūn had no words,
only drinking one cup of rice gruel a day.
After several days,
he was as thin as a chicken bone lying on the bed,
even worse than before.
The matchmaker suddenly arrived,
and exclaimed in surprise,
“Why are you so wasted away?”
Wángsūn shed tears,
and told her his situation.
The matchmaker laughed and said,
“Foolish young master!
The other day, when someone came seeking you,
you deliberately rejected them;
today you seek someone,
can you be sure to succeed?
Nevertheless,
there is still something that can be done.
If you had consulted me earlier,
even if she had been promised to the Imperial Prince of the capital,
I could have gotten her back.”
Wángsūn was greatly pleased,
and asked for a plan.
The matchmaker ordered a letter to be sent to request a meeting the next day at the Zhāng [張] family’s residence.
Guì'ān [桂庵] feared that such an abrupt approach would lead to rejection.
The matchmaker said:
“Previously, I had a firm agreement with Zhāng Gōngyè
for a few days, but then suddenly he regretted it. Moreover, his daughter is betrothed to another family,
and there has been no letter or message.
The proverb says, ‘He who cooks first eats first.’
What is there to doubt?”
Guì'ān followed this advice.
The next day,
two servants went.
Everything was as expected,
and after being generously rewarded, they returned.
Wáng Sūn's illness immediately cleared up,
and from then on, his thoughts of the guīxiù were completely dispelled.
Initially,
when Zhèng Zǐqiáo declined the betrothal,
the guīxiù was quite displeased.
When she heard that the marriage with the Zhāng family was settled,
her heart became even more depressed,
and she fell ill,
wasting away day by day.
Her parents questioned her,
but she would not speak.
A maid, perceiving her feelings,
secretly informed her mother.
Zhèng, hearing of this,
furiously refused to allow treatment,
letting her die.
The Èrniáng comforted him, saying,
“My niece is not so bad either.
Why adhere to such a rigid vow,
killing our beloved daughter!”
Zhèng angrily replied,
“If you bear such a daughter,
it is better for her to die early
to avoid becoming a laughingstock!”
Because of this, the couple quarreled.
The Èrniáng spoke with her daughter,
proposing to send her back to Wáng Sūn,
to be a concubine.
The daughter bowed her head and said nothing,
implying great willingness.
The Èrniáng discussed it with Zhèng,
but Zhèng grew even angrier,
leaving it entirely to the Èrniáng,
disregarding his daughter completely,
and refusing to hear any more of it.
The Èrniáng loved her daughter dearly
and wanted to make her words a reality.
The daughter then rejoiced,
and her illness gradually recovered.
Secretly, they inquired about Yù Sūn,
and the day for the wedding procession was set.
When the day arrived,
after completing her niece's wedding,
feigning a wish to visit her parents,
at dawn,
she sent someone to ask her brother for a sedan chair and servants.
Her brother was most affectionate,
and since their villages were close,
he used the carriages and horses prepared for his own wedding procession
to first welcome the Èrniáng.
Once she arrived,
a woman in wedding attire was placed in the carriage,
and two servants and two old women were sent to escort her.
Upon arriving at the gate,
felt mats were laid on the ground for her to enter.
At that moment, drums and music had already assembled.
The accompanying servants shouted for them to play and beat,
and immediately, the sound of human voices grew boisterous.
Wáng Sūn rushed to see,
and saw a girl with a red veil covering her head.
Extremely alarmed,
he wanted to flee;
but Zhèng's servants held him firmly,
immediately making them perform the ceremonial bows.
Wáng Sūn, not knowing what was happening,
completed the bows.
The two old women helped the girl
directly into the wedding chamber,
and only then did he realize it was the guīxiù.
The whole family was in a state of confusion,
not knowing what to do.
As dusk gradually approached,
Wáng Sūn no longer dared to perform the wedding procession ritual.
Guì'ān sent a servant to inform Zhāng of the situation;
Zhāng was enraged
and wished to break off the engagement.
Wǔkě refused,
saying,
“Although she arrived first,
the ceremonial wild geese have not been presented;
it is better to still have the wedding procession.”
Her father accepted her words
and conveyed them to the messenger.
When the messenger returned,
Guì'ān still dared not comply.
Facing each other, they pondered,
unable to express either joy or anger.
Zhāng held out for a long time,
knowing that he would not comply.
So, he also sent Wǔkě in a carriage and horses,
and then set up another green tent in a separate room.
Wáng Sūn wandered between the two rooms,
feeling at a loss, unable to settle.
His mother then mediated between them,
arranging for them to proceed by age,
to which both daughters agreed.
When Wǔkě heard that the guīxiù was slightly older,
she found it difficult
to call her "elder sister"
and showed reluctance.
Her mother was very worried about this.
By the time of the third day's formal meeting,
Wǔkě saw that the guīxiù's demeanor was pleasing,
and she unconsciously favored her,
and from then on, things settled.
However, the parents feared that over time they might not get along,
but the two daughters had no discord,
exchanging clothes and shoes,
loving each other like younger sisters.
Wáng Sūn then asked Wǔkě the reason for rejecting the matchmaker.
She smiled and said,
“No other reason, I was just repaying you for rejecting the old woman.
Before I had even seen your humble servant,
my mind only held the guīxiù;
even after seeing your humble servant,
I still held back a little
to observe how you would regard your humble servant
compared to the guīxiù.
If you were ill for her,
but not ill for your humble servant,
then there would be no need to force acceptance.”
Wáng Sūn laughed and said,
“What a cruel repayment!
However, if not for the old woman,
how could I have glimpsed your beautiful face?”
Wǔkě said,
“It was your humble servant who wished to see you;
what could the old woman do?
When you passed by my gate,
did you not know that someone was eagerly watching inside?
We already met in a dream;
why do you still not know the truth?”
Wáng Sūn asked in surprise,
“How do you know?”
She replied,
“While ill, your humble servant dreamed of coming to your house,
and thought it was an illusion;
later, I heard that you also had that dream,
then your humble servant knew that my soul truly came here.”
Wáng Sūn was astonished by this
and then recounted his dream,
and the times and days all matched.
The good fortune of both father and son
was achieved through dreams;
it is truly a strange affair.
Therefore, it is recorded together.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“The father was infatuated by love,
and the son nearly died for love.
This 'seed of love'
refers to Wáng Sūn, indeed.
If there had not been a father with auspicious dreams,
how could there have been a son with a soul departing his body!”
According to the Chuīxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Zhōu Shēng,
a retainer in Zīyì.
When the magistrate left,
his wife, Xú Fūrén,
had a wish to pay homage to Bìxiá Yuánjūn.
As the journey was long,
she intended to send her servant Jìyí to go in her stead.
She asked Zhōu Shēng to compose a prayer.
Zhōu Shēng wrote a proud piece,
recounting his life,
which often delved into vulgar proverbs.
Among them were lines such as:
“Cultivating flowers throughout Bānyáng Prefecture,
yet particularly doting on cut sleeves;
setting up straw effigies all over Jiágǔ Mountain, yet only loving leftover peaches.”
This was a complaint about what angered Xú Fūrén,
and there were many such instances.
After drafting it,
he showed it to his fellow retainer Líng Shēng.
Líng Shēng deemed it blasphemous
and warned him not to use it.
He didn't listen
and gave it to the servant before leaving.
Soon after,
Zhōu Shēng died in the yámen;
presently the servant also died;
after childbirth, Xú Fūrén
also fell ill and died.
People still didn't find this strange.
Zhōu Shēng's son came from Dū to retrieve his father's coffin,
and that night he shared a room with Líng Shēng.
He dreamt that his father warned him, saying:
“One must be careful with writing!
I did not heed Líng Jūn’s words,
and so by using blasphemous words,
I angered the deities,
and my natural lifespan was cut short;
I also brought harm to Xú Fūrén,
and even afflicted the servant who burned the text: I fear my punishment in the underworld is still not averted!”
He woke up and told Líng Shēng,
who had the same dream,
and then recounted the text.
Zhōu Zǐ was greatly alarmed by this.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“To indulge one's emotions and write freely,
often expressing oneself for one's own pleasure,
this is common for literary men.
However, how dare one use lewd and disrespectful words
to address the deities!
Ignorant madmen deserve the retribution of the underworld.
But for the worthy夫人 and the servant who traveled a thousand *lǐ*
to die from this prideful act without knowing their sin,
is this not similar to the many confused cases
of principals and accessories being indistinguishably judged
in the justice system?
What an injustice!”
Based on the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* Chùxuězhāi manuscript.
A man named Zhào Mǒu from Chángshān
rented a house from a prominent family.
He suffered from a gējié illness
and was also poor and alone,
on the verge of death.
One day,
mustering his strength despite his illness, he sought coolness,
moving to lie beneath a beam.
When he awoke,
he saw a peerlessly beautiful woman sitting beside him.
He questioned her,
and the woman said:
“I have come specifically to be your wife.”
Zhào Mǒu was surprised and said:
“Not only do the poor dare not harbor such extravagant hopes,
but I am also on my last breath;
what good would a wife be!”
The woman said:
“I can cure you.”
Zhào Mǒu said:
“My illness is not something that can be quickly cured; even if there were a good remedy,
what good is it if I have no money to buy medicine!”
The woman said:
“I treat illness without medicine.”
Thereupon, she placed her hand on Zhào Mǒu's abdomen
and massaged it vigorously.
He felt her palm hot as fire.
After a while,
the lumps in his abdomen
began to dissolve with a faint sound.
After another short while,
he needed to go to the latrine,
so he got up quickly,
walked a few paces,
removed his clothes, and relieved himself greatly;
mucus and liquid flowed out,
and all the lumps were expelled.
He felt refreshed all over.
Returning to lie in his original spot,
he said to the woman:
“My lady, who are you?
Please tell me your name
so that I may make offerings to you.”
She replied:
“I am a fox immortal.
You were Chú Suìliáng in the Táng Dynasty,
and once showed kindness to my family,
which I have always kept in my heart, wishing to repay it.
I have been searching for you daily,
and now I have finally found you;
my long-cherished wish can now be fulfilled.”
Zhào Mǒu felt ashamed of his unkempt appearance,
and also worried that the soot from his thatched hut's stove
might stain her splendid clothes.
The woman merely urged him to proceed.
Zhào Mǒu then led her into the house,
where the earthen bed had no mat,
the stove was cold and smokeless.
He said:
“Not only is the situation like this,
unfit to bring shame upon you,
but even if you could bear it,
please look at the empty bottom of the jar;
how then could I support a wife and children?”
The woman merely said:
“Do not worry.”
As she spoke,
she turned her head,
and saw that a felt mat, quilt, and bedding were already laid on the couch;
just as he was about to question her,
she turned her gaze again,
and saw that the entire room was covered in shiny silver paper, like mirrors,
and all the objects had been changed.
The tables and desks were clean and elegant,
and dishes and wine were set out.
Thereupon, they happily drank together.
At dusk,
they slept together intimately,
like husband and wife.
The landlord heard of their strangeness
and asked to see her.
The woman immediately came out to meet him,
showing no reluctance.
From then on, the news spread far and wide,
and many people came to their door.
The woman did not refuse anyone.
Sometimes, a feast was arranged to invite them,
and the woman would always go with her husband.
One day,
among the guests was a Xiàolián
who secretly harbored lustful thoughts.
The woman knew this
and suddenly rebuked him.
She pushed his head with her hand;
his head passed outside the window lattice,
but his body remained inside the room,
making it impossible for him to move in or out or turn around.
So everyone pleaded for his release,
and only then did she pull him back in.
More than a year passed,
and the number of visitors seeking them grew increasingly bothersome,
which the woman found quite annoying.
Those who were refused often cursed Zhào Mǒu.
On the day of Duānyáng Festival,
they were drinking at a grand gathering,
when suddenly a white rabbit hopped in.
The woman stood up and said,
“Chūnyào Wēng has come to summon me!”
She said to the rabbit:
“Please go first.”
The rabbit scurried out
and went straight away.
The woman ordered Zhào Mǒu to fetch a ladder.
Zhào Mǒu brought a long ladder from behind the house,
several *zhàng* high.
There was a large tree in the courtyard,
against which he leaned it;
the ladder was even taller than the treetop.
The woman ascended first,
and Zhào Mǒu followed her.
The woman turned and addressed the guests, saying:
“Any relatives or friends who wish to follow
should step forward immediately.”
The crowd looked at each other, not daring to climb.
Only a young servant of the landlord
eagerly followed behind them.
They ascended higher and higher,
and when the ladder ended, the clouds connected,
and they were no longer visible.
Everyone looked at the ladder,
and it was just an old broken door,
its white plank removed.
The crowd entered their room;
the grey walls and dilapidated stove were still there,
nothing else.
They still hoped the servant would return so they could ask,
but he never reappeared.
Based on the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* Chùxuězhāi manuscript.
In Zōupíng, there was a veterinarian named Hóu
who carried food and plowed for others.
When he reached the wilderness,
a whirlwind appeared before him.
Hóu immediately scooped up some juice with a dipper, made an offering, and poured it out for it.
When he had used up several scoops,
the wind finally departed.
One day,
