he happened to visit the City God Temple.
As he strolled along the corridor,
he saw a statue of Liú Quán presenting melons inside,
which had been soiled by bird droppings,
obscuring its eyes.
Hóu felt sorry and said:
"Liú dàgē, how can you suffer such defilement!"
So he used his fingernail to clean it off.
Several years later,
he fell ill and lay in bed,
and was seized by two yāmén runners.
When they reached the front of the yāmén,
they pressed him hard for bribes.
Hóu had no idea what to do,
when suddenly a green-clad man emerged from within.
Seeing Hóu, he exclaimed in surprise:
"Hóu wēng, what brings you here?"
Hóu then told him his story.
The green-clad man reprimanded the two yāmén runners, saying:
"This is your Hóu dàye,
how dare you be so disrespectful!"
The two yāmén runners bowed and scraped,
apologizing for their ignorance.
Soon, a drum roll like thunder was heard.
The green-clad man said:
"It's time for the morning session."
So he entered with Hóu,
and had him stand at the foot of the steps,
saying:
"Just stand here;
I will inquire for you."
Then he ascended to the hall, gestured,
and summoned a clerk down.
He briefly spoke a few words.
When the clerk saw Hóu,
he cupped his hands and said:
"Hóu dàgē, you've come?
You don't have any major issues.
There's a lawsuit involving a horse;
you can return after a single cross-examination."
Then he took his leave.
A short while later,
Hóu's name was called from the hall.
Hóu knelt,
and a horse also knelt.
The official asked Hóu:
"The horse claims it was poisoned to death by you.
Is this true?"
Hóu replied:
"It contracted a plague.
I treated it with a plague remedy.
Since the medicine didn't cure it,
it died the next day.
How is that related to me?"
The horse spoke in human language,
both complaining bitterly.
The official ordered the records to be checked.
The records stated that the horse's lifespan was a certain number of years,
and it was destined to die on a certain year, month, and day.
The numbers matched exactly.
So he roared:
"Your allotted lifespan is over!
How dare you make a false accusation!"
He dismissed it with a shout.
Then he said to Hóu:
"You have a benevolent heart;
you can avoid death."
He then ordered the two yāmén runners to escort him back.
The two former men also exited with them,
and were instructed to treat him well on the way.
Hóu said:
"Although I've received your protection today,
I've never actually met you in my life.
Please tell me your name,
so I may repay your kindness."
The green-clad man said:
"Three years ago,
I came from Tài Shān,
parched and dying of thirst.
Passing by your village,
I was offered juice from a dipper,
which I have not forgotten to this day."
The clerk said:
"I am Liú Quán.
I was once covered in bird droppings,
which was unbearably stifling,
and your hand cleansed me.
That is why I remember it so clearly.
However, the food and drink in the underworld
cannot be offered to guests,
so please take your leave now."
Hóu then understood,
and returned.
Upon reaching home,
he tried to keep the two yāmén runners for a meal.
But they dared not even drink a cup of his water.
Hóu revived,
for he had been dead for more than two days.
From then on, he practiced even greater kindness.
Every festival,
he would offer juice and wine to Liú Quán.
At eighty years old,
he was still robust
and capable of mounting a horse and riding.
One day,
he saw Liú Quán riding a horse on the road,
as if preparing for a long journey.
After exchanging greetings,
Liú said:
"Your time is up;
the summons has been issued.
The underworld escorts wanted to summon you,
but I forbade them.
You can return home to prepare for your final affairs.
In three days,
I will come and accompany you.
I've already bought a small plot of land for you below,
so there will be no hardship."
Then he departed.
Hóu returned home and informed his wife and children,
and bid farewell to relatives and friends,
preparing everything, including his coffin.
On the fourth day, at dusk,
he said to the assembled crowd:
"Liú dàgē has arrived."
He then entered the coffin and passed away.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
When Jìngnì Hóu Zhāng Yǒng was stationed in Lánzhōu,
he went hunting and caught many rabbits,
some of which had half their body or both hind legs still made of earth.
At that time, it was widely rumored in Qínzhōng that earth could transform into rabbits.
This is another one of those inexplicable physical phenomena.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi handwritten manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
Shǐ Wúchéng of Yuànchéng was at home,
when suddenly a bird,
fragrant and black like a crow, perched on his roof.
Shǐ saw it,
and told his family:
"Madam has sent a bird messenger to summon me.
Quickly prepare for my funeral;
I shall die on a certain day."
On that day, he indeed passed away.
On the day of the funeral,
the crow returned,
slowly flying alongside the coffin
from Yuàn to Xīn.
After the burial,
the crow finally disappeared.
Wú Mùxīn of Chángshān witnessed this personally.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
The È clan of Nányáng
was troubled by a fox spirit.
Gold coins and various items
were frequently stolen.
They moved,
but the haunting grew worse.
È had a nephew, Jī Shēng,
an unconventional scholar.
He burned incense and prayed on their behalf for deliverance,
but received no response.
He also prayed to invite his maternal ancestral spirit to his house,
but that also yielded no response.
Everyone laughed at him,
but Jī Shēng said:
"It can conjure illusions,
so it must have a human mind.
I will certainly guide it
to achieve enlightenment."
For several days, he repeatedly offered prayers.
Although there was no visible effect,
wherever Jī Shēng went,
the fox spirit would not bother them.
Because of this,
the È clan often kept Jī Shēng to stay overnight.
At night, Jī Shēng looked up at the sky and requested to see the spirit,
his invitation growing more fervent.
One day,
Jī Shēng returned,
and sat alone in his study.
Suddenly, the room door slowly opened by itself.
Jī Shēng rose,
and respectfully said:
“Brother Hú, have you come?”
Utter silence.
Another night,
the door opened by itself.
The scholar said,
“If it is truly Brother Hú who has graced us with your presence,
which this humble student has prayed and wished for,
why not immediately grant us your radiant presence?”
But again, there was silence.
On the table lay two hundred coins,
which were gone by morning.
When night came, the scholar
added several hundred more.
In the middle of the night,
he heard the rustle of the curtain.
The scholar said,
“Have you come?
I have respectfully prepared several hundred current coins for your use.
Although I am not affluent,
I am not a miser.
If you have any urgent needs,
feel free to speak plainly,
why resort to theft?”
A short while later,
he checked the money,
and two hundred had been taken.
The scholar still placed them in the same spot,
and they were not lost again for several nights.
There was a cooked chicken,
which he intended to offer to a guest, but it went missing.
That evening, the scholar
also added some wine.
From then on, the fox stopped appearing.
The haunting at the È family continued as before.
The scholar went again and prayed, saying,
“I offered money, but you did not take it;
I offered wine, but you did not drink it.
My maternal grandfather is old and infirm,
please do not haunt him for long.
I have prepared some humble provisions,
tonight you may take them yourself.”
So he took ten thousand coins, a jar of wine,
and two chickens, all chopped up,
and placed them on the table.
The scholar lay beside them,
there was no sound all night,
and the money and items remained untouched.
The fox haunting also ceased from then on.
One evening, the scholar returned home,
opened the study door,
and saw a pot of wine on the table,
a platter full of warmed chicken;
four hundred coins,
strung together with a red cord,
which were exactly the items lost the previous day.
He knew this was the fox’s repayment.
He sniffed the wine and found it fragrant,
poured it out and its color was bluish-green,
drank it and found it very mellow.
When the pot was half empty, he was half-drunk,
he felt a sudden surge of greed in his heart,
and abruptly desired to commit theft.
So he opened the door and went out.
In Ēncūn, there was a wealthy household,
so he went and climbed over its wall.
Although the wall was high,
he leaped over it with ease,
as if he had wings.
He entered its study,
stole a mink fur coat,
and a golden tripod, then exited.
He returned and placed them at his bedside,
then finally lay down to sleep.
At dawn,
he brought them into the inner room,
his wife asked in surprise,
the scholar stammered and told her,
with a look of joy.
His wife exclaimed in shock,
“You have always been upright and honest,
how could you suddenly become a thief!”
The scholar remained calm and unperturbed,
and then recounted the fox’s affection.
His wife suddenly realized, saying,
“This must be the fox poison in the wine!”
She then remembered that cinnabar could ward off evil,
so she ground it into the wine,
and
gave it to the scholar to drink.
A short while later,
the scholar suddenly cried out,
“How could I have become a thief!”
His wife explained the reason for him,
and he was utterly crestfallen.
Then they heard that the wealthy household had been robbed,
and the news spread noisily throughout the neighborhood.
The scholar ate nothing all day,
not knowing what to do.
His wife devised a plan for him,
to throw the stolen items back over the wall at night,
and the scholar followed her advice.
The wealthy household recovered its old possessions.
The matter then subsided.
The scholar became the champion in the annual examination,
and was also praised for his conduct,
deserving of a double reward.
When the day for the announcement arrived,
a note was stuck on a beam in the prefectural office, saying:
“Jī Mǒu committed theft,
stealing a fur coat and a tripod from a certain family.
How can he be praised for his conduct?”
The beam was very high,
not reachable by standing on tiptoes.
Wénzōng was suspicious,
held the note and questioned the scholar.
The scholar was astonished,
thinking that no one knew about this matter except his wife;
moreover, the office was very secure,
how could it have gotten there?
He then realized, saying,
“This must be the fox’s doing.”
So he recounted everything without concealment,
and the literary award and ceremonies were even increased.
The scholar often thought to himself: I did not intend to offend the fox,
so the reason it repeatedly shamed me
was also to prevent me, a humble person, from being the only humble person.
Yìshǐshì says:
“The scholar wanted to lead the evil to righteousness,
but was instead deluded by evil.
The fox’s intention may not have been greatly malicious,
perhaps the scholar provoked it with familiarity,
and the fox also played a trick on him.
However, if he did not have innate good roots,
and his home did not have a wise helper,
how many would, like Yuán Shè said,
once a family member or widow is tainted by theft,
then engage in debauchery!
Alas!
How frightening!”
Wú Mùxīn says:
“In the Jiǎxū year of Kāngxī,
a provincial judicial official in Zhèzhōng
inspected prisoners.
There was a thief
who had already been tattooed.
According to custom, he should have been released.
The official disliked that the character ‘qiè’
(theft) had a simplified stroke according to common practice,
and was not the official standard character,
so he ordered it to be scraped off;
after the wound healed,
he was to be tattooed again according to the exact strokes and form in the dictionary.
The thief recited a quatrain by mouth:
‘Holding the mirror, I look closely,
old scars stained with fresh blood.
Had I known the pain of retattooing my face,
I would have first guarded against the literate official when stealing.’
The jailer laughed and said, ‘
A poet who does not seek fame and fortune, but instead becomes a thief?’
The thief then recited a reply by mouth: ‘
In my youth, I studied the Dao, aspiring to fame,
but poverty ruined my life.
Hoping to gain wealth to leverage capital,
I roamed the marketplaces of Yān to seek favor and honor.’ ”
From this perspective,
a scholar becoming a thief also stems from the ambition for advancement.
The fox provided Jī Shēng with the means to acquire wealth,
but he then regretted being misled.
How迂!
(A laugh).
According to the Jiànxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāizhìyì.
A certain scholar from Ānqīu
was skilled in divination.
He was dissolute and unrestrained in his conduct,
and whenever he had an urge to drill holes or climb walls (to steal),
he would divine it.
One day he suddenly fell ill,
and medicine could not cure him.
He said,
“I have truly seen something.
The underworld is angry with me for trifling with divine numbers,
and is about to mete out a severe punishment;
what can medicine do!”
Before long,
his eyes suddenly failed,
and both his hands inexplicably broke.
There was a certain
Mǒu Jiǎ. His paternal uncle had no
heir. Mǒu Jiǎ coveted his
possessions and wished to become his heir.
After the uncle died,
all his land and property became Mǒu Jiǎ's.
Mǒu Jiǎ then went back on his former promise.
He also had a paternal uncle
whose family was quite wealthy
and also had no son.
Mǒu Jiǎ again adopted him as a father.
When he died,
Mǒu Jiǎ again went back on his word.
Thus, he merged the properties of the three families,
and Mǒu Jiǎ alone dominated the entire village.
One day,
he fell ill with a sudden illness, as if mad,
and said to himself:
"Do you wish to enjoy wealth and live on?"
Then, with a sharp blade, he cut his own flesh,
throwing the pieces to the ground.
He also said:
"You cut off the heirs of others,
do you still wish to have heirs?"
He then disemboweled himself, spilling his intestines,
and died.
Not long after,
his son also died,
and the property returned to others.
Such retribution is
truly terrifying!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Bǎodìng, there was a gongsheng
who was preparing to go to the capital to pay for
a county magistracy.
Just as he was preparing his luggage, he fell ill
and did not recover for over a month.
Suddenly, a servant announced:
"A guest has arrived."
Mǒu also forgot his illness,
and hurried out to greet the guest.
The guest was dressed in fine clothes, like a noble.
After three bows, he entered the house.
When asked where he came from,
the guest said:
"I am
Gōngsūn Xià,
a retainer of the Eleventh Prince.
I heard you are preparing to seek a county post.
Since you have this ambition,
would not a prefectural magistracy be even better?"
Mǒu humbly declined,
only saying:
"My capital is meager,
I dare not have such extravagant wishes."
The guest offered to help,
offering to pay half the capital,
with the agreement to take the remainder from the profits of his post.
Mǒu happily sought his advice.
The guest said:
"The Governor-General and Governor are both my brothers-in-arms.
If you can temporarily raise five thousand strings of cash,
the matter will be settled.
Currently, there is a vacancy in Zhēndìng,
which you can quickly pursue."
Mǒu was surprised that it was in his home province.
The guest laughed and said:
"You are being naive!
As long as you have 'Master Kong Fang' [money],
why ask if it's Wú or Yuè, Sāng or Huái?"
Mǒu still hesitated,
doubting its authenticity.
The guest said:
"There's no need to doubt.
I'll tell you the truth: this is a vacancy for a City God in the underworld.
Your lifespan is at its end;
you have already been marked in the death register.
By taking this opportunity to manage affairs,
you can still achieve high rank in the underworld."
He then rose to bid farewell,
saying:
"You consider it for yourself;
we shall meet again in three days."
Then he left the door and rode away.
Mǒu suddenly opened his eyes,
bidding his wife and children a final farewell.
He ordered his hidden money to be brought out,
and bought ten thousand strings of paper money,
emptying the supply in the entire prefecture.
He piled it up in his courtyard,
along with straw figures and ghost horses,
burning them day and night until
the ash was as high as a mountain.
After three months,
the guest indeed arrived.
Mǒu presented the money for exchange.
The guest then led him to a department,
where he saw a high official sitting on the dais.
Mǒu immediately prostrated himself in homage.
The high official briefly questioned his name,
then exhorted him with words like
"integrity, diligence, and caution."
Then he took out the official document,
called Mǒu to the desk, and handed it to him.
Mǒu bowed and exited the office.
He thought to himself that as a lowly gongsheng,
without ostentatious carriages and attire,
he would not be able to impress his subordinates.
So, he bought even more carriages and horses;
he also dispatched ghost servants with a decorated palanquin to fetch his beautiful concubine.
Just as his arrangements were complete,
the Zhēndìng retinue arrived.
For more than a li along the road,
the procession stretched, one after another,
and he was immensely pleased.
Suddenly, the vanguard halted, their banners drooping.
Amidst surprise and doubt,
he saw all the riders dismount,
prostrating themselves along the roadside;
the men were less than a foot tall,
the horses as large as civet cats.
The one in front of the carriage exclaimed in alarm:
"Lord Guān has arrived!"
Mǒu, afraid,
also got out of his carriage and prostrated himself.
From afar, he saw the Emperor Lord, followed by four or five riders,
slowly approaching with loosened reins.
His beard wrapped around his cheeks,
unlike the depictions of him in the human world;
but his divine presence was mighty and awe-inspiring,
his eyes long, almost reaching his ears.
From horseback, he asked:
"Who is this official?"
A retinue member replied:
"The Prefect of Zhēndìng."
The Emperor Lord said,
"A mere prefecture,
why does it deserve such an ostentatious display!"
Upon hearing this, Mǒu
was startled, his hair standing on end;
his body suddenly shrank,
and he saw himself as a child of six or seven.
The Emperor Lord commanded him to rise,
and made him walk alongside the horses.
By the roadside was a temple.
The Emperor Lord entered,
sat facing south,
and commanded a brush and paper to be given to Mǒu,
ordering him to write his native place and name.
After Mǒu had written it,
he presented it.
The Emperor Lord looked at it and said angrily:
"The characters are erroneous and do not form proper images!
This is a mere huckster,
how can he be fit to govern the people and the altars of soil and grain!"
He also ordered to check his record of virtues.
One person beside him knelt and reported,
the words of which were unknown.
The Dìjūn said in a stern voice:
"Illegally seeking advancement is a minor offense,
selling titles is a grave offense!"
Soon, a golden-armored deity was seen shrinking back and leaving with a lock.
Then two men seized Mǒu,
stripped him of his cap and robes,
gave him fifty strokes,
his buttocks were almost torn off,
and he was driven out of the gate.
He looked around, and the carriages and horses were all gone.
The pain prevented him from walking,
so he lay down to rest in the grass.
He carefully identified the location;
it was not very far from home.
Fortunately, his body was light as a leaf,
and he only reached home after a day and a night.
It was as if he had awakened from a dream,
groaning on the bed.
His family gathered and asked,
but he only said his buttocks hurt.
He had been in a coma, as if dead,
for seven days,
and only now had he recovered.
He immediately asked:
"Why hasn't Ālián come?"
— This was the pet name of his concubine.
Earlier,
Ālián was sitting and chatting,
when she suddenly said:
"He has become the Grand Administrator of Zhēndìng,
and an envoy has come to fetch me."
She then entered her room to dress meticulously;
after dressing, she died,
only the night before.
His family recounted her strangeness.
Mǒu regretted deeply, clawing at his chest,
and ordered the corpse to be kept and not buried,
hoping she would return.
After several days, realizing it was futile,
he buried her.
Mǒu's illness gradually improved,
but the sores on his buttocks were extremely severe,
and he only recovered after half a year.
He often said:
"All my official emoluments are exhausted,
and I suffered a hidden punishment,
this much is still bearable;
but where my beloved concubine went is unknown,
this is what is truly unbearable on clear nights."
The Yìshǐ Shì says:
"Alas!
A huckster is indeed unfit to sit facing south (i.e., rule)!
Since there are already clues in the underworld,
I fear that even Fūzǐ's investigations would not reach such depths.
Those who wield power and privilege
are indeed inexhaustible in number to be punished.
My fellow countryman, Mr. Guō Huáyě, recounted an incident
quite similar to this,
he was also a divine being among men.
The gentleman was known to his lord for his uprightness and integrity,
and was again appointed to supervise Jīngchǔ.
His travel luggage was sparse,
with only four or five people accompanying him,
their clothes and shoes all worn out and simple,
so people on the road did not even know he was a high official.
Coincidentally, a new magistrate was on his way to his post,
and their paths crossed.
There were more than twenty camel carts,
several tens of horsemen leading the way,
and hundreds of attendants.
The gentleman also did not know what official he was,
sometimes preceding him,
sometimes following him,
sometimes a few horsemen mingled among his entourage.
The horsemen in front were annoyed by the disturbance,
and often shouted to drive them away;
the gentleman paid no heed.
Before long,
they arrived at a large town,
and both stopped to rest.
He then sent someone to discreetly inquire,
and found it was a Guó Xuéshēng [student of the imperial academy] who had paid for an appointment in Húnán.
He then sent a messenger to summon him.
The magistrate heard the summons with surprise and doubt,
and upon questioning his status,
he realized it was the gentleman,
and was so terrified he couldn't find his footing.
He put on his cap and robes, and prostrated himself forward.
The gentleman asked: 'Are you the magistrate of a certain county?'
He replied: 'Yes.'
The gentleman said: 'A small district
how can it support so many attendants?
When you assume office,
the entire region will be plunged into misery!
You cannot be allowed to bring disaster to the people and the altars of soil and grain,
you must return immediately,
and not proceed further.'
The magistrate kowtowed and said: 'Your humble official still has his official credentials.'
The gentleman immediately ordered the credentials to be brought,
and after examining them,
said: 'This is also a minor matter,
I can submit them on your behalf.'
The magistrate prostrated himself in obeisance and left.
On his way home, he didn't know how to feel,
while the gentleman had already departed.
That there are those in the world who receive an assessment before even assuming office
is truly unheard of,
but the gentleman was an extraordinary man,
which is why such a delightful event occurred."
According to the Liaozhai Zhiyi manuscript from Shandong Provincial Museum
In the late Míng dynasty,
in several prefectures and counties north of Jìjùn,
an evil plague raged,
affecting every household.
Hán Fāng, a farmer from Qídōng,
was extremely filial.
Both his parents fell ill,
so he prepared offerings and silk,
and wept as he prayed at the temple of Gūshí Dàfū.
On his way home, tears streamed down.
He met a person,
dressed cleanly and properly,
who asked:
"Why are you sad?"
Hán told him everything.
That person said:
"The spirit of Gūshí is not here,
what good will praying to him do?
I have a small technique
that you can try."
Hán was pleased,
and asked his name.
That person said:
"I seek no reward,
why bother with my hometown and name?"
Hán earnestly invited him to his home.
That person said:
"No need.
Just go home,
place a yellow paper on the bed,
and loudly declare: 'Tomorrow I am going to the capital,
to report to the Yuè Dì!'
The illness will surely be cured."
Hán feared it would not work,
and insisted on him coming in person.
That person said:
"I will tell you the truth: I am not human.
The巡環使者 (Xúnhuán Shǐzhě) appointed me as the Tǔdì of the southern county
because of my sincerity.
Moved by your filial piety,
I instruct you in this method.
Currently, the Yuè Dì is gathering the spirits of the dead,
those who have benefited the people,
or who are upright and do not cause mischief,
are appointed as Chénghuáng or Tǔdì.
Those afflicted today
are all spirits killed by the northern soldiers of the prefectural city,
who are eager to go to the capital to present themselves,
hence they are soliciting bribes along the way
to make a living.
When you say you will report to the Yuè Dì,
they will surely be afraid,
and thus the illness will be cured."
Hán was awestruck and filled with reverence,
prostrating himself to express his gratitude.
When he rose,
the person had already vanished.
He returned, astonished and amazed,
followed his instructions,
and both his parents recovered.
He spread the word to neighboring villages,
and it never failed.
Xià Lían-Zhī felt pity for her: Looking at the girl,
so graceful and lovely,
she felt even more sorrowful and sympathetic.
So she invited them into her home,
treated them to food and wine,
and comforted them, saying:
"Mother and daughter, do not grieve;
I will do my utmost."
Before Fàn could express her thanks,
the girl had already collapsed in tears on the ground,
which increased Xià's pity.
She thought to herself:
"Though I have some meager savings,
thirty pieces of gold is still a great sum;
I must pawn things and give it to them."
The mother and daughter bowed in thanks.
Xià set a three-day deadline.
After they parted,
she devised every possible scheme to raise the money,
and did not dare tell her husband.
On the third day,
still short of the full amount,
she sent someone to borrow from her mother.
Fàn's mother and daughter had already arrived,
so Xià told them the truth,
and arranged for the next day.
By dusk, the borrowed gold arrived;
she wrapped it all and placed it by the bed.
That night,
a thief dug a hole in the wall
and entered with a light.
Xià awoke,
and peered at him.
She saw a man with a short saber slung over his arm,
looking fierce and vicious.
Greatly frightened,
she dared not make a sound,
and feigned sleep.
The thief approached the trunk,
intending to unlatch it.
He looked back,
and saw a wrapped object by Xià's pillow.
He reached out, snatched it,
and opened it by the lamp to examine it.
It was merely a money pouch,
so he did not bother to open the trunk and left.
Xià then got up and called out.
Her household had only a small maidservant.
She called out to her neighbor through the wall.
The neighbors gathered, but the thief was already far away.
Xià then wept by the lamp.
Seeing the maidservant deeply asleep,
she took a white ribbon and hanged herself from the window frame.
At dawn, the maidservant awoke,
called for help to cut her down,
but her limbs were already cold.
Yú Wén rushed over,
questioned the maidservant, and only then learned the reason.
He was shocked and tearful as he arranged the funeral.
It was summer at the time;
the corpse did not stiffen
nor decay.
After seven days,
she was interred.
After the burial,
Rèn-Zhēn secretly went out
to weep at her grave.
A sudden torrential rain gathered,
and great thunder and lightning struck,
splitting open the grave,
and Rèn-Zhēn was struck dead.
Yú Wén heard about it,
rushed to examine it,
and found that the coffin was already open.
His wife was groaning inside;
he carried her out.
He saw a female corpse,
but did not know who it was.
Xià carefully examined it,
and only then recognized it.
They were both greatly astonished.
Not long after,
Fàn arrived.
Seeing her daughter dead,
she cried, saying:
"I suspected she was here,
and now it has indeed come true!
I heard that Madam hanged herself,
and her voice never stopped day and night.
Tonight, she told me she
wanted to cry at the burial hall,
but I did not agree."
Xià was moved by her righteousness,
and spoke with her husband,
then buried Rèn-Zhēn in the same grave she had prepared for herself.
Fàn bowed in thanks.
Yú Wén carried his wife home,
and Fàn also returned to tell her husband.
They heard that a man north of the village had been struck dead by lightning on the road,
and there were characters on his body saying:
"The thief who stole Xià's gold."
Soon after, they heard a neighbor woman crying,
and then knew that the one struck by lightning was her husband, Mǎ Dà.
The villagers reported it to the officials.
The officials detained the woman and interrogated her in shackles.
It turned out that Fàn had redeemed her daughter with the gold Xià had raised,
and spoke of her gratitude to people.
Mǎ Dà, a dissolute gambler,
heard of it and thus conceived the idea of stealing.
The officials ordered the woman to produce the stolen goods,
but only twenty-some pieces remained.
They also searched Mǎ Dà's corpse and found four more.
The officials ruled that the woman be sold to compensate for the loss and return the money to Yú Wén.
Xià was even more pleased.
She gave all the gold back to Fàn,
who then repaid her creditors.
Three days after Rèn-Zhēn's burial,
there was great thunder, lightning, and wind at night.
The grave was opened again,
and the girl suddenly came back to life.
She did not return to her own home,
but went and knocked on Xià's door,
for she recognized the grave
and suspected Xià had revived.
Xià rose in surprise
and questioned her through the door.
The girl said:
"Madam, have you indeed come back to life?
I am Rèn-Zhēn."
Xià was terrified, thinking she was a ghost.
She called a neighboring old woman to question her,
and realizing she had revived,
happily let her into the room.
The girl herself said:
"I wish to serve Madam;
I will not go back home."
Xià said:
"Do you perhaps think I spent money to buy a maidservant?
After you were buried,
the debts were already paid on your behalf;
you need not be suspicious."
The girl was even more moved to tears,
and wished to serve her as a mother.
Xià did not agree.
The girl said:
"I can work,
and will not eat idly."
At dawn, Xià told Fàn.
Fàn was happy
and rushed over.
She also agreed with her daughter's wishes
and entrusted her to Xià.
After Fàn left,
Xià insisted on sending the girl back home.
The girl cried, missing Xià.
Wáng Xīn-Zhāi then carried the girl back,
entrusting her to the gatekeeper and leaving.
Xià was surprised to see her and asked,
only then learning the reason,
and thus allowed her to stay.
When the girl saw Yú Wén arrive,
she quickly bowed,
calling him father.
Yú Wén had no children of his own,
and seeing the girl clinging to them so dearly,
he was quite pleased.
The girl spun, wove, sewed,
and worked diligently to the utmost.
When Xià fell seriously ill,
the girl served her day and night.
Seeing Xià not eat,
she also did not eat.
There were often tear stains on her face.
She said to people:
"If anything should happen to mother,
I swear I will not live again!"
When Xià recovered slightly,
the girl finally smiled cheerfully.
Xià wept upon hearing this,
and said:
"I am forty without children.
If only I could give birth to a daughter like Rèn-Zhēn, it would be enough."
Xià had always been infertile;
a year later, she suddenly gave birth to a son.
People considered this the reward for her good deeds.
Two years passed.
The daughter grew older.
Yú and Wáng discussed,
unable to firmly uphold the old alliance.
Wáng said:
“The daughter is in your house;
her marriage is solely at your command.”
The daughter was seventeen,
unrivaled in grace and beauty.
When these words were out,
those who came to ask for her hand crowded the gate,
and the couple began to choose a suitor.
Huáng Mǒu also sent a matchmaker,
but Yú disliked him for being rich yet unkind,
and firmly rejected him.
He chose for her a man from the Féng clan.
Féng
was a famous scholar in the town,
and his son was intelligent and skilled in writing.
Yú was about to inform Wáng;
but Wáng had gone out to hawk wares and had not returned,
so he simply assented.
Huáng, unable to obtain her from Yú,
also pretended to be a merchant,
tracked Wáng’s whereabouts,
set up a feast to invite him,
and further helped him with capital,
gradually becoming familiar and close.
Then he spoke of his son’s intelligence, acting as his own matchmaker.
Wáng was moved by his sentiment
and also admired his wealth,
so he entered into an alliance with him.
Upon returning,
he went to Yú,
only to find that Yú had already accepted the Féng clan’s marriage contract the day before.
Hearing what Wáng said,
he was displeased,
called the daughter out,
and told her the situation.
The daughter angrily said:
“The creditor
is my enemy!
To make me serve my enemy,
there is only one death!”
Wáng was ashamed.
He asked someone to inform Huáng of the alliance with the Féng clan.
Huáng angrily said:
“The daughter’s surname is Wáng,
not Yú.
My agreement was first,
their agreement was later;
how can he go back on his word?”
He then reported it to the Yì Zǎi,
who intended to rule in favor of Huáng based on the prior agreement.
Féng said:
“Wáng Mǒu entrusted his daughter to Yú,
and indeed said he would no longer concern himself with the marriage.
Furthermore, I have a formal marriage contract,
while his was merely a talk over drinks.”
The Zǎi could not decide,
and planned to simply follow the daughter’s wish.
Huáng again bribed the official with gold,
seeking his full support,
and because of this, the matter remained unresolved for over a month.
One day,
a Xiàolián traveling north,
by public carriage, passed through Dōngchāng,
and sent someone to ask for Wáng Xīnzāi.
They happened to ask Yú,
who in turn questioned them,
and it turned out that the Xiàolián’s surname was Fù,
who was indeed Āmǎo.
He was from Mǐn Province,
and had passed the provincial examination at eighteen.
His previous engagement was still unmarried.
His mother had instructed him to visit Wáng on his way,
and ask if the daughter had been betrothed to another.
Yú was overjoyed,
invited Fù to his house,
and recounted all that had happened.
However, the son-in-law had come thousands of miles,
and they worried about lacking proof.
Fù opened a basket
and took out the marriage agreement Wáng had assented to that day.
Yú summoned Wáng,
verified it was indeed genuine,
and they were all happy.
On that very day, the case was to be reviewed by the official;
Fù presented his calling card to visit the Zǎi,
and the case was finally dismissed.
He selected an auspicious day and scheduled a date, then departed.
After the metropolitan examination,
he returned with gifts of silks,
resided in his old residence,
and performed the personal welcoming ceremony.
News of his Jinshì status had already reached Mǐn,
then it reached Dōng,
and Fù had again triumphed in the Nángōng (palace examination).
He then entered the capital for official observation before returning.
The daughter was unwilling to move south,
and Fù also had ancestral tombs there,
so he went alone to retrieve his father’s coffin,
and brought his mother back with him.
After several more years,
Yú passed away.
His son was only seven or eight years old,
and the daughter raised him with greater care than her own younger brother.
She made him study,
and he was able to enter the district school (yìkù),
and the family was renowned for its wealth,
all thanks to Fù’s efforts.
The Yìshǐ Shì said:
“Are there also chivalrous figures among the divine dragons?
They champion good and expose evil,
and their actions in life and death are all like thunder and lightning.
This is the ‘Qiántáng Pòzhèn Wǔ’ (Qiántáng battle-array dance).
Repeatedly striking with thunderous force,
all for one person;
how do we know that the needle-threading girl was not a dragon maiden banished to the mortal realm?”
According to the Zhùxuě Zhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Péng Hàoshì of Jīngzhōu,
returned from drinking at a friend's house.
He dismounted to relieve himself,
and his horse nibbled grass by the roadside.
There was a clump of fine grass,
shaggy and lovely,
just starting to bloom with yellow flowers,
whose radiant glow was dazzling.
The horse had already eaten more than half of it.
Péng pulled up the remaining stems,
smelled an unusual fragrance,
and tucked them into his bosom.
He remounted and rode on,
the horse galloping at full speed.
Feeling quite pleased,
he did not calculate his return journey,
letting the horse go where it pleased.
Suddenly, he saw the setting sun on the mountains,
and only then prepared to turn his reins.
He saw only a jumble of mountains and apricot trees,
and had no idea where he was.
A man in blue clothes approached,
and seeing the horse snorting and neighing,
took its bridle for him,
saying:
"It's getting late,
my master invites you to stay the night."
Péng asked:
"To what place does this belong?"
He replied:
"This is Lángzhōng."
Péng was greatly alarmed,
as he had already traveled over a thousand *lǐ* in half a day.
So he asked:
"Who is your master?"
He replied:
"You'll know when you get there."
Again he asked:
"Where is it?"
He replied:
"It's very close."
Thereupon, he took the reins and sped off,
man and horse flying.
Passing over a mountain peak,
he saw buildings piled up halfway up the mountain,
interspersed with screens and draperies.
From afar, he saw a cluster of people in official attire,
as if waiting for someone.
When Péng arrived and dismounted,
they greeted him with clasped hands and respect.
Presently,
the master came out,
his demeanor fierce and powerful,
his clothing utterly unlike that of the human world.
He cupped his hands to the guest,
saying:
"Today's guest,
none is more distinguished than Lord Péng."
Then he bowed to Péng,
and asked him to go first.
Péng humbly declined,
unwilling to precede him.
The master grasped his arm and led him,
Péng felt as if his arm where it was held was in shackles,
and his arm was about to break.
He dared not contend further,
and so he went.
Those below him,
still pushed and yielded to each other,
the master sometimes pushing them,
sometimes pulling them,
and the guests all groaned and stumbled,
as if unable to bear it,
and proceeded entirely according to the master's command.
Ascending the hall,
the furnishings were dazzlingly splendid,
with two guests per table.
Péng secretly asked the person sitting next to him:
"Who is the master?"
He replied:
"This is Zhāng Huánhóu."
Péng was stunned,
and dared not cough again.
The whole company was silent.
Once the wine was served,
Huánhóu said:
"Year after year, I trouble my relatives and friends.
I have prepared a humble feast
to express my small intentions.
That a distant guest deigns to visit
is also a fortunate encounter.
I secretly have an impertinent request;
if you have even a little attachment,
then I will not force it."
Péng rose and asked:
"What is it?"
He said,
"Your esteemed mount already possesses immortal bones;
it is not something that can be driven in the mortal world.
Would you like to exchange it for a horse from the market?
How about it?"
Péng said,
"I respectfully offer it as a gift;
I dare not exchange it."
Huán Hóu said,
"I shall repay you with an excellent horse,
and moreover, bestow upon you ten thousand gold coins."
Péng rose from his seat and bowed in thanks.
Huán Hóu ordered someone to help him up.
In a moment,
wine and food flowed abundantly.
As the sun set,
candles were ordered.
The guests rose to take their leave,
and Péng also bade farewell.
Huán Hóu said,
"Sir, you have traveled far; where are you returning?"
Péng looked at his table companion and said,
"I have already asked this gentleman to be my host for a stay."
Huán Hóu then personally poured a large goblet of wine for each guest,
and said to Péng,
"Of the fragrant herbs you carry,
the fresh ones can lead to immortality,
and the withered ones can turn things into gold;
seven stalks of the herb
are worth ten thousand gold coins."
He then ordered an attendant to bring them out and present them to Péng.
Péng bowed in thanks again.
Huán Hóu said,
"Tomorrow, when you visit the market,
please feel free to choose the best one from the horse herd,
without needing to discuss the price with them;
I will pay for it myself."
He then told the crowd,
"Our distant guests are returning home;
a small amount of travel money can be of assistance."
The crowd assented.
After finishing their drinks,
they thanked him and departed.
On the way, Péng finally asked for the surname and given name;
his table companion was Liú Zǐcuì.
They walked two or three *lǐ* together,
and after crossing a ridge, they saw village houses.
The guests accompanied Péng Jǐng to Liú's residence,
and only then did they recount the strange events.
Before this,
the villagers would hold an annual communal sacrifice at Huán Hóu's temple,
slaughtering animals and performing plays,
considering it a fixed custom;
Liú was among the most virtuous of them.
Three days prior,
the communal sacrifice had just concluded.
That afternoon,
each household had one person invited to cross the mountain.
When asked,
the explanations were vague and perplexing,
but the urging was very urgent.
After crossing the mountain, they saw pavilions and dwellings,
and were mutually astonished and suspicious.
As they approached the gate,
the messenger finally told them the truth;
the crowd also dared not refuse or retreat.
The messenger said,
"Gather here for now;
the two distant guests are on their way."
This referred to Péng.
The crowd recounted their astonishment.
Those among them who had been gripped
all suffered from arm pain;
when they uncovered their clothes and examined them,
a bluish-black mark was visible inside.
Péng examined himself, and it was the same.
When the crowd dispersed,
Liú immediately arranged for Péng's lodging.
When morning came,
the villagers eagerly invited the guest to stay;
they also accompanied Péng to the market to look for a horse.
For over ten days,
he inspected dozens of horses,
but unfortunately found no good ones;
Péng was even resigned to settling for an ordinary one.
Again, he went to the market
and saw a horse whose bones looked excellent;
he rode it to test it,
and it was incredibly spirited and swift.
He rode it directly into the village,
waiting for the seller;
when he went to look for him again,
the person had already left,
so he bid farewell to the villagers, intending to return home.
The villagers each presented him with money,
and so he returned.
The horse could travel five hundred *lǐ* in a day.
Upon arriving home,
he recounted where he had come from,
but people did not believe him.
When he took out the items from Shǔ from his bag,
everyone was finally amazed.
The fragrant herbs had long withered,
and he happened to have seven stalks;
following the method to transform them,
his family became instantly wealthy.
He then respectfully went to the former place,
personally attending Huán Hóu's shrine,
and performed plays for three days before returning.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Observing Huán Hóu entertaining guests,
one then believes that the 'slow pavilion' of Wǔyí is not a myth.
However, the host's solemn treatment of guests
caused those who received his favor to almost break their arms;
one can imagine the strength of those days."
Wú Mùxīn said:
"There was a scholar named Lǐ,
whose lips did not cover his front teeth,
which protruded by a full finger's width.
One day,
at a banquet gathering somewhere,
two guests yielded to each other regarding their seats,
their dispute was very intense.
One pulled forcefully to make him go forward,
the other pulled forcefully to make him go backward.
When the force was violent, they slipped,
and Lǐ happened to be standing behind them;
at that moment, he was struck on the snout,
and both front teeth fell out,
blood flowed like a gush.
Everyone was stunned,
and their dispute then ceased."
This, and Huán Hóu's gripping of arms and causing swelling,
are equally humorous.
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
According to the *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
Yáng Yuēdàn
was a scholar from Qióngzhōu.
He happened to be returning from another prefecture,
sailing by boat on the sea,
when he encountered a hurricane.
His boat was about to capsize;
suddenly, an empty boat drifted over.
He quickly leaped onto it.
Looking back,
he saw that everyone on his former boat had drowned.
The wind grew even more furious,
and he resignedly let it blow him where it would.
Before long,
the wind subsided.
Opening his eyes,
he suddenly saw an island
with continuous houses stretching along it.
He rowed his oar closer to the shore,
straight to a village gate.
The village was silent;
he sat and walked for a long time,
but not a single chicken made a sound.
He saw a gate facing north,
obscured by pines and bamboos.
It was already early winter,
but inside the wall, he didn't know what kind of flowers
were blooming, covering the trees with buds.
His heart delighted in them,
and after lingering for a moment, he entered.
From afar, he heard the sound of a qín,
and his steps paused slightly.
A maidservant emerged from inside,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
graceful and beautiful.
Seeing Yáng,
she quickly turned and went back in.
Soon, the qín music ceased,
and a young man came out,
asking with surprise where the guest had come from.
Yáng told him everything.
He then inquired about Yáng's family and clan,
and Yáng told him that too.
The young man joyfully said:
"You are my relative by marriage!"
He then bowed and invited him into the courtyard.
Inside the courtyard, the exquisite house was beautiful,
and the sound of a qín was heard again.
Once he entered the house,
he saw a young woman sitting upright,
just adjusting her red strings.
She was about eighteen or nineteen,
with a radiant charm.
Seeing the guest,
she pushed her qín and intended to leave.
The young man stopped her, saying:
"Don't flee;
this is precisely your family's kin."
He then explained their relationship on her behalf.
The young woman said:
"He is my nephew!"
She then asked:
"Is your grandmother still healthy?
How old are your parents?"
Yáng replied:
"My parents are over forty,
and both are well;
only my grandmother, at sixty,
has contracted a chronic illness
and needs assistance with every step.
Nephew truly doesn't know which branch of the family my aunt belongs to,
so I earnestly request you to inform me clearly,
so I can relate it upon my return."
The young woman said:
"The journey is long and distant,
and communication has been blocked for a long time.
When you return, just tell your father,
'Your tenth aunt sends her regards.'
He will know it himself."
Yáng asked:
"What is my aunt's husband's family name?"
The young man said:
"On this sea island, his surname is Yàn.
This place is called Shénxiān Dǎo (Immortal Island),
three thousand lǐ from Qióng.
I haven't been living here long either."
The tenth aunt quickly went inside
and had a maidservant bring food and wine for the guest.
The fresh vegetables were fragrant and delicious,
and he didn't know what they were called.
After eating,
they led him to look around.
He saw peach and apricot trees in the garden with buds,
which he found quite strange.
Yàn said:
"Here, there is no great heat in summer,
nor great cold in winter;
flowers bloom without ceasing."
Yáng happily said:
"This is truly an immortal realm!
When I return, I will tell my parents
that we can move our family here and be neighbors."
Yàn merely smiled.
Huánzhāi lit a candle.
He saw a qín lying across the table
and asked to hear its elegant playing.
Yàn then strummed the strings and twisted the pegs.
Shíniáng came out from inside.
Yàn said:
“Come,
come!
My dear, play for this excellent person.”
Shíniáng immediately sat down
and asked her nephew:
“What do you wish to hear?”
Yáng said:
“Your nephew has never studied the Qíncāo,
so I truly have no specific wish.”
Shíniáng said:
“Just name any topic at will,
and it can all be turned into a tune.”
Yáng smiled and said:
“Can ‘Sea Wind Pulling a Boat’
also be made into a tune?”
Shíniáng said:
“Yes.”
She immediately pressed the strings and plucked them,
as if following an old score,
the melody surging and crashing.
Quietly listening to it,
it was as if his body was still in the boat,
being tossed and buffeted by a hurricane.
Yáng was astonished and awestruck to the point of collapse
and asked:
“Can this be learned?”
Shíniáng handed him the qín
and had him try plucking and strumming,
saying:
“It can be taught.
What do you wish to learn?”
He said:
“The ‘Hurricane Tune’ you just played,
I wonder how many days it would take to learn?
Please first record the tune,
so I can hum and recite it.”
Shíniáng said:
“This has no written notation;
I compose it by feeling.”
Then she took another qín
and demonstrated plucking and picking techniques,
making Yáng imitate her.
Yáng practiced until after midnight,
and the rhythm and melody were roughly correct.
The couple then departed.
Yáng gazed with concentrated longing,
playing by himself facing the candle.
After a long time,
he suddenly gained a wonderful insight,
and unconsciously began to dance.
He raised his head
and suddenly saw a maid standing under the lamp.
Startled, he said:
“My dear, have you really not left yet?”
The maid smiled and said:
“Tenth Aunt told me to wait until you were asleep,
then close the door and move the lamp.”
He scrutinized her carefully;
her eyes were clear like autumn waters,
and her will was utterly captivating.
Yáng’s heart stirred,
and he subtly provoked her.
The maid lowered her head and smiled.
Yáng was even more enchanted,
and abruptly rose to embrace her neck.
The maid said:
“Don’t!
It’s already the fourth watch of the night,
the master will soon rise.
If we both have feelings,
tomorrow night is not too late.”
Just as he was about to embrace her tightly,
he heard Yàn calling
“Fěndié.”
The maid changed color and said:
“This is disastrous!”
She hurried away.
Yáng secretly went to listen.
He only heard Yàn say:
“I always said that girl’s worldly attachments were not extinguished,
and you insisted on taking her in.
Now what?
She deserves three hundred lashes!”
Shíniáng said:
“Once this sentiment sprouts,
she cannot be used as a servant.
It would be better to send her away for our nephew.”
Yáng was deeply ashamed and fearful,
returned to his study, extinguished the candle, and went to bed.
At dawn,
a young servant came to attend to his washing,
and Fěndié was no longer seen.
He was anxious and afraid of being blamed and expelled.
Soon, Yàn and Tenth Aunt came out together,
seemingly untroubled by anything,
and then tested his progress.
Yáng played a tune for them.
Shíniáng said:
“Although it hasn’t reached divine mastery,
you’ve already achieved nine-tenths of it.
With diligent practice, you can reach perfection.”
Yáng then requested another piece to learn.
Yàn taught him
the tune of
“Celestial Maidens Descending,”
with intricate finger techniques.
After three days of practice,
he could finally complete the tune.
Yàn said:
“The main points have all been covered.
From now on, you only need to practice diligently.
Once you are proficient in these two tunes,
there will be no difficult melodies on the qín.”
Yáng thought of his home quite a bit
and told Shíniáng:
“Living here,
I’ve been very happy under your care;
however, my family at home is worried.
Having been away from home for three thousand lǐ,
when can I return?”
Shíniáng said:
“This is not difficult.
The old boat is still here;
I will assist it with a sail and a fair wind.
Since you have no family,
I have already sent Fěndié to you.”
Then she gifted him a qín
and also gave him medicine, saying:
“When you return, treat your grandmother.
Not only will it cure her illness,
but it can also prolong her life.”
Then she saw him off to the coast
and had him board the boat.
Yáng looked for an oar.
Shíniáng said:
“There’s no need for that.”
She then untied her skirt and made it into a sail,
tying it to the boat for him.
Yáng worried about getting lost.
Shíniáng said:
“Don’t worry;
just listen to the sail guiding you.”
Once it was tied,
he boarded the boat.
Yáng felt a pang of sadness.
Just as he was about to bow in thanks and bid farewell,
a south wind suddenly rose,
and the boat was already far from the shore.
He looked at the provisions in the boat, which were just enough for one day’s meal.
He resented her stinginess in his heart.
Fearing hunger, he dared not eat much,
only worrying it would quickly run out.
He only ate one flatbread,
feeling it sweet and fragrant inside and out.
The remaining six or seven pieces
he cherished and saved,
and he no longer felt hungry.
Soon, he saw the setting sun
and regretted not having asked for a lamp and oil when he left.
In an instant,
he vaguely saw signs of human habitation;
upon closer inspection,
it was Qióngzhōu.
He was overjoyed.
Soon he was near the shore.
He unwrapped the skirt, wrapped the remaining cakes in it, and returned home.
Rén mén,
the whole family was astonished and delighted,
for she had been away from home for sixteen years.
Only then did they realize she had encountered an immortal.
She saw her grandmother was even more frail with age and illness;
she took out medicine and gave it to her,
and the chronic illness was immediately cured.
They all marveled and questioned her,
so she recounted what she had seen.
Her grandmother, with tears in her eyes, said:
“That is your paternal aunt.”
Initially,
the old lady had a young daughter,
named Shíniáng,
born with an immortal appearance.
She was betrothed to a man surnamed Yàn.
The prospective husband, at sixteen,
went into the mountains and never returned.
Shíniáng waited until she was over twenty,
then suddenly died without illness.
She had been buried for over thirty years.
Hearing Dàn's words,
they all doubted she had died.
They took out her skirt,
and it was still the one she usually wore at home.
She divided the cakes among them to eat;
one cake kept them from hunger all day,
and their spirits were greatly invigorated.
The old lady ordered the grave to be opened and inspected,
and indeed, an empty coffin remained.
Dàn was originally betrothed to a daughter of the Wú family, but they had not yet married.
As Dàn did not return for several years,
she subsequently married someone else.
They all believed Shíniáng’s words,
and waited for Fěndié to arrive;
but after more than a year, there was no news,
so they began to consider other plans.
A scholar from Línyì, Qián Xiùcai,
had a daughter named Héshēng,
whose beauty was widely renowned.
At sixteen,
before she was married, she had already lost three fiancés.
So they arranged a marriage,
chose an auspicious day, and performed the ceremony.
When she entered the door,
her radiance was unparalleled.
Dàn looked at her,
and it was Fěndié.
Startled, he asked about the events with the bag,
but the girl was completely unaware.
This was because the moment she was banished
was precisely the time of her birth.
Whenever he played for her
the tune of “Celestial Maidens Descending,”
she would lean on her hand and ponder deeply,
as if she understood something.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Tánsī from Chángshān,
was a student of the Imperial Academy.
There was an old woman in their village who "ran into the impermanent ones" (had a near-death experience)
and told people:
“Tonight, an old Tán from the human world will be reborn with me into a new household in Bájiāzhuāng, Zīchuān.
His body will be heavy and cumbersome,
almost suffocated by the bed.”
At that time, Lǐ Tánsī was happily drinking with guests,
and everyone dismissed the old woman's words as nonsense.
That night,
he died without illness.
At dawn,
they went to inquire as she had said,
and indeed, that family had given birth to a daughter during the night.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Shēng from Yí,
was orphaned young
and raised himself.
His family was poor;
however, his bearing was elegant and clean,
a graceful and upright youth.
A wealthy man, Lán Shì,
saw him and was pleased,
giving him his daughter in marriage,
and promising to build him a house and establish his estate.
Not long after the marriage, the wealthy man died,
and his wife's brothers disdained and ignored him.
The wife, in particular, was arrogant towards her husband,
often treating him like a servant;
she enjoyed delicious food herself,
but when Wáng Shēng arrived,
she would place before him
only coarse grain and a gourd of water,
with a broken stalk of grain as a spoon.
Wáng Shēng endured it all.
At nineteen,
he went to take the prefectural examination for child students,
but was rejected.
Returning from the prefecture,
his wife happened not to be in the room,
and a cooked mutton stew was in the pot.
He helped himself to some.
When his wife entered,
she said nothing,
but moved the pot away.
Wáng Shēng was greatly shamed,
threw his chopsticks to the ground,
and said:
“To suffer thus,
it is better to die!”
His wife, enraged,
asked when he would die,
and immediately handed him a rope to hang himself.
Wáng Shēng, in a fit of anger, threw the soup bowl,
injuring his wife's forehead.
He left, seething with resentment,
thinking to himself that indeed it would be better to die,
and so he took his belt and went into a deep ravine.
He reached a clump of trees.
Just as he was selecting a branch to tie his belt to,
he suddenly saw, from a dirt cliff,
a corner of a skirt faintly showing.
In an instant,
a maid appeared.
Seeing Shēng, she quickly turned back,
vanishing like a shadow.
The dirt wall showed no trace of an opening.
He knew for sure it was something supernatural.
However, desiring to seek death,
he had no fear.
He untied his belt and sat down to watch.
After a short while,
half a face reappeared,
peeking once before shrinking back.
He thought, "This ghostly being,
following it will surely lead to the joy of death."
So he picked up a stone and knocked on the cliff wall, saying,
"If this place can be entered,
please show me a way!
I do not seek pleasure,
but rather death."
For a long time,
there was no sound.
Wáng spoke again,
and from within came a voice,
"If you seek death, please withdraw for now;
you can come tonight."
The voice was clear and sharp,
fine like a wandering bee.
Shēng said,
"Understood."
Then he withdrew to await the evening.
Before long,
the stars were already numerous,
and suddenly, in the cliff, a grand mansion appeared,
with silently open double doors.
Shēng ascended the steps and entered.
After only a few steps,
there was a flowing gush of water,
its steam like that of a hot spring.
He touched it with his hand;
it was as hot as boiling soup.
He did not know its depth.
Suspecting that the ghosts and spirits were showing him the place of death,
he leaped in.
The heat penetrated his heavy clothes,
and his skin hurt as if it would melt.
Fortunately, he floated and did not sink.
He swam submerged for a long time;
the heat gradually became bearable.
He struggled to climb and grab,
finally reaching the south bank.
His body was fortunately not scalded.
As he walked,
he saw a distant light in a mansion,
and hurried towards it.
A fierce dog suddenly rushed out,
biting his clothes and tearing his socks.
He groped for a stone and threw it,
and the dog retreated slightly.
Then a pack of dogs barked at him,
all as large as calves.
In this critical situation,
the maid came out and scolded them away,
saying,
"So the young master who seeks death has come!
My lady pities your dire predicament,
and has sent me, your servant, to escort you to a peaceful haven,
where you will be free from misfortune henceforward."
She lit a lamp and led him.
She opened a back door,
and they walked on in the darkness.
They entered a house;
bright candlelight shone through the window.
She said,
"You may enter by yourself;
I will leave now."
Shēng entered the room and looked around;
it turned out he had returned to his own house.
He ran back out.
He met an old woman who worked for his wife, who said,
"We've been looking for you all day,
where are you going again?"
She pulled him back in.
His wife, her wound bandaged,
got out of bed and smiled, greeting him,
saying,
"After more than a year as husband and wife,
can it be that in jest you don't recognize me?
I know I am to blame.
You suffered a false accusation,
and I received a real injury.
Perhaps your anger can now somewhat subside."
Then she took two large ingots of gold from beside the bed and placed them in Shēng's bosom,
saying:
One night,
as he was about to sleep,
he heard shouts and clamor from the inner residence.
He quickly got up,
grabbed a knife and went out,
seeing torchlight illuminating the sky.
He entered to investigate,
and found the courtyard filled with numerous bandits,
while the servants fled in terror.
One servant urged him to escape with him,
but he refused.
He smeared his face and tied a sash around his waist,
mingled among the bandits and shouted:
"Don't scare Xuē Niángzǐ!
Just divide and seize the property,
don't leave anything behind."
At that time, the various bandits in the other rooms were still searching for Jǐnsè without success.
He knew she hadn't been captured yet,
so he quietly entered the back of the residence to search for her alone.
He encountered a crouching old woman,
and then learned that the girl and Chūnyàn had both climbed over the wall.
He also climbed over the wall,
and saw the mistress and maid crouching in a dark corner.
He said,
"How can you hide yourselves here?"
The girl replied,
"I can't walk anymore!"
He threw away his knife and carried her on his back.
After running for two or three *lǐ*,
sweat pouring all over his body,
he finally entered a deep valley.
He released her from his shoulders and bade her sit down,
when a tiger suddenly approached.
He was greatly alarmed,
and wanted to go forward to face it,
but the tiger had already seized the girl in its mouth.
He quickly grabbed the tiger's ears,
stretched his arm with all his might into the tiger's mouth,
to substitute for Jǐnsè.
The tiger, enraged,
released the girl,
and crunched his arm,
with a sharp sound.
His arm broke and fell to the ground,
and the tiger also turned back and left.
The girl cried,
"You've suffered!
You've suffered!"
He was in such a hurry that he didn't yet feel the pain,
but only felt blood gushing like water.
He told the maid to tear her collar to wrap the broken part.
The girl stopped her,
bent down to find the severed arm,
and reattached it herself;
then she wrapped it.
As dawn gradually broke in the east,
they slowly walked back.
The hall was like a ruin when they entered.
When the day was bright,
the servants and old women gradually gathered.
The girl personally went to the west hall,
to ask about his suffering.
When the wrapping was undone,
his arm bone had already rejoined;
she then took out medicine powder and sprinkled it on his wound,
and then left.
From then on, she respected him even more,
making sure all his comforts
were equal to her own.
When his arm healed,
the girl prepared wine in the inner chamber to reward him.
She granted him a seat,
and after three refusals, he sat in a corner.
The girl raised her cup as if deferring to a guest.
After a long while,
she said:
"My body has already attached itself to yours,
and I wish to emulate the daughter of King Chǔ towards Chén Jiàn.
However, without a matchmaker,
I am ashamed to recommend myself."
He said in alarm:
"I have received such great kindness,
even dying would not be enough to repay it.
What I did was out of place,
I fear divine lightning,
and dare not obey your command.
If you pity my unmarried state,
bestowing a maid would already be more than enough."
One day,
the girl's elder sister, Yáotái, arrived;
a beautiful woman of about forty.
In the evening,
she summoned him in.
Yáotái bade him sit,
and said:
"I have come a thousand *lǐ* to arrange my sister's marriage,
tonight she can be matched with a gentleman."
He again rose to decline.
Yáotái insisted and ordered wine,
making the two exchange cups.
He resolutely refused,
but Yáotái forcibly exchanged them.
He then prostrated himself to apologize,
and accepted the drink.
When Yáotái left,
the girl said:
"Let me tell you the truth: I am an immortal maiden,
who was banished for a crime.
I willingly reside beneath the earth,
to take in and nurture wronged souls,
to atone for the Emperor's punishment.
I happened to encounter this calamity from celestial demons,
and thus have this fate of attachment to you.
I invited my elder sister from afar,
not only to preside over the marriage,
but also to have her manage the household in my stead,
so that I can return with you."
He rose respectfully and said,
"Beneath the earth is most joyful!
My family has a fierce wife,
and the house is narrow and crude;
it would be impossible to accommodate
and cherish her life."
The girl laughed and said:
"No matter."
After getting drunk,
he returned to his bedchamber,
and their joyous affection reached its peak.
A few days later,
she said to him:
"Our underworld union cannot last long,
please return, my lord.
When you have finished managing your family affairs,
I will come myself."
She gave him a horse,
opened the gate herself and went out,
and the wall closed up again.
Shēng rode his horse into the village,
and all the villagers were startled.
When he reached his home gate,
the tall mansion was brilliantly lit.
Previously,
after Shēng had left,
his wife summoned her two elder brothers,
intending to punish him with a whipping.
By evening,
he had not returned,
so they finally left.
Someone found Shēng's shoe in a ditch,
suspecting he had died.
After more than a year, there was no news.
A certain merchant, Jiǎ, from Shǎnmò,
arranged a marriage with the Lán clan,
and then proceeded to Shēng's residence and cohabited with his wife.
Within half a year,
they had built and expanded continuously.
Jiǎ went out on business,
and also bought a concubine,
and from then on, he was not at peace in his home.
Jiǎ also frequently did not return for several months.
Shēng inquired and learned the reason,
became angry,
tied his horse, and entered.
He saw the old maidservant,
who, startled, prostrated herself on the ground.
Shēng scolded and cursed for a long time,
then made her lead him to his wife's quarters,
but she had already fled.
He later found her behind the house,
where she had already hanged herself.
He then sent someone to send her back to the Lán clan.
He called out the concubine,
who was eighteen or nineteen years old,
and her demeanor was also excellent,
so he took her to bed.
Jiǎ, through a villager,
sought to reclaim his concubine,
but the concubine wept and refused to leave.
Shēng then drew up a detailed complaint,
intending to sue him for the crime of seizing property and occupying his wife.
Jiǎ dared not speak again,
packed up his shop, and went west.
He was still wondering about Jǐnsè breaking her promise;
one evening,
as he was drinking with the concubine,
a carriage and horses arrived at the door, and the woman (Jǐnsè) appeared.
The woman only kept Chūnyàn,
and sent the rest back.
Entering the room,
the concubine bowed to her.
The woman said:
"This one has the appearance of bearing sons;
she can take my place in suffering."
She then bestowed upon her silk robes and pearl ornaments.
The concubine bowed and received them,
standing to serve her;
the woman pulled her to sit,
and they spoke and laughed very happily.
After a long while,
she said:
"I am drunk and want to sleep."
Shēng also removed his shoes and went to bed,
and the concubine then left;
entering the room,
Shēng was lying on the couch;
she was surprised and peered back,
but the candle had already been extinguished.
Shēng did not spend a single night without sleeping in the concubine's room.
One night,
the concubine got up,
and secretly peeked into the woman's (Jǐnsè's) place,
only to find Shēng and the woman laughing and talking together.
She was greatly astonished.
She rushed back to tell Shēng,
but there was no one on the bed.
At daybreak,
she secretly told Shēng;
Shēng himself was unaware,
only feeling that he sometimes stayed at the woman's place, and sometimes lodged with the concubine.
Shēng instructed her to hide this strangeness.
After a long time,
the maidservant also secretly bore Shēng's child,
and the woman seemed unaware of it.
The maidservant suddenly had a difficult labor and childbirth,
only calling out
"Niángzǐ."
When the woman came,
the fetus descended immediately;
she picked it up,
it was a boy,
cut the umbilical cord and placed it in the maidservant's arms,
and smiled saying:
"My little maid, do not do this again!
If you have too many [children],
then it will be difficult to part with them."
From then on,
the maidservant bore no more children.
The concubine bore five sons and two daughters,
and after thirty years,
the woman (Jǐnsè) would occasionally return to her home,
coming and going always at night.
One day,
she took the maidservant and left,
and never returned.
When Shēng was eighty years old,
he suddenly took an old servant and left at night,
and also did not return.
Based on the Xuezhai manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Tàiyuán there was a common family,
where both the aunt (husband's sister) and niece-in-law (brother's wife) were widows.
The aunt was middle-aged,
unable to maintain her chastity,
and a village ruffian frequently called on her.
The niece-in-law disapproved of her conduct,
and secretly placed obstacles at the doors and walls to deter him.
The aunt was ashamed,
and used an excuse to expel the niece-in-law.
The niece-in-law refused to leave,
leading to considerable strife.
The aunt grew more resentful,
and in turn falsely accused her,
reporting her to the authorities.
The official asked for the lover's name.
The aunt said:
"He comes at night and leaves at dawn,
I truly do not know who he is.
The niece-in-law certainly knows."
Thereupon, the niece-in-law was summoned.
The niece-in-law indeed knew him,
but attributed the illicit affair to the aunt,
bitterly disputing it.
The ruffian was apprehended and brought in,
and he loudly argued:
"Neither of them has a secret lover.
The aunt and niece-in-law simply cannot get along,
so they are making false accusations to slander each other."
The judge said:
"In a village of a hundred people,
why would they single out only you with false accusations?"
He was severely questioned again.
The ruffian begged for leniency,
admitting to having an affair with the niece-in-law.
The niece-in-law was shackled,
but she still refused to admit guilt.
She was banished.
The niece-in-law, in indignation, reported it to the Xiànyuàn,
where the case remained as before,
unresolved for a long time.
At that time, Sūn Jìnshì Liǔxià, from Zīyì, was now administering Línjìn.
Recognized for his talent in solving difficult cases,
this case was therefore sent down to Línjìn.
When the accused arrived,
the duke briefly interrogated them once,
then committed them to prison.
He then ordered his subordinates to prepare bricks, stones, knives, and awls,
to be used as instruments of justice.
Everyone doubted, saying:
"Severe punishments already involve shackles and manacles,
why would he use unusual instruments to resolve the case?"
They did not understand his intention,
but nevertheless prepared them.
The next day,
when he ascended the hall,
he inquired whether all the implements were ready,
and ordered them all placed in the hall.
Then he summoned the offenders,
and interrogated each of them briefly again.
He then said to the aunt and niece-in-law:
"It is not absolutely necessary to clarify this matter completely.
Though the identity of the adulterous woman is not yet certain,
the adulterous man is confirmed.
Your family was originally respectable,
it was merely for a time that you were enticed by this scoundrel.
The blame rests entirely with him.
The knives and stones are here in the hall.
You may personally take them and strike him to death."
The aunt and niece-in-law hesitated,
fearing that they might accidentally be liable for compensation.
The duke said:
"Do not worry,
I am here."
Thereupon, both the aunt and niece-in-law rose,
picking up stones and throwing them.
The niece-in-law had harbored resentment for a long time,
and lifted large stones with both hands,
wishing she could instantly kill him.
The aunt, however, only used small stones to strike his buttocks and legs.
He then ordered them to use knives.
The niece-in-law grasped a knife and thrust it at his chest,
while the aunt still hesitated to strike.
The duke stopped her, saying:
"I know who the adulterous woman is!"
He ordered the aunt to be seized and severely shackled,
and thus obtained the truth.
The ruffian was given thirty blows,
and the case was finally closed.
Appended Note: One day, the duke sent an attendant to collect rent.
The tenant was out,
and his wife answered.
The attendant, unable to get a bribe,
detained the wife
and brought her in.
The duke angrily said:
"A man will return in his own time,
how can you disturb a household!"
He then flogged the attendant
and sent the wife away.
He then ordered craftsmen to prepare many hand shackles,
to be used for beating.
The next day,
the entire town spread stories of the duke's benevolence.
Those who owed taxes, hearing this,
all sent their wives to respond.
The duke arrested them all and shackled them.
I once said: The talent of Duke Sūn was not lacking,
but if he obtained the truth,
he rejoiced and had no time for pity or compassion.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Shí Jìnshì Zōngyù from Chángshān,
served as the magistrate of Xīnzhèng.
It happened that a distant traveler named Zhāng,
who was trading abroad,
wished to return home due to illness.
Unable to ride or walk,
he rented a hay cart,
carrying five thousand in capital,
and traveled with two large men pulling it.
Upon reaching Xīnzhèng,
the two men went to the market for food and drink,
while Zhāng, guarding his capital, lay alone in the cart.
Someone named Jiǎ passed by,
glanced at him,
saw no one else around,
and snatched the capital and left.
Zhāng could not prevent it,
but with effort, rose despite his illness,
and distantly followed him.
The man entered a village;
Zhāng followed him again,
into a gate.
Zhāng did not enter,
but peered through a low wall.
Jiǎ put down what he was carrying,
and turning his head, saw the peeper.
Angrily, he seized him as a thief,
bound him, and brought him before Duke Shí,
then recounted the situation.
When Zhāng was questioned,
he fully described his grievance.
The duke, having no concrete evidence,
scolded him and sent him away.
As the two men left,
they both felt the official was unjust.
The duke acted as if he heard nothing.
He somewhat recalled that Jiǎ had long-standing unpaid taxes,
and sent an attendant to rigorously pursue them.
The next day,
Jiǎ immediately paid three taels of silver.
Duke Shí asked where the money came from.
Jiǎ said:
"I pawned clothes and sold goods."
He named specific items to substantiate it.
Duke Shí sent an attendant to see if any taxpayer
was from the same village as Jiǎ.
Coincidentally, Jiǎ's neighbor was present,
so he was called in and asked:
"Since you are Mǒu Jiǎ's close neighbor,
you should know where his money came from."
The neighbor said:
"I don't know."
The duke said:
"If a neighbor doesn't know,
its origin is ambiguous."
Jiǎ, frightened, looked at his neighbor and said:
"I pawned such-and-such an item, and sold such-and-such an article,
surely you know?"
The neighbor hastily said:
"Yes,
that is indeed true."
The duke angrily said:
"You must have stolen with Jiǎ,
interrogation by unusual punishment is unavoidable!"
He ordered shackles and manacles to be brought.
The neighbor, frightened, said:
"Because he is my neighbor,
I dared not incur his resentment;
but now punishment has reached my own body,
why should I conceal it?
He truly robbed Zhāng Mǒu of his money to buy these things."
Thereupon, Jiǎ was released.
At that time, Zhāng, having lost his capital, had not yet returned,
so Jiǎ was ordered to compensate him.
This also shows Shí's ability to truly administer justice.
The Historian of the Unusual comments:
"When Duke Shí was a scholar,
he was earnest and refined,
suggesting he would excel in the Hanlin Academy,
but be inept at judicial matters.
Yet, once he became an official,
his reputation as a 'divine magistrate'
was widely proclaimed throughout Héshuò.
Who says literary talent has no practical use!
Therefore, I record this to inspire those in power."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Fēng Xiàngxiān
was a renowned man from Shòuguāng.
In a previous life, he was a violent monk in a certain monastery,
who passed away without illness.
His soul emerged and dwelled above the monastery.
From there, he looked down upon the pedestrians in the market,
all of whom had a fiery glow emanating from their heads.
This was presumably the yang energy within their bodies.
As night fell and it grew dark,
he realized he could not stay long above the monastery.
But all the houses were dark,
and he did not know where to go.
Only one house still had a bright lamp.
He floated towards it.
Upon reaching the door,
he found himself already an infant,
being breastfed by a mother.
He was frightened by the sight of the milk;
but his stomach could not withstand the hunger,
so he closed his eyes and sucked forcefully.
After more than three months,
he no longer nursed;
when offered the breast,
he would cry out in fear.
His mother fed him with rice gruel mixed with dates and millet,
and he grew up.
This was Xiàngxiān.
As a child, when he visited that certain monastery,
he could recognize the monks
and call them by name.
Even in old age, he still feared milk.
The Historian of the Strange says:
“Xiàngxiān was profoundly learned,
a pure scholar of Hǎidài.
His sons achieved high status early,
while he himself merely ended his life as a man of letters.
Is this what the Buddhists call 'one whose meritorious karma has not yet been cultivated'?
His younger brother was also a famous scholar,
who had a hidden illness from birth,
moving only once every few months.
When it moved, he would get up quickly,
disregarding guests,
and call from outside to be let in.
Then, all the maids and matrons would avoid him.
If he reached the door, he would become limp again,
and if he entered, he would not go into the room but turn back.
Both brothers were extraordinary men.”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Dèng Chéngdé from Kāifēng,
while studying and traveling to Yǎn,
lodged in a dilapidated temple.
He was hired to transcribe records for those compiling the dental registry (census).
At the end of the year,
his fellow clerks each went home for the holidays,
leaving Dèng to cook alone in the temple.
At dawn,
a young woman knocked and entered.
She was extraordinarily beautiful.
She burned incense and kowtowed before the Buddha, then left.
The next day,
she did the same.
That night,
Dèng got up and lit a lamp,
as he had some work to do.
The woman arrived even earlier.
Dèng said:
“Why are you here so early?”
The woman replied:
“During the day, people are numerous;
it's better at night.
Too early,
and I fear disturbing your peaceful sleep.
I just saw the lamplight,
knowing you were already up,
so I came.”
He joked:
“There's no one in the temple;
staying here overnight would save you the trouble of running back and forth.”
The woman smiled:
“There's no one in the temple,
are you a ghost?”
Dèng, seeing she was amenable to familiarity,
waited until she finished her worship,
then pulled her to sit down and sought intimacy.
The woman said:
“How can this be done before the Buddha?
You don't even have a roof tile to call your own,
