yet you harbor such extravagant thoughts!”
Dèng persistently begged.
The woman said:
“Thirty li from here, in a certain village,
there are six or seven boys
who haven't found a tutor yet.
You go visit Lǐ Qiánchuān,
and you can get the position.
Say you are bringing your family,
and ask them to provide a separate house.
I can then cook for you.
This is a long-term plan.”
Dèng feared that if the matter came to light, he would be punished.
The woman said:
“No harm.
My surname is Fáng,
and my given name is Wénshū.
I have no relatives,
and I have always stayed at my uncle's house for the entire year.
Who would know?”
Dèng was delighted.
After parting with the woman,
he immediately went to the certain village,
met Lǐ Qiánchuān,
and his plan indeed succeeded.
He promised to bring his family before the year's end.
After returning,
he told the woman.
The woman arranged to wait for him on the way.
Dèng bid farewell to his companions
and borrowed a horse to depart.
The woman was indeed waiting halfway.
He dismounted and handed the reins to the woman,
who drove the horse onward.
Upon reaching the study,
they were extremely happy together.
For six or seven years,
they lived harmoniously as husband and wife,
and no one pursued or looked for a fugitive.
Suddenly, the woman bore a son.
As Dèng's wife was infertile,
he was overjoyed at this,
and named him
“Yǎnshēng.”
The woman said:
“A false match can never become real.
I am about to bid farewell to you and leave,
so why give birth to this troublesome child?”
Dèng said:
“If our fate is good,
and we can gather some spare money,
I plan to return to our hometown with you.
Why speak such words?”
The woman said:
“Thank you,
thank you!
I cannot bow my shoulders and force a smile,
or look up to the mistress's eyebrows,
to be a wet nurse for others.
That wailing child is unbearable!”
Dèng believed his wife would be understanding and not jealous,
but the woman said nothing further.
More than a month later,
Dèng closed his school
and planned to go into business with Lǐ Qiánchuān's son.
He told the woman:
“I think teaching in a school
will never lead to wealth.
Now, learning to trade as a peddler,
I hope to have a time to return.”
The woman also did not reply.
At night,
the woman suddenly got up, holding the child.
Dèng asked:
“What are you doing?”
The woman said,
“I want to leave.”
Dèng quickly got up,
and pursued her, asking,
but the door was not open,
and the woman had already vanished.
Extremely startled,
he then realized she was not human.
Dèng, finding the situation suspicious,
therefore dared not tell anyone,
and simply claimed she had returned to her family.
Initially,
Dèng left home,
and made a pact with his wife, Lóu,
that he would definitely return by year-end;
but then several years passed without news,
and it was rumored he had died.
His elder brother, seeing he had no son,
wished to arrange a new marriage for Lóu.
Lóu, however, set a new three-year term,
living solely by her spinning and weaving.
One day,
as dusk fell,
she went to bolt the outer door.
A woman slipped in,
carrying a swaddled infant,
saying:
“I’m returning from my mother’s home.
It’s getting late.
Knowing that elder sister lives alone,
I ask for a night’s lodging.”
Lóu let her in.
Entering the room,
she looked at her and
saw a beauty of over twenty years.
Joyfully, they shared the bed,
and together they played with the child;
the child was as white as a gourd.
Lóu sighed, saying:
“This widow has no such blessing!”
The woman said:
“I actually find him a burden;
why not adopt him as your heir,
how about that?”
Lóu said:
“Regardless of whether young madam can bear to part with him;
even if she could,
I have no milk to sustain him.”
The woman said:
“That’s not difficult.
When the child was born,
I worried about lacking milk;
I took half a dose of medicine and it worked.
Now some of the medicine is still left,
I will give it to you.”
Thereupon, she produced a packet
and placed it by the window.
Lóu responded casually,
not yet finding it strange.
After sleeping,
when she awoke and called out,
the packet was there, but the woman had already opened the door and left.
Lóu was extremely startled.
It was already mid-morning,
and the child cried from hunger.
Lóu had no choice
but to take the medicine;
in a short while, milk flowed,
and she nursed the child.
Over a year passed,
the child grew plumper and healthier,
gradually learning to speak.
She loved him as if he were her own.
From then on, her intention to remarry was completely abandoned.
But rising early to hold the child,
she couldn’t work to earn food and clothing,
and her predicament worsened.
One day,
the woman suddenly arrived.
Lóu feared she had come to reclaim the child,
so she first reproached her for leaving without explanation,
and then spoke of the hardship of raising him.
The woman smiled, saying:
“Elder sister tells me of her difficulties,
and I should then leave the child and not reclaim him?”
Then she beckoned to the child.
The child cried and buried himself in Lóu’s embrace.
The woman said:
“The calf doesn’t recognize its mother!
This child cannot be exchanged for a hundred pieces of gold;
you can bring the gold,
and I will sign a bond of guarantee.”
Lóu thought it was true,
her face turned crimson,
the woman smiled, saying:
“Elder sister, do not fear,
I have come precisely for the child.
After I left, I worried elder sister had no means to raise him,
so I managed to gather more than ten pieces of gold.”
Then she took out the gold and handed it to Lóu.
Lóu feared that by accepting the gold,
the woman would have grounds to reclaim the child,
so she firmly refused it.
The woman placed it on the bed
and left through the door without a trace.
Lóu, holding the child, chased after her,
but she was already far away,
and did not look back when called.
Lóu suspected her intentions were malicious.
However, having received the gold,
she could temporarily sustain herself and the child,
and the household became prosperous.
Another three years passed,
Dèng, having made a profit in trade,
prepared his return.
As they were comforting each other,
he saw the child and asked whose son it was.
His wife told him the story.
He asked:
“What is his name?”
She replied:
“His mother called him Yǎnshēng.”
Dèng exclaimed in surprise:
“This is truly my son!”
He asked about the date,
and it was the very night he had left.
Dèng then recounted his love and separation from Fáng Wénshū,
and they were all the more delighted.
They still hoped the woman would return,
but she remained elusive.
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
In Qīngzhōu, at the home of FÉNG Zhōngtáng,
a pig was slaughtered.
After scalding and removing its hair and bristles,
there were characters inside the meat which read:
“Qín Huì’s seventh incarnation.”
It was cooked and eaten,
but the meat was foul and smelled bad,
so it was thrown to the dogs.
Alas!
Qín Huì’s meat,
one fears even dogs should not eat it!
It is said in Yìdū: Zhōngtáng’s ancestor,
in a previous life in the Sòng dynasty, was harmed by Qín Huì,
which is why he was born to revere Yuè Wǔmù most.
North of Qīngzhōu city, by the main thoroughfare, he built a Yuè Wáng diàn (Temple of King Yuè),
where Qín Huì and Wàn Sìqì knelt prostrate on the ground.
Passersby would venerate King Yuè,
and then throw stones at Qín Huì and Wàn Sìqì;
the incense offerings were continuous.
Later, in the seventh year of a great military campaign,
the FÉNG family descendants destroyed the statue of Yuè Wáng.
A few *lǐ* away,
there was a folk shrine
to “Zǐsūn Niángniáng” (Goddess of Descendants),
so they carried Qín Huì and Gāo there,
making them kneel in front.
A hundred generations later,
there will surely be the mistake of “Shì Shíyí” and “Wǔ Zīxū,”
which is truly laughable.
Also, within Qīngzhōu city,
there used to be a temple to TÁNTÁI Zǐyǔ.
During the peak of Wèi Dāng’s power,
his family was powerful.
There were those in the family who flattered him,
so they defaced Zǐyǔ by removing his cap and beard,
and remade him into a Wèi監 (Wèi Supervisor).
This too is something truly shocking to hear.
According to a Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A scholar from Zhèdōng, Fáng Mǒu,
was a guest in Shǎn,
teaching students.
He often boasted of his courage and daring.
One night,
he lay naked,
when suddenly a furry creature fell from the sky,
hitting his chest with a thud;
he felt it was as big as a dog,
its breath was clammy,
and its four paws thrashed about.
He was greatly frightened,
and tried to get up;
the creature used two paws to pin him down,
and he died from extreme terror.
After about an hour,
he felt someone piercing his nose with a sharp object,
he gave a loud sneeze,
and then revived.
He saw the lamp in the room dimly lit,
and a beautiful woman sitting by his bed,
who smiled and said:
“Good man!
Is your courage truly like this?”
The scholar knew it was a fox spirit,
and was even more terrified.
The woman gradually played with him.
His courage began to loosen,
and they soon became intimate.
After half a year,
they were as harmonious as zithers.
One day,
while the woman lay on the bed,
the scholar secretly covered her with a hunting net.
The woman awoke,
dared not move,
but only pleaded mournfully.
The scholar laughed and did not come forward.
The woman suddenly transformed into a white mist,
emerged from under the bed,
and angrily said:
“We are certainly not good acquaintances!
You can send me away.”
She dragged him by the hand,
and his body involuntarily moved along.
Leaving the door,
they flew rapidly through the air.
After a short while (the time it takes to eat a meal),
the woman released his hand,
and the scholar, dizzy, plummeted.
He happened to fall into a tiger pit in a wealthy family's garden,
which had a wooden frame
and a rope net covering its mouth.
The scholar fell onto the net,
which tilted under him;
he received the net with his abdomen,
and his body was half-inverted.
Looking down,
a tiger squatted in the pit,
looked up to see the person lying there,
leapt up,
nearly a foot away,
and his heart and gall shattered.
The gardener came to feed the tiger,
saw him, and found it strange.
He helped him up,
he was already dead;
after a while,
he gradually revived,
and recounted the entire story.
That place was in the Zhè district,
only four hundred *lǐ* away from his home.
The master of the house gave him money to return home.
Upon returning, he told people:
“Although I died twice,
if not for the fox, I would not have been able to return home due to poverty.”
According to a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Mǒu, a commoner from Bóxīng,
had a daughter who had reached marriageable age.
A powerful local magnate spied her beauty,
and when the girl went out,
he abducted her,
without anyone knowing.
Upon reaching his home, he forced himself upon her,
but the girl screamed and resisted;
the magnate strangled her.
Outside his gate, there was a deep abyss,
so he tied a stone to her corpse
and sank it into the abyss.
Wáng searched for his daughter in vain,
and had no recourse.
Suddenly, the heavens rained,
thunder and lightning encircled the magnate's house,
with a clap of thunder,
a dragon descended and snatched the magnate's head away.
When the sky cleared,
the girl's corpse floated out of the abyss,
one hand clutching a human head,
upon careful inspection,
it was the magnate's head.
The officials were informed,
interrogated his family,
and only then learned the truth of the matter.
Could it be the girl's transformation?
Otherwise,
how could it have happened?
How miraculous!
According to a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wú Gōng, the Vice Prefect of Jǐnán,
was upright and unyielding.
At that time, there was an illicit custom:
whenever a corrupt official embezzled funds and committed a crime of bribery,
the superior official would invariably shield him,
distributing the embezzled money among his subordinates,
and no one dared to object.
They ordered Wú Gōng to do so,
but he refused;
they could not force him,
and angrily scolded him.
Wú Gōng also retorted with harsh words,
saying:
“Although my office is humble,
I also receive the sovereign's mandate.
You can impeach and punish me,
but you cannot revile me!
If I must die, then so be it,
I cannot diminish the court's salary
to cover up other people's illegal embezzlements!”
The superior official then changed his expression and appeased him.
People all say that in this world, one cannot follow the straight path;
it is people themselves who lack the straight path,
why blame the world for being impassable?
At that time, there was a man named Mù Qínghuái in Gāoyuàn,
possessed by a fox spirit,
who would often speak eloquently with people,
his voice resounding from the seat,
but his person was unseen.
When he happened to arrive at the prefecture,
during a conversation among guests,
someone questioned him, saying:
“The immortal surely knows everything;
may I ask how many officials there are in the prefecture in total?”
He immediately replied:
“One official.”
Everyone laughed.
When asked the reason again,
he said:
“Although there are seventy-two officials in the entire prefecture,
in reality, only one can be called an official:
Vice Prefect Wú alone.”
At that time, Zhāng Gōng, the Prefect of Tài'ān,
was called
“Juézǐ”
by people because of his stubbornness.
Whenever high-ranking officials and grand dignitaries ascended Mount Tài,
they would demand many horses, palanquins, and other such things,
and the common people of the prefecture suffered from these provisions.
Zhāng Gōng abolished all of these.
Someone demanded sheep or pigs,
and Zhāng Gōng said:
“I myself am a sheep,
I am a pig,
please kill me to feast your retinue.”
Even the grand dignitaries could do nothing.
Zhāng Gōng had been serving in distant posts,
separated from his wife and children for twelve years.
When he first arrived in Tài'ān,
his wife and eldest son came from the capital to visit him,
and they met very happily.
After six or seven days,
his wife calmly said:
“Your 'dusty cauldron' is still as it was;
why are you so old and muddled, not thinking of your descendants?”
Zhāng Gōng became enraged,
cursed loudly,
called for a stick,
and forced his wife to lie down and receive the beating.
His son covered his mother, weeping,
and begged to take her place.
Zhāng Gōng beat him mercilessly,
and then stopped.
His wife immediately took her son and ordered the carriage to return,
vowing:
“Even if he dies here,
I will never come again!”
More than a year later,
Zhāng Gōng died.
This cannot be said to be an example of a strong-willed person of today.
However, regarding a couple long separated,
how could a single remark provoke such violent anger,
is that human nature?
And to wield authority and power even in the bedroom,
this matter is even stranger than ghosts and spirits.
According to a manuscript copy from the Zhùxuězhāi Studio of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Gāo Yùchéng
was the son of a prominent family
residing in Guǎnglǐ, Jīnchéng.
Skilled in acupuncture and moxibustion,
he treated people indiscriminately, regardless of their wealth.
One day, a beggar came to the village.
He had a festering wound on his leg,
lay by the roadside,
and was covered in pus and blood,
stinking so much that one could not approach him.
The residents, fearing he might die,
fed him once a day.
Gāo saw him and took pity on him,
sending someone to help him home
and placing him in a side-chamber.
His family members, disgusted by the smell,
stood far off, holding their noses.
Gāo personally took out moxa and treated him with moxibustion
and fed him plain food daily.
After several days,
the beggar asked for soup and cakes (tāngbǐng).
The servant angrily chided him.
Gāo heard this
and immediately ordered the servant to give him soup and cakes.
Before long,
he again begged for wine and meat.
The servant ran to report, saying:
"This beggar is absolutely ridiculous!
When he was lying by the roadside,
he couldn't even get one meal a day;
now, after three meals, he still complains about the food being coarse.
We've already given him soup and cakes,
and now he's begging for wine and meat.
Such a glutton
should just be thrown back onto the road!"
Gāo asked about his wound.
The servant replied:
"The diseased flesh is gradually falling off;
he seems able to walk.
However, he deliberately makes groaning noises, feigning pain."
Gāo said:
"What does it cost!
Just give him wine and food.
When he gets well,
perhaps he will not resent us."
The servant pretended to agree
but ultimately gave him nothing.
Moreover, he often whispered with other servants,
all laughing at their master's foolishness.
The next day,
Gāo personally went to check on the beggar.
The beggar rose with a limp
and expressed his gratitude, saying:
"I am deeply grateful for your noble kindness.
You bring the dead back to life and put flesh on white bones;
your benevolence is as profound as the heavens and earth.
But I am newly recovered and not yet strong,
so I foolishly craved delicious food."
Gāo realized that his previous orders had not been followed.
He called the servant and severely punished him,
immediately ordering him to bring wine and roasted meat to the beggar.
The servant resented this.
In the middle of the night,
he set fire to the side-chamber,
then deliberately cried out.
Gāo got up to look;
the chamber was already burned to ashes.
He sighed, saying:
"The beggar is done for!"
He urged the crowd to put out the fire.
They saw the beggar sleeping soundly in the fire,
snoring like thunder.
When they woke him up,
he feigned surprise, saying:
"Where has the house gone?"
The crowd then realized his extraordinary nature.
Gāo esteemed him even more.
He housed him in a guest room,
dressed him in new clothes,
and sat with him daily.
When asked his name,
he said:
"Chén Jiǔ."
After several days,
his complexion became more radiant,
and his speech showed great character.
He was also skilled at 'hand talk' (chess or a similar game).
Gāo played against him
and always lost;
so he learned from him daily
and gained much of his profound knowledge.
After half a year like this,
the beggar did not speak of leaving,
and Gāo also felt unhappy whenever he was away for a short time.
Even when important guests arrived,
he would always invite Chén to drink with them.
Sometimes they would throw dice for a drinking game,
and Chén would always shout out the winning number for Gāo,
and 'pheasant-deer' (a high roll in dice) was always achieved as desired.
Gāo found this extremely astonishing.
Each time he asked to perform a trick,
he would refuse, claiming ignorance.
One day,
he said to Gāo:
"I wish to bid farewell.
I have received much kindness from you,
and now I am hosting a small invitation,
please do not take it as a trivial matter."
Gāo said:
"We have been enjoying ourselves greatly,
why such a sudden parting?
Moreover, your staff head is empty,
so you need not trouble yourself to be the host."
Chén resolutely invited him, saying:
"It's just a cup of wine,
there will be no great expense."
Gāo asked:
"Where?"
He replied:
"In the garden."
It was severe winter,
and Gāo worried that the garden pavilion would be bitterly cold.
Chén insisted:
"It will be fine."
So he followed him into the garden.
He felt the weather suddenly warm up,
like early March.
Upon reaching the pavilion,
it was even warmer.
Exotic birds flocked together,
singing in clear tones,
as if it were late spring.
The tables and desks in the pavilion
were all inlaid with agate and jade.
There was a crystal screen,
so clear it could reflect: within it, flowering trees swayed,
blooming and falling unevenly;
and white birds like snow
flew back and forth, tracing paths upon it.
When he touched it with his hand,
there was nothing there at all.
Gāo was astonished for a long time.
Sitting down,
he saw a mynah bird perched on a stand,
which called out:
"Bring tea!"
Immediately, a crimson phoenix of the morning sun
appeared, holding a red jade tray
on which were two glass cups,
filled with fragrant tea.
It stretched its neck and stood tall.
After drinking,
he placed the cup in it,
and the phoenix carried it away,
flapping its wings.
The mynah bird called out again:
"Bring wine!"
Immediately, green luan and yellow cranes
flew gracefully from the sun,
carrying a pot and cups,
and placed them on the table.
A moment later,
various birds brought forth dishes,
flying back and forth without resting their wings;
rare delicacies were piled up,
instantly filling the table.
The food was fragrant, and the wine was pure,
all were extraordinary items.
Chén saw Gāo drinking heartily,
and said:
"You have a grand capacity,
you should have a larger goblet."
The mynah bird called out again:
"Bring the large goblet!"
Suddenly, a flash appeared near the sun,
and a giant butterfly, seizing a parrot-shaped cup
that held about a *dǒu*,
flew and landed on the table.
Gāo saw the butterfly was as large as a wild goose,
its two wings graceful,
its patterns brilliant and beautiful,
and he praised it highly.
Chén called out:
"Butterfly, persuade him to drink!"
The butterfly spread its wings and flew once,
transforming into a beautiful woman,
her embroidered clothes fluttering,
and she came forward to offer wine.
Chén said:
"There must be something to accompany the wine."
The woman then danced gracefully.
When the dance was at its height,
her feet would leave the ground by more than a foot,
and she would bend her head back,
straightening it with her feet,
then flip over and stand up,
her body never touching the dust.
She also sang:
"Fluttering and laughing, treading through fragrant thickets,
bending down flower branches to brush my red face.
Unaware in my turning and twisting that my golden ornaments have fallen,
I follow the butterflies over to the east of the fence."
Her lingering notes were ethereal,
more than echoing around the beams.
Gāo was greatly pleased,
and pulled her to drink with him.
Chén ordered her to sit,
and also gave her wine.
After Gāo drank,
his heart and mind swayed,
and he abruptly rose to embrace her intimately.
He looked,
and she had transformed into a yakṣa,
her eyes bulging from their corners,
her fangs protruding from her mouth,
her black flesh lumpy and uneven,
hideously grotesque beyond description.
Gāo, startled, released his hands,
and crouched trembling by the table.
Chén struck its mouth with a bamboo leaf,
and scolded:
"Begone quickly!"
As he struck, it transformed,
again becoming a butterfly,
and fluttered away.
Gāo, regaining his composure from the shock,
excused himself.
Seeing the moonlight like washed silver,
he casually said to Chén:
"Your excellent wine and fine dishes
come from the sky;
your home must be in heaven.
Why not take your old friend for a visit?"
Chén said:
"Alright."
Then he took his hand and leaped up.
He then felt his body in the vast emptiness,
gradually approaching the heavens.
He saw a high gate,
its opening round like a well,
and people within were bright as day.
The steps and path were all paved with blue stone,
smooth and clean without a speck of dirt.
There was a large tree,
several *zhàng* tall;
it bloomed with red flowers at the top,
as large as lotuses,
profusely covering the entire tree.
Below, a woman
in crimson clothes was pounding clothes on an anvil,
peerlessly beautiful.
Gāo stood rooted,
completely forgetting to move.
The woman saw him,
and angrily said:
"Where does this mad fellow
presumptuously come from!"
Then she threw her pestle at him,
hitting him in the back.
Chén quickly dragged him to an empty space,
and severely reprimanded him.
Gāo, struck by the pestle,
sobered up immediately,
and felt very ashamed and embarrassed.
Then he followed Chén out,
where white clouds received them underfoot.
Chén said:
"We part ways here.
I have something to instruct you,
remember it carefully and do not forget: your life will not be long;
tomorrow, quickly hide in the Western Mountains,
and you may be spared."
Gāo wanted to hold him back,
but he turned and left immediately.
Gāo [Gāo] felt the clouds gradually recede,
and his body landed in a garden.
The scenery was vastly different.
He returned home and spoke to his wife,
and they were both greatly astonished.
He looked at the spot on his clothing where the pestle had touched,
which was a striking red like brocade,
and had a strange fragrance.
Early next morning,
he followed Chén [Chén]'s advice,
packed food, and entered the mountains.
A thick fog obscured the sky,
so vast and indistinct that he could not discern the path.
He quickly trod through the wilderness,
when suddenly he lost his footing
and fell into a cloud-filled grotto.
He felt it was unfathomably deep;
yet his body was fortunately unharmed.
He settled down and sobered up for a long while,
looking up to see the cloud-vapor like a shroud.
Thereupon he sighed to himself,
"The immortals made me escape,
but great destiny cannot ultimately be avoided.
When shall I get out of this grotto!"
He sat for another moment,
and saw a faint light in the depths.
So he rose and gradually went in,
discovering a completely different world.
There were three elders playing chess.
When they saw Gāo [Gāo] arrive,
they did not even ask him anything,
continuing their game without interruption.
Gāo [Gāo] squatted down and watched.
When the game ended,
they gathered the pieces into the box,
and only then asked the guest how he came to be there.
Gāo [Gāo] said,
"I got lost and fell, losing my way."
The elders said,
"This is not the human world,
and you should not linger.
We will send you home."
Thereupon they led him to the bottom of the grotto,
and he felt the cloud-vapor envelop him and lift him up,
until he stepped onto level ground.
He saw that the mountain trees had deep yellow leaves,
and the trees were rustling and shedding their foliage,
seemingly the end of autumn.
He exclaimed in great surprise,
"I came in winter,
how has it become late autumn?"
He rushed home,
where his wife and children were all startled,
gathering and weeping.
Gāo [Gāo] asked them in bewilderment,
and his wife said,
"You left three years ago and did not return;
we all thought you had become a spirit!"
Gāo [Gāo] said,
"How strange,
it was only for an instant."
He took out his provisions from his waist,
which had already turned to ashes.
They were mutually astonished.
His wife said,
"After you left,
I dreamt of two men in black robes with sashes,
resembling officers of the underworld,
who boisterously entered the room and looked around,
saying, 'Where did he go?'
I scolded them, saying, 'He has already gone out.
If you are government officers,
how dare you enter a woman's chambers!'
The two men then exited,
talking as they went, saying 'Strange, strange'
and left."
Thereupon Gāo [Gāo] realized that what he encountered
was an immortal;
and what his wife dreamt
was a ghost.
Whenever Gāo [Gāo] met guests,
he would wear the pestle-scented garment inside,
and everyone in the room could smell its fragrance,
which was neither musk nor orchid,
and became more intense with sweat.
According to a manuscript of chapter 24 of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì* [Liáozhāi Zhìyì]:
Mǎ Shēng Wànbǎo [Mǎ Shēng Wànbǎo],
a native of Dōngchāng [Dōngchāng],
was free-spirited and unconventional.
His wife, Tián [Tián],
was also unrestrained and elegant.
They were a very affectionate couple.
A young woman arrived
and lodged with a certain neighbor, an old woman [Mǒu Ào],
claiming she was abused by her in-laws [wēnggū]
and had temporarily fled.
She was extraordinarily skilled at sewing,
and readily performed tasks for the old woman,
who was pleased and kept her.
After several days,
she claimed she could perform massages at midnight
to cure women's wasting diseases [zhàigǔ].
The old woman often visited Shēng's [Shēng] home,
extolling her skills,
but Tián [Tián] never paid much attention.
One day, Shēng [Shēng] peeped through a crack in the wall and saw the woman.
She was about eighteen or nineteen,
and quite graceful.
He secretly admired her.
He privately conspired with his wife
to feign illness to summon her.
The old woman arrived first,
and after comforting and questioning Tián [Tián] by the bed,
she said,
"Since the mistress [niángzǐ] has invited her,
she will come.
But she fears men,
so please do not let the young master [lángjūn] enter."
His wife said,
"There is no spacious room in the house,
and he often comes and goes,
what can be done?"
She then pondered and said,
"This evening, my uncle [ājiù] in Xīcūn [Xīcūn] has invited him for a drink,
so I can easily instruct him not to return."
The old woman agreed and left.
The wife and Shēng [Shēng] used the strategem of "replacing the Zhào [Zhào] banner with the Hàn [Hàn] banner"
and carried it out with smiles.
As dusk fell,
the old woman led the young woman there,
and asked,
"Will the young master [lángjūn] return home tonight?"
Tián [Tián] said,
"He will not return."
The young woman happily said,
"That's good then."
After a few words,
the old woman bid farewell and left.
Tián [Tián] then lit a candle and spread out the quilt,
inviting the young woman to get into bed first.
She also undressed and extinguished the candle.
Suddenly she said,
"I almost forgot,
the kitchen door isn't closed,
to prevent the dogs from stealing food."
She then got out of bed, opened the door, and replaced herself with Shēng [Shēng].
Shēng [Shēng] rustled in,
got into bed, and lay beside the woman.
The woman said tremblingly,
"I will cure mistress's [niángzǐ] ailment."
She interspersed her words with endearments.
Shēng [Shēng] remained silent.
The woman then stroked Shēng's [Shēng] abdomen,
gradually moving to below the navel.
She stopped massaging,
and suddenly explored his private parts.
Her wrist touched something that surged and throbbed.
The woman's reaction of terror
was no less than someone who had accidentally grabbed a snake or scorpion.
She quickly got up, intending to flee.
Shēng [Shēng] stopped her,
and put his hand between her thighs,
finding a pendulous object that filled his grasp;
it was also a magnificent organ.
She cried out for a light in great alarm.
Shēng's [Shēng] wife, thinking the plan had failed,
quickly lit a lamp and came,
intending to mediate.
She then saw the woman, naked, throwing herself on the ground begging for her life.
The wife, ashamed and frightened, rushed out.
Shēng [Shēng] questioned her,
and she said she was Wáng Èrxǐ [Wáng Èrxǐ] from Gǔchéng [Gǔchéng],
whose elder brother Dàxǐ [Dàxǐ] was a disciple of Sāngchōngmén [Sāngchōngmén],
and thus she had learned their art through him.
He also asked,
"How many people have you defiled?"
She replied,
"I haven't been practicing this art for long;
only sixteen people."
Shēng [Shēng], believing her actions punishable by death,
considered reporting her to the magistracy,
but pitying her beauty,
he instead tied her hands behind her back and castrated her [gōng zhī],
and she bled profusely and fainted.
After a short while, she revived,
and he laid her on the bed,
covered her with a quilt,
and instructed her,
"I will treat you with medicine.
When your wounds heal,
you may follow me from then on,
otherwise if this matter is exposed, you will not be forgiven."
Wáng [Wáng] agreed.
The next day,
the old woman came.
The scholar explained to her,
"This is my maternal cousin's daughter, Wáng Èrjiě.
She was driven out by her husband's family because of his congenital impotence.
Last night, she told my family the reason,
and only then did we learn of it.
She's suddenly a little unwell;
I'm going to buy medicine for her,
and also send for her family,
to have her stay and keep my wife company."
The old woman entered the room,
looked at Wáng,
and saw that her complexion was ashen like dust.
She immediately went to the bed and questioned her.
She said,
"Her private parts are severely swollen;
I fear it is a malignant carbuncle."
The old woman believed her and left.
The scholar gave her a medicinal decoction,
and sprinkled her with powder,
and day by day she recovered.
Every night, he would draw her close and be intimate with her.
In the morning, she would draw water from the fields, mend clothes,
sweep and clean,
and prepare meals,
just like a concubine or maid.
Not long after,
Sāng Chōng was executed,
and seven of his accomplices were publicly beheaded.
Only Èrxǐ escaped the net.
Warrants were issued to all jurisdictions for his strict arrest.
The villagers secretly began to suspect her.
They gathered the village old women to examine her private parts through her skirt,
and then all doubts were dispelled.
From then on, Wáng felt indebted to the scholar,
and thus followed Mǎ until the end of her life.
After she died,
she was buried next to the Mǎ family tomb west of the prefectural seat.
Today, it is vaguely still there.
Yìshǐ Shì said:
"Mǎ Wànbǎo can be said to be skilled at utilizing people.
Children like to play with crabs,
but they also fear their claws.
So they break off their claws and keep them.
Alas,
if one can grasp this idea,
one can govern the world well."
According to a manuscript of volume 24 of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
